## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

*The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, diligently corrected by comparison with one another and with certain manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the three most recent centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of significance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, together with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers commented on the individual biblical texts, and in which places in their works they did so. An edition incomparably accurate and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of its type, the quality of its paper, the integrity of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, systematic, and chronological—which brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.*

*Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold at 1,200 francs per thousand volumes; the Greek-Latin at 1,300 francs per eight hundred volumes. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.*

# Complete Works of Saint Peter Damian

## Prolegomena to the Works of Saint Peter Damian

[Col. 0009]

### Notice of the Venetian Printer’s Edition of the Year 1743

[Col. 0009A] **I.** Since many works of the Fathers of the Church have already been brought to light from the Venetian presses, and others are soon to be published, I thought it worthwhile to make some works public from my own printing house as well. I chose first the writings of the holy Peter Damian, perhaps more agreeable to students of sacred literature, since he was a man so learned and eloquent that he must rightly be regarded as easily the foremost of his age.

The first person who, not without care and toil, gathered these works of Saint Peter into something like a single body and distributed them into four volumes was the most distinguished man, Dom Constantine Cajetan of Syracuse, abbot of the Cassinese Congregation of the Order of Saint Benedict. Pope Clement VIII summoned him to Rome to advance this labor more vigorously, as Pope Paul V, of blessed memory, testifies in his own [Col. 0009B] letter, which is reproduced here from the Roman edition, where alone it exists.

These four volumes, or rather tomes, did not appear in the same format or at the same time. The first tome, containing the eight books of the Letters, was published in 1605 from the printing house of Aloysius Zanetti. Then, in 1608, the second appeared from the press of William Facciotus; it contains the Sermons on the saints and the Histories of the saints. The third was printed from Mascardi’s press in 1615 and contains the Moral, Theological, and Miscellaneous Minor Works. Finally, the last was made public only in 1640, likewise at Rome, as were the other three; it presents certain pious prayers and poems and rhythms of various kinds, and Cajetan himself dedicated it to Pope Urban VIII. In 1610 [Col. 0009C] the first tome, containing the letters, appeared from the Nivellian printing office in Paris, published by Sebastian Cramoisy, in quarto. In 1623 the first three tomes were printed at Lyon in folio; Labbe speaks of this edition in volume II, page 201. But all the works of Saint Peter, divided into four tomes, were published at Paris by Charles Chostelain in 1642; and finally they were reprinted in the same format and place by Aegidius Tompere in 1663.

**II.** My edition, too, is now being brought to light according to the model of these editions; in everyone’s judgment it will be the more accurate because it will be compiled from both—the Roman and the Parisian—and will moreover include many additions. To speak of each tome individually: after Cajetan’s letter to Paul V, of blessed memory, mentioned above, and that pontiff’s reply, there is presented the dissertation of the highly celebrated Guido Grandi, *On the Camaldolese Institute of Saint Peter Damian*, published at Lucca in 1707 by the press of Marescandoli, together with three other Camaldolese dissertations. Then follows the preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Peter Damian, composed by Godefrid Henschenius, S.J., and already published in the Bollandist February, together with his notes [Col. 0010B] on the Life of Saint Peter himself written by Saint John of Lodi.

The Life itself follows immediately; afterward comes a neatly collected series of testimonies from both ancient and more recent authors, compiled by Cajetan. Here I remark in passing that Saint Peter Damian may be called Damian just as well as Peter Damian, as Sirmond defends in his *Antirrheticus* I, part II, chapter 6, against Peter Aurelius.

Finally, the letters of the holy Father themselves appear, in the same order that Cajetan gave them, perhaps because he found them arranged in that way in manuscript codices, although it must be admitted that chronological order is scarcely observed in them. Part of Letter 12 of Book I, page 6, written to Alexander II, has appeared more than once under the title of a certain minor work, *On the Correction of a Bishop and of the Pope*, [Col. 0010C] especially in Goldast, volume II—elsewhere numbered III—page 42 of *On the Monarchy of the Empire*, as the distinguished Johann Albert Fabricius notes in his *Latin Library of the Middle and Lower Ages*, published at Hamburg in 1734. If that part of the letter is identical with the minor work, Cave is wrong to assert that this work is missing among Damian’s writings; and Possevinus, Labbe, and Natalis Alexander are also wrong to claim that it was falsely attributed by heretics. Many of these same letters, being longer or of greater importance, were transferred to the third tome under the title of minor works. Nevertheless, so that this separation might not cause confusion, readers are warned at the places where they ought to occur and are directed to the place where they should seek them.

The final letter, which Saint Peter wrote for a certain dying man, the Church still uses in the Roman Ritual as the third prayer for commending the soul of the dying, as Gavantus observes in section 9, chapter 5, number 4, of his notes on the rubrics of the Roman Missal and Breviary, and Baruffaldi in his commentary on the Roman Ritual. Cajetan published it at the beginning of the third tome of the Works; it is absent from the Nivellian edition of Damian’s letters because the aforementioned third tome had not yet [Col. 0011B] been made public at that time. Cajetan’s notes and observations are added—learned and imbued with true and orthodox teaching, whatever Gaspar Ziegler may babble to the contrary in *Ecclesiastical Sidirolizus*, published at Wittenberg in 1672, chapter 2, from section 7 through section 16, as Armellinus writes in the *Cassinese Library*, page 125, in his *Eulogy of Cajetan*.

**III.** In the second tome, however, the sermons occupy the first place. Yet not all of them have Peter Damian as their author. In this matter Cajetan—otherwise a man outstanding in learning and highly deserving for his work on the arrangement of Damian’s writings—was seriously mistaken. Nineteen of them must be restored to their true and legitimate author, Nicholas of Clairvaux, a monk and the notary, or secretary, of Saint Bernard. [Col. 0011C] The following is the series of Nicholas’s sermons:

1. Sermon on the feast of Saint Benedict the abbot, 21 March.
2. On the Advent of the Lord, concerning blessed Mary, placed under the feast of the Annunciation of the same Virgin, 25 March.
3. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, 24 June.
4. On the feast of Saint Peter in Chains, which is simply entitled *On Saint Peter*, 29 June.
5. On the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, on the same day.
6. On Saint Mary Magdalene, 22 July.
7. On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 25 August.
8. On Saint Victor, 1 September. Concerning this sermon, however, it should be observed that the first paragraph, which begins “This great man” and ends “fragrant,” was perhaps added by some copyist. For this sermon of Saint Victor, in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers of the Cistercian Order*, where Nicholas’s sermons are found, begins only with the second paragraph, namely with the words: “It is at hand,” and so forth.
9. On the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 8 September.
10. On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, 14 September.
11. On the feast of the holy angels, entitled *On Saint Michael the Archangel*, 29 September.
12. On the feast of All Saints, 1 November.
13. On the feast of Saint Martin, 11 November.
14. On the feast of Saint Andrew, 30 November. [Col. 0012A]
15. On the feast of Saint Nicholas, 6 December.
16. On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, 24 December.

These last four sermons are included among the works of Saint Bernard in the ancient editions. The first of them, namely the sermon on Saint Martin, could never have been attributed to Peter Damian, but belongs to a man named Gaul, who reveals himself in these words: “The clemency of the Divinity has mercifully provided both for kings and for our kingdom,” and so forth.

17. On the Nativity of the Lord. Cajetan recognized that this was not a sermon of our Peter Damian, but did not know to whom it should be attributed. Nevertheless, beyond doubt it must be assigned to Nicholas of Clairvaux.
18. On the feast of Saint Stephen, 26 September. This, too, was once listed among Bernard’s sermons. [Col. 0012B]
19. On the Dedication of a church. This occupies the first place among those published in this tome.

These sermons, I say, belong to Nicholas, who, as Mabillon writes in the second part of the Preface to volume III of the Works of Saint Bernard, was made a monk of Clairvaux from Arremar and was employed by Saint Bernard as his notary. He enjoyed the holy man’s favor and was dear to others distinguished for learning and holiness, especially Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.

Yet he lamentably defected from the order. The highly distinguished Mabillon and others doubt whether he ever seriously corrected this defection. Nevertheless, the most learned Martene observed, with sufficiently clear arguments, in the Preface to volume I of the *Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*, that he returned to his former monastery at Arremar [Col. 0012C], and that from there he acquired great renown and won the allegiance of princes, bishops, and even supreme pontiffs.

Besides these sermons, there is a book of Nicholas’s letters in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, Lyon edition of 1677, volume XXI, page 517. The highly distinguished Baluze also published two other letters of Nicholas, never before edited, in volume II of his *Miscellanies*.

**IV.** But to return to Damian’s sermons: several had already been published by Surius. Among them Vossius, on page 118 of *On Latin Historians*, enumerates sermons on Saints Eleuchadius, Benedict, George, Mark, Vitalis and Valeria, Anthimus, Apollinaris, Cassian, Fidelis, Nicholas, Barbatianus, Odilo, Maurus, Romuald, Rodulphus, and Dominic Loricatus. Possevinus, however, lists many more. [Col. 0012D]

Moreover, the distinguished Dacherius published five sermons on the Lord’s Prayer under Peter Damian’s name in volume VIII of the *Spicilegium* in 1666. But he himself later recognized that they belonged to Saint Peter, bishop of Ravenna, surnamed Chrysologus. They are accordingly restored to him in the new edition of the same *Spicilegium* and are found in nearly all editions of Chrysologus’s sermons as numbers 67, 68, 70, 71, and 72.

**V.** Following the sermons are the Histories of the saints written by Saint Peter Damian. First among them is the Life of Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, copied after Surius by Bollandus in the *Acts of the Saints*, by Barale in the *Lerinian Chronology*, and by Marrier in the *Cluniac Library*. [Col. 0013A] In the present edition we append to it the notes of the distinguished Andrea Duchesne, as they appear in the aforementioned *Cluniac Library*, together with other recent notes by an anonymous man, from whom I obtained these and the notes that follow through my own efforts, when the publication of this volume was already well advanced.

Next follows the History or Life of Saint Maurus, bishop of Cesena, with the notes of the distinguished John Bollandus from volume II of the January volume. Third comes the Life of Saint Romuald, already printed many times, but now published with notes by the same anonymous author. Fourth are the Lives of Saints Rodulphus and Dominic Loricatus, followed by the notes of that anonymous author. Fifth is the Passion of Saints Flora and Lucilla, with the notes of the most learned William Cuperus, which are found in volume VII of the Bollandist July.

It must be observed here, however, that Peter Damian was not certainly the author of the final chapter, which concerns the translation of their bodies [Col. 0013B], since a serious anachronism is detected in it. On this matter, see Cuperus’s commentary in the aforementioned Bollandist volume.

Finally, in the last place, there is the *Explanation of the Visions of Saints Marianus the Lector and Jacob the Deacon*, written by Peter Damian himself while he was serving as the prior of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana. Surius included it in volume III of his collection, and Cajetan published it out of its proper place.

**VI.** The third tome presents sixty minor works on various subjects. The fourth among them is the *Synodal Discussion on the Election of the Pontiff*, sent in 1062 to the Council of Osbor, commonly called Osbori, in Alemannia. By that council the election of Alexander II, of blessed memory, was confirmed [Col. 0013C], while Cadalo, the pseudo-pontiff, was rejected. Goldast also presents it in volume II—elsewhere III—of the *Monarchy of the Empire*, page 45.

The sixth is the book called *Most Welcome*, which treats of ecclesiastical institutions. It first appeared at Cologne in 1536, in an octavo volume in which sermons on the excellence of Saint John the Baptist—placed in our edition in tome II, page 116—were also included, together with Saint Prosper’s book *On the Contemplative Life*. This minor work was later printed in Belgium together with other books on the same subject.

The eighth treats of degrees of relationship and degrees of consanguinity. See Benedict Pictet’s *History of the Eleventh Century*, pages 636 and following.

The eleventh is entitled *The Lord Be with You*, because in it he most learnedly discusses that expression and the other, *Jube, domne, benedicere*—“Give the order, lord, to bless.” It was first published in 1549 by Johann Cochlaeus in *A Mirror of Ancient Devotion Concerning the Mass*, Mainz, in folio, page 143. It was then published with the same Cochlaeus at Venice in 1572, in octavo, page 98. It appeared again among the authors *On Divine Offices*, Rome, 1591, in folio.

Concerning the Decree of Pope Boniface IV, which is found placed at the end of the twenty-eighth minor work, see Franciscus Hallier near the end of his work entitled *Ecclesiastical Defense of the Hierarchy*, Paris, published by Charles Morel in 1632, in quarto; there, on page 781, he gives a lengthy judgment concerning this Decree.

The thirty-fifth minor work deals with paintings of the chief Apostles. [Col. 0014A] Besides the arguments brought forward by our holy writer concerning the question why the Apostle Saint Paul is placed on the right and Saint Peter on the left, other discussions may be consulted in Molanus, *On Sacred Images*, II, 46; III, 24; Allatius, *On the Agreement of the Two Churches*, book I, chapter 6; the Macri brothers, *Hierolexicon*, under the word “Bull”; Pagi, for the year 49, number 3; Papebrochius, in the *Paralipomena* to the *Propylaeum* of the *Acts of the Saints* for May; and elsewhere.

The forty-third discusses the praise of scourges and discipline. Jacques Boileau of France, in his *History of the Flagellants*, first published in Latin at Paris in 1700 and later also in French, chapter 7, denies that before our Peter Damian the practice of beating oneself with scourges as a penitential measure existed in the Church. But, together with Baronius, for the year 1056, number 5, volume XI [Col. 0014B], there can be no doubt that, even if we do not wish to regard him as the originator of this voluntary flagellation, he was nevertheless its propagator and certainly its defender against those who attacked it.

Finally, the fifty-second minor work contains a sermon on the goodness of the religious state. With regard to this work, where an allegorical interpretation of various animals is discussed, one may consult the *Physiologus* of Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, volume II of his works, and the minor work *On Beasts*, which occupies a place among the works of Hugh of Saint Victor in volume II, although it should rather be attributed to Hugh of Fouilloy. Whoever this Hugh may be, he imitated Damian’s minor work and excerpted much from it.

**VII.** Finally, the last tome, namely the fourth, [Col. 0014C] contains first of all prayers, supplications, hymns, readings, Masses, responsories, and poems. Several of the hymns were republished by the most learned and venerable Cardinal Thomasius, a cleric regular, in the *Hymnary* at the end of his Psalter.

Next follow *Collections on the Old Testament*, excerpted from the letters and minor works of Peter Damian by a monk who was his disciple and sent to Damian, the nephew of Saint Peter through his brother. The minor work 47 is addressed to this Damian by Saint Peter himself. The distinguished Grandi, in his dissertation presented here, chapter 1, number 5, endeavors to prove with considerable learning that Damian was made a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church by Pope Gregory VII, of blessed memory.

Finally, Cajetan thought it appropriate to insert the *Rule of the Regular Canons* of Peter de Honestis of Ravenna, [Col. 0014D] since some had attributed it to Saint Peter Damian. The similarity of their names, homeland, and humble subscription, “Peter the Sinner,” could easily have provided an occasion for error. Yet everyone can see that it can never belong to Peter Damian, but only to the other Peter de Honestis, since the rule itself is addressed to Pope Paschal II, who was elevated to the government of the Catholic Church in the twenty-seventh year after Peter Damian’s death—which occurred in 1072—namely, in 1099.

**VIII.** I thought it worthwhile to divide into two parts the tables both of the passages of Sacred Scripture and of the subjects, which are relegated to the final tome in the Parisian edition, so that—as will be a considerable convenience to you—you may easily find after the second tome what pertains to the first two tomes, and after the fourth what pertains to the two later ones.

There, most courteous reader, is everything I have wished and, for the time being, been able to note concerning the Works of Peter Damian. For the rest, I would have wished that someone should subject all the writings of this outstanding author to renewed examination; compare them with the manuscripts perhaps lying hidden in libraries [Col. 0016A]; bring forward any new materials that might exist; and enrich them with fuller observations and notes. I admit that something is lacking even from this edition, so that it cannot rightly be called fully complete. Nevertheless, I trust that in other respects it will prove more accurate, fuller, and more polished than all those that preceded it. Farewell.

[Col. 0015]

# Cajetan’s Dedication Letter

Constantine Cajetan, monk of the Cassinese Congregation, offers greetings and prays God for health and happiness for our most holy lord Pope Paul V, supreme pontiff.

With the greatest justification, most blessed Father, I dedicate to you the first fruits of my labors, since by divine providence you have not only succeeded to the place and the most exalted office of Clement VIII, but are also the supporter and enlarger of the plans and well-ordered undertakings of that pontiff, who deserved so well of you.

Among these is the blessed Peter Damian, whose publication was chiefly urged by me. Therefore, to free myself from every obligation, I present to his most merciful successor the work that I cannot return to Clement. I might call Damian Clement’s work, for Clement always embraced him with such love that some portion of that benevolence flowed even to me, who had labored greatly on him.

But I do not know whether I should call him yours rather. For if we consider his person, he is a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Ostia. If we consider the purpose of this book, it is the correction of the conduct of the rulers of the Church and of corrupt morals. If we consider the men to whom it is written, they are princes and, above all, supreme pontiffs. All these matters it is your duty to care for and your dignity to embrace.

Added to this is your extraordinary ardor of spirit and your zeal for defending and enlarging the Christian religion. This ardor rightly demanded such a man as the holy Doctor is commended to be: a most vigorous defender of the faith and divine law, and most devoted to uprooting the corrupt way of life that dominated his own age. It will be pleasant to observe this in his letters, and more useful and glorious to imitate it.

Receive, therefore, most holy Father, your Damian, who is joined to you by so many and such great titles that I rejoice that, while I am concerned for Damian’s patronage, you are his glory; and that before Your Beatitude he has found a patron for his own affairs and for other matters that are with me and require your aid and assistance.

For I have at hand the Histories of very many saints, which are lacking—not without great injury to the saints themselves and loss to piety and holy emulation. I have noted much from approved writers that ought to be added to the Roman Martyrology, material pertaining partly to the number of the saints and partly to the truth concerning the times and places in which they gloriously died.

Finally, I have collected certain monuments of the ancient Fathers which, if they were brought into public view, would enrich many good readers either through their novelty or through their usefulness. All these works, most holy Father, when they saw you occupied in restoring and adorning the temples of the Blessed Virgin and of the chief of the Apostles, came to the firm hope that through you they would be brought back into the light and restored to life; and that the devotion to holy men conceived in human hearts through your worthy deeds would produce abundant fruits for the universal Church and everlasting glory for their author.

For my part, I can promise all my assistance, whatever its worth may be. To approve and foster the enterprise itself belongs to your judgment and authority. Finally, it is my part to pray to God Almighty that he grant you firm health and prosperity in your wisely and piously begun counsels and undertakings. Farewell.

[Col. 0017]

# Dissertation of Guido Grandi of Cremona, Abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict and of the Camaldolese Congregation, on Saint Peter Damian and the Institute of the Avellanites in the Camaldolese Order

## Chapter One: The Aim, Subject, and Occasion of Writing

[Col. 0017A]

### Synopsis

The various aims of writers: which of these was proposed by the author? No. 1. His confidence in Peter Damian. 2. The importance of the question. 3. The eulogy of Peter Damian. 4. The glory of the Avellanites from their great number of saints and bishops, and from the cardinals taken from the same monastery. 5. Jacopo Laderchi’s attempt to detach all the Avellanites from the Camaldolese Order. 6. Our undertaking to refute him justly, necessarily, and modestly; ibid. Concerning other apologies that have appeared against Laderchi.

## Dissertation

**I.** Those who endeavor to claim for a family, homeland, or order men distinguished by holiness, learning, or other notable achievements are accustomed to be moved to write by various motives. Most undertake such a task for the display of glory; some out of love of truth; very few for the sake of edification.

For my part, just as I strive with all my strength to avoid the vanity of the first group, so I desire with the greatest ardor of spirit to imitate the zeal of the second and to obtain, through this dissertation, the benefit sought by the last.

I wish to demonstrate, against the arguments of Jacopo Laderchi, a priest of the congregation of the Roman Oratory and the most recent author of a Life of the same Peter Damian, that Peter Damian and the other Avellanites belonged to the Camaldolese institute. I undertake this both so that truth may not in any respect be prejudiced and, above all, so that our Camaldolese may continue to recognize themselves as the sons and successors of such Fathers and predecessors, [Col. 0017C] and may not dare to separate themselves from the imitation of those from whom they proudly derive their common monastic or eremitical discipline, received from that most holy Father Romuald.

For that grave admonition of Peter Damian seems to belong no less to us than to the ancient Avellanites, with which the holy Doctor concludes his minor work 13, *On the Order and Resources of Fonte Avellana*, namely: “Let it shame you to become degenerate in your way of life from the nobility of those whose dwelling you have succeeded.”

**II.** I wish to establish this as the aim of the present dissertation, and I hope to direct the entire course of its treatment exclusively toward it, if he himself who supplies this study with its principal subject will not disdain to favor my desires, support my feeble efforts, and guide the pen consecrated to him: [Col. 0018A] blessed Peter Damian, the principal light and ornament of our order. I earnestly beseech him for this as I humbly prostrate myself before his altar.

For I did not undertake this kind of writing without first invoking his patronage, whose presence I have so often felt to be favorable to me. Nor, except under his auspices, do I trust that amid so many occupations wholly foreign to such studies, and leaving scarcely any leisure suitable for a more careful investigation of these matters, I could have composed this apology in any fashion and finally brought it to completion.

Especially since I approach this fourth part of the course I have set before me with my strength almost exhausted by the preceding stages. I could scarcely hope to traverse and complete it in its entirety unless the aid of that holy Doctor whose cause is at issue should raise my prostrate spirit, renew my vigor, restore my strength, and steady my faltering step, so that I might reach the desired goal with an easy and unhindered stride. [Col. 0018B]

**III.** Lest anyone should perhaps judge the controversy I have proposed to be of slight importance and little weight because he has insufficiently considered the outstanding merits of our Peter Damian toward the Church, and the distinguished qualities of his predecessors and successors—those who have rendered illustrious the celebrated monastery of Fonte Avellana, the monasteries dependent upon it, the famous hermitage of Sitria, and other related solitudes—for this question touches all of them alike, and the case of each is the same—qualities worthy of eternal remembrance [Col. 0018C] and deserving the highest praise, I therefore think that I should first place before the reader a brief and almost cursory outline both of them and of him.

Nevertheless, for a fuller knowledge of Peter Damian, I refer the reader to the most learned and devout Cardinals Baronius and Bellarmine, and to the other ecclesiastical writers cited by Abbot Constantine Cajetan at the beginning of volume I of the Works of that outstanding Doctor. Their works contain very frequent eulogies of him, although they fall far short of his merits.

For a fuller understanding of the Avellanites—it being understood that I do not at all distinguish among the praises of the Avellanites, the Sitrines, and similar groups, whose intermingled praises are confused with one another through the communion of their institutes—it will be sufficient to recommend the reading of the three volumes on the Saints of Umbria formerly published by the learned Ludovico Jacobilli.

For I do not undertake to write their complete history, but only to demonstrate their kinship with the Camaldolese institute. [Col. 0019A]

**IV.** Blessed Peter Damian was certainly a man far more learned than any other of his age, endowed with singular holiness and authority. If you consider his eloquence, you will rightly call him second only to Gregory; if you consider his zeal, equal to Jerome; if you attend to the austerity of his life and his devotion to extending the eremitical discipline, you will rightly say that he resembled Romuald.

Virtue alone raised him from the hiding places of solitude to the Roman purple and the primacy of the Church of Ostia. His renowned prudence brought him to undertake the most difficult papal legations; his proven humility led him back from the highest summit of dignity to the squalor of the hermitage.

Finally, only one who has not read his Life, Minor Works, and Miracles, who has not weighed the many institutions established through him for the advancement of divine worship and received by the universal Church, and who has not heard how highly he was esteemed by all the Roman pontiffs with whom and before whom he lived, can be ignorant of his praises.

Of these, it is sufficient to report the declaration of Alexander II, who, in a letter to the bishops of Gaul, published this magnificent testimony about him while he was still living:

> “We have taken care to send you such a man that, plainly, after us no greater authority is held in the Roman Church: namely, Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, who is both our eye and the immovable support of the Apostolic See.”

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

### V

[Col. 0019C]

As for the remaining companions of Peter Damian and followers of the same institute, they are so numerous and so distinguished that it seems almost miraculous that all could have come from that one Avellanese asceterium. Nor will it be easy to find another monastery—excepting one or two of the principal houses of the orders—which was adorned with men so illustrious for holiness and ecclesiastical rank. For this one solitude sent more than forty monks to the heavenly homeland, whose names have been consecrated to the veneration of posterity among the lists of saints and blessed; and approximately as many bishops of various cities are recorded as having been taken from its cloisters.

Four of these, on account of their merits, were enrolled in the senate of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church: namely, the man of whom we are speaking chiefly, Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia; Damian, the son of the holy doctor’s sister Rodelinda and therefore his nephew—whom Peter himself mentions in volume I, book II, letter 11; book VI, letters 3, 2, 22, and 29; and volume IV, poem 219, to whom the *Collections from the Works of Peter Damian* are addressed, in volume IV of his Works, and whom Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, also mentions in his *Commentary on Isaiah*.

[Col. 0019D]

That he was created cardinal by Gregory VII in memory of his uncle is clear from Roger, the author of the *Life of Saint Anselm, Bishop of Lucca*, as Constantine Cajetan notes in the preface to the aforesaid *Collections*. It is confirmed by the instrument of agreement between the provost of the Florentine church and the abbot of Saint Minias, where this Damian is read among the other cardinals as a subscriber in the year 1087, in Ughelli, volume VII, in the appendix to volume III on the bishops of Florence.

Also Guitmund, bishop of Aversa—whom some call Sigismund. Trithemius indeed believed him to have been a monk of Holy Cross of Leufridus, whereas Arnold Wion writes that he belonged to Holy Cross at Fonte Avellana and thinks that Trithemius was misled by the similarity of the monastery’s name. Jacobilli, however, maintains that he passed from the Leufridian monastery to Avellana, attracted by the reputation for holiness of Blessed Ludolphus, and that he was elected cardinal. This is established from the *Library of the Fathers*, in the *Works of Writers of the Eleventh Century*, volume XVII, page 469, and from Ughelli in his account of the bishops of Aversa, as well as from William Cave’s *Literary History* under the year 1066.

[Col. 0020A]

And finally Gebiosus, bishop of Cesena—who was summoned from the monastery of Avellana to Rome, where he was made abbot of Saint Alexius and then bishop and cardinal, as well as legate of Dalmatia and Sclavonia by Gregory VII, according to Ughelli, Jacobilli, and Ciacconius. Thus, as if by four purple gems, the diadem of the Avellanese cross is illumined.

### VI

[Col. 0020B]

Whether, then, James Laderchius was justified in striking so many and such great men from the register of the Camaldolese—*Life of Saint Peter Damian*, volume I, book I, chapter 8—is something to be investigated in this fourth dissertation. I maintain that I can undertake the task without offending him; whether I may also hope to succeed, I do not know. For although I am sufficiently confident in the fairness of my cause, I do not wish to flatter myself so far as to promise that he will treat me more mildly than his customary character would lead one to expect.

Whatever the outcome, it will be enough for me that I have undertaken—and necessarily undertaken—the defense of a just cause, and that I have kept within the limits of legitimate self-defense. Even if I were to exceed them, the right of complaint would belong to the man who, though he was the first to give offense and had in no respect been provoked by our side, attacked the order by attempting to erase and remove Peter Damian and the entire company of saints from its calendars, thereby striving to overturn its chief glory and utterly ruin its honor.

[Col. 0020C]

Just as we have endured this prejudice with due moderation, so it will be fair that he deal with us according to the same right and measure, and not take it ill that in the present dissertation we endeavor both to establish, by arguments of our own, the Camaldolese character of Peter Damian’s institute and to defend it against each of his objections and criticisms. Our aim is that the glory of our religion—which shines most brilliantly in Peter Damian and in his most celebrated followers—may remain intact and secure, and that in one and the same work we may defend the prudent judgment of so many distinguished writers who agree with us, as well as of the supreme pontiffs—whom we shall cite in chapter 6, section 19—and of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, which granted our order permission to recite the offices of Peter Damian on 22 February and of his disciple Dominic Loricatus on 17 October.

[Col. 0020D]

### VII

And although, while these pages were at press, a brief apology written in Italian appeared in defense of Saint Peter Damian against the same Laderchius, published by Filippo Maria Macchiarelli, a Camaldolese hermit of the Congregation of Monte Corona, who on page 9 considered himself the first of all Peter Damian’s defenders—as though he alone, while everyone else slept, had awakened to defend the entire order—he evidently did not know that others had long since taken up this task. Among them, the author of the *Dialogue between Sejanus and Rufinus* had already accomplished it deftly but vigorously.

[Col. 0021A]

I say nothing of the present Dissertation, which was then close to publication and which, if it could have been contained in three little sheets—as Macchiarelli’s *Apology* was—or if it had not had to await the remaining parts with which it was to be joined, would certainly have anticipated not only this author’s work but also his intention and conception.

Although, I say, Macchiarelli’s *Apology* preceded this dissertation of ours, just as the *Dialogue of Sejanus and Rufinus* already mentioned did, I nevertheless do not find that the subject has been so exhausted that no room remains for my own study. It is true that much of what I shall say must be shared with him and with the author of that dialogue; for those laboring to defend the same cause cannot fail to encounter the same arguments, drawn from the same quarters, and the same considerations derived from the same sources.

[Col. 0021B]

This should be regarded as an indication of truth. For several writers, composing their works in different regions separated by long distances and without communicating their studies to one another, could not agree almost simultaneously on the same principles unless the unity and constancy of truth—which speaks everywhere with a similar voice—compelled agreement in their opinions and words.

## CHAPTER II

### The origin and institution of the Avellanese hermitage, deriving from the holy father Romuald

[Col. 0021C]

### Synopsis

The origin of Avellana according to Fortunius, sections 1 and 2. Observations on his account, 3. It is shown that the monastery of Avellana was founded around the year 1000, 4. Whether Blessed Ludolphus fled the Arians, 5. Saint Romuald’s residence at Avellana, also on Mabillon’s testimony, 6. His residence near Catria is not to be interpreted as a residence at Sitria, 7. From Fortunius’s own principles, the foundation of Avellana is to be attributed to Saint Romuald, 8. Thomas Minius supports the same view, 9. The same is confirmed by the authority of Ludovico Jacobilli, 10. The same truth is strengthened by the calculation of Julius Ambrosius Lucentius, 11. A more certain determination of the year in which these events occurred, 12.

[Col. 0021D]

### I

To come closer now to the matter itself, we must trace back somewhat further the foundation of the monastery—or hermitage—of Saint Andrew, now of Holy Cross, at Fonte Avellana, where, as is related in the *Life of Peter Damian* published by John, his disciple and companion, chapter 4, Peter assumed the monastic habit.

Our Fortunius, in his *Camaldolese History*, part II, book V, chapter 5, speaks of it as follows:

> Those who mention the origin of the venerable hermitage, or monastery, of Holy Cross at Avellana attribute the matter to Ludolphus, or Candulphus, a man most distinguished for singular innocence and holy works. On account of these merits he deserved to be promoted to the chair of the Church of Gubbio, approximately thirty years after the hermitage itself had been founded. Yet no one identifies his lineage or original condition; he is believed to have been born of noble stock and to have been religious.
>
> The following eulogy concerning him survives: “In the year 1000, the building of the hermitage of Avellana beneath Catria was begun by Candulphus, or Ludolphus, as a simple chapel and hut, in order to flee the sect of the Arians.”
>
> But since the Arian plague, which began to weaken the Church of Christ around the year 320, had long since been extinguished before the year 1000, we have no doubt that this building was erected long before the time of our holy father Romuald.

[Col. 0022A]

### II

He continues as follows:

> Moreover, Ludolphus—whether fleeing persecutors or making a pilgrimage with a certain faithful companion—was accustomed, wherever he found a place suitable for an eremitical life among the forests and valleys, to be uncertain whether he should settle there and end his wandering. When he seemed unable to establish his path anywhere, it happened that, traveling over the ridges of the Apennines, he descended to a pleasant spot in a curved valley situated amid very dense forests between Mount Catria and Corno.
>
> As he paused there, more exhausted than usual by the journey, he came to a spring that gushed in great abundance at the roots of the hazel trees. After taking food, and when he had begun to fall into a little sleep, a voice from heaven came to him in these words: “Ludolphus, a dwelling has now been prepared for you here; at last spare yourself the labor of wandering.”
>
> Rising and giving thanks to God, he first erected there, as has been said, a chapel and hut in honor of Saint Andrew the Apostle. From the spring just mentioned the place received the name Fonte Avellana, which it has retained to this day.
>
> Ludolphus lived there for some time as though unknown, but was exposed by shepherds and then, entirely against his will, drawn to the episcopal chair of the Church of Gubbio, in whose diocese the place lies. Consequently his hermitage of Avellana, transformed into a famous monastery by the multitude of disciples, retained that title—the Order of the Dove, owing to the founder’s incredible, dove-like simplicity—even down to the time of the Tuscan poet Dante,

and so forth.

[Col. 0022B]

### III

The first point to be noted in this account is that Fortunius, with excessive carelessness, assumes as unquestionable that the foundation of the Avellanese hermitage occurred long before the time of Saint Romuald, since the inscription he cites seems to attribute to Ludolphus, the founder of the place, a flight from the long-extinct sect of the Arians.

Since that eulogy expressly affirms both that the building of the Avellanese hermitage was begun by Ludolphus in the year 1000 and that it was undertaken in order to flee the sect of the Arians, and since our historian judges these two statements incompatible, he ought to have considered more cautiously which of them he regarded as fictitious: the first, which is confirmed by countless other monuments, or the second, which rests on no testimony other than that of the polished inscription. He would then have discovered that the former should not be called into doubt on account of the latter; rather, the latter ought to be corrected in light of the former.

[Col. 0022C]

### IV

In fact, it is established that the sacred house of Avellana was truly built around the year of Christ 1000—or certainly a little earlier, as we shall determine below—and that its foundation cannot be referred to the age of the Arians.

This is clear first from Blessed Ludolphus himself, the founder of that hermitage. He was transferred to the episcopate of Gubbio in the year 1009, and after sending word in 1012, he is said to have returned to his hermitage, where he died most holily on 20 January 1047.

It is also clear from Ludolphus’s disciples: Julian, who governed the hermitage in Ludolphus’s absence from 1009 to 1012, succeeded him in the episcopate of Gubbio, and died on 7 May 1032; Blessed Guido of Arezzo, who in 1022 dedicated his *New Treatise on Music* to Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, and in 1030 was appointed by Blessed Ludolphus as his coadjutor or vicar, succeeding him also in the priorship in 1047 and continuing until he went to God on 17 May 1050; and Blessed Fortis the hermit, who offered himself as Ludolphus’s disciple in 1030 and departed this life on 9 May 1040, as the ancient inscription on his tomb in the cathedral of Gubbio attests.

[Col. 0023A]

I omit the weighty writers who maintain that Peter Damian devoted himself to divine service there in the fiftieth year after the foundation of the Avellanese hermitage. That claim would certainly be false unless the beginnings of that venerable solitude, established by Blessed Ludolphus, were placed around the year of Christ 1000.

### V

Meanwhile, what the author of that eulogy meant when he said that Ludolphus built the little chapel at Fonte Avellana in order to flee the sect of the Arians is not easy to determine, unless we say that some remnants of the Arians—perhaps remnants still surviving or revived—were present. Even in our own age this impiety was renewed, especially in England and Poland, through various sectarians: Faustus Socinus, John Crellius, Brennius, Eniedinus, Smalcius, Schlichting, Ostorod, and Christopher Sand.

For Peter Damian appears to speak of the Arians as still existing in volume III, *Opusculum* VI, chapter 22:

> On the contrary, the Arians, who openly and utterly impiously contend against the divinity of the Holy Spirit, cannot, when they return to the Catholic faith, remain in the dignity of the order they wrongly received. For, as their sacrilegious assertion makes clear, they believe that the Father is creator, the Son a creature, and damnably maintain that the Holy Spirit is the creature of a creature.

[Col. 0023B]

An anonymous panegyrist of Henry IV likewise mentions the Arians as existing in his own time; Pagius cites him from volume I of Freher’s *Collection* under the year 1058, section 5.

Or, finally, unless we interpret this clause to mean that Ludolphus, devoted to divine worship, demonstrated by that chapel that he was alienated from the Arian superstition, which he especially abhorred, and that he there bore witness to the divine honors due to Christ and to the proper veneration of Saint Andrew, his apostle.

[Col. 0023C]

It is not worth lingering over the interpretation of that inscription, however, since its authority is so obscure that I see no one relying on it or commending it for this purpose except Fortunius and those who took the account from him.

### VI

A second observation concerning Fortunius’s account is that he omitted an important circumstance expressly noted by other writers: namely, that this Ludolphus was himself a disciple of the holy father Romuald and had been instructed by him in the laws of eremitical discipline. Indeed, Saint Romuald himself stayed in the very solitude established near Catria with Ludolphus’s assistance, as Peter Damian relates in the *Life of Saint Romuald*, chapter 19:

> At one time, however, the holy man stayed not far from Catria.

[Col. 0023D]

Various authors explain this passage as referring to a residence at Avellana, among them Ludovico Jacobilli in his *Saints of Umbria* and John Mabillon in his preface to the sixth Benedictine century, where he writes concerning the Avellanese monastery:

> Around the year of Christ 1000 it began to be built—namely, in Umbria, in the diocese of Gubbio, at the foot of Mount Catria, where Saint Romuald likewise had a retreat.

[Col. 0024A]

I pass over authors of lesser prominence, such as Portesanus and Crucettus.

### VII

Indeed, scarcely any witnesses are needed where the matter itself speaks: first, from the agreement between the Avellanese institute and the Romualdine laws, which we shall discuss more fully below; and second, because that residence of Romuald near Catria cannot be explained in any other way than as a residence in the solitude of Avellana.

Fortunius, in part VII, book I, chapter 11, interprets that place as referring to the hermitage of Sitria. This opinion appears to conflict with Peter Damian’s authority, for in the *Life of Saint Romuald*, chapter 49, he reports that Romuald turned aside to inhabit the solitude of Sitria as though he had not previously lived there, but were then beginning to fill the place with his disciples.

Damian’s words are as follows:

> Afterwards, when Romuald had left the Apennines, he climbed Mount Sitria in order to inhabit it. Great care must be taken, however, lest anyone, hearing that the holy man changed so many places, attribute the burden of a pious work to the fault of fickleness. Without doubt, the cause of these changes was that wherever the venerable man lived, an almost innumerable crowd of people gathered around him. Reason therefore required that when he saw the space of one place filled with inhabitants, he should establish someone there and hasten immediately to fill another.

[Col. 0024B]

If Romuald had already founded a hermitage at Sitria while he was staying at Catria, as Fortunius teaches, this new journey to Sitria would have had to be attributed not to a new change of place but to a visitation of his former disciples. Damian’s explanation would then have been unnecessary, and the reason he gives—the multitude of disciples—would not fit the matter itself.

[Col. 0024C]

Therefore the residence near Catria must certainly be understood not as a residence at Sitria—which lies two miles away, toward the town of Sassoferrato—but in the solitude of Fonte Avellana, which clings directly to the side of Mount Catria.

### VIII

I do not think Fortunius himself would have failed expressly to concede this, had his preconceived opinion—that Ludolphus’s flight from the Arians meant that Avellana had been founded before the time of Romuald—not persuaded him to place the foundation of Avellana in an earlier period. From this he falsely concluded that Romuald’s residence near Catria could not refer to the Avellanese solitude, already occupied by other monks, but had to be twisted into a reference to the hermitage of Sitria.

[Col. 0024D]

For elsewhere he admits that monasteries constructed in Romuald’s age derived their discipline chiefly from him. He says in part I, book I, chapter 23:

> So great was the reputation of the most holy Romuald throughout Europe that there was nowhere in the world, in his own time, any monastery, any solitude of the desert, or any congregation of religious persons that either did not have Romuald as its teacher and father or did not seek counsel from him through envoys concerning how one ought to conduct oneself in the sacred army and how one might resist diabolical attacks.

[Col. 0025A]

He ought to have affirmed this especially, and with still greater justification, of the Avellanese hermitage. It was established not merely during Romuald’s lifetime, but in Italy itself, indeed in Umbria, under the eyes of the holy father; and it could receive appropriate laws for eremitical living from no one except Romuald, the great restorer of the eremitical life.

### IX

For this reason our monk Thomas Minius, in his *Camaldolese History*, preserved in manuscript in the Library of the Angels at Florence, where he renders Fortunius verbatim in Italian—correcting only certain passages and supplying some omissions, as we noted above in Dissertation I, chapter 1, section 6—interprets and restores the foundation of the Avellanese monastery, which we cited above from Fortunius in section 1, as follows. He presents Ludolphus as a disciple of Romuald, instructed by him in the precepts of eremitical life:

[Col. 0025B]

> Those who mention the origin of the venerable hermitage, now an abbey, of Holy Cross at Avellana, maintain that its founder was Blessed Ludolphus, otherwise Candulphus, a man endowed with singular innocence. Through his holy works he was made bishop of Gubbio in the thirtieth year after the foundation of that hermitage. But they give no account whatever of his origins; they say only that he was of noble stock and religious, producing this record:
>
> “In the year 1000 the building of the hermitage of Avellana beneath Catria was begun by Candulphus, or Ludolphus, as a simple chapel and hut, in order to flee the sect of the Arians.”
>
> At that time the fame of the holiness of our father Saint Romuald, who was still living, and of his disciples was celebrated not only in Italy but throughout almost all Europe. There is no reason for doubt; rather, I firmly believe that Ludolphus too was his disciple, and that he not only fled the persecution of the sect but, following the example of his master Saint Romuald—and indeed with his blessing and consent, like another Saint John Gualbert—went in search of solitary places remote from every worldly tumult, intending to settle there with his companion and attract others to the service of God, since they possessed an ardent desire for the salvation of souls,

and so forth.

[Col. 0025C]

Minius adds below:

> As confirmation of what I have said—namely, that Blessed Ludolphus was a disciple of our father Saint Romuald and lived with his disciples under such protection—this is seen clearly in the person of Peter Damian, insofar as Father Friar Paolo Morigia states in his *History of the Religions* that Peter Damian was a Camaldolese monk. Pope Pius V held the same opinion. This is confirmed by the fact that Peter Damian was abbot and superior in several monasteries of the Camaldolese order, as will be said in his Life.

We shall also say something about this in chapter 6.

### X

[Col. 0025D]

Ludovico Jacobilli confirms the same point in volume III of his *Saints of Umbria*, page 324:

> Many came to do penance and joined their company, building there a monastery for many monks. Blessed Ludolphus clothed these monks there around the year 1000 of Our Lord, and with the authority of Pope Sylvester II established the congregation of Fonte Avellana, also called that of the Dove, under the rule of Saint Benedict, with certain constitutions of Saint Romuald, abbot, who had founded the Camaldolese order for his monks and hermits as early as the year 953 and was living at that time,

and so forth.

[Col. 0026A]

These are his words. He relates similar things elsewhere and likewise places Peter Damian among the Camaldolese absolutely, especially in volume II, under 13 July, in the *Life of Saint Romuald*, page 32.

### XI

It is useful to cite in support of the same opinion what the most reverend abbot Julius Ambrosius Lucentius, a Cistercian and consultant of the Sacred Congregation of the Index, wrote for this purpose in a book entitled *The Splendor of Foligno*, printed at Rome in 1703, and therefore after the publication of Laderchius’s work.

[Col. 0026B]

In the notes following Eulogy XVIII, page 102, he writes:

> Under Ludolphus’s direction his school began to be frequented by many, with the approval of John, bishop of Gubbio, in the year 976. What began at first as a rough and undeveloped undertaking grew, with the subsequent approval of Sylvester II, Roman pontiff, into the head and principal house of the most renowned congregation of Holy Cross at Avellana, under the rule of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino, with certain constitutions added—some dictated by Saint Romuald, the first abbot of the Camaldolese, and some written by Ludolphus himself.

Thus far Abbot Lucentius.

### XII

[Col. 0026C]

If the beginnings of Avellana are to be brought within more certain chronological limits, then, since Ludolphus was appointed to the episcopal see of Gubbio in 1009, those who think that he was called to the episcopate in the thirtieth year after the construction of that sacred solitude must place its foundation in 979. This is not far removed from the year 976 expressly given above by Ludovico Jacobilli and Abbot Lucentius.

[Col. 0026D]

Accordingly, those who wish the Avellanese hermitage to have been founded in the year 1000 must either be understood as referring to the building which was later reduced to the more definite form of a hermitage or monastery, or else their date must be interpreted as not precisely determined but only approximately indicated.

It must nevertheless be admitted that until the years 989 and 990 Ludolphus governed the disciples who had joined him without any fixed rule, following only the guidance of his own spirit. For it was only then that Saint Romuald lived near Catria, from whom Ludolphus received the rule of Saint Benedict and at the same time learned the complete norm of eremitical life and the most salutary institutions by which he would thereafter train his pupils.

[Col. 0027A]

Since Romuald became prefect of the monastery of Classe in 995—and this had been divinely revealed to him by Saint Apollinaris five years earlier, therefore in 990, according to chapter 22 of his Life—and since this occurred while Romuald was staying at Catria, according to chapter 19 of the Life, it follows that Romuald must have stayed at Mount Catria with Ludolphus and his companions in 989, and that in 990, warned by that same Saint Apollinaris, he departed from there, drawing nearer to the monastery of Classe while awaiting the prefecture divinely assigned to him.

## CHAPTER III

### Comparison of the institutes of the Avellanese and Camaldolese

[Col. 0027B]

### Synopsis

The purpose of this chapter. Section 1: The union of hermitage and monastery at Avellana. 2. The institute of monks, hermits, and enclosed solitaries flourished at Avellana. 3. Obedience inculcated upon the hermits among both the Avellanese and the Camaldolese. 4. A particular comparison of the two institutes. 5. What abstinence and fasting—including two-day and three-day fasts—mean in Blessed Rodulphus, Camaldolese prior, and in Peter Damian. 6. At what time the fasting prescribed by Romuald was observed by the Avellanese and Camaldolese. 7. Abstinence was relaxed by both for three octaves. 8. The discipline of fasting during the Easter season. 9. What was customary among both during the rest of the year. 10. The observance of the two Lents. 11 and 12. The custom concerning Holy Saturday and the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. 13. The scales used in the cells of the Camaldolese and Avellanese to measure the weight of bread. 14. The measure of bread prescribed by Saint Benedict, clarified from these facts. 15.

[Col. 0027C]

### I

Lest anyone think that I rely merely on the arbitrary imagination of writers when I say—as I explained in the preceding chapter—that Blessed Ludolphus merited to be trained under the discipline of Saint Romuald and received from him the rules of eremitical living to be handed on to his Avellanese followers, it is useful in the present chapter to compare the two institutes.

On the one hand, we shall compare the practices of the unquestioned disciples of Saint Romuald and the first Camaldolese; on the other, those of the followers of Blessed Ludolphus and Peter Damian, namely, the ancient Avellanese. It will immediately become clear that both groups spread from one and the same root: the holy Romuald, leader of all hermits.

[Col. 0027D]

Although this is already sufficiently evident from Dissertation I—especially where, in chapter 4, sections 8 and 21, and elsewhere throughout, we showed that the institute of Romuald was observed exactly at Fonte Avellana no less than in the sacred hermitage of Camaldoli—it must nevertheless be demonstrated here more specifically from the records of Peter Damian, Blessed Rodulphus, and others. We shall not provide a long and exact enumeration of every detail, but at least a brief sample of the principal rules.

[Col. 0028A]

### II

Let us therefore first compare the more general matters.

We proved in Dissertation I, chapter 4, that Romuald’s institute comprised a union of cenobitic and eremitical life. For this reason Saint Romuald established monasteries near hermitages in many places and placed both the community of social discipline and that of solitary discipline under one superior. Thus in chapter 30 of his Life we are told that:

> He ordered the abbot to withdraw into the hermitage and remain in his cell throughout the entire week, but on Sundays to come to the monastery and visit the brothers.

[Col. 0028B]

Damian likewise arranged for a cloister to be built beside the church at the solitude of Avellana for those who preferred to live cenobitically and, following monastic custom, enjoyed conducting processions on solemn feast days. He himself testifies to this in volume III, *Opusculum* XIV:

> We also judged that a cloister should be built beside the church for this purpose: that if anyone still took pleasure in the long-established custom of the monastic order, he might have a place where, on the principal festivals, he could solemnly proceed according to custom. We also procured for this procession a sufficiently suitable silver cross.

He also mentions these monks, living a cenobitic life near the church, in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 7, where, speaking of the servants, he says:

> Some also rise earlier to hear the vigils of the psalter, namely, with those brothers who live near the church.

### III

[Col. 0028C]

Since the Camaldolese institute, by Romuald’s direction, embraces three kinds of religious persons—cenobites, open hermits, and enclosed anchorites—as we already explained in the place cited, it is perfectly clear that all three lived at Fonte Avellana in Peter Damian’s time.

Thus in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 18, he enumerates these three degrees when he says:

> In the cells themselves they should never speak to anyone, unless perhaps they are entirely enclosed or are established near the monastery.

That is, he commands open hermits to observe silence in their cells, except when they live wholly enclosed—those who are not forbidden to converse with visitors in the cell—or when they live among the cenobites, who are not bound by so strict a censure of silence.

[Col. 0028D]

Peter Damian instructs the monks in *Opusculum* XIII, *On the Perfection of Monks*, where he also discusses the various offices of the monastery. He instructs the hermits in *Opuscula* XIV and XV, openly laying out all the rules of fasting and other austerities.

He directs the enclosed solitaries both in book VI, letter 30, addressed to Theuzo, adducing various examples of them—such as Martin Storax, “who has not come out for three lustrums,” and Lupus, “who enclosed himself for eternal freedom” in “the prison” of his own cell—as well as in *Opusculum* 9, where he teaches that solitaries, in the celebration of the divine offices and sacred mysteries, cannot alter the formulas used by the Church, such as *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) and *Jube, domne, benedicere* (“Command, lord, a blessing”), even though these formulas may seem to presuppose the presence of others.

[Col. 0029A]

That work is addressed “To Leo, enclosed for love of the freedom above,” just as *Opusculum* XV is addressed “To Stephen, enclosed for love of the charity above.” Peter praises Stephen because:

> Fleeing the spaciousness of monastic life, he immediately enclosed himself, with fervent spirit, within the prison-like narrowness of a little cell.

### IV

Again, just as Romuald directed the principal concern of his efforts toward recalling hermits—who had formerly lived according to their own judgment—to the yoke of salutary obedience, so that, without the command or consent of a superior, they would not hope that even very great works would profit them toward merit, as we explained in Dissertation I, chapter 5, section 6 and following, so Peter Damian inculcates this same virtue of obedience upon the hermits above all else.

[Col. 0029B]

In *Opusculum* XV, chapter 18, he writes:

> This must be guarded against with the greatest care: that no one, under the pretext of the eremitical life, refuse the yoke of obedience. Rather, he should bind himself by a stricter law of obedience in proportion as he knows that this institute surpasses the rule of the cenobites. For obedience both commends our good works and excuses offenses arising from negligence. Therefore, if our withdrawal or affliction is to be fruitful, let it always be seasoned with the salt of salutary obedience; and whatever branches of good work our life may spread, they must always grow together at the root of obedience.

These words correspond exactly to the admonitions of Blessed Rodulphus, Camaldolese prior, in the constitutions of 1080, chapter 40:

> This virtue is very necessary for solitaries, so that the harder a life they lead, the more complete an obedience they observe. Some, under the pretext of a holier life, refuse the yoke of obedience. They think themselves released from the law of obedience because they know themselves bound by a stricter zeal for the eremitical life. But obedience must certainly be more carefully observed where the manner of life is more fervent and austere.

### V

[Col. 0029C]

But, to descend to particulars, let us compare the discipline of Romuald and the ancient Camaldolese with the manner of life of Peter Damian and the ancient Avellanese. We shall discover that the one agrees so completely with the other that both seem to have been dictated almost by the same pen, certainly by the same spirit. If there is any difference, it is so slight that scarcely any greater distinction could be observed between different monasteries of the same indivisible congregation, and no greater agreement could be expected on account of differences of place.

[Col. 0029D]

It would be too long to pursue every detail. We shall review the main points, which will prove to correspond almost word for word. From these the reader will easily infer the rest, which at least agree in meaning.

We shall begin with the discipline of abstinence or fasting, which is the chief of eremitical customs. First, however, let us hear the definitions of the terms supplied by each side; then we shall proceed through the remaining matters in order.

### VI

Blessed Rodulphus, the fourth Camaldolese prior, says in the constitutions of 1080, chapter 11:

> Abstinence is said to occur in this place when nothing is served to those eating except bread and water, or, if anyone wishes, the addition of salt.

[Col. 0030A]

Peter Damian, however, says in *Opusculum* XIV, *On the Order of the Hermits of Fonte Avellana*:

> We call those people fasting who take bread with salt and water. When anything else is added besides these, it is not called a perfect fast—or, as *Opusculum* XV, chapter 6, has it, “fasting in the hermitage.”

Thus Rodulphus’s term *abstinence* has the same meaning as Damian’s term *perfect* or *eremitical fasting*. When any cooked dish is omitted while a single meal is retained, Rodulphus calls this a simple fast, whereas Peter Damian calls it a single meal.

Again, the five-day fast per week in Peter Damian has the same meaning as the two-day and three-day abstinence in Rodulphus. For, as Paulus Justinianus says in *Rule of Eremitical Life*, chapter 27:

> Two-day and three-day fasts were so called when they fasted on bread and water on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, and afterward on Friday and Saturday: the abstinence of the first three days being called three-day abstinence, and that of the following two days two-day abstinence.

[Col. 0030B]

These points needed to be stated lest a difference in the sound of the words lead anyone to infer a difference in meaning.

VII. Now let us learn from Peter Damian’s Opuscula XIV and XV, chapter 6, during what season of the year this abstinence of three, two, or five days per week—prescribed by Romuald himself for all followers of his eremitical discipline (as stated above, Dissertation I, chapter 3, no. 3)—was observed among the Avellanites:

> “From the Ides of September,” he says, “until the Resurrection of the Lord, a fast is customarily kept here on five days each week.”

How long the Camaldulenses observed this is taught by Blessed Rudolph the Prior in the aforementioned Constitutions, chapter 11, where he says:

> “From the beginning of the greater Lent until the Paschal solemnity, a three-day and two-day abstinence is customarily observed in this hermitage each week.” [Col. 0030C]

He adds in chapter 14:

> “From the solemnity of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Savior, the Lenten observance is made, as it was prescribed above for the greater Lent.”

And in the Constitutions of the year 1085:

> “In these aforesaid Lents,” he says, “it is customary to fast for five days on bread, water, and salt.”

Thus the Avellanites came even closer than the Camaldulenses to the institution of the blessed Romuald in this respect. They observed the perfect eremitical fast instituted by the holy Father—distributed over five days of the week through three-day and two-day fasts, according to chapter 9 of his Life—not only during both Lents, as did our people, but also for two months before the feast of Saint Martin. Thereafter, from the octave of the Nativity of the Lord—which they wished to exempt from fasting, as will be explained below—until the beginning of the greater Lent, that is, altogether from the Ides of September until the Lord’s Pasch, they were subject to the rigor of this abstinence. [Col. 0030D]

VIII. Three octaves alone—the octaves of the Resurrection, the Nativity of the Lord, and Pentecost—were exempted from the common abstinence and eremitical fast, both among the Avellanites and among the Camaldulenses. Concerning the first, Peter Damian writes in Opuscula XIV and XV, chapter 5:

> “Only three octaves are celebrated during the year in such a way that no one here is compelled to fast: namely, those of the Lord’s Resurrection, holy Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord. Although during the octave of Pentecost both ecclesiastical tradition and the authority of the Fathers decree that one should fast—for the four Ember seasons—during the other octaves of whatever feasts, we observe the ecclesiastical Office, as the regular order requires, but we do not alter the course of the customary fast.” [Col. 0031A]

Concerning the second, Blessed Rudolph the Prior states in the Constitutions of the year 1085:

> “It is customary to fast each week on bread, water, and salt, except during the octave of the Nativity of the Lord, his Resurrection, and Pentecost, and to celebrate no other octave in this manner except these three, which we have just mentioned above.”

In the other Constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 12, he says:

> “During the Paschal week, not only is abstinence relaxed, but the fast is also suspended. At Pentecost the same observances are to be maintained that were mentioned for the Paschal solemnity, except that the fasts of the four Ember seasons during this week are simply observed according to ecclesiastical rite on Friday, which is assigned to abstinence.” [Col. 0031B]

And shortly afterward, in chapter 15:

> “On the day of the Nativity itself the fast is also suspended; on the other days throughout the octave, only abstinence is relaxed.”

IX. Again, throughout the entire Paschal season, the discipline of fasting was maintained for only four days of each week, both at Avellana and at Camaldoli: Tuesday and Thursday were assigned to two meals, in addition to Sunday. Hence Peter Damian says in the places cited above:

> “From the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection until the holy day of Pentecost, you fast four days each week; but apart from Sunday, concerning whose reverence no one has any doubt, on Tuesday and Thursday you eat on these days.”

Saturday’s fast, however, was not a perfect fast but a simple one, restricted to a single meal; wine and cooked food were nevertheless permitted to the hermits. Damian writes in Opusculum XV, chapter 15:

> “Let it not seem burdensome to a brother to defer his meal even on Saturday until the ninth hour, so that he may eat only once on that day, but may nevertheless not be forbidden, by the indulgence of our institution, to receive wine and cooked food.” [Col. 0031C]

Blessed Rudolph the Prior expresses the same matter more briefly in the cited Constitutions, chapter 12:

> “Afterward, from the octave of Easter, abstinence is resumed for three days of the week—namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—until Pentecost; Saturdays, however, are assigned to a simple fast.” [Col. 0031D]

X. From the octave of Pentecost until the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, abstinence—or the perfect fast—was observed in both places on only four days. In addition, Tuesday was devoted to a simple fast; thereafter, from the feast of Saint John until the Ides of September, it was assigned to two meals, exactly as we noted was customary during the Paschal season.

Here are Peter Damian’s words in Opuscula XIV and XV, chapter 6:

> “From the octave of Pentecost until the Nativity of Blessed John, cooked food is given to the brothers on Tuesday at the ninth hour, while on Thursday the meal is repeated. From the feast of Saint John until the Ides of September, two meals are taken each day on Tuesday and Thursday, while on the other four days the customary fast is observed.” [Col. 0032A]

Blessed Rudolph agrees with this in the cited passage, chapter 13:

> “Thereafter, from the octave of Pentecost until the feast of Saint John, with four days of the week assigned to abstinence, Tuesday is observed as a simple fast, while on Thursday the meal is doubled. For the remainder of the time until the Ides of September, the same abstinence of four days is maintained, with Tuesday and Thursday assigned to two meals.”

XI. Since such a distribution of the eremitical abstinence instituted by Saint Romuald prevailed among the Avellanites and Camaldulenses throughout the entire year, with the same measure of moderation observed in both places, let us now see with what strictness both groups were accustomed to complete the course of the two Lents. Concerning Saint Romuald’s disciples we read in his Life, chapter 9:

> “During the two Lents of the year, not only he himself, Romuald, but most of his disciples were accustomed to continue the fast throughout the entire week.”

Blessed Rudolph the Prior likewise testifies to this concerning some Camaldulensian hermits of his own time in the Constitutions of the year 1085. Peter Damian speaks as follows of the Avellanites in Opusculum XIV:

> “Concerning those two Lents that precede either the Nativity of the Lord or holy Easter, although I remain silent, you nevertheless know that there are some here who customarily pass through that entire double Lenten period fasting, apart from Sundays, except for three solemnities: namely Saint Andrew’s, Saint Benedict’s, and [Col. 0032C] the Lord’s Annunciation.” [Col. 0032B]

And in Opusculum XV, chapter 6:

> “During those two Lents that precede either the Nativity of the Lord or holy Easter, there are some brothers here who pass through the entire week fasting and live each day on bread and water, except on Sundays.”

XII. The others, however, who could not endure the continuation of so rigorous a fast, contented themselves with a three-day and two-day abstinence. On Thursdays and Sundays during both Lents they added vegetables or some kind of broth to their meal. Both the Avellanites and the Camaldulenses nevertheless abstained equally from fish and wine, except on certain more solemn days.

Concerning the former, Peter Damian says in both Opuscula XIV and XV, chapter 6:

> “During the aforesaid two Lents it has been customary that neither monks nor laypeople be permitted to receive wine or even fish, except on these four feasts: namely Saint Andrew’s, Blessed Benedict’s, Palm Sunday, and the Lord’s Supper. On these most sacred days, they receive fish and wine, invited to do so by the joy of the outstanding solemnities.” [Col. 0032D]

Concerning the latter, Blessed Rudolph the Prior says in the Constitutions of the year 1085:

> “It is customary during the two Lents never to eat fish or drink wine, except on the solemnities of Saint Andrew, Saint Benedict, Saint Mary, Palm Sunday, if the Lord should send it from some quarter, and the Lord’s Supper.”

Likewise, in the other Constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 11, he says:

> “Wine also is not given after the beginning of the great Lent and of the Advent of the Lord, except on Palm Sunday and the designated feasts, and on the Lord’s Supper, on the feasts of Blessed Mary and Saint Benedict.” [Col. 0033A]

XIII. Specifically, however, on Holy Saturday and the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the institution of both places permitted them to take wine and bread in a more generous measure because of the labors of the choir. Thus Damian speaks of his Avellanites in Opuscula XIV and XV, chapter 6:

> “On Holy Saturday, and likewise on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, so that the labor of the ecclesiastical Office may be relieved, they eat as much bread as they wish; but they admit no other food at all, whether they are laypeople or monks.” [Col. 0033B]

Blessed Rudolph the Prior makes the following provision for the Camaldulensian hermits in the passage cited immediately above, chapter 11:

> “Holy Saturday ought to be assigned to the abstinence of sacred baptism; but, because of the labor of the Office that follows at Easter, twice-baked bread, with a moderate consumption of wine, may be granted to the brothers.”

And shortly afterward, in chapter 14, he says:

> “On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity the same observance is to be maintained that we said was to be observed on Holy Saturday.”

XIV. Damian and Rudolph specifically note that an entire, unbroken quantity of bread was permitted only on the day preceding the Resurrection and on the day preceding the Nativity of the Lord because on the other fasting days they devoted only five eighths of a loaf, weighed according to a fixed measure and prescribed weight, to their single meal.

Hence Peter Damian says in Opusculum XV, chapter 8:

> “The measure of bread is the same in the hermitage as in the monastery, with this distinction: on days of meals, whether there is one meal or two, if a brother wishes to eat the whole portion, he is not obliged to incur blame. On fasting days, however, since each brother has scales in his cell, he always weighs what he is going to set before himself for supper. The measure has this form: with half a quarter added—that is, an eighth—it weighs half of a whole loaf, with a quarter and a half-quarter remaining intact”—that is, three eighths remain. “And so that no doubt may remain concerning this measure, nine ornix eggs [the bird is uncertain], or three goose eggs weigh exactly the same on the balanced scales.” [Col. 0033C]

Blessed Rudolph the Prior similarly says in the Constitutions of the year 1085:

> “Each brother has scales in his cell, with which he weighs three loaves, all of which he receives on Sundays and Thursdays.” [Col. 0033D]

The same is also attested by Paul Justinian in the Rule of the Eremitical Life, chapter 29, and by Fortunatus in the History of Camaldoli, part I, book I, chapter 58.
