All this is derived from the institution of Saint Romuald, who prescribed the provision of those fasting with such a fixed measure that he initially confined his disciples to half a paximatius—that is, a twice-baked loaf—and then granted a quarter of the same loaf in addition to those who needed more abundant food, as happened in the case of Blessed Peter Urseolus. After he had thrown himself at the feet of the holy Father and disclosed his need, he said:

> “Father, because I have a large body for my sins, I cannot sustain myself on this half of a paximatius.” [Col. 0034A]

Romuald immediately and compassionately took pity on his weakness, added a quarter of a paximatius to the customary measure, and thus extended the hand of mercy to the failing brother so that he would not perish altogether,” and so forth, as we read in the Life of Romuald, chapter 8.

XV. It is worth noting in passing that from the passage of Damian cited shortly beforehand one can derive the precise measure of bread prescribed by Saint Benedict in chapter 39 of the Rule:

> “One weighed pound of bread is sufficient for the day, whether there is one meal or both lunch and supper.”

Saint Benedict entrusted this weight, together with the measure of a hemina of wine, to Blessed Maurus when he sent him into Gaul, as Faustus relates in his Life in Surius. The monks of Cassino, fleeing the invasion of the Lombards, likewise carried that same weight and [Col. 0034B] measure with them to Rome, according to Leo of Ostia in the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, book I, chapter 2, and Regino, book I of his Chronicle, as well as Sigebert under the year of Christ 596.

Moreover, monks sent by Theodemar, abbot of Cassino, to Charlemagne in Gaul to restore monastic discipline brought with them a weight of four pounds and the measures for lunch and supper.

Although the Council of Aachen decided in canon 57:

> “That a pound of bread be measured at thirty solidi by twelve denarii,”

nevertheless, since the weight of those solidi is unknown, that ancient monastic measure of bread likewise remains obscure.

From the preceding text of Peter Damian, however, at least this can be deduced: in his time five such pounds corresponded in equal weight to twenty-four goose eggs. For when [Col. 0034C] he testifies that the measure of bread “in the hermitage was the same as in the monastery” outside the fasting days, and says that during fasts this measure was diminished by one quarter and one half—“with the quarter remaining whole and a half,” that is, reduced to five eighths—and that this weighed the same as three goose eggs, he plainly indicates that the complete measure was equal in weight to five such eggs less one-fifth of a single egg. Accordingly, five complete monastic measures of bread were equivalent to twenty-four eggs, as can easily be established by calculation.

But let us pass on to other matters, having briefly recovered our breath.

# CHAPTER IV  
## Other Points of Agreement between the Avellanites and the Camaldulenses

[Col. 0034D]

### SYNOPSIS

Similar abstinence from wine among the Avellanites and Camaldulenses. 1. The same discipline for servants. 2. Equal observance of vigils. 3. Likewise, the distinction of feasts. 4. The custom of transferring feasts among both groups. 5. Equal practice of going barefoot. 6. Likewise, the discipline of metanies and the use of the chapter. 7. The measure of scourging and other exercises of this kind left in both places to the discretion of individuals. 8. A discreet and hidden relaxation for the weak likewise accepted. 9. The discipline of chanting prescribed by Romuald for both groups. 10. The Office of Blessed Mary the Virgin proposed by Peter Damian for both groups. 11. Equal piety toward the dead in both places. 12. Equal avoidance of sleep after the night Office. 13. The same rigor of silence. 14. Similar avoidance of instability and wandering. 15. The use of the cell commended in like manner to both groups. 16. The value of perseverance [Col. 0035A] impressed upon both groups. 17. Other admonitions of Saint Romuald common to both. 18.

I. In this chapter we shall pursue the remaining customs of the ancient Avellanites and the corresponding practices of the Camaldulensian hermits. Above all, we shall note that the use of wine was initially completely unknown to both groups, but was later permitted in moderate measure, outside the days of abstinence—that is, those devoted to the perfect fast, discussed above.

Concerning Saint Romuald’s disciples at Sitria, Damian himself testifies in chapter 64 of his Life that:

> “There no one knew wine, even if someone suffered the most serious illness.”

Soon afterward, Blessed Rudolph, Prior of Camaldoli, is recorded as having decreed in the Constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 23:

> “Wine is known to be foreign to hermits, but because the decline of our age, [Col. 0035B] as well as the weakness of nature, does not permit this altogether, they customarily receive such a drink rarely and moderately—those who cannot preserve frugal abstinence with John, or practice moderate restraint with Timothy.”

Peter Damian likewise says the following when reviewing the institutions of his congregation, in Opuscula XIV and XV, no. 15, chapter 6:

> “As you know, we abstained from wine for some time, so that neither laypeople nor visitors from outside, nor even on the Pasch of the Lord, drank anything here apart from water; wine was kept here only for the sacrifice. But because those who remained here began to weaken through illness, and because some who desired to pass into the hermitage utterly recoiled from observing this rigor, we mercifully accommodated the weakness of our brothers—or, more truly, the common weakness—and allowed wine to be drunk here, provided that moderation was preserved. Since we cannot wholly relinquish it with John, let us at least strive, with Timothy, the disciple of Paul, to administer it soberly and humbly to the weak stomach; and since we cannot be completely abstinent, let us at least strive to be sober.” [Col. 0035C]

II. No one should be surprised that formerly even the laypeople at Avellana abstained from wine, since the discipline of fasting was extended even to the servants themselves, both there and among Romuald’s followers. For after Damian had described the strict manner of life of the disciples at Sitria, he adds in chapter 64 of the Life of Saint Romuald:

> “But why am I speaking of the monks, when the servants of the monks themselves, and even the keepers of the sheep, also fasted?” and so forth. [Col. 0035D]

Concerning the servants of the hermitage of Avellana, he likewise says in Opusculum XV, chapter 7:

> “The servants who serve this place also do not depart from the order of life assigned to them. Throughout the entire course of the year they customarily fast for three days each week. During those two Lents, however, they devote four days to fasting,” and so forth.

It is unnecessary to repeat that fasting here always signifies fasting on bread and water, not merely eating only once during the day.

III. In addition to the days of such abstinence prescribed for each week, the vigils of the saints were also customarily celebrated with the same strictness, both at Camaldoli and at Avellana. This applied not only to those vigils that are universally observed with fasting, but also to those that ecclesiastical law does not prohibit from having two meals, such as the vigil of Epiphany and those of the holy apostles Philip and James.

Hence Blessed Rudolph the Prior says in the cited Constitutions, chapter 17:

> “The vigils of the saints that have been established in the Church, as well as the vigils of Epiphany and of the holy Philip and James, although they are not observed among secular people, are to be assigned to abstinence in this hermitage”—that is, at Camaldoli. [Col. 0036A]

And Peter Damian, writing in volume I, book VI, letter 35 to the hermits of his congregation concerning the fast of eight vigils, commends these among others, but especially those of Epiphany and of the holy Philip and James, saying:

> “It is also worthy to fast on the vigil of Epiphany, because of the greatness of the solemnity in which so many mysteries converge into one.”

Further on he says:

> “Therefore we also bear it heavily that many brothers, when they shrink from fasting on the vigils of the blessed apostles Philip and James, put forward the solemnity of Pentecost as an excuse for their laxity, saying that no one ought then to be constrained under the discipline of fasting, since the season dictates that one should rather feast in Paschal rejoicing.” [Col. 0036B]

The holy Doctor later refutes this with various arguments and examples.

IV. If the vigils were devoted to a perfect fast of bread and water, conversely the feast days were exempted from both abstinence and the simple fast of a single meal from Easter until the Ides of September. From the Ides of September until Easter, they were free only from abstinence involving bread and water; they were nevertheless assigned to a single meal, except on certain principal solemnities.

Blessed Rudolph the Prior says in the Constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 13:

> “On the feast days that occur from Easter until this limit—the Ides of September—it is customary both to relax abstinence and to suspend the fast. After the Ides of September and until Lent, the feast days that occur within this period relax abstinence to some extent, but do not suspend the fast.”

Peter Damian says in Opusculum XV, chapter 6:

> “On the feasts with the Office of twelve lessons, wherever they occur from the Ides of September until the Resurrection of the Lord, let the brothers eat only once, except, of course, the solemnities of All Saints and Saint Martin,” and so forth. [Col. 0036C]

[Col. 0036D]

V. At that time, however, feasts celebrated with the Office of twelve lessons did not occur as frequently as they do now in many places. They were much rarer, and even those were not always observed in the hermitage as in the monastery. When they fell on a day assigned to abstinence, they were transferred to a more suitable day for observing the fast.

Peter Damian says in the cited passage:

> “It should be noted that not all the feasts celebrated in the monastery are also celebrated in the hermitage; and those that are celebrated there are often transferred so that they may be celebrated either on Tuesday or on Thursday, except, of course, the principal feasts, which cannot be changed because of the reverence due to their dignity.” [Col. 0037A]

Blessed Rudolph the Prior of Camaldoli agrees with this in the Constitutions of the year 1085, saying:

> “If, as usually happens, a feast on which the twelve lessons ought to be read falls on one of these weekdays—namely, those assigned to fasting—the customary practice is as follows: if it falls on Monday, transfer it to Tuesday; if it falls on Wednesday, transfer it to Thursday; and if it falls on Friday, move it to Saturday, and use cooked food and wine. This was done so that the fast might be observed on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. These feasts—namely, that of the holy Savior and the four feasts of his Mother, and so forth—are never to be transferred.”

VI. Enough concerning the manner of abstinence. [Col. 0037B] Let us likewise note a few things about the other exercises of the Camaldulenses and Avellanites.

Damian notes that Saint Romuald’s disciples observed the practice of going barefoot. For at Pereo he describes them in chapter 26 as:

> “Enclosed, barefoot, and unkempt.”

At Sitria he testifies in chapter 64 that they remained:

> “All going barefoot and unkempt.”

At least reclusive hermits are still commanded to observe this practice in Paul Justinian’s Rule of the Eremitical Life, chapter 54:

> “They shall always remain barefoot; nevertheless, they may wear leggings up to the ankles if this has been granted to them by their superior for some reason, provided that they always keep their feet entirely without shoes.”

All hermits, including those living openly, were accustomed on days assigned to abstinence to take their meal in their own cells, “sitting barefoot on the floor,” as Blessed Rudolph teaches in the Constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 20. Justinian likewise confirms this in the cited work, chapters 32 and 38.

Concerning the Avellanites, Peter Damian transmits the same discipline in Opuscula XIV and XV, chapter 11:

> “It is also no small part of penance that at all times, whether summer or winter, they use neither shoes nor boots in their cells, but customarily remain always with bare legs and feet, except those who are afflicted by severe illness.” [Col. 0037C]

VII. The degree of zeal that existed in both places for metanies, prostrations, disciplines, and other pious exercises of this kind can be understood from the following words of Rudolph the Prior concerning his Camaldulenses in the Constitutions of the year 1085:

> “For who could worthily describe the things that the brothers of this hermitage customarily do at all times: namely, works of goodness; blows with scourges, flowing tears, countless metanies, sighs of the heart, continuous psalmody, persistence in prayer, sacred vigils?” and so forth. [Col. 0037D]

Peter Damian writes similarly of the Avellanites in Opusculum XIV:

> “As for the other pursuits of spiritual exercise, what continual fervor and persistence, what vigilance and energetic frequency there may be, I fear to say . . . Yet let me say this, because such diligence is shown in the bending of the knees, in disciplines with scourges, and in other practices of this kind,” and so forth. [Col. 0038A]

The extent of their voluntary scourging—both that undertaken publicly in the chapter and that inflicted privately upon themselves in the cell—was the same in both hermitages and can scarcely be described. Nothing is more clearly evident from Peter Damian’s letters and opuscula than the custom of discipline, as it was called. It was established, expanded, and defended against all detractors by his fervent admonitions and by the examples of his holy disciples, especially Dominic Loricatus and Rudolph, bishop of Gubbio, whom he treats at greater length in book I of his letter to Alexander II.

That this practice was likewise in use among the Camaldulenses is clear from the Life of Saint Romuald, chapter 38, where Blessed Guido “had been ordered by the Prior to receive I do not know how many strokes of the scourge,” and chapter 64, where “even the servants of the monks themselves inflicted disciplines upon one another.” It is also clear from the Constitutions of the year 1080 of Blessed Rudolph the Prior, chapter 19, where it is stated that the Camaldulensian hermits:

> “Meeting in chapter every Sunday, after a fraternal exhortation has been given, ought charitably to accuse one another; finally, after a common confession has been made, they receive blows of the scourge upon their naked limbs—not so much to torture their bodies, since they inflict more severe punishments upon themselves in their cells, as to pursue the example of the divine Passion and humility, for the confusion of him who is the king of pride.” [Col. 0038B]

Concerning the Prior of the Camaldulensian hermitage he likewise decrees in chapter 53:

> “Let him often meet in chapter with the brothers, and after making metanies, confess his own excesses, so that he may be corrected from his vices and show others a model of correction.”

[Col. 0038C]

Peter Damian’s admonition to the Prior of Avellana in Opusculum XV, chapter 31, is similar:

> “Let chapter with the brothers be held either never or rarely, without your accusing yourself after a metany has been made.”

VIII. Such exercises were not imposed upon either group by command, but were customarily left to the discretion of each person. For Damian says of his Avellanites in Opusculum XV, chapter 18:

> “Concerning metanies, disciplines, prostrations, extending the arms in prayer, and the other exercises of holy fervor, we bind no brother by any law. Rather, we judge that these matters should be entrusted to his own prudent discretion. There are some for whom certain of these practices are unsuitable; therefore it seems safer and freer that in such matters a choice be offered rather than that a definitive ruling of the Rule be prescribed.” [Col. 0038D]

Concerning the Camaldulenses, Rudolph writes in the cited passage, chapter 35:

> “In metanies, prostrations, blows with scourges, and other similar services, works, or practices, each person ought to exercise himself according as ability permits, usefulness advises, or divine grace inspires. In such matters a voluntary offering is encouraged, not compulsion imposed. Let each person measure his strength in this respect, calculate the cost, and moderate his feelings.”

IX. Whatever was prescribed by common law for the hermits of both congregations was nevertheless tempered, out of consideration for the weaker, by a discreet dispensation according to the superior’s judgment. This was done secretly and quietly, without the knowledge of the others, lest the discipline accepted by most solitaries be weakened by the examples of a few and gradually fall into disuse.

Let us hear Damian in Opusculum XV, chapter 16:

> “If one person, or perhaps several, need what those who are healthy do not need, let pious kindness be offered to the sick in such a way—quietly and secretly—that the healthy may remain, without the spur of envy, in the discipline of their own rigor. For what necessity imposes upon one person need not immediately become a rule for everyone.” [Col. 0039A]

Blessed Rudolph agrees with him in the Constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 30:

> “If the weak and more delicate require some dispensation in food or clothing, it must be done wisely and cautiously, so that pious discretion may be shown to those in need without thereby generating harmful laxity in the stronger. For a special or individual concession ought not to be drawn into a precedent for the others, lest from the indulgence shown to one or a few there arise the disorder of many.” [Col. 0039B]

X. No less agreement between the two communities can be observed in the discipline of chanting. They had two kinds of psalmody, private and public.

The private psalmody was contained in two psalters. One was for the living, with certain additions that Saint Romuald had ordered to be appended; this they recited daily. The other was for the dead, and each person recited it in his own cell every day, sometimes in its entirety and sometimes in part.

Blessed Rudolph says in the Constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 35:

> “Accordingly, during both Lents each brother shall recite each day two psalters with their additions”—what these were we shall learn from Damian below. “At other times he ought to celebrate one psalter for the living; for the dead, however, the whole, or half, or at least a third part.” [Col. 0039C]

Peter Damian says in Opusculum XIV:

> “Concerning psalmody, the custom is that when two brothers live together in a cell, they recite two psalters each day, one for the living and the other for the dead. The psalter for the living is recited with those additions that Blessed Romuald appended; the one for the dead is recited with nine lessons, three lessons for each group of fifty psalms. Whoever lives alone completes the entire psalter for the living each day; for the dead, either half or the whole, according to what his strength permits.”

He repeats all this in Opusculum XV, chapter 9, explaining more fully those additions, or appendices, of Blessed Romuald—which Rudolph calls additions—to be joined [Col. 0039D] to the psalter for the living. He says:

> “The psalter for the living is recited with those additions that Blessed Romuald appends. Let us also not be reluctant to insert them, lest a novice perhaps complain that we have passed over what he especially needs to know. After five psalms have been completed, the following is immediately inserted:
>
> ‘Glory to you, Trinity, equal and one Godhead, before all ages, and now, and forever; pray for us, all holy ones of God, that we may be made worthy of the promises of our Lord God Jesus Christ; Our Father.’
>
> When these have been completed, the following is immediately added:
>
> ‘Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.’
>
> After another five [Col. 0040A] psalms have been completed, the following is then said:
>
> ‘You, God the Father unbegotten, you the only-begotten Son, you the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, the holy and undivided Trinity, we confess, praise, and bless with all our heart and mouth; to you be glory forever. Amen. Lord, God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me. Let my enemies be confounded and put to shame, those who seek my soul. Be my helper and deliverer, Lord; do not delay. Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’
>
> When this has been completed, the following is again said:
>
> ‘Our help is in the name of the Lord.’
>
> These additions are therefore always inserted alternately after every five psalms, until the psalter is completed, together with the three Sunday canticles and the canticles of the entire week. The following additions, which appear at the end of the psalter, are also not to be neglected: ‘We praise you, God’; ‘Now dismiss your servant’; the two Creeds; ‘Glory to God in the highest’; the Lord’s Prayer with the Catholic faith; and finally the Litanies with the prayers. All these conclude the whole with the customary ending.” [Col. 0040B]

### XI

Furthermore, following the institution of the same Peter Damian, the followers of both places recited the Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary daily, either communally in choir or individually in their own cells, as may be gathered from Damian’s Life, chapter 15, and from book VI, letter 32. There he also relates that the monastery of Saint Vincent was divinely afflicted because the daily Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary, instituted by him, had been discontinued, and asserts that the monastery was restored to its former tranquility only after the penance imposed for neglecting this duty had been completed and a solemn promise had been made thereafter to observe this custom inviolably [Col. 0040C]. This same daily obligation of the Hours of the Blessed Virgin, transmitted to us by right of inheritance, remains in force today. Concerning it, the Constitutions of the Camaldulensian monks under Pius V, chapter 18, state:

> Our Fathers determined that this should be placed before our eyes: namely, that all professed monks who, without legitimate impediment, knowingly omit to recite, either wholly or in part, the Office both of the Lord himself and of his Mother commit mortal sin. For this is contrary to the ancient and praiseworthy custom both of the hermits and of the monks of our congregation, who have always endeavored to perform and devoutly celebrate both Offices.

Thus our Fathers spoke—not indeed imposing a new obligation concerning this burden, but explaining by an authoritative declaration the ancient obligation that had prevailed by force of longstanding custom, of which they are the most abundant witnesses. It was most recently confirmed by a response of the Sacred Congregation of Rites dated 12 March 1616, in which these two points are decreed. First:

> By the constitutions of their rule, Camaldulensian monks are bound under pain of mortal sin to recite daily the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Second, they are bound to this duty

> even after accepting the Benedictine Breviary, just as they had been bound previously.

Nor, indeed, had Leo X supposed that the Marian Office was incumbent upon us with any less solicitude. He established that the divine Office itself could be dispensed from by the prelates of our order, but made no such provision concerning the Marian Office. For he says in his bull *Et si a summo*, § 70:

> And although those monks mentioned above, who are so occupied with the duties of their monasteries, etc., provided that they have not been constituted in sacred orders, even if they have made profession, are nevertheless not at all bound to perform the entire and complete Divine Office, their prelates, taking into consideration the condition of their subjects—and apart from the Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary, to which they remain obliged—should, according to the dispensation granted to them, impose upon them something to be recited, if it seems expedient for the salvation of their souls, which they may be able to fulfill with willing hearts.

### XII

Moreover, due piety toward the deceased of their own congregation shone forth among both the Camaldulensians and the Avellanites through equal observances. Damian says in *Opuscula* XIV and XV, chapter 12:

> When one of our brothers dies—that is, one who lives with us—each person fasts for seven days, undergoes seven disciplines with a thousand blows of the broom, makes seven hundred prostrations, chants thirty psalters according to custom, and each priest offers seven Masses for him individually; in addition, for thirty consecutive days the solemnity of Masses for him is celebrated communally in the convent.

Rodulphus, however, in the constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 35, decrees something not very different when he commands:

> For the departure of any brother who dies in the hermitage or at Fonte Buono, each person must offer thirty psalters or Masses; but for those who die in other places of the congregation, three psalters or Masses are to be said by each person. As for prostrations, palm-beatings, strokes of the scourge, and other similar services, everyone must practice them according to his ability.

### XIII

The same practice of public psalmody was certainly in use not only among both of these families of Romuald but among all monks, so that no distinctive agreement is revealed by it. Nevertheless, at least this may be observed: just as Romuald, according to Damian in his *Life*, chapter 9,

> strongly recommended that vigils be performed moderately and with great discretion, lest it happen to someone that, after completing the nocturnal offices, he should give himself over to sleep,

because

> the holy man detested such sleep to such an extent that if anyone confessed to him that, after keeping vigil through twelve psalms and especially toward dawn, he could not celebrate the sacred solemnity of Mass that day with his permission,

so Paul Justinian, in his *Eremitical Rule*, chapter 40, inculcates this same example of Romuald upon hermits.

Peter Damian likewise prescribed to his Avellanite monks a similar discretion concerning sleep and its avoidance after the morning vigils. He writes in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 16:

> As for sleep, a severe restriction is not necessary for everyone. It is better to grant the flesh sleep through a certain measured dispensation and afterward to keep fervent vigil in the praises of God. It should be noted, however, that before the office of the nocturnal assembly, if the night is still very deep or if the vigils seem burdensome for any reason, it is permissible to return to bed; after the nocturnal office, it is altogether forbidden.

Hence, in volume I, book VI, letter 17, he says:

> He who, while chanting psalms at night, falls asleep again does not violate the canon.

### XIV

There is no need for me to add anything concerning the discipline of silence, since it is proper to hermits. Let Rodulphus, the Camaldulensian prior, be heard in the constitutions of the year 1080, chapter 21, where he prescribes:

> When they leave their cells and return to them, they must be restrained by the discipline of silence. In the oratory and in the refectory, the rule of silence must be preserved inviolate at all times.

The Blessed Peter Damian agrees with this, both in *Opusculum* XIV and in *Opusculum* XV, chapters 11 and 18:

> In the chapter house, in the oratory, and in the refectory, they must not set aside the customary rule, so as not to speak with guests. Therefore, from their cells to the church, whether coming or returning, they must not depart from the discipline of silence.

### XV

Rest and the avoidance of all wandering were likewise imposed with equal diligence upon the followers of both hermitages, by Rodulphus in the place cited, chapter 32, in these words:

> Let him flee the vice of wandering and instability in such a way that he not only does not roam about externally with Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, but also remains stable and fixed within his own cell. For he could, within that same cell, as though driven by Vertumnus and the spirit of wandering, circle around all day.

Peter Damian says in *Opusculum* XII, chapter 24:

> It is by no means pleasing that even among the most holy hermits some seem to have been admitted whom the same plague of wandering torments and whom—as one may say—Vertumnus, a certain kind of demon, afflicts. Among the ancients, Vertumni were said to be demons whose instigation rendered men, placed in a state of dizziness, unstable.

And in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 18:

> Let the hermit place beside him whatever necessities are most familiar to him, so that when necessity demands their use, he himself may not have to rise frequently to fetch them. Wandering must be avoided so completely that it is not even permissible to stroll idly through one’s cell.

### XVI

In order that solitaries may become accustomed to resting in their cells, Rodulphus attempts to strengthen them with this golden admonition in the place cited, chapter 36:

> Moreover, let the solitary strive to maintain continual and uninterrupted diligence in his cell, so that, through God’s grace and the constancy of remaining there, the dwelling in his cell may become sweet to him. For just as, to a restless and unstable monk, the cell supplies punishment like a prison and the material of penal affliction, so to one who is quiet and persevering it offers refreshment of sweetness and the silence of blessedness, as though a portion of paradise.

Damian had asserted the same in *Opusculum* XII, chapter 25:

> In addition, for those who alternate their life under this inconstancy of change, the life of withdrawal becomes more severe in proportion as they are drawn away from their ingrained habit of wandering, so that the strictness of the eremitical life and the cell itself seem to them exceedingly difficult and dreadful. Custom makes the cell sweet to a monk; wandering makes it seem horrible. To those who wander, the cell is a prison; to those who remain, it is a pleasant chamber.

[Col. 0043A]

### XVII

Again, just as Romuald, according to his *Life*, chapter 9,

> considered it of little value if someone began something great for a time but did not also persevere in it patiently,

so Damian inculcated the same perseverance upon his Avellanites in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 27, saying:

> Hold perseveringly to the manner of life that you have once undertaken; carry it out steadfastly, lest—God forbid—you seem to differ from yourself through a theatrical kind of fickleness. Persevere, therefore, in what you have begun, and hold to the straight line of your accustomed life, lest the diversity of a life continually changed always make you a new man; rather, let the custom of the established rule stabilize you upon the foundation of holy constancy.

### XVIII

Finally, whatever the most blessed hermit Romuald is said to have taught his hermits who gathered at his cell in the Camaldulensian wilderness, as reported by Jerome of Prague in Bollandus under 7 February, in his sermon on Saint Romuald, chapter 11—and likewise whatever is inserted in chapters 6 and 9—is found almost entirely, and in the same or similar formulas, in Damian’s instruction of his Avellanites.

Thus, what is said in the cited chapter, no. 69, concerning the rest, silence, and fasting necessary for hermits, Damian expresses in exactly the same words in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 5. What Jerome adds there, from the mouth of Romuald, concerning the poverty and meanness of clothing that ought to be loved, Damian again inculcates in the same words in the place cited, chapter 21. What Jerome adds in no. 70 concerning those who come from the world to the hermitage, Damian here recommends in the same words and with the same wording in chapter 29 of the aforementioned *Opusculum*. Finally, what Jerome decrees in no. 71 concerning those who come to the hermitage from a cenobitic way of life, Damian likewise sets forth in the very same words and formulas in chapter 30 above. It is therefore immaterial whether one transcribes from one source or the other, since not only the meaning but also the words and the very order of the words are found unchanged in both.

# Chapter V. Synopsis

The affinity of the Camaldulensians and Avellanites is further illustrated by other considerations.

## Synopsis

1. The rule of each place was common to both.
2. Peter Damian mentions Saint Romuald more frequently than Rodulphus, the Camaldulensian prior.
3. Peter Damian often employs the authority of Saint Romuald.
4. Conversely, the authority of Peter Damian is cited in the statutes of the Camaldulensians.
5. The eremitical rule of Saint Peter Damian acquired the force of law in the Camaldulensian hermitage through Blessed Rodulphus, its prior.
6–7. This is demonstrated.
8. According to Ludovicus du Pin, the congregation of the Avellanites was a form of the same kind of hermits instituted by Romuald.
9. According to Ludovicus Thomassinus, the institution of Romuald was the same as that of Peter Damian.
10. Peter Damian himself bears witness to this affinity.
11. Community of hospitality and suffrages was established in ancient times between the Camaldulensians and the Avellanites.
12. The habit of the Avellanites was very similar in color and form to the clothing of the Camaldulensians; they likewise used a belt, as we do.
13. Peter Damian is shown to belong to the Camaldulensian order with even greater right than the other Avellanites.

### I

What was briefly touched upon in the two preceding chapters concerning the ancient manner of life of our Camaldulensians and Avellanites abundantly demonstrates the agreement between the two institutions. It shows that the constitutions of both families, being framed by similar or scarcely differing precepts—or, for the most part, written in exactly the same words and formulas—were conceived under the direction of the same spirit and derived from the same source, Romuald.

Hence each rule rightly obtained equal authority among both groups, and statutes concerning the manner of eremitical life, whether established by Romuald or by Peter Damian, were accepted by both with virtually no distinction. It is therefore not surprising that Jerome of Prague, in the passage cited in the preceding chapter, at its final number, attributed to Romuald an exhortation taken almost word for word from the rule of the Avellanites.

### II

Certainly, Rodulphus, the Camaldulensian prior, mentions Romuald no less frequently than Damian himself when strengthening eremitical customs by his authority. For, as we saw in the preceding chapter, no. 10, Damian derives the practice of private psalmody from the institution of Saint Romuald. In *Opusculum* XIV he says:

> The psalter, which is that of the living, is recited with those additions that the Blessed Romuald appended.

And again, in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 9:

> The psalter, which is that of the living, is recited with those additions that the Blessed Romuald appends.

He notes that these additions must be observed with such care that he counts them among the matters most important for novices to learn, using the words that immediately follow:

> Let us not consider it burdensome to insert these also, lest the novice perhaps complain that we have passed over matters which it is greatly necessary for him to know.

That all of Romuald’s admonitions, examples, and counsels were of no less importance for instructing his hermits is sufficiently indicated when, in chapter 16 of the same *Opusculum*, Damian brings forward the opinions of the Blessed Romuald concerning the discretion to be imposed upon prelates in moderating the life of their subjects, and declares that he adheres to them:

> We approve, he says, what the Blessed Romuald is reported often to have said to his disciples: “Provided that a brother does not leave his cell, he may, by discretion, even be permitted to eat meat if an utterly unavoidable necessity appears to threaten.” He added: “For it is almost the same thing to return from the hermitage to the monastery as to be carried from the monastic order into the world.” A little later he adds: “The Blessed Romuald himself, as his disciples customarily report, alternated the weeks of the summer season in such a way that he spent one week, from Sunday to Sunday, fasting on bread and water, while during the other week he ate a cooked dish on Thursday.”

### III

Similarly, in volume I, book VI, letter 26, Damian sets before his cousin, the monk Marinus, the example of the Blessed Romuald, who prudently rebuked a disciple for excessive curiosity, in order to commend modesty in conversations with women. A little later, to urge the same man to preserve moderation and avoid hypocrisy, he adds:

> Nor should you apply this ineptly—that is, do not hear it idly, but attend to it seriously—what the man of God Romuald often said to his disciples: “Brothers,” he said, “when you are eating in any assembly while the others are intent upon their food, refrain at the beginning of the meal; but when they have already been satisfied to some degree, begin your meal, so that you may both escape the charge of hypocrisy and preserve the rule of moderation without giving offense.”

And in the same book VI, letter 30, addressed to the hermit Theuzon, he says that, setting aside arguments, he took refuge in the authority of Saint Romuald in order to establish his position:

> Finally, he says, when we were placed in difficulty and hemmed in by the narrow confines of many objections, once the opportunity for reasoning had ceased, we immediately took refuge in the examples of the saints, so that at least credence might be given to those whose authority is readily admitted for proving any matter. And when Saint Romuald was summoned as a witness concerning a certain point of dispute, etc.

### IV

Conversely, the authority of Damian is frequently invoked in the statutes of the Camaldulensians. Thus, in the constitution promulgated by Placidus, prior of the Camaldulensian hermitage, and Martinus, administrator of the same hermitage, one century after Blessed Rodulphus, the discipline of silence and its necessity are confirmed. They say:

> Peter Damian says: “It is the duty of the hermit to rest in fasting and silence.”

In the eremitical rule published by Paul Justinian, the authority of “Peter Damian” is proposed in chapter 47, in the words already cited in Dissertation I, chapter 4, no. 14, concerning the discipline governing the reception of secular persons into the hermitage. Elsewhere, too, his authority is repeatedly invoked, for example concerning the qualities required of the prior of the hermitage and many other matters, reference being made to the decrees of the same “Peter Damian.”

Moreover, Justinian did not hesitate to publish the “eremitical rule of Peter Damian” in its entirety and to join it to the eremitical rule of Saint Romuald in the same volume, while placing entirely after them the other constitutions of Rodulphus, Placidus, Gherardus, and Martinus—as though he understood that whatever was contained in the decrees of all our Fathers could be found more fully and abundantly in the institutions of Peter Damian alone, as in its source. He did not consider his own eremitical rule sufficiently perfect, although collected from the traditions of Saint Romuald and from the writings—or orally transmitted customs—of all his predecessors, unless it were joined to Peter Damian’s related treatise, *On the Institutions of His Congregation*, from which it would receive greater light and firmness.

### V

Indeed, the “eremitical rule of Peter Damian” itself was once proposed as the sole rule to be observed in the Camaldulensian hermitage, namely until Blessed Rodulphus, its prior, issued his own constitutions. Its force was not thereby wholly abolished. Apart from one or another article, it remained expressly approved in all other respects by Rodulphus, who says in the constitutions of the year 1085:

> Each brother has scales in his cell, with which he weighs the three loaves that he receives every Sunday and Thursday. There are also many other things necessary for these brothers, all of which the prudent reader will find sufficiently set forth in the eremitical rule. But care must be taken lest, because that rule says that one should eat at table on Saturday, or because of other matters that seem contrary to the practices of this hermitage and that we have briefly described on this page, these practices be neglected. For, as you yourselves see, these practices are more important and stricter, and they were observed in this hermitage before the Rule itself had been written down. But all the remaining matters that agree with and resemble the practices of this hermitage—how it teaches us to remain in the cell and outside it, to resist inwardly, to acquire virtues, and always to retain discretion in all things—we must continually observe with Christ’s help and never abandon the pious custom of Saint Romuald and our other predecessors.

### VI

It follows first that the “eremitical rule” of which Rodulphus speaks can be none other than that of Peter Damian, which Paul Justinian later judged worthy of publication after his constitutions. For it is the very rule that speaks of “having scales in the cell for weighing the measure of bread,” as Damian says in *Opusculum* XV, chapter 8, whose text we cited above in chapter 3, no. 14.

This follows secondly from the fact that it is also the very rule that always grants a relaxation of the Saturday fast outside Lent, both in summer and winter, on account of the weak, assigning that day to a simple meal with a cooked dish and wine. This is what Rodulphus intended by the formula “to eat at table on Saturday.” For in the constitution of the year 1080, chapter 20, he says:

> At table, on all days of either a double or a single meal—that is, not of a complete fast—the brothers eat together.

On days of abstinence, however, each person was refreshed in his cell with bread and water, sitting barefoot upon the pavement and looking at a book of sacred reading, as Rodulphus says in the same place.

Damian says in the aforementioned *Opusculum* XV, chapter 15:

> We believe that each brother who remains in his cell, unless he is altogether sick and confined to bed, can very easily, with God’s help, fast three days each week throughout the whole year—whether summer or winter—on bread and water. Since fasting on Saturday is established by canonical tradition, it should not seem burdensome for a brother to defer his meal even on Saturday until the ninth hour, so that he may eat only once on that day; nevertheless, by the indulgence of this institution, he is not forbidden to take wine and a cooked dish. This applies in summer. From the Ides of September until the joy of Easter, he should know that he must fast four days each week. But if at some time such weakness should occur that, even in winter, it is permissible on Saturday to temper the customary fast somewhat with soaked legumes, the roots of herbs, or even fruits, this must be done in such a way that, if he takes one of these, he does not add another unless true necessity dictates it. Finally, for the sake of the fainthearted, if necessity should altogether demand the concession permitted in summer, the same discretion concerning Saturdays is to be observed in winter.

Rodulphus therefore established that this very general relaxation of the Saturdays was not to be admitted in the sacred hermitage, since it was contrary to its custom. According to his earlier constitutions, chapter 12, which we cited above in chapter 3, no. 9, Saturday abstinence could be relaxed only “during the Easter season,” “on the octaves of saints,” “on days of bloodletting,” because of the arrival of a distinguished person, in consideration of extraordinary labor, or on the Saturdays preceding both Lents, as is clear from the constitution cited above, chapter 16.

### VII

This is shown a third time by the fact that the eremitical rule of which Rodulphus speaks had been composed during the period between the foundation of the Camaldulensian hermitage and the age of Rodulphus. He says:

> In this hermitage these practices were first observed by holy men before the rule itself had been written down.

No rule composed during that period is known to us other than the eremitical rule of Peter Damian. This, therefore, is the very rule that had until then been in use among the hermits at Camaldoli and that Rodulphus afterward proposes for continued observance in those matters that did not conflict with the older customs of that hermitage.

Finally, the doctrines said to be contained there—concerning withdrawal into the cell, conduct outside the cell, the acquisition of virtues, and the discretion of the prelate—are in fact found in Peter Damian’s *Opusculum*, as is evident to readers. It is therefore completely established that in Rodulphus’s time Peter Damian’s rule itself had been received in the sacred Camaldulensian hermitage, just as in the solitude of Avellana, and was being observed almost in its entirety.

[Col. 0047C]

### VIII

Rightly and deservedly, therefore, the institution of the Camaldulensians and Avellanites ought to be regarded as having proceeded from Saint Romuald. Hence the most learned Ludovicus Ellies du Pin, in *Nova Bibliotheca Auctorum Ecclesiasticorum*, volume VIII, part II, *The Church of the Eleventh Century*, chapter 14, § 10, after describing the foundation of the Camaldulensian order by Romuald, says that another special congregation of hermits “of the same kind” was instituted by Peter Damian. Here are the author’s complete words:

> He [Romuald] placed himself under the guidance of a holy hermit named Marin, who lived in the region of Venice, and embraced the eremitical life, which he restored in the West. Their institution did not consist in living alone in solitudes, like the ancient hermits, but in several living together in one place, separated from other men and in individual cells, under the guidance of one superior and practicing the same rule. Such monasteries were formerly called lauras. Saint Romuald established a very large number of them in Italy. One of the most famous was built on the Apennine near Arezzo, in a place given to them by a man named Mandol, from whom the order took the name Camaldoli. Saint Romuald lived for a hundred years after his religious profession and saw his order flourishing. Peter Damian also instituted a kind of congregation of hermits of the same type. These hermits practiced great austerities and performed very extraordinary things.

### IX

The most learned Ludovicus Thomassinus likewise indicates, in *On the Ancient and New Discipline of the Church: Concerning Benefices*, part I, book III, chapter 25, no. 7, that the institution of Romuald and that of Peter Damian were the same. After recounting the restoration of the eremitical life and its union with the Benedictine rule accomplished chiefly by Romuald in Italy, he says that those who attacked this institution were silenced by Peter Damian in book VI, letter 12. There Damian clearly defends himself and his followers against the attack of a certain abbot who had complained that Damian had received a monk who had departed from his monastery, contrary to the rule of Saint Benedict:

> You are angry, he says, and accuse us in your complaint because we ought not to have received your monks into the hermitage contrary to the precepts of our Blessed Father Benedict.

He then shows that our most holy lawgiver wished only to prevent wandering from one monastery to another, not to prohibit the transfer of men from the cenobitic life to the more perfect life of hermits; indeed, he wished to encourage all to make that transfer. Thus the institutions of Romuald and Damian coincide so closely that the defense of one must equally be regarded as an apology for the other.

Here are Thomassinus’s words in the cited passage:

> Peter Damian wrote the life of Romuald, and he also wrote an apology. For these anchorites, striving immediately toward the summit of perfection, soon began to be criticized on the ground that they were following a path that Blessed Benedict had neither shown nor followed, and that they were gathering into their community deserters from the monasteries of Blessed Benedict. Peter Damian stopped their mouths with this response: Blessed Benedict had taken precautions against abbots receiving one another’s monks when they were known to one another—“Let the abbot beware,” he says in chapter 61 of the Rule, “of ever receiving a monk from a known monastery to dwell there without the consent of his abbot”—but the priors of anchorites were not included under this prohibition.

### X

Peter Damian himself does not deny that this common fellowship of institution existed between him and the disciples of Saint Romuald. Indeed, in the prologue to the *Life* of that holy Father Romuald, indicating that he had been compelled by the distinguished disciples of the holy man who were still alive to commemorate his deeds, he says:

> Bound by the prayers of many brothers and by genuine charity, I shall undertake, with God as my guide, to describe what I learned concerning that remarkable man from his distinguished disciples.

He considered himself joined to them by the same bond of religion by which “kinsmen and brothers,” begotten by the same father, ought to be bound to one another by certain ties of love and charity.

### XI

Conversely, our Camaldulensians regarded the Avellanites themselves as “brothers” and considered them shoots of a related stock propagated by Romuald as their common trunk, even after they had transferred from eremitical discipline to cenobitic life and had departed from the original institution of Saint Romuald and Peter Damian. This occurred contrary to the warning of Peter Damian, who had gravely rebuked them toward the end of *Opusculum* XIV:

> Therefore, do not desire to descend from eremitical strictness to monastic laxity.

Even in this condition, I say, the Avellanites, joined to us as though by a fellowship of genuine charity, were customarily received in our monasteries in the refectory under the same right of hospitality as the monks of Vallombrosa, instituted by Saint John Gualbert, the disciple of the Lord Romuald. The souls of the deceased of their congregation were likewise accustomed to be purified by equal suffrages of Christian piety.

For in the constitutions issued in 1253 by Blessed Martin III, the general, book III, chapter 23, it is prescribed:

> We decree that the brothers of our order, the Vallombrosans and those of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana, as though united by one office of charity, whether monks with monks or lay brothers with lay brothers, be received cheerfully and kindly by all the prelates and subjects of our order.

Again, in the general chapter held on 27 May 1372 in the monastery of Saint Michael in the Borgo of Pisa, under John III, the general, it was decreed:

> That the monks of Vallombrosa and of the Holy Cross of Avellana, both in the hermitage and in the monasteries of the order, be received in choir and refectory as though they belonged to the Camaldulensian order, and that the brevia of those same orders—that is, the diptychs indicating the names of deceased brothers—be carried by the order’s keeper of the brief, etc.

The act was recorded by the hand of Leonardo, formerly Francesco of Castiglione Aretino, the appointed notary and secretary, from the Camaldulensian archive, book R. 18, folio 80, and its index under “Statutes,” page 2, no. 9.

Therefore, all the more, while they still followed the original form of eremitical life in which the Avellanites had been instructed by Blessed Peter Damian according to the precepts of Romuald, they deserved to be regarded by the Camaldulensians as companions in a similar discipline.

### XII

This was all the more the case because the habit of the ancient Avellanites, both in color and in form, entirely agreed with the habit of the Camaldulensians. For, as we demonstrated in Dissertation III, chapter 2, nos. 9 and 10, the white color appropriate to their monastic garments is established from ancient monuments and other reliable authorities. Peter Damian himself, in volume I, book VI, letter 14, warned the abbot Mainardus not to despise the white garment of monks as something lowly, citing the example of Christ, who allowed Herod to mock him in a “white garment,” as we noted in Dissertation III, chapter 2, no. 7.

Peter Ricordatus, Silvester Maurolycus, Paulus Morigia, Constantinus Cajetanus, and the Benedictine chronicler likewise testify, in the prolegomena by the same author to volume I of the works of Blessed Peter Damian, that the tunic, scapular, and cowl of the Avellanites were entirely white. Thus, according to the cited Morigia, *History of Religion*, chapter 58, the blue mantle that they most recently used in place of the cowl was introduced solely through the abuse of later times.

This confirms that their ancient habit was formerly related to our Camaldulensian habit and corresponded to it in every respect, both in color and in form. Indeed, it may be added that the habit of the Camaldulensians is distinguished from the clothing of the other monastic congregations—even from that of the monks of Montevergine and Monte Oliveto, who likewise use white garments—by this particular feature: our monks do not wear the scapular loose and hanging freely from both shoulders, but fasten it beneath the chest with a woolen belt. After the knot has been tied as simply as possible, this belt extends in two strips hanging down in front.

The Avellanites, too, are found formerly to have been accustomed to gird themselves with a similar belt. For when Peter Damian and his companion Albizo visited the hermit Theuzon at Florence, were harshly treated by him, and were finally expelled after many quarrels, Damian testifies that both were seized by their belts. He says in book VI, letter 30:

> Finally, seized violently by our half-belts, we were driven out.

Therefore, there was no difference in the clothing of the Avellanites and Camaldulensians, and consequently no difference ought to be judged to have existed in their life, institution, or profession.

### XIII

Whatever may be true concerning the other alumni of Fonte Avellana, there is certainly a much stronger reason in the case of Peter Damian for judging that he belonged to the Camaldulensian order, or to the institution of the Lord Romuald.

First, he was instructed directly by Saint Romuald himself—or at least through his disciples—in the rudiments of the eremitical life, which he later transmitted to others. Hence the most reverend abbot, Lord Secundus Lancellotus of the Olivetans, says of Peter Damian in his congregation’s *History*, book II, chapter 22:

> In monastic matters he heard Romuald, the founder of the Camaldulensian institution, and first lived at Fonte Avellana, where he spent many years amid a great multitude of monks or hermits. Then Stephen IX added him to the college of cardinals.

Second, he himself actually lived for some time in the Camaldulensian hermitage, as follows from the conjectures cited in Dissertation III, chapter 2, no. 8. To these may be added the explicit assertion of Antonius Maria Bonuccius in *Ephemerides Eucharisticae*, volume I, under 22 February, that Peter Damian wished to renounce the cardinalitial dignity

> in order to return to his Camaldulensian hermitage.

Therefore, both before and after renouncing the cardinal’s hat, it is probable that he lived in the Camaldulensian hermitage.

Finally, third, Damian may have spent his life in other monasteries built by Saint Romuald or organized for regular observance. Since this matter requires a longer treatment, it will be reserved for the subject of the following chapter.

# Chapter VI

Blessed Peter Damian lived chiefly among the disciples of Saint Romuald and in his monasteries.

## Synopsis
## On the Monastery of Avellana and Pomposa, in Which Peter Damian Lived: By Way of Reference

1. In the monastery of Saint Vincent of Petra Pertusa, Romuald lived with his disciples.  
2. In that same place Peter Damian wrote the Life of Saint Romuald.  
3. From the Life of Peter Damian it is clear that he stayed at the monastery of Saint Vincent.  
4. The same habit was worn by those living in that monastery and at Avellana. [Col. 0051A]  
5. The distinction between the colors *candidus* and *albus*. *Ibid.* Peter Damian is sent back to the same monastery.  
6. On other occasions he lived there, and his statutes were received there.  
7. That monastery was punished with the greatest severity by divine judgment because the observance of Damian’s decrees had been violated.  
8. Damian’s love and solicitude toward that monastery.  
9. He resided there for a very long time.  
10. The monastery of the Savior in the Perugian territory, constructed by Saint Romuald, over which Peter Damian presided.  
11. The hermitage of Mount Pregius was first inhabited by Saint Romuald and afterward by Damian.  
12. Other places constructed by Romuald in which Damian and his disciples lived.  
13. Blessed Dominic Loricatus, living under Damian’s direction, was made prior of the hermitage of Sitria, constructed by Saint Romuald.  
14. When near death, he withdrew to the hermitage of Mount Suavicinus, which Peter Damian had founded.  
15. The people of Sitria are mentioned by Peter Damian as his own pupils.  
16. Blessed [Col. 0051B] Leo, a recluse of Sitria, was Peter Damian’s teacher. *Ibid.* Peter Damian lived in our monastery of Classe.  
17. Conclusion of our position from the evidence.  
18. The authority of many writers and of three supreme pontiffs in support of our view.  
19. All the people of Avellana, together with their monastery, passed into the jurisdiction of the Camaldolese.  
20.

### I

Nothing proves more decisively that Peter Damian earned his place under Romuald’s discipline and ought to be numbered among his followers than a consideration of the places over which he presided or in which he spent a very long time. From this it will become clear that he could have followed no institution other than that of Saint Romuald, among whose disciples he lived every day and whose way of life he adopted.

As for the monastery of Fonte Avellana, which he inhabited most frequently, [Col. 0051C] there is no need to repeat anything, since enough has already been said about it to settle this matter completely, clearly demonstrating that its institution was derived from Saint Romuald. Nor will we say anything here about the monastery of Pomposa, where Damian spent nearly two years, according to his Life written by John, a disciple of the holy man, chapter 6, lest we seem to wish to resolve this already ambiguous controversy by means of still more ambiguous examples. Nevertheless, from what was said in Dissertation I, chapter 4, number 8, page 70, it has become sufficiently clear that, according to Romuald’s pattern, the union of eremitical and cenobitic life had taken root there and had been put into practice, in Damian’s own time, under Saint Guido, who, from being a monk of our monastery of Saint Severus, became abbot of Pomposa.

### II

[Col. 0051D] We shall begin with the monastery of Saint Vincent of Petra Pertusa, which once stood in the territory of Urbino, eight miles from Urbino, but which is now assigned to the canons of that city and displays only the remains of its former greatness.

Damian relates in the Life of Saint Romuald, chapter 43, that Saint Romuald settled there and attached a hermitage to that monastery itself:

> “Romuald moved to Mount Petranus, not far, that is, from the monastery of Saint Vincent, which is situated beside the Candilian River. Wishing to find a suitable place for establishing a hermitage, he ordered a certain priest,” etc.

In chapter 57 he mentions Blessed Gaudentius and Berard, who had lived in the same monastery of Saint Vincent under the direction of Dom Romuald [Col. 0052A] and had likewise been buried in that monastery’s cemetery. When one of them—namely Gaudentius—resenting the withdrawal by Romuald, at Tedald’s instigation, of a permission for abstinence that had previously been granted to him, defected to Ingelbert, and therefore seemed to have “ended his life in the transgression of disobedience,” Romuald “completely forbade prayer to be offered for him,” although he had ordered that Gaudentius be placed in the cemetery of Blessed Vincent beside the body of the venerable Berard, “who had likewise been a disciple of Romuald.”

But because of a vision shown—not to Berard, as our Macchiarellus thinks in his *Apologia*, page 22 (for from the words of Damian just quoted and from the whole context, Berard had died earlier), but to another monk who was praying at the two tombs and had been freed from toothache—“Romuald immediately ordered the brothers to show brotherly charity toward Gaudentius and to pray for him more earnestly.”

### III

Peter Damian therefore lived in this monastery of Saint Vincent, and consequently among the surviving disciples of Romuald. Indeed, he wrote the Life of Saint Romuald in that very place, as Fortunius noted in *Camaldolese History*, part II, book V, chapter 6. This is also clearly inferred from the beginning of the cited chapter 57 of the Life of the holy Father, where Damian says:

> “Another brother, named Gaudentius, was the father of the abbot of this monastery of Saint Vincent.”

Since no mention of such a monastery had occurred immediately before, but the discussion had dealt almost entirely with events at Sitria, the demonstrative expression “of this monastery” cannot be understood in any other way than as referring to the monastery present to him, where the holy doctor was actually writing.

Thus the distinguished title *egregius*, with which he honored the disciples of the holy Father in the prologue to his Life, applies to these monks of Saint Vincent:

> “Bound by the prayers and brotherly affection of many brothers, I shall undertake, with God as my guide, to describe what I learned concerning that remarkable man from his excellent disciples.”

Accordingly, in the dedicatory preface to the Roman edition of 1656 of the Life of Saint Romuald written by Peter Damian, the author addresses Romuald himself as follows:

> “After he”—that is, Damian—“had adopted your customs together with the garments of your order, while living in the monastery of Saint Vincent, where you, Romuald, had lived a most holy life and where other men, renowned for the holiness of their lives and formed in your discipline, had closed their final day, he observed there the deeply impressed traces of outstanding virtues. The very walls breathed upon him the sweetest fragrance of your blessed life, and he resolved to commit your heroic deeds to public records,” etc.

### IV

In the Life of Peter Damian written by John, his disciple, Peter is also said to have gone twice to the monastery of Saint Vincent. He went there once during the first years of his novitiate, as is related in chapter 5 in these words:

> “When Peter Damian was once about to depart with his teacher, he was ordered to put on a softer and more attractive scapular than he desired and to mount a horse. He therefore began to ask his teacher with humble prayers not to deem it appropriate to command this of him, since he abhorred it exceedingly as something unbecoming. His teacher, however, was unwilling to yield to his requests, lest he seem to despise a disciple whom he loved as his only one if he allowed him to proceed with him, unkempt according to his desire.
>
> “The disciple, thinking very differently and turning the whole matter in another direction, was deeply ashamed to appear already polished before secular people, lest he, who had formerly seemed to have renounced the world, be thought still carnally to seek worldly display. Nevertheless, he preferred to endure that reproach rather than incur the charge of disobedience, which he feared above all.
>
> “For, as he himself related, it seemed to him that anyone who saw him riding in such finery would point him out with a finger and mock him as a worldly man. They would therefore apply to him not the name of monk but that of bridegroom. Such shame suffused his face that he could scarcely raise his head or direct the gaze of his eyes toward anyone.
>
> “When they were returning and had reached the monastery of Saint Vincent, which was given its name by the neighboring rock called Petra Pertusa, the servant of the Lord could no longer endure the disgraceful ornament of the elegant garment. Finding an opportunity to remain there briefly, the teacher continued on his journey toward the hermitage, while Peter obtained another scapular, more humble in its weave and color, and put it on. Thus relieved, as though of a huge burden under which he had until then been weighed down, he returned as quickly as possible after his teacher to his own monastery. For he could not bear to visit again those who wore squalid garments while he himself was dressed in attractive ones; they were more eager to be adorned by their conduct than by their clothing.”

### V

From this passage it is plainly evident that both the people of Avellana and the monks of Saint Vincent wore the same habit in appearance, color, form, and customary use. Damian is said to have found at Saint Vincent a suitable tunic in which he could appear among them—not in a fresh or recently washed garment woven of finer wool, white and shining, but in one made of coarser thread, rough and unkempt with the natural whiteness of sheep, and matching all his other brothers.

Thus, among both groups, the color in use was not an exquisite or affected brilliance—one especially akin to light, as we proved in Dissertation III, chapter 6, number 16—but a simple whiteness more closely associated with pallor. In order to reconcile this distinction with numerous texts of the *Monastic Antiquities*, with the authorities of Peter of Cluny, book IV, letter 17, and of Smaragdus in his *Exposition of the Rule*, chapter 55, where they disapprove the white color of clothing “because it signifies glory more than lowliness,” as well as with the monuments and traditions supporting the ancient custom of white monastic dress cited in Dissertation III, chapter 7, beginning at number 14 and following, it will be useful to read what the distinguished grammarian Servius writes in his commentary on Book III of the *Georgics*:

> “It is one thing to be *candidus*, that is, suffused with a certain shining light; it is another to be *albus*, which is understood to be close to pallor.”

Cornelius Fronto likewise distinguishes the two terms in his discussion of their difference, saying that “*candidus* properly describes what results from care, whereas *albus* describes what results from nature.”

But it is enough to have noted this in passing.

### VI

Peter Damian is recorded to have been sent a second time to the same monastery of Saint Vincent, both to instruct those monks in sacred letters and to advance them more fully toward monastic perfection. John, Peter Damian’s disciple, testifies to this in chapter 6 of his Life:

> “After the period of time allowed for him to remain with his fellow brothers had been completed, he was again ordered, for the same reason for which he had gone to Pomposa, to proceed to the monastery of Saint Vincent, mentioned above. Having remained there for some time, he did not cease diligently cultivating the Lord’s vineyard until, with the Lord’s cooperation, he had produced an abundant fruit of his service.”

It is clear that on this second occasion Damian, asked by the monks of this monastery—disciples of Dom Romuald—to write Romuald’s Life, undertook the task. On the one hand, he appears not to have composed it at the beginning of his conversion, as is evident from these words of the prologue:

> “For us, sitting in the narrow corner of a cell, it was more useful, as we had resolved, constantly to recall our own sins before the eyes of our mind than to weave a history of another’s virtue. It would be more expedient to lament the darkness of the guilt we had committed than to obscure the splendid insignia of holiness with inept speech.”

On the other hand, he could not have written it during his first visit to this monastery, since he had merely been present there in passing and had not stayed long enough to complete the work.

### VII

It is also established from volume I of the same holy doctor’s works, book VI, letter 32, that Damian lived for a longer period at the monastery of Saint Vincent on other occasions and, after undertaking the governance of hermits, carefully watched over its spiritual direction. There, when he relates examples of events that had occurred in that monastery, he notes that they were domestic examples and narrates how certain matters depended upon precepts he had established there by his authority, which were eventually divinely punished because of the obstinacy of certain men and their neglect. He says:

> “To provide an example from our own household as well, in the monastery of Blessed Vincent, which is situated not far from the mountain called Petra Pertusa, we had established this rule as a disciplinary ordinance: that the beginning of Lent should be observed under the strictest severity. Specifically, for three days all the brothers were to eat nothing but a little bread with water; they were to utter no words except those of readings or of the appointed offices; barefoot, mournful and grieving, they were to walk about; and after completing the Psalter with the customary communal chant, they were to cleanse themselves by mutual scourging with brooms.
>
> “The brothers carried this out diligently, with vow, intention, and spiritual joy, and even went beyond what had been prescribed, doing more than enough from the wealth of their goodwill. But one of them secretly violated the rule while eating.”

He then describes the extremely bad death of this transgressor, which occurred in his presence:

> “Let those hear and fear,” he says, “who break the rule of discipline imposed upon them through impatience with their own pleasure.”

It is therefore clear how strictly Peter Damian’s statutes were to be observed in this monastery of Saint Vincent, and how God himself demonstrated, by a terrible vengeance upon this monk, that they were not to be violated rashly or with impunity.

### VIII

God also chastised the entire monastery with the gravest punishment because the daily custom of the office of Blessed Mary, which Damian had introduced, had been discontinued. The holy doctor continues in the same place:

> “I shall also relate another event that occurred in the monastery mentioned above. It had been established and had already been observed for nearly three years that the offices of Blessed Mary, ever Virgin, should be recited together with the canonical hours.
>
> “Among them was a man named Gozo, a monk by habit, indeed of blameworthy life, but eloquent in speech, sharp-tongued, and polished in expression. He began to complain that what Saint Benedict had commanded was more than sufficient; that the burden of a new invention ought not to be added; and that we were not holier than the ancient Fathers. Those Fathers, judging such practices superstitious and superfluous, had fixed for us the limit of psalmody and the whole rule of life. We ought surely to be content with this, lest, carelessly departing from it, we be led astray through winding paths and impassable places.
>
> “What more need be said? He seemed to have gone to war against the Queen of the World, and he prevailed. By crafty contrivance he enticed the brothers to stop offering the customary praises of Blessed Mary.
>
> “But divine judgment was not asleep, nor did it disregard our wickedness. Immediately so many hailstorms of adversity and so many storms of wars [Col. 0055C] and conflicts arose on every side against the monastery mentioned above that threatening swords daily menaced the monks with death. Plunder and robbery occurred everywhere; threshing floors were burned together with the crops; servants and dependents of the holy place were cruelly slaughtered. It was no longer the image of death but death itself that raged, so that the monks were already weary of living, since they could in no way preserve, amid the preparations for battle, the peaceful service of their profession.
>
> “At great expense the emperor was sought from the German lands, and pragmatic sanctions bearing the imperial seals were brought in; but it was all in vain. In every effort there was not fruit but useless labor.”

He then adds that, chiefly in response to his admonitions, the monks recognized the divine vengeance and humbly atoned for their fault, whereupon the entire storm was calmed:

> “At last,” he says, “they come to their senses, prostrate themselves humbly on the pavement, and, having undertaken penance, unanimously promise that henceforth they will never neglect the customary praises of the Mother of God. Immediately, I confess, after such flashes and such thunder, so great a calm returned to the sky that from then until today the brothers have enjoyed the leisure of a joyful peace and have rejoiced that, under the guidance of the Virgin’s Son, they have been brought from the whirlpool of Scylla into harbor.”

Finally he concludes:

> “Let those who therefore easily overturn the statutes of their elders consider this; and, lest the sword of divine anger come upon them, let them fear—not without reason.”

### IX

The holy man burned with such love for this monastery of Saint Vincent that he undertook to commend it to Duke Boniface more earnestly than any other. This is clear from book VII, letter 15, where he says:

> “Concerning the monastery of Saint Vincent, I ask your Excellence above all and before all to love it especially. Restore to it, by legal right, the estates held by invaders, and defend it from all mortals with the shield of your protection. Let it become evident in this monastery whether my humility can obtain something greater from the ears of your Highness.”

Certainly, he never showed equal solicitude for the very seat of his own profession—namely, the hermitage of Avellana—nor for any of the many monasteries specifically founded by him, as he did for the monastery of Saint Vincent, highly praised above, which Romuald had consecrated through his distinguished institutions and through the relics of his disciples.

### X

Finally, it seems possible to infer that Damian lived in the monastery mentioned above for a very long time, perhaps longer than anywhere else, from the case of Arduin. In book V, letter 16, Damian relates that Arduin, who for ten years postponed the vow of conversion he had promised to Damian and mocked the holy man’s repeated urgings, was punished by God’s just judgment:

> “I shall relate,” he says, “what is known to have happened recently among us in a matter not unlike this. A certain man named Arduin, distinguished by a celebrated reputation for prudence and wealthy in possessions, had promised me with genuine devotion that, if he could not do so earlier, then at least after ten years had been completed he would withdraw to the monastery of Blessed Vincent, situated in the territory of Urbino, in order to assume the monastic habit.
>
> “When the agreed term had finally expired and I pressed him continually as one demanding the fulfillment of his promise, he withdrew from the matter and, by flattering words, promised every good thing, while postponing the actual effect of his conversion through various evasions. The rector of the said monastery also favored his wishes and discouraged his conversion, since he was supported by Arduin’s very necessary assistance. Meanwhile, when bodily illness attacked him, he took to his bed,” etc.

But enough has now been said about the monastery of Saint Vincent.

### XI

Let us turn to the monastery of the Savior of Mount Acutus in the Perugian territory. Ludovicus Jacobillus, in volume II of *The Saints of Umbria*, asserts that it was built by Saint Father Romuald. Although in volume III he later writes that this same monastery was constructed under the Cistercian order in the year 1008, it is clear that this resulted from a printing error, whereby “Cistercian” was substituted for “Camaldolese.”

Indeed, Saint Robert, the father of the Cistercians, could not even have been born in 1008, much less could that monastery have been founded for the Cistercians at that time. The author himself admits elsewhere that it was granted to the Cistercians only in the year 1394. In 1504 it was granted in commendam by Julius III and passed into the hands of Galeazzo Gabrieli of Fano. In 1522, with the approval of Clement VII, Gabrieli resigned the abbey to the Camaldolese hermits of the Coronese Congregation, among whom, taking the name Peter of Fano, he assumed the monastic habit and flourished with outstanding titles to holiness.

Therefore Peter Damian also spent considerable time in this monastery, which had once belonged to the Camaldolese and has now returned to their ownership, as the cited Jacobillus notes. Indeed, he was at one time its abbot, as is gathered from volume I of the works of the holy doctor, book VI, letter 30, where he says:

> “In the Perugian monastery, namely that of the Holy Savior, over which I myself recently presided, there had shortly before been a certain monk named Guinizo,” etc.

### XII

Furthermore, in the same territory of Perugia, at Mount Pregius, Damian lived in the hermitage of Saint Vincent, which Saint Father Romuald had founded on the property of Marquis Rainier, as is gathered from the end of chapter 39 of his Life and from the following chapter 40. Cosmas of Arena confirms this in part I of his *Series of the Dukes of Etruria*, page 183. Jacobillus, in volume II of *The Saints of Umbria*, likewise lists it among the places built by Saint Romuald.

John, Damian’s disciple, relates in Damian’s Life, chapter 7, that the same place was not merely inhabited by Peter Damian but was expanded by him to provide more cells and a larger community of servants of God:

> “He therefore reached Mount Pregius in the territory of Perugia, and there he founded other dwellings of hermits”—in addition, evidently, to those already existing—“where he found a certain cell in which Blessed Romuald was said once to have lived.”

### XIII

Jacobillus further adds that Damian then went to Perugia and lived for some time in the Camaldolese hospice near the church of Saint Matthew in Campo d’Orto, now granted to the Friars Minor of Saint Francis. He also repeatedly states that Peter Damian lived at other times in the monastery of Saint Gismund at Marsciano, on Mount Regius, of the Camaldolese order, where Saint Father Romuald had lived.
