He likewise asserts that the holy doctor lived in the hermitage of Serra Santa, or Serra Sanctorum, near the Apennine mountain in the region of Tadinum, in the diocese of Nocera, together with Saint John of Lodi, his disciple. Saint Romuald and Saint Facundinus, the bishop, had previously lived there.

Similarly, either Peter Damian himself or certainly Saint Dominic Loricatus lived in the hermitage of Luceoli. According to the same Jacobillus, Saint Romuald built it—after the destruction of that very ancient city, ordered by Otto III around the year 996 because it had supported Crescentius, the Roman consul—in order to restore the ancient religious life of the place. He divided it into eighteen cells.

After Dominic Loricatus had lived there “for many years under the direction of the holy man John, who was called of Montefeltro,” Peter Damian says in book I, letter 19, Dominic submitted himself to Peter Damian’s direction:

> “Much later, with his teacher’s consent, that holy man deigned, with truly extraordinary humility, to commit himself to me, wretched and unworthy though I was—whom he himself had chosen to receive—and to subject himself to me as a monk to an abbot. To him he gave himself; he did not receive him. I had accepted him as a dependent subordinate, but I rejoice that in Christ’s school I truly found in him a teacher of philosophers.”

This certainly could not have happened if Dominic, a disciple of Romuald and a pupil of Romuald’s followers, had differed from Peter Damian in religion, institution, or habit.

### XIV

After Dominic Loricatus had lived in the neighboring cell under Damian’s direction, Damian says of him in book VI, letter 30:

> “But why, while commemorating holy men, do I range through different places here and there? I have someone within my threshold and before my hands, someone whose praises I am unequal to proclaim with due dignity. Indeed, since our cells are situated opposite one another, separated only by the intervening basilica, he and I are divided from each other. If I devote myself to enumerating his virtues, the days will pass before the material for writing appears capable of being exhausted. I speak of Dominic, my teacher and my lord.”

Later, as I have said, Dominic became prior of Saint Mary of Sitria. This was the famous hermitage constructed by Saint Father Romuald, as is clear from his Life, chapter 49. There Dominic also “remained enclosed for nearly seven years and inviolably maintained continuous silence,” according to the same Life, chapter 52. The hermitage is praised by Peter Damian as filled with Romuald’s most holy disciples in chapter 64 of that Life:

> “Such was life at Sitria that, by the likeness not only of its name but also of its work, it seemed to be a second Nitria. O golden age of Romuald! Although it did not know the torments of persecutors, it nevertheless was not without voluntary martyrdom. Golden, I say, was that age which among the wild beasts of mountains and forests nourished so many citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.”

Dominic Loricatus therefore became prior of this monastery or hermitage, as is clear from the title of book VI, letter 31:

> “To Dominic Loricatus, prior of Saint Mary of Sitria, and to his hermits.”

At that time both he and his subjects depended upon Peter Damian’s will and direction, as is inferred from the beginning of the same letter, where Damian says:

> “You have written to me, most beloved, that the envy of so many perverse and violent men assails you, and that unless I hasten quickly to your aid, you will abandon the place and provide yourselves with another man who will not be exposed to these robberies and troubles.”

### XV

It is therefore clear that the care of the people of Sitria belonged to Damian. This proves the mutual communion between Romuald’s places and Peter Damian’s, and the indiscriminate movement of monks from the former to the latter and in turn from the latter to the former.

Thus Dominic Loricatus certainly left Sitria two years before his death and withdrew to the hermitage of Mount Suavicinus, now called Frontalis, which Peter Damian had founded. Damian himself relates this in volume III, short work XV, chapter 6:

> “In that hermitage,” he says, “which, with God as author, we built on the slope of Mount Suavicinus.”

Dominic died there. He was first buried in his cell and then, on Peter Damian’s order, buried in the chapter house on the ninth day, as Peter Damian himself relates in book I, letter 19, to Alexander.

Peter Damian likewise lived there indiscriminately at this time and mentions the monastery of Sitria in many places as though it belonged to him. Indeed, from the frequent examples and conversations of the people of Sitria that he reports, he seems to indicate that he spent time among Romuald’s disciples and their successors at Sitria more often, perhaps, than among the people of Avellana.

### XVI

Certainly, in volume III, short work XIII, chapter 22, the holy doctor speaks of this monastery of Sitria as his own:

> “Finally, we have an old man in the monastery of Sitria, named Mainardus, whom, while he was still wearing secular dress, I admonished to become a monk,” etc.

For the purpose of suppressing the pride of Theuzo, a Florentine hermit, he presents the examples of Leo of Sitria and of other hermits of that place as domestic examples in volume I, book VI, letter 30:

> “Would that you were present and could judge with your eyes what is done in these woods by unknown and despised men! Nevertheless, so that the swelling of arrogance, if it exists in you, may be brought low, do not hesitate to learn briefly something about their way of life,” etc.

Then, speaking of Martin Storace, he says:

> “We have in a cell a certain rustic and ignorant man,” etc.

Next he turns to Leo of Sitria:

> “I shall come to Lord Leo—and truly to a lion,”

whose counsel he often says he used. He likewise mentions Lupus, who was enclosed, and Peter the hermit, of the same hermitage of Sitria.

There is no doubt that the Leo mentioned above was Peter Damian’s principal director. For in volume III, short work XI, in the dedicatory address of the little book he inscribed to this hermit, he speaks to him as follows:

> “I regard you as no ordinary companion or friend, but as a father, a teacher, a master, and a lord, chosen by me above almost all mortals. What more shall I say? I have established you as my angel, so that in doubtful matters, whatever counsel might proceed from your mouth to me hesitating and asking questions, I would accept it immediately and without hesitation as though the voice of an angelic heavenly oracle were sounding for me.
>
> “Therefore, whenever a difficulty in any matter creeps upon me, before I approach you to seek counsel, I implore divine mercy from you: that, making you the instrument of its will, it may command me through your mouth what I should do and what it determines in the ambiguity confronting me.”

### XVII

Nor should our monastery of Saint Apollinaris in Classe at Ravenna be omitted among the places of the Camaldolese order in which Peter Damian had his dwelling. It was consecrated in the earliest beginnings of Romuald’s conversion, according to his Life, chapter 1; it boasts that it had him as abbot for at least two years, according to chapter 22 of the same work; and it owes to his vigilance the fact that it was cleansed of a certain simoniacal prefect, as related above in chapter 41.

At the same time, it owes no less to Peter Damian the immediate assistance he provided in a serious crisis, as is evident from his letters of recommendation to Boniface, bishop of Albano and cardinal of the Roman Church, and to Stephen, the priest, on behalf of the abbot of Saint Apollinaris. These letters are found in volume I, book II, letter 4:

> “I do not want you, my most beloved brothers and lords, to be unaware that this present Jacob, the rector of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris, has crept into the summit of our mountain. Show him mercifully the compassion which you possess and in which you abundantly overflow, so that he need not fear the ruin of his place or the destruction of his dwelling. Let it therefore benefit him that he has undertaken the summit of so great a mountain,” etc.

The monastery of Classe can also boast that it received such a man as Peter Damian. For in letter 1 of book VII, writing to Emperor Henry, he notes that he stayed at the monastery of Classe:

> “Let it return to the memory of my lord the king that, when I was about to depart from you at the monastery of Classe…”

Again, in book VI, letter 26, he writes “to Marinus, his cousin, a monk of Classe,” then still a novice. The letter begins:

> “An inexperienced recruit is easily struck down in the first encounter of battle,” etc.

He testifies that he himself had placed the monastic habit upon Marinus with his own hands in the monastery of Classe:

> “Especially since I myself also gave you the monastic habit, I do not without reason confess that I am released from your consultations.”

He also sufficiently implies that he had lived there at other times, when he says:

> “In that same monastery of Classe, which you now inhabit, in our time”—that is, while he was living there—“a certain monk held the office of prior,” etc.

Near the end he indicates that he had enjoyed the companionship and association of the people of Classe, when he concludes:

> “Greet all the holy brothers of your monastery on my behalf. But if you happen at some time to see my very dear brothers Boninus and Peter singing more loudly than usual, place this distich in my name into their hands,” etc.

This certainly indicates that great familiarity existed between these men and the holy doctor. I say nothing of the mutual movement of the people of Classe to Avellana and of those of Avellana to Classe, which is evident from book II, letter 12, and book VI, letter 15. We also touched upon this matter in passing in Dissertation III, chapter 7, number 8.

### XVIII

If, then—to reduce everything to a brief summary—the following conclusions are drawn from what has been set forth at length, it follows that the monastery of Fonte Avellana, where our Peter was initiated into the monastic habit, had once been inhabited by Saint Father Romuald and had been instituted by Blessed Ludolphus, his disciple.

The way of life of the people of Avellana agreed generally with the way of life Romuald prescribed for hermits and specifically with the customs of the Camaldolese. Damian repeatedly appealed to Romuald’s authority while attempting to regulate the conduct of his monks. Peter Damian’s own rule possessed the force of law among the Camaldolese. In former times the people of Avellana were joined to the Camaldolese by mutual fellowship, admitted into a common participation in hospitality and suffrages, and used a habit extremely similar to theirs, whether one considers the habit itself, its color, or its form.

Peter Damian himself, if not a direct hearer of Romuald, was certainly a pupil of his disciples and, in all likelihood, lived in the Camaldolese hermitage, and most clearly in many other hermitages and monasteries constructed by Romuald or operating under his discipline. He was nourished by the milk of the same institution.

What further doubt can be permitted concerning the fact that he lived as a follower of the discipline transmitted by Saint Romuald and therefore ought truly and properly to be called a Camaldolese, according to the general meaning of that name explained in Dissertation I, chapter 2, number 21?

### XIX

For this reason, with the very greatest justification, Peter Damian has been regarded and called a Camaldolese by the agreement of so many foreign writers. It is sufficient here to list Gabriel Pennottus, cited by Father Laderchius; Ludovicus Jacobillus, *The Saints of Umbria*; Paulus Morigia, *History of Religions*, chapter 58; Cornelius a Lapide, on Revelation, chapter 3; Martin Baronius, in the *Life of the Five Polish Brother Martyrs*; Joannes Paulus Portesanus, in the *Life of Saint Theobald*; Joannes Petrus Crescentius, *Roman Defense*, book I, part II, narrative 2; Stephanus Demalevicius, *Life of Saint Bogumilus*, chapter 28; Secundus Lancellotus, *Olivetan History*, book II, chapter 22; Ludovicus Tomasinus, *On Benefices*, part I, book III, chapter 25; Ludovicus Du Pin, *Ecclesiastical Bibliotheca*, volume VIII, part II, chapter 14, section 10; Antonius Maria Bonuccius, *Eucharistic Calendar*, 22 February; Augustinus Lubin, *Information on the Abbeys of Italy*, letter A.

The same view was held by the supreme pontiffs Pius V, Gregory XV, and Urban VIII. The last two called Peter Damian the honor and glory of the Camaldolese order in their diplomas, cited by our abbot D. Andreas Vallemannius, both in the Life of the same Peter, arranged into narratives together with the eulogies of other saints of the order, and in the sermon on Saint Dominic Loricatus, page 84.

The first of these pontiffs, as our Ractius testifies in *Description of the Sacred Hermitage*, chapter 19, and in the *Life of the same Peter Damian*, page 50, and as Thomas Minius testifies in *Camaldolese History*, book VIII, chapter 1, was so firmly convinced that Damian belonged to the Camaldolese institution and that the abbey of Avellana had long flourished within our order that he decreed its restoration to that same order after assigning an apostolic visitation of the monastery to Giovanni Battista Novarese, the general, on 22 December 1568.

He completed this restoration through other diplomas dated 1, 10, and 14 December 1569.

XX. Hence, even from this very fact—that the Camaldolese have now fully succeeded to the places inhabited by Saint Peter Damian and other illustrious men of his congregation, and that all their rights have passed to us—someone might reasonably judge that Peter Damian himself, together with his disciples and successors, ought to be admitted into our catalogues; that their cult and their glory belong to us, lest we seem to have inherited merely their temporal possessions while leaving to the original occupants what is more valuable. Whether this observation deserved to be added in jest or in earnest, let each person judge according to his own discretion.

I shall bring forward a similar observation by that most serious and learned man, Jean Mabillon, from his preface to volume I of the *Monastic History*, which agrees exactly with our purpose. He writes:

“What I have said thus far proves the unity of the monastic order—let us say, of the Camaldolese Order—during those times, a unity which the diversity of rules in no way invalidated. Therefore, in distinguishing the holy or illustrious men who followed the Rule of Saint Benedict—or, as we may say, the discipline of Blessed Romuald—or in distinguishing the monasteries that from their foundation were subject to that same rule, I shall be neither excessively scrupulous nor overly exacting. I am certain that knowledge of both belongs to our history: first, because, as I have said, there was one order embracing them all; and second, because, even if they had then belonged to different orders, once all those monasteries had been transferred to our order, the honor belongs to those to whom the inheritance came. Our order’s history would therefore be mutilated and incomplete if we omitted mention of those monasteries and monks. This would not only seriously damage our history, but would also expose us to the fault of ingratitude. In this matter we follow the custom of the Christian Church, which claims the holy and illustrious men of the Old Testament as its own because the Church of both Testaments is one. For the same reason we receive the ancient monks as our fathers,” and so forth.

# CHAPTER VII. Laderchius’s Principal Arguments Are Refuted

## Synopsis

The confusion of congregation and order introduced by Laderchius. No. 1. Whether the kinship of the Avellanites and Camaldolese is proved from the Rule of Saint Benedict. 2. Whether it is proved from the identity of their Constitutions. 3. Laderchius attempts to prove that these were different. 4. Several congregations, with different constitutions, serve under the same order. 5. Likewise, several monasteries of the same order. 6. By Laderchius’s argument, even the Camaldolese monks and hermits would not belong to the same order. 7. Different constitutions were subsequently proposed both for the hermits and for the monks of the same congregation. 8. The constitutions of the Avellanites and Camaldolese were not different. 9. Laderchius denies this gratuitously, since he has not read either set. 10. Romuald is cited more often in the Avellanite rule than in the Camaldolese constitutions. 11. Why Damian does not expressly refer everything to Romuald. 12. Laderchius’s observation and contradiction. 13. Even if Damian had special constitutions for the Avellanites, they could nevertheless have concerned Romuald’s common eremitical discipline. 14. Damian approves not merely some things but everything pertaining to Romuald’s institution. 15. Whether Damian names the disciples of Saint Romuald as though they had no connection with him. 16.

## I

Let us now hear Laderchius’s arguments, by which he has attempted to attack this position. He says in book I, chapter 8, no. 6:

“We nevertheless think it should not be passed over that certain persons have attempted to fuse disorderly into one those bodies which remain like stars in their own order and course—namely, the Camaldolese and Avellanite congregations. Although we think they should be forgiven, since the fraternal charity and fellowship that the Lord established between the Avellanite and Camaldolese families deceived them, we ask them to examine more carefully the face of heaven and of the earth. Among these is the Gabriel Pennottus mentioned above, by whom the hermits of Fonte Avellana are commonly called Camaldolese, together with others.”

Here, at the very threshold of the controversy and in the very formulation of the question, the author appears to have fallen conspicuously into error. For we are not attempting “to fuse the Camaldolese and Avellanite congregations disorderly into one” when we assert that Saint Peter Damian was Camaldolese. Rather, we bring together both of them: that is, the Camaldolese in the narrower sense, which embraces only the hermits of the sacred Tuscan hermitage, according to the distinction explained elsewhere, and the Avellanite congregation instituted by Blessed Lodulphus, a disciple of Saint Romuald, and especially illumined by Peter Damian.

In the same way we have brought together the Coronese, Taurinese, French, and our own monastic Family of Saint Michael in Murano into one order instituted by Romuald. We call it Camaldolese in the broader sense, taking its name from the noblest and most celebrated of all these places, as we noted in Dissertation I, chapter 2.

This has been done with the greatest justice on the basis of that very “fraternal charity which the Lord established between the Avellanite and Camaldolese family.” For the social bond between the two families could not have existed through any other bond than that of the same institution and through their common emulation of the discipline of Saint Father Romuald—a bond such as did not exist between us and the other monastic congregations that are entirely independent of our order.

## II

Our author continues in no. 7:

“But that this unity is not clearly proved by the identity of the rule is evident. For if, from the fact that the same Rule of Saint Father Benedict was observed by both congregations, one infers that they were only one, then the congregations of the Cistercians, Cluniacs, Vallumbrosans, and Sylvestrines—all of which profess the same Rule of Saint Father Benedict—will not be several congregations but only one. Nothing more absurd can be said.”

Yet no one has imagined that, merely from their profession of the Benedictine Rule, one could infer that the hermits of Fonte Avellana belonged to the Camaldolese institution—unless someone added or at least assumed from elsewhere that the Avellanites also practiced the eremitical life, whose conjunction with the canons of the Benedictine Rule acknowledges Saint Father Romuald alone as its author and institutor, as we observed in Dissertation I, chapter 5, no. 10. From this it is clear that no inference can be drawn from the Avellanites to the other monks whom Laderchius lists.

## III

He nevertheless proceeds in no. 8:

“Still less is such unity proved by the identity of the constitutions when the constitutions themselves are compared. Through their constitutions each congregation differs from the other as star from star. For if, with Augustine Fortunius, we admit that Saint Romuald did not issue constitutions and did not hand them down to his Camaldolese, then the Camaldolese congregation is not the same as the Avellanite congregation. The former, as will be seen, had its own institutions, whereas the latter did not. What shall we say to this?

“We shall certainly answer that Saint Romuald issued no constitutions, but also that he had none—not merely Camaldolese constitutions, but not even Avellanite ones. This follows from Peter Damian himself, who, in his work *On the Order of the Hermits of Fonte Avellana*, says the following when discussing the institutions of his congregation:

‘But I wish, my brothers, to touch briefly upon the order of your way of life, so that what is now read in your living practices may also be handed down in writing for the knowledge of those who will succeed us in this place. Thus, even if they should not happen to ascend to higher things, they may at least strive faithfully to observe the same rule of life that they will have learned you to have maintained, so that those who succeed to your dwelling may nevertheless be heirs also of your way of life.’

“From this it is clear that, before these times, the Avellanite hermits had no fixed constitutions, but were led to obedience in all things to the faith by customs rather than by laws. Therefore nothing can be proved from constitutions against the unity of these congregations, since neither the one nor the other possessed them. Rather, it must be said that both walked rightly before God in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord that Saint Romuald had taught them, without blame, and that both proceeded in this manner throughout their days.”

## IV

He undertakes to refute this response in the following no. 9, saying:

“But if we maintain that the Avellanite and Camaldolese families came simultaneously from one master, why did the former begin to live by laws, while the latter remained content with traditions? The institutions of his congregation are said to have been written down by our Peter Damian in or about the year 1040—or, more safely, in 1071 or 1072, since it is clearly gathered from his own words that he wrote them when near death. He was addressing his successors in the office of prior:

‘Behold, my brothers, I was what you are, and I have measured out what you are passing through; what I left is at hand for you, and what I have reached is near.’

“And in the year 1100 and afterward, according to Augustine Fortunius, the Reverend Father Rodulphus, prior of the Camaldolese hermitage, promulgated the eremitical rule, with the consent of Helempertus, bishop of Arezzo. Why, then, was this new rule of Rodulphus composed to no purpose, if Peter Damian had committed it to writing so long before? If, as is assumed, the Camaldolese and the Avellanites alike received that very rule which the Camaldolese had received from the mouth of Saint Romuald?”

Thus far he.

## V

First, it must not be concealed that this writer is wasting his effort in proving a distinction between the congregations of Avellana and Camaldoli—that is, the sacred Tuscan hermitage—for this is not at all the question. The question is only whether both belong to the same order instituted by Saint Romuald, which we call Camaldolese.

He therefore misleads his readers when he anxiously investigates whether both, or neither, lived at the same time according to written constitutions, and whether Blessed Rodulphus wrote down the customs of Camaldoli to no purpose after Saint Peter Damian had set forth the institutions of Avellana. As though the unity of the order depended upon this! It is abundantly evident that many congregations of the same order are commonly found that do not use institutions written at the same time or identical with one another.

Thus the laws of the Capuchins differ from those of the Observant Friars Minor, and both differ from those of the Conventuals, although all serve under the same order of Saint Francis. Likewise, the constitutions of the Carmelites whom they call Calced differ from those of the Discalced. There are also the customs of the Barefoot Augustinians and those of the congregations following the ancient eremitical institution.

I say nothing of the monastic order, or of the Camaldolese order itself, in which the ways of life differ among the coenobites, the hermits of the sacred Tuscan hermitage, the congregation of Monte Corona, the Taurinese, and finally the French hermits, although all acknowledge the same common Father Romuald as their master in the way of life and all glory in the same surname, Camaldolese.

## VI

Second, since, as we said in Dissertation I, chapter 2, no. 11, all the monasteries formerly existed independently of one another, as though each were a congregation in its own right, it was entirely appropriate that each should use its own written constitutions. Martene mentions many such examples from manuscripts in his *On the Ancient Rites of the Monks*: the Corbie, Dijon, Toul, Compiègne, Laon, Lérins, and other monasteries.

What, then, is surprising if the Camaldolese hermitage had its own customs, while the solitude of Fonte Avellana likewise preserved its own—first received from Romuald by oral tradition alone, and later set forth in writing, first by Peter Damian for the Avellanites and somewhat later by Blessed Rodulphus for the Camaldolese?

Although all might agree in substance, something could nevertheless arise in the circumstances that would have to be adapted differently to places, times, and persons according to regional diversity. This is demonstrably what happened in our case. For Damian himself admits in work XV that he did not extend his constitutions beyond the hermitage in which he lived:

“We prescribe not so much by a general definition what ought to be done by hermits as we specifically explain what is done in this hermitage, both with regard to the place and with regard to the person.”

Likewise, the statutes of Blessed Rodulphus exercised their force no farther than the sacred hermitage and the adjoining monastery of Fontebuono. Luke the Spaniard says in book I, chapter 12 of his *History of Romuald*:

“For the constitution of subjection that exists under Rodulphus does not extend beyond the inhabitants of Fontebuono.”

Nothing, therefore, required the constitutions of one place to become known in another, much less required that what was promulgated in one place should immediately be adopted in another and at once bind those living there.

## VII

Third, if Laderchius’s argument had any force, it would equally prove that the Camaldolese coenobites did not belong to the Camaldolese order itself, even during those first five centuries when they were most closely joined by a social bond to the hermits of the sacred Tuscan hermitage and lived under the same general prior.

For, according to Laderchius’s admission, Blessed Rodulphus the prior proposed the first constitutions to the hermits. The coenobites, however, until Martin III, rendered their vows to the Lord without any particular written customs of their own, retaining only the observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Fortunius testifies to this in book II, chapter 40 of part I of his *Camaldolese History*, where he says of Martin III:

“At the general council held at the sacred hermitage in the year 1254, he promulgated for the first time constitutions for the Fathers, in which he encompassed in five books the entire arrangement of a truly coenobitical life, both with regard to divine matters and with regard to morals, and so forth.”

Thus one could say here with Laderchius:

“Therefore the congregation of Camaldolese monks is not the same as the congregation of Camaldolese hermits, since the latter, as has been seen, had its own institutions—from the time of Blessed Rodulphus until 1234—but the former did not. What shall we say to this?”

Likewise one could say with the same Laderchius:

“But if we maintain that the family of Camaldolese hermits and monks came simultaneously from one master, why did the former begin to live by laws, while the latter remained content with traditions? And why was this new rule of Blessed Martin III composed to no purpose, if Blessed Rodulphus had committed it to writing so long before? If, as is assumed, the monks also received that very rule which the hermits had received from the mouth of Saint Romuald?”

Yet the coenobites and the hermits alike belonged not only to the same order but also, at that time, to the same still-undivided congregation, even with regard to its ultimate government.

## VIII

To prevent anyone from quibbling about a difference in the argument on the ground that these men followed different ways of life while living under the government of one congregation, we shall observe, fourth, that places belonging to the same congregation and serving under the same general superior, even when following the same kind of discipline, were nevertheless accustomed at times to have and preserve different constitutions suited to their regions.

Thus Martin III, who, as we have said, compiled the constitutions of all the monks in 1254, had already added particular constitutions in 1248 for the monastery of Saint Matthias in Murano alone. These can be read in Fortunius, *Camaldolese History*, part II, book III, chapter 5.

Indeed, it is worth noting that the same religious, living in the same places, repeatedly revised their constitutions according to changing circumstances. Thus Blessed Rodulphus, after his first constitutions, later proposed a milder rule of life to his hermits, as is clear from Fortunius, part I, chapter 65 of the *Camaldolese Histories*. These were later followed by the statutes of Placidus, then the constitutions of Gherardus, next the rule of eremitical life by Paul Justinianus, and finally the declarations concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict that appeared under Clement X for those same Tuscan hermits, which they now use.

Likewise, in addition to the constitutions for the monks composed by Blessed Martin III, others were added under the emperor Octavianus, others under the generals Bonaventura and Ptolemy, others under Cardinal Gallio, others under Pius V, and some even under Clement VIII.

I say nothing of Peter Damian himself, who is found to have written the institutions of his Avellanite congregation twice, namely in works XIV and XV. Would Laderchius’s exclamation not apply here as well—an exclamation imitated from the ill-considered and feigned zeal of Judas the traitor:

“Why this waste?”

For sufficient laws of life had already been committed to writing for the hermits, for the Camaldolese monks, and for the Avellanites themselves. The Camaldolese order, therefore, can no more be proved different from the Avellanite order on this account than the Camaldolese themselves can be proved different from the Camaldolese, or the Avellanites from the Avellanites.

## IX

But fifth, I answer that, although Peter Damian issued one set of constitutions for the disciples of Fonte Avellana and Rodulphus another for the Camaldolese, they were nevertheless not different or divergent in essentials. Rather, both alike derived from Romuald’s institution, as we demonstrated at length above in chapters 3 and 4. Therefore, the constitutions of Damian and Rodulphus demonstrate not the diversity but the identity of the institution of the Avellanites and the Camaldolese.

This is especially true because the same constitutions of Saint Peter Damian had been received in the sacred Camaldolese hermitage and possessed the force of a rule, both before Blessed Rodulphus and after him. Rodulphus himself established in his own constitutions that the hermits were still to observe them, except for the relaxation concerning Saturday and a few other provisions that did not entirely accord with the customs of the sacred Camaldolese hermitage, as we demonstrated above in chapter 5, nos. 5–7.

## X

From this the answer is clear to what Laderchius adds in no. 10 in confirmation of his position:

“But the sequence, order, and other features of the constitutions themselves, when compared with one another, abundantly demonstrate that they did not proceed from one source. And although it is true that Peter inserted some of Saint Romuald’s admonitions into his constitutions and elsewhere, it does not follow that all the constitutions handed down by Peter himself to the Avellanites were Romuald’s. On the contrary, it follows that only those which he expressly names were Romuald’s. For if all had been Romuald’s, no reason can be devised why he should have attributed only some to Romuald rather than all, if they were his.

“It is clear to readers that, whenever he states something said by Romuald, he reports it not as the command of a master but rather in the manner in which, in most rules, the admonitions and sayings of Augustine, Jerome, the Fathers, or the elders are stated. These are not therefore rightly called the Rule of Augustine or Jerome, and so forth, merely for that reason.”

As I have said, the answer to all this is evident from what was stated above. These claims are wholly fabricated and gratuitously invented against the manifest evidence of the matter. Still, something must be conceded to a man who, placing excessive confidence in his cause, ventured to pronounce—before he had read even the smallest line of Blessed Rodulphus’s constitutions or seen even the external covers of their codex—as though he had compared them with Peter Damian’s rule, that “the sequence, order, and other features of the constitutions themselves, when compared with one another, abundantly demonstrate that they did not proceed from one source.”

## XI

As for his further claim—that Romuald’s sayings are cited in Peter Damian’s constitutions not as the precepts of a master but as the admonitions and sayings of holy doctors of the Church, and that therefore not everything contained there should be asserted to have proceeded from Romuald’s institution, but only those few things expressly referred to Romuald—that claim would plainly demonstrate that the Camaldolese hermits and monks belonged, or once belonged, even less under the banners of the same Saint Father Romuald.

Indeed, in their constitutions you will scarcely find Romuald cited as many times as he is in the Avellanite laws described by Peter Damian. In the latter, Damian expressly mentions Romuald four or five times; in some of the former, once or twice; in others, Romuald’s name is not heard even once.

Therefore, if Laderchius’s judgment were accepted, neither would the whole discipline of the Camaldolese depend upon Blessed Romuald, nor would Romuald’s institutions have to be regarded by our hermits as the commands of a master and institutor, but merely as the counsels and opinions of some particular saint. Nothing more absurd could be said.

But whether Damian invoked Romuald’s authority as that of a master can be sufficiently gathered from what was said above, especially from what we noted in chapter 5, nos. 2 and 3.

## XII

The reason why Peter Damian expressly attributes only a few things among many to Romuald’s institution is that the remainder had not been specifically conceived or newly invented by that holy Father. Rather, they had been imitated from the way of life of the ancient anchorites and most suitably adapted to his own institution.

Damian relates in chapter 8 of the *Life of Saint Romuald* that Romuald was accustomed to occupy himself with reading the histories of the ancient Fathers and to use their examples in restoring and perfecting the eremitical discipline throughout the West. We have already discussed this matter at greater length in Dissertation I, especially chapter 5.

Accordingly, Damian himself, in work XV, chapter 2, traces the more ancient origin of the eremitical life back to Paul and Anthony. And in chapter 18 he says:

“Whatever is said in the Rule of Blessed Benedict, whatever is said in the institutions or conferences of the Fathers, we judge to belong to this discipline.”

Yet Laderchius dares to portray Damian to us everywhere as though he were the Father of the eremitical life, as when he declares in book I, chapter 14, no. 7:

“Before Peter Damian, no one from the Order of Saint Benedict, at least in Italy, had handed down such outstanding eremitical institutions.”

This ought with still greater justice to be said of Saint Father Romuald, the pioneer of the hermits of the West:

“Before all others,” as Blessed Paul Justinianus notes in the preface to his rule, “he handed down to his contemporaries and left to all posterity rules and institutions for living the eremitical life—not in writing, but through the example of his life and through his instructions and admonitions. Perhaps he imitated Christ the Lord, who did not commit to writing what he established by doing and teaching it himself, but left it to others after him to write.”

It is therefore clear that nothing prevents Peter Damian’s constitutions from being called a product of Romuald’s discipline, even if not everything was Romuald’s own. Romuald’s own contribution was only the method collected from the institutions of Blessed Benedict and the ancient Fathers, together with its application to monks, enriched by certain distinguished admonitions from that holy Father himself.

Damian wished to refer those admonitions expressly to Romuald in order to secure greater authority for them, since the rest had already been consecrated by the customs of the ancient Fathers, and since he had once indicated— in chapters 8 and 9 of the *Life of Saint Romuald*—the source of all those practices, from which Romuald had transferred them into the use of the western hermits whom he undertook to instruct.

## XIII

Laderchius continues in the same chapter 8, cited no. 11:

“And Peter himself, writing to the monk Stephen about the institutions of his congregation, suggests this when he says:

‘We prescribe not so much by a general definition what ought to be done by hermits as we specifically explain what is done in this hermitage, both with regard to the place and with regard to the person.’

“Those institutions he wrote were therefore particular to his own place, not common to all who lived under Blessed Romuald’s discipline. For in that case he ought rather to have said that he was explaining everything that was observed both in his own place and by all the hermits who followed Romuald. Nor could he call the rules of his own place particular if he found that they were common to other places.”

Here it must be observed that this writer is not sufficiently consistent with himself. Above, in the words reported in no. 4, he wondered that Rodulphus had prepared new eremitical constitutions for the Camaldolese, when Peter Damian had already committed them to writing so much earlier. Now, however, he admits with us that Damian’s rules were written for the Avellanite hermitage alone, and therefore that there was room for other constitutions to bind other followers of Romuald outside Avellana.

## XIV

Moreover, just as there could be special constitutions for the Camaldolese hermitage, as we observed in no. 6, so there could likewise be the first constitutions of Blessed Martin III, discussed in no. 8, specifically for the monastery of Saint Matthias in Murano. Although these conformed to the discipline of Saint Romuald, they therefore could not bind other places founded by Saint Romuald or belonging to the Camaldolese order.

Similarly, although the constitutions of Blessed Peter Damian contained observances common to the Romualdians, they could nevertheless, in the primary intention of their author, be particular to the hermitage of Fonte Avellana. This could be so either because, besides the common customs of the order, they also included certain provisions suited only to the persons of that place, appropriate to the region, and established by use; or because, even if they prescribed nothing there beyond the common way of life, nevertheless, by the very fact that they were proposed by the superior who governed that particular place, they necessarily became special—with regard to their binding force—and could not be regarded as general and common to all who belonged to the same order, because the authority of the one issuing them was particular and his jurisdiction was restricted by definite limits of persons and places.

## XV

As for what Laderchius adds in no. 12, where he says of Peter Damian:

“There, also, speaking of the discretion of the superior—and we approve this—he says that Blessed Romuald is reported to have often told his disciples”—

by approving this one thing that Saint Romuald told his disciples, and the few other matters that he expressly distinguishes, he thereby shows, according to Laderchius, that all the institutions were not Saint Romuald’s, as we have said. Nor, he claims, should he have said that Romuald taught these things to his disciples, naming them as though they had no connection with him, especially since at that time many of them were still alive, from whom he admits that he learned the outstanding deeds of so great a Father, which he committed to writing.

And below, when he says what we quoted above—

“We do not describe in detail all the precepts of this institution, but deliberately omit many that occur to us frequently. For whatever is said in the Rule of Blessed Benedict, whatever is said in the institutions or conferences of the Fathers, we judge to belong to this discipline; nevertheless, we consider it superfluous to gather everything together here in one place”—

he plainly indicates, according to Laderchius, that he issued institutions particular to his own place, based not only on what he had expressly received from Romuald, but also on the Rule of Saint Benedict, the institutions of the Fathers, and especially the holy customs and practices of the hermitage that he cultivated.

As I have said, part of this has already been refuted above, and there is no need to repeat what we have demonstrated so clearly so many times. The remainder has an easy and obvious answer: Damian, in the passage cited by Laderchius, does not at all imply that he approves precisely that one thing which Saint Father Romuald had taught concerning the discretion of the superior. He simply approves it by assertion, without denying that the other matters also derived from Romuald.

This is shown by the matter itself, through a comparison of the two institutions in chapters 3 and 4, apart from the express mention of Blessed Romuald that occurs in Damian concerning the discipline of psalmody and other matters that we examined in chapter 5, nos. 2 and 3. Damian seems at least tacitly to indicate this in the very words quoted by Laderchius:

“We do not describe in detail all the precepts of this institution, but deliberately omit many that occur to us frequently,” *On the Order of the Hermits*, XV, chapter 18.

For what other eremitical institution could this have been than the one recently restored by Blessed Romuald and then in force? Although Romuald imitated many elements pertaining to this discipline from the ancient Fathers of the East, he nevertheless reduced everything to a more certain method and a perfect, regular norm of life, and he was the first to bring it into practice in these western regions.

Paul Justinianus says in the preface to his eremitical rule:

“The eremitical life in the Western Church perhaps had some follower, but it had no institutor. Its first author and institutor, however, was a man conspicuous for every holiness and altogether most admirable, the most blessed Romuald,” and so forth.

## XVI

Whether Damian names the disciples of Saint Romuald as though they had no connection with him, as Laderchius quibbles, we have already observed elsewhere, especially in chapter 5, no. 10, and chapter 6, no. 3.

For in the preface to the *Life of Saint Romuald* he calls them his brothers and asserts that, compelled by their prayers and urged by genuine charity, he was led to commit the deeds of the holy Father to writing.

If he does not expressly repeat this every time he mentions the disciples of Saint Romuald and endeavors to report what the most holy man taught his disciples, he should not for that reason be considered to mention them as though they were strangers to him.

Otherwise we would have to say that the Evangelists declare themselves alien to the discipline of Christ whenever they recount the parables that Jesus spoke to his disciples. Or we would have to assert that Peter Damian himself separated himself from the discipline of Saint Benedict when he called the disciples of Saint Benedict disciples in volume II, sermon 8, without expressly joining himself to them, and that he therefore mentioned them, in Laderchius’s judgment, as though they had no connection with him.

But how could Damian name the disciples of Romuald as though they had no connection with him? He lived with them most frequently, as was demonstrated throughout chapter 6, and he also made use of their instruction and guidance, as we proved from Damian with respect to Blessed Leo of Sitria in the cited chapter, no. 16.

Yet this Leo, according to Damian himself in book VI, letter 17, “had already spent nearly seventy years in the monastic habit.” He had therefore begun his training in the eremitical life while Romuald was still alive and under Romuald’s auspices, and among the disciples of Romuald who survived at Sitria he was perhaps the oldest of all.

# CHAPTER VIII. The Remaining Objections of Laderchius Are Examined

## Synopsis

What argument most seriously presses Laderchius. No. 1. How the author attempts to resolve it. 2. Refutation of the proposed solution. 3. For the foundation of his order, Romuald did not need to write down distinctive institutions of his own. Ibid. Two other statements by Laderchius are refuted. 4. Laderchius’s further attempt to evade the principal argument. 5. Why the monastery of Classe was joined to the Camaldolese hermitage. 6. Other unions of monasteries within the same order. 7. Another quibble by Laderchius is refuted. 8. Another challenge by the adversary against our position, again resting on a false supposition. 9. The two differences brought forward by Laderchius for this purpose are refuted. 10. Two further objections by Laderchius. 11. The solution of the first of these. 12. Refutation of the second. 13. Laderchius’s final argument is dissolved. 14.

## I

The force of truth radiates with such powerful light that it strikes even the eyes of those who flee from it. Thus it could by no means have escaped our Laderchius that one of the principal arguments customarily brought forward to prove Peter Damian’s Camaldolese institution is based on the fact that Saint Dominic Loricatus, prior of Sitria, was a disciple of that same Peter Damian, as we demonstrated in chapter 6, no. 14.

Our writer therefore leaves no stone unturned to remove this prejudice against his position and turns in every direction to crush this exceedingly troublesome obstacle. For I remember that, as early as 1699, when Laderchius was occupied with compiling the life of Saint Peter Damian—although in the preface to this work, published in 1702, he claims to have devoted only three months to its composition—I was then living in Rome and heard from the mouth of the same author, while we were discussing this very controversy with one another, that of all the arguments advanced for our position, this one caused him the greatest difficulty, although he would not allow its force to move him from his preconceived opinion.

## II

Thus Laderchius presents the matter and undertakes to disentangle this difficulty in paragraph 13:

> “You will say that Romualdus founded the hermitage of Sitria, in which Dominicus Loricatus, Damianus’s disciple, subsequently lived; therefore he lived under the constitutions of Romualdus, since he was in a hermitage founded by him.”

He immediately replies to this argument as follows:

> “But the conclusion is denied on the basis of what was said above: Romualdus did not give constitutions, but taught by keeping silent with his tongue and preaching by his life; and although he founded many places under the Rule of Saint Benedict, nevertheless the practices observed in them beyond the Rule were commanded by the master himself more by example than by word—or, if by word, by a word not bound by fixed constitutions—so that they were received from an abbot, not from the founder of a new Rule, but rather as from the particular instructor and master of this or that place. This continued until, moved by the spirit of Romualdus, they committed his constitutions to writing; and Peter likewise gave his own. From these the Camaldolese congregation is distinguished from that of Avellana, just as, under the Rule of Saint Benedict, the Cistercians, Cluniacs, and Vallombrosan congregations are separated from one another.”

So much for him.

## III

In these statements, I confess that I am uncertain which point I should admire first, or more: whether the fact that he denies that the hermitage of Sitria was founded by Saint Romualdus and that its inhabitants belonged to the Camaldolese order, because the holy Father did not set down his constitutions in writing; or the fact that he presents this same holy Father to us not as a restorer of eremitical life, but as the particular instructor of this or that place; or, finally, the fact that he asserts that this state of affairs continued until the Camaldolese applied themselves to writing down their constitutions.

But what kind of monstrosities of fact and opinion are these? We already said in the preceding chapter, paragraph 12, together with Paulus Justinianus, that Romualdus indeed did not publish his constitutions in writing, following the example of Christ our Lord himself:

> “What he established by doing and teaching, he did not hand down in writing, but left to others after him to commit to writing.”

Nor did the great abbot Antonius, the father of so many monks, commit any Rule or institution to writing. Rather, through the examples of his life and the teachings impressed more deeply upon the minds of his disciples, he thoroughly instructed his followers, as the author—and Athanasius—states:

> “For the life of Antonius,” he says, “is a sufficient pattern for monks pursuing the ascetic life.”

The same can be said of Romualdus, who earned, by his example of life and his most salutary admonitions, the title of father and founder of all Western hermits, as we proved in Dissertation I, chapter 5. Damianus himself likewise asserted in chapter 9 of his Life that Romualdus had nonetheless

> “set forth a rule of life for all who pursued the solitary life,”

a rule that we have received as shining forth in that same admirable History. Hence Blessed Rodulphus, in the constitutions of 1085, describes the first inhabitants of the Camaldolese hermitage as

> “continually recalling the life and teaching of the ever-venerable Romualdus.”

I pass over the fact that neither Saint John Gualbert left written constitutions to the Vallombrosan family, nor Saint Robert the abbot to the Cistercians, nor Saint Stephen, the father of the Grandmontines, committed his institutions to writing. We have heard that these were once collected by his disciples and recently translated into French, and were printed by Augustinus Mercier in 1704.

It is therefore clear that the fact that Romualdus did not write down his constitutions is wholly irrelevant to separating the monastery of Sitria from his order. By the same reasoning, the Camaldolese hermitage would also have to be excluded, since Romualdus wrote no Rule there either, nor is he found anywhere to have set down particular canons of his discipline in writing.

## IV

As for the second point—whether Romualdus presided over the inhabitants of Sitria as the master of a single private house, or should rather be regarded as the common abbot of all and the founder of eremitical discipline—one should consult what we expressly observed in Dissertation I, chapter 3, paragraph 14, against this very assertion of Laderchius. There is no reason to repeat it pointlessly here.

What shall I add about the third point, except that by this observation Laderchius seems to imply that we derive our origin not from Romualdus, but from those who committed his constitutions to writing? That would be to wrest from Romualdus a distinguished tribute to a patriarch and transfer it to Rodulphus. By the same reasoning, Romualdus would not merely be excluded from the founders of religious families; so too would John Gualbert, Robert, Stephen, and almost all the founders of monastic branches, who likewise handed down nothing in writing. In their place, their disciples and successors—whoever established any statutes concerning their orders—would have to be installed and regarded as the patriarchs of the Vallombrosans, Cistercians, or, respectively, Grandmontines.

This is utterly ridiculous.

## V

Laderchius continues in paragraph 14:

> “Besides the fact that the constitutions of Romualdus, whether handed down by word of mouth or subsequently committed to writing, were not received by all the places that he is said either to have founded or to have governed, we therefore clearly infer, leaving other matters aside, that those who lived in those hermitages or monasteries did not belong to his Camaldolese congregation. For although it is certainly held that he governed the Classense monastery at the command both of the emperor Otto and of Saint Apollinaris himself, nevertheless that same monastery, which Saint Romualdus governed, was not handed over to his Camaldolese congregation by Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, until the year 1138, that is, one hundred and more years after the death of Romualdus. For this new transfer would surely have been superfluous if that place had already received the precepts of its most blessed founder for so long a time, namely when he governed it as abbot. Therefore, just as it is clear from this that the monks living in the Classense monastery could not have been called Camaldolese either during Romualdus’s lifetime or after his most blessed death, until the aforesaid year 1138, so likewise we think that Dominicus Loricatus cannot be called Camaldolese merely because he was in the hermitage of Sitria founded by Romualdus. Rather, he should be regarded as belonging to the congregation of Avellana, since he was a disciple of Peter Damianus, who instructed him through his particular Institutions, distinct—as we see—from those of the Camaldolese, when Dominicus submitted himself to his instruction.”

## VI

These arguments collapse completely in light of what was said in Dissertation I about the twofold meaning of the name “Camaldolese,” which we distinguished there in chapter 2, paragraph 21, and which Laderchius repeatedly confuses.

The observation he adduces proves only that the Classense monastery long remained separate from the congregation of the sacred Camaldolese hermitage, just as many other places built by Saint Romualdus did—at a time, namely, when individual monasteries formed as many mutually independent congregations, although belonging to the same institute, as we have often pointed out. It does not prove that the same Classense monastery should not be referred to the same Camaldolese order insofar as that order embraces all the places that had received the discipline of Blessed Romualdus.

Indeed, Romualdus had begun his conversion in this distinguished asceterium, and is said to have governed it for two years. Fortunius, *History of Camaldoli*, part II, book I, chapter 15, testifies that his successors were Ardefadus and Bonus, his disciples. Although Romualdus had relinquished its governance, he nevertheless showed such concern for it that, when he heard that the most noble monastery had been polluted by the invasion of a certain Venetian simoniacal abbot,

> “that tireless soldier of Christ hastened to go there and attempted by various means to cleanse the monastery of him,”

as Damianus reports in the *Life*, chapter 41.

But the holy Father had not joined that same Classense monastery to the Camaldolese hermitage. Why, then, should it be surprising if Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, wished to establish such a union?

Fortunius preserves an entire charter of union in the place cited, book II, chapter 17. From it, it is clear that the archbishop entrusted the Classense monastery, with all its appurtenances, to Azo, prior of the Camaldolese hermitage—not by transferring it from one order to another, but so that, through the agency of its members, it might flourish again with richer fruits of observance and receive greater growth in virtue:

> “For the reform and preservation of religion”—

these are the words of the charter—and below:

> “Solely with a view to, and for the purpose of, reforming religion.”

Nor do we read that, as a result of the execution of this union, there was any displacement of the monks or innovation of their habit in the Classense monastery.

## VII

Indeed, if what we demonstrated in Dissertation I, chapter 2, paragraph 14, concerning the monastery of Vallis Castri—which Saint Romualdus had built and where he had laid aside his mortal remains—namely, that it was incorporated into the places of the sacred hermitage only after 360 years, and if what we generally observed there in paragraph 23 concerning various monasteries of an order coming together into a particular congregation of that same order, is applied to the present case, it will certainly be evident that such unions of monasteries offer no obstacle to attributing the Camaldolese institute to those monasteries even in the periods preceding those unions.

Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that the Camaldolese themselves first collected a congregation of nine places and then one of seventeen monasteries; afterward, when other monasteries of the order were added, the congregation of Saint Michael was formed. Yet no one would dare claim that these same monasteries did not belong to the Camaldolese institute even before the time of Leo X, when this congregation was fully formed, even though, as Fortunius says in part I, book III, chapter 1, most of them could seem to have forgotten their former communion and were striving to resume their original freedom and gradually return to their native independence:

> “So that there were, in a certain sense, as many bodies within the Camaldolese religion as there ought, by the strictest right, to have been members within a single body.”

## VIII

But let us hear what Laderchius adds in paragraph 15:

> “Furthermore, even if it is admitted that Dominicus was in the hermitage of Sitria, and that this same hermitage belonged to the Camaldolese rather than to the Avellanans, it nevertheless follows only that he was once among the Camaldolese. For when he submitted himself to Peter, he did not always live in the hermitage of Sitria; rather, according to that same Peter, he was at one time in Avellana, separated from him only by the intervening space of the basilica; at another time he was remote from him; and at another he had a cell near the monastery of Conjunctuli. This is confirmed by the fact that he did not die and was not buried in the hermitage of Sitria, but rather in a place that is found in no way to have belonged to the aforesaid hermitage.”

Thus, lest he admit that Peter Damianus was Camaldolese, this author presents Dominicus Loricatus to us as a sort of deserter from the Camaldolese. But he labors in vain and with needless effort. For we showed in chapter 6, paragraph 14, that Dominicus Loricatus lived under Damianus’s instruction while he inhabited Sitria, not after he had departed from Sitria. This is clear from letter 31 of book VI, which Damianus wrote to Dominicus, prior of Saint Mary of Sitria.

Peter Damianus himself speaks of the inhabitants of Sitria as his own, as I demonstrated in the place cited, paragraph 16, from *Opusculum* XIII, chapter 22:

> “Finally, we have an old man in the monastery of Sitria,”

and so forth. There I also noted that Damianus himself lived very frequently among the inhabitants of Sitria and was the spiritual son and disciple of the hermit Leo. Therefore the author ought rather to have asserted that Peter Damianus became Camaldolese from being an Avellanan than that Dominicus Loricatus moved from the Camaldolese to the Avellanans.

Nevertheless, as we have said so often, whether one calls this man or that one a Sitrian or an Avellanan, both will equally be shown to be followers of the Camaldolese institute.

## IX

Having thus disposed of the matter of Dominicus Loricatus, Laderchius turns to other weapons in order to attack our teaching.

> “Finally,” he says in paragraph 16, “how shall we suppose that Peter N. Damianus, the most vigorous teacher of humility, was ashamed of the master from whom his congregation of Fonte Avellana had drunk all that it had learned, making no mention of him when writing its Institutions, especially since he honored him so magnificently and even wrote his life?”

But it is clear that this is false. For, as has often been said, Peter Damianus mentions Saint Romualdus repeatedly in both Rules contained in *Opuscula* XIV and XV. Laderchius himself had observed this earlier in the same chapter, paragraph 10, in these words:

> “And although it is true that Peter inserted certain admonitions of Saint Romualdus in his constitutions and elsewhere,”

as we reported in the preceding chapter, paragraph 10.

It is astonishing that what the author had stated only five paragraphs earlier could so quickly have slipped from his memory. Hence it is clear that this feeble weapon falls completely without striking its target. Even if Damianus had nowhere mentioned Romualdus, the argument would have no force in itself, since the matter itself speaks plainly, and this truth becomes evident from the comparison of the two institutes made in chapters 3, 4, and 5. The example of Blessed Ludulphus, the founder of Avellana, who is likewise nowhere mentioned, proves that no such mention was required.

## X

Because Laderchius had foreseen that this very parity would be brought against him, he attempts to present and diminish it in the same paragraph by devising a twofold distinction:

> “But you will say that he likewise made no mention of Ludulphus, who is assumed to have been the founder of the congregation of Avellana. We do not admit the comparison. For the authority of Ludulphus was not equal to that of Romualdus, who had already been numbered among the saints by the Apostolic See; or one must say, on account of those who still represent Ludulphus as alive when Peter N. Damianus published the Avellanan Institutions, that he rightly kept silent about Ludulphus because he judged it too inappropriate to praise a man before his death. For they reckon that Ludulphus lived until the year 1047, whereas Peter wrote those Institutions in the year 1042.”

So much for him.

But neither distinction proves sustainable. Peter Damianus speaks repeatedly in his works, and even in the constitutions of *Opusculum* XV, chapter 14, about Blessed Dominicus Loricatus. He likewise often mentions other living men—Leo of Prêza, Mainardus, Martin Storax, Lupus, Leo of Sitria, and others—who were no greater in authority or reputation than Blessed Ludulphus, the founder of the place, and who were still alive.

The holy doctor therefore could not have been deterred from mentioning Ludulphus either because of his lesser authority or because he was still living. This is especially so since, in the same *Opusculum* XV, chapter 28, he considered the example of the living more effective than that of the dead for encouraging souls:

> “The examples of our contemporaries,” he says, “provide stronger encouragement than those of the ancients; and it is a source of great shame if, while living in the same age as holy men, we are not found in some respect their equals in the pursuit of upright conduct.”

## XI

In paragraph 17 Laderchius also turns two weapons against our position. One is based on his claim that Damianus asserts in the *Life* of Romualdus that Romualdus never stayed at Avellana; the other is that he mentions the Camaldolese as though they had no connection with him.

Here is the first:

> “From the very *Life* of Saint Romualdus, which, as we have said, Peter N. Damianus wrote, it can easily be inferred that Romualdus himself never visited the hermitage of Fonte Avellana. For although he reports in such detail many places on Mount Catria that the beloved one of the Most High traversed, leaping upon the mountains and crossing the hills, he nevertheless never mentions Fonte Avellana, even though it is evident that the name of the place that he himself revered and so frequently mentions in his writings could not have escaped him.”

Here is the second:

> “To this one should finally add that he mentions those dwelling in the Camaldolese hermitage as though they had absolutely no connection with him, as can be seen in letter 29 of book VI of his Letters. Certainly he does not do this when he mentions hermits who belong to him; for he expressly calls them his own, as may be gathered from letters 34 and 56 of the same book VI.”

## XII

There is an obvious answer to both points.

To the first: those “places on Mount Catria that Romualdus traversed” indicate the very solitude of Avellana, where the holy Father stayed, according to chapter 19 of the *Life*, as we demonstrated in chapter 2, paragraphs 6 and 7.

Even if we granted Laderchius that Romualdus stayed not at Avellana but only at Sitria, would it follow that Ludulphus, the founder of Avellana, could not have been imbued with Romualdus’s eremitical institutions and required his disciples to follow the discipline that he had learned from the holy Father either at Sitria or elsewhere?

Romualdus certainly never lived in Poland. Would it therefore be judged that the followers of his holy disciples John and Benedict, who flourished in holiness in the hermitage of Casimir, belonged any less to Romualdus’s institute?

## XIII

With regard to the second point, we likewise deny that Damianus indicates the Camaldolese as though they had no connection with him. For, by the very fact that he indicates that the inhabitants of Sitria belonged to him, as we have proved, he certainly asserts that the Camaldolese were related to him, since they had truly been instituted by Romualdus and were consequently included under the general name “Camaldolese.”

If Laderchius is speaking of the Camaldolese in the narrower sense—that is, of the inhabitants of the sacred Camaldolese hermitage—I deny that Damianus mentions these men as strangers. For in the cited letter 20 of book VI he describes Martinus the Camaldolese only in these terms:

> “The lord Martinus, who dwells in the Camaldolese hermitage, a man adorned with various virtues and especially watered by continual streams of tears, told me what I am about to relate.”

What, I ask, appears in these words to indicate that Martinus was regarded by Damianus as an outsider?

But suppose that our exceedingly acute opponent discovers some distinction between the way Damianus mentions the Camaldolese and the Avellanans. At most, this distinction would be that he differentiates subjects from non-subjects, or the members of one congregation from those of another congregation of the same order.

For the Avellanans or the Sitrians could not otherwise be said to be more closely connected with Damianus than the Camaldolese, except in the sense that other Camaldolese monks are more closely related to me than hermits are. Likewise, each inhabitant of the sacred Camaldolese hermitage seems to be more closely connected with other hermits of that same congregation than with the Coronans, the monks, or the members of other congregations of the same Camaldolese order.

## XIV

Finally, in paragraph 18 Laderchius advances his last and decisive argument in these words:

> “Moreover, Arnoldus Wion admits that the monks of Avellana were united in his own time to the Camaldolese congregation; therefore they had previously been separate from one another. Otherwise it would have been superfluous and pointless to join together those who were already united.”

But this objection clearly vanishes in light of what was said above in paragraph 6 on the occasion of the union of the Classense monastery, and of what we observed in Dissertation I, chapter 2, paragraph 23.

Monasteries belonging to one congregation can be joined to another congregation of the same order. In our own days, for example, the illustrious piety of His Royal Highness Cosimo III, grand duke of Etruria, arranged for the celebrated monastery of Buon Solazzo, administered by Italian Cistercian monks, to be joined to the Trappists—solitaries of the same order whom that most munificent and religious prince wished to bring from France into Etruria.

In the same way, Pope Pius V, believing that the monastery of Avellana had flourished under the eremitical discipline of Romualdus in the time of Peter Damianus, but that it had long since departed from the observance of its former fervor, entrusted it to the general visitation of the Camaldolese and finally subjected it entirely to our congregation, as Fortunius testifies shortly above in *History of Camaldoli*, part I, book III, chapter 27:

> “The same pontiff brought about the extinction of the conventual Camaldolese, assigning their benefices to the congregation.”

This was done so that, through the work of our monks, the ancient institute and the primitive religious observance of the place might be restored.

I therefore believe that it is clear from everything said thus far that none of Father Laderchius’s objections retains any force against the position that we have attempted to establish on its grounds in the present Dissertation.

Certainly, much stronger arguments could be brought against the various assertions of his that occur in this very History—not to mention the other works subsequently published under his name. But, on the one hand, we do not wish to exceed the limits of the defense we have undertaken by assuming the role of aggressor; on the other, we do not wish to appear to be reworking what has already been done, since the dialogue of Sejanus and Rufinus has largely exhausted this material. Nor is it our task to subject each of Laderchius’s opinions to examination. We shall therefore gladly leave this concern to others whom our author has likewise provoked and who have more leisure than we do.

For the same reasons, we shall make no observation here about the elegant character of Laderchius’s style. It will be sufficient to consult the aforementioned dialogue and to consider the judgment—reported there—of the author of the *Journal des Savants* in its review of Laderchius’s work, *Journal* 34, year 1704. There is no need for us, at the cost of time, to digress into these matters or to beat the same anvil with repeated blows.

Nevertheless, wishing to grant something to the wishes of our friends, we shall not hesitate to supply, in the form of an appendix, several observations that concern us more directly and that we noticed had either been treated less accurately by the aforementioned dialogist or omitted altogether, since we do not expect to find elsewhere a more suitable opportunity for illuminating the truth.

# APPENDIX

Containing several observations on the *History of Peter Damianus* described by Laderchius.

## SYNOPSIS

Certain errors to be noted in Laderchius’s History in order to obtain a more perfect edition of the *Life of Peter Damianus*.

1. Laderchius incorrectly determines the number of Blessed Peter Damianus’s brothers.
2. Laderchius is mistaken concerning the institute of Saint Clare.
3. He is likewise mistaken concerning the Rule of Saint Peter Celestine.
4. He falsely reports that Albizo, the companion of Blessed Peter Damianus, was the abbot of the hermit Theuzo.
5. Other errors concerning Saint John Gualbert and Atho, bishop of Florence.
6. The year of Saint Dominicus Loricatus’s death should be determined more accurately.
7 and 8. The proposal and solution of certain difficulties.
9 and 10. Saint John of Lodi is wrongly confused with John, the author of the *Life of Peter Damianus*.
11. Saint John of Lodi was summoned to the see of Gubbio after the year 1076. Likewise, he immediately succeeded Peter Damianus in the priorship and must therefore be distinguished from the John who, in obedience to Prior Liprandus, wrote Damianus’s *Life*.
12. It is shown that this same *Life* was written after the death of Saint John of Lodi.
13. Other distinctions between the two Johns.
14. Conclusion.
15.

## I

Just as we acknowledge Peter Damianus as a follower of the Camaldolese institute and regard him as the foremost imitator of Saint Father Romualdus, so we are deeply devoted to him and rejoice exceedingly that his veneration is promoted.

Laderchius would therefore have earned our great gratitude if he had undertaken both to describe the life of this outstanding doctor in a more polished style and to cleanse it of every stain of falsity.

But such is the condition of human affairs: our first attempts are never ordinarily granted the achievement, or even the hope, of complete perfection; rather, they always leave many matters to be corrected by further efforts. It is therefore not surprising if Laderchius himself, having little confidence in this first edition of his History, promises to produce a second one—“with greater diligence and more exact study, and also enlarged in certain respects”—in the *Admonition to the Reader* appended to its index.

So that he may achieve this more perfectly, for the glory of so great a Father, whose most devoted admirers we also are, it seemed appropriate to propose for his consideration, in addition to the matters noted by the author of the dialogue between Sejanus and Rufinus, the following points, which concern us more directly.

## II

First, concerning the number of Blessed Peter Damianus’s brothers, we affirm that Sejanus rightly reproached Laderchius—not merely for the reason that anyone may read there, namely, that the brother by whom our Peter was treated so harshly, before he came under the care of another brother, Damianus the archpriest, could not have been that Marinus whom Sejanus, along with many other writers, considered religious, but whom we believe died as a layman, that is, a secular person, on the basis of the circumstances of his death narrated by Peter Damianus in book II, letter 11.

Peter Damianus describes Marinus as so fearful of God and so devoted to the service of the Blessed Virgin Mary that, at his death, he deserved to be visited by her. It therefore follows that at least three brothers must be assigned to our Peter Damianus, not merely two, as Laderchius asserts in book I, chapter 2, paragraph 1:

> “We have learned with certainty that he had two brothers, namely Damianus and Marinus, whom he himself mentions in book II of the Letters, letter 14 to Desiderius.”

This assertion of Laderchius is refuted not only for that reason, but for an additional one. If the words of John, the author of the *Life of our Peter Damianus*, which Laderchius cites in chapter 3, paragraph 3, are considered, it will easily become clear that Peter had at least four brothers.

John, the disciple of the holy shepherd, says in chapter 1 of his *Life* that our Peter,

> “having been prematurely deprived of both parents, was left to the care of his brothers. One of them, who beneath a sheep’s clothing concealed a savage character despite the honorable conduct of the others, now under the guise of fraudulent kindness took him into his charge to raise him in place of a father; and while pretending to adopt him as a co-heir, consigned him like a purchased slave to harsh servitude. His wife shared his household, and she differed from her husband’s cruelty in no respect for compassion.”

For if our Peter had had two brothers, one of them—the one who first took him in to be fed—would certainly have been described not as “savage among the others,” but as savage in comparison with another, or as more savage than the other.

The author of Peter Damianus’s *Life* therefore indicates that, besides this brother to whose care Peter was entrusted, there were other brothers still alive at that time, indeed present there. Yet Damianus the archpriest does not seem to be included among them. For, as Laderchius reports on page 22:

> “He had been absent from his homeland for several years. When he returned and took pity on the sufferings of his brother Peter, moved by paternal affection, he soon rescued him from his miserable servitude, clothed him in new garments, and sent him to school,”

and so forth.

The pious archpriest would certainly have carried this out from the beginning if he had been present.

Therefore, if we connect with Damianus the archpriest the married brother by whom Peter was treated so savagely, and add at least two others whom John, the author of the *Life*, compared with this man when he called him savage “among the others who possessed honorable character”—one of whom I believe was Marinus, praised by the holy doctor, and the other somewhat older than Peter himself, who, envying his other brothers, caused by his complaints the mother to wean Peter prematurely and abandon him impiously—we must acknowledge that Peter Damianus had four brothers, or certainly more than two.

John, the author of the *Life* and disciple of the holy man, narrates this at Laderchius’s page 17:

> “For when one of the children, who had by then grown somewhat older, complained and cried out: ‘Shame! Look, there are already so many of us that we scarcely fit in this house,’”

and so forth.

## III

Second, as Sejanus very correctly observed, there is a notable error in those whom Laderchius followed in good faith in book I, chapter 14, paragraph 3, where he reports that Saint Clare, the Assisian virgin and sister of Saint Francis, gave her name to the Rule of Saint Peter Damianus because both she and her sisters are called by Gregory IX the Order of Saint Damianus.

In fact, the passage concerns the order of the monastery of Saint Damianus the Martyr, built near Assisi, not the institutions of Saint Peter Damianus, as is perfectly clear from the Bulls reported by Wadding at the end of volumes I and II of the *Annals of the Friars Minor*.
