It is nevertheless entirely true that the nuns of Saint Clare professed the Rule of Saint Father Benedict and the monastic order for at least twelve years, namely from 1212 to 1224; some did so even until 1239, as Wadding shows in the cited place and Jacobillus confirms in volume III.

Nor are there lacking those who think that during that period they should be referred to the Camaldolese institute—not because of the Rule of Saint Peter Damianus, after whom they would have been named, but because of the Camaldolese constitutions that Cardinal Hugolinus, our own cardinal, had prescribed for them to observe.

According to Jacobillus, Hugolinus had been summoned to the purple from the abbacy of the monastery of Saint Silvester on Monte Subasio, built by the holy Father Romualdus and still then flourishing under the Camaldolese order. Certainly, the Poor Clares seem during that period to have observed the law of enclosure in imitation of the Camaldolese.

Hence the same Cardinal Hugolinus, later Gregory IX, wished to insert this clause in their privileges, as Wadding testifies in the *Apologeticus on the Monasticism of Saint Francis*, section 6, paragraph 5, number 9:

> “The monastic order, which is known to have been instituted according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the enclosed nuns of Saint Damianus of Assisi.”

Therefore, by order of Gregory IX himself, Blessed Pacifica and Blessed Balbina—the first of that name among the Damianists—were sent from the family of Saint Clare to reform the monastery of the Camaldolese nuns of Saint Mary of Valle Gloria, which flourished under the jurisdiction of the abbot of Saint Silvester on Monte Subasio, as Jacobillus demonstrates.

## IV

Third, Sejanus likewise shows that Laderchius was mistaken concerning the institute of Saint Peter Celestine. Celestine and his followers had no association whatsoever with the Rule of Peter Damianus, although the common people sometimes confused the Celestines with the Avellanans.

It should be observed that, in addition to the reason for this confusion supplied by Papebrochius and reported by Sejanus, the origin of the ambiguous designation may have depended on the fact that the Avellanans, as we observed earlier from Morigia on page 64 and in Dissertation III, page 11, wore a blue mantle.

Since this color is called *celestial* among the Italians, it could have given the ignorant populace occasion first to begin calling our Avellanans Celestines, then to take the genuine Celestines themselves for Avellanans, as though they too had been propagated by Peter Damianus and followed his Rule. For this reason they came to be called by some the Order of Saint Damianus.

## V

Fourth, concerning the hermit Theuzo, Laderchius is not merely mistaken in denying that Theuzo spoke with Peter Damianus at Florence, contrary to the opinion of Baronius, which Sejanus has defended very well. It is additionally worthy of notice that it is false that Albizo, the companion of Peter Damianus, was the abbot of that same Theuzo, as our historian asserted, with Sejanus’s agreement, in book III, chapter 5, paragraph 9.

In fact, no Albizo governed the monastery of Saint Mary at Florence. Rather, in Theuzo’s time Peter was in charge of that abbey, as is shown by the records cited by Puccinello in the *Chronicles* of that monastery, published in 1664.

Nor do the words of Peter Damianus in letter 30 of book VI, addressed to Theuzo, or in *Opusculum* LI, signify anything of the kind:

> “At last,” he says, “we were scarcely admitted, as though we were importunate nuisances [the text literally has ‘a man’s head’]”—for Albizo was then accompanying me—“but, intent and by no means lacking in eagerness to receive the lessons of edification, we were immediately compelled, at the very beginning of our mutual conversation, to devote ourselves to certain contentious disputes,”

and so forth.

It is clear that he is speaking of himself and Albizo as a companion on the journey and partner in the conversation, not as Theuzo’s superior.

When he adds below:

> “For there was an intolerable hostility and an old disagreement between them and the abbot of your monastery. He, being a man of virtue and simplicity of spirit, surpassed all the requirements of satisfactory reconciliation and humility by his promises, and appointed us”—that is, Peter Damianus and his companion Albizo—“as mediators to carry out the reconciliation between himself and you. But while we rashly attempted to serve the friendships of others,”

and so forth, it seems perfectly clear that Theuzo’s abbot was someone distinct from the two mediators appointed to reconcile the parties, namely Damianus and Albizo.

I shall add nothing except that this Albizo was not an abbot but a hermit, as is clear from *Opusculum* XII of volume III, addressed directly to “the venerable hermit Albizo” and “the monk Peter.” There Damianus calls Albizo “an example to be imitated of eremitical conduct,” just as he calls Peter “a polished model of cenobites.”

### VI.

Fifth, regarding what Laderchius says in the same chapter 5, nos. 6 and 7—namely, that Saint John Gualbert became a monk at the monastery of San Miniato in the year 1003, that he advised the hermit Theuzo to make a public proclamation against the simoniacal abbot Uberto and the bishop Atho in 1007, and that the first Atho of this name preceded Hildebrand the Florentine bishop—it is entirely fabricated and rests on false foundations, as is clear from our Dissertation II, chapter 4, beginning at no. 4 and following; especially since Theuzo did not enter his hermit’s cell before the year 1020 [Col. 0083A], as we proved there at no. 13. Nevertheless, I do not wish to decide whether, on the occasion of the controversy of the Florentine clergy concerning Peter, the simoniacal bishop of Ticinus, Peter Damian’s conversation with the hermit Theuzo took place; nor whether Damian, on that occasion or at another time, contended with the monks of Saint John Gualbert, or attacked them in Book VIII, Letter 11. Let others investigate these matters more inquisitively. Whatever judgment is to be formed concerning them, we meanwhile congratulate Laderchius that Peter Damian has here and elsewhere been vindicated from the calumnies of Didacus Francus.

### VII.

Sixth, it deserves more careful consideration whether Saint Dominic Loricatus truly ought to be said to have died in the year 1061, as Laderchius, following Baronius, asserted in Book II, chapter 24, beginning at no. 2, and in Book III, chapter 1, no. [Col. 0083B] 12. For Peter Damian relates in Book I, Letter 19, that Dominic died on the day before the Ides of October. If this had occurred in the year 1061, when the solar cycle was 6, and therefore the Dominical letter corresponding to it in the old calendar was G, he would necessarily have departed to heaven on a Sunday, since this letter is found assigned precisely to 14 October. Moreover, the ninth day after his burial—namely, 22 October—would have been Monday, or the second feria, which is marked by the letter A. Both conclusions are false. For the holy doctor testifies in the passage cited that Dominic departed this life on Saturday, in these words:

> “Accordingly, throughout the whole of Friday he scarcely ceased either to devote himself to chanting psalms or to scourging himself with blows from leather straps. During the night, after setting aside sleep, he took an antidote; then he began to suffer distress and complained bitterly of pain in his stomach. When the office of the nocturnal synaxis had therefore been completed, and after the morning hymns, while the first hour was already being sung for him by the brothers who were present, he gave back his holy spirit to God.”

And he testifies that the ninth day after Dominic’s burial was a Sunday:

> “On that Sunday itself, then, the day on which we entered the hermitage, we reverently removed the holy body from that place and buried it in the chapter house, as was fitting; and when it was the ninth day after his burial, we found the aforesaid body sound and uncorrupted.”

### VIII.

Hence it is plainly evident that the death of Dominic Loricatus must be assigned either to the year 1060 or to 1066, so that these circumstances may agree with one another [Col. 0083D]—namely, that 14 October fell on a Saturday and 22 October on a Sunday.

But the former possibility cannot have occurred in 1060 for another reason. The death of Blessed Rodulphus, bishop of Eugubium—which, according to Damian’s testimony, occurred on 26 June in the year after the death of Dominic Loricatus—would then have fallen in 1061. At that time Nicholas II, supreme pontiff, had not yet departed this life; his death occurred on 3 July, and in October Alexander II was consecrated Roman pontiff. Yet it is evident from the period when Alexander II had already long been reigning that Rodulphus had died. In the letter of Damian cited above, he addresses that same pontiff as follows:

> “Having recently departed from you, most dear lord, when I entered the walls of the city of Florence, I was immediately met by a sudden messenger, namely, that the bishop [Col. 0084A] of Eugubium had died,” etc.

It therefore remains that the death of Dominic Loricatus must have occurred in 1066, and consequently that of Saint Rodulphus in 1067. Thus the argument by which Laderchius attempts in Book III, chapter 5, no. 12, to prove that Damian’s letter to Theuzo was written before the controversy concerning the simony of Peter, bishop of Pavia and Florence, arose—because that letter mentions Dominic Loricatus as still alive—seems to collapse.

### IX.

I know that this conclusion may be opposed by the fact that Rodulphus, according to Damian’s own testimony, “nearly seven years earlier” (and therefore, on this hypothesis, in 1060), “coming to the hermitage, had received the habit of monastic profession.”

Nevertheless, Ughellus, in his account of the bishops of Eugubium [Col. 0084B], testifies that Rodulphus is found subscribing to the Roman synod of Pope Nicholas II in 1059, while in a bull of Alexander II for the Church of Forosempronium, dated 1062, there is mention of Hugo, bishop of Eugubium. Ughellus supposes that Hugo was elected not immediately after Maynardus but after him in 1061, and that he succeeded Rodulphus.

Yet it is too evident that Rodulphus had departed this life during the time of Alexander II, and therefore after the year 1061. What if, then, I say that the succession of the bishops of Eugubium has been corrupted in this place in Ughellus, no less than shortly before, where he assigns Ludulphus, elected in 1012, as successor?

Furthermore, neither in Baronius nor in Labbe does there occur any record of Rodulphus, bishop of Eugubium, as subscribing to the Roman synod in 1059. Nor, in Ughellus’s account of the bull of Alexander II—which he reports as inserted in another bull of Honorius III dated 19 May 1224, in the second volume of *De Episcopis Forosemproniensibus*—is the year 1062 or any other year explicitly given. Indeed, the only note found there is:

> “It was enacted in this month of May, on the tenth day, in the thirteenth indiction.”

That indiction corresponds neither to the aforesaid year 1062 nor to any year of Alexander II’s pontificate, but only to the years 1060 and 1075, between which the pontificate of that pope falls. It certainly does not seem reasonable, on account of these uncertain documents reported by Ughellus, to abandon the evident force of the reasoning set forth above or to conceal its significance [Col. 0084C].

### X.

Yet, if Ughellus’s documents are admitted, this dispute may perhaps be suitably resolved if, for the present, we grant that Hugo—whom Ughellus indicates, on the basis of the bull of Alexander II, as having governed the Church of Eugubium after Maynardus in 1062—was the immediate predecessor of our Rodulphus, but not his second successor. Thus Rodulphus may have been promoted to the see of Eugubium after the year 1062, perhaps in 1063 or 1064, and may have survived until June 1067, being succeeded by Dominic or by another bishop.

Although I would rather believe that the bull of Alexander II belongs to the year 1070, which was marked by the eighth indiction—so that, by the change of V into X, the copyists produced indiction 13, which is now read in this document in Ughellus [Col. 0085A]—Hugo could therefore very well have succeeded Maynardus in the bishopric of Eugubium after Rodulphus had died in 1067.

As for the fact that Rodulphus is said to have subscribed to the Roman synod in 1059, if this is indeed true, it may easily be understood of another predecessor named Rodulphus—or Reginaldus, Raynerius, or some similar episcopal name beginning with the letter R. For such a subscription may have been written, as is customary, in this form: “I, R., bishop of Eugubium.” This could have provided the occasion for interpreting the name as Rodulphus. Thus, from the subscription “W., bishop of Humanata,” made to the same Roman synod of 1059, Ughellus himself had interpreted the name as Willelmus in volume I, p. 804; shortly afterward, in the appendix to the same volume, p. 419, he observed that it should be corrected to Wido on the authority of Peter Damian [Col. 0085B].

Nor will arguments be lacking to confirm this conjecture. The first arise from what we examined above concerning the year of Saint Rodulphus’s death; the second from Book IV, Letter 2, of Peter Damian to R., bishop of Eugubium, who appears clearly to have been someone other than our Rodulphus. For that bishop R . . . did not seem particularly favorable to Peter Damian, since he had subjected Damian’s church to ecclesiastical interdict. Damian therefore entreats him humbly:

> “We beseech you, therefore, most beloved one: restore the ministry of our Church, which has been placed under interdict; and defend by your authority not only that small possession which is undoubtedly within your diocese, but also whatever else we possess,” etc.

But our Rodulphus always revered Peter Damian as his father, even after his episcopal consecration; he determined everything according to Damian’s direction and counsel. Living in the hermitage more than in the palace of his church, he “considered the Church a lodging, but decreed the cell of solitude to be his dwelling,” as Peter Damian himself relates. He adds below:

> “Compelled by my insistence, he retained in office the church which he had relinquished by vow; yet he continued to dwell in the hermitage with greater perseverance.”

It is therefore likely that he would not have subjected Peter Damian’s church to interdict before learning from Damian himself why he had allowed it to be consecrated by the bishop of Forosempronium.

Another bishop R . . . therefore governed the Church of Eugubium before our Rodulphus, and he could have subscribed to the Roman synod under Nicholas II.

### XI.

Seventh, concerning John, Peter Damian’s disciple and the author of his *Life*, Laderchius is seriously mistaken when, in Book VI, chapter 28, he confuses him with Saint John of Laude, bishop of Eugubium. This also gave our Machiarellus and the author of the *Diario Gallico* an occasion to make the same assertion. Although the author of the *Dialogue* sufficiently refuted our historian on this point, he nevertheless used arguments which, as the saying goes, serve to prove a point *ad hominem*, not to establish it by an appeal to judgment.

For it is clear that John of Laude did not ascend the Eugubian see in 1076, as Laderchius determines from Ferrarius, but much later, namely in 1105, as Ughellus records. This is shown, among other things, by an authentic document of a transaction in the Classense archive, box 94, no. 67, which demonstrates that in 1084 the same John was serving as prior at Avellana. It reads:

> “In the name of the Lord. In the time of Lord Gregory, supreme pontiff, in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1084, while Henry, son of the late Emperor Henry, was reigning, in the seventh indiction, at Eugubium: I, Thebaldus, by the name of God, son of the late Paganus of Nartianula, make a renunciation, transaction, and settlement with the church of Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana, and with you, John of Laude, prior, and your successors in perpetuity—namely, concerning the church of Saint Apollinaris, situated at Nartianula,” etc.

The same is evident from other documents of that period and from the *History* of Saint John of Laude itself. These likewise show that he did not live thirty-six years in the episcopate, but only one year, or at most a few additional months, and that he went to God not in 1116 but in 1106, as Ughellus also confirms.

### XII.

Moreover, not only does Laderchius himself admit in Book III, chapter 27, no. 2, that this same John of Laude immediately succeeded Peter Damian in the priorate of Avellana; the author of John’s own *Life* also states this. Constantine Cajetanus quotes a fragment of it at the beginning of volume II of the works of Blessed Peter Damian. It says that after the death of the holy doctor:

> “The brothers, inspired by the Lord and acting in concord and unanimity, elected the holy man John of Laude as their chief prior, so that, just as he was like the holy father Peter Damian in holiness and wisdom, so he might succeed him in the priorate.”

But John, the writer of Peter Damian’s *Life*, admits that he was a monk subject to the obedience of Prior Liprando, and that he had been compelled by the command of Liprando and the other elders of Fonte Avellana to gather the material for that history. For he says in the preface:

> “John to Lord Liprando, prior, and the other elders of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana. Fathers, it is a wonderful work that you have chosen to impose upon my insignificance . . . But since I do not presume to refuse anything to your command . . . the merits of Peter Damian, whose deeds you summon my obedience to record,” etc.

It therefore remains evident that this John, the author of Damian’s *Life*, cannot be the same as that John of Laude, bishop of Eugubium, who immediately after Damian’s death became prior of Avellana and soon afterward a bishop, and who never lived as a simple monk subject to the commands of others.

### XIII.

The same conclusion is demonstrated even more clearly by the fact that this *Life* of Peter Damian was certainly written after 1110, and therefore long after the death of Saint John of Laude, which occurred in 1106, as we have said. It is consequently far from being attributable to John of Laude himself.

The chronology of Prior Liprando clearly establishes this. In the catalogue of the priors of Avellana, compiled from the records of that monastery, his name is entered under the year 1110. As we have noted, John of Laude is recorded as having immediately succeeded Peter Damian. But when John was promoted to the bishopric of Eugubium in 1105, Peter of Rimini succeeded him in the priorate; then, in 1110, Liprando succeeded Peter. At Liprando’s direction, John, Damian’s disciple, undertook the plan of writing the *Life* of the holy doctor and dedicating it to Prior Liprando.

Since Saint John of Laude had laid aside his mortal remains four years earlier, it is evident that the John who wrote Peter Damian’s *Life* was entirely different from Saint John of Laude, bishop of Eugubium [Col. 0087A].

Even if we followed Jacobilli’s reckoning, according to which Liprando is said somewhere to have immediately succeeded John of Laude in the priorate, it would still be clear that, once John had become a bishop and had survived for a year and a few months, the task of compiling Peter Damian’s *Life* could not have been imposed on him by Liprando [Col. 0087B].

### XIV.

I add that the distinction between the two Johns may also be inferred from their different homelands and different times of death. Writers report that John, Peter Damian’s disciple and the author of his *Life*, was also Damian’s fellow citizen, namely a man of Ravenna. John, bishop of Eugubium, however, was born in his homeland of Laude, in Insubria, not in Emilia.

The former is recorded in the Avellana calendar as having died on 26 May 1115. The latter went to God on 2 September 1106. The former died at the hermitage of Avellana; the latter at the cathedral of Eugubium. The former was a private monk; the latter became a bishop after serving as prior. The former was distinguished by some reputation for holiness, but never acquired the title of saint or blessed; the latter, famous after his death for many miracles, was entered by Paschal II in the catalogue of the saints.

The two Johns therefore ought not to have been confused by Laderchius, especially since he alleged no foundation for his assertion against the evidence of so many differences [Col. 0087C–0088A].

### XV.

Let it suffice to have noted these matters, among many others, in Laderchius’s *History*. Other concerns, which draw me more powerfully away from this kind of study, compel me to withdraw. If I should at some time again enjoy the leisure I desire, and if Laderchius himself should once more order me to turn over this stone, I shall not allow my assistance to be lacking in supplying what I have now omitted or neglected.

I ask P. Laderchius to judge this work favorably. The zeal for truth and the counsels of friends have drawn it from me, especially since he will find it written not with a jealous or hostile spirit, but with an open and friendly one, and entirely free of those bitter jokes with which the *Dialogue of Sejanus and Rufinus* bristles and overflows with excessive abundance. For what need is there of insults in defending the truth?

Perhaps, however, that dialogist should be spared, if we can reach anything by conjecture: either he himself belongs to, or emerged from, the school whose master Laderchius had previously attacked most bitterly in volume III, pages 315 and 323.

The case of our own cause is altogether different, and therefore its disposition is milder, so long as we differ only in our opinions, not in our intentions. Would that these observations might contribute to the clarification of truth and to the glory of the eminent doctor Peter Damian, which alone we have sought in this dissertation, and that they might provide no occasion either for quarrels, from which I have always recoiled, or for insults, from which I have hitherto abstained.

This is my greatest desire, and I wish it to be fixed and certain for everyone who disputes with me: that on both sides alike, “without prejudice against persons, the claims of truth may be vindicated.”

[Col. 0087]

# Godefridus Henschenius, S.J.  
## Preliminary Commentary on Blessed Peter Damian

*(From the February volume of the Bollandists, under day 33.)*

### § I. The Hermitage of Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana in the Diocese of Eugubium, Attached to the Camaldolese Order: Its Foundation and Growth; Holy Monks under Blessed Peter Damian

[Col. 0087D]

#### 1.

Inguvium, or Iguvium, a town of Umbria on this side of the Apennines, situated at the very foot of the mountains and known to Caesar in Book I of *The Civil War*, to Cicero in Book VII, Letter 13, *To Atticus*, to Silius Italicus in Book VIII, and to other ancient writers, is today called Eugubium, and by the Italians Gubbio or Agubio. It is nevertheless thought to have been restored from the ruins of the ancient town nearby after the barbarian invasion of Italy.

An episcopal see was once established there, and during the eleventh century several bishops were drawn from the monastery of the Hermitage of Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana, or Avellana. This monastery lies fourteen miles from the city of Eugubium, situated at the foot of Mount Catria toward the east, in the region which the *Chronicle of Gualdo*, an ancient writer, calls a part of the Apennines. The anonymous hermit of that same place likewise describes it in Cajetanus’s preface to the works of Blessed Peter Damian [Col. 0088D–0089A].

Petrarch, writing in the fourteenth century in Book II, Treatise III, chapter 17, *On the Solitary Life*, called it

> “a most peaceful solitude in the middle of Italy, on the left side of the Apennines, which still retained the ancient name of Fonte Avellana.”

Augustine Florentinus observes that it now bears the title of Holy Cross in Book V, chapter 7 of his *History of Camaldoli*. He adds that the designation “Holy Cross” was adopted because of the Friday fast begun there in the time of Blessed Peter Damian.

#### 2.

This hermitage of Fonte Avellana, as some call it, is said to have been built around the year 1000, or somewhat earlier, by a certain Lodulphus, son of Gesso. He was elected bishop of Eugubium but voluntarily renounced that honor. Julianus, Theobaldus or Tedaldus, Saint Rodulphus, and Maynardus received him into that hermitage of Fonte Avellana. Blessed Peter Damian lived during their times, and, with the exception of the first of them, after he had embraced monastic discipline in that hermitage.

He writes that some care of that same Church had also been entrusted to him in Letter 14, Book I, to Pope Alexander II:

> “The Church of Eugubium, which was formerly entrusted to me by your predecessors, is now, alas, entirely disordered and cast aside like a threshing floor trampled underfoot. I attribute this to my sins, which have demanded it.”

In the same way, in Letter 8 of Book IV, he gives these instructions to Maynardus, bishop of Eugubium:

> “Restore, venerable brother, the estates of your Church, recklessly handed over to secular persons; recall the ornaments of various kinds that have been wickedly dispersed; and at least let all the distinguished and best things be restored, whose removal during the time of your governance we deeply lament.”

Thus he wrote out of concern for the Church entrusted to him. But he appointed as judges and, as it were, censors of the books he had composed Saint Rodulphus, bishop of Eugubium, and Theodosius, bishop of Senigallia, whose diocese is also near the hermitage of Fonte Avellana on the Adriatic side. A letter to them is preserved in Book IV, no. 11. On the bishops of Eugubium and Senigallia, consult Ughellus’s *Sacred Italy*.

#### 3.

We have not yet read who governed this hermitage of Fonte Avellana as priors—that is, as they called the superiors—before Blessed Damian. Blessed Peter himself says in *Opusculum* XXXIV, chapter 6:

> “In this hermitage of Fonte Avellana, where I now live, there had previously been a certain prior named John.”

In *Opusculum* XV, chapter 28, he explains what sort of person should be elected prior among the hermits and how an elected prior should exercise the office of the priorate. In the *Life* below, however, he is also called abbot and master.

After Blessed Peter’s death, Prior Liprando governed those hermits. John dedicated Peter’s *Life* to him; John himself was later, as will be said below, appointed prior of Fonte Avellana and finally created bishop of Eugubium. Perhaps this is how most of the bishops of Eugubium mentioned above were chosen from among the priors of Fonte Avellana.

#### 4.

Blessed Peter also presided as supreme superior over other disciples gathered in different places, as is said in chapter 7 of the *Life*. There five monasteries, or dwellings of hermits, built by him are mentioned [Col. 0089D–0090A]. Together with several others, these coalesced into a single congregation whose head was the hermitage of Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana.

Thus the monastery of Saint Mary at the gates of the city of Faenza—now enclosed within the walls, and the place where Blessed Peter ended his life—is called a monastery of the congregation of the monks of Holy Cross of Avellana in the *Monastic History* of an anonymous Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint Justina, quoted by Cajetanus in the preface to the works of Blessed Peter. Cajetanus says that this anonymous writer flourished around the year 1480.

Blessed Peter prescribes and explains the rule and manner of life of this congregation in *Opusculum* XV, divided into thirty-one chapters. In *Opusculum* XIV, however, he sets forth, for the example and imitation of posterity, the rules and manner of life followed in his own time by the hermits of Fonte Avellana. He earnestly urges those who would live there after him to observe them and not decline to a looser standard of life.

This hermitage of Fonte Avellana was attached to the Camaldolese order about one hundred years ago, chiefly through the efforts of Peter Franceschini of Balneocavallo, its visitor, and of Cardinal Julius Roboreus, bishop of Urbino, created in 1548. He later became bishop of Vicenza and then archbishop of Ravenna, and died in 1578.

Peter Ricordatus, in the fourth book of his *Diary of Monastic History*, cited by Cajetanus, mentions this union, as do Augustine Florentinus in Book III of his *History of Camaldoli* and others.

We discussed the Camaldolese Order on 7 February in the *Life* of Saint Romuald, its founder, written by Blessed Peter Damian, “compelled,” as he testifies in the prologue, “by the prayers of many brothers and bound by genuine affection.”

In the previously cited *Opusculum* XV, chapter 16, concerning the institutions of his congregation, Peter teaches that discretion regarding the weak should be left to the judgment of the prior, adducing the discipline of Saint Romuald as an example. Below, in the *Life*, no. 19, it is said that at Mount Pregium he

> “found a cell in which they said Blessed Romuald had once lived,”

and that there he

> “founded dwellings for hermits.”

#### 5.

Blessed Peter discusses the possessions acquired for this hermitage in *Opusculum* XIV:

> “In this place, called Fonte Avellana, about twenty monks, more or fewer, live in cells or under the obedience assigned to each one, so that all together, including lay brothers and servants, we scarcely reach or briefly exceed the number thirty.”

After explaining the rule of life, he addresses the successor who was to be appointed to govern the community:

> “So that no one may have any excuse for failing to observe these things, we have taken care to acquire possessions, insofar as was appropriate to the modest size of the place, so that you may be able to support the aforesaid number of brothers, provided that you do not lack the diligence to exercise this responsibility.

> “We have also left behind a considerable number of books, so as to provide our brothers, who may deign to pray for us, with abundant opportunity for meditation. We have taken care to correct, though only hastily and therefore not exactly, the library of all the books of the Old and New Testament. You also possess many books from the passions of the blessed martyrs, from the homilies of the holy Fathers, and from the commentaries of those who explain the allegorical meanings of Sacred Scripture—namely, Gregory, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Prosper, Bede, Remigius, Amalarius, Haimo, and Paschasius—our labors growing white through divine grace. You can devote yourselves to these books, so that your holy souls may grow not only through prayer but also be enriched through reading.

> “Of these books, we corrected several as far as we were able, so that we might open for you a path to understanding in the study of sacred discipline.”

#### 6.

> “We also decided that a cloister should be built beside the church, so that, if anyone still takes pleasure in the long-established custom of the monastic order, he may have a place from which he can proceed solemnly according to custom on the principal feast days. For this procession we also procured a sufficiently suitable silver cross.

> “With the same intention, taking thought for the weakness of the frail, we acquired bells, *bechinia*, and various utensils for the divine house. We also provided you with two silver chalices, beautifully gilded, so that, whenever you wish to receive the sacred mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, you would not be forced to bring pewter or any cheaper metal to your lips.

> “We likewise supplied conspicuous coverings for the sacred altar and precious ornaments for the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass. We sought all these things, brothers, not without labor, so as to remove from you the burden of labor and to allow your minds to rise toward higher things with that much greater freedom, the less they were weighed down by the poverty of their material resources in providing for their lowest needs.”

Thus far Blessed Peter, who, when summoned by Gebehard, archbishop of Ravenna, excuses himself in Book III, Letter 2, on account of the poverty of those for whom he had to provide:

> “You commanded me, most beloved Father and lord, and by commanding you ordered me to come to you. But I undertook the governance of a poor little place. Previously I had been poor only on my own account; now I have become poor through as many people as I have received to govern. I therefore consider how difficult it is to govern many and not possess the means by which their necessities may be supplied.”

This is what Blessed Peter says. In the *Chronicle of Gualdo*, written around the year 1325 and preserved by Cajetanus, he is called the founder of this hermitage of Holy Cross near Fonte Avellana. This cannot in any way be understood as referring to the original foundation of the eremitical life [Col. 0091D].

#### 7.

Among the men who rendered good service to that hermitage was Saint Rodulphus, his disciple and later, as we have said, bishop of Eugubium. Blessed Peter dedicated the *Life* he had written of him to Pope Alexander II, and at its beginning relates:

> “Nearly seven years earlier, Rodulphus, together with his mother and two brothers slightly older than himself, and with servants who had been granted their freedom, handed over to me his castle, fortified by an impregnable defense, together with all the estates belonging to him; and, coming to the hermitage, he received the habit of monastic profession.”

This is found there. Saint Rodulphus is commemorated on 26 June.

Another was Saint Dominic Loricatus, whose *Life* is read together with the *Acts of Saint Rodulphus*. He too became a disciple of Blessed Peter Damian, as the latter testifies in these words:

> “Much later, when the master had given his consent, the aforesaid holy man deigned, with extraordinary humility, to entrust himself to me, wretched and unworthy as I was to be accepted by him, and to subject himself to me as a monk to an abbot—though he gave me more than he received from me. I had received him as a dependent subordinate, but I rejoice that in the school of Christ I found in him a truly philosophical teacher. For his entire life was preaching and edification, teaching and discipline.”

This is said there of Saint Dominic Loricatus, whose feast falls on 14 October.

#### 8.

A third disciple enrolled among the saints was John of Laude [Col. 0092B], born of an illustrious family among the Insubrians at Laude Pompeia. His *Acts* relate that:

> “Having learned of the fame of so great a man, and animated by his example, he fled to him. He withdrew from the world, departing from his native land and kindred; he came to the land which the Lord revealed to him; and he humbly presented himself to the venerable Father Peter Damian, prior of the hermitage and master of the devout brothers. Kneeling, he earnestly begged that he might be received as a disciple and brother under the discipline of the sacred rule of the most blessed Father Benedict, in order to serve Christ the King perpetually.

> “But the reverend priest of God, Peter Damian, seeing in John the purity of his simple heart, the fervor of his spirit, his readiness for obedience, and his genuine contempt for the world, received him kindly.”

Blessed Peter dedicated *Opusculum* XLIV, *On the Ten Plagues of Egypt and the Decalogue*, to him, and addresses him as follows:

> “To his most beloved brother John, no longer of Laude and therefore a laudable man: Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of paternal love. Recently, my son, you despised Pharaoh and at once abhorred the slavery of the proud king and of oppressive Egypt. It is therefore necessary now that, as you proceed through the desert, you undergo many kinds of temptation, endure the deprivation of thirst and hunger, and thus reach the promised land through perilous hardships and the distress of various calamities.”

More may be read there, both in the prologue and in the final chapter, concerning Blessed Peter’s singular affection of charity toward this disciple. The author of Saint John’s *Life* expresses it in these words:

> “The reverend prior Peter, and John, the cleric of God, were two shining pillars of the brothers of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana. Like two Seraphim inflamed with divine charity, they continually praised the Most High God in heart and mouth, and kindled the minds, hearts, and mouths of the brothers with the fear of God and fraternal charity. O how good and how pleasant it was for such brothers to dwell together!”

The *Chronicle of Gualdo* says the following concerning the same Saint John:

> “In that same hermitage, among the other holy prior monks, the servant of God, Lord John of Laude, flourished in great holiness, and through severe penance and abstinence he chastised his body amid those dense forests and steep mountains. Later, having been taken from the priorate of Holy Cross and made bishop of Eugubium, he lived and died in great holiness.”

His feast day is assigned to 7 September.

## § II. The Works of Peter Damian; The Published *Life*; His Feast Day

#### 9.

Pope Paul V, in a brief to Constantine Cajetanus, a Benedictine monk of the monastery of Saint Nicholas of the Arena at Catania, testifies that

> “the works of Blessed Peter Damian had lain scattered in various ways in darkness, to the detriment of ecclesiastical letters,”

and asserts that they had been “collected and gathered from many libraries through the labor and diligence” of Cajetanus.

Before this, however, Aloysius Lippomanus, first bishop of Verona and later of Bergamo, had excerpted various treatises of Blessed Peter from manuscripts in the libraries of Cassino and Capranica, as well as those of the canons of the Church of Saint Peter and of another monastery in Italy. He had arranged for them to be printed at Rome in 1560, in the fourth part of volume eight of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers of Antiquity*.

Margarinus de la Bigne likewise added various letters of Blessed Peter in the enlarged edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*.

Cardinal Baronius, under the year 1047, no. 15, says that one ought to relate “almost every year” how “Blessed Peter benefited the Catholic Church in those most depraved times in many ways, since he was often summoned from the hermitage to undertake ecclesiastical affairs.” He frequently cites his letters and other short works from manuscript codices.

Cajetanus, however, collected all his works from every source and divided them into three volumes. The first contains eight books of letters; the second [Col. 0093C] contains various sermons and histories of the saints; and the third finally contains sixty distinguished short works on various subjects. All of these were later revised and enlarged through renewed study and labor and were published in France.

10. Preceding these works is the Life of Blessed Peter Damian, published from two manuscript codices, one from Ravenna and the other from Faenza, and reprinted in the third edition of Surius. We too present it here, divided into chapters according to our custom, and enriched with notes, marginal annotations, and brief summaries of the events described. We believe its author to have been Saint John of Lodi, first prior of that same hermitage and later bishop of Gubbio, as we said above. He discloses his name in the heading of the Life, and shortly afterward says in the prologue that he had “clung to so great a Father as his constant companion, although only in the final period of his life.” [Col. 0093D] For Saint John himself, as his Life relates, “having learned by report of so great a man,” when Peter “with the permission of the Lord Pope abandoned the glory of the cardinalate and shut himself away in the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, animated by his example, fled to him.” After recounting in chapter 8 of Saint Peter’s Life his return to the hermitage, he immediately reports, at no. 42, what he had seen Peter doing: “I saw it indeed,” he says, “and afterward, being myself present, I recognized this.” Finally, he remained Peter’s constant companion until death, when Peter, at no. 49, “recognizing that the hour of his departure was approaching, immediately ordered us, who were standing around his little bed, to perform the office of Matins”; and at no. 21 he says: “After we had celebrated his burial at Faenza and, returning from there, had lodged for our first stop at the monastery of Acereta, there it happened that we learned not only this but also certain other matters, which we shall take care to add to this miracle, from the reports of certain brothers of that monastery and also of the aforementioned hermitage, who had then gathered there.” From the accompanying miracles he says at no. 24 that one was reported to him by a brother when he had returned from the forest with Peter. He relates another at nos. 27 and 28, just as the man to whom that benefit had been granted, after becoming a monk, “related the whole matter to us in due order, as we have arranged it.” Thus, at no. 42, he says: “I shall report what I heard from my senior fellow disciples when they related it.”

But “what preceded his conversion,” he says at no. 2, he “heard from the report of one of his relatives, a serious and honorable man.” Yet “part of what I am about to relate,” he says, “came from certain of my fellow disciples who, before me, had been closely attached to his companionship; part I remember receiving from Peter’s own mouth.” And at no. 18: “He often used to relate to us.” He also excerpted other material from the works of Blessed Peter himself. Thus, at no. 10: “Indeed, he himself,” he says, “inserted in his works, by writing it down, both this matter and another which I recently related above concerning his rejection of the newly born child.” What is narrated in chapter 7 about the reconciliation of the Church of Milan, he says, “is clearly set forth in the book entitled Acts of Milan,” which he transcribed while preserving the same wording throughout. Similarly, what is related at no. 16 about the establishment of Fonte Avellana, although he himself had witnessed and observed it in person, was nevertheless taken from works XIV and XV.

[Col. 0094C] 11. Ughellus, in volume I of *Italia sacra*, in the section on the bishops of Gubbio, calls Saint John of Lodi “the Grammarian,” on account of the elegance and gravity of his style, which in this Life is expressed in a manner almost beyond the practice of his age. This diligent lover of truth therefore dedicated, with a flourishing pen, an account of Blessed Peter’s deeds, written soon after his death, to Liprandus, the prior who succeeded him. This may perhaps be Ariprandus, the man to whom Blessed Peter addressed works XLV and XLVI, the latter of which begins as follows: “You demand, dearest son, that I write something to you; and although you frequently write to others at my dictation, you beg that something also be written for you.” To him, in letter 19, he sets out the course of his illnesses. The material placed near the end concerning an apparition of Blessed Peter in the year 1080 seems to have been added later by someone else, as we observe there and indicate by giving it the title “Appendix.”

12. In the sixteenth century, others embellished the Acts of the same Blessed Peter in their own style. They were printed by Cajetan together with the Roman edition of the letters, but were later omitted from the Lyon edition because they narrate the deeds of that same Damian which his disciple John recounts in precisely the same sequence. The first of these was John Anthony Flaminius of Imola, between whom and Leander Albertus of the Order of Preachers there existed a profound bond of affection and a mutual exchange of scholarly work. In 1516 Leander dedicated to him the *Lives of the Masters General of the Order of Preachers*, from Blessed Jordan, the successor of Saint Dominic, down to Thomas Cajetan. These Lives appear in Book I of the *Illustrious Men of the Order of Preachers*.

[Col. 0095A] Flaminius also composed various Lives of Fathers of the Order of Preachers edited by Leander, including those of Albert the Great, Vincent of Valencia, James of Venice, Maurice of Pannonia, Venturino of Bergamo, and James of Germany; the latter, however, he rendered into Latin from Italian. He likewise testifies in the prologue to the Life of Blessed Peter Damian that he had written the Lives of the four most holy patrons of the city of Faenza, in these words:

“I am accustomed to be filled with great pleasure, men of Faenza, whenever I recall how agreeable and delightful a work I have undertaken for you, and how eagerly I began to perform it in writing the Lives of the Saints whom you venerate with the greatest devotion—indeed, with such enthusiasm of spirit that it could scarcely be surpassed by anyone who loves you. I observed this in the Life recently written by me of Blessed Terentius the Confessor, who was the first presented to me, and in that of Blessed Sabinus, bishop and martyr. Therefore, when I heard that you expected from me similar work on the two saints who still remained, I thought that I ought, with the same devotion, to respond to your expectation and desire. Accordingly, I added Blessed Peter Damian and Saint Aemilian, who made episcopal dignity illustrious by his holiness, to the two whom I have mentioned, so that, if I am not mistaken, you may daily perceive by clearer signs the love I have already demonstrated toward you and my willingness to gratify you in every way that lies within my power.”

Such were the words of Flaminius. The other saints mentioned are venerated together with Blessed Peter as protectors of the city of Faenza: Terentius on 30 July, Sabinus—or Savinus—on 7 December, and Aemilian on 6 November. [Col. 0095C] The author of the manuscript Life of the latter is said to be John Anthony Flaminius, a priest of the Church of Faenza, whom Leander Albertus calls a learned man.

He concludes the Life of Blessed Peter as follows:

“Finally, they placed his body in a marble tomb, where, even to the present day, God makes his holy bishop illustrious and venerable to the people through many wonders. Those who have read what we have briefly written about him, and his splendid and salutary sermons, will, I think, be fully able to testify—on the strength of the great proofs of his remarkable holiness and eloquence—what a luminary he was in the Church of God. Blessed Peter died around the year of Christ 1080, a great protector and guardian of the city of Faenza.”

This is what is found there. We shall discuss the year of Blessed Peter’s death below.

13. Cajetan also preserves another “Life of Blessed Peter Damian, from Book V of the Camaldulian Histories of Augustine Fortunio, a monk of the Camaldulian Congregation, and from the second part, chapters 6 through 14.” The first part, in three books, was published by its author under the name Augustine of Florence in 1575, dedicated to the Grand Duke of Etruria. At the end of this Life, after the account of Blessed Peter’s apparition—which we have relegated to the Appendix—the following is added: “Blessed Peter, therefore, from that time onward—that is, from the year 1080—was regarded as a saint by the whole Church and was received among the inhabitants of heaven.”

Another Life of the same Blessed Peter was compiled by James Mosander from Jerome Rubeus’s *History of Ravenna*, and published in volume VII of the *Lives of the Saints* in the Supplement to Surius; it was also reprinted by Lipelous. Cajetan published from the same Rubeus the same Life, but arranged in a different order, together with the works of the preceding authors. Since all these accounts are either derived from the earlier Life written by John or excerpted from other ancient authors, whom we shall discuss below, and since they have often been printed, we omit them here, relegating some matters to the notes and the following sections. Silvanus Razzi, Camaldulian abbot, also published the same Life in Italian in his book *On the Saints and Blessed of the Camaldulians*, where he states in the preface that he translated it chiefly from Rubeus.

14. John in the Life, no. 49, and others who follow him relate that Blessed Peter Damian gave up his spirit to the Lord on the anniversary of the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle. Nevertheless, because of the solemnity of the Chair, the people of Faenza transfer the veneration of Blessed Peter to the following day, 23 February. On that day Ferrarius records in his *General Catalogue*: “At Faenza in Aemilia, Saint Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia and protector of that city.” He celebrates the same saint with a longer encomium in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, and even honors him with the title “saint,” although he admits that Peter had not yet been formally numbered among the saints. Jacobillus likewise calls him a saint in *On the Saints and Blessed of Umbria* under 23 February; on that date he also gives one of his Lives, asserts that Peter is venerated among the people of Faenza, and cites the ancient manuscript lessons of the Church of Faenza, which at that time used to be read from his Life.

Together with the people of Faenza, we too give his Acts on 23 February. Calvisius, under the year 1072, and Schmidius in his *Historical Diary* assign his death to that day; yet they had not read this in Baronius, whose testimony they follow. On the other hand, under 22 February, the day on which we have said he died, our Balinghem, Ghinius in the *Calendar of the Canons*, Wion, Dorganius, Menardus, and Bucelinus in the Benedictine Martyrologies, as well as Surius, Haraeus, and others, place him and have published his Life.

§ III. Blessed Peter’s reverence toward Saint Benedict, his Rule, and his Order. Another Peter, Peter de Honestis. The surname Damian.

15. The Benedictines are entirely justified, moreover, in claiming the worship and veneration of Blessed Peter Damian, since he followed the most holy patriarch Benedict with solemn devotion. For this reason, in his work XIV, *On the Order and Rule of the Hermitage of Fonte Avellana*, Peter prescribed that the strict fast of Lent might be relaxed somewhat on Saint Benedict’s feast day.

“In the two periods of Lent,” he says, “which precede either the Nativity of the Lord or holy Easter, it has been customary that neither monks nor laymen be permitted to partake of wine or even fish. During those same Lents, there is likewise never to be more than one cooked dish, except on these four feasts: namely, those of Blessed Andrew and Saint Benedict, Palm Sunday, and the Lord’s Supper. On these most sacred days, fish and wine are consumed with thanksgiving.”

Indeed, he says that “some people customarily complete that entire double period of Lent, apart from Sundays, by fasting throughout, except for three solemnities: namely, those of Saint Andrew, Saint Benedict, and the Annunciation of the Lord.”

That hermitage was dedicated to Saint Andrew; hence it is also said, in the account of Augustine of Florence cited by Wion in Book II, chapter 9 of *The Tree of Life*, to have been called the monastery of Saint Andrew of Avellana. But in the congregation of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana they honored Saint Benedict as patron, not as cenobites but as anchorites or hermits. Blessed Peter Damian teaches at length that the life of the latter is more perfect than that of cenobites, in Book VI, letter 12, using the very words of Saint Benedict:

“These, therefore, are not our words but those of the same Father of us all: ‘The second kind,’ he says, ‘is that of anchorites, that is, hermits. They are those who, no longer in the first fervor of their conversion, but after having been tested in the monastery, have learned to fight against the devil, trained by the support of many others; and, well prepared, they go forth from the battle line of their brothers to the solitary combat of the desert, already secure without another’s consolation, and by their own hand or arm, with God’s help, suffice to fight against the vices of the flesh and of their thoughts.’”

[Col. 0097C] These words Blessed Peter took from chapter 1 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. In the same letter he also writes:

“Moreover, we know this: Blessed Benedict was a cultivator of the desert, and certainly wished us to become what he himself had been; but . . . in his prudence he first established the level ground of monastic life, so that there, worn down by the blows of discipline and tested by exercises, we might more easily ascend from there to the summit of the desert. In this respect Benedict did what blessed Paul had also done. He was [ἄγαμος—unmarried], indeed, an apostle; yet he urged people to marry. ‘Let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband’ (1 Cor. 7:2). A little later, however, he says: ‘I wish that all men were as I myself am’ (ibid., 7). The Apostle wanted one thing and commanded another. He wanted us to be celibate, as he was, because of the outstanding merit of flourishing chastity; but he wanted us to enter marriage because he feared the danger arising from our weakness . . . . Thus Blessed Benedict, although he more earnestly wishes us to be what he himself was—that is, followers of the desert—nevertheless considers it more tolerable for us, weak and infirm, to live even ignobly in the harbor of a monastery than to perish in the stormy abyss of the world’s shipwreck.”

Finally, he concludes:

“Therefore, just as we must urge the brothers to ascend from monastic life to the desert, so we must receive them with charity, lest they appear to depart from the blessed man as enemies, with a schismatic aversion—which God forbid—but rather appear as true disciples, and agree unanimously with him in turn.”

16. Thus far in that letter of his wrote Blessed Peter. Besides the customary exercises of the monasteries of Saint Benedict, he relates in work XIV that in his own hermitage of Fonte Avellana many other observances, and far more excellent ones, were practiced.

“Concerning psalmody,” he says, “the custom is that when two brothers live together in a cell, they recite two psalters each day, one for the living and the other for the dead. Whoever lives alone, however, is to complete the entire psalter of the living each day; as for that of the dead, either half or the whole, according to what his strength makes possible. As for the canonical psalmody of the Hours, it is completed here in its entirety, in due order, just as it is done in the monastery.”

A little farther on he says:

“It is the rule in monasteries that those who are sent out on a journey do not eat outside if they hope to return on that same day. To this observance we add among ourselves that, whether someone has gone out on that day or another, he must always return to the hermitage fasting.”

Indeed, as we read in the Life, no. 43, Blessed Peter “established this standard of observance in certain monasteries whose members embraced it with pious devotion, and he decreed that the distinguished coenobium of Monte Cassino should have certain matters ‘written down’ among its regular commands.”

Leo of Marsica, himself also bishop of Ostia, confirms this admirably in Book III, chapter 21 of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, in these words:

“Moreover, when Lord Peter Damian came to the monastery, he fervently kindled in the service of God as many people as he could, by word and example alike. Finally, with the permission of Abbot Desiderius, he obtained from the entire congregation, by voluntary offering for the remission of all sins, that every Friday throughout the year they should be content with bread and water, receive the discipline after making confession, and in addition observe a three-day fast each year at the beginning of Lent.”

Desiderius was abbot, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and later Roman pontiff under the name Victor III. Blessed Peter visited him frequently and wrote him numerous letters and short works. Leo dedicated his *Chronicle of Cassino* to Oderisius, Desiderius’s successor among the people of Cassino.

17. At that time the monastery of Cluny, founded in the tenth century as we said on 13 January in the Life of Blessed Berno, its first abbot, flourished above all the monasteries of Gaul. Berno was succeeded by Odo, Aymard, Majolus, Odilo, and Hugh, men illustrious for holiness.

Concerning Blessed Peter Damian’s visit to the monastery of Cluny, the following is related in the *Library of Cluny*, column 460, in an account of the miracles of Saint Hugh written by a contemporary author:

“At a certain time it became necessary for the holy man, in order to protect his sons, to return to the mother Church and call upon the patronage of the Roman See. Therefore, seeking refuge in that city, he obtained with great labor and difficulty that Lord Peter—drawn away from his side, namely Peter, bishop of Ostia, surnamed Damian—be given to him to fight on behalf of the great Peter and overthrow his adversaries by his remarkable prudence and eloquence.

“That man was accustomed to singular abstinence and was so worn down everywhere by the bonds of iron that it was scarcely possible to find a way to support the weakness of his body sufficiently for him to bear, however inadequately, the heavy burden of riding. And because he could often be offended by the slightest cause of scandal, he frequently had to be appeased by some satisfaction. Venerable Hugh inclined himself to this task so readily that he restored his spirit to tranquility, as though he were another Martin, who considered nothing unworthy if humility advised that it be done.

“When he had come to Cluny, that other Gregory—similar in the abundance of his eloquence, though not equal in apostolic life—had observed their humanity and discipline, and had seen the rod and staff brought together. He began to hesitate and wonder how those who possessed such abundance of goods could be saints or have holy founders. Then again he wondered how those could fail to be saints, or could perish, who so devoutly endured so heavy a burden of labor and guarded monastic discipline.

“At one time he judged the quantity of their food excessive; at another he was amazed that the grace he saw them possess was lacking to those who fasted. Nevertheless, if it could be done, as he himself said, so that both virtues—obedience and abstinence—might be joined in them, then certainly nothing would be lacking to apostolic perfection.”

18. “For this reason he approached and entreated the lord Abbot that those who were so perfect in all other respects, and owed nothing to anchorites, should at least abstain from fat on two weekdays.

“To him venerable Hugh, an outstanding guardian of discernment, replied: ‘If, dearest Father, you wish to increase our crown of reward by adding fasting, first try with us the burden of labor, at least for a period of eight days; afterward you will judge what you ought to consider should be added. For as long as you have not tasted the cooked dish, you cannot know what seasoning of salt it requires; and if you have not applied even the smallest part of your finger, you will in no way be able to judge clearly and properly the burden borne by a brother.’

“When he heard this, and realized that the weight of such burdens was beyond what his own strength could bear, he abandoned his request to increase the burden and began to strike himself with the weapon by which he had wished to strike others, since he could not direct the arrow against them without wounding himself. He understood that this was a great task and that it ought to suffice that he himself was unable to undertake it, although he seemed to stand at such a height of virtues. Thus the learned bishop returned far more learned than he had come, carrying back with him a great treasure: the avoidance of empty glory and the pursuit of true humility.”

This comes from the *History of the Miracles of Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*. At Hugh’s request, Blessed Peter testifies that he himself wrote the Life of Saint Odilo, beginning it as follows:

“Hugh, rector of the monastery of Cluny, leader and foremost instructor of spiritual warfare, imposed upon me the labor of briefly treating in my own style the Life of Blessed Odilo, his predecessor, and of selecting in a short summary from what was more fully spread out in the preceding pages whatever was most useful and necessary.”

19. These few remarks have been made concerning Saint Benedict, his Rule, and his Order because some have transferred Blessed Peter from the hermitage of Fonte Avellana to the canons of Porto in the diocese of Ravenna, and from the anchoritic institution of Saint Benedict to the Rule of Clerics, or Regular Canons. They also maintain that he prescribed constitutions and decrees for proper living to those canons and wrongly call them the “Damian Rule.”

For information about this congregation of the Canons of Porto, one should consult Gabriel Pennotus, Part II of the *History of the Order of Clerical Canons*, chapter 47. At no. 2 he lists various proponents of this error. Following their opinion, Ciaconius, in his *Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs and Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church*, under Stephen X, confuses the deeds of Blessed Peter Damian with those of another Peter, Peter de Honestis. Ughellus corrected him in the second edition, also removing the insignia of the House of Honestis, in which a red lion, standing upright on a white field, holds a golden pine cone between its forefeet as though they were hands.

Arnold Wion, as though attempting to reconcile the opinions of everyone, begins Book II, chapter 9, as follows: “Saint Peter de Honestis, surnamed Damian and the Sinner, a nobleman of Ravenna, monk of the monastery of Saint Andrew of the hermitage of Avellana, of the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of the Dove,” and so forth.

But Peter de Honestis was a different man. Both were natives of Ravenna, and both assumed the name “the Sinner”; but the former customarily subscribed his letters “Peter the Sinner, monk,” while the latter subscribed his “Peter the Sinner, cleric.” Both were priors: the one of the monks of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana in the diocese of Gubbio, the other of the clerics or Regular Canons at the Church of Blessed Mary at Porto in the Ravenna region. He also prescribed constitutions for them, which Pope Paschal II approved on 10 Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1116.

Finally, Peter de Honestis died in his monastery at Porto in the year 1119, that is, forty-seven years after the death of Blessed Peter Damian. The previously mentioned Pennotus records the epitaph of Peter de Honestis, his letter to Pope Paschal, the pope’s reply, and various monasteries attached to this congregation at Porto. He also calls Peter de Honestis “Blessed” and says that he died on 4 Kalends of July; Ughellus, however, printed 4 Kalends of April, a matter that will be examined in its proper place.

20. Authors differ as to how Blessed Peter acquired the surname Damian. Ciaconius and Bellarmine, together with several others, call him the son of Damian. Fortunio and others prefer to say that he took the name from his brother Damian, through whose efforts he was instructed in the liberal arts; perhaps for this reason some write “Peter Damiani” rather than “Peter Damianus.”

Yet, unless the manuscripts—which have been printed with the utmost accuracy—are frequently in error, Peter is called “Petrus Damianus” by Leo of Marsica and by the ancient author of the miracles of Saint Hugh cited above; also in the Life of Pope Stephen X and in the letters of Pope Alexander II. Later authors followed this usage: Helinandus, Antoninus, Lipomanus, Bergomensis, Ricordatus, Rolewinchus, an anonymous Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint Justina, and an anonymous author of Fonte Avellana, in the testimonies printed by Cajetan before the works of Blessed Peter.

§ IV. Earlier deeds of Blessed Peter Damian; his relations with Popes Gregory VI, Clement II, Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, and Nicholas II; his episcopate of Ostia and cardinalitial dignity. The schism of the antipope Benedict abolished through his efforts.

21. “That Peter Damian was an outstanding teacher and a noble member of the Christian commonwealth and of the Apostolic See” was testified by Paul V in the aforementioned Brief to Constantine Cajetan.

He was born at Ravenna, perhaps around the year 988 of Christ, as will become clear below from the account of his death. In the first years of adolescence he had to tend pigs, even after he had grown somewhat older. Later, having been instructed in letters and the liberal arts, and then excelling in knowledge, he is said to have taught others, as related at no. 7.

Finally, embracing the eremitical life, he put on monastic clothing at Fonte Avellana. Since he “devoted himself to sacred reading with assiduous meditation,” he is said at no. 17 to have “shone with such knowledge of the divine Scriptures as no one previously versed in secular learning had shone.” There he taught the brothers of his hermitage, and afterward the monks of Pomposa, having been summoned by Abbot Guido. This abbot died in the year 1046, but Rubeus, in Book V of his *History of Ravenna*, says that he had presided over the monastery of Pomposa for more than forty-eight years.

After spending two years among the people of Pomposa, partly teaching and partly preaching, Peter returned to the hermitage of Fonte Avellana. After enjoying some peace there, he was sent to the celebrated monastery of Saint Vincent. Rubeus likewise asserts that Blessed Peter Damian wrote the Life of Saint Romuald in this monastery around the thirteenth year after Romuald’s death. We published the Life of Saint Romuald on 7 February, and said that he had died in the year 1027. Thus the thirteenth year after his death falls in the year of Christ 1040, confirming the chronological epoch of Blessed Peter’s activities, which Augustine Fortunio also observed from certain larger chronicles.

22. He was subsequently made prior of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, after having for some time been placed in charge of administering temporal affairs. When Archbishop Gebehard of Ravenna invited him to come to Ravenna—this man died on 16 February 1044 and was buried in the monastery of Pomposa—Peter replied with the letter mentioned above, excusing himself on the grounds that, since he had now become prior and was obliged to govern others and provide for their needs, he could not easily come to him. These events occurred before the year 1044.

In that year, after three false pontiffs had simultaneously invaded the Roman Church and the schism had been removed, Gregory VI was elected legitimate pope. Two letters of Blessed Peter to him are found at the beginning of the book. In the first, Peter shows himself delighted to have heard of Gregory’s election and hopes that through him the Church of God, cleansed of its filth, will recover its former beauty.

After citing these letters under the year 1044, no. 8, Baronius adds concerning Blessed Peter:

“Such statements are worthy only of a legitimately elected pope; indeed, if there were no others, these alone would suffice to demonstrate that his canonical election was entirely pure in every respect. For Peter Damian was not the sort of man who, when writing these things, would shamefully flatter the pontiff. Burning with zeal for ecclesiastical discipline, he knew how to spare no one and most bitterly rebuked anyone whom he knew to oppose it.”

This is what Baronius says. Under the year 1046, no. 3, he states that Gregory VI, “following the example of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, who voluntarily abdicated in order to restore peace to the Church, likewise resigned the pontifical throne of his own accord, with the same spirit and the same virtue.”

23. Gregory was succeeded by Svidgerus, bishop of Bamberg, called Clement II, who was consecrated on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord, 25 December. He soon crowned the emperor Henry, son of Conrad the Salian, and his wife Agnes during the celebration of Mass.

Baronius writes under the year 1047, no. 13:

“It is reported that Peter Damian, then a famous inhabitant of the hermitage, distinguished both by holiness and by learning, wrote to Clement himself a letter whose opening is as follows: ‘Let Your Beatitude know, most excellent lord, that the most invincible lord emperor has commanded me, not once but often, and, if I may dare to say so, has deigned to ask me to come to you and communicate to your ears what is being done in the churches of our regions and what I thought necessarily needed to be done by you.’”

That letter carries out this task diligently. Peter also sends with it letters from the emperor that he had received on the journey, and asks Clement to write back whether he thinks Peter should continue the journey he has undertaken.

24. Clement II died in the same year, on 9 October. After the Church had been afflicted for some time by Benedict, who had invaded the Roman See for the third time, Damasus II was elected in the year 1048. When Damasus died within the first month of his pontificate, and the See had then been vacant for five months, Saint Leo IX finally succeeded him. Previously called Bruno, he was bishop of Toul in Belgica Prima.

Blessed Peter wrote to him against malicious detractors. Leo replied with an excellent letter in which he praised the holy man’s zeal, condemned clerical incontinence, and wrote that it ought to be punished. He concluded with these words:

“My dearest son, I rejoice beyond description because, by the example of your way of life, you teach whatever you have taught by eloquence. For teaching by deeds is greater than teaching by words. Therefore, with God as your author, you will obtain the palm of victory, rejoice with the Son of God and of the Virgin in the heavenly dwelling, and be heaped with as many rewards as there are people whom, having been snatched from the devil’s snares through you, you have gathered together and, in a certain sense, crowned.”

This was Saint Leo, who held a Roman council against the Simoniacs in the year 1049. Blessed Peter Damian praises its decree in work VI, chapter 35. A letter of that same Leo, letter 10 to the people of Osimo, in which he rebukes, after the death of a bishop, those who plundered episcopal houses, is included among the letters of Blessed Peter Damian in Book V, no. 6, and is said to have been written by him under the pope’s name.

Saint Leo died in the year 1054, on 19 April, distinguished by the praise of his virtues and miracles, as the tables of the Roman Martyrology proclaim. He was succeeded by Gebehard, bishop of Eichstätt in Germany, later called Victor II. He was consecrated on Maundy Thursday, in the following year, 1055. In the following year, 1056, on 5 October, the emperor Henry surrendered his spirit to God in Victor’s hands.

This Victor, too, died as pope at Florence the following year, 1057, on 28 July. One letter of Blessed Peter to Victor is extant, written in a rather bitter spirit but with zeal burning on behalf of violated justice, for an illustrious man who had been despoiled and unjustly harassed.

25. In the same year, 1057, Frederick, formerly abbot of Cassino and a cardinal priest, was elected pope unwillingly on 2 August and was called Stephen. He is commonly called the ninth, but should actually be reckoned the tenth, since Stephen, successor of Zacharias, was established in 752 and, although he lived in that dignity for only a few days, was a legitimate pontiff; he was improperly omitted because his successor was also named Stephen.

Under this pope, Blessed Peter, compelled by a precept of obedience, was ordained bishop of the Church of Ostia, as will be related below in the Acts. Since the bishopric of Ostia is customarily assigned to the dean of the cardinals, by whom the supreme pontiff is consecrated, Blessed Peter is also rightly numbered among the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, although this dignity is not mentioned in his Life or in the letters of the pontiffs then living. Nor does Blessed Peter himself call himself a cardinal in his writings.

His letter 1 of Book II is addressed to “the venerable bishops, cardinals of the Lateran Church.” Cajetan comments on it that Peter’s status as a cardinal bishop may be inferred from these words:

“Therefore, my brothers—and so that I may boldly insert myself among you, I mean we who are like seven eyes upon one stone, who bear the image of the stars, who hold the dignity of angels through the office of the Annunciation—let us see, let us shine, and let us proclaim the words of life to the peoples, not only with our voices but also by our conduct.”

This is found there. We shall soon provide clearer indications from his works.

Berthold of Constance, consecrated priest in 1084 by Otto, bishop of Ostia, later Pope Urban II, calls Peter Damian “the cardinal bishop of pious memory” in the Appendix to the *Chronicle of Hermann the Lame*, under the year 1100. The author of the Life of Saint John of Lodi, his disciple, followed him, as did Francesco Petrarch, John Trithemius, Aloysius Lipomanus, and others.

Cardinal Baronius, however, under the year 1057, no. 19, explains at length the structure of the Roman Church at that time, according to which he places the bishop of Ostia first among the cardinal bishops. Augustine Fortunio, in the Life published by Cajetan, says:

“Pope Stephen joined the Church of Ostia to him and made him dean of the sacred college in the year 1058, at the beginning of Lent, in March, on Ember Saturday.”

Ciaconius asserts that the first creation of cardinals took place under Stephen on that day, and that six others were made cardinals together with Blessed Peter Damian. In the aforementioned Brief of Paul V to Cajetan, Peter is called “cardinal bishop of Ostia of the Holy Roman Church.”

“Pope Stephen,” as it is read in his Life published together with the Councils, “having held many councils in the city against concubinage and many other vices of the clergy, reformed the morals of the Church. He drew Peter Damian from the hermitage and created him cardinal bishop of Ostia . . . . While traveling to Florence to visit Saint John Gualbert, renowned for the fame of his holiness, he fell ill and, after being sick for a few days, died on 4 Kalends of April in the year 1058.”

26. The schism that arose immediately afterward is described as follows by Leo of Ostia, book II, chapter 102:

“In the meantime, Gregory, count of the Lateran and Tusculum, having learned of the Roman pontiff’s death, joined by Gerard of Galeria [Col. 0104A] and several Roman nobles, entered the church by night with crowds of armed men and, together, installed John, bishop of Velletri—later called Mincius—as pope, giving him the name Benedict III. When Peter Damian, a very religious man (whom Pope Stephen had at that time drawn from the desert and made bishop of the Ostian Church), learned of this, he began, together with the cardinals, to resist and protest, and to pronounce an anathema. But all these men, nevertheless compelled by terror, fled to various places.”

Blessed Peter wrote about the schism of the said Benedict in Letter 4 of Book V, under this heading: “To the lord H., most reverend archbishop: Peter the sinful monk, the service of due submission.”

Cajetan thinks that this letter was sent to Henry, archbishop of Ravenna, and that it concerns the schism of the antipope Cadalus. He addressed to Henry his Opusculum VI, *Against the Simoniacs*, when he had newly received the priesthood, in the year 1051. But in the Appendix, or chapter 39, he laments that he had done this, since “he could not extract even the slightest spark of a solution.” Therefore, it does not appear that he later supported him or maintained his friendship.

That the subject is rather the schism of Benedict, not that of Cadalus, is clearly indicated by these words:

“Moreover, since Pope Stephen of pious memory, after assembling the bishops within the Church, the Roman citizens, the clergy, and the people, had established under the threat of strict excommunication that, if it should happen that he departed this world before Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Roman Church, who had been sent with the common agreement of all, returned from the empress, no one should elect a pope, but that the apostolic see should remain vacant and untouched until his return.”

When therefore Hildebrand—later Pope Gregory VII—had returned from Germany, he summoned the cardinals and Roman nobles to Siena. By their votes Gerard, bishop of Florence, was proclaimed Roman pontiff and called Nicholas II.

Meanwhile, since Benedict still held the occupied Roman see by force, Peter wrote the aforementioned letter, in which he plainly indicates his own cardinalitial dignity:

“But as for what you added at the end of your letter, asking me to write to you what I think of the man who now presides in the apostolic see, or of the one who has been elected to that same see—although you might already have learned from some sons of your Church what our judgment is concerning the difference between the two men—nevertheless, because you command it, we also record it in writing.

“That man is unquestionably a Simoniac, because, while all of us, the cardinal bishops of that city, protested, resisted, and pronounced a fearful anathema, he was enthroned at night, amid crowds of armed men who were making tumult and raging on every side.”

The remaining passages being omitted, these words show that the subject is the schism mentioned above.

27. When Benedict, the false pope and schismatic, had been condemned at the Council of Sutri and deprived of every priestly office, and when Nicholas had been received by the clergy and Roman people with due honor and inaugurated as pontiff by solemn coronation in January of the year 1059, a council of one hundred and thirteen bishops was held at Rome in the same year. At it Berengar abjured his heresy, a constitution concerning the election of the Roman pontiff was issued, and a decree was made against the Simoniacs. Blessed Peter mentions it in his *Opusculum* XXX, chapter 1.

Later, sent by Pope Nicholas to the Milanese, he freed that Church from a twofold stain. These events are related in chapter 7 of his *Life*. They are also recalled by the legates of Alexander II, who had succeeded Nicholas, in the constitutions prescribed in 1067 to the clergy and people of Milan, where these prudent words were inserted:

“Since, therefore, certain matters were formerly corrected in this city through our brother, the lord Peter, bishop of Ostia, a man of reverend holiness, there is no need to repeat either them or the former disputes, which are known to all.”

The letter found in Book VII, Letter 9, was written by Blessed Peter in the name of Pope Nicholas to Anna, daughter of Jaroslav, king of the Russians, queen of France and wife of Henry I.
