He praises her piety and generosity toward the poor and urges her to inspire her husband, the king, to administer the state justly, protect the Church, and undertake other works of piety; he also urges her to educate her sons in the virtues with which she herself was imbued.

King Henry died in the year 1060, and Philip I, still a child, succeeded him. The monastery of Saint Felicity near Florence, which the same pontiff had formerly arranged to have rebuilt, he endowed with a privilege dated at Florence on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the thirteenth indiction—that is, in the year 1060. Yet because the year at Rome was reckoned from the feast of the Annunciation, the privilege is inscribed with the year 1059. [Col. 0105C] Together with four other bishops, Peter the sinful monk subscribed it. He is the Damian whom we are discussing.

§ V. The schism of the false pope Cadalus extinguished by Blessed Peter; his return to the hermitage of Fonte Avellana. His legation to the Cluniacs, the archbishops of Gaul, and King Henry under Pope Alexander II.

28. When, under Nicholas II’s rule of the Christian world, the Church of God had begun to enjoy greater tranquility and prosperity, Blessed Peter congratulates him in Letter 7 of Book I. At the same time, he prays for the Anconitans, who had been removed from Catholic communion, asking that the unhappy men be rescued from the danger of eternal death.

He addressed to the same pontiff, Nicholas, *Opusculum* XVII, *On the Celibacy of Priests*, and urges him, setting aside every human consideration, to rise against this abuse, inflamed with apostolic zeal, and not to fear powerful men who defiled the Church with disgrace.

But Blessed Peter’s principal request of this pontiff was that he be permitted to lay down the episcopal burden. Letter 8 of Book I survives on this matter, addressed to the same Pope Nicholas and to Hildebrand, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. There also survives *Opusculum* XIX, dedicated to the same pontiff, *On the Abdication of the Episcopate*. In its preface, among other reasons, he gives this one:

“Since, under your holy pontificate, the universal Church enjoys a delightful peace, may rest also not be denied to my gray hairs and already advanced old age.”

Finally, with great humility, he concludes this little book in chapter 11:

“Supported, therefore, by the authority of these and other Fathers, I irrevocably renounce in your holy hands both the episcopate and the monasteries, and I cut off from myself every right to raise any future question or claim. And because, on account of my countless sins, I am not worthy to remain in ecclesiastical dignity, may divine mercy grant me, through your holy prayers, venerable Father, to remain for the rest of the life allotted to me in mourning and repentance. […] Almighty God, who by the incomprehensible design of his dispensation has cast me down from the ambition of obtaining rule and has raised you to the summit of ecclesiastical dignity, may he inspire your holy heart, whose inhabitant he is, to send me through sacred letters commands capable of agreeing with my vows and desires.”

29. Blessed Peter did these things in support of his abdication from the episcopate, but he did not obtain what he desired, perhaps because of the death of Pope Nicholas. Nicholas died toward the end of July 1061. After an interregnum of two months, he was succeeded by Anselm, bishop of Lucca, lawfully elected by the cardinals around the Kalends of October and called Alexander II.

Anselm had been Blessed Peter Damian’s companion in the celebrated legation to the Milanese, and Peter bears witness in the *Opusculum* called *The Acts of Milan* that he was distinguished for prudence and holiness.

Against this pontiff, when a new schism had been fomented, Cadalus, bishop of Parma, was made false pope on 28 October, assuming the name Honorius II. In two letters addressed to him, Blessed Peter warned him by setting before his eyes the enormity of his crime and threatening him with the near thunderbolt of divine vengeance. These are Letters 20 and 21 of Book I.

Since he had learned that Cadalus’s cause was being wickedly defended by the followers of Henry, king of Germany—then still an adolescent and not yet raised to the imperial office—he tried in Letter 3 of Book VII to impel the king’s mind, as though with certain spurs, to bring aid to the Church. His exceptional zeal and devotion toward the Church shine forth in the following brief words taken from the epilogue:

“Would that I might be judged guilty of treason before your tribunal, while you nevertheless sit as the arbiter of justice to punish the adversaries of the apostolic see! Let a swung axe rage against my neck, provided only that the Roman Church, restored through you to the summit of its proper dignity, may ascend it. Moreover, if you quickly destroy Cadalus, like another Constantine destroying Arius, and strive to restore peace to the Church for which Christ died, may God soon make you ascend from kingship to the imperial throne and receive from all your enemies the honors of distinguished glory. Otherwise, if you continue to dissemble, if, though able to abolish it, you refuse to remove the error of a world in peril; and so forth. I restrain my spirit and leave the meaning of what follows to the readers.”

30. Blessed Peter wrote these things to the king. There is also his Letter 6 of Book III to Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne. He praises Anno because he had persecuted Cadalus and, with the ecclesiastical sword, cut him down as far as his strength allowed; he urges him to put the finishing hand to the work. This would happen, he says, if Anno’s efforts brought about a general assembly of the Fathers.

And this was done. For in Germany the Council of Osbor is said to have been convened on the authority of Saint Anno. In it, with King Henry present, a synodal disputation was read which Blessed Peter Damian had composed as though it had been held between the royal advocate and the defender of the Roman Church. There, by the unanimous consent of all, the condemnation of the false pontiff Cadalus was proclaimed, and Alexander’s election was approved.

Consult Baronius under the year 1061, number 21, where he writes that these events took place on 27 October, on the very vigil of the holy apostles Simon and Jude. That synodal disputation is also included among Blessed Peter’s works in volume III, *Opusculum* IV, and in volume XXV of the royal edition of the Councils, beginning on page 638.

Likewise, at Saint Anno’s urging, when German nobles had been sent as legates to Rome, the Council of Mantua was held in 1064. Pope Alexander attended with the cardinals. At his request, Blessed Peter Damian and Saint Anno, archbishop, were also present. There, after the false pope Cadalus had again been condemned, the scandal of the Church and the Empire was removed.

Meanwhile, in those years Blessed Peter underwent many dangers in his life, which he calls in Letter 5 of Book VI to the Cluniac monks “the accumulated snares of Cadalus’s fury.” Because Duke and Count Gothfrey of Tuscany had received Cadalus as a guest, Blessed Peter admonished him in Letter 10 of Book VII.

31. As stated above, Alexander II had been elected around the Kalends of October in the year 1061. He postponed his consecration until it could be ascertained that his election had been canonically conducted by synodal decree and likewise confirmed as valid.

Indeed, when the schism of Cadalus had arisen, he fled from the City lest he be overwhelmed by certain Romans who favored Cadalus. Blessed Peter writes that he had then been freed from the episcopal burden in *Opusculum* XX, which he addressed to “Alexander, elect of the apostolic see, and Hildebrand.” He begins chapter 1 as follows:

“Blessed be the dispensation of the almighty Creator, because, when I recently ascended to you, weighed down by the burden of two episcopates—one requiring governance, namely Ostia, and the other visitation, namely Gubbio—I crossed the precipitous Alpine ridges. Soon, casting off the burden of tribulation, unloaded and free, I returned as a fugitive to my beloved solitude, as though restored to my former place. […]

“Therefore, when I resolved to renounce ecclesiastical governance to you, I did not err, because I worthily restored to the Roman Church, which you are, what belonged to it. And, to profess that I have made confession to you, as a consequence of this renunciation a penance of one hundred years has been imposed upon me, through those remedies, namely, which are established by the monastic rules.”

How this penance of one hundred years is fulfilled, Blessed Peter explains in the *Life of Dominic Loricatus* in these words:

“Among us, three thousand strokes of the discipline regularly complete one year of penance, while the recitation of ten psalms permits one thousand strokes. Since it is undisputed that the Psalter consists of one hundred and fifty psalms, those who calculate correctly find that five years of penance are contained in the discipline of one Psalter. But whether you multiply five by twenty or twenty by five, the result is one hundred. Therefore, whoever chants twenty Psalters with the discipline may be confident that he has completed one hundred years of penance.”

But at what age Blessed Peter undertook this penance he indicates in the same *Opusculum* XX, chapter 5:

“Look,” he says, “my eyes are already dim, and the humors of phlegm abound more than usual. Wrinkles are appearing, and my gums threaten the ruin of my teeth. Finally, the head that until now was scattered with white hairs is already becoming snowy with the whiteness of a swan; my voice is hoarse, and my strength is failing.”

And in chapter 7, during his concluding appeal, he declares that he desires, as he had been ordered, “to ordain”—that is, consecrate—“the pontiff of the apostolic see,” and immediately to withdraw from the stronghold of his own Ostian pontificate.

32. Yet although Blessed Peter had been granted permission to remain in the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, he himself indicates in Letter 15 of Book I, addressed to Alexander, the prelate of the supreme see, already consecrated, that he had not been entirely freed from the episcopal burden. Near the end he writes:

“O how joyful, how pleasing, and finally what a sweet report has recently reached my ears—that you had removed the Ostian county from me and entrusted it to another. […] I also freely implore divine mercy that you do not delay assigning the bishopric as well, and that you quickly take from my hands the plow of a barren, sandy shore.”

It does not seem that he obtained this request. For, apart from what he undertook against the antipope Cadalus, he was employed in various legations. Perhaps the first of these was to the monastery of Cluny, since, as we stated above from his *Life*, its abbot Saint Hugh “called upon the protection of the Roman see and, with great labor and difficulty, obtained from the pope’s side the lord Peter, namely the bishop of Ostia, surnamed Damian.”

Blessed Peter recalls the labor he undertook at that time in Letter 2 of Book VI, addressed to Saint Hugh, abbot:

“When already my bent old age was weighing me down, and my body, exhausted of strength, caused the steps of one walking to totter and falter in uncertain strides, at the command of your order I placed my soul, so to speak, in my hands. Covered with summer snows, I climbed the precipitous Alpine ridges and, for the benefit of your venerable monastery, penetrated deep into the lands of Gaul, which lie quite near the ocean.”

That he remained there for a long time he indicates in Letter 5 of the same Book VI, addressed to the Cluniac monks:

“I had been promised that I would return home by the Kalends of August. But after three months had subsequently run their course, although I made every effort with all possible speed, I scarcely climbed the summit of Fonte Avellana, from which I had departed, before the fifth day before the Kalends of November.”

Blessed Peter also recalls this journey in *Opusculum* XXXIV, chapter 6, and in *Opusculum* XXXIX.

33. A second legation of Blessed Peter to Gaul is described, together with his exceptional commendation, in Letter 21 of Pope Alexander to five archbishops of Gaul. We reproduce it here in full:

“Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to G., archbishop of Reims; R., archbishop of Sens; B., archbishop of Tours; M., archbishop of Bourges; and T., archbishop of Bordeaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Your holy fraternity, most beloved, is not unaware that, by the authority of the apostolic see, to which divine mercy has appointed us, responsibility for governing and ordering the condition of the entire universal Church rests upon us.

“Since, therefore, being occupied with many matters of the Churches, we ourselves cannot come to you, we have taken care to send you such a man that, after us, no greater person is found in the Roman Church—namely Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, who is both our eye and the immovable foundation of the apostolic see.

“To him, therefore, we have entrusted our place with full authority, so that whatever, with God’s help, he establishes among you shall be held as valid and firm, as though it had been promulgated by a judgment of our special examination.

“Therefore, we admonish your venerable holiness in fraternal charity and, moreover, command you by apostolic authority to receive such a great and distinguished man with the devotion due to our own person, and humbly to obey his decisions and judgments out of reverence for Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

“For whoever, inflated by the arrogance of pride—which God forbid—should become a contradictor or adversary of his judgment shall not have our favor or that of the Roman Church until he has made worthy satisfaction.

“But because, when we sent Girelmus to you, we did not yet at all hope that we could obtain the arrival of the aforesaid lord Peter, we wish that, if Girelmus began anything among you, it should come under the direction of the lord Peter, and that whatever must be done should be done through his hand.”

Thus far the letter of Alexander II.

Among the other notable achievements accomplished by Blessed Peter in Gaul was the sentence of execution issued with other bishops against Reginald, the invader of the monastery of Saint-Médard. Alexander II confirmed this sentence in Letter 22, addressed to Gervasius, archbishop, and his suffragans, and ordered it to be carried out. For the sake of brevity, I omit the letter.

34. Blessed Peter was again sent as legate across the Alps, this time to King Henry, when, carried away by youthful frenzy, Henry had decided to repudiate his wife Bertha, whom he had married two years earlier.

Lambert of Hersfeld, who was living at the time, relates the event in his *Chronicle* under the year 1069, when it occurred:

“After Pentecost, the king held a conference with the princes of the kingdom at Worms. There he first discussed the matter privately with the bishop of Mainz and earnestly implored his assistance in accomplishing what he was plotting in his mind. […]

“He summoned a synod at Mainz for the week immediately following the feast of Saint Michael, to settle the affair. […]

“When the appointed day for dissolving the king’s marriage was approaching, the king hurried toward Mainz. And behold, while he was on the way, he learned that a legate of the apostolic see was awaiting his arrival at Mainz in order to prevent the separation and to threaten the bishop of Mainz with the judgment of apostolic censure because he had promised to be the author of so wicked a separation.

“Immediately dismayed at having lost from his hands the matter he had long desired, he wanted to return to Saxony by the route he had come. Yet, overcome with difficulty by the advice of his friends, lest he frustrate the princes of the kingdom whom he had ordered to meet him in great numbers at Mainz, he went to Frankfurt and ordered those who had gathered at Mainz to be present there.

“When they had arrived in large numbers, Peter Damian—who was the legate of the apostolic see, a man greatly revered for his age and innocence of life—set forth the mandates of the Roman pontiff. He declared that the deed Henry was attempting was utterly evil and far removed from the Christian name, much more from that of a king.

“If he was not restrained by human laws or the sanctions of the canons, he should at least spare his own reputation and standing, lest the poison of so disgraceful an example, begun by a king, contaminate the entire Christian people, and lest the man who ought to be the avenger of crimes become himself their author and standard-bearer.

“Finally, if he could not be moved by counsel, Peter said that he would necessarily employ ecclesiastical force and prohibit the crime by the law of the canons.

“He added that he would never consecrate as emperor a man who, by so pestilential an example, had betrayed the Christian faith as far as lay within him.”

This was the substance of Blessed Peter’s legation. The princes judged it just, and the king himself at last yielded. He received the queen into partnership in the kingdom and marriage bed, and by her fathered an heir and successor to the kingdom.

35. The mother of this King Henry was Agnes, daughter of William IV, duke of Aquitaine. Together with her husband, Henry, son of Conrad the Salian, she had been crowned empress by Pope Clement I, as stated above, in the year 1046.

She had also taken amiss that, without her permission, Pope Alexander II had been created against the will of herself and her son, and she had joined and given support to the false pope Cadalus. To expiate this offense, she came to Rome to the thresholds of the apostles, where she sought the counsel of Blessed Peter Damian, whom she had taken as her spiritual father. She confessed to him all the sins she had committed from her earliest childhood.

Blessed Peter himself testifies to this in chapter 5 of *Opusculum* LVI, *On the Fleeting Glory of the World and Contempt for the Age*, which he addressed to her. There are also four letters of his to this empress in Book VII. In the last of them, when she had gone to Germany, he urges her to return to Rome. She did so, and, remaining at Rome, died distinguished for holiness in the year 1077.

§ VI. Blessed Peter’s legation to the Florentines and Ravennates; his death, burial, and veneration.

[Col. 0110D]

36. During the final years of his life Blessed Peter accomplished many notable things in Italy. Some are related in chapters 8 and 9 of his *Life*; others, omitted there, we touch upon briefly here.

Around the year 1063 a major schism arose in the Florentine Church, when monks dissented from their bishop. Among them, Saint John Gualbert, founder of the order of Vallombrosa, is said to have held the leading place. In his *Life*, to be commemorated on 12 July, the matter is stated in these words:

“The blessed man asserted that Peter, bishop of Florence, a native of Pavia, was guilty not only of simony but also of heresy on account of that vice together with his brothers, and he declared that the sacraments were not to be received from him. Consequently, a violent dispute arose among the clergy and people of Florence: some defended the bishop, while others praised the monks because they detested that vice with such freedom.”

The bishop’s father, being an exceedingly simple man, is said falsely to have given three thousand pounds to the king.

Alexander II, sending Blessed Peter Damian, attempted to reconcile the dissenting parties, but, having accomplished nothing, he was compelled to return. The monks opposed him, proclaiming that their bishop—who had not yet been condemned by the Catholic Church—was to be avoided, and that his blessings and sacraments were curses and sacrileges. For this reason they forbade the people to receive the sacraments from the bishop or from those ordained by him.

As a result, many died without the sacrament of the Eucharist, and the baptized were not anointed with chrism. Blessed Peter discusses these matters at length in *Opusculum* XXX, *On Sacraments Administered by Wicked Men*, which he sent to the Florentines.

The monks, corrected by Blessed Peter’s just rebuke because they had pursued the bishop’s cause with zeal that was not properly ordered, went to Rome and accused the bishop before the pontiff. After the sacrifice of the Mass, Peter, a monk of Vallombrosa, still clothed in the sacred vestments but having removed only the chasuble, passed unharmed through fire. Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, describes this at greater length and affirms that the same Peter, bishop of Albano, was still alive when he was writing.

Baronius, under the year 1063, number 58, asserts that “Peter, bishop of Florence,” whom the *Acts of Saint John Gualbert* report to have been “removed by Pope Alexander from every episcopal office,” was afterward “reconciled and received into communion by those same monks.” Ughelli, in *Italian Sacred History*, volume III, denies this and maintains that another bishop, also named Peter, was soon substituted.

37. On account of this Florentine bishop, a council of one hundred and more bishops was held at Rome against the Simoniacs. At it, canon 4 also established that clerics should eat and sleep together and possess their goods in common.

Baronius, under the year 1063, number 37, asserts that this was “done at the suggestion of Peter Damian, who, in his writings, urged Pope Alexander to enact these provisions”—namely, in *Opusculum* XXIV, *Against Clerics Who Possess Property*.

To the same pontiff he dedicated *Opusculum* XXIII, *On the Shortness of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs and Divine Providence*. For the same pontiff, in response to a question from a certain patriarch, he also published *Opusculum* XXXVIII, *Against the Greek Error Concerning the Procession of the Holy Spirit*.

There survives, in the name of that same pontiff, Letter 7 of Book V, addressed to the clergy and people of Milan. After showing in the most humane words the paternal concern that the pontiff, a Milanese by birth, felt for their salvation, he urges them, thinking nothing low or earthly, to raise themselves toward heavenly things with the full force and fervor of their souls.

He also sent various letters to the pontiff himself, printed in Book I. In some he explains the need to eradicate corrupt customs; in others he attacks the Simoniacs; elsewhere he carefully commends to him a bishop of Orléans whose Church, afflicted by wicked men, was being shaken by many storms and tempests of calamity; and elsewhere he pleads for the bishop of Ravenna, asking that he be released from the bond of anathema.

“For it is unworthy,” he says, “that on account of the offense of one little man so countless a multitude of people should perish, and that so great a labor of Christ, for which he shed his precious blood, should be overturned by the guilt of one pitiable person.”

This was Henry, who had been made archbishop in the year 1051 and died around 1070. Pope Alexander, writing about him to Valerian, bishop, says:

“We were astonished that Henry, called archbishop of Ravenna, attempted to excommunicate you. But since one who is excommunicated could not excommunicate you, by apostolic authority we absolve you and your people and command you henceforth to pay no attention to it.”

Thus according to Ivo, Gratianus, Rubeus, and Ughelli.

“Once the profaner had been removed,” as the *Acts* below state in section 49, “he was ordered, at the command of Alexander II, to proceed to Ravenna. Although already worn out by age, he undertook this legation.”

38. “After these and several other matters had been accomplished,” the account continues in section 49, “when he had made his first stop at Faenza, he was seized by a fever and took to his bed; and on the anniversary of the Chair of Saint Peter, he gave up his spirit to God.”

Berthold of Constance, a contemporary author, as we have shown above, gives the year of his death. In his continuation of Hermann’s chronicle, under the year 1072, he writes:

“Peter Damian, cardinal bishop of pious memory, long since crucified to the world, departed to the Lord on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. Lord Gerard succeeded him in the episcopate—a true monk, distinguished in knowledge of the Scriptures and not inferior in conduct to his predecessor.”

Thus far Berthold.

These facts agree remarkably with Blessed Peter’s *Life*. It is therefore surprising that Fortunatus, Rubeus, Ricordatus, Wion, and many others postpone his death until the year 1080 and assert that he was sent to Ravenna by Gregory VII, Alexander’s successor, after the death of Archbishop Wibert.

Since such claims rest on no foundation, they require no further refutation. The successor whom Blessed Peter, while alive, long and earnestly requested but was never able to obtain, he finally received through death. This was Gerard—also called Gerald and Gerold—“a German by nation, a native of Regensburg, a monk and senior prior of Cluny.” Pope Alexander sent him as legate to Gaul, and Gregory VII sent him to Spain and Germany. According to the same Berthold, he died on the ninth day before the Ides of December in the year 1077.

Consult Ughelli in *Italian Sacred History* and in the additions to Ciaconius’s *Lives of the Pontiffs and Cardinals*.

39. Baronius, under the year 1072, number 34, asserts that “Blessed Peter died in the sixty-sixth year of his age, since he himself testifies in a letter to the Senate that he was born five years after the death of Emperor Otto III, namely in the year of our Lord 1006, for it has been demonstrated above that the same emperor died at the beginning of the second year after 1000.”

But we have nowhere been able to find this letter of Blessed Peter to the Senate in the accurate edition of his works and letters.

On the contrary, Blessed Peter, writing to Alexander II after his election—therefore toward the end of 1061 or the beginning of the following year—describes his old age and says that “the head that until then had been scattered with white hairs was already becoming snowy with the whiteness of a swan.” Yet he would have been only fifty-five years old, or at most just completing his fifty-fifth year.

What if he meant that he had been born five years after the death of Emperor Otto II? That would be the year 988. In that case, he would have had the swan-white hair and the other signs of old age mentioned above in the seventy-third year of his life, and would have died in the eighty-fourth year, worn out by age, as we have already stated from the *Acts*.

The same Baronius concludes the notable works of Blessed Peter that he has recounted in the aforesaid number 34 with these words:

“Thus God, in this most lamentable age, when a flood of flesh had grown so great that it threatened to overwhelm the Church, gave the world such a man that, by the example of his most austere life, by the preaching of his word, and by his writings, he might dry up so great a corruption and at the same time fight against the Simoniac heresy, which was raging everywhere with impunity.”

Thus far Baronius.

40. Concerning the translation of the sacred body, Ughelli reports the following in his additions to Ciaconius:

“At Faenza, torches burn around the tomb of this holy man, and the people gather. The following inscription, effaced by the use of lights, recalls the translation of his body.””

“In the year of our Lord 1354, on the thirteenth day of April, the body of Saint Peter Damian of Ravenna, doctor in sacred Scripture and bishop of Ostia, legate of the apostolic see, of the Order of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana, was translated into this present ark by the Reverend Father Lord Matthew of Callio, abbot here.”

The following verses are found beneath the same tomb:

After thirteen hundred and fifty-four years had passed,

When the third of April had risen after the tenth,

The clergy translated you, learned in the sacred page,

Bishop of Ostia, whom the cardinalate adorns.

O Peter Damian, the Cross blesses you

In the Order of Fonte Avellana; you also became at last

A legate of the apostolic see, and now this stone encloses you.

Now Matthew, abbot, born of Callio, presides.

41. The same Ughelli adds another inscription, displayed on a certain column of the principal church of Faenza. It testifies that the people of Faenza counted Blessed Peter among the patrons of their city. It reads as follows:

“When the danger of slaughter, destruction, and flames from the French threatened the city, the entire people of Faenza vowed that, if almighty God turned away the ruin, they would celebrate the feast days of Saints Savinus, Emilianus, Terentius, and Peter Damian no less solemnly than it was customary and required to celebrate Sundays. 1512.”

[Col. 0113]

LIFE OF BLESSED PETER DAMIAN, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, by John, a monk, his disciple,

from two manuscripts, one from Ravenna and one from Faenza.

[Col. 0113C]

To Lord Liprandus, prior, and the other elders of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana: John.

A remarkable work, Fathers, which it has pleased you to impose upon my inadequacy, is something whose difficulty for my abilities and disproportion to my talent I myself clearly recognize. Yet because I do not presume to refuse anything to your command, although the dullness of my understanding avoids committing the deeds of so great a man to an inept pen, lest, while undertaking matters beyond it, it seem to provoke the reader more to nausea than to reading, nevertheless, trusting in your holy prayers and in the worthy merits of that pious father of ours, Peter Damian—to whose deeds you summon my obedience—I will dutifully undertake to obey your commands.

I myself had judged it more prudent to make temporary notes of these matters in whatever rough style I could, so that later, properly clarified by more skilled writers, they might usefully reach the knowledge of those yet to come, rather than, by excessively avoiding the mark of incompetence, leave them entirely untouched. Otherwise, after a short time they might be covered by the darkness of oblivion and slip entirely from everyone’s memory, bringing no small danger upon me.

For since it is evident to all that no one who knows the deeds of illustrious men may conceal them in cowardly silence without the stain of guilt, how much more will it be clear that I would be liable to no small offense if, although I remained his constant companion almost until the end, I preferred to pass over in silence the wondrous deeds of so great a father rather than make them known?

Of the matters I am about to relate, I remember receiving some from his own mouth; some from one of my fellow disciples who had lived in his company more familiarly before me; and some I heard from a certain relative of his, a serious and honorable man, concerning events that had preceded his conversion. The rest I myself recorded from direct personal observation.

But now let the point of our discourse turn toward the beginning of his history.

CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the parents and childhood of the blessed man.

A man of God, then, Peter, surnamed Dannanus, a by no means unknown citizen of the very famous city of Ravenna, thoroughly instructed in the liberal disciplines, after he had crossed a little beyond the fork in Pythagoras’ summit-road, wisely abandoned the left-hand path he had begun and prudently seized the right-hand way. Inflamed by divine grace amid the very fervor of youth, he renounced worldly pomp and eagerly hastened toward monastic perfection.

Born, to be sure, of respectable parents, he began to be beset by adverse circumstances from the very cradle of his birth. For when his mother, already weary of her children, and with her house filled with heirs, had given birth to him as the last of them, one of the children, who had by then grown fairly large, complained and cried out:

“Shame! Look, we are already so numerous that we scarcely fit in this house; and how badly a multitude of heirs agrees with a narrow inheritance!”

At these words his mother, overcome by vehement indignation and inflamed by the zeal of feminine jealousy, clasped her hands and loudly declared that she was wretched and unworthy to live any longer. Immediately—if I may put it so—she weaned him before he had scarcely been nursed, and, uttering certain evil imprecations against herself, drove him entirely away, as though she would never again touch him with her hands. Thus she emancipated her son before he had learned to live, and disinherited him from the possession of his mother’s breast—the only possession he could have held.

> **[Col. 0115D] Note:** “With her house filled with heirs.” Two sons are soon mentioned among them; but he himself mentions two daughters, or sisters of blessed Peter, in Letter 14 of Book VIII, which he wrote to them when they were widows, exhorting them to continence. They are called Rodelinda and Sufficia. He mentions the brothers Damian and Marinus in Book II, Letter 14.

When, therefore, that tiny creature, deprived of every service of nourishing care, was growing black from hunger and cold alike, and a thin sound—not, I should say, a voice, but almost a hiss—issued hoarsely from his little breast, which still scarcely trembled with life, a woman of a certain priest, who was almost a member of the household of his native home, arrived. With severe reproach, insofar as she was able, she rebuked the inhuman hardness of his mother.

“Madam,” she said, “is this the conduct of a Christian mother, which is not found even in a tigress or lioness? Those animals nourish their cubs, while we cast away from our wombs those whom we have brought forth, though they were made in the image of God? And perhaps this child, who is now being thrown away in this fashion, if he reaches the growth of maturity, will hold no lowly place among his own. Take care, too, lest you be rightly judged a child-killer, since you refuse to be the mother of one whose mother you are.”

> **[Col. 0115D] Note:** “The priest’s wife.” She is soon called a sinful little woman. The abuse of priests who at that time kept concubines as though they were wives is discussed below. Fortunatus and Rubeus call her a *pellex* (“concubine”); Flaminius calls her “a certain woman.” Blessed Peter, *Opusculum* VI, chapter 18, says: “The priest Marinus was not ashamed publicly to possess his wife as though she were legitimate.”

The priest’s wife thus performed the office of a priest: she softened the mother’s feelings toward compassion and restored the dying child to life. At once, then, the brave woman freed her arms from her flowing garments; she stretched the child’s limbs out on a skin laid near the fire; and, rubbing the little body all over, she drove away a considerable amount of *songia*.

> **[Col. 0116D] Note:** “*Songia* was driven away.” Rather, we think *rongia* should be read, that is, scabies. In Italian, *rogna*; in French, *rogne*; in Spanish, *rona*.

You would have seen the tender limbs absorbing the warmth of the melting fat, growing red as their vital heat returned, and the brightness of raw infancy suddenly blooming again in him. Here it should be noted that his mother had become a Herodias, while that woman had become an Elijah; thus, through the efforts of the sinful little woman, one despaired of was snatched back from the jaws of death, and the mother was freed from child-murder.

When she realized that she was now a mother, she recalled to the embrace of tender love, with the feelings of a mother’s heart, the child whom she had harshly rejected as though he were a stranger, and she did not cease to provide him diligently with every care of nourishment. The boy enjoyed this care until he was weaned; but shortly afterward, deprived of both parents, he was prematurely bereft of them while still within his childhood.

Left, therefore, to the care of his brothers—O incomprehensible mystery of divine providence!—one of them, who beneath a sheep’s clothing concealed a savage character among the rest, who were endowed with respectable morals, took him under his protection, by a deceitful show of kindness, to raise him in place of a father. Pretending to adopt him as a co-heir, he instead subjected him to a cruel slavery as though he were a purchased servant. His wife clung to him as his companion, differing from her husband’s cruelty in no respect of compassionate feeling.

Both of them, therefore, attacking the innocent boy with united savagery and treating him with a grim and stepmother-like gaze, impaired his precarious strength with harsh afflictions. They continually supported him with the food of slaves and with whatever was more suitable for pigs and for a malicious sour wine; he went barefoot and unkempt in his clothing; he was beaten with blows; and he was subjected to frequent strikes of fists and heels. At length, when he had grown fairly large under such unjust burdens, he was driven out to tend pigs and was indiscriminately subjected to the other conditions of slaves.

What should be considered in all this except that the Lord was allowing his soldier to be harshly afflicted so that he might learn to be more strictly trained for the campaign of spiritual warfare, in order that his courage might afterward endure every difficult task more robustly because he himself had experienced such things from childhood?

Here, too, we think it worthwhile to relate briefly something noteworthy.

## CHAPTER II. His devotion toward his deceased father, his progress in learning, and his mortification of himself.

[Col. 0116D]

One day, while he was still suffering the aforementioned hunger, he happened by chance to find a coin. Suddenly, as though he had become rich, he rejoiced and began for a long time to turn over in his mind what he could most suitably purchase with it. Since he lacked every pleasant thing, a sweet appetite was drawing the boy’s mind toward all manner of soft delights.

When this deliberation continued at length and he was uncertain what he ought to choose, he was finally inspired by God and said:

“What is this that I am turning over in my mind? Whatever of these things I take, its pleasure will certainly not last long. It is better, then, that I give it to a priest, who may offer a sacrifice to God for my father.”

What could be wiser than the simplicity of this boy? What more frugal than this needy orphan? He rejected everything he recognized as perishable and chose only what he hoped would remain forever. What should we think this was except a certain foreshadowing of things to come—namely, that he would despise temporal things that flatter through desire for eternal things?

To return to the order of the narrative: after the Lord, who does not abandon the care of his own, had rescued him from the calamities just described, it pleased Him mercifully to withdraw him, almost consumed by the attacks of the wicked, and place him at last in the bosom of another brother of his, named Damian, to be comforted and cherished.

> **[Col. 0117D] Note:** “Named Damian.” This Damian was his brother and later became archpriest of Ravenna. Peter wrote to him in Letter 2 of Book V under this heading: “To the lord Damian, dearest brother, Peter the sinner, a monk, whatever a servant and son may be.” He later calls him “the sweetest and dearest father and lord in Christ,” confesses his own negligence to him, and asks for his prayers. The same Damian is said to have become a monk after having been an archpriest in Book II, Letter 14. He mentions another Damian, his nephew, in Letter 11 of Book I, addressed to Pope Alexander II, and in Letter 29 of Book VI, addressed to the monk Stephen, where he calls him the son of his sister. He wrote Letters 21 and 22 of the same Book VI to this man after he had become a monk.

This man embraced him with sufficiently dear affection and devoted such great diligence to his care that he seemed to surpass a father’s love. Although the boy was already fairly grown, he handed him over to the letters for instruction.

> **[Col. 0118D] Note:** “He handed him over to the letters.” He says in Letter 30 of Book VI that he was “established in the city of Faenza for the study of letters”; but in Letter 16 of Book V he says that, “while he was in the very flower of adolescence, when new puberty was clothing his face and the heat of lust was inflaming his flesh, he pursued the studies of the liberal arts near the town of Parma.” He also mentions these studies in Book II, Letter 17. He calls Ivo his teacher in Book VI, Letter 17. Rubeus likewise reports that his studies were completed in the places mentioned.

He also subsequently trained him in the liberal studies. In these he was found to be so teachable and industrious that he was considered remarkable even by his own teachers. When he had completed his learning and become skilled in every liberal science, he soon began to teach others, with a crowd of clients flocking from every direction to hear of his learning.

Meanwhile, as he was exalted by popular favor and enriched by an abundance of wealth, he could almost have been drawn away by the enticements of worldly pomp or entangled by the allurements of sexual pleasure. But since no one belonging to the number of the elect can be wholly diminished, he was immediately forestalled by divine regard and began to reason with himself:

“Why should I take pleasure in present things, as the flesh suggests and age demands? Surely I ought not to cling to these perishable things, but rather, renouncing them, provide for better ones. Yet if I promise that I shall do this later, why do I not now strive to do what is much dearer and much more acceptable to God, while my age is vigorous and while prosperity delights me?”

From then onward he gradually began to be withdrawn from worldly studies and girded for divine service. Although in outward appearance he still seemed to cling to fleeting things, in the entire affection of his mind he aspired to eternal goods. Under soft garments he put on a hair shirt; he devoted himself diligently to fasts, vigils, and prayers. Since, in the heat of youth, he was sharply pressed by carnal goads, he would rise from his bed in the middle of the night and immerse himself in the waters of a river. He remained there naked until his chilled limbs grew stiff and the harmful warmth had departed.

Afterward he would return and, going around all the venerable places while singing psalms, complete the entire Psalter before the night office. He also devoted himself constantly to almsgiving for the poor, feeding them at frequent banquets, and rejoiced to minister to them with his own hands as though they were Christ.

## CHAPTER III. Through victory over himself he is freed from grave danger to his life.

Meanwhile, I think it should not be passed over that which, as I do not doubt, will benefit the edification of many.

One day he was dining privately, and no one was reclining with him except a certain blind prebendary, who was accustomed, as was his daily practice, to sit beside him as his regular table-companion. It happened that at that time there was no more than a single loaf of wheat bread. This was therefore set before him alone; but there was nothing available to give his table-companion, who was not accustomed to being fed on foods different from his own.

The other man, therefore, was set a household-servant’s loaf, an inferior bread made from second-grade flour. He looked upon it with displeasure and took it badly. Gradually, however, fear entered him, and he began to think within himself:

“Is Christ inferior to me at my table? Am I to eat like a lord, with fine and delicate bread, while he eats the bread of my servants?”

As he turned over many such thoughts in his heart, the idea occurred to him that he should exchange the other man’s bread for his own, and his own for the other’s.

What, then, was he to do? Where should he turn? Should he take the other man’s bread? Shame held him back. Should he eat his own? Conscience gnawed at him. What more need be said? At last the flesh prevailed, and his mind, having struggled feebly, succumbed.

Both therefore began to eat: the one, as lord and master of the table, the bright, fine bread; the other, after the fashion of clients or slaves, the coarse bread. But as he ate, fear gradually overtook him, and an extreme horror shook the inner parts of his whole body. For he was afraid that the divine judgment against him would awaken, and he certainly suspected that sudden vengeance of just severity was impending—and so it happened.

A fishbone became dangerously lodged in his throat, and no effort whatsoever could draw it inward. He swallowed his food deliberately, but it would not descend; he cleared his throat, but it remained just the same; he tried to spit it out, but the affliction, fixed in place, nevertheless remained immovable.

Yet he was ashamed to say what he was suffering within. A hidden hook held him and, like an unwary fish, dragged him by the throat toward death. His distress increased on every side, and he was terrified not so much by death as by the disgrace of dying. He would have preferred weapons to pierce him rather than be defiled by the shameful death brought on by a greedy throat.

His breath came in anxious gasps, and the darkness of grief swirled around his eyes. Why delay with further details? At last he appealed to Christ and clearly recognized that he was unequal to Him—not in bread, but in power. He hurriedly set his own morsel before the poor man and placed it before him by a reciprocal exchange.

And O God, easily appeased in the face of our wickedness! At the very first taste of the bread he had received, that plague passed away, and the obstructing fragment fell, clearing the passage within. Thus the delicate bread became a wound to him, while the coarse and hard bread became medicine. He changed the food, and the snare that had cruelly bound him was loosened.

He laid aside his pride and perceived the heavenly medicine of humility and the healing of heavenly mercy. When he realized that he had obtained this remedy so wonderfully, he immediately burst forth in praise of his liberator with words such as these:

“Blessed is almighty God, who helps those in danger and turns grief into joy; who tramples arrogance underfoot, humbles the proud, and grants mercy, so that He Himself may invite us to mercy: ‘Be merciful,’ He says, ‘just as your heavenly Father is merciful’” (Luke 6).

He then joyfully related to everyone the danger of his tribulation, which until then he had concealed out of shame. What the force of pain had been unable to accomplish, the greatness of his joy extracted. He himself, indeed, inserted this event in his writings, as well as the other incident concerning his exposure when newly born, which I related above.

## CHAPTER IV. His desire to renounce the world and his entry into religious life.

But, to let our narrative return now to its proper course, this soldier of Christ, raising the flame of his heart toward higher things through continual aspirations, ardently desired to accomplish what he had conceived in his mind: namely, to renounce this world completely and assume the habit of spiritual warfare.

Nevertheless, he absolutely refused to do this in his native region, lest the affection of relatives or friends prepare some obstacle harmful to him as he pursued perfection. While he was meditating on this and asking through continual prayers that an avenue of salvation might be opened to him by the Lord, behold, two brothers from the hermitage of the Holy Cross at Fonte Avellana arrived, having been sent there.

> **[Col. 0119D] Note:** “From the hermitage of the Holy Cross at Fonte Avellana.” It is often called simply Fonte Avellana. We have discussed it above.

When, by divine direction, he encountered them and began to enjoy the long-desired association with them, he revealed the secret of his heart. They listened gladly to what he disclosed and, strengthening him in the same purpose with pious counsels, inflamed him further.

He therefore asked whether their holy abbot, whose praiseworthy reputation had already come to his knowledge, would receive him if he wished to enter his community. When they assented and urged him to do this, he promised that, with God’s help, he would come to them as soon as possible so that he might fulfill his desire.

He offered them a silver cup, asking them to take it to the lord abbot when they received him. But when they saw the size of the vessel, they complained of its weight, claimed that it would hinder their longer journey, and said that they could not burden themselves with so heavy a load or impede their extended journey.

When he persisted in asking them to accept him, they said to him:

“If, then, you press us so insistently and will not permit us to depart entirely without a gift from you, provide something else of this sort which we can carry for your devotion more lightly and without inconvenience on the journey.”

Hearing this, he was greatly astonished and amazed, and began to say to himself:

“Who are these men who, although they appear poor and needy, despise the things of this world so thoroughly that they refuse to undertake even the smallest exertion to carry an excellent vessel? May I not truly call them free, and truly blessed, since they are seen to have shaken the yoke of ambition from their necks with such strength and to have trampled down the vain pomp of the world with such greatness of mind?”

Thus greatly edified by this, he was inflamed still more intensely with contempt for worldly pomp.

From that point onward, anxious about his firm promise, he first wished to test whether he would be able to endure the hardship of the cell he had heard about. He entered a certain cell, where he diligently exercised himself for forty days, in imitation of the regulations of that hermitage.

> **[Col. 0120D] Note:** “He entered a certain cell.” “The cell of the monastery of Saint Mary on the shore of the Adriatic,” says Fortunatus from Dante, Book V of his *History of Camaldoli*.

Strengthened considerably by this experience, he no longer feared that eremitical austerity; rather, he began to desire it eagerly with his whole heart. When the desired time arrived—namely, when he could undertake the matter suitably without the knowledge of any of his people—he took from his property whatever he wished and secretly set out.

When he reached the hermitage, he disclosed the desire of his heart to those elders and devoutly asked to be received into their fellowship. His wholesome request was immediately granted with joy, and he was entrusted to one of the brothers for instruction, according to the custom for novices.

After leading him to the cell, the brother, as he had been ordered, stripped him of his linen garments and clothed him in a hair shirt, then brought him back to the abbot. Without delay the abbot ordered that a cowl be put over him.

Astonished at this, he said within himself:

“What has happened to me? Should I not first have tested this discipline and afterward approached, of my own accord, to ask to receive this habit? Can I obey when I have been taken by surprise so suddenly?”

While he was thinking this, he immediately came to himself, began to rebuke himself sharply, and said:

“If circumstances required you to offer your head to be struck off for Christ, would you flee in the same way or stubbornly resist? Did you not promise a little earlier that you would endure everything steadfastly for Christ? Why are you not afraid to succumb so quickly and feebly? But perhaps, judging that first course harmful, you may admit this one more willingly, so that the more harshly you endure it, the more favorably you may receive your recompense.”

## CHAPTER V. His progress in the virtues, especially humility, prayer, mortification, and obedience.

Recalled by these self-reproaches, he immediately submitted to the elder’s command and obeyed calmly and gladly.

Once he had assumed the habit, he was instantly inflamed with such fervor that, disregarding care of the body, he sought only the things of the spirit and compelled the flesh with all his strength to serve the spirit. He rejected everything delicate or costly and sought whatever was rough and despised.

You can observe what I mean in the following example. Once, when he was about to travel with his teacher, he was ordered to put on a softer scapular and mount a horse finer than the one he desired. He began to beg his teacher earnestly not to command him to do this, since he recoiled from it as something unbecoming.

But his teacher did not wish to yield to his request, lest he seem to despise the disciple whom he loved as an only son if he allowed him to proceed with him in such an unkempt condition, contrary to his own desire.

The disciple, however, felt quite differently and turned the whole matter in another direction. He was extremely ashamed to appear handsome and well-groomed before worldly people, lest he, who had once seemed to renounce the world, be thought still carnally to seek worldly pomp.

Nevertheless, he preferred to endure that disgrace rather than incur the reputation of disobedience, which he feared intensely. For, as he himself related, it seemed to him that whoever saw him riding well-groomed would point at him, mock him as a worldly man, and apply to him not the name of monk but of bridegroom.

His face was therefore covered with such deep blushes that he could scarcely raise his head or direct the gaze of his eyes toward anyone.

When they returned and had reached the monastery of Saint Vincent, to which the nearby rock gave the name Petra Pertusa, the servant of the Lord could scarcely bear any longer the shameful adornment of the elegant garment.

> **[Col. 0121D] Note:** “To the monastery of Saint Vincent.” Blessed Peter discusses this monastery in Letter 32 of Book VI and implies that he presided over it with supreme authority, prescribing a Lenten fast and other practices.

Finding an opportunity to remain there for a little while, the teacher continued the journey toward the hermitage. Peter, however, obtained and put on another scapular, humbler in its weave and color.

> **[Col. 0121D] Note:** “A scapular humbler in weave and color.” He discusses the humble clothing of monks in *Opusculum* 12 and that of ecclesiastics in *Opusculum* 29.

Thus freed, as though from a massive burden under which he had until then been weighed down, he quickly followed his teacher and returned to his own monastery. He could not bear to revisit them while wearing elegant clothing if they were using shabby garments, since they desired to be adorned by their conduct rather than by their clothes.

To return to what came before: this soldier of Christ, of good character, immediately began to wear himself down with such labors of fasts, vigils, and other afflictions that those who had already been trained by long practice were forced, when they observed his conduct and life, to despise their own achievements.

While he strove to banish the deep-rooted vices completely, he eagerly sought with all his strength to complete every kind of moral exercise practiced in that place through tireless labor.

> **[Col. 0121D] Note:** “The institution of the place.” Two treatises by blessed Peter are extant on the order of the hermits and the resources of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, and likewise on the institutions of his congregation: *Opuscula* 14 and 15 of Volume III. The present account appears to be excerpted from them.

The institution of the place was recognized as follows: two men, living in separate cells, stood day and night as though in battle formation, engaged in spiritual combat, and did not relax their arms. Girded with the unconquerable weapons of psalmody, prayer, reading, abstinence, and obedience, they fought without truce against the aerial powers.

Their rule of abstinence was this: on four days of the week they were content with bread and water; on Wednesday and Friday they took a little legume, which each cooked in his own cell. On fasting days no one was permitted to take bread according to his own desire, but only what the prescribed measure provided.

As for the use of wine, why should I speak of it, when it is reported that wine was entirely absent there at that time except for the sacrifice, or perhaps for the sick?

They practiced going barefoot throughout the hermitage at all times; in their cells they did not even put on leggings.

> **[Col. 0121D] Note:** “They did not put on leggings.” *Opusculum* 14 reports that they were accustomed to remain with bare legs.

They devoted themselves also to the other spiritual exercises: scourgings, *metanoeae*—μετάνοιαι, “repentances,” here meaning prostrations or the bending of the body to the ground—*palmatae*, and prolonged extensions of the arms, diligently according to the fervor and strength that each possessed.

> **[Col. 0121D] Note:** “Metanoeae.” *Metanoea*, μετάνοια, means repentance; here it signifies prostration, or inclination of the body to the ground. Thus blessed Peter writes in the *Life of Saint Dominic Loricatus* that Dominic performed a thousand *metanoeae* while reciting one Psalter, and in the aforementioned *Opusculum* 14 he says that each brother performed seven hundred *metanoeae* for a deceased brother. Saint Simeon Stylites, according to Theodoret, chapter 26: “Philotheus made very many inclinations every day; when these had been counted up to 1,244, the exhausted observer stopped counting.” Consult Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers*. [Read Cajetan’s Scholium, p. 240, vol. II of the *Opera horarum*.]

> **[Col. 0122D] Note:** “Palmatae.” *Palmatae*, so called from the palm of the hand, are performed when someone strikes his palms against the ground. Thus blessed Peter writes in Book VI, Letter 27, to Peter Cerebrosus, a monk: “A cuirass is a man clothed against the flesh: it encircles limbs torn apart by iron rings; with effort he performs *metanoeae* and repeatedly strikes his palms against the pavement.” Burchard, Book XIX, chapters 17 and 25, says: “One day of penance can be redeemed by twenty *palmatae*.” Some understand this as blows inflicted on the palms with a rod.

> **[Col. 0122D] Note:** “With prolonged extensions of the arms.” Blessed Peter says in the *Life of Saint Dominic Loricatus*: “He recited twelve psalms twenty-six times every day without any interval at all, in one continuous effort, with his arms extended in the form of a cross; another young brother held his arms raised from the beginning to the end of the Psalter, so that his hands often touched the wooden ceiling of the cell.”

They also observed this custom of vigils: when the signal of the hour sounded, they completed the entire Psalter before dawn, after the night office. Peter, however, anticipating this common signal by keeping vigil much longer, strove to spend whatever remained of the night after the night office in continuous watchfulness, lest he seem to break the common rule, which he tried to extend even to things that had not been commanded.

For he knew that what was prescribed by a public rule would be more sacred than what was paid out under a private arrangement, and that voluntary gifts, however great, could in no way absolve one who offered them from fulfilling the command of the rule. Rather, one must diligently perform what the rule has established. It is permissible to add anything through devotion, but not to remove the institutions of one’s predecessors by one’s own practices. Voluntary additions may rightly increase what is required, but they cannot at all excuse what belongs to the rule.

Finally, while he spent nights in such vigils, he contracted such an affliction of the brain that he could scarcely recover even with a little sleep. After he had recovered from the illness he had incurred through the help of God and the application of medicine, he learned to act with such discretion that he strove both to avoid the torpor of excessive relaxation and to restrain the course of undue haste through prudent moderation.

While he maintained the discipline of his cell with rigid severity and, after completing his accustomed psalmody, prayers, and devotions, devoted himself assiduously to reading and meditation, he became distinguished by such knowledge of the divine Scriptures as he had not previously possessed of secular learning.

## CHAPTER VI. The fame of his holiness spreads far and wide, and he is compelled to watch over the salvation of others.

[Col. 0123C]

When the time had come for the lamp of the Lord’s house, raised upon its lampstand, to shine for everyone, he began, at his teacher’s command, to offer words of exhortation to those few brothers.

> **[Col. 0123D] Note:** “Those few brothers.” Usually about twenty monks, more or less, lived there; but including lay brothers and servants, the number mentioned above was thirty-five.

As his reputation spread ever more widely and grew, the venerable Guido, abbot of Pomposa, a most holy man, sent his envoys to this abbot and asked that, out of love for the brothers, he send Peter to his monastery and permit him to remain there for some time. He was to distribute the nourishment of the sacred word to the brothers who requested it.

His pious request, made in the charity he sought, was not frustrated by God’s providence. Peter was sent there, where a crowd of brothers was said to approach the number of one hundred.

> **[Col. 0124C] Note:** “The venerable Guido.” Saint Guido, or Guy, surnamed Stambiatus, died on April 2, 1046, but is chiefly commemorated on March 31. His body is preserved at Speyer on the Rhine, in the cathedral church dedicated to him.

> **[Col. 0124D] Note:** “The abbot of Pomposa.” “Pomposa,” says Ferrarius under March 31, “is a village with a monastery and a distinguished abbey in the territory of Ravenna, between Ravenna and Adria, about fifteen Roman miles from Ravenna, and approximately the same distance from Comacchio.” In Letter 6 of Book VI, blessed Peter “sends a gift to the monks of Pomposa and asks them to pray for him in death, as they do for their own.” He also dedicated *Opusculum* 13, *On the Perfection of Monks*, “To O . . . the abbot of Pomposa and his holy community.”

After he had been kept there for nearly two years and had brought no small fruit to the Lord, the faithful laborer, from the seed of the word he had sown, he received a command from his abbot, accompanied by the obligation of obedience, that he should return to him. Although bound by the prayers of many, he could not be detained any longer. Like a man full of God, entirely subject to obedience and afraid not to heed his teacher, he hurried back to him.

He often used to relate this to us whenever the occasion of speaking seemed to demand it, so that by his example, as though from close at hand, he might provoke us more effectively to obedience. If it ever happened that a command was given to him with the added word “obedience,” that word immediately shook his inner being with such terror that no difficulty in the assigned task could delay him from carrying it out.

When the period he had been permitted to spend with his fellow brothers had ended, he was again ordered, for the same purpose for which he had gone to Pomposa, to proceed to the monastery of Saint Vincent, which we mentioned above. The more abundantly that monastery appeared to flourish in its multitude of monks and breadth of resources, the more narrowly it declared that the monastic rule of discipline was to be observed there.

He also remained there for some time.

> **[Col. 0124D] Note:** “He also remained there for some time, by no means idle, and so forth.” We stated above that he wrote there, around the year 1040, the *Life of Saint Romuald*.

By no means idle, he did not cease cultivating the Lord’s vineyard until, with the Lord assisting him, he had produced an abundant fruit of his service.

## CHAPTER VII. He is made prior; after many monasteries have been built, he enlarges the eremitical discipline.

[Col. 0124C]

But when his master observed such prudence and zeal in him, he rejoiced that he had received so energetic a disciple, to whom he could safely entrust the governance of the hermitage. Having therefore taken counsel with the disciples, he commanded him—though he denied and refused—to undertake the administration of the hermitage after him.

After his master’s departure, when he assumed control of the place [Note: “[Col. 0124D] When he assumed control of the place.” This has been established above as occurring before the year 1044.], he enlarged it considerably both in spiritual and temporal cultivation [Note: “[Col. 0124D] He enlarged it considerably.” The property he acquired for the monastery is explained by Blessed Peter in *Opusculum* 14, as we indicated above.]. And because divine grace had kindled his mind toward a richer harvest of souls, he began to seek out other places where he might gather a company of monks to serve God.

Thus, in the diocese of Camerino [Note: “[Col. 0125D] Thus, in the diocese of Camerino.” Camerino is a city in the March of Ancona, at the foot of Mount Apennine. At that time its bishop was Romuald, to whom Blessed Peter is said by Ughellus to have addressed a surviving letter. Blessed Peter describes the monasteries founded by Saint Romuald in this diocese in chapter 12 of his *Life*.], as a careful investigator he found a suitable place for hermits’ dwellings, beside his own neighboring crag; and there, after gathering the brothers and founding and arranging an oratory, he appointed a prior under whom they were to serve God. He then proceeded again to investigate another site.

Accordingly, he reached Mount Pregium [Note: “[Col. 0125D] To Mount Pergium.” Blessed Peter writes as follows in book VI, letter 30, to the monk Teuzo: “In the monastery at Perugia, namely that of the holy Savior, which I myself recently governed, there had been a certain monk,” and so forth. Was this at Mount Pregium? The Camaldolese monastery now situated in the city of Perugia, dedicated to Saint Severus, is said by Crispoltus in *Perugia Augusta*, book I, chapter 18, to have once stood outside the gate of Saint Peter.] in the Perugian territory, and there he founded other dwellings for hermits, where he found, as they said, a certain cell in which Blessed Romuald had once lived.

After placing other brothers in that location, he moved once more to another place and found, in the territory of Faenza, a suitable site called [Col. 0125B] Gamonium [Note: “[Col. 0125D] Which is called Gamonium.” Gamonium is called Gamunium by Flaminius, Ganvinium by Fortunius, and Gaviumum by Rubeus, who says that according to some it is now called Cavina. In *Opusculum* 44, *On the Fast of Saturday*, Blessed Peter writes: “For the brothers established in the hermitage of Gamagnum”; and his letter 31 in book VI was written to the hermits of the monastery of Gamugnum of Saint Barnabas. These references appear to concern this place.], where, after preparing dwellings, he installed others to serve God.

He also built near this place a monastery called Acereta [Note: “[Col. 0126D] A monastery called Acereta.” This is encountered by those returning from Faenza to Gubbio as their first stopping-place, as is said below. See also chapter 9.]. He built another in the territory of Rimini, at a place called Murcianum [Note: “[Col. 0126D] At a place called Murcianum.” Murcianum, still a village, is found not far from the sea, almost on the borders of Romagna, toward the Duchy of Urbino.].

He rejoiced to devote himself constantly to such pursuits, seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Philippians II). Although this prudent servant of God was zealous in carrying out these works, he nevertheless took care to visit frequently the beloved place and community of the Holy Cross at Fonte Avellana, which he loved above all others as something uniquely his own, wherever he happened to go.

He certainly could not forget those with whom he had lived from the beginning of his conversion, remembering that they had been entrusted to him by his master’s command. Yet he did not permit the other disciples whom he had gathered in various places to be deprived of his more abundant visitation. Sometimes by his presence, sometimes by letters, and sometimes by sending one of the spiritual disciples attached to him, he visited them all in turn with paternal care.

Nor did he cease to extend this solicitude only to his own foundations, but also to many other places, both monasteries and houses of canons, as the common father of all, according as each appeared to require it.

But let us set these matters aside for a little and now speak of some of the things that the Lord is said to have done through him. In reporting them, with God’s help I shall take the utmost care not to mingle any falsehood of my own, faithfully following the account of those who said either that they themselves had been present at these events, or that they had received the account from those who had been present, or even that the events being reported had taken place in relation to them.

## CHAPTER VIII. Through the merits of the blessed man, water is twice changed into wine.

One day, while he was staying in his cell at the aforesaid Gamonium [Note: “[Col. 0126D] At the aforesaid Gamonium.” Flaminius wrongly attributes this miracle to Acereta, whereas the author means Gamonium.], he ordered the brother who served him to bring him drinking water from the spring. The brother immediately went and hastened to carry out the command. When the master tasted it, it was found to be wine. He therefore began to rebuke the disciple for having brought him wine instead of water.

But when the disciple insisted that he had drawn from the spring what he had offered, the master handed the same drink to him and ordered him to test by tasting it what it was, so that, with himself as witness, he might be convicted of deceit. Although the disciple tasted it and it had the flavor of wine, he nevertheless, being fully conscious of the truth, maintained that he had drawn that drink from the spring.

Since he was not believed, another brother was sent to the same spring, and he was ordered to observe his steps so that he could not similarly deceive them. Drawing a full vessel immediately from the same spring, the brother hurried back and handed the drink he had drawn to the master. But when this too was tasted, it was equally truly found to be an excellent kind of wine.

The brothers who were with him also tasted it, discovered that it was excellent wine, and all together praised God with joy. Peter immediately prostrated himself before them and begged—or rather, under obedience, forbade and commanded them—not to reveal to any mortal, while he remained in the flesh, what they had learned had happened.

Consequently, the matter could not come to our knowledge before his death. Only after we had celebrated his burial at Faenza and, on our return, had stayed at his aforesaid monastery of Acereta as our first lodging, did we happen to learn there, from certain brothers of that monastery and also from members of the aforementioned hermitage who had gathered there at the time, not only this event but also several others that, by the Lord’s working, we shall relate in connection with this miracle.

## CHAPTER IX. Soldiers cannot forcibly draw the holy teacher’s wine from the cask, but afterward a devout pilgrim succeeds.

On one occasion the man of God had a wine cask stored near one of his chapels. [Note: “[Col. 0126D] A wine cask.” In the glosses formerly appended to Cyril, *boûtis* (Βούττις) means a large cask, and *bouttion* (Βούττιον) a small cask. Hence the Latin words *buttis* or *butis*, which also occur in Marculfus’s formulas, and *butto*, or *buto*, meaning a silver vessel, in Anastasius’s accounts of Leo III and Leo IV. Here the word is used for a cask.]

It happened one day that a troop of soldiers passed near the chapel. As they were burning with thirst, they asked the priest whether he could provide them with wine. He replied that there was absolutely no wine there except one vat belonging to Lord Peter [Note: “[Col. 0127D] Except one vat.” *Tina* occurs in the *Acts of Saint Thyrsus and His Companions*, 28 January, p. 820, no. 25; in the *Life of Saint Philibert*, 20 August, it is written *tonna*, where it is added that this is the name for a wine vessel; the word *tina* is also attributed to Festus and Varro.], which he himself did not dare to touch.

When he heard this, the man in charge of the others, who, as they say, bore a grudge against the same man of God, replied: “If it belongs to Lord Peter, then I shall drink from it all the more willingly.” Immediately he ordered those serving him to draw wine from it and pour it for him and his companions.

They eagerly rushed to perform this service, as men of that sort are accustomed to do. But when they pulled out the small stopper [Note: “[Col. 0128D] But when they pulled out the small stopper.” The *tenellus* is understood to be the stopper at the mouth of the cask, in place of which a tap is fitted.], they drew absolutely no wine. They turned to another opening and found the same thing [Col. 0127B]. Then they opened every aperture—and, O marvel!—the entrances to the cask stood open, yet the liquid within remained concealed as though it were something solid.

They therefore opened the upper vent and carefully searched to see whether any wine was contained inside. They found the vessel half a palm deep, but empty [Note: “[Col. 0128D] An empty vessel.” Three editions read *semum* for “empty”; perhaps *semotum*, *semiplenum*, or something similar should be read.].

Amazed at this occurrence, yet still supposing that some obstacle might be hidden inside and preventing the liquid from flowing out, they thrust individual rods through the open openings. When they withdrew them, they saw that the rods were wet, but the wine nevertheless remained enclosed within.

The power that had once suspended the waters of the Red Sea like walls on the right and left for the Israelite people who were treading its depths (Exodus XIV) had restrained the flow of this liquid. He who then plunged the hostile ranks of the adversaries forcefully into the waters, so that the footsteps of the righteous might not be hindered, now wonderfully opposed the insolence of these men, lest they harm his servant.

For just as the savage hunger of those men could not be satisfied by the spoils of plunder after God’s people had been slain, so the mad thirst of these men could not at all be quenched by robbing God’s servant. When they perceived that their insane attempts had been mocked and frustrated by heavenly power, they yielded in confusion to the divine power and departed parched.

After they had gone, a certain traveler arrived and begged the same priest to assist him with whatever quantity of wine he might graciously provide. The priest replied to him with the same words he had spoken to the soldiers. When the traveler continued to entreat him to help him from the same supply as an act of charity, the priest carefully recounted to him, one by one, what had happened to the soldiers, so that he would not continue to press him.

The traveler nevertheless did not abandon his request. He said that he now had even greater hope in the priest’s kindness, because what had been withheld from the rapacity of the arrogant had been so protected, whereas he himself had long been well known to him and had often rendered him service [Col. 0128A].

At last the priest, overcome by such persistent pleading and softened by faith, approached the cask, though timidly. And because, as it is written, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6), the flow of liquid immediately followed the hand of the one drawing it with the slightest touch.

Thus the gentle and unarmed man obtained what had been denied to the armed and proud.

## CHAPTER X. In a time of extreme scarcity of bread, an abundance of food is brought from heaven.

One day, as evening was falling, the same father returned from the forest, tired, with the same brother who related this to me. A single piece of bread with raw vegetables was set before them for supper. He gave the whole piece to his companion, eating only the vegetables himself, and urged his fellow diner to endure patiently that poor supper, since he would have a table at his disposal on the following day.

And so it happened. For on the next day such an abundance of food was brought that it could have sufficed for several days for all who lived there.

## CHAPTER XI. Through the merits of the blessed man, a man who was bringing him a fish is freed from danger of death.

A certain man, greatly devoted to the man of God, was accustomed on the principal solemnities to send him a load of fish as a gift [Note: “[Col. 0128D] A gift of fish.” *Exenia*, or *xenia*, means hospitality gifts; the initial *e* has been prefixed through error.]. But on one occasion, when the Lord’s Nativity was approaching, he could not find the sort of fish that he could suitably send him according to custom.

Since this caused him considerable distress, at last, on the very sacred night of the Lord’s Nativity, a large fish was brought to him. Delighted and greatly rejoicing, he ordered that it be taken immediately to the man of God.

But the night, thickened by dreadful darkness, gave off no light from the stars. The road was also extremely difficult and arduous, entirely covered with the roughness of muddy snow. Nevertheless, the bearer of the fish was not permitted to wait for daylight.

As he proceeded along the route he had begun, he came to a certain dark and deep ravine. While he followed its edge too closely, like someone unaware of the danger, his footsteps suddenly slipped and he plunged to the bottom. Although the fall was so great that all the joints of his body might have been dislocated, through the merits of the man of God and by divine power he was preserved completely unharmed.

Safe and strong, he joyfully took up again the load that had been shaken from his shoulders. He then hastened cheerfully to the man of God, presented his master’s gift, and gave thanks because he had been snatched from the jaws of death through the latter’s merits.

But Peter said to him: “Do not, my son, do not attribute to a sinful man what God has graciously granted you through his own mercy alone. Give thanks only to him for the gift of the salvation bestowed, for he is never absent from those who serve him in tribulation.”

## CHAPTER XII. Another man, halted at a fork in the road, is directed onto the right path through his aid.

On one occasion Peter sent one of his disciples to a certain abbot. When the brother did not find him at the monastery, he anxiously inquired where he had gone. After doing this, his return was delayed so long that he could not return on the day he had been expected. Since he began to fear correction on that account, he took a companion and set out on his journey beneath the darkness of the silent night.
