After they had gone forward together for a little while, his fellow traveler gradually withdrew and secretly departed. The monk, now completely unaware of the road he had taken, began to grieve intensely, since he knew neither how to go farther nor how to return by the way he had come.

Placed in this difficulty, he begged the Lord to grant that, through the merits of the man whose obedience he was striving to fulfill, his journey might be directed. After making this prayer, he began to leave and came upon a fork in the road. He paused there for a little while, uncertain which path he should take, and finally chose one that he thought would be more suitable for him.

When he tried to direct his beast onto it, the animal would not consent. Instead, taking the other path, it began obstinately to proceed. The rider strained with all his might, urging it with his heels and blows to return to his chosen route, but it continued toward the place where it had begun to go.

After they had struggled in this way for a long time, and the rider had been unable by any means to bring the beast back to obedience, he finally suspected that perhaps the dumb animal was resisting him against its custom by divine impulse. He therefore loosened all the reins, so that it might proceed freely wherever God wished to direct it.

When morning came and the dawn began to brighten, he raised his eyes, recognized the familiar landmarks, and realized that by divine favor he had been guided along the most direct route. Thus, recognizing that his prayers had been heard through his master’s merits, he joyfully gave thanks to God and also to his master, whom he perceived to be so worthy of God.

## CHAPTER XIII. The blessed man’s messenger is pulled from the mud and freed from nighttime terror, after the author of that great evil is warned by the holy man in a vision with blows from rods.

At another time Peter sent a certain messenger to a bishop. On the road the messenger came upon a stream, which he crossed easily. But immediately after leaving it, his horse became so deeply stuck in the mud that it could not rise by any effort.

Seeing himself thus impeded and utterly unaware of what to do, the rider begged the Lord to grant him aid through the merits of the man whose obedience he knew himself to be carrying out. After this prayer had been poured forth to the Lord, the horse immediately sprang forward, quickly reached dry ground, and, covering the intervening distance at a swift pace, arrived at the city.

When he reached the bishop to whom he had been sent, he did not find the bishop he was seeking. He did, however, find one of the bishop’s paternal relatives—or household members—and was honorably received by him. Out of reverence for so great a man, the host and his entire household served him most attentively.

In one respect, however, he failed him seriously: after having given him a bed, he allowed him to sleep alone in that spacious lodging once everyone else had departed. When the messenger became fully aware of this, such terror seized him that he could scarcely admit any sleep at all that night.

The young man who had shown him this negligence did not escape unpunished. That same night, while he lay relaxed in sleep on his bed, God’s servant Peter violently leapt upon him, threatened him harshly with stout rods, and terrified him because by his negligence he had caused the holy man’s envoy such immense distress.

When this vision was over, the young man immediately awoke and began to await daylight so that he could visit and speak with his guest. At the first light of dawn he hurried to him and carefully asked what negligence or offense had been committed in his service, that Lord Peter had inflicted such terror upon him and had rebuked and frightened him with such threats and insults.

The messenger immediately replied: “I was so terrified last night when all of you had departed and I had been left alone that, in great distress, I spent almost the entire night without sleep.”

When these matters had been revealed to each other, the men marveled at the power of God’s servant and glorified God, who displays himself as wondrous in his saints and servants through such great miracles.

The man who had been sent was so deeply moved by this sign that, returning to the man of God, he immediately placed himself under his direction, promising that he would renounce the world and, with Peter’s blessing, assume the monastic habit in order to serve God. He fulfilled this promise shortly afterward, and he himself related the entire matter to us in the order in which we have set it down.

## CHAPTER XIV. In obedience to Pope Stephen IX, he is made cardinal-bishop of Ostia of the Holy Roman Church; and his dream concerning this matter.

When the fame of his great holiness and prudence could no longer remain hidden, it was clearly conveyed to the ears of the Holy Roman Church. [Note: “[Col. 0129D] To the ears of the Holy Roman Church.” Blessed Peter was known to various pontiffs, since letters of his survive to Gregory VI, Clement II, Saint Leo IX, and Victor II, all of whom occupied the see before Stephen, who is discussed here.]

And because so great a man was considered suitable for the priesthood and extremely necessary for ecclesiastical affairs [Note: “[Col. 0130D] Extremely necessary for ecclesiastical affairs.” He had previously been sent by Clement II to the emperor Henry II—who was King Henry III of that name—as he himself says in book I, letter 3.], he was brought before the supreme pontiff, namely Stephen IX [Note: “[Col. 0131D] Namely Stephen IX.” Stephen was elected on the fourth day before the Nones of August 1057 and died on the fourth day before the Kalends of April 1058.], and was compelled by the other bishops and ecclesiastical men, as well as by the supreme pontiff himself, to accept the episcopal chair.

But he, remembering the solitude and quiet in which he had been accustomed to devote himself sweetly to divine reading and contemplation, and greatly dreading its loss and a return to worldly turmoil, resisted their demands with all his strength and effort.

When they saw that neither their exhortations nor their prayers achieved anything at all, they began to threaten him with a sentence of excommunication if he decided obstinately to continue resisting. What more is needed? At last the apostolic lord added one command that he could in no way disregard. Under the authority of obedience, he ordered him to comply with the brothers and peacefully accept what was being commanded. Then, taking his right hand, he endowed it simultaneously with a ring and a staff [Note: “[Col. 0131D] He endowed it simultaneously with a ring and a staff.” He was made cardinal in the year 1058, as established above.].

By these tokens he joined him to the Church of Ostia. When he had assumed this episcopate in this manner, he immediately recognized that what had been revealed to him in a vision three years earlier had been fulfilled.

The vision had been as follows: he thought that he had a most illustrious bride, richly endowed, whom he could neither touch nor even look upon with a calm gaze; yet he did not dare renounce her in any way, as though she were joined to him by right. We perceived that this corresponded exactly to the matter at hand.

For we learned that he had often complained about this, yet had never dared to shake from his shoulders the burden of the obedience imposed upon him, however heavy it might be.

## CHAPTER XV. He labors for the salvation of souls and the expansion of the worship of Christ and the Blessed Virgin, even at the risk of his own salvation.

When he realized that he had thus been bound by such perpetual bonds and was no longer free to devote himself to his accustomed contemplation, he judged that the losses of the past should be compensated by the gains of what followed, so that the fruitfulness of Leah might be compared with Rachel’s beauty. [Note: “[Col. 0131D] So that the fruitfulness of Leah might be compared with Rachel’s beauty.” Blessed Peter discusses the active and contemplative life splendidly under the figures of Leah and Rachel in *Opusculum* 13, *On the Perfection of Monks*, chapter 8.]

Recognizing himself, therefore, as a faithful and prudent servant appointed steward of the Lord’s household, he began diligently to discharge the ministry entrusted to him, so that he might await the Lord’s coming without fear and present his fellow servants with such a full and perfect measure of grain that, when the Lord came, he might deserve to hear: “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew XXV; Luke XIX).

Nor did he judge it sufficient to devote his administrative care only to the people of the one Church over which he presided [Note: “[Col. 0131D] Only to the people of one Church.” We said above that the Church of Gubbio had also been entrusted to him.]. Since he knew that he was responsible to all his fellow servants enrolled with him in one household, he showed himself solicitous for them all. Desiring to win them all for God, like a skillful searcher of the fish-filled deep he diligently investigated whether a crowd of people might gather anywhere for a solemnity, so that, casting the nets of the divine word, he might catch many and lift them, as it were, from the depths of the worldly sea to the heights of heavenly love.

For the sake of such gain, we often saw him anticipate the daylight by a long interval when such a gathering was to take place some distance away, lest the suitable hour for preaching pass him by. We also very often knew him, exhausted at night by severe fevers, to enter the church as soon as the sun had risen, begin the solemnities of Mass, and continue preaching in a loud voice almost until the sixth hour, offering us a considerable miracle in himself, since we saw him stronger in bodily power and clearer in speech even though we had thought he was already about to collapse.

This clearly showed that it was not another who preached through his mouth, but the one who, teaching his disciples, said: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X).

He dispensed the words of this Spirit, as though they flowed from the most abundant spring, in a form suited to the capacity of each person. Although these words were sometimes more extended, they could nevertheless be burdensome to no one. What burden could there be in sermons to which everyone listened with attentive ears as though they were divine inspirations? Or how could the words of one with whom the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperated be fruitless? Certainly not.

Hence it is that the Day of the Cross [Note: “[Col. 0131D] The Day of the Cross.” That is, every Friday, as is discussed again below, nos. 43 and following.] is observed throughout this entire province by countless faithful through abstinence, out of reverence for the Lord’s Passion. The same man preached and urged this observance everywhere.

It is likewise clear that the offices of all the hours [Note: “[Col. 0132D] The offices of all the hours.” Blessed Peter reveals his devotion to the Hours of the Blessed Virgin, the Mother of God, in *Opusculum* 10, *On the Canonical Hours*, chapter 10, where he relates that a devotee of the Blessed Virgin’s Hours obtained forgiveness of sins through her. Fortunius says: “Blessed Peter was sent as legate *a latere* throughout all Italy to promulgate decrees concerning the recitation of the Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and at the same time he decreed the Friday fast in honor of the Holy Cross.” But because he says that this legation was instituted by Gregory VII, the account is suspect, since it is certain that Blessed Peter died before Gregory’s pontificate. We believe that the chronology has been carefully preserved in this *Life*.] in honor of the gracious Mother of God are observed with zeal in many churches, largely through his efforts.

We see the clergy of the mother churches gathered from every part of the Roman province contiguous with him, and, with God’s favor, we applaud them as they imitate certain traces of the canonical rite—those who had once abandoned all canonical institutions, completely withdrawn from the order of common life, and lived in a worldly manner in their individual houses together with women.

## CHAPTER XVI. He uproots the heresies of simony and the Nicolaitans and reconciles the Ambrosian Church with the Roman Church.

He also labored greatly to uproot the stain and heresy of simony [Note: “[Col. 0133C] The stain of simony.” Blessed Peter relates that Simon Magus was the originator in the New Testament of simony, which was named after him, in chapter 4 of *Opusculum* 3, addressed to the cardinal bishops of the Apostolic See; in that treatise he argues against avarice and the desire for gifts.] and of the Nicolaitans [Note: “[Col. 0133C] The Nicolaitans.” Christ says in the Apocalypse of Saint John, chapter II, verse 7, that he hates the deeds of the Nicolaitans; see the commentators and Baronius under the year 68, no. 9 onward. In the letter of Saint Ignatius of Antioch to the Trallians—but interpolated by later writers—the following is read: “Flee also the most impure Nicolaitans, falsely so called, lovers of lust and wicked slanderers.” In any event, Blessed Peter’s letter 13 in book V, addressed to the chaplains of Duke Gotifred, survives against the Simonians and Nicolaitans of his own time.].

These plagues had grown powerful through such a pernicious custom and had so impudently defiled almost the whole Church [Note: “[Col. 0133D] Almost the whole Church.” Blessed Peter writes the following in *Opusculum* 6, called *The Most Gracious Book*, chapter 27: “For who does not know that, until the reign of this most merciful King Henry and the episcopate of Clement, of revered memory, and of that most blessed apostolic Leo—under whose episcopate, namely, the holy Church now rejoices that it is governed—throughout the western kingdoms the poison of the simoniacal heresy boiled up lethally, so that what was commonly done and freely admitted was in no way considered subject to punitive correction, and what was almost universally accepted was held as a rule, as though decreed by legal sanction?” Saint Leo IX occupied the see from 1049 to 1056, dying on 19 April.] throughout the Roman world that they scarcely feared a reprover any longer, treating their conduct as lawful.

O good Jesus, we rejoice that through this outstanding champion of yours and the few who adhered to him, with your cooperation, these evils have now been expelled; and we gladly exult over them once they have been overthrown.

We must not pass over in silence the great danger into which he plunged himself in order to drive these evils from the Ambrosian Church as well. As he himself clearly expressed in one of his books, which he composed specifically for this matter and entitled, according to its subject, *Acts of Milan* [Note: “[Col. 0134C] *Acts of Milan*.” *Acts of Milan*, on the privilege of the Roman Church, was addressed to Cardinal Hildebrand, later Pope Gregory VII. It survives as *Opusculum* 5, whose very words are inserted here.], a considerable dispute had arisen between the people and clergy of that Church on account of these two heresies, namely simony and that of the Nicolaitans.

For this twofold execrable plague had taken such deep root among them and assumed such freedom that, in carrying out the wickedness of its filth, it no longer sought any hiding place, but publicly practiced it as though it were lawful and honorable business.

If anyone was to be promoted to any ecclesiastical order, he could not approach the hands of the consecrator—or rather, the contaminator—without a commercial exchange involving sale. The filth of the other evil had spread itself so shamelessly that the marriages of priests seemed no different from the ambitions of worldly men.

Accordingly, by divine impulse, the zeal of the faithful laity against these detestable stains was kindled with pious fervor, and they sought the assistance of the Apostolic See to wash away such crimes. [Note: “[Col. 0134C] They sought the assistance of the Apostolic See.” The ancient deeds of the Roman pontiffs, collected by Cardinal Niccolò d’Aragona, contain the following: “The Milanese legates came to the same pontiff, Pope Nicholas, earnestly beseeching him to have mercy and compassion on the afflictions of the Church of Milan. For this reason Pope Nicholas sent there the venerable Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, and granted him his own authority for correcting and establishing whatever concerned that Church.” Consult Baronius under the year 1059, no. 44, and Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, who adds: “Ariald the cleric was sent to Rome by Landulf Cotta, prefect of the people.”]

To carry this out, Pope Nicholas II [Note: “[Col. 0134D] Nicholas II.” Nicholas II occupied the see from 1059 to 1061. Blessed Peter himself also writes in *Opusculum* 53, chapter 4, that he came to the city of Milan as its legate.] arranged to send this man, whom he knew to be endowed with authority both of wisdom and holiness.

When Peter had departed [Note: “[Col. 0134D] When he had departed.” The remainder is related by Blessed Peter in the same words, in the aforementioned *Opusculum* 5.], and had been received with the honor entirely appropriate both to himself and to the Apostolic See, he explained the purpose of his embassy to the ears of the whole Church.

As a result, on the following day a murmur suddenly arose among the people through the faction of the clergy: the Ambrosian Church ought not to be subject to Roman laws, and the Roman pontiff possessed no right to judge or regulate that see.

“It is utterly disgraceful,” they said, “that the Church which under our ancestors always existed in freedom should now, to our shame and confusion, be subjected to another Church—God forbid!”

At last the shouting of the rioters grew louder, and people gathered from every side at the episcopal palace. Then the bells rang out, and the entire city resounded with the blasts of trumpets. Everything, so to speak, threatened him with death, and some of his own friends, grieving in sympathy, told him that certain men thirsted for his blood.

When the clergy and people had gathered in the church, he mounted the pulpit. After the tumult had at last been quieted with difficulty, he began in these words:

Your charity should know, dearly beloved, that I have come here not for the honor of the Roman Church, but wholly to seek your glory and to procure for you, with his help, salvation and the grace that is in Christ Jesus, if you permit it. For how can she need the honor of a puny man, when she has received proclamations of praise from the very mouth of the Savior? And what province throughout all the kingdoms of the earth is found to be outside his dominion, at whose judgment even heaven itself is both bound and loosed? (Matthew 16.)

For the other Churches, whatever their dignity, were founded either by a king or by some mere human being, and, according as there was willingness or ability, their rights were established with particular prerogatives. But the Roman Church was founded by him alone, and he raised it upon the rock of the faith that was just coming into being (ibid.), he who entrusted to blessed Peter, the heavenly key-bearer, the rights of earthly as well as heavenly rule. It therefore enjoys his privilege and is supported by his authority. Hence there is no doubt that whoever deprives any Church of its rightful jurisdiction commits an injustice; but whoever attempts to remove the privilege of the Roman Church, handed down by the supreme Head of all the Churches himself, certainly falls into heresy. For he violates the faith who acts against her, since she is the mother of the faith; and he is shown to be rebellious against the one who is known to have preferred her to all the Churches.

When these and many other arguments had thus been presented concerning the prerogative and primacy of the apostolic see, the people became entirely well disposed and unanimously promised that they would carry out whatever he should choose to command.

[Note: “When these and other matters, etc.” Other arguments are examined in the said treatise 5.]

Why delay over details? That very large assembly of clerics was present, summoned from the whole Ambrosian diocese as though to a synod. They were therefore examined both collectively and individually, and among so great a number scarcely anyone promoted to orders was found who had not paid for it. Who could explain how many cares afflicted him, how many goads of thought wearied him? For, to use his own words, it seemed the overthrow of Christian religion to profane, in a manner, the sacred mysteries in all the churches of so extensive a diocese and so noble a city. Yet it was contentious to show indulgence to a few, since almost everyone shared the guilt; nor did it seem lawful to issue a different sentence against them, since the cause was the same for all. This too increased his anxieties. For unless this matter received some sort of decision, the quarrels of the raging people could not be quieted except at the cost of a great slaughter of men.

Thus placed in a difficult position, because he could not correct the evils of that Church by the authority of the canons alone, he at least endeavored to put an end to its corrupt practices and to provide for the future that promotion to orders should be free. He therefore exacted—not only from the archbishop but also from all his officials to whom the matter seemed to belong—an inviolable pledge, recorded in writing,

[Note: “Not only from the archbishop.” Wido Valvassorius was archbishop of Milan; according to Hermannus Contractus in his *Chronicle*, he was appointed in the year 1045.]

by the touch of a sacred hand, and finally by an evangelical oath,

[Note: “By written documents.” Blessed Peter inserted Wido’s pledge in treatise 5 in the form of a letter to the clergy and people of his diocese. Various members of the clergy subscribed it after him; it also contains the form of the oath, the testimonies of the holy Fathers, and the penance undertaken both by the archbishop and by the clergy.]

that from that time forward the stain of simony and the heresy of the Nicolaitans should be abolished and faithfully rooted out entirely, insofar as they could do so.

After these matters had been accomplished, the authority of the canons of many holy Fathers was sought. Having considered them, it seemed, with the moderation required by prudent judgment, that all those clerics, after receiving penance, should be reconciled during the solemn celebration of Mass, receiving the vestments from the bishop’s hand by the authority of the Council of Toledo. Once they had thus been reconciled, it was decreed that ecclesiastical office should not immediately be restored indiscriminately to all, but only to those who appeared to be learned in letters, chaste, and honorable in the gravity of their conduct. For the others, it was sufficient that by divine grace they had again been inserted into the holy Church, from which they had previously been cut off by the sickle of divine knowledge.

Those bishops to whom permission to administer was restored were not reinstated in the office they had lost on the basis of their old ordination, improperly purchased, but rather by that most effective authority of the blessed prince of the apostles which he suddenly exercised toward blessed Apollinaris, saying: “Rise, receive the Holy Spirit, and likewise the pontificate.”

I have briefly touched upon these matters so that his other deeds may be understood by examining them. For how could I express individually the deeds of one who never ceased in the holy Church to overthrow whatever evil or improper thing arose, and to establish for the glory of Christ whatever was observed to be pious and religious? In carrying out these works, he was accompanied by no small ability granted by God, since the judgment of his authority determined what the canonical decrees required to be admitted or done.

The entire Church of the city of Rome bears witness to this assertion. Enlightened by a certain radiance of his teaching and supported by his authority, she lamented that, after his departure, she had almost fallen silent in the word of exhortation and had been deprived of the protection of an irreplaceable authority. His authority refuted every error: confirming those who wavered, it stabilized uncertainties; restraining the mouths of quarrelsome men, it pressed down the necks of the proud; and encouraging the minds of the humble, it strengthened them.

## CHAPTER XVII. His piety and generosity toward the poor and toward religious men

Who could adequately describe what kind and how great he was in works of mercy? Who was more inclined to the practice of almsgiving,

[Note: “More inclined to the practice of almsgiving.” He displays his affection for almsgiving in treatise 9, *On Almsgiving*, addressed to Mainardus, bishop of Urbino.]

who more devoted to washing the feet of the poor? Who could ever have been more ready than he to clothe the naked, refresh the needy, and visit the sick? Almost no day was free from such works for him, wherever the suitability of time or place permitted them. And since he did not cease to perform them everywhere, what must we suppose he did when he remained at the episcopal residence?

There, while a crowd of poor people daily frequented the episcopal doors, some were refreshed with food that had been set before them, while others returned after receiving a charitable gift. From among these he regularly selected twelve whose feet he washed. Moreover, at his little meals, which according to custom he always shared with guests, he could not forget any needy people lying on beds throughout the surrounding region, since he always had one of his own men whom he knew to fear God more strictly specially assigned to serve them.

Persisting in such pursuits with constant practice, he rejoiced to fill the treasuries of the Church with the wider riches of heaven, while he scrupulously avoided taking such riches for his own expenses. For he used to say that he had been appointed a minister, not a lord, of the Lord’s possessions; a steward, not an owner.

To kindle in the minds of his own dependents a devoted zeal for carrying out these duties faithfully, he frequently strove to admonish them in words such as these:

“You should know, sons, that all these things are sacred and the price of sins. Therefore you must take the greatest care that nothing belonging to these resources be taken away from Christ’s poor through avarice or through any careless negligence. Everything that remains to us is owed to them intact.

“Since we have sufficient resources by which the needy and miserable can be refreshed, diligently seek out and piously consider who in the neighboring regions is sick, and who is suffering either from hunger or from the distress of any kind of poverty. By compassionately assisting such people and supplying what is necessary, you may acquire in heaven the fruit of an eternal reward shared by us and by you. For if you prove faithful fellow workers with us now in sowing, you will unquestionably rejoice with us in the blessed recompense over the common harvest.”

With such admonitions the pious Father urged his companions to works of mercy. From this we should judge what he is believed to have been in providing what his brethren needed, since he is known to have shown such kindness toward all. But why should I speak of those attached to him, when toward all servants of God established in the purpose of the sacred warfare he was bound by such an affection of love that he rejoiced more in their consolation than in his own?

## CHAPTER XVIII. He withdraws to his monastery, where he is trained by fasts, prayer, and other exercises of body and soul

Moreover, when he had resolved to return from these outward affairs,

[Note: “Moreover, when he had resolved to return from these outward affairs.” He had obtained permission from Alexander II, as stated above.]

although they were holy and pleasing to God, to the sweet solitude of the desert, both for the refreshment of his mind and for washing away whatever dust he had contracted, he tormented himself in the prison of his cell by excessive hunger: every day, except feast days, he fasted, living on *cantabrum* bread,

[Note: “Coarse bread.” Blessed Peter says in treatise 15, chapter 14, that a certain man lived each day on one small loaf of *cantabricius* bread. In the *Life of Saint Rodulfus, Bishop of Gubbio*, he says that this man used to eat, “whenever he could obtain it, bread made either from pure barley or rather from *cantabrum*, which had remained from children’s loaves and ought to have been thrown to the dogs.” Gononius, in the published *Life*, book 5 of *Lives of the Western Fathers*, says that “*cantabrum* is the refuse of flour or wheat, or is food for dogs.” There are also *cantabra*, military standards, in Tertullian’s *Apology* and in Minucius Felix; to the latter Rigaltius remarks that “*cantabra* are banners which served soldiers as a sign not only by their color, but also by a chant or by some name, which they sang or proclaimed to signify something pleasing and delightful to them.” But why should they not have been military standards adopted from the Spanish Cantabri? Should the same be said of the coarser bread?]

and drinking yesterday’s water. Though his body was already worn out by old age and bound everywhere by many iron chains, he never spared it its allotted blows of discipline and palm-strikes. He devoted himself continually to singing psalms, praying, reading, and dictating.

Nor should it be omitted that he ate bread for refreshment in the same little basin in which he washed the feet of the poor, and took the rest of his sleep upon a bare mat of rushes.

[Note: “Upon a mat of rushes.” Among other meanings, *biblea* signifies a reed and bark; hence *biblea cratis* means a reed mat, the use of which Pliny describes in book 21, chapter 14.]

On one occasion, when he had decided to go to the brothers’ chapter, he gave an exhortation and then immediately rose from his seat and accused himself of his faults. For these he received the judgment of discipline according to custom and was beaten with blows on both sides. Returning again to his place, he did not cease to instruct them by his speeches,

[Note: “To instruct them by his speeches.” On this subject treatise 13, *On the Perfection of Monks*, is especially notable; it contains distinct chapters for adolescents, novices, the elderly, and others.]

speaking now to some, now to others, and now to all together.

To the younger men he therefore said:

“You should know, sons, that each of you ought to begin the novitiate of this sacred warfare with such fervor and vigor, and exercise himself with such labor in striving toward higher things while bodily strength is available, that the entire course of his future life may be shaped for courageous action, as though by the impression of a true seal.”

To those more advanced in age he discoursed more subtly on the struggle against vices, the discernment of thoughts, and the need to seek the grace of compunction or contemplation and purity of mind.

Whenever a passage of this sort occurred in his conversations, one in which the minds of the brothers ought to be stirred to greater strength, he would usually say:

“Every vigorous leader in the divine warfare ought to recognize his strength in every spiritual struggle. It is utterly shameful for a monk both to profess the profession of spiritual warfare and, through the cowardice of refusing to test himself, to remain ignorant of what he is capable of in combat.”

What he urged his disciples to do by such words he clearly demonstrated by his examples. I do not think it pointless to recall some of them. I myself saw him spend forty days without taking any food that had passed through fire, content only with raw fruits and things growing from the earth, and entirely without drink. I witnessed this myself.

I heard another matter from my older fellow disciples, namely, that on one occasion he spent just as many days without taking any food except a small quantity of legume steeped in water,

[Note: “Except a small quantity of legume steeped in water.” Blessed Peter says in treatise 15, *On the Institutions of His Congregation*, chapter 6, that many monks during Lent ate only “fruits, the roots of plants, and legumes soaked in water or even boiled.” Hence *infusidarium* seems to designate every kind of liquid food macerated in water but not boiled. Vossius did not understand this distinction in book 3 of *On the Faults of Language*, chapter 16.]

though if he noticed that he was being excessively exhausted by such practices, he by no means regarded it as contemptible to assist bodily weakness somewhat by a measured relaxation, so that, having regained his strength, he might return more vigorous to another contest. He used to say that it should be attributed not to vice but rather to virtue if someone relaxed his tired arms for the purpose of rising afterward stronger for courageous action.

Furthermore, it was his custom not to lean on any lectern while singing during either the night or the day offices. At the beginning of both Lents he abstained entirely from food for three days. Although he himself persuaded no one to do this, he nevertheless thought that something should be handed down to those seeking progress in spiritual devotion, by which they might commend themselves to the Lord at the very beginning of their undertaken fast.

He established this rule of voluntary observance in certain monasteries by rousing them to embrace it with pious devotion, so that during the aforesaid three-day fast the entire brotherhood would preserve an unbroken rigor of silence in the cloister. No one was to put on footwear without unavoidable necessity until they had all completed the Psalter each day. All were also to receive the discipline of the broom,

[Note: “The discipline of the broom.” For a deceased brother, Blessed Peter prescribes in treatises 14 and 15, chapter 12, that “seven disciplines, each with a thousand strokes of the broom,” should be received. He indicates the manner in which the discipline was to be administered in book 6, letter 34, addressed to the hermits of his Congregation.]

and they were to abstain alike from everything except bread and water.

## CHAPTER XIX. He establishes the Friday fast in honor of the holy cross, and this is confirmed by heavenly visions

He also instituted that every Friday throughout the year, except during Easter and on the other solemn days, should be observed by them under the same rule of discipline and abstinence, out of reverence for the cross.

Finally, all his exhortation is known to have borne fruit so abundantly, with the Lord’s cooperation, that even that celebrated monastery of Monte Cassino

[Note: “That celebrated monastery of Monte Cassino as well.” Desiderius, appointed in 1058, was in charge of the monks of Cassino. Blessed Peter was very close to him; several of Peter’s letters and works to him survive. We have confirmed the present account above from Leo of Ostia, who writes that this visit of Peter to the monks of Cassino occurred in the fifth year of Abbot Desiderius; therefore in the year of Christ 1062 or 1063.]

adopted the rule with such fervor that it decreed all the aforesaid practices should be written among its regular commands.

We do not think it idle to add here certain records of revelations that he himself wrote, by which that holy man was confirmed with great determination in this observance of Friday. Let us therefore set down his own words:

“In the cell of the sick there was an old father named Leo, who devoted himself especially to fasts, psalms, and prayers. Although his bodily strength had failed, he was nevertheless strong in the vigor of a youthful and fervent spirit.

“On the night before this rule of fasting was to be established, he saw in a dream a great choir of brothers standing in the church. They were splendidly dressed in bright white garments and sang with a sufficiently sweet and honeyed melody the Alleluia called ‘Sweet wood, sweet nails,’ and so forth.

“He also saw that loaves had been placed upon all the tables of the refectory, shining in appearance and sweetened with the taste of nectar. Among the brothers reclining everywhere at table there was also, if I remember correctly, a man of great distinction and conspicuous beauty. When asked where such loaves had come from, since he had never before seen loaves like them, he replied: ‘These are the loaves by which the children of Israel, receiving manna from heaven, were nourished in the desert’ (Exodus 16).

“This man also took the abbot’s table, which had been set toward the west, and placed it on the eastern side of the refectory, where an image of the crucified Lord had been depicted on the wall.

“Consider, therefore, the mystery and understand the sacrament of the mystical revelation. What does it mean that the choir of singers resounded with melodious voices in praise of the cross, except that, when they had established a solemn fast in honor of the cross, they would sing to it sweet melodies of praise? He sings a hymn in honor of the blessed cross who celebrates a fast on the day when Christ was suspended upon the cross.

“And what does it mean that the loaves appeared honey-sweet, except that they were to eat the sweet nourishment of the spirit while, through the bitterness of the flesh, they sounded sweet melodies of praise to God? The taste becomes sweeter upon the palate of the heart in proportion as the greater bitterness of austerity disturbs the wantonness of the flesh.

“What does it also mean to place the abbot’s table beneath the feet of the crucified Redeemer, except that through the Friday fast, which is the day of the cross, the entire refectory was to be dedicated by the saving sign of the cross? And what does it mean to sit beneath the feet of the crucified Lord, except to follow in his footsteps and continually walk along the path by which he went before us?”

To commend this matter more firmly, it also most appropriately happened that another holy brother named Peter was absent when this was established. Returning afterward on a certain Thursday, he saw that night in a dream that Lord Peter was inviting him to dinner and that he himself was reclining at table as Peter’s guest.

On the following day he came to the chapter with the other brothers, received the discipline of the new rite, and, becoming joyful and glad, rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, saying:

“Behold, thanks be to God, the dinner to which Lord Peter Damian had invited me.”

And rightly indeed our affliction of the flesh is called a table or a meal, since by that through which our body is worn down by abstinence, the spirit is nourished with the richness of heavenly grace.

When all had clearly recognized from such revelations that the practices recently proclaimed to them through the mouth of the most blessed man had been handed down by heaven, they were not only inflamed to observe them more fervently, but also asked him to command whatever still seemed lacking among them, remove whatever was excessive, and, with the approval of all, correct whatever required correction.

As a result, among other things, they threw away the *copulae* with which they covered their heads as though with caps, deciding henceforth to be content with hoods alone, in the respectable manner of monks. They also decreed that they would no longer buy costly garments made from foreign fabrics, but would instead purchase cheap, native garments from the looms of country people.

## CHAPTER XX. He frees certain boys afflicted by demons on Monte Cassino, where they were helping to build the basilica of Saint Benedict

[Col. 0141B]

When the same Lord Peter had once visited the aforementioned monastery of Cassino according to custom,

[Note: “When Lord Peter had once visited according to custom.” This visit was different from the preceding one, as the following account makes clear.]

the basilica of the most blessed Benedict was then being founded there,

[Note: “The basilica of blessed Benedict was being founded.” That basilica began to be built in 1066 and was consecrated by Pope Alexander II in 1071. Ten archbishops, fourteen bishops, princes, dukes, abbots, and many others attended the solemnity. It may be read about in Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Cassino*, book 3, chapters 26–28, and in other writers on Cassinian affairs.]

the building which is now visibly adorned with gold and precious stones. There he found several boys who had come to carry stones and were being violently tormented by demons. Although their limbs were small, such strength was imparted to them by the demons that each boy, seized by two or three very strong men, could scarcely be restrained at all.

One day, when Lord Peter happened to go out to inspect the work, Desiderius, the venerable abbot of that monastery of Cassino, greeted him cheerfully by name, as he was accustomed to do, and said:

“Lord Peter, why do you not care for these workers of ours?”

He replied:

“They have here the presence of the most holy Benedict, who, if he wishes, is able to grant them healing. For what am I?”

Nevertheless, the abbot thought that some of them should be sent to Peter’s lodging, so that, seeing their affliction, he might feel compassion for them more attentively and pray for them. Peter absolutely forbade this—not from the harshness of inhumanity, but from his observance of humility, which was more deserving of regard.

Yet since it happened that he remained there for nearly twenty days out of love for the brothers, and during that same period all those possessed persons were completely healed, who would not faithfully believe what the monks then asserted: namely, that he had secretly prayed for them and thus obtained their healing from the Lord?

But since it is difficult, indeed impossible, for us to narrate all his deeds, we think it appropriate now to direct our pen toward the final events and, with the Lord’s help, to relate how he completed his course and departed from here to the realms above.

## CHAPTER XXI. As legate of the Roman pontiff, he absolves the city of Ravenna from the censures imposed because of the fault of its archbishop

While, therefore, the pious priest of Christ eagerly devoted himself to such efforts for winning souls, and the labor of the present life was already delaying him almost at its final boundary, he was ordered by Alexander II,

[Note: “By order of Alexander II.” Alexander II occupied the papal see from 1061 to 1073. To him Blessed Peter dedicated, besides letters and works that he sent, the *Lives of Saints Rodulfus, Bishop of Gubbio*, and *Dominicus Loricatus*. As is clear here, Peter died under Alexander.]

the Roman pontiff, to go to Ravenna, his native city, to carry out a matter of great necessity for the salvation of the whole city, its clergy, and its people.

At that time the archbishop of that city had died,

[Note: “The archbishop of that city.” Henry died in the year 1070, on the first of January.]

having previously been deprived of communion by the sentence of a Roman synod because of his arrogance. Yet, since he had not been shaken by the sentence imposed upon him,

[Note: “Because of the sentence imposed upon him, etc.” We said above that he had been excommunicated by Pope Alexander.]

and had by no means refrained from the archiepiscopal office, he miserably defiled the people who followed him by his contagion and profaned the entire Church by his unlawful presumption.

At last the profaner was removed from their midst. The aforesaid apostolic pontiff, moved by brotherly compassion for the deadly contagion of so numerous a people, decided to delegate to them such a father as would absolve and reconcile them by apostolic authority. He judged no one more worthy or more suitable for carrying out this task than Peter, because he was supported by considerable authority, was by the grace of regeneration a son of that Church, and had also repeatedly urged the pontiff toward this clemency.

[Note: “And also at his urging.” In letter 14 of book 1, addressed to Alexander II, Blessed Peter says the same, as related above. From this it is clear that Fortunatus and Rubeus wrongly transfer all these events to Gregory VII, Alexander’s successor, as though Peter had been sent to Wibert, Henry’s successor as archbishop.]

Although already worn down by age, Peter gladly accepted this legation, like a vigorous son who was not ungrateful for the benefits received from his mother. He rejoiced that he had at last found something by which he could repay his mother for the duty he owed her.

When, with the Lord’s assistance, he arrived by a prosperous journey, the citizens received him into their hands with immense joy. He explained the purpose of his arrival. The citizens were exceedingly delighted and gave boundless thanks to God, who had looked upon them, and to Christ’s vicar, who had sent such a great and distinguished man to them. They humbly performed penance for their transgression; and thus they deserved, with rejoicing, to receive the pardon of their guilt, which they humbly requested, and absolution by virtue of apostolic authority.

Once it had been released from the bond of that excommunication and the gift of motherly grace had been granted to the whole Church, immense rejoicing arose throughout the entire city.

## CHAPTER XXII. He dies most holily at Faenza and is buried with the greatest honor in the church of the Blessed Virgin

After completing these and several other matters appropriate for so great a man to undertake, he left the city and began to proceed along the route of his legation.

[Note: “He left the city and began to proceed.” “He was returning to Rome,” says Fortunatus.]

When he had stopped for his first lodging at Faenza, he was courteously received at a certain venerable monastery of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, which is called “Outside the Gate,”

[Note: “Which is called Outside the Gate.” Blessed Peter places it beside the walls of the city of Faenza in treatise 6, chapter 18. Fortunatus and Rubeus report that this monastery has since been incorporated within the city.]

and soon afterward he was seized by a fever and took to his bed.

As the fever grew stronger each day, around the middle of the silent eighth hour of the night, which was leading into the annual celebration of the feast of the Chair of Blessed Peter the Apostle, he recognized that the hour of his departure was approaching. Immediately, while we stood around his bed, he ordered the entire nocturnal, or matutinal, office to be performed, wishing first to offer his vows to the apostolic solemnity and only then to depart in security.

When the entire assembly of prayer had been completed, he shortly afterward returned his holy spirit to the Lord, freed from the bonds of the body.

[Note: “His spirit to the Lord.” In the year 1072, as was established above.]

Thus, on the very day when the Church on earth had been found worthy to place Peter in the pastoral seat, the heavenly court received Peter’s disciple into the blessed seat.

As soon as his death had been announced in the city by those keeping watch around the same house, lest his lifeless body be secretly carried away by his monks,

[Note: “By his monks from his nearby monastery.” Gamon or Acereta, discussed above. Wion seems to understand this monastery of Saint Mary as one or the other of these when he says in book 2, chapter 9 of *The Tree of Life* that it was built by Blessed Peter.]

who had come from his nearby monastery, the entire city suddenly hurried to his funeral in a great throng.

When the church in which he had been placed was suddenly filled by their multitude, and all eagerly wished to approach the pious funeral, they pushed one another backward like waves. The more each person tried to arrive quickly amid the tumult, the more slowly access was granted.

Those who were fortunate enough to approach him and touch his bier rejoiced in pious kisses and fastened their gifts to his feet or to the very cloths covering him.

Meanwhile, a mausoleum was prepared with the greatest care. From another basilica some distance away, an immense stone basin, remarkable for its shining whiteness, was brought with astonishing ease and speed—even to the wonder of those carrying it—as though it were some extremely light material. It was suitably placed in the very basilica of the blessed Mother of God, in front of the choir, beside the steps by which one ascends to the altar.

There the venerable body of the priest of Christ was reverently laid to rest amid the greatest rejoicing of all. Everyone raised his voice on high with psalms and hymns, offering with all his strength worthy proclamations of praise to God, by whose gift they rejoiced that they had been enriched with so great a benefit.

To him be glory, praise, power, honor, and splendor and dominion, now and always and throughout every age. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Blessed Peter Damian reproves an abbot in a vision for ingratitude, and chastises and heals him by swelling of the throat

In the year one thousand and eighty after the Lord’s incarnation, in the month of August, in the fourth indiction,

[Note: “In the year one thousand, etc.” The following material appears to have been added to the *Life* and, as we have seen, concluded with the author’s customary phraseology.]

[Note: “In the fourth indiction.” It was in fact the third indiction; moreover, John, the author of the *Life*, nowhere uses either the indiction or the year of Christ.]

after the death of the aforementioned Lord Peter Damian,

[Note: “After the death of the aforementioned Lord Peter Damian.” The ninth year seems to be missing.]

there was a certain monk who had once been abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Gregory, situated in the territory of Rimini.

[Note: “The monastery of Saint Gregory.” This is the village of Saint Gregory near the monastery at Murciano, built by Blessed Peter.]

He saw Lord Peter, himself wearing a mitre, seated among a multitude of white-robed bishops, holding a pastoral staff in his hand and teaching them the things that pertain to God.

When that abbot greeted him with bowed head, Lord Peter said to the other fellow bishops:

“This is a monk whom I loved greatly. But after he withdrew from me, he never returned to me. And not only he, but many others whom I educated and nourished, proved ungrateful for the benefit they had received.”

Then he said to him:

“Why did you not come to me, to the place where I was?”

He replied:

“O my lord, ever since you withdrew from us, we have not known the place in which you dwell. How, then, could I come to you?”

Then Lord Peter said to him:

“Fool, do you not know that I dwell in the chamber of the Virgin Saint Mary and remain in her sanctuary? For I live in her house and profess myself to be her chamberlain.”

After he saw this, he immediately awoke from sleep.

A little later, falling asleep again, he saw the same Lord Peter saying these words to him—for it seemed to him that he had heard the same words from him several days before:

“Did I not tell you to come to me? And why did you not come?”

But he stood there like a mute.

Immediately Lord Peter, apparently in anger, pricked him below the left ear with the tip of the staff that he held in his hand. From that blow he felt so disturbed that it seemed as though he had been pierced by a lance or bored through by a terrible point.

Finally, his entire jaw and throat swelled so much that people nearly despaired of his life.

Then, prostrate before the altar of that church and turned toward God with his whole heart, he said to him with a great groan:

“Lord, almighty God, who created heaven and earth and all that is in them, if the service of my lord Peter was pleasing to you, as we believe, free me through his merits from the pressing pain that I suffer.”

He said this and began to stand. And behold, after no long time, all the swelling and pain fled from him as though someone had come and removed the wound from his jaw or throat with his hand.

He immediately began to glorify God and his servant Peter Damian, who had deigned first to chastise him and then to heal him.

On the following day he rose, well chastised by the blow, and went to Faenza. Coming before the altar of Saint Mary Outside the Gate, where the body of Lord Peter had been laid to rest, he prostrated himself on the ground, his face drenched with tears, and worshiped, praised, and blessed God for the judgments of his justice.

Afterward he went outside to his brothers and began to relate to the superior and to the other brothers everything that had happened to him. When they heard it, they praised and blessed God, who had deigned to display such wonders through his servant.

Finally, the superior, together with the aforementioned abbot, named Ugano,

[Note: “Together with the aforementioned abbot Ugano.” Fortunatus calls him Urbanus.]

and the brothers entered the church of the holy Mother of God. They rang all the bells and placed wax torches

[Note: “They placed wax torches.” *Ceroptata*: torches made of wax.]

with lamps before the shrine of Saint Peter Damian. Celebrating Masses, they offered solemn sacrifices to God as a pleasing fragrance for the absolution of his soul.

[Note: “For the absolution of his soul.” Was this the soul of Abbot Ugano, whom Blessed Peter had rebuked?]

Amen.

[Col. 0145]

# Another Life of Blessed Peter Damian

By Giovanni Antonio Flaminio of Forlì.

From the author’s autograph manuscript preserved at Faenza.

[Col. 0145C] I am accustomed to being filled with great pleasure, men of Faenza, whenever I recall how welcome and agreeable to you is the work which I have undertaken to perform in describing those whom you most devoutly venerate—with such eagerness of spirit that scarcely could anyone who loves you more perform it with greater zeal. I observed this when I recently wrote the life of Blessed Terentius the Confessor, who was first presented to me, and that of Blessed Sabinus, bishop and martyr. Therefore, when I heard that you expected from me a similar labor concerning the two saints who still remained, I thought I ought to respond to your expectation and desire with the same devotion. Accordingly, I have added Blessed Peter Damian and Saint Aemilianus—whom the episcopal dignity made illustrious together with their holiness—to the two whom I mentioned first, so that you may daily experience, through clearer signs, my already demonstrated love for you and my desire to gratify you in everything that I am able to accomplish. Farewell.

The beginnings of the life of the most illustrious and most holy man Peter Damian can bring great wonder to everyone. They were so humble and difficult that those who know them can understand that it happened only through divine providence that he was able to become such a great man, one who would illuminate the Church of God both by his eloquence and by the holiness of his life.

His mother had scarcely brought him forth into the light of day when, weary of her numerous offspring, she began to persecute the infant with the hatred of a stepmother. For after she had borne this child as well, following many others, one of the older sons exclaimed indignantly: “And how will this one house contain so many heirs?” From that moment the mother began to nourish the child with hostile feeling, so that she gave him her milk only with the greatest reluctance. Thus the infant was gradually wasting away from hunger and cold. But almighty God, who had willed that he be born for the adornment of his Church, did not permit him to remain any longer deprived of every assistance.

For he stirred the spirit of a certain woman, who approached the mother and sharply rebuked her cruelty, saying: “Lionesses and tigresses nourish their cubs with marvelous care and affection, yet you treat your own son, created in the image of God, so cruelly, with the maternal affections of your heart dulled? You do not know that it may happen that this boy will one day hold an illustrious place among his people.”

The mother was moved and ashamed by this rebuke; and, as though awakened from a deep sleep, she began to recover her senses and to show the infant maternal care. But he, who shortly before had been so badly treated that he had grown stiff and seemed more a shadow of a boy than a boy, soon regained his strength and appearance. Yet the hatred begun during his nursing years was also stirred against him during his childhood.

After his parents had died, one of his brothers, the eldest, and that brother’s wife began to harass him in extraordinary ways and to exercise against him, as though he were a worthless slave, contempt and cruelty. I say nothing of food more suitable for pigs than for a human being; there was no care for his body, his clothing was filthy, and his feet were bare. I omit the other things that one could scarcely endure in the utmost poverty, even as a beggar. I pass over the beatings, blows, and kicks that he frequently suffered, as well as many other things scarcely tolerable to relate or hear, much less to see.

Such was his childhood. When he reached adolescence, his condition did not improve in the least. From this one may form some idea of what he suffered when he was sent to tend pigs. Anyone who knows what preceded may imagine how harsh everything was for him there. But divine Providence wished in this way to exercise its athlete and put him to the test, so that it might heap upon him all these things for the sake of more abundant grace and finally make him, from one so ignoble and despised, glorious to his entire Church.

It is worthwhile to know by what beginnings he attained this. One of his brothers, embracing him with the affection he owed him, began to treat him humanely and carefully arranged for him to be educated in letters. In a short time he progressed so far that he became an object of admiration even to his teachers. Once he had been thoroughly instructed in the liberal arts, so that he could now teach others, a multitude of students began to flock to him from every side; and as his reputation and the favor of the people grew daily, his wealth also increased.

But divine Providence took care that he not be held back by earthly attractions. It instilled in his mind a complete contempt for earthly things and inspired in him an extraordinary desire for heavenly things. Gradually abandoning human studies and devoting himself to divine ones, he began to wear a hair shirt beneath soft and delicate clothing, to devote himself to fasting, prayer, and vigils, and through continual mortifications to compel the flesh to obey the spirit.

When youthful ardor began to rise within him and he was driven by the sharp impulses of his age, he would rise from bed in the middle of the night, angry with himself, go out of the house, and plunge into the river water until his limbs grew stiff from the extreme cold; thus the dangerous warmth and softness within him would completely disappear.

He relieved the poverty of the needy by almsgiving, prepared banquets, and with his own hands ministered to them as though they were Christ. But a higher concern and the thought of finding a way to serve God more freely and attentively, after removing worldly hindrances, had already taken possession of him. God himself, who had placed this thought in his mind, immediately showed him the path by which he could satisfy his desire.

Two monks from the hermitage of Fonte Avellana—for that was the name of the place—happened to encounter him. He disclosed to them what he was considering and desiring. Since the fame of the holy man had already reached their abbot, they received the news joyfully and, through much conversation, inflamed his desire even more.

When they were leaving, he tried to give them a certain silver vessel, a valuable gift for them to offer their abbot, but he could not persuade them to accept it despite all his entreaties. Astonished at their great contempt for earthly things, he resolved all the more firmly to embrace Christ’s poverty and to renounce entirely worldly possessions and all their attractions.

Before, however, he went to the hermitage mentioned above and entered the monastic life there, he wished to test whether he could endure the austerity of that life, having heard how severe it was. He therefore entered a certain cell and spent forty days disciplining his body there, mortifying and afflicting it in every way available to him.

Thus confirmed still more firmly in his resolve, he waited for the time when he could most suitably carry out his holy plan. Then, taking with him some necessities from his possessions, he secretly set out for the desired hermitage, without the knowledge of any of his family. He was received there with great joy and cheerfulness and was entrusted, according to custom, to one of the elders for instruction. When the elder had led him to his cell, he stripped him of the clothing he had brought with him, clothed him in a hair shirt, and returned him to the abbot, who immediately ordered that he be dressed in a cowl.

During these events his spirit began to waver, and he almost regretted what he had done, as though he had hurried too much into this undertaking when he ought first to have tested what he could do in the monastery. But he soon came to his senses. Accusing himself of a kind of cowardice and of forgetfulness of the holy purpose that had driven him to come—so that, in such austerity, his tamed body might be subjected to the spirit and to Christ’s gentle yoke—he offered himself willingly to the battle like a strong athlete girded with spiritual weapons. How great he proved himself in that battle will be shown by what follows.

For he immediately began to afflict his body, wearing it down with prayers, fasts, vigils, and various other mortifications, and sparing himself none of the monastery’s labors, so that those who had long lived and been trained in the monastery marveled and accused themselves as though they were slothful.

It is pleasant at this point to describe the rule of life of that most holy monastery, so that it may be clear to what austerity the blessed man subjected himself.

Above all, this was their established discipline: two monks were to live in each cell, and day and night, fighting in spiritual combat as though in battle formation, they were never to relax their arms. Armed without ceasing with psalmody, prayer, reading, hunger, and obedience, they fought against the aerial powers.

Their practice of hunger, which they call abstinence, was as follows. On four days of each week they ate bread and drank water. On Tuesday and Thursday they added a small quantity of legumes, which each man cooked in his own cell. On the days appointed for fasting, no one was permitted to take bread according to his own desire, but only as much as the decree of the Fathers commanded. No one was permitted to drink wine except at the sacrifice or in illness. They walked barefoot in winter and summer; no one used leggings.

They also devoted themselves to other spiritual exercises: scourging, genuflections, and extending their arms for long periods in the form of a cross, according to each man’s fervor and strength. They observed this custom of vigils: when the signal was given earlier than usual, after certain other offices they would complete the entire Psalter before dawn.

But Saint Peter, without waiting for the common signal and anticipating the others by a long interval, spent whatever remained of the night after the regular offices in vigil, and undertook many other tasks without being ordered to do so.

Since he kept vigils more frequently than was healthy, he contracted a dangerous illness of the head, so severe that he could scarcely obtain even a brief sleep. After medicines had been administered and he was restored to health, he began to be gentler and more moderate toward himself.

After psalmody, therefore, he rarely left his cell and devoted himself with intense zeal to reading. In a short time he progressed so far in it that he became as distinguished in sacred Scripture as he had formerly been in human letters.

As a result, at the command of his teacher, he frequently addressed the monks who lived together in the manner of a public declamation. When his reputation grew, the venerable abbot Pomposianus sent messengers to his abbot, asking him to allow Peter to come to him and remain there for several days.

The abbot graciously permitted this, as charity required. The monks there, whose number was very large—about one hundred—were so attracted and delighted by Peter’s presence, his conduct, the holiness of his life, and especially by the nourishment of the divine word that flowed from his mouth like honey, that after two years they were reluctant to let him return to his own monastery.

But he was recalled at the command of his teacher, and since he was devoted to inviolable obedience and held it in honor, he could not be detained any longer.

Shortly afterward he was ordered to go to the monastery of Saint Vincent. This monastery was more crowded in proportion to the abundance of its monks and more illustrious in wealth, and it was consequently more admirable in monastic austerity and discipline. There too he remained for some time as a diligent laborer in the Lord’s vineyard.

His teacher, who rejoiced in his disciple’s great progress, as well as in his prudence and the admirable integrity of his life, instructed him to take charge of the hermitage after him.

Peter refused and resisted as much as he could; but when obedience pressed him, he could no longer oppose it. Having accepted the administration of the place, he began to look around and diligently inquire where he might gather other communities of monks, so as to increase the number of God’s ministers.

Through this zeal and careful investigation he built eremitical monasteries in many different places: in the region of Camerino; in the territory of Perugia, where he found a cell that was said to have been inhabited by Blessed Romuald; also in the district of Rimini; and in the territory of Faenza, in two neighboring places, the first called Gamunium and the second Acereta.

Although he was deeply occupied with administering and directing these establishments, he frequently visited the monastery where he had first entered and took special care of it. He also visited the other monks, greatly consoling them by his presence and daily inflaming them more fervently to serve God. Whenever he could not go to them, he sent letters or messengers.

He cared not only for his own monasteries but also for those of others, like a common father of all, constantly striving by whatever means he could to increase the honor of God.

I must not pass over in silence a remarkable example of his holiness, which occurred in the monastery of Faenza, in the place called Acereta, as we have said.

He had sent one of his disciples to draw water for him from a nearby spring. The disciple brought it. When the holy man had tasted it, he turned to the disciple and said: “I did not order you to bring me wine.”

The disciple replied: “I drew water from the spring and brought it.”

The holy man denied this, but the disciple firmly insisted that it was so. To discover the truth, Peter sent another man to the spring and instructed him not to turn aside elsewhere. The man brought water, and Peter himself tasted it. As though he did not trust his own senses, he gave it to those who were present to taste. All affirmed that it was excellent wine, and they marveled with immense joy.

But he, displaying his customary humility and recognizing the divine generosity toward him, imposed silence on everyone who knew what had happened, lest anyone reveal it to another while he was alive.

Nor is what follows worthy of less admiration.

Blessed Peter had an amphora of wine in the house of a neighboring priest. A troop of soldiers arrived and began insistently to demand wine from the priest. He replied that he had no wine except what we have just mentioned, and that he did not dare draw anything from it.

But when the soldiers pressed their demand still more and accomplished nothing by asking, they hurried to draw the wine themselves. As they attempted to do so, they saw that nothing flowed and were astonished. They tested many places on the amphora to see whether it might be leaking, but in vain, for nothing flowed. Finally, after removing the vessel’s cover, they examined it to see whether wine was inside. They found that there was wine, but were astonished that it did not flow. After repeatedly laboring in vain, they departed.

Later a certain pilgrim came and asked the same priest for a drink. The priest refused, repeating what he had told the soldiers and what had happened when they made their demand. But the pilgrim did not stop asking. He reproached the soldiers’ arrogance and insolence, saying that he was humbly asking for a drink because he was being tormented by excessive thirst.

Not to prolong the story: overcome by the pilgrim’s entreaties, the priest, although very fearful, dared to test whether he could draw the wine. As soon as he tried, the wine immediately followed his hand. The pilgrim drank and, filled with wonder, gave thanks to God and to the priest.

On another day, when he was about to dine, Peter had only one loaf and one guest; there was no other dish except vegetables. He therefore chose to eat the vegetables himself and offered the bread to his guest, encouraging him to endure the poor meal with a cheerful spirit, since he would have an abundant one the next day.

The prophet was not mistaken. For on the following day such an abundance of food was brought that it could have sufficed for many days.

A certain noble and wealthy man was accustomed to send a large quantity of fish on solemn feast days. The most celebrated day of Christ’s Nativity had arrived, but he had been unable to find any fish. He was distressed and could not rest. During the night a large fish was brought to him, for God had come to the aid of his desire.

He immediately ordered one of his servants to take the fish to the holy man. It was nighttime, and the light of the stars, weakened by the clouds, made the road much more difficult. In addition to the other obstacles, the servant had to cross a very high cliff. After he had already climbed part of it, he slipped while making his way—or rather crawling—along the treacherous path and fell into a deep ravine, where he ought to have been torn limb from limb. Nevertheless, through the merits of the holy man, he emerged unharmed and reached him with the fish.

[Col. 0151A] Blessed Peter had sent one of his disciples to a certain abbot. The disciple set out but did not find him. He searched carefully to see whether he could locate him, but could not, and the time prescribed for his return was already passing.

Fearing a reprimand, he began the journey in the stillness of the night. After he had gone a short distance, his companion and guide abandoned him, and the darkness of night was dense. He did not know the road. Sad and uncertain, he did not know what to do; he knew neither how to proceed nor, if he wished, how to return.

He therefore began to ask God not to abandon him. As he gradually moved forward, he came to a fork in the road and hesitated about where to direct his journey. Finally he entered one of the two roads. After he had proceeded a short distance, the animal began to refuse to go forward, and he could not force it to advance even with the spurs. Overcome by its stubbornness, he loosened the reins and allowed it to go wherever it wished.

When dawn was breaking and he looked around, he saw that he had been carried to places he knew. He rejoiced greatly and gave God the thanks that were due. He did not doubt that, through the merits of his teacher, he had been brought to the place where he wished to be.

He then sent another messenger to a certain bishop. This man reached a stream in which the water was shallow, but near the farther bank there was deep mud, so adhesive that the horse could not free its feet from it by any effort.

Since no other means of escape presented itself, he prayed God that, through the merits of the one by whom he had been sent, God would assist him so that he could continue the journey he had begun. He had scarcely finished praying when the horse leapt out onto dry ground.

[Col. 0151C] But when the fame of so great a man and the magnitude of his miracles began to spread, and the reputation of his holiness increased daily, Pope Stephen IX summoned him to his presence. The pope judged—and rightly—that such a man was greatly needed in the Church of God and would become a great light. Since many other bishops held the same opinion and urged the pope to do so, he made Peter a bishop, although Peter resisted and absolutely refused.

He saw that he would be deprived of the sweetness of the solitary peace in which he had continually devoted himself at one time to divine contemplation, at another to sacred reading and other spiritual exercises, and would be called back to the turmoil of public affairs.

But when neither the exhortations of the other prelates nor threats of excommunication achieved anything, the pontiff, who thought that a treasure once found must not be abandoned under any circumstances, drew him to his own decision by the command of obedience. Taking Peter’s hand, he invested him with a ring and staff, as pledges of episcopal dignity, and placed him over the Church of Ostia.

Thus, as Peter himself later used to say, what he had seen in a dream three years earlier was fulfilled. He had thought that a most illustrious bride was being assigned to him, whom, once joined to him, he could neither put away nor look upon willingly.

He therefore humbly subjected his neck to what he considered an exceedingly heavy yoke. Although he believed that he was suffering a great loss of his customary contemplation, he nevertheless compensated for the losses of the past with the gains of what followed.

He therefore began with the greatest vigilance to devote himself to the flock entrusted to him, directing them into the way of salvation and keeping them in it through frequent exhortations and repeated public addresses. Desiring with extraordinary zeal to win everyone for God, he made no distinction of persons and was loved by all.

In return, the people showed him extraordinary reverence, extraordinary love, and extraordinary devotion. They listened to him with such attention, pleasure, and admiration that he might have seemed an apostle sent down from heaven.

This should cause no surprise. The holiness of his life, proven to all, the integrity of his conduct, and the gravity evident in all his words and deeds were so great that his words possessed immense weight, and prayer sweeter than every kind of honey flowed from his mouth.

The sermons that survive also clearly testify to this. Consequently, his most wholesome and eloquent addresses, however long they might be, never seemed long to those who came to hear them; they seemed extremely brief, and nothing could be heard with greater eagerness and attention.

No labor tired him. When he was going to address the people, he spent almost the entire night sleepless. He did not spare himself even when he was often suffering from fever; indeed, he seemed at such times stronger and more eloquent.

He made the venerable day of the Lord’s Passion throughout the entire province a day of the highest observance and fasting. He also restored to their former observance the Office of the Blessed Virgin and the canonical rites, whose neglect had gradually crept in.

He labored greatly and achieved much in removing the stain of simony and the heresy of the Nicolaitans, which had infected not only other places but even the city of Rome, so that scarcely anyone remained to rebuke it.

Because of these evils the supreme pontiff also sent him to Milan. There they had taken such deep root that Peter attempted to eradicate them only with immense labor and great danger to his life.

For the Milanese had become so proud and rebellious toward the Roman pontiff that a great dispute arose. The people and clergy shouted that an utterly unworthy and intolerable thing was being proposed: that the Ambrosian Church had never previously been subject to the Roman Church and ought not to be subject to it thereafter.

The holy man gathered the people in the church and imposed silence. Through the clearest arguments, the testimonies of sacred Scripture, and authoritative texts—which his eloquence made still more powerful—he demonstrated to all that the Roman Church was the sovereign and head of all Churches, and that the Roman pontiff presided over all by divine right.

He had obtained this prerogative from the mouth of the Savior himself, who said:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

“For what province,” he said, “among all the kingdoms of the earth can be said to be outside this dominion and power, by whose judgment heaven itself is opened and closed?

“As for the other Churches, whatever their dignity may have been, the one who established them was merely a human being. But the Roman Church was founded by that one alone, who built it upon the rock of the faith as it arose and entrusted to the blessed keeper of the keys the rights of both the earthly and heavenly kingdom.

“The Roman pontiff therefore exercises his privilege by Christ’s privilege and is supported by Christ’s authority. Whoever dares to weaken the right of the chief Church is undoubtedly acting unjustly and giving himself bad counsel.

“For whoever attempts to violate the privilege of the Roman Church, granted by the supreme head of all Churches himself, undoubtedly falls into heresy, for he violates the faith. Whoever therefore rises up against that Church which is the mother of faith is also found rebellious against him who willed it to preside over and command all Churches.”

The prayer of so great a man was effective and penetrated the hearts of the people. They ended the dispute and submitted themselves to the greater authority.

But when a careful investigation of the sacred ministers was undertaken, scarcely anyone was found who had attained sacred orders without payment. The holy man was tormented by great anxieties because of this. He saw that so broad a diocese, together with so noble and extensive a city and so many churches, was being profaned, and he thought that the Christian religion was thereby being overthrown.

Yet it was highly contentious to show indulgence to a few when almost everyone shared the guilt; nor did it seem just to pronounce a different sentence against them when the case of all was one and the same.
