Placed therefore in such a difficult situation, since he could not correct the evils of that Church without great danger while preserving the authority of the canons, he at least endeavored to put an end to the corrupt custom and to ensure that henceforth advancement to sacred orders would be free of charge.

He therefore demanded from the archbishop of Milan and from the others who held any office under him an inviolable pledge that henceforth the entire stain of simony and the heresy of the Nicolaitans would be completely abolished.

When their minds had thus been reconciled and matters settled, it was decreed that the office of ministering should immediately be restored to all indiscriminately—but only to those who appeared worthy through learning, gravity of conduct, and honesty. For the others, it would be enough that, by divine grace, they had been incorporated into the holy Church from which they had been cut off by the divine judgment.

Even those to whom the power of ministering was restored received it not on the basis of their former advancement, acquired through wrongdoing, but through the blessed authority of the chief of the apostles, which he exercised toward Blessed Apollinaris when he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit, together with the pontificate.”

We have touched on these matters briefly so that from them everyone may form some idea of the nature of his other deeds. I do not think anyone could recount them all, since in the holy Church he never ceased entirely to remove and uproot whatever was corrupt or insolent, and to establish for the glory of Christ whatever he observed to be pious and religious.

In all these matters divine favor and overflowing grace were present with him, since his judgment, determining what ought to be admitted, done, or avoided, was in accord with the canonical sanctions.

[Col. 0154A] No one could easily express in words how greatly, and through how many works pleasing to God, the holy man shone forth—whether by washing the feet of the poor, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, or consoling the afflicted.

The needy frequently came to his door. Some he refreshed with food; others he sent away happily after distributing alms. No one left his doorway without receiving a gift.

It was his constant custom to wash the feet of twelve poor men. If there were any lying on beds, he took particular care of them, assigning someone to them who would remain with them and provide what they needed.

Thus he distributed the goods of the Church—which are the goods of the poor—for pious uses, sparing his own expenses. He reminded the sacred ministers, saying:

“Know, dearest brothers, that all these goods of the Church are sacred and are the price of sins. Therefore the greatest care must be taken that none of these things be taken away from Christ’s poor, whether through the impulse of greed or through any negligent carelessness, for whatever remains to us is owed to them.

“Since we have sufficient means by which the needy may be helped and supported, diligently inquire whether there are any who are ill in neighboring places, or who suffer from hunger or any other form of poverty. If you provide them with what they need, you will prepare treasures for yourselves in heaven.”

Through such holy admonitions the devout father urged his people toward works of compassion and daily inflamed them to greater zeal by his exhortations.

Remembering his former life in the hermitage, he was always possessed by an extraordinary longing for it. Since he could no longer live there, he at least represented its austerity in every way available to him.

Except on feast days, he mortified himself by a daily fast, and that fast was exceedingly severe and rigorous: although already worn out by old age, he ate coarse bread and drank water from outside sources. In addition, he bound and constricted his body, already mortified in many ways, with iron chains over his bare flesh, and frequently afflicted it sometimes with blows from the palm of his hand, sometimes with straps.

When his limbs had been exhausted by so many harsh practices, he did not lie on feathers or straw, but took his very scant sleep on a bare grating.

What can I say of his marvelous zeal in singing psalms, praying, reading, and dictating? Nor should it be passed over that he himself took his food from the same basin in which he washed the feet of the poor.

[Col. 0154D] Whenever in earlier times he attended the synod of the monks—which the cenobites call the chapter—he would rise from his seat, go into the midst of them, humbly confess his sins, ask for much penance for them, and with holy exhortations instruct now one, now another, and now all together.

Turning to the younger men, he would say:

“You must know, dearest sons, that each of you ought to begin the novitiate of this warfare with such zeal and ardor, and exercise himself with as much labor as his bodily powers permit, so that the entire course of his future life may be shaped for courageous action.

He would inflame those more advanced, with grave and eloquent speech, to combat vices, to discern thoughts, to cultivate compunction and contemplation, and to preserve purity of mind with all their strength. He would add that everyone ought to recognize his own strength in spiritual combat. For it is disgraceful for a monk to profess spiritual warfare and, through cowardice, to remain ignorant of what he is capable of testing.”

Certainly, he himself wished to test his strength in great struggles. For his most faithful witnesses asserted that for forty whole days he regularly ate no cooked food, but only fruit and raw vegetables, without any drink; and, more astonishing still, that for an equal number of days he took no food at all, contenting himself only with a small infusion of legumes.

If at any time, while maintaining the austerity of life that he constantly observed, he felt his strength failing, he did not think it a fault to relax something of such severity so that he might return stronger to his former contest. He used to say that it should be counted as a virtue if someone relaxes his weary arms a little because of excessive labor in order to rise afterward more vigorous for courageous action.

Moreover, whenever he attended the offices of day and night, it was his custom to stand and lean on no support.

At the beginning of both Lents he abstained from food for three entire days. Although he never urged anyone else to do this, certain people thought they should imitate him for the sake of greater spiritual progress.

Consequently, some monasteries also adopted, following the example of so great a man, a rule of this voluntary observance. Throughout the entire three days, complete silence was rigorously maintained within the monastery precincts; and no one put on his footwear, unless unavoidable necessity intervened, before completing the entire Psalter.

When, in the place called the chapter, they underwent the use of brooms—a practice which the cenobites call discipline—all observed a fast of bread and water.

He also made every Friday, except during Eastertide and on other solemn days, venerable out of reverence for the holy cross by means of the same discipline and fasting.

These practices were approved with such universal agreement among religious men that even the renowned monastery of Monte Cassino decreed that all of them should be observed there and wished them to be written among its regular precepts.

I wish to recount at this point a vision through which the custom of observing Friday was wonderfully confirmed. Since he himself recorded it, I shall append his own words:

> “In the cell of the sick there was an old father named Leo, who devoted himself earnestly to fasts, psalms, and prayers. Although his bodily strength was exhausted, he was nevertheless strong with the vigor of a youthful and fervent spirit.
>
> “On the preceding night, when this regulation of fasting was to be established, he saw in a dream a great choir of brothers standing in the church. They were splendidly clothed in bright white garments and sang with the sweetness of a most melodious and honeyed harmony that Alleluia which is called ‘Sweet wood, sweet nails,’ and so forth.
>
> “He also saw that loaves had been placed on all the refectory tables, shining in appearance and sweetened with the flavor of nectar.
>
> “Among the brothers reclining all around was a distinguished man of striking beauty. When he was asked where such loaves had come from—loaves like which they had never seen before—he replied: ‘These are the loaves by which the children of Israel, receiving manna from heaven, were nourished in the desert’ (Exodus 19).
>
> “This man also took the abbot’s table, which had been set toward the west, and placed it on the eastern side of the refectory, where the image of the crucified Lord had been represented on the wall in a painting.
>
> “Consider therefore the mystery and understand the sacrament of the mystical revelation. What else does it mean that the choir of singers resounded with melodious voices in praise of the cross, except that, when a solemn fast was to be instituted in honor of the cross, they would sound forth, as it were, sweet melodies of praise to it?
>
> “For the one who celebrates a fast on the day when Christ was hung upon the cross sings a hymn in honor of the blessed cross. And what does it mean that the loaves appeared sweetened with honey, except that they were to eat sweet spiritual nourishment while, through the bitterness of the cross, they resounded with sweet melodies of praise to God?
>
> “For the sweeter the taste that arises on the palate of the heart, the greater the bitterness of strict discipline that disturbs the wantonness of the flesh.
>
> “What also does it mean to place the abbot’s table beneath the feet of Christ the Redeemer, except that, through the Friday fast—the day of the cross—the entire refectory was to be dedicated to the saving sign of the cross?
>
> “And what does it mean to sit beneath the feet of the crucified Lord, except to follow in his footsteps and walk by the path along which he went before us?”

[Col. 0156C] This was the life of that most holy man; these were his deeds, worthy of remembrance and of every admiration. By these steps he opened for himself a way to the immortality of his name and to eternal blessedness. When the appointed time had come, Almighty God, intending to pay the servant his established reward, caused his vicar, Alexander, supreme pontiff, to order him to depart for Ravenna.

The reason for sending him was this. The archbishop of that city had died; while alive, he had raised his horns against the Roman pontiff and had therefore been condemned by the judgment of the Roman synod. Yet he bore so insolent a spirit that he did not on that account cease from his episcopal duties, but continued to exercise them with a certain contempt for the Roman see, [Col. 0156D] and had a people obedient to him. The devout pontiff, moved by compassion for so great a loss of souls, ordered the most holy man—whose authority and fame were renowned throughout all Italy—to go there, reconcile the rebellious people to the apostolic see, and release them from the sentence of excommunication. For the supreme Father believed that no one could be more suitable or more effective than he.

Although already worn down by old age, he willingly accepted this mission, as he was an ardent champion of the salvation of souls; and divine grace did not fail him in it. Indeed, on his arrival he found the city wonderfully rejoicing and asking pardon for its offense. When this pardon had been graciously granted, the applause and rejoicing of the people were so great that [Col. 0157A] no one could easily express them in words.

After completing his mission, he was returning to Rome. When he had reached Faenza, a city especially dear to him, and had turned aside to the monastery of the Mother of God, which at that time lay outside the city walls, he fell ill with the sickness that was to end his life. As it grew worse day by day, on the night of the eighth day—the day of the celebrated Chair of the blessed prince of the apostles being at hand—he asked the monks standing around his bed, in the silence of the dead of night, to perform the nocturnal Office of the holy Chair. When it was finished, after a brief interval, he gave his blessed spirit back to God, so that on the very day when the Church had enthroned blessed Peter in the pastoral chair, she might enthrone Peter’s disciple in the heavenly seat.

When his blessed death was announced, almost the entire city went out to the venerable body, so that the sacred building in which he lay could not contain the surging crowd. Like waves, people now approached more closely, now were driven farther back. Each person considered himself fortunate if he could kiss his hands, his feet, or his linen wrappings.

Because people had come from neighboring places where he himself had once lived for a long time, the people set monks as guards, lest his sacred body be carried away by them. At last they placed it in a marble tomb, where, even to the present day, God makes his holy and venerable bishop illustrious to the people through many miracles.

Those who have witnessed his extraordinary holiness and eloquence through great proofs, and who have read the clear and salutary sermons he composed—those, that is, which we have briefly described—will, if I am not mistaken, be fully able to testify what a star he was in the Church of God. Blessed Peter died about the year 1080 of Christ, a great protector and guardian of the city of Faenza.

[Col. 0157]

## ANOTHER LIFE OF BLESSED PETER DAMIAN

From the fifth book of the *Camaldolese Histories*, by Augustine Fortunatus, a monk of the Camaldolese congregation of the Order of St. Benedict, specifically from the latter part, chapters 6 through 144.

[Col. 0157C] Peter Damian was born at Ravenna to respectable parents, though they possessed only modest means and resources. When his mother had given birth to him as her last child, it happened one day that her rather older son, distressed by their poverty, complained and exclaimed: “Look, there are already so many of us that the house can scarcely contain us.” By these words the mother accused herself of being most unfortunate because she was excessively fertile, and from that moment began to deny milk to the infant Peter. Moved by none of his cries or wailings, she took no care whether he should perish from cold and hunger.

A certain neighboring concubine heard of this, hurried to him, and sharply reproved the mother’s cruelty. After much exhortation she finally softened the woman’s savage disposition, joined herself to her with great charity, and, applying warm water, cloths, and other suitable remedies, became the means of restoring to life the half-dead infant, who scarcely breathed and could not even utter a sound.

Afterward, when the boy had been weaned, he lost both parents and was entrusted to the care of his elder brother. When that brother married, he never ceased to oppress Peter, whom he regarded as a superfluous brother, with harsh servitude and beatings, until he even made him keeper of the pigs.

While Peter was occupied in this ignoble service, he one day found a silver coin and, congratulating himself, began to consider what he might buy with it. At last, out of the piety of his heart, he said to himself: “It is better to give this to a priest, who may perform a sacred act for the soul of my father.”

He had another brother named Damian, who had been away from his homeland for several years. When he returned and pitied the sufferings of his brother Peter, moved by affection for his family, he immediately freed him from his wretched servitude, clothed him in new garments, and sent him to school to be instructed in grammatical studies. Recognizing that he possessed an excellent talent and was suited to embrace other disciplines, he sent him first to Faenza and then to Parma, and supported him there so that he could most readily study under learned men.

When Peter had made great progress there in a short time, he adopted the name Damian from his brother’s name, so that he always signed himself “Peter Damian.” His learning in grasping the disciplines of the liberal arts was so great, and the eager and eloquent young man acquired such a reputation and renown, that he was compelled to expound works of rhetoric and eloquence before large gatherings of students, both by his fellow students and by distinguished men.

When his favor and influence increased day by day, together with his wealth and authority, he was suddenly inspired by the divine Spirit and rebuked himself, saying: “Must I cling forever to these fleeting and perishable things? Should I not rather reject them and pursue heavenly things while my age is vigorous and prosperity is pleasant?”

From that day, although he tried to conceal outwardly what he had conceived in his heart, he nevertheless gradually sought to recall himself from worldly studies to sacred philosophy. With all the affection of his mind he aspired to heavenly goods, put on a hair shirt beneath his clothing, and devoted himself diligently to fasts, vigils, and prayers.

When he felt himself fiercely harassed by the impulses of the flesh in the course of his youth, he would rise even in the middle of the night and plunge himself into the waters of a river. Then, returning, he would not go back to bed but would visit the churches and strive to complete the Psalter before the hour of Matins.

[Col. 0159A] He also became generous toward Christ’s poor and frequently invited them to dinner. One day, when he was dining with a companion, he had nothing other than a single loaf of fine wheat bread, while an inferior loaf—the bread of servants—had been set before his companion. Peter immediately began to say to himself: “Is Christ inferior to me at my table?” As he noticed that he had done an injustice to his companion, he felt a fishbone fixed in his throat, choking him. Believing that this had happened because the inferior bread had been assigned to his companion, he at once exchanged the bread with him and discovered that he recovered with his very first bite. Overjoyed, he disclosed the miracle to everyone.

Thus, standing at Pythagoras’ crossroads and deciding to seize the right-hand path, while considering within himself renunciation of the world and how he might accomplish it outside his native land, it happened that two brothers from the solitude of Fonte Avellana, inspired from heaven, came to him by chance. In conversation he asked them about the conversion of certain people and also whether he himself would be received into the monastery by the abbot. When they replied that he certainly would be received, he wished to give them a silver cup to take to the abbot.

When they refused to do this, explaining that neither did the abbot drink from silver nor was it lawful for monks who had professed the vow of poverty to possess gold or silver, Peter praised their answer, and his opinion of the sanctity of the place was strengthened more and more.

[Col. 0159C] Yet, lest he seem to undertake so great a matter without foundation, he wished first to test, as is proper for a prudent and wise man, whether he could endure the labor of monastic life. He therefore went to the monastery of Saint Mary at the shore of the Adriatic—as Dante states (*Paradiso*, canto 21)—and there for forty days exercised himself in a manner resembling the rigor of the eremitical life. Greatly strengthened, he then secretly left his parents and acquaintances and moved to the hermitage of Avellana.

There he was gladly received and became a humble and despised monk. Like a novice, he was assigned a discerning master, who always esteemed his virtue highly.

One day he was ordered to ride with the master and to put on a finer garment. Peter humbly begged him not to give such an order, since it was unbecoming. Finally compelled, he put on the garments that had been offered; but [Col. 0159D] out of shame he did not dare look at anyone during the entire journey. For it seemed to him that everyone was pointing at him with a finger, as though he were a bridegroom rather than a monk.

On the return journey, when they had reached the monastery of Saint Vincent, he devised a suitable pretext for remaining there. With the master’s assent and permission, he quickly asked for rougher, cheaper garments of uniformly colored fabric. He immediately put them on, leaving all the monks an example that each person should strive to be adorned more by character than by clothing.

The rule of the sacred place at that time was as follows. Two brothers lived together in separate cells, girded with the weapons of psalmody, prayer, reading, abstinence, and obedience, to fight against the powers of the air. Four days a week they lived on bread and water. On Tuesday and Thursday each added a small quantity of legumes. On days of fasting, bread was supplied not as much as each person wished, but in a fixed measure. Wine was permitted only in the sacrifice of the Mass and, as was known, to the sick; to no one else. They went barefoot at all times, having rejected footwear.

Peter practiced himself most diligently in this way of life. He added the following. Since, according to custom, each monk recited the Psalter before the nocturnal synaxis, and since the signal for it was sounded early, he anticipated the signal by too great a margin. Because of his excessive vigils, he fell ill, losing the benefit of sleep because his brain had been damaged. Yet, after medicines had been applied, he recovered by God’s grace.

Since he could scarcely obtain any rest from teaching and writing, he began to be regarded as illustrious for such knowledge of the divine Scriptures as he had previously possessed of human learning.

[Col. 0160B] In the earliest period of his career, around the year 1040 of the Lord, he published the life of Saint Romuald, having received it from the lips of Romuald’s disciples, who lived in the neighboring hermitage of Sitria. We read the same account of the date in the *Greater Chronicles*, at Venice, in the house of Francesco Giustiniani.

Moved by this reputation, Wido Strambiatus, abbot of the monastery of Pomposa, sent envoys to the abbot of Avellana and, with many prayers, begged that Peter be given as a teacher to his young men. After Peter had spent two years there, bringing great benefit to the monks, he was recalled to his beloved solitude when his own abbot died, and Peter was appointed in his place.

[Col. 0160C] Having therefore assumed the insignia and administration, he first of all strove to reform the monastery into a better condition of complete holiness. But as the number of disciples grew, he was compelled to seek other places where he could establish them.

He therefore rose up and, having discovered a particularly suitable site in the diocese of Camerino, built a monastery beside his nearby rock and established there a community of disciples under a prior. Then he went into the Perugian territory and built another at Mount Regius, beside the cell where Saint Romuald was said to have lived. Next he built another in the territory of Faenza, at a place called Ganuinium, now Gavina. Then another nearby, called Arcere. After that, Marciano in the territory of Rimini.

While he was building these places and striving everywhere to organize monks who were thoroughly instructed in holiness and in the true service of God, he nevertheless could never forget the community and place of his beloved monastery of Avellana. He often hurried back to visit them and refresh them with the nourishment of heavenly discourse, either by his presence or through letters, with a singular paternal affection and charity. Thus, becoming daily more filled with God, he also began to grow more renowned for miracles.

One day, while he was staying in a cell at Ganuinium, he became thirsty and ordered water to be brought to him from the spring. The servant hastened to fulfill the order; but when the master tasted what had been brought, it was discovered to be wine. The servant, rebuked by him, insisted that he had drawn water. Another was sent to the spring, and when he likewise brought wine—which all the monks tasted—the holy man, recognizing the miracle, ordered everyone to keep the matter silent. This was done until his death.

[Col. 0161A] On another occasion the holy man had a cask full of wine near one of his chapels. A band of soldiers happened to pass by, and some of them forced a priest to pour them a drink from that very cask. When he insisted that he did not wish to touch the holy man’s wine, they attacked the cask, opened all its apertures, and inserted rods, but could never draw out any wine. Struck by an inward trembling, they immediately withdrew from the place.

Shortly afterward, a pilgrim passing by asked insistently for a drink out of love of God. The priest went back to the cask, saw that its openings were closed, and drew wine from it. Recognizing the miracle, he refreshed the hungry pilgrim, giving thanks to God.

At another time a nobleman, who was accustomed occasionally to send gifts of fish to blessed Peter, sent his servant to him on Christmas Eve. The servant set out at night in darkness, while deep snow was falling; his foot slipped and he fell headlong at a remote point along the road. Because he could not easily have been torn apart, he escaped unharmed through the merits of the holy man. Taking up again the burden on his shoulders, he reached Peter and gave him thanks. Peter replied:

“My son, do not—do not attribute to this sinful man what God in his mercy has deigned to grant you. Give thanks for the gift of the salvation bestowed upon you to him who is never absent from those who serve him.”

[Col. 0161C] On another occasion Peter sent a disciple to one of the abbots. When the disciple did not find him at the monastery and wished to return to his master because of the delay, he obtained a guide for the journey. But after they had gone some distance, the guide disappeared from his sight because the sky had become exceedingly dark.

Unfamiliar with the road, the disciple reached a fork and, uncertain which path to take, finally directed the animal along the one he judged to be more heavily traveled. The horse constantly resisted, wishing instead to take the other path. At last, overcome, the disciple slackened the reins. As the sky soon began to brighten, he realized that, by divine prompting, the dumb animal had taken the right road. He was brought directly to the master and gave thanks to God and to the blessed man.

On another occasion he sent a messenger to a certain bishop. While crossing a river, the messenger’s horse became deeply stuck in the mud and could not get out. He invoked the holy man, and the horse immediately extricated itself from the mud.

When the messenger reached the bishop’s residence, the bishop was absent. The bishop’s cousin received him kindly but left him alone for the night in a large room. The messenger was overcome by nighttime fear and could not sleep at all. Behold, in the middle of the night blessed Peter appeared to his host and sharply rebuked him.

In the morning the host went to him and asked what negligence or fault he had committed, that blessed Peter had come to rebuke him during the night. This gave the entire household an opportunity to praise God.

[Col. 0162A] Finally, during the reform of the monastery of Saint Benedict, Abbot Desiderius discovered that certain workers there were possessed by demons and asked blessed Peter to deign to cure them. Peter replied that he was unworthy to lay his hands upon the harvest of Saint Benedict. Nevertheless, by remaining there for a longer time, he obtained that God should free them on account of his merits.

During those days the fame of Peter’s holiness resounded far and wide. Stephen, supreme pontiff, judging the good man worthy of the priesthood, invited him, together with the most sacred order of the purple-clad cardinals, to accept an episcopal chair. When Peter refused, the pontiff judged that his virtue was supremely necessary for the correction of the Church. Under threat of anathema, [Col. 0162B] he ordered him to do so. Having summoned him to Rome, he took him by the right hand and, through his ring and staff, joined the Church of Ostia to him, making him dean of the sacred college of cardinals. This occurred in the year 1058, at the beginning of Lent, in March, on the Ember Saturday.

Thus compelled, he held the episcopate. As a good shepherd, he took particular care that whatever revenues remained should be devoted to the benefit of Christ’s poor. Every day he washed the feet of twelve people, also providing them with a meal, and diligently exercised his protection on behalf of orphans and widows. When he ministered to the poor, he often ate with great eagerness from the basin in which he had washed their feet, and he slept on a bare lattice.

After Pope Stephen died at Florence, Peter took part in the election of Benedict X, his successor. When the other cardinals were compelled by the influence and care of the counts of Tusculum, by the distribution of money, and by force to adore Benedict, Peter protested vigorously. He succeeded in removing the counts themselves from their abominable undertaking and brought it about that Nicholas II was substituted for Stephen according to the election, shortly afterward, on 3 January 1059.

[Col. 0162C] But when he saw how the See of Peter was being oppressed by powerful laymen, and on the other hand how sacred men indulged every kind of lust and kept numerous prostitutes in place of wives, and when he saw no one capable of correcting them, he grew disgusted with the customs of the curia. He judged it better to return to his beloved solitude, where he could freely devote himself to his customary contemplation and compare the fecundity of Leah with the beauty of Rachel, than to remain any longer amid the upheavals of the world. He therefore voluntarily renounced both the sacred hat and the episcopate.

Here it is evident how plainly those are mistaken who have thought that blessed Peter Damian became a hermit only after being made a cardinal, since Peter himself, his disciples, and Dante—as noted above (*Paradiso*, canto 21)—remove every doubt on the matter.

But Pope Nicholas, unwilling to accept his resignation, compelled him to resume the insignia of his dignity. When he saw that he could not persuade him, he finally yielded to Peter’s perseverance, but imposed upon him a punishment of a hundred years: namely, that for one hundred years he should recite Psalm 50 every day, accompanied by scourging.

The devout supreme pastor did this in order that, by imposing so great and almost impossible a task, Peter might abandon his obstinacy and show the reverence owed to pontifical majesty. But Peter eagerly accepted the penance and, wonderfully enough, completed it within a year. He also wrote to the pontiff most elegant letters, full of humility and holiness, in which he diligently sought to justify himself, recalling that he had acted according to the example of holy men.

Among these letters are the following words:

“Finally, to leave aside the rest and return to a domestic example, Lambert of venerable memory, who was the third bishop of the Church at Florence before us, rejected the office of princely authority and subjected himself to monastic discipline.”

These words led some people to suppose that Peter Damian had been a bishop of Florence, or else that “Faventinus” had been corrupted in its first syllables. But this is certainly not so. Since Lambert held the chair of the Church of Florence from 1026 to 1037, and was succeeded by Atto, and Atto by Gerard, who was later raised to the summit of the pontificate and became Pope Nicholas II, it is perfectly clear that the error lies in the word “us,” where perhaps “you” ought to be read.

Peter wished to defend his case by taking an example from the pontiff’s predecessor, as being nearer to him. Nor is there evidence that Florence had any Peter at that time before the year 1064, by which time Nicholas himself had already died, unless perhaps Saint Peter Damian held both the Florentine [Col. 0163C] and Ostian chairs simultaneously—a claim supported by no other testimony.

He also resigned the administration of two other monasteries entrusted to him, as is evident from the following words near the beginning of that letter:

“Therefore, for the remission of all my sins, which I have wickedly committed, I surrender by this ring the rights of the episcopate; you have taken away the staff, and, abandoning every hope of making a further complaint, I renounce it. I also return both monasteries.”

But the pontiff, wishing to reform the Church of Milan, which differed from the Roman Church and was infected both with the stain of simony and with the heresy of the Nicolaitans, again brought Peter out of his hermitage and sent him to Milan as a legate *a latere*, so that he might recall the entire clergy and people there to the correct position.

Compelled to obey, Peter went there, taking Bishop Anselm of Lucca as his colleague. When he had been received with appropriate honor and had explained the purpose of his mission, a rumor was stirred up in the city by a faction of the clergy: that the Ambrosian Church was free according to the ancient institutions of the Fathers; that the Roman pontiff had no right to regulate it; and that, without delay, as a crowd of people gathered at the bishop’s palace, death was being threatened against Peter the legate from every side with great violence.

Suddenly the whole city was filled with the clamor of bells and the din of the crowds. Voices were repeatedly heard declaring that the injury done to Archbishop Wido should be avenged, because the day before the legate had seated him on the left rather than on the right.

Then blessed Peter, placed in such great danger and relying on divine aid, summoned the people to the church. He mounted the pulpit, and, when silence had been made, spoke these very brief words before the gathering of the entire city:

“Most exalted Pontiff Nicholas, dearest brothers, has sent me to you not to serve the honor and greatness of the Roman Church, but to care for your glory and salvation. What need has the Roman Church of the honor of a most insignificant man, since it has received the proclamation of praise from the very mouth of the Savior? (Matthew 16.) What province on earth is found to be free from the jurisdiction of him whose authority opens and closes heaven itself?

“If you pay proper attention, you will find that the other Churches were founded by human beings, but that the Roman Church was founded by God himself. From it the others, and especially this Church of Milan, received the beginnings of their origin and the rudiments of their discipline.

“For did not Peter and Paul, who consecrated the Roman Church with their blood, also establish this Church through their disciples? Nazarius, after being washed in the sacred font by Linus, Peter’s disciple, suffered holy martyrdom in this city. Gervasius and Protasius, whose holy bodies are venerated in this city, had no other teacher than Paul.

“Finally, the divine Ambrose, in whom you glory so greatly, when he could not suppress and restrain the heresy of the Nicolaitans, sought help from the Roman Church; and three men sent by Siriacus, who was then pontiff, brought immediate aid to the city for the cleansing of this error.

“Therefore, since both the first authors of your salvation and the later reformers of your fallen discipline proceeded under the Roman Church, why do you now refuse, with untimely obstinacy, to obey its decrees?”

With these words, by divine grace, he bent the proud people. Immediately voices broke out in the gathering, and throughout the entire city people everywhere repeated that the people of Milan were bound to the obedience and authority of the holy apostolic see, and that both clergy and laity were ready to receive the commands of the apostolic legate.

The case of the clergy was therefore examined before the legate. Scarcely a single person was found who had not either purchased holy orders or had relations with a woman. But the legate embraced mercy and promised to grant pardon to all if they would bind themselves by oath to abstain from such offenses.

When the archbishop first made this profession in solemn words, and then all the clergy did likewise, each was assigned a salutary penance, and Peter the legate departed from Milan.

Afterward, however, the archbishop was misled by the barbs of the clergy’s tongues and their insults and returned with the clergy to his vomit. The following year blessed Peter wrote this letter to certain men who persisted in the matter:

“We give thanks to God, etc.” It is found in Book 5, Letter 84.

In the year 1068 from the incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, when Alexander II wore the triple tiara of Saint Peter, Emperor Henry IV pressed the bishop of Mainz to summon a council of bishops, because Henry wished to divorce his wife, the empress Bertha, and was fiercely oppressing the liberty of the Church, being especially hostile to monks.

Wishing to provide against these injuries, the pontiff sent blessed Peter Damian as legate to Germany. When Peter had arrived, he fearlessly set forth the pontiff’s commands to Henry at Frankfurt, where the assembly was being held, under the following headings, as Sigonius writes:

“What he was undertaking was a most evil act, alien not only from the Christian name but even from that of a king. If he was not frightened by human and divine laws, he should at least take account of his reputation and standing, lest the entire Christian people be infected by such a foul poison concocted by the king; and lest a prince who ought to punish crimes bind himself to them.

“If he could not be swayed by advice, he should know for certain that the pontiff would employ ecclesiastical force, and that he would never consecrate him emperor with his own hands.”

When the princes who were present had cried out in response to this speech that the Roman pontiff was issuing just commands, and said that he ought not to provide the empress’s relatives with an opportunity to disturb the state by force of arms, the emperor, leaving no other argument available, placed himself entirely under the pontiff’s authority.

During this mission Peter had as his traveling companion in the kingdom of Burgundy, as he himself records in the *Miracles*, Adraldus, a prudent and religious man who presided over the monastery of Bremet. On the journey he related two miracles to Peter, which it will not be pointless to add here.

A certain cleric was crossing a river when he encountered Saint Severinus, the bishop. At the bishop’s request he gave him his hand, and the bishop pressed it into the current. Suddenly such a burning seized the cleric that the flesh of the entire hand dissolved and flowed away on every side, leaving only bones scarcely held together by their joints.

Then the cleric cried out in pain: “How is it that you, whose name is associated with such blessing, are confined by so deadly an abyss?”

The bishop replied: “In purgatory I am punished only by this remaining penalty, because I wished to entangle myself in worldly affairs at the royal court, and negligently performed my canonical duties not at their appointed hours but in accumulated batches. You, however, humbly implore God’s mercy, so that he may restore your hand to its former health.”

When this had been done, the cleric asked him to pour forth prayers to God, to have the brothers offer sacrifices for him, and to give assistance to the needy, since he had obtained from God the grace that he would soon be purified.

Likewise, a brother of the Cluniac monastery, of upright mind and honorable conduct, was traveling through the place where Peter and Adraldus were conversing. He encountered a long-haired pilgrim carrying a palm in his hand. As he passed, the pilgrim said:

“To complete Compline in bed is neither salvation nor progress.”

At once he disappeared from the brother’s sight. The brother was astonished at this unexpected encounter and at how he had lost sight of the man. Then he remembered that on the previous evening, tired from his journey, he had thrown his limbs onto the bed and had completed the canonical hours while lying there. He therefore strove to erase his fault through the proper penance.

He left all religious people and those initiated into sacred orders an example of how each person ought always to keep the prophet’s words before his eyes: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118); and of how great the reverence and devotion should be with which the divine work is performed everywhere, as the same prophet admonishes us: “Sing to God, sing; sing wisely” (Psalm 46); and elsewhere: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Psalm 137).

Returning from his mission in Germany, Peter hurried back to his hermitage at Avellana, thinking that at last he would be able to devote himself wholeheartedly to the rest he desired. But he was recalled by Pope Gregory VII, who occupied the Chair of Peter in 1073, and was sent as a legate *a latere* throughout Italy to promulgate the decrees concerning the recitation of the Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which had everywhere fallen silent. At the same time he was to proclaim the Friday fast in honor of the holy cross, which seemed to have been forgotten.

Peter undertook this task with the most ardent charity and, with God’s help, overcame many and great difficulties.

Concerning the fast of the cross, what happened at the hermitage of Avellana must not be passed over in silence. An old man named Leo was sick there in his cell. He prayed constantly to God for blessed Peter, for the congregation, and for the Church. When he did so with greater fervor than usual, on the night preceding the day on which Peter was to promulgate the decree concerning the Friday fast, he saw in a dream a large gathering of monks in the church.

They were dressed in white garments and, with voices of the sweetest sound and a very harmonious chant, were singing these words of the hymn of the cross:

“Sweet the wood, sweet the nails, bearing sweet burdens.”

Loaves of bread had likewise been set out in the refectory on very clean tables. Among the monks stood a venerable man dressed in white, who said:

“These are the loaves with which the children of Israel were fed in the desert” (Exodus 16).

After saying these words, he moved the table, which had been situated toward the west, toward the east, where an image of Christ crucified had been placed on the wall.

Another monk, also named Peter, returned to the monastery on Thursday, unaware of the new institution. During sleep he was invited by blessed Peter to dinner. On the following day, after learning the discipline of the new observance, he disclosed the mystery to the monks.

Moved by these visions, the monks immediately all begged blessed Peter to decree and command in all their remaining food and clothing whatever he judged could be most beneficial.

From that day onward, the refectory was arranged according to the vision, and the Friday fast was adopted as inviolable. The monastery of Avellana acquired the name and title of the Cross, which it retains to this day. Previously it had borne only the title of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, as is clear from the life written by a disciple; or, as Dante’s interpreters wish, it had adopted the surname “Columba,” from the institution of blessed Candulf.

At that time blessed Peter also wished to prescribe for the place a definite form of life. He spoke these words in the assembly and issued the following decrees:

“When I carefully consider the fervor of your holy way of life, dearest brothers…”

The remainder is found in volume 3, *Opusculum* 14.

Blessed Peter, wishing still further to encourage his disciples by his own example to observe his precepts and to endure every hard and difficult thing insofar as Christ might grant grace, spared himself no labor. Secretly, too, he wore an iron breastplate next to his flesh, fastened around his body by two iron bands and around his upper arms by two others. He never ceased from divine conversations and prayers.

His disciples therefore reported that it often happened that, after suffering from fever at night because of the excessive labor of speaking, he nevertheless never failed, after completing the solemnities of Mass in the morning, to give a sermon again until the sixth hour. He often provided a great miracle in himself, since he always appeared before everyone as though renewed, precisely when they thought he was almost at the point of death.

But all unanimously proclaimed this as his greatest marvel: although he always delivered long sermons, he never became burdensome to anyone. On the contrary, he affected each person with such great delight that his discourse seemed to everyone very brief. They recalled what is written: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10).

He also gave the brothers a good example in the chapter. After delivering an exhortation, he would rise and publicly accuse himself of his own excesses. Then he would return to his place and, in a more concise speech, urge everyone to imitate the holiness, obedience, and holy charity of the Fathers, and to consider attentively the divine mysteries. Immediately afterward he would go to the sick and the elderly who had been unable to assemble with the others, clearly confirming by his actions the things he had spoken in admonition.

The disciple who first wrote his life noted that during Lent Peter never wished to eat anything cooked by fire. He was content with fruit and no other drink, and, because of his extreme weakness, scarcely took a little cooked legume infusion. He did this in imitation of Saint Romuald, whom he always strove to imitate as far as his strength allowed, since he had written his life—and especially by always standing during the divine offices, so that shortly afterward, strengthened as though renewed, he might return to the interrupted task.

Now, as he was already advancing into old age and worn out by the excessive austerity of his life, when he had begun to consider more attentively the imminent cutting loose of the tent of his body, Pope Gregory again sent him as an apostolic legate to Ravenna. The people there had condemned their archbishop, and together with him required the expiation of the offense. When the blessed man had gone there and, after convening an assembly, had restored everything to good order by papal authority, he departed from Ravenna and wished to visit the monks whom he had established at Faenza. At that time there was a monastery outside the city gate, which is now seen enclosed within the city. There, seized by fever and exhausted by his labors, he completed the pilgrimage of this life together with his legation, passing most happily and angelically to heaven, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, during the preceding night, in 1080.

When his death became known, the whole city hastened to venerate and bury his body, with such a multitude rushing together that, as they approached the bier, some impeded others amid incredible tumult, like waves. A tomb of the whitest marble having been prepared, his body was placed there amid hymns and songs.

In the following month of August, Blessed Peter appeared to Urban, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gregory at Rimini, amid a multitude of bishops clothed in white, with a mitre on his head and a pastoral staff in his hand. He was teaching them the things that pertain to God and reproving Urban because he had never gone to him, although he had nourished him along with many others. When Urban replied that he did not know where Peter was, he heard him say: “Indeed, I dwell in the house of Saint Mary, and I profess to be her chamberlain.” Then, appearing to him a second time, he struck him beneath the left ear with his staff. When the place swelled and caused great pain, Urban prayed to God and spoke these words:

“Lord God, who created heaven and earth and all that is in them, if the service of my father Peter was pleasing to you, free me through his merits from the pain that now afflicts me.”

After he had prayed thus, he immediately felt all the pain disappear. He went to the sacred tomb, prostrated himself on the ground, and gave thanks to God; then he disclosed the miracle to the monks and to the entire city. The solemn rites of Mass were celebrated with the greatest magnificence and with the devotion of the whole people. From that time Blessed Peter was regarded by the whole Church as a saint and was received among the inhabitants of heaven.

He left many volumes that he had published, the better-known ones being entitled as follows:

*Book of Sermons and Homilies.*

*Book of the Miracles of His Times.*

Two books addressed to Leo the hermit, on whether *Dominus vobiscum* should be said at Mass.

Three books of *Apologies.*

One book *On the Continence of Priests.*

One book *On the Rule of the Solitary Life.*

One book *On the Good Conduct of Monks.*

One book *On the Progress of the Same.*

One book *Against the Jews.*

One book *On the Avarice of Prelates.*

One book *On the Terror of Death.*

One book *On the Life of Saint Romuald.*

One book *On the Life of Odilo, Abbot of Cluny.*

One book *On Saint Cassian the Martyr.*

One book *On Saints Flora and Lucilla.*

One book *Against Simoniac Bishops.*

One book *Against Another Bishop, Unnamed.*

One book *On the Insolence of the Wicked.*

One book of *Rhetorical Exclamations.*

One book *On the Nature of Certain Animals,* along with many others.

# ANOTHER LIFE OF BLESSED PETER DAMIAN

From the fifth book of the *Histories of Ravenna* by Jerome Rubeus.

After two years, when Pope Victor II had died, Stephen IX was substituted in his place. During his pontificate, while he flourished in holiness and learning, Peter Damian of Ravenna, who had professed the monastic life and lived in the wilderness at the Fonte Avellana of Mount Catria in Umbria—although, amid the severity of such a harsh life, detractors and the fiercest insults of the impious had not been lacking against him before Pope Leo IX—had himself repeatedly and urgently requested the pontiff by letter not to give easy credence to them but to investigate the matter carefully. Nevertheless, as his authority and reputation grew more illustrious each day, and as Pope Stephen considered his assistance especially suitable for establishing the Church, in this year, 1058, at the beginning of Lent, he made him a cardinal. Peter was not summoned to the cardinal’s hat, but, as he himself writes, was dragged to it. Stephen did not consider this sufficient in view of the man’s integrity and learning, and therefore added the bishopric of Ostia and appointed him prince and dean of the sacred college of cardinals.

Soon afterward Stephen died. The Tusculan counts, as they were accustomed to do, created John, their relative, pope—an armed retinue supporting them—from the bishop of Velletri, despite the opposition of the cardinals. They forced Peter Damian, who protested and pronounced dreadful curses upon them all, to pay him homage; then, having distributed money throughout the neighborhoods, they invited the people to adore him. He was called Benedict X.

Meanwhile, in the following year, when the Benedictine monk Hildebrand, a truly extraordinary man, had come to Rome with Duke Godfrey, and chiefly at Peter Damian’s urging, Gerard of Burgundy, bishop of Florence, was proclaimed supreme pontiff under the name Nicholas II, and Benedict abdicated the papacy.

Nicholas, in order to restore the commonwealth, which was greatly shaken and disturbed by the most serious calamities, sent Peter Damian to Milan. He was to reconcile that Church, which held erroneous opinions, had been separated from and at variance with Rome, and was infected with the stain of simony and the heresy of the Nicolaitans, to the Roman Church and lead it back to the right judgment.

For because the pontiffs, through the disturbances of war and the power of the seditious, had connived at these abuses and were not sufficiently able to prohibit them openly, many princes had begun, by usurped authority and with little regard for divine religion, to bestow churches and episcopates, as well as the lesser orders, not on the basis of men’s virtues but for payment. The clerics who had purchased churches and orders, once they had crossed the boundaries of shame, gradually allowed themselves to slide further into other crimes, to such an extent that they openly kept wives and concubines. They did not hesitate to defend both disgraceful practices with stubborn argument, as though they had been permitted by an honorable custom. Hence they easily fell into the two grave crimes of heresy: the first of those called simoniacs, the second of the Nicolaitans.

Peter Damian, taking Bishop Anselm of Lucca as his associate, went as legate to Milan. The citizens received him with dignity. On the following day, when he had explained the purpose of his legation in an assembly, he perceived a serious tumult arising throughout the city. At the sound of the church bells, and at the signal being given, the people—incited by the clerical faction—rushed to arms. They approached angrily the praetorium where Peter was staying and threatened him with death, asserting that the Ambrosian Church was free according to the ancient institutions of the Fathers and that the Roman pontiff had no authority to reform it.

Peter summoned the people into a church and handled their feelings so prudently and gently that, at last, all came over to his opinion and did not refuse to obey the apostolic see. He said that he had been sent by Pope Nicholas to consult their glory and salvation, not to serve the multitude or to enlarge the power and dignity of the Roman Church. Since, in the words of the Savior himself, it had acquired praise and primacy over all the Churches, it had no need of the proclamation of so insignificant a man as himself.

He said that the first authors of their salvation and restorers of their declining discipline had proceeded from the Roman Church. Saint Nazarius, whom Saint Linus, the disciple of Saint Peter, had washed in the sacred waters of baptism, had taught this, as had the saints Gervasius and Protasius, who had Saint Paul the Apostle as their teacher. Moreover, Saint Ambrose himself—of whom they boasted so greatly and justly—when he was unable by himself to overthrow the heresy of the Nicolaitans, had sought assistance from the Roman Church.

After Peter had addressed the people in this sense and by such words, and their waves of agitation had consequently been calmed, the case soon began to be debated. Yet scarcely a single person was found who had not either purchased an ecclesiastical order or engaged in shameful relations with women.

Peter judged that, given the circumstances of the times and the multitude of the guilty, he ought to act with moderation. He promised them pardon if they confirmed by oath that in the future they would abstain from such crimes. First, Archbishop Guido professed this in solemn words, publicly detesting the heresy of simony and that of the Nicolaitans; afterward all the clerics did likewise.

The archbishop threw himself upon the ground and asked that a penance be imposed upon him. Peter imposed one hundred years, but decreed that it could be redeemed by the payment of a fixed sum for each year. The clerics were bound to various fasts throughout their lives.

Then the archbishop ascended the platform and, with the clergy and people present, ordered his cleric to swear that he would do everything in his power to extirpate these two heresies. The people bound themselves by the same oath.

From that point the clerics regained their former vestments; those who were learned and chaste also had their office restored, while the rest were merely associated with the Church. The archbishop further promised that he would send them to Rome or Tours for the sake of religion, while he himself would go to Saint James in Spain. Yet although he made these promises at such length, not long afterward, when Peter had departed and he was wearied by the continual complaints and almost reproaches of those who had received holy orders, he returned to his former ways.

Therefore, in the following year, Peter, deeply angered, wrote about this matter to Rodulf, Vitalis, Ariald, and Erlembald Cotta, who had remained firm in their position. After praising them, he began to speak of the others, saying that what had happened was not new in the Church of Milan, which had always contained men of differing doctrines, beginning with Auxentius and Ambrose.

Peter writes that these things had been accomplished by him at Milan. In order to give himself wholly to God and devote his days and nights to meditation on divine matters, he renounced the cardinal’s hat, the episcopate, and the administration of the two monasteries entrusted to him.

When Pope Nicholas, who had especially approved his legation to Milan, compelled him to return to those dignities and insignia of honor, Peter consistently—and perhaps more obstinately than the circumstances and the majesty of the pontiff allowed—refused. The pontiff yielded to his perseverance, but imposed upon him a penance of one hundred years. By this penalty Peter was bound to recite every day, with accompanying scourges, the fiftieth psalm, which David used when he had committed adultery with Bathsheba, brought about the death of her husband, and had been severely accused and threatened by Nathan, who declared that God would by no means leave such grave crimes unpunished or unavenged (2 Samuel 12).

Peter willingly undertook this penance. His ardor for repentance was so great that he completed it within a year. Vincent, as he testifies from Helinand in his *Speculum*, gives the example of Dominic: wearing an iron coat of mail next to his flesh, girded with two iron bands and with two more around his upper arms, holding brushes armed with bristles in both hands, naked, reciting twelve psalters and sleeping not at all throughout the entire night, he completed the task the following day and proceeded from the thirteenth to the *Beati quorum*.

He reports that, following this man’s example, the practice became established in his regions, so that not only men but noble women as well willingly undertook this form of penance. The wife of Cechaldus, a woman of great rank, after her husband’s death, completed this hundred-year penance by counting three thousand scourges—called disciplines—for one year.

Accordingly, after completing his penance, Peter sent Pope Nicholas an elegant letter full of duty and piety. In it he carefully cleared himself and testified that he had done this no less on rational grounds than following the example of holy men.

Nevertheless, whether Pope Nicholas agreed to this is somewhat doubtful, although almost everyone asserts that he did. The diploma of Alexander II, however, preserved in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, is a source of uncertainty, since Peter signs it as “Peter the sinner, bishop of Ostia.” John Trithemius, too, when he records Peter Damian’s legation to Germany to King Henry in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, under the year 1069, calls him a cardinal bishop.

Yet I do not agree with those who say that, in the year 1078 from the birth of the Virgin, he both laid down the episcopate and sent the letter concerning its resignation—which we have mentioned—to Gregory, then pope, since in all the manuscripts I have read these letters are addressed to Nicholas, and the testimony of the most serious authorities establishes that Gerard was made bishop of Ostia by Pope Alexander II.

I also consider it necessary not to omit that Peter always called himself a monk in his letters and withdrew into the solitude of Catria, which he desired above all.

Meanwhile Pope Alexander was seriously troubled by the dispute with Cadalous of Parma, whom the Germans had made a false pope and whom they were attempting to have accepted even by the Roman nobles. Although Cadalous had been rejected at the council held at Mantua in 1064, which Alexander himself had attended, he nevertheless retained the insignia of the papacy.

For this reason Peter Damian, deeply lamenting so great a disturbance of the Church of God, wrote to him. He declared that Cadalous had already been condemned by three assemblies and had been deposed three times—if not by the judgment of priests, at least by the authority of the laws. Since the council of Osbor was now imminent, Peter said that he wished, as a kind of preliminary exercise, to set out what could be said on behalf of each side. Having carefully weighed the legal claims, he demonstrated with complete clarity that Cadalous had become pope through wrongdoing.

In the same year, 1069, Peter Damian—whom, as we have shown above, John Trithemius here calls a cardinal bishop—was sent as a legate to Germany by Pope Alexander. The reason was that Caesar Henry omitted no form of avarice toward God or human beings; that he favored the common people against the nobility and the princes; that he conducted everything by force rather than by law; that he openly sold bishoprics and abbeys; and that he bestowed the rich estates of monks upon his followers in shameful generosity.

In addition, because he had grown weary of his wife Bertha, the daughter of Otho the Margrave, to whom he had been betrothed not long before, and wished to divorce her, he had urged the archbishop of Mainz to summon an assembly at Mainz concerning the matter.

Thus, when Peter opportunely arrived in Germany, he immediately recalled the archbishop of Mainz from holding the council by threatening him with the danger of severe punishment. Soon afterward he went to Frankfurt, where Henry was then holding an assembly of his nobles. Admitted to the gathering, he explained the pope’s commands and severely rebuked both the numerous princes who were present and Henry himself for the wicked undertaking he was planning, declaring it utterly foreign not only to a Christian but even to a king.

If he was not terrified by human or divine laws, Peter said, he should at least take account of his reputation and standing. He should not allow the Christian people to be infected by such a foul poison administered by a king, nor should so great a prince bind himself to the very crimes he ought to avenge. If Henry could not be moved by counsel, he should know for certain that the pontiff would employ ecclesiastical force and that Henry would never be consecrated by his hands.

This speech, delivered, as Trithemius says, with the greatest authority and wisdom, was followed by the grave voices of the princes who were present. They declared that the Roman pontiff was issuing a just command; that Henry should not stain the majesty of the royal name with the disgrace of so shameful an act, nor give the queen’s parents cause for revolt and a legitimate occasion for disturbing the commonwealth. If they were men of substantial power, they seemed undoubtedly prepared to expiate so great an insult to their daughter by some distinguished action and to avenge it with the utmost force at their disposal.

Broken by these arguments rather than persuaded, Henry affirmed that he would submit to the authority of the pontiff. This was the outcome of Peter Damian’s German legation.

In the following year, 1080, when Pope Gregory VII heard that Archbishop Wibert had departed from Ravenna, he sent Peter Damian as legate to Ravenna, although Peter was worn out by age. Peter departed with great willingness, moved both by love for his native city and by the zeal for religion with which he had always burned, now inflamed in him to an extraordinary degree.

The citizens received him humanely and with the greatest courtesy. They listened kindly as he discussed Wibert’s impiety, since Wibert seemed, through perverse judgment and neglect of religion, to have followed Henry’s party. Peter therefore urged them earnestly to accept the devout plans of the most holy pontiff and to favor the just cause, and by the salutary decree to withdraw their pious and courageous minds from Wibert’s discipline.

When he saw that all had been deeply humbled by these words, he received the people, corrupted by the contagion of the condemned archbishop, back into the Church’s favor and, by papal authority, freed them from the offense they had contracted.

At last, as he was leaving Ravenna to go to the pontiff, he visited the monks whom he had established at Faenza outside the city gate, in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which we now see brought within the city. He did this so that his journey would not be entirely fruitless. There he was seized by fever and, on the eighth day after he had fallen ill, departed this life during the night preceding the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in that same year, 1080 from the birth of Christ.

When those keeping watch beside the monastery announced his death, lest the sacred body should be secretly carried away by his monks, who had come from nearby places, all the citizens suddenly hastened to his funeral rites. In a short time the church was so filled with the multitude of the people that they pushed one another like waves, and anyone who was allowed to touch the casket of the holy man, offer gifts to him, or kiss his feet was plainly considered blessed.

Meanwhile, a tomb of the whitest marble was transported with great ease from another monastery some distance away, to the astonishment of the very men who brought it. It was placed opposite the choir, beside the steps leading up to the altar. While everyone sang hymns and psalms and praised God, the body of the holy man was laid in it.

Since this most distinguished bishop and monk has frequently been mentioned above, and since his death falls in the present year, I think it will be neither unwelcome nor wholly unrelated to our purpose to write somewhat more carefully about him.

According to John the monk, who had once been his companion and wrote his life, Peter was born at Ravenna in an obscure place because of his poverty, though of free birth. Some, however, believe that he came from the noble family of the Honesti. They are mistaken, for this claim belongs to Peter the Sinner.

His elder brother Damian carefully nourished him with every duty of charity and instructed him in good letters, so that Peter took his surname from him and wished to be called and written “Peter Damian.” We read that something similar happened with Eusebius of Caesarea, who, after his friend Pamphilus, always wished to be called and to be Eusebius Pamphili. In Peter Damian’s case, however, it may be observed that he himself calls himself only Peter, while others add “Damian.”

Before he took the monastic habit, he publicly taught many of the liberal arts, in a style sufficiently elegant for those times, which were filled with barbarism. This can readily be recognized from his letters, which he sent to many people, from the books he wrote, and from the sermons he delivered to the people.

From his earliest age he began to be harassed by adversity. His mother had borne him last, after many other children. One day, after their father had died, his eldest brother complained about the number of siblings and the smallness of the inheritance. His mother, who had long been tortured by the anguish of poverty, became so indignant and distressed that, crying out that she was wretched and unworthy to live any longer, she refused milk to Peter, who had only just been born. Unmoved by the infant’s continual crying, she seemed to desire his death; and she would certainly have brought it about soon if the concubine of a certain priest had not arrived.

She sharply rebuked the mother’s cruelty, lamented the child’s tears and misery, and softened the heart made savage by such monstrous cruelty. Joining herself to the mother, she restored the half-dead infant to life by means of warm water and other remedies.

Not long afterward his mother died, and his elder brother married. Although the couple pretended that they wished to care for the boy, they oppressed him with such harsh and severe servitude that they fed him not only bread and other foods but also bad and spoiled wine. He went about perpetually barefoot and dressed in rags, suffered many beatings, and, when he grew somewhat older, was put in charge of feeding the pigs.

While engaged in this degrading service, one day he found a silver coin. As though he had suddenly become rich, he rejoiced and, with the sweet impulse that drew his childish mind—deprived of all pleasant things—toward soft and agreeable thoughts, considered for a long time what he might most suitably buy with it. At last, inspired from heaven, he said: “Why am I turning these things over in my mind? Their pleasure will certainly not last long. It will be better to give this to a priest who may offer sacred worship to God.”

Meanwhile another of his brothers returned. His name was Damian, and he had been away from Ravenna for several years. Taking pity on his brother’s hardships, he received him under his protection and patronage, treated him affectionately and like a father, and arranged for him to be educated in letters.

After keeping him at Ravenna for some time and recognizing the boy’s excellent disposition, he first sent him to Faenza and then to Parma, so that he might hear learned men there. Peter himself testifies to this in his letters.

Within a short time he had learned all the liberal arts and acquired such reputation and renown among everyone that, afterward, as he explained them to others with the greatest usefulness and to crowded audiences, he was easily regarded as the foremost teacher in all Italy.

As he increased day by day in favor, the grace of princes, wealth, and authority, he reproached himself, saying: “Have I perhaps clung forever to these fleeting and perishable goods? Should I not instead bid them farewell and pursue heavenly things?”

As he repeated these thoughts more and more often, he gradually began to devote himself to divine study and service. Thus, beneath a costly garment, he wore a hair shirt. He devoted himself frequently to fasting, vigils, and divine hymns. When, as was natural at his age, he was troubled by the heat of sexual desire, he would rise from his bed in the middle of the night and immerse himself in water until his whole body became cold. Afterward he would not return to bed but would worship God with psalms and hymns.

It would be astonishing to relate how generous and munificent he was toward the needy, and how kindly and piously he received them at his table.

On this subject, the following incident certainly must not be passed over in silence. One day, while he was dining with a companion whose services he used, he had no bread other than a single loaf of fine wheat bread. For his companion, who normally ate the same food, a coarse and inferior loaf had been set before him.

Peter began to say to himself: “Christ is inferior to me at my table.” After repeating this and similar thoughts in his mind, he decided to exchange his loaf with the companion’s, but shame held him back. As he ate, fear gradually seized him and terror shook his inward parts. At last a fishbone, lodged crosswise in his throat and yielding to no remedy, began to strangle him.

Believing that this had happened to him because he had not given his companion the loaf made of fine wheat, he exchanged the breads and recovered at the first bite. For this reason, happier than words can express, he disclosed the miracle to everyone.

As he became increasingly inflamed by these and other deeds of service to God, he resolved to withdraw completely from fleeting things and become a monk. Yet he judged that doing so in his homeland was unsafe because of certain relatives and other obstacles. While he was thinking about these matters and striving through constant prayers that God might open for him a path to eternal salvation, two monks from the solitude of the Holy Cross at Fonte Avellana, which lies in the diocese of Gubbio, concerning whom he had already heard many excellent things, came to him, divinely impelled.

After Peter had spoken with them at length about God, he disclosed his state of mind and asked whether their abbot would receive him if he wished to become a monk. They assured him that he would be received, and he gladly promised that he would go there as soon as possible.

Meanwhile he gave the departing monks a silver cup. But when they persistently refused it, leaving no room for his entreaties, and thereby strengthened even more the religious opinion Peter had formed of them and his conviction of their holiness, they caused him to develop an even greater contempt for these fleeting things, so that he thought of nothing but heavenly matters.

After the monks’ departure, in order to discover by experience whether he was capable of enduring the labor and hardship of this life, he shut himself in a rather cramped cell. There, for forty days, he lived according to the rules of the hermits of the Holy Cross.

Greatly strengthened by this manner of life, and no longer fearing the difficulties or harshness of that way of living, he secretly departed for the solitude of Mount Catria without the knowledge of any of his family. The abbot gladly received him, clothed him in the cowl, and entrusted him to one of the monks for instruction in the manner of a novice.

How greatly he advanced, and how much obedience and reverence he showed toward his teacher, can easily be understood from the following incident. When he was about to set out on horseback with his teacher and was ordered by him to put on softer and finer clothing, Peter humbly begged the master not to command what he himself thought unbecoming.

The master, however, who loved him dearly because he had recognized his virtues, and who did not want him to appear in public so poorly groomed, refused for a long time to yield to his repeated entreaties. Peter therefore, lest his stubborn obedience oppose the command too strongly, although covered with the greatest shame and blushing deeply because he seemed to have resumed the ornaments he had rejected, dared not look at anyone out of embarrassment. Dressed in the finer cowl, he accompanied his master.

Yet, as he himself later related, he seemed to see everyone pointing him out with their fingers and calling him “bridegroom,” not “monk,” wherever he went.

When he returned to the monastery, he applied himself each day more intensely to holiness and the highest good through greater abstinence and vigils.

At that time the monks spent four days of the week on bread and water. On Tuesdays and Thursdays they took a small amount of legumes cooked separately in their own cells. On the days of the sacred fast, bread was supplied not according to each person’s desire but in a fixed measure and quantity. Wine was known only for the celebration of the divine service and for the sick; no one else received it.

Their custom during vigils was that, when the signal was given, after the morning prayers had been completed, everyone recited David’s hymns. Peter anticipated this common signal and spent whatever remained of the night in continuous watching. As a result, he fell ill and passed days and nights without sleep; but after adopting a more moderate regimen, he recovered.

Within a short time he had acquired the highest reputation for holiness. At last, through the earnest petitions of Guido Strambiato of Ravenna, abbot of Pomposa, the head of the monastery of the Holy Cross was persuaded to send him to Pomposa, so that he might instruct those monks in divine commandments and sacred letters.

He spent two years there. When they had elapsed, he was recalled by the head of the Holy Cross, who had sent him there, and by his monks. After the head died soon afterward, Peter repeatedly and carefully refused the position, but at last he was placed in charge of the monastery.

After establishing it, he founded monasteries first at Camerino, then at Mount Regius in the Perugian territory, where he found a cell said to have been inhabited by Saint Romuald; afterward in the territory of Faenza, then at Acereta, then at Gaviunium, which they now think is called Cavina; and finally in the territory of Rimini at Murcianum.

While he was at the monastery of Gaviunium, he one day ordered the monk who usually served him to bring him a drink from the spring. The servant obeyed, but when the water had been changed into wine, Peter sent another of the monks who were sitting nearby to bring water. When that water likewise had been turned into wine, Peter ordered them not to disclose it to anyone. They did so, and no one learned of it until after his death.

Another incident was also quite famous. Peter had a full cask of wine beside his chapel. Some soldiers passed by and arrogantly demanded a drink from the priest who served as guardian of the chapel. When the priest pointed out the cask and they opened all its holes, no wine came out.

At first they suspected that the priest had deceived them. They therefore uncovered the upper opening and saw that only a little wine was missing. Yet although they thrust rods into the openings, no wine came out anywhere, even though the rods themselves were soaked with wine.

The miracle seemed all the greater because, a few hours later, a pilgrim passed by the same place and asked to be given a drink for God’s sake and in his name. When the priest told him what had happened to the soldiers, the pilgrim, terrified, declared that he hoped to receive a great benefit because the wine had been preserved safe and intact from the robbery of insolent men. He added that Peter had long been known to him and that the priest had often offered him hospitality.

Although the priest was afraid and thought that he would not drink any wine, the persistent pleas of the needy guest moved him. He went to the cask, opened one of its holes, and drew wine from it.

Nor was the following event less astonishing. A certain distinguished man, rich in wealth and resources, was accustomed to send Peter fish as a gift on the more solemn feast days. On the night preceding the day of the birth of Christ God, since he had been unable to obtain fish earlier, he sent a servant with a large fish.

The sky was foul that night, illuminated by no rays of the moon or other stars, and deep snow added to the continuous difficulty of the road. When the servant reached a high bank and followed its edge too closely, his foot slipped and he was hurled down below.

The fall was such that he could easily have been torn apart and crushed. Yet through the merits of the holy man and by divine power he escaped unharmed and uninjured. Strong and vigorous, he lifted the load that had been thrown from his neck and placed it back upon his shoulders.

When he came to Peter and presented his master’s gift, he gave immense thanks because he had escaped death. Peter replied:
