“My son, do not attribute to a wandering man stained with the filth of crimes what the almighty God, in his single mercy, did not disdain to grant you. Give thanks to him, who is never absent from those who humbly implore his aid in calamities and dangers.”

Likewise, not many days later, Peter sent one of his monks to a certain abbot. The monk had to wait a long time for the absent abbot and, at last, had to find him wherever he might be. Realizing that, unless he traveled by night, he would not return by the day Peter had appointed, he took a guide and set out in the evening.

He had not gone far when the guide secretly disappeared from sight. The monk, unfamiliar with the road, was therefore extremely anxious and uncertain where to go. He asked God to provide a guide to lead him, through the merits of the man whom he was striving to obey.

Not long afterward he came to a place where the road divided into two branches. After hesitating for a while, uncertain which one to take, he finally chose the one that he saw was more traveled and considered more suitable. But when he tried to direct his animal onto it, the animal not only refused but entered the other road.

The monk feared that the animal was doing this because it was accustomed to take that road on other occasions. He therefore tried, with kicks and blows, to force it onto the other path, but the animal would not yield. After struggling for a long time without success, he finally began to suspect that perhaps the brute animal was resisting him contrary to its habit through divine inspiration.

He loosened the reins, though at first to no purpose. When the sky began to grow light, he realized that he had entered the correct road. A little later, when he reached the monastery, he related everything that had happened to Peter and gave everlasting thanks to God and to him.

By an equal power of merit, with God’s gift, Peter rescued a young man whom he was sending on business to a certain bishop. After the young man had crossed a river, he became deeply stuck in the mud and called upon Peter; Peter brought him out safe and unharmed.

When the young man had traveled farther toward the city and had not found the bishop, he was received by the bishop’s young cousin. Yet the cousin appeared to have failed in his duty because, after everyone else had departed, he left the young man alone in a large room. Seized by great fear, the young man spent the entire night without sleep.

Then Peter Damian appeared to the sleeping cousin of the bishop. With a fierce expression, threatening and reproving him for having treated his messenger so badly through rustic negligence, he terrified him greatly.

The cousin awoke and waited for daylight so that he might visit his guest and ask what these things meant. When this had been done, and the young man had recounted his own journey and the hardships he had suffered, the cousin admired the power of the holy man and exalted the glory of God, who is wondrous in those who serve him wholeheartedly.

The young man whom Peter had sent was so moved by this event that, when he returned to Peter, he committed himself wholly to him and, shortly afterward, put on the monastic habit there.

After Gregory VII had urged him, he returned from his German mission and instituted throughout Italy a sacred fast and abstinence from food on Friday in honor [Col. 0179B] of the cross—or rather, restored a practice instituted in antiquity but by then almost entirely forgotten. The same was done with the prayers of the canonical hours, through which due worship is offered each day to the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of Christ; and the pontiff ordered all who had been initiated into holy orders to recite them devoutly and piously every day.

Regarding the sacred fast on Friday instituted—or rather restored—in honor of the cross, we thought it necessary to omit nothing of what happened in connection with it. In a room set apart for the sick there was an elderly monk named Leo, who, with unremitting prayers, vigils, and abstinence from food, devoted himself to these practices with almost youthful fervor. During the night preceding the day on which this sacred fast in honor of the cross was to be instituted, he saw in sleep a large gathering of monks [Col. 0179C] in a church. Clad in white garments, they sang in the sweetest voices and with a most melodious chorus: “Sweet wood, sweet nails,” and what follows.

In that same place, where they had been accustomed to eat, he saw tables spread with loaves of bread, most clean, sweet, and savory. Among the monks reclining on every side was a man of exceptional beauty and venerability. When Leo asked where such loaves—never seen before that day—had come from, the man replied: “These are the loaves with which the children of Israel, receiving manna from heaven, were fed in the wilderness” (Exod. 16).

The same man moved the abbot’s table, which had stood toward the west, toward the rising sun in the east, where an image of Christ fixed to the cross had been painted on the wall. A little later, another monk named Peter returned to the monastery on Thursday. Since he still knew nothing about this fast, he saw in sleep that Peter Damian was inviting him to dinner and reclining at table with him. Thus, on the following day, when he learned the discipline of the new observance, he exclaimed joyfully and eagerly: “Behold, by divine grace, the dinner to which Peter Damian had invited me.”

After seeing these things, all his monks were deeply moved. They seemed thereby to perceive with their own eyes that this institution was plainly divine, and they begged him that, if he thought anything else in their remaining food or clothing ought to be changed, corrected, or removed, he should remove, correct, or change it. For this reason, after establishing an even humbler and more abject form of dress and habit, he continued to raise them toward the rewards of heavenly life no less by his constant teachings than by the examples of his life.

When he was a cardinal and held the bishopric of Ostia, he poured out abundantly among the needy whatever he had left over, washed the feet of those twelve continually, provided them with a meal, and searched throughout the whole city for orphans and widows in order to help them. At the monastery he sometimes ate nothing cooked by fire for forty days, but subsisted only on raw fruits, without any drink. His disciple—the man who wrote this life—is a witness to this.

He was also accustomed, while reciting the daytime canonical prayers and hymns, to cling to no lectern or bench [Col. 0180C], and at the beginning of each of the two Lents to abstain completely from food for three days. Although he himself did not persuade anyone to adopt this observance by words, he nevertheless strongly praised certain monasteries that subsequently kept it after his example, so that silence might be maintained more diligently within the monastery throughout those three days. He established that no one should put on footwear, except in the utmost necessity, before they had each day jointly completed all the psalms of David. But enough concerning Peter Damian.

[Col. 0179]

## SOME MATERIALS CONCERNING THE LIFE AND PRAISE OF BLESSED PETER DAMIAN, DRAWN FROM AUTHORITATIVE WRITERS

### I. Pope St. Leo IX (year 1019), formerly a monk of the Order of St. Benedict, in a letter written to him, preserved as Opuscle 7 in volume III of the works of that same holy doctor

**LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, PETER the hermit: joy of eternal blessedness.**

My most beloved son, the little book that you published against the pollution of the fourfold contagion of the flesh, in a style indeed honorable but with an even more honorable purpose, commends by clear evidence that your mind has reached, through pious struggle, the splendid and shining bed of chastity. You have subdued the barbarism of the flesh, since you have raised the arm of the spirit against the obscenity of lust. And after much else:

But, my most beloved son, I rejoice indescribably because, by the example of your way of life, you teach whatever you have taught by your gift of speech. For to teach by one’s deeds is greater than to teach by one’s voice. Therefore, with God as your author, you will obtain the palm of victory; you will rejoice with God and the Son of the Virgin in the heavenly dwelling; and you will be heaped with as many rewards as the people whom you have snatched from the devil’s snares, gathered about yourself, and, in a sense, crowned.

### II. Pope Alexander II (year 1061), who greatly benefited the most religious family of the Benedictine Fathers, in one of his charters. In my manuscripts

**ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the people of Gubbio, clergy and people—namely, the faithful of St. Peter and of ourselves—greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Let your holy devotion, dearly beloved brothers and sons, not be unaware that we have received under our protection and defense, and that of the Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the church of our dearest brother and fellow bishop, Peter Damian, consecrated in the name of Blessed Luke [Col. 0181B] the Evangelist, etc.

### III. Desiderius, abbot (year 1062) of the sacred monastery of St. Benedict on Monte Cassino, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church with the title of St. Cecilia, later Pope Blessed Victor III, in book II of his *Dialogues*. In my manuscripts

I learned these things from the testimony of many brothers, and I took care to record them in my little book. Although the venerable Peter, bishop of Ostia, inserted this matter elegantly and appropriately in the sermon that he most brilliantly composed to be read at the vigils of Blessed Father Benedict, nevertheless, among the other miracles that Almighty God, for the praise of his name, also in our memory, etc.

### IV. Leo of Marsica (year 1088), monk and librarian of the sacred monastery of Cassino and cardinal-bishop of the holy Roman Church of Ostia, chapter 101 of book II of the *Cassinese Chronicles*. In my manuscripts, from the autograph

Meanwhile, Gregory, count of the Lateran and Tusculum, having learned of the death of the Roman pontiff, joined by Gerard of Galera and several of the powerful Romans, invaded the rights of the Church by night with bands of armed men. They appointed John, bishop of Velletri, later called Minelus, pope, imposing upon him the name Benedict.

When Peter Damian learned of this—he was a very religious man whom Pope Stephen had at that time taken from the desert and made bishop of the Church of Ostia—he began, together with the cardinals, to resist, protest, and anathematize it [Col. 0181D].

And in book III he writes:

“Moreover, Lord Peter Damian, whom we have already mentioned above, came to this monastery of Cassino. By word and example alike, he kindled with fervent zeal for the service of God as many people as he could. At last, with the consent and permission of Lord Desiderius, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, etc., and abbot, he obtained from the whole congregation, by voluntary offering and for the remission of all their sins, that throughout the Fridays of the entire year—unless they were feast days—they should be content with bread and water alone, and that each should receive discipline individually after making confession. In addition, they were to observe a three-day fast every year at the beginning of Lent.”

### V. Lambert of Aschaffenburg (year 1069), monk of Hersfeld, of the Order of St. Benedict, in his *History of the Deeds of the Germans*, under the year of Christ 1069

As the day already approached that had been designated for dissolving the marriage of King Henry III, later emperor, the king hurried toward Mainz. Then, while still on the way, he learned that the legate of the Apostolic See was awaiting his arrival at Mainz, intending to prevent the separation and to threaten the bishop of Mainz with the sentence of apostolic condemnation, because he had promised to become the author of so wicked a separation.

Immediately dismayed that he had lost from his grasp the matter he had long desired, he wished to return to Saxony by the route he had come. Yet, scarcely and with difficulty overcome by the advice of his friends, lest he disappoint the princes of the kingdom whom he had ordered to meet him at Mainz in great numbers, he went to Frankfurt [Col. 0182B]. There he ordered those who had assembled at Mainz to be present on the appointed day.

When they had come in large numbers, Peter Damian—the legate of the Apostolic See, a man highly revered for his age and blameless life—set forth the commands of the Roman pontiff. He declared that the king was attempting something utterly wicked and far removed from the Christian name, let alone from a king. If he was not deterred by human laws or the sanctions of the canons, he should at least spare his own reputation and good name, lest the poison of so foul an example, beginning with the king, stain the entire Christian people; and lest he who ought to have been the avenger of crimes should himself become their perpetrator and standard-bearer [Col. 0182C].

Finally, if he would not yield to counsel, Peter said that he would necessarily have to employ ecclesiastical force and prohibit the crime by the law of the canons. Moreover, he would never consecrate with his own hands an emperor who, by so pestilential an example, had betrayed the Christian faith as far as lay within him.

Then all who were present—the princes—joined in addressing him. They said that the Roman pontiff judged rightly, and they begged him by God not to bring disgrace upon his glory or stain the majesty of the royal name with the filth of so shameful a deed. They added that he should not give the queen’s parents cause for revolt or a legitimate occasion for disturbing the state. If they were men, since they possessed great arms and resources, they would undoubtedly expiate such an insult to their daughter by some notable deed [Col. 0182D].

Broken by this speech more than converted, he said: “If this is firmly and obstinately resolved by you, I shall command myself and bear as best I can the burden that I cannot lay down.” Thus, driven more by his zeal for concord than softened in his hatred, he did indeed agree that the queen should be recalled into partnership in the kingdom.

### VI. Berthold, priest of Constance (year 1090) and apostolic penitentiary, in the continuation of Herman the Lame, under the year of Christ 1061

At this time the venerable Peter Damian, a cardinal-bishop formerly a hermit, wrote many works and refuted the incontinence of priests quite reasonably in his writings.

Again, under the year 1070 [Col. 0183A]:

Peter Damian, cardinal-bishop of pious memory, long since crucified to the world, departed to the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. Lord Gerold—Gerald, a monk of the Order of St. Benedict and of the monastery of Cluny, truly a monk distinguished by knowledge of the Scriptures and not inferior in character to his predecessor—succeeded him in the bishopric.

### VII. Sigebert the Gaul (year 1100), monk of Gembloux, of the Order of St. Benedict, book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 103

Peter Damian, the seventh deacon of the Roman Church, wrote the life of Odilo, fourth abbot of Cluny. Homilies composed by him in a polished style are also found.

### VIII. Honorius of Autun, priest (year 1120), monk and abbot of the Order of St. Benedict, near the end of his book *On the Luminaries of the Church*

Peter, surnamed Damian, a bishop formerly a monk and hermit, wrote a book against those accustomed to reordain simoniacs, and many other works. He flourished under Henry the Pious.

### IX. Helinand the Gaul (year 1200), monk of Frigidmont, of the Order of St. Benedict, in his *History*, whose words are given by Vincent of Beauvais, of the Order of Preachers, in the *Historical Mirror*, book XXV, chapter 52

At this time Peter Damian wrote to Pope Hildebrand, giving an account of why he had resigned the bishopric. For he was a man highly renowned for religion and wisdom [Col. 0183C]. There he relates certain things that I have decided to excerpt in this place:

“Because,” he says, “I rejected ecclesiastical government, a penance of one hundred years was imposed upon me, according to the remedies of the monastic rule.”

### X. Francesco Petrarch (year 1370), most distinguished orator and poet, chapter 17, treatise 3 of book II, *On the Solitary Life*

Now Peter appears—the one who bears the surname Damian—although there is also much disagreement concerning this very matter and concerning the life and deeds of the man: some say that he was drawn from the leisure of solitude to the cares of ecclesiastical business, while others say that he was drawn from the very citadel and tumult of those cares to the peaceful silence of leisure.

The commendation of both forms of life either made him worthy of so great an office or made the office itself seem worthy to be preferred to so great a man. Others confuse the matter. For when, seeking the truth more exactly, I had sent people as far as the monastery where he flourished, to bring me a report of everything they discovered, I learned from the testimony of the religious men of that place that he had first been a solitary, had then been raised to a higher position, and had finally returned of his own accord to solitude.

If this is so, the evidence of his final years is clear, and a double glory of solitude comes together in one example: solitude lends such men to the world and then receives them back in this manner. His letters encourage me to believe that this is indeed how it was. Now, especially after hearing these things, I recall them to mind—letters issued at different times and in different conditions of life [Col. 0184A]. In some, as it seems to me, when occupied, he sighs for the rest of his lost leisure; in others, when at leisure, he remembers the agitation of his completed business.

I have a more certain recollection of this latter matter. Omitting, therefore, what lies outside my purpose, I say that this Peter, so far as I gather from his latest writings, had held the Roman cardinalate with no small distinction: a man no more distinguished by rank than by language.

But you shall now hear what decision he made even in this matter. Leaving to his fellow citizens that condition and the pomp of the world, he himself chose, in the middle of Italy, on the left side of the Apennines, a most peaceful solitude—about which he wrote much and which still preserves the ancient name of Fonte Avellana—as preferable to honors destined to perish. There he afterward lay hidden no less gloriously than he had first become known at Rome [Col. 0184B]. Nor was it a disgrace for him to exchange the radiant splendor of a high office for a ragged hair shirt.

### XI. St. Antoninus (year 1450), archbishop of Florence from the Order of Preachers, part II, title 16, chapter 8 of his *Chronicles*

In the year of the Lord 1068, Peter Damian, distinguished in life and learning, was held in Italy. Here he published many sermons in an elegant style on various subjects. He resigned the bishopric with which he had been invested, so that he might devote himself more freely to God.

He also wrote several short works, namely: the first book, *On the Perfection of Monks*; another entitled *Most Welcome*, or *Most Approved*, and against the simoniacs; a book *On Contempt of the World* [Col. 0184C]; a short work entitled *The Lord Be with You*, addressed to Pope Leo; a book *On the Customs of the Church*; he also wrote a rule for hermits and *On the Order of Hermit Life*; a book in dialogue form against the Jews; a short work of narratives; a book *On the Dissolution of Marriages*; a book *On the Discussion of the Canonical Hours*; and an invective against a certain bishop who was recalling monks to the world.

He also recounts many highly noteworthy examples of things that happened in his time in various places, some of which are set forth in this chapter. In his *Apology*, that is, his defense of himself concerning his resignation of the bishopric, Helinand says of him:

“This Peter wrote to Pope Hildebrand, who was Gregory [Col. 0184D] the Seventh, giving an account of why he had resigned the bishopric. For he was a man highly renowned for wisdom and religion.”

And below:

“He also described the life of St. Romuald and of Odilo.”

### XII. An anonymous Benedictine monk (year 1480), of the Congregation of Unity of St. Justina, now Cassinese, in a *Monastic History*, in my manuscript

Saint Peter Damian, distinguished in life and learning, flourished in Italy. After resigning the bishopric, he became a monk in the monastery of St. Mary situated at Faenza, of the Order of Monks of the Congregation of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana. They wear white garments and a white cowl. Having performed much penance there, he died a monk in the aforesaid monastery, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, and is venerated and worshiped by the people [Col. 0185A]. He wrote many works of the highest excellence, according to Vincent and the archbishop, to whom I refer the reader.

### XIII. Werner Rolewinck (year 1494), a German Carthusian, in the *Fascicle of Time*, under the year of Christ 1054

Peter Damian, a doctor of very great authority and a highly religious man, shines forth.

### XIV. Johannes Trithemius (year 1497), abbot of the Order of St. Benedict, of the Congregation of Bursfeld, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Peter Damian, formerly a monk and later bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, was a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures [Col. 0185B], and not ignorant of secular literature. He was gentle and keen in intellect, calm and composed in speech, and sufficiently well suited to persuade; he shone forth and was distinguished no less by holiness than by learning.

Following the example of Gregory the Great—he means Gregory of Nazianzus—through love of solitude and quiet, he relinquished his bishopric after governing it vigorously for several years and returned to his monastery. Thereafter he spent his life with his brothers in tranquility of mind.

When the supreme pontiff reproached him in a charitable admonition for having resigned his bishopric, although he was a useful and capable man, out of love for his private salvation, he composed *Apologies* for three successive Roman pontiffs: Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII. In them, humbly defending his action by authority, reason, and example, he appeased their minds.

The following works are attributed to him:

To Leo the Hermit, whether a solitary praying the canonical hours should also say “The Lord be with you” when there is no one to respond: an instructional work entitled *To the Lord Leo, Out of Love*, book 1.

*Antilogium Against the Jews*, book 1.

*Against a Certain Bishop*, book 1.

*On the Natures of Certain Animals*, book 1.

*Apologies*, book 3: “To his lord Nicholas.”

*On the Continence of Priests*, book 1: “Recently, having had dealings with certain men.”

*On the Wives of Clerics*, book 1: “I address you, O hares.”

*Rule for Solitaries*, book 1: “While the holy zeal…”

*Exhortation to Monks*, book 1: “To the brothers at Gangres.”

*Miracles of His Own Time*, book 1: “To the most beloved Gerard.”

*On the Progress of Monks*, book 1.

*On the Avarice of Prelates*, book 1.

*Life of Abbot Odilo*, book 1: “Hugh, abbot of Cluny.”

*On the Terror of Death*, book 1: “To Blanche, formerly countess.”

*On Meditation on Death*, book 1: “For it must be considered.”

*Against Simoniacal Bishops*, book 1.

*On the Insolence of Wicked Men*, book 1.

*Most Welcome*, or *Most Approved*, book 1: “To Lord H. of Ravenna.”

*Rhetorical Declamations*, book 1.

*On Saints Flora and Lucilla*, book 1: “Still, most beloved…”

*On St. Cassian the Martyr*, book 1: “Wonderful and glorious.”

*On St. Boniface*, book 1: “The glorious [deeds] of Blessed Boniface.”

*On St. Anastasius*, book 1: “To the beautiful one, dearest brothers.”

*Sermons and Homilies.*

And many other works that I have not seen.

He flourished under King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1050.

### XV. The same Trithemius, book II, chapter 93, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*

Peter Damian, a monk of the monastery of Vivarium, bishop of Ostia and cardinal, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, sweet and adorned in the manner of Gregorian eloquence, and sufficiently persuasive.

After governing the pontificate vigorously for several years and correcting the vices of the wicked without regard to persons, he finally, worn out by old age and wearied into consulting for his own salvation, abandoned the bishopric. Following the example of Gregory the Great, formerly bishop of Nazianzus, he returned to the pursuits of monks.

For this reason three Roman pontiffs reproached him for having abandoned the bishopric, although he was a man so learned and useful to the Church, and for having placed his private advantage before the common good, when by word and example he was suited to govern souls [Col. 0186B]. But Peter humbly excused himself and wrote *Apologies* on behalf of his action, by which he made the pontiffs tranquil through reason and example.

He wrote many other volumes, of which I have found only the following:

*Apology to Pope Nicholas II*, book 1.

*To Alexander II and Gregory VII*, book 2.

*On the Progress of Monks*, book 1.

*Antilogium Against the Jews*, book 1.

*On the Avarice of Prelates*, book 1.

*Against Simoniacal Bishops*, book 1.

*On the Continence of Priests*, book 1.

*On the Wives of Clerics*, book 1.

*To Leo the Solitary*: whether a solitary praying the canonical hours should also say “The Lord be with you” when he has no one to respond, book 1.

*Rule for Hermits and Recluses*, book 1.

*Exhortation to the Brothers*, book 1 [Col. 0186C].

*On Certain Incredible Things Done in His Time*, book 1.

*Life of St. Odilo, Abbot of Cluny*, book 1.

*On the Terror of Death*, book 1.

*On Meditation on Death*, book 1.

*On Saints Flora and Lucilla*, book 1.

Another work entitled *Most Grave*, or *Most Approved*, book 1.

*Against a Certain Bishop Who Was Recalling Monks to the World*, book 1.

*On the Insolence of Wicked Men*, book 1.

*Rhetorical Declamations*, book 1.

*On the Nature of Certain Animals*, book 1.

*A Treatise on St. Cassian the Martyr*, book 1.

*On St. Boniface*, treatise 1.

*On the Situation and Foundation of the Monastery of Vivarium*, book 1.

He wrote nearly innumerable sermons and homilies, as well as many letters to various people, and many other works that have not yet come into our hands [Col. 0186D].

He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

### XVI. In the same series, Trithemius himself gives this in book IV, chapter 35, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*. But in the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Hirsau*, under the year of Christ 1056, he writes as follows

Peter Damian also, formerly a monk of our order and now bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, is regarded as distinguished in these times: certainly the most learned among the learned men of his age, and venerable no less for holiness than for learning. He published many excellent volumes of his intellect, whose titles we have set out fully elsewhere.

Out of love for holy religion, he abandoned his bishopric and returned to the monastery.

And a little later:

Therefore, in the first year of William, the twelfth abbot of Hirsau [Col. 0187A], Peter Damian, of our order, cardinal-bishop of the most holy Roman Church, whom we mentioned much earlier, was sent by Pope Alexander II as legate to King Henry in Germany. At Frankfurt, in the presence of many princes, he set forth the commands of the Apostolic See to the king with great authority and wisdom.

### XVII. Jacobus Philippus Bergomensis (year 1500), Augustinian hermit, book XII of the *Supplement to the Chronicles*, first edition, under the year of Christ 1070

Peter Damian, doctor and cardinal-bishop of the Roman Church, most learned in the divine Scriptures, was highly esteemed in those times for these reasons. He also published several short works worthy of praise.

As Vincent the Gaul reports in book XXVI [Col. 0187B], he was a man highly renowned for religion, humility, and wisdom. While he was a cardinal-bishop, he resigned the bishopric so that he might serve God alone in humility. When Pope Gregory reproved him for this, he wrote a beautiful book to that same pontiff, giving an account of why he had resigned the bishopric.

### XVIII. The same Jacobus Philippus of Bergamo, in the cited place, second edition

Peter Damian, formerly a monk and cardinal-bishop of the Roman Church, was a doctor most learned in the divine Scriptures and was highly esteemed in those times for these reasons. Besides his exceptional learning, he was everywhere renowned for religion and wisdom. He was also exceedingly gentle and keen in intellect, calm and composed in speech, and sufficiently capable of persuading [Col. 0187C]. Out of love for solitude and quiet, he abandoned both the bishopric and his very high dignity.

Since he was a man of outstanding intellect, he published the following volumes:

*Apologies*, book 3.

*On the Incontinence of Priests*, book 1.

*On the Wives of Clerics*, book 1.

And many other works.

### XIX. Hartmann Schedel (year 1505), in his *Universal History*, under the year of Christ 1068

Peter Damian, cardinal legate, carried out his legation with the greatest courage against the emperor, who wished to separate from his queen and lawful wife.

And a little later, under Pope Alexander II:

Peter Damian, doctor and cardinal-bishop of the Roman Church, most learned in the divine Scriptures, was highly esteemed in Italy in those times for these reasons. Distinguished in life and learning, he published several short works worthy of praise [Col. 0188A]; he also wrote elegant sermons, a rule for hermits, and a work on the order of hermit life; likewise, a book against the Jews. He also recounts many examples that occurred in his own times.

For he was a man highly renowned for religion, humility, and wisdom. When he was a cardinal-bishop, he resigned the bishopric so that he might serve God alone in humility and devote himself more freely to God. When Pope Gregory reproved him for this, he wrote a beautiful book to him, giving an account of why he had resigned the bishopric.

### XX. An anonymous monk of the monastery of the Holy Cross, from Fonte Avellana (year 1537), in a certain treatise concerning that same monastery. In my manuscript

Formerly, a thousand years after the birth of the Virgin, there was a place called Fonte Avellana, on the Apennine mountain [Col. 0188B], at the foot of Mount Catria, facing east and fourteen miles distant from the city of Gubbio. There a certain house had been built with a small oratory, which was the benefice of a certain Ludolf, son of Gesso, with a few inhabitants there.

Later, in the year 1047, the venerable hermit Peter Damian, surnamed the Sinner, from Ravenna, of the Order of St. Benedict, an outstanding doctor and a man distinguished for religion, conduct, and charity, who by his virtues became bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church—though unwillingly, on account of his humility—and who therefore resigned the bishopric a few years later, to the great displeasure of Pope Gregory VII, withdrew to the aforesaid place of Fonte Avellana. He judged it sufficiently suitable for the service of Almighty God [Col. 0188C].

There he enlarged the houses and the oratory. From the year 1047 until the year 1100 and beyond, he remained there almost continually with about twenty monks, hermits of the same order associated with him, serving God alone through continuous prayers and penances, and with fifteen lay brothers together with servants.

He himself was the first to adorn this sacred hermitage with holy works and divine worship. Through the offerings of the faithful he acquired possessions for it in various places. He left a library containing nearly all the volumes of the Old and New Testament; built a cloister beside the church; procured a sufficiently suitable silver cross; acquired bells and various furnishings for the house of God; and also provided two beautifully gilded silver chalices [Col. 0188D], as is more fully recorded in his volumes.

At last, in the year 1100, on 10 April, he closed the final day of his life, and his blessed body was committed to ecclesiastical burial in the abbey of St. Mary at Faenza, its members being perpetually united to the aforesaid hermitage of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana. May the Lord, through the prayers of the Virgin, lead his soul and those of his companions to the place of eternal blessedness.

With these facts established, who could doubt that Peter Damian was both, as it were, the founder of this sacred hermitage and the instructor of the eremitical life—especially since no memory has been preserved of anyone having lived under any rule at the aforesaid place of Fonte Avellana before his time?

### XXI. Aloysius Lippomano (year 1550), bishop of Bergamo and soon afterward of Verona, in a letter prefixed to part IV of volume VIII of the *Lives of the Saints*

While I was still a young man, I had heard that Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, who had flourished around the year of the Lord 1050 under the Roman pontiffs Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII, was a most learned man and highly practiced in sacred letters. I had also heard that he had left behind many monuments of his intellect, and indeed distinguished ones—works that could not easily be obtained for consultation because they had never previously been committed to print.

After I had undertaken the task of bringing together into a single body the lives of the holy Fathers written by worthy men, I made every effort, if possible, to bring to light some of the writings of this blessed Father in this field—for I had heard that many existed.

Nor, as you will see, did the kindness of Almighty God fail, a kindness that habitually favors pious desires. Through the diligence of my most beloved Francis Torres of the Capranica Library in Rome, a man distinguished by piety no less than by learning; through the renowned library of the monastery of Cassino, with the Fathers of that congregation kindly consenting; from a certain distinguished monastery of Italy, whose name I do not rashly mention at present; and finally from the library of the venerable canons of the church of the divine Peter, prince of the apostles, at the indication of that most learned man Guillelmo Sirleto, apostolic protonotary, many works of this most holy Father relevant to the present undertaking came into our hands [Col. 0189C].

We now gladly publish them with open-hearted generosity to the whole Church of God, for the benefit and usefulness of all the faithful—first those we obtained from the city of Rome and the monastery of Cassino, and then those we acquired from that monastery and the aforesaid library of St. Peter.

Read these works, therefore, kindly reader. For in this most holy man you will find no less learning, elegance, piety, and devotion than in the Fathers mentioned above.

The works published by Lippomano from manuscripts of the Cassinese and Capranica libraries are these:

*On St. Eleuchadius, Bishop.*

*On St. George the Martyr.*

*On St. Rufinus the Martyr.*

*A Hymn on the Same.*

*On St. Mark the Evangelist.*

*On St. Apollinaris, Bishop and Martyr.*

*Another Work on the Same.*

*A Third Work on the Same.*

*A Hymn on the Same.*

*Life of St. Dominic Loricatus.*

*Life of St. Romuald, Abbot.*

From a manuscript of a certain Italian monastery and from the library of the canons of the church of St. Peter:

*At the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.*

*On the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ.*

*On St. Stephen the Protomartyr.*

*On St. John the Evangelist.*

*Another Work on the Same.*

*On the Epiphany of the Lord.*

*On St. Severus, Bishop.*

*On Palm Sunday.*

*On the Lord’s Supper.*

*On the Resurrection of the Lord* [Col. 0190A].

*On St. Victor the Confessor.*

From that volume Surius and various others subsequently drew their material, as we shall soon explain.

### XXII. Onuphrius Panvinio (year 1560), Augustinian hermit, in the *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 1056

Peter Damian, formerly a monk and later bishop of Ostia; Lanfranc, formerly abbot of Bec and later archbishop of Canterbury; and Anselm, a monk of Reims—men most learned and most holy.

### XXIII. Johannes Rioche (year 1565), Franciscan Friar Minor, chapter 5 of book IV of the *Compendium of Times and Ecclesiastical Histories*

Peter Damian, formerly a monk of St. Benedict and later bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, was a learned and educated man, but also distinguished in his way of life. Following the example of Gregory of Nazianzus, however, he abandoned the bishopric out of love for solitude and returned to the monastery.

When Nicholas II, Alexander, and Gregory VII reproached him for this, he composed a satisfactory *Apology* addressed to them, by which they were appeased. He composed many learned and devout short works under Henry III, around the year 1050.

[Col. 0190D]

### XXIV. Carlo Sigonio (year 1570), *Histories of the Kingdom of Italy*, book IX, from A.D. 1058 to 1080
But when many other Churches rejected the new and renewed decrees against the heresies of the Simonians and Nicolaitans, the Church of Milan did so above all: although it had long since abandoned the authority of the Roman Church, it in no way obeyed its commands, and yet was, if any other [Church] was, infected with this kind of poison. Believing this matter to be both grave in itself and disgraceful to the name of the Milanese clergy, Artaldus, a cleric and tithe-collector, urged Landulfus Cotta, prefect of the people, to undertake its public opposition. When Landulfus had begun to do this with the favorable ears and minds of the people, Archbishop Wido took the opposing side, relying especially [Col. 0191A] upon the support of the nobility. Thus the matter was brought by mutual disputes and quarrels to such a degree of infamy that priests who had wives were compelled, out of shame, to celebrate the divine offices separately from the others in a place called Pataria. Hence they were commonly called “Patarines” by the boys as an insult.

Wishing to apply an appropriate remedy to this evil, Wido summoned an assembly of his bishops at Fontanetum, a town in the territory of Novara; and, following their judgment, he decreed that clerics might have wives, though unjustly. At that time Peter Damiani of Ravenna flourished in holiness, learning, and administrative ability. He had embraced the eremitical life and was living in the wilderness at Fonte Avellana. Stephen, judging his services suitable for restoring the Church, upon returning to the city at the beginning of Lent, honored him with [Col. 0191B] the Church of Ostia.

When Landulfus had sent Arialdus to Rome to report the insane contumacy of the Milanese Church and at the same time to request judges to investigate the charge of heresy, the pontiff appointed Peter Damiani, bishop of Ostia, as his legate for this purpose. Meanwhile Peter Damiani, taking Bishop Anselm of Lucca with him, went as legate to Milan. He was received there with due honor and explained to them in an assembly the purpose of his legation.

After this had become known, a rumor stirred up the following day in the city by the clerical faction grew widespread: the Ambrosian Church, they said, was free under the ancient institutions of the Fathers and was not subject to Roman laws; nor did the Roman pontiff possess any right to regulate or [Col. 0191C] establish his Church. Accordingly, amid loud cries, the rioters hurried from every direction to the episcopal residence; the whole city was filled with the clamor of bells and the blare of a huge trumpet, and everyone threatened the legate with death.

The flame of resentment had been kindled by the fact that on the previous day, when Peter presided over the assembly, he had placed Bishop Anselm at his right hand, while he ordered Archbishop Wido to sit at his left. Perceiving the will of the people, the legate summoned them to the church the next day, ascended the pulpit, and, when the tumult had at last been quieted, spoke as follows:

“Pope Nicholas, most beloved brothers, has sent me to you, not to serve the honor and greatness of the Roman Church, but to care for your glory and salvation. For what need has the Roman Church of the [Col. 0191D] honor of the lowliest man, when it has received the proclamation of praise from the mouth of the Savior himself? And what province on earth is found to be free from the authority of the one by whose decision heaven itself is opened and closed? (Matthew 16.)

“Indeed, if you attend carefully, you will find that the other Churches were founded by men, whereas the Roman Church itself was founded by God, and that from it all the others—and especially the Milanese Church—received the beginnings of their origin and the rudiments of their discipline. For what of Peter and Paul, who consecrated the Roman Church with their blood? Did they not also establish this Church through their disciples? Nazarius, washed in the sacred font by Linus, Peter’s disciple, suffered a holy martyrdom [Col. 0192A] in this city; and Gervasius and Protasius, whose holy bodies are venerated in this city, had no other teacher than Paul. Finally, the blessed Ambrose, in whom you take such great pride, when he was once unable by himself to restrain the heresy of the Nicolaitans, sought assistance from the Roman Church; and three men sent by the then-pontiff Siricius to expiate this error brought immediate aid to the city.

“Therefore, since both the first authors of your salvation and those who later corrected its failing discipline came forth from the Roman Church, why do you now refuse, through untimely contumacy, to obey its decrees?”

By these words he so moved the defiant people that they replied that they were prepared to obey all his commands. An inquiry into the clergy [Col. 0192B] was then instituted, and scarcely a single man was found who had not either purchased his orders or shared in relations with a woman.

Then the legate perceived that, if he removed the sacred ministry from the city while condemning everyone, but absolved only a few, he would wrong the rest, since the case of all was alike. He therefore declared that he would grant pardon to everyone if they bound themselves by an oath and a penance to abstain from such offenses in the future.

The oath was threefold. First the archbishop swore as follows:

“I confess that a custom has arisen in the Church whereby anyone who receives clerical orders pays twelve coins for the title of subdeacon, eighteen for that of deacon, and twenty-four for that of priest. Therefore, in the presence of Lord Peter, bishop of Ostia and legate of Pope Nicholas, and of Lord Anselm, [Col. 0192C] bishop of Lucca, and of all of you, I condemn and detest every Simoniac heresy, and I promise that neither I, nor my clerics, nor my successors will exact anything of this kind in the future. I likewise condemn the heresy of the Nicolaitans, and I promise, insofar as I am able, to drive priests, deacons, and subdeacons away from the company of wives and concubines.”

Then, before the altar and in the presence of the bishop of Lucca, he said: “If I fail in these matters, then may God and the saints cast me out from the communion of the righteous.”

Finally, his nephew Arnulfus, a cleric, held the archbishop’s hand with one hand and touched the sacred Gospel book with the other, and spoke as follows:

“Lord Wido the archbishop will observe what he has promised concerning the chastity of clerics, and he will ordain no one except monks, unless he binds them by the preceding [Col. 0192D] oath.””

The clerics swore the same oath.

When these proceedings had been completed, the archbishop threw himself upon the ground and ordered that a penance be imposed upon him, because, although he himself had not introduced those disgraces into the Church, he had nevertheless failed to remove them when he could have done so. The legate imposed a penance of one hundred years and decreed that it could be redeemed by the payment of a fixed sum for each year. The clerics were bound to various fasts during their lives.

The archbishop then ascended the pulpit and, in the presence of the clergy and people, ordered his cleric to swear that he would eradicate these two heresies to the best of his ability. The people likewise bound themselves by the same oath.

Finally, the clerics’ former privileges were restored to those who were learned and chaste. The others were merely admitted to the fellowship of the Church; the archbishop also promised that, for the sake of religion, he would send them [Col. 0193A] to Rome or Tours, while he himself promised to go to Saint James in Spain. Peter himself wrote that he had carried out these actions as legate at Milan.

After the legate’s departure, the archbishop, assailed by the harsh insults of his own clerics because he had betrayed the liberty of the Milanese Church, did not persevere in the decision concerning chastity but permitted indiscriminate relations with women. Accordingly, in the following year, 1060, Arlembaldus Cotta was chosen in place of his deceased brother Landulfus. At the urging of the same Arialdus, he revived the dormant cause and stirred up serious riots in the city; he even prevented the abbot of Saint Celsus from being consecrated by the archbishop. Peter Damiani therefore sent them this letter:

“Peter Damiani, etc.” It is found in Book V, Letter 84.

[Col. 0193B] The same Henry III, emperor, devoted to evil counselors, especially Adalbert, archbishop of Bremen, omitted no form of avarice, lust, or insolence toward human beings or God. He supported the common people against the nobles and princes, conducted everything more by force than by law, openly sold bishoprics and abbeys, and bestowed the richest estates of the monks upon his followers in disgraceful generosity.

Moreover, having grown weary of his wife Bertha, daughter of the margrave Otto, to whom he had recently been betrothed, and wishing to divorce her, he induced the archbishop of Mainz to summon an assembly at Mainz to discuss the matter. When Alexander learned of this, he sent Peter Damiani as legate to Germany to prevent it. Peter set out the following year for Mainz [Col. 0193C] and, by threatening the danger of a more severe punishment, dissuaded him from holding the council.

At Frankfurt, however, where Henry had summoned the assembly, Peter delivered the pontiff’s instructions in these terms: what Henry was attempting was a most wicked act, alien not only to the Christian name but even to the royal one. If he was not restrained by human or divine laws, he should at least consider his reputation and standing, lest, by allowing such foul poison to spread from a king, he infect the entire Christian people; and lest a prince bind himself to offenses which he ought to punish. If he was not moved by advice, he should know for certain that the pontiff would employ ecclesiastical force and would never consecrate him as emperor with his own hands.

After this speech came the grave [Col. 0193D] voices of the princes who were present, declaring that the Roman pontiff was right to command such things. They urged Henry not to stain the majesty of the royal name before God with the pollution of so shameful an act, nor to provide the queen’s relatives with a cause for rebellion and a legitimate occasion for disturbing the state. If they were men, possessing great power in arms and men, they would undoubtedly expiate such a conspicuous insult to their daughter through some conspicuous deed.

Broken more than persuaded by these arguments, Henry said that he would remain under the pontiff’s authority.

In the following year, namely 1080, when Gregory VII heard that Archbishop Gilbert had gone to Ravenna, he sent Peter Damiani there as legate, although Peter was worn out by age. Peter departed and was graciously received by the city. He received back into the Church the people, who had been corrupted by contact with the condemned [Col. 0194A] archbishop, and the condemned archbishop himself, and, by pontifical authority, released him from the penance he had incurred. Soon after leaving Ravenna, when he had reached Faenza, he was overcome by fever and died. He was a man distinguished in those times both for holiness and wisdom. After his death, people regarded him as a saint, renowned for miracles.

### XXV. Petrus Ricordatus (1578), a Tuscan from Bojano, monk of the Cassinese Congregation, in the fourth journal of *Monastic History*

Speaking of Peter Damiani, distinguished both for learning and holiness, we say that he was from Ravenna and a monk of the monastery of Saint Mary at Faenza. Because of his outstanding virtues, he was made by Stephen IX bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and he discharged this office worthily for a very long [Col. 0194B] time.

Among the matters concerning him that I find worthy of notice in Trithemius’s *Hirsaugia*, it is recorded that, sent by Alexander II as legate to Henry at Frankfurt, he explained the entire course of his legation to the king before the nobles and princes of the empire with the greatest authority and learning. Later, seized by love of solitude, he freed himself from such affairs and, resigning his bishopric, withdrew to the monastery of the Holy Cross at Avellana mentioned above.

This monastery lies in the mountains of the territory of Urbino. There our poet Dante, delighting in that solitary region, lived for a long time while composing most of his works. Evidence of this still exists today in a certain cave called Dante’s chamber. [Col. 0194C] The poet described this place in his *Paradiso* in the verses in which, in Canto XXI, he introduces Peter himself speaking, namely:

> Between the two shores of Italy rise rocks  
>   
> (and not far distant from your homeland)  
>   
> So high that thunder there sounds much lower, etc.

In our own time this monastery was restored to regular observance under the Camaldolese Congregation by the illustrious and most reverend Julius, cardinal of Urbino.

To return to our subject: Peter, having returned to the monastery, held a private position. Later, when he was admonished by Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII because it was unfitting for a man endowed by the good and great God with such learning and eloquence—and therefore especially suited to persuade peoples to live rightly—to abandon the bishopric, while concerned with his own advantage, even though he could be of assistance to many in such a dignity, to have resigned [Col. 0194D] the bishopric, he replied by letter. In it he gives both excellent and appropriate reasons for his departure.

He wrote to the hermit Leo, *Whether “The Lord Be with You” Should Be Said in the Divine Office*, Book II; *Apologetics*, Book III; *On the Continence of Priests*, Book I; *On the Rule of Solitaries*, Book I; *On the Miracles of His Time*, Book I; *Monastic Exhortations*, Book I; *On the Progress of Monks*, Book I; *Against the Jews*, Book I; *On the Avarice of Prelates*, Book I; *The Life of Odilo, Abbot of Cluny*, Book I; *On the Terror of Death*, Book I; *Against Simoniac Bishops*, Book I; *Against an Unnamed Bishop*, Book I; *On the Insolence of the Reprobate*, Book I; *On the Exclamations of Rhetors*, [Col. 0195A] Book I; *On the Nature of Certain Animals*, Book I; *On Saint Cassian the Martyr*, Book I; *Sermons and Homilies*, Book I; *On Saints Flora and Lucilla*, whose bodies rest in our monastery at Arezzo, Book I.

He wrote many other works, which it would be tedious to enumerate. He died during the reign of Henry III, around the year of our Lord 1080, and was enrolled among the saints.

### XXVI. Arnoldus Wion (1294), a Belgian, monk of the Cassinese Congregation, Book II, chapter 9 of *The Tree of Life*, treating of the cardinals of the Order of Saint Benedict, writes the following about Blessed Peter Damiani:

Saint Peter of Honestis, surnamed Damianus, and “the Sinner,” a nobleman of Ravenna, monk of the monastery of Saint Andrew in the wilderness of Avellana, of the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Columba, was created cardinal of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 0195B] and bishop of Ostia in the year of our Lord 1058, in March, on the Saturday of the Ember Days of Lent. Finally, having resigned the dignity of cardinal, he returned to his monastery in 1072 and died at Faenza in the monastery of Saint Mary, which he had built with five others, in the year 1080, on 22 February.

Volaterranus, in Book XXI of his *Anthropology*, and several others, list our Damian among the professors of the Rule of Saint Augustine. We demonstrate from many sources that they are mistaken. First, Leo of Ostia, Book II, chapter 102, reports that he was taken from the wilderness and raised to the dignity of cardinal, saying:

> When Peter Damiani, a very religious man, whom Pope Stephen at that time had drawn from the wilderness and made bishop of the Church of Ostia, learned of this, he began, [Col. 0195C] together with the cardinals, to resist and protest, etc.

Berthold of Constance confirms this in his appendix to Hermannus Contractus under the year 1066, in these words:

> In these times the venerable Peter Damiani, a cardinal-bishop from an eremite, wrote many works, etc.

It is manifest from the histories that no hermits, especially at that time, observed the Rule of Saint Augustine; many, however, pursued this profession under the Rule of Saint Benedict. The authorities are Peter the Deacon, in *The Saints of Monte Cassino*, chapter 4, in the *Life of Saint Martin, Hermit of Monte Marcisi*; John Dubravius, Book VI of his *Bohemian History*, in the *Life of the Five Holy Monk-Hermits of Broumov*; Martin Kromer, in his *Polish History*, where he discusses the same subject; and other Polish writers. [Col. 0195D]

Damianus was called a hermit because, as his Life relates—and Augustine of Florence reports in Part II, Book V, chapter 7 of his *Camaldolese History*—the monks of the monastery of Saint Andrew at Avellana, which now bears the title of the Holy Cross, lived at that time in pairs, dwelling in separate cells and devoting themselves to psalmody, prayer, reading, abstinence, obedience, and other such works of piety and religious duties.

That he was a monk, and an abbot, is proved both by his Life by Hieronymus Rubeus, Book V of the *History of Ravenna*, which appears in Volume VII of Surius as edited by Mosander, and also by the same Augustine, in the book cited, from chapter 6 to chapter 15, and by Jacobus Philippus in his *Supplement of Chronicles*, Book XII, who says:

> Peter Damiani, a cardinal-bishop of the Roman Church from a monk, a most learned teacher in the divine Scriptures, was highly esteemed in these times for these reasons.

Honorius likewise says so in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Panvinus in his *Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs*; and others.

Trithemius, in Book II, chapter 93, and Book IV, chapter 35 of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, identifies him as a professor of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Panvinus does the same in the *Epitome*, when he says: “Peter Damiani, [Col. 0196A] a Cassinese monk, of the Order of Saint Benedict, cardinal-bishop of Ostia.” He is called a Cassinese monk because he led the monastic life in those monasteries that were subject to the monastery of Cassino.

I shall add, omitting the other recent authorities, Damianus’s own testimony in his sermon on Saint Benedict, where he calls Saint Benedict his master and father. It may be found in Volume VII of Mosander’s edition of Surius, under 21 March, [Col. 0196B] and reads as follows:

> To whom, then, can the whole course of evangelical reading be assigned in such a special way as to our Father and master, Blessed Benedict?

Likewise, in a letter to a certain Peter, abbot, found in the appendix to Margarini de la Bigne’s *Library of the Holy Fathers*, he speaks even more clearly, saying at the very beginning:

> For you are angry and accuse us in our complaints because we ought not to have received your monks contrary to the precepts of our blessed Father Benedict.

And below, after quoting the words of Our Father Benedict, he says:

> These words, therefore, are not ours but the words of that same Father of ours, etc.

In other [Col. 0196C] letters also found there, he repeats the same thing again and again, calling Saint Benedict his Father and master.

Finally, the monasteries in which Damian himself lived as a monk and not yet as an abbot—such as Saint Vincent’s, Cassino, and Pomposa—clearly demonstrate that he was a disciple of Saint Benedict. Moreover, the monks of Avellana openly profess that, down to our own times, when they were united with the Camaldolese Congregation, they had observed the rule of our holy Father Benedict from the original foundation of their monastery.

He received the surname Damianus not, as Panvinus says, because he was the son of a man named Damianus, but because, when he had first been sent by his brother Damianus to Faenza and then to Parma to study, he adopted the name Damianus as a testimony of his gratitude toward his brother, using it from his brother’s name, so that he always wrote himself “Peter Damiani.” [Col. 0196D] Augustine correctly teaches this in chapter 6.

The Congregation was called Columba because of the extraordinary simplicity of Ludolfus, its first founder at Avellana. Augustine himself discusses this in chapter 5, as does Benvenutus of Imola in his commentary on Dante’s *Paradiso*, Canto XXI.

Trithemius, Book II, chapter 93, considers him a monk of Vivarium; Volaterranus, a monk of Saint Mary of Ravenna; and Bugianus, a monk of Saint Mary of Faenza. These three accounts may be reconciled by saying, with Trithemius, that after making his profession at the monastery of Saint Andrew at Avellana, he lived for some time in the monastery of Vivarium; but before his profession he tested himself for forty days at the monastery of Saint Mary of Ravenna, in imitation of eremitical rigor, to discover whether he could endure the labor of monastic life, as Augustine says in chapter 6. [Col. 0197A]

Dante Alighieri says this in the following words:

> In that place I was Peter Damiani,  
>   
> And Peter the Sinner was in the house  
>   
> Of Our Lady upon the Adriatic shore, etc.

He finally died in the monastery of Saint Mary at Faenza in the year 1080, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, as Augustine, Book V, chapter 14, and Rubeus in his Life most correctly report.

Berthold of Constance, however, in his appendix to Contractus, reports that he died in the year of our Lord 1072, saying:

> 1072: Peter Damiani, cardinal-bishop of pious memory, long since crucified to the world, departed to the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends [Col. 0197B] of March.”

I think these words should be explained in such a way that the meaning concerns not temporal death but the death of an office and dignity—namely, when, having rejected the honor of the cardinalate, he died to the world and its splendors. For that he lived after the year 1072 is proved by his legations, which he undertook during the time of Pope Gregory VII, who was not proclaimed pontiff until the year 1073.

As for Trithemius’s statement that Damianus resigned the bishopric out of love of quiet and solitude, following the example of the great bishop Gregory, and returned to his monastery, it should not be understood as though Trithemius were speaking of Saint Gregory the Great, pope. Rather, he meant Gregory of Nazianzus, who, inflamed by the same spirit as Damianus, resigned his bishopric and returned to the solitary life.

[Col. 0197C] ### XXVII. The same author, *The Tree of Life*, Book III, under the eighth day before the Kalends of March

The deposition at Faenza of Saint Peter Damiani, surnamed “the Sinner,” most holy cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. Because of his desire for a stricter life, he had said farewell to the cardinalate and could be diverted from his original purpose neither by threats nor by blandishments. When the supreme pontiff rebuked him for this action with charitable correction, he issued apologies to three successive Roman pontiffs. In them, humbly excusing his action by authority, reason, and example, he calmed their minds; and thus persevering in his good work, he fell asleep in the Lord. (Peter Damiani.)

[Col. 0197D] The Camaldolese registers sent to me discuss the same man on this day. Mosander reproduces his life from Book V of Hieronymus Rubeus’s *History of Ravenna* in Volume VII of Surius’s *Lives of the Saints* under this day; Dom Augustine Fortunius treats it more fully in Part II of his *Camaldolese History*, Book V, chapters 6–14. Leo of Ostia, bishop, also discusses him in Book II, chapter 102 of the *Cassinese Chronicle*. Trithemius treats him in Book II, chapter 93, and Book IV, chapter 35 of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, as do innumerable others.

He was first a monk of Saint Andrew’s, now called the Holy Cross of Avellana, of the Order of Saint Benedict, as he himself testifies in his sermon on Saint Benedict, which appears in Volume VII of Mosander’s edition of Surius, where he calls Benedict his father and master. He died at Faenza in the year 1080. For the rest of his deeds, see above [Col. 0198A] in the description of the second branch of this Tree and in the treatise on the cardinals.

### XXVIII. The same author, *The Tree of Life*, Book V, explaining the second branch of his Tree; this is its head, chapter 31

Saint Peter Damiani, the magnificent restorer of the Milanese from schism to the Catholic Church.

> For God gives a good man wisdom, knowledge, and joy in his sight (Ecclesiastes 2).

My mind falters, my pen fails, and my hand stiffens when I consider writing about Saint Peter Damiani, monk and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, bishop of Ostia, who occupies the first place in the third order of the present branch. For he was so great and so distinguished, and so useful and necessary to the holy Church, that I do not know where to begin the account of his deeds.

[Col. 0198B] His learning and eloquence are known from his many writings, which still survive today. His holiness was shown by the fact that, after serving for a long time as cardinal and bishop of Ostia, he finally grew weary of that life and, following the example of Nazianzenus, returned to his former monastic pursuits. He also explained the reasons for this action in a splendid written work, making them clear to everyone.

Shall we remain silent, then? Far from it. There remains that distinguished action for which this cardinal is represented here in his cardinal’s habit, carrying in his hands the arms of the bishopric of Milan: those arms are a human hand holding a golden whip of netting over a blood-red field.

For Pope Nicholas II, wishing to restore the state, which was greatly shaken by the most serious calamities, sent Peter Damiani to Milan in the year 1059 [Col. 0198C] so that he might reconcile that Church, which held erroneous views, had been separated from and at variance with Rome for two hundred years, and was infected with the stain of simony and the heresy of the Nicolaitans, with the Roman Church and bring it back to the correct position.

Peter summoned the people to the church and handled their minds so prudently and gently that at last they adopted his view and did not refuse to obey the apostolic see. First Archbishop Wido professed this in solemn words and publicly detested the Simoniac and Nicolaitan heresies; afterward all the clerics did the same. The archbishop threw himself upon the ground and asked that a penance be imposed upon him. Peter imposed a hundred years and decreed that it could be redeemed by the payment of a fixed sum for each year; the clerics were bound to various fasts during their lives.

There survive letters on this matter from Peter himself, [Col. 0198D] who everywhere calls himself “the sinner,” to Pope Nicholas, and from Nicholas to him, in Book V of Hieronymus Rubeus’s *History of Ravenna*, from which we have taken this account. Paul Morigia also confirms this action by Peter in Book I, chapter 58 of *On the Origin of Religion*, as do other recent writers, though some present the matter differently.

They attribute all the glory to Pope Stephen X, called IX, whom they make the author of this reconciliation. I think their position should be understood as follows: Stephen began this action but, because of the brevity of his life, could not complete it; after his death, Peter Damiani, acting by the command of his successor Nicholas II, brought it to [Col. 0199A] completion, as Peter himself demonstrates at length in the treatise he composed *On the Reconciliation of Wido, Bishop of Milan*, which is preserved in manuscript in the Cassinese library.

Since Peter was a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, acquainted also with secular literature, gentle and acute in intellect, calm and composed in speech, and well suited to persuasion, he composed many works highly useful to pious minds. Some have already been printed, while others remain to be printed in due time.

Among the printed works I have seen are the following:

* *On Ecclesiastical Institution and the Refutation of the Simoniac Heresy*, Book I, printed at Cologne by Gymnicus together with three books of Prosper, in octavo; also printed in Flanders, though I no longer recall the place, together with other works on the same subject.
* Two homilies *On the Excellence of Saint John the Baptist*, printed at Cologne by Gymnicus.
* *The Lord Be with You*, Book I: whether a solitary praying the canonical hours should also say *Dominus vobiscum* when there is no one to respond. Printed at Venice by Zilettus in 1572, in octavo.
* *The Mirror of the Mass*, also printed at Rome with other authors on the divine offices in 1591, in folio.
* *On the Epiphany of the Lord*: “When he had been born.”
* *The Life of Saint Maurus, Bishop of Cesena*: “Desiring.”

All these sermons were printed at Cologne in Surius’s *Lives of the Saints* and at Venice in folio. I have seen fifteen of his letters to various persons printed at Paris, in folio, in Volume VII of Margarini de la Pigne’s *Library of the Holy Fathers*.

The following works are also attributed to him:

* *On the Last Judgment*: “I am not unaware that when…”

All these sermons, homilies, and letters are found in manuscript copies in my possession and in that of Lord Constantine Cajetanus of Syracuse, a monk; also, to a considerable extent, in the Cassinese library and elsewhere.

*On the Miracles of Our Holy Father Benedict*, Book I.

*On Penance*: “One must consider.”

*A Sermon Against the Simonians*: [Col. 0200D] “The turbulent crowd of the world.”

These are in manuscript in my possession and likewise in our library of Saint Benedict at Mantua.

In the Cassinese library, on the sixth desk to the left, the following manuscripts are found: a certain sermon and poems addressed to Cadalus, bishop; a synodal disputation between the king’s advocate and the defender of the Roman Church; a disputation on the question “Whether God exists”; several letters and certain other short treatises; *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son*; a sermon *On Saint Mark the Evangelist*; *On Saint Alexius the Confessor*; *On the Duties of the Pontiff*; [Col. 0201A] many of his letters; three sermons *On Saint Matthew*; *On the Cassinese Monastery and Certain Miracles*, addressed to Desiderius, abbot; *On Certain Beasts*, though its beginning is missing; a sermon *On Saint Columba, Virgin and Martyr*; a sermon *On Almsgiving*; and many of his letters.

### XXIX. In another manuscript book, on parchment, the following are set down.

Sermon on Saint Boniface the Martyr. Two sermons on Saint John the Baptist. On Saints Donatus and Hilarinus. Hymn on Saint Antimus. Homily on the Gospel: “The Book of the Generation.” Two sermons on the Nativity of Blessed Mary. Three sermons on Saint Apollinaris. Two sermons on Saint Vitalis. Three hymns on Saint John the Evangelist. [Col. 0201B] One book of his letters. On the incontinence of bishops. On the property of clerics. Two sermons on Saint Bartholomew, and collects concerning him. Hymn on Saint Ursicinus. The Miracles of Saint Ruffinus. Letter to the Empress Agnes. A pious treatise to monks. Another on the perfection of monks. Dialogue between a Jew and a Christian. Invective against a bishop recalling monks to the secular world. A little work to the hermit Teuzo. A disputation on the canonical hours. That marriages can take place without intercourse. Sermon on the vigil of Saint James. On the vigil of Saint Bartholomew, several letters. On the discipline of monks. A disputation on the degrees of patience. On the privilege of the Roman Church, to Archdeacon Hildebrand. On reconciling heretics; a long letter on resigning the episcopate. Some treatises to monks, and several questions. Many letters to the monks of Pomposa and others. On various histories, verses, and letters. Sermon on readiness more toward evil than toward good, and on eight vigils to be observed by fasting, beginning as follows: “Yet human weakness naturally labors in this way.” [Col. 0202A] A mournful lament over a soul devoted to the filth of uncleanness, beginning: “I, I bewail you, unhappy soul.” Three sermons against the Sodomites: the first begins, “Those who irrationally”; the second, “But the cleric of the Lord”; the third, “This vice indeed.”

The following works are also cited by Trithemius: *On the Situation and Foundation of the Monastery of Vivarium*, book 1. *Apologetics*, book 3, to his lord Nicholas. *On the Incontinence of Priests*, book 1, beginning: “Recently having.” *On the Wives of Clerics*, book 1, beginning: “I address you.” *Rule of Solitaries*, book 1, beginning: “While the fervor of holy…” [uncertain]. *Miracles of His Time*, book 1, beginning: “To the most beloved Gerard.” *An Exhortation to Monks*, book 1, beginning: “To the brothers at Ganges.” *On the Progress of Monks*, book 1. *On the Insolence of Wicked Men*, book 1. *On the Avarice of Prelates*, [Col. 0202B] book 1. *Rhetorical Declamations*, book 1. *Most Welcome*, or *Most Approved*, book 1, beginning: “To Lord N. of Ravenna.”

His letters concerning the whole of life and religion exist in manuscript, in folio, on parchment, in the emperor’s library at Vienna.

A certain treatise, or little book, was printed at Strasbourg in 1562, in folio, in the *Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth*, as they themselves call it, under his name, *On the Correction of a Bishop and of the Pope*. I do not know whether it is his work; nevertheless, it seems to me that it must be avoided, since heretics thrust many such spurious offspring upon us in order to defend their impostures as though by the authority of holy men and doctors of the Church, as also happened with that spurious letter of Saint [Col. 0202C] Ulrich, bishop, and similar works. [Note: [Col. 0202C] I have forborne to cite here the authority of the most illustrious Lord Cardinal Baronius because anyone can easily consult his *Ecclesiastical Annals*. For in volume XI he writes much about the holiness, learning, and deeds of blessed Peter Damian.]

[Col. 0201]

## A Brief Notice to the Reader

We did not wish you, friendly Reader, to be unaware that, after the author of the preceding Life, who was his contemporary (*sýnchronos*) and disciple, John Anthony Flavinius of Forlì, Augustine Fortunius, a Camaldolese monk, and Jerome Rubeus also wrote the Life of the same Blessed Peter. Since their labors, set out more fully in the Roman edition of the letters, recount the deeds of Damian in the same way as his disciple, whom they followed, and in precisely the same sequence, we have, on the advice of learned men, excerpted only those details that seemed to be lacking in the preceding account—and these are quite few—lest the length of the same story, repeated so many times, bring readers more weariness than eagerness to read.

We have observed the same principle in the ancient testimonies concerning the author, from which, for the sake of brevity, we selected only those passages commended by the authority of the witnesses or those that contribute more substantially to the commendation of the author himself. These are the passages that you will gladly receive as an appendix.

[Col. 0201]

## Supplements to the Testimonies

### I. From Book V of Augustine Fortunius’s *History of Camaldoli*, a monk of the same congregation

Peter had another brother named Damian, who had been away from his homeland for several years. On his return, and moved by compassion for the sufferings of his brother Peter, touched by natural affection, he immediately freed him from the miserable servitude in which his elder brother—into whose care, after the death of both parents, the child, scarcely weaned, had been entrusted—was cruelly keeping him oppressed. He clothed him in new garments and sent him to school to be instructed in grammatical studies. When he recognized that he was endowed with an excellent intellect and suited to embrace other disciplines, he sent him first to Faenza and then to Parma, and supported him so that he might most conveniently devote himself to learned men. When he had made great progress there in a short time, he adopted the name “Damian” from his brother’s name, so that he always signed himself “Peter Damian,” and so forth.

### II. From Book V of Jerome Rubeus’s *History of Ravenna*

Meanwhile, Pope Alexander was troubled by the grave dispute with Cadalo of Parma, whom the Germans, after making him a false pope, were striving to have accepted even by the Roman nobles. Although he had been rejected at the council held at Mantua in 1064, which Alexander himself also attended, he nevertheless retained the insignia of the pontificate. Therefore Peter Damian, pitying the great disturbance of the Church of God, wrote to the man that he had already been condemned by three assemblies and had three times been deposed—if not by the judgment of priests, at least by the authority of the laws.

[Col. 0203B]

### III. An anonymous Benedictine, circa 1125, in the *Life of Blessed John of Lodi*, disciple of the same holy doctor and bishop of Gubbio

At that time the venerable man and priest of the most high God, Lord Peter Damian, adorned with virtues and learned in the sacred Scriptures, flourished in holiness and knowledge in the vast wilderness of Santa Croce at Fonte Avellana. And Peter himself, when he was a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and had been sent as a legate by the lord pope, traveled through the county and bishoprics of Gubbio, Nocera, and Cagli, and through Romagna and the Marches. When he learned of the admirable words and works concerning the perfection of the poor brothers of Fonte Avellana, attracted by their conversation and angelic way of life, he abandoned the glory of the cardinalate and, with the permission of the lord pope, shut himself away in the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, serving God day and night.

Many, stirred by his example, despised the glory of the world and devoted themselves entirely to the service of God. The man of God John, having learned of the fame of so great a man, encouraged by his example, fled to him and withdrew from the world. Leaving his own land and kindred, he came to the land that the Lord had revealed to him and humbly offered himself to the venerable Father Peter Damian, prior of the hermitage and master of the devout brothers. Falling to his knees, he earnestly begged him to receive him as a disciple and brother under the discipline of the sacred Rule of the most blessed Father Benedict, so that he might serve Christ the King forever.

The reverend priest of God, Peter Damian, seeing in John the simple purity of his soul, the fervor of his spirit, his readiness for obedience, [Col. 0204A] and his genuine contempt for the world, received him kindly.

(And shortly afterward.) The two luminous pillars of the brothers of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana—the reverend prior Peter and John, the cleric of God—like two Seraphim inflamed with divine charity, continually praised the most high God with heart and mouth, and kindled the minds, hearts, and mouths of the brothers with the fear of God and fraternal charity. Oh, how good and pleasant it was for such brothers to dwell together, with Christ Jesus as their Lord and Master in their midst!

When almighty God had determined to reward the venerable Peter for his labors, while he was absent from the hermitage and staying for a time with the brothers at the monastery of Faenza, God brought his life to a good end. The man of God, happily departing from the world, flew up to the heavenly realms and lives with Christ forever. Although all the brothers greatly rejoiced in his happiness at his departure, they nevertheless lamented that his absence would bring them many losses. But divine providence did not fail them. For, inspired by the Lord, they unanimously and concordantly elected the holy man Lord John of Lodi as their principal prior, so that, just as he was like Saint Father Peter Damian in holiness and wisdom, he might succeed him in the priorship.

### IV. An ancient author of the manuscript *Chronicle of Gualdo*, circa 1325

The venerable cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, God’s servant Peter Damian, in the fervor of the Holy Spirit given to him by God, abandoned the glory and dignity of the Roman curia. Within the Apennine mountains of Catria he built the venerable hermitage of Santa Croce beside the spring of Avellana and established there a community of many holy monk-brothers in holy perfection, under a very strict and ordered way of life. He himself also lived there for many years in great holiness and became renowned for many miracles.

### V. Cardinal Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume XI, under A.D. 1072

Thus, in that most lamentable age, when a flood of the flesh had grown to the point of overwhelming the Church, God gave the world such a man, who by the example of his most austere life, by the preaching of his word, and by his writings dried up so much corruption [Col. 0204D] and at the same time fought against the simoniacal heresy that was raging everywhere with impunity.

## Letters of Saint Peter Damian

[Col. 0205]

# Eight Books of Letters of Saint Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church

## Book One: To the Supreme Pastors of the Christian Commonwealth and to Cadalo the Antipope

[Col. 0205]

### 1–2. First Letter: To Gregory VI, Roman Pontiff

#### Summary

With the care of the sacred affairs and the Christian commonwealth entrusted to Gregory VI, he declares himself greatly rejoiced and hopes that henceforth everything will be administered better, with criminal transactions and bribes removed and room given to virtue alone.
