He especially urges him to restore the condition of the Churches of Castellana, Fano, and Pesaro: if a beginning is made with these, the others can readily be corrected.

To Lord Gregory, most holy pope, Peter the sinful monk offers the service of due obedience.

Most reverend lord, I give thanks to Christ, King of kings, because I thirst with the parched throat of my desire always to hear good news from the apostolic see. I drink deeply of the generous cup of your praise, since many are already offering it. This draught refreshes the stomach of my mind with such sweetness that, while my mind rejoices inwardly, my tongue immediately bursts into this song of praise: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

For truly he, as it is written, changes times and transfers kingdoms. Truly, what he foretold long ago through his prophet, he has now, with the world as witness, wonderfully fulfilled: “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and he gives it to whomever he wishes” (Deuteronomy 4; Daniel 2). Let the heavens therefore rejoice, let the earth exult, and let the holy Church rejoice that she has recovered the ancient privilege of her own right.

Let the thousand-formed head of the poisonous serpent now be crushed; let the commerce of wicked dealing cease; [Col. 0205C] let the counterfeiter Simon no longer mint any currency in the Church (Acts 8); let no Gehazi (2 Kings 5), in the absence of a watchful teacher, carry away stolen gifts. Let the dove now return to the ark and, with green olive leaves, announce that peace has been restored to the earth (Genesis 8). Let the golden age of the apostles be restored, and, under the presidency of your prudence, let ecclesiastical discipline bloom again.

Let the greed of those panting for episcopal miters be restrained; let the chairs of the money-changers who sell doves be overturned [Col. 0206A] (Matthew 21; Mark 11; John 2). Yet whether it is permissible for the world to hope for these things about which we write, the Church of Pesaro will first give a clear indication of good hope. For unless that Church is taken from the hand of that adulterer, incestuous man, perjurer, and ravisher, all the hope of the peoples that had been raised by the prospect of the world’s restoration will be utterly weakened. All indeed direct their eyes toward this end; all raise their ears to this one voice. And if a man wrapped in so many crimes is restored to the fortress of the episcopate, it is wholly denied that anything further can be accomplished for good by the apostolic see.

There are, indeed, three seats that will give testimony: Castellana, Fano, and Pesaro, so that “by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand” (Deuteronomy 19; Matthew 18). In these three it is plainly shown how much hope remains for the future.

May almighty God, supreme Father, guard you for the preservation of the rights of his Church, and permit his people to rejoice, not unjustly, under so great a pontiff.

## Second Letter: To the Same

#### Summary

He writes that he does not entirely approve of a certain man who, elected bishop by his own people, was coming to Rome to be confirmed by the pontiff; nevertheless, when compared with others, he does not seem unworthy of that dignity. He asks that, if the pope rejects him, he defer the matter until Peter’s arrival.

To Lord Gregory, most holy pope, Peter the sinful monk offers the service of the most devoted obedience.

Let your Beatitude know, most pious lord, that because of our sins clerics worthy of the office of bishop are not found in our regions. For all seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2). Inflamed by the fire of avarice and pride, they indeed strive to be promoted to the priesthood, but do not endeavor to become worthy of the priesthood. They long to preside; they do not care to be useful.

Nevertheless, given the circumstances of the times and the scarcity of suitable persons, it seems to me that this archpriest could be advanced to the summit of the episcopate, [Col. 0207A] if the authority of your holiness so decrees. The only objection is that he burns with a desire for honor and eagerly longs to ascend to the height of pastoral office. Let this, however, be left to your judgment.

But if this is not an obstacle, when I consider the clerical order of the Church of Sempronius, this man appears somewhat better than the rest. Therefore, if it may please your most prudent holiness, since he has been elected by clergy and people, and since many have judged him at least somewhat suitable for this office, let him repent of his ambition and receive the blessing of consecration.

Nevertheless, may almighty God teach you by the grace of his Spirit what must be done in this matter and establish in the temple of your breast the laws of his will. There is one thing, however, for which I ask the mercy of your piety: if you do not consecrate this man, grant no one the chair of the aforesaid bishopric until you have seen me, your servant.

## Third Letter: To Clement II, Roman Pontiff

#### Summary

Ordered by the emperor to visit the pontiff and inform him about the deplorable condition of certain Churches, he received, while already on the journey, letters from the same emperor to deliver to the pontiff. He now sends them to him and asks him to write back whether he thinks Peter should continue the journey he had undertaken. At the same time, he diligently fulfills the task entrusted to him and, as a pious man, laments with great sorrow the calamities and disturbances of the Churches caused by the crimes and offenses of their bishops. He therefore implores the pontiff, to whom the entire care of sacred affairs has been entrusted, to bring aid to the holy Churches weakened by wicked men and to endeavor to restore them to their former tranquility.

To Lord Clement, prelate of the highest see, Peter the sinful monk offers the service of the deepest devotion.

Let your Beatitude know, most excellent lord, that the most invincible emperor, my lord, ordered me—not once but often—and, if I may say so, deigned to ask me to come to you and report to your ears what was being done in the Churches of our regions and what I thought ought to be done by you. Although I feared the difficulty of the journey and absolutely refused to come to you, he did not abandon his purpose; rather, he ordered me to set out on the journey by an unequivocal command.

After I had returned to the hermitage following a three-day journey, behold, these letters of his, to be offered to your sacred hands, were brought to us. We do not dare to tamper with them before seeing you. If you please, inspect them first, and together with them deign to order me by your own letter whether or not I ought to come to you.

For, placed between the two alternatives, I fear wasting my days by running here and there; yet I waste away in excessive grief and sadness out of compassion for the Church of God, which in our regions has been utterly thrown into confusion by wicked bishops and abbots. And what does it profit, my lord, for us to say that the apostolic see has returned from darkness to light, if we still remain in the same [Col. 0208A] darkness? What good does it do if someone locks away an abundance of vital food under a bolt, while he himself nevertheless perishes from hunger? What good does it do when someone is girded with the steel of a polished blade, if he does not wield it against the enemy formations surrounding him?

For almighty God has, in some sense, set you as food among his people in his own place; through you he has armed the side of his Church against every assault of her adversaries, so that you may strive to pierce with heavenly power the breast of those who resist God and satisfy the hungry stomach of our humility with the dishes of the sacred word.

But when we see the robber of Fano, cursed and excommunicated even by those who were not apostolic but were called apostolic, and likewise the man of Osimo, entangled in so many unheard-of and such great crimes, together with others who ought to be condemned by a similar sentence, returning from you with such arrogance and exultation, the joy of our hope is compelled to turn into mourning. For we hoped “that you were the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 14).

Therefore, most blessed Lord, strive to raise up justice so trampled upon and cast down; display ecclesiastical vigor with such discipline that the unjust party may fall from its proud position and the minds of the humble may grow more confident in hoping for good things.

## Fourth Letter: To Leo IX, Roman Pontiff

#### Summary

In this letter he devotes himself entirely to showing that he was falsely accused of certain crimes. He mildly excuses Pope Leo, the Supreme Pontiff, for being too ready to believe them. He says that it was easy for a man occupied with such great affairs to be deceived for a time by slanderers, and he confirms this even by the example of David. He then demonstrates, with arguments drawn from Holy Scripture, how cautiously credence should be given to the accusations of others. Finally, he calls God as witness to his innocence and adds that, if it should please that supreme ruler, he is prepared to endure any punishment, though innocent.

To Lord Leo, most blessed pope, Peter the sinful monk offers the service of the most devoted obedience.

I shall say at least this to my accusers, which the Israelite people said to their preachers: “May the Lord see and judge, for you have made our odor stink before Pharaoh and his servants” (Exodus 15). For the ancient enemy, fearing that by bringing suggestions to you I might destroy what he never ceases daily to fabricate in these regions through new inventions, sharpened the tongues of the wicked against me. He made his accomplices into a kind of instrument for composing lies, rattled through his vessels, and poured the venom of his malice into sacred ears.

And what wonder is it if the cunning of men was able to creep upon my lord, oppressed by such great affairs, when even David, who was filled with the prophetic spirit, rashly believing Ziba, immediately delivered the innocent Mephibosheth to a sentence of proscription? (2 Samuel 16.) The word of false accusation prevailed so greatly with him that he admitted a punishable servant into the fellowship of his master’s inheritance and judged a man guilty of infidelity worthy of the reward of freedom.

Nevertheless, if we attentively consider the deeds of our Creator, we ought not readily to give credence to the evil of just anyone. For he, before whose eyes all things are naked and open (Hebrews 4), did not disdain to say: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I shall descend and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Genesis 18).

This was surely said for no other reason than to teach human ignorance not to believe what it hears without examination, not lightly to pass judgment on what is unknown, and not to pronounce a sentence before it has confirmed a doubtful matter by testimony. Since we plainly know that you exercise this caution wisely in other cases, because it was not observed toward us, we do not attribute it to you but undoubtedly charge it to our own merits.

Nevertheless, in these matters I return to my conscience and withdraw into the secrets of my mind, certain that, except for the love of Christ, whose bad servant I am, I seek the favor of no mortal man and fear the anger of none. Therefore I call him himself as witness to my conscience, and I humbly ask him—whom it is pious to believe dwells in the sanctuary of your breast—that, if he judges it conducive to my salvation, he may immediately command you by his authority to grow gentle toward me and make the countenance of your serenity favorable to me. Thus may he unite me with you in reconciliation, he who frightens me lest I stand rigid and drives me to seek the favor of your mercy.

Otherwise, if he still decrees that I must be scourged by the harshest rod of your aversion, I humbly submit my bruised shoulders, place my finger upon my mouth, and make no complaint. But I raise the eyes of my hope to him himself, whose hidden judgment I understand to have justly ordained these things to be done against me. Therefore I do not ask you, but him, without whose will I believe not even a leaf falls from a tree, to incline toward my good will the heart that he holds in his hand, if this is my salvation.

## Fifth Letter: To Victor II, Roman Pontiff

#### Summary

He remonstrates with the Supreme Pontiff because he allowed a certain illustrious man named Henry, who had despised human affairs and fled to the service of Christ, to be unjustly harassed and oppressed by certain people. In Henry’s defense he also introduces Christ speaking in the gravest terms. He warns the pontiff to consider again and again lest, when Henry complains about him, he have no answer to give. Finally, he deflects any suspicion of arrogance from himself and shows, by Christ’s own example, that those placed in some high authority ought not to become angry if they are reminded of their duty by people inferior in rank.

To Lord Victor, prelate of the highest see, Peter the sinful monk offers due service in Christ.

The world wonders, most pious lord, why your clemency has not shown compassion for this wretched man for so long and why zeal for justice has not moved you to avenge the crime of so bloody a robbery. For as long as he served in the warfare of the earthly world, he possessed all his goods diligently [smoothly] and peacefully. But after he sought refuge beneath Christ’s wings, after he followed Peter’s example and, having abandoned everything, hastened to follow the footsteps of the Redeemer [Col. 0210A] (Matthew 19), a cruel robber immediately expelled him from his possessions and, as though he were lamenting under the protection of an invalid defender, stripped him of all his goods.

Thus it seems that it is no longer Henry who suffers the injury, but Christ. Christ, I say, suffers prejudice during the time of your episcopate: he who “does justice for all who suffer wrong” (Psalm 145) does not obtain justice for himself in the examination of your severity.

What if the Savior himself were to confront you with these words and pour out these reproachful complaints? “I,” he would say, “not to begin from the very beginning, raised you from the common herd of clerics to the priestly eminence and promoted you from the clientele of a bishopric to obtain the rights of episcopal office. I established you as the emperor’s father, so to speak, and inclined his heart toward favoring you above almost all mortals. I placed the keys of my entire universal Church in your hands and set you over her as my vicar—the Church I redeemed by the shedding of my own blood. And if these things are few, I also added monarchies; indeed, after removing the king from the scene, I granted you the rights of the entire vacant Roman Empire.”

“I, therefore, who bestowed such great and such remarkable things upon you, find neither law nor justice in your judgment. Disregarded and neglected by your tribunals, I depart. If, then, most pious lord, he who will judge the living and the dead were to attack you with these words, what excuse would your holiness offer in reply? What argument or defense would you find to clear yourself before him who cannot be deceived by argument?”

Let zeal for the execution of justice now inflame your most sacred heart; let the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline come forth to punish the crime that deserves punishment; and, setting aside the evasions of wicked men, restore Christ to his rightful claim in the person who has been despoiled. Let justice be shown to the wretched man with priestly compassion; let your censure proceed against the perverse with the severity of royal judgment, so that he who entrusted you with power over men may find in himself a defender of legal justice.

Spare my mouth, venerable Father, and do not disdain the words of a man humbly offering counsel to a man, since almighty God himself says to human beings: “Come and reason with me” (Isaiah 1).

## Sixth Letter: To Nicholas II, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0210D]

(This appears in volume III and is little work 17.)

## Seventh Letter: To the Same Nicholas II, Roman Pontiff

#### Summary

First, he congratulates Pope Nicholas, the Supreme Pontiff, because, while he guides the reins of the whole world, the Church of God enjoys great tranquility and happiness. Then, moved by mercy, he pleads for the people of Ancona, who had been removed from Catholic communion. He therefore asks the pontiff to deal more gently with them and, after taking very serious men into counsel, finally decide how he may rescue these unhappy people from the danger of eternal death. Finally, he asks pardon for his boldness, using the example of Christ, who, although he was God, did not refuse to be challenged by human beings.

To Lord Nicholas, most blessed prelate of the highest see, Peter the sinful monk offers the service of the most devoted obedience.

Because the celebrated fame of your prosperity has spread widely through our regions, our heart is suffused with great joy and delight. With all our inmost being we rejoice in the Lord, who is the author of these gifts, so that while our mind rejoices inwardly, our tongue also bursts into this song of divine praise: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

But concerning the people of Ancona, venerable lord, I grieve deeply each day over their perishing, and I tremble from the depths of my being at the confused and mingled danger of sinners and innocent people alike. For by the condition of their flesh their bodies die each day, while by your sentence Peter’s sword rages in the death of their souls.

We sleep, indeed, but the drawn sword of the apostolic see does not sleep; it strikes down so many thousands of people in one bloody slaughter—not in bodies destined at some time to die, but, alas, and grievous to say, in souls destined to live without end.

Indeed, I shall say boldly that, since my lord ascended to the summit of the apostolate, he has never done anything that ought to be so greatly feared by us, who ought to keep watch over him. They wished to submit to you, to surrender their city to you, and humbly to subject themselves and their possessions to you. [Col. 0211C] But because of their faults, not only was the door of your mercy not opened to them; when the sentence was issued, it also excluded them from the kingdom of God and from the lights of the Church as though they were rebels and contumacious in the opposite camp.

Far be it from my lord that, when the raised hand of some tyrant is soon restrained by fear after the slaughter of two or three men, the sword of him who is the teacher of all Christian piety should rage everywhere in the destruction of so many souls.

For when Abner, in the very midst of battle, said to Joab, “Must your sword rage forever unto destruction?” (2 Samuel 2), Joab immediately replied, “As the Lord lives, if you had spoken, the people would have withdrawn from pursuing their brother in the morning” (ibid.).

Far be it, I say, that while he wishes to please the eye of one man, so great a multitude of those for whom Christ’s blood was shed should perish. For you hold the place of him who, while still poor and insignificant, did not fear to say in a free voice to supreme princes and magistrates: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). And again: “If it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than to God, judge” (Acts 4).

Therefore, if it pleases my lord, summon Lord Hildebrand, a man of most holy and pure counsel, and also the reverend bishops Humbert and Boniface, who are, as it were, your keenest and most perceptive eyes. Share with them the mystery of your counsel, and together deliberate by what remedy the death and destruction of so many perishing souls may cease.

Let the sentence issued by the apostolic see therefore be moderated according to its customary practice, and let the discipline of ecclesiastical vigor temper itself, so that those whom hostile cruelty strives to scatter may be gathered into the bosom of priestly mercy.

Spare my mouth, most clement Father, and consider not the clamor of an impudent tongue but the secret of a devoted heart. Do not be displeased to be humbly admonished by your servant, since almighty God himself says to human beings: “Come and reason with me.”

## Eighth Letter: To the Same Nicholas II, Roman Pontiff, and to Hildebrand, Cardinal and Archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church

#### Summary

Having been stripped of not only the fruits and revenues of his episcopate but also all his furnishings and priestly vestments, he seizes this opportunity to write to Pope Nicholas and to the archdeacon Hildebrand, who at that time held almost the foremost place with the pontiff in favor and dignity, asking them to allow him to be free and exempt from the burden of the episcopate.

To the most blessed Pope Nicholas and to Hildebrand, venerable archdeacon, Peter the sinful monk offers service.

Blessed be almighty God, because, while everything that had been given to me as a benefice is taken away, and while even the priestly vestment itself is removed, clear signs are becoming evident to me that the episcopal dignity is soon to be completely taken from me.

For when the sons of Jacob resolved to destroy their brother Joseph, they first stripped him of his long, many-colored tunic (Genesis 37). The Lord also, when he ordered Aaron the priest to die, said to Moses (Numbers 20): “Let Aaron go to his people”; and shortly afterward: “When you have stripped your father of his garment,” he said, “you shall clothe Eleazar his son with it, and Aaron shall be gathered to his people and shall die there” (ibid.).

Clearly, the one whom he wished now to rest from priestly office he first stripped of the sacred garment, and, clothing his son in it, appointed him to minister in his father’s place. Thus, in the removal of the vestment, the loss of dignity becomes clear.

The same is also found in the *Tripartite History* (book 5, chapter 37): when famine had seized the province of Jerusalem, the crowd of needy people looked to Cyril, who then presided at Jerusalem, truly as to a bishop, for food. Since he lacked money with which to assist them, he sold the sacred vessels and hangings. In this way he provided aid to the people who were suffering from want.

For this reason the emperor Constantius was provoked to anger, especially because Acacius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, is known to have plotted against Cyril. For Acacius alleged that Cyril had sold the sacred vestment which the most renowned Emperor Constantine had given to Macarius, bishop of that city, for the honor of the Church of Jerusalem—woven with gold and silk, so that, clothed in it, he might perform the ministry of sacred baptism—and that a certain stage-dancer, Thymelicus, had then bought it. While this man, clothed in it, was dancing in his customary fashion, as Acacius testified, he immediately fell, was crushed, and, struck by divine vengeance, breathed his last. Acacius therefore brought this charge against Cyril and thus deposed him from episcopal dignity.

If, then, those great pontiffs, Aaron namely and Cyril, after losing their garments also consequently lost the priestly insignia of their dignities, what else is given to me, a small and unworthy man, to understand except that, while I am stripped of priestly ornaments, I am undoubtedly being deposed from priestly dignity?

Moreover, by lodging guests and confiscating property, you have taken away gifts; from the episcopate also you have consumed whatever income could be found. What therefore remains, except that a veteran soldier should cast away his belt together with his cloak, having lost the donative of his military pay? Let the episcopates, then, and likewise the monasteries, now pass into your uses; and let no one henceforth reproach me with the empty name of a benefaction, but let it become clearer than daylight to your [Col. 0213B] [Note: [Col. 0213D] Something seems to be missing here.] Let the kindness of you both know, then, that I return these things to you so irrevocably that, as long as life remains with me, I shall hold them no longer.

## LETTER IX. TO THE SAME NICHOLAS II, ROMAN PONTIFF

(This is found in volume III and is opusculum 19.)

## LETTER X. TO ALEXANDER II, ROMAN PONTIFF, AND HILDEBRAND, CARDINAL AND ARCHDEACON OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

(This is found in volume III and is opusculum 20.)

## 11. LETTER XI. TO THE SAME ALEXANDER II, ROMAN PONTIFF

**ARGUMENT.**—He carefully commends to the supreme pontiff the bishop of Orléans, whose Church, harassed by wicked men and shaken by many storms and whirlwinds of calamity, was being battered, so that, rescued and raised up by his help from the waves, she might at last rest in the harbor of tranquility and security.

To his lord ALEXANDER, prelate of the supreme see, PETER, a sinful monk, offers his service.

Let your blessedness know, venerable Father, that this bishop of the Church of Orléans came to me and, finding me lying sick in bed—for he hoped that I might have some influence with you—asked for the assistance of my intercession. Having finally rescued himself, not without great tribulation, from the many calamities and afflictions inflicted not only upon him but also upon his Church by depraved and perverse men, he judged it best, spurning the aid of the deceitful world, to seek only the remedy of the apostolic see, to fall at your holy feet, and, as to the safest harbor, to hasten beneath the shelter of the holy Roman Church from the many storms, reefs, and whirlwinds of a sea tossed by waves. He wished, of course, that she who, through the privilege of divine grace, comes to the aid of all in tribulation might also receive him with maternal affection and defend his Church from the invasion of violent and wicked men. Therefore I humbly beseech your holy clemency, and humbly ask also the fraternity of my hostile friend, the lord archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0214D] He means Hildebrand.], and of your other holy associates, that for love of me you deign to assist this brother who seeks my help, and strive to temper toward him the rigor of justice, insofar as this does not displease God.

That you may know what concerns me: for nearly seventy days I have scarcely been able to lie down or sit, much less stand, except with difficulty. What shall I say? I loathe wine because my stomach is nauseated; and I recoil also from various kinds of honeyed and spiced drink. But I will not enlarge upon these matters, because while I seek groans and compassion from the fraternal affection of my other companions, I have no doubt that I must draw laughter from the greatest of my friends, namely, the lord archdeacon.

[Col. 0214B] Concerning the aforesaid bishop, I ask you to decide in such a way that almighty God may rejoice in the judgment of your discernment, and that he, with the entrails of the apostolic see—so to speak, of maternal affection—poured out over him, may grow joyful. Since I do not presently have our seal, I have instructed my nephew Damian to provide the authentication of the seal.

## 12. LETTER XII. TO THE SAME

**ARGUMENT.**—He censures two wicked customs that had then become established in the Church and requests that they be abolished. First, he shows that it is a dangerous and, so to speak, perilous undertaking to append the penalty of anathema at the end of every decree. For, striking against this penalty as against a reef on the lightest of grounds, people would very often suffer shipwreck. He then vigorously rebukes the other custom—namely, that bishops could not be accused before the archbishop and primate by priests. In this way, he argues, impunity for crimes and a freer license to run riot in every kind of wickedness are granted.

To his lord ALEXANDER, pope, PETER, a sinful monk, offers his service.

You wrote that I should write; you commanded me often to send you, however unpolished, the little pages of my foolishness. Yet I would rather weep than write; indeed, I weep more grievously for this reason: that I cannot weep. Thus, plainly, I recently departed from the synod over which the authority of your holiness presided, crushed and dried up, so that my mind, burdened by so many affairs and hardened like flint, is neither softened by the rain of compunction nor raised, however little, above itself by the grace of inward contemplation. This, therefore, is given me as punishment, which is promised to be given to the saints by grace. “God,” he says, “will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints” (Revelation 21). And in the Psalm it is said: “He rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears” (Psalm 114). What, therefore, is granted to holy men as a reward is inflicted upon my merits as torment. For this reason I have settled this decision in my mind: henceforth, unless unavoidable necessity compels me, for as long as I live I shall keep myself entirely absent from Roman counsels.

Moreover, two practices have become frequent at the apostolic see which, if your holy prudence judges as we think it should, are altogether deserving of correction. One is that anathema is appended to almost every decretal page; the other is that a son of any Church, whether cleric or layman, is forbidden to lay before a greater Church the offenses of his own bishop. Your merciful kindness does not fail to understand how the first of these is a monstrous danger to human salvation, an infinitely gaping abyss for those who fall, and a destruction of souls. It is said: whoever does not do this or that—or certainly whoever regards as void, or violates in any respect, what has been established above—let him be anathema. Here one must note how slippery and precipitous an opportunity for sudden ruin is prepared, so that a person may fall into the abyss of eternal death before realizing that he has even stumbled slightly; and, as though into a snare laid beneath him, his foot is already caught while he imagines that he is still walking with free steps.

Whoever he may be, then, transgresses that decree of the apostolic constitution, perhaps by some slight and very small offense; and immediately, as though he were a heretic and held guilty of every crime, he is condemned by the sentence of anathema. Although justice dictates that one who commits a greater offense should be punished by one penalty and one who offends less by another, an equal and undifferentiated penalty—namely, anathema alone—is imposed upon those who sin gravely and those who sin lightly. Not according to the practice of tribunals or a forensic examination is a free man beaten or property confiscated, nor is the guilty party subjected to a monetary fine; rather, he is deprived of God, the author of all good things.

Thus one human being inflicts upon another a penalty which almighty God himself does not presume to impose for the transgression of his commandment. “Whoever loves,” he says, “father or mother more than me” did not immediately add, “let him be anathematized or accursed,” but only said: “He is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10). And in the Law (Exodus 21), “eye for eye, tooth for tooth, blow for blow, burning for burning” is required; nor is the guilty person immediately cast out of the synagogue or condemned by a curse. For, contrary to the Stoics, not all sins are equal and therefore to be punished by an undifferentiated penalty; rather, the measure of vengeance must always be proportioned to the degree of guilt (Cicero, *Paradoxa* 3).

Furthermore, neither the blessed Pope Gregory nor the other Fathers who flourished at different times in the government of the apostolic see are found to have observed this custom in their decrees; and anathema is scarcely ever appended to their enactments, except when the text ends with a clause concerning the Catholic faith. Therefore, if it pleases your holy prudence, let it order that this custom henceforth be removed from the decretal pages, and let it establish in cases of transgression either a monetary penalty or the assessment of some other punishment, lest what has been provided for the protection of some should result in the destruction of souls for others.

That other provision also, which says, “It is not permitted for a son of any Church to bring before a greater Church the guilt of his own bishop or matters requiring correction,” is shown to be exceedingly absurd and altogether contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. For to whom should what a bishop does wrong be reported more appropriately than to one who performs the office of a teacher? He therefore stands above the other brothers so that, by the privilege of his own see, he alone may correct the errors of priests, though what is not permitted to others is permitted to him.

What is this swelling of arrogance? What is this pride of exaltation? What, finally, is such great arrogance that a bishop may live according to his own will, by right or wrong, and disdain to hear from his subjects what he has insolently done? Especially since they have not gone to the tribunals of secular governors or knocked at the courts of forensic judges, but rather approach the Church and lay before priests matters concerning their priest that are subject to judgment, so that what might become a laughingstock among secular officials may be corrected gravely and honorably through priestly office. [Col. 0216B] It is certainly appropriate that the one who is accused should either show himself innocent by reasoned explanation or humbly confess himself a sinner.

Nor should one make use of such arguments [the text reads “live by”]: that he ought not to be accused by those subject to him, lest he appear to cover his excesses and evade judgment while attempting to turn against another the injury of the question raised against him.

For who does not know that Peter, prince of the apostles, received the power of the kingdom of heaven? He obtained the power of binding or loosing whatever he wished in heaven and on earth. He walked upon the sea with his feet. By the mere shadow of his body he raised up the sick. He struck dead liars with the dart of his bare word. By prayer he raised the dead (Matthew 14, 16; Acts 5:9).

When this man, therefore, a person of such exalted merit, had entered the house of Cornelius—a gentile—at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, a question was raised against him by the faithful who were of the circumcision, because he had entered among foreigners, dared to eat with them, and had even received them in baptism (Acts 10–11). This man, I say, supported by the incomparable power of so many heavenly gifts and distinguished by the display of so many miracles, did not resist the complaint of his subjects by appealing to his authority; rather, he humbly satisfied them by giving an account, and, as a truthful narrator, explained the matter in order: how he had seen a certain vessel, like a linen sheet, lowered from heaven, containing four-footed animals of the earth, reptiles, and birds; and how he had heard a voice: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”

He also explained how three men had come and summoned him to Cornelius; and finally, how the Holy Spirit had commanded him to go with them, and how that same Holy Spirit, who had been accustomed to descend upon those already baptized in Judea, had come upon gentiles even before baptism.

If, then, when he was blamed by the disciples, he had wished to invoke the authority he had received in the holy Church, he could have answered that the sheep entrusted to him ought not to dare reproach their shepherd. But if, in the complaint of the faithful, he had thrown up the title of his power, he would certainly not have been a teacher of gentleness. He therefore did not restrain them by the authority of his privilege; rather, he appeased them by humble satisfaction. And, as though he alone were not sufficient to establish the truth, he brought forward witnesses as well: “These six brothers,” he said, “came with me.”

Let a bishop, therefore, when questioned about his actions, learn to give an account humbly, not to grow proud of the eminence of his primacy; and let him not consider it an injury when he is corrected by an inferior, but rather regard that person as an adviser or physician of his wound.

For did the prophet Nathan incur the anger of the king when he rebuked David with such a stern denunciation? Did David set against him the height of royal excellence and repel, as an insult inflicted by his subject, what had been said? Rather, as soon as he recognized himself as sick, he willingly accepted the remedy, exposed his wound, and did not shrink from the instrument of the incision.

See the humble sick man: “I have sinned,” he said, “against the Lord.” Hear also the swift remedy: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Samuel 12). By contrast, King Ahab, who scorned to listen to the prophet rebuking him, did not escape the sword of vengeance that the prophet threatened: “Because you have let a man worthy of death go from your hand, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people” (1 Kings 20).

David, therefore, calmly hearing his guilt, escaped the sentence of death that he deserved; but Ahab, impatient of correction, found no pardon for the impious clemency he had shown to an unworthy king.

Did not those women, the hostesses of the Savior, quarrel with each other when one complained against the other because she was forcing her to serve alone? (Luke 10.) Mary could have said, in the manner of our pontiffs: “You have accused me and condemned me for sluggishness and negligence.”

Not every complaint should immediately be called an accusation. A complaint arising from compassion is one thing; an accusation arising from hostility and hatred is another. The former is made so that an offense may be corrected; the latter so that the offender may be condemned.

Paul plainly rebukes Peter to his face and judges him blameworthy before everyone (Galatians 2). Peter did not take this as an injury of accusation, but accepted it kindly and patiently, clearly recognizing that it proceeded not from ill will but from charity.

But now it is said: “I am a bishop; I am the shepherd of the Church. I ought not to be exposed to the annoyances of accusations by the sheep entrusted to me; indeed, in a matter of faith I deserve to be borne with calmly even in bad morals.”

But tell me, whoever you are, have you not read what is written in the Gospel? “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. If he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. If he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church” (Matthew 18).

If, then, the case of any brother is to be referred to the Church, how can the case of priests not be referred as well? Furthermore, if a priest who sins in the Church disdains to be examined in the Church, who will henceforth tolerate his being restrained by the laws of the Church?

And if, as you claim, the sons of your Church are not permitted to murmur against you, are witnesses then to be brought from elsewhere—people who, because they do not live with you at home, are ignorant of you and your actions?

Blessed Job says: “If I have disdained to enter into judgment with my servant” (Job 31); and you say: “Far be it from me to submit to examination with my cleric.”

Almighty God cries out through Isaiah: “Judge the orphan, defend the widow, and come, let us argue together” (Isaiah 1). If the one who judges all things does not disdain to be challenged by servants, do you, though yourself a servant, refuse to come to judgment with your fellow servant? And though you are earth and ashes, a worm and dust, do you disdain to humble yourself according to the image of your Creator?

Especially since Scripture says: “They have appointed you a ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Sirach 32).

Who does not know that the Israelite people brought a charge against Samuel and unjustly removed him from his leadership? Though he could rightly have rebuked them, he voluntarily offered himself for accusation without anyone accusing him, and asked whether he had violently oppressed any of them: “Behold, I am present,” he said; “speak against me before the Lord and his anointed: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey, whether I have calumniated anyone, whether I have oppressed anyone, whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand. I will reject it today and restore it to you” (1 Samuel 12).

When men so incomparable, eminent, and exalted do not disdain to give an account of their actions to their subjects, what arrogance is this, what pride of such great presumption, that a priest of the present time, swollen with self-importance, should set up the title of his prelacy and refuse to answer on equal terms before judgment to the sons of his Church who assert that they have been burdened?

Let the rule of this pernicious custom therefore be excluded from ecclesiastical discipline; let this crafty cunning of evasion be removed, so that the person who uses such perverse arguments of audacious pride may not gain immunity for the sin committed.

Let the way be open, then, to just complaints; let a Church that sees itself oppressed by its own pontiff be permitted to complain before the primate, lest one who refuses, through arrogant pride, to place himself on an equal footing with his brothers grow proud of the singularity of his exalted prerogative.

And let the person who shakes the censor’s rod over others also feel upon himself the discipline of ecclesiastical severity. Let the one whose voice does not sound human but thunders over others like a terrifying lightning bolt learn, at some point recognizing himself as human, to form human words through humility. Thus, while every arrogant prelate is brought down from the swelling of exaltation and assistance is given to subjects through the authority of the superior Church, with quarrels everywhere quieted and fear of synodal examination laid to rest, all the members of the Church may be united together in peace.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE SAME

**ARGUMENT.**—John and Tudetchinus—one a Venetian, the other barbarian by nationality—both exercising the priestly office under Duke Godfrey, had once dared, in the presence of Blessed Peter Damian, obstinately to assert that those who purchased episcopates from kings or princes did not fall into the crime of simoniacal heresy, since, they claimed, through that purchase they acquired only possession of the Church’s goods and estates, while through the laying on of hands performed by priests they acquired the full right of the episcopate.

After brilliantly refuting this opinion of theirs, no less impious than foolish and ridiculous, he asks Alexander, the supreme pontiff, to strive, before it spreads more widely in human minds, to suppress and eradicate it by the authority of his sacred power. He also earnestly commends to him that he permit no one to be brought to the episcopate by money or by service at court, or to remain in it once brought there by such means.

To his lord ALEXANDER, prelate of the supreme see, PETER, a sinful monk, offers his service.

Just as the loss of any household property is reported to the head of the household, so it is fitting that the injury of a suffering Church be reported to the supreme pontiff. Just as the former, insofar as his strength permits, confronts the evils threatening his house, so likewise the latter should restore the foundation of wavering faith, or even the order of religion that had begun to be thrown into confusion.

Alas, a new heresy has arisen in our time. Unless the vigor of your authority confronts it as quickly as possible, there is reason to fear that it will spread like a deadly cancer to the destruction of the Christian religion and the peril of souls.

Some clerics, plainly counterfeiting a religious life by the appearance of their outward habit, but inwardly so utterly cold toward God and inflamed by the torches of ecclesiastical ambition, obstinately proclaim this doctrine: that it does not belong to simoniacal heresy if someone acquires an episcopate from a king or any worldly prince through a purchase, provided only that he receives the consecration free of charge.

Thus, when we recently found ourselves in conversation with the most excellent Duke Godfrey, two of his chaplains—one a barbarian, named by a barbarian name, Tudetchinus; the other a Venetian by nationality, called John—like Hymenaeus and Philetus in Paul’s preaching (2 Timothy 2), or certainly like Jannes and Jambres in the time of Moses (Exodus 7; 2 Timothy 3), resisting the truth, did not cease to spread this doctrine. They acknowledged it as the Catholic and canonical judgment: namely, that no one should rightly be called a simoniac unless he could be proved to have purchased an episcopate without the laying on of hands.

They said that when this occurs, it is not the Church that is sold, but its property; not the priesthood that is bought, but possession of estates. Under this payment of money, they claimed, only wealth is redeemed, not the sacrament of honor or of the Church. What makes people rich is for sale, they said; what makes them priests they receive free of charge.

O new kind of schismatics, and sacrilegious mouth deserving condemnation by the judgment of eternal silence! In one human person they establish two persons: one, a priest sold under the burden of sin; the other, a rich man purchased at a price. Let the former, like another Sardanapalus, belch amid the pleasures of banqueters; let the latter preside, like an apostle, over the government of souls.

By this reasoning, then, someone who purchases a field must be said to have acquired only the dust of the earth, not the produce of its crops. A slave-dealer who sells a human being must likewise be judged to have sold not a soul but flesh.

Indeed, since we read that the body is fully formed, with the members distinctly arranged, on the forty-sixth day after the beginning of conception, and is then divinely animated—and since it is not the soul but only the flesh that proceeds from the father’s seed—the father must therefore be said to have begotten only flesh, not offspring, which consists of soul and body.

Since this is utterly absurd, and that man is rightly called the father from whose thigh only flesh, not the soul, has emerged, so without doubt the other must be called a merchant of the Church who ascends to the summit of honor through the earthly goods he has redeemed and, through the commerce of bodily profit, nevertheless becomes a buyer of the sacrament.

Say, then, whoever you are who boast that you are only the purchaser of earthly property, through which you nevertheless aspire to climb to the dignity of episcopal excellence; and while you say that you received from the prince only the earthly advantages of the Church, you claim to have been appointed in some fashion as a steward, not to exercise the priestly office.

Tell me, I say, what shape did this investiture have, and what appearance did it truly possess, when that prince placed it in your hands? If it was a shoot or a simple staff, rightly rejoice and applaud yourself, because, as you claim, you were initiated not into the office of a priest but into the stewardship of an administrator; and therefore it is no longer necessary for you to be subject to the bishop who ought to be placed over you.

But if that secular prince, after receiving or being promised money, handed you a pastoral staff, with what face will you be able to excuse the purchase of episcopal office? Indeed, unless by this investiture he first impressed upon you the title of the priesthood you were to receive, the man who was to ordain you would in no way have handed you the sacrament of the priesthood through the laying on of hands.

Through what you accepted for sale you are subsequently promoted to the priesthood. Therefore, although that laying on of hands was not itself sold but given freely, nevertheless, as far as you are concerned, it is in no way free from the filth of venality. If venality is known to the one receiving it, it contaminates the one consecrating; a free consecration cannot cleanse the buyer. The obscenity of an impure and filthy transaction stains what is clean; a free laying on of hands cannot purify what has been polluted.

Perhaps I am accused of lying if I do not affirm what I say by the testimony of sacred Scripture. Through the prophet Haggai it is said:

“Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man carries sanctified flesh in the fold of his garment and touches with its edge bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, will it be sanctified? The priests answered, ‘No.’ And Haggai said: If one who is polluted in soul touches any of these things, will it be defiled? The priests answered, ‘It will be defiled.’ And Haggai answered and said: ‘So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord; and so is every work of their hands, and everything they have offered there: it will be defiled’” (Haggai 2).

In these prophetic—indeed divine—words it is therefore clearly shown that this buyer, who is polluted in soul, pollutes the dignity of the order he has received. Although the dignity has been received freely through the laying on of hands, it nevertheless does not cleanse the buyer.

I return again to the investiture, and I ask you, who boast that you purchased not the Church but the estates of the Church: when that man handed the staff to you, did he say, “Receive the lands and wealth of that Church,” or rather, as is certain, “Receive the Church”?

If you received the Church’s goods without the Church, you are a schismatic and sacrilegious person, separating the goods of the Church from the Church and violently turning what is another’s into rights for your own use.

But if you received the Church—which you cannot deny at all—you have undoubtedly become a simoniac; and venality made you a heretic before the laying on of hands made you consecrated. You plainly bought the consecration at the moment when you accepted for sale that for which you were to be promoted to consecration.

For the one thing hangs upon the other, so that the person who receives the earthly goods of the Church aspires to the grace of consecration, while the person who is perfected through consecration should preserve the Church’s goods for distribution to the needy and for other works of piety.

In this way, then, although no mention of the Church’s property is made in the laying on of hands itself, the person being consecrated is nevertheless made the steward of the Church’s goods; and when he receives the Church, even though nothing is then said about consecration, he is nevertheless chosen for the purpose of being consecrated.

From the very beginning of the Church’s birth, this salutary custom of the faithful began: each person sold his possessions and placed the money at the feet of the apostles and apostolic men, so that they might provide assistance for the needs of the poor (Acts 4).

Later, however, the holy Fathers who succeeded them in the order of sacred governance judged that those who were converted to the Lord should not sell their estates, but should hand them over to the holy Churches, not merely for temporary benefit but by perpetual right, so that they might serve the needs of the needy.

And certainly through Moses the Law commands: “Everything,” he says, “that is consecrated to the Lord, whether a human being or a field, shall not be sold or redeemed. Whatever has once been consecrated shall be holy of holies to the Lord” (Leviticus 27).

Here it is most clearly forbidden that things consecrated to the Lord should either be sold or redeemed; rather, they are commanded to remain continually holy of holies.

Why, then, do you boast that you redeemed the holy of holies for a price, and that you received for sale what belongs to God, contrary to the law of God, though it is to be received freely and given freely? As though it were not a sin because such a transaction takes place without consecration?

Perhaps you do not fear it for this reason: that the old Law indeed prohibits the offense but does not impose a penalty. Hear, then, what Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church, writes about this in a decretal letter:

“No one,” he says, “should be permitted to be ignorant that everything consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a human being, an animal, a field, or anything else that has once been consecrated, shall be holy of holies to the Lord and belongs by right to the priests.”

For this reason, because everyone who takes away, lays waste, invades, or seizes what belongs to the Lord and to the Church to which it pertains will be without excuse, he is to be judged a sacrilegious person until he makes amends and satisfies the Church; and if he refuses to make amends, let him be excommunicated.

Pope Anacletus, much earlier, adds among many other statements:

“For whoever takes away the Church’s possessions commits sacrilege and must be regarded as sacrilegious.”

Pope Lucius likewise says in his decree:

“We anathematize and expel from the thresholds of the holy Church, by apostolic authority, those who seize ecclesiastical things and property, and we condemn them and judge them to be sacrilegious.”

We could gather many other examples from the Catholic Fathers, were it not clear that this would in no way suit the brevity of an epistolary work.

By these statements of the holy pontiffs and by others like them you are plainly convicted: either you received the goods of the Church without the Church, and therefore, as a plunderer and sacrilegious person, you ought to be anathematized and expelled from the thresholds of the Church; or—and this is clear and cannot be denied—you redeemed the Church together with the Church’s goods for a price, and therefore it is fitting that you be condemned as truly a simoniac and heretic by the judgment of canonical rigor.

The canonical judgment is certainly that which says:

“If any bishop, or presbyter, or abbot has obtained this dignity through money, let him and his ordainer be deposed, let him be cut off in every way from holy communion, and let him be anathema, like Simon Magus by Peter” (Acts 8).

Here one must note that it does not say, “If anyone has obtained this consecration or laying on of hands,” but rather: “If anyone,” it says, “has obtained this dignity through money.”

It is also asserted as canonical that the following was promulgated by the holy Fathers in a council:

“Bishops, kings, and all higher powers, as well as all supporters, electors, consenters, and ordainers of anyone in an ecclesiastical rank, must beware, must take the greatest precautions, and must forbid by the power of Christ’s blood that anyone obtain a place of governance through simoniacal heresy, by any arrangement, cunning, promise, benefit, or gift, either personally or through an intermediary.”

Here too one must note that, after mentioning bishops, the text immediately adds kings and all higher powers, so that this heresy is not to be avoided only by bishops who lay hands upon those to be consecrated, but also by secular princes who, although unjustly, nevertheless in some fashion hand Churches over to future rulers.

For when something is received through venality, what necessarily follows from it is undoubtedly purchased as well. A pastoral Church is entrusted to someone for this purpose: that he may be confirmed by consecration in order to obtain its governance. And the exchange involving money certainly aims at this, which is what the person to be promoted aspires to obtain.

This is plainly why not only those who are placed over greater Churches, but also those who pestilentially acquire rural congregations or canonical prebends through the intervention of money, do not escape the snares of simoniacal heresy. Through what they obtain by sale they reach the orders of the sacred ranks; and they are already designated for those orders when they receive the means by which they reach the advancement of the sacred ranks. A person is initiated into the rank of a dignity when he is appointed to obtain the dignity of that rank.

Let this brief statement against those who dogmatize that acquiring a Church for sale without the laying on of hands is not simoniacal suffice. If they expressed this simply, as it seemed to them, they would rightly be called foolish or dull-witted. But since some of them assert it boldly and obstinately strive to defend it with various sophistries and argumentative tricks, they not undeservedly incur—as we say reluctantly—the name of heretics.

It is not error that makes a heretic, but obstinate persistence. Nor are all who hold an erroneous opinion to be called heretics, but only those who pertinaciously and boldly preach falsehood.

Therefore, venerable Father, meet these preachers of Satan and apostles of Antichrist, girded with the sword of heavenly eloquence; and, like another Joshua fighting the Amalekites who attacked Israel (Exodus 17), strike them down with the drawn blade of canonical rigor.

Let the aconite of hellish bitterness be removed as quickly as possible, lest—God forbid—the deadly poison flow into the throats of the little ones. Moreover, let an antidote of such an aromatic medicine be offered by your hands to all who are sick, an antidote that will remove the filth of poisoned error and restore the purity of a sound and sincere faith.

At the end of this letter I suggest one matter to the sacred ears of your clemency: insofar as your power permits, never allow anyone either to become or to remain a bishop who is known to have risen to the summit of honor through payment—or, what is more damnable, through service at court.

Far be it that one who has courted a secular prince through ambition for preeminence should obtain the spiritual dignity of an ecclesiastical office.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE SAME

**ARGUMENT.**—Having suffered some injury from Alexander, the supreme pontiff, and with the Church of Gubbio, over which Alexander presided, greatly disturbed, he protests against him more mildly than bitterly, reproaching him with his own merits and the labors he had endured for the apostolic see, for which he complains that an inadequate reward had been returned. He therefore asks that some satisfaction be made to him, lest he be compelled to disclose publicly to others his indignation and just grief, which he had hitherto concealed. He also pleads for the bishop of Ravenna, that he may be released from the bonds of anathema, lest the whole city be endangered because of the fault of one person. He writes that he had entrusted the bearer of these letters with several further messages for him.

To the lord Alexander, bishop of the highest see, Peter, sinful monk, offers his service.

[Col. 0224A] That the Church of Gubbio, which was formerly entrusted to me by your predecessors, is now, alas, utterly confused and cast down like a threshing floor trampled underfoot, I attribute to my sins, not—God forbid—to any fault of your smallness [variant: fatherhood]. The multitude of my crimes demands that even the man for whom I undertook, standing firm and without weakness, a struggle against the whole world, and against whom I set myself as a hard and unconquerable combatant with the swords and arrows of almost the entire human race, should inflict a wound upon my breast with his own hands.

Is this the reward you have given me, venerable Father, for having so often stood forth as the advocate of your cause in the councils of holy pontiffs? For having, in the concerns and business of your legation, frequently declaimed before assemblies of secular persons and laymen [Col. 0224B], as though I were some legal advocate? Are these, I ask, the gifts returned to me for having violently attacked your enemies and destroyed them most bitterly in speech and writing; for having exalted you through the several sections of my writings, and, as far as lay within me, extended your memory and the praises of your excellence [addition: the proclamations of praise] even among posterity?

Let the judgment of your examination weigh what I have done and what I have endured, so that I may not be compelled to overflow in a complaint as fitting as it is grievous—something which, suppressing it in silence until now, I can scarcely conceal any longer. For as yet Rome has not learned of this, either from me on my return or through my writings; nor has this matter, which would wound the reputation of your holiness, become known to others through me. Let the one who has caused the injury therefore do penance as is fitting, so that the one who has been injured may not be compelled [Col. 0224C] to enlarge upon a fitting complaint.

May the sweetness of oil soften the sharpness of biting vinegar, and may the gentle and soothing liquid of benefits pour forth mildness upon bruises swollen from the harshest blows; otherwise it will now be necessary for one who has endured the blows of so many strokes to say also—[Note: [Col. 0223D] Aposiopesis.] … But now I restrain my freedom, repressing the boldness of my tongue; I place a finger upon my lips, and I, who have suffered misery, in turn beg for mercy.

Moreover, I implore the clemency of your holiness on behalf of the most unhappy bishop of Ravenna, and I humbly beseech you to deign to release him, as you once decreed. For it is unworthy that, because of the offense of a single insignificant man, so immeasurable a multitude of people should perish, and that the fault of one pitiable person should overthrow so great a labor of Christ, for which he shed his precious blood, and so many innocent souls [Col. 0224D].

We do not wish to burden your holy eyes with a longer letter, but entrust everything that must be said to the experience of the bearer. Let your holy clemency therefore attend carefully to this man as though I were speaking, and grant these two petitions of ours, which we have touched upon here briefly and swiftly: so that we may not regret having sent messengers and vehicles across so many stretches of land, and so that our mind, which had begun—let me not say to grow lukewarm toward you, but rather to grow cold [Col. 0225A]—may grow warm again with longing for your former affection.

## LETTER XV. TO THE SAME

### Argument

He replies to the supreme pontiff, who had asked him by letter not to become so absorbed in the practice of contemplation that he would forget to write to him. He explains, however, that he is so obstructed by profane cares and affairs that he has no time for contemplation; moreover, that he cannot devote himself to divine matters with a tranquil and secure mind in places where everything is threatened by brigandage, robbery, and plunder. On this occasion he digresses into enumerating the crimes and outrages continually committed by the people of that age. Those were indeed calamitous times, when everything was permitted to weapons and audacity, while the laws had little or no authority. Blessed Peter Damian records these things so that the pontiff might attempt, as time and place required, to remove and restrain them. Amid these evils, he says that he was filled with no ordinary pleasure when he was informed that the administration of the county of Ostia had been taken away from him and entrusted to another. He also asks that the burden of the episcopate be removed from him. Finally, he appends a few verses that may serve the pontiff as an oracle.

To the lord Alexander, bishop of the highest see, Peter, sinful monk, offers his service.

I joyfully seized the letters of your holiness, brought by a rather disorderly priest; I kissed them, unfolded them, and eagerly read them through. But although the weight of your authority is such that it is enough for anyone even to receive a brief note of your decree in a few lines, there were in that letter so many flowers of eloquence [Col. 0225C], so many sweetnesses—not, I should say, of a master’s, but rather of a father’s affection—that what was sent to a poor little man would have sufficed for royal dignity.

Nevertheless, I found two things inserted there which, I confess, forced me to blush. For you said—if not in these exact words—that, because of the practice of contemplation to which I devote myself vigilantly, I ought not altogether to omit visiting you from time to time through written compositions. As far as concerns you, venerable Father, who agreed with me wholeheartedly about laying aside the burden of the episcopate, I do indeed enjoy leisure for contemplating and composing; but I cannot draw breath under the oppressive arrival of visitors and the onrush of legal affairs.

Furthermore, when I shut myself within the boundaries of my cell, I remain as though in the shelter of a harbor or at an anchorage by the shore. But what does it profit me? For when I desire there to enjoy the tranquility of a secure and resting leisure, behold, the blasts of the raging world shake me; the waves of surging lawsuits swell more fiercely; I am dashed against the storms of inflicted wrongs, and I am troubled by the violent diminution of estates or of any revenues whatever, saying with the prophet: “We hoped for peace, and there is no good; for the time of healing, and behold, disturbance” (Jer. VIII).

Meanwhile, there are also those who demand counsel concerning the salvation of their souls; and, what is harder still, they strive to extort pontifical judgment from one who is not a pontiff. Thus I, who flee the episcopate, do not escape being a bishop, and I am wearied beneath a priestly burden although I have been dethroned from the dignity of the priestly seat.

Surrounded by such narrow straits [Col. 0226A], I strive, and soon collapse; I attempt, but immediately fail; I do not penetrate the summit of contemplation, nor do I break forth into tears of compunction. For a mind darkened by earthly affairs strives in vain to raise itself to the height of contemplation, while it is weighed down by the merit of secular actions, as though by heaps of stones and rubble.

Just as the leather of a shoe, after passing through muddy streams of mire, does not admit grease, so the human mind, unless it has been stripped of the moisture of worldly care, does not receive the grace of heavenly richness. Dry leather absorbs grease; when moistened, it repels it. So long as the human heart swells with the dampness of worldly cares, it does not admit the nourishment of inward grace.

Hence we read that the law was given on Mount Horeb (Exod. XX), a name which is interpreted as “dryness.” That mind, finally, which through the love of the spirit is lifted from earthly things to what is on high (Ps. XVIII), is a mountain on which the law of the Lord, irreproachable and undoubtedly charity, is divinely proclaimed. And this mountain is truly Horeb, which is called “dryness,” for there the moisture of every vice is boiled away, and, under the rays of the sun of justice, all the rheum of lust and carnal allurements is dried up.

This is why Hiram, at Solomon’s command, made the vessels of the Temple from clayey earth, which eagerly absorbs water (III Kings VII). Among these vessels is also that one which longs to be filled by heavenly rain, when it says: “My soul is before you like land without water” (Ps. CXLII); and therefore, burning with thirst, it cries: “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI.)

Of these vessels the Third Book of Kings says: “For in the plain country of the Jordan the king cast them, in clayey earth, between Succoth and Zarthan” (III Kings VII). Succoth is translated “tents”; Zarthan, however, is interpreted as “their tribulation,” or “those who demolish,” or “those who confine.”

What, then, do we understand by Succoth, which we have said is interpreted “tents,” except holy men who say: “We have here no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come”? (Hebr. XIII.) Hence Peter also says: “I am certain that the laying aside of my tent is soon to come” (II Pet. I).

What, then, is designated by Zarthan, which is called “their tribulation,” except the persecution of the wicked who trouble us? They are indeed both demolishers and those who confine, because while they attempt to demolish and destroy the structure of our faith or good work, they hem us in with harsh calamities of injuries and pressures.

The vessels of the Temple, therefore—that is, all the elect—are cast in the plain country of the Jordan, that is, in the humility of baptism, between Succoth and Zarthan, that is, between the righteous and the perverse. Thus the example of the good may be set before the wicked for imitation as a model of upright conduct, and the persecution of the wicked may contribute to the increase of the good’s merits. “The furnace tests the potter’s vessel, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Eccli. XXVII).

The vessels of the Temple are therefore cast in dry earth, because the human mind is not fit to receive the gift of heavenly grace unless it has first been dried of all moisture of carnal allurements [Col. 0227A]. A dry string produces a clear harmonious sound; a damp one gives a dull sound. A drum also sounds muffled if any liquid moistens it. So the human mind must be dry of carnal pleasure, so that its prayer may be sharp in the ears of almighty God.

Indeed, just as the eye, when it exposes itself to the rays of the sun, strives in vain to see, and attempts to open its hollow sockets and empty eyelids, yet cannot at all look upon the brilliance with which it is flooded, so one who has lost the vision of the heart through the conduct of secular life raises himself vainly to behold the light of contemplation.

For if some unknown person bursts into the king’s chamber and stands before him as though he were a familiar, he does not enjoy the king’s conversation, because he is not dear to him through the favor of prior acquaintance. So we, unhappy and wretched—as I speak of people like myself—often remain alone in the seclusion of a narrow cell; we stand trembling before the gaze of divine majesty alone; yet, because sins stand in the way, we are not found worthy either of the spark of inward brightness or of the grace of compunction.

Thus we seem to stand before the presence of the king, but because we are not known to him through the uprightness of our lives, we do not taste the sweetness of inward conversation. But, O honey-flowing sweetness, when the Lord delights in the servant and the servant delights in the Lord! Hence the Psalmist says: “May my praise be sweet to him; but I will delight in the Lord” (Ps. CIII).

For me, wretched man, the desire is indeed present, but I do not find the ability to accomplish it (Rom. VII). For I do not find what is good in my flesh. I desire these things, I sigh for them with my whole heart, but impeded by my merits I do not rise to attain them. I am hindered both by the guilt of a blameworthy life and by outward affairs, which do not permit me to behold the splendor of the inner light.

This same earthly disturbance, which overwhelms the mind’s vision and prevents it from contemplating, likewise takes away my ability to write. To this is added the fact that, although I may perhaps be able to dictate something, there is no copyist to transcribe it. But why should I complain of the negligence caused by the lack of transcription, when no one has time not only to copy what I write, but even to run through it in a quick reading?

Indeed, the leaders of the churches, upon whom the chief care of this matter ought to have rested [Col. 0227D], are daily whirled about by such an impulse of worldly turbulence that a clerical shaving indeed separates them from secular persons, but their conduct does not distinguish them. They do not meditate on the words of the sacred Scriptures, but on legal devices and forensic litigation.

The tribunals of judges and royal halls are not enough for the multitude of priests, while they vomit forth crowds of clerics and monks and complain of the narrowness of their own courts. The cloisters are empty, the Gospel is shut up, and forensic laws stream from the mouths of the ecclesiastical order.

Would that we were content merely with a lawsuit under the authority of a legal decree. Rather, we seize weapons—weapons!—we hurl weapons bristling with missiles against one another, and fight not with words but with iron, contrary to the rule of our order. To such men the Apostle says: “The word of God is the sword of the Spirit” [Col. 0228A] (Eph. VI).

And indeed so monstrous a calamity of oppression weighs upon the churches that they seem to be besieged, as though surrounded by the battle lines of a Babylonian army, together with Jerusalem and its citizens.

For any secular persons scrape together ecclesiastical rights, withdraw stipends, invade possessions, and thus boast of carrying away the provisions of the poor as though they were spoils from enemies. Secular people themselves likewise plunder among one another the property belonging to each; they trip over one another as each steps over another’s rights, and, confined together in the common world, since they cannot be alone, they collide through mutual assault.

Soon they attack and burn the thatched shelters of peasants, and the gall of the most savage resentment—which they cannot vomit upon their own enemies—they are not ashamed to pour out upon defenseless peasants [Col. 0228B]. Then literally comes to pass what is sung through the Prophet: “When the wicked man exalts himself, the poor man is set on fire” (Ps. IX).

In this respect, the venom of a serpent is more noble than human cruelty. A serpent flees from a naked man; it attacks with bites one whom it sees clothed. Every strong and well-born warrior avoids the unarmed and attacks one who brandishes weapons against him. A hawk, too, wherever it nests, does not deign to practice plunder within a wide surrounding circuit, so that it may nobly pass over what is easy and readily available and seek what is distant, where the labor of victory is greater.

These men, however, take up weapons against the unarmed; while enemies flee, the innocent are beaten. Moreover, when one has first inflicted an injury, another immediately rises against him; and instead of returning an eye for an eye, according to the law (Exod. [Col. 0228C] XXI), he returns the injury with interest.

The retaliation decreed by the law of Tully is unknown in our times, and the discipline of vengeance, once observed under pagan rule, is now ignored, while the Gospel thunders forth forgiveness with terrifying force. Therefore, instead of the rod they return a bull-hide whip, instead of the scourge a club, instead of a word iron, instead of a staff a sword.

They are ashamed of not exceeding the measure of the injury; they disdain the fairness of the danger inflicted. They strive to appear victorious and terrifying; they covet the titles of triumphal glory. Thus, while one person grows angry, another is provoked to madness; rage generates rage, and fury inflames fury.

This may also be recognized from the following experiment: if a rabid dog happens to bite a person, its rabies is immediately transferred with such force into the human entrails that soon puppies are generated in the very receptacle of the urine [Col. 0228D]. This is proved by the clear evidence that, if the person seized by the bite of a dog drinks cantalenas—this is a kind of fly—ground up in water, he soon gives birth, together with his urine and amid groans of great pain, to puppies.

Certainly it is a remarkable matter, worthy of attention: how offspring can be generated from the dry bone of teeth, in which there is no moisture of seed; and how what nature could not easily accomplish through the genital organ, it forms through the passage of the teeth, producing a similar kind of thing in a different species. Perhaps it is not without a mystery that, through this animal called a cantalena, the poison conceived from canine rabies is expelled.

For an “incantator,” that is, a preacher, is so called in divine discourse. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Like the deaf asp that stops its ears, which does not hear the voice of charmers, or the spells that are chanted by the wise” (Ps. LVII). And concerning a preacher inwardly wounded it is elsewhere written: “Who will heal the charmer wounded by the serpent?” (Eccli. XII.) And in Proverbs: “As vinegar to soda, so is one who sings songs to a perverse heart” (Prov. XXV).

Therefore, just as the poison of rabid fury is expelled by cantalenas, so through the exhortation of a holy preacher the anger of resentment that has been conceived is calmed.

To return, then, to what the discourse began. With the world inflamed by these and similar furies, and its limbs everywhere torn apart by mutual conflict, it shakes us also, as well as those to whom a bill of repudiation has been given [Col. 0229B], and dulls the mind’s acuity for composing or for the inward vision of contemplation. Add that, even if there should perhaps be someone to write, as we have already said, there is entirely no one to copy; and finally there is no one even to run through the text in a quick reading.

Indeed, when a storm rises with raging winds, and the shifting whirlwind of storms lifts the waves into heaps, the sea boils more mildly in the very depth of its waters; but near the shore it rises so much more fiercely that it breaks even ships if they come alongside. Hence, at such a time, rowers flee places near the shore as though they were the danger of the Syrtes, and climb into the deeper and quieter sea.

So, as the end of this age now approaches [27], the worldly heat boils up as though around its own shore, and raises itself into heaps of disturbance and pride. The world, which in past ages had been somewhat tranquil, as though in the depth of the sea, now pestilentially seethes near the shore of its end, so that those who come alongside may rightly escape the danger of shipwreck.

This shaking and disturbance arises from luxury; and, contrary to nature, affliction is generated from pleasure. Hence Solomon says: “This is the worst occupation God has given to the children of men, to be occupied with it. I saw all that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccl. I).

For while all strive to acquire the things in which they delight, they are necessarily compelled to labor in affliction of spirit; and while one person is obstructed in what he seeks by another, he reaches what delights him only without escaping the weariness of labor.

Again he says: “When I turned to all the works that my hands had done, and to the labors in which I had toiled in vain, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in everything” (Eccl. I).

Yet this affliction itself delights hard and reprobate minds, since they take pleasure not only in the sweetness of delights but also in the sharpness of labor.
