Hence the Israelites, enticed by the itching stimulus of appetite, complained that they lacked not only meat and the delicacies of fish, but also leeks, onions, and garlic (Num. XI). These plants, while by the natural force of their sharpness they bite the taste of the throat, provoke tears from the eyes.

Do those who abandon the more nourishing foods of the household table, who think little of the delicacies of fatty sauces voluntarily offered by a lavish host, not hunger for the sharpness of onions and garlic? They pursue wild beasts with hunting spears through bristling thickets and mountain crags; they disdain what is brought out of storerooms and hunt birds of prey with hawks sent wandering through the air [Col. 0230A].

Although they could usually rest in tranquil peace, they consider it pleasant and delightful to sweat through the labors of riding or litigation. They judge the leisure of rest flaccid, and confess it to be dull, ignoble, and slack. So that people also said: “Our soul is dry; our eyes look upon nothing but manna” (ibid.). Elsewhere, murmuring, they say: “There is no bread, there is no water; our soul is nauseated by this very light food” (Num. XXI).

They regard food as very light if it happens to lack the weight and hardness of labor. They are dissolved by labor and wearied by leisure.

It is plainly worth examining how small a part of the body it is for which the substance of the whole world is not sufficient, although it desires all the resources of earthly wealth. For while the other members of the body appear in some way brute and stupid, scarcely half a cubit can be found in the body which the totality of all things cannot satisfy.

From the eyes down to the genitals, every human desire holds sway. This is enclosed within a narrow space by natural necessity, but it is not held within the laws of the natural limit; rather, it spreads through all external things. What proceeds from a small root is not content with small or few things but gapes after everything; it pants after all things in order to enjoy and gorge itself.

The eyes feed upon the beauty of things; the ears are soothed by the ringing sounds of harmony or by the flattering agreement of words; the nostrils take in fragrances; the throat delights in the flavors of feasts; the heart turns over the secret of its thoughts; the tongue pours forth speech; and what the heart meditates is brought forth into the midst through the interpretation of the mouth. “Out of the abundance of the heart,” of course, “the mouth speaks” (Matt. XII).

Now the genitals are urged toward intercourse with greater ardor in proportion as the stomach is filled either by an abundance of food or by an inundation of drink. Gluttony is a kind of leech with two daughters, namely drunkenness and lust. Concerning them Solomon says: “The leech has two daughters, saying, ‘Bring, bring’” (Prov. XXXVI).

For the more immoderately one eats, the more necessarily one is inflamed with thirst for drink. And while the accumulated mass of food is cooked in the boiling cauldron of the stomach, it must necessarily be irrigated by frequent draughts. But when the belly swells with food and drink, it follows that, through alternating passages on either side, it expels feces through the anus into its channels and pours moisture from the genital receptacle through the private parts.

For just as in wine presses the wine is separated from the wine, so in the intestines dung is separated from the food [viru: the text appears corrupt]. The leech, therefore, which is gluttony, has two daughters: drunkenness and lust; for while one disease conceives pleasurably, it necessarily gives birth to twin offspring.

These say, “Bring, bring,” because, being insatiable, they are also violent exactors. This part of the body, from the private parts to the eyes, destroys the whole human being and utterly overturns in him the dignity of natural excellence. Through these channels of the senses, the unhappy human condition allows what belongs to salvation to flow out and admits what belongs to destruction.

The Apostle John briefly encompasses all these things when he says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (I John II). The desire of the flesh pertains to bodily pleasure; the desire of the eyes to the beauty of visible things; but the pride of life expresses the elevation of earthly honor and rank.

The first human being is recognized as having been tempted through these things, as Scripture testifies (Gen. III): “The woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was good for food”—there is the desire of the flesh. Then it continues: “And beautiful to the eyes and delightful to behold”—there is the pride of the eyes. For whoever delights in things forbidden by God is convicted of taking pride through the eyes. The pride of life was present when that same woman willingly heard from the mouth of the serpent: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid.).

The whole world, then, at this time is nothing other than gluttony, avarice, and lust. And just as once the world was divided into three parts so that it might be subject to three rulers, so now the human race, alas, alas, bows its servile neck to these three vices and obediently obeys the laws of as many tyrants [Col. 0231C].

“For all,” as Scripture says, “from the least to the greatest, pursue avarice” (Isa. LVI; Jer. VI). What shall I say about gluttony, when all the wealthy know nothing of hunger and never wait for the appetite to arise? Their swollen bellies, unless they quickly disgorge through both outlets, fear a rumbling in the intestines; and thus the health of life consists in their hands like a tube.

Their flaming mouths gorge themselves, yet because disgust prevents them, they should not be said to eat, but rather to nibble greedily [29]. And so, while almost all penitents reject the affliction of the flesh, the force of the canons is utterly weakened in assigning penalties for repentance. Therefore either the book of the canons must be closed altogether, or the assessment of penance to be imposed must cease.

For what secular person could endure it if you ordered him to fast even for three days in a week [Col. 0231D]? At one moment they pretend to suffer from the stomach; at another they complain of the destruction of the spleen or bladder; at another they claim that the defect of a decayed lung blocks their breathing. On one side they produce the many cares of household property; on the other they plead the burdensome services of their master’s household.

Why say more? They construct labyrinthine scenes of arguments, put on the guise of Proteus, and transform themselves into monsters of various shapes. They feign every kind of illness so that they may not incur what they fear most: the weakness caused by fasting. But while they serve not nature, which makes no such demand, but their impatient appetite with such devotion, whether they wish it or not, they loosen the reins of lust.

For the belly and the private parts are contiguous and closely related; and when the former is restored without the discernment of temperance, the latter are immediately aroused to insults. Foods are, of course, the allurements of lust; and when consumed immoderately, they soon transmit an excess of their own moisture to the private parts. When these fluids, heaped up, itch and titillate, they demand with increasing urgency that they flow forth through intercourse.

Hence many, while they know the permission to enter marriage granted by law, display no discipline in rendering the marital debt; nor do they use marital intercourse temperately, since they serve not the begetting of offspring but an innate pleasure. Such men are plainly—not, I will say, husbands, but prolectarii [term uncertain]; not spouses, but rather lovers. They prolong every period into intemperate intercourse, so that, shameful as it is to say, they do not spare their wives even when pregnant.

Nor are men ashamed to violate the rule of chastity which even dumb animals observe with respect to their pregnant females. Look, O man, whether a dog mounts a bitch after she has conceived; observe whether a heifer, or indeed a mare, is pursued by her males after conception. They know nothing of the lust of intercourse when they see that the capacity for begetting is lacking.

When, therefore, bulls, dogs, and the other kinds of beasts show reverence toward their offspring, human beings alone—whose Teacher was born from a Virgin—do not fear to crush and kill their little ones, who are formed in the image of God, in order to fulfill the desires of their lust.

Hence some women miscarry before the time of giving birth, or certainly discover the tender limbs of those same little ones mutilated or injured [Col. 0232C]. Thus, while they rush headlong toward the incentives of lust, they are parricides before they are parents; and, what is extremely dangerous, while they attribute this to the fault of sinful nature, they do not recognize themselves as liable to so heinous a crime.

Nevertheless, sometimes they are not ignorant of this either; but while they profit from the ignorance of the people, they pretend not to confess it to priests.

The barrus, also called the blephas, is said to love the purity of chastity uniquely and to abominate the obscenities of lust to such an extent that, when compelled to mate for the propagation of its kind, it turns its face behind its back. Thus, compelled in a sense by the command of nature, it shows that it does not wish or feel ashamed to do what it is doing.

Every beast, therefore, mates only in order to beget; man alone begets in order to mate. For beasts, the culmination of intercourse is offspring; for human beings, the culmination of begetting is intercourse.

Vultures produce offspring without corrupting themselves through intercourse. Bees nourish offspring destined to continue their posterity so that they may remain virgins. Thus creatures without reason imitate the Son of the Virgin, while human beings, for whom he was born, delight in the mire of lust.

Who casts seed upon seed? Who judges that a field clothed in the beauty of blooming grain should be furrowed again by plowshares? He sends in the sickle first, so that when the field is empty, sowing may soon follow and produce a crop; otherwise, if seed is cast upon seed, it may happen that, I will not say an abundant yield from both, but not even a harvest from either, may be gathered.

Consider, therefore, weak man—or rather, emasculated man—what you desire, and know that the one toward whom you pant, inflamed by the torches of lust, is dust and ash. When you embrace a woman’s limbs, you should contemplate what she will shortly become: worms, corruption, and intolerable stench, so that consideration of the future decay may cause you to despise the cosmetics of theatrical beauty.

For in the judgment of the wise, not only what flatters the eyes is subject to scrutiny, but also what lies hidden in the substance of truth. Nevertheless, all those pleasures which wives now provide for their husbands must necessarily be provided for other men as well, if after their husbands’ death they happen—as is customary—to become twice-married or even thrice-married. They have no fidelity at all after death; and while they eagerly desire to please later husbands, they are shamelessly ashamed, with faces flushed, even to hear the names of their former husbands.

[Col. 0233B] I certainly know of a man who, while trying to avenge an injury inflicted upon his wife, was killed with swords; yet she is said to have moved to a second marriage before the year’s cycle had been completed. Let men therefore go and, abandoning God, place their hope in their wives; for while they love them too immoderately, they often transmit through them their own property not only to unrelated men but also to their enemies.

Furthermore, if a woman violates the marriage bed, although the report already flies through the mouths of all her neighbors, the husband alone remains ignorant; and the man who first suffered the disgrace of his own household scarcely discovers it last.

Thus the incentives of lust are the fuel of avarice and the material of greed. For since luxury plainly requires many expenses, its pleasures cannot flow unless resources abound through manifold advantages [Col. 0233C]. But just as those who are proved to be natives of this world strive to burden themselves with earthly things, so, conversely, the mind that gapes toward heavenly things boasts of stripping itself bare.

O how joyful, how welcome the message, and finally how sweet to my ears, that recently reached me—the report, namely, that you had taken the county of Ostia away from me and handed it over to another! A certain Roman, as though accusing you before me, and as though offering me counsel and sympathy, informed me of what had happened; but, not realizing whom he thought he was accusing, he commended you instead. At first I pretended to take it gravely, but when certain signs of joy broke forth, I could not even outwardly simulate grief. Indeed, I gladly implore the divine mercy that you not delay in arranging the bishopric as soon as possible, and that you take from my hands the plough of this barren, sandy shore.

For this is not a time in which one who desires to keep to the path of purity and innocence can consent to bear the governance of the Church, when nearly everyone is rushing headlong over the precipices of vice and, like maddened horses, is carried unchecked across the fields of his pleasures. And what else do we discern amid all these evils of such countless crimes, except that a road is already being paved for the Antichrist, who will soon arrive, so that he may walk along it with the footprints of his wickedness unobstructed?

For as the Apostle says: “The mystery of iniquity is already at work” (II Thess. II). The world borrows light from darkness when its end is already drawing near. And just as twilight seems to waver between day and night, so, when the light of virtues is setting, the night of vices rises. This was surely foreshadowed by what Scripture declares concerning Abraham: “When the sun was setting,” it says, “a deep sleep fell upon Abraham, and a great and dark terror seized him” (Gen. XV). The setting of the sun signifies the setting of the world; the great and dark terror, however, represents the darkness of vices and crimes, which daily grow horribly through the feverish depravity of reprobate people.

Hence, a little later, it is added there: “When the sun had set, a dark gloom came to be, and a smoking furnace appeared” (ibid.). For just as smoke comes forth from the fire of a furnace that is giving off heat, so the darkness of all vices and crimes is generated from the furnace of burning avarice, as the Apostle says: “For avarice is the root of all evils” (II Tim. VI). And this occurs toward the end of the day—that is, toward the end of the world.

The smoking furnace, therefore, generates dark gloom, because the furnace of avarice, which burns in the breasts of wicked people, darkens the world with the pestilential darkness of many perversions. Does it not blind the minds of the wretched—avarice, which both removes faith and extinguishes the light of every virtue in their hearts? Hence, after the Apostle had said this, he immediately added: “By desiring it”—namely, avarice—“some have gone astray from the faith and involved themselves in many sorrows” (ibid.).

For they involve themselves in many sorrows when, for the sake of temporal gains, they recoil from one another in irreconcilable hostility. And often, while they rush into armed conflict over bodily possessions, their souls depart from their bodies. Those, however, who burn only with heavenly desires obtain delights in place of sorrows, because they live united in the sweetness of fraternal charity.

This is why, in that evening sacrifice which Abraham then offered, he arranged the earthly animals separated from one another, but did not divide the birds. Hence Scripture says: “Taking all these, he divided them through the middle and set the two parts opposite one another, but he did not divide the birds” (Gen. XV). The earthly animals are set against one another and placed opposite one another because all earthly people rage against their neighbors with quarrels and disputes, or at least burn inwardly against them with hidden kindling of hatred. But those who raise themselves aloft on the wings of heavenly desire, while offering themselves to God as a sacrifice, do not withdraw from the bond of mutual love.

**32** These are the complaints I make to you, venerable Father, about the madness of the raging world, which I am compelled both to endure daily and to hate. I do not fear the accusation of being a detractor when I expose the crimes of sinners to one who holds pre-eminent authority to correct what is wrong. For that person is not to be called a slanderer who takes care to lay the guilt of the erring before one who can amend what has been rashly undertaken.

These, moreover, are the words of Elijah (III Kings XIX): “They have destroyed your altars, Lord, and slain your prophets with the sword, and I alone am left.” To him the Lord replied: “I shall leave for myself seven thousand in Israel whose knees have not been bent before Baal” [Col. 0235A]. Although the prophet says that he alone has remained, while the Lord replies, by contrast, that seven thousand still survive, Elijah is nevertheless not accused of lying, because, inflamed by the fire of heavenly zeal, he believes that what he says is so.

If Elijah therefore did not sin because, driven not by hatred but by zeal, he exceeded the proper measure of accusation, ought I to be accused of presumption when I have reported a few matters out of many to one who above all possesses the right to correct? It was therefore my task to bring these things, in whatever manner, to your sacred ears; it is yours, insofar as your ability permits, to restrain them.

It must therefore be our concern, and we must labor persistently, so that, at the dread judgment of the supreme Shepherd, either the intimate fervor of zeal may excuse you with Elijah, or—what is more glorious—the abundant fruit of the flock entrusted to you may adorn you with Peter.

Do not, I beg you, be surprised if the course of this letter runs in an unpolished style, because while my hand hastens to form its letters, on one side Cadalous, that most dreadful dragon, blows, and on the other a venomous swarm of serpents has emerged from its caves and hisses. Since we cannot break them by incantations, we prepare to cut off their scaly necks with swords.

But since a synod is approaching, I also append these pedestrian verses:

> Whoever wishes to preserve the authority of the apostolic see  
> must weigh the equal measures of stern justice.  
>   
> For he does not know how to suspend equal scales of law  
> whom favor bends or greedy hope draws away.  
>   
> To him whose purses, filled with gifts, loosen his lips,  
> justice, left empty, destroys his wretched soul.  
>   
> Rome of heaven holds the bars of heaven and governs the reins of the world;  
> whoever desires more than this seeks Tartarus alone.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE SAME ALEXANDER II, ROMAN PONTIFF, AND HILDEBRAND, CARDINAL ARCHDEACON OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

**SUMMARY.**—Rebuked by Pope Alexander and by the archdeacon Hildebrand for having written a certain letter to the bishop of Cologne, he sends them a copy of that letter. Then, because they had asked him to travel with them to Rome and from there to Mantua, where a meeting of bishops was to be held, he declines the journey to Rome as less necessary and excessively burdensome to his old age; but he entirely refuses to reject the hardship of the journey to Mantua, since it appeared to be in the interest of the Christian commonwealth. Until the arrival of both men, who were to pass through that way on their journey to Mantua, however, he postpones deliberation on so important a matter.

**To the father and son, the pope and the archdeacon, Peter, sinful monk, offers service.**

I send you the letter about which you taunted me, so that you may see it and clearly establish what I did in it against you. But if I sent another letter to that region, or if anything in this very letter, knowingly on my part, was increased or diminished by even a single letter, or altered in any way, and if it was not sent to you straightforwardly, exactly as it was then addressed to the lord bishop of Cologne, may the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian (IV Kings V) cover me, or may the blindness of Bar-Jesus (Acts XIII) cover the eyes of my brow.

I call Jesus and his holy angels to witness that in this declaration I am not lying. If I must die for this letter, I offer my neck; drive in the dagger.

Henceforth, I humbly beseech my holy Satan [Note: He means Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church.], that he not rage so fiercely against me, nor that his venerable pride wear me down with such prolonged beatings, but that, now at last, sated, he may grow gentle toward his servant. For my bruised shoulders are already failing, and my back, furrowed by so many blows and swollen with so many livid welts, can no longer endure. Hence the wise man says: “The wound of a scourge produces a bruise, but the wound of the tongue crushes the bones” (Ecclus. XXVIII).

Come, then; it is time that I now . . . [Note: Aposiopesis.] But I still restrain my spirit and place my finger upon my lips; and although it is late, wretched as I am, I still seek mercy.

As for your command that I come to Rome to meet you and then go with you to Mantua, each journey seemed to me exceedingly difficult and far too burdensome for my old age. Thus I omitted coming to Rome, since it would have benefited you less; but I judged the undertaking of the journey to Mantua more necessary for you.

Yet in assigning me the oracle of your holy legation, the two of you divided the matter between yourselves with sufficient inequality. One of you, it seems, has flattered me with the friendliness of paternal affection, while the other has terrifyingly threatened me with hostile reproaches. One of you shines upon me like the sun with the warmth of flashing brilliance; the other, like the raging north wind, blasts me with the violent gusts of his force.

This brings to mind what is related in fables. It is said that, while a traveler wearing a cloak was walking along, the Sun and the East Wind proposed him as the object of a contest between them, to see which of the two could take his cloak away. After they had established this agreement between themselves—that a green laurel would crown whichever one proved victorious—the East Wind began to roar violently and stir up masses of clouds. The traveler, on the other hand, tightened his cloak and huddled himself together on every side so as not to lose his garment.

When the disciple of Aeolus, exhausted by fruitless effort, began to despair completely of accomplishing what he had begun, the Sun immediately began to uncover his golden face and illuminate the earth with his gleaming heat. Soon, when the traveler was drying out under the fires of excessive heat and abundant sweat was boiling forth from his moistened entrails, he threw off his cloak in order to moderate the burning heat of the oppressive warmth.

Thus the victor in the agreed contest was the one who acted gently, not the one who attempted to conquer by raging and inflicting violence.

But, to offer a more honorable example from the sacred Scriptures: if Rehoboam, accepting the counsel of the elders, had given a mild answer to the people, he would have subjected all Israel to his rule. But because he trusted the pride of his contemporaries, and ten tribes were separated from him, he made the lofty power of his kingdom humble (II Kings XII; II Chronicles X).

The rhinoceros, too, which with swift speed scorns the raging mouths of pursuing dogs, does not fear being captured in the embrace of a gentle maiden. But since I have returned to you everything that belonged to you, why do I still suffer persecution?

Those who investigate the natures of things certainly report [PLIN. book XII, chapter 1]—I do not know whether hunters also support the account—that when a beaver realizes by its natural instinct that it is being pursued for no other reason than its testicles, which are sought in order to be cut off and preserved for medicinal use, it suddenly rushes to the stump of a tree and, striking itself violently against it, throws off its testicles. Then, leaping farther away, it turns toward the hunter and rises onto its two hind feet, showing that it no longer possesses what is being sought.

Is a harsher satisfaction, then, demanded from a human being than is required from brute animals? But, lest this letter exceed the proper brevity, we shall await your arrival in our region in order to make these complaints.

## LETTER XVII. TO THE SAME ALEXANDER II

(It is found in volume III and is work 23.)

## LETTER XX. TO CADALOUS, BISHOP OF PARMA, ALSO HONORIUS II, ANTIPOPE

**SUMMARY.**—Besides the other vices that were numerous in him, Cadalous, bishop of Parma, inflamed by the great torches of ambition, stirred up immense disturbances in the Roman Church. After rejecting Alexander, the legitimate pontiff, he used largesses and every sort of wicked device to have himself proclaimed by certain Cisalpine bishops like himself—although they had no right of election at all—as the true and genuine pontiff.

Having therefore achieved the object of his criminal desire, he began openly, and in the sight of everyone, to commit the crimes that he had previously practiced more secretly. He defiled everything with plunder, slaughter, and devastation; he allowed ecclesiastical property to be seized by his soldiers and retainers; in short, to sum it up in a single word, he mingled human and divine things.

At first gently admonished, and then, when this accomplished nothing, publicly condemned three times in assemblies of the fathers—at Pavia, Mantua, and Florence—and removed from Catholic communion, he did not cease from his madness and fury.

To this man, so impious and so stubborn in rejecting salutary counsel, Blessed Peter Damian writes. After placing before his eyes the enormity of the crime he had committed, and after attempting by every means available to recall him to sanity, he finally concludes the letter with a prophecy of his grievous death.

**To the one called Cadalous, bishop, Peter, sinful monk, [Col. 0237D] sends what is fitting and just.**

One who does not correct a boy stealing eggs later suffers a great robber breaking into his stables. If a powerful matron neglects to keep an insolent man away from her own *corynetes* (club-bearing attendants) [the reading is uncertain; the printed conjecture suggests *famulab.*], what wonder if he later extends toward her also the desire of his madness?

And, to introduce something from Scripture: King David, who does not avenge the fratricide committed by Absalom, is subsequently driven out by him and deprived of the dignity of the royal throne (II Kings XIII). Adonijah, son of Haggith, while insolently raising himself in the pride of arrogance, and while, with his father conniving, promising himself the kingdom with horses and chariots prepared, eventually advances so far as to seek Abishag the Shunammite in marriage and desire to profane his father’s bedchamber (I Kings I).

In many matters, brother, the Roman Church spared you and frequently restrained the discipline of legitimate rigor against you, to such an extent that those who confess that they were present assert that in three synodal councils already—namely, at Pavia, Mantua, and Florence—a clear sentence of condemnation against you was pronounced. Everywhere, nevertheless, the apostolic see mercifully indulged you with the affection of a mother.

But while it sought to restrain the rigor of the canons toward you, you are not afraid to return hostile tyranny against it.

Moreover, if the sequence of Scripture is carefully considered, David is found to have been anointed king three times: first by Samuel at Bethlehem, second by the men of Judah at Hebron, and third, again at Hebron, before all the tribes of Israel (I Kings XVI; II Kings II; II Kings V).

And, to say something similar about our fisherman, whose place you are so eager to take, Peter held three sees: the see of Antioch, where, after he himself had laid the foundation of the faith, he soon ordained Ignatius as bishop in his place [Note: Rather Evodius, as Ignatius himself and others testify.]; also Alexandria, where Saint Mark the Evangelist, after sowing the seed of the new faith, faithfully dedicated it to the glorious name of his blessed master Peter; and finally he presided over the city of Rome for five periods of five years, adorning it with his fellow apostle Paul in the blood of a precious triumphal victory.

But why do we introduce either that man, anointed three times, or this one, presiding three times, into the argument of this discussion, unless so that you may meanwhile return to your conscience and yourself consider how far you are from holy men, having been deposed as many times—not by the judgment of priests, but by the authority of the canons?

For although the triple promotion of both of those men was in a certain sense no more than one promotion, since it represented no increase either of kingdom or priesthood, it was nevertheless an indication of fuller holiness. Just as the former surpassed all kings in piety or justice, so the latter surpassed all priests in privilege.

This is why, together with the other saints, we do not celebrate such a feast for any of them, but celebrate the feast of the chair of Blessed Peter alone.

Since, then, your priesthood is burdened by such great infamy, how did you dare—or, to speak more gently, how could you consent—to be elected Roman bishop without the knowledge of the Roman Church?

Let us meanwhile say nothing of the senate, the clergy of the lower order, or the people. What do you think of the cardinal bishops? They are the ones who principally elect the Roman pontiff, and who, through certain other prerogatives, surpass the rights not only of any bishops but also of patriarchs and primates.

With due regard for the sacrament of the universal Church, these are the eyes of the one stone—that is, of the Roman Church. Of them Zechariah says: “Behold,” he says, “the stone which I have set before Jesus” (Zech. III). “Upon the one stone are seven eyes.” They are also the lamps of one candlestick, of which he later speaks, saying: “I saw, and behold, a wholly golden candlestick, and its lamp above its head, and seven lamps upon it” (Zech. IV).

They are also the candlesticks in whose midst Jesus, according to the words of blessed John (Rev. I), moves about, and he directs to you, in a certain special sense, the words that immediately follow there: “Remember,” he says, “from where you have fallen, and do penance” (Rev. II).

Clearly, if anyone who inflicts an injury upon any priest whatsoever is rightly punishable by penance, what sentence do you deserve, who have inflicted prejudice upon those priests by whose counsel and judgment the condition and discipline of the entire Catholic Church ought to be governed?

And since canonical authority decrees that even the clergy of any humble church may freely judge the one who ought to be placed above them, with what audacity born of arrogance did you presume to thrust yourself violently upon those who, beyond the common rule of the Church, are even able to issue an authoritative censure against pontiffs themselves?

Why, through ambition to attain a position of power and an inaccessible height, have you stirred almost the whole world into dispute over your condemnation? So that, as though crying out, they might exclaim the words of the prophet Jeremiah: “Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Write this man down as childless, a man who will not prosper in his days” (Jer. XXII).

And you, in turn, might aptly respond in the words of the same prophet: “Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife, a man of discord throughout the whole earth! I have not lent at interest, nor has anyone lent at interest to me; everyone curses me” (Jer. XV).

Again, there is that equally prophetic saying: “Cursed be the day on which I was born; let not the day on which my mother bore me be blessed” (Jer. XX). Immediately afterward he adds: “Cursed be the man who announced to my father, saying, ‘A male child has been born to you,’ and made him rejoice as though with joy. Let that man be like the cities which the Lord overthrew and did not repent. Let him hear a cry in the morning and a wailing at noon, who did not kill me in the womb, so that my mother might become my grave and her womb an eternal conception” (ibid.).

It is not the day on which the man was born that is cursed here; rather, it is the prosperity by which he was enticed into sin and is condemned. On that day, so to speak, you would die in the womb if you withdrew from the fault that you had undertaken—or rather, in which you were wrongly born.

For when strangers, and not sons of the apostolic see, elected you, and deposed you from the see that you held, promoting you to another not by judgment but by uproar, it was as Scripture says: “You cast them down while they were being raised up” (Ps. LXXII).

We restrain laymen from the thresholds of the Church when, having dismissed their own wives, they unite themselves to other women. But how much worse is the adultery committed by the one who, without a synodal sentence, abandons his own Church and, like a robber, invades a Church belonging to another jurisdiction?

The prophet laments this adultery when he says: “My heart is broken within me, and all my bones tremble. I have become like a drunken man and like a man intoxicated with wine, because of the Lord and because of the words of his holiness” (Jer. XXIII).

He immediately discloses why he wastes away in such an exhaustion of grief when he adds: “For the earth is full of adulterers; because of the curse the earth mourned; the fields of the desert have dried up” (ibid.).

What kind of men perpetrate this adultery, and why the earth mourns and human hearts, like the fields of the desert, dry up under the inundation of preaching, he reveals at once when he continues: “For prophet and priest have been polluted, and in my house I have found their wickedness, says the Lord” (ibid.).

But what awaits those same adulterous priests and prophets he declares immediately afterward: “Therefore their way shall be like slippery ground in darkness; they shall be driven on and fall upon it. For I shall bring evils upon them, the year of their visitation. They prophesied in Baal and deceived my people Israel, and in the prophets of Jerusalem I saw the likeness of adulterers and the way of falsehood” (ibid.).

You hear the likeness of adulterers; you hear the way of falsehood. One plainly depends upon the other. For the person who defiles the purity of ecclesiastical chastity through the circuitous excesses of luxuriant desire strays from the path of truth.

Now, alas, we mourn that the Church has been polluted to the very summit, just as Jeremiah once complained that this had happened to Jerusalem: “The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have polluted you to the crown of your head” (Jer. II).

Jerusalem is polluted to the crown of its head when the luxury of venality extends from the smallest churches to the apostolic see, which is the head of all the churches. But the divine voice immediately adds into what bitterness the sweetness of this adultery is turned: “Behold,” it says, “I shall feed them wormwood and give them gall to drink” (Jer. IX).

Do, then, brother, according to the voice of the prophet who says: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. LVI). Examine your conscience, I beg you, and carefully consider with what tranquility and refreshment you have been endowed since you plunged yourself into this perilous undertaking as though into the waves of Scylla’s whirlpool.

The coins of greed are squandered; bags swollen with metal of various kinds are emptied; the resources of the Church, which ought to be distributed to the poor, are wasted on troops. You obey everyone and become subject to everyone, so that you may surpass everyone in dignity, and the ambition for domination makes you a slave by right of servitude.

Let one thing not be hidden from you: whoever once slips into the Church through venality will not cease buying it back as long as he presides over it. For by the just judgment of God it happens that whoever undertakes the governance of the Church after bargaining for it does not gain from his transaction the tranquility or prosperity that he had hoped for. Instead, sitting in the seat of pestilence, he is always wielding the smith’s hammers, and the stream of filthy pre-eminence, running down through foul channels, always answers to its own deadly source.

Indeed, when every religious man shudders at taking upon himself the burden of such a laborious see and scarcely consents to be placed there despite the prayers of men, why do you not merely fail to prepare to flee the burden of burdens, as Pope Leo called it, but even anxiously strive to force yourself into it by offering prayers and a price?

Thus it plainly appears that the sentence which the divine word pronounces through Ezekiel against Jerusalem fits you: “To all prostitutes wages are given; but you have given wages to all your lovers. In this, that you gave wages and received no wages, the opposite has occurred in you” (Ezek. XVI).

Moreover, if the sacred canons label as heretics those who do not agree with the Roman Church, what sentence will you deserve, when you thrust yourself upon one that resists you and obstinately struggles against you—not as a shepherd but as a tyrant—and, together with Satan’s retainers, overthrow the Church that Peter the preacher raised upon the rock of faith?

And, in order to obtain the undeserved name of shepherd, do you not fear to confuse and tear apart the very pasture with its flocks?

But hear what the Lord says through the prophet to you and your kind: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and tear apart the flock of my pasture, says the Lord. Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel to the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, driven them away, and not visited them; behold, I shall visit upon you the evil of your endeavors” (Jer. XXIII).

What you are now attempting is not to visit the Lord’s flock but rather, like a robber and thief, to destroy and slaughter it. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy” (John X).

Were you born for this: to shake the world into wars, destroy the labors and works of the apostles, and confuse the entire Church of Christ through the ambition of one man—your own? Perhaps this disturbance is foreshadowed by the omen of your name.

For you are called Cadalous. (Consult the Scholia at the end of the work.) The first part of this name plainly announces a fall; the second signifies “people,” for *λαός* (*laos*) means “people” in Greek. And what else is expressed in this name except what Scripture says (Ezek. VII): that wicked priests are the ruin of the people?

Thus, you who had been a son of the holy Church have become a sword against her. **39** And perhaps you are that sword of which the prophet Ezekiel says: “A sword, a sword has been sharpened and polished” (Ezek. XXI).

Why this sword has these two qualities—namely, that it has been polished and sharpened—he explains in what follows: “It has been sharpened,” he says, “to slaughter victims; it has been polished to shine” (ibid.).

Do these words not seem to fit you, who, in order that you alone may shine in dignity, are striving to gather the entire kingdom for battle, like victims for slaughter?

But hear also what he immediately adds (ibid.): “You who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree, and I gave him to be polished, so that he might be held in the hand.” Then it follows: “This sword has been sharpened, and it has been polished, so that it may be in the hand of the one who kills.”

You, surely—you are that sword which moves the scepter of the Son of God: that is, you stir up the people in whom he reigns and rules. The scepter of the Son of God is the Catholic Church; she is his kingdom, she is the dominion of our Redeemer. You are rightly said to move her when you strive to harass and disturb her.

It is not my purpose to expound the prophet’s words in the manner of a commentator, so that I would also have to discuss the trees from which the Church is now fashioned after Noah’s ark. Let it be enough for me merely to touch upon those matters that seem to suit your madness.

Moreover, since this attempt of yours will never reach its intended result but will finally end in an ill-fated outcome, and since you who advance proudly against the Roman strongholds will return with disgrace to your own soil, hear what follows.

After the divine voice says (ibid.): “Sword, sword, draw yourself for slaughter; polish yourself so that you may kill and shine,” a little later it continues: “Return to your sheath, to the place in which you were created. In the land of your birth I shall judge you, and I shall pour out my indignation upon you, and I shall blow the fire of my fury upon you.”

Perhaps you now have a mitre and, according to the custom of the Roman pontiff, a red cloak. Take care lest the divine word, through the same prophet, pronounce this sentence against you: “But you, profane and wicked prince of Israel, whose day has come at the time appointed for iniquity, thus says the Lord God: Remove the tiara, take away the crown. Is this not the thing that raised up the lowly and humbled the exalted?” (ibid.).

As though it were openly declaring that whoever arrogantly pants after this tiara or priestly crown is rightly brought low, while whoever cries out that he is unworthy and refuses it is deservedly exalted.

It is indeed a great source of joy that such pontiffs elected you—namely, the bishops of Piacenza and Vercelli—men so very insolent and common that, just as they know how to discuss the appearance of women, so, if only they had been able, they might have possessed penetrating judgment in electing a pontiff.

Behold again those two elders of whom the Lord spoke: “For iniquity came forth from Babylon, from the elders and judges who seemed to govern the people” (Dan. XXV).

Behold again Susanna brought forward, accused before the court; behold a false charge directed against an innocent woman, and innocent blood condemned. But will Daniel also be absent—the one whose spirit will suddenly be stirred up to avenge the wickedness of false witnesses?

He will certainly be present; that true man of desires will be present, of whom the prophet says: “Behold, the Desired One of all nations will come” (Haggai II). That more powerful Daniel will be present, I say, who will prove that the wicked elders judged perversely and will absolve our Susanna from the sentence of unjust condemnation.

Of his sudden judgment another prophet says: “Behold, the whirlwind of the Lord’s indignation will go forth, and a storm breaking forth will come upon the head of the impious. The Lord’s fury will not return until he acts and until he fulfills the thought of his heart” (Jer. XXIII).

With due reverence for our kings, who, whether because of weakness of sex or of age, may perhaps have been misled in this matter (consult the scholion), all those who drove you toward this crime must be called sons of Caiaphas, firstborn of Satan, helpers of the Antichrist, and adversaries of the truth.

Therefore I am moved to cry out: O heaven! O earth!—together with which, surely, all the elements must be thrown into confusion. O tragedy unheard of in all the ages before us—that a foreign bishop, disregarding his own see, with God ignorant of it, Peter ignorant of it, and the Roman Church ignorant of it, should be set over the Roman Church! And that what no church of the lowest rank can endure should be endured by the one who is the mother and teacher of the whole Christian religion!

But someone might perhaps object that some Roman took part in this disorderly ordination. Let the frenzied tongue blush at this, and let the tongue that does not know how to be eloquent learn at least to be silent: if it does not know how to say anything useful, let it at least know how to keep silent without causing harm.

For since the principal judgment in that election must be made by the cardinal bishops, the clergy should lawfully give its assent in the second place, and popular favor should raise an acclamation in the third; and thus the matter must be suspended until the authority of the royal majesty has been consulted—unless, as recently happened, danger perhaps threatens and compels the matter to be hastened.

Moreover, just as the devil gave a plural number to the divine name when he said to the woman, “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III), so you have added something new to the rules of grammarians, so that children may now say *papae paparum*—“of or to a pope; of popes”—in the declension of *papa*. Through you, therefore, the aged world is learning what it had hitherto not known.

And just as, according to Paul’s words (Hebr. IX), the high priest entered the holy place every year with the blood of another, so you now perform the slaughter of wretched men as though they were pigs, and shed blood in order to enter the shrine of Blessed Peter covered in blood.

Beware, brother, beware lest you rise so rashly as an enemy against Peter, who certainly pierced Ananias and his wife with the weapon of his word, and plunged Simon, arrogantly seeking the stars, into the depths of Gehenna (Acts V).

I report what was told me by elders: In the regions of Babylonia the Apostolic See possessed an estate from which it received each year so much balsam that it was sufficient as an unfailing fuel for the lamp that gleamed, suspended before the altar of the blessed chief of the apostles. That estate the pope sold for money that he received, and he lost the annual measure of aromatic substance that he had been accustomed to receive. Some time afterward, when that same pope was standing and praying before the aforesaid sacred altar as though devoutly, behold, a certain terrifying and very old man, whose face even appeared to have a beard, raised his arm and struck him a mighty blow on the cheek, saying: “You have extinguished my lamp before me, and I shall extinguish your lamp before God.” Then he immediately disappeared. The pope at once collapsed, and shortly afterward ended his days.

Thus, surely, he deserves correction who sets himself against him who holds the primacy of heaven and earth. Which of the two popes, I ask, seems to you deserving of punishment with the harsher severity: the one who dared to extinguish the lamp of the sacred altar, or you, who are striving to obscure the whole universal Church from the beginning of your furtive promotion? For, according to the word of Truth, “he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep; but he who enters by another way is a thief and a robber” (John X). But just as light is poured into the house through the door of the shepherd who already presides, so through your “other way” nothing is introduced except smoke, darkness, chaos, and the horror of shadows.

Moreover, when someone is in a low position, his vices are in a sense hidden; but when he climbs to the summit of dignity, they immediately burst into view. What had previously been unheard of is now worn smooth and made public by the mouths of the rowing populace. How many thousands of people now enumerate your deeds who, until this time, knew them utterly not at all? For the condemnable transactions involving the prebends of your Church and of other churches, and other matters far more disgraceful, which we blush to mention, were previously being recounted only in your little town. Now, throughout every part of this kingdom, merchants speak of them in the marketplace and diggers in the fields. Boys who practice rhetoric in the schools, citizens who gather at the crossroads—all but everyone tears you to pieces and passes judgment on you.

What has happened to you is proved to be what Jeremiah says to every transgressor: “Because of the multitude of your iniquity, your shameful parts have been exposed; your feet have been polluted” (Jeremiah XIII). A little later he also says: “This is your lot and the portion of your measure from me, says the Lord, because you have forgotten me and trusted in falsehood. Therefore I also stripped your thighs before your face, and your disgrace appeared, and your adulteries, and your neighing, the crime of your fornication” (ibid.).

Yet if I decided that I ought to confront you and reproach you to your face with these words, would I not say to you: “Have you not sold what ought to have been offered freely in the Church? Have you not committed this and that, with heaven and earth as witnesses?” If I said these things to you, I know well that, since you could not deny them before a world that bore witness, you would immediately flee to the protection of future correction. For every seeker of high office, when shame overwhelms him because his conscience reproaches him for his past life, promises himself amendment in the future. But when the summit of high rank becomes an opportunity for sinning, how will one who stumbled while walking on level ground avoid falling over the precipitous crags of a rugged mountain?

I could also reply that the Lord says through the prophet to you and to those like you: “If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots, then you also will be able to do good, when you have learned to do evil” (Jeremiah XIII). Of this diversity he says elsewhere: “Is a variegated bird my inheritance? Is it a bird dyed all over?” (ibid. XII). But the variety of guilt immediately brings with it the sentence of vengeance: “Come,” he says, “assemble yourselves, all the beasts of the earth; hasten to devour” (ibid.). To whom this devouring punishment threatens, he makes clear by adding at once: “Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have trampled my portion; they have made my desirable portion a desert of solitude; they have laid it waste” (ibid.).

All these things indicate nothing other than the Church scattered by evil shepherds. Since I believe that you know this too, and since no lengthy explanation is needed, I shall not expound it. But I will not allow this one thing to remain hidden from you: both you and whoever else like you seeks the summit of the Church through ambition are, beyond doubt, tearing the Church apart while ignorant of God. Hence it is said through the same prophet: “Because the shepherds acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord, therefore they did not understand, and their whole flock was scattered” (Jeremiah X).

You now promise amendment so that you may obtain the dignity you covet. You speak humbly so that you may be raised to exaltation. But since this humility is born from the root of pride, it does not appear suitable for making satisfaction.

Meanwhile, the history found in the Book of Genesis comes to mind (Genesis XXXIV). When Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of that land, saw Dinah, the daughter of Leah, he loved her, seized her, and slept with her, violating the virgin by force. His soul became attached to her, and he soothed her grief with endearments. He loved her so passionately that he circumcised not only himself but all the males of his city, so that he might obtain her in marriage. But this satisfaction did not please God, nor did it appease the hearts of her brothers, because it was done not out of religious devotion but to obtain the pleasure of the flesh. Her brothers, enraged over the rape, killed with the sword all those who had been circumcised.

You, then—you are the new Shechem, the corrupter of Dinah, the violator of the Church. You circumcise the flesh so that you may fulfill the desire of the flesh. You promise that you will cut away your wicked conduct so that afterward you may be permitted to remain in wickedness with impunity. But behold, Simeon and Levi attack Shechem with swords, because the Old and New Testaments, condemning you by their judgments, cut you down like brothers armed with so many swords. Or, so that the avengers may be acquired more closely, let Peter and Paul, who are judges of the world, themselves also become the avengers of your transgression. For you have done a foul deed in Israel.

But lest someone perhaps object to me that those killers of Shechem—namely Simeon and Levi—deserved a sentence of condemnation when the patriarch Jacob departed, let him know that there the prophetic spirit looked forward rather to the future death of the Savior than condemned in due measure the slaughter already committed against a lustful man. Simeon signifies the scribes of the Jews; Levi, the tribe of the chief priests. Concerning them it is written: “They took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him” (Matthew XXVI). Of that counsel it is said: “Let my soul not come into their counsel, and let my glory not be in their assembly. For,” he says, “in their fury they killed a man, and in their will they undermined a wall” (Genesis XLIX)—that is, the man of whom Wisdom says: “Let us oppress the just man, because he is contrary to our works” (Wisdom II).

They undermined the wall—that is, that strongest and spiritual bulwark which guards Israel. Therefore, leaving the rest to the commentators, let it suffice to understand here that it is not vengeance for the rape but the sacrileges of Christ’s murderers that are being condemned.

Judith also showed that this vengeance was pleasing to God, saying: “Lord God of my father Simeon, who gave him a sword for vengeance upon the foreigners, who proved violators in their defilement and uncovered a virgin’s thigh to her shame, and gave their women for plunder, their daughters into captivity, and all their spoil for distribution among your servants, who were zealous with your zeal” (Judith IX).

Moreover, you are not content with the measure of a human being; you desire to appear as a mountain among humankind, and you raise yourself to the summit of power like a promontory of pride. You do not wish to be among the valleys, of which it is said: “The valleys will abound with grain” (Psalm LXIV). But hear what the Lord says to you through the prophet: “Behold, I am against you, pestilential mountain, says the Lord, which corrupts the whole earth. I will stretch out my hand over you, tear you away from the rocks, and make you a mountain of burning. They will not take from you a stone for a corner or a stone for foundations, but you will be lost forever” (Jeremiah LI).

And again: “Behold, I am against you, proud one, says the Lord, for your day will come, the time of your visitation. The proud man will fall and collapse, and there will be no one to raise him up” (Jeremiah L).

Has the heat of condemnation burned so fiercely within you? Has the arrogance of pride and ambition for exaltation provoked you to such a degree that you dared the rule of the queen of Churches—or, to speak plainly, of all kingdoms? But “the virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; after you the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head. Whom have you reproached and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel? You said: ‘With the multitude of my chariots I will ascend the height of the mountains, the ridges of Lebanon’” (Isaiah XXXVII)—namely, the Roman Church, established at the summit of the whole world and made white with the radiance of virginal chastity.

But hear what the divine voice says to you through the same prophet (ibid.): “I know your dwelling, your going out, and your coming in, and your madness against me. When you raged against me, your pride rose up into my ears.” Immediately he adds the sentence in conclusion (ibid.): “Therefore I will put a ring in your hands and a bridle on your lips, and I will lead you back by the way you came.”

But behold, although the subject matter dictates much more to us, we have not yet fulfilled our purpose, and already we have exceeded the brevity proper to a letter. We must therefore ask almighty God only that he recall to you the spirit of humility and, when the errors of quarrels have been put to sleep, establish in his Church the foundation of the peace and concord that has been torn apart through you. At the end I gladly lament these things:

Alas, Apostolic See,

once the glory of the world,

now, alas, you have become

the workshop of Simon.

Hammers wear down the anvil;

the coins are infernal.

By the just judgment of God

this condition has come to be.

Whoever once buys

the Apostolic See

does not cease to redeem it

until he perishes miserably.

He holds the chair of pestilence,

burdened by an anathema,

with the priests

who have slain Christ.

The earth becomes iron for him;

the seat of heaven, bronze.

Pay close attention, therefore, to what I say:

A smoky life flies away; unforeseen death draws near;

the winged end of your completed life threatens you.

I do not deceive you: you will die in the year you have begun.

[Note: [Col. 0247B]

“Addressed to Bishop Cadalous, Peter the sinful monk,” etc. The parents and homeland from which Cadalous—whom some more recent writers call Cadalus or Cadaleus—was descended have been taught to me most accurately by the old records of the archive of the monastery of Saint George at Braida in Verona. He was the son of Lord Ingo, Lord Guizard, count of Sabulon, a castle not far from that same city. After his father and grandfather had died, Cadalous went with his brothers to live in Verona. He lived in the district of Saint Faustinus, in the ducal court. In the year of Christ 1042 he was enrolled in the clerical order; and not long afterward, around the year 1045, he was made bishop of the Church of Parma. He considered nothing more important than to establish a monastery for those serving under the rule of Saint Benedict, and he successfully accomplished this. First, from Walter, bishop of Verona, he obtained a site on the bank of the river Adige near that same city, a place called Braida; endowed with his paternal goods, he consecrated it to the most holy martyr George. From these facts it is easy to correct the more recent writers who record different things. Concerning Cadalous’s elevation to the antipapacy, more is found in Distinction 23, chapter “In the name of the Lord.”

“Perhaps now you have a mitre; you have, according to the custom of the Roman pontiff, a red cloak.” This red cloak was rightly adopted by the greatest pontiffs of the Church as a badge of royal power, especially because this color was prescribed by God for the clothing of the pontiff of the Hebrews: “They shall make,” says Exodus XXVIII, “the ephod of gold, violet, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and fine twisted linen, in embroidered work.” And also: “Its woven work, and all the variety of its workmanship, shall be of gold, violet, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted fine linen.”

For the significance of this color, see Philo (Book II, *Allegories*) and Saint Jerome (in the Letter to Marcella). Certainly the pagan pontiffs in the city of Rome also used a purple robe, as Aurelius Prudentius mentions (in *Peristephanon*, the poem on Saint Stephen the martyr), as do more recent writers (in the notes on Tacitus, near the beginning of Book II), where the following is read: “That same night brought Germanicus a joyful rest, and he saw himself performing the rite and, with his purple-bordered robe sprinkled with sacred blood, receiving from the hands of his grandmother Augusta another, more beautiful one.” And the historian Zosimus (Book IV), when he mentions that the pontifical bordered robe was brought to Gratian, the Christian emperor, and rejected, says: “When, therefore, the pontiffs according to custom had brought Gratian such a garment, he rejected what they requested, judging that it was not lawful for Christians to use such attire.”

As for this red cloak that the Roman pontiffs wore, you have clear testimonies among our doctors. Peter the Deacon, concerning Victor III (*Chronicle of Cassino*, Book III, chapter 65): “With one mind and equal agreement, they seize him and, although unwilling and resisting, lead him to the Church of Christ’s martyr Saint Lucy. There, according to the custom of the Church, they give him the name of Victor after his election. But since all these things, as we have said, were happening against his will, he put on the red cloak, but they could never persuade him to put on the white one.” And in chapter 67: “Victor yielded to prayers and arguments, and by taking up again the former election, the cross, and the purple, confirmed it.”

In Book IV, chapter 2, concerning Urban II, he says: “He is seized by everyone, and after being stripped of his woolen garment, he puts on a purple cloak.” Otto of Freising, concerning Leo IX (*Chronicle*, Book VI, chapter 83): “He had been designated for the See of blessed Peter, and when, having assumed the pontifical purple, he was traveling through Gaul,” and so forth.

Charles Sigonius, writing about Calixtus XI, says in a manner relevant to our subject (*On the Kingdom of Italy*, Book X, under the year 119): “But he, fearing that his election might be annulled by the Romans, resisted and refused to be adorned with the scarlet cloak unless letters and messengers had been received from Rome concerning this matter.”

The final mention of this purple garment occurs in the chapter “Constantinus,” in Gratian, Distinction 96, in these words: “Nevertheless, the purple cloak and scarlet tunic,” and so forth. Understand that the emperor granted the supreme pontiff the right to use these, just as the pontiff himself of the Holy Roman Church granted them also to the cardinals.]

## LETTER XXI. TO THE SAME CADALOUS, BISHOP OF PARMA, ALSO THE ANTIPOPE HONORIUS II

### Argument

He writes again to the same most wicked Cadalous, who, after receiving the preceding letter, had not only made no concession concerning his impiety but, daring worse things, had violently entered Rome with an army and, after engaging his opponents in battle, had become the author of a most bloody slaughter. Now he does not deal gently with him as he had done before, but accuses him with the severity he deserves; and, unless at last he comes to his senses, he threatens him with the imminent thunderbolt of divine vengeance.

Peter, the sinful monk, to Cadalous the pseudo-bishop: what he deserves.

If Nineveh, after Jonah’s preaching, had corrected itself so steadfastly from its wickedness that, having once rejected its vices, it had in no way entangled itself in them again, the prophet Nahum would certainly not have taken up this burden against it, so as to burst out immediately at the beginning of his book in these words: “God is jealous and the Lord takes vengeance; the Lord takes vengeance on his enemies and is angry with his adversaries” (Nahum I).

I wrote to you recently, before you attacked Rome with Satan’s minions, warning and solemnly declaring that you should restrain yourself from the purpose of so bloody an undertaking, confine yourself within the limits of your own measure, and stir up neither the movement of divine wrath against you nor the world against the Church in wicked wars.

But you, like Vesuvius [Vesuvius] spewing forth the flames of Gehenna, do not cease. You scatter, so to speak, the sparks of money among the people, and through the heat of greed corrupt the hearts of miserable men. You lay waste your own Church in order to obtain another’s. On one side gold and silver are weighed in balances; on the other, contracts, ratifications, and seals are issued, and documents are drawn up under mortgage law. Thus the estates of the collapsing Church are sold.

You lead behind you military camps armed more with gold than with iron, and coins are drawn from purses as though swords were being brandished from their sheaths. The phalanxes that follow you are roused to the standards of your warfare not so much by the blast of the *lituus*, the trumpet, or the horn as by the lure of the vein of ringing metal. For, as the peasants say, “Having a fistful of gold, you break an iron wall.”

But “riches,” as Solomon says, “are kept to the harm of their owner” (Ecclesiastes V). For what did gold profit Ptolemy, king of Egypt (Eutropius, *Roman History*, Book VI, at the end), who, after the naval war that he had treacherously and arrogantly waged against Julius Caesar, was killed by the waves and lay neglected and despised on the shore without a guardian? He was recognized among the others only because he was girded with a golden cuirass. It would have been better for him to live under a ragged covering than to perish in purple or gold.

The emperor Nero fished with golden nets (Eutropius, *Roman History*, Book VII), and, as histories relate, drew them from the deep with ropes of scarlet thread. Yet neither riches nor luxuries could free him in any way from the danger hanging over him. For when the Romans sought him for the unparalleled enormity of his crime and punishment, he fled in terror from the palace and inflicted death upon himself in the suburbs.

The emperor Justin possessed such a great abundance of treasure (Paul the Deacon, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 11) that his wife had iron chests made to guard the wealth. But afterward, when he lost his mind and destroyed himself, he also lost everything he possessed, together with the royal scepters themselves. Hence the prophet rightly says: “Their silver shall be thrown outside, and their gold shall be like refuse; their silver and gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. They shall not satisfy their soul, and their bellies shall not be filled, because it became the stumbling-block of their iniquity, and they set the ornaments of their jewelry toward pride” (Ezekiel VII).

The Gothic leader Alaric, as authentic history testifies (Jordanes, *On the Origin of the Goths*, chapter 30), while boasting that he possessed unexpected riches, died a sudden death in the region of Consentia. The Goths immediately diverted the river Busento from its channel into another course through the labor of captives. Thus, when the water in the channel had run dry, they buried Alaric there with many riches, and soon restored the river to its customary course. To prevent anyone from learning the place, they killed all the captives who had taken part.

Would that your own soldier likewise bury your money for you, so that through it, as it has already begun, the condition of the Church might not perish; so that what is recorded as having been said to your master might rightly also be said to you: “May your money perish with you” (Acts VIII).

The mother of Micah, as we read in the Book of Judges (Judges XVII), had silver from which an idol was cast. But far be it from us to say that as much sacrilege came from that silver as has come from your money. From that sum, scandal was produced in only one tribe of Israel; but your money is striving to overturn the foundation of the Christian faith and of the whole holy Church.

And, O unheard-of crime! Pilate’s soldiers did not dare to tear the seamless tunic of the Lord (John XIX), yet you divide the Catholic Church between two popes. They did not break the bones of the Savior hanging on the cross, yet by cutting the members of the Church—which is undoubtedly his body—you violate the sacrament of unity.

When the ark of the God of Israel had been captured in war, the princes of the Philistines did not dare profane it, but preserved it closed on every side and undefiled (1 Kings V). Yet you strive to vex and dissolve the mystery of Christian piety—not a mystery of stone tablets, but a heavenly mystery of the living and abiding word of God—with the wedge of roaring warriors.

If Uzzah dies because he puts out his shoulder so that the ark of the Lord may not fall (2 Samuel VI), what will rightly happen to the man who exalts himself over the Church of Christ so that he himself may appear elevated in its ruin?

Hear what the divine voice says to you through Obadiah (Obadiah 3–4): “The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rocks and raise your throne on high, who say in your heart: ‘Who will bring me down to the ground?’” Immediately it follows: “If you are exalted like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.”

It is clearer than light that David was anointed king through the ministry of Samuel, while Saul was rejected by the sentence of divine judgment. Yet as long as Saul lived, David did not presume to usurp even the smallest portion of the kingdom for himself.

But what shall we say? While Saul lived, David did not ascend to the summit of royal power; and even after Saul had died, he did not immediately set out to obtain the royal scepters. Instead, he humbly inquired whether he at least deserved the right to live in any city of the kingdom, saying (2 Samuel II): “Shall I go up to one of the cities of Judah?” When he was told by divine command, “Go up,” he did not at once suppose that he should go up wherever seemed best to him, but repeated his inquiry so as to gain certainty. He still asks where he ought most particularly to go up, lest he offend in even the smallest matter, God forbid, the judgment of the one directing him. “Where,” he says, “shall I go up?” The Lord replies: “To Hebron.”

Thus David, king in a kingdom divinely entrusted to him, does not presume not only to reign but even to dwell anywhere unless the divine command is renewed. Yet we, who are called priests, invade other people’s Churches like bandits and robbers and, while the world looks on and God forbids it, hasten to purchase them through a sale contrary to the decrees of the laws and the judgments of the canons.

Of such men Jeremiah says under the figure of adulterers: “I fed them to the full, and they committed adultery; they rioted in the house of the prostitute. They became lustful stallions, each neighing after his neighbor’s wife” (Jeremiah V). It follows: “Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord? And shall not my soul take vengeance on such a nation?” (ibid.).

Indeed, just as by amplification we say “Holy of holies” and “Song of songs,” so for the Roman Church to be sold for money is certainly the sin of sins. Whoever buys any Church is a Simoniac; but whoever reduces the Roman Church to a monetary valuation—what else does he attempt than to usurp for sale all the Churches throughout the world over which it has been set?

Just as Judas Iscariot sold the Lord for thirty denarii, so no fewer than thirty curses are found in the psalm that the prophet composed against him. These curses begin with the verse where it says (Psalm CVIII): “Appoint a sinner over him,” and end where it adds: “Let them be clothed with their shame as with a double cloak.”

If, then, the weight of a curse or condemnation is measured according to the measure of the sin, how great a destruction will the merchant of the Roman Church deserve, who, while trading in one Church, is shown to be purchasing all Churches together?

Therefore, I do not doubt that the sentence which the Lord threatens through Ezekiel rebounds upon you, saying: “The time has come; the day of slaughter is near, and not of the glory of the mountains. Now I will pour out my wrath upon you from nearby, complete my fury against you, judge you according to your ways, and lay all your crimes upon you. My eye will not spare, nor will I have pity; I will lay your ways upon you, and your abominations will be in your midst. Then you will know that I am the Lord who strikes you” (Ezekiel VII).

When Caesar Augustus died—the emperor under whom the Savior of the world deigned to be born—the Roman people, mourning, cried out in grief: “Would that he had either not been born or had not died” (Roman Martyrology, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; and Cardinal Baronius there; Eutropius, *History*, Book VII).

But concerning you, Cadalous, we may rightly say: Would that you had either not been born or had died at once. According to Scripture (Jeremiah XX), “may your conception have been an eternal conception”; may your mother have miscarried and not given birth; may she have brought forth a miscarriage rather than begotten offspring.

Eutropius relates (*History*, Book IV) that shortly before the Saguntines were captured by Hannibal through lack of food and forced to perish by the most extreme punishments, when a certain woman had almost given birth, the infant suddenly returned into her womb and portended the destruction of that city.

We would also wish that you, having returned to your mother’s womb, might have portended a sad omen over one city rather than, after reaching maturity, destroy the whole Catholic Church—not now by a sign but by living action.

For the furious desire to rule and the madness of an exaltation that ought not to be sought have plunged you into this, so that you are not content with the measure of one bishopric but aspire to universal dominion over the Church; and, so that you alone may stand out, you do not fear to plunge the whole world into ruin.

Certainly the emperor Diocletian, as ancient history records (Eutropius, *History*, Book IX), laid aside the insignia of royal power and, not far from Salona, remained a private citizen for almost nine years until his death, occupied with cultivating the pleasant greenery of a little garden. When Herculius and Galerius repeatedly begged him to resume the empire, he is said to have replied, as though shrinking from some plague: “If only you could see the vegetables planted by my hands at Salona; surely you would never judge that this burden should again be placed upon our shoulders.”

When Constantius, the father of the great Constantine, and Galerius were created Augusti (Eutropius, *History*, Book X), the Roman world was divided between them in such a way that Constantius held Gaul, Italy, and Africa, while Galerius held Illyricum, Asia, and the East. But Constantius, content with the dignity of an Augustus only together with Gaul, declined the burden of administering Italy and Africa as well. That excellent man, and one of the highest civic virtue, while caring for the wealth of private persons and provincials, did not greatly covet the advantages of the treasury; he judged it better for public resources to be held by private people than to be locked within the confines of a single treasury.

Thus the kings of nations, wearied by the burden of cares that press upon them, scorn the rights of more extensive rule and flee the summits of imperial dignity. But the priests of God, who ought especially to have preached this, raise themselves upon the horns of pride and pant to seize over the human race not a priestly staff but a royal—or rather a tyrannical—rod.

Those men lay down the weapons granted to their rank so that they may enjoy the leisure of peace; these, surrounded by legions of armed men like enemy camps, attack the Churches of Christ and fatten themselves on the blood of those falling by the sword as though on the fat of brute animals.

Even the evil owl, though it sheds another’s blood, spares its own offspring (Ovid, Book VI, *Fasti*). Saturn, when he tries to devour his own son, is astonished to find Abbadir [Ἀβαήρ; Latin: *tenuis, minutus*, “thin, small”] among his teeth.

You claimed that the Romans were your children, yet you resolved to devour them in the mouth of the sword—not as a father but like a cruel stepfather. Against the strong you found a hardness like stone, but against the miserable and weak you rejoiced to carry away a triumphal victory.

In this contest you are judged plainly to have surpassed the tyranny of King Totila, and your soldier exceeds the savagery of the Goths. For Totila, as a well-known history relates (Paul the Deacon, *Roman History*, at the end of Book XVII according to Eutropius), when he was besieging Rome with his soldiers surrounding it, and the enclosed people were suffering such famine that mothers had already resolved to consume the limbs of their own children, eventually entered through the Ostian gate. Wishing to spare the Roman citizens, he ordered the trumpet to sound throughout the night, so that, while they learned that the enemy had broken in from the continual blaring of the horn, they might hide themselves wherever they could from the swords of the Goths (Procopius, *Gothic War*, Book III).

But you and your soldier inflicted such slaughter in war upon the weak and untrained populace that the number of the slain is unknown. Certainly, when Pompey was fighting a civil battle against Caesar (Eutropius, *History*, Book VI), amid the horror he kept saying to everyone only: “Spare the citizens.” Caesar, by contrast, pressed on, saying: “Soldier, strike the face.”

You, therefore, driven by Caesarean cruelty, while inflaming the spirited hearts of your followers, brought back spoils and booty from the bodies of the slain, so that of you it may be said by analogy: “All the nations recounted the battles of Judah” (1 Maccabees III). And in all these things you strive for nothing else than to expel the pontiff of the Apostolic See and seize, as an invader of another’s rights, a non-vacant chair.

But so that you may know that this undertaking will by no means grant you a fortunate outcome, let us offer you an example from the neighboring and adjoining region.

The region of Piacenza borders upon you. Its bishop [Note: [Col. 0253] John, bishop of Piacenza, the antipope, concerning whom Cardinal Baronius, *Annals of the Church*, year 10] not long before our time proved to be an artificer of deceitful cunning and, like you, burned with more than sufficient ambition for exaltation and glory. So much so that he first obtained a silver cross to be carried before him, just as you are now said to be doing. He was also said to have had some disgraceful relationship with the empress who was then in power. Then, gradually advancing toward greater things, he finally violently invaded the Apostolic See with the support of money familiar to him.

After Gregory had been expelled—Gregory, a relative of the emperor Otto—he obtained the chair of the Roman Church, not as a great priest but as a thief and tyrant. But shortly afterward, when the Roman people came to their senses and unanimously burned with zeal for deserved vengeance, they rushed upon him, laid hands on him, tore out his eyes, and cut off his ears and nose.

Thus he experienced what the Lord, through the prophet Ezekiel, threatened both to him then and to you now, saying: “Against you will come those equipped with chariots and a multitude of peoples. They will be armed on every side with breastplate, shield, and helmet; I will set judgment before them, and they will judge you with their judgments.
