I will set my zeal against you, and they will deal with you in fury; they will cut off your nose and your ears, and what remains they will cut down with the sword” (Ezekiel XXIII).

And, to pursue to the end the history worthy of your attention: after the Romans had answered the pontiff as stated [perhaps: had repaid him], they immediately placed the illustrious rider backward on a little donkey. They made him hold the tail of his mount in his hands and compelled him to sing these words as they led him through the public road of the entire city: “Let such punishment be suffered by anyone who strives to drive the Roman pope from his seat.”

Let every fornicator of the Church hear this example. Let him tremble at the realization that even today the judgment of divine severity watches over him. Let him hear what the divine voice says to him through the same prophet: “Your final end will be consumed by fire; they will strip you of your garments and take away the vessels of your glory. I will make your crime and your fornication cease from you, from the land of Egypt, because thus says the Lord: Behold, I will deliver you into the hands of those whom you hate, into the hands of those from whom your soul has turned away. They will deal with you in hatred, take away all your labors, leave you naked and full of disgrace, and the disgrace of your fornications will be exposed. Your crime and your fornications have done these things to you” (Ezekiel XXIII).

To abandon one’s own Church and profane another Church with Simoniacal contaminations is recognized as a form of the most extreme fornication.

Moreover, if you should obtain the summit of the Apostolic See while God disregards the world, all the wicked rejoice and all the enemies of the Christian religion exult. Conversely, all who hunger and thirst for God’s justice, and who long to see works of piety, believe that, when you have attained the summit of affairs, the whole Church has reached its precipice.

## BOOK TWO. TO THE CARDINAL BISHOPS OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0253]

### 51–52. FIRST LETTER, TO THE CARDINAL BISHOPS OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0253D]

## Argument

He exhorts the cardinal bishops to order their lives, amid so corrupt an age and such widespread license in conduct, in such a way that all the others may regard them as models of character and set them before themselves for imitation. He briefly demonstrates how great is the obligation of integrity imposed upon priests, and especially upon bishops, since their office is to entreat God for the forgiveness of sins and faults on behalf of other human beings. If they wish to obtain that forgiveness, they must necessarily keep themselves, as far as possible, wholly free and untainted by every crime.

To the venerable and holy bishops in Christ, the cardinals of the Lateran Church, Peter, unworthy, sends an expression of profound devotion.

The guards of military watchtowers or of towers, so that they may present themselves more promptly, keep vigil through the untimely hours of night and often direct loud cries to one another: [Col. 0254D] thus, while rousing others, they certainly make themselves more watchful for carrying out their own sentry duty. So I too, who have been compelled to share, however inadequately, in standing guard for the camp of the ecclesiastical militia, write these things to you, venerable Fathers, and, with an unpolished pen, make a noise as though with hoarse cries—not so that sleep may leave you, since you are vigorously watchful, but rather so that I may awaken myself, yawning unawares beneath the torpor of sloth. For often we ourselves learn better while teaching, and are compelled, as it were by our own mouths, to carry out what we impress upon others, as Solomon bears witness when he says: “The soul of the laborer labors for himself, who compels his mouth” (Prov. XVI).

You see, therefore, beloved, that the whole world, bent toward evil, is rushing headlong through the slippery paths of vices; and the nearer it comes, now at last, to its end, the more heavily it heaps upon itself each day a mass of graver crimes. Indeed, almost everywhere the discipline of the ecclesiastical order is neglected, the reverence due to priests is not shown, the ordinances of canonical sanction are trampled underfoot, and care worthy of God is devoted only to the eager satisfaction of earthly [substance or desire, or something similar has been added in the source]. Moreover, in contracting marriages the legitimate order is confused; and—shame upon it!—those who outwardly cloak themselves under the Christian name live in truth like Jews. In fact, where are rapacities absent? Where are thefts guarded against? Who fears perjuries, pandering, or sacrilege? Who, finally, shudders at committing any of the most atrocious crimes? Long ago, plainly, we repudiated the pursuit of virtues, and the plagues of every perversity have emerged savagely, as though in a sudden assault. But lest we seem, like tragedians in high boots, to be raising a tragedy, let it be enough for us merely to repeat the Apostle’s words concerning these matters. For, as though drawing forth a prophetic oracle, he says:

> “But know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, accusers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, insolent, puffed up, lovers of pleasures more than of God, having indeed an appearance of holiness, but denying its power” (II Tim. III).

Amid, therefore, these profound and shipwreck-like dangers of a world in peril, amid so many yawning chasms of human ruin, the Roman Church alone and uniquely stands open as a harbor. To speak frankly, it is the net prepared by a poor fisherman, which rescues all who sincerely flee to it from the waves of the swelling storms and sets them ashore in the life-giving tranquility of safety. Hence this Church itself is distinguished by privileges superior to those of all the other Churches throughout the world; nor is it doubtful that it has also been founded and ordered according to mystical sacraments. To touch briefly on a few points among many: just as the Lateran Church is marked by the name of the Savior, who is indeed the head of all the elect, so it is the mother, and a kind of summit and pinnacle, of all the Churches throughout the world. It has seven cardinal bishops, who alone, after the Apostolic [one; the noun is absent in the source], are permitted to approach that most holy altar and celebrate the mysteries of divine worship. In this, surely, the oracle of Zechariah is clearly contained:

> “Behold,” he says, “the stone that I have placed before Jesus: upon the one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. VIII).

This stone is undoubtedly that rock concerning which the true Jesus makes a promise to Peter, saying:

> “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI).

This rock therefore has seven eyes, because the holy Church shines with an equal number of gifts of the Holy Spirit. Like a golden lampstand shining unquenchably, it drives away the darkness of ignorance and illuminates human minds so that they may contemplate the sun of justice. Concerning this the same prophet says:

> “I saw, and behold, an entirely golden lampstand, and its lamp upon its top, and its seven lamps upon it” (Zech. III).

Blessed John also did not conceal that he had learned this mystery in the Apocalypse, where he was told:

> “The mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven Churches” (Apoc. I).

This Church, therefore, founded in honor of the Holy Savior and made, so to speak, the height and summit of the whole Christian religion, is the Church of Churches and the holy of holies. On either side it has the Churches of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, established in different places but united by the structure of their sacramental meaning; for, situated, as it were, at a central point, it rises above them as the head above its limbs. With these two arms, as it were extended by divine mercy, that supreme and universal [Col. 0256B] Church embraces the whole expanse of the world. It cherishes and protects all who desire to be saved in the lap of maternal devotion. Supported by this citadel, Jesus, the supreme pontiff, binds his entire Church throughout the world together in sacramental unity, so that one priest and one Church may rightly be believed to exist. Hence the prophet says:

> “Behold the man whose name is Orient, and beneath him he shall arise; he shall build a temple to the Lord, and he himself shall construct the temple, and shall bear glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne, and he shall be a priest upon his throne” (Zech. VI).

But since it is not our purpose to comprehend all the mysteries of his figures, we leave these matters for others to consider and, as we began, turn back to the course of exhortation. [54]

We, then, my brothers—to bring myself boldly into your company—we, I say, who are like the seven eyes upon the one stone, who bear the image of the stars, who hold the dignity of angels through the office of proclamation: let us see, let us shine, and let us announce the words of life to the peoples not only with our voices but also by our conduct. The tongue of preachers indeed announces the sermon, but life commends it. Moreover, since people stream into the Lateran palace from different nations and from every part of the world, it is necessary that there, more than anywhere else, the pattern of right living should always be found, and that strict discipline should constantly be maintained in honorable conduct. And just as a coin lies continually in the furnace so that it may restore the image on damaged coins, so in the priestly household people ought to correct every falsity of their corrupted life. But if the standard of the coin itself has been obliterated or worn away, then, after it is impressed upon the metals, what is found is not a coin but a *paracaraximus*—that is, “without a mark.” The perversity of priests, when they are set forward as examples, is therefore more harmful than that of ordinary people. For when the person appointed as guide of a journey himself falls into a precipice, everyone who follows his footsteps must necessarily be plunged into the depth of the same ruin.

Meanwhile, let us consider what the outstanding preacher says concerning this statement:

> “Whoever desires the episcopate,” he says, “desires a good work” (I Tim. III). [Col. 0257A]

Here he plainly shows that a pontiff is nothing other than a pursuer of good work. For he did not say, “He desires a good dignity,” or “He desires a good honor,” but: “Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work.” It is as though he said: Whoever longs to possess the episcopate without good work wishes to put on an empty name without the truth of the thing itself.

The episcopate therefore does not consist in the turreted caps of the Gebellini or of overseas barbarians, nor in the flaming roses beneath the chins of Mars’ warriors, nor in the trappings of flowing gold ornaments, nor, finally, in the packed ranks of clustered soldiers, nor in raging horses champing their foaming bits; it consists in honorable character and the practice of holy virtues. Immediately he adds:

> “It is necessary that the bishop be irreproachable” [Col. 0257B] (ibid.).

Here the Apostle wishes the bishop to possess such perfection that he almost seems to speak beyond the limits of nature. For who, living in the flesh, can live so cautiously and look so carefully all around himself that he can never be found blameworthy? Woe to those who live blameworthily and yet, even more blameworthily, desire a position in which they may live irreproachably!

Among these are those who, forgetting affection for kin and homeland, follow the camps of kings through unknown and barbarous kingdoms of the earth. The ambition for perishing dignities drives them to this—something that the promise of heavenly rewards could not extort from them. Thus, unwilling to be content with their domestic means, they become foreigners among strangers; and, in order to seize a [stern?] rod over others, they render hard service to those set over them. Indeed, their departure would have been easier if they had once weighed out money to purchase honors at a price, rather than endure the hardships of so many labors and so many pressures. For when the prophet says of the righteous man:

> “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. XXXII),

who will defend from the giving of gifts the man who both subjects himself to the command of another’s servitude and, moreover, squanders the profits of his resources on the expenses of a prolonged expedition? [55]

[Note: [Col. 0257D] See Letter 3 of Book II.]

That prophetic statement is plainly expounded in such a way that three kinds of gifts are identified: a gift from the hand, a gift from service, and a gift from the tongue. A gift from the hand is money; a gift from service is obedient submission; a gift from the tongue is the favor of flattery. Since the prophet declares that one’s hands must be shaken free from each of these, the man who pursues the camps of exalted powers through ambition to obtain a dignity is proved to have entangled his hands in all of them. For when a considerable sum is poured out on acquiring conveyances and arranging various expenses, he is undoubtedly found liable for money given. Nor can anyone doubt that he also offers service to the person whose follower he has become, laboring under so great a burden of toil and travel. Finally, while striving to flatter his master and conform in everything to his will, he often assents to him through various favors of flattery.

Moreover, whoever, in giving or receiving ecclesiastical dignities, is corrupted by even one of the plagues mentioned above is judged to be held guilty of the crime of Simoniac heresy. What excuse, then, will those offer who, although they have not contracted a sale by words, are nevertheless shown by their actions to be caught not in one but in all of these snares? Yet they boast and glory in their innocence because they claim that they have not agreed to pay any sum of money for receiving honors. But tell me, cleric—whoever you are—if, after buying some golden vessel or estate, the seller demanded that, instead of the price retained by you, you provide him with such an expenditure of devoted service, would you not afterward assert firmly that you had acquired what you received at a just price? Not, evidently, because you paid money, but because you rendered service. You would say—and perhaps not shamelessly maintain—that it was bought more dearly when you afflicted yourself with so much labor and spent the resources of your means so many times than if you had counted out once the money of the stipulated amount.

Let them therefore by no means promise themselves innocence or trust that they are clean from the stains of Simoniac heresy, those who, although they do not weigh out glittering metals, nevertheless pay a price for receiving honors in certain quasi-talents of submission and service. Let this suffice as spoken against those who deny that they are guilty of a sale, although they have been burdened for a long time with harsh servitude through ambition for domination.

But you, beloved, to whom it has been given, by the authority of the apostolic see, to correct these and other wrongs, offer yourselves as a certain rule of living not only to the other faithful but also to priests. Let what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided be read in our life. Let no idle words flow from our lips; let the priestly tongue be restrained by the judgment of disciplined silence. Let jokes not release it; let immoderate joy not shake our breast. Let childish play depart; let biting eloquence and urbane wit vanish. Let obscene words be avoided, and let fictional conversations never be mixed in. For how can a prayer be directed pure from a priest’s mouth to God when that mouth is polluted by the filth of corrupt speech? Or how can a tongue become a mediator between God and human beings when, because of its own guilt, it itself deserves the judge’s anger? A guilty person uses supplications in his case; he is not himself found to be a culpable intercessor. [Col. 0258D]

Remember what is said to priests (Matt. V):

> “You are the salt of the earth.”

But, as the Truth says:

> “If the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned?”

A great deal is sweetened by a little salt, and by the small number of priests the whole multitude of the Christian people is purified and instructed. For just as bishops are known to hold the primacy of the twelve apostles, so the priests of the Church represent the order of the seventy disciples. This is certainly figured by that encampment of the Israelite people at Elim. There, twelve apostolic springs flowed forth, to drench the parched hearts of human beings with the rains of the divine word; there, seventy palms flourished—namely, the same number of disciples, who, when the world was oppressed by the slavery of the devil’s tyranny, would bring the palms of Christ’s victory. Those springs water the palm trees, because the sacred pontiffs overflow with words from which the other priests of the Church continually grow green in hope of heavenly rewards. They appear, by the number seventy—seven multiplied by ten—to signify that through the sevenfold Spirit of grace the tenfold law may be fulfilled.

Since, therefore, beloved, it is fitting that you should be not only priests but also teachers of priests, it is necessary that your life be a kind of line and, as it were, a seal of adamant, providing others with a pattern for living. An adamant seal impresses its own image upon other things, but receives an image from no metals. When, therefore, a multitude of people arriving from different parts of the world presses in upon you, when people of many different mixtures make a din, when each person importunately urges you to accommodate yourselves to him, let your countenance always shine with the same festive serenity, lest—God forbid—some childish frivolity break out in anything. Let mature gravity so compose the priestly face that the weakness of those who look upon it does not dread excessive severity. Let the sweetness of our cheerfulness charm others without allowing our seriousness to dissolve into insolence or wantonness. If someone begins to laugh or speak lightly and suddenly sees us, let him suppress his word, place a finger upon his mouth, and fall silent in fear. Thus indeed we become rightly sharers with Peter in the keys of the Church: when we present ourselves to all the other faithful as a fixed pattern and seal of living.

## Epistle II. To the Cardinal Bishops of the Holy Roman Church

(It is found in volume III and is work 31.)

[57]

## Epistle III. To Boniface, Cardinal Bishop of the Holy Roman Church of Albanum

(It is found in volume III and is work 22.)

## Epistle IV. To the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, Boniface, Bishop of Albanum, and Stephen the Priest

### Argument

He writes this letter on behalf of a certain abbot of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris, asking Boniface and Stephen, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, to show him humanity and clemency. But since he himself does not indicate why or in what matter he wishes humanity to be shown to him, it is certainly not permissible to guess.

To the holy and most reverend priests of the apostolic see, Boniface and Stephen, Peter, sinful monk, sends servitude.

I do not wish it to be hidden from you, my beloved brothers and lords, that this modern Jacob—namely, the rector of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris—has crept up to the summit of our mountain; indeed, he who is accustomed to crawl through level and unobstructed valleys, driven on by the spurs of fear, has been forced, as though by the rowing of wings, to fly swiftly over the steep mountain cliffs; and he who scarcely crawls, limping, across level ground now traverses the rocky ridges of the mountains by leaping.

Therefore I beseech the clemency of your brotherhood: since you two, like Peter and John, compel the lame man to run, offer him not gold or silver—which perhaps you do not possess with you (Acts III)—but the mercy that you do possess and in which you abound. Let his foundations and feet therefore be strengthened, so that he need not tremble at the ruin of his place or the destruction of his dwelling. Let it benefit him, then, to have climbed the summit of so arduous a mountain, and let him have cause to give thanks to God as he enters his temple again, walking, leaping, and praising God.

## Epistle V. To the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, Hildebrand the Archdeacon and Stephen the Priest

[Col. 0260B]

### Argument

He interprets the hidden mysteries of the whole creation of the world, and especially the Sabbath, on which day the Creator of all things ceased from every work. Through the Sabbath he teaches that Christ is understood: in him, after setting aside the pleasures of this world and laying down love of earthly things, the human mind rests most happily as though on holiday. Nevertheless, in order to attain this rest, it is necessary to reclaim our spirit from profane thoughts and the allurements of the world as from unjust possessors, and to reserve it sincere and undefiled for Christ its true Lord. For thus the true sabbath-rest will be fulfilled, when we establish an eternal dwelling both in him and he in us.

To Hildebrand, the twin of the apostolic see, Peter, sinful monk, sends an unbreakable bond of charity.

It is a common observation, beloved, that no wealthy person would overflow with abundant riches if the poor did not offer him, from their small resources, at least humble gifts or presents. Often, too, some delicate person is pleased by a poor man’s small vegetable and immediately has his fallen stomach refreshed by it, although until then a rich man’s food, as it were, had nauseated him like something sickening. Why, then, should I, although clipped in eloquence and poor in understanding, fear to address distinguished and learned men, since they themselves, together with us, are disciples not of philosophers but certainly of fishermen? Especially since Paul also says: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. I).

But since recently I have been separated from you in body, though not in heart, through my love of quiet, and have resolved to keep a spiritual Sabbath, I wish to discuss briefly with your holy prudence what concerns this Sabbath. Therefore, as one who celebrates the Sabbath, I explain what I think of it.

For throughout the whole law of the Old Testament I find no command laid down so strictly, enjoined so frequently, or impressed through so many admonitions. It is mentioned not only very often among the sanctions and ceremonies of the law but also in the frequent oracles of the prophets:

> “Keep the Sabbath day. Every person who does not observe the Sabbath day shall perish from his people” (Exod. XXXI).

What, then, ought we to understand by the Sabbath except Christ? In this Sabbath we rest when we place our hope in him alone, when we love him with all the affection of our heart, and, setting aside desire for temporal things, cease from the labor of servile works.

It is one and the same command of the law both to keep the Sabbath and to obey the words of the angel who goes before us:

> “Behold, I will send my angel, who shall go before you, guard you on the way, and bring you into the place that I have prepared. Observe him and listen to his voice, and do not think him contemptible, because he will not forgive when you sin, and my name is in him. But if you hear his voice and do everything that I speak, I will be an enemy to your enemies and afflict those who afflict you, and my angel shall go before you” (Exod. XXIII).

Hence, on the first of the tablets given to Moses, where only three commandments are written, this is found as the third. After it is written there:

> “You shall have no other gods;”

and:

> “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain;”

it immediately adds:

> “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX).

On the other tablet, where there appear to be seven commandments concerning not the divine substance but external matters, it begins:

> “Honor your father and your mother” (Deut. V),

concerning which the Apostle says that it is “the first commandment with a promise” (Eph. VI), because it is placed first in the order of the second tablet. Otherwise it ought rather to be called fourth than first, except with respect to the promise of longevity. For elsewhere he says:

> “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. XX).

Since, therefore, Christ is indicated by the Sabbath, the commandment of the Sabbath is rightly placed on that tablet where the faith in God alone is contained.

Even at the beginning of the world’s birth, when Scripture assigns morning and evening to each day, once it reaches the Sabbath it names neither of them, so as to show that the Sabbath is, as it were, wholly without beginning or end. For the historical text keeps this order (Gen. I):

> “There was evening, and there was morning, the sixth day. Thus the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were completed;”

and immediately it adds:

> “And God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made, and he rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had done.”

It had not first said anything concerning the creation of the Sabbath in the manner of the other days, but suddenly moved toward it as though toward something already known. And by mentioning neither its morning nor its evening, it showed in a certain way that it had neither beginning nor end.

Moses introduces the Sabbath in the likeness of the priest Melchizedek, concerning whom the Apostle says to the Hebrews:

> “King of Salem, which is king of peace, without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever” (Hebr. VII).

And rightly, things that signify one another under an allegorical figure do not disagree in the very order of the writing either. This too is shared by both: just as Melchizedek, king of Salem, is called king of peace, so the Sabbath is likewise interpreted as rest. These two, therefore, which express peace or rest in their names, fittingly converge in him who is supreme peace, through a typological signification:

> “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II).

And rightly the Creator of all things rested on this Sabbath, because in Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, the almighty Father found nothing at all by which he could be offended. Finally, he rightly rested in him concerning whom, in the hearing of the disciples, he thundered:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III).

In him he rested sweetly, and he commands us to rest. Hence in Leviticus he says:

> “Keep my Sabbaths and fear my sanctuary” (Lev. XIX).

For the one who is the Sabbath is also the sanctuary:

> “In whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II),

and concerning whom the Apostle likewise says:

> “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V).

But the same Truth also says in the Gospel:

> “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us” (John XVII).

And again:

> “I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected in one” (ibid.).

But how a human being can be perfected, and how he ought to be made complete, I wish to touch upon briefly, insofar as it can be found in the very order of the world’s creation. Since the human being is asserted to be a *microcosmos*—that is, a smaller world—it is necessary that, striving toward the growth of his fullness, he imitate the form of the world’s creation. Just as this visible and bodily world was completed through the mass and multitude of its parts, so our inner human being must gradually come to his fullness through the increase of virtues.

Concerning this spiritual fullness the Apostle says:

> “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV).

Then God said:

> “Let there be light” (Gen. I).

Light is said to be made in a human being when it is granted that the illumination of faith may shine upon him. For the first light of the mind is faith. Hence the Apostle says to those who already believe:

> “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

And this is the first commandment in the law:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI).

Thus the first day comes to be in a human being when someone newly comes to faith.

On the second day God made the firmament, which is heaven, and he made divisions of the waters, so that some flowed down through the lower regions while others remained in the higher places. What, then, is the firmament except the strength of the Scriptures? Hence it is read (Isa. XXXIV) that heaven will be folded up like a book on the day of judgment. What are the lower waters except the multitudes of human beings? And what are the upper waters except the choirs of angels? For the angels do not have the heaven of the Scriptures above them but beneath them, because they do not need to hear the word of God by reading it: they clearly behold God himself present and continually burn with his love.

When, therefore, a human being begins, through the firmament—that is, through the instruction of heavenly speech—to divide the lower and upper waters, separating carnal things from spiritual and earthly things from heavenly, then the second day comes to be in him, because he begins to possess not only the light of faith but also discernment of things.

Then God said:

> “Let the waters that are beneath the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear” (Gen. I).

After the division, therefore, between earthly and heavenly things, as has been said, the human mind must further divide these same earthly things among themselves in finer distinctions. Thus it must distinguish wicked people, itching with the brine of earthly wisdom, from the just who thirst for the fountain of faith, as the sea is distinguished from dry land.

For unbelievers, or any carnal people, are shaken by the bitter waves of temptations and swell like storms of desires or arrogance. [Col. 0263B] But all the holy and just, like dry land, thirst for God and, like fertile earth, strive to produce the green fruits of good works. Therefore God commands that on the same day the earth should bring forth green grass producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit. Whoever diligently carries these things out, whoever meditates on them subtly, undoubtedly sees the third day already rising for him. Let each person therefore separate himself from the bitter brine of those who think carnally; having become dry land, let him thirst from his inmost being for God, the fountain of life; let him bring forth the shoots of good fruits, so that the third day may dawn for him.

When these things have been arranged and healthfully ordered in this way, the human soul, as though the darkness of vices had been removed and put to sleep, begins to shine with the brightness of virtues. [Col. 0263C] Hence it is said that on the fourth day the luminaries were made in the firmament of heaven. For what does it mean that the earth first brings forth plants and immediately afterward the luminaries are created, except that, when the shoot of good work emerges, a more abundant light rises in the soul, so that it may be able to imitate the footsteps of its Redeemer?

Let the earth of the human mind therefore hasten to produce the yield of spiritual crops, so that it may be illuminated by the glowing rays of inward light, and, while enjoying the light of the fourth day, may also be carried away, like spiritual birds, to contemplate heavenly things.

Hence on the fifth day fish were created, by which those who receive the sacraments of baptism are signified; and birds as well, which signify those who raise themselves on the wings of virtues to contemplate heavenly things. [Col. 0263D] Whoever, after despising love of this world, disdains to tread the earthly mire and through the grace of contemplation lifts himself toward desire for heavenly glory possesses the fifth day together with the birds. Such a person no longer walks upon the earth but flies through the air, because, scorning all earthly things, he thirstily longs for heavenly things:

> “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI).

Such a person is formed, as a perfect man, into the image of his Creator, since he possesses so great a dignity of spiritual gifts that he is no longer merely instructed to maintain the rule of any of the saints, but strives, insofar as is lawful, to imitate God’s own example. As the Apostle says:

> “Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us” (Eph. V).

There was, indeed, a difference between Paul, who imitated Christ, and those whom he urged to imitate himself:

> “Be imitators of me,” he says, “as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XI).

Hence on the sixth day the human being was created according to the likeness of his Creator. Just as this was then accomplished at the beginning of human creation, so it is now brought about through the inner mystery of restoration. Moreover, among all the living creatures of earth, water, and air, the human being receives something like a monarchy and a position of superior excellence, because every perfect person, made complete in virtues, knows how to pronounce a right judgment concerning each of them. As the Apostle says:

> “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (I Cor. II).

For this reason the almighty God establishes the man who is dead to the world but alive to himself as his throne, and through him often publishes the decree of his justice. Hence, too, that angelic order through which almighty God most frequently determines his judgments is called the throne, because the supreme arbiter presides among them when he exercises judgments of equity through them.

God therefore establishes the perfect man as his throne, so that he may rest sweetly in him. Hence through the prophet:

> “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and gentle person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

It should also be noted that for each day it is said: [Col. 0264C] “There was evening, and there was morning.” Evening signifies the perfection of the good work itself; morning, the light of the mind. For when a good work reaches perfection, then the light of spiritual grace rises in the mind of the one who acts, so that, while he carries out the work outwardly, he himself is illuminated inwardly by the grace of the Spirit.

Thus one reaches the Sabbath, in which God, after completing his works, rests himself and commands the human being to rest. In this way the human being becomes God’s Sabbath, and God becomes the human being’s Sabbath, when the human being rests in God and God rests in him.

> “Remain in me,” he says, “and I in you” (John XV).

He himself is for us both a timeless time and a non-spatial place: non-spatial because he is not circumscribed; timeless because he never ends. He is time for us when he says:

> “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John XI).

By “the day” he means himself, and by the twelve hours he means the twelve apostles. A place, however, is unmistakably expressed where the prophet, after saying:

> “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail,”

immediately adds:

> “The children of your servants shall dwell there” (Ps. CI),

without doubt meaning “in you.”

God therefore made heaven and earth, and he is not said to have rested; he made the plants of the earth and the luminaries of heaven, and he is not said to have rested; he made all that feeds upon the earth or moves in the waters, and nowhere in all these things is he read to have rested. But after the human being had been formed according to his image, the Sabbath of rest immediately dawned, and thus the Creator of the universe rested. And although he himself says through the prophet:

> “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI),

what is not said concerning their creation is declared concerning the creation of the human being alone: that he rested. And, so that you may marvel more and more at the remarkable dignity of this day, Scripture says:

> “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work” (Gen. II),

something that is in no way found to have been done on the other days.

For what is it for God to sanctify the Sabbath except to build for himself a temple in the mind of a holy and perfect man? As the Apostle also says:

> “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (I Cor. III).

Moreover, just as we spoke of the Sabbath, so reason also requires us to speak of the temple, because God is the temple of man, and man is the temple of God; as it is said in the Apocalypse of John: “I saw no temple in it. For the Lord God almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. XXI).

God, therefore, is the temple of man; man becomes the temple of God. This temple of man is the spiritual paradise: namely, a holy mind, a perfect mind, a pure mind, distinctly formed in the image of its Creator. This mind, I say—or rational soul—is rightly called paradise, since it is watered by streams of heavenly gifts and adorned, like fertile trees or herbs, with the fresh growth of holy virtues. For that fountain, or river, which is said there to go forth from the place of delight to water paradise and which is divided into four heads, is the mind’s reason. From it, as from an original fountain, four virtues—justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance—flow forth like four life-giving torrents, making the soil of our heart fertile. The tree of life, moreover, is the wisdom of good things, concerning which Solomon also says: “She is a tree of life to those who have grasped her, and whoever holds her is blessed” (Prov. III). The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, however, is the transgression of the law that was enjoined, and the experience of misery. But since it is not our purpose to explain everything in order, it will suffice to have briefly previewed what is relevant to this subject.

It should be noted, moreover, that the soul of anyone who is reprobate becomes a confusion of Tartarus, while the holy, pure, and perfect soul becomes a likeness of paradise. For does not a mind that is hateful, greedy, devoted only to worldly cares, and inflamed by the fire of lust seem to you to be hell—in which, evidently, the devil dwells and the fires of desire never cease to burn? From luxury there arises a sulphurous stench, and from the dark gloom of ever-increasing thoughts volumes of smoke, as it were most hideous, are produced. For while it loves this thing, fears that one; rejoices in some matters, hates this one; eagerly desires that one—the mind becomes unhappy, always suspicious and restless, inquisitive, anxious and troubled at once. Driven by its cares, it is divided among many things and torn by the bites of different passions. Thus this lamentable soul has become Gehenna, Tartarus, and hell; it is tortured by the torments of cares and ravaged by the conflagration of vices.

But that soul which enjoys the light of its Creator, which is adorned with the fresh shoots of spiritual virtues, which, finally, the fountain of wisdom waters with four streams flowing from it and makes fruitful with the moisture of heavenly grace for producing the fruits of good works—this is unquestionably paradise; this is the garden of delights. Concerning it the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will pour out my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring, and they shall spring up among the grasses like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. XLIV). Then what is promised through the prophet Hosea is effectively fulfilled in it: “I will be like dew; Israel shall blossom like a lily, and his root shall burst forth like Lebanon. His branches shall spread, and his glory shall be like an olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon. They shall return, sitting in his shade; they shall live on grain and blossom like a vine; his memory shall be like the wine of Lebanon” (Hos. XIV).

This soul, then, just as it is read concerning the Sabbath, almighty God sanctifies and blesses, and in it he delightfully rests. This, truly, is the Sabbath; this is the temple; this is the sanctuary of its Creator.

Moreover, just as Egypt was struck by the plague of flies (Exod. II), while the Israelite people received the Sabbath as a gift, so the reprobate mind is always eagerly dispersed amid the restless affairs of this world, whereas the holy soul delights in the repose of its Redeemer alone. Hence it is that nowhere else, but at Reblatha, the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah and afterward put out his eyes (IV Kings XXIV). Clearly, while sacred Scripture narrates Zedekiah’s captivity, it announces the order of inward captivity.

For the king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, the possessor of intimate confusion. He first slaughters the sons before the eyes of the one who is watching, because he often kills good works in such a way that the captive himself sees with grief that he is losing them. 64 For the spirit often groans and yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, lovingly loses the good things it has begotten; it considers the losses it suffers, but nevertheless does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. Then, while it is struck by the perpetration of wickedness before its own eyes, it is eventually brought to the point where it too is deprived of the light of reason.

Thus the king of Babylon first destroys Zedekiah’s sons and then puts out Zedekiah’s eyes, because the evil spirit first removes good works and afterward takes away the light of understanding. This is rightly suffered by Zedekiah at Reblatha. For Reblatha is interpreted as “many things.” The light of reason is deservedly closed to the one who, setting aside the rigor of holy repose, is swept away amid worldly affairs. He is rightly made blind at Reblatha when, having despised the one, his restless and impatient mind is scattered among many things.

The Israelite soul, therefore, keeps the Sabbath when, removed from the noise of worldly affairs, it devotes itself to readings and prayers. But the Egyptian soul is struck by the infestation of swarming flies when it delights in the restlessness of earthly actions. For what in this life is more laborious than to burn with earthly desires? What is more peaceful and sweeter than to desire absolutely nothing of this world?

Solomon says: “Dying flies ruin the sweetness of perfume” (Eccl. X), because superfluous thoughts, which are continually born and perish in a mind thinking about carnal things, destroy that sweetness with which each person has been inwardly anointed by the Spirit. Hence, when truth comes to the heart through a wondrous work of mercy, it first drives out from it the heat of carnal thoughts and afterward arranges in it the gifts of the virtues. The sacred history of the Gospel aptly suggests this to us. When the Lord is said to have been invited to raise the ruler’s daughter, it immediately adds: “And when the crowd had been put outside, he entered and took her by the hand, and the girl arose” (Matt. IX).

The crowd is therefore driven outside so that the girl may be raised, because, unless the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the heart’s innermost chambers, the soul that lies dead within does not rise again. For while it disperses itself through innumerable thoughts of earthly desires, it does not gather itself together at all for consideration of itself. No one fully perceives wisdom, which is God, unless he strives to withdraw himself from all fluctuation of carnal actions. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Write wisdom in a time of leisure, and whoever is less occupied with activities will perceive it” (Ecclus. XXXVIII).

Since, therefore, we cannot be Israelites without the worship and observance of the Sabbath, let us celebrate the Sabbath of spiritual leisure, so that we may not, like the Egyptians, be disturbed by the intrusion of swarming flies. Since, by the gift of divine mercy, we have now reached the point of entering the Israelite land, it is not permissible for Israelites to be ignorant of its worship. Otherwise, if we do not learn their ceremonies, we shall be exposed to the bloody teeth of invisible lions.

For, as the sacred history of Kings testifies, it was reported to the king of the Assyrians: “The nations whom you transferred and settled in the cities of Samaria do not know the ordinances of the God of the land. And the Lord sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the rite of the God of the land” (IV Kings XVII).

Whoever, however, is established in the spiritual order and serves God through the outward appearance of his way of life, yet does not abandon the old habits of secular life, is in a certain sense judged to be ignorant of the worship and ceremonies of the one God and attempts, as it were, to serve several gods. Hence it is also said of them: “While they feared the Lord, they also served their own gods, according to the custom of the nations” (ibid.).

Anyone is in a certain sense convicted of worshiping the Lord and the gods of the nations if he administers the office of the sacred order in which he stands in such a way that he nevertheless does not withdraw from secular affairs and the habits of carnal life. “No one,” says the Lord, “can serve two masters” (Matt. VI).

Or does it seem more tolerable for someone to live carnally, or to offer the world the services of servitude, than to sacrifice to demons according to the rite of the nations? Yet the same Prophet who says, “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. XCV), also says: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). The same Apostle who says, “What agreement is there between the temple of God and idols?” (II Cor. VI), also says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. VIII). And again: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II).

The evil spirit, moreover, which is the author of the idol, is called the prince of the world. And James says: “Whoever is a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. IV). What difference, then, does it make whether someone rushes into enmity with God through sacrilegious offerings or through a reprobate life?

As we have already said, it profits us nothing that we have begun to inhabit the land of Israel unless we worship the one and only God of Israel without admixture of the gods of the nations. But what is the land of which we speak except that which Naaman the Syrian signified when he said to Elisha: “I beseech you, grant your servant that I may take away a burden of two mule-loads of earth” (IV Kings V)?

What, allegorically, does Naaman the Syrian signify except the human race? For just as Naaman, previously a leper, is cleansed of all the filth of leprosy as soon as he is washed seven times in the water of the Jordan, so the worldly people, receiving the seven gifts of that dove which descended upon the Lord in the Jordan, laid aside the contagion of sins through the washing of sacred baptism.

What, then, does the earth that Naaman requests signify except the incarnation of the Redeemer? This is, mystically, that promised land said to flow with milk and honey. Milk flows from the flesh; honey comes from above. Since, therefore, in the one mediator between God and human beings the milk of humanity and the honey of divinity are recognized to be present, the mystery of his incarnation is rightly prefigured by the land flowing with milk and honey.

But when he asks from this land for the burden of two mule-loads, what else does he request except the teaching of the two apostles, Peter and Paul? Hence one of them says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. II). And because not only apostles but all preachers must possess both knowledge and action, the Lord sent two disciples into the town that lay opposite them (Matt. XXI), and, as Luke testifies, he sent pairs into every city and place where he himself was about to come (Luke XII).

Thus, when Naaman seeks from the holy land a load carried by two mule-bearers, the human race appears to be demanding apostolic teaching concerning the Lord’s incarnation, so that these pack animals may transport into the world the earth from which an altar may be made in the sight of the Creator for the offering of sacrifices. Hence he commands the children of Israel, saying: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exod. XX).

To make an altar of earth for God is, of course, to hope in the incarnation of our Redeemer. For our gift is then received by God when, upon this altar—that is, upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation—our humility has placed whatever it accomplishes. We therefore place our gift upon an altar of earth if we make our actions firm through faith in the Lord’s incarnation.

Concerning this altar Isaiah says: “On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the Lord beside its boundary. And it shall be for a sign and for a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt” (Isa. XIX). That Naaman had requested the prophet’s land for no other reason than to build an altar to the Lord from it, he himself demonstrates in his words, when he immediately adds: “For your servant will no longer offer holocaust or sacrifice to foreign gods, but only to the Lord” (IV Kings V).

In this land, then, let us also worship God—not according to our own law, but according to his—so that what was said of them may not also be said of us: “They do not know the ordinances of the God of the land” (IV Kings XVII).

For the one who worships God according to his own law is seen to be someone who outwardly obeys his commandments, but in what he does chiefly looks to the advantage of his own profit. While he displays the external rule of Christianity, he conceals himself beneath the appearance of honesty, but inwardly he strives for this: to prosper in this life.

We worship God according to his law and ceremonies if we fulfill with every desire whatever we recognize him to will, entirely neglecting what belongs to ourselves; if we do not carefully consider how extensive our possessions may be, but how simple, how pure, and finally how sincere our conscience is inwardly; if we do not concern ourselves with how lofty horses gather their steps while we sit upon them, or how they seem to revel with their gilded necks, but with how we ourselves may deserve to have God as our rider; if we do not embrace every dead piece of metal, but store a living stone in the chest of our breast; if it is not the ornaments of gems that shine in our garments, but the pearls of virtues that gleam in our minds; if in our hearts there shines both the glass of purity and the gold of saving wisdom, so that it may now imitate that city of which it is said in the Apocalypse through John: “The structure of its wall was of jasper; and the city itself was of pure gold, like pure glass; the foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone” (Rev. XXI).

This soul, therefore, which is such, is unquestionably paradise; it is the garden of delights, whose inhabitant is God. While it enjoys the contemplation of its Creator, it is restored to that dignity in which the first human being had been created.

Hence, when the Lord was about to say in Leviticus, “I will place my tabernacle in your midst, and my soul will no longer reject you; I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people” (Lev. XXVI), he first said: “You shall eat the oldest of the old, and when new things come upon you, you shall cast away the old” (ibid.).

For the very oldest things for us are that the first human beings saw God in paradise; the old things are that the Israelite people kept the rite of circumcision and sacrifices and the commandments of various ceremonies. We therefore eat the oldest of the old with the mouth of the mind when, in the likeness of our first parent, we contemplate the appearance of God. We cast the old things far away when new things come upon us, while, as the grace of the Gospel flashes forth, we pay no attention to the observance of the Mosaic law.

Therefore, if we seek to possess the glory of paradise with God, it is necessary first that we offer ourselves as a dwelling place to him, so that, while he dwells in us and we in him, we may strive to celebrate not the Sabbath of ignoble leisure but of laborious repose, and thus deserve to pass into the Lord’s Day, which is enclosed by no end.

May almighty God, beloved, who has made you distinguished before human beings, grant that you may also truly be worshipers of his law in his sight.

## LETTER VI. TO THE SAME HILDEBRAND AND STEPHEN, CARDINALS OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

**SUMMARY.**—He bitterly complains that a book which he had recently completed through many labors and vigils was fraudulently taken from him by Alexander II, Roman pontiff, and earnestly begs Cardinals Hildebrand and Stephen to see that it is restored to him.

To his lord HILDEBRAND and his sweetest brother STEPHEN, invincible shields of the Roman Church, PETER, a sinful monk, offers servitude.

I lay before almighty God and before you, who are his members, a complaint against our lord the pope, who so frequently disturbs my heart with sorrow and provokes the soul of an already very old man to bitterness. For he took our book, which I had plucked with great labor from the scant resources of my poor little intellect and embraced like an only son in the arms of maternal tenderness. It is worthwhile for you to learn how he took it.

He knew that he could not obtain it from me in any other way. In my presence he handed it over to the lord abbot of Saint Saviour, ordering him to transcribe it. But during the night, without my knowledge, he took it and stuffed it into his own chests. Truly, this is priestly cleanliness of character—or rather, this is an indication of papal purity.

Yet when he is confronted about these things, he smiles and strokes my head, as though with oil, with the pleasant sweetness of playful courtesy. He regards the priest as a stage-player: while he attacks me with deeds, he sweetens me with words; his hand delivers a slap, while his face is roused to laughter.

Solomon compares such a man in Proverbs to one who says: “As one is guilty who throws spears and arrows toward death, so is the man who deceitfully harms his friend and, when he has been caught, says, ‘I was only playing’” (Prov. XXVI).

Roman history, moreover, records (Suetonius, ch. 48) that when Tiberius Caesar, because he too often stuffed himself with a great quantity of wine, was called Claudius Tiberius Nero, the stage-players said: “Caldius Biberius Nero”—a punning “Hot-Drinker Nero.”

Since I do not know how to dance but do know how to write, I too may perhaps one day write not what befits a priest but what befits a stage-player. I could easily sprinkle my lord’s name with playful wit, unless the excellence of such great dignity prevented me.

For Alexander is interpreted as “lifting the distress of darkness,” as is found in the interpretations of Hebrew names. What else is signified by these distresses of the darkness than the many labors and calamities that the madness and frenzy of Cadalus has inflicted upon us? Cadalus plainly aroused the distresses of darkness, which, according to the etymology of his name, Pope Alexander lifted, because while that man attempted, so to speak, through the sulphurous smoke of an Aetna-like desire to extinguish the light of the apostolic see, he compelled all of us to endure the distresses of darkness.

For this reason, not only our lord the pope but all of us may be called Alexanders in the presence of Cadalus, because while he imposes upon us the distresses of darkness, and we share in his labor, we are rightly judged to share also in his name.

But since one name signifies “to lift” and the other “to fall,” this struggle between the one who lifts and the one who falls forces us to recall the conflict that John narrates: “There was a battle in heaven: Michael and his angels battled with the dragon” (Rev. XII). Shortly afterward it is added: “And that great dragon was cast down, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (ibid.). Following his example, Cadalus also fell from heaven into Tartarus, when from the height of the apostolic see, which he hoped to attain, he plunged into the abyss of anathema.

Furthermore, no pontiff of this name is recorded to have presided over the apostolic see except that famous martyr whom we know to have been set fifth after blessed Peter in his chair and to have been pierced through in every part of his body. Since I am being forced into play, this name on the apostolic see claims for itself every kind of torment and does not depart from the ancient custom, possessing tribulation by inheritance.

Indeed, according to the interpretation of this name, the whole world has become Alexandria, since throughout the earth the entire universal Church is placed beneath the distress of various pressures. Here and there it is exposed to the plundering of reprobate people, torn by injuries, weighed down by the burden of calamities, and narrowed by possessions taken away day after day. While it suffers the winding arguments and tumult of perverse speakers, it is blackened, as it were, by the darkness of burning brands, saying through Solomon: “I am black but beautiful, O daughter of Jerusalem. Do not look upon me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me” (Song I).

But when our aforesaid lord hears these words, perhaps, as is his custom, he will immediately answer: “You speak harshly. What have I done? What serious wrong have I committed against you?” His response would resemble that of the sons of Dan to Micah, from whom they had taken everything he possessed: “What do you want? Why are you crying out?” (Judg. XVIII). He replied to them: “You have taken away my gods, which I made, and my priest, and everything I possess, and you ask, ‘What is the matter with you?’” (ibid.).

But since, as the wise man says, “Music in mourning is an untimely story” (Ecclus. XXII), although I am a stage-player, I do not wish to play while I am compelled to mourn in my heart; nor does one whose friend’s book has been lost take pleasure in plucking the strings of a lyre.

Let him therefore return the book if he wishes to possess a book-maker. And because of the brief sequence of a worthless little tract, let him not lose the poor author of that same style. Such, indeed, is the reward earned by so many labors and so many dangers of death, when we are forced to sing in a mournful voice the words of the Prophet: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. XLIII; Rom. VIII).

Just as the Gospel enumerates eight beatitudes (Matt. V), so Cicero, in his laws, describes no fewer than eight kinds of punishment. Since those beatitudes are as familiar to us in knowledge as I wish they were present in practice, let us here, according to the Ciceronian order, enumerate only the kinds of punishment: loss, bonds, scourging, retaliation, disgrace, exile, death, and servitude.

Since we have endured nearly all these things in the service of the apostolic see, it is, I ask, fitting that, as though the debt of punishments had been paid, we should now pay to that same see, above all, the interest of injury. Yet in the service of that same pope we do not seem entirely without the Gospel’s beatitudes either. For we possess the first and the last—poverty and persecution—and in these beatitudes we abound.

The Romans do not want Alexander, but the coppersmith—the one whom the Apostle condemns (II Tim. IV)—not the one who proceeds along the path of the apostles and apostolic pontiffs. They do not want Alexander presenting the Gospel money of the ecclesiastical table, but rather weighing the coins of sordid avarice. They reject Peter’s successor and embrace the disciple of Simon, who offers money for the sale of the Spirit (Acts VIII).

Therefore, since our lord has no time to give us what is his, let him at least not take away what is ours. For the apostolic sentence says: “Children ought not to store up for their parents, but parents for their children” (II Cor. XII).

But since, in presuming to speak against so great a father, we have exceeded our measure by accusing him, we ask from you, beloved, with impudent lips, the penance of repentance. In a dispute between servant and master, satisfaction is owed to the offender and repentance to the one who has been struck.

## LETTER VII. TO HILDEBRAND, ARCHDEACON AND CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

(It is found in volume III and is opusculum 32.)

## LETTER VIII. TO THE SAME HILDEBRAND, ARCHDEACON AND CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

70 **SUMMARY.**—He complains to Hildebrand that he has discovered himself to be little loved by him: first, because Hildebrand never wrote to him; then, because in his speeches he spoke of him disparagingly. He shows how undeservedly this has happened to him, since he had always striven to obey Hildebrand to the best of his ability and loved him with the greatest affection. Finally, he renounces the episcopate. This, evidently, is believed to have been the reason why Hildebrand showed himself angry with him: in that necessity of the times and scarcity of good priests, he did not wish the Church to be deprived of so holy a prelate.

To his lord HILDEBRAND, archdeacon, PETER, a sinful monk, offers servitude.

I wonder, venerable brother, why your holy mind cannot be softened toward me by any circumstance, so that you do not utter even one word—especially when I am absent—either to me or about me that appears to belong to the office of charity. Whenever either a delegation is sent to me or some mention of me perhaps arises in your presence, the name of my insignificance is immediately rejected, my reputation spat upon, my levity mocked, and such things are said about me that they are a pleasant story to my enemies but a sorrowful disgrace to me.

Clearly, after I was bound to the Roman Church [Note: He means the cardinalate, so to speak.], would that I had always striven to obey God, or Peter, as much as I obeyed your initiatives and efforts, and that in all your struggles and victories I had thrown myself in—not as a fellow soldier or attendant, but like a thunderbolt. What contest did you ever begin in which I was not immediately both litigant and judge? In such matters I followed no authority of the canons except the judgment of your will alone, and your mere will was authority for me as though it were the canons themselves. Nor did I ever judge what seemed right to me, but what pleased you.

Moreover, inquire at least of the lord Cluniac, who is not unknown to you, in how great a blessing your name was upon my lips. For once, when I was discussing you, he said: “He does not know that such sweetness of his love exists in you; if he knew it, he would surely burn with incomparable love for you.”

But why am I prolonging this section of writing, when I do not expect you to read it? Certainly no one lives in the flesh to whom I would write more willingly, if you would deign to cast your eye upon it. But since there is no such hope, see how careful and polished the style is—what flowers of eloquence it contains, how the elegance of its diction shines.

But whether you see it or do not see it, through these letters I return to you the episcopate that you gave me, and cut away from myself every right and power that seemed to belong to me over it.

71 ## LETTER IX. TO THE SAME HILDEBRAND, ARCHDEACON AND CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0273C]

**SUMMARY.**—Again he complains to the same Hildebrand that he had placed faith in the malicious statements of certain people who falsely asserted that the holy man had built a monastery on another person’s land. He plainly demonstrates that this was false.

To his lord HILDEBRAND, the immovable pillar of the apostolic see, archdeacon, PETER, a sinful monk, sends greetings.

I give you abundant thanks, venerable brother, because when you were striving toward the summit of the royal court, I perceived the love that burned around me radiating from the sanctuary of your heart. Nor is this surprising: since God is said to be a consuming fire (Deut. IV; Heb. XII), the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit may appear to be set aflame by certain sparks bursting forth.

For wherever mention of my name occurred along that journey, my memory was held by you in blessing. This both raised the spirits of my friends and closed the lips of my detractors with barriers of fitting reply.

Nevertheless, [f. “it is reported,” or something similar] at Florence your mind, which had always been accustomed to be cautious and firm against empty talkers and liars, seems to have been softened by the persuasive influence of certain detractors. For the followers of Count Guido, with their servile herd, were calumniating me, saying that I had built a monastery from those estates which they had once granted, out of their lord’s generosity, as a stipend for his dependants.

[Col. 0274A] Why, I ask, did you not then remember that saying: “Food, a rod, and a burden are for the donkey; bread, discipline, and work are for the servant” (Ecclus. XXXIII), where it immediately follows: “Loosen his hand, and he seeks freedom” (ibid.)? Why did that little verse also slip from your memory: “The yoke and the strap bend the hard neck, and continual labors incline the servant”? (ibid.) Why did your memory not recall this as well: “Torture and fetters for a wicked servant. Send him to work, so that he may not be idle”? (ibid.)

But what wonder if crafty servitude and cunning were able to deceive you, although you are a prudent and holy man, when they compelled David himself, full of the prophetic spirit, to depart from justice through the sly lies of Ziba, Saul’s servant? “You and Ziba,” he said, “shall divide the possessions” (II Kings XIX).

That man falsely accused the innocent Mephibosheth of acting against the royal majesty; these men assert that I have renounced the condition of servitude. But, I ask, brother, could not Tethgrimus, this Guido’s uncle, who died without children, have bequeathed at least some small portion of his many fields and estates—those, at any rate, that seemed to border the monastery? Or will he still be judged unworthy of an obedient group, since when he himself departs from this life no posterity succeeds him?

Will it not be permitted even to him who helped, since dependants possess everything, to offer something to God from his own allodial property? Would you judge it proper that those who are assigned to turn spits over the fire or wash cauldrons should possess their lords’ goods in such a way that their masters, when departing from the world, leave nothing of their own property to the holy churches?

Do you consider it fitting that our slaves should display blazing faces and put on ornaments of precious attire, while we endure the punishments of burning hell? Shame! That they should flow in abundance while we are constrained by poverty! They should belch up yesterday’s banquets while we seek a crumb among the dead!

He rightly loses his inheritance who leaves a slave as heir. He deserves to be excluded from the number of sons who, disregarding his own salvation, substitutes a servile slave for himself.

Let the mouth of those who speak wickedly therefore be stopped; and, in accordance with the Prophet, let ears be hedged about with thorns against the lies of deceitful detractors (Ecclus. XXVIII). They present flattering words to the face, but conceal within the poison of malice; like bees, they carry honey in their mouths but sting with their barbs.

And what wonder if we, who are striving toward the land flowing with honey, are torn by the stings of bees flying around us? The man who said this was certainly hastening toward that land: “They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns” (Ps. CXVII).

To this is added that, since we are striving to hasten toward the honey of the land of the living, and since, while offering the sweetness of the divine word, we also carry honeycombs in our mouths, swarms of bees fly around us here and there to sting us with the barbs of their detraction. For it is written: “Honey proceeds from the mouth of the prudent” (Prov. XVI). And the Beloved says to the bride: “Your lips drip with a flowing honeycomb, O bride; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song IV). She in turn says of the bridegroom: “His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable” (Song V).

What wonder, then, if, as we hasten toward honey and carry honey in our mouths, swarms of bees fly around us on every side to pierce us with the stings of detraction?

Hence it is that when the Israelite people were hastening through the desert toward the promised land, they first camped, as the old edition has it, at Gai; then they came to Dibongad (Num. XI). Gai is interpreted as “chaos.” And what is meant by chaos except the heart of perverse people—dark, foul, and deep? For the heart of man is perverse, as Scripture says, and inscrutable; who among human beings can know it? (Jer. XVII.)

Dibongad, however, signifies “an apiary of temptations.” After chaos, therefore, one comes to the apiary, because once a dark, deceitful, and deep heart, after the manner of Gai, has been overshadowed by the darkness of malice and fraud, it eventually advances through an increase of wickedness to the point where the wicked flatter their neighbors, like bees, with the honey of their presence, but sting those who are absent with the barbs of detraction.

From Gai, therefore, one comes to Dibongad; from chaos one comes to the apiary, because from the fraudulent malice of a dark heart a wicked person advances to inflicting the arrows of detraction.

What, then, shall I say of you? Although at first you preserved toward me the rights of our united concord, eventually you nevertheless neglected to break the jaws of barking dogs, and did not shrink from granting faith to detractors. “Many calves and fat bulls surrounded me” (Ps. XXI), and you listened patiently.

I shall therefore say of the archdeacon of the highest see what was then said of the apostle James: “O, even the just man has gone astray.”

But since we must pray impartially both for those who favor us and for those who harm us, I shall conclude the complaint I have laid down with the ending of a prayer.

May almighty God, venerable brother, both repay you with a manifold reward for the service of the great love you have shown and mercifully forgive you for having agreed with detractors.

## LETTER X. TO PETER, CARDINAL ARCHPRIEST OF THE LATERAN OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

(It is found in volume III and is opusculum 18.)

## LETTER XI. TO DESIDERIUS, ABBOT OF THE SACRED MONASTERY OF CASSINO, PRIEST AND CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, TITLE OF SAINT CECILIA

**SUMMARY.**—He instructs Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, with most salutary admonitions. First, that he should always keep his own faults before his eyes and his virtues behind his back; that he should not take others’ corrections badly but embrace them; that, according to his office, he should not neglect the faults of his subjects but correct them; that he should not disparage those who are absent but rebuke them to their face; that he should love fasting; and, finally, that he should continually celebrate the sacrifice of Christ’s passion.

To the most reverend abbot DESIDERIUS, PETER, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

Sacred history bears witness (2 Kings XIV) that Absalom repeatedly sent messengers to request that Joab, the commander of the army, come to him; yet Joab scorned to come. When Absalom sent for him again, but Joab, obstinate and unyielding, absolutely refused, Absalom immediately sent to his field and set fire to the barley harvest, [Col. 0276A] with which it was full. Joab came at once to confront Absalom; and Absalom rejoiced that he had won his approach by such benefits—namely, that what he had not obtained by requests, he had secured by injuries.

But I, venerable brother, have written to you not twice but many times; nevertheless, up to this day I have not wrung from you even a single jot, so that you might deign to write back. You yourself also promised that you would send me a secretary who would at least transfer onto parchment at your expense those things I had written specifically to you. Yet you have entirely refrained either from replying to one who writes or from sending the secretary, as you promised. Of these alternatives, one is demanded by charity, while the other is urged by truth as the payment of a debt.

What, then, shall I do? Since I cannot rouse you by striking and tickling you as though you were asleep, I shall prick you, and in this way at least I shall succeed in making you wake. I shall therefore take up the rod of instruction toward you as a teacher, and, as though you were my equal or dependent, I shall presume to remind you of matters that perhaps are more familiar to you than to me. Let this be my pricking: that I wish to teach one who is more learned. Perhaps, awakened by this affront, you will wake up, so that, having denied charity its due, you may at least repay the one who injures you in kind. Nevertheless, let younger brothers regard the one whom you see cheerfully offering you these suggestions as plainly giving serious counsel.

Come, then, brother: do not do what most people do, attending only to whatever virtue there may be in you, and neglecting to judge your vices as though they had been placed behind your back. Imitate the natural example of the peacock’s diversity. [Col. 0276C] It always keeps its dark-colored and, as it were, undistinguished feet before its eyes, while displaying behind itself the conspicuous beauty of its tail. In its feet it sees something rustic to despise; in its tail it fails to recognize what makes it remarkable. It has at hand what should humble it; behind its back it carries what might make it boast, as though it were superior to the other birds.

You, too, should in some manner keep hidden whatever virtue there is in you; but whatever is vicious and deserving of correction should never leave the judgment of your sight. Do not take the zeal of fraternal correction amiss, but embrace it with joy, and pour it into the inner parts of your languishing soul like the antidote of a sure cure. Remember, therefore, what is said through Solomon: “Open correction is better than hidden love. The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates” (Prov. XXVII). And elsewhere: “Sudden destruction,” he says, “will overtake the man who stubbornly despises one who corrects him, and healing will not follow him” (Prov. XXIX). Attend also to what he says: “He who hides his crimes will not prosper; but he who confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Prov. XXVIII). And again: “He who loves discipline will love wisdom; but he who hates reproof is foolish” (Prov. XII).

Glass, indeed, because it admits the sharpness of vision and reveals whatever is hidden within it, would seem superior to all metals, if it did not break so easily when struck. But because it shatters immediately at the first blow of the one who strikes it, a talent of glass scarcely equals three-quarters of a talent of silver. A purple rose appears more radiant than scarlet dye; but because it withstands no hardship, it is counted among stalks of rubbish.

Moreover, since you have been appointed ruler of a holy community, do not overlook guilt; but as soon as it emerges, apply discipline, so that zeal may advance you, like Phinehas, to the rights of the eternal priesthood (Num. XXV), and so that sudden vengeance may not strike you, like Eli, ignobly yawning beneath the torpor of sloth (1 Sam. IV). Hence it is said through Solomon: “Do not withhold discipline from a boy. If you strike him with the rod, he will not die. You strike him with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from hell” (Prov. XIII).

Nevertheless, beware lest excessive severity in discipline become harshness, [Col. 0277B] and lest the uncontrolled fervor of zeal turn into anger; otherwise, while the rust of guilt is being scraped away, the fragile vessel may be shattered. Hence Solomon also says: “Do not befriend an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his ways and bring a stumbling-block upon your soul” (Prov. XXII). Elsewhere: “It is better to dwell in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and angry woman” (Prov. XXI).

Some people, plainly, when they recoil from the charity of their brothers because of the fuel of impatience, turn to their own defense the fact that Paul and Barnabas separated from one another because of Mark the disciple (Acts XV). It is certainly clear that this happened not through the fault of discord but by the judgment of divine dispensation, so that the holy apostles, like grains of wheat scattered for the sowing of faith, [Col. 0277C] might produce a richer harvest precisely because a breeze of disagreement blew them far apart from one another.

Never disparage those who are absent, but rebuke them to their face, appropriately, as circumstances dictate. Hence we read in Proverbs: “Remove a crooked mouth from you, and let deceitful lips be far from you” (Prov. IV). And in Ecclesiastes: “If a serpent bites in silence,” he says, “he is no worse than one who secretly slanders.” A wise man also says: “The whisperer and the double-tongued are accursed; they have disturbed many who were at peace” (Ecclus. XXVIII). But to the one who listens he says: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue; make doors and bolts for your mouth and for his ears” (ibid.). We are commanded to hedge our ears with thorns against a wicked tongue, so that we may blunt every slanderer with the point of a thorny reply.

Love fasting, so that while the body is worn down by hunger, the soul may be fattened with the richness of heavenly grace. And let that serpent, which had struck down the man who ate with the weapon of food (Gen. VIII), now succumb to the one who fasts, overcome by the arms of sobriety.
