For the serpent, as those who have diligently investigated the nature of things report (Pliny, book XXVIII, chapter 4), dies immediately if it tastes the spittle of a fasting man. If fasting has such power over this beast that crawls bodily, how much greater must we believe its force to be against that dragon which crawls invisibly?

But so that you may break this serpent more effectively, strive to offer frequently the saving victim of the sacrifice, so that when it sees your lips reddened with the blood of Christ, it may tremble in terror, flee at once, and not presume to approach more closely the sacrament by which it was taken captive. Thus, its strength immediately exhausted, let it collapse, and, so far as you are concerned, let it remain perpetually hidden and buried in the pit of its own wickedness.

But now I impose silence on my pen, because I myself reproach my audacity in this presumption, and, like one who has sent fire into a harvest, I flee immediately, lest I be caught burning the yield of a fertile field when I ought to have set fire only to thorns and wild shrubs.

## LETTER XII. TO THE SAME DESIDERIUS, ABBOT AND CARDINAL

**Argument.**—This letter, like the preceding one, is entirely exhortatory. For it urges the same Desiderius to care tirelessly for the monastery entrusted to him, to avoid flattery, to think humbly of himself, to direct the monks—especially those who are simpler—along the way of perfection, and finally to raise himself to the summit of contemplation.

To the venerable lord DESIDERIUS, abbot, PETRUS, the sinful monk, offers his service.

Although fire consumes everything around it, it nevertheless naturally rises above itself and always strives toward higher things. So too fraternal love, which burns in my heart for you, is by no means content with you alone or establishes its end in you; through you it is also transferred to the common Creator. For love is useless, arid, and tasteless when it occupies itself with one’s neighbor in such a way that it is not also extended to God. And although the love of God is primary, through love of the neighbor whom we see we arrive at love of God, whom we do not see (1 John IV).

Meanwhile, as I attend closely to you, whom I love, I always raise my eyes to him whom I long to reach together with you. Join and clasp hands, therefore, and, to lighten the labor of the journey, let us encourage one another with mutual exhortations. But because you are bound by the obligations of governing a most distinguished monastery, beware lest, amid the labors of this road, weariness weaken your courage, or the soothing words of flatterers enervate the strength of a mind that gives them an evil assent.

I therefore recall to your memory what Scripture testifies concerning the righteous man Tobias: “It happened,” it says, “that one day, wearied from burying the dead, he came home, threw himself down beside the wall, and fell asleep; and from a swallow’s nest, hot dung fell upon the eyes of the sleeping man, and he became blind” (Tob. IX).

Weary from burying the dead, when he throws himself down even with his strength broken, he loses the light. Whoever perseveres indefatigably in good works preserves the eye of his heart unharmed; but when he is broken by faintheartedness, he is rightly deprived of light. Hence it is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance!” (Ecclus. VIII). Hence Paul says: “Watch, stand firm in the faith, act courageously” (1 Cor. XVI).

But what do lightly flying swallows signify except the frivolous conduct of flatterers and smooth speakers? While they charm with the sweetness of their flattering speech, while they grease the head of the listener with the oil of flattery, they blind the inner eyes so that they cannot enjoy their accustomed light: “Let the righteous strike me,” he says, “in mercy and reprove me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. CXLVIII). And they thrust dung into the eyes when, with the bland verbosity of seductive speech, they smear anyone with their wheedling eloquence.

From them these things are often said: “Live while you live; refresh your body with food, lest, if it wear itself down too rigorously, fragile flesh, oppressed by so many labors, soon succumb.” “Let your person be adorned with more gracious clothing, so that the dignity of the rank you hold may retain its proper character. Let a crowd of clients gather at your sides like a wedge, so that, when the multitude of visitors adorns you, the lofty honor of your office may not become insignificant.”

But when this bitterness of diabolical malice is exposed to us, the darkness of the temptation introduced vanishes completely. Hence it is also said there: “Then Tobias took some of the fish’s gall and anointed his father’s eyes; and immediately the white film began to come out of his eyes like the membrane of an egg, and at once he recovered his sight” (Tob. XI).

For the fish’s gall is the malice of Behemoth, which is the head and beginning of all iniquity. [Page 77] The blind man is therefore anointed with the fish’s gall, and blindness is immediately dispelled, because when the bitterness of diabolical cunning is set before our eyes and exposed, the darkness of shadows is at once driven away, and the inner light, which had seemed to undergo an eclipse, is restored.

It should also be noted that it is said first that the white film came out of his eyes, and that only then was the light immediately restored. He bears a white film in his eyes who has an opinion of holiness concerning himself. Whoever, therefore, wishes to recover the light must first cut away from himself the white film of pretended esteem, so that he may not deny himself to be a sinner if he wishes to escape the blindness of sin.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). These are the eyes of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within” (Song IV). For although the saints now behold their Creator through the grace of contemplation, something great still remains hidden, to which the keen sight of the human mind in this corruptible flesh does not aspire.

Immediately thereafter it says: “Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Gilead” (ibid.). Just as the doctors of the Church are understood by the eyes, because they are appointed over the lower members in order to see higher and spiritual things, so by the hair and the flocks of goats are signified the simple and the subject. Although, by reason of their simplicity, they penetrate every mystery and exalted reality, by their number and arrangement they adorn the holy Church as hair adorns the head.

A goat, because it is often offered with sin, is a figure of sin; Gilead means “heap of testimony.” Through Gilead, therefore, we understand Christ, to whom the multitude of all the saints bears witness; through the hair, or the flocks of goats, we understand the multitude of subjects. The flocks of goats therefore ascend from Mount Gilead, because the multitude of all the saints strives to climb to the heights of virtue from Christ, whom they make their foundation.

But why has the course of this discourse brought this example into the middle of its exposition, except so that you may understand that just as there is a distance between the eyes and the hair, so there should be, almost to the same degree, a difference in the practice of contemplation between rulers and subjects? Thus you should be the eye of those entrusted to you: intent upon spiritual pursuits, seeing both for yourself and for them.

From this there frequently arises an outpouring of tears, a salutary compunction. Hence we read in Genesis: “This is Ana, who found warm waters in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of Sebeon his father” (Gen. XXXVI). Taken literally, this plainly seems empty and frivolous. For what relevance does it have to Sacred Scripture to report that a keeper of asses found water in the desert? But where no usefulness appears in the written words, the mind must necessarily turn to spiritual understanding.

What does it mean figuratively for Ana to pasture the asses of his father in the wilderness, except for a spiritual man, whose father is God, to guard simple brothers under the discipline of a more secluded way of life? And what does it mean to find warm waters except to break forth into tears of compunction, which are drawn out by the fervor of the Holy Spirit?

The very interpretation of the names does not resist this understanding. For Ana is interpreted as “pain,” or “their sadness,” and also as “muttering” or “murmuring.” Whoever is saddened by the pain of compunction is, as it were, compelled by a kind of plaintive muttering to murmur against the wickedness of his own life. Sebeon, however, is interpreted as “standing in equity,” which no one at all is unaware is fitting for God. For he principally stands in equity who, compelled by no necessity, deviates from the straightness of justice.

When, therefore, Ana pastures the asses of his father Sebeon in the wilderness, he finds warm waters, because whoever shows himself to be God’s son through the uprightness of his life and grieves from the depths of his being over his sins, while making himself solicitous in the constant care of his brothers, receives by divine gift the grace of tears. For that blessed sinner first anointed the Lord’s feet with ointment, and afterward poured an alabaster jar of precious ointment over the head of the one reclining at table (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; John XII).

The head of Christ is God; the feet of Christ are the servants of God. Just as that woman, while rendering service to Christ’s humanity, was deemed worthy to attain an understanding of his divinity, so likewise the teacher of the Church, while guarding Christ’s members, receives the grace of contemplating the divinity.

Moreover, there are some simple brothers who do not know what contemplation is and therefore cannot in any way exercise themselves in spiritual pursuits. Yet while they mortify themselves completely to this world, while they strive to weary themselves through various labors in obedience, and while they burn to obey their superiors in all things, they obtain a place of intimacy with almighty God, so that through them signs of virtue are sometimes even performed.

Just the other day, when the sun was already inclining toward setting, a certain brother named John came to me and told me of a miracle that had happened to him some time before, one worthy of celebrated remembrance. “When I was living,” he said, “in the monastery at Classe, and was guarding the sacred chamber entrusted to me, one day after Compline I gathered the church books into the archive. Then, pressing in the key, I locked it, as I was accustomed to do every day. But, as later became perfectly clear, a flame had escaped without my knowledge from the candle I was carrying and had breathed upon the cloth with which the book was covered.

“When morning came and I opened the chest to remove the books, smoke and fiery vapor suddenly met my face. Immediately astonished and terrified, I began carefully to search whether anything might still remain of the books. But—O the incomprehensible effect of divine power!—although all the approximately twenty cloths in which the codices had been wrapped had been burned and reduced to ashes, the codices themselves were entirely unharmed.

“Furthermore, the fire had penetrated the chest and left a broad circle of combustion on its bottom. When the brothers learned this, they praised divine power, because just as God had protected the Hebrew boys in the Chaldean furnace (Dan. III), so now, amid the blaze of a burning chest, he had also preserved his own books.

“That brother who told me these things is indeed unlearned, but his obedience is so fervent and his life so devout that it does not at all seem unworthy that God should have deigned to display a marvel through him.”

You, venerable brother, should therefore guard the house of God with the flock entrusted to you in such a way that you do not abandon yourself through negligence. Cultivate Leah’s fecundity in bearing offspring, but do not withdraw from the embraces of beautiful Rachel (Gen. XXIX). Do not throw yourself into the flatteries of flatterers, lest, while the empty words of frivolous people delight you, the eyes of your mind, like those of Tobias, be covered with swallow dung (Tob. II).

If there is someone who corrects you in a friendly manner, lend him your ears with equanimity. But turn away from flatterers as though spitting and nauseated, lest what Solomon says apply to you: “Sudden destruction will overtake the man who stubbornly despises one who corrects him, and healing will not follow him” (Prov. XXIX).

Of such people Isaiah also says: “For this is a people provoking to anger, and lying sons, sons unwilling to hear the law of God; who say to the seers, ‘Do not see,’ and to those who behold, ‘Do not behold for us the things that are right. Speak to us pleasing things, see for us errors; remove from me the way, turn aside from me the path; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before my face’” (Isa. XXX).

Therefore, as we have already said above, [Col. 0281D] let us approach with confidence the throne of grace (Heb. IV). Let us abandon the darkness of the world; let the gloom of earthly desire be removed from our eyes, so that, when the darkness of carnal passions has slipped away, the splendor of the true Sun may burst upon us. Let us pant for him who dwells in inaccessible light (1 Tim. VI), and let us hasten with the innermost approach of our heart toward him who awaits us, the author of true light.

If we earnestly seek warm waters in the wilderness, we can find them, so that, when we are withdrawn from the world, the fervor of the Holy Spirit may kindle us and the moisture of salutary compunction cleanse us from defilements, as Isaiah says: “The Lord will fill your soul with splendors and deliver your bones; and you will be like a watered garden and like a spring of waters whose waters will not fail” (Isa. LVIII).

When this has happened, the human soul becomes a paradise, and truly becomes, as it were, a garden of delights. Then love of this world is turned into bitterness; the mind, freed from the bonds of carnal affection, is lifted on high and delights in the ineffable companionship of its Creator alone, as the same prophet says: “Then you will delight in the Lord, and I will raise you above the heights of the earth and feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father” (ibid.).

Let us strive toward this, dearest brother: let us extend ourselves toward the banquet of inner refreshment; let us never cease hungering for these delights of heavenly food, so that, while we fail through this seemingly small breakfast lest we faint on the road, we may be nourished by that full dish of the wedding feast which is in heaven.

And although the care of government may oppress you with various affairs, let your mind nevertheless return, whenever it can, to the bosom of inner quiet. Imitate Moses, who frequently entered and left the tabernacle of the covenant (Exod. XXXIII). What does his repeated entering and leaving the tabernacle mean except that he provides an example: the one who is carried away inwardly into contemplation is frequently pressed outwardly by the affairs of the weak; inwardly he considers the secrets of God, while outwardly he bears the burdens of those subject to the flesh.

He also always returns to the tabernacle concerning doubtful matters and consults the Lord before the ark of the covenant, plainly offering rulers a model: when they are uncertain outwardly about what they should arrange, they should always return inwardly, as if to the tabernacle, and consult the Lord, as if before the ark of the covenant, if in their inward uncertainty they seek the pages of sacred speech concerning the matters about which they doubt.

Hence Truth itself, shown to us through the assumption of our humility, spends the nights in prayer on the mountain, while by day it shines forth in the cities through signs of miracles. In this way it lays out a path of imitation for good rulers, so that, even if they desire to contemplate the highest things, they may nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak through compassion. For charity rises wondrously to high things when it mercifully draws itself down to the lowly, and the more kindly it descends to what is below, the more vigorously it returns to what is above.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE SAME DESIDERIUS, ABBOT AND CARDINAL

**Argument.**—In the fragments of this letter, in which, as the superscription testifies, he was discussing the renunciation of dignities, he interprets certain passages of Sacred Scripture mystically from the Books of Kings.

To the lord DESIDERIUS, abbot . . . PETRUS, the sinful monk:

Who would not be built up and stirred toward the perfection of charity by this passage (1 Sam. XXVIII)—who, I say, would it not urge not only to practice the dutiful devotion of humane kindness, but also to return good for evil? It concerns that famous Pythoness, clearly worthy of the praise of great acclaim. In imitation of God, she treated Saul so well, although he had already been abandoned at the royal summit and was destined on the following day to be killed by the swords of the Philistines; and, like a prudent serpent according to the Gospel (Matt. X), she bestowed a benefit on one from whom she hoped to receive no advantage.

Moreover, as she herself complains, he had exterminated all the diviners and magicians from the land of Israel, and by this means had deprived that same little woman of all the income of her accustomed divination. She cooked the young calf that remained to her from her scarcely surviving poverty, and, mixing unleavened bread from a very small quantity of flour, set it before him to eat.

When he, mourning and terrified by the nearness of death, rejected this and absolutely refused to take food, she, on the contrary, persisted without ceasing with urgent prayers and with certain arguments, as it were, so that he might repay the one who was asking as she had repaid him, and, just as she had obeyed his command, so he might yield to the requests of the woman pleading with him:

“Behold,” she said, “your maidservant obeyed your voice, and I placed my life in your hand, and I heard the words that you spoke to me. Now, therefore, you too hear the voice of your maidservant, and I will set before you a morsel of bread, so that, when you have eaten, you may regain your strength and be able to make the journey” (1 Sam. XXVIII).

Who, when the Gospel was shining forth, would do what this woman is described as having done beneath the shadow of the Law—especially since the Old Testament offers the saying: “You shall love your friend, and hate your enemy” (Lev. XIX; Matt. VI; Mark XII), whereas the evangelical trumpet thunders terribly: “For your Father will not forgive you your sins if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts”?

Saul was so hostile to diviners and magicians that he killed all of them indiscriminately, and scarcely any one of them remained except this poor woman. Even this one who remained was so tightly constrained by the ferocity of the royal persecution that, since she did not dare to practice divination at all, she had completely lost the customary income of her own art.

Yet she cheerfully offered good for evil, returning what remained to her, and fed her enemy, as though the Apostle were already commanding this (Rom. XII; Prov. XXV). And this praiseworthy woman did these things at a time when she knew that he would immediately die, and therefore neither hoped that he would become peaceful nor feared him when angry.

People use arguments to drive from their own houses guests who are unwilling to lodge there, sending them to nearby taverns or shops. One place, they say, is inferior, another preferable. Here, they claim, because of the harshness of last year’s weather, a sickly crop is said to have denied food to the farmers; there, the yield of fertile grain is said to have overflowed. Sometimes the shortness of the journey is praised; sometimes the sun is said to occupy the higher spaces of heaven. With such careful arrangement of words, nothing else is accomplished except to compel those who arrive to provide themselves with lodging elsewhere.

This prudent and noble woman, however, so to speak, engages in rhetoric and employs the speeches of orators, so that her enemy, while resisting and recoiling, may be induced to eat.

### 2 Kings XIII, throughout

Absalom is interpreted as “peace of the father.” Through him the Jewish people are signified, for they persecuted Christ even unto death. Concerning this people Isaiah says: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. I). It is rightly called “peace of the father,” because in that people especially God seemed to have rested through the Law that was given, through the sacrifices of victims, and finally through the tabernacle or temple.

As David says: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV). And so that this people may seem to be the peace of the father, hear what follows: “And his place has been made in peace” (ibid.).

Alternatively, Judas the traitor is signified by Absalom. He too is not improperly called “peace of the father,” as Christ himself complains of him in the psalm, saying: “For even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, magnified his deception against me” (Ps. XL).

Nor is Christ inappropriately asserted to be the father, as the prophet testifies: “He will be called,” he says, “Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX). Thus Christ is called the Prince of Peace, and Judas the peace of the father. To Judas, moreover, at the very moment of his persecution, Christ did not deny the kiss of peace (Matt. XXVI).

Nor is it surprising that Absalom represented the figure of Judas the traitor, whom he expressed not only in David’s persecution but also in the very manner of his death. Absalom clung to an oak when he tried to pass by; Judas, as Scripture testifies, hanged himself with a noose. Thus, because each was overflowing with the viperous gall of wickedness and unworthy both of earth and heaven, suspended between the two, he would lose the earth and be unable in any way to reach heaven (Matt. XXVII; 2 Kings XVIII).

Achitophel also, who similarly desired to persecute David (2 Kings XVII), chose the same kind of death, as his merits demanded. For Achitophel gave Absalom, who was pursuing David, the counsel that he should pollute his father’s concubines, whom David had left to guard the house, with sacrilegious intercourse, and should disgracefully commit incest with his stepmothers in order to defile his father (2 Kings XVI).

What, then, are signified by David’s ten concubines except that part of the Jewish people which does not follow Christ, the true David fleeing into the deserts of the Gentiles, because it boasts that it possesses the Decalogue of the Law? By the number of the concubines, the number of the commandments is expressed. The concubines, therefore, who do not follow David but guard the house are those who persevere in the guardianship of the Old Law.

Absalom therefore enters David’s concubines, because the devil, who was in Absalom, fornicates with such people through the excesses of various crimes. And it is rightly said that David had left them to guard the house. For by the provident dispensation of our Redeemer, it is divinely arranged that the remnants of the Jews should be preserved, as it were, to guard the house of the Law, so that they may in some manner be our scribes and carry throughout the world the books of heavenly speech in the very language in which they were composed. Thus those who are our enemies may, whenever a scruple of doubt arises, remove every ambiguity for us.

Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, show me good things among my enemies; do not kill them, lest at some time they forget your law” (Ps. LVIII). For the authority of the Christian faith is greatly assisted by the Hebrew language, which is dispersed throughout the whole world. If that testimony were not added—the testimony that is written among us—it could in some manner be thought a fabrication. But when that testimony is brought forward, doubt is immediately removed.

Hence there too it openly adds: “Scatter them in your strength” (Ps. LVIII), as though the Son were saying to the Father: Scatter and disseminate throughout the whole world those who remain from the Jewish people, so that they themselves may bear witness from the ancient books to the truth of the new faith.

When David came to the camp, Sobi son of Naas, Machir son of Ammiel, and Barzillai the Gileadite brought him bedding, carpets, earthen vessels, and so forth (2 Kings XVII). What else do the Midianites who provided King David with bedding and carpets signify except Gentiles converted to the faith? While they persist continually in devout actions, they prepare, as it were, the linen cloths of a weaver’s work, on which the Lord may rest sweetly.

These are those evangelical garments that the apostles place upon the donkey and make Jesus sit upon (Matt. XXI; Mark XI; Luke XIX).

As for what follows—“For they also gave David earthen vessels, wheat and barley, flour and beans, lentils and roasted chickpeas, honey and butter, sheep and fattened calves” (2 Kings XVII)—the many kinds of foods are the diverse dispositions of holy people. David is fed with these together with his fellow soldiers, because our Redeemer, together with his saints, feasts as though hungry upon the righteous works of the just.

Berzellai the Gileadite, very old—eighty years of age, as sacred history attests—coming down from Rogelim, led King David across the Jordan. The king said to him: “Come, he said, so that you may rest with me in Jerusalem” (II Kings 19). But he declined, pleading the excuse of old age, and, leaving the king, soon returned to his own home.

There are, then, some who, following King David—that is, our Savior—cross the streams of the Jordan: that is, they either receive the sacrament of baptism or undertake what is, in the second place, a spiritual way of life. Since Christ, the author of baptism, was baptized in the Jordan (Matthew 3; Luke 3), baptism is rightly understood through it. But these people, changing their clothing but not their mind, altering their outward appearance but not their disposition, return to their former ways and resume secular activities. Since they cannot rest from the turmoil of worldly affairs, they do not wish to dwell with the king in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace.

For they are old and aged, and therefore cannot be changed from their long-standing way of life into something new. They cross the Jordan and are eighty years old, because they have been baptized and believe in the future resurrection, which is signified by the number eight. Yet although they speak humbly and courteously to the king, they abandon him and return to the habits of their customary way of life. For what is it to offer the king flattering words except, as it is said in the Gospel, to excuse oneself craftily rather than humbly? “I ask you,” he says, “to have me excused” (Luke 14).

Berzellai said to the king: “Why should your servant become a burden to my lord the king? Your servant will go forward a little way with you from the Jordan, and I do not need this exchange of service” (II Kings 19). Those who assume his role address some spiritual man, who urges them toward higher things, as though humbly singing: “We are indeed sinners, Father, and we obey you, but we cannot keep the rule of a stricter discipline. We are weak and fragile, and therefore we judge it better to live somehow without distinction under a light burden than, under the weight of a heavy load, to perish utterly while appearing strong.”

What this same Berzellai had said earlier also agrees with the old age of their inner person: “How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?” (Ibid.) And he added: “Are my senses still vigorous enough to distinguish what is sweet and bitter? Or can food and drink delight your servant? Or can I hear the voice of male and female singers?” (Ibid.)

Truly, the inner senses of such people are dulled, because they do not discern the spiritual nourishment of the mind or the instruments of inward rejoicing. That heavenly food does not taste good to them, the food to which the Prophet invites spiritual banqueters: “Taste,” he says, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33). Nor do their throats discern those honeys of which he said: “How sweet are your sayings to my palate, Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Psalm 118).

They have not yet reclined at that banquet of Wisdom of which it is said in the Book of Proverbs: “For Wisdom has sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table” (Proverbs 9); and it continues: “She sent her maidservants to call from the citadel and the walls of the city: Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Ibid.).

These people do not hear the voices of male and female singers either, because they cannot comprehend the melody with which holy martyrs and holy virgins rejoice before God. Since they live carnally and do not raise their hearts to the Lord in contemplation, they are unaware of the measures of heavenly harmony and the honey-sweet delights of angelic song.

It is therefore not without reason that the old man Berzellai is said to have been from Rogelim, which is interpreted as “feet.” Such people walk on foot; and because they do not know how to lift themselves above the path of earthly conduct, they do not rise to grasp the songs of heavenly melody. They wish always to proceed only on foot, and therefore cannot penetrate the lofty inner joys of rejoicing. Since earthly actions, in which they are scattered, make them hard and insensitive, they cannot contemplate the subtle things of spiritual gladness.

For this reason, too, this Berzellai the Gileadite is said to have been so called because the name is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Since that heap of testimony, called Gilead, is known to have been made by Laban and Jacob from stones (Genesis 31), the Gileadite aptly signifies hard and stony people who, because they do not soften their hearts toward the love of spiritual life, become like stones and grow hard in the stubborn rigidity of worldly affairs.

The same hardness is also indicated by the fact that Berzellai is said to mean “my iron.” What is harder than iron? And what is more obstinate than a perverse heart? “Wisdom will never enter a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1). Appropriately, “my iron”—as though any hard and obstinate person were speaking of himself—because, while he resolves to persist in his own hardness, he never commits himself to the counsels of another.

Because he is rigid and inflexible, he does not proceed with King David toward the heavenly Jerusalem; from the road that he had begun with Berzellai he is recalled to the land of Madian (II Kings 20), that is, to the beginnings of his former life.

When King David had entered Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines whom he had left to guard the house and placed them under guard. He did not go in to them, but they remained confined until the day of his death, living in widowhood.

The concubines who do not follow David but guard the house are those who persevere in guarding the old law. Of these concubines it is expressly said: “David no longer went in to them; they remained confined until the day of his death, living in widowhood.”

The Jews are plainly now confined and live in widowhood, because they do not approach the husband of the holy Church. Nor does that heavenly bridegroom enter in to them, since he disdains to share his dwelling with them as with little women prostituted by the devil; and because they have been polluted by adultery, he gives them a bill of repudiation.

Those who do not follow the husband are rightly called concubines and are not called wives, because, wholly unworthy of the marriage covenant and nuptial union, they do not produce that offspring which might possess the inheritance of the father’s blessing. To us, by contrast, it is said: “For you have been called to possess the inheritance of blessing” (II Peter 3). The Apostle likewise says: “Therefore those who are of faith will be blessed with faithful Abraham. But whoever is of the works of the law is under a curse” (Galatians 3).

## LETTER XIX. TO PETER, CARDINAL DEACON AND CHANCELLOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

**SUMMARY.**—He praises Peter, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, very highly, and says that he desires to be joined to him in friendship; at the same time he commends to him the condition of the holy Church.

**86** To Lord Peter, chancellor of the sacred palace, Peter, servant of the servants of Christ, offers the service of most fervent devotion.

Dearest, since I am not unaware of what Rome is at this time, and since I also frequently hear who you are, my mind returns to this one thought: he who can cause a shining lily to grow amid dense thorns (Song of Songs 2) also wished to display you as such a man amid the Roman strongholds [variant: arts]. Therefore know beyond doubt that I desire to possess your charity, and that I greatly long to be joined to you by a special friendship and a bond of united concord.

The distance between our places cannot hinder this desire of mine. I do not see the eye of my own head, through which I see, yet I nevertheless enjoy the benefit of its service; and because an eye comes before me when I speak words of example, may you be my eye in this matter, may you be my teacher, so that through you I may be permitted to see whether I can accomplish anything in the presence of this most blessed apostolic lord.

Unless the Roman See returns to a state of uprightness, it is certain that the whole world will remain sunk in its error and fall. It is already necessary that the same see should be the beginning of renewal which was the foundation of the birth of human salvation.

But since a man of such prudence is satisfied with little, let rusticity not offend urbanity. I ask that you not disdain to write back to the reader. Understand, in this very brief parchment of my writing, the extensive library of my heart.

## LETTER II. TO GEBEHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

**SUMMARY.**—Having been recalled to his homeland by the archbishop of Ravenna, he excuses himself for not yet having obeyed, being detained by the needs of the monks entrusted to his care. He then praises and exhorts the same archbishop. Finally, he asks that the burden of his journey be for the time being remitted, if this can be done.

To Lord G., bishop of the second see in Italy, Peter, the least of hermits, offers the service of most devoted servitude.

You commanded me, dearest Father and lord, and by commanding me ordered me to come to you. But when I undertook to govern a poor little place—having previously been poor only by myself—I have now become poor through as many people as I have received to govern. I therefore consider both what it means to govern many people and not to possess the means necessary to provide for them.

Therefore, while I attended to the brothers’ needs, I could not easily come to you. Nevertheless, while I carefully consider this very matter, I in a way regard it as sacrilege if I postpone obeying your holiness on any pretext. For who could safely disobey one whom he does not doubt obeys God through holy works?

To you, who by God’s appointment preside over the See of Ravenna, the entire holy Church in Christ has given thanks—especially since, at a time when the Simoniac dragon pours venom through the twisted coils of his greed, you alone, almost among them all, remain unharmed as an invincible soldier of Christ: you pierce the throat of that most wicked beast with Peter’s spear, keep your Church pure from all its poisonous contagion, and preserve inviolate through the chair of a noble disciple what the fault of shepherds—or rather, of robbers—caused the master’s see to lose.

Amid all these efforts of your holiness, however, this is much dearer to me: that your pastoral eye watches over the salvation of the monks and does not cease to bring hidden wounds, long concealed, into the light and cut them away with the surgeon of discipline.

Come, soldier of Christ, gather your strength courageously and, surrounding everything with the eye of your prudence, fight manfully against all the devices of the devil. Slaughter avarice, trample down pride, raise up the fallen, and extend the right hand of holy exhortation to those who waver, so that you may both protect yourself with the shield of holy virtues and defend others from every assault of the ancient enemy.

I ask you, dearest, if it can be done with your permission, not to allow me to be troubled at this time. If not, command with full authority whatever you wish.

## 89 LETTER III. TO THE SAME GEBEHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

**SUMMARY.**—He shows that he is held by such love for Archbishop Gebehard that he can scarcely endure longing for him in his absence. He urges him immediately to set right the condition of the Churches of Pesaro and Fano by removing their disgraceful rulers. Finally, he commends to him the abbot of Classe.

To Lord G., most reverend archbishop, Peter offers the service of most devoted servitude.

My dearest Father and lord, the tongue that so frequently complains of your absence bears witness to the longing with which I burn for you and to the flame of your love that consumes my breast; my conscience also bears witness, for it contemplates so clearly the serene and angelic appearance of your face.

In that chamber of my heart—not where my father or mother is, but where I myself am—I carry you, another self, hidden within me. Therefore I humbly ask that you return to me the due of mutual love, and that the grace which proceeds from you in simplicity may return to me doubled.

Those who come to you from our region, seeking to conduct some business in the presence of my most holy apostolic lord, will easily be able to persuade me of this.

Therefore, dearest Father, present yourself in the matter of the condemned bishops of Fano and Pesaro in such a way that I may truly find you fearing God’s judgment, fighting manfully against the ministers of the devil, tearing up the withered shrubs of the devil’s plantation, and willing to bring Christ’s Church back from darkness to the light.

But I do not want you to be unaware of one thing: if those infamous and criminal men remain in the fortress of the episcopate, the reputation of the pope, most illustrious lord, will suffer no little; and you, who are his counselor and possess the wisdom of such comprehensive learning, will undoubtedly incur the stain of reproach.

I ask and humbly entreat you to receive my dearest father, the abbot of Classe, in my person, and to understand that whatever benefit or affection you extend to him, you extend personally to me.

## LETTER IV TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

**SUMMARY.**—Consulted by Archbishop Henry about Cadalous the antipope and Alexander II, and asked which of the two ought to be judged the legitimate pontiff, he replies—as was just—that Alexander should be regarded as the true pontiff, while Cadalous, as a Simoniac and schismatic, must be condemned and rejected by everyone. This can also easily be recognized from the conduct of the two men. He rejects as unbecoming the advice given to him by the same archbishop, namely, that he should disapprove of Cadalous’s election secretly and not openly. He says that one must fight for the Church of God not in secret but in the sight of men.

To Lord H., most reverend archbishop, Peter, sinful monk, offers the service of due submission.

Venerable Father, as soon as I saw the letter stamped with the seal of your holiness, I eagerly took it up, gladly unfolded it, and read it carefully. In it I clearly discovered both the affection of your piety toward me and the definite promise concerning what I had previously requested of you.

At the end of the letter you added that I should write to you what I thought about the man who now presides over the apostolic see and about the one who appears to have been elected to that same see. Although you could already have learned from some sons of your Church what our judgment is concerning the difference between these two men, nevertheless, since you command it, we set it down even in writing.

The former, so far as I can judge, is a Simoniac without any excuse, because, while all of us—cardinal bishops of that city—protested, resisted, and pronounced terrible anathemas, he was enthroned at night while armed bands raged and raised tumult on every side.

Afterward he hastened to the fatal protection of purses: money is distributed among the people through the regions, streets, and alleys; the venerable treasury of blessed Peter is invaded; and throughout the whole city, as though it had been turned into a workshop of the evil craftsman Simon, scarcely anything but the ringing of hammers and anvils [variant: anvils] is heard.

And, O wickedness and dreadful portent! Peter is forced to pay the fairs of Simon out of his own resources, although he is known to have condemned Simon and all his commerce to perpetual curse.

As for the fact that he disguises this crime and excuses himself with whatever words he can, claiming that he was dragged and compelled by force, I do not know the matter in full detail, yet I do not entirely deny it myself. He is so foolish, sluggish, and lacking in intelligence that one might believe he did not know how to contrive such things on his own.

Nevertheless, he is guilty in this respect: in the mire into which he was once violently thrown, he now rolls of his own accord, and he persists with delight in the adultery that he had previously committed unwillingly.

To avoid prolonging, as they say, tearful words about his own promotion: while we bishops were fleeing through various hiding places, the priest of the Church of Ostia—who, if only he knew how to read one page properly, letter by letter—was seized and dragged away by the satellites of Satan and violently brought forward to raise him to the summit of the apostolate.

And behold: although the decrees of canonical sanction are not unknown to you, even if every objection that can be brought against him were suppressed, this one matter alone is sufficient, and he can in no way escape from it. If a priest must certainly be deposed because he usurped the privilege of the pontiff for himself, how can the man who was ordained by him stand, when the very person who ordained him has been judged to have fallen from his dignity because of him?

To this is added the fact that Pope Stephen, of pious memory, after gathering bishops, Roman citizens, clergy, and people inside the church, had established under the strict sentence of excommunication that, if he should happen to depart from this world before Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Roman Church, who was being sent with the common agreement of all, returned from the empress, no one should elect a pope; rather, the apostolic see should remain vacant and untouched until his return.

There is much more that could be said about these matters. But lest your holiness, occupied with many affairs, should become weary of lengthy words—and lest the briefness of a letter exceed the limits of its rule—let this suffice for now.

To satisfy your inquiry also in this respect, this is my opinion of the elected man: he is well educated, quick-witted, chaste without suspicion, and generous in distributing alms. I add no more, lest I seem a lover of the whole rather than an advocate of one individual.

As for the other, by contrast, if he can fully explain to me a single verse—not of a psalm, but even of a homily—I will do nothing more against him: I surrender, I kiss his feet, and I shall call him not merely apostolic but even an apostle, if you command it.

As for what you wrote—that I should send you a letter marked by silence, advising me as a father lest I perhaps encounter adversity if I expressed the thoughts of my heart freely—far be it from me in such a matter to evade enduring what is harsh and bitter, or, by neglecting the incest of so noble a mother, to hide like a degenerate son under a shadow.

Rather, I ask that this letter be made public, so that through you all may know what ought to be thought about this danger to the whole world. Concerning the blessing of yours which I requested, venerable Father, I say only this: whatever is given to the one who is sent is undoubtedly placed into the hands of the one who sent him.

## LETTER V. TO WIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

**SUMMARY.**—He asks Archbishop Wibert, who was coming to visit his monastery, not to take away the money he had intended to take, out of consideration for the monastery’s poverty and need; he should be content with the things he had taken previously.

To Lord W., most reverend archbishop, Peter sends greetings.

We give thanks to God, King of kings, because, while the approaching day of the Lord’s Nativity is already illuminating the whole world, your illustrious arrival also brightens our city. Thus I am glad to exclaim: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

Nevertheless, venerable Father, I am greatly surprised that after I came to you, and after I was recalled from another journey and obeyed your commands, I have deserved to receive no word of your embassy and no sign of your friendship.

There are certainly several witnesses to what I say. For when your predecessor of blessed memory confirmed here, by a firm promise, that he would dwell here for the sake of his soul’s salvation and the ordering of spiritual matters, you, by contrast, scourge me daily and inflict upon me every day the sharp blows of a whip; and he who does not deserve to hear a tongue receives severe discipline from holy hands.

While I carefully consider this, I often turn these words over silently within the secret recesses of my heart: “My lord does to me,” I say, “what almighty God is read to have done to Elijah: ‘Go,’ he said, ‘to Sarepta of Sidon; there I have commanded a widow to feed you’” (III Kings 17).

After that widow received the prophet at God’s command, she judged that both she and her household would be blessed by the companionship of so great a guest. Yet while she diligently served him and ministered with devoted service, her son was suddenly seized by death; and the one through whom she had hoped that her son would flourish for a long time in this life, she began to accuse as though he were the author of his death, saying: “What have I to do with you, man of God? You have come to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and my son might be killed?” (Ibid.)

Behold, most merciful lord: the other monasteries remain unharmed beneath the wings of your mercy and serve God in security and freedom from interference. This one alone, ever since you commanded me to enter it, is exposed to so many invasions and acts of plunder that, unless your mind is even now bent toward mercy, it already appears utterly desolate.

Thus the house of God seems to be cast down through me, the very person through whom it was hoped—God cooperating with you—that it would be exalted to heaven.

Therefore, most glorious lord, I fall with tears at your feet and implore the inward compassion of your holiness: according to the prudence appropriate to your dignity, remember now to restrain the whip and put an end to so many persecutions. For the Lord says through the prophet: “When you are troubled, you will remember mercy in anger” (Tobit 3; Habakkuk 3).

Do not burden the holy place further by taking away money, when you know that it has already suffered such a great loss of ecclesiastical possessions.

## LETTER VI. TO ANNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

**SUMMARY.**—He praises the archbishop of Cologne because he had admirably protected the emperor’s orphaned son, entrusted to his faith, and, when the boy had grown, restored his father’s imperial authority to him. He then praises him because he had persecuted Cadalous, the false pontiff, and, insofar as he could, struck him down with the ecclesiastical sword. He urges him to put the finishing hand to the work, since the fury of the same Cadalous is still raging with greater danger against the Christian commonwealth; yet it can be restrained if, through the archbishop’s efforts, a general assembly of the Fathers is convened.

To Lord Anno, most reverend archbishop, Peter, sinful monk, offers the service of worthy devotion.

Being engaged in the conduct of an expedition, we cannot fittingly weave the thread of a flowing pen with the same hands with which we properly attend to the tossing reins of horses. Yet although it is better to speak clearly than to mutter, when necessity presses it is nevertheless better to mutter somehow than to fall completely silent.

When, venerable Father, your labor and zeal come to mind, the noble faith and prudence of the priest Jehoiada immediately occur to us (IV Kings 11). As sacred history testifies, as you know well (II Chronicles 22), when Athaliah, the wife of Joram, saw that her son Ahaziah—the king of Israel—had been killed, she began savagely to rage against all the royal offspring, and cruel Bellona attempted to wipe out the descendants of David completely.

But that distinguished priest Jehoiada rescued Joash, the son of Ahaziah, by a pious fraud worthy of much praise, and secretly kept him within the precincts of the temple for seven years. Later he restored to him the rights of the royal scepter and strengthened him to preside over the people of Israel according to the custom of his ancestors.

Soon, as though this noble achievement were not enough for the priest, once the king’s authority had been confirmed he extended his diligence to the benefit of the priesthood and the temple, and together with the aforementioned king devoted himself to ordering and regulating the discipline of his fellow priests. He also arranged for the sacred roofs of the temple to be restored and issued certain decrees concerning matters that belonged to the priests.

For he knew that each dignity requires the other’s mutual assistance: the priesthood is protected by the kingdom’s defense, and the kingdom is supported by the holiness of priestly office.

But why should I run through the sequence of sacred reading, except that I see in you a likeness of the same work suited to our own time? Venerable Father, you preserved the boy entrusted to your hands, strengthened the kingdom, restored to the orphan the authority of his paternal right, and immediately extended the hand of your prudence also to the priesthood. You strove both to cut off the scaly neck of the Parmese beast with the strength of the evangelical sword and to restore the bishop of the apostolic see to the throne of his dignity [f. *solium*].

But unless a final hand is added to the work begun, unless the remaining measures are also undertaken, the sacred structure of your work threatens to collapse.

For that Cadalous—the disturber of the holy Church, the destroyer of ecclesiastical discipline, the enemy of human salvation, that is, the root of sin, herald of the devil, apostle of Antichrist, an arrow drawn from Satan’s quiver, the rod of Assyria, the son of Belial, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped as God (II Thessalonians 2)—still breathes like a most dreadful dragon; still fouls human nostrils with the stench of poisonous money; and, as a new heresiarch, disturbs the faith of many, which wavers in the wind of perfidy.

For just as the inventions of fable falsely imagine that Jupiter descended into Diana’s lap through a shower of gold (Apollodorus, *Library*, book II), so this man, through gold obtained from the sacrilegious expulsion of his own Church, seeks an adulterous intercourse with the apostolic see; and, like a wanton adulterer, he burns to the marrow to satisfy his lust through the violation of the Roman Church.

Therefore, venerable Father, so that the holy labor of your zeal may entirely reach its fulfillment, so that the Roman Church may not be made contemptible in the eyes of men through this tail of a burning brand—or rather, through this one rotten member of the devil—and so that, God forbid, the Christian people may not remain in error on this account, your prudence must strive with all its strength to ensure that a general council be held as quickly as possible and tear out the thorns of this destructive error in which the miserable world is entangled.

I would also gladly come to speak with your holiness, if an opportunity were given, so that the counsel which absence prevents us from sharing could be exchanged in living and connected conversation. But since perhaps I do not deserve this, I ask, entreat, and humbly suggest that your holy prudence make every effort to extinguish the Cadalousian fury, which never ceases to bark, so that the Christian religion may be able through you to rejoice in peaceful tranquility. Then, while kingdom and priesthood enjoy through you the peace they desire, may the author of both dignities bestow upon you worthy rewards of eternal peace.

But while a horse is being brought forward and all my companions are setting out on the journey, behold, I disregard brevity; I spread [uncertain: *strevi*] the tracks of my footsteps.

## LETTER VII. TO VIDO, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN

**SUMMARY.**—He silently gives thanks to Archbishop Vido because, while he was staying with him, he generously presented him with sacred vestments. He shows that he remembers this benefit and continually pours out prayers to God for him; he also takes care that his monks and friends do the same.

To Lord G., most reverend archbishop, Peter, sinful monk, offers the service of most devoted servitude.

Let your holiness know, venerable Father, that I have repented greatly and, so to speak, that my heart has severely struck me because I did not restrain your generosity, so lavish and munificent.

For, in the likeness of the future resurrection, you decided to clothe me in two stoles. Overcome by your authority, I offered no resistance and withdrew no hand; forgetting the genuine rigor proper to God’s servants, I readily accepted everything.

When I recall this, my conscience bites and rebukes me, I am drenched with shame, and I blush beneath accusations that seem to come from myself as though from others.

Nor is this without reason. If King David’s heart, as Scripture testifies, struck him because he silently cut off only the edge of Saul’s cloak (I Samuel 24), what should I deserve, who extorted from my lord not a piece of clothing but whole and even costly garments, and, under the pretext not of giving but of receiving charity, clothed myself while stripping another?

If I were truly a priest, I ought surely to seek to be clothed in justice rather than to pursue woven ornaments.

Yet while I stand to be examined before the tribunals of my mind and scrutinize myself with the strictest judgment, I have this defense, and it speaks on my behalf: at that time certain gifts were offered to me, but since no opportunity for acceptance was found among us, they were sent back with all speed to those who had sent them.

From this I can perhaps conclude that the charity which prompted my lord to confer a blessing was the same charity that persuaded his servant to accept what had been conferred.

But while we recall the manner of your gift, my mind returns to that oracle of Zechariah: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the face of the angel” (Zechariah 3). The angel answered and said to those who stood before him: “Take the filthy garments away from him” (Ibid.). Then, as Scripture continues, he was clothed in changing garments.

Blessed will be that day on which this exchange of garments is celebrated, and the body of Jesus, which is the Church, having laid aside every squalor of mourning and sadness, will be clothed in the splendor of blessed immortality; just as it already joyfully proclaims in the psalm of dedication: “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that I may sing to you, my glory” (Psalm 15).

But to whom am I speaking of such things? Let it suffice merely to say that you, venerable Father, have become an angel of the Lord to me: out of love for Jesus, removing what was filthy from me, you adorned that same Jesus in me with priestly vestments.

For these gifts, however, I did not remain wholly ungrateful; I repaid them in this way, inscribing your name in many places—not only among our own, but also in foreign and distant regions, deserts, and monasteries—and commending you to the prayers of the brothers with humble devotion.

# BOOK FOUR. TO THE BISHOPS

## 97–98 LETTER I. TO ALBERT, BISHOP

**SUMMARY.**—I readily persuade myself that this Albert, to whom he is writing, was a bishop and Damian’s disciple before Damian himself became a bishop. With great authority he not only admonishes him but also commands him to do nothing avariciously or greedily in administering the souls entrusted to him; rather, he should strive to conduct himself innocently, so that from his life and conduct not infamy but glory may redound to his most holy teacher.

To Lord Albert, bishop … Peter, sinful monk …

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

I appeal to your experience, venerable brother Albert, and by the authority of paternal firmness I command you: do not be so intent upon temporal affairs that you fail to be sufficiently vigilant in guarding the souls entrusted to us, [Col. 0297B] for souls have been entrusted to us, I say—just as they were entrusted by God to me, so they have been commended by me to you. Yet beyond all doubt, both of us will render an account to God alone. Let your fraternity therefore strive both to lead a religious life and to possess an honorable reputation. The life is for your sake; the reputation for your sake and mine—or rather, not so much for ours as also for those who have been entrusted to us. For if, God forbid, your name should be disfigured by foul infamy, disgrace immediately redounds upon me, and, like a deadly cancer, it spreads as an example among those whom we have endeavored to form in virtue. Thus Peter, after first saying, “Having your conduct honorable among the Gentiles, so that, when they speak against you as evildoers, observing you in your good works, they may glorify [Col. 0297C] God on the day of visitation” (I Peter III), added shortly afterward: “With modesty and fear, keeping a good conscience, so that in the matter in which they slander you, those who malign your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame” (I Peter III). Paul also says to Timothy: “A bishop must have a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (I Timothy III).

Moreover, dearest brother, diligently guard against and carefully attend to this: when you distribute tithes, or whatever offerings of the faithful there may be, among the churches, do not presume to diminish anything from my fellow priests on the pretext that you might thereby increase what belongs to me, as though you were faithfully acting in my interest. Far be it from us that what belongs to another’s right should become an addition to my profit, or that what is sacred through the merit of those who offer it should become sacrilege in the hands of priests. “For I,” as the Apostle says, [Col. 0298A] “have all things and abound” (Philippians IV); nor do I wish to supplant by power or cunning my brothers in those things which God has granted to us for common use. I ought to surpass them in the simplicity and humanity of Christ, and before their eyes I must clearly imprint upon myself the mark of Christ’s poverty. Far be it from me to permit their poverty to pass into my profits, so that, with the same Apostle, I may be able humbly to glory before them with an open face: “I have learned,” he says, “in whatever state I am, to be self-sufficient. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (ibid.).

I also wish that in those same diocesan churches where, on the occasion of the more solemn festivals, loaves have been offered—and if there are other offerings that appear to pertain to food or drink—these should be distributed to the poor. Otherwise, while we heap together offerings to be given to other poor people, we may leave the populace grounds for complaint and be judged, through avarice, to be stuffing our purses. Certainly it is fitting that the poor of Christ should chiefly experience refreshment from the alms of the church which they attend.

Take care also that, following the custom of certain men—not pastors, I will not say, but smiths—you do not impose upon any priest, under the pretext of money, some accusation of guilt, suspend him from his administration, and afterward restore him to the rights of his rank in exchange for some earthly financial advantage. Gehazi deserves leprosy (IV Kings V), since he changes his judgment out of desire for money. Whoever takes a payment and restores an office does not escape the dart hurled by Peter’s mouth against Simon (Acts VIII). He is compelled to bear simoniacal leprosy . . .

[Note: [Col. 0297D] The end of this letter is missing in the manuscripts.]

## LETTER II. TO B., BISHOP

**Argument.**—He gives thanks to Bishop B. for the alms bestowed upon himself and his monastery. Yet he admonishes him to join to mercy and beneficence toward the poor the other virtues as well, lest, God forbid, the merit of his almsgiving be blotted out by a life burdened with faults. Finally, he asks him to promote two clerics to the order of the diaconate.

To B., lord bishop, Peter sends faithful prayer in Christ.

Dearest friend, whenever I recall the benefits bestowed upon me through your generosity, I confess that I turn wholly toward love of you in order to repay them with the gifts of daily prayer. Although that prayer, because of my sins, is hindered from benefiting anyone, your devotion nevertheless merits that it may benefit you. Take care, therefore, dearest friend, lest the incentives of vices consume the good that your generosity in almsgiving could have conferred upon you, and lest the building constructed by the hand of mercy be destroyed by the battering ram of lust. Let good things therefore be done in such a way that evil things are not mingled with them. Temporal goods are given for this purpose: that through them eternal goods may be acquired. Otherwise, God forbid, while [evil and avarice] outweigh them on the scales of the strict Judge, the weight of the good work may become worthless.

For what benefit is it to offer temporal goods to God while denying him the most precious soul—that is, money? The omnipotent God indeed delivered all created things to human use, but he reserved souls alone for his own use. Therefore, dearest father, strive to give what is yours in such a way that you also endeavor to offer yourself. For by the dignity of episcopal office it has been granted to you that you should feed us, who are younger, at the rich breasts of holy preaching, and offer the tender inward parts of maternal affection to our infant-like weakness.

We therefore ask your holiness to promote to the order of the diaconate these two clerics, who acknowledge that they have received permission from their bishop, and to determine that they should freely receive the due consecration of this office, as is fitting.

## LETTER III. TO CUNIBERT, BISHOP OF TURIN

(It is found in volume III and is treatise 18.)

## LETTER IV. TO G., BISHOP OF AUXIMUM

**Argument.**—Having recently departed from the Bishop of Auximum, whom he had persuaded to renounce the vanities of this world, and having returned to his own people, he found many of those whom he himself had known there dead. Taking this as his occasion, he exhorts the same bishop not to defer his conversion any longer, nor to allow himself to be tossed for so long by the storms and waves of the treacherous Ocean, but to hurry to the harbor of the monastery. If he does so, he promises him all his zeal, service, and goodwill; if not, he orders him to keep his possessions for himself and declares that henceforth he will have nothing more to do with him.

To G., most reverend Bishop of Auximum, Peter, servant and son, sends every good wish.

Dearest friend, after I departed from you, I found that very many people had died in our region. Turning the eye of my mind toward you also, I was greatly terrified, lest, God forbid, something similar should happen to you, and lest the divine judgment should condemn me, for prolonging your conversion through delay upon delay, by another’s death. Therefore I beseech you, dearest father, by almighty Jesus, by his holy angels, and by the fiery throne of his majesty, on which he will judge the living and the dead: do not deceive yourself; do not delay any longer; do not seduce your soul by postponing its remedy of salvation from day to day. Enter quickly, while it is permitted, into the harbor of conversion, lest sudden misfortunes overtake you in your delay, lest the wave of unexpected death swallow you, and the abyss of the burning Gehenna devour you.

Alas, alas, my father! Why can I not obtain from God that he open the eyes of your heart and permit you to see the bed of your calamity on which you lie secure? Certainly, if you clearly perceived how near death is—the death that now lies in ambush behind you—you would immediately abandon whatever the world makes pleasing to you, whatever this deceitful life caresses you with. But I act foolishly if I presume to teach one who is more learned than I. I say one thing, my father, and do not be angry: if you wish to convert, keep me, your servant, your son, your most worthless attendant, beneath your feet always, for as long as you live. But if not, I will no longer join myself to you, lest, God forbid, by disagreeing with my God I should scatter; nor do I ever wish to be joined in love to anyone who has been separated from the fellowship of God.

## LETTER V TO G. . . , BISHOP

**Argument.**—He vividly describes that terrible and fearful day for mortals when the whole human race will be gathered before the tribunal of the supreme Judge, like the sand of the sea, to render the most exact account of the life spent in this valley of miseries; and he places it, as if in a painting, before the eyes of Bishop G. He urges him to contemplate its form and image with the eyes of his mind as though it were present, and not to permit it, once fixed in his spirit, ever to be displaced or torn away by any sight of the world’s false, painted happiness.

To G., most reverend bishop, Peter sends the service of due obedience.

Dearest father and lord, while the world smiles upon you, while the health of your flesh is vigorous, and while earthly prosperity caresses you, consider what follows after these things. Regard with prudent care, as though what is present had already passed, what will succeed the present. Therefore decide already that whatever is transitory has passed away according to a higher counsel, and count it as the dream of a deceptive illusion. Let your mind return there; direct the anxious eyes of its keen understanding there—to what, once it has occurred, knows no passing away.

Place also the terrible day of the last judgment already before your eyes, and reflect with trembling inward parts upon the sudden arrival of such majesty. Do not think that day far away: the prophet, so many ages before us, proclaimed it near, as though it were already at the threshold, saying: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and very swift; the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be afflicted there. A day of wrath is that day, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery; a day of darkness [Col. 0300D] and gloom; a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zephaniah I).

Consider, dearest friend, the last day of judgment over the hearts of the reprobate: with what bitterness the prophet saw it become bitter, though he could not explain it by so many names. Indeed, to say nothing now of those never-ending punishments of eternal damnation, if only the terror and horror of that last day are diligently examined as they deserve, the whole deceitful and false happiness of this world will be judged as though it were mud or barren seaweed on the shore.

For whom will that voice not terrify? Who will not tremble to the marrow when he hears the Lord himself saying in the Gospel: “For just as lightning comes forth from the east and appears in the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” [Col. 0301A] (Matthew XXIV)? Who, I ask, will not be afraid when the same Truth says: “For the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken” (ibid.)?

Of this Peter also says: “The day will come like a thief, on which the heavens will pass away with great force, and the elements will be dissolved by heat” (II Peter III); and again he says: “The heavens and earth that now exist have been reserved by the same word, kept for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly men” (ibid.). Hence the Apostle Jude also says: “Behold, the Lord will come with holy thousands to execute judgment against all, to convict all the ungodly of all their works of ungodliness by which they acted ungodly, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him” [Col. 0301B] (Jude I).

Oh, if only we could taste upon the palate of our hearts how great is the bitterness of what is said through John: “Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Apocalypse I). Then the loins of those who now do not fear will be loosened by terror; then the inward parts of those who now lie softly in the pleasures of carnal allurements will be filled with bitterness. Then, shedding bloody tears, they will begin to say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Apocalypse VI; Luke XXIII).

Then there will be nowhere to flee, no hiding place in which anyone may conceal himself. For the gates of hell will be opened, hostile death will be destroyed, and the dust that had decayed—that is, human flesh—will be brought to life upon hearing the sound of the trumpet. Those whom the earth had received into its bosom, whom the water had swallowed, and whom the devouring flame had consumed will all render them back, as a deposit entrusted to them, and restore them to life without any diminution of their substance.

Then the earth will be shaken, the air disturbed by a sudden storm, thunder will roar, and flashes and lightning will confound human breasts with terror. “For God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him. He has summoned heaven above and earth, to distinguish his people” (Psalm XLII).

On that dread day he will appear with angels and archangels, with thrones and dominions, with principalities and powers; the heavens will flash, the earth will burn, and all the elements will be stirred in terror to serve him. The distinguished prophet Isaiah rightly announces that day, saying: “Behold, the day of the Lord will come, unendurable; a day of fury and wrath, to make the world desolate and destroy sinners from it” (Isaiah XIII). “The stars of heaven will not give their light, the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not give its light. I will command evils against the whole world, and against the ungodly for their sins; I will destroy the insolence of the wicked, and humble the arrogance of the proud. Those who are left will be more precious than gold refined by fire, and a human being more precious than a sapphire stone. Heaven will be shaken, and the earth will be moved from its foundations because of the fury of the wrath of the Lord of hosts, on the day when his anger comes upon it” [Col. 0302A] (Isaiah XIII).

The prophet Malachi also speaks in agreement with these things, saying: “Behold, the almighty Lord comes, and who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will bear his sight? For he will enter the refiners’ fire and be like the chaff of those who veil (velantium; variant: winnow, ventilantium), and he will sit refining and cleansing like gold and silver” (Malachi III). And again he says: “Behold, the day of the Lord will come, burning like a furnace, and it will burn them: all foreigners and all who commit iniquity will be like straw; that day which comes, says the almighty Lord, will burn them, leaving neither root nor branch” (Malachi IV).

But another, the man of desires, says: “And behold, I was watching, and thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head was like clean wool” (Daniel VII). His throne was burning fire; a stream of fire flowed before him. Judgment was established, and the books were opened. Shortly afterward he says: “I saw in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven. He came as far as the Ancient of Days, and he was presented before him; and to him were given dominion, honor, and a kingdom. All peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed. My spirit shuddered; I, Daniel, was troubled by my dullness and by the visions of my head” (ibid.).

When these things begin to take place, the gates of heaven will undoubtedly be opened—or rather, heaven itself will be removed from the midst, as though the curtains of a tabernacle were being gathered up, so that it may be repaired and transformed for the better. Then everything will be filled with fear, dread, and trembling, when he judges who needs no witness, seeks no arguments, and requires no advocate for the case. With all such things removed, he himself will judge deeds, words, and thoughts, place them in the midst, and display them as though painted on tablets before the eyes of those who committed them and of all who appear to stand by.

How, then, will the whole of creation be shaken and filled with fear at that time? Come, therefore: when we have come to that unique judgment, we will be judged by a Judge who can neither be deceived by the concealment of crimes nor corrupted by anyone’s offering to obtain impunity. When all secrets begin to be revealed, and not only acts and words but even thoughts themselves are displayed, what will we do beneath the majesty of so great a Judge? What excuse will we be able to offer? By what art of defense will we cleanse ourselves? What repentance, which we despised in this flesh, will come to our aid? What good works, which we did not perform in this life, will defend us? To which apostles, or to which other saints, will we flee, whose examples and words we despised?

Or perhaps some weakness of the body will excuse itself? But all the examples of the saints will protest against that excuse: they conquered the weakness of the flesh while still in the flesh and taught us that what they did we too were able to do. Especially since they themselves resisted sin not by their own power but by the help of the merciful God, who reveals himself even to those who do not seek him, so that he may be sought and believed in; and he defends those who believe in him with unconquerable protection, lest they be overcome by sin.

What, then, will they answer if the Lord says to them: “If you were able, why did you not resist the desires of sin? If you were unable, why did you not seek my help against sin? Or, when wounded, why did you not apply the remedy of repentance to your wound?” Having none, he says: “Bind them hand and foot and cast them into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew XXII), “where their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isaiah LXVI).

It must therefore be pondered [Col. 0303B] and turned over with the utmost care what terror there will be on that day, when punishment will contain no remedy; what shame will come upon each person, as his guilt demands, when he must blush in the assembly of all human beings and angels; and what fear it will be to see him angry whom the human mind cannot contain even when tranquil.

Of that day it is rightly said through Isaiah: “The Lord alone will be exalted on that day, because the day of the Lord of hosts is against every proud and lofty person, against every arrogant person, and he will be humbled; against all the lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon, against all the oaks of Bashan, against all the lofty mountains and raised hills, against every high tower and every fortified wall, against all the ships of Tarshish, and against everything beautiful to the eye. The loftiness of human beings will be bowed down, the height of men will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day. The idols will be utterly crushed, and they will enter into the caves of the rocks and the hollows of the earth, away from the face of the Lord’s terror and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth” (Isaiah II).

Now the Lord sees the sins of sinners and is silent; “then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his fury he will trouble them” (Psalm II). As he himself says through the prophet: “I have been silent; I have always kept still; I have been patient. Like a woman in labor, I will speak” (Isaiah XLII).

Whoever now pants after earthly advantages, whoever feeds upon the pleasures of wanton flesh, will then be consumed by the fire of eternal burning and devoured by the sword of divine fury. For as the prophet says: “All the earth will be devoured in the fire of the Lord’s zeal, and all flesh by his sword” (Zephaniah I).

There, the person who refused here to hear what the Lord commanded will no longer be able to obtain from the Lord what he requests. Those who despise the divine voice in this life will then come before the door with their false humility and prayers, but they will not be heard. Instead it will be said to them: “I do not know you. Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV).

And truly the Lord says through Solomon: “I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes. I also will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you—when sudden calamity rushes upon you and destruction comes like a storm.
