When tribulation and distress come upon you, then they will call upon me, and I will not hear. They will rise early and will not find me” (Proverbs I).

In what, then, will we place our confidence? Where will we have hope of obtaining salvation? In the treasures of money that we store in a chest? In the abundance of riches, which, empty within, we wickedly possess outwardly?

But hear the Apostle James, and how little he esteems human riches, and what merit he assigns to the possession of earthly substance: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and it will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days” (James V). And shortly afterward: “You have feasted upon the earth, and in luxury you have nourished your hearts; you have brought yourselves to the day of slaughter” (ibid.).

Alas! What will those wretched people say then, when they see that they have both irretrievably lost temporal goods and that perpetual evils inevitably threaten them? What will their mind be like when they see that the acceptable time and the day of salvation (II Corinthians VI) have completely flowed away, and that the time has arrived in which they can do no good and find no remedy for their destruction? How bitter will their conscience be; how mournful their complaint!

Then, as Solomon confesses, weeping and groaning in anguish of spirit, they will say: “We have gone astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us. We have grown weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we have walked difficult paths; but we did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed like a shadow, and like a messenger running ahead, and like a ship that passes through the tossing water, whose trace cannot be found once it has passed, nor the track of its keel in the waves. Or like a bird flying through the air, no sign of its journey is found, but only the sound of its wings beating the light wind and cleaving the air by the force of its passage; it flew across with beating wings, and afterward no mark of its journey is found. Or like an arrow shot toward its appointed place: the divided air quickly closes back upon itself, and its passage is unknown. So we too, once born, immediately ceased to be, and we were unable to display any sign of virtue; instead, we were consumed in our wickedness” (Wisdom V).

Such things were said in hell by those who sinned, because the hope of the impious is like down, which is lifted by the wind; like thin foam, which is scattered by the storm; like smoke, which is dispersed by the wind; and like the memory of a passing guest who stays for one day.

[Note: [Col. 0305] The end of this letter is lacking in the manuscripts and appears to be recoverable from the end of Letter 8 of Book VIII below, which concerns the same subject and uses the same thoughts and words.]

## LETTER VI. TO JOHN, BISHOP . . . .

**Argument.**—He sends certain little works of his to Bishop John, whom he exhorts to despise human affairs. He also shows that he desires John’s friendship and communicates certain matters useful to the salvation of them both.

To John, most reverend bishop, Peter, the last servant of the monks, sends the obedience of due reverence.

Dearest friend, whoever hastens to climb a lofty mountain must ascend to its summit by means of intervening steps. Therefore I desire to reach the knowledge of your eminence—as a churchman and one divinely raised upon Mount Zion—and I send ahead an ecclesiastical little gift in the manner of steps. Since I direct these little works to you and seek your favor neither to display vain glory nor for bodily advantage, I better satisfy the one whom I know without doubt to judge the eyes of hearts.

Moreover, dearest father and lord, you yourself see that all temporal things flee; what we possess in this world cannot remain with us for long. Earthly honors and dignities, like smoke, return to nothing the higher they are raised, and nothing worldly can endure when the world itself has already descended toward its end. We too, who begin here with such great desire, are suddenly struck down by a momentary fever and abandon everything; then, without doubt, we learn that the things we considered greatest were nothing.

Our works alone, whether good or evil, do not perish; they are kept to be sifted in the strict examination of the dread Judge. Therefore, dearest friend, return within your conscience and, while it is permitted, carefully meditate what you must answer to such majesty. Consider who will come to settle accounts with you and what manifold fruit he will require in return for such an extensive stewardship.

Know beyond all doubt, dearest father, that I always desire to have your favor and goodwill, and that I desire your salvation from the depths of my heart—not only of your soul but also of your body. Therefore confidently command me regarding your service, and know without hesitation that I will gladly obey you.

Since I possess no earthly gifts, I send you the contemptible gifts of my little works—not to seek through them the protection of your defense, but to open, by the traces of my tongue, an entrance to the chamber of your heart; not so that assistance may benefit me, but so that my counsel may be able to benefit you. Indeed, my humility has certain matters to suggest to you that are highly necessary not only for the future life but also for the present. I would write part of them even in this letter if I were not afraid of the curious eye of someone who might arrive unexpectedly.

Set a time for me after Easter, and command me by the authority of your holiness to come to you. I also ask, if it pleases you, that what the bearer of this letter says aloud be heard effectively.

## LETTER VII. TO N. . . , BISHOP . . . .

**Argument.**—He wrote this letter while on a journey, as he himself says. He admonishes a certain bishop to refrain from accepting gifts from the impious, lest he become a participant in their sins. He proves this both by the authority of sacred Scripture and by several examples. Great caution must therefore be exercised, he says, lest gifts be indiscriminately accepted from everyone, but only from those whose gifts are undoubtedly acceptable to God as well.

To N. . . , bishop of venerable holiness, Peter, sinful monk, sends greetings.

Dearest friend, although I am on a journey and unable to write anything polished, I nevertheless judge it better to mark out, however inadequately, what is necessary than to pass it over entirely in silence. What I have often admonished you face to face, I now repeat in writing, and I categorically forbid you to pollute yourself with gifts from any guilty persons.

For it is written: “The offering of one sacrificing (immolans; variant immolantis) from injustice is defiled, and the mockeries of the unjust are not pleasing” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV). Why, then, do we not fear accepting what we know God rejects? Again it is written: “The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked, nor does he regard the offerings of the impious; nor will he be appeased for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord” (Proverbs XV). The Psalmist says: “He will not give God his appeasement, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Psalm XLVIII).

Why do we not also recall that Gehazi put on the scab of perpetual leprosy when he desired the gifts offered by Naaman the Syrian? (IV Kings V.) But, so that ruin may be avoided, let another example be added.

Gerard, a devout canon of the Church of Florence, recently related to me the following account, which I now report. Count Hildebrand of Tuscany [variant: “into Tuscany”], who was said to be of Capuana, was so rich and powerful that he boasted of having more estates and castles than there are days counted in the year. He had therefore made a certain priest, a devout, honorable, and spiritual man, his spiritual father, and from him he customarily received penance.

Another priest, named Rainerius, saw the following vision concerning this priest. A loud voice sounded, calling him to ascend: “Peter,” it said, “priest”—for, if I remember correctly, that was his name—“come up here.” The voice is said to have been so loud that several people were awakened from sleep by its force.

At the command of this voice the priest ascended to a certain promontory of extraordinary height. The one who had called him appeared to be Saint Benedict. After climbing this mountain, the priest immediately discovered that his entire body was leprous. Breaking out at once, he said: “Alas, alas! Why has the plague of this disease destroyed me?”

Blessed Benedict replied: “The cloak that you received from the alms of Count Hildebrand—for Hildebrand himself had recently died—has been turned into leprosy for you. Therefore return the transient garment, if you wish to avoid the itching of perpetual leprosy. This hateful and destructive garment has harmed you, as you see, but it has done him no good at all. Why, then, do we seek the gifts of wicked men of every kind, when every offering of theirs can neither erase their contagion nor avoid being turned into leprosy for us?”

To continue the whole sequence of the vision: Blessed Benedict immediately brought him down from the mountain and led him into the lower parts of the valley beneath it. Meanwhile the priest saw a certain dreadful river, dark, pitch-black, and sulfurous. As he proceeded beside it under the guidance of the blessed man, a voice sounded from the river and called him.

When the priest immediately stopped and asked who had called him, the voice answered: “I am that most wretched Count Hildebrand, to whom you were accustomed to impose penance, though it was without fruit.”

The priest said to him: “How are you Count Hildebrand, when you have such an obese and mutilated body that you appear to possess not a human form but rather the likeness of a yew tree?”

The count replied: “I am worn down by so many punishments and afflicted each day by so many new and carefully devised torments [Col. 0307C] that it is not surprising that the form of my body should perish, but rather that its very substance should remain in any way. I was so cruel while I lived in the body that now I am hated by all the saints. Their just severity despises me unanimously in such a way that none of them has yet interceded for me with the divine mercy.”

Near the river mentioned above there appeared innumerable birds, apparently like doves, mottled with a variety of feathers, so that in one place their appearance seemed white and in another black. All of them, as though deeply sad and mournful, twisted their beaks toward their little feathers, as if out of grief.

When the count was asked what those birds were, he replied: “They are the souls assigned to various purgations in this gulf. Just as they are not entirely white but varied by blackness interspersed here and there, so they are partly purified and partly still subject to sins. For the greater the expanse of whiteness seen in the variety of their feathers, the greater is the erasure of their sins understood to be; and to the extent that blackness is seen to remain, to that extent they are still marked by the stains of sins.”

Afterward, proceeding farther on, the priest saw Count Lothair, who had died not long before. He was still being tormented in the gulf up to the groin and protruded nearly halfway from it. When the priest asked him how he was being treated, he replied that he had first been completely submerged beneath sulfurous waves, but was gradually being raised and that his severe punishment was becoming milder day by day.

“But I beg you,” he said, “tell my household to return to Blessed Mary the property that I took away, if perhaps I may deserve to be released from the punishments in which I am held.”

The priest did not learn which church of Blessed Mary he meant and could not specifically identify it to the living.

Moreover, as the priest pressed forward, he saw a very horrible and terrifying house, and several servants of that house who were equally fierce, grim, and frightening to behold. They hurried back and forth in great numbers, anxious and panting, preparing I know not what great thing, as though for a distinguished guest.

When the aforementioned priest, astonished, asked what this meant, he was told that they were expecting Count Guido on the coming Wednesday. Just as abundant and luxurious provisions are prepared for guests who are about to arrive, so the malignant spirits were providing the wretched man with a banquet consisting only of punishments and torments.

After this vision, therefore, the priest Rainerius awoke, recounted what he had seen, and the count died on Wednesday, exactly as had been foretold.

So, to return to what we began: do not, brother, do not tolerate gifts; let not every gift that is offered have free access to you, but let some be admitted, so that they may relieve necessities, and let others be rejected, lest the weight of another’s guilt burden us. Therefore, while we receive what is offered, we must first examine the merits of those who offer it. Let our hand, then, not accept indiscriminately everything that is offered; and let it distinguish, by careful examination, not what is offered but rather by whom it is offered [Col. 0308C] 109. Scripture says: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Genesis 4, according to the Septuagint). And we say something similarly necessary: if you accept what is offered but do not distinguish the merits of those who offer it, you have sinned more seriously. Do you wish to hear what recently happened to me concerning a certain gift that was presented?

A certain leading man named Rodulphus, sufficiently powerful and prudent, reverently offered me at his monastery a cloak which, according to the character of its material, is called a *triblathon*. It is of three colors; for *blathon* means “cloak,” and hence a *triblathon* is called a cloak that is seen to be of three colors. As that man humbly offered it, he fell prostrate and, lying face down before me, begged me with all the humble intention of heart that he could summon: “Carry,” he said, “this little gift, my lord, to your holy brothers.” I ask nothing else from them except that they strive to obtain this one thing from the divine mercy: that it remove from my heart the darkness that afflicts it. For the love of the world holds my heart blinded and inflicts upon me a darkness which, he adds, he desires may be driven away by their holy prayers, so that at least I may deserve to be enlightened by some small spark of divine light.””

But when I both promised the requests of their prayers and repelled the gift that had been pressed upon me, not only with words but also with my hands, we have decided to leave unrecorded what words were poured forth on both sides, rather than write them out in order. What more need be said? I carried the gift to the brothers, but found them ungrateful; I performed the office of an envoy, but was not received cheerfully. They railed against it rather than giving thanks; they complained rather than speaking graciously; and they judged the offering of such a man not a gift but filth and a contagion of souls. They could not rest by any means until I promptly returned the gift, which had been imprudently accepted, to the man who had given it, and promised him—under words of apology, as though I were not returning it nevertheless—that the prayers would be offered freely. I confess that it pleased me greatly that I had been rebuked, corrected, and sprinkled with biting words.

You too, brother, guard yourself from the gifts of the impious, so that, while you beware of your own crime, you may dread bringing another’s guilt upon yourself; and, in accordance with Paul’s saying, “Do not share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5), may you be able to say to such people with a clear conscience: “I am clean from the blood of you all” (Acts 20).

## LETTER VIII. TO MAINARD, BISHOP OF GUBBIO

**SUMMARY.**—He advises Mainard, bishop of Gubbio, to try to recover the estates and resources of the Church that were taken away during his episcopate; he exhorts him to correct his conduct and undertake the arduous path of life, so that, tossed amid all the rough and difficult rocks of this world, he may more easily reach the harbor of rest and happiness in heaven.

**110 To Lord Mainard, bishop … Peter, a sinful monk.**

Because I know, brother, that you are not lacking in prudence, I apply correction to you confidently and without fear of rebuke. For Solomon also says in Proverbs: “Correction benefits the prudent more than a hundred blows do the fool” (Proverbs 17). And again: “If you rebuke a wise man, he will understand discipline” (Proverbs 19). He says once more: “The ear that hears the reproofs of life will dwell in the midst of the wise” (Proverbs 15). And immediately he adds: “He who rejects discipline despises his own soul; but he who accepts reproofs is the possessor of a sound heart” (ibid.). What I have often warned you face to face, I repeat in this letter, and I fasten the movement of fleeting speech, as it were, to the anchor of a fixed station with the letters of the page.

Restore, venerable brother, the estates of your church that have been lavishly handed over to secular persons; recall the ornaments of various kinds that have been wrongfully disposed of [or, according to the variant: exposed]; and at least let all the distinguished or finest things be restored, which, during the period of your rule, we deeply lament having been taken away. [Col. 0309D] Correct yourself also in your conduct, and, cautious and watchful on every side, shape yourself entirely according to priestly gravity and decency. Do not take pleasure in the abundance of deceptive riches that may perhaps be pressed upon you; and do not strive to rejoice in the honor of the chair over which you preside.

For often almighty God—may this be far from you—closes every avenue of effort begun by a reprobate mind when he sees it taking the path through the precipices of its pleasures. And just as he often prevents one who is already presiding from rejoicing, when he wishes to rejoice, so he restrains one who pants for authority, lest he climb to the summit of the dignity he desires.

John, formerly archpriest of the Church of Marsica and now a religious monk in the monastery of Monte Cassino, taught me yesterday, in a report, what I am relating. “Alberic,” he said, “was encroaching upon my church under the title of episcopal office.” He clung to a certain obscene little prostitute, acting as her procurer. When he feared the impending arrival of Otto Augustus, he falsely pretended to be celibate. He therefore removed the prostitute from his companionship and, deceitfully clothing her in a sacred veil, established her as a nun. Yet after the emperor’s departure he returned both to the disgrace of his former foulness and, to increase the infamy of his shame, fathered a son by the same victim of that infernal brothel.

“As soon as the boy had grown larger with the passage of time, his father substituted him for himself in episcopal dignity. But when the long habit of ruling returned to his memory, and he was ashamed that he was no longer celebrated and reverently honored as he had previously been, he found a plan issued from the innermost gall of the devil’s heart. First speaking with certain utterly pestilential monks, then with some laymen who knew nothing of God, he finally entered into a pact under an agreed bond of pledged assurance: the wretched buyer was to weigh out a price of one hundred pounds in Pavia coin, and those men, after first blinding the abbot who was then in charge, were to hand over the monastery of Monte Cassino to him securely, so that thereafter, supported by their assistance, he could possess it without any obstacle of opposition.

“These firstborn sons of Satan added this to the arrangement of their contrived pact: he was to send only part of the stipulated price through his servants, and until he saw the abbot’s eyes placed in his own hands, he was in no way to send the remaining part. What more need be said? Having scraped together and amassed from wherever he could golden female ornaments, he sent, through his accomplices, valuables worth sixty pounds to the town of Saint Germanus, and vomited upon them the serpent’s poison that the wicked disciple had imbibed from the devil’s counsel, telling them what they were to say and to whom.

“When they arrived at the town and had communicated with those who had been instructed in the unspeakable mystery, they were immediately sent into a certain crypt in that town, where they were hidden for several days. Meanwhile, Satan’s attendants violently seized the abbot, gouged out his eyes, promptly wrapped them in a linen cloth, and secretly sent them to those who were staying in the crypt. They, now elated and greedily embracing them as a long-desired treasure, began hastening back to their own place.

“When the greater part of the journey had already been completed and only the final stretch remained, and when, as though their wish had been fulfilled, they were already eating their provisions in security, a certain traveler suddenly arrived. Asked about a new matter, he replied that Alberic, who had once been bishop, had died. They, deeply indignant and greatly stunned, could not believe it at all. Then, learning the matter more certainly, they carefully discovered the number of days during which he had lain ill, and clearly recognized that he had miserably breathed his last at the very hour when the abbot’s light had been torn away.

“Behold how bitterly he ended who had desired to live joyfully and pleasantly; and at the very moment when he hoped that he would climb to what he regarded as a lofty summit, the man who had blinded another was himself, as though truly blinded and suddenly overtaken, plunged headlong into Tartarus.”

That prophetic saying rightly applies to him: “While I was still beginning, he cut me down” (Isaiah 38).

His son, that apostle of Antichrist whom his father had enticed to the pinnacle of ecclesiastical dignity, suffered many bitter calamities and conflicts for as long as he survived. Finally, pierced on every side by the swords of his own men, he died. It is fitting that such an end of life should overtake those who pant against God’s will for the summit of sacred rank. Thus the sweetness of life that they had conceived in their minds turns for them into bitterness, and the prosperity that had smiled upon them under the appearance of falsehood becomes calamity. [Col. 0311B] To them the saying of Jeremiah also rightly applies: “We hoped for peace, but there was no good; we sought good things, and behold, disturbance” (Jeremiah 14). And that of the Psalmist: “You cast them down when they were being exalted” (Psalm 72).

You, on the other hand, venerable brother, despise every sweetness and falsely pleasing attraction of this world; scorn the abundance of passing things and the seduction of worldly glory; and, following the footsteps of the Savior, set before yourself every rough and difficult path, so that, walking through hardships, you may reach delights, and, traversing rough thickets as it were, bring your journey to a sweet conclusion.

## 112 LETTER IX. TO OLDERIC, BISHOP OF Fermo

**SUMMARY.**—He writes this letter to the bishop of Fermo, first saying how greatly he welcomed the very pleasing letter sent to him by the bishop; then saying that he deeply resents the title of holiness attributed to him in it. He therefore attempts, by several arguments, to draw him away from this opinion, although he consoles himself with the thought that the bishop did not really believe it, but wrote it to urge him more sharply onward. He adds that he has been distressed by the calamities of the Church, since he was being compelled to defend sacred matters by arms. For this reason he says that the Church must be defended not by weapons and bodily strength but by prayers and divine arms; and he endeavors to prove this by sacred witnesses and arguments.

**To Lord Olderic, bishop of Fermo, Peter, a sinful monk, sends an inexhaustible affection of devotion.**

How eagerly my heart received the honey-sweet letter of your holiness is shown by my perseverance. I keep it continually as a companion dwelling with me in my cell; I often converse with it; and in it I clearly contemplate the likeness of your inner man and the image of your true face. Yet there is something in it that I bear heavily, namely, that I find myself not so much honored as burdened by the praise of so holy a name. My calamity is more grievous in this respect: not only do my own sins hinder me, but, alas, holy men also err in their estimate of me.

Let me not, however, admit that so great a man is lying even while praising me; but because you are human, you can at least be mistaken through goodwill. Since to lie means to speak contrary to one’s mind, it sometimes happens that the same statement is true according to the speaker’s opinion and false according to the nature of the matter itself.

I confess before my Lord that this thought often occupies my mind: whoever praises me to my face undoubtedly accuses me of being desirous of flattering praise. As conscience immediately bites me, I say: “When this man comes to speak to me according to his wishes and tries to make me favorable to him, he would never sprinkle me with the oil of soothing sweetness if he did not hope that I delight in the favors of praise.” Thus I am ashamed of my own praise; and while I seem to be magnified, I blush. The very favor that judges me considers me eager for praise, even as the one who appears to have been praised.

Furthermore, any human mind that is sound and supported by sound counsel, if it examines itself subtly and carefully, scarcely finds in its own capacities anything from which it can deservedly hope for praise. Mortal nature, hemmed in and constrained on every side, what does it know from which it could be exalted? For who knows what existed in eternity before God created this world? Yet although a person does not know what existed before the beginning of the world, perhaps he knows what will be after its end—whether, that is, the stars will continue to serve in the ministry of their course, and whether other elements will again succeed those that now exist.

For this reason the Seraphim whom the prophet Isaiah saw standing in the presence of the Lord are described as having six wings: “With two,” he says, “they covered their face; with two they covered their feet; and with two they flew.” They covered, moreover, not their own face or feet, but those of God. And what ought “the face of God” to mean except the beginning of the world? What “the feet” except the end of that same world? Thus the Seraphim have many wings that cover and few that fly, because, although a very few things are permitted to fly into our knowledge from the loftiness of divine works, very many remain hidden in the treasuries of heavenly secrets.

Isaiah likewise testifies that we are wholly ignorant of what existed before the beginning of the world and what will exist after its completion: “Declare to me the former things,” he says, “and the latter things that are to come, and I shall say that you are gods” (Isaiah 41). Of the intermediate things we know something, however imperfectly, insofar as they are disclosed to us by the testimony of Scripture. Yet how great our poverty of knowledge is even in these matters was not something that the wisest among human beings was ashamed to confess. Solomon says: “There are just men and wise men whose works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things remain uncertain for the future” (Ecclesiastes 9).

Here it should be noted that, while he speaks of just and wise men—who ought, of course, to know themselves more subtly—he nevertheless declares that they are ignorant of what is to come.

Indeed, when you praised me not only for wisdom but also, as it were, for holiness of life, you did not do so because your prudence believed this, but perhaps for this purpose: to spur me more sharply toward the battle-line of holy struggle. With what confidence can I assent to this even in the slightest, when an account must be given for every idle word; when merely calling someone a fool threatens the punishment of Gehenna; when not one apex or one iota of the divine law may pass away; and when the mere sight of desire incurs the crime of adultery?

Whoever weighs these and similar matters with worthy consideration may indeed presume upon divine mercy, but I do not know whether he can sleep in any security whatsoever because of an abundance of his merits—especially since the world roars on every side and, like a vast sea, rises with swelling storms, imposing such troubles upon all of us that it often compels us to serve earthly affairs rather than devote ourselves to divine service or strive for purity.

Clearly the malignant spirit is now hurling the human race more violently than usual down every precipice of vice; yet it disturbs everyone more savagely with the rancor of hatred and hostility. So many wars rage daily, armed lines surge forward, and hostile attacks bristle that the sword seems to destroy more military men than bodily illness ends among those resting on their beds, so that this world is conducted almost in the manner of the sea.

For just as, when a storm of winds arises, a stronger swell is stirred near the shore even while the sea is more gently ruffled, so now, at the end of the world, as though beside the shore of a nearby sea, all human hearts are tormented and battered like foaming waves by the storms of dissension and discord.

The unstable murderer searches everything and traverses every place of the world as though it were one field, lest anything unfruitful escape the sowing of his envious tinder. Hence, to the universal danger of the ecclesiastical order, the priesthood and the empire recoil from one another; and, to the injury of almighty God, now that one pope is seated upon the apostolic throne, another has been sent from the northern regions as the elected one [Note: [Col. 0313D] He means Cadalous.].

But he who first declined the name of almighty God in the plural number—saying, “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3)—undoubtedly adds a usurping pope to the pope. On this matter we are compelled to weep rather than take pleasure in writing at greater length. Therefore, when several days ago I was bringing forth rhythmic hymns through tears:

> Alas, apostolic see,  
> Once the glory of the world,  
> Now, alas, you have become  
> The workshop of Simon.  
>   
> Hammers wear away the anvil;  
> The coins are infernal.  
> By the just judgment of God  
> This condition has come to be:  
> Whoever once purchases  
> The apostolic see  
> Does not cease to redeem it  
> Until he perishes miserably.

After these words, I wasted away from grief and refrained from adding more.

But since, among the other evils that arise in our times, violent men also insolently oppress the churches themselves and invade their estates—or any goods belonging to sacred right (consult the Scholia at the end of the little work)—some people ask whether the rulers of the churches ought to seek vengeance, returning evil for evil in the manner of secular men. For many, as soon as force is inflicted upon them, rush immediately to declare war, assemble bands of armed men, and thus perhaps take revenge upon their enemies more fiercely than they themselves had been injured.

This seems to me plainly absurd: that the priests of the Lord should attempt what is forbidden to common crowds, and should affirm by their deeds what they attack in words. For what appears more contrary to Christian law than the repayment of injuries? Where, I ask, are all those proclamations of Scripture? Where is what the Lord says: “If anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6)? If we are not permitted to reclaim the very things that have been taken from us, how can we be permitted to inflict upon others the wound of retaliatory punishment for them?

And where is this saying: “If he strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also; if he forces you to go one mile, go with him two more; if he takes your tunic, give him your cloak also” (Matthew 5)?

Perhaps someone objects that these commands were given to secular crowds, not to priests—so that the bishops of churches should preach them, not observe them. But who, even if foolish, could think this, when the Lord says: “Whoever relaxes one of these least commandments and teaches people so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great” (ibid.)?

Therefore, a priest who wishes to be great in the kingdom of heaven should go before the people, so that what he dictates by his voice to those who follow him, he himself may first fulfill through living deeds.

Accordingly, to remove every opportunity for a perverse interpretation, the first among the priests of the Church did not say, “Lord, how often will a brother sin against his brother and he will forgive him?” Rather, making the cause of all priests his own in his single person, he said: “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I shall forgive him? Up to seven times?” (Matthew 18). When he was answered that forgiveness was to be granted “up to seventy times seven” (ibid.), no uncertainty seems to remain about the universal command that priests must observe.

The evangelist Luke also teaches us, by his testimony, that when the Lord was going to Jerusalem, the disciples who went ahead entered a Samaritan town in order to prepare it for him (Luke 9). When the Samaritans would not receive them at all, James and John, prompted by human feeling, said: “Lord, do you wish us to say that fire should come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” (ibid.). Immediately he turned and rebuked them, saying: “You do not know what spirit you are of. The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them.” Immediately afterward it is added: “And they went to another village” (ibid.), as though he were saying not by words but by his action: “Give place to anger”; or rather, as he himself says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10).

The life that our Savior lived in the flesh is set before us as a rule of discipline to be maintained no less than the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore, just as he overcame all the obstacles of the raging world not through the vengeance of a strict judgment but through the unconquered majesty of unshaken patience, so he teaches us to endure the world’s fury with equanimity rather than seize weapons or answer injury with injury.

This is especially so because “between the kingdom and the priesthood the proper duties of each are distinguished,” so that the king may use the weapons of the world, while the priest girds himself with the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6).

Paul says of the ruler of the world: “He does not bear the sword without cause. For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil” (Romans 13). King Azariah, because he usurped the priestly office, was covered with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26); and if a priest takes up arms, which certainly belong to laymen, what does he deserve?

David too is believed to have lived evangelically before the Gospel, for he is found to have spared not only Shimei and Saul but also many of his enemies. I would briefly touch here upon some examples concerning him and the other holy Fathers, if I were not certain that these matters and similar ones are incomparably better known to you than to me.

Who does not clearly see how shameful a confusion it is when the Church itself shamelessly commits what it denies should be done, and, while preaching patience to others, is itself inflamed with irreconcilable anger against the innocent? What happens to one who does this is what the Apostle says: “Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9); or rather, what he says to the Romans: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Romans 2).

Above all, the statement that follows immediately seems applicable to a priest: “You who glory in the law dishonor God through transgression of the law” (ibid.). A priest rightly glories in the law of God, since he has received the office of ministering the commandments of the law; but he is convicted of dishonoring God through transgression of the law when he does not fear violating its ordinances.

While doing one thing and preaching another, he disturbs everyone, so far as he is able, from observing that same law, just as the Lord says to the scribes and Pharisees: “Woe to you, who have taken away the keys of knowledge and understanding; you yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who wished to enter” (Matthew 22).

Indeed, with what face and boldness of freedom can any priest toil in the alliance of dissidents when he does not grant the forgiveness of mercy to those who injure him, but is fiercely driven to vengeance?

Among all the jewels of virtue that our Savior brought from heaven, he showed two shining more prominently and brilliantly: charity and patience. He first expressed them in himself and taught them so that they might be impressed upon us.

Of charity the Apostle says: “Because of his great charity with which God loved the world, he sent his Son” (Ephesians 2). Of patience he says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15). Through the charity of God the Son descended from heaven; through patience he overcame the devil.

Armed with these virtues, the apostles, as founders, established the holy Church; and its defenders, the holy martyrs, triumphantly endured various punishments of death. [Col. 0316A] (Consult the Scholia.)

If, then, for the faith by which the universal Church lives, no one is ever permitted to take up iron weapons, how can armored lines rage with swords for the earthly and transient resources of the Church? Moreover, when holy men prevail, they do not kill heretics or worshipers of idols; rather, they do not refuse to be killed by them for the Catholic faith. How, then, can a faithful person attack another faithful person with swords over the loss of worthless possessions, when he knows that the other has likewise been redeemed with Christ’s blood?

In the regions of Gaul I heard that the following occurred. A serious dispute over a possession arose between an abbot and a certain powerful secular man. After the supporters of both sides had long contended with threats and quarrels, it was finally agreed that the matter should be decided by arms on both sides.

The secular man, having prepared a force of soldiers, entered the field to fight; he drew up his battle line, arranged his formations, and, as an exceedingly zealous exhorter, inflamed everyone’s minds to act bravely. Everything bristled with swords, shields reddened, the shouting of those who cried out rose up, the threatening growls of the armed men were terrifying, and weapons were drawn. They awaited only the attack of the opposing side, their hands already eager to strike.

But the abbot, placing his hope not in earthly arms but in the author of human salvation, forbade all who had gathered to fight on his behalf to accompany him. He placed only his monks upon horses, ordered their heads to be covered with hoods, and thus came with them to the place of battle, as though they were helmeted and armored with the protection of faith and bearing the banner of the cross.

When that man saw that the expected iron weapons were absent, but perceived at close range what seemed to be a heavenly and angelic army approaching, such terror of divine fear seized him and all his men that they immediately dismounted, threw down their weapons, prostrated themselves humbly on the ground, and begged forgiveness.

Thus, truly, he obtained the marks of a triumphal victory—not by placing his hope in numerous horses or flashing swords, but by trusting solely in the power of God.

If someone objects that Pope Leo often involved himself in military affairs and nevertheless was holy, I say what I think: Peter did not obtain apostolic primacy because he denied the Lord (Mark 14), nor did David deserve the prophetic oracle because he invaded another man’s bed (2 Samuel 11). Evil and good are not judged according to the merits of those who possess them, but according to their own qualities.

Is it read anywhere that Gregory, who endured so many plunderings and acts of violence from the ferocity of the Lombards, either did such things or taught them by his writings? Did Ambrose wage war against the Arians who were cruelly harassing him and his Church? Is any pontiff among the saints said to have risen up in arms?

Let the laws of the forum or the decrees of a priestly council settle the causes of any ecclesiastical dispute, lest what ought to be conducted in the tribunals of judges or proceed from the judgment of pontiffs be turned, through armed conflict, into our reproach.

But behold, while my eagerness to speak with you prolongs the thread of my discourse, as I see, beyond the limit of a concise letter. May almighty God preserve you, venerable father, safe for governing the state of his Church; and may you also deign to remember me in your holy prayers. [Note: [Col. 0317A]

But since, among the other evils that arise in our times … This part of the letter should be read attentively, lest anyone either take from it an occasion for error or think that the author has deviated in doctrine. For it may appear that he believed that a pontiff, or other ecclesiastical rulers, could not defend ecclesiastical possessions through war if necessity required it, because the Church has not a temporal sword but only a spiritual one.

Hence, in the section beginning “Therefore, just as,” midway through the letter, he intends the duties of kingdom and priesthood to be divided in such a way that the king uses the weapons of the world while the priest girds himself with the spiritual sword. And below: “If, then,” he says, “for the faith by which the universal Church lives, no one is ever permitted to take up iron weapons, how can armored lines rage with swords for the earthly and transient resources of the Church?” and so forth.

Before we draw these words of Damian, and others that he expresses with considerable exaggeration and without distinction, toward a pious and true meaning that is not foreign to the words themselves, it is necessary briefly to set forth the true and Catholic doctrine.

First, then, it must be established that the subject here is an ecclesiastical ruler as such, or a pontiff insofar as he is a pontiff. For if he is considered as a temporal lord, possessing direct and proper temporal dominion and jurisdiction in his own lands, there is no doubt that he has the same right of war that other supreme kings and temporal lords possess, insofar as the requirements of justice are concerned.

Even so, in conducting military affairs, he must preserve the religious character and decorum appropriate to pontifical dignity—which is preeminent in him—and this obliges him to observe, in the use of the temporal sword, a manner appropriate to pontifical dignity. It is unnecessary to say more on this point, because blessed Peter Damian does not treat it, nor does he touch upon any statement that requires interpretation from this perspective.

Second, it must be established that, by virtue of pontifical dignity, the pontiff possesses not only a spiritual sword but also, in some manner, a temporal one, as Pope Boniface expressly teaches in *Extravagantes* 1, *On Majority and Obedience*. Gregory, in Book 12, Letters 21 and 22, teaches the same; and this is a view approved by the common consensus of Catholics.

Gregory IX says in a letter to the patriarch of Constantinople that this was signified in the Gospel when the disciples said to Christ: “Behold, here are two swords.” He himself replied: “It is enough” (Luke 22). Later he said to Peter: “Put your sword into its sheath” (Matthew 26; John 18).

The Church also speaks thus concerning Peter: “You are the shepherd, the leader of all the apostles; God has entrusted all the kingdoms of the world to you.”

The reason is that, unless spiritual power had temporal power joined to it in some manner, it would be ineffective and weak. Therefore, since God’s works are perfect and rightly ordered, when he gave Peter supreme spiritual power, or the spiritual sword, he also gave him the temporal or material sword, insofar as this is appropriate to the end of the other power.

Hence the Gloss on chapter *Auctoritatem*, under the word *Materiali*, distinction 15, question 6, notes that an ecclesiastical judge can declare war, citing Pope Nicholas in the text there, where he says to the archbishop of Trier that the defenders of the Church should use both the spiritual and material sword until they recover ecclesiastical goods.

Third, it must therefore be established that the pontiff, insofar as he is pontiff, possesses the spiritual sword in one way and the temporal sword in another. He possesses the spiritual sword in itself and directly; but the temporal sword only indirectly—that is, on account of the spiritual sword, and insofar as it is appropriate to the latter’s end.

Therefore, he alone possesses the spiritual sword immediately from God, and through him it is transmitted to ecclesiastical persons, who participate in it; in laymen it is found in no way. But the temporal sword is found in itself and directly in the emperor and in temporal kings or princes—not through emanation from the pontiff, but through other titles and means by which that power is customarily justly acquired or obtained by hereditary right.

For that supreme power which the pontiff possesses indirectly in temporal matters does not take away the proper rights of other princes, nor deprive them of their direct dominions and authority. For this reason the laws commonly say that the pontiff—formally speaking, always with regard to his pontificate—does not possess jurisdiction in temporal matters, as is gathered from chapter *Si duobus*, section *denique*, *On Appeals*, together with the concordant passages cited there by the final Gloss, and frequently by the jurists, especially in chapter *A nobis*, *On Judgments*, and in chapter *Licet ex suscepto*, *On the Competent Forum*. [Col. 0318B] 119
Therefore Damian’s words are to be understood according to the truth: “The respective duties of kingship and priesthood are distinct,” and so forth. For he is speaking of duties that are proper in themselves and, indeed, directly suited to the dignity in question. Nor is this manner of speaking foreign to the pontiffs themselves. For Pope Nicholas, in a celebrated letter to the emperor Michael, writes near its end as follows:

“When the matter came to the true King and Pontiff alike—that is, in the time of the law of grace—the emperor no longer seized for himself the rights of the pontificate, nor did the pontiff usurp the title of the emperors; for that same mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, so distinguished the offices of each power by their own acts and dignities that Christian emperors needed pontiffs for eternal life, [Col. 0318C] while pontiffs used imperial laws only for the course of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain separate from carnal incursions, and therefore one serving God might not at all involve himself in secular business,” and so forth.

In discussing this passage, the Gloss on chapter *Cum ad verum*, distinction 96, under the word *Usurpavit*, gathers from it that these powers are divided, and that the emperor does not have the temporal sword from the pope [[Col. 0317D] see chapter *Duo sunt*, distinction 96, with the other passages there]. The same point is made in chapter *Quoniam*, distinction 10, where it is also added: “The pope does not possess both swords.” This must be understood as referring to direct and proper possession, lest the statement be erroneous. Moreover, insofar as the temporal sword is in the pontiff, it is in a certain way one with the spiritual sword, because where one thing exists for the sake of another, there is, in a sense, only one thing. Otherwise, as we have said, it is certain that the pontiff possesses both swords, spiritual and temporal; and the Gloss likewise asserts this in the words of the text there, in chapter 1, distinction 22.

Finally, it must be established that although the pontiff, by virtue of [Col. 0318D] his own power, possesses the material sword in the manner already explained, he ought not to use it himself, nor through ecclesiastical persons, except for his own defense in a case of extreme necessity. Rather, he ought to use secular princes, whom he can command to employ it in his defense or in just vengeance whenever necessity requires.

Boniface expressly said this in the passage cited above. For after stating that both swords, spiritual and temporal, are in the power of the Church, he adds: “The one is to be exercised for the Church, the other by the Church; the one belongs to the priest, the other is wielded by the hands of kings and soldiers, but at the priest’s command and with his approval.” Gregory IX uses nearly the same words in the said letter to Germanus.

[Col. 0319A] That pontiffs were accustomed to rouse temporal princes in this way and to declare war through them is sufficiently clear from ecclesiastical histories, as well as from Gregory’s letters: book IV, letter 31; book VII, indiction 1, letter 20; indiction 2, letters 2 and 3; book XI, letter 43; and book XII, letters 21 and 22; and from many other passages collected by Gratian, 23, question 5, chapters *Principes* and *Omnium*, with others, and 23, question 8, chapter *Igitur*, with the following three chapters.

Indeed, in all these passages one may observe that pontiffs almost always deal with defensive war when they declare it or exhort others to it, because such war is not only just but also extremely necessary. Thus, when they call even for offensive war, it almost always has the character of defense, because the injury done to the Church continues: either her goods are unjustly withheld, or the obedience owed to her is denied, or some other harm is inflicted upon the Christian religion.

They rarely, or never, call for war that is purely vindictive—not because such war could not be declared by one possessing supreme power, but because it is not equally necessary, nor so consonant with ecclesiastical piety and gentleness; and because it carries so many disadvantages and even spiritual harms that [Col. 0319B] ordinarily it is judged better to leave certain offenses unpunished than to bring about wars of this kind.

Accordingly, in those same histories it may also be observed that pontiffs rarely declare war, especially among Christians and the faithful, for the sake of a merely temporal end, but rather for a spiritual one. For although at times they may initially intend the recovery of the Church’s temporal goods, they do not stop at that objective; they always consider the spiritual benefit or harm that will result from it. Thus they never declare war unless, after everything has been weighed, a greater spiritual benefit for the Church is expected from it than the harm of the war.

Damian, therefore, never doubted the Church’s right to declare war in these just and honorable ways, nor did he discuss anything concerning that matter in this letter. He dealt only with the fact itself and with a certain abuse or excess that some prelates of his time were committing in this business.

Thus, if the holy doctor exceeded the proper bounds in this respect [Col. 0319C]—which I do not decide—his error concerned the fact, not the doctrine; and this is sufficiently clear from his words. First, he censures ecclesiastical persons who wage war to avenge their own injuries, as is evident from these words:

“Some people ask whether the rulers of the Churches ought to seek vengeance, repaying evil with evil after the manner of secular people. For many, as soon as the force of an injury is inflicted upon them, immediately rush to declare war and organize bands of armed men; and so they take revenge upon their enemies, perhaps more fiercely than they themselves were injured. This seems absurd to me,” and so forth.

Observe that he is not dealing with the right to do so, but with the fact itself; and he censures the circumstances of the deed rather than its substance—namely, that it is carried out in revenge, with excessive readiness and severity or cruelty, and, finally, that it is undertaken personally by ecclesiastical persons.

Later he draws an argument from King Azariah, by way of contrast:

“For because he usurped the priestly office, he is covered, he says, with leprosy; and if a priest takes up arms—which is properly the work of laymen—what does he deserve?”

This, then, is what he censures in the bishops of Gaul or Germany [Col. 0319D]: that they used the material sword with their own hands, which ought not to be done. Indeed, at the end of the letter he dares to criticize Leo IX for personally accompanying an army against the Normans, although he did not enter into the actual engagement of battle. With what justice Damian wrote this, let the prudent reader judge.

Certainly Herman the Lame, recounting that history, says:

“It was said that this befell Leo by the hidden judgment of God, either because it was more fitting for so great a priest to fight a spiritual battle rather than a carnal one for perishable things, or because he was leading wicked men with him,” and so forth. (HERM. CONTRACT., *Chronicle*, under the year 1053.)

[Col. 0320A] I therefore consider this to have been the sound meaning of the holy doctor. If at times he seems to introduce testimonies, examples, or arguments that appear to imply something more, one ought not to take and apply each of them with such rigor, but only according to the purpose and intention of the writer. He did not weigh each word or testimony in the scholastic manner, but rhetorically gathered together everything that could in any way contribute to persuading his readers of what he intended or to heightening his criticism.

## LETTER X. TO R., BISHOP

### ARGUMENT

It is credible that this letter was written to the bishop of Eugubium. In it he excuses himself for having allowed his church to be consecrated by the bishop of Forosempronius, although the right of consecrating it seemed to belong to the bishop of Eugubium, since the church had been established within his diocese.

He says that he did this first because he had heard that the same bishop regarded himself as having, so to speak, possession of the right to consecrate the churches of that place. Secondly, he did it so as not to make more hostile someone whom he had previously found insufficiently well disposed toward him. He therefore asks that the right to celebrate Masses, which had been taken away, be restored to the church, and that the bishop undertake the protection of his monasteries.

[Col. 0320B] To his lord, the lord Bishop R., Peter, in every respect a servant and son.

Most dear father, my conscience bears witness that, although I allowed the church to be consecrated by the bishop of Sempronius, I did not do so in order to diminish your prerogative, but because I heard from the inhabitants of a custom, though a new one, associated with his predecessor [the wording is corrupt]. They admitted that, ever since the aforesaid bishop entered upon the estate of Sorbitulus, he had acquired the custom of consecrating the churches himself. And who was I to impose another bishop upon one possessor, whether justly or unjustly, and to sow a quarrel between two bishops while I was a monk?

[Col. 0320C] Moreover, I did not doubt that scandals had to come, but I feared what follows: “Woe to the one through whom the scandal comes” (Matthew 18). Certainly, this scandal, however unwelcome it may seem to anyone insofar as it was carried out with God and justice, was not a little necessary for me.

For ever since you came to this episcopate, by God’s authority—ask whether this is true—I have been unable to maintain charity with the bishop of Sempronius. He who had until then been most devoted to me has now become, no longer secretly but most openly, my enemy. Happy am I in such misfortune! For from the very source from which your spirit is stirred against me, I, who desire to flee from an enemy, gain the fruit of advantage.

For Saul was killed without David’s knowledge (1 Samuel 31; 1 Chronicles 10); and this sinful monk has likewise been freed from the snare of the bishop of Sempronius, not through any effort of his own, but solely by God’s will.

[Col. 0320D] Know without doubt, most beloved father, that I love your Church and faithfully desire your salvation and honor according to God. Nor do I in any way refuse to show obedience to your see; rather, I run to offer it eagerly.

Therefore, most beloved, I earnestly beg you: restore the ministry that has been forbidden to our church. And not only defend that little possession, which is undoubtedly within your diocese, by your authority, but also defend everything that we possess; in every respect regard it as yours. Thus the brothers who serve God with us may rejoice that they have you as their father and defender, and may not cease to implore divine mercy for you.

## LETTER XI. TO THEODOSIUS OF SENIGALLIA AND RODULPH OF EUGUBIUM, BISHOPS

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0321A] He appoints Theodosius, bishop of Senigallia, and Rodulph, bishop of Eugubium, as judges and, as it were, censors of his books. He orders them, after reading them carefully, to correct and amend whatever seems necessary, whether before or after his death, by whatever means they deem appropriate.

To the most reverend bishops, Theodosius of Senigallia and Rodulph of Eugubium, Peter, a sinful monk, offers his service.

Let your holiness know, most beloved fathers and lords, that I have presumed to write certain little works—not so much, obviously, to add anything to the ecclesiastical laws, which would have been rash, as chiefly because I could not endure the tediousness of idle leisure and a more secluded cell without some form of exercise. Since I could not labor usefully with the work of my hands, I sought to restrain my wandering and wanton heart with a kind of bridle of meditation, and thus more easily to drive away the clamor of invading thoughts and the persistence of creeping listlessness.

[Col. 0321B] But since I am already approaching the tribunal of that judgment where, I do not doubt, an examination will be conducted not only of words and writings but even of the smallest thoughts, I earnestly entreat your holiness’s prudence, insofar as I am able, that either while I am still alive, if you have the opportunity, or after it happens that I die, you carefully read through whatever little works of mine you can find.

[Col. 0321C] And if anything in them is found to be discordant with the Catholic rule, or opposed to the authority of the sacred Scriptures, then, as seems best, either cut it out entirely or restore the corrected statement to a sound meaning. Thus, whatever has been distorted through the ignorance of my foolishness may be reformed according to the line of the right faith through the diligence of your holiness. In this way, the charity that builds up may correct through you what the knowledge that perhaps puffed me up has done wrong.

For what wonder is it if I, an unlearned and merely natural man, appoint holy men as judges of my little compositions, when Luke and Mark had the apostles Peter and Paul as censors of the Gospels that they had written under the dictation of the Holy Spirit?

[Col. 0321D] Moreover, since among those who are practiced in meditation upon the Scriptures I do not believe that anyone exists with a purer faith concerning me or more abundant charity, I therefore impose this burden of labor upon you above all.

So, most beloved, remain faithful to me in this work of piety even after my death, and discharge the final obligations of our old friendship in such a way that neither the guilt of my error, if any is found, may cling to me, nor may the reward of heavenly prizes fail to increase for you through the service of charity that you have rendered.

## LETTER XII. TO V., BISHOP

### ARGUMENT

He rebukes a bishop who is alienating the goods of his church and, setting the magnitude of his offense before his eyes, urges him not to commit anything similar in the future.

[Col. 0322A] To his lord V., most reverend bishop, Peter the sinner sends greetings.

I do not want you to be unaware, venerable brother, that considerable rumor has grown concerning the estates of your church, which you are said to be disposing of; indeed, that report recently pierced my heart with no slight sting of sorrow.

Have you forgotten that about five years ago Victor, bishop of the Apostolic See—Pope Victor II—prohibited this under penalty of excommunication at the plenary council held at Florence, which the emperor Henry also attended? Or are you unaware that estates are given to churches for this purpose: that the poor may be supported from them, the needy fed, and assistance provided from them to widows and orphans?

At the beginning of the rising Church, this custom took root: that all who came to the faith should dispose of the rights to their possessions and offer at the apostles’ feet the price received from them. Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles:

[Col. 0322B] “As many as were owners of fields or houses, selling them, brought the prices of the things they sold and laid them at the apostles’ feet” (Acts 4).

In a later period, however, the holy rulers of the Churches judged that the estates themselves should rather be transferred to the churches. This was so that the Church might not only feed clerics who kept vigil at the sacred offices, but also provide a contribution for refreshment to various needy persons and to those suffering from want.

Consider, therefore, venerable brother, how many murders the person will be guilty of on the day of judgment who now deprives so many orphans and various poor people of the means by which they ought to live.

[Col. 0322C] With what conscience does he come before the tribunal of the one who loves the poor in a special way, who declares that he is refreshed in the poor and hungers in the poor (Matthew 25)—before the tribunal, I say, of the one who recognizes that he has taken away the poor people’s means of sustenance?

If the one who kills even a single person with a sword is condemned, what sentence will be deserved by the person who, by squandering the goods of the Church, kills many with the sword of hunger and want?

To every such seller, the divine voice already says:

“Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Genesis 4).

That man killed his brother out of envy, because his sacrifice was not accepted when God rejected it. These people, for the most part, do such a thing out of love of money, “which is the service of idols” (Ephesians 3).

But because I confronted you and rebuked you concerning these matters with as much severity as was permitted, you replied that what had been given was insignificant and that the report brought to me had exaggerated the extent of the matter.

[Col. 0322D] To this I answer: sometimes liquid trickles out drop by drop, yet eventually empties the vessel completely; even a well-stocked storeroom, from which a small amount is removed each day, is eventually found empty. Yet the very thing you call small and insignificant does not escape the knowledge of the Judge of all.

Hear what Jeremiah says:

“The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Behold, Hanamel, the son of Shallum, your paternal cousin, will come to you, saying: Buy for yourself my field which is in Anathoth, for the right of kinship belongs to you, so that you may buy it” (Jeremiah 32).

[Col. 0323A] A little later he adds:

“I understood that it was the word of the Lord, and I bought the field from Hanamel, my paternal cousin, which is in Anathoth, and I weighed out to him seven staters and ten pieces of silver” (Jeremiah 32).

Observe how small and insignificant that field is understood to have been, since it was bought for only ten pieces of silver and seventeen shekels; and yet the prophet testifies that the word of the Lord concerning it had been addressed to him.

The same field was nevertheless of such importance to Jeremiah that he says of it:

“I wrote it in a book, sealed it, called witnesses, weighed out the silver on the scales, and took the sealed book of purchase, with its stipulations, ratifications, and external marks” (ibid.),

along with many other details that we postpone recording here, lest we burden the readers.

If such a small possession was bought by the prophet with such solemnity, and was even proclaimed by an oracle of the divine voice, how much more ought any inheritance belonging to ecclesiastical right to be a source of dread when it is to be sold—an inheritance from which Christ is to be supported in his needy members?

[Col. 0323B] But why speak of sale, when not only those properties that are leased by a contract of emphyteusis, or that come by right, and even those that are held under the name of a *libellus* and pay a fixed rent, but also those that secular persons receive under the bare title of a benefice, can in no way thereafter be recalled and restored to the churches?

Thus the hands of those who seize such goods become stuck fast with the devil’s glue of tenacity, so that once they have received them in any manner, they are in no way willing to return the Church’s goods. Not only do they themselves possess them while they live, as though by proprietary right, but they transmit them to the descendants of their lineage to be possessed by them in turn.

[Col. 0323C] Secular persons ask you for ecclesiastical estates; they thrust themselves forward importunately and persist in their pleas. They do not ask for them under formal written guarantees, but merely, perhaps, in the name of a benefice—which amounts to the same thing as if they were written with a diamond stylus on bronze tablets.

They come to you, therefore, saying with Ahab, king of Samaria:

“Give me your vineyard, so that I may make it into a garden of vegetables, because it is nearby and close to my house” (1 Kings 21).

You, with Naboth the Jezreelite, ought to answer at once:

“May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (ibid.).

[Col. 0323D] Furthermore, you are not unaware that when we receive lands from penitents, we lessen the measure of their penance in proportion to the size of the gift, as it is written: “A man’s wealth is his redemption” (Proverbs 13).

Consider, therefore, and reflect with appropriate reasoning: just as the one who provides estates to the churches is rightly lightened of the burden of his penance, so the one who takes them away is weighed down by a fitting burden of penance that he must undergo.

For if the giver is absolved, it follows that the one who seizes the property is bound in chains, and that he is held liable to a debt as great as the other is undoubtedly held absolved.

Whoever, therefore, is prodigal with ecclesiastical territory gathers many evils together upon a single head. At the terrifying judgment of God, the saints, whose honor is diminished by the poverty of the clergy, will be angry; the poor, widows, orphans, and all manner of guests will cry out that they have been killed by the sword of hunger.

Thus a person will be guilty of many murders even though he may never have shed blood.

[Col. 0324A] There are also those who hand over parishes to secular persons. These plainly sin more gravely, insofar as they are also convicted of committing sacrilege: they profane holy things and offer deadly poison to those to whom they appear to grant a benefice.

For what is it to turn tithes to secular use except to provide them with deadly poison by which they may perish?

To this is added the fact that a just occasion is given to the parishioners to withdraw obedience from their mother churches and to refuse to pay them the lawful tribute of tithes.

These truly are the outstanding gifts of a pontiff: the honor of the churches is taken away; those who receive what is given turn it to their destruction; and the people are recalled from obedience to Christian practice.

[Col. 0324B] Therefore, most beloved brother, withdraw your hand from these sacrilegious gifts. Guard yourself from these wicked and profane contracts with ever-watchful and most diligent care.

First govern the souls entrusted to you, and then also the resources of the Church, with such constant vigilance that, when you have completed the course of your stewardship, you may be called—not, God forbid, the destroyer of the Church, but its guardian and pastor, as the testimony of an illustrious reputation confirms.

I beg you, brother, not to regard this correction as too severe. Since you know that through our efforts you were advanced to the summit of the episcopate, it is fitting that, just as you calmly endured the one who advanced you, so you should also at times calmly endure the one who rebukes you.

The Lord himself first raised Peter above the universal Church and then struck him with a severe rebuke. For when he said:

“I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind or loose on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16),

shortly afterward he rebuked him so sternly that he said:

[Col. 0324C] “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings” (ibid.).

In this he plainly gave us an example, so that those whom we raise to the summit of honor we may always restrain under the instruction of discipline; and so that they may not, with the height of their position flattering them, raise themselves into a tyranny of pride, their teachers may press them down with the heels of their guardianship.

## LETTER XIII. TO V., BISHOP OF SARSINA

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0324D] He gives thanks to the bishop of Sarsina because he had willingly received and continued to support with every service of generosity a certain young man of outstanding character but reduced by misfortune to extreme poverty, whom Peter himself had commended to him.

He urges him to continue to earn merit by works of piety on the young man’s behalf—indeed, on God’s behalf. He also begs him not to neglect his own salvation, nor to lie as though sunk in the sleep of lethargy, but to set before his eyes the fleeting hopes of mortals, the brevity and uncertainty of life, and the nearness and certainty of death; and by constant reflection to meditate upon the heavenly and eternal riches prepared in heaven for the pious in place of earthly and perishable goods.

To V., most reverend bishop of the Church of Sarsina, Peter the sinner offers his dutiful service in Christ.

I return worthy thanks to you, most beloved father, because you gladly received, for the love of Christ and out of affection for me, this poor young man whom I sent to you. As a true governor of the poor and father of orphans, you have offered him every service of humanity and piety.

[Col. 0325A] Now, therefore, most beloved, I humbly beg your Reverence: complete what you have begun. Plant in the garden of your Church the shoot that, cut off from every root of human assistance and hidden beneath the shadow of your mercy, you have not allowed to die until now, lest the moisture of your compassion preserve for a time one whom the later heat of extreme poverty might burn.

But why am I teaching a master? Take care of him, most beloved, not according to what my ineptitude stammers out in asking, but as your keen prudence sees to be expedient for his soul.

For the rest, most beloved, consider what you are doing, and reflect toward what end this tranquility of yours is tending. O how miserable it is to live for a short time amid the prosperity of this age and to hurry daily, with closed eyes and as though lying in a litter, toward the burning of eternal fire!

[Col. 0325B] Who knows how near death is, which now lies hidden like an ambush, or how short life is, which, deceptively flattering, supplies every prosperity?

But since I perhaps have greater influence with one wiser than myself by praying than by preaching, I beg you, most beloved father and lord, through Jesus: rouse yourself, awaken, become fully awake, open your eyes, look toward heaven, and do not lose the reward of eternal true blessedness through the dream of a momentary illusion.

I also ask you concerning our most beloved and sweetest brother Henry: keep him with you as a most beloved son, and bestow upon him the affection of paternal charity, so that he may never regret the praise and commendation that he continually reports about you wherever he goes.

May you be well; and in your holy prayers, I beg you to keep in mind me, a sinner.

## LETTER XIV. TO V., BISHOP

[Col. 0325C]

*(It is found in volume III and is opusculum 26.)*

## LETTER XV. TO V., BISHOP

### ARGUMENT

He prudently admonishes that the five bodily senses, when neglected, cause human beings to slide into the most shameful crimes, and that they must be restrained by the strictest guard of discipline.

He urges the bishop not only to practice this himself, but also to compel others entrusted to his care to do the same. Above all, he insists that, in this matter, he must take the strictest action against presbyters and priests who are especially guilty, without regard to their dignity or age; indeed, the greater a person’s rank, the more severely he should be punished.

[Col. 0325D] To V., most reverend bishop, and to the holy canons of his church, Peter, a sinful monk, offers his service.

In the forefront of a marching army, trumpets, horns, bugles, and military instruments are carried for this reason: that by their blasts the watches of the camp may be roused, and the soldiers may be able to protect themselves from the nighttime assault of the enemy. We too, who have sworn the military oath of the heavenly army and have entered battle against the rulers of the world and the spiritual forces of wickedness, must rouse one another with mutual cries, so that the nocturnal assailant may not find us weighed down by ignoble sleep, but, discovering us always prepared and ready in the battle line, may be afraid.

For we live, as it were, in a city of five gates, since we dwell in a body encircled by five senses. To these gates, therefore, we apply bolts; to them we add barriers, bars, and locks, when we carefully guard the entrances of our senses against invading vices and the vanities of the world. Our Pentapolis then remains safe and whole when it is content within its own boundaries, neither insolently going out against its enemies nor opening itself to those attempting to break in—so that our mind, established in the citadel of Mount Zion, may seek the things above and not descend to the flowing pleasures of carnal allure. Let it sigh for that Jerusalem which is above, which is free and is our mother; but let it despise and trample that which is enslaved, together with her children.

Otherwise, if it advances, following the example of the Gomorrites, into the wooded valley that is now the Salt Sea—that is, if it casts itself down into the depths of an unfruitful life, if it seeks the saltiness of earthly wisdom—it is immediately laid low when the enemy wins the victory, because it is not fortified when the walls of its own city are barred.

Does the prophet not close the gates of our city when he says: “He who stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed, and closes his eyes so as not to see evil, he shall dwell on high” (Isa. XXXV)? Does the Lord not also fortify the entrance of our taste when he says: “Beware lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness!” (Luke XXI). Concerning the sense of smell the Apostle says: “For we are the good aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved” (II Cor. II). But those who said, “Let us fill ourselves with perfumes, and let no flower of the season pass us by; let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither” (Wis. II), had opened the foul exhalations of their sense of smell.

Our sense of touch, however, ought to desire the same thing as our sense of taste. For what the Prophet says, “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. XXXIII), John likewise says: “What our hands have touched concerning the Word of life” (John II).

This contest, waged against the five senses of the body, is mystically represented by the five kings of the Midianites. “Arm from among yourselves men for battle,” Moses says, “who may exact the vengeance of the Lord from the Midianites” (Num. XXXI). When they had fought against the Midianites and conquered them, as sacred history relates, they killed all the males and their kings—Evi, Recem, Sur, Bur, and Rebe—the five princes of the nation.

Evi is plainly interpreted as “beastlike” or “wild.” We transfix this king within ourselves with a spiritual sword when we cut away wild behavior from ourselves, when we sever the rage of bestial anger from our breast. For when the Lord says, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V), how will you be able to obtain the blessedness of the meek unless you restrain within yourself the savagery of the beastlike spirit?

Recem—or, as it is called in the Old Translation, Rocon—is interpreted as “emptiness.” And what else is everything done in the world out of worldly desire than what Scripture says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity!” (Eccles. I). Vanity produces vain people, and vain people produce vanity, since the world, which is transient, makes vain the people whom it deceives, while people turn into vanity the world that they foolishly love.

Therefore, the soldier of God kills this king, and the true Israelite cuts him down, if he does nothing superfluous, nothing empty, nothing irrelevant, but strives seriously and rationally to fulfill the commandments of the divine law.

The third king of the Midianites is called Sur, which is certainly interpreted as “wall,” “strong,” or even “distress.” What should be understood by “wall” or “strong” except the obstinacy or stubbornness of a hardened mind?
