And since it is also interpreted as “distress,” this too is not far removed from the vice of hardness, because whoever is hard and stubborn about forgiving debts to his neighbor is constricted by distress of mind, since charity is not expanded in any breadth. Concerning this charity the Prophet says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII). It may also be understood in this way: distress of condemnation follows hardness of mind. Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful, but he who is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. XXVIII).

Moreover, the fourth king of the Midianites is called Bur, which is interpreted as “provocation.” You see, then, that the names of the kings are shadows and images of vices. For those who bring heavy burdens in through their gates pour into the secret places of their hearts, through the entrances of their senses, what is noisily clamoring outside; without doubt they provoke God, whom they thereby incite to pronounce a sentence of vengeance. Hence it is written: “The deceitful and the crafty provoke the anger of God” (Job XXXVI). And of such people it is often said in Ezekiel: “For it is a provoking house” (Ezek. II). The Psalmist likewise says: “Why, O God, has the enemy reproached you? Why does the adversary provoke your name continually?” (Ps. XXXIII).

Rebe, however, is said to mean “ordered.” Here this can proceed only if the expression is understood as irony or antiphrasis, so that the one called “ordered” is, on the contrary, disordered and confused. For every vicious person, even if outwardly he pretends to display an orderly way of life, nevertheless turns over in his heart the darkness of confused and disordered thought.

Through the five kings of the Midianites, therefore, the five bodily senses are signified, because every vice that reigns in the body depends upon these five senses. They must then be extinguished by us and cut down with swords when they rise up against us in battle, when they do not cease to scandalize us.

Does the Lord not command these kings to be extinguished and killed by the sword of the spirit when he orders the scandalizing eye to be plucked out and the hand or foot to be cut off? “It is better,” he says, “to enter life with one eye or maimed than, possessing two eyes, feet, and hands, to be cast into hell” (Matt. V).

These, plainly, are the kings of the Midianites. Midian, however, is interpreted as “judgment,” for all who are not ruled by the spirit as kings but obey the senses of the flesh show that they belong not to mercy but to judgment. Thus it is said of every unbeliever: “He who does not believe has already been judged” [Col. 0328A] (John III). But of the one who hears the Savior’s word it is said: “He does not come into judgment, but passes from death into life” (I John V).

Rather, each person should strive to exercise himself in holy works, and to endeavor to purify and sanctify himself in all things. He should never cease to rebuke and judge himself. For whoever judges himself perfectly does not await judgment. To judge oneself perfectly means both not to do what deserves reproach and to reconsider fearfully what has been done irreproachably.

Whoever does this truly kills the kings of the Midianites; he lays low the princes of the Amalekites and excludes from himself all the plagues of vice. Hence the same sacred History testifies: “The children of Israel went out and came to the fountain of judgment”—that is, Kadesh—“and killed all the princes of Amalek and the Amorites who dwelt in Tharansem [Asasonthamar]” (Gen. XIV).

Kadesh is interpreted as “sanctification.” At Kadesh, therefore, which is the fountain of judgment, we spiritually kill the Amalekites and Amorites when we strive both to sanctify our life through pious works and nevertheless judge ourselves as guilty and blameworthy. While we labor always to live irreproachably, through the vigilance of strict examination we do not cease to accuse our works.

It should also be noted that the fountain of judgment and Kadesh, which is called “sanctification,” are one and the same place, because every just person, while living holily, accuses himself and, by judging or accusing himself, sanctifies himself more and more.

Thus the life of the saints is both reproved in their own thoughts and found irreproachable in their works. Hence that chief city of the kingdom of Sihon is called Heshbon, which is interpreted as “thoughts.” This signifies that the greatest part of the devil’s power reigns in thoughts. Through Sihon the spirit of wickedness is represented; but Heshbon is transferred from the dominion of Sihon into the possession of the Israelites when our thought, which had swollen with the plague of pride, inclines itself by grace of true humility to the judgment of its own reproach—so that what once exalted itself arrogantly now humbly reproves itself, judging and carefully examining its own deeds.

At Kadesh, therefore, which is the fountain of judgment, we cast down the Amalekites and Amorites with the devouring sword, because then we overthrow the barbarism of every vice and wage unconquerable war against the aerial powers, if we live innocently and nevertheless judge ourselves guilty and subject to sins, saying with the Apostle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I).

Then Heshbon, which we said is interpreted as “thoughts,” is compelled to pass into the dominion of the Israelites, when our mind is transferred from pride and every earthly desire into love of the kingdom of heaven. The struggle of thoughts can never be absent from Christ’s soldiers, because the uprightness of our deeds does not free us if our mind, armed with virtues, does not resist its own evil thoughts.

It was enough for the observers of the ancient Law merely to do what was right outwardly. But when the Gospel thunders fearfully at us, we are commanded that, while stripping off evil works, we also keep watch against and fight our thoughts: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

Hence John the Baptist, through whom the Old Law is expressed, is said to have worn a leather belt around his loins (Matt. III). Our Savior, who is the author of the Gospel, was seen by John among the seven golden lampstands, clothed in a long robe and girded at the breast with a golden belt. What, then, is the leather belt around the loins except what was said to the ancients: “You shall not commit adultery”? And what is the golden belt at the breast except what is said to the observers of the Christian faith: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart”?

For this reason also the prophet gives the divine command: “Wash your heart, Jerusalem, from wickedness; how long will harmful thoughts remain within you?” (Jer. IV). And elsewhere: “I attended and listened; no one opened his mouth concerning what is good” (Jer. VIII). Solomon says: “The holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. I).

Let us therefore seize the sword of the spirit and fight without compromise against the phalanxes of thoughts that assail us. We read (Num. XXV) that Phinehas the priest, when he saw an Israelite having intercourse with a Midianite woman, suddenly seized a dagger and pierced the sacrilegious pair of fornicators through their joined bodies, between the private parts.

May this deed have built up the former people. But you, who have been instructed in the leadership of another kind of battle and are a spiritual leader of the flock, not a bodily [uncertain reading]: if you see anyone from your people going after the senses into love of the Midianites and wallowing in seductive thoughts, I do not want you to spare him; I do not want you to pretend not to see. Strike him immediately; pierce him without delay.

Investigating and penetrating that very womb—that is, the secret places of nature—pierce through the very tinder of sin, so that it may no longer be able to conceive or generate a poisonous offspring that would defile the Israelite camp. Let the sword of the spirit strike the very receptacle of sin and extinguish the delights of the wanton flesh’s licentiousness.

Although everyone must do this according to his own measure, it especially falls upon those who hold a position of governance and preside over the brothers entrusted to them. It is necessary that the fervor of priestly zeal kindle them against the vices of their subjects, and that they possess with Phinehas the rights of an everlasting priesthood. If, however, through laziness toward delinquents they grow weak with sluggishness, they are stripped of the priesthood and, like Eli, are struck down with their necks broken against the ground (II Kings IV).

Hence, when that Israelite people had been initiated into the worship of Beelphegor in the desert and had shamefully fallen into the prostitution of Moab, the Lord, angered and enraged against Israel, said to Moses: “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on gallows before the sun, so that my anger may be turned away from Israel” (Num. XXV).

What does it mean that the people fall into the abyss of lust, while vengeance is exacted upon their superiors? The subjects sin, and the leaders are hanged on gallows? Clearly, one is the person who sins and another the one who is punished. Why is this, unless it is because the guilt of the subjects redounds to the reproach of their superiors, and what the sheep do in straying is attributed to the negligence of the shepherd?

And see how dreadful is the condition of those who preside: they are punished not only for their own offenses but also for those of their subjects. Moses accuses them, because the law of God charges them with negligence and sluggishness. He hangs them before the sun because they are brought out for examination and reproved by the light. “For everyone,” as the Lord says, “who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be reproved; but whoever does the truth comes to the light” (John III).

The one who opens his hidden things through the entrance of pure confession comes to the light.

The rulers of the churches must therefore take care to beget children in Israel—not just any offspring, but male offspring, which may grow strong for fighting the battles of the Lord. For whoever, through the office of preaching entrusted to him, urges others to fight but does not fight himself is like one who makes a noise with the blasts of a bugle but does not dare to engage in close combat.

Such a man does not beget male offspring, since he is himself a cowardly father. He was signified by that Salphaad who, when he died, left behind not a son but five daughters (Num. XXVII). Salphaad is interpreted as “shadow in his mouth.” Whoever preaches courageous things but lives feebly hides himself, lest he appear shameful, as though beneath the leaves of honorable speech; he conceals himself in the shadow of his own mouth, since through the cowardice of his sluggishness he does not advance into the field of battle.

Thus, so far as he is concerned, he begets not a male but a female offspring, and this under the number five, when he trains his followers not for the strength of spiritual courage but for the idleness of an ignoble life. Since he does not take care to train them in the diligence of spiritual warfare, he compels them to serve outward affairs, as though they were subject to the five bodily senses.

Beloved, therefore, close these gates of the bodily senses against the phalanxes of invading vices, and open them to the ranks of spiritual virtues. The mind of Christ’s soldier ought to be spread out like a net, so that it may both divert the streams of empty thoughts and, conceiving the impulses of the Holy Spirit, enclose them as fish.

Let the nocturnal assailant find you strong and watchful, so that he may not break into the camps for which you stand—that is, into the entrances of your hearts. Let him always see the triumphant banner of the cross raised against him, so that—God forbid—he may not carry away the spoils of victory from you, but, fleeing at once, may disappear.

Always persevere in doing what is right, and nevertheless weigh the same deeds under the strict examination of the heart, so that you who now stand trembling before your own tribunals may behold the examination of the final necessity without fear—not to be judged again, but to receive glory.

## LETTER XVI. TO BISHOP V.

**Argument.**—He maintains that the octave of the nativity of Saint John the Baptist ought to be celebrated with the same veneration as the nativity itself. He then discusses the eight festivals of the Old Testament and transfers and adapts them allegorically to the standard of evangelical faith.

To the lord V., bishop of venerable holiness, and to the religious canons of his church, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the service of a servant.

The service of divine worship is unquestionably worthy of praise when it has been laudably completed. But what does it profit anyone to begin any work correctly unless he brings it to a proper conclusion? We know, therefore, beloved, that you reverently celebrate the feast of blessed John the Baptist as is fitting, but that, content with the brevity of three readings at his octave, you do not offer it the reverence it deserves.

For if the substance of the Gospel reading is carefully considered, no saint’s feast is celebrated in the Church whose octave deserves such reverence. The angel says to Zechariah: “It shall be joy and exultation for you, and many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke I). This was unquestionably fulfilled not on the very day of his birth but rather on the eighth day.

On the eighth day, when he was circumcised, it was announced by the angel to Zechariah, not without the joy of many; Elizabeth, inspired by God, gave the child his name; and the mouth of his father, which had long been closed, was opened. He who until then could not utter even ordinary words now poured forth the mysteries of a prophetic oracle.

All the joy, therefore, that had been promised by the angelic announcement is shown to have been bestowed on the eighth day of the nativity. The nativity of blessed John is thus exalted not so much by the grace of its own dignity as by the privilege of its octave.

For this reason equity dictates that, just as the nativity itself is honored, so also its octave should be honored, since the nativity itself is illuminated by it and receives from it the source of its celebration and distinction. This venerable nativity receives from its octave what makes it surpass the nativities of all the saints. Therefore it deserves from the octave an honor equal to that which, from itself, gives the octave its dignity of honor and solemn reverence.

Nor is it surprising that every especially distinguished and notable feast is now extended in the Church through a cycle of eight days, since Scripture says that in the ancient Law the Lord instituted eight principal solemnities through the course of each year. These festivals are, in the diversity of times, common both to us and to them. They belong to them through the rite of carnal observance, and they belong no less to us through the mystery of spiritual understanding.

The first of their festivals is the continual sacrifice, which is commanded to be offered throughout successive days at the morning and evening hours (Lev. XXIII; Num. XXVIII–XXIX). The one who continually celebrates the solemnity of the continual sacrifice to the Lord is the one who perseveres unceasingly in meditating upon the heavenly word.

Since the morning of our light is the Law and the Prophets, while the evening of this light, with regard to the order of the ages, is the Gospel—as the Apostle says, “upon us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X)—David likewise says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL).

He offers the morning and evening sacrifice to the Lord continually who, sacrificing himself by withdrawing from worldly affairs, remains constantly engaged in meditating upon the new and the old Scriptures. Or we continually offer the morning and evening sacrifice to the Lord when we render him worthy thanks for our redemption and, fearing his terrible judgment, stand trembling before him as though he were already presiding at the tribunal.

After the continual sacrifice comes the Sabbath, namely, so that one may abstain from every performance of servile work. For a Christian to keep a spiritual Sabbath is to rest from the laborious desire for temporal things, to toil only at prayer and reading, to cast the burden of worldly affairs from the neck of the mind, and to devote oneself with the whole intention of the heart to contemplating heavenly things. It is to despise the pleasures of the flesh and rejoice in spiritual delight from the sole hope of heavenly things.

Concerning this the Apostle says: “Therefore a Sabbath-rest remains for the people of God” (Heb. IV). He truly celebrates the Sabbath for the Lord who abstains from the works that belong to the world in such a way that he does not cease from spiritual actions.

Hence the Truth says: “Have you not read that the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are without blame?” (Matt. XVIII; John VIII). Whoever therefore ceases from the labors of worldly actions and devotes himself to works of divine service celebrates the Sabbath of the Christian religion.

He does not perform servile work, because he guards himself against committing sin. For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin. He does not light a fire in his house, because he extinguishes from the dwelling of his mind every fuel of vice and every spark of anger and hostility, guarding against that fire of which it is written: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isa. L).

Finally, he does not carry a burden on the road, because through repentance he lightens the heart bowed down by the rubble of iniquities. Concerning these the Prophet says: “For my iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they weigh heavily upon me” (Ps. XXXVII). And shortly afterward: “I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly” (ibid.).

Moreover, sitting in his own place, he does not proceed farther away, because he makes Christ his foundation, upon which he constructs the firmest dwelling of his rest. He is that place of which it is written: “The children of your servants shall dwell there” (Ps. CI). He is the foundation of which it is said: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Cor. III).

The third festival is the Neomenia, that is, the new moon. The moon is said to be renewed when it is joined to the sun and is restored by him to receive brightness, as though its lost light were recovered.

Christ is the Sun of righteousness (Mal. IV); the moon is first the holy universal Church, and then every faithful soul, enlightened by his rays, who is the splendor of glory and the figure of substance (Heb. I).

When any holy soul is truly joined to its Redeemer in love, when, as in a bridal chamber, it is united to him through the innermost bond of delight, then without doubt it celebrates the solemnity of the Neomenia, presenting itself renewed by heavenly light to the sight of its brothers, as the Apostle says: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI).

For if in all these matters only the outward rite of the solemnities is accepted, it now seems that no benefit can be derived from them for us; rather, they would have to be judged superstitious and frivolous. Hence the Apostle says: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or with regard to a festival, or a new moon, or a Sabbath, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. II).

What was then a shadow of things to come for the Jew is now the manifestation of present realities for the Christian; and what was given to them under outward ceremonies has become for us an instrument of spiritual understanding. We celebrate the rising of the Neomenia, that is, of the new moon, when we lay aside the old person and put on the newness of holy conduct.

In fourth place comes the Paschal festival among them, in which that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world is now sacrificed among us for the salvation of the whole age (John I). “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V).

Joined to this is the festival called the Azymes, in which it is commanded that all leaven be cast out of every house. We truly celebrate this festival—which is to be understood together with Passover—if we cast the leaven of malice and wickedness out of the tabernacle of our heart and preserve the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

We must therefore beware that there be in our minds no shadow of disguise, corruption of leaven, or cavern of falsehood; rather, in the house of our breast let both the integrity of purity and the solidity of truth flourish.

After this comes the festival called that of the New Produce, when firstfruits are offered from the new crops. When the grain has reached maturity, the festival is celebrated for God, the author of all good things, in the perfection of good fruits.

We too celebrate the solemnities of the New Produce if, first breaking up the field of our heart with the plow of discipline, we scatter the seeds of virtues, so that afterward we may reap the grain of good works. Hence the prophet says: “Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jer. IV).

Concerning the good farmer Solomon says: “He who cultivates his land will heap up a harvest; he who practices righteousness will himself be exalted” (Ecclus. XX). Concerning the negligent worker he likewise says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, it was entirely overgrown with nettles, thorns covered its surface, and its stone wall was destroyed” (Prov. XXIV). And again: “Prepare your work outside and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (ibid.).

But whoever renews his inner person from day to day according to the Apostle’s teaching (II Cor. IV), whoever furrows his heart with the mattocks of divine fear—he sows not upon thorns but upon new ground, so that he may reap a harvest yielding a hundredfold.

Hence the Apostle says: “He who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. VI). What fruits are gathered from the Spirit in this life he carefully enumerates elsewhere, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, meekness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. V).

Whoever, therefore, gathers these fruits into the granary of his mind undoubtedly celebrates the solemnity of the New Produce to his salvation.

Next follows the festival of the seventh month, which is called that of the Blast or of the Trumpets. Just as every seventh day is called a Sabbath, so likewise among the months the seventh is called the Sabbath of the months, and even the Sabbath of Sabbaths.

What is that blast of trumpets to which we ought to pay our annual festival observances, except evangelical and apostolic teaching? Like heavenly thunder and a terrifying trumpet, it summons us to the readiness of spiritual warfare and urges us to fight without compromise against the spirits of wickedness on behalf of the camp of the eternal emperor.

Who, then, legitimately celebrates the festival of the trumpets or of the blast, except the one who strives to enclose the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments in the treasury of his mind and to entrust the heavenly commandments always to tenacious memory?

To those celebrating these feasts properly the Prophet says: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of your solemnity” (Ps. LXXX).

After this comes the festival celebrated on the tenth day of the seventh month, on which the Jews are commanded to afflict their souls. We too properly celebrate this solemnity when we chastise our flesh through fasting and mortification; when we restrain ourselves under the strict custody of discipline; when, finally, we crucify the wanton enticements of carnal passions; when we wear down our body through labors and hardships for the Lord; when we sacrifice the inner person through the lamentation of contrition and tears.

When we celebrate this festival in this way, the one whom God appointed as an expiation through faith in his blood is reconciled to us.

The eighth solemnity, which is also the last, is called Scenopegia, that is, the festival of Tabernacles. It begins to be celebrated on the fifteenth day of the same seventh month.

God rejoices in you when he sees you as a pilgrim and exile, and sees you dwelling not in the houses of your homeland but in the tabernacles of exile. “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. XIII).

When, although we see ourselves here through the mass of the body, we dwell in heaven through the intention of our desire; when, as travelers and sojourners, we pass through all present things by despising them in our minds, but hasten toward our heavenly homeland with anxious steps of longing—then we spiritually celebrate Scenopegia, which formerly was observed among them carnally through the ceremonies of the prescribed rite.

This festival begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month; and since it is celebrated for eight days, it unquestionably ends on the tenth day before the Kalends of October. For it is said in the Book of Numbers: “On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, which shall be holy and venerable for you, you shall do no servile work on it, but you shall celebrate a solemnity to the Lord for seven days” (Num. XXVI). A little later it adds: “On the eighth day, which is the most celebrated, you shall do no servile work on it” (ibid.).

On this holy and most celebrated day, blessed John the Baptist is said to have been conceived. For this reason we were moved to write this letter: so that we might place its conclusion where its writing had its origin.

Here a not-simple question arises: how was blessed John conceived while the festival had not yet ended but was still continuing, when the evangelist Luke says: “And when the days of his service were fulfilled, he went”—there is no doubt that this means Zechariah—“to his house; and after these days Elizabeth his wife conceived” (Luke I)?

How were the days of his service fulfilled when the festival itself had not yet been completed? The festival called Scenopegia began on the fifteenth day of the aforesaid month and was celebrated for eight full days, so that the eighth day before the Kalends of October, on which blessed John was conceived, might be regarded among the other days of the same festival as the more festive and, as it is called there, the most celebrated.

But if it should perhaps be said that the Church’s tradition is mistaken, so that he was conceived on that very day but afterward, once the entire solemnity had run its course, this . . . .

[Note: At this point the manuscript is mutilated.]

It is also worthy of consideration that, if the number of days is carefully examined—whether those during which the Lord remained in the virginal womb or those during which blessed John remained in the womb of the aged woman—the number of the Lord’s days is found to exceed John’s by two days.

From the conception of the Lord until his birth there are 276 days; from John’s conception until his birth there are found to be only 274 days. For since the Lord was conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, while John was conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of October and came forth from his mother’s womb on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, the number of the Savior’s days nevertheless exceeds John’s number by two days.

This is because of the month of February, which contains only twenty-eight days in its reckoning, whereas all the other months contain either thirty or thirty-one days. Since blessed John lay hidden in his mother’s womb during this month—after it had elapsed the Lord was conceived, and before the annual cycle was completed John was born—the two days by which this month is shorter are found to be lacking from the conception of blessed John.

The brevity of this month therefore explains why the number of the Savior’s days exceeds John’s number. Once this explanation has been given, it is believable that blessed John the Baptist was conceived before the solemnity of Scenopegia had run its course.

The fact that the Lord remained longer in his mother’s womb while John came forth more quickly was not an accidental coincidence but a dispensation suited to the persons. The one, like a surveyor preparing a lodging, left the house earlier, so that he might immediately prepare the way for the emperor who was to follow; announce his coming to kingdoms, provinces, and cities; direct the crowds of the gathered peoples to meet such majesty; and quickly prepare everything necessary for his reception.

But our emperor, remaining in the bridal chamber of the virginal palace, stayed a little longer, and judged it better to proceed more slowly, he who had sent ahead the surveyor and steward. But . . . .

[Note: The end of this letter is missing in the manuscript.]

## LETTER XVII. TO BISHOP A.

(It is found in volume III and also in tract 40.)

## BOOK FIVE. TO ARCHPRIESTS, ARCHDEACONS, PRIESTS, AND CLERICS.

[Col. 0335]

139–140—FIRST LETTER. TO THE ARCHPRIESTS ANDREW, V., AND C.

[Col. 0335C]

**Argument.**—He vehemently attacks certain slanderous and unlearned persons because they were attempting maliciously to bring into disrepute certain words taken from his own sermon. In those words he had maintained that human souls leave this world in such a condition as they are brought before judgment; he shows that this saying was not first uttered by himself, but by Gregory the Great, and that it accords with Holy Scripture.

To the venerable brothers in Christ, the archpriests Andrew, V., and C., Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of brotherly charity.

Although I am now confined to my bed by no slight illness and, as has been said, another brother is to take up the remainder, it should not be surprising if I do not arrange a lucid or polished composition in this feeble discourse. Indeed, since I am speaking against rustic and uneducated people, utterly ignorant of letters, it is fitting that I speak rustically, in a manner suited to them; and, as they themselves say, that I carelessly pour out whatever comes into my mouth.

Nevertheless, before I come to the matter itself, I shall briefly set down what my mind suggests. A certain philosopher [Note: [Col. 0337D] Thales the philosopher, concerning whom Plato writes in the *Theaetetus*], while carefully examining by night the courses of the stars and the movements of the constellations, suddenly fell into a well, gaping open—as the saying goes—of monstrous depth and full of filthy, indecent squalor [Note: [Col. 0338D] Diogenes, *On the Lives of the Philosophers*]. This philosopher had a household maid named Iambe, who freely and intelligently mocked her master. In iambic meter—which afterward received its name from her—she amusingly said of him:

> “My master,” she said, “did not know the dung that lay beneath his feet, yet he was trying to learn about the stars.”

So it is in our own days. Rustic and foolish men, who know almost nothing except how to cleave the fields with ploughshares, to tend pigs, and to guard the pens of various livestock, now do not blush to debate the pronouncements of the sacred Scriptures at crossroads and in the streets before little women and their fellow herdsmen. Indeed—and this is shameful to say—though they lie all night between women’s thighs [f. “who lie all night”], by day they are not ashamed to discuss the sayings of angels; and in this way they sit in judgment on the words of holy teachers. [Col. 0337A–B]

For your holiness has informed me by letter that, because of the statement which we included in the sermon of blessed Stephen—namely, that each person’s soul is presented at the judgment in the condition in which it departs from this world—such scandal has arisen among certain people that they say the prayers, offerings, and sacrifices presented for the souls of the dead accomplish nothing for them before the judgment. [Col. 0337C]

And what wonder if the same thing has happened to me, a sinner, that is known to have happened to the very author of the whole Christian religion? For he says:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

When nearly seventy men heard this, they said:

> “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (ibid.)

And, as Scripture testifies, they no longer walked with him. Christ the sun therefore scorched them, for he is the Sun of Justice (Malachi 4); but the moon scorched these people. I belong to the moon—that is, to the body of Christ, which is the Church. You, on the contrary, while blessing me, deign to say:

> “By day the sun shall not strike you, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 120).

Behold how far the learned and prudent men of these regions have advanced: they know all the depths of heavenly speech and comprehend all the mysteries of the divine books, yet in one single statement of my discourse they fall into the darkness of blindness. [Col. 0337D]

And if it pleases them to be heretics, do my friends love me so greatly that they cannot pass into heresy without me? For whoever maintains that prayers, offerings, and sacrifices cannot benefit the dead, and rashly attempts to assert this, is plainly shown to be an Aerian. Aerius, in his discussions of his error, teaches that these works of piety are altogether vain and futile and will later benefit no one in that world. [Col. 0338A]

Can these vigorous investigators of the divine utterances not find many statements throughout the fields of sacred Scripture by which they might construct snares and nooses for themselves, if they wish to become heretics? Moreover, if they delight in finding grounds for abandoning Christianity, let them judge what the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Concerning that day”—that is, the judgment—“neither the angels in heaven know, nor the Son himself, but the Father alone” (Matthew 24).

And how could the Son be ignorant of the day of judgment, since he created that very day, and all times and all visible and invisible things, together with the Father? Let them also reject what he says elsewhere:

> “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7). [Col. 0338B]

O Lord Jesus, we, your simple and dull servants, believe you in whatever you say. For we know that you are the truth (John 14) and cannot lie. But how will the wise men of this earth, those most dark and profound investigators of the divine books, be able to place faith in your words? According to their own cleverness, they will be able to question you with crafty malice: how can it be true that you said, “My teaching is not mine”? If it is yours, how is it not yours? But if it is not yours, how will it be yours? It remains, therefore, either that you plainly assert your teaching to be yours and no longer say that it is not yours, or, if you establish that it is not yours, that you altogether deny that it is yours. [Col. 0338C] Thus we must fear that they may ensnare you by the crafty argumentation of their syllogisms and entangle the author of wisdom in the traps of deceptive quibbling.

Moreover, to return also to the history in the Book of Kings, the Lord sent word to Josiah, king of Judah, through Huldah, the wife of Shallum:

> “Because you heard the words of the book, and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard the words spoken against this place and its inhabitants—that they would become a desolation, a curse, and an astonishment—and because you tore your garments and wept before me, I also have heard you, says the Lord. Therefore I shall gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your tomb in peace, so that your eyes may not see all the evil which I am about to bring upon this place” (2 Kings 22). [Col. 0338D]

A little later the same history adds:

> “Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Assyria at the river Euphrates; and King Josiah went out to meet him, and he was killed at Megiddo when he had seen him” (2 Kings 23). [Col. 0339A]

Here, surely, is where the censors of other people’s actions and the detractors of their brothers sharpen their teeth. For, as David says:

> “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56).

Here, I say, with puffed-out cheeks they may belch forth fiery flames, vomit the bitterness of their innermost gall, and confuse heaven and earth with their shouting, saying:

> “How did the divine utterance avoid falsehood and effectively fulfill what it had promised to the king? How, indeed, did Josiah rest in peace in his tomb, when he fell by the sword of the Egyptian king in the fortunes of war?”

Thus that prophetic saying may be applied to them:

> “They have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has traversed the earth” (Psalm 72). [Col. 0339A]

But you, my most beloved and like-minded brothers, from whom nothing must be concealed, know with certainty that that statement is Gregory’s, not ours. Therefore search carefully through the fourth book of the *Dialogues*, and there, among other things, you will find the following:

In the Gospel the Lord says:

> “Walk while you have the light” (John 12).

Through the prophet he also says:

> “At an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah 49).

Paul, explaining this, says:

> “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 5).

Solomon also says:

> “Whatever your hand can do, do it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes 9).

David likewise says:

> “For his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 165, 166).

From these statements it is plainly established that each person is presented at the judgment in the condition in which he departs from here. A little later he adds:

> “Yet this must be known: there, at least, no one will obtain any purification from the least sins unless, while still placed in this life, he has earned through good works what he is to obtain there.” [Col. 0339C]

And, so that these men may rage in the madness of even fiercer anger, let them hear what the same Gregory says in the *Moralia*:

> “For every wicked person, as soon as he has died, immediately finds that which he can no longer change.”

Let them therefore cry out, shout, and say:

> “If I cannot be changed, what use are offerings to me? What use are prayers? What use are sacrifices?”

Let the Church now close her doors, then, and henceforth I shall be content with the walls of my own house. For why should I enter churches here, if there I can in no way be changed?

Let them therefore cease their spiteful persecution of a little man, and not wish to stir up envy against me * as though over a word. Let them tear Gregory apart; let them bite Gregory; let them sink the teeth of their most bitter jealousy into him. Let them read him and find this in his writings; and, holding the censor’s rod of judgment over him, let them sharpen against him the teeth of the condemnation he deserves and seize him by the mouth like mangy dogs. [Col. 0339D–0340A]

Let them hear what the same Gregory says elsewhere:

> “Whenever the hand is extended to food through immoderate eating, the fall of our first parent is repeated.”

I do not exaggerate how harsh this is, since I have no doubt that it is evident to every reader; nor do I mention how much of this sort he writes, which we omit for the sake of brevity, lest we exceed the limit of the concise letter—a tedious thing.

But these men love me so greatly that they read only me; content with me alone, they despise all the volumes of sacred Scripture. Though they scarcely know how to run through the alphabet syllable by syllable, they do not hesitate, having made themselves judges over me, to pronounce sentences against me.

Far be it from blessed Gregory, the illustrious and distinguished teacher of the Church, or from us, humble and insignificant men who desire, insofar as we are able, to hasten along in his footsteps, to forbid sacrifices or prayers to be offered continually to almighty God for any of the dead, even if they were grievous sinners, and thus to have them helped by the devotion of the faithful who are alive. [Col. 0340A]

Indeed, those who understand that statement in this way wander like travelers by night and, like the blind, grope along the wall with their hand. We do not wish to be their teachers in resolving this question, because through the arrogance of their hearts they disdain to be disciples.

But you, my most beloved, implore the mercy of almighty God for me, his servant. Commend our monastery and hermitage to Lord Drudro, to his brother and vice-count, and to the other noble men. May almighty God guard you by his protection and grant you a share with his chosen priests. [Col. 0340B]

## LETTER II TO DAMIAN, HIS BROTHER, ARCHPRESBYTER OF RAVENNA

### Argument

He confesses his sins and negligences with no small grief of heart, and especially gravely accuses and emphasizes his excessive sociability—or rather, his inclination toward laughter. He entreats his brother Damian to pour out prayers to God on his behalf, offering in this an outstanding example of modesty and humility.

To Lord Damian, my dearest brother, Peter, a sinful monk, sends whatever a servant and son can send.

I do not wish you to be unaware, my sweetest father and lord in Christ, that my mind is continually weighed down by sorrow as it constantly contemplates the day of my own departure, already impending and almost placed before my eyes. For as I count my many years, as I await the spreading of gray hairs, and as, wherever I am in any gathering of people, I consider nearly everyone to be younger than I am, I set aside every other concern and think only of death. I meditate upon the tomb; I do not withdraw the eyes of my mind from the tomb. [Col. 0340C]

Nor is my unhappy mind content with this fear alone, fixing the limit of its reflection at the death of the body. It is immediately carried on to the judgment and considers, with no small dread, what may be brought against it and what defense it might itself offer.

But alas for me, wretched man, worthy of mourning with an inexhaustible fountain of tears! I have committed every evil, and throughout so many years of life I have fulfilled scarcely any commandment of the divine law. What evil, miserable man that I am, have I not done? With what vices, with what crimes, have I not entangled myself? I confess:

> “My life has fallen into a pit of misery; my soul has been destroyed in my iniquities” (Lamentations 5).

Pride, lust, anger, impatience, malice, envy, gluttony, drunkenness, desire, robbery, lying, perjury, foolish speech, buffoonery, ignorance, negligence, and the other plagues have overthrown me; all the vices, like roaring beasts, have devoured my soul.

My heart and lips have been polluted. I have been defiled in sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. In every way—in thought, speech, and action—I have been ruined. I committed all these evils. But alas! What grief! I have never brought forth worthy fruits of repentance. [Col. 0340D–0341A]

Among all these things, I mourn one more bitterly, recognizing by the testimony of my conscience that it has bound me more perniciously: buffoonery, namely, has always been familiar to me, and even after my conversion it never completely abandoned me. Although I have often fought against this savage monster, although I have battered the most wicked teeth of this beast with the hammer of severity, I was able to restrain it for a time but never to win a complete victory over it.

For the ingrained habit of any vice, even when it has been driven from the inner chambers of the soul with every effort, nevertheless often remains, as though importunately before the doors. If it is forbidden to seize its prey with its teeth, it at least attempts to lick the surface.

Under the appearance of spiritual joy, while I wish to show myself cheerful to my brothers, I slip into words of vanity. While, supposedly with discretion and for the sake of brotherly love, I decide to descend from my customary severity, I indiscreetly release my tongue to utter useless things. [Col. 0341B]

But since the Lord says:

> “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5),

what judgment threatens those who not only do not devote themselves to weeping but even willingly serve laughter and empty mirth like actors? Since consolation is owed not to those who rejoice but to those who mourn, what consolation can they expect from the coming Judge who now dissolve themselves in the honeyed delight of foolish merriment?

Again, since the same Truth says:

> “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6),

what will they say at the terrifying judgment who not only laugh themselves but, by uttering buffooneries, violently force laughter from their hearers? [Col. 0341C]

Here it must be noted that, although laughter is an enemy of the soul, it is more pernicious still to utter buffoonish words. For one who serves buffoonery destroys others along with himself through empty amusement, and is additionally guilty because he uselessly pours forth idle words, whereas it is written:

> “Every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12).

Indeed, when I consider these words of the Gospel, what else do I perceive than that a kind of exchange has been set before us? A perpetual weeping is bought with a momentary laugh, and everlasting joy is acquired through temporal weeping. [Col. 0341D]

This is why holy men now sow weeping and tears with every effort, so that they may reap the harvest of eternal joy, as the Prophet bears witness when he says:

> “They went forth, going and weeping, scattering their seed; but they shall come, coming with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125).

We must arrange the green shoots of virtues in the field of our hearts, as though by propagating them, and water them with the frequent inundation of suitable rains. We must devote ourselves ardently to radiant works, while always possessing the health-giving water of tears in which every superfluous thing may be extinguished.

Hence it is read (Exodus 25, 37) that Moses made seven lamps in the tabernacle, with their snuffers, and vessels in which what had been snuffed might be extinguished, all of purest gold. For what do we understand by the seven lamps except the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit? We make seven lamps in the tabernacle when, by divine gift, we establish within our minds the charisms of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0342A]

But because, in the very holy works to which we devote ourselves ardently through the breathing of the Holy Spirit, certain superfluities of earthly corruption become interwoven, snuffers must necessarily be made along with the lamps. For what do the snuffers signify except the strictness of repentance? With the snuffer what is superfluous in the lamp is cut away; through the strictness of repentance the guilt of human perversity is erased.

Thus Peter says to certain people who were committing superfluous things:

> “Repent, therefore, and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3).

It is as though he said openly: “Tighten the snuffer and cut away the excesses of wicked action.” [Col. 0342B]

The snuffers are rightly made with the lamps, because we who strive to make the grace of the Holy Spirit shine through the light of good works nevertheless need the remedies of repentance when human corruption produces excess.

But since these very excesses, which the discipline of repentance cuts away, must be extinguished by the weeping of a contrite heart, Moses is rightly said to have made, after the lamps and snuffers, vessels in which what had been snuffed might be extinguished.

Our vessels are hearts that ought always to be filled with an inundation of tears and weeping. In these vessels that oil is also stored of which the Gospel says:

> “The wise virgins took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matthew 25). [Col. 0342C]

If even those who shine with illustrious works still need tears, what must be thought of a wretch like me and those like me, who have committed many dark deeds and possess no good works that shine? With what abundant streams of tears ought we always to overflow! To what continual sorrow should we have constantly devoted ourselves! We should not compel others to laughter by the witty urbanity of a talkative buffoon, but should ourselves rather always appear mournful, with downcast face, so that even our outward appearance might express the form of perfect repentance that principally burns within the hidden bitterness of the heart. In this way it might not only bring us the remedy of the healing we desire but also offer others a fruitful example of repentance. [Col. 0342D]

Therefore I beg your holiness, dearest Father, and prostrate myself at your feet, that you may set before me the shield of your holy prayer against this savage monster, and by wisely driving out the serpent’s poison through your incantation, remove it from me. Not only for this, but also for all the things I have confessed to you above, strive to pour out continual prayers to God and obtain for me a place before the divine ears of mercy.

## LETTER III TO P., ARCHPRESBYTER

### Argument

In the fragments of this letter, by adducing two passages from the prophet Jeremiah, he shows how mournful the soul’s departure from the body will be for sinners and with how many torments they will be afflicted after death.

To P., archpresbyter …, Peter, a sinful monk. [Col. 0343A]

> “Behold, I shall summon all the clans of the kingdoms of the north,” says the Lord; “and they shall come, and each shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its surrounding walls, and upon all the cities of Judah. And I shall speak my judgments with them concerning all their wickedness, because they abandoned me” (Jeremiah 1).

If these words did not look beyond the citizens of earthly Jerusalem to others, they would certainly not resound today in the holy Church.

What, then, are those clans of the kingdoms of the north except the multitudes of evil spirits reigning proudly in minds so cold? Each of them sets his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem when, surrounding the unhappy soul as it departs from the body, they guard it with a siege so that it may not go forth freely, intending now to drag it with them to the punishment of fire, in which they had previously reigned over its cold mind. [Col. 0343B]

Oh, how mournful and sorrowful is that late and fruitless repentance, when the sinful soul, already beginning to be released from the prison of the flesh in which it was confined, looks behind itself and directs its eyes before itself! Behind it, it sees the very narrow and very short course of mortal life that it has traversed; before it, it sees the length of endless ages. It considers that the brief moment in which it lived has swiftly flown past, while it contemplates the immeasurable expanse of time that it is now beginning. The briefest thing, which is like a point, passes away; but the life it is now entering has no end at all. [Col. 0343C]

> “Behold,” says the Lord, “I shall send against them”—that is, against the citizens of Jerusalem—“the sword, famine, and pestilence; and they shall become a curse, an astonishment, a hissing, and a reproach” (Jeremiah 29).

He explains why this happens when he adds:

> “Because they did not hear my words,” he says, “which I sent to them through my servants the prophets, rising early and sending them” (ibid.).

When he says “rising early,” he indicates the solicitude and speed of the one sending, so that sluggish negligence may be found not in the preachers of the word but rather in those who hear them.

Since almighty God, speaking to human beings in human fashion, complains that he has risen early and thus, as it were, interrupted his sleep, what reproach could he bring against us if, established in the final peril of necessity, he were to answer us as follows? [Col. 0343D]

> “For your sake, although I was the Creator, I became a creature. For your sake I endured mockeries and insults, underwent the cross, and passed through all the torments that were owed to you. Yet you did not listen to me; you despised the ceremonies and commandments of my law.”

If he reproached them with servants sent by him, how much more terrifyingly will he reproach us with himself? If he reproached them with interrupted sleep, how much more can he reproach us with having died and been buried for our sake?

God does not free the Jews enclosed by the siege of surrounding enemies because they despised the servants appointed for them; how, then, will he hear Christians who have rejected the Gospel commandments sent through the Son? For whoever does not hear God is not heard by God. [Col. 0344A]

There is one thing that every faithful person ought constantly and carefully to attend to and investigate anxiously within himself: whether what he has done pleases God, and whether God delights in his life or in his works. For what does anything a person does profit him if it does not please God?

Thus it is said of David:

> “God sought for himself a man according to his own heart” (1 Kings 13; Acts 13).

For if the Creator does not now delight in a person, that person will not afterward be able to delight in the Creator.

Hence it is read in the *Life of the Fathers* that, when a certain false, famous, and highly renowned solitary was approaching death, a Tartarean spirit came to him, carrying a fiery trident in his hands. And behold, a voice came to him:

> “Just as this soul,” it said, “did not permit me to rest in it even for one hour, so neither should you have mercy when you tear it out.”

Then the wicked spirit drove the fiery trident into the heart of the dying man and, as he had been commanded, tore out his soul … [Col. 0344B]

## LETTER IV TO P., ARCHPRESBYTER

### Argument

In the fragment of this letter, from a passage in Jeremiah, he shows how detestable is the intemperance of clerics.

To P., archpresbyter …, Peter, a sinful monk … [Col. 0344C]

> “Go,” the Lord says to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 13), “and acquire for yourself a linen loincloth, and place it around your loins.”

A little later he says:

> “Rise, and go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole in the rock.”

When he had done this and had hidden it in the Euphrates as he had been commanded, after many days the Lord said to him:

> “Rise, and go to the Euphrates, and take the loincloth from there.” And I went, he says, to the Euphrates, and took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it; and behold, it had decayed, so that it was fit for no use.

And the Lord said:

> “So shall I make the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem rot, this very wicked people who refuse to hear my words and walk in the perversity of their hearts; and they shall be like this loincloth, which is fit for no use.”

What does Jeremiah’s person signify here except the Lord? What does the loincloth signify except the order of clerics? The whole Church is the garment of Christ, concerning whose members the prophet says:

> “You shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament” (ibid.). [Col. 0344D]

But just as the loincloth is closest to the human body and clings to it more tightly than the other garments, so the clerical order is more familiarly attached to divine service than other people are.

As the divine voice says there concerning the people of Israel:

> “For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I attached to myself the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, that they might be to me a people, a name, praise, and glory; but they did not listen” (ibid.).

To whom, I ask, can these words fit so suitably and expressly as to clerics, who have been specially appointed to proclaim the name, praise, and glory of God?

Just as Israel and Judah were God’s special people among all the nations of the earth, so now clerics are specially attached to Christ above all the members of the Church. They are the linen loincloth joined to the divine body by a closer familiarity. Linen reaches whiteness only through labor; so clerics, now laboring in the study of letters, now ascending through certain degrees at intervals of time, are with difficulty advanced to the dignity of the sacred order. [Col. 0345A]

Otherwise, if some contentious person asserts that this happened historically according to the literal sequence of Scripture and is not to be understood spiritually, how could Jeremiah have gone out, girded with a loincloth, amid the countless nations of Assyrians and Chaldeans that were besieging Jerusalem in tightly packed armies, and have hidden it in the Euphrates, which flows so far away? Later, after the long passage of time had run its course, how could he have returned almost safely and found it decayed, as Scripture testifies, when Jerusalem was surrounded by a ditch, a rampart, fortresses, and such frequent defenses on every side? [Col. 0345B]

For when the same prophet once attempted to leave for his native village of Anathoth, situated three miles from the city, he was immediately seized at the gate, dragged before the princes, severely beaten, and thrust into prison as a deserter or traitor to his country (Jeremiah 37).

Since, therefore, it does not follow that the event should be understood historically, it is beyond doubt that the mystery of a typological figure is present. Accordingly, in keeping with what has been said above, the choir of clerics is well represented by the linen loincloth.

But what is signified by the command that this loincloth be placed in the Euphrates—that is, in a watery place—and in a hole in the rock—that is, in darkness and shadow—except that part of the clerics which dwells under the shadow of self-will [variant: “pleasure”] and in the flow of luxury? [Col. 0345C]

Concerning their leader the Lord says in the Book of Job:

> “He sleeps under the shadow, in the secret place of reeds and in moist places” (Job 40).

The shadows protect his shadow; the willows of the stream surround him. And, to show how much he delights in dwelling in the river with his companions, he immediately adds:

> “Behold, he will swallow the river and not be astonished” (ibid.),

for he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.

That it is said to have been placed in a hole in the rock may suitably be understood as referring to the enclosure of the church. Clerics are, as it were, shut within a hole in the rock when they are commanded to keep watch over their ministries within the thresholds of the church through assiduous attendance. [Col. 0345D]

The loincloth placed in a moist place therefore decayed, because the prophet testifies concerning those who linger in the flowing waters of luxury:

> “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1).

Beasts rot in their dung when carnal and filthy people bring their lives to an end in the stench of luxury.

It was also found fit for no use, because the Lord says:

> “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

It is as though he said openly:

> “Whoever, instructed by the rule of his order, has once taken up the plough of chastity, if afterward, through the burning of lust, he turns his eyes back toward Sodom—because he now despairs of the highlands—shows that he has become wholly useless to the kingdom of God.”

Thus, in the likeness of a loincloth placed in a moist place, clerics rot when they fill their moist bellies with gluttony and drunkenness, when they inundate themselves with the filth of lust and the muddy floods of luxury. In this way they are rendered useless for every purpose, because the more they seem to flourish in the flesh, the more disastrously, withering away, they grow old in the foulness of their squalid soul. [Col. 0346A]

Concerning them the Psalm says:

> “They have become corrupt and abominable in their pleasures” (Psalm 13).

## LETTER V TO ALMERIC, ARCHDEACON

### Argument

He shows with what affection he cherishes Almeric, saying that he loves him more than his brothers. He praises him and asks him to send his book back to him; he also asks him to send some fish necessary for the monastery’s use.

To Lord Almeric, archdeacon, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of brotherly love. [Col. 0346B]

Let the Holy Spirit, author of love, make known to your most sincere heart how great is the love of my mind toward you, and how firmly and persistently your memory remains in our heart. With my conscience as witness, I am not lying: in my estimation the power of your affection surpasses even that of those whom the bond of blood relationship unites to me. And certainly it is fitting that spiritual love should surpass bodily love.

Nevertheless, I grieve that an aromatic sprig, recently sprung up among the pebbles of the shore, is seen to be rooted more deeply in that same dry soil. If it were transplanted from the barren sands in which it somehow lives into the garden of spiritual warfare, it would undoubtedly produce a shoot of which, in accordance with the oracle of the preceding Psalm, I will not say that its fruit, but not even that its leaf, would perish. It would always grow green like the cedar of Lebanon or like the palm, and, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, would produce shoots of oil for everlasting beauty. [Col. 0346C]

But enough, and more than enough. It wearies the writer to labor over what he knows the hearer is unwilling to receive gladly. And when the heart of the listener is not stirred by the subject, an extended composition is not pleasing. Yet if I knew that you willingly lent your ear to such things, I should think that, in abundance of speech, I could easily rival Demosthenes or Cicero.

Send back my little book to me. And since we do not eat meat on the second feria, we ask that some fish be sent to us for the glory of the Lord’s Nativity, so that what is sent to the brothers may benefit both your parents: while earthly refreshment restores the brothers, they may offer prayers for your parents.

Greet on my behalf my dearest and sweetest brothers Julian and Fuscard, the excellent Philomela, and Lord Corbulon [variant: “lord Corbulon”], who refreshed me with his generous hospitality; and assure them that I am not cold in my affection for them. [Col. 0346D]

Greetings to the pious reader. We have inserted the following two letters here under the names of Leo and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, because the style shows that they were written by the holy Doctor in their names, and manuscript codices clearly attest this.

## LETTER VI OF POPE LEO IX TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF AUXIMUM

### Argument

Leo IX writes to the people of Auximum, commanding under penalty of anathema that they correct and abolish a very wicked custom which had especially become established in their city: namely, that after the death of a bishop they should plunder the ecclesiastical goods in a popular uprising. [Col. 0347A]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to all his beloved sons in Christ at Auximum, clergy and people.

Because, by God’s authorship, the care of one Church has been specially entrusted to us in such a way that, through the dignity of the apostolic see, the general oversight of the other Churches has also been delegated to us, it appears to belong to our office not only to correct whatever has hitherto been seized from those same Churches by rash acts of usurpation [Col. 0347B], but also to take measures lest they presume to do the same again in the future.

We have learned, through widespread report, of a perverse and utterly detestable custom among certain peoples: namely, that when their bishop has died, they burst into the episcopal residence and seize it, plundering his possessions like brigands; they set fire to the buildings on the estates, and, with a savagery more brutal than that of beasts, cut down the vines and orchards as well. Unless this is corrected by ecclesiastical discipline, there is no doubt that the sword of sudden fury threatens those regions.

If, then, the first commandment is said to be to honor one’s parents, and if the one who curses father or mother is ordered to be punished by death, what punishment do those deserve who do not seek to persecute their fleshly [Col. 0347C] parents, but strive to destroy their very mother, the Church, in which they have been regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit (I Pet. II), like a brood of vipers? Although any priest has died by the necessity of human condition, Christ, who is the bishop of our souls, lives eternally by the power of his divinity. For, as Paul says: “Many became priests according to the law because they were prevented by death from continuing; but Jesus, because he remains forever, possesses an everlasting priesthood” (Heb. VII).

Therefore, the man who, while the mortal bishop [“while living,” added] was alive, restrained himself from injuring the Church because he was oppressed by earthly fear is convicted of dishonoring God if, after the bishop’s death, he pours out against Christ—the immortal bridegroom of the Church—the gall of hatred and the poison of malice that he had until then concealed. Perhaps the bishop injured someone during his life; but what sin did Christ commit, who was left as guardian of the Church? If evil is not repaid with evil to the man who caused harm, why is reverence not shown to the eternal Pontiff, who repaid us good for evil?

Yet if the Church’s plunderer truly believed that the immortal Son of God is certainly its pontiff, and if he considered him present everywhere, knowing and able to do all things, he would not dare to commit so impious and sacrilegious a crime before his eyes. But in him is truly fulfilled what is said through the Psalmist: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. XIII).

Moreover, if those who bestow their possessions upon the Church obtain absolution from their own guilt by this blessed exchange [Col. 0348A], then, correspondingly, those who plunder ecclesiastical goods with barbarous savagery fall into the abyss of eternal damnation. In a new and incomparable kind of crime, they surpass Jewish faithlessness, so that they exceed not only the error of the Gentiles but also the depravity of heretics in detestability. By them Christ is crucified again, and his body, which is the Church, is cruelly torn apart.

Let unlawful presumption therefore be restrained, and let the wicked excess of diabolical instigation be held in check. Let the bold hand abstain from ecclesiastical property, lest the sustenance of the poor perish; lest what has already been made a sacrifice to God through the offering of the faithful become the spoil of robbers.

But whoever proves to be an impious violator of this decree of ours [Col. 0348B], we decree, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, that he is to be anathematized; and, as a truly rotten member, we cut him away from the body of the holy Church with the sword of excommunication. Therefore, unless he repents, let him be anathema maranatha (I Cor. XVI), and let him know that all the curses of Ebal (Deut. XXVII) have descended upon his head. But to those who observe it, glory, honor, and incorruption, who seek eternal life. Amen.

## Letter VII. Pope Alexander II to the Clergy and People of Milan

### Summary

Alexander II, a native of Milan who was created Roman pontiff, writes this letter [Col. 0348C] to his fellow citizens. After displaying in the most humane words his paternal concern for their salvation, he urges them, thinking of nothing low or earthly, to raise themselves toward heavenly things with the full force and ardor of their souls.

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the Milanese, clergy and people: greetings and apostolic blessing.

By the providence of divine judgment it has been arranged that, although unworthy, I—son of the Milanese Church and nourished at the breasts of Ambrose [152]—should rise to the service of the apostolic see and serve the mother of all Churches through the anxious care of pastoral responsibility. Since the care of the entire universal Church rests heavily upon us, nature itself urges us to be especially vigilant concerning you, so that where it is clear that we have drawn the beginning of our origin, there too we may have a greater increase of concern for eternal salvation.

For fire first consumes the wood from which it arises, and a spring pours its waters first into those veins of the earth from which its flowing course is derived. Therefore, beloved, in the zeal of paternal affection we exhort you: let your spirit rise toward heaven; let it despise the deceitfulness of earthly things and their fleeting profits; let it wisely free itself from love of this muddy world; let it burn to the depths of its being with desire for its Creator.

For you are, as the blessed Apostle says, “a holy nation, a people for acquisition, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (I Pet. II). Since an undefiled and unfading inheritance is being preserved for you in heaven [Col. 0349A], far be it from you that your minds should be entangled by love of earthly things.

Since we are also speaking to ordinary people, we gladly make use of a testimony of Scripture that is familiar to all. Remember, therefore, my brothers, that in the Lord’s Prayer you say: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. VI; Luke XI). Since we call him our Father, we ought to hasten toward his inheritance with the whole desire of our minds.

Of an earthly inheritance, however, it is written: “An inheritance toward which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. XX). Why, then, when we say “Our Father,” do we immediately add “who art in heaven,” and not rather “who art on earth,” since earthly things are more familiar to us? Or “who art in the waters,” or “in the abysses,” since God is everywhere and nothing is empty of his omnipotence [Col. 0349B]?

When we say “Our Father,” we add “who art in heaven” for this reason: so that our spirit may raise itself toward that heavenly inheritance, and, having been adopted into so exalted a lineage as to be God’s heir, may not ignobly seek earthly things.

Indeed, Abraham, the father of faith, had several sons, but only the one who was the son of his wife was noble; those who were born from the ignobility of concubines are read to have been excluded from succession to their father’s inheritance. While Abraham was supporting them, all were called sons of Abraham; but when the time came for the testament, it was plainly shown who was the legitimate heir and who were to become heirs.

For, as Scripture testifies: “Abraham gave all his inheritance to his son Isaac; but to the sons of the concubines he gave gifts, and he separated them from his son Isaac” (Gen. XXV). Behold: all were called sons, but not all obtained a share in the rights of their father’s inheritance.

So indeed, brothers, there are many today adorned with the title of Christian profession who by no means deserve to be enrolled among Christ’s heirs. Even now they boast in the name of fatherhood, but they do not attain to inheriting their father’s goods, because, like illegitimate children, they ignobly desire not heavenly but earthly things.

But you, beloved, my members, the inward parts of my soul, strive to walk along the way of the heavenly commandment, so that our mind may always rightly rejoice in the holy conduct of its kindred. We hope in him who deigned to be born of the Virgin that, during the period of our ministry, the holy chastity of the clergy will be exalted, and the lust of the incontinent will be confounded along with the other heresies.

May almighty God, my beloved brothers, guard you from every depravity and lead you by the path of justice to the heavenly kingdom.

## Letter VIII. To the Clergy of Florence

### Summary

In this letter he vigorously rebukes those who ridiculed the practice of voluntarily beating the body with scourges as something new and contrary to the sacred canons.

To the religious brothers, the clerics of the holy Florentine Church, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of sincere charity.

[Col. 0350A] It is fitting that an innocent man should satisfy even those who make no request, since everywhere a livid slanderer accuses even those unwilling to listen. Nor is it useless if a clear conscience explains the order of evident truth to the same ears into which a liar pours falsehood, so that the hearer may not sin by believing vanity and the reputation of the accused may not work harm to others.

What I wrote about the exercises of the monastic order, and especially about the disciplines of the broom, I sent specifically as one monk to another monk; I did not entrust it for publication to the knowledge of laypeople or even of clerics. But urban hermits, that is, worldly solitaries and universal monks, sought to extract from the flowing text only what could cause scandal among those who did not know the secrets of monastic fervor.

But my witnesses are the brothers who live regularly under the institution of the holy Rule: I committed to writing what they themselves strive daily to practice in their deeds. The sequence of my account reported nothing other than what the custom of a well-trodden and long-established practice dictated.

But those who command the crowds under the name of monastic profession—those who, stationed in corners as though in tribunals or praetoria, promulgate the laws of pragmatic sanction; those who, tearing and biting others, arrogate to themselves alone the privilege of strict justice—do not know what is done among monks in the humility of Christ’s cross. They regard as a monstrosity what others practice through the constancy of daily observance.

“Behold,” they say, “a ship wandering abroad; behold a new penance, unheard of until now after so many centuries. If this is admitted even once, if it is accepted, if it is maintained, all the sacred canons are destroyed, the commands of the ancient Fathers perish, and, as the Jew had said, the traditions of the fathers are reduced to nothing.”

Such words plainly do not boil forth from charity, from which they are utterly remote, but from a brutish and bestial folly. Did our Redeemer not, as the Gospel testifies, undergo scourging? (John XIX.) Did Paul not receive five times forty less one? (II Cor. XI.) Were not all the apostles beaten with scourges? (Acts V.) Did not the holy martyrs also experience insults and beatings? (Heb. XI.) Did not Moses command in the Law that the guilty be beaten? (Deut. XXV.) Is it not reported, under God’s guidance, that blessed Jerome and certain others were beaten with scourges? [Col. 0350D]

Or will almighty God refuse to accept from those who offer it willingly the same penance that he sometimes exacts even from the unwilling? But perhaps the detractor will say that, since Scripture teaches us that the saints were beaten not by themselves but by others, we ourselves ought not to chastise ourselves with our own hands outside their example.

An easy answer to this objection presents itself: when we voluntarily bear the Lord’s cross through mortification, unless we are fastened by persecutors to the wood of the cross in imitation of him, then, once persecution has ceased and crucifiers are absent, it would henceforth be vain to command that the cross be borne, since no punishment is inflicted by torturers upon the combatant.

If it is insane and absurd to believe that the Lord despises in our affliction the kind of penance that he deigned to endure in himself for our salvation, what is surprising if a man, by punishing what he has done, presents himself as his own torturer and appoints himself judge in order to escape judgment? The Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI).

Just as one should not be accused of rashness who fasts not only at a priest’s command but also voluntarily, so he should not be considered to labor in vain who chastises himself by afflicting himself not only with another’s hands but also with his own.

If divine mercy did not despise the sackcloth of Ahab, that reprobate king (III Kings XXII), how kindly and mercifully must we believe that God looks down from above upon the man who, as though discovered in the most atrocious crime, presents himself naked before the divine gaze, making himself both accuser and torturer, defendant and witness, and likewise censor and executioner?

He rightly repents who, while slaughtering the flesh with blows, repays through affliction the profit he had lost through the pleasure of the flesh, and now inflicts upon it a healing bitterness, although he once sinned through its harmful delight. It makes no difference by what punishments the flesh of the penitent is disciplined, provided that the enticement of the former pleasure is exchanged for the affliction of the body that has been restrained.

If the discipline of rods seems new, and therefore reprehensible, to those who do not practice it, and is judged, according to the stupidity of livid persuasion, to be a destruction of the canons and an abolition of decrees, should venerable Bede perhaps be rebuked because, after citing the judgment of the ancient canons, he asserts that certain penitents ought to be bound with iron rings?

Should the life of the holy Fathers rightly be spat upon, since it testifies that some completed the penance for their guilt by standing among thorns for periods of eight and fifteen days, others by suspending their rigid arms in the air from sunrise to sunset, and others by continually hiding in excavated caves?

Should that blessed Macarius also rightly be mocked because, when he repented of having committed some minor offense, he exposed his naked limbs for six months to the sharpest bites of gnats—bites that could pierce even wild boars? (Palladius, *History of the Holy Fathers*, section 17.)

And is the penance of the Ninevites to be despised, since for three days they did not even permit their animals to be fed? (Jon. III.) Since these and many other kinds of penance are not found inserted in the sacred canons, are they therefore to be utterly detested and declared contrary to the decrees of the Fathers?
