Let the frenzied tongue, then, be ashamed; and let the tongue that does not know how to speak eloquently learn at least to remain silent. It does not know how to produce useful words; let it at least know how to keep silent without causing harm.

But let this censor of the brothers and teacher of an unknown doctrine tell me—he who arrogates to himself such an untimely rod over his disciples, although he has not yet offered himself as a pupil to his teacher—let him tell me, I say: when the priests of the Church impose a lengthy penance upon certain sinners, do they not sometimes prescribe a fixed sum of money as redemption for the years, so that those who dread prolonged fasting may redeem their crimes through almsgiving? [Col. 0352A]

But because this monetary redemption is not found at all in the ancient canons of the Fathers, will it be judged absurd and frivolous? If this is permitted to laypeople, so that they may redeem their sins through almsgiving and, should death suddenly overtake them, may not depart this life without absolution from their guilt—which God forbid—what should be prescribed for a monk who perhaps receives a long penance because his sins require it, and who long ago entirely cast away the money by which he might be redeemed?

If, out of consideration for human frailty, redemption of sin through a sum of money is prescribed, is affliction of the flesh therefore rightly rejected for sin? What is surprising if the flesh that once happily cast us into exile now, in turn, brings us back to our homeland through affliction? And through the very thing to which we once consented harmfully and by which we sinned, let us now make wholesome correction by chastising it.

Or, to put it this way, why should it be surprising if the same beast, now made humble, carries to the physician the man it had earlier struck with an impatient kick in its unrestrained and raging madness? Indeed, what is new if the earth that previously produced thorns and buckthorns, cultivated after those thistles have rotted, later grows fertile and rich?

Therefore, let the mouth of those who speak iniquity be stopped. Let those who do not know how to correct their own errors cease at least to tear apart another’s justice with biting words. Let them fear to ridicule slanderously among secular people what they themselves do not know how to practice among spiritual persons.

But you, beloved, whom religious life sanctifies and the splendor of heavenly wisdom enlightens, restrain the hissing mouths of serpents. By your authority oppose the pestilential poison, lest it flow forth with such freedom to the ruin of many. Since, according to the Lord’s word, “you are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V), let the flavor of your most prudent seriousness sweeten whatever bitterness the rusticity of ignorant people displays.

I intended to write more, but while my hand hastens to cast down the letters, the sheet has ended, and a messenger, already equipped for a speedy journey, is eager to ride.

## Letter IX. To the Clergy of Fano

(It is found in volume III and is treatise 27.)

## Letter X. To the Clergy and People of Faenza

### Summary

Called by the people of Faenza after the death of their bishop, he excuses himself because, being greatly weakened at present by illnesses suffered in the past and by exhaustion, he is unable to come to them. Meanwhile, he urges them to defer the election of a bishop until the emperor’s arrival, by whom the condition of that Church was to be settled, and to choose a suitable priest to administer the bishopric in the interim. He also promises that he will be present at the appropriate time.

To the holy and venerable brothers, the sons of the Church of Faenza, clergy and people, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

When we learned that your bishop, the lord P., of holy memory, had died, our mind was suddenly disturbed and withered; astonishment at the sudden calamity seized us, and the grief of fraternal compassion stirred our inward parts.

But our venerable son, the abbot whom you sent to me, found me so shaken and broken not only by illnesses of the past but also by certain labors that I cannot now come to you so quickly. Therefore, until it happens that we can come into your service—something that, according to our limited ability, we believe ought to be done for you—we send through this little letter a brief statement.

As far as we can discern, it was one spirit that touched the small understanding of our heart and unanimously impelled your holy prudence toward what was agreed and settled among you: namely, that you should not elect a bishop until the king’s arrival. He will remove the error and, after calming disputes on every side, settle you and your Church in tranquility and peace.

Therefore our lord the pope should be asked not to impose a bishop upon you for the time being, but to decree that your Church remain vacant meanwhile and that you remain under the shelter of his blessing.

Since, by God’s mercy, you have among you capable, prudent, and learned clerics, if it pleases you, let one of them be chosen who is found more useful for carrying out this business. The care and responsibility of the entire bishopric can be entrusted to him, and through him all the necessary affairs of the Church can be administered.

Meanwhile, if you command it, I will come into your service when the opportunity arises, and perhaps, for the love of God and of you, I will labor to some extent either in confirming children or in other episcopal duties.

## Letter XI. To V. and P., Clerics of Faenza

(It is found in volume II and is treatise 41.)

## Letter XII. To G., Treasurer of the Church of Ravenna

[Col. 0353C]

### Summary

Lord Peter Damian, summoned to his homeland by his fellow citizens and the archbishop, where nevertheless he was neither honored nor effective for the salvation of souls, writes this letter to the treasurer of Ravenna, uncertain what he should do. He asks his advice: whether he ought to remain in his homeland or return to his monastery.

Eager for the salvation of others, he could not remain at Ravenna with equanimity, where there was no opportunity for his preaching. On the other hand, if he returned to his monastery, the most modest of men feared that, amid the great attention everyone paid to him, something of his humility might be endangered. Nevertheless, he appears inclined to the view that he should place the gain of souls before his own danger. He leaves the entire matter to the counsel of the man to whom he writes.

To Lord G., a religious priest, Araeque Seth, treasurer, Peter, the least servant of the monks, offers the service of fervent devotion.

You know, beloved, that in former times I was often and earnestly asked by Archbishop Gebehard, and recently by this new archbishop, who was appointed through zeal for the divine Spirit, as well as by many of the citizens of Ravenna. At last I consented; leaving the wilderness, I came to live in the city, hoping to gain souls.

But when I saw the aforesaid man doing not what he had been sent to do, but rather what he had been permitted to do, and when I saw that the people possessed neither zeal of charity toward me nor concern for their own salvation, I repented, I confess. While I had trusted human vanities, I recognized—though late, yet clearly—that I had wandered from the path of the divine will.

While, eager for an accumulation of fish, I sought a fishpond, I was frustrated and lost even the few fish that I had been accustomed to enclose amid the far-reaching waters of the sea. Meanwhile, however, I enjoyed a kind of consolation: although I could not exercise myself in gaining souls, I did not have to bear the extremely burdensome weight of popular reverence.

The two things hung almost evenly in the balance of my mind, and I happily compensated for the misfortune of sterility with the gain of denied veneration. For popular favor is truly no small danger to the imperfect: it either casts those who delight in it into the abyss of vainglory, or pierces even those who resist it with fear of losing the reward they have received.

On the occasion of a certain festival, when some religious men invited me and sent a vehicle, I returned to the region of Urbino. A wave of brothers—both monks and secular persons—flooded over me and swallowed me up so completely that it did not allow me to turn my sails back toward the haven of greatest safety. It was as though an estate surrounded by sand had been set before me upon the very marble, while the untimely affection of so many brothers implored me not to go elsewhere.

But, as I think, almighty God allowed me to approach that place where I ought not to remain so that, when I saw the precipitous rocky cliffs, I might judge a field of scantier harvest not wholly contemptible and therefore capable of being furrowed. When the rocky field is taken into account, the land that produces thirtyfold fruit would be judged, by comparison, a most fertile African fallow.

At last I had been anxious to discover where I might obtain richer fruits of souls, and, driven by zeal for my neighbors, I surveyed various regions of Italy with the attentive light of my mind. While I sought to recall others to a state of uprightness, I myself nearly incurred the blemish of wandering.

Now, so to speak, a kind of ballast outweighs the skiff of my mind; or, like an anchor fixed in the ground, it constrains me with a threefold cord of perseverance. Only one scruple still troubles me, and it compels me, dearest Father, to ask for the hand of your counsel.

If this scruple is shaken from the foot of my mind by the indication of your reply, I do not doubt that, through God’s mercy, I shall afterward walk firmly along the straight path.

Let your wisdom therefore answer me: what is more useful for me? Should I live where both the fruit of souls is gained and the people’s devoted reverence is shown to me, or rather where I remain without either fruit or honor? Either choice seems dangerous to me; while I fear one, I nevertheless fear the other from the opposite direction.

For if I live without fruit, I dread the evangelical axe laid at the root of the tree, concerning which Truth thunders terribly, saying: “Cut it down; why does it even occupy the ground?” (Luke XIII.) But if, while fruit is gained, honor is already shown to me, I scarcely escape the sentence that says: “Amen, I say to you, you have received your reward” (Matt. VI).

This, then, is the question that I desire you to resolve. This alone is why I decided to write to you and set down everything related above. But since I know that you are occupied with the office of ecclesiastical prior, and perhaps will not easily find leisure to write back, I myself meanwhile write what I think on this matter—not so that a disciple may teach a master, but so that I may learn whether the judgment of my understanding should be followed.

I leave the choice to your prudence, so that you may either restrain me from it with the authority of your own writing or establish that it should be approved by the full weight of your judgment.

All the words of divine Scripture have been written in their many volumes for no other purpose than the salvation of souls. Whatever is commanded in them, whatever is forbidden, is unquestionably done for the advancement of souls, as Paul testifies: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. XV).

If, because of the threats of Scripture, honor is so completely avoided that the benefit of souls is also neglected, it is plainly evident that the purpose for which Scripture ought to be observed is not being maintained. If all sacred Scripture is directed toward this end—that through it the salvation of the soul may be sought—then, while fleeing honor, if we set aside the gain of souls, we do not preserve the very thing for which Scripture was made.

In a perverse manner, while striving to obey the sacred books, we fight against those same sacred books. The one who says, “Do not recline in the first place” (Luke XIV), himself commands, saying: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. XXII). And the one who forbids you to be called masters (Matt. XXIII) himself commands the disciples: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII).

Therefore, while the fruit of souls is sought, neither human praise, nor popular favor, nor any honor or reverence should be sought with the mind’s intention. If honor is thrust upon us against our will, it must be trampled under the strict foot of discipline upon the pavement of the heart; like a poisonous serpent, it must be struck on the very head of its suggestion, lest—God forbid—it presume to bite our heel at the end of a good work.

Yet the benefit of souls must not for that reason be abandoned. Rather, like vigorous soldiers, while protecting ourselves with the shield of humility from the weapon of pride hurled against us, we should rouse our neighbors to act bravely through words of holy exhortation.

Nevertheless, let the shield of our prudence protect our neighbors, lest the enemy, hiding behind us, inflict a concealed wound from ambush. Let us fight our adversary in such a way that we also provide help to our fellow soldiers. Let brotherly charity watch over our comrades, lest it expose our own side to hostile swords. In this way, indeed, a double reward is acquired for us: from the very duty of charity that we piously perform for our neighbors arises the struggle of warfare, which we overcome by resisting.

But lest we appear to insist upon argument rather than solid truth, let us not hesitate to demonstrate what we have proposed through examples from sacred Scripture.

The holy man Joseph, in order to relieve the people’s dangerous hunger, does not refuse to accept a position second only to the king; he who had previously been an inhabitant of a narrow prison now became ruler of all Egypt. Hence his brothers say joyfully to Jacob: “Joseph your son is alive, and he himself rules in the land of Egypt” (Gen. XLV).

Moses, who had once humbly tended the flock of his kinsman in the wilderness, did not refuse the service of the whole Israelite people, so that he might later become the leader of a better flock. He was raised to such a height of honor that the entire multitude of the Hebrews depended upon his words of command and obediently submitted to his laws (Exod. III and following).

Yet it is unquestionably recognized how great a gentleness each of them maintained amid such exaltation. One voluntarily offered himself to be recognized by foreign brothers, although he could have remained concealed; the other humbly disclosed his own humility as though it belonged to someone else: “Moses,” he says, “was a very meek man, more than all the men who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. XII).

Joshua too, who had been Moses’ servant, did not refuse to undertake the office of rule when Moses died (Josh. I). If, in order to preserve humility, he had rejected the rights of leadership, he would have exposed the multitude of the people to be slain by the many kings whom he killed, himself guilty in the eyes of all; while guarding himself against the fall of vainglory, he would have neglected the danger to his brothers’ lives.

What should I say of Samuel? As long as he had not been cast down by the people themselves from the height of leadership, he was exalted in public but humble in secret. He left the position of rule he had assumed so reluctantly that, when the elders of Israel asked him for a king, Scripture immediately says of him: “The word displeased Samuel, because they had said, ‘Give us a king, to judge us’” (I Kings VIII).

What should I say of Elijah? What of Elisha? So that they might benefit their neighbors through their preaching, they were not afraid both to shine with many miracles and to appear venerable to the kings themselves and to the whole people.

And, passing over so many Fathers of the Old Testament and coming now to the Gospel, was the Lord’s forerunner able entirely to avoid the reverence of honor, when he scarcely persuaded the crowds who believed him to be Christ that he was not Christ himself by denying it? (John I.)

Did Peter lack the favor of popular reverence, when he healed so many sick people merely through the shadow cast over them by his body? (Acts V.) Was honor not shown to Paul when, as soon as the man who had been weak in his feet rose at Paul’s command in Lystra, the entire crowd cried out in astonishment to his praise: “The gods have come down to us in human form” (Acts XIV)? Hence, as is added shortly afterward: “The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was before the city, brought bulls and garlands before the gates and wanted to sacrifice with the crowds” (ibid.).

But how unbendingly Paul remained upon the height of his humility is shown by him and Barnabas when, tearing their garments in grief, they said: “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are mortal human beings like you” (ibid.).

Could the beloved of the Lord, John the Evangelist, entirely escape the reverence of honor, when, on his return from exile, he found the whole people, men and women, coming out to meet him with hymns and praises? To him also that singular proclamation of Christ was sung—not as an act of presumption, but from an overwhelming desire for devotion: “Blessed,” they say, “is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXIII).

And should Andrew the Apostle be thought to have lacked the service of the people, when, while the people of Achaea were tumultuously trying to rescue him as he hung upon the cross, they threatened to kill the governor of the province himself?

And, so that our argument may be more firmly strengthened by an appeal drawn from the very head of all the saints, the Jews wanted to make our Redeemer king, unless he had fled to the mountain (John VI).

Therefore, if the Mediator of God and human beings had wished to cast aside human reverence in order to display only an example of humility—so that he neither showed the powers of miracles nor uttered words of preaching—what salvation, I ask, or what benefit would he have provided for the human race, dead in sins? But for this reason he wished to appear venerable and wondrous: so that he might turn toward himself the hearts of those who marvelled, and then recall those who had been converted to their homeland by the path along which he walked.

Thus, when we greatly fear human reverence, [Col. 0357C] by it our virtue may be exercised and the reward of those who show devotion may increase. Indeed, whenever it murmurs before the door of our mind, as though blown by the wind of vainglory, the shield of humility is immediately held up; and the more violent the blow that strikes it, the more richly our reward is increased after victory has been won.

Moreover, unless the person of the preacher appears in some way venerable to his hearers, the word of preaching, not admitted to their minds, does not work within them. For if the person speaking is despised, it follows that the speech itself will be judged despicable by those who hear it. Paul could not make progress among those who despised him, saying: “His letters, they say, are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (II Cor. X). [Col. 0357D] Yet he had made great progress among those to whom, giving thanks, he said: “You received me as an angel of God; for I bear you witness that, if it were possible, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me” (Gal. IV).

Did the Apostle wish to be held in contempt, when he complains of it? Did he avoid the service of devoted obedience, when he gives thanks for it? Neither was for his own sake. For he was not seeking what was his, but what belonged to another. He therefore wished to be honoured by his disciples so that he could also be heard attentively; and he refused to be despised by his hearers because he feared that his message would likewise be held in contempt.

Hence he says to the Thessalonians: “We ask you, brothers, since you know those who labour among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you, to hold them in the greatest esteem in love because of their work” (I Thess. V). [Col. 0358A] Hence, concerning Epaphroditus, he says to the Philippians: “Receive him,” he says, “with all joy in the Lord, and hold such men in honour” (Phil. II).

If, then, the Apostle had decided that reverence must be avoided altogether, when he commands hearers to show honour to their teacher, he would surely be urging them to drive him from their territory while honouring him. But the excellent preacher seems to advise that a discerning man should outwardly accept the honour shown to him for the benefit of his brothers, while inwardly despising that same honour out of humility, so that, watchful in every direction, he may provide for their salvation without himself succumbing to the vice of pride.

Nor, in order that we may be more cautious against such a vice, ought we therefore to deny our brothers the help of preaching, since Moses says: “I beseech you, Lord: this people has sinned a great sin; they have made gods of gold for themselves. Either forgive them this offence, or, if you will not, erase me from your book which you have written” (Exod. XXXII). [Col. 0358B] With what conscience, then, can we place the gains of our brothers’ salvation below private affection, when this man does not hesitate to perish utterly from the book of divine remembrance for the salvation of those near him?

Paul also says: “I myself was wishing to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. IX). Since holy men, in order to care for their brothers, do not fear even to undergo danger to their souls, what else are they doing than imitating the example of their Head? He laid down his life for the sheep and, in order to redeem us from death, did not shrink from enduring the punishment of death (John X). [Col. 0358C] Therefore, far be it from us to withhold words of edification from our brothers because of the honour shown to us; rather, for their salvation, let us consent to bear that honour with equanimity.

Venerable Father, I have said these things not to follow stubbornly the judgment of my own understanding, or to presume to affirm them, but so that you, according to the ability divinely given to you, may either indicate that the matter is otherwise, or confirm what has been said by the very great authority of your judgment.

Please greet on my behalf my dearest father and teacher, the presbyter Mainfrenus, and my most beloved brother Gerard of Blanca. May almighty God repay them for all the good things they have done for me out of love for him.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE CHAPLAINS OF DUKE GOTHIFRED

### Summary

He defends himself against the slander of the chaplains of Duke Gothifred, who accused him of avarice; he also refutes two very wicked opinions of theirs. For they maintained that clerics could take wives, and that those who purchased bishoprics and priestly offices were not Simoniacs provided that they received the laying-on of hands gratuitously. He clearly demonstrates that both positions are heresies.

To his beloved brothers in Christ, the chaplains of Duke Gothifred, Peter, the sinful monk, sends greetings.

Whenever I am accustomed to write something that lies close to my heart, I usually surround myself with a library of many different books, recall the opinions of the ancients, and, whenever necessary, always return to their examples. But now, standing on the summit of a steep and snow-covered mountain, while I am striving to build the structure of a monastic building, I am unable not only to occupy myself with the pages of books, which are far away, but, overwhelmed by the clamour of the shouting masons and stonecutters, I am almost compelled to be unaware of what is within me. Therefore I fear writing to you, lest, while the rough joint of my pen is not fortified by impregnable—such as befits such matters—testimonies of Scripture, you should soon read it with raised eyebrows and wrinkled forehead, spit upon it as though it were the delirious nonsense of dreams and the ditties of an old woman’s foolishness. [Col. 0359B]

Nevertheless, I would rather, with David, be called mad before Achish, king of Gath, with saliva running down my beard (I Kings XXI), and, with Jesus, be called deranged among the Jews, as Mark relates (Mark III), than, fearing the mark of ignorance, be condemned for my silence at the judgment of supreme Majesty, saying with Isaiah: “Woe is me, because I was silent, for I am a man unclean of lips” (Isa. VI).

Moreover, “what is foolish of God is wiser than men” (I Cor. I). And, as the same Apostle says: “Because the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching” (ibid.).

That is also signified by Samson, who, with the jawbone of a donkey, miraculously killed a thousand Philistines (Judg. XV). [Col. 0359C] Samson—for his name is interpreted as “their sun”—is Christ, who with the jawbone of a donkey, that is, of a brutish and simple animal, slew very many: when, through the mouths of fishermen and simple people, he crushed the human race in its rigidity of pride, so that he who had come to defeat the powers of the air might triumph not with orators and philosophers but with the meek and unlearned.

You plainly make three assertions to which, while preserving your charity, I must respond. For you maintain that sacred ministers of the altar may lawfully associate with women. You add this further, attempting to affirm it with certain arguments: that the man should not be called a Simoniac who accepts the governance of a Church in exchange for money, but only the man who enters into the laying-on of hands and consecration through a commercial transaction. Finally—and this is the least important matter—you brand me with the mark of greed. Why you presume to do so, since it is of little importance to me, I shall briefly explain; and thus, having cleared myself of the remaining two objections, which concern the common affairs of the Church, I shall address them.

“For it is a very small matter to me to be judged by you or by a human day” (I Cor. IV).

Come, then. While I was celebrating the mysteries of the Mass, the wives of the princes—the duke’s and the marquis’s—offered me Byzantine gold coins. Our fellow monk Paul, after the mysteries had been completed at the altar, went out with us and left them there. But one of your number, while you not only were unaware of the matter but were also absent, stole them by clandestine fraud. Although you had committed no fault whatsoever, because he was nevertheless your associate, he in a certain way brought a stain of guilt upon you. [Col. 0360A]

As soon as he was caught in the offence, and violently overcome by the threatening terror of Beatrice, the most excellent duchess and a courageous woman, he secretly brought the gold to our brother and begged that intercession be made on his behalf. As soon as we learned of this, we ordered the entire sum to be returned to that same cleric, and we encouraged him not to despair of recovering his lady’s favour. While he kept pressing the matter and could not force the money upon us by any prayers at all, he finally gave it secretly to our brother on the following day, and thus lightened himself of the burden of a gnawing conscience.

Why, then, do you accuse as avaricious a man whom you know to have so thoroughly despised the acquisition of money? [Col. 0360B] Why do you sharpen your tongues against me and hasten to inflict upon one who does not resist the wound of biting reproach? For Solomon also says: “A dart, a sword, and a sharp arrow is the man who bears false witness against his neighbour” (Prov. XXV). And the Psalmist says: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons, and their tongues arrows, a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI).

Am I to be accused of greed, when I refused to accept what had been stolen, forgave the crime, and, returning good for evil, restored the master’s favour to the guilty man? Am I, I ask, to be branded with avarice, when I bore the loss with equanimity—or is it he who, stealing the sacred from the sacred, profaned the office of the priesthood in which he served? [Col. 0360C]

Brothers, I am not attacking him in this speech; provoked by your slander, I am compelled only to clear myself. I am plainly a disciple of fishermen, and therefore I stir up neither the sea of Demosthenes nor the torrent of Cicero. And because I owe compassion to a delinquent brother, I do not long to return an injury with a fitting retaliation.

Let me say only this: if arguments are to be drawn from companions and close associates, as orators and rhetoricians maintain, then the charge of avarice is not rightly brought against us, since our brother, treating money as though he regarded and despised it as a trifling thing, left it in the Church. But, if it may be said, the charge should rather be assigned to you, whose associate stole by cunning contrivance what belonged to someone else.

As for your shameless assertion that ministers of the altar ought to be joined in marriage, we consider it unnecessary to draw the sword of your own words against you, since we see the battalions of the whole Church, armed against you, and the serried line of all the holy Fathers standing in resistance. [Col. 0360D] When so great a cloud of heavenly warriors is arrayed against you, it is astonishing if the temerity of any new presumption does not yield to such authority.

Although the body of the canons is not presently at hand, we shall nevertheless not hesitate to set down certain testimonies of the Fathers, which we can find either by repeated recollection or in some little parchment booklets.

Indeed, blessed Clement writes the following in his letter (Epistle 2, to James, the brother of the Lord):

“Presbyters, or deacons, ministers of the altar, should be chosen for such offices of the Lord as have left their wives before ordination. [Col. 0361A] But if, after ordination, a minister should happen to uncover his own wife’s bed, he shall not enter the thresholds of the sacristy, nor become a porter of the sanctuary; he shall not touch the altar, nor receive from those offering sacrifices the offering of a holocaust, nor approach the portion of the Lord’s body. He shall pour water into the hands of the priests, close the doors from outside, and perform lesser offices; but he shall not supply the ewer to the saving chalice.”

A little later he says:

“Let a cleric alone not approach a woman’s dwelling, nor hasten there without the command of a superior ruler. Let neither a presbyter alone converse privately with a woman alone, nor an archdeacon or deacon, under the pretext of humility and service, frequent the homes of married women. Or perhaps let a married woman communicate some secret matter through clerics or household servants. If this is discovered, let the man be deposed and let the woman be barred from the thresholds of the Church.” [Col. 0361B]

The Council of Nicaea likewise says:

“But to the unmarried men who have been advanced to the clergy we prescribe that, if they wish, they may take wives, but only if they are readers or singers.”

From the Council of Carthage (Apostolic Canon 25; Council of Carthage V, chapter 3):

“Furthermore, when a report was made concerning the lack of continence of certain clerics, even readers, with regard to their own wives, it was resolved that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should, according to their own statutes, also abstain from their wives; and if they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.”

Likewise, from another council held at Carthage (Council of Carthage II, chapter 2), Bishop Aurelius said among other things:

“It was resolved that sacred bishops and priests of God, and also Levites, or those who serve the divine sacraments, should be continent in all things, so that they may obtain simply what they ask from God; so that we too may observe what the Apostles taught and antiquity itself preserved.” [Col. 0361C]

To this Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Pontiana in the province of Picenum and legate of the Roman Church, said:

“It is pleasing that the bishop, presbyter, and deacon, or those who handle the sacraments, should be guardians of chastity and abstain from their wives.”

All the bishops said:

“It is pleasing that chastity be preserved in all things and by all who serve at the altar.”

And so that no doubt could remain concerning subdeacons—that they too ought to abstain from marital relations—the same Aurelius adds after much else:

“It was resolved, as was also confirmed in various councils, that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, as well as deacons, presbyters, and bishops, should, according to their own statutes, also abstain from their wives, so that they may appear to be as though they did not have them; and if they do not do so, they are to be removed from the office of the Church.” [Col. 0361D]

Pope Gregory also writes to Peter the subdeacon, among other things, saying (Gregory, *Register*, Book VIII, Epistle 42; Distinction 31, *Ante*):

“Three years ago the subdeacons of all the Churches of Sicily had been forbidden to associate in any way with their wives, according to the custom of the Roman Church.”

It seems harsh and inappropriate to me that someone who has not found the practice of this same continence, nor previously undertaken chastity, should be compelled to separate from his wife—and thereby, God forbid, fall into something worse. [Col. 0362A] Hence it seems to me that from the present day all bishops should be told not to presume to make anyone a subdeacon unless he has promised to live chastely, so that past obligations, which were not sought by a deliberate resolve of the mind, may not be exacted by force, and future obligations may be carefully guarded against.

Those who, after the prohibition made three years ago, had lived continently with their wives are to be praised and rewarded, and encouraged to remain in their good conduct. But those who, after the prohibition had been made, refused to abstain from their wives, we do not wish to see attain the sacred order, because no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been proven before he receives the ministry.

Likewise, there is a decree of Pope Leo (Epistle 82, chapter 4, to Anastasius of Thessalonica):

“For whereas those established outside the clerical order are free to devote themselves to the partnership of marriage and to the begetting of children, nevertheless, for the display of perfect continence, even subdeacons are not permitted carnal marriage, so that those who have wives may be as though they did not have them, and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried” (I Cor. VII). [Col. 0362B]

If this is rightly observed in the order that is fourth from the head, how much more must it be observed by the first, second, and third orders, lest anyone be judged suitable for Levitical or priestly honour, or for episcopal excellence, who is found not yet to have restrained himself from conjugal pleasure?

Likewise, Pope Sylvester says (Roman Synod, canon 8):

“We permit none of the subdeacons to proceed to marriage, and we prescribe that no one presume to do so by any transgression.”

If you should judge so many decrees of apostolic men worthy of contempt, and despise their statutes as though through so many instruments of the Holy Spirit speaking through their mouths, you ought to hear what blessed Pope Damasus pronounces concerning you:

“Voluntary violators of the canons,” he says, “are judged severely by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift they have been enriched.”

For those who, not compelled by necessity but willingly, as has been stated, act insolently against the same holy canons, presume to speak or act in opposition to them, or freely consent to those who wish to do so, seem not improperly to blaspheme the Holy Spirit. Such presumption is plainly one kind of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, since, as has already been mentioned, it acts against the one by whose command and grace these holy canons were produced. [Col. 0362D]

Let those who resist us, who quarrel with us over this question, hear this: while they are our adversaries, by their manifest rebellion they are blasphemers against the Holy Spirit. In blaspheming him, they offend the one whose offence is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

But we shall now omit adding the sanctions of more holy pontiffs, lest we be judged to exceed the limit of an abbreviated letter. For excessive, ragged prolixity produces weariness. Certainly, whoever is not satisfied by the testimonies of the saints, however they may have been gathered from every source, will not be satisfied by a greater number either.

Furthermore, concerning what you object—that the canons provide that whoever rejects the office of a married priest should be deprived of communion—if I may speak with your permission, while you attend carelessly to the surface of the words, you do not retain the sobriety of ecclesiastical understanding. [Col. 0363A] A “married priest,” to be sure, means not one who now has a wife, but rather one who had a wife before receiving the dignity of priestly office. If we despise him, it follows that we must also despise blessed Paul the Apostle—which is an unspeakable thing.

Nevertheless, you also brandish in your hands, as though it were an outstanding and famous sword of Goliath, that passage from the blessed Apostle’s Letter to the Corinthians, and, waving it, attempt to scatter the battle line of the Israelite people:

“Because of fornication,” he says, “let each man have his own wife; let the husband render the debt to his wife, and the wife to her husband” (II Cor. VII).

In this statement, where it says “each man,” you infer that ministers of the altar are included together with laypeople. [Col. 0363B] And while, in the Apostle’s sentence, you gnaw at the chaff of the letters as though with the teeth of beasts of burden, you do not taste the marrow of spiritual understanding with the palate of human piety. Indeed, you do not distinguish refuse from grain at all; setting aside the rule of discernment, you mix everything together.

The Apostle was saying to those to whom he was speaking: “Let each man have his own wife.” But that he was speaking in this letter not to priests or preachers, but rather to the people, he makes clearer than daylight at the very beginning of the same letter:

“It has been reported to me,” he says, “about you, my brothers, by those who are of Chloe, that there are disputes among you. I mean this: each one of you says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ ‘I to Apollos,’ ‘I to Cephas,’ ‘I to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (I Cor. I.) [Col. 0363C]

These words plainly show that the Apostle was rebuking not priests but the people, who were creating sects and schisms by claiming to be disciples of different teachers. Therefore, when he said, “Let each man have his own wife,” he was granting marriage to those to whom he was directing his words.

Moreover, “each” or “every” does not always embrace the totality of a multitude; it is often confined within the measure of a definite quantity, as reason dictates. Such is what the Lord says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII). For he did not draw Judas the traitor to himself, nor associate the wicked thief with himself; rather, “all things” means all the elect, whom he raised to the height of his own fellowship.

And the Apostle testifies that God desires all to be saved (I Tim. II), and that he desires no one to perish. But when the Prophet says, “For the Lord has done whatever he wished” (Ps. CXXXIV), why does he permit the reprobate to perish? Clearly, although he desires no one to perish and can undoubtedly do whatever he wishes, when it is said that God wishes all to be saved, it must be understood of the elect alone.

According to this rule, when the Apostle says, “Let each man have his own wife,” he does not include all human beings, but only those to whom, according to the norm of lawful sanction, it is permitted to have wives. Otherwise, how will those join themselves in the bonds of marriage who defile their fathers’ beds, who—oh, wickedness!—commit incest with their sisters born of the same mother? [Col. 0364A]

Let the monks now go forth, publicly produce marriage contracts, and contract marriages; and, according to the judgment of your sanction, let them not blush in the least to soothe wailing children in tender embraces.

Indeed, since canonical authority frequently places monks and Levites on an equal footing, whether in sinning or in doing penance, how can you forbid conjugal unions to monks while allowing them to deacons? For how can those who are equal in other excesses be different only in the matter of intercourse with women? It must therefore be decreed either that monks enter marriages—which is sacrilegious to say—or that deacons completely restrain themselves from the obscenity of this disgraceful shamefulness.

The same must likewise be understood of subdeacons, as the various decrees of the holy Fathers confirm, as shown above. Some people suppose that they hold the office of the Nathinaeans, but this does not follow. For Nathinaeans, as Jerome asserts in the *Hebrew Questions*, means “the given ones.” They are the Gibeonites, because they were given by Joshua to serve the tabernacle of the Lord.

Between these, then, and the others there is demonstrably this difference: the former served the tabernacle or temple of the Lord as servants; the latter perform the fourth office of the altar, namely, that of those equal in rank to deacons and of ministers. [Col. 0364C] Therefore, just as they are commanded to take part with priests and Levites in the sacred mysteries of the Mass, so it is necessary that they also share with them in guarding perpetual purity of chastity.

Finally, concerning what you say—that it does not belong to the offence of the Simoniacal heresy if someone accepts the governance of a Church without the transaction being wholly free of purchase, provided only that he acquires the laying-on of hands gratis—how great a scandal this generates in the Church, and how far it strays from the path of ecclesiastical discipline, is so clear to everyone that it needs no lengthy explanation.

For whoever buys the Church at a price is also shown to purchase its consecration, through the acceptance of which he is promoted to that Church. In the commerce of the Church he plainly also purchases the consecration, without which he does not hope to preside over that same Church.

In opposition to this you contend that a man receives the investiture of ecclesiastical property, not the gift of spiritual grace. He acquires the estate of the Church, you say, not the sacrament of ecclesiastical charisma. [Col. 0364D]

Anyone who divides the Church through the brine of this tartarean wisdom—or rather, this poisonous cunning—is a heretic through the sale and also incurs the crime of schism through the division.

There were indeed certain people, ignorant of sincere faith and Catholic confession, who divided human and divine nature in such a way that they asserted that two persons existed in the Mediator of God and human beings. But those who were granted, with the penetrating gaze of the mind, to penetrate the mystery of the incarnate Word truthfully maintained that both natures came together in so inseparable a union that not even in Christ’s death could the divinity be separated from the flesh; otherwise he would not be true God if, even at the very moment of death, he ceased to be God.

Hence blessed Ambrose says:

“Christ’s flesh indeed tasted death, but the impassible power of God did not depart from the body.”

The great Pope Leo likewise expressed a similar judgment on this matter in one of his sermons:

“Unless the Word became flesh,” he says, “and there were so solid a unity in both natures that not even the brief time of death could separate the assumed nature from the one who assumed it, mortality would never have been able to return to eternity.”

The same man says elsewhere:

“The divinity, which did not withdraw from either substance of the humanity it had assumed, joined by its power what it had divided by its power.”

But you do not divide Christ; you do not fear dividing the Church, which is his body. [Col. 0365B] For the Apostle says:

“I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ, for the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Col. I).

Indeed, the soldiers feared to tear the Lord’s tunic, but you do not fear rending the Church. You do not seek the profits of Churches in order to rise to the grace of consecration; rather, compelled by necessity, you tolerate consecration only so that you may not lose possession of ecclesiastical property. You do not aspire to become priests of the Church, but only to be possessors of the sanctuary, as though by a kind of hereditary right.

You imitate those who, according to the prophetic utterance of David, said:

“Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance” (Ps. LXXXII).

Concerning them it is said to God in the same psalm:

“For they have plotted together in agreement; against you they have made a covenant” (ibid.).

This sentence strikes you, for you plot agreement together when, in what you say against the sacred canons, you unanimously agree among yourselves with no difference of zeal. And you make a covenant against God when you promulgate a new law contrary to ecclesiastical rule.

The prophet goes on to enumerate and reveal who those people are who do such things against the Lord:

“The tents of the Edomites, and the Ishmaelites; Moab and the Hagrites; Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, and foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre. Assur also came together with them. They became a refuge for the sons of Lot. Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They perished at Endor” (Ps. LXXXI), and so forth. [Col. 0365D]

If we explain the interpretations of these names, we undoubtedly find that they correspond to your conduct.

The Edomites are called “blood-red” or “earthly.” This certainly suits you, who, while you argue these matters, openly demonstrate that you are flesh and blood and altogether earthly.

You are also Ishmaelites—that is, “obedient ones”—not obedient to God but to the world; not to the divine law but to the flesh.

Moab means “from the father,” by which paternal incest is understood; and therefore your lust is also condemned.

Hagrites means “proselytes” or “newcomers.” This name designates those who, through outward association, pretend to be fellow citizens with the Christian people, but, being opposed to the law of Christ, persist among them with a foreign and adventitious mind.

Gebal means “a vain valley,” by which those who falsely pretend to be meek and deceptively humble are designated.

Ammon is interpreted as “a turbulent people” or “a people of sorrow.” These are understood to be those who, while they disturb the people with new teaching, generate sorrow and sadness for the Church of God.

Amalek means “a people who lick.” By them the enemies of Christ are designated, concerning whom it is said in the psalm: “And his enemies shall lick the earth” (Ps. LXXI).

Although the foreigners indicate themselves as foreigners even by the Latin name, and consequently as enemies, in Hebrew they are called *Philisthiim*, which is interpreted as “falling through drinking.” They represent those whom the luxury of the flesh intoxicates and, as though falling from excessive drinking, casts down into the depths.

Tyre, which in Hebrew is called “lot,” is interpreted as “anguish” or “tribulation.” By it those are plainly represented who, through works of impiety, are shown to be subject to perpetual tribulation or anguish. [Col. 0366B]

Madian is interpreted as “turning aside from judgment.” Those plainly turn aside from judgment who, by teaching perversely, violate the justice of the divine law.

Sisera means “exclusion of joy.” Whoever wantonly immerses himself in wantonness and carnal allurements excludes from himself the joy of heavenly happiness.

Jabin means “wise,” which, by antiphrasis, is to be understood of those concerning whom the Apostle says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age?” (I Cor. I.) “Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish?”

Oreb is interpreted as “dryness.” Whoever is burned by the heat of carnal desire does not deserve to be moistened by the rain of the Holy Spirit.

Zeb means “wolf”; Zebee, “victim.” The reprobate, who are rapacious in the world, are both wolves and themselves victims: for while they strive to devour the weaker, they themselves are exposed to the teeth of the spiritual wolf, that is, the devil.

But so that this interpretation of the names may not depart from the order of the present discussion, the perverse teachers of the Church are like wolves of the forest. They are both wolves and victims, because while they slaughter the innocent like sheep with the bloody teeth of wicked preaching, they themselves become prey and are carried into the entrails of the devouring devil, refreshing his insatiable greed.

The Psalmist says of them:

“They are placed like sheep in the underworld; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. [Col. 0366D] XLVIII).

For the devil is called death, as it is written in the Apocalypse:

“There was a pale horse, and the one seated upon it had the name Death” (Apoc. VI).

Beware, therefore, lest, while you satisfy your hunger by feeding upon the deaths of little ones, you yourselves become victims of the hidden ravager, whom that voracious and insatiable murderer may transfer into his own food.

Salmana means “the shadow of disturbance.” Whoever is carnal, while pursuing a shadowy happiness and despising the truth, is disturbed by the various desires of the world.

Kishon, the torrent in which all those men were defeated, is interpreted as “their hardness.” In their hardness they perish who, teaching perverse things, resist the truth stubbornly and obstinately.

Endor, where they perished, is also interpreted as “the fountain of generation”—but specifically of carnal generation. To this they devoted themselves with delight and deserved to be struck down by a deadly slaughter, not seeking to germinate where they will neither marry nor take wives, nor begin to die, but rather there where whatever is born must necessarily dissolve into death. [Col. 0367A]

You, therefore, fall at Endor under the innermost slaughter of the divine sword, because you teach that ministers of the sacred altar should enter into the unions of incestuous marriage and beget illegitimate children.

Finally, because you assert that the sanctuary of God should be administered not with spiritual governance and forethought but possessed as though by hereditary right, all these interpretations of the names briefly set forth above plainly apply to you.

Although many further arguments remain for refuting those propositions to which we have responded briefly and quickly, we now restrain our hand from the freedom of writing, so that we may restore the strength of dictation more abundantly—if, indeed, it should still be necessary—during a period of respite for the breathing spirit.

Spare your insolent lips, beloved ones; and if you see the brine of some harsher word flowing forth against you, rebuke not me but yourselves, who compelled me to write.

## LETTER XIV. TO RODULPH, VITALIS, ARIALD, ERLEMBALD, AND OTHERS

### Summary

First he congratulates those to whom he writes on their faith and courage. Then he complains about the dissensions and scandals of the Milanese Church. Finally, he seems not only to pray for but also to predict their steadfastness in defending the truth and their heavenly happiness. For many of them, having fought bravely for the faith of Christ, were crowned with martyrdom and enjoy the eternal vision of God.

To the holy brothers Rodulph, Vitalis, and Ariald, and Erlembald, and the others who fight with unconquered faith for the camps of Christ, Peter, the sinful monk, sends greetings in Christ.

We give thanks to almighty God, dearly beloved, because through the reports circulating about you we frequently hear that you persist with pious fervor in that which you have conceived through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and that with the strength of an unwavering spirit you contend against the enemies of ecclesiastical discipline. For the most wicked money-changer does not cease to build the workshop of his perversity within the bounds of the Church; he does not stop manufacturing, with striking hammers, coins of infernal currency. [Col. 0367D]

The heresy of the Nicolaitans also, which seemed to us to have been uprooted while we labored together with you, is still sprouting with renewed shoots, and savagely suffocates Christ’s already ripening, golden harvest beneath the shadow of weeds rising up. Hence we fall before the Lord with plaintive lamentation, saying: “Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, has it weeds?” We add also: “Do you want us to go and gather them?” But he immediately answers us with a consoling voice: “Let both grow until the harvest, and at harvest-time I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn; but gather the wheat into my barn” (Matthew 13).

For although God can undoubtedly do all things, he could certainly cast far from the field of the Milanese Church the contagions of every heresy and preserve unharmed the grain of its flourishing faith. Yet he wishes to test the steadfastness of his faithful: how violently they seize their weapons, how vigorously they join hand to hand, and, finally, with what tireless hostility they fight against the devil and his satellites. They could also have prevented their master—namely Simon, who once opposed the apostles—from rising into the air; but I allowed him to be lifted up for this purpose, so that, to God’s greater glory and Simon’s disgrace, he might be compelled to sink into the depths (*Acts of Saint Peter*).

Therefore, dearly beloved, as you fight against the twofold battle-line of the devil’s legion, do not cease; do not fail through ignoble faint-heartedness. Rather, like the true sons of Benjamin—whose name is said to mean “son of the right hand”—fight with customary fervor using both hands, and with the swords of the divine word cut off the head of the two-headed monster. Behold, surely, Jesus, from whose mouth proceeds a sword sharpened and honed on both sides, mowing down whatever it encounters and laying low the bloodstained barbarity of his enemies (Judges 3).

And if perhaps the multiplied words of the wicked seem to assail you from the opposite side, confidently proclaim that saying of Elisha: “There are more with us than with them” (2 Kings 6). What more shall I say? I add the apostolic saying: “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what I preached, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1).

For behold, those who had previously been held fast in the snares of the Nicolaitan and Simoniac heresies are now, to the accumulation of their destruction, also perjurers after violating the sanctity of their oath, so that in them the saying made in the Apocalypse through John may be fulfilled with the greatest clarity: “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy” (Revelation 22). But in you, by contrast, the following saying is fulfilled: “Let the one who is righteous continue to be justified, and let the one who is holy continue to be sanctified” (ibid.).

It was always familiar and characteristic of the Milanese Church that men of differing doctrines should exist within it, and that both Auxentius and Ambrose should be present: the former barking at the faithful like a rabid little dog, while the latter drove him back, as it were, with the horned fork of the testimonies of the Old and New Testaments; the former offering the error of a viper’s gall, while the latter poured forth the pure water of the heavenly fountain; the former plunging his followers, nourished on poisonous milk and enticed by fraudulent cunning, into Tartarus, while the latter raised them through the sweetness of apostolic teaching to the rewards of heavenly glory; the former clothing those who believed him in the darkness of blindness, while the latter recalled those obedient to priestly commands to the splendor of the true faith and the light of eternal grace.

Therefore I gladly cry out in praise of him with whatever praises I can offer at this time:

“May almighty God, dearly beloved, through the keys of blessed Peter the apostle, open for you the door of the heavenly kingdom; and through the prayer of blessed Ambrose, your bishop, may he mercifully wipe away from you every defilement of the spirit of darkness. May he grant you to persist in inviolate truth, which you once began to embrace, and, founded upon the rock of the apostolic faith, to withstand invincibly every error of perverse doctrines. May he grant that throughout your passage through this life you live in such a way that, together with him who is the author of life, you may deserve to rejoice without end in that heavenly Jerusalem. Amen.”

## EPISTLE XV. TO THE SAME MEN

**Summary.**—This epistle contains the same matters as the preceding one, but more briefly.

Peter Damian sends greetings in the Lord to the brothers Rodulphus, Vitalis, Arialdus, and Erlembaldus.

We give thanks to God because, according to the steadfast report we hear, you steadfastly contend against the enemies of ecclesiastical discipline. The heresy of the Nicolaitans, which seemed to have been uprooted while you labored together with us, is sprouting again. God wishes to test the steadfastness of his own. Behold, those who had previously been held in the snares of the Nicolaitan and Simoniac heresies are now, to the accumulation of their destruction, also perjurers after violating their oath. Yet this is not new in the Milanese Church, which has always possessed men of differing doctrines, beginning with Auxentius and Ambrose.

## EPISTLE XVII. TO SAINT THE PRESBYTER

(This is found in volume III, in opusculum 8.)

## EPISTLE XVIII. TO UBERTUS, THE PRESBYTER

[Col. 0369C]

**Summary.**—In this epistle he responds to the questions of the presbyter Ubertus concerning baptism and the sacrifice of the Mass.

To the lord Ubertus, a presbyter of religious character, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the bond of indivisible charity in the Lord.

I do not doubt, venerable brother, that your little questions arise from the fervor of the spiritual study that nobly burns within you. Since the bearer of this letter is hastening to return, I must answer them briefly, especially since their solution requires no extended discourse, as everything is so clear that anyone who is not ignorant of the rule of ecclesiastical order will find no difficulty in these matters.

For we are not introducing a new custom into the Church; rather, we preserve what has been established by the Fathers. And because we have received the faith from the apostles, and from apostolic men the order of conduct in the Church, we change the mode of discipline handed down by our forebears no more than we preserve the very foundation of the faith unaltered. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Timothy 3).

For the later members of the Church are no longer permitted to choose whatever seems best to them; rather, it is necessary to preserve what was ordained in ancient times, especially as the Roman Church observes it. Heresy, indeed, is called “choice.” And those who presume to choose what seems better to them are rightly marked as heretics; they disdain to remain in what has been established by the holy teachers.

But because I profess myself to be a disciple not only of the ancient saints but also of those of the present day, and do not usurp for myself the chair of a teacher, I do not devise a new rule for you concerning the matters about which you consult me, nor do I promulgate legal enactments. Rather, I simply make known what I have become accustomed to do in the Roman Church while the attendants of the apostolic see themselves taught me, or what I have learned and repeatedly practiced in other churches.

Accordingly, in the sacred washing of baptism, following the custom of the Roman Church, I have always mixed in chrism alone; I have never seen wine or oil being added. For that writing which is read on the day of the Lord’s Supper and is entitled *A General Sermon on the Preparation of Chrism* seems to express the view that we ought to mix nothing besides holy chrism into the baptismal font. For among other things it says:

“By the oil of sacred chrism the water of baptism is prepared, and it becomes a fountain of heavenly grace.”

Since the author of this sermon speaks sufficiently above about consecrated oil, but when he comes to baptism says that it is prepared with chrism alone, mentioning no oil, it is beyond doubt that he intended only what he named to be mixed in. For if he had decided that wine or oil should be poured in, he would not have remained silent about this after mentioning chrism.

As for celebrating the solemnities of the Mass, we have both learned and observe this rule of custom in disciplined churches: we defer rinsing the chalice at the end of Mass if we hope to offer the sacrifice again ourselves on that same day. Otherwise, whenever we sacrifice the sacred offerings, we always rinse the chalice at the end according to custom. Moreover, whether we are fasting or have eaten, we do not change this rule concerning rinsing it.

But as to your report that some say that, after someone has rinsed the chalice, he should no longer be said to be fasting, and that by these frivolous absurdities they attempt to provoke a dispute in the guise of questions, you should take care to observe what the Apostle says: “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels; but the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all” (2 Timothy 2).

It should therefore be enough for you to hear briefly arranged the custom that the Church now observes; do not insist that an explanation be supplied to you in due sequence, since this matter requires many words and is more easily completed through a conversation in ordinary speech than it can be finished in the moment of dictation.

Nor should you be surprised if this little written piece, dashed off with such haste, is insufficient for you or even reveals the defect of rusticity. Ask the bearer of the letter: since, when the day was already nearly half gone, he had climbed to the summit of our mountain, he received this little sheet before sunset.

Nevertheless, ask further about baptism if something perhaps escaped me concerning what is observed in the Roman Church. I beg divine mercy, venerable brother, to visit the sanctuary of your heart and illuminate it with the rays of his brightness, so that that Key of David who opened the sealed book with seven seals (Revelation 5) may also open for you what is still closed, and powerfully release what is bound.

## EPISTLE XIX. TO CLERICS AND CANONS

(This is found in volume III and is opusculum 28.)

# BOOK SIX. TO ABBOTS AND MONKS

[Col. 0371]

## EPISTLE ONE. TO THE MONKS OF THE SACRED MONASTERY OF SAINT BENEDICT AT MONTE CASSINO

[Col. 0371B]

(This is found in volume III and is opusculum 43.)

## EPISTLE II. TO HUGO, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF CLUNY

**Summary.**—The monks of Cluny, who had received the greatest benefits from the holy doctor, since he had not refused, on their account, to cross the Alps in his old age and go to Gaul, had granted him that the day of his death should perpetually be celebrated in their monastery each year with prayers poured out to God and with funeral solemnity. He now recalls this very matter to Hugo, abbot of Cluny, and begs him to ensure that the same should be done in the other monasteries subject to Cluny.

To the lord U., abbot of venerable holiness, Peter [Col. 0371C], a sinful monk, sends whatever a servant can send.

When one thing is sought and another is found, the petitioner’s wish is by no means fulfilled. Paul, indeed, complains that, while he asks for the angel of Satan to be taken away from him, the thorn in his flesh that he requested is not removed; rather, he is warned that divine grace is sufficient for him (2 Corinthians 12). Moses likewise asked the Lord, who spoke with him, to show him his face, and he did not obtain this (Exodus 33). Elsewhere, however, because the Lord would make him into a great nation if he himself wished, Moses heard: “Let me alone, he said, so that my anger may burn against this people and I may destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation” (Exodus 32). To this Moses replied in a free voice: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, blot me out of the book that you have written” (ibid.).

Here, therefore, divine generosity freely offered what Moses did not want; there, it did not grant in any way what he had earnestly demanded. Solomon, however, was happier than both in his petition, for he obtained both the understanding heart that he wanted and the glory and riches that he had not asked for. The divine voice said to him: “Behold, I have done for you according to your words, and I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that no one before you was like you, nor will anyone like you arise after you. And I have also given you what you did not ask for, namely riches and glory, so that no one among all the kings of former days will be like you” (1 Kings 3; Wisdom 7; Matthew 6).

Why I have prefaced this, I shall explain briefly. Your holy prudence has not forgotten, venerable Father, that when old age was already bending me down, and my body, exhausted of strength, caused the steps of my faltering walk to stagger uncertainly, I placed my soul, so to speak, in my hands at your command. Covered in summer snow, I climbed the precipitous heights of the Alps and, for the benefit of your venerable monastery, penetrated deep into Gaul, close enough to the Ocean.

In return for this labor, I asked chiefly that your incomparable and holy community should promise me, together with you, through written assurances, that throughout all the changing succession of times it would always honor the anniversary of my death with renewed remembrance and commend me to the dreadful Judge through the pious rites of prayer. To this promise was then added the provision that one poor man should be continuously supported for my sake with both food and clothing.

This is the fruit of my labor, this the reward of my work, this the reciprocal recompense. But while your generosity showers me with so many abundant and precious gifts, I fear—not without reason—that when the amount of earthly payment assigned to a completed labor is repaid to me, the salutary benefit of your prayer may be withdrawn from me. For when a daily wage is paid for a day’s work, nothing remains thereafter for the laborer’s hope—unless perhaps that lot which befell Solomon should also be mine, by which he obtained both what he desired and, in addition, received what he had not asked for (Wisdom 7).

But I am content with one and take no pleasure in the other. While I earnestly request the gift of your holy prayer and desire it with all my longing, I regard as insignificant every earthly advantage, however difficult to obtain or however costly. For although your charity is so full and perfect that it willingly and abundantly bestows both gifts upon those who deserve to be its friends, one of them is nevertheless so valuable to me that I do not seek the other.

A sinister suspicion troubles the secrets of my fearful mind: I fear that while earthly means are offered to me, the spiritual gift may in some way be diminished. For on the scales of my judgment, the small coin of holy prayer weighs more heavily than a talent of gold or a great multitude of glittering gems.

That gold I seek; that is what I long desirably to receive, of which it is written: “The elders had golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 3). I prefer this gold to every acquisition that can be desired; I eagerly embrace it, and in comparison with it I count all the advantages of earthly gain as worthless.

Therefore I implore the mercy of your holy charity, venerable Father, that the little indication of your promise, as it has been written in the holy monastery of Cluny, should likewise be written in the other monasteries subject to your authority. I humbly reveal this further to your piety: falling at your holy feet with streaming tears, I embrace them, asking you to order that what you graciously promised me in the form of a written memorial should also be transcribed in the other monasteries subject to your laws.

And if rustic speech does not obtain the fulfillment of this request, may the Holy Spirit, who possesses the sanctuary of your heart, mercifully inspire you to grant my prayers. Thus, just as I did not hesitate to offer my body to cruel dangers for your sake, may heavenly mercy through you deign to free my soul from infernal torments, and may I deserve to be recorded, through the instrument of your writing, among the lot of the righteous.

## EPISTLE III. TO THE SAME HUGO, ABBOT

**Summary.**—He shows, as can easily be inferred, how greatly he loves Hugo, the abbot of Cluny, and at the same time commends to him his nephew Damian, his sister’s son, whom he had sent to Gaul to learn the liberal arts, asking him to care for him in all matters, both those pertaining to the cultivation of the body and those pertaining to the cultivation of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] The beginning is missing in the manuscripts.] …has instilled—how utterly effaced, how, so to speak, obliterated from the innermost wax tablets of my heart! Indeed, witnesses to the great blessing in which your name is held upon my lips, and to the praises with which that angelic community of yours is celebrated by me, are both those who dwell with me in the service of Christ and those who visit me for love of him.

I also ask the mercy of your holiness concerning this young man, namely the son of my uterine sister, that you provide him with a teacher and with food through fatherly kindness. Receive him, unformed and unskilled, and, like Jacob simply leaning upon his staff (Genesis 32), send him back later to his own home with the twofold spouse of the trivium or quadrivium.

In this boy, then, look upon my image; in him consider the likeness of my face. Whatever kindness is expended upon him, attribute it entirely not to himself but to me.

Would that I could send you what I wrote to the holy men of Cluny, or the many other things that I composed from various themes after returning from Gaul! May almighty God, venerable Father, preserve you unharmed for a long time for the protection of his servants, and make me see in your presence the angelic appearance of your face.

## EPISTLE IV. TO THE SAME HUGO AND THE MONKS OF HIS MONASTERY

**Summary.**—When the most holy doctor was serving in Gaul as legate of the apostolic see, he conferred many benefits upon the monastery and the monks of Cluny. In return, so that they might show him some gratitude, they had unanimously promised that for themselves and their successors the day of his death would be solemn each year, with prayers poured out to God. Since he sensed that his final day was approaching, he now reminds them of this promise and earnestly urges them not to neglect fulfilling it. This epistle is chiefly concerned with commemorating the praises of those monks and the holiness of that place.

To the lord U., archangel of the monks, and to the holy community, Peter, a sinful monk, sends whatever a servant can send.

Once a hunter has caught a wild animal in a snare and fastened the knot around its feet, he allows it to wander farther under a kind of freedom, without fear of losing it. The man who delights in bird-catching likewise, while holding a bird by a cord tied around its feet, pretends confidently to grant it the freedom to fly away. The bird indeed attempts flight and, as usual, balances the oar-like movement of its wings; but when it tries to leap upward, it is pulled back as the bird-catcher tightens the cord.

You too have safely sent me back to my own place, though you retain me inseparably bound by the bond of your charity. For I was able to withdraw in body, but in mind I did not escape from your hands. The lure of your wondrous way of life so ensnared me, the cement of your angelic life so glued me, and the noose of sincere charity so entangled me that my mind could more easily forget itself than be torn away from the memory of you.

Indeed, I saw a paradise watered by the streams of the four Gospels—or rather, overflowing with as many channels of spiritual virtues. I saw a garden of delights putting forth the varied graces of roses and lilies and sweetly exhaling the honeyed fragrances of spices and perfumes, so that almighty God could truly say of it: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field that the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 29).

And what else should I call the monastery of Cluny but a field full of the Lord, where, like a heap of heavenly harvests, there is a choir of so many monks dwelling in charity? That field is cut each day with the hoe of holy preaching, and the seeds of heavenly eloquence are scattered in it. There the yield of spiritual fruits is heaped up, so that afterward it may be carried into heavenly barns.

Therefore, when I consider you, fortunate Cluny, I reflect that this name was assigned to you not without the arrangement of divine foreknowledge. For this name is composed from *clunes* and *acus*, by which the work of oxen plowing is signified. An ox is pricked in the haunches with a goad so that it may pull the plow and cut open the fields.

For there the field of the human heart is cultivated, from which that harvest is gathered that is packed into the chambers of the heavenly storehouse. There is applied that goad with which the still proud Saul was addressed: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9). For he, like a proud and savage bull, was still tossing about the Lord’s threshing-floor, which is the Church, with the horns of his pride; but he is divinely subjected to the yoke of faith, so that he is compelled to pull the plow in the Lord’s field.

Hence afterward he says of evangelists, as of plowmen: “The one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes ought to do so in hope of sharing in the harvest” (1 Corinthians 9). Concerning this plow the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

The Israelite people were pulling the plow of the Law through the desert when Pharaoh pricked them from one side with the goad of the harshest slavery, while Moses from the other drew them forward with heavenly commands as though with ropes. The former, while they built cities with mud and bricks, beat them as if from behind; the latter, promising a land of milk and honey, drew them forward as their guide.

But we, who plow in the field of the Church like the Lord’s oxen, are pricked from behind when we are terrified by the final scrutiny of the last judgment. The goad of terror drives us from behind so that our neck, worn down—or [as the textual variant has it, “bound”]—by the yoke of divine law, does not grow weary in its labors.

Appropriately, then, I would call Cluny a field in which the Lord’s oxen plow tirelessly while the goad of divine terror urges them on. As with a needle, the rear part of the haunches is pierced when the human mind is terrified by the fear of the final judgment. It is pierced from behind so that it may press forward, because the life already passed terrifies our heart so that it fears the scrutiny of the final examination.

Paul was pierced by this goad when he said: “I do not consider that I have grasped it. But forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling; I pursue it, if I may grasp it” (Philippians 3). A thorn in the flesh had been given to him so that he would not collapse in labor but would plow tirelessly in the field of the Lord’s harvest.

This notable and wondrous ox bore two horns on its head, because through the office of preaching he wielded the two Testaments. When he said to the Galatians (Galatians 4) that one son of Abraham was born from a slave woman and the other from the freedom of a noble and legitimate marriage, he immediately added: “These are the two covenants” (Philippians 1).

He also plowed while bound like an ox, for he often mentions his chains. Was he not plowing in chains when, bound by fetters, he said to Philemon: “I appeal to you for my son, whom I have begotten in chains, Onesimus” (Philemon 1)? He was also led to sacrifice like an excellent ox when he said: “For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice, and the time of my release is at hand” (2 Timothy 4).

Rightly, therefore, the venerable place received a name where the plow of spiritual oxen is now drawn, and where the heap of heavenly harvests is accumulated—or, as the reading *accuminatur* has it, “sharpened”—up to the one grain who is Christ Jesus. He says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12).

Cluny is also a certain spiritual plain where heaven and earth meet, like an arena of combat in which fragile flesh, after the manner of a wrestling school, struggles against the powers of the air. “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

There Joshua—not that son of Nun, but the heavenly leader of the army and instructor of spiritual warriors—teaches his soldiers to trample upon the necks of the five proud kings. Those are known to obtain a triumphal victory over them who restrain the same number of bodily senses through the discipline of strict custody.

There the walls of Jericho collapse at the blasts of trumpets, and its inhabitants are killed by the swords of the Israelites. There Joshua pronounces this terrible curse: “Cursed before the Lord is the man who rises up and rebuilds the city of Jericho. Upon his firstborn shall he lay its foundations, and upon his youngest child shall he set up its gates” (Joshua 6).

That man rebuilds Jericho upon his firstborn who loves this world above all, after it has been overthrown by the blast of the apostolic trumpet.
