But the man who sets its gates upon his youngest child is the one who despises the world, considers it of little worth, and places it after everything that is truly to be loved. He has this world for use, but does not have it in love; and while he nourishes the love of the heavenly kingdom as his firstborn and heir, he despises the world like a filthy child crying in its cradle.

“Seek first,” says the Lord, “the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6). Thus the kingdom of God should be firstborn in our heart, while the world should be regarded as last through an addition at the extremity.

There also Adonibezeq is cut off at the extremities of his hands and feet, while the evil spirit among holy men is deprived both of the power to walk and of the power to act. When he suffers these wounds, he boasts that he had inflicted the same upon others: “Seventy kings,” he says, “with the extremities of their hands and feet cut off, gathered the scraps of food beneath my table. As I did, so the Lord has repaid me” (Judges 1).

The seventy kings are the seventy nations of differing languages, from which the ancient enemy had entirely taken away, until the coming of the Savior, both the ability to walk rightly and the ability to do good. The physician of souls, Paul, heals both of these paired wounds when he says: “Raise up the slack hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not go astray but rather be healed” (Hebrews 12).

Adonibezeq is interpreted as “Lord of lightning,” or “Lord content with vanity.” Lightning vanishes as soon as it begins to flash. By this the Jewish people can be understood: they flashed, as it were, with a certain brilliance when they said, “All that the Lord has commanded us, we will both hear and do” (Deuteronomy 5); but this light soon faded and fell when they bowed their necks to dark demons.

By the expression “content with vanity,” the Gentile people are signified. Content with visible idols, they did not care to return to the mercy of the Creator; and, while they were ignorant of the worship of truth, they persisted in the vain ceremonies of idols. Of them the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Romans 1).

Thus Adonibezeq, that is, the reprobate spirit of wickedness, held dominion over these two peoples for the most part: the one began to flash like lightning and then ceased, while the other, content with the vanity of demons, did not seek the help of its own Creator.

And, to return to my subject, there Eglon, in the type of lust, is pierced through by the strong Ehud’s dagger driven into his belly (Judges 3); there proud Sisera’s brain is pierced by the tent-peg (Judges 4); there, as a sign of avarice, stones crush Achar, son of Carmi, and the plagues of every vice, like hostile battle-lines in revolt, do not escape the swords of the strong Israelites (Joshua 7).

There the true David, as though stationed upon the summit of the citadel of Zion, with the two-edged sword that proceeds from his mouth, slaughters on every side the adversaries who resist him and cuts off the necks of all who oppose him. In these *galgals*—a word said to mean “revelation” [or, according to the variant, “revolution”]—the reproach of Egypt is removed from us Israelites, while the second circumcision is celebrated with stone knives; there the Paschal solemnity is observed, and, under the leadership of Jesus, we pass from Moses’ veil to the mirror of revelation (Exodus 34).

Moreover, dearly beloved, you know how much labor has worn me down for the sake of preserving your salvation: how in my extreme old age I crossed so many precipitous mountains and so many terrifying ridges of the Alps. To sum everything up briefly, I endured the bitterness of death so that you might live pleasantly; I placed my life in my hands and, through the help of him whom you serve, freed you from the hands of your persecutors.

Therefore all of you who were sitting in chapter established by common judgment and resolved to have it entered on written slips, through the instrument of a written record, that both you and your successors should always observe some special rite on the anniversary of my death, so that all the trumpets might sound more festively and the brothers might celebrate solemn rites of prayers and sacrifices for their brother.

This decree of your agreement has been inserted in the margin of your heart, so that forgetfulness might never at any time intercept it. Therefore I tearfully implore the sweetness of your holy charity, and, prostrate with a bowed heart, I throw myself at your feet: as soon as you know with certainty that my summons has come, effectively fulfill what you promised your servant.

May my lord also, your venerable Father and abbot Hugo, as he promised me, cause this same token of his promise to be proclaimed orally throughout his monasteries and order it to be transcribed in their books by a flowing pen, so that the true disciple may keep faith and not violate the security of the pledged covenant.

I ask this by Jesus, who gives testimony before Pontius Pilate (1 Timothy 6); by his terrible judgment, by which he will judge the living and the dead; by the angels and archangels, by Peter and Paul, and by all the apostles and martyrs; I appeal by the name of the holy consubstantial Trinity: may both you and your successors remember me in your holy prayers.

And what has been written by you to me under threat of anathema, may you faithfully fulfill. To induce you to do so, I impose upon you the adjuration of this entreaty. Yet if you do not do it, although by the authority of the apostolic see I could properly threaten the choir of the angelic host with such a terrible sentence, I do not threaten it.

Let only the one who has disdained to favor me in this request be—let him, I say, be—guilty of falsehood and liable for a violated promise at the final judgment of truth.

I am tempted to add: “Let him be blotted from the book”; but while I keep your reverence before my eyes, I do not presume to utter what my mind suggests.

If you do not deny fulfillment to my request, and after my death you continually provide me with the assistance of your holy prayer each year, as was agreed and prescribed, may the protection of almighty God always watch over this monastery. May it defend you from the snares of invisible enemies and guard your goods from external adversities.

May the almighty Spirit possess your hearts and rise within them through the continual fervor of his love. May he now build a temple for himself in your breasts, and afterward bring you into the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem. Amen.

## EPISTLE V. TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF CLUNY

**Summary.**—In this epistle he praises the monks of Cluny, with whom he was joined by great goodwill because, when he was legate in Gaul from the apostolic see, he had freed them from the attempt of a certain bishop to usurp jurisdiction over them, praising them in the name of holiness and piety. He exalts to heaven the order and discipline that he had himself observed being maintained in their monastery, as most beneficial and consonant with the commands of the holy Fathers and of sacred Scripture. Finally, he begs them to remember him and not to cease assisting him with their prayers before God, as though he were one of their number.

[183] To the truly holy brothers of the monastery of Cluny, worthy of angelic veneration, Peter, a sinful monk, sends perpetual service in the Lord.

I do not want you, beloved, to be unaware that, as I was returning from you, a grievous sorrow of weariness overwhelmed me, and that a dense darkness of thoughts wore down my impatient heart, cast into dejection by faintheartedness. Indeed, when I recalled myself as though I had been deceived like a child by an egg, and bound by flattering words as though by silken cords or by the soft bands of a delicate hyacinth, promised one thing in speech but shown something altogether different in reality, I was tossed in mind; and at that time, I confess, everyone who strayed from the straight line of truth displeased me more than usual.

For, to note only one example by which the others may be gathered together: I had been promised that I would have returned to my own place on the Kalends of August. But after nearly a three-month period had subsequently been exhausted, although I hastened with all the speed I could, I nevertheless climbed to the summit of Fonte Avellana, from which I had set out, only on the fifth day before the Kalends of November. Thus, while our spirit proceeded anxiously through so many channels of swollen torrents, through so many rocky precipices of the snowy Alps, and—what was worse—through so many ambushed conspiracies of Cadaloic fury gathered together, it endured, so to speak, a dense hailstorm of inward conflict.

Although in this matter it always remained stern and unbending, and had resolved, unquestionably, not to return evil for evil, nevertheless, however hard it strove to forget the injury, it could not wholly achieve this. But after I had reached my cell—or rather, after I myself, who had been shut out, had entered into myself—the heat of my seething spirit was immediately extinguished; the complaint of contentious dispute was stilled; swelling, clamour, and indignation were at once laid aside; and everything that had been bitter in my inward parts was sweetened by divine action.

For, like a contentious litigant brought before a judge’s tribunal, I did not dare to present my useless complaint before the majesty of the strict cell. And just as some sick person, entering an apothecary’s shop, recovers before receiving the medicines of an antidote, having laid aside the sickness of his illness, so I, as soon as I touched the threshold of my cell—before I had opened any book at all, and, O blessed result!—found myself healthy and unharmed, as though by the power of the place, with the wounds of my soul set in order. Thus, at the sight of the divine books, which were still being kept closed, I drank in salvation as though before drinking a medicinal draught, inhaling only the fragrances of sweet-smelling spices.

Therefore, to your holy superior [Note: He means Saint Hugh, the abbot.], who brought upon me the burden of so great a calamity, I not only restore the due measure of injury, but, for the sake of your love, bring him back into the rights of our former friendship. For since we ask that our sins be forgiven by God not absolutely, but in the same way that we forgive others (Matthew 6; Luke 11), while seeking God’s grace together with the remission of sin, it is fitting that we too, after forgiving our enemies their offence, should restore them wholly to the fullness of our former friendship.

For just as forgetfulness of God’s commandments is undoubtedly a vice, so forgetfulness of an injury inflicted is no small virtue. Moreover, thanks must also be given to the man who crushed me beneath the pressure of so great a labour, because, by the arrangement of him who makes good use of our evils, through that man’s offence it happened that I came to know your holiness. I rejoice all the more in this because my labour granted you the leisure of pleasant security, and my distress procured sweet holidays for your laborious rest.

In this way, then, he inserted me into your pious works. Although I did not remove from you the traces of holy living, I nevertheless brought you assistance so that you might be able to live holily. Thus Obadiah, steward of the house of Ahab, while hiding in caves the prophets who were fleeing Jezebel’s swords, fifty at a time, later earned the grace of the prophetic spirit in a glorious exchange (1 Kings 18). And now he refreshes the Church with the fare of spiritual food who at that time supplied bread and water to those who were hungry.

Thus Elisha, while offering his master the service of devoted diligence, obtained a double grace in the power of miracles (2 Kings 2). Thus Rahab, because she concealed the Israelite spies from the face of the raging tyrant, escaped the swords of Jericho’s slaughter; and the Gentile prostitute was transferred into the company of the Israelites because she supplied their messengers with the means of escaping alive (Joshua 2).

I too, as I hope, have entered into the merits of your holiness, since I drove away the yoke of the Church of Matica which was being attempted to be imposed upon you. I believe that through you I am to be guarded against the wiles of demons, since I seized from the hands of the clerics the club of Hercules, already brandished against you, and struck down, like Jesbibenob rising against David (2 Samuel 21), and intervened lest the lamp of Israel should be extinguished.

Furthermore, when I recall the strict and highly ordered pattern of your holy way of life, I recognize that it contains not human ingenuity but the instruction of the Holy Spirit. For such was the length of the continual persistence with which the order was observed, and such especially was the prolonged diligence devoted to the ecclesiastical offices, that even in the heat of Cancer or Leo, when the days are longer, scarcely half an hour in the whole day remained in which the brothers were permitted to exchange conversation in the cloister.

This exercise of such unbroken labour, it seems to me, was provided with sufficiently careful and prudent skill of instruction for this purpose: to restrain the frailty of weak and infirm brothers and almost to remove the opportunity for sinning, so that, even if they wished to do so, they could scarcely sin beyond the realm of thought.

The weakness of the frail is therefore taken into account when the entire span of both day and night is spent in fulfilling the appointed burden of the continuous order. For almighty God himself was pleased to use this as an instrument of human salvation when he imposed so many commandments upon the people travelling through the wilderness (Exodus 36): namely, that an elaborate and inexplicable tabernacle should be constructed; that different sacrifices should be offered to him through so many ceremonies and rites; and that the arrangement of the camps, whether of those remaining in place or of those moving about, should be distinguished by such an artful and mystical variety that, while the people continually exercised themselves in these matters, the carnal multitude could not relax into the worship of idols.

Indeed, since that people was not occupied with textile work, did not practise any other craft, and did not devote itself to agriculture, nor labour at any tasks necessary for making provision, it had to be occupied with many commandments when God promulgated the law, so that, while fulfilling these with labour, it would not, relaxed through idleness, turn aside into sacrilege.

Nor is it surprising that Pharaoh too attempted to appropriate this very principle when he said: “You are idle, and therefore you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord’” (Exodus 5). But that they did not need to do anything earthly except observe the precepts of the law that had been imposed is testified by Moses, who addressed him in these words: “The Lord gave you manna for food, which neither you nor your fathers knew, to show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deuteronomy 8; Matthew 4; Luke 4). Immediately he adds:

“Your garment, with which you were covered, did not wear out through age, and your foot was not worn down. Behold, it is the fortieth year, that you may reflect in your heart that, just as a man instructs his son, so the Lord your God has instructed you, so that you may keep the commandments of the Lord your God, walk in his ways, and fear him” (Deuteronomy 8).

In these words, special attention must be paid to what he says: “He gave you manna to show that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” Here it is perfectly clear that the manna by which they were nourished physically signified the food of the divine word by which we are now renewed in soul.

It should also be noted that the book of Exodus says of this manna: “When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, ‘Manhu?’”—which means, “What is this?” (Exodus 16). Those, therefore, truly eat manna—that is, “What is this?”—who, when they read or hear, diligently seek out the mystery of the divine word. Within the sheath of the literal straw, they strive to extract the sweet kernel of spiritual understanding.

This person truly feeds upon “What is this?” who is occupied in diligent, continual inquiry into Holy Scripture. For we eat, as it were, a question—“What is this?”—with the eager mouth of the heart when we apply ourselves vigilantly to penetrating the mysteries of Scripture, when we subtly chew over the feasts of heavenly speech.

And how fittingly does the monastic profession correspond to that Israelite people, since what nourished them then in the wilderness is now our feast in the cloister! For what is the wilderness except a place separated from human habitation? And what is the cloister except a place enclosed away from every activity of worldly business?

And just as a fiery light shone upon those travelling through the wilderness amid the darkness of night, so those dwelling in spiritual cloisters are often illuminated by the rays of heavenly light, which drive away the darkness of bodily passions and suffuse them with the radiance of innermost contemplation.

The world, therefore, must be fled: it gives birth to darkness. Retirement must be sought, where, as in a wilderness, the true light breaks forth. He must be driven entirely from our friendship who, while continually inserting the darkness and gloom in which he himself always remains, extinguishes the light in those who agree and obey him. Indeed, we ought always to wage irreconcilable war against him [the text lacks *indicere* or some similar verb], since he blinds the eyes of his friends.

Hence we have learned from the sacred history of the Kings that when Naas the Ammonite went up to attack Jabesh-gilead with his forces, all the men of Jabesh said to Naas with one voice: “Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.” He replied to them: “On this condition will I make a covenant with you: that I remove the right eyes of all of you and make you a reproach throughout Israel.” The elders of Jabesh said to him: “Grant us seven days, so that we may send messengers throughout all the territories of Israel; and if there is no one to defend us, we shall come out to you” (1 Samuel 11).

When Saul heard this, he gathered a multitude of troops, seized weapons, and, after striking down the Ammonites with a very great slaughter, triumphed gloriously.

What, then, do we understand by Naas the Ammonite—that is, the proud king—except either the world rebelling against its Creator or the devil, its prince? Of him it is said: “He is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41). And because *Naas* is interpreted as “serpent,” the poisonous and slippery snake is rightly represented by him.

What, moreover, is suggested by Jabesh, which was an Israelite city, except the Christian soul intent upon seeing God through the practice of contemplation? And because *Jabesh* is interpreted as “dried up” or “dryness,” that soul is suitably understood through Jabesh which abandons the richness of heavenly grace and withers in the heat of carnal desire. For when it withdraws from longing for the dew of the divine gift, it becomes dry, although previously, while receiving that dew, it flourished healthily, watered by it, as the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will pour water upon the thirsty and streams upon the dry ground” (Isaiah 44).

But Naas refuses to make a covenant with Jabesh unless it agrees that its right eye be torn out, because whoever submits either to the ancient enemy’s perverse suggestion or becomes entangled in the restless activities of this world, when he shamefully makes a covenant with it as with a proud king, must lose his right eye—that is, the light of contemplation.

Thus he is made a reproach in Israel: for when he descends from the stronghold of contemplation to perform earthly or any filthy tasks, it follows that in the Church he is bitten by the reproaches of disgraceful ridicule.

They ask for seven days’ respite. Since God is read to have rested on the seventh day from the works he had made (Genesis 2), what is signified by the number seven except rest? The disobedient Saul did not understand this number when Samuel ordered him to await him: “For seven days,” he said, “you shall wait until I come to you and show you what you must do” (1 Samuel 10). But because the reprobate man despised spiritual rest, an evil spirit seized him to torment him.

Thus, through the number of seven days, the city of Jabesh is liberated from the wicked king. For any soul whom the world, at the devil’s urging, attempts to draw to itself and blind with the darkness of worldly affairs preserves its eye of contemplation unharmed if, resisting completely, it perseveres in its resolve of quiet. Our Redeemer rescues it from the temptation it suffers when he finds it resting within the discipline of its withdrawal.

Hence it is written there: “When the next day had come,” it says, “Saul divided the people into three companies, and entered the middle of the camp during the morning watch, and struck down Ammon until the day grew hot” (1 Samuel 11).

What, then, is signified by Saul, who was called the Lord’s anointed, except the one who is the true king of Israel, the mediator between God and human beings? What does it mean that he divided the people into three companies except that there are three principal virtues of the soul, namely faith, hope, and charity?

Victory is therefore obtained in the threefold divisions of the warriors, because every demonic temptation is conquered by these three virtues, with Christ as leader.

Nor is the number of the warriors proclaimed by Scripture without its own mystery. “There were,” it says, “three hundred thousand of the children of Israel, and thirty thousand men of Judah” (1 Samuel 11). Since the thousand and the ten are perfect numbers, they signify the perfection of the saints; while three hundred and thirty, which arise from three, signify the divine Trinity.

What, then, are signified by the three hundred thousand or thirty thousand warriors except the holy teachers of the Church, who are orthodox in faith and perfected in works of religion? With these, therefore, Saul overcomes the hostile forces of King Naas, because Christ, together with the teachers of his Church, triumphs over the crafty machinations of the aged serpent.

For when their teachings or examples are carefully considered, immediately the torpid hearts which a harmful sluggishness had already invaded grow warm again, and the spirit is kindled, as though with a drawn sword, to cut down the ranks of the vices that attack us.

Hence those very warriors of Israel and Judah say to the messengers who had come to them: “Thus shall you say to the men who are in Jabesh-gilead: Tomorrow you shall have salvation, when the sun has grown hot” (ibid.).

For when the mind, at first weakened by sloth, has returned to itself and grows warm again with desire for its Creator; when it abandons the torpor of negligence and the flame of holy love kindles the former coldness of insensibility, then, as the sun grows hot, victory is taken from the enemies and the besieged city is freed from the hands of the proud king.

Hence it is written of Abraham: “The Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre in the very heat of the day” (Genesis 18). Hence it is said of Lot: “The sun rose over the earth, and Lot entered Segor” (Genesis 19).

Rightly, therefore, do we reject friendship either with the world or with its prince, and refuse to have any covenant of fellowship with them, lest, while we join ourselves to darkness, we be deprived of light.

It should also be noted that the wicked king does not demand that both eyes of his enemies be torn out, but only one, so that he may make them a reproach in Israel. For the evil enemy often takes away from any reprobate person who consents to him the better part of holiness and of shining work, while leaving the lesser part behind through a certain artful device of his cunning.

Thus, in what is taken away, there may be an occasion of condemnation by which he perishes; while, in what remains, he may presume upon a confidence of hope, so that the sinner does not return to repentance. Instead, relying like a transgressor upon the remnants of his lost holiness as upon a staff, he is torn by infamy among those who know that he has fallen. Thus the loss of pious work becomes a deserved reproach of ridicule.

Something similar also happened to David’s messengers when, after the death of that same Naas, his son succeeded him in obtaining the royal sceptre. He said: “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Naas, as his father showed kindness to me” (2 Samuel 10). David therefore sent servants to console him over his father’s death. To compress the account into a brief narrative, Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved off half of their beards, cut their garments in half up to their buttocks, and dismissed them.

What is signified by Hanun except the spirit of wickedness? What by the beard, which is proper to men, except the strength of holy virtues? And what by the garments except the clothing of holiness? As the Psalmist testifies: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131).

Hanun therefore shaves away half the beard of those seeking a covenant of friendship, because the ancient enemy sometimes diminishes the strength of one who is acting courageously. But after shaving the beard, he also cuts the garments, because as soon as the evil spirit takes away the inner strength, it consequently strips away the outward dignity of conspicuous conduct.

For what does it mean to cut men’s garments up to their buttocks except to strip them, from the covering of righteousness placed over them, down to the disgrace of obscene and shameless conduct?

Let Andreas hear this—he who recently departed from the fellowship of your holiness, entered into a covenant of friendship with the king of the Ammonites, and now runs about within the walls of Rome, as though shaven of beard and mutilated in clothing, not without bringing shame upon David.

Let those also hear it who perhaps still desire to go out into public, lest, while they eagerly long to gaze freely upon empty things, they extinguish their right eye—that is, the power of inward contemplation.

Nor should their appetite itch after those things of carnal Israel—leeks, onions, and garlic (Numbers 11)—whose intense bitterness troubles the eyes and provokes tears. For worldly activity, while surrounded by many narrow pressures and harassed by the repeated disturbance of hardships that descend upon it, often compels those whom it promised joy to weep.

Certainly, if the exercise of labour is pleasing, holy rest has its own labour. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Go and say to them, ‘Return to your tents’; but you, stand here with me, and I will speak to you all the commandments, ceremonies, and judgments” (Deuteronomy 5).

While the others rest with pleasure in the tent of their flesh, the servant of God is not ordered to sit but to stand with the Lord, so that, the farther he withdraws from the labours of the world, the more vigilantly the ardour of holy rest may exercise him in divine service.

But now I return to myself and prostrate myself at the feet of your holiness, so that, just as you unanimously promised me orally, you may extend to me, plunged into the yawning abyss of sins, the arm of diligent prayer.

For although I could not dwell with you, I nevertheless secured tranquillity for your dwelling. The Gileadite Barzillai, descending from Rogelim, supplied David with provisions while he was fleeing from the face of Absalom (2 Samuel 17). When the king, after victory had been accomplished, invited him to cross over with him to Jerusalem in order to rest there, he refused to consent, but entrusted his son to him in his place:

“I beg you,” he said, “to let your servant return, that I may die in my own city and be buried beside the tomb of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham: let him go with you, my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you” (2 Samuel 19).

I too am not unlike Barzillai in this example. I came to your aid in the persecution of the enemy, but, once God had granted the triumph, I returned to my own place, saying to the Cluniacensians what Paul said to the Colossians: “For although I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Colossians 2).

As he therefore handed over his son to the king, so I hand over my own soul to your hands, and I implore you to nourish it at the table of your prayer.

Indeed, since the divine law commands that good be returned for evil, how much more does it command that good be rendered for good? What wonder is it if human reason fulfils this under the law imposed upon it, when even irrational animals, subject to no laws, sometimes fulfil the same thing?

For, as I have learned through a brother’s report, certain Venetian merchants were cutting through the dangers of the sea by the labour of rowing. When they had come ashore, they saw not far from the sand of the shore a frightening and astonishing portent: a lion, apparently wrapped in the intertwining coils of a huge dragon.

When the dragon was violently dragging its captured prey toward its cave, while the wretched lion resisted with whatever strength it possessed, at last, as the lion began to weaken through its desperate struggle, the dragon, binding it with ever more inextricable knots, became increasingly confident of securing victory.

But the innkeepers, who had suddenly come upon this spectacle, took pity on the lion’s unhappy condition, boldly seized their weapons, killed the dragon, and allowed the lion, rescued from the jaws of death, to depart.

But the lion—so to speak, the noblest of beasts (Proverbs 30)—proved grateful to the authors of its life. For the several days during which they remained there, it brought them each day a single skin of the animal it had captured.

What wonder, then, if holy men, instructed in divine laws, respond with grateful reciprocity after receiving an act of charity, when even an irrational animal appears to have fulfilled the same duty?

And perhaps this example may suitably apply to you in a certain respect. You are signified by the lion, not without reason, because you sleep away from the world in such a way that you always keep watchful eyes upon God, singing with the bride: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5).

You tread upon the asp and basilisk and trample the lion and the dragon (Psalm 10); finally, you trust like a lion without fear and are not afraid to meet the wickedness that opposes you (Proverbs 30).

Michal placed a skin at the head of David, by which he escaped the swords of King Saul (1 Samuel 18). Almighty God also clothed our first parents in tunics of skin (Genesis 3), by which, once they had become mortal, he marked them as required by the guilt of transgression.

You, therefore, having been freed by me from the dragon’s coils, return a skin in payment for the benefit and obtain for me, through your prayers, a life-giving mortification, so that the world may no longer live for me; but if anything of it still remains for me, may it advance toward the gain of eternal salvation.

Although the Apostle says, “Without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the better” (Hebrews 7), nevertheless, because charity compels me, I cannot refrain from blessing you.

May almighty God protect you from all the assaults of the wicked Satan and cleanse you from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Amen.

May he extinguish in you the companions of seething vices and make you flourish with the beauty of budding virtues. Amen.

Through the intercession of his apostles Peter and Paul, may he absolve you from all sins and make you fellow citizens with himself of his elect, who reign without end. Amen.

May the blessing of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit descend upon you and remain with you. Amen.

EPISTLE VI. TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF POMPOSA.

SUMMARY.—He sends some gift, I know not what, to the monks of the monastery of Pomposa and declares his goodwill toward them. He also begs them to remember him after his death by offering prayers for him, as they were accustomed to do for their own monks.

To all the most religious and holy men who serve God at Pomposa, PETER offers the service of most devoted submission.

Most beloved fathers and lords, I do not wish to write how my heart burns with the fire of your charity, or with what torches of love it is inflamed toward the monastery of Pomposa, lest perhaps I seem to be serving flattery. My own conscience is witness to this; nor is it wholly hidden from those who can often converse with me. You also, beloved, although I am separated from you in bodily dwelling, must not judge me to be a stranger. Do not reckon me merely some friend or whatever kind of companion; rather, recognize without doubt both us and our whole community as a possession belonging to you by your own right, and command without any hesitation whatever may please you, as though we were your subjects and household members.

Therefore, beloved, I beseech you tearfully and, prostrate, cast myself at your holy feet: deign always to pray for me, your servant; and especially when I have died, strive to do for me, miserable man that I am, whatever you do for a monk of your community. I ask, moreover, my lords, that you kindly receive the small blessing from the hand of your servant [or some similar addition], and consider not what it is, but from whom; not how much, but from how much it is offered.

EPISTLE VII. TO ABBOT ALTIZO.

SUMMARY.—He writes to Abbot Altizo that he is deeply distressed because he did not immediately give him a horse when he needed one, and generously offers himself, the horses, and all the goods of the monastery to him.

To Lord A., his lord, PETER, a sinful monk, whatever a servant may offer.

Dearest one, it seems better to me to have no charity than to feign it; and I think it more tolerable for anyone to lack charity than to pretend to possess its fullness. For where charity is absent, it can be born through divine grace; but where it is feigned, the more it lies about truth beneath the colour of pretence, the more it is either never, or only with greater difficulty, corrected. Let, therefore, your most sweet holiness know that I have greatly repented because, when I heard you complain of a lack of horses, I did not at once dismount from my own horse, did not voluntarily offer both, and did not compel you, willing or unwilling, to accept them.

But amid this I also consider, not without reason, that already for a long time my heart has been consumed by so great a fire of repentance for this fault, and, with sighing and the gnawing of conscience as by a worm, laments most grievously that it did not fulfil the office of charity. What will he do after passing from this life who will lament that the time for bestowing charity has elapsed, yet will be unable to amend his negligence because he has lost the acceptable time and the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6)? For if it seems so grievous and bitter to our mind to have sinned here, where we can still correct sins, what must be done there, where no one will be able to amend his guilt?

But enough of this for another time. Now, dearest one, if you have found a horse, thanks be to God; otherwise, if you still lack one, send to us, with your letter, a monk who may carefully inspect all our horses and mules and take whichever one pleases him. We also have an excellent cloak; have it brought to you by the same messenger and put it up as a pledge, and procure another horse for yourself. For it is not fitting that we who serve God in the spirit should defile our souls with the gifts of wicked men because of a lack of temporal goods. And if, in order that you may not believe what we say to be feigned, you have none from elsewhere, yet do not accept what we gladly offer, you take away the confidence by which we ought also to presume concerning you without any doubt. Far be it that earthly substance should be divided from one with whom my mind is one, or that I should deny any outward thing to him for whom I would not hesitate, and rightly so, even to die should necessity arise. I ask that this little letter not perish, but be copied into some book, so that the memory of my devotion toward you may be preserved.

EPISTLE VIII. TO ABBOT B.

(It is found in volume III and is treatise 21.)

EPISTLE IX. TO ABBOT GEBIZO.

SUMMARY.—He charges the monk Gebizo with pride, because he had abandoned the care of the hermits entrusted to him by the holy doctor in order to preside over another monastery recently built by his brother, evidently seeking to be called the founder of monks. He exposes his feigned humility and shows the gravity of the offence. Finally, he commands him either to resume the government of the hermitage which he laid down or to live in a monastery under another’s discipline.

To Brother GEBIZO, PETER, a sinful monk, greeting.

Brother, what you are doing seems a prodigy and a portent; the road upon which you now enter as a new traveller is impassable. Ordered by me—indeed, asked—and chosen without distinction by the brethren, you accepted the government of the hermitage; but afterwards, like one sick and weak, asserting yourself unequal to such great labours, you cast off the burden of the office laid upon you. Yet now, made a superior elsewhere, you plainly show that you disdain to hold office under another’s authority, lest you beget offspring under another’s name and, while striving to extend the name of your own household, refuse to raise up seed to your dead brother. You imitate, that is, Onan, Judah’s son, who, according to the sequence of the sacred history, when he went in to his brother’s wife spilled his seed upon the ground, lest children be born in his brother’s name (Genesis 38). But observe what follows: “Therefore,” it says, “the Lord struck him, because he did a detestable thing.”

You shrink from and disdain that those who belong to Gebizo should be called Peter’s disciples; and, because you seek singular glory, you are ashamed, despising others, to share the renown of your name with another. Indeed, the sacred canons provide (canon *Requisisti*, 33, question 1) that whoever, being impotent, cannot have intercourse with his wife must not reject her by divorce and pass on to second marriages. For it was a pretence that he could not lie with the first if he can join himself to the second. You likewise, if you are sufficient there to govern a community, could have done so here also; but though you could have governed this one, you transferred yourself, by an adulterous flight, to the government of another community. Therefore you ought not to hold the one which you have, since, having scorned your lawful wife, you cling in union to a harlot; especially since canonical authority further decrees (text in chapter *Quanto*, On the Translation of a Bishop) that whoever transfers from one church to another shall also lack the one he despised and in no way retain the one he newly acquired.

Clearly you seek to acquire the private name of your own glory and disdain to beget offspring for another’s name. So too the man to whom, by right of kinship, it belonged to take Ruth as wife said to Boaz: “I yield to you the right of kinship” (Ruth 4), for I ought not to destroy the posterity of my family. That vain and glory-seeking man tried to extend his family’s posterity for his own name; but Boaz, a good and just man, making little of the renown of his own name, was content merely to keep the commandments of the divine law. Yet behold: the name of the one who longed to leave a memorial of himself to posterity is not even known; while the other is numbered with glory not only in the catalogue of the fathers but of the patriarchs. The former lost the renown of the posterity for which he provided; the latter received the paternal name which he had disregarded for observance of the sacred law. The former is not known to be the parent even of any human beings; the latter became the brother of most mighty kings. While the former desired a memorial in posterity, he fell from remembrance; the latter, who did not provide for the propagation of his line under his own name, begot, through the succession of David’s stock, the Saviour of the whole world.

Cease, brother, cease arrogantly to lift up the neck of your heart and so openly exalt yourself upon the horns of pride. For once pride has fixed its root in anyone’s heart, although it may at times be coloured with certain thin plates of imposed humility, it is nevertheless never restrained on every side from issuing forth, even slightly, and secretly breaking out.

Remember, brother, that when you recently sat with the brethren in chapter, you burst out, as though asking counsel, with these words: “Father, is there a reward if we give assistance by building a monastery?” And you said this not in order to untie a knot of rushes in which you were entangled, but in order to open a way for the words that followed. For who does not know this, unless he is wholly ignorant of the practice of piety? But so that what was bubbling up might flow out, you immediately added: “For my brother has recently caused the monastery of Saint Lawrence, built by him, to be dedicated, and generously offered twelve cloaks there.” What concern was it of ours, in so fearsome a place, either to hear what your brother had offered or to calculate the amount of the offering, except only that you might appear high-born and eminent in your brother, and your brother wealthy and liberal in his gift?

The same coinage was also evident in what you shortly afterward contrived to add: “My brother so-and-so married Vassus’s only daughter”; and immediately you added: “only daughter,” I say—for that Vassus had no other offspring—so that, unless shame had flushed your face and you feared being exposed, you would consequently have added, had you given vent to the thought that was rising in your mind: “For he would not have joined her to himself by the right of dowry if he had co-heirs in his parents’ succession.” You did not express this in words, but you carefully left it clear to us, so that we might understand it implicitly. Whatever a person utters through the organ of his speech, God, the searcher of the reins (Ps. VII), considers only the secrets of the mind; and in the ears of the hidden Judge it is not so much the noise of the voice as the cry of the heart that resounds.

Hence it is said through the Prophet: “Your ear has heard the desires of their heart” (Ps. IX). Hence Daniel says of the proud king Nebuchadnezzar: “And the king, answering, said: ‘Is this not great Babylon, which I built as a royal residence by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?’” (Dan. IV). To whom, I ask, did this boastful and arrogant man reply in the words of his expressed pride, except to the swelling thought that had already been shouting within his mind? For that spirit of perdition, of whom it is recorded that he said, “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV), did not utter these things with his lips—for he is not clothed in flesh—but burst forth as a tyrant into sacrilegious thought.

If, then, that exalted angel perished irrecoverably for this reason—not because he uttered or did anything wicked against the Author of the universe, but solely because he swelled up through the evil of his thought—what benefit is it to us to cast ourselves down outwardly in garment or word as though humble, while inwardly we arrogantly exalt ourselves above others through the titles of our forefathers or through the conceit of singular wisdom? We strive to speak humbly and to appear humble. Let the root of pride planted in the heart be torn out, and at once, even if our own effort is lacking, humility will also be visible in our speech.

But when liquid turns sour in the vessel, no one can draw sweet wine from the cup. Who can make flour from bran? Who can fashion the brightness of silver from a vein of iron? Indeed, to return to the Gospel example: “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” (Matt. VII). “For,” as it continues there, “a bad tree cannot produce good fruit” (ibid.). The tree, certainly, is to be understood as the will, not the person. For the same human person can perform both good and evil, just as from the same earth both a fig and a thorn are produced. But just as a bad tree never produces good fruit, so from a proud will—which is unquestionably bad—pure and uncontaminated humility never proceeds.

And just as, when the root is damaged, the branches of the whole tree consequently wither, so, if some good work is seen to flourish for a time from a proud mind, it dries up like a valley drained of its moisture amid the aridity of a precipitous rock. “But the seventy-two returned,” as the Evangelist Luke testifies, “with joy, saying: ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name’” (Luke X). What did he who attends to the secrets of the heart answer them? “I was watching,” he said, “Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (ibid.). As though he were saying: “Take care, lest, while the spirit of wickedness is subjected to your authority, your minds be crushed beneath the yoke of elation.” For if Satan lost the heaven that he possessed through pride, a proud human being will certainly never be able to find what he hopes for.

Certainly, when Joab was vigorously fighting against the Ammonite king Rabbah and was enclosing the royal city with a siege, he arranged for messengers to go to David and invited him to come and transfer the victory to his own name: “I have fought,” he said, “against Rabbah, and the City of Waters is about to be taken. Now, therefore, gather the rest of the people, besiege the city, and capture it, lest, when the city has been devastated by me, the victory be attributed to my name” (2 Kings XII). A military man gladly transfers the victory of his labor to his king’s renown; and does a servant of God, in governing the brethren, disdain to render this service to his superior?

Herod and Philip gave cities constructed by their own labor the name “Caesarea,” one in honor of Augustus and the other of Tiberius (Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book I, chapter 10, and *Antiquities*, book XVIII, chapter 3). And we, who have cast away the pomp of this life—indeed, who have sworn that we would be dead to the world—covet little glories of an empty name and are inflamed by mere twigs of frivolous praise.

Take care, brother, lest your mind bear heavily what we say, lest, pulverized beneath the hammer of correction, it burst apart; and lest, through this very reaction, it become even clearer that you are what is being reproved. Pride makes the human mind like glass, so that through impatience it cannot endure the blow of correction. Glass is so called because vision penetrates it; and therefore, if it possessed the strength of solidity, it could surpass other metals. But because it breaks more quickly, it is valued at a low price.

Thus one who is shattered by the blows of correction through impatience demonstrates that he does not possess strength’s solidity, even if he excels in other virtues. Hence the Lord says through the Prophet concerning the proud people of Israel, afflicted with the disease of impatience: “The house of Israel has become dross to me” (Ezek. XXII). Dross, plainly, is the refuse of any metal; when struck by a pounding hammer, it is immediately crushed into dust. Therefore, let your mind not turn itself into dross before the Lord, but endure with equanimity the blows of friendly reproof.

To conclude the letter with a pronouncement of judgment: either restore yourself to the office of prior that you rejected, or, content with your own salvation, live as a monk under the former prior, so that either the labor of a chaste priorate may make you fruitful through the legitimate education of spiritual sons, or the abasement of true humility may exalt you before the eyes of the Redeemer who was humbled for you.

## LETTER X. TO GEBIZO, THEOBALD, AND JOHN, ABBOTS

**Summary.**—The humble teacher instructs his disciples to correct what he had falsely said about the day of Saint John the Baptist’s conception, or whatever errors they may find in his other little works.

To the holy abbots Gebizo and Theobald, and also to John of Lodi (Laudensis), indeed a praiseworthy brother in Christ, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the service of a servant.

Let your holy charity know, most beloved, that yesterday, when I was overcome by midday sleep, it seemed to me that, being aboard a ship, I held in my hands part of a book that I myself had dictated, and that I feared the assault of a raging storm no less than I feared for those pages themselves. And when, utterly stunned and gripped by the terror of impending danger, my entrails shaken with fear, I dreaded the shipwreck of the threatening waves, suddenly the surge of the waters swelled violently and submerged both me, holding the book in my hand, and the very vessel in which I then was.

When I awoke, I began to reflect and diligently turn over in my mind what mystery the event contained and, finally, what this vision signified. Today, as I was carefully meditating upon it, that letter came to mind,

*[Note: Column 0391D: Letter 16 of Book IV.]*

in which I had spoken about the eight festivals of the Old Testament and the birth of Blessed John the Baptist; and immediately, like an inundation of sea waves, an abyss of sudden grief swallowed me. There I discovered, I confess, that I had erred, had spoken foolishly, and had plainly departed from the rule of sound understanding.

For I had said that Blessed John was conceived on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, which is evidently the most celebrated of its days. But when this is weighed with careful consideration, it is found to be discordant with the truth. The day of Blessed John’s conception, which is the eighth day from the Kalends of October—that is, the third day after the eighth day of the Feast of Tabernacles—is therefore unquestionably shown to have no connection with that festival. Since, then, the Feast of Tabernacles ends on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, while Saint John’s conception occurs on the eighth day of the same month, it is perfectly clear that blessed John was conceived from the embrace of an aged couple well beyond the limits of the Feast of Tabernacles.

Behold: what I did wrong by writing carelessly, with God mercifully calling me back to repentance, I have corrected. Now, therefore, most beloved, I impose upon your holy prudence this work of obedience—or rather, as a servant and disciple, I humbly beg you—to bring this letter into conformity with the form in which it has been corrected among us, and, carefully reading through the other little works of my dictation, to hasten either to cut out entirely whatever may be found absurd or to arrange it in a more polished style.

For we must not fear that, if the hand of a corrector is applied, the writing will lose the beauty of its native elegance. Rather, we must strive for this: that, while no indulgence is shown to the urbanity of the running pen, the rule of sober understanding may be preserved inviolate. Since “every word shall stand upon the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XIX), I entrust this work of examination by my voice to you three, whom I know to possess spiritual prudence (Gal. VI), so that, if anything still remains in those little works that strays from the path of truth, it may through you be brought back to the rule of rectitude, and so that, through the diligence of your examination, the book may grow strong for a complete edition and the authority of being read.

## LETTER XI. TO JOHN OF LODI (LAUDENSIS), HIS DISCIPLE

(It is found in volume III and is little work 44.)

## LETTER XII. TO ABBOT J.

**Summary.**—He defends himself against the attack of a certain abbot who had complained that he had received a monk who had left his monastery, contrary to the rule of Saint Benedict. He therefore demonstrates that Saint Benedict does not prohibit a monk from passing from a monastery to the hermitage, but rather that he permits one who has left one cenobium to be received in another; indeed, he proves that Benedict strongly commends the eremitical life as more perfect and recommends it to monks—if any are capable of it.

To the lord J., venerable abbot, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of the sincerest charity.

We have received, revered Father, the letter of your Holiness with the devotion it deserves, and we answer it briefly, as the matter requires. For you are angry and accuse us in your complaint, saying that we ought not to have received your monks in the hermitage, contrary to the commands of our Blessed Father Benedict (Rule, chapter 16), since he decrees that those coming from a known monastery are not to be granted access to a dwelling among strangers.

With your permission, we shall easily repel the obstacle of this accusation, because that holy man established monasteries according to the commands of his teaching, but claimed no authority over hermits. For after enumerating four kinds of monks, he immediately added (Rule, chapter 1): “Having omitted these, let us proceed, with the help of God, to establish the most valiant kind, that of the cenobites.” Since, then, he devoted himself to organizing only the kind of cenobites, it is plainly evident that he did not apply his institution to hermits.

But let us set down the blessed man’s own words here, and clearly discern whether he wrote for cenobites or for hermits (ibid., chapter 61): “Let the abbot,” he says, “take care never to receive a monk from a known monastery to live there without the consent of his abbot.” Since he addresses the abbot of a monastery, not the prior of a hermitage, he evidently shows that whatever he wrote he enjoined not upon hermits but rather upon cenobites, so that they might follow it.

Moreover, since we have already plainly demonstrated that Saint Benedict did not prohibit the reception of another’s monk in the hermitage, let us now show how he even encouraged this to happen—that is, how he urged a monk to hasten from a monastery to the hermitage. These words, then, are not ours but those of our same Father (Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 1):

“The second kind,” he says, “is that of anchorites, that is, hermits. These are no longer moved by the first fervor of their conversion, but have learned through long testing in the monastery how to fight against the devil. They have been well taught by the support of many and, well trained in the fraternal battle line, are now sufficiently strong to fight alone, without another’s consolation, against the vices of the flesh or of their thoughts, with God’s help, by their own hand or arm.”

From these words it is certainly and plainly gathered that the gracious teacher not only did not prohibit any brother from ascending from the monastery to the hermitage, but even advised, taught, and encouraged some to do so. For he gives authority for a brother first to learn in the monastery, through long testing, how to fight in the hermitage against the stratagems of the crafty tempter. Here he begins the fight relying upon the support of many, so that there, afterward, exercising himself tirelessly and unceasingly by his own hand or arm, he may not succumb to the vices or thoughts of the flesh that assail him.

Here he is a recruit; there, a soldier. Here he is inexperienced and tender, becoming accustomed to combat under a trainer in the field; there, strengthened, he fights at close quarters and, as a monk of Christ, does not refuse the solitary contest. Here, as if in the preliminary exercise of a simulated battle; there, his trained hand brings weapons to the fighting and does not fear the packed assaults of warriors. There a man coming from the world enters as though he were the little city of Zoar, departing from Sodom; but when he passes to the hermitage, he ascends the mountains with that same Lot (Gen. XIX).

For one striving toward the summit of perfection, the monastery is said to be a passage, not a sojourn or dwelling, but a lodging; not the end of his purpose, but a certain rest along the journey. A person is marked out as suitable for this so that priestly election may advance him to the ecclesiastical order; he enters the schools of grammarians for this purpose, so that, once perfected in the discipline, he may depart; someone studies the knowledge of the laws for this purpose, so that he may be able to plead legal disputes eloquently before the tribunals of judges.

Just as these people do not fix the purpose of their minds upon the activity they are undertaking, but undoubtedly strive toward another end, so, indeed, so must a monk—unless age or illness weighs him down—both live bodily in the monastery and yearn from the depths of his being for the hermitage with his whole desire, so that there he may cling by the intention of his mind, rooted like a noble tree; while here, for a time, he exercises himself under the discipline of regular obedience. Thus the life of the monastery should be nothing other than preparation for the hermitage, and he should serve wholly toward the higher purpose for which, having first been established in the monastery, he trains himself.

Thus Jacob intended the fourteen years during which he served Laban in the manner of a shepherd solely to earn the union with Rachel. He had indeed already received Leah by marital right, but through the desire of his inmost love he rested in the embraces of beautiful Rachel (Gen. XXIX).

In those words of the holy rule that we quoted above, it is plainly declared that Saint Benedict, when he places a man in the monastery, directs him toward the hermitage. Here he establishes him, but there he urges and invites him. Here he teaches him to begin the spiritual contest; there, to complete it. Here he admonishes the recruit to seize his weapons, so that there he may know how to cut down without weakness the battle lines of his enemies and the barbarity of vices.

But perhaps it may be said that we forcibly bend the holy man’s words to suit our own will and rely more upon arguments than upon truth supporting us in this interpretation of the words. Let us question the most blessed man further, so that what he thinks concerning this point of dispute may shine forth more clearly. Those words of his that we quoted above are found at the very beginning of the holy rule. Let us now see with what conclusion he ends that same rule:

“We have written this rule,” he says, “so that, by observing it in monasteries, we may show that we possess to some extent a beginning of a good way of life or of moral conduct. But for those who hasten toward the perfection of the way of life, there are the teachings of the holy Fathers, the observance of which leads a person to the height of perfection.”

You see, then, that the distinguished teacher establishes in the monastery the beginning of a good way of life, but afterward calls the person onward to the institution of a more exalted life in holy religion: so that there he may begin to live honorably and order his conduct, as though in the valley of an initial way of life; then, strengthened by spiritual exercises and passing from milk to solid food, he may ascend to the summit of perfection.

An animal is conceived in its mother’s womb so that it may emerge. And certainly the mother must miscarry unless the fetus grows to its full development. Yet we want the womb always to swell, and what has once been conceived never to emerge. He is a child of poor nature whose teeth do not emerge from his gums even when he has grown older, and whose knees do not grow strong enough for walking.

Moreover, since the rule of the cenobites itself acknowledges that it does not possess perfection, but plainly sends anyone who wishes to be perfected on to the institutions of the hermitage, why do we regard it as worthless for us ourselves to climb to the summit of perfection, and why do we continually envy others lest they advance to better things?

When John saw Jesus walking, he cried out: “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John I). Immediately the Evangelist adds: “And two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus” (ibid.). What complaint, I ask, could John have had when he himself plainly placed Jesus before them, and they followed the one who was unquestionably superior?

If, then, the rule that presides over them sends those who flock to it on toward the hermitage, with what recklessness, with what presumption, can one who is subject to the rule resist? It is now clearer than daylight that whoever forbids those seeking the hermitage is unquestionably attacking the rule itself as a rebellious detractor; and, while stripping the words of the rule of authority, condemns the author of the holy rule itself.

A true mother hands over her son so that he may live; a false one asks that a public sword divide him (1 Kings III). The eighty-year-old Barzillai, so that he might provide for the needs of his son Chimham [Channa is printed in the source], does not care to support him with the burden of his own bent old age; provided that the son remains familiarly attached to King David, he himself does not refuse to be deprived of his support (2 Kings X).

Let Antony allow Hilarion to depart, so that Hilarion may ascend alone to higher things. We, however, love monks like asses, or at least like slaves. People love these animals not for their sake but for their own, either to turn them into their own flesh or to enjoy their help in labor. People love them so that they themselves may be well, while the animals either may not exist or may exist in misery.

We too, merely to enjoy the obedience of monks, entirely disregard their progress in salvation. Furthermore, we know that Blessed Benedict was a cultivator of the hermitage, and certainly did not desire to be what he was. But since, as he himself testifies (4 Kings XL), each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that, and not all receive this word, he providentially established first the level ground of monastic life, so that there, worn down by the lashes of discipline and tempered and strengthened by exercises, we might more easily ascend to the summit of the hermitage.

In this, Benedict did what blessed Paul had also done. For the Apostle was unmarried, yet he nevertheless encouraged people to marry: “Let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband; let the husband render the debt owed to his wife, and the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. VII). Shortly afterward, however, he says: “I want all people to be as I myself am” (ibid.).

The Apostle wanted one thing and commanded another. He wanted us to be celibate as he was, because of the outstanding merit of flourishing chastity; but he wanted us to marry because he feared the danger of our weakness. By wishing me to be like himself, he urges me to ascend; by offering marital union, he holds me up and sustains me so that I do not fall. He ardently desires the former on his own initiative; he grants the latter reluctantly. For he would rather I be what he is than what I am not. Yet he chose that I remain near him in either condition rather than be entirely distant as a stranger.

Thus, just as Blessed Paul prefers celibacy to monogamy or digamy, but nevertheless grants wives lest the weak fall into concubinage, so Blessed Benedict, although he more earnestly wishes us to be what he was—that is, followers of the hermitage—nevertheless considers it more tolerable for us, weak and feeble, to live even ignobly in the harbor of the monastery than to perish in the stormy abyss of the world’s shipwreck.

Brothers who remain immovably in the monastery are therefore to be tolerated; those who migrate to the hermitage with fervent spirit are to be exalted with applause and praise. The former hide beneath the shield of divine protection; the latter, advancing into the field of battle, are adorned with the titles of victory. The former defend their own possessions; the latter bring back spoils. The former, protected by God, are unconquerable; the latter daily strive to trample the necks of their enemies.

The former, stationed before the walls and besieging them, prevent the enemy from entering; the latter drive away the threatening battle lines of their enemies, turning them back far from their own boundaries.

And why should I say more? The former, certainly, are removed from the world; the latter already converse inwardly with God, joined to him by intimate charity. The former guard the bronze altar; the latter already enter the Holy of Holies.

To append an epilogue at the end of this letter: since we are accused of having received monks from a known monastery, it is clearer than daylight that we have in no way offended Saint Benedict in this matter. For just as, being established in the hermitage, he imposed nothing upon us that we were to carry out, so he prohibited absolutely nothing that we were to avoid.

As we have sufficiently and more than sufficiently taught above, the distinguished teacher not only did not reject the passage of a brother from the monastery to the hermitage, but even suggests, encourages, and urges it. To show clearly how great a force of desire this possessed for him, he placed it at the beginning of his rule and concluded the written work with it at the end. That holy book begins from this point and ends with this subject by a rhetorical crescendo, so that it seems in a certain way to command the very thing throughout its entire text.

Moreover, since this is a rule for beginners, so that, by making the hearer attentive, it may commend what is to be written, he not only diminishes and lowers the value of his entire work at the very beginning of the opening rule, but does so also at the end, making the order of the cenobites equal to the eremitical life.

Therefore, we ought both to encourage brothers to ascend from monastic life to the hermitage and, with charity, to receive them, so that they may not seem to depart from the blessed man as enemies through a schismatic rejection—which God forbid—but may appear, as true disciples, to agree unanimously with him.

## LETTER XIII. TO M., ABBOT OF THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY

**Summary.**—In this letter he strongly commends the Latin monks who lived in the monastery of Saint Mary at Constantinople because in those regions they maintained the right path of faith and life. Concerning the question about which they had consulted him, he says that he had fully satisfied them through their messenger, who was to carry this letter.

To the lord M., venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary in Constantinople, and to the rest of the brothers, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

We rejoice, most beloved brothers, because, although you live among foreign peoples and in a region of an alien language, you have not, as we have learned through widespread report, been exiled from the Catholic Faith or from pious works. Thus, citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, you do not depart from your own home, since, established within the bosom of Holy Church, you hasten abroad along the path of an upright way of life.

In whatever region of the earth one may be, the court of heaven is equally open. And where the merit of right faith and holy conduct is the same, no difference or variety of languages causes prejudice. Wherever God’s servant may dwell, he must cut off from himself worldly and carnal acts and, having been put to death to this age, walk always with tireless steps along the straight path of holy works.

Hence it is that the hands and feet of King Adoni-bezek are cut off (Judg. I), so that this clearly signifies that the steps and actions of worldly life must be cut away from us. Adoni-bezek is interpreted as “lord of lightning.” Through him, what else is understood but the devil? He is the lord of lightning, the author alike of impulse and fury; whereas, conversely, our Lord is called through the Prophet “Father of the coming age, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX).

This Adoni-bezek, as Scripture testifies, said: “Seventy kings, with the tips of their hands and feet cut off, gathered the scraps of food beneath my table. As I did to others, so the Lord has repaid me” (Judg. I). What, then, do we understand by the seventy kings except the nations of the seventy languages? The evil spirit had cut off the tips of their hands and feet, because he allowed no nation either to perform any good work or to walk along the path of justice.

But from this Adoni-bezek, the enemy of the human race, our Redeemer cut off the tips of both hands and feet when he restrained his wicked deeds and steps among his chosen ones.

Therefore, most beloved, do not permit this tyrant to preside over you, whom you do not doubt has been cut down by the sword of the divine sentence. Conceive in your minds the force of heavenly desire; burn with kindled hearts for the glory of the heavenly kingdom; carefully suppress the incentives of carnal allurements; hasten always toward God by the path of a singular life and in the footsteps of the holy Fathers, so that, while you strive to hold to the path of justice, you may reach the very author of justice and of all holiness.

May Almighty God, most beloved brothers, snatch you from the hands of the ancient enemy, make you citizens instead of strangers, and lead you within the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem, where there is no diversity of languages or of wills.

Concerning the question about which you decided to consult us, carefully question this brother Peter, your messenger, and observe whatever he may tell you in person.

## LETTER XIV. TO MAINARD, ABBOT

(It is found in volume III and is little work 29.)

## LETTER XV. TO P., ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT APOLLINARIS AT CLASSIS

**Summary.**—He earnestly implores the abbot of Classis, who was detaining a monk who had fled from his monastery and was bound by many bonds of excommunication, not to allow him to remain with him. If the monk wishes to return to his own monastery, he promises that he will be gentle and merciful toward him.

To the lord P., venerable abbot, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

I marvel at your holy prudence, venerable brother, because, although the whole earth is filled with monks, you cherish my monk against me—a man whom I have repeatedly demanded from you, who has been sought out and wounded by so many darts of excommunication from the Apostolic See and the Roman pontiffs.

Indeed, when the first parent of the human race was permitted to eat from all the trees of paradise except one, he scorned the fruits of the other trees but chose to eat from the one tree that had been forbidden him (Gen. II and III). In the same way, although you perhaps do not admit those whom you are permitted to receive, you do not fear taking in the one whose reception is forbidden you so terribly; and, merely so that you may possess him under your authority, you care nothing if the soul perishes for which Christ died (1 Cor. VIII).

In the case of Solomon, the prostitute who had stolen another woman’s child preferred that it be cut in two by the royal sword rather than returned to its mother’s breasts (1 Kings III). She cared little about the destruction of the dying child, provided that she herself did not lose the name of mother.

Following her example, why do you nurse one whom you did not beget? Or, like a partridge, why do you cherish one whom you did not hatch? For this is the nature of the partridge: it secretly steals the eggs of others and warms them as though they were its own until the offspring emerges. But when the chicks hear the mother’s voice, they recognize her by the sign of nature’s teaching; and, rejecting the false mother, they swiftly return to the true one.

Hence Jeremiah also says: “The partridge hatched what she did not lay; she made riches, and not with justice; in the middle of her days she will abandon them, and at her end she will be a fool” (Jer. XVII).

Apart from the legitimate possibility that this may be understood of those who steal the offspring of others, it nevertheless appears to be said principally of the author of all wickedness. For the devil, like a teacher in the chair of pestilence, usurped teaching authority over human beings whom he himself did not create; and by teaching us error he cherished, as it were, those whom he did not beget by creating.

Thus he made riches, and not with justice, because, wishing to grow rich through things belonging to another’s right, he violated the judgment of equity. “But in the middle of his days he will abandon them.” For the devil is as though still alive, since the sword of the final judgment has not yet pierced him. Not yet dead, he already abandons his riches, because the human race has for the most part already returned to its Creator.

“But at his end he will be a fool,” whom, as the Apostle says, “the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming” (2 Thess. II). And the Prophet says: “With the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked” (Isa. XI).

A human being therefore abandons an abusive teacher and returns to his rightful one when he condemns a new error and returns to the origin of his own creation. Hence the passage fittingly adds: “The throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our sanctification, the expectation of Israel” (Jer. XVII).

God, therefore, who is the beginning of glory, is himself the expectation of Israel, because the human race returns through the mystery of its creation to the one from whom it came forth. The one who sat upon the throne of exalted glory from the beginning and taught humanity is himself the expectation of Israel, so that in the place of our sanctification—that is, in Holy Church—he may teach that same humanity once again.

Hence the Psalmist says: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence” (Ps. XXI).

Whoever, therefore, steals another’s disciple by violating faith unquestionably imitates the example of Antichrist. And just as that one loses what belongs to another, after the manner of the partridge, so this one will not retain what he has usurped when the judgment of equity intervenes.

Remember, venerable Father, that, in your presence, that brother first before the holy altar of the church and afterward before the cross of the cell bound himself under a solemn declaration of excommunication, if he knowingly violated the obedience owed to our priorate thereafter.

Take care, therefore, lest he who is entangled in so many bonds of excommunication pollute so holy and venerable a monastery, and lest the itch of a deadly leprosy spread through so religious and holy a community, just as the divine voice says to the people of Israel: “The anathema is in your midst, O Israel; you will not be able to stand against your enemies until the one contaminated by this crime is removed from you” (Josh. VII).

But I, who ought not to thirst for the death of a fallen brother, groan with moved compassion, sympathizing with his misfortune; and I am prepared not only to forgive him mercifully, but, if he repents, even to lay down my life for his salvation.

For the sake, therefore, of your charity and that of your holy brothers, whose servant I am, let him come to me with only a letter from you, and let him not doubt that I will be gentle, mild, and benevolent toward him; otherwise, with the Roman synod now approaching . . . if . . . But I do not wish to make threats. For the time being, let it suffice humbly to ask that no prejudice be caused to me.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE SAME

(Column 0399C: It is found in volume III and is little work 46.)

## LETTER XIX. TO RODULPH AND ARIPRAND, MONKS

**Summary.**—He sets out the course of his illnesses, by which he had been severely afflicted for many days. He says nothing angrily or impatiently, but, like another Paul, glories in his infirmities, everywhere blessing and praising God and giving thanks to the Most High, so that he offers a notable example of endurance and courage.

To his dearest brothers Rodulph and Ariprand, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of intimate love.

It is characteristic of united friendship that brother should share with brother both favorable and adverse circumstances, so that the heart may faithfully sympathize with one who reports adversity and likewise rejoice together with him in prosperity. I, however, overwhelmed by both alike, relate to you the blessed story of my calamity, so that you may grieve that I was severely battered by the scourge from above, and rejoice with me that, by the power of that same God of ours, I was mercifully rescued. “For the Lord has chastened and punished me, but he has not delivered me to death” (Ps. CXVII).

I had often prayed that the force of heavenly discipline might descend upon me and chastise the insolence of my wanton body with no light illness. In this God’s mercy did not disregard me; rather, assenting to my prayers beyond hope, it fulfilled my requests with interest. For he gave me a mournful Pentecost, not a Paschal one, and, so to speak, bestowed upon me a jubilee—not one resounding with the blasts of priestly trumpets (Lev. I), but one stealing upon me tearfully amid sighs and lamentations. On the Lord’s Day, feverish, I fell into bed; and after seven weeks had passed, on the Lord’s Day again—the fiftieth day, to be sure—when God raised me up, I arose.

Nevertheless, because, as the physicians maintained, the prescribed diet had been carelessly violated, barely three or four days flattered me deceitfully under the allure of an apparent recovery. Then, falling into a relapse, I did not cease suffering the distress of the same illness for another twenty days. Thus, after a jubilee not of rest but of turmoil, the seventieth day of captivity was, in a certain sense, completed.

Moreover, while the heat of so great a disease consumed me, while I spat blood mixed with phlegm, while I displayed so many signs of imminent death that even the physicians standing around were almost despairing, almighty God granted me this: that I did not break out into the murmur of any complaint, but willingly and wholeheartedly endured everything.
