I give you thanks, merciful God, because, although you deigned to drag me away to punishment from beneath the ruins of my sins, you also deigned to cook me in the fire of paternal severity and purge the rust from my soul as though by the blows of a hammer striking upon an anvil. Therefore, Lord, let not my will be done—for it is always perverse and unjust—but rather yours, which must be humbly adored by the powers of heaven and by human beings. Burn, cut, hack; search out every fold and hiding place of my wounds, so that nothing rotten whatsoever may lie hidden in me which the instrument of your healing passes over.

Yet while I endure these blows of heavenly discipline with equanimity, I do not, God forbid, attribute this to my own patience. You, Lord—you temper your scourges as you strike, so that when I am brought to the utmost point of pain and anguish, and, suffering spasm, am almost compelled immediately to expire, I at once feel the weight of the inward pain diminish and the hand of the striker suspended by a certain measured gentleness—as though someone were holding a four-thonged whip in the act of beating and, moved by compassion, restrained one of those thongs from striking.

It is not I, then, but you, most merciful one, who are the author of this patience; under such moderation you order the scourges of your wrath. For although, at times overcome by the excess of my illness, I am compelled to utter something elegiac and mournful—“I burn, I die, I am cut down”—this is merely the body’s simple groaning, not the complaint of a grumbling mind.

Furthermore, most merciful one, I ask you for one thing: either now bring my life to an end, and do not permit me to live any longer in the lukewarmness of my customary negligence; or, if it pleases the incomprehensible judgment of your majesty to prolong me longer in this prison of flesh, grant me, I beg, a stronger force of your love, a richer grace of compunction, or certainly an increase of some virtue that I have not hitherto possessed. Otherwise, may it never please your mercy that I escape unless some small measure of the grace of virtue, which I have not yet attained, increases within me.

[Col. 0401A] While I repeated these and similar words more and more frequently, funeral rites were being prepared for me. I was anointed with the application of sacred oil and laid out upon a bed of ashes and haircloth, as though I were about to die there. For just as, when an egg’s shell is broken and a knife is turned, the yolk comes forth, so my soul, torn from the entrails of the flesh, was threatening to depart.

Meanwhile, a certain brother named Leo was in the desert. He was advanced in years, but still more venerable for the strictness of his way of life and the purity of his simple heart. A splendid and radiant man appeared to him in a vision and asked him what he was doing. The brother replied that he was indeed sleeping, but was very sad because of the imminent death of his prior. The man said to him:

“Tell Peter Damiani, of whom you speak, to place no hope in physicians; let him feed only one hundred poor people, and immediately he need not doubt that he will recover from the illness he suffers.”

When Leo, concerned as he was for the man’s better life, asked him, “Will he have paradise, my lord?” he replied:

“He will indeed be in paradise very soon; but tell him that as soon as he has given food to the poor, he will immediately regain his health and rejoice.”

The brother awoke and immediately went to the church. Since he could not enter it—the silence of night forbidding this—he nevertheless remained astonished by the vision and did not return to his cell. What more need be said? The brother recounted the vision to the brethren, and fraternal charity, with ardent desire, supplied alms to the needy. He also added money in abundance for them. Thus, on the following day, as the illness departed, I recovered. The restoration of my health therefore confirmed the truth of the vision.

But since fish were entirely unavailable and, with my stomach weakened, I could not take food, the brothers began to press me insistently with urgent prayers to permit myself, at least for three days, to eat meat for the restoration of my wasting and exhausted body. They promised that, if I yielded to their prayers, they would willingly and devotedly bear whatever burden of penance I wished to impose upon them.

I gave them an example of ridiculous deception such as Pharulphus, count of Urbisvetus—said to possess one hundred thousand estates—had once experienced. As the story was related to me, while that count was reclining at table, a certain monk sat beside him. The count began to urge him, since fish were lacking and necessity required it, to eat meat. At first the monk refused; then gradually and little by little he softened; finally, with the pleasant pressure of their encouragement driving him on, he began to incline his mind toward it.

Meanwhile, a boar’s callus [the reading is uncertain] was set before him, and the foolish monk was deceitfully persuaded by the seductive arguments of his advisers that it was not meat and therefore could be eaten without reproach. Thus what is said through Solomon about the foolish man deceived by a prostitute happened to him:

“She ensnared him with many words and drew him along with the blandishments of her lips. Immediately he follows her, like an ox led to the slaughter, and like a playful lamb that does not know what is happening; nor does he know that the fool is being dragged to bonds until the arrow pierces his liver. He is like a bird hastening to the snare, and he does not know that his life is at stake” (Prov. VII).

[Col. 0402A] In this way, then, that brother was enticed by crafty and flattering persuasion, struck as though a tender bird caught in the fetters of a fishmonger. At last, first covering his bashful face with a blush and becoming frightened by the eyes of those looking at him from all around, he began by merely tasting a little. Then, once he had conceived the freedom to eat, he loosened the reins of his itching appetite.

When he was already satisfied and had fulfilled his desire for the allurements of meat, behold, the steward brought in a very large pike, and the eyes and mouths of his fellow diners turned toward it. When the monk marveled at it and fixed his eyes upon it with gaping, curious eagerness, the count said:

“Since you have eaten meat like a layman, why are you staring at the fish like a monk? If this is permitted you, you may appropriately sing that verse: ‘Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine’ (Ps. XIX).”

Moreover, if you had abstained from meat, this fish would have been deliberately reserved for you. But because you satisfied your appetite for flesh with meat, this fish will not pass your throat after the food of carnal gluttony.

He therefore deserved, and not undeservedly, the disgrace of this shameful confusion: he had softened the strength of his native rigor by the degenerate persuasion of flatterers, and deservedly endured the reproach of manifest embarrassment because he had not restrained the appetite for flesh that enticed and secretly tickled him.

So, I say, perhaps the Lord will deal with me, my brothers, in this same way: when you have succeeded in making me agree to eat meat, may he deign to display to me a blessing of fish; and thus may I repent of having violated my resolve through impatience of appetite, when I see that, by God’s gift, an abundance of fish has flowed to me.

And so it happened. For on the third day after these words were spoken, both from Guido, count of Cornelium, and from the city of Faenza, so many fish were brought to me that I did not lack food from them for many days. Thus, through the example of Pharulphus’s monk, who had been mocked, I escaped the disgrace of a worse confusion. It is more tolerable, after all, to be despised by human beings than to be put to shame before the majesty of God.

I have related these things to you, my beloved, as companions in suffering and friends; like brothers born of the same womb, I have arranged the story of my visitation with united affection. May almighty God, through your holy prayers, restore me sound in soul, but inflict upon my body a punishment worthy of my wickedness, so that the most merciful Judge—whom here I shall have felt moved against me by sterner breasts—may deem me worthy there to find him tranquil.

I am sending this son of ours, my beloved, to you, after God, in the confidence I place in you. For whatever progress he makes in the matter for which he is being sent will be attributed especially to you.

## LETTER XX. TO BROTHER B.

### Argument

He urges a certain monk not to undertake the task of cleansing another person’s faults; but, if he has undertaken it, to atone for it through sudden and complete penance. For this purpose he adduces the example of a monk who, having been more negligent in washing away his friend’s offenses, underwent the punishments of purgatory.

[Col. 0403A] To the lord B., his dearest brother, Peter the sinful monk sends greetings and the affection of fraternal charity.

What I often impressed upon you when present, I now write while absent. And so that the matter may not run on like a fluctuating stream, I tie together the thread of this letter: namely, that you should by no means, through disordered charity, undertake a penance which you are able to fulfill. But if you do undertake it, discharge it with the greatest possible urgency and energy, insofar as your strength permits.

Moreover, since canonical authority forbids a priest to relax even a single day’s fast for a penitent unless he compensates for it at once through almsgiving of an appropriate value, with what conscience do we subject ourselves to so fearful a precaution, when we do not know how near the end of our life may be?

The lord Martin, who lives in the hermitage of Camaldoli, a man adorned with various virtues and, above all, abundantly watered by continuous streams of tears, told me what I am about to relate:

“There was a monk,” he said, “in a monastery in the coastal region called ad Pinum, entangled in many bonds of sin. Since a harsher and prolonged penance had been imposed upon him according to the measure of his falls, he asked for help in bearing its burden from a certain brother to whom he was closely attached in familiar friendship.

“That brother devoutly undertook the request, bore the agreed portion of the penance, and instructed him to remain secure by fulfilling this part of the debt. But while the other, relieved by the division of the burden, was released from the discipline of a stricter life, the brother who had taken on the longer repayment promised himself a longer span of life. A little later he fell ill and suddenly encountered the death which he had hoped was far away.

“That brother had, for his own part, lived an irreproachable life and enjoyed an honorable reputation among the brethren. Not many days afterward, he appeared in a dream to the penitent monk, who immediately asked him:

“‘How are things with you, brother? How are you?’

“‘Badly and harshly,’ he replied, ‘but because of you. For, although I was free from my own sins, I bound myself with your chains. I did not make myself liable for another person’s debt, nor did I pay it; therefore I am being battered by scourges and constrained by a sufficiently bitter punishment. I beg you, and with all the supplication I can offer, I implore you: be vigilant for yourself and free me. Go, then, and ask the holy community of this place to pay on my behalf the debt of my pledge which I neglected, and thus rescue me from the punishments that now await me.’”

When he awoke, he told the brothers what he had seen and made known what he had heard. He set forth his request and obtained it effectively.

After the brothers had fulfilled the amount of penance prescribed for that monk through various exercises of specific kinds, the brother appeared to the monk again in a vision and displayed to him the appearance of a very serene and cheerful countenance. Asked once more what he had, he replied that, through the prayers of the brothers, he had not only been freed from penal sufferings but had recently been transferred, by a wondrous transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High, into the lot of the elect.

Blessed is the administration of divine mercy, which instructs the living even through the dead and, while scourging some, teaches others how they may be rescued from scourging.

You have heard the story, brother; be prudent for your own protection.

## LETTER XXI. TO DAMIAN, A MONK AND HIS NEPHEW ON HIS SISTER’S SIDE

(Held in volume III, and is opusculum 47.)

## LETTER XXII. TO THE SAME

### Argument

He praises the same Damian for his fervor, although excessive; for he says that among recruits in spiritual warfare it is better to exceed the bounds of discretion than to grow lukewarm through coldness. Nevertheless, he advises him to restrain himself with the bridle of discretion whenever his superiors command it. He then reproves him for having moved from the desert to a monastery and orders him to return to the desert, where he should strive to crucify himself with Christ to the world. Taking this as his occasion, he shows what is spiritually signified by the figure of the cross.

[Col. 0404B] To Damian, his nephew, Peter the sinful monk sends the affection of paternal love.

If God, who led his people out of Pharaoh’s prison, were to cease being their guide in the desert, Israel could never have reached the promised land. They needed to have as guide on their journey the one whom they had had as the author of their departure. Hence he had also said to Abraham: “Come into the land that I shall show you” (Gen. XII). For he did not say, “Go,” but rather, “Come,” promising to be his companion on the journey that lay ahead. And when he adds, “into the land that I shall show you,” he plainly demonstrates that he would be the guide of the one whom he summoned to leave the land of his birth all the way to the goal of completed perfection.

I have greatly rejoiced that something similar has begun to happen to you, when I learned, through the report of our brother Hubald, a most trustworthy man, certain notable signs of your youthful fervor. Among other things, he says that when the severity of winter’s cold was then raging in those Alps to such an extent that the accumulated mass of snow surpassed the roofs of any huts or houses, you threw off your clothes and secretly plunged your naked body into the depths of that snow. There a certain brother found you almost half-dead.

When he rebuked you more severely, as was proper, you are said to have replied: “The flesh is trying to kill me, but I shall kill it first.” Later you were found, not indeed under the open sky but beneath some building—I do not know which—lying in the snow in the same manner.

Although regular correction must not be concealed in this deed, I nevertheless prefer that excessive fervor should exceed the measure of discretion in some respect rather than that torpor born of sluggish idleness should bind degenerate souls. It is easier to remove from an overflowing vessel what exceeds its capacity than to fill what is empty within it. It is more laborious to graft onto a trunk branches that it does not possess than to cut off those that are superfluous from a tree.

The horse is also of greater value when it requires restraining reins because of its impatience to run than when, through the idleness of immense torpor, it exposes its flanks to be pierced by spurs. The former, while it rapidly and lightly gathers the turns of its swift steps, is easily restrained by drawing back the bridle a little; the latter is beaten and pounded, yet does not hasten with equine agility, but through the sluggishness of its natural torpor presents itself like a donkey.

Although it is therefore also a fault that you exceed the limit of discretion, it is nevertheless better for you to be accused of excessive fervor than to be branded with the foul disease of sloth. I do not wish, then, that this praiseworthy flame of zeal should cool within you; nevertheless, let the severity of your superiors restrain the excess of indiscretion wherever necessary.

Through this zeal, which is said to live within you, I have understood that the spirit which admonished you, as it admonished Abraham, to leave your homeland (Gen. XII), has not departed from you. Rather, having become the guide of your journey, it has not ceased to go before you.

I was nevertheless displeased to learn that you had entered the monastery of Blessed Bartholomew in order to learn the melodies of ecclesiastical chant. When I heard this, it seemed to me, in a certain way, that a tender little lamb had leapt from the sheepfold and fallen into the bloody jaws of a ravening wolf.

At that time, when brother Hubald brought me this news about you—not, of course, the news I had desired—there was with him Peter, abbot of the monastery built in the city of Salerno and flourishing under the title of Blessed Benedict, a man memorable for great sweetness and distinguished by the propriety of religious conduct. He told me that a ravenous wolf of human beings secretly attacked a small boy from his monastery’s household, snatched him away, and departed.

After this, the boy’s mother, pierced with grief, cried out:

“By Blessed Benedict, whose servant he is, I adjure you, beast: do not carry my son away any farther, but release him immediately.”

When the wolf heard this, he immediately dropped from his open mouth the child he was carrying. But he suddenly sprang upon another boy, swiftly tore him apart, rejected his mutilated corpse, and carried away the severed head, seized between his teeth, to his hiding place.

I too, who fear that you have been seized by the tooth of the invisible wolf, trust in your rescue through that same holy father Benedict, whose servant you have become. For how else would you have descended from the desert to the monastery unless the cunning ambusher had drawn you on by the bite of his pernicious cunning?

Nevertheless, I do not wish to pursue this first fault any further. For, as I believe, it did not arise from the instability of your levity but proceeded from the ill-considered measure of those giving orders, especially since the aforementioned Hubald told me that you agreed to this command only reluctantly and under compulsion.

Return, then, dearest son, to the desert with all speed, lest, while the spaciousness of monastic life delights your youth, the rigor of the desert, through the forgetfulness of disuse, should eventually—even God forbid—come to be hated.

There fix the trophy of your cross immovably; there suspend yourself together with Christ, so that, rooted and founded in love, as the Apostle says, you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth (Eph. III).

This is undoubtedly the cross of the Redeemer. In its heavenly figure of victory, the whole Christian religion is depicted; in the character of this life-giving sign, the entire perfection of spiritual virtues is represented.

Since all divine law consists in these three virtues—hope, faith, and charity—and since from them proceeds the multitude of all virtues, faith, which is the foundation of the Christian religion, is represented in that part of the cross which is fixed in the earth. Upon this foundation the entire structure of good works rests, and, so that it may stand, the whole machinery of spiritual virtues is sustained. Hence the Apostle says to his disciples: “For by faith you stand” (I Cor. I).

By the uppermost horn, which rises above the others, hope is understood; through it our spirit is summoned to attain heavenly things. By the wood placed in the middle and extending on both sides in two arms, the breadth of twofold charity is signified.

By this same sign of the life-giving cross, the number of the four principal virtues is undoubtedly expressed; from these, as from seeds, the harvests of all virtues spring forth: namely, justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance.

By the uppermost horn, which looks toward heaven, justice is represented, as may be gathered from the words of the Redeemer himself. After saying, “The Holy Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning justice, and concerning judgment” (John XVI), he shortly afterward added: “Concerning justice, indeed, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me” (ibid.). The wise man also says: “Justice elevates nations” (Prov. XIV)—and there is no doubt that he means toward heaven.

The lower part of the cross, which supports the upper mass, signifies fortitude, which patiently endures whatever things are difficult and adverse. The right arm of the cross expresses prudence, by which we repel the darts cast by the evil spirit, as though by the rejection of the right hand; and, striking him through with the weapon of a fervent spirit, we overthrow him bravely, fortified by divine protection, and carry away the spoils of victory.

By the left horn, temperance is not improperly signified. In the left hand there is lesser strength than in the right. Through temperance, therefore, we in a certain way draw strength into our virtue, when we live temperately and modestly; when we often soften the rigor and strictness of justice through the art of discretion, which acts as a teacher.

Why should I mention that the law of the Old Testament already breathed the mystery of the cross at the very beginning of its promulgation? For just as this cross is joined together from pieces of wood, so that law too is known to have been inscribed by the finger of God upon two tablets.

And since the number ten is expressed by the letter X, which represents the sign of the cross, while it is beyond doubt that the law was given through the Decalogue, it is clear that that law, although secretly, contained within itself the mysteries of the saving cross. Later, the brightness of evangelical grace revealed them as it flashed throughout the world.

Hence it is said through Zechariah: “On that day, what is upon the horse’s bridle will be called holy to the Lord” (Zech. XIV). The horse’s bridle is the Gospel, which restrains the appetite of the unbridled horse of carnal desire. The cross is therefore above the bridle, because whatever is commanded through the evangelical precepts undoubtedly pertains to the cross, as the Lord himself bears witness:

“Whoever wishes,” he says, “to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke IX).

This cross is rightly called holy to the Lord, because through it the world, which had been so greatly profaned, is blessed. But since we have written elsewhere at greater length about the holy and precious cross, lest the same matter happen to intrude here, we judge it sufficient to have passed over these points briefly in this epistolary summary.

This sign of your life, dearest son, just as you depict it upon your forehead, so also impress it upon the thresholds of your heart, so that the avenging angel, seeing it, may pass by without harming you (Exod. XII). Let these protective tokens hang before your eyes without ceasing; let these marks brand your body everywhere, as the Apostle testifies concerning himself:

“I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. VI).

Break your body through fasts; abstain from your own wills; submit yourself to the command of another’s order with the readiest devotion; let the excesses of a brazen tongue be restrained by the modest discipline of silence; let the seductive attractions of playful speech not burst forth; let the enticing impulses of carnal passions be crushed by the rigor of strict continence. Thus, since you now willingly die with Christ, the more heavily his cross is seen in your way of life, the more fully the glory of his resurrection will be heaped up for you.

## LETTER XXIII. TO WILLIAM, A MONK

### Argument

He gently reproves as excessively delicate a monk who had promised to come from the monastery to the desert but kept postponing the matter from day to day; moreover, he could not bear with sufficiently even temper to renounce drinking wine and drink water instead. By introducing a personification of water, in which both the great dignity and supreme usefulness of this element to human beings, as well as the many harms of wine, are set forth, he concludes that water is not a beverage from which the monk should recoil. Finally, he teaches that all the difficulties presenting themselves along the way of the spirit must be overcome with the weapons prescribed by the Apostle.

To his dearest brother William, Peter sends perpetual charity in Christ.

I wonder, dearest brother, why you did not come to the desert as you promised—or rather, why you did not fulfill what you had agreed with me, not through a messenger but by pledging your own faith. Tell me, I beg you, what deterred you from the austerity of the desert? Why did a base fear seize the heart of a soldier of Christ?

Could the taste of wine, with womanly blandishment, have held a stern soldier within the barriers of his house, and not allowed him—already helmeted, already girded with weapons, already breathing great things—to go out to battle?

But alas! What shame will invade the mind of this soft man, what blush of embarrassment will suffuse his face, when he sees others return from battle laden with rich spoils, victorious, enriched with abundant rewards, and crowned after their triumph with such glory? How much will a little wine cost the man who will wish that he had drunk so much poison for himself?

Hear what the wise Solomon says:

“Who has woe? Whose father has woe? Who has quarrels? Who has pits? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Is it not those who linger over wine and devote themselves to emptying cups?” (Prov. XXIII.)

For if woe—which is plainly a cry of lamentation—is threatened to those who linger over wine, joy without any doubt is promised to those who drink water for the love of God. Aptly, the text adds:

“Do not look upon wine when it becomes golden, when its color shines in the glass; it enters gently, but at the end it will bite like a serpent and spread poison like a basilisk” (ibid.).

We do not speak against the liquid mentioned above in order to obscure God’s creation, which is certainly good. Rather, we judge that wine, meat, marriage, and many things like them ought to be placed after other concerns by monks, so that by abstaining from created things we may please the Creator more closely.

But since you hate water, let water itself address you as though with a living voice and convict you, by its own assertion, of being ungrateful for its benefits.

“Come now,” it says, “good man, why do you look down upon me with raised eyebrows? Why do you despise me with curses, irritation, and a wrinkled brow? Why do you drive me away so forcefully from your companionship? If I deserve this from you, I do not resist or grieve, since I justly suffer this insult. Answer me: what evil have I ever done you? Rather, what good have I not bestowed upon you?

“I made you, through the power of the Holy Spirit who consecrated me, from a slave of the devil into a son of God. I brought you forth from being an occupant of hell to be an heir of the heavenly kingdom; from a tenant of hell I made you a citizen of paradise; from the dark straw of eternal fire I displayed to you the light of new grace. ‘For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’ (Eph. V).

“I fashioned you from a vessel of wrath into a vessel of mercy. I stripped from you the ancient tunic of condemnation and clothed you in the light of the new man. I released you from the bond of the ancient transgression and, having regenerated you through me, joined you to the sons of divine adoption.

“You yourself are my witness, because you descended into my womb with the seven original vices and emerged immediately purified and clean, entirely without the contamination of sin. When I found you filthy and foul-smelling, I did not hesitate to wash both your soul and body; and now you disdain to bring me even to your lips.

“I enable you to take part in divine banquets, and you are not ashamed to cast me away from human tables. Very well, let it be so; let the other things retain their rights, while from me alone, as I deserve, the privilege of proper honor is taken away! Is it perhaps because I am younger than the other elements in time that I must therefore be inferior to all of them in dignity?

“But ask Moses, I beg you; inquire what element the Holy Spirit chose for his dwelling at the beginning of the world. Was it earth? Was it air? Was it fire? Surely, unless I am mistaken, he will answer you: ‘The Spirit of God was borne above the waters’ (Gen. I).

“And, to say nothing now of spiritual matters, I wash your body, your clothing, and everything you use. I never cease irrigating your fields so that they may produce crops. I provide a route for ships; I refresh all living creatures of the earth; I bring the fruits and vegetables on which you feed to maturity.

“I say nothing of birds; I pass over the fish, which are born daily throughout my realms and are not at all ashamed to acknowledge themselves the servants of my household. Finally, the very vines that you love with insane desire while despising me would, unless they grew strong from their roots with my help, immediately dry up and feed the fire rather than fill the bellies of drinkers with overflowing cups.

“But why should I linger over brief matters? Even the mass of earth itself, where all visible things are born, relies upon my supports, as though upon foundations placed beneath it, in partnership with the air, so that it may stand; it is upheld by my power.

“While I support the earth, I am by no means content with the depths below; I also claim the summit of heaven for my domain. As it is read in Genesis: ‘God also divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament’ (Gen. I). The whole earth would indeed be scorched by heavenly fire unless our moisture continually tempered the force of the conflagration.

“But perhaps, because you see that liquid lacks strength, you believe it weak. Yet if my strength were lacking for you, who, I ask, would turn the heavy millstones for grinding grain?

“The power of liquid must not, therefore, be despised, since it so easily moves the hardness of stone. And, so that you may not fail to recognize the marvelous power of my nature, fire itself—which, according to the dialecticians, is seen to be opposed even to me—is certainly drawn from me and brought forth from my entrails.

“For if crystal, which without question becomes hard from ice, is exposed to the sun’s ray, no one doubts that fire immediately arises from it. Stones too, which have been baked in a kiln to make lime, if I touch them after any long interval, you will immediately see them both smoke and burn; and those that until then were cold, after the command of our touch are brought back to their former heat.

“I ask you, if you know: what is it that in many rivers, when the moon is increasing or rising, you see me rise high, but, when that same moon is waning, cease? What is it also, if you have learned it, that makes springs in winter, when almost everything is stiff with cold, render me warm and steaming, but in summer make me cold?

“Or perhaps you believe the vain claims of philosophers, who think that summer exists among the antipodes when, among those above, the setting sun produces winter? But if you examine the matter carefully, you will find this entirely false and contrary to solid truth.

“Inquire into these matters diligently, then, and when you cannot unravel them completely, conclude that the deepest power of my nature is impenetrable.

“But while, in the interest of brevity, I pass swiftly over the rights of my majesty, I do not want you to remain unaware that I also hold no ordinary primacy in the studies of the liberal arts. For when geometers or astrologers strive to construct a clock—to learn the intervals of the hours, to compare the sun’s sphere with the sphere of heaven, to measure the zodiac and all its signs, to distinguish the circles of the planets, and to compare the dimensions of the earth with the regions of heaven—they immediately turn to our element.

“Why should I say anything about music, when its very name testifies that it is subject to our laws and arose from our beginning? For if *musa* in Greek means ‘water,’ then music is plainly marked by the title of our name.”

Nor does Pythagoras himself, the author of this discipline, disagree with my argument. In order to discover its method, he carefully fashioned certain vessels for measuring water, and thus, with me as his guide and presiding authority, at last successfully attained the full realization of his purpose in all the expertise of harmony. Even today, whatever is pleasingly played on hydraulic instruments or organs is likewise sustained by my power.

And, to reveal now the most distinguished privilege of my dignity: when the Lord was hanging upon the cross, I came forth from the side of my Creator himself (John 19), and, joined to his most precious blood, consecrated the whole earth and all the air. Hence the apostle John says: “This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ” (1 John 5); and shortly afterward he adds: “There are three that bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood” (ibid.).

Now, if you attend to everything comprised above, consider that all the remaining elements are subject to my dominion. Yet while I enumerate the praises of my excellence, I may perhaps better teach you who I am and what power I possess if I bring you back to yourself, so that when you have perceived my rights ruling within you, you may no longer doubt my other powers.

You do not, then, fail to know that you yourself consist of four elements. But while three of them are distributed among the other members of the body, the Almighty Creator has bestowed upon me a more excellent dignity and, as it were, a citadel of primacy among the others, by appointing me a seat in the head itself. Since it is agreed that phlegm is generated from the moisture of water, and phlegm is in the head, no one can doubt that the throne of water appears to preside in the head.

It is therefore sufficiently astonishing that liquid moisture should be suspended with such mastery in the upper part, so that it does not descend at all to the lower regions, except that it gently flows down through the arteries of the brain and seeks, as it were, the mouth’s breathing passage as an outlet through which it may escape. In this, surely, your pride is plainly humbled. Although it scorns to drink me when I am placed outside, it is nevertheless continually compelled to have me moving among the barriers of the mouth; and, so to speak, you flee with me within you, since wherever you turn, you cannot be without me.

For just as a water-mill can in no way grind grain without the flooding of the torrent, so I must continually run between the two millstones of the human mouth, so that the speaking tongue may form its words. If, then, you need my help in all these things and necessarily employ my services, why do you disdain to have my companionship in the single matter of drinking? Return, then, to me, fugitive; come back, ungrateful man. You who are wholly dependent upon me for your health—do not appear to be nauseated by me.

“But perhaps,” you will say, “my head hurts; my stomach is weak.” These are the poultices of the soft, these are the excuses of monks living according to the flesh. This excuse is plainly very meager, since water often refreshes the sick, while wine frequently kills them.

Did the Lord’s Forerunner ever languish in sickness, though he never drank wine or strong drink? Is James the son of Alphaeus ever said to have sought physicians, although he is reported to have been ignorant of these liquids from his mother’s womb? Now, if we go back to the beginning of the world, it is recognized that this world remained entirely ignorant of wine until Noah’s six-hundred-and-third year, although throughout all those stretches of time human beings are indeed said to have died, but no one is recorded to have fallen sick.

But when Genesis says, “Noah, a husbandman, began to cultivate the land, and he planted a vineyard,” it immediately adds, as though in praise of water: “And drinking wine, he became drunk, and he was uncovered in his tent” (Genesis 9). It is as though it plainly said: “The one whom water long kept clothed without shame, wine suddenly stripped of his private parts.”

Solomon also aptly agrees with this judgment, saying: “Wine,” he says, “causes even the wise to apostatize” (Sirach 19). Lot, too, who lived chastely even among the Sodomites, afterward drank wine on the mountain and, without knowing it, slept with both daughters. Wine persuaded him to lose the purity of his modesty in a single night of solitude; Sodom itself, amid so many adulterers, had been unable for a long time to violate that purity.

Thus it came about that Lot, who until then had been righteous in all things, by a perverse right in this one matter became father and grandfather of Moab and Ammon, each separately. Hence Solomon not inappropriately says: “Wine is a luxurious thing,” he says, “and drunkenness is tumultuous; whoever delights in these will not be wise” (Proverbs 20).

At this our weakling replies: “But the Apostle,” he says, “commanded his disciple, saying: ‘Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses’” (1 Timothy 5).

Would that, brother, we remembered by heart the other sayings of Sacred Scripture that commend fasting as readily as this single passage, which relaxes the rigor of abstinence out of discretion. Why do we not remember in the same way what Paul says elsewhere: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5)? Why do we not recall in the same way what Isaiah says: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness!” (Isaiah 5.) Why do we not remember what Solomon says: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns. Lest they drink and forget judgments and pervert the case of the poor man’s children” (Proverbs 31)?

But Paul himself, whose saying you so willingly set against me, and other statements like it, reveals elsewhere by what principle of discretion he gives this command, when he says: “I say this,” he says, “according to indulgence, not according to command” (1 Corinthians 7). Indeed, in matters permitted according to indulgence, the disciple is more pleasing if he simply passes over the command than if he eagerly obeys it.

This can easily be understood if what Jeremiah relates is brought back to memory. He says: “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Go to the house of the Rechabites, speak to them, and bring them into one of the chambers of the treasury of the house of the Lord, and give them wine to drink” (Jeremiah 35). A divinely given command is evident here; and shortly afterward it adds: “I set before the sons of the house of the Rechabites bowls full of wine and cups, and I said to them: Drink wine” (ibid.).

Here is what is commanded by God’s authority and announced through the prophet’s ministry; yet it is by no means found to have been carried out. For Scripture continues and says: “They answered: We do not drink wine, because Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, saying: You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your children, forever” (ibid.).

But was God offended by this resistance? Was it counted against them as disobedience? Hear instead what the divine voice later says to them: “Because you obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his commandments, therefore thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: A man from the stock of Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not fail to stand in my sight all his days” (ibid.).

O happy disobedience, which was deemed worthy of the proclamation of so great a Judge and earned the perpetual service of divine obedience! Happy, I say, the disobedience that experienced not the judgment of punishment but carried away the reward of divine recompense.

I would gladly continue for a long time to play with you in such familiar conversation while preserving due seriousness; but, as you yourself know, one may not dispute briefly except briefly. Nevertheless, I still exhort you; I still entreat you:

> Break the delays of sloth; shatter the chains of torpor.

Do not let the flashing arrows of the enemy terrify you; do not let the blandishments of domestic presumption relax you; do not let the violent blast of the trumpets deprive you of breath; do not let the dense forest of weapons keep you within the privacy of your chamber.

Now, now, distinguished warrior, lay aside all fear, engage the enemy, and burst into the midst of their ranks like lightning sent down from heaven. Seize your weapons manfully and, raising Christ’s banner, rush fervently wherever the line appears most tightly massed. Hasten to cut down with the sword whatever lies nearest, and always remember to protect yourself on every side by turning your shield about. And, lest fear of inflicting wounds shake your heart, hear what Wisdom promises you through Solomon’s testimony: “Do not,” it says, “fear the sudden terror of the powers rushing upon you, for the Lord will be at your side and will guard your foot, lest you be ensnared” (Proverbs 3).

But lest anyone assert that I have invented this manner of engagement through some novel notion of my own, note what Paul, instructor in the sacred warfare, says: “I therefore run not as uncertainly; I fight not as one beating the air” (1 Corinthians 9). And again: “Put on,” he says, “the armor of God, so that you may stand against the deceits of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.” Then he adds: “Therefore take up the armor of God” (Ephesians 6).

He plainly enumerates what weapons these are, for which he urges us to seize arms with such zeal: “Stand,” he says, “with your loins girded in truth, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one; and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6).

Solomon, too, had by no means been ignorant of this warfare when he said: “Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed, among the strongest of Israel; all hold swords and are most learned in warfare, each man’s sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” (Song of Songs 3).

But while he enumerates the swords with which adversaries are to be pierced, he also describes the shields by which we are to be protected, when shortly afterward the voice of the bridegroom says to the bride: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with battlements; a thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty” (Song of Songs 4).

What these shields are to be understood as signifying, Solomon himself plainly declares in Proverbs when he says: “Every word of God is a shield for those who hope in him” (Proverbs 30).

It has been a long time, dearest brother, since I thirsted to speak to you with the dry throat of my desire. Now, having received the opportunity, when I drove wine from the monks’ table, I have satisfied myself with abundant streams of discourse.

## LETTER XXIV. TO HONESTUS, A MONK

(This is found in volume III and is opusculum 48.)

## 218. LETTER XXV. TO JOHN, A MONK

**SUMMARY.** He defends himself against a certain monk named John, who had reproached him because he intended to resign the episcopate.

[Col. 0413C] To the lord John, a religious man, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

Because you are angry that I wish to leave the episcopate, and because, concerned for my interests, you give me advice, you are not, if I may speak with your permission, attending to the matter with spiritual eyes. Overwhelmed by the darkness of so many secular affairs, I cannot see the clarity of the innermost light; I raise the mind’s vision, excessively confused and dull, toward the contemplation of spiritual things.

Nearly seven years ago, the abbot of the monastery established in the suburb of Perugia in honor of Blessed Peter rejected responsibility for the government entrusted to him and, by authority of the Apostolic See, appointed another as rector of the place. Concerning this, Rainerius the judge—a distinguished man, conspicuous for the charm of his eloquence—recently related to me the story I am about to tell.

“The abbot,” he said, “after ceasing to administer the government he had laid down, celebrated Mass every day in a twofold office. My father, already a veteran, whom that abbot had once made a monk, continually assisted him in the service of divine worship.

“One day, then, after the Gospel had been read and he was about to offer the heavenly victims, my father saw a lamb standing beside the altar. When he suddenly wished to seize it, he was shaken with fear and did not dare to stretch out his hand toward it. When the moment came for the Lord’s body to be broken, he saw the aforesaid lamb upon the altar table. As he gazed at it again fixedly, it suddenly disappeared.

“When the venerable abbot learned of this from the report of the man who had seen it, he ordered that it be kept secret and absolutely forbade anyone to speak of it for as long as the abbot lived. Shortly afterward, the abbot, devoted to the pursuit of holy conduct, died; and not long thereafter the man to whom the vision had appeared also departed from this life to the Lord.”

What else does this example summon me to do, unless to abandon the anxious burden of ecclesiastical occupation and hasten with complete freedom of spirit toward the repose of contemplation?

But while this was being told to me in due order, another event was also related from nearly the same period. I do not think it useless to commit it to memory, because although it does not pertain to this matter, it is not without relevance to the praise of Almighty God, for whom everything we write is engaged in service.

Richard, rector of the monastery called Camporizano, said that he had learned this from reliable reports of certain people:

A man from the regions of Lombardy was traveling with his wife to the venerable thresholds of the blessed apostles. When the traveler came upon Lake Bolsena, he boarded a fisherman’s boat and bought fish. But after returning to the shore, he discovered that he had lost his purse, in which he had possessed twenty-four Pavia solidi.

His wife complained that, because of a cheap meal, she had suffered a serious loss. But the magnanimous man bore this calmly and sought to soothe his wife’s grief with gentle encouragement. “We still have,” he said, “six pounds of Lucchese denarii; with no more than this sum we can manage to complete our journey honorably. For divine clemency will deign by its blessing to compensate for the loss of our misfortune.”

When the journey had been completed, and the man was seeking lodging near the same lake, he began cheerfully to say to his companions: “Since this lake has brought us loss, it is surely fitting that, with God’s help, as we return home it should provide us with a joyful and solemn banquet.”

Then, turning to the inhabitants, he said: “Who will sell me a fish for twelve coins?”

A fisherman standing nearby immediately replied: “I certainly have an excellent fish for sale, but you will undoubtedly pay me fifteen denarii if you wish to claim it for yourself.”

Without hesitation the man paid the sum and instructed that the fish he had bought be prepared for his wife in the most appetizing manner possible. When the woman gutted it, she found in its intestine a little pouch containing twenty-four solidi of Pavia currency.

Then all who were present together gave thanks and clearly recognized that in all losses occurring one after another, hope must always be placed in God.

[Note: The remainder of this letter is missing in the manuscripts.]

## LETTER XXVI. TO HIS COUSIN MARINUS, A MONK OF CLASSIS

(This is found in volume III and is opusculum 49.)

## LETTER XXVII. TO PETER CEREBROSUS, A MONK

**SUMMARY.** This entire letter is written against the monk Peter Cerebrosus. After first admonishing him concerning the restraint of the tongue and the reckless pouring forth of words, Peter then severely rebukes him for disparaging the voluntary infliction of blows. He demonstrates by very strong arguments and examples that the remedy of scourging is not absurd, as the other man thought, but pious and highly suitable for cleansing sins.

To Peter Cerebrosus, a monk, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings.

Whoever thinks that clever talk is eloquence goes astray, led by the similarity of things. For, as the Wise Man says: “The lips of the imprudent recount foolish things, but the words of the prudent are weighed on the scales” (Sirach 21).

Just as an unbridled horse passes through winding paths and trackless flats, or over every kind of height, so the tongue of fools, whether speaking directly or frivolously, flows out indifferently and lightly with whatever happens to be available. But the prudent man weighs what ought to be said and, like a cautious traveler, carefully considers where to place the footprint of his tongue.

The former, through impatience to speak, brings into the open whatever is hidden; the latter, when usefulness requires it, keeps the secret under the key of silence. Hence the same Wise Man says: “In the mouth of fools is their heart, but the mouth of the wise is in their heart” (ibid.).

You recently vomited much gall upon us, brother, saying and writing what seems certainly to boil over from the fury of a deranged mind. We pass over the rest, in which you raged with the fiercest venom of hostility. But concerning the disciplines of scourging that the brothers customarily inflict upon themselves, where you have pressed the foot of detraction for so long, we reply with God’s help.

This kind of discipline was by no means newly invented by modern practices, but was rather brought forth from the authority of Sacred Scripture. We know that the Lord and Savior was scourged by the soldiers of the governor; that the blessed apostles were beaten in councils by the chief priests; and we read that some of the holy martyrs were torn by rods and harsher whips. Paul, too, was beaten with rods three times and received five times “forty lashes less one” (2 Corinthians 11).

In Deuteronomy the Lord commanded, saying: “If they judge the one who has sinned to be worthy, they shall throw him down and have him scourged in their presence.” And immediately afterward it is added: “The number of blows shall be according to the measure of the sin, provided that they do not exceed forty, lest your brother, disgracefully lacerated, depart before your eyes” (Deuteronomy 25).

That which was a legal command for that people is for us a mystery of allegory. For the number forty signifies the course of human life. Hence Israel travels through the desert for forty years; hence Moses and Elijah, and also the Lord himself, prolonged their fasts for that many days.

Just as he lay dead in the tomb for forty hours, so likewise after his resurrection he remained with his disciples for the same number of days, so that the merciful teacher might instruct us, his members, to follow the footsteps of our Head, to be dead to the world, and to live as pilgrims and strangers in this age.

Mystically, too, when the sinner in the Law is commanded to be beaten, the number of blows is forbidden to exceed forty, because whoever has performed perfect penance in this life will afterward suffer no punishment for his offenses.

Moreover, the number three, because of the mystery of the Holy Trinity, pertains to faith; the number five, because of our five senses, pertains to action. And because every person, when he sins, either errs in faith or commits an offense in action, it was fitting that Paul, who had sinned in both respects, should, for the effect of perfect cleansing, be beaten with rods three times and be scourged five times with forty lashes less one (2 Corinthians 11).

As for the phrase “less one,” this undoubtedly means that the judges of the Jews decreed that one blow should be subtracted from forty, so that, while they did not reach the legal total, they could in no way exceed the command of the Law; and while they remained below it, they would not go beyond it.

[Col. 0416B] Since not only the authority of the ancient Law but also evangelical grace commends the infliction of blows, sometimes through commands and sometimes through examples—for we read that the holy apostles were beaten in council and that the blessed martyrs were very often scourged—“Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Romans 15).

What is absurd or foolish if now the holy Church, in the leisure of peace, uses what it once used in war? For the Apostle also says again: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9). And elsewhere: “The saints experienced mockery and scourging” (Hebrews 11).

Now that the executioner’s hand has ceased to inflict blows upon martyrs, what harm is there if holy devotion offers itself the means by which it may deserve to become a participant in the lot of the holy martyrs? When I voluntarily scourge myself with my own hands before God’s presence, I openly show the desire of sincere devotion: if an executioner were present, I would be ready.

If punishment is so sweet to me for Christ’s love when it is absent, with what spirit would I receive it if a persecutor offered it? I would wish to undergo martyrdom for Christ, but because the opportunity is lacking, I have no means to do so. By wearing myself down with blows, I at least display the will of a fervent spirit.

Indeed, if a persecutor were to strike me down, I would scourge myself, because I would willingly present myself to be scourged. For if Scripture is examined carefully, Christ himself, the King of martyrs, is found to have been handed over not only by Judas but also by the Father and by himself.

Concerning the Father, the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8). Concerning the Son, he says elsewhere: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Galatians 2).

Therefore, whether my own hand afflicts me or an executioner inflicts a blow, I myself am especially the author of this testing, since I voluntarily offer myself to be tested.

Furthermore, because a tambourine is made of dried skin, he truly praises the Lord on the tambourine, according to the Prophet, who scourges his body, worn out by fasting, through discipline (Psalm 150).

The sacred canons also command certain offenders to be beaten. Hence many holy pontiffs order some who come to penance first to be scourged before their eyes, and then impose the judgment of penance upon them.

Before our time, this rule of discipline was by no means unknown in nearly all holy monasteries, although it was not practiced so frequently. Hence they were accustomed to redeem each year of penance with a thousand strokes of the scourge.

You, too, do not detest the rule of discipline but the madness of excessively prolonged discipline. You do not disapprove of saying a psalm together with discipline, but you shudder at having the Psalter continued along with discipline.

But tell me, I beg you, brother—speaking with your permission—do you detest those disciplines that are customarily performed in the chapter house? Do you perhaps condemn the fact that we often command a brother who has confessed some slight offense to undergo twenty strokes, or at most fifty?

But since these disciplines are light and small enough to bear and are regularly customary among the brothers, it is evident that you do not disparage or criticize them, lest you seem to act against the common custom of the holy order.

Come, then: if, as has been said, it is permissible to impose fifty strokes, why not sixty, or, if we dare say so, as many as a hundred? If it is permissible to reach the number one hundred in this sacrifice of pious devotion, why not two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred? Why certainly should it not be permissible to add a thousand, and thereafter any number?

For it is sufficiently absurd that the smallest part of something should be gratefully accepted while the greatest is rejected. It is exceedingly foolish to suppose that something good ought to be begun but not allowed to increase.

How can it happen that, if a small discipline purifies, it becomes defiled in God’s sight when multiplied? If a one-day fast is good, a two-day and three-day fast are better. The same is true of keeping vigil, singing psalms, laboring, obeying, and persistently applying oneself to meditation upon the Scriptures.

Every pious labor is worthy of a more abundant glory of reward in proportion as it is longer. Is this one kind of piety alone to be judged worse the more it increases?

You say: “Why am I striking the flesh?” I answer: “Why am I striking the spirit?” For the Psalmist says: “I exercised myself and swept my spirit” (Psalm 76).

I sweep both flesh and spirit when I recognize that I have sinned through flesh and spirit: the spirit with corrections, the flesh, along with other afflictions, also with the blows of rods, so that, because my joyful flesh drew me into guilt, when afflicted it may lead me back to forgiveness.

A man clothed in a coat of mail surrounds his various limbs with iron rings; he drives himself through the labor of *metanoia*—repentance—and repeatedly strikes his palms against the pavement. Why do these things, and others like them, occur, unless so that, while the body is afflicted through them, refreshment may be procured for the soul?

Whatever it may be by which the flesh is torn and struck for the sake of repentance, through that very means a person is undoubtedly cleansed of the foulness of contracted guilt.

Hear what I happened to learn on the third day after the frenzied heat of your—let me not call it maliciousness, but simplicity—had blazed up against me.

[Note: The remainder is missing in the manuscripts.]

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0418A]

**SUMMARY.** He resolves two questions proposed to him by the monk Peter. The first was why Gregory the Great had said that the rich man who had refused to help the beggar Lazarus had been condemned to eternal torments because he had been born under the New Testament, in which mercy toward the poor is commanded. The second question concerns the vice of curiosity, which the same holy teacher had mentioned; here it is shown what this means.

To Peter, his dearest brother, Peter sends greetings.

You ask me, dearest son, what is meant by what Blessed Gregory says in his homily on the rich man (Homily 40 on the Gospels): “Some think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New; but they are certainly deceived by careless consideration. In the former, it is not hoarding but robbery that is punished; there, property unjustly taken is punished by fourfold restitution. Here, however, this rich man is reproved not for taking another’s property but for not giving his own.”

By these words the distinguished teacher is attempting to establish only this: if that rich man had been found under the Old Testament, he would in no way have been consigned to Tartarean punishments. According to this assertion, then, he perished because, established under the new grace, he refused to keep the Gospel.

But you are troubled by the contrary consideration and say: How can the New Testament be said to have dawned already, when Christ had not yet been hung upon the cross and had not yet been exalted through the glory of his resurrection and ascension? Indeed, the very Gospel that is commanded to be kept had not yet been spread throughout the world through the mouths of the apostles. Finally, the Holy Spirit had not yet filled human hearts—the Spirit who supplies minds with strength to keep the commandments: “The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7).

To this question, with due reverence for the teachers, we give the brief answer that now occurs to us. The Lord says in the Gospel: “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Matthew 11). John, however, commands: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none; and let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke 3).

Just as there are two commands of John under this saying, so there are two sins of the rich man. John says: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none”; but the rich man was clothed in purple and fine linen. “Let the one who has food do likewise”; but the rich man feasted splendidly every day.

He is convicted of being hard and inhuman in both respects: he neither clothed the naked Lazarus, whom the dogs licked, nor gave food to the man who desired to be satisfied with the crumbs falling from his table, but entirely denied him nourishment.

A great matter—no wonder if it has a long beginning. The New Testament, at least insofar as this humanity is concerned, had already begun, even if it had not yet everywhere been brought to perfection. It is therefore understood that this rich man lived in the time of John but refused to obey his commands.

Concerning that time the Savior says: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11). From the time when the kingdom of heaven is said to suffer violence, it is clear that the Gospel was already succeeding the Law; and after the Old Testament, the New Testament is rightly said to shine forth.

The rich man was therefore justly condemned with the reprobate to Tartarus, because he was unwilling, with the elect, to do violence to the kingdom of heaven.

If someone objects to us that Abraham says to the rich man, “They have Moses and the prophets” (Luke 16), this very point works in our favor. Since John is not only a prophet but more than a prophet, whatever is referred to John is undoubtedly directed to a prophet, especially since John’s statement does not disagree with the oracles of the ancient prophets.

Among those prophets we often find something of this kind: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house; when you see the naked, cover him” (Isaiah 58).

Moses also says: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me” (Deuteronomy 18). And the Lord himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5).

Those, therefore, who are sent to Moses and the prophets are certainly sent to John and Christ.

As for what you ask again—what is meant by the vice of curiosity found in another saying of the aforementioned teacher—what he set forth obscurely for the sake of brevity, I shall unravel from the knot of this question with the words of Blessed Augustine.

While expounding the epistle of Blessed John the Apostle, Augustine says that “the desire of the eyes” means every kind of curiosity. How broadly curiosity itself extends! It is present in spectacles, in theaters, in diabolical rites, in magical arts, and in sorceries. Sometimes curiosity also tests the servants of God, making them wish, as though to perform a miracle, to test whether God will hear them.

Curiosity in miracles—this desire—is not from the Father.

Having resolved the questions, I ask in return the favor that I may deserve a share in your holy prayer. When the interest of the reward has increased, repayment is made if the obedience of a sinner is compensated by the prayers of a holy man.

## LETTER XXIX. TO STEPHANUS, A MONK

[Col. 0419D]

**SUMMARY.** He especially commends two things to a certain monk named Stephanus as highly beneficial: that he recite the office of Blessed Mary the Virgin every day and diligently devote himself to reading Sacred Scripture. He teaches how great the usefulness of both is.

To the lord Stephanus, a religious man, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

Since you diligently exercise yourself in the study of psalmody and in divine praises, I exhort and admonish you, venerable brother, not to omit the daily office of Blessed Mary, ever-virgin.

For it is fitting that she who deserves the proclamations of praise from the angels should also be frequently honored by human service, and that the whole world after God should offer praise to her, through whom it received the author of its own salvation.

It is certainly an excellent hope to take refuge with her who, among all the senators of the heavenly court, holds the first place in obtaining favors from God.

My sister’s son Damianus, a young man of religious character, reported to me that, while I was writing these things in his presence, he had learned the following by widespread report while engaged in literary studies in Gaul.

A certain cleric of the Church of Nevers was weakened by illness and languished; as the affliction grew worse and worse, he reached his final extremity, already dying. He had imposed upon himself this rule of holy service: to offer daily, at each hour, vows of praise to the blessed Mother of God.

When scarcely anyone had any confidence in his life remaining, and as though his spirit were about to leave his breast, it anxiously fluttered, behold, the glorious Mother of God visibly stood beside him. Pressing milk from the nipple of her sacred breast, she dripped it upon his lips. Immediately, through the antidote of divine power, he recovered strength and was restored from his illness.

Soon afterward, dressed in clerical vestments, he went to the church and joyfully joined himself to the choir of singing brothers, presenting a wondrous spectacle to those who saw him. It is also said that traces of milk could still be seen upon his lips.

Although I have been told, in some fashion, what words the Blessed Virgin spoke to him, I do not place faith in them, since I am not certain of them; for I fear even slightly striking against the line of truth. Yet from this it may be inferred that, with the same lips with which he had praised and honored her, the glorious Virgin milked the milk of salvation for him, so that through that bodily member with which the venerable cleric had offered her the glory of praise, he might, in fitting reciprocity, receive the medicine of restored health.

It seemed necessary, moreover, to suggest to your holy prudence that the page of Sacred Scripture should always be in your hands. Be wholly occupied with it; linger over it; continually rest in it. Nor should you take pleasure in mingling conversation with worldly people, since such conversation often strikes back at and confuses the vision of a mind seeking God. Let your mind occupy itself with the divine books; intent upon them, let it persevere always with wakeful diligence.

When the ancient tempter sees you intent upon these things, he flees like an armed enemy and fears to attack you at close quarters, until he sees you fortified with these weapons and, so to speak, with an impenetrable cuirass. My Exadelphus, the same man mentioned above, related that he had learned this from a trustworthy report. A certain Northman, while possessing a considerable hoard of gold and attempting to return to the place from which he had originated, began to fear equally for his property and his life—[the passage is corrupt: “locus, cor.”]—lest, if he travelled burdened with it, he should encounter an attack of unjust robbery.

While he was anxiously turning this over in sustained meditation, now travelling and now not travelling, wavering amid various deliberations, and Saturday evening was already approaching, the ancient enemy appeared to him in the guise of a traveller. Having learned his desire by questioning him, he agreed with his future companion on a payment of ten bezants, and thus promised to be both his guide on the journey and the guarantor of unquestionable security.

“On the following night,” he said, “gather together your little bundles of belongings, rest, and await me without doubt, so that I may come to you in the silence of night; and, when I have found you, we shall both set out on the journey together.”

The man believed the words of his speaker and, surrendering himself to sleep, waited as he had been instructed. That same night the shape-shifting spirit came to him as it had promised and said: “Behold, without any effort on your part, I have brought you back to your homeland without your knowledge, and I have not been slow to fulfil what I promised you.”

When the man found himself beside a certain stream that he had formerly known very well, and unexpectedly and suddenly recognized the neighboring places as having been revisited by this return, he was shaken with fear. He recognized without doubt that this was the malignant spirit which had transported him so suddenly from distant regions.

Then the spirit, deceitfully truthful—or rather, truthfully deceitful—said to him: “See that you do not neglect to come here to me next Thursday and pay the debt of my stipulated payment.”

Having heard this, the man hurried to a certain priest and reported in order everything that had happened to him. He also carefully asked what he ought to do concerning the debt mentioned above. The priest sprinkled him with sanctified water, fortified him beforehand with certain sacred writings and the patronage of the saints, and, sending him back to the appointed place, ordered him to take the agreed amount of the debt—not to hand it over to the most wicked collector, but to throw it into his mouth.

When both had met one another at the appointed place, and the man scattered the bezants into the air, saying, “Take your debt,” the devil stood at a distance, afraid to come nearer. He began to complain and protest bitterly, saying: “You come armed against me; girded with weapons and swords, you confront me as though you were about to fight. Where is your faith? Since I dare not come near you, I shall depart frustrated of my payment.” Then he stirred up the dark air in a whirlwind and, with a great rush of fury, vanished from the sight of the terrified man.

The man immediately gathered the gold from the ground as it lay there and, returning again to the priest, earnestly asked what he should do with it. The priest severely rebuked him for collecting the bezants, but nevertheless gave him this advice: that he should use them to build a bridge at a particularly necessary place, one that would serve the needs of travellers.

He humbly obeyed the priest’s words and built the bridge as he had been ordered. But whatever he constructed by laboring with stonecutters and masons, the devil violently buried and destroyed during the silence of night. The aforesaid man attempted to rebuild it as many as three or four times, it is said. But whatever he had constructed on the preceding day with no small labor, he found destroyed on the following day by the devil’s nocturnal machinations.

To omit the other examples of this, if the man who possessed the sacred writings and the relics of the saints appeared armed and terrifying in the eyes of the ancient enemy, so that the enemy could neither approach nor draw near him, with what diligence ought we to gird ourselves with the weapons of heavenly speech, so that we may triumph over malignant spirits in an unrelenting struggle? The Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one, and take up the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6).

Therefore, beloved, always gird yourself with this sword, so that the cunning tempter may be pierced and perish, and Christ may stand victorious within you, as in the most strongly fortified bulwark of his camps.

## LETTER XXX. TO TEUZON, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF FLORENCE OF ST. MARY

(It is found in volume III and is opusculum 51.)

## LETTER XXXI. TO DOMINICUS LORICATUS, PRIOR OF ST. MARY OF SITRIA, AND TO HIS HERMIT BROTHERS

[Col. 0422B]

(It is found in volume III and is opusculum 53.)

## LETTER XXXII. TO HIS HERMIT BROTHERS OF THE MONASTERY OF GAMUGNO OF ST. BARNABAS

### Argument

He rebukes the monks living in the hermitage of the neighboring mountain because they completely neglected and violated certain rules he had established in their monastery, and because in some worldly matters they caused scandal. He also severely reproves them because they were too desirous of earthly riches and used more delicate foods than suited their strict manner of life. Finally, he shows, by the unhappy end of certain monks, how great must be the caution used in uprooting things rightly established by their predecessors.

[Col. 0422C]

Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings to the brothers established in the hermitage of Gamugno.

“‘A wise son,’ says Solomon, ‘makes his father glad, but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother’ (Proverbs 10).” He also says: “‘He who gathers in harvest is a wise son; but he who snores in summer is a son of confusion’ (ibid.).”

Why I say this I shall explain. A certain man, setting out from the city of Milan while seeking me, passed through your midst; indeed, as he himself admitted, he desired to live with you under that name. While, tired from his journey, he prolonged his stay as though resting, yet did not keep his eyes closed to the observation of your conduct, he noticed—I do not know which of you—spouting childish old men’s chatter and idle nonsense, and he saw you mingling vulgar jokes and urban mockeries with laymen.

As a result, he not only despised us and all our fellowship on your account, but also, as far as he could, completely lost the intention of conversion itself. Clearly, our life bears fruit in such a way that it not only continually turns aside from the path of justice through winding ways and trackless places, but also, through examples of its perversity, drives people away from entering the worship of God.

We pay sufficient and vigilant attention to what we hear in the prophet’s reproachful threat: “Through you the name of God is blasphemed” (Isaiah 52; Romans 2). We also hear what Scripture testifies concerning the sons of Eli: “The sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, because men withdrew from the sacrifice of the Lord” (1 Samuel 2).

There are, moreover, very many who are tossed about in the turbulent world as in the storms and waves of a foaming sea, so that unless they make their way to the quiet harbor of this sacred order, they have no confidence that they can escape the shipwreck of their salvation by any means. How great, then, is the guilt of the man who, under the appearance of the sacred habit, through negligence of the profession he has undertaken, presents himself in such a way that, by living perversely, he disturbs those who are seeking to approach?

The Gospel sentence certainly applies to him: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18). For it would have been more tolerable for him alone to be whirled about in the turning world he had abandoned than for him now to turn many back from approaching the station of salvation.

If, then, our life appears so perverse and filthy that it stinks even to men clothed in flesh, what do you suppose it is to the angels, who continually stand at the summit of spiritual purity? What is it to God, who surpasses even the dignity of the angels? Therefore we must also consider with fear lest the angels appointed to guard us be offended by the stench of our life, so that they may be more inclined to complain against us before God than to protect us by their testimony.

It has also come to our knowledge, as an addition to the praises of your holiness, that many chapters concerning the discipline of continence, which we regularly established among you, have now been handed over to oblivion—as though they had been entrusted to the forgetfulness of some madman. Namely: that wine should not be drunk during either of the two Lenten periods; that no fish should be eaten; that legumes should not be ground in the mill except on the principal feast days; that no stew should be prepared for the evening meal; that frying in olive oil should be permitted only very rarely; and many similar matters, which we decided should be observed rather than written down.

Nor is it surprising that this is now presumed, with me away, when, as it happened, even on the very Nativity of the Lord, while I was present but unaware of it, mulsum was prepared with honey and various kinds of spices. When I learned of this, I was struck with horror all the more because of the novelty of the prodigy, since until then it had not even happened that I should hear of such a thing being done in the hermitage.

In saying these things, however, let no one suppose that we agree with those who prohibit foods that God created (1 Corinthians 10), or that we oppose the apostolic sentence which commands us to eat whatever is set before us and to reject nothing that is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4). For it is one thing to assert that God’s creatures are good without distinction; it is another to provide for the preservation of chastity and sobriety through the disciplining of the body.

The tree in paradise was good, for it had been created by the good Artificer; nevertheless, eating it was not good, since the same Artificer had imposed the command (Genesis 2). But when what was good was not rightly joined to what was good, death immediately arose from the poisonous seed of pride. What had been good by nature became evil through the guilt of disobedience; and what had been salutarily forbidden by the Creator became deadly to man through the exercise of usurped freedom.

This sin of the first man, my brothers—to speak with your peace—you do not cease to repeat even today, if through the itching of enticing allure you taste what has been forbidden to you. Whenever the hand of disobedience is stretched toward this food, without doubt the guilt of the first parent is repeated, and the seed of the stock consequently breaks forth into the branches. Thus, as the vein flows, the stream corresponds to the spring and the course to its origin.

This also moves me no less: having crossed the boundary of disobedience, you accept alms from secular people indiscriminately, greedily extend the cords of your possessions, and, to sum everything up in a brief statement, hasten to become rich both secretly and publicly.

By doing these things, you tear us apart with the bitterest impulses of foul desire.
