You deprive not only yourselves but also your successors of the sweetness of quiet; you bind yourselves with the snares of worldly cares; and, worst of all, you establish the material for perpetual combat with secular people—or rather, for serving them. You do not consider what the eminent preacher says to true renouncers: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into the snares of the devil and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and perdition” (1 Timothy 6).

There he continues: “The root of all evils is avarice; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows” (ibid.).

Indeed, to receive gifts or offerings from an evil person—what is it other than to stain one’s own soul with the filth of the giver? Hence it is written: “The offering of one who sacrifices from what is unjust is defiled, and the mockeries of the wicked are not pleasing” (Ecclesiasticus 34). And again: “The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked, nor does he look upon the offerings of the wicked; he will not be propitiated for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices” (ibid.).

And truly, what benefit is there in building up a righteous person by prayer, if a wicked person hastens to destroy him by living perversely? Hence the same Wise Man says: “One builds and another destroys; what do they gain except labor? One prays and another curses; whose voice will God hear?” (ibid.)

Moreover, why do we accumulate the profits of riches? Is it because, since nature—content with little—prevents us from spending them for our own needs, we anxiously and continually seek those upon whom they might be squandered? Meanwhile, by gazing upon them we feed only the allurements of our unhappy eyes, since we cannot turn them toward the expenses of our own necessity.

Thus, when Solomon had said: “The miser is not filled with money, and he who loves riches gains no fruit from them” (Ecclesiastes 5), he immediately added: “Where there are many riches, there are also many who consume them. And what benefit does the possessor receive except that he sees his riches with his eyes?” (ibid.)

But let the monks hear that riches bring anxiety to their possessors and do not permit them to rest securely. Their profession certainly serves not anxiety but quiet: “Sweet is sleep to the laborer, whether he eats much or little. But the abundance of the rich does not permit him to sleep” (Ecclesiastes 5).

Furthermore, even if a person does not seize violently or secretly, and even if he deceives no one by lying or fraud, he nevertheless does not sin lightly if he simply desires another’s property. Hence, too, among the catalogue of the Ten Commandments it is written: “You shall not desire your neighbor’s property” (Deuteronomy 6).

What guilt is involved in coveting what belongs to another is clearly shown—leaving aside many other considerations—by one example from blessed Peter: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a slanderer, or one who covets what belongs to others” (1 Peter 2). By placing the coveter of another’s possessions among murderers, thieves, and slanderers, who certainly do not possess the kingdom of God, he plainly shows by comparison with such people how grave and condemnable this crime is.

This becomes even clearer if what follows these words is carefully considered. For he immediately added: “But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this name, because it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God” (ibid.).

Therefore, when we speak of those who covet what belongs to others, the person who suffers anxiety because he longs for other people’s possessions suffers not as a Christian but, without doubt, as an Antichrist. Christ came to give himself and heavenly glory; but the Antichrist, when he comes, attempts to take away human souls, that is, their precious substance.

If, then, the person who covets what belongs to another is not a Christian, by what reasoning should he be called a monk?

Nevertheless, it must be noted that anyone who takes something from men—not criminals but honorable men—for this purpose, namely, to provide assistance to brothers in need, or to supply the expense of some pious work, or, what is more distinguished, to assist the poor in their necessity, should not be said impudently to covet what belongs to another. Rather, he justly transfers what is held in common from brothers to brothers.

For this reason one person is richer than the others: not merely so that he may possess what has been entrusted to him, but so that he may distribute it to those who have nothing. As a minister, not a master, he dispenses what belongs to others—not merely piously but justly.

Thus, when the Prophet said, “He distributed; he gave to the poor” (Psalm 111), he did not add, “his gifts,” but rather: “His righteousness remains forever and ever” (ibid.). Likewise, when the Lord spoke about giving alms, he said: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6). That he especially wishes the giving of alms to be understood here as righteousness, he himself indicates when he immediately adds: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet” (ibid.).

Thus it is righteousness to return what belongs to others. Therefore, the person who takes from the rich and gives to the needy should not be called one who covets what belongs to others, but rather a distributor of goods held in common.

[Note: The holy Doctor uses the verb *aufero*—“to take away”—to mean receiving something not from unwilling rich people, but from those who themselves wish it to be received. For he contrasts good rich men with wicked rich men: from the latter, whose gifts he had forbidden to be accepted, he permits gifts from the former to be accepted for the benefit of the poor.]

We have said these things briefly in order to show the difference between coveters of what belongs to others and faithful distributors, lest someone at some point conceal his vice under the guise of virtue, or, conversely, the purity of genuine virtue be obscured by a false name of vice.

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, would certainly not have incurred the sentence of leprosy if, by receiving talents of silver—as he lied, allegedly for the sons of the prophets—he had been seeking their welfare. He was struck with the plague that the giver had escaped because he did not accept what belonged to another in order to spend it on a work of piety, but in order to satisfy his own desire and possess the money as his personal property.

Therefore, after the man of God had deservedly rebuked him, saying: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?” (2 Kings 5), he immediately added: “Now, therefore, you have received silver and garments, so that you may buy olive groves, vineyards, sheep, cattle, male servants, and female servants. But the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your offspring forever” (ibid.).

The offspring of Gehazi are those who preserve for themselves, to their own future harm, what they had received for expenditure on a work of piety. For a posterity answering to an ignoble and degenerate parent is covered with the leprosy of another’s crime, when it attempts to transfer heavenly resources into its own profits.

Nor should what is said there be passed over: “And Gehazi went out from him leprous, white as snow” (ibid.). Snow is white but cold. So too the hypocrite, who transforms himself into an angel of light through the fiction of an outward appearance of holiness, burns with no heat of charity. Like snow, he is at once white and cold: he pretends to devote himself to works of piety, but he knows nothing of the inward substance of steadfast piety.

Why should I mention more? I spoke when present; I speak now when absent, yet in both circumstances I bring the matter to completion: Despise riches, lest you beg forever. Be voluntarily poor, so that you may reign without end. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5; Luke 6). Solomon also says: “He who hates avarice will have long days” (Proverbs 28). And again: “Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance, but righteousness will deliver from death” (Proverbs 11). [The printed text reads *tristitia*—“sorrow”—but the context and parallel tradition require *justitia*, “righteousness.”] And again: “Better is the poor man in his simplicity than the rich man in his crooked ways” (Proverbs 28). And elsewhere: “The man who hastens to become rich and envies others does not know that poverty will overtake him” (ibid.).

Let discipline, moreover, restrain the itching of gluttony with a bridle. For he attempts in vain to build a summit who places his foundation on shifting sand. Whoever hastens to construct a lofty hall with the stones of virtues must first clear away the bristling thickets of carnal pleasures.

Hence Solomon says: “Cultivate your field diligently, so that afterward you may build your house” (Proverbs 24). He builds the house of the mind well who first clears the field of the body of the thorns of vices. Otherwise, if the prickles of carnal desires and passions are allowed to sprout in the field of the flesh, as the hunger for goodness grows, the entire structure of the virtues collapses within.

Again he says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, it was completely filled with nettles; thorns had covered its surface, and the stone wall had been destroyed” (ibid.).

What is the field or vineyard of a lazy man except the flesh of anyone who is unwilling to sweat in the labors of spiritual cultivation? What are the nettles except the itchings of gluttony and carnal allurements? What, finally, are the thorns except the stings of carnal passions? And what is the stone wall except the structure of virtues that adhere together through charity?

The field of a lazy and foolish man is therefore filled with nettles and thorns when the flesh of someone living idly is not cultivated through the discipline of continual labor, but is softened and nourished in the desire for pleasure and wantonness. The wall of stones also collapses when it is weakened, because the entire edifice of virtues is scattered as though battered by the rams of incontinence.

The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem. The chief of the cooks is rightly understood as the belly, since the cooks serve it with laborious effort. Whoever therefore desires to grow rich in the abundance of spiritual crops should now sweat over the field of his body, furrowing it with the plow of discipline and continence through constant labor. Like the clods of his fallow land, let him break it with a wise hoe [or “with a scraping tool,” according to the printed variant *sarriente*]. Whatever he finds sterile within himself, let him wear down through continual blows of penitence. Let him never cease to uproot completely the nettles of itching gluttony and the bristling hedges of carnal desires, so that the fields of his heart may produce abundant harvests of spiritual grain.

Hence the same Solomon says: “He who cultivates his land will be filled with bread; he who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty” (Proverbs 12).

Joshua also urged the sons of Joseph toward this cultivation through allegorical exhortations: “If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and cut out spaces for yourself in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, because the possession of Mount Ephraim is too narrow for you” (Joshua 17).

When they complained there and said: “We cannot go up to the mountains, because the Canaanites who inhabit the level country use iron chariots,” Joshua replied: “You are a numerous people and of great strength; you shall not have one lot only, but you shall pass to the mountain and cut down and clear spaces for yourself in order to inhabit them. You will be able to proceed farther when you have overthrown the Canaanite whom you say has iron chariots and is very strong” (ibid.).

I might perhaps explain these matters at length, since they require many words, if the limit of epistolary brevity did not stand in my way. Let this brief treatment, as though touching the matter only from above, suffice: when Joshua commands the people to cut down the dense growth of the forests, he indicates that our Jesus, who bears the same name, commands those who follow him to uproot the badly growing shoots of forest-like vices.

He urges them to wage not treaties but war against the Canaanites, to climb the mountains, so that they may labor to conquer the barbarism of vices and hasten to attain the lofty summit of virtues.

When they faintheartedly complain that they cannot rise against those who use iron chariots, this means that we, weak and fragile, often despair of enduring the attacks of malignant spirits that oppose us like iron chariots. For when the insolence of gluttony, the gulf of lust, and the plagues of every vice gather against us like the tightly packed ranks of roaring Canaanites, what else is happening than that the Canaanites attack us with iron chariots and block the paths of salvation, lest we be able to climb from the level ground of carnal life to the heights of virtue?

But the good commander of our warfare raises our weakness to steadfastness in action and drives us forward against the attacks of our enemies, so that we may advance to higher things.

How, however, can we gain a triumph over our enemies if we always want to lie at feasts and always gorge ourselves on an abundance of cups? Concerning such people Solomon says: “He who loves feasting will be in poverty; he who loves wine and rich foods will not become rich” (Proverbs 21). And again: “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous; whoever delights in these will not be wise” (Proverbs 20).

To accustom the belly to wine and feasts—what else is this than to open an entrance for the enemies of the soul, so that they may enter? Hence the same Solomon says: “He who pampers his servant from childhood will afterward find him rebellious” (Proverbs 29).

Paul kept this servant well restrained with the cords of fasting when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9). He argued against this servant when he said: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians 6). He showed that this servant must be restrained under the heel when he said: “For many walk—of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears—as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3).

It must also be noted here that two terrifying things are being said, and that the same Apostle expresses a dreadful judgment against an enemy of the cross of Christ when he says: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: Maranatha” (1 Corinthians 16). Whoever venerates the belly as God is thereby shown in a certain sense to deny God. Thus these two things appear full of terror: namely, God forbid, to be both an enemy of Christ and a worshipper of another god.

Two brothers, one young and the other old, were staying in charge of a property of the monastery of Classis called the Ravenna property. Eight days before the Nativity of the Lord, on Friday—the day that customarily precedes the Saturday of the twelve readings—the young man said to the elder, whose name was Leo: “Brother Leo, how shall we live today?”

The old man replied: “Live as you wish. For I shall both drink wine and shall not live on bread alone, as it is written” (Deuteronomy 8; Matthew 8).

He was vigorous, stout, healthy, and robust. When the table had been set, both reclined at it. The young man, content with bread and water, restrained himself by the discipline of the regular fast; the old man allowed himself wine and, in addition, whatever else seemed appropriate.

If he had recognized what was impending, he certainly would not have softened the rigor of abstinence into an enticement to wanton gluttony. On the eighth day, when the glory of the Lord’s Nativity shone forth and the world rejoiced, he died. While the joy of the festival invited and drew the others to the table, he was carried out for burial, with his fleshly relatives weeping everywhere.

A certain monk told me that, while he was carrying some fried foods in a little vessel to the refectory, the sting of itching gluttony pricked him, and he immediately threw one into his mouth and secretly ate it. At once such a great heat of lust seized him that he could not restrain himself by any means, though he had never before done such a thing, until he had discharged the flow of impurity with his own hands.

Thus he rightly experienced his servant as rebellious, because, according to the saying of the wise man, he had nourished it gently (Proverbs 29). Of him it can rightly be said that “after the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John 13). The belly and the genitals are naturally close to one another; when the one is refreshed in the flesh, the other is aroused to acts of shame.

Therefore let avarice be extinguished, so that we may be free from worldly things and live in quiet. Let the voracity of gluttony be restrained, so that we may be conspicuously victorious in sincere chastity. Let no idle words flow from our mouths; rather, let the strict judgment of divine fear always restrain us from everything superfluous.

Let us therefore be ashamed to yield disgracefully in the encounter of this inward war when our adversaries attack. Instead, let us strive to carry back to the Author of all things the trophies and emblems of triumph and glory.

Furthermore, the fact that certain practices, as was said above, were regularly established by us among you but have now been handed over to oblivion and negligently omitted both aggravates us with no slight sorrow and accuses you of no small offense.

What was once approved for admission by my direction ought never to have been violated without my consent. Whatever is established by public judgment among many must either be observed by everyone, or, if it should be appropriate to violate it, be reconsidered by common judgment. Otherwise, if it is broken at the discretion of any individual, it deserves to be punished with severe correction.

Achan, son of Carmi, because, contrary to the common command, he did not restrain his hand from the anathema of Jericho, did not escape the burning of fire after the casting of stones (Joshua 7). He had been inflamed by the torches of avarice; therefore, in the punishment of vengeance, he also fed the flames with his own flesh.

Jonathan deserved the sentence of death because he changed a decree issued for the community by anticipating the appointed time for eating (1 Samuel 14). The man who presumed, in the wilderness, to gather wood on the Sabbath was stoned and, because he alone transgressed the common command, alone underwent the punishment deserving death (Numbers 15). It was not because gathering wood in a time of necessity is a crime, but because it is no slight crime to violate through disobedience a rule once established by decree.

To provide an example from our own household as well: in the monastery of blessed Vincent, which is situated not far from the mountain called Petra Pertusa, we had established this as a rule: that the beginning of Lent should be observed under the strict judgment of rigor. For three days all the brothers were to eat nothing but a small amount of bread with water; no words were to be spoken except words of readings or of the offices; they were to walk barefoot, in mourning and sorrow; and, after completing the common chanting of the Psalter, they were to cleanse themselves by mutual correction with brooms.

The brothers carried this out diligently, with vow, intention, and spiritual joy, and even went beyond what had been prescribed, doing more than enough from the treasury of good will. Yet one among them arose who secretly violated the rule while eating.

He was a brother gifted in many kinds of practical exercises: writing and notation, turning on the lathe, and also fabrication, so that the following saying seemed in a certain way to fit him:

“Augur, rope-walker, physician, magician—he knows everything.”

As usually happens with such men, because he was supported by expertise in many necessities, whatever he wished was for the most part permitted with impunity.

When Lent was already halfway over, he appeared in every respect vigorous, stout, cheerful, and robust. Suddenly he was overtaken by a mild and moderate illness. When I came to visit him, it occurred to me to tell him what I had happened to hear: that, because of certain offenses, he ought not to minister at the holy altars.

Fearing to exasperate him, I hesitated for a long time and deliberated even longer. What more is there to say? At last I hardened my face, judging and deciding that it was safer to offend a man than the majesty of almighty God.

I therefore said to him: “Dearest brother Maure”—for that was his name—“confess, do penance, and if there is anything in you that perhaps prevents you from the fearful celebration of Mass, let not your venerable brotherhood disdain to obey the sacred canons.”

He replied: “I have made all my sins known to very many spiritual men, but I have not received an order to withdraw from the ministry of offering sacrifice.”

On the second day of his illness, scarcely at dawn, behold, though he was not lying down but sitting on his little bed, he anxiously demanded the sacrament of the Lord’s Body. When the abbot was present with us and with the other brothers, sitting beside the bed, he began to rebuke him: why was a man who showed no signs of death asking so insistently for viaticum?

Nevertheless, the man persisted in his request. When the priest was already approaching with the ministers, the sick man drew one of the brothers close to him and whispered some grave sin into his ear.

The brother was immediately struck with astonishment. As he later reported to me, he did not know so suddenly what definite measure of penance to impose. Though uncertain, he spoke quietly into the man’s ear and imposed fifteen years of penance upon him.

As soon as the sick man received the most holy mystery from the priest’s hand—alas, woe! I shudder to report it—he breathed out his soul together with bile. The bile did not cease to flow from his mouth until his burial, so that, while the corpse lay lifeless in the coffin, that continual discharge kept wetting the church pavement farther and farther.

We have taken care to report this in accordance with the truth of the matter so that not only those who break a prescribed rule of discipline through impatience with their own pleasure may hear and fear, but also those who nurse an admitted crime at the breasts of their conscience and wait until death to confess it. The former are guilty because they postpone what must be observed; the latter undoubtedly pay in the next life, with interest increased, the debt of the penance they do not discharge here.

I shall also relate another event that occurred in the monastery mentioned above. It had been established and was observed for nearly three years that, together with the canonical hours, the offices of Blessed Mary, ever-virgin, should be recited daily. Among them was Gozo, a monk by his habit, indeed of disreputable life, but of fluent and precise speech. He began to complain that what Saint Benedict commands is always sufficient, that no burden of novel invention ought to be imposed, and that we are not holier than the ancient Fathers, who, judging such practices superstitious and superfluous, prescribed for us the whole measure of psalmody and the entire rule of life; surely we ought to be content with this, lest, imprudently turning aside from it, we wander through winding and impassable paths.

What more need be said? [Col. 0431C] He appeared to wage war against the Queen of the world and brought the matter to completion. By crafty contrivance he enticed the brothers to cease offering the customary praises of Blessed Mary. But, O divine judgment, which does not sleep when it observes our perversity! Immediately there arose against the aforesaid monastery such hailstorms of adversity and such storms of wars and conflicts on every side that threatening swords of death daily menaced the monks themselves. Plunderings and robberies took place everywhere; threshing floors were burned together with the crops; the retainers and servants of the holy place were cruelly slaughtered; and it was no longer the image of death but death itself that raged. The monks had grown so weary of living that, amid the imminence of conflict, they could by no means preserve the congenial duty of their peaceful profession.

[Col. 0431D] At great expense an appeal was made to the emperor in the German regions, and pragmatic sanctions were brought with individual imperial seals attached; but it amounted to nothing. For in all these efforts there was not fruit, but useless labor. Therefore, when I was often pressed by the brothers’ requests to intervene and, if possible, restore the bonds of peace among them, I answered those who asked me in these words:

“Christ,” I said, “is our peace; and of him, newly born from the Virgin, it was also said by the angels: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace’ (Luke II). Since, therefore, they have cast the mother of true peace out of their monastery, it is fitting that they should be shaken by the restless storms and whirlwinds of calamities and tribulations.”

But, not to detain the reader longer, [Col. 0432A] those brothers, recognizing that what I had said was true through unmistakable signs that broke forth, and at last brought to their senses by their desperate situation, prostrated themselves humbly on the pavement. Having accepted penance, they unanimously promised that henceforth they would never neglect the customary praises of the Mother of God.

Immediately, then—to speak frankly—after the flashes and thunder, such calmness of sky returned that from that time until today the brothers have enjoyed the leisure of a joyful peace and have rejoiced that, under the guidance of the Virgin’s Son, they had been carried from the Scylla-like abyss to harbor. Thus was fulfilled what is said through the prophet: “Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord” (Malachi III). Let those who easily tear down the statutes of their elders consider this, and let them fear, not without reason, lest the sword of divine fury come upon them.

[Col. 0432B] Spare my mouth, dearest brothers; and if perhaps in some respect I have exceeded the bounds of moderate correction, attribute it rather to the zeal of fraternal love than to ill will. Remember what is said through Solomon: “Open correction is better than hidden love; the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates” (Proverbs XXVII); and again: “Sudden destruction will overtake the man who stubbornly despises the one correcting him, and healing will not follow him” (Proverbs XXIX).

May almighty God, the physician of souls, dearest brothers, turn this wormwood of my speech into sweetness for you, and may the wondrous flame of his Spirit illuminate and kindle whatever in you is cold and whatever is obscure.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO THE SAME HERMIT MONKS OF THE GAMUGNENSE MONASTERY

[Col. 0432C]

(It is found in volume III and is treatise 54.)

## LETTER XXXIV. TO THE HERMIT MONKS OF HIS CONGREGATION

### Summary

He prescribes for all the hermits who follow his way of life the measure of discipline to be imposed, beyond which they may not proceed. He establishes that henceforth this discipline is to be voluntary, according to each person’s judgment, and not, as previously, compulsory.

To the holy brothers established in the desert, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings.

Among spiritual brothers, the order of discretion is properly maintained when the superior’s moderation imitates the diligence of a horseman. The latter uses spurs to drive forward and reins to hold back; he urges on the horse that proceeds too slowly and restrains with the bridle the steps of the one that advances while snorting proudly. In the same way, the superior of the brothers ought to drive on those who are slower with his exhortations, as with certain spurs, and to restrain with the rein of discretion those who proceed more fervently than is necessary.

Did not Moses urge the people of Israel with certain, so to speak, spurs when he said: “Set aside among yourselves first fruits for the Lord; let every willing person, and everyone of ready mind, offer them to the Lord: gold, silver, bronze, violet, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, acacia wood, and oil for preparing the lamps” (Exodus XXXV)? Did he not restrain that same people, running as though without measure, with the bridle of moderation when he prohibited them from offering gifts?

For it is written: “While they were urging on the work, the people were bringing offerings every morning” (Exodus XXXV). Therefore the craftsmen were compelled to come and say to Moses: “The people are offering more than is necessary.” Then it immediately adds: “So Moses ordered this proclamation to be made by the herald: ‘Let neither man nor woman offer anything further for the work of the sanctuary’” (ibid.).

[Col. 0433A] To come, then, to the matter for which we have offered these preliminary examples: let your holy devotion, dearest brothers, not be unaware that this discipline of scourging, which you pursue so fervently, is recognized as capable of doing good when moderated, but of doing harm when indiscreet. For this reason your bodies, exhausted of strength, grow weak; and sometimes, as some believe, they languish, worn away by so many blows—especially since certain of you go through one complete psalter, or even two, every day with the discipline.

Moreover, many brothers who wish to come to the desert are deterred by fear when they hear of these practices. Since this discipline is believed to be harsher than it is felt and inspires greater fear than pain, whenever weak brothers hear that it is so prolonged among you, they tremble to the marrow and are immediately called back from approaching the desert.

Therefore, having applied the moderation of discretion, we establish that no one in the desert is to be compelled to undertake the discipline upon himself. Whoever, however, is impelled to it by holy fervor may perform the discipline upon himself for forty psalms each day, provided only that he does not exceed this number of forty psalms.

[Col. 0433B] During the two Lents—that is, those preceding the Nativity of the Lord and the most holy Easter—it may proceed as far as sixty psalms with the discipline; and let no one, God forbid, presume rashly to exceed this rule of the measure we prescribe.

In this way, then, we do not remove what is good, but restrain what is excessive. Nor do we begrudge the brothers their salvation; rather, we impose a measure of discretion, below which it is certainly permissible for anyone who wishes to afflict himself, but beyond which it will not be permissible to proceed.

In doing this, we do not arrogate to ourselves the authority of personal judgment, but imitate the example of divine law. For through Moses in Deuteronomy the Lord says: “But if they judge the one who has sinned worthy of lashes, they shall throw him down and have him beaten in their presence” (Deuteronomy XXV). [Col. 0433C] Immediately it is added: “The measure of the punishment shall correspond to the measure of the sin, provided only that they do not exceed the number of forty, lest your brother, disgracefully torn, perish before your eyes” (ibid.).

Behold: the Lord both commanded the offender to be beaten and nevertheless set a limit to the blows, so that punishment might proceed against the guilty person while discretion tempered the severity of the punishment. Hold fast, therefore, dearest brothers, to this measure for carrying out the discipline; chastise the spirit rather, and devote yourselves vigilantly to the other good works, so that the supreme Rewarder may deign to repay your transitory labor with rewards that endure without end.

## LETTER XXXV. TO THE SAME HERMIT MONKS OF HIS CONGREGATION

(It is found in volume III and is treatise 55.)

## LETTER XXXVI. TO ALL THE HERMIT MONKS OF HIS CONGREGATION

[Col. 0434B]

### Summary

He commands, under penalty of excommunication, that the monks who lived in monasteries established under his authority should not retain with themselves after his death property belonging to others, but that each should restore his own goods to the monastery to which they belong.

To all the brothers established in any desert under the protection of our ministry, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the bond of undivided charity.

You know, dearest brothers, that these places entrusted to us are, while I live, as one; and whatever things are necessary pass indiscriminately from here to you. From you, too, as fraternal unanimity requires, things are brought here. And I pray the Holy Spirit that, when I am dead, the same harmony may prevail among you which now fuses you into one heart and one soul through the bond of charity.

But now I must prudently make provision for you, lest, if charity should perhaps grow cold, private affection over the retention of some object should be able to generate scandal among you. Therefore we adjure you and beseech you by the tribunal of the dread Judge: whatever each of you may happen to find in his possession after my death that belongs to another place, let him restore it at once; and, removing every scheme and crafty argument, let him return purely and simply what belongs to another.

By “belonging to another,” I mean whatever I did not give to be held perpetually as a gift, but allowed to remain in one place as the property of another place, because both places were ours. Whoever, therefore, proves to be a violator of this judgment of ours shall remain subject to excommunication until he has made suitable satisfaction.

# BOOK SEVEN. TO SECULAR PRINCES

[Col. 0433]

## LETTER I. TO HENRY II, EMPEROR

[Col. 0433D]

### Summary

He entreats Emperor Henry to pardon a certain Gislerius, who was being held captive in Germany at his command, as he had promised him while he was in Italy, and to permit him to depart free.

To Lord Henry, unconquered emperor, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of due obedience.

Most excellent and most pious lord, if it pleased you, the time would now have come for that wretched Gislerius to obtain mercy; it would now be fitting for him to leave the bonds of such prolonged captivity and, after a long exile, return to his own country.

Let my lord the emperor not forget what King David did when he was fleeing from the face of Absalom. For while Shimei was throwing stones at him and hurling still harsher darts of cursing against the king, saying, “Go out, go out, man of blood and man of Belial” (2 Samuel XVI), David, though advancing surrounded by such powerful troops of warriors, not only did not kill him but also severely rebuked Abishai, who wished to kill him, saying: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him alone, that he may curse me. The Lord has commanded him to curse David; and who is there to dare say, ‘Why has he done so?’” (ibid.).

Nor are you unaware how he spared foolish Nabal when Nabal said against him: “Today there are many servants who flee from their masters” (1 Samuel XXV), after Abigail intervened. You also know how, when Saul was savagely persecuting him and he could have killed him, he did not dare to lay a hand upon him (1 Samuel XXIV, XXVI).

Set these and other examples of holy kings before you, my lord, and after judgment show mercy to sinners. “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Romans XV).

And since, as the whole world bears witness, your most abundant piety fills all the kingdoms of the earth subject to your empire, how will Gislerius alone be deprived of such mercy, unable to find a place for pardon with you either through secular men or through the servants of God? Let the piety of the Roman Empire now shine forth; and may God’s mercy happily conquer even the one to whom God subjects all adversaries by his own strength. For this is perfect victory: that he to whom victory is granted by Christ’s gift should be conquered by Christ’s mercy alone.

Most pious lord, I implore your mercy with tears and, prostrate, throw myself at your feet. For the love of Christ, now mercifully release that wretched man, and allow me, your servant, to rest in peace and pray for your holy empire. But if this seems preferable to you, promise me by your letters, without any uncertainty, his release, and order me to hasten to you.

Let the king remember that when I was departing from you at the monastery of Classe, you said to me: “Know for certain that I shall at some point grant pardon to this man for whom you are pleading, and whatever I mercifully do concerning him, I shall most certainly do for the love of Christ and out of affection for you.”

Now, therefore, most eminent lord, mercifully extend your mercy to that most unfortunate man, and effectively fulfill for me, your servant, the truth of your holy mouth, for as the Prophet says: “God loves mercy and truth; may the Lord grant you grace and glory” (Psalm LXXXIII).

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME HENRY II, EMPEROR

[Col. 0436A]

### Summary

He praises the virtues of the same Henry, especially his piety and his zeal in protecting religion, because he expelled the barbarous Wiquerius from the archbishopric of Ravenna, which he had acquired wrongfully and was retaining still more wrongfully. He urges him not to allow this same man, who was attempting to return to the dignity from which he had justly been deprived, to do so in any way.

To Lord Henry, unconquered emperor, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of due obedience.

We offer immense praises to Christ, King of kings, because we now approve by living deeds, not merely by words, the holiness and gifts of virtue that we had learned from the reports of many concerning your royal majesty.

For at the expulsion of Wiquerius [also Widquerius], everyone’s voice is raised in praise of his Creator; the Church is rescued from the hand of a violent plunderer; and your safety is judged to be the salvation of the whole world. “Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult” (Psalm XCV), because Christ is recognized truly to reign in his king, and under him, now at the end of the age, the golden age of David is renewed.

For he who once drove from the temple those selling doves, making a whip from cords (Matthew XXI; Mark XI; Luke XIX; John II)—he, I say, and no other—has now overturned, in his king, the chair of Wiquerius, who was trafficking in the Church. And he who once rejected the arrogance of proud Saul (1 Samuel XIII; 1 Chronicles X) has now trampled underfoot the similar wickedness of a reprobate man.

Nevertheless, I do not want my lord the king to be unaware that this pestilential man composed letters to the city of Ravenna—some secretly to individuals, others openly to everyone—in which he promised that he would do whatever they themselves wished with the property of the Church. And if they did not believe his words, he ordered his messenger to swear accordingly.

Therefore I have no doubt that some of the Ravennese are urging your majesty to enable him to return to the same chair. The plunderers of the world who desire to seize ecclesiastical goods naturally want such a bishop, one who would not be able to oppose their robberies.

But you, most excellent lord, close your ears to their poisonous counsels, and do not allow the splendid fame of your glory, which flies throughout the breadth of the whole world, to be darkened on account of one man. For if he returns to the summit of the episcopate, the hope of the whole people, which had been raised up, will collapse; joy will be taken from the servants of God; and the wickedness of the depraved, which had already begun to fear, will be strengthened with confidence to dare worse things.

Therefore, unconquered king, carry through to the end what you began for the praise of God and the salvation of humanity. Reject the robber and appoint a shepherd in whom the Church may rejoice.

May almighty God, who grants the governance of earthly empire, preserve you for a long time in this life to do his justice, and after the course of mortal life lead you to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

## LETTER III. TO HENRY, SON OF HENRY II THE EMPEROR, KING OF THE ROMANS

[Col. 0437A]

### Summary

This letter was written to Henry, the son of the preceding Henry, who, after his father’s death, had not yet been called emperor but bore the royal title, which is the rank immediately preceding imperial dignity. At that time he was a young man, and his age was governed by certain chosen nobles of the highest rank. The holy teacher therefore attempts to urge this young man’s mind, as with certain spurs, to bring aid to the Church, which was being grievously afflicted by the fury of that most wicked pseudo-pontiff, Cadalo.

But because he had learned that this same Henry, both through the evil counsels of certain of his associates—who valued everything above honesty and piety—and also of his own accord, as later events revealed, was more inclined to defend the worse cause, he intersperses sharper and, so to speak, more bitter words among his gentler ones, so that one whom he could not recall to duty through shame he might at least recall through threats and fear.

To Lord Henry, most excellent king, Peter, a sinful monk, offers service.

Every subject fears the king; the king necessarily must fear the Creator. But since Scripture says, “From the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required” (Luke XII), it is especially necessary for the king to fear him who does not deceive himself about the secrets of the heart, because he is compelled to render an account for more things.

When, then, the king examines a man in judgment, God examines the king. Is it fitting that dust should fear dust, and that the same dust in the king should despise the divine majesty?

In your days, O king, a danger has arisen such as scarcely surpasses the wickedness of all the ages of the world: the apostolic see is being torn apart by the heresiarch [Note: [Col. 0437D] He means Cadalo.] of the Church of Parma; Christian religion is thrown into confusion; the labor of the apostles is overturned; and the universal splendor of the Church is darkened by the sinister desire of one schismatic man.

What will you say to this, you who exercise the duty of defending the Church, who succeed to the rights of your father’s or grandfather’s scepter? Do you perhaps complain that the strength of full maturity is still lacking in you?

But behold: Joash, king of Judah, while still a child, discusses with the priests the speedy restoration of the temple’s damaged roofs (2 Kings XII). He also forbids them to retain the money collected from the people and judges that it must all be handed over to the craftsmen for the work.

David, scarcely entering the threshold of adolescence, fights against Goliath not with a sword but with pebbles, almost like a child; yet, like a strong man, he cuts off his head with a sword-stroke (1 Samuel XVII). Josiah, still a young boy, casts all the vessels of Baal out of the temple of the Lord together with the priests and burns them in the valley of Kidron, where the flame consumes them (2 Kings XXIII).

They honored the temple in which the blood of brute animals was poured out; will you not come to the aid of the Church in which Christ’s body is offered for the salvation of the world?

To turn also to the history of the gentiles: that Hannibal who became commander of the Carthaginians, when he was still nine years old, swore to his father Hamilcar at the altars that, as soon as he first had the power, he would fight the Romans with the utmost ferocity (Livy, Third Decade, book I).

Feeble boys already breathe war for the honor of one earthly city; and you do not rouse yourself to battle for the defense of the liberty of the universal Church!

Furthermore, certain counselors of yours—administrators, that is, of your courtly service—are rejoicing, as a shameful rumor spreads among the people, over the persecution of the Roman Church. They flatter both parties and sing sweetly, so that at one moment they may claim through the enticement of flattery to be supporters of the venerable pope, and at another promise false successes joyfully to the firstborn of Satan.

Yet it is wicked to believe this of certain holy men who are accustomed to attend your councils. Clearly, whoever attempts to divide the holy Church must fear that, according to the evangelical sentence, he himself will be divided: “The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and he will divide him and assign him his portion with the unbelievers” (Luke XII).

Moreover, it is written of Peleg, son of Eber, that in his days the earth was divided (Genesis X). You too must beware lest it be said of you: “In your days the Church was divided.”

Let annals be written and history woven, saying that the most merciful emperor Nerva pacified the Church, Constantine confirmed it, Theodosius exalted it; and when they come to you, will it be glorious for you if it is said: “Henry divided it”? Far be this from you, so that posterity may not read such a history about you.

Do not therefore be Peleg, who divides what has been joined (Genesis X); be instead a disciple of Christ, who joins what has been divided. Let those who are inflamed by a diabolical impulse to divide the apostolic see recall Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, and let them infer from their destruction (Numbers XVI) what end also awaits those who pursue similar things.

They made a schism in the Synagogue; these are plotting division in the Church. Therefore, just as the earth swallowed those men alive, so these, knowingly and deliberately, are engulfed in Tartarus through the merit of schismatic wickedness.

Nor should those who do not openly create a schism in the Roman Church boast, while by acquiescing in and neglecting to resist those who divide it. For just as not only the one who said, “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne” (Isaiah XIV), but all his supporters as well were suddenly cast down from heaven, so not only Korah but also his accomplices—namely, two hundred and fifty men—were consumed by the fire of heaven.

[Col. 0438D] Therefore one must beware lest the wickedness of subjects overflow upon the king—even if he is not himself offending, yet is not doing everything in his power to prevent it. For it is a Gregorian maxim: “He bears the guilt of the deed who neglects to correct what he can.”

Beware, I say, O king, lest while you permit the priesthood to be divided, your own empire also, God forbid, be divided. For, as sacred history testifies, as soon as Saul seized the edge of Samuel’s cloak and tore it, Samuel immediately said to him: “Thus the Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you” (1 Samuel XV).

Moreover, just as that cloak was Samuel’s garment, so the holy Church is truly the garment of the Redeemer. To him it is said through the Prophet: “You have clothed yourself with confession and beauty” (Psalm CIII). The Lord clothes himself with confession when he joins sinners to himself after they have been healed through repentance; he puts on beauty when he mercifully attaches to himself the innocent, made splendid by the radiance of justice.

Saul tore Samuel’s cloak and lost the kingdom. Christ’s garment is being torn; and although you are not the one tearing it, will your empire stand when you permit it to be torn? The gentile soldier feared to tear Jesus’ seamless garment, yet Christians are not afraid to separate the Church through schismatic error?

Since, then, the Church is called Christ’s holy garment, the tearing of the garment threatens the division of royal power. Perhaps this is why we see the cities, towns, and provinces of this kingdom daily being seized by foreign nations.

Belshazzar, because he brought the vessels of the Lord to be defiled by the lips of gentiles, immediately heard from Daniel’s mouth: “Your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians” (Daniel V).

Eli was removed from the dignity of the priesthood because he did not inflict blows upon his sons but flattered them. He did rebuke them to some extent, but with a father’s gentleness, not with a pontiff’s severity (1 Samuel II); and for that reason he died with his neck broken (1 Samuel IV), because he indulged sinners without sternness.

The prophet Ahijah tore his cloak into twelve pieces and said to Jeroboam: “Take ten pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘Behold, I will tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and give you ten tribes’” (1 Kings XI).

The division of a garment therefore signifies the tearing apart of royal dominion. Since the Lord by no means fulfilled this during Solomon’s days, but this sentence took effect in his descendants, it is pious to believe concerning you, who are innocent, that the kingdom will remain intact for you; but after you, because of the merits of your subjects—unless perhaps they correct themselves—it will be transferred and surrendered to foreigners.

For as it is said through Daniel: “The Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wishes” (Daniel IV). The kingdoms of the Assyrians, the Lacedaemonians, and other peoples endured for fixed periods of time, nor could they extend the limit of their duration beyond what their annals testify was prescribed.

The Greeks at one time ruled this Italian kingdom, the Gauls at another, and the Latins for the most part. I beg you, glorious king, close your ears to wicked counselors as though to the poisonous hissing of serpents. Rouse yourself to manly strength through the ardor of the spirit; extend your hand to your fallen mother, the Roman Church; and, like the archangel Raphael driving the demon from Sara, daughter of Raguel, by whom she was widowed (Tobit VIII), drive out from the Church the demon by whom it is bereaved.

Then, just as Octavian Augustus boasts in this inscription: “I found Rome built of brick; I leave it marble” (Suetonius, *Augustus*), so you may say, much more gloriously and nobly: “I found the Roman Church, though lying prostrate, while still a boy; but before I had fully reached manhood, by God’s authority, I restored it to its former state.”

[Col. 0440A] So that one day the people may say of you, as they did of him, with celebrated devotion: “Would that he had never been born, or never died.” Rather, to apply an example from the sacred pages, may this be fulfilled in you which David recalls that the God of Israel said to him: “As the light of dawn, when the sun rises, shines on a morning without clouds, and as grass springs from the earth through the rains” (2 Samuel XXIII). Thus, with that same David, may you rightly be able to sing: “All my salvation and all my desire—there is nothing of it that does not flourish” (ibid.).

Moreover, just as the two dignities—royal and priestly—are principally joined to one another in Christ by the unique truth of the sacrament, so among the Christian people they are joined together by a certain mutual covenant. Each needs the other for reciprocal benefit: the priesthood is protected by the kingdom’s defense, and the kingdom is supported by the holiness of priestly office.

The king is girded with a sword so that, protected by it, he may confront the enemies of the Church. The priest devotes himself to the watchfulness of prayer so that he may render God favorable to the king and his people. The king, under the scales of justice, must settle earthly affairs; the priest must offer the streams of heavenly eloquence to those who thirst.

The king is appointed so that he may restrain the harmful and wicked by the severity of legal sanctions; the priest is ordained for this purpose: through the keys of the Church that he has received, to bind some with the zeal of canonical rigor and to release others through the gentleness of ecclesiastical piety.

But hear Paul discussing kings and laying down the straight line of royal office. For after much else he says: “He is God’s minister for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid. For he does not bear the sword without reason; he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil” (Romans XIII).

If, then, you are God’s minister, why do you not defend God’s Church? Why are you armed if you do not fight? Why are you girded if you do not resist those who engage in battle? Who, safe beneath a summer shade, will be able to discuss war?

Truly, you carry the sword without cause unless you pierce the necks of those who resist God; and you are not an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil when you do not rise against those who adulterate the Church and, with Simeon and Levi, do not drive away from the house of Israel the disgrace of their violated sister (Genesis XXXIV).

Let your trained hand therefore turn to the hilt, and rush upon the Amalekites with David in a flash of force (1 Samuel XXX). As he subdued the bandits, so you too should pierce the enemies of the Church by brandishing the sword of justice.

Let that ancient dragon—namely, Cadalo, the disturber of the Church, the destroyer of apostolic discipline, the enemy of human salvation—feel, yes, let him feel it. Let the root of sin, the herald of the devil, the apostle of Antichrist feel it—and what more shall I say?—the arrow drawn from Satan’s quiver, the rod of Assyria, the son of Belial, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped (2 Thessalonians II), the abyss of lust, the shipwreck of chastity, the disgrace of Christianity, the shame of priests, the offspring of vipers, the stench of the world, the filth of the age, the dishonor of all humanity.

Let further epithets be added to Cadalo: a catalogue, as it were, of his dark name—slippery serpent, twisting snake, human excrement, latrine of crimes, sewer of vices, abomination of heaven, outcast of paradise, food of Tartarus, straw for eternal fire.

Let this man feel the movement of royal majesty and fear the earthly prince, since he boldly provokes the heavenly one to war. And because the fool says in his heart, “There is no God” (Psalm XIII), let him discover that the royal breast contains the piety of Christian faith and fights with vigor for the camps of the divine army.

Let your kingdom therefore take up arms, so that the priesthood may stand with Melchizedek (Genesis XIV); and let the priesthood pray so that the empire of your ancestral David may be exalted.

For the universal Church prays for you to this end: that your labor may produce rest for it, and that its prayers may increase triumphal glory for you, just as Moses prayed and, while he prayed, Israel conquered; but when Moses lowered his hands, Amalek immediately prevailed (Exodus XVII).

Hence the Apostle also says: “I urge first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy II). Why? Hear what follows: “So that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity” (ibid.).

Moreover, since your father, of splendid memory, that magnificent emperor, exalted the Church in a lofty manner, you too, as heir to his empire, should likewise succeed to the rights of ecclesiastical protection.

Therefore, in preserving the safety of the ecclesiastical order, let the illustrious offspring answer to his father’s institutions; and let the branch of his tree not fail to produce fruit when the beauty of virtue and grace adorns it through the continuity of its stock. But as once through him, so now through you, let the fallen Church rise again, and let the ecclesiastical discipline that has been thrown into confusion blossom anew.

Perhaps I have spoken too harshly to the king, especially since Solomon says: “In your thoughts do not revile the king, and in the privacy of your bedchamber do not curse the rich, because a bird of the sky will carry your voice, and one with wings will report your judgment” (Ecclesiastes X).

And indeed, whoever incurs the crime of embezzlement is compelled to stuff what he has taken into a *diacoposis* [uncertain reading; the term is retained as printed]. But it is right to report this to the king when the king obeys the Creator; otherwise, when the king rebels against divine commands, he is rightly despised by his subjects.

For he who does not stand in the day of battle for the camps of the Church is shown to be a king of his own, not of God; he fears his own interests so particularly that he does not come to the aid of the Church in danger of ruin.

And when the Lord says through Isaiah, “Come, let us reason together” (Isaiah I), why should a human being refuse to be reproved by another human being, when it is clear that both are bound by the same law of mortality?

And since forensic law provides that one who does not avenge the slayers of his parents is in no way admitted to the right of hereditary succession, shall I, who cannot avenge the murderer of my mother—the Roman Church—not at least attempt to urge avengers onward?

Consider me, therefore, O king, a faithful counselor, not an insolent reviler; or, if you prefer, regard me as mad with grief over my murdered mother, not insolently exalted against the excellence of royal majesty.

[Col. 0442A] But O, would that I be judged guilty of treason before your tribunal, provided that you remain the arbiter of justice in taking vengeance upon the adversaries of the apostolic see! Let an axe brandished against the throat of my neck rage as it will, so long as the Roman Church, restored by you to the summit of its own dignity, ascends it once more.

But if you swiftly destroy Cadalo, like another Constantine destroying Arius, and strive to restore peace to the Church for which Christ died, may God soon cause you to ascend the height of imperial power and to carry away from all your enemies the titles of distinguished glory.

Otherwise, if you continue to dissemble, if you refuse to abolish the error of the world in peril when you are able to do so—and so forth. I restrain my spirit and leave the consequence to the readers’ understanding.

## LETTER IV. OF HUMBERT, ARCHBISHOP, BONIFACE OF ALBANO, AND THE OTHER CARDINAL-BISHOPS, TO AGNES, EMPRESS AND WIFE OF EMPEROR HENRY II

[Col. 0442B]

## ARGUMENT

The Empress Agnes had requested by letter that the pallium be sent to the archbishop newly elected for Mainz. The most blessed doctors, the cardinal bishops who serve as confidential advisers, reply that this cannot be done. For the Roman Church is not accustomed to grant the pallium to any absent prelate unless he has first been examined by the supreme pontiff or his legate and found suitable for so great a dignity. The same archbishop of Mainz must therefore travel to Rome, so that, after being approved there and obtaining what he desires, he may return to his homeland.

To the most serene Empress Agnes: Humbert, archbishop, and Boniface of Albano, together with the other cardinal bishops, offer the service of most harmonious fidelity.

[Col. 0442C] For a long time now the Roman Church has owed no greater debt to the imperial majesty than to your glory, from whose devout and holy zeal it has received many and great benefits. Thus, indeed, you may rightly be called the daughter of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the faithful handmaid of almighty God in the administration entrusted to you.

Therefore, if your magnificence asks something of the Roman Church that conflicts with the canonical regulations, we do not attribute it to malice—God forbid—but rather to the ignorance of your advisers. You requested that the pallium be sent to the lord of Mainz, a request that is undoubtedly shown by the decrees of the holy Fathers to be contrary to established practice. For the pontiffs themselves, according to the custom of ancient tradition, must hasten to the threshold of the apostles [Col. 0442D] and receive there the sign of the completion of their dignity, without which they cannot be metropolitans.

If someone should perhaps object to this assertion that the pallium has often been sent by Roman pontiffs through messengers to many places, the matter seems to be distinguished by the following explanation: at that time the legates of the Roman Church, appointed throughout the provinces, exercised the pope’s authority. They examined those who were being promoted to the summit of the episcopate, and thus obtained the pallium from the apostolic see through messengers.

Moreover, to make our meaning clear with a single example: Queen Brunhild of the Franks could not obtain a pallium from blessed Gregory for her brother Syagrius, namely the bishop of Autun, in any other way [Col. 0443A] (Gregory, *Register*, book VII, letter 5), except that, although he was good and just, he first went to Candidus, the defender who was exercising the office of apocrisiarius in those regions, in order to be examined by him; and, receiving the pallium in this manner, he showed fitting reverence to the Roman pontiff in his legate.

The emperor Maurice also, after petitioning the same Gregory for a long time, did not obtain in any other way what he had requested concerning the pallium, except that Maximus, bishop of Salona, traveled as far as Ravenna and cleared himself with a proper defense of the charges that had been brought against him before those to whom this judgment had been entrusted (the same, *Register*, book V, letter 25, and book VII, letter 129).

Indeed, blessed Pope Damasus also decreed this (in Ivo of Chartres, book I): whoever among the metropolitans delayed for more than three months after his ordination [Col. 0443B] explaining his faith to the Roman pontiff and asking for the pallium was to lose the dignity entrusted to him.

Therefore, your elected lord of Mainz should not delay coming to the threshold of the apostles, so that the completion of his dignity may take place canonically and in proper order. Whether it is we or our lord, we do not hesitate to do whatever must be done for any mortal, for the glory of your highness.

## LETTER V. TO THE SAME

(Found in volume III; it is treatise 56.)

## LETTER VI. TO THE SAME

### ARGUMENT

He consoles the same Agnes, who had previously been accustomed to converse about matters relating to piety and to share all her counsels with Rainald, bishop of Como, Hermisinda, a relative by marriage, and Peter Damian himself, but now seemed somewhat saddened because she was deprived of their presence. He exhorts her to draw herself wholly into Christ’s friendship and to seek all consolation from him; as long as she is with him, she should never consider herself alone.

To his lady, the Empress Agnes: Peter, sinful monk, offers service.

I think, venerable lady, that since the lord Rainald, bishop of the see of Como, and the holy woman Hermisinda, once the widow of your brother, and I also, your servant, have each returned to our own places, your mind is now troubled and, deprived as it were of every consolation, laments that it has been left alone.

Perhaps the long judgment of silence weighs upon you, and you are wearied by the absence of those who used to converse with you—those whom, when they were present, you often avoided, seeking the hiding place of some more secluded corner. We often tolerate what is freely offered; we enjoy what we obtain only with difficulty; we make little of what is abundant; and what we see lacking we eagerly desire.

But let your pious mind, burning with the fire of divine love and fervent with every desire, not wither because of the absence of human companionship. Rather, the more it considers earthly consolations lacking, the more confidently let it trust in the near presence of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.

Therefore, when the Savior declared that he would go to the Father after the glory of the resurrection, and saw that this would greatly disturb the minds of the disciples, he immediately added: “Because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart; but I tell you the truth: it is better for you that I go. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you” (John X).

If, then, the Spirit who enlightens minds could not pour himself fully into apostolic hearts unless Truth itself, which was to send him to them, withdrew his bodily presence from their sight, how much more necessary is it for a mere human being to withdraw from the company of human beings in order to become capable of the heavenly gift? Thus, when the human mind is free from the sight of others, it becomes worthy of the entrance of the Holy Spirit.

Do not therefore reckon the absence of those who lived with you as a loss. Rather, let it be counted an occasion of salvation, a gain in perfection, and an indication of the growth of our merit, because, when the noise of human conversation ceases, the temple of the Holy Spirit is built within you.

Hence sacred history bears witness concerning the construction of the Israelite temple that “neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house of the Lord while it was being built” (1 Kings VI). The temple of God grows through silence, because when the human mind does not pour itself outward through external words, the structure of the spiritual building rises to a lofty height. The more it grows and is raised upward, the more it is enclosed by the guardianship of silence and prevented from pouring itself out externally.

Silence is the guardian of justice. And through Jeremiah it is said: “It is good to await the salvation of the Lord in silence. It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he will sit alone and keep silent, because he will lift himself above himself” (Lamentations III).

The solitary person plainly lifts himself above himself while he is silent, because the human mind, enclosed on every side within the barriers of silence, is raised sublime into higher things, is carried toward God by heavenly desire, and is set aflame with love for him by the ardor of the Spirit. Like a living spring, when it is not permitted to flow here and there through circuits of words, it rises into the heights in swelling waves.

Let the temple of your heart therefore now grow through silence. Let the structure of spiritual virtues, like heavenly stones, rise within you, so that the heavenly bridegroom whom you love with your whole being may rest there joyfully as in his bridal chamber.

Remember, then, what the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. If anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, the quality of each person’s work will be tested by fire” (1 Corinthians III).

What is signified by gold, silver, and precious stones except the strength and adornment of virtues? And what is indicated by wood, hay, and straw except the frailty of vices? Take care, therefore, that the building being formed in you is not made from fragile material that can be exposed to flames and will collapse when driven by winds.

Wood, hay, and straw can easily be consumed by devouring fire; gold, silver, and precious stones, however, do not succumb to burning. And certainly the same Apostle says: “Taking up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the wicked one” (Ephesians VI).

Therefore, let the fire that the hidden enemy sends find in you the precious metals of virtues, not the straw and kindling of vices. When the raging flames blown by the crafty enemy attack, let not rotten and fragile material yield weakly, but let the strength of an impenetrable and firm solidity resist, so that the virtue of the Most High, which overshadowed the womb of the virgin (Luke I), may also preserve your mind in the perpetual verdure of flourishing chastity and—God forbid—not allow it to be overshadowed by the harsh vapors of spiritual wickedness [f. something such as “to be overshadowed” is required].

Take comfort, therefore, venerable lady, and drive every weariness of harmful grief from your heart. Let Christ be your companion in conversation; let Christ be your housemate and your table companion. Indeed, let Christ himself be your delight, himself the feast of your daily refreshment, himself the nourishment of your intimate sweetness.

Read with him, sing psalms continually with him; finally, prostrate yourself with him on the floor to pray, and rise with him. Let your bed receive you as you sleep with him; let sleep find you with him. Let his chaste and virginal embrace bind you, so that what is said through Isaiah may truly be fulfilled in you: “The bridegroom will rejoice over the bride, and your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah LXII). And may you be able to say in a particular way what the universal bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved will dwell among my breasts” (Song of Songs I).

For it is clear that the human heart is situated between the breasts. The beloved therefore dwells among the bride’s breasts when Christ is loved with the whole heart by any faithful soul.

Let your holy soul therefore say to this bridegroom: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely; our couch is covered with flowers” (ibid.). For he is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm XLIV).

And because for love of him you have despised royal headgear and looked down upon imperial majesty, let him himself be your crown, himself your purple robe; let him prepare for you the blessed ornaments of all glory, so that you may rightly sing with the Prophet: “The Lord has clothed me with the garment of salvation and covered me with the robe of gladness, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride adorned with her jewels” (Isaiah LXI).

Let him console you for the absence of human companionship; let him suffice for you in place of everyone’s commands and conversation. Let him, like another but far greater Elkanah, truly say: “Not Anna but Agnes, why do you weep, and why do you not eat, and why is your heart troubled? Am I not better for you than ten sons?” (1 Samuel I).

And since Elkanah is said to mean “zeal of God,” may the zeal of God, the love of the Redeemer, console your soul in all the weariness and distress of grief, so that in every adversity you suffer you may cast yourself upon him, flee beneath his shelter from the heat of human persecution, and rest safely and sweetly in his embraces. Thus may he himself offer the harbor of deepest rest—he who for your sake deigned to suffer shipwreck amid the worldly waves and surging storms.

## 251. LETTER VII. TO THE SAME

### ARGUMENT

He indicates how painful it is for him to be separated from her and promises hope of a near return. Meanwhile, considering the greatness of the rewards prepared in heaven for those who love God, he exhorts her, following Christ’s example, not to be ashamed to endure, for the time being, every labor, inconvenience, and hardship while she remains in this narrow dwelling of the body.

To his lady, the Empress Agnes: Peter, sinful monk, offers whatever service a servant can give.

Because I am far from your holy presence and cannot be with you at this time, I grieve greatly and sigh with daily lamentation. Meanwhile, before I return to you, I exhort your holy patience not to find it burdensome to endure any hardships and difficulties, and for love of the heavenly bridegroom to bear anxiety and even the lack of necessary expenses.

Since Christ bore the cross for you, what is remarkable if you endure poverty for love of him? If he, whom Virtues and Dominations served in heaven, suffered spittle, scourges, insults, blows, and slaps in the world, is it a great thing if you, who are earth, cast away the empty pomp of imperial glory and show yourself not as the queen of the world but—as is far more glorious—as the handmaid of the eternal King?

Recall what the Apostle says: “Let us therefore go out to him beyond the camp, bearing his reproach; for here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews VIII, 13).

A happy exchange indeed, in which clay is given and gold is taken up; in place of darkness we obtain light, and in place of earthly honors we acquire the dignity of heavenly glory. For, as the prophet says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass; the grass withers and its flower falls, but whoever keeps the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah XL).

Moreover, the person who is clothed in purple today is enclosed in a tomb tomorrow. Today someone rules over human beings; tomorrow, having become rotten, he is gnawed by worms. Today he is encircled with royal headgear; tomorrow his lifeless corpse is wrapped in mean rags. Today he shines, crowned, on the throne of royal excellence; tomorrow he stinks, decaying in the grave.

Weigh these things and others like them carefully, my lady, and now endure the labors of this life with Jesus in calmness, so that when he who was judged comes to judge, you may meet him worthily like one of the wise virgins adorned with lamps (Matthew XXV), and in place of temporal purple receive the robe of immortality, and in place of the crown fashioned from earthly metal receive that diadem made in heaven from precious stone.

## 252. LETTER VIII. TO THE SAME AGNES, EMPRESS

### ARGUMENT

He exhorts the same Agnes, who has departed for Germany, to return, indicating with what grief all Italy, and especially Rome, has been afflicted by her departure. In that city, all were stirred toward the true path of virtue by her most holy example.

[Col. 0447A] To his lady Agnes, the Empress: Peter, sinful monk, offers service.

I can scarcely express how greatly my heart is overwhelmed with grief while, with my whole being suspended in expectation day after day, it awaits the joy of your return. Alas for me! Why, senseless and foolish, did I consent to your journey? Indeed, why did I not violently oppose myself to your departure? Why did I not seize the horses’ reins and, with my hands placed before them, delay your journey as far as I could?

In the absence caused by your departure, Rome mourns, the Church of blessed Peter grieves, and all Italy laments through its holy men and women. You seemed to illuminate, like a golden star, the darkness of those who seek earthly things, and, calling them toward God, you poured the brightness of a shining example upon those who followed you.

And, to pass over much else, while I sigh because you are far away, I too shudder to look upon the walls of Rome. Return, therefore, my lady, return, and restore festive joy to those who mourn you, who in Rome, the head of the world, are in a way weeping because we see the radiant jewel of heaven torn away.

May the court of imperial power bring you nausea; may only the fisherman’s net smell sweet to your nostrils. May you desire to share burial there with Petronilla, so that that distinguished father may rejoice to have resting beside him his twofold daughter, one of flesh and one of spirit.

I also greet my lord Bishop Lopertus and beg that he return quickly.

## LETTER IX. OF POPE NICHOLAS II TO … THE QUEEN OF FRANCE

[Note: [Col. 0447] I believe this was Anna, wife of King Henry and likewise mother of King Philip.]

[Col. 0447C] ### ARGUMENT

The holy doctor writes in the name of Pope Nicholas II to the queen of the Gauls. He praises her piety and generosity toward the poor and exhorts her steadfastly to retain to the end the most praiseworthy way of life that she once undertook. At the same time, he urges her to inflame her husband the king to administer the state justly, protect the Church, and perform works of piety, and to train her sons in the same character with which she herself is imbued.

## 253. NICHOLAS, BISHOP, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD, TO THE GLORIOUS QUEEN: GREETING AND APOSTOLIC BLESSING

Let us give worthy thanks to almighty God, the author of good will, because we hear that the strength of virtue lives in a woman’s breast with the courage of a man.

For it has reached our ears, most excellent daughter, that your serenity overflows toward the needy with the generosity of pious liberality, labors diligently in the practices of devoted prayer, exercises the force of strictness on behalf of those violently oppressed, and, insofar as is fitting for you, fulfills the office of royal dignity through other good works.

We therefore exhort you to hold to the path that, inspired by God, you once entered. Strive also to urge your most invincible husband, our son the king, to guide the reins of piety and justice and to preserve the condition of the Church.

For if Abigail’s eloquence preserved foolish Nabal unharmed from the sword of the angry David (1 Samuel II), how much more will your holy devotion render your wisest husband pleasing in the sight of God? You truly love him if you cause him, through pious exhortations, to preserve the things that belong to God.

Otherwise, how are those wives to be believed to love their husbands who love in them, so to speak, only the containers of their bodies but pay no attention to the gold of their souls stored within them? For, according to the Apostle, “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians IV).

Such women embrace only what worms devour in tombs; in their madness they despise that for which unfading glory is reserved in heaven. She had established her love in the flesh who, when David despised her, said mockingly: “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the eyes of his servants, and being naked as one of the buffoons might be naked?” (2 Samuel VI).

Because she had placed her desire in the flesh alone, she was deservedly deprived of the fruit of the flesh as punishment. Thus Scripture adds shortly afterward: “Therefore Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child to the day of her death” (ibid.).

But you, glorious daughter, because you have deserved by divine favor the gift of fertility, train your illustrious offspring so that, from the earliest beginnings of nursing infancy, they may be nourished in love for their Creator. Through you, let them learn to whom above all they owe both the nobility into which they were born on the throne of the royal court and the far greater nobility into which they were reborn in the bosom of the Church through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Do not ever prefer money to justice, but eagerly acquire the treasure of true wisdom. The queen of Sheba came not to see riches but to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings X). Yet although she had not asked for riches, she carried them away in abundance.
