You too, daughter, by obeying divine commands, possess wisdom, so that you may deserve both to enjoy earthly abundance suitably for the salvation of your soul and to pass from the summit of a transient kingdom to the heavenly one.

## 254. LETTER X. TO GOTHIFRED, DUKE AND MARQUIS OF TUSCANY

### ARGUMENT

In this letter he writes to the duke and marquis Gothifred that he was deeply distressed to learn that Gothifred had received into his hospitality Cadalo, the false pontiff who had defected from the Catholic faith. He reinforces the accusation with several examples from sacred Scripture and admonishes him to acknowledge his fault, wipe it away with tears, and return once more to the favor of the holy blessed Church.

[Col. 0448D] To Lord Gothifred, most excellent duke and marquis: Peter, sinful monk, offers an admonition born of fervent zeal.

A new and unheard-of report about you has recently spread among us. It has brought us no small grief and sorrow, shaken our trembling inmost parts, restrained our mouth from its customary praise of your glory, and pierced our enfeebled heart like the sharpest dagger of inward pain.

You have, it is said, entered into fellowship with Cadalo, whom, as you clearly know, the universal Church long ago vomited out like deadly poison, cut off from its own entrails like a putrid limb, plunged into the depths of the abyss of Gehenna, and, like human refuse buried in the channels of a latrine lest it stink any longer to human nostrils, sealed off from breathing.

That you have shared your prudence with such a man, diggers in the fields, merchants in the marketplace, and soldiers in public are proclaiming. Alas, what grief! Most eminent man, where then were those abundant streams of tears which you used to pour forth like a torrent from the fervent charity of your pious heart, and in which, set aflame by love of the Holy Spirit, you never ceased to bathe your tear-wet face?

To what have the fruits of your almsgiving been reduced? Through the continuous course of Lenten fasting, your generous and most pious clemency not only relieved the poverty of the needy but, following the example of our Redeemer, did not blush both to wash their feet and to imprint kisses upon them.

Therefore you must fear what is said through Haggai about that man: “He who had money put it into a bag full of holes” (Haggai I). For whatever is put into a bag full of holes through its opening must necessarily escape through the rupture by which it leaks out. What good is it if at first the purse swells through the accumulation of money, only to become empty and collapse soon afterward through the loss caused by carelessness?

You did indeed fight manfully against this Antichrist and, together with your most serene and illustrious wife, frequently resisted his sacrilegious and perverse efforts. But now I do not know what has restrained the steadfastness of your holy religion from this resolve, softened the strength of your honorable firmness through its poisonous suggestions, and persuaded you, as it were, to bury the work you had begun.

Hence Solomon also says: “Whoever is slack and careless in his work is a brother to the one who destroys his own work” (Proverbs XVIII). For whoever does not carry out the good he has begun with strictness imitates, through negligent dissolution, the hand of the destroyer.

Tell me, magnificent man: if someone tried to inflict an injury upon your honorable and most chaste marriage chamber, what kinsman of yours, what member of your household, would dare to join himself to that person in friendship? Which of them would presume to enter into a bond of friendship with him?

If, then, a human being does not dare to make a treaty of peace with his master’s enemy, how did your highness not fear to enter into fellowship with one who presumed to violate Christ’s bride, namely the holy Church, as though by the defilement of obscene seduction?

The enemy of God is plainly shown to be the one who joins himself in friendship to God’s enemy. Hence, when Joram, king of Israel, a thoroughly wicked and impious man, consulted Elisha, saying, “Why has the Lord gathered these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab?” Elisha replied: “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand, if I did not respect the face of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor pay attention to you” (2 Kings III).

Hence, because Jehoshaphat had assisted Ahab, Jehu son of Hanani the prophet is said to have told him: “Do you give help to the impious and join friendship with those who hate the Lord? Therefore you deserve the wrath of the Lord. But good works have been found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah and prepared your heart to seek the Lord, the God of your fathers” (2 Chronicles XIX).

Hence, because Ahab allowed Ben-hadad, king of Syria, whom he had defeated in war, to depart unharmed, he heard from the prophet’s mouth what he deserved: “Because you have let go from your hand a man worthy of death, your life shall be for his life and your people for his people” (1 Kings XX).

Hence Saul lost the kingdom because, in an impiously misplaced piety toward Agag, king of Amalek, he did not punish him as he deserved (1 Samuel XV).

But if almighty God were now to demand an account from you for an injury done to him and set before you this complaint worthy of retribution, what would you answer? “I,” he might say, “raised you above all the princes of your kingdom; I made you renowned and conspicuous throughout all the boundaries of the Roman Empire; I bestowed upon you, in foreign lands, far more wealth than you would have inherited by paternal right; and, apart from the rank of royal power, I permitted no one—not merely to surpass you, but even to equal you.

“And if these things are few, add that I gave you an acute intelligence and eloquence for speaking, strength for waging war, and laid the stiff necks of many enemies beneath your feet. I bestowed all these things upon you, together with many other gifts of virtue, and you have decided to receive into communion my adversary, whom I had cast away from me, utterly severed from my members, and condemned by the common judgment of my priests?”

If God himself, I say, were to set these and similar matters before you, illustrious man, what excuse could you offer? What escape through evasion could the subtlety of your prudence discover?

Consider these things and others like them that could be brought against you, illustrious and exalted man. Wash away the guilt of your offense with the tears of fitting repentance. Break off the pact of deadly friendship; confess openly before everyone that you have sinned; and return swiftly to the favor of the apostolic see, whose noble and distinguished son you are.

Thus, when you cast out what was being praised by the members of the devil and are yourself corrected through the lamentation of repentance, you may obtain, together with King David, not only forgiveness from God but also his favor (2 Samuel XII).

May your highness, magnificent man, pardon my speech, and understand that I have spoken not against you but for myself; and may you attribute what I have said not to the fuel of envy or hatred but rather to the cauterization of medicinal care.

## LETTER XI. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0450D]

(Found in volume III; it is treatise 57.)

## LETTER XII. TO THE SAME

(Found in volume III, in treatise 57.)

## LETTER XIII. TO THE SAME AND TO HIS WIFE BEATRICE

### ARGUMENT

He asks that she and her husband give money to the abbot of Saint John the Baptist so that he may pay the price of a library he has purchased; at the same time, he teaches how great is the usefulness of such works of piety.

To Lord Gothifred, marquis and duke, and to Beatrice, his most serene wife: Peter, sinful monk, offers the service of prayer.

[Col. 0451A] This son of ours, namely the abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist, has purchased a library. But because, constrained by poverty, he cannot pay the price, necessity compels him to ask me for help in supplying the amount.

Since what is needed at present is not available to me, I grant permission for him to seek it from others. What he does not obtain from us—namely, from wealthy bishops—may at least be supplied in some measure by you, though you are small and poor.

If someone says, “The world rages against us, war is pressing upon us, and it does not permit us leisure to offer gifts to God,” let him hear that Joshua, the leader of Israel, was fighting in the desert while Moses prayed on the mountain with his hands extended toward heaven (Exodus XVII).

But, as Scripture relates, whenever Moses lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed; when he raised his hands, Amalek fell and Israel conquered. Hence the prophet says: “Lift up your hearts with your hands to God” (Lamentations III).

A person lifts his heart to God with his hands when, while offering vows of prayer to God, he also sends him gifts from his possessions, either for the adornment of churches or for the support of the poor.

Let us therefore put on the breastplate of good works, and we shall not fear the darts of the impious. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “Do not fear the sudden terror of the powers of the wicked when they rush upon you; for the Lord will be at your side and will guard your foot, lest you be taken captive” (Proverbs III).

He immediately added why we should conceive this confidence in our minds: “Do not hinder the one who can do good. If you are able, do good yourself. Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back; tomorrow I will give to you,’ when you are able to give at once” (ibid.).

We must therefore place our trust not in iron or weapons but in works of piety.

I would come at the command of your instruction if old age, bent with years, did not restrain my trembling step. Nevertheless, let this brother see and judge whether a reasonable cause summons me.

Furthermore, I humbly beseech your excellence that, if you send anyone to the German lands, you send this letter, for the sake of our charity, to my lady Agnes the Empress.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] This letter is the eighth in this book.]

## LETTER XIV. TO BEATRICE, DUCHESS, WIFE OF GOTHIFRED, DUKE OF TUSCANY

### ARGUMENT

He writes to Beatrice, the wife of Duke Gothifred, that he was greatly delighted to learn that she was preserving continence by common agreement with her husband. He sets before her the examples of holy women and exhorts her to keep them before her eyes and strive to imitate them. Above all, he commends hospitality toward the poor and generosity toward churches.

To Beatrice, most excellent duchess: Peter, sinful monk, offers the persistence of daily prayer.

I rejoice greatly in you and in your most glorious husband, and I marvel profoundly at the disposition of almighty God. When he established you in so lofty a fortress of earthly dignity and also granted you to produce the fruits of good works, what else did he display to the wonder of the world than fruitful fir trees?

The vine is small but fruitful; the fir is tall but barren. The former compensates by the abundance of its flowing grapes for what it lacks in strength; the latter, although it contributes nothing to the setting of tables, is nevertheless suitable for building, and what it does not provide for delights, it supplies for structures.

When these two qualities meet—when the height of the tree and the abundance of its yield are found together—the rarer the combination, the more worthy it is of wonder.

This distinguished double grace is therefore found in you: humble and holy devotion toward God, and the exalted height of power toward the world. Thus you may rightly be called both lofty vines and fruitful fir trees.

Concerning the mystery of the mutual continence that, with God as witness, you maintain between you, I confess that for a long time I held a twofold opinion: I supposed that your husband would gladly offer this gift of chastity, but that you, because of your desire to bear offspring, would not willingly accept it.

[Col. 0452B] But when that same glorious man recently revealed to me, before the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, your holy desire and your resolve to preserve chastity perpetually, I confess, “I rejoiced in those things that were said to me” (Psalm CXXI), and I exulted exceedingly.

The saying of the ancient curse has now been removed from you—the saying addressed to the first woman: “You shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis III).

It is entirely clear that Sarah had already formed the purpose of chastity when the event occurred that sacred history relates about her, namely, that Sarah’s womanly functions had ceased. She herself also says: “After I have grown old, and my lord is old, shall I give myself to pleasure?” (Genesis XVIII).

These words plainly show that she had already undertaken the purpose of chastity. After this God said to Abraham: “In all that Sarah has said to you, listen to her voice” (Genesis XXI).

Behold: the woman whom Abraham had previously commanded and whom he was called her lord is now to be obeyed because of the merit of her chastity, so that in all things he who had previously commanded her as lord may now obey her words.

Learn from these same patriarchs also this example of salvation: do not neglect to extend the duty of human kindness to guests. For concerning this the Apostle, after first saying, “Let brotherly love continue among you, and do not forget hospitality,” added specifically: “For through this some, by receiving angels in hospitality, were pleasing to God” (Hebr. XIII).

As sacred history relates: “When three men had come to Abraham, he hastened into the tent to Sarah and said to her: ‘Quickly, mix three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes.’” Then it continues: “He himself ran to the herd, took from it a tender and excellent calf, etc.” (Gen. XVIII). In these words of sacred eloquence one must observe that Abraham, in order to show kindness to his guests, did not command this of Hagar the maidservant, did not assign it to his servants, and did not order it of any of his household dependants; rather, he himself personally, together with his wife, carried out this work of piety. Hence the text immediately adds: “He also took butter and milk, and the calf which he had prepared, and set them before them; but he himself stood beside them under the tree” (Gen. XVIII). He himself, together with his wife, ministered to the guests, and did not decide that the service of human kindness should be delegated to lowly persons.

The wife of the emperor Theodosius plainly followed their example. Concerning her, to add the same words, the Tripartite History bears witness (book IX, chapter 31): “She had the greatest care for the lame and the weak, using neither servants nor other attendants, but doing the work herself, going to their dwellings, and providing each person with whatever he needed.” Soon afterward it adds: “Thus also, going through the guest-houses of the churches, she ministered to the sick with her own hands, cleaning their pots, tasting their broth, offering spoons, breaking bread, serving food, washing cups, and doing all the other things which it is customary for servants and attendants formally to perform.”

Woe to us, the lazy, sluggish, and proud, who can scarcely force ourselves to do this one thing: scatter simple fare and the leftover scraps of our food into the laps of the needy. But if some flatterer happened to stand by and, on account of the dignity of her royal rank, tried to prevent her from undertaking this diligent service, she would say: “To distribute gold is the work of imperial authority; but for the empire itself I offer this work to him who bestows every good upon me.”

Nor was it enough for her merely to devote herself to works of piety unless she also urged the emperor—her husband, of course—to the same holy devotion and eagerness. Hence these are her words: “You ought always, husband, to consider what you once were and what you now are. If you always consider this, you will not be ungrateful to your benefactor; rather, you will govern the empire that you have received lawfully and will appease the Author of these things.”

Of this woman, then, we may say that she was wholly unlike the first woman: she spoke differently and acted contrary to what the first woman had done. The first woman ate the forbidden fruit, and then persuaded her husband to eat it as well (Gen. III); but this woman supplied her husband both with an example of conduct to be imitated and with words of holy exhortation. The first, by both her actions and her words, drove her husband from possession of paradise; this woman recalled her husband by her words and deeds.

[Col. 0453D] Moreover, my lady, do not—do not, like most of the powerful of this world, grow rich by confiscating ecclesiastical property; rather, strive to enrich impoverished churches through the donation of your estates. Give earth, and receive heaven. Let transient possessions be transferred into titles of eternal inheritance.

I shall certainly relate what Heinricus, the venerable rector of the monastery established in the territory of Arezzo in honor of the blessed virgins Flora and Lucilla, told me. “Do you see,” he said, “the basilica standing nearby? That was the road by which we were traveling. In ancient times it was commonly called Saint Mary the Poor. When Guilla, the mother of the illustrious marquis Hugo, happened to pass through these confines, it also happened that the name of this church came to her ears. As soon as the noble and distinguished woman heard it, she was exceedingly indignant and, as though recoiling in disgust, said: ‘Far be it—far be it—that we should call poor the one who gave birth to the giver of heavenly glory. Far be it, I say, that she should deserve the name of poor on earth, since, raised above the angels, she possesses immortal riches in heaven.’ Immediately she added: ‘Is there here any possession belonging to me?’ She was told that she had there a village divided, according to ancient custom, into nine homesteads, which later, according to modern usage, had been divided into very many parts. ‘Let this church,’ she said, ‘immediately possess it by lawful right, and from now on let no one dare call it Poor.’”

Therefore, always emulate noblewomen of this kind. Let not the nobility of the flesh, but rather the lineage of holiness, spur you to action. It is trivial to boast of the titles of one’s ancestors; it is glorious to equal the triumphs of the saints who came before.

Roman history relates that Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine, was a stable-girl. Hence these are nearly the words of Eutropius (History, book X): “After Constantine’s death, his son Constantine was made emperor from a less distinguished marriage, in Britain.” The blessed Ambrose also supports this assertion in his letters (St. Ambrose, *On the Death of the Emperor Theodosius*). Yet she transformed the obscurity of her lineage through such outstanding moral excellence that very many basilicas throughout the world are found adorned with the title of her name; and what empresses born from exalted and noble lines were unable to attain, this stable-girl deserved to obtain through, so to speak, a noble ancestry of life.

I therefore beseech you, distinguished lady, and humbly exhort you: gather the testimony of holy princesses, and place the pattern of their conduct before your eyes, so that by contemplating them you may discern what you ought to hold fast and what you ought to avoid. Do not take as much delight in the exaltation of your birth as in the beauty of spiritual virtues, so that you who now excel among human beings in earthly dignity may also be enrolled before God—which is far more glorious—in the catalogue of holy women.

## LETTER XV. TO B., DUKE AND MARQUIS

**SUMMARY.**—He urges him, despising present things, to turn with the whole attention of his mind toward the future; not to remain intent upon the earthly riches in which he abounded, but to raise his mind toward heavenly and eternal things and meditate on them continually.

To the lord B., most excellent duke and marquis, Peter, the least of the servants of the monks, offers faithful prayer in Christ.

I do not fail to recognize, most excellent lord, that if almighty God did not love you to some degree, he would never have entrusted so many thousands of people to your governance, laid the necks of your enemies beneath your feet, and exalted you with such glory above all the powerful men of the kingdom. But divine compassion has raised you up temporarily for this reason: that, if you strive to keep his commandments, he may advance you through earthly goods to heavenly things and lead you through temporal matters to eternal ones.

Therefore, dearest one, in accordance with the prudence of your exceptionally keen intellect, look toward heaven, place the end of this exceedingly brief life before your eyes, and carefully consider with whom you must render an account of so extensive and prolonged a stewardship. For what benefit is it if someone today is covered with gold, gems, and purple, frequently surrounded by companies of soldiers, if tomorrow he is dragged naked, guilty, and deprived of every consolation to the punishments of hell? What advantage is it if today someone endowed with temporal power makes the earth tremble beneath his feet, and tomorrow is compelled to leave this world as a beggar and a pauper?

Hear what Solomon says: “Even if a man lives a hundred years and rejoices throughout them all, he must remember the days of darkness and the evil days, which, when they come, expose the past” (Eccl. XI). Where now are all those powerful men of the world, all those unconquered kings, who seemed to surpass the heavens and to possess almost the entire breadth of the world under the command of their power? If you look at their tombs, is not that whole body, beneath which the world was compelled to tremble, scarcely found to weigh a single pound?

Consider these things carefully, therefore, beloved, and review them with diligent attention of mind. Examine closely not what you are, but what you will be forever.

Regarding the monasteries that are now near you, I beseech you on God’s behalf and humbly ask you to extend to them the protection of your hand, and not permit them to be plundered or harassed by the multitude of the army that is with you. Above all and before all else, I ask your excellence to love especially the monastery of Saint Vincent. Restore to it by lawful right the estates held by invaders, and defend it from all mortal men with the shield of your protection. Let it be clearly evident in this monastery whether my humility is able to obtain anything greater from the ears of your highness.

## LETTER XVI. TO ADELAIDE, DUCHESS AND MARCHIONESS OF THE COTTIAN ALPS

(It is found in volume III, treatise 18.)

## LETTER XVII. TO RAINER, MARQUIS

[Col. 0455D] **SUMMARY.**—He endeavors to urge the marquis Rainer, whom he had ordered to go to Jerusalem in order to expiate his sins, but who was delaying and bringing forward the difficulties and dangers of the journey as an excuse, to carry out the penance imposed upon him. To encourage him to undertake so long a journey cheerfully, he demonstrates by examples that no dangers are to be feared, because God cares for devout people.

To the lord Rainer, most illustrious marquis, Peter, sinful monk, greetings.

I charged you, magnificent man, to seek Jerusalem on account of the sins that you confessed to me, and to appease divine justice through the satisfaction of a distant pilgrimage. But you, since, according to Scripture, you do not know what tomorrow may bring (Jas. IV), defer the matter to the future; and while you fear the uncertain accidents of the journey, you do not provide for yourself a secure abode. Thus that saying is fulfilled in you: “Whoever watches the wind will never sow, and whoever considers the clouds will never reap” (Eccl. XI).

In moderating this penance, we plainly maintain a certain distinction: we neither restrain indiscriminately from this journey all who seek our counsel, nor loosen the reins of unrestricted permission to everyone who wishes to go. To those who live according to a rule and lawfully observe the statutes either of canonical or monastic religion, we advise that they remain in the vocation in which they have been established, and that they not abandon, for these reasons, what is set before them as necessary by human judgment.

Thus, as it is said through John: “Let those who possess hold fast, and let no one take their crown” (Rev. III). But those who either serve the world in the garb of office or bear the title of spiritual warfare while failing to observe the discipline of their profession, we urge to undertake the journey of spiritual exile and to make satisfaction abroad to the terrifying Judge, whose laws and commandments they do not keep within the responsibilities, cares, and obligations of the Lord. By wandering in this way, let them provide themselves with rest; by pilgrimage, with a dwelling in their true homeland.

Therefore, dearest one, do not set before yourself adversities that can be imagined or devised; do not, like a woman, fear the misfortunes of various accidents. Rather, “hope in the Lord and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). Often, precisely where human reasoning most distrusts, heavenly clemency comes to the aid of those in distress; and where we despair of human consolation, we frequently perceive divine protection to be present.

To speak, then, of the journey about which we are now concerned: our brother and fellow monk Richard, a man of religious life and honorable gravity, told us that eight men, having fulfilled the vow of their devout desire, were returning from Jerusalem. As they were traveling through uninhabited places and had already been afflicted by four days of severe hunger, they unanimously began to implore divine clemency, asking that it come to the aid of those laboring in extreme distress and that he who gives food to all flesh (Ps. CXXXV) not refuse them at least some kind of nourishment in so great a necessity.

Immediately after completing their prayer, they saw a loaf of bread lying on the road, enormous in size and of marvelous whiteness. They marveled at the sight shared by all, certainly not unaware that a mass of such weight could never have slipped from the pack of an unsuspecting bearer. Then they recognized the benefit of heavenly mercy and, since they were eight, divided the bread into eight parts. They were so pleasantly and sufficiently filled by it that throughout their entire lives they were never restored by more abundant fare.

Our same brother Richard also related another event that I do not think should be passed over in silence. He says that our brother Agius, a man advanced in age and distinguished in religion, while still living in the world, was traveling out of devotion to prayer to the church of the blessed archangel Michael, built near Sipontum on Mount Gargano.

He had only one horse with his brother, who was a secular man. They took turns riding it, each in succession, and thus somehow moderated the labor of the journey. But when he saw that his fellow travelers needed help in carrying their bundles, he urged his brother that they both cease riding the animal and make it available for carrying the burdens of their companions, out of charity.

While they rested, exhausted by the labor of the long road, and refreshed their failing stomachs with food, the aforementioned brother Agius mixed bread with wine in a cup. He placed it beside him, postponing his own refreshment for the moment, and fell asleep. While they were thus resting, behold, bandits arrived in a sudden attack and, seizing everything belonging to them together with the horse, departed.

One of them, however, remained behind and consumed Brother Agius’s food and drink. Immediately afterward an intolerable pain seized him, and a savage agony did not leave his bowels until he was forced to vomit everything up. Then, springing up with agile speed and quickly overtaking his companions, he persuaded them that unless they returned God’s animal to his servant as quickly as possible, they would not escape the imminent danger of divine vengeance.

Shaken by God, they immediately returned to the man of God, sorrowfully sought pardon for their presumption, and at the same time restored the horse together with the other things that had likewise been taken. Thus divine mercy does not withdraw the help of its protection from those whom it sees laboring in the service of devotion to God.

Our brother Bonizo also, a veteran and holy man who has persevered for many years in the desert, and whose old age has not relaxed the rigor of his more continent life, related to us that, while returning by sea from Jerusalem, he suffered shipwreck.

When the storms swelled, the ship sank, and all his companions perished in the violence of the sea, he seized a sack filled with cotton wadding. Resting upon it amid the surging heaps of the waves, he struggled against the sea like a fighting man for nearly three days and two nights, contending with death.

It happened that certain rowers, cutting across the sea, saw him from a distance. They compassionately lifted him aboard, refreshed him with food, and provided him with the attentions of human kindness. Thus he who preserved Paul unharmed day and night beneath the depths of the sea (Acts XXVII; 2 Cor. XI) also kept this brother from being swallowed by the sea’s abyss, suspended amid the very flood of the battling storms. And by whose power Jonah was vomited from the throat of the voracious beast (Jon. VIII), by that same command the gentle wave was spread beneath this man—not to swallow him, but to preserve him.

Bring these and similar flowers of heavenly mercy before your inward sight, illustrious man. Doubt, as is fitting, in your own strength; but place your confidence in the unfailing protection of him who is almighty everywhere. Degenerate flesh may tremble, but let the noble fervor of a ready spirit blaze forth. Go out, strive, contend. He will be the guide of the journey who is the author of the will that is to be rewarded.

It is yours to undertake the journey; it is God’s to direct the footsteps of one who seeks him. He brings good works to completion who moves the affection of a devout heart. And he who stirs the human spirit to do good unquestionably brings the vows of a devout intention to fulfillment.

## LETTER XVIII. TO GUILLA, COUNTESS, WIFE OF THE MARQUIS RAINER

**SUMMARY.**—He instructs Guilla, recently married to the marquis Rainer and therefore, as it were, a novice, concerning what she ought to do: namely, not to covet the property of widows and orphans, as had been customary in her husband’s household, but rather to see that everything unjustly taken be restored. He writes that a great aid in avoiding such robberies in the future will be for her to order agriculture to be diligently practiced; he also urges her to give alms.

[Col. 0458B] To Guilla, most illustrious countess, Peter, sinful monk, offers the persistence of prayer.

Since, in relation to the matter from which conflict arises, it is better to possess gratuitous ignorance than always to struggle to acquire forgetfulness, we safely offer the address of letters to young women whose appearance we fear. I, certainly, now an old man, can safely gaze at the face of an old woman marked with wrinkles and wet with the discharge of bleary eyes, and can look upon it freely. But from more beautiful and painted faces I guard my eyes as one guards children from fire.

For my unhappy heart, which is not satisfied with holding the mysteries of the Gospel even after reading them a hundred times, does not lose the memory of a face seen once; and where the law written by the divine finger has not remained, forgetfulness does not intercept the image of vanity. But these matters belong elsewhere. Here I have judged it appropriate to describe not what is harmful to me, but rather what may be beneficial to you.

You have passed, my daughter, through the obligations of a marital union into a household sufficiently spacious, indeed, but—let me confess—badly ordered; conspicuous in wealth and dignity, but confused by a corrupted rule of life. Therefore break the rule of the perverse custom that you found there; abolish the confiscations of the poor; restrain unjust exactions and levies upon the peasants; and, following the example of King Josiah, establish an institution of a new order.

He found the kingdom of Judah devoted to the worship of idols and polluted not only by the long-standing contamination of his father’s but also of his grandfather’s sacrilege. But as soon as Scripture bears witness, he burned with fire in the valley of the Kidron all the vessels that had been made for Baal; he destroyed the diviners who sacrificed on the high places and demolished the altars; he shattered the statues, cut down the sacred groves, polluted the altars, and profaned the little buildings of the effeminate. Since it would take too long to enumerate everything he did, it is enough to summarize by saying that he overturned all abominations and splendidly restored the temple of the Lord with its lawful ceremonies (2 Kings XXIII).

You too, emulating the holy king, destroy the order of ancient confusion that you have found, and introduce the newness of a saving innocence. For even if you have not found there an idol to destroy, you have found what deserves equal punishment: avarice, which, as the Apostle testifies, is the service of idols (Eph. V).

Do not let the little possessions of orphans or the fattened portions of widows be sweet in your mouth, while the Lord thunders terribly through Moses: “You shall not harm a widow or an orphan. If you harm them, they will cry out to me, and I will hear their cry; my wrath will be kindled, and I will strike you with the sword, and your wives will be widows and your children orphans” (Exod. XXII).

It is as though he were saying: If you harm those deprived of the support of a husband and bereft of parents, I will also strike your wives and children with a punishment worthy of my wrath; likewise, you will leave widows and orphans behind, so that someone may be able to harm them with impunity, just as you confidently suppose that you may safely oppress these people as though they were without the possibility of retaliation.

To support this judgment of the Lord not with a distant example but with one drawn from the household itself: your father-in-law, namely Margrave Uguizo, once had as his brother by the same mother Count Ubertus. While his wife was living in the fortress called Sciffena, she took a pig from a certain widow. After it had been prepared as food through the efforts of the cooks, she reclined to dine.

The widow had often asked that the victim be returned to her, but had not even been able to obtain a patient hearing. Pierced with grief, she presented herself to the woman solemnly feasting and asked her to offer at least a thin fragment of her own nourishment. “Since I did not deserve,” she said, “to rejoice, as is customary, in the nourishment of my accustomed hope, may I at least taste the final morsel of its flavor?”

The proud and arrogant matron despised this request and, with insulting abuse, declared to her that she would never eat from that pig. But O divine justice, always armed with the sword of vengeance to punish impiety and pride! On that very day, after the meal, while the aforementioned countess was sitting on the fortress rampart, secure upon the rampart and with her entrails fattened by another’s misfortune, fearing no danger of ruin, the ground was suddenly overwhelmed by a collapse of the fortification. An immense mass of the falling promontory was heaped upon the unhappy woman.

Crowds of people rushed together, resounding on every side; diggers approached and searched the bowels of the earth. As the collapsed mass of earth was pierced here and there with various kinds of tools, scarcely a slight trace of the crushed corpse was found. The fragments of bones and limbs that, with great exertion, they were able, so to speak, to carve out were committed to burial.

Thus she deserved to be divided into fragments of her own body because she had denied the widow who asked it the fruit of the flesh of a pig.

Do not, therefore, noble daughter, live on the plunder of the poor, but dread as the venom of serpents the food acquired through violence. And since the Apostle commands each person to labor with his own hands so that he may have something with which to assist one suffering want (Eph. IV), you should see that agriculture is pursued vigorously, so that your granaries may be filled with the blessing of produce to provide relief for the needy.

Indeed, as is recorded in the *Book of Illustrious Men*, Hilary, bishop of Arles, was so concerned to assist the needy in their distress—not only through the piety of his mind but also through the exertion of his own body—that he himself cultivated fields beyond his strength. Though distinguished by birth and educated in a very different manner, he subjected himself to rural labor.

But it is not enough that you be warned merely not to seize what belongs to others; it must also be added that whatever you discover was taken before your time, you should restore. For that ancient Roman commander, Scipio, when he had victoriously captured Carthage, returned all the spoils to the cities of Italy, Africa, and Sicily that he learned had once been taken from them by the Carthaginians (Livy, *Decade* 3, book X). What the followers of the Gospel today can scarcely be compelled to do, a pagan accomplished before the Gospel had yet shone forth.

But perhaps you might respond that unless a man takes the lead in all these matters, a weak vessel does not aspire to carry them out. Certainly, we do not deny that, since God has ordained that a woman should be subject to a man, the weaker sex often needs masculine authority. But when a woman judges more rightly, it is fitting that the man not oppose her by the laws of his authority. Such judgment is for the man, not against the man.

The priest Ozias established a term of five days while awaiting the Lord’s mercy, but the magnanimous Judith rebuked and rejected this judgment: “This is not speech,” she said, “that calls forth mercy; rather, it provokes anger and kindles wrath” (Judith VIII).

Abigail, likewise, when she changed the foolish judgment of Nabal, turned back David’s drawn swords from the destruction of her household. She acted for Nabal precisely by refusing to preserve his perverse judgment (1 Sam. XXIII).

When Manoah saw the angel, he began to despair; but his wife raised up his weak and vacillating spirit: “We shall surely die,” he said, “because we have seen God.” To him the woman replied: “If the Lord had wished to kill us, he would not have received from our hands burnt offerings and libations” (Judg. XIII).

Moreover, if a man ought never to have obeyed a woman, the Lord would never have said to Abraham: “Everything that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Gen. XXI).

It is therefore fitting that whatever you discover to have been acquired through injustice, whatever to have been violently taken from others, and whatever to be attached to the household over which you now preside, you should not delay restoring, insofar as it is possible for you. Otherwise, what is written may seem to apply to you: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke XVI).

Thus, venerable daughter, establish the customs of your household. Restrain plunder and violence; curb unbridled service under discipline. In this way, I say, arrange everything entrusted to you according to the will of God, so that, when your stewardship of this exceedingly brief time has been completed, you may deserve to soar to the height of an eternal inheritance.

## LETTER XIX. TO BLANCA, FORMER COUNTESS, NOW A RELIGIOUS

(It is found in volume III and is treatise 50.)

# BOOK EIGHT. TO ILLUSTRIOUS MEN AND OTHER PRIVATE PERSONS

[Col. 0461]

## LETTER ONE TO CINTHIUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

[Col. 0461A]

**SUMMARY.**—He praises Cinthius, prefect of the City, as a defender of justice and equity, instructing the people entrusted to him no less by his example than by his words. Taking this as his occasion, he discusses the duty of the preacher. Finally, he urges him to persevere steadfastly on the path he had once begun, and to protect the poor, the one who has no helper, and above all the resources of the Church.

To the lord Cinthius, prefect of the City, Peter, sinful monk, greetings.

Hearing a proclamation of one’s own virtue, just as it raises the vain to boastfulness, kindles the good and sober to the grace of humility; indeed, they are provoked even more to increase their right conduct when they hear the gifts of virtue bestowed upon them praised.

Yesterday, while we were preaching to the people in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, concerning the solemnity of the Epiphany then being celebrated, as divine mercy suggested, you spoke in a manner befitting not a prefect of the state but rather a priest of the Church. It was not the word of a secular man that was heard, but the eloquence of apostolic preaching.

In this, whom should you be judged to imitate except him who is both king and priest, who governs the world by the command of divine virtue and offered himself to the Father for us as the sacrament of a saving sacrifice?

Through the grace of the same Redeemer, whose members we are, we have received the same thing that he is, so that we might be (1 Cor. VI). Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests for God and his Father” (Rev. I). And Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his wonderful light” (1 Pet. II).

It is therefore established that every Christian is, by the grace of Christ, a priest; hence he ought, not without reason, to proclaim Christ’s mighty deeds (see the scholia at the end of the treatise). You, in particular, clearly imitate the example of this priesthood and kingdom, when in the tribunals you promulgate the laws of legitimate sanction, and in the church, pursuing the urgency of exhortation, build up the minds of the assembled people.

I, however, to whom the office of preaching has been entrusted through the rank of the priestly order, suffer an impediment of voice, and therefore do not rise to satisfy the ears of the very large congregation. Yet when I consider the priests of apostolic grace—Gregory and Ambrose, namely—lamenting a broken stomach and the failure of their voices, I set despair aside and raise my mind into a state of living consolation. Nor do I charge the anger of the terrifying Judge against myself, since I consider that such things came upon those men of such eminence as a safeguard of humility.

What troubles me more, what pierces the secret places of my heart more grievously, is that, while I am hoarse and do not abound in the capacity to teach, I likewise emit not even the slightest spark of a life radiant with good conduct.

Two things are supremely necessary for a perfect preacher: namely, that he abound in the teachings of spiritual doctrine and shine with the splendor of a religious life. But if some priest is unequal to both—if he cannot be distinguished both for his life and for the fluency of his doctrine—life is unquestionably better than doctrine.

The fruit of deeds is sweeter than the bare leaves of words. The radiance of a life is more powerful for example than eloquence or the carefully polished refinement of speech.

Therefore, at the very moment of the Lord’s birth, as the Gospel history bears witness: “An angelic power appeared to the shepherds, and the glory of God shone around them” (Luke II). Immediately afterward it adds that the angel said to them: “Do not fear; for behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (ibid.).

At the manifestation in which he was shown more clearly to those seeking him, the star, herald of that same Redeemer of ours, shone with light but uttered no words. What, then, is signified by the angel, who both shone with splendor and announced the Lord, except the preacher endowed with a twofold grace—one who both abounds in the words of doctrine [Col. 0462C] and radiates with the splendor of holy religion? And what else is indicated by the star except any straightforward priest of honorable life, who, although he does not possess the power of fluent eloquence, nevertheless gleams through his virtuous deeds like the rays of a praiseworthy life, and confirms by the example of his living conduct those whom he does not instruct by his word?

Since, therefore, the priests of the Church are the heavens “which declare the glory of God” (Psalm XVIII), it is necessary that the priest who performs the office of preacher should both rain down the showers of spiritual doctrine and shine with the rays of religious life, like that angel who, announcing the newborn Lord to the shepherds, both flashed forth with the splendor of his brightness and expressed in words what he had come to proclaim. Hence it is said through Malachi: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi II).

But if he cannot be an angel who energetically fulfills the office of preacher by his tongue, let him at least be a star that sends forth the rays of holy conduct. Indeed, the star became more widely known through its brightness because the speaking angel announced it to the shepherds. Hence it is said through Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for everlasting ages” (Daniel XII).

Nevertheless, the one who does not abound in the fluency of eloquent preaching must shine more brightly through the merit of his life. Hence, when Moses said of himself to the Lord who was speaking: “I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday or the day before; and since you have spoken to your servant, I have become more impeded and slower of tongue” (Exodus IV), his face afterward shone so greatly with glory that it dazzled the sight of the children of Israel, and because of the greatness of its splendor they could not look upon him (Exodus XXXIV). But no splendor of heavenly brightness was added to Aaron, of whom the divine voice answered him: [Col. 0463B] “Aaron your brother, the Levite—I know that he is eloquent” (Exodus IV).

When I carefully consider what task was divinely assigned to each of them, I perceive that you fulfill the office of both through a certain imitation in your conduct. “I,” he says, “will be in your mouth and in his mouth, and I will show you what you must do; he will speak for you to the people and will be your mouth, but you will be for him in matters pertaining to God” (ibid.). For when you restrain the multitude of the people through the jurisdiction of your prefecture and the force of judicial authority, what else are you doing than fulfilling Aaron’s office? And when you urge that same people toward the things of God by holy exhortations, what else are you undertaking, as a devoted imitator, than Moses’ spiritual purpose?

Act, then; courage, valiant man, and exercise yourself in the Lord’s field as a worker with a double task. Advance, strive, labor; and in the things you have begun gloriously, persevere still more gloriously. At one time, distinguish a legal dispute by the judgment of justice; at another, preserving the measure proper to your rank, bring forth words of salutary exhortation in the Church; at another, follow Moses’ footsteps in matters pertaining to God; and at another, set before yourself the examples of Aaron the priest in the reckoning of secular cases and business. Be therefore a Benjamin [Benjemini], using both hands as your right hand, so that you may restrain the quarrels of a turbulent people through the vigor of discipline and, insofar as the capacity of your office permits, also set in order the rights of the ecclesiastical state.

May a sword, sharp on both sides, be seen coming from the mouth of Jesus in you (Revelation I), so that the blade with which you are girded may both terrify the swelling hearts of rebels and defend the poor, orphans, and especially ecclesiastical rights from the violence of every kind of evildoer. Let transgressors of the laws recognize in you the avenger of violated justice; let the rulers of the churches rejoice that an energetic and vigilant guardian watches over them.

Be a disciple of David in the art of holy discernment: he mercifully granted pardon to those who persecuted him, yet maintained strict judgment in avenging the slaughter of another (Reg. XVI). Also show yourself a follower of Judas Maccabee (I Maccabees V), who did not cease to rush like lightning against his enemies and to cut down the swollen necks of tyrants with avenging swords, so that he might protect his fellow tribesmen from the impending slaughter of the savage [Col. 0464A] barbarians.

Therefore, fighting without compromise for the protection of the resources of the Churches, avenge the violent oppressors of the poor. Take up the breastplate of equity and justice; devote yourself wholly, not to domestic concerns, but steadfastly to the commonwealth. Thus may Rome call you her savior and father of the fatherland, and may the holy Church rejoice that she has in you a suitable defender. After your death also, may your memory remain in praise with both, and your name in blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0464A] It is therefore established that every Christian is a priest by the grace of Christ; hence he ought rightly to proclaim his mighty acts. For the heretics of our time, not acknowledging with the Catholic Church the sacrament of orders, misuse that testimony of Peter in which he calls all the faithful “a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” although in that passage Saint Peter uses a customary manner of speaking, by no means unfamiliar in sacred writings, whereby something is said indefinitely to exist among all when it is found among some of the multitude. Thus we say, in a proper and true sense, that empire exists among the Germans, not that all Germans are emperors.

Augustine discusses this phrase in Book [I] Against the Donatists, after the conference, chapter 20, and other Fathers readily acknowledge that Saint Peter indicated a certain mystical priesthood, by which a layperson is considered to sacrifice evil desires and offer pure offerings of good works to God. On this priesthood, see Leo the Great, Sermon 3, On the Anniversary of His Assumption. Cardinal Thomas of Saint Sixtus, in his third Jentaculum, explaining Peter’s words, “To whom you come, a living stone rejected indeed by men but chosen and honored by God, and you yourselves, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices” (1 Peter II), makes it clear from these very words that they must be understood of a priesthood not properly but metaphorically. For Saint Peter metaphorically says that living stones are built up into spiritual houses, and in metaphorical language he adds “spiritual sacrifices.” It is therefore evident that Peter speaks metaphorically of the priesthood—namely, of the priesthood of virtue, by which someone offers works of virtue to God. There can be no doubt that our cardinal also speaks of this mystical or metaphorical priesthood, not of priesthood properly so called.]

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME MAN

[Col. 0464D] **Summary.**—He reproves the same Cinthius because, perhaps out of devotion to prayer, he was not fulfilling the duty entrusted to him of rendering justice to the people. He therefore shows how praiseworthy it is, and how great its merit, to administer justice.

To the lord CINTHIUS, prefect, Peter, sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

Most beloved, since you administer an office of such great dignity, it is exceedingly fearful if you should ever allow yourself to be relaxed through the torpor of negligence. For I hear that many complaints are being made against you by those who have cases in litigation, because they are unable to obtain from you the decision of a lawful judgment.

Hear, then, what the wise man says: “A wise judge will judge his people, and the rule of a sensible man will be stable upon the earth. As is the judge of the people, so are his ministers; and as is the ruler of the city, so are those who dwell in it” (Ecclesiasticus X). From these words it is plainly gathered that if you preserve justice and prove yourself truly just, not only your ministers but also all those subject to you among the urban population will become just.

Take care, therefore, lest because of your devotion to private prayer, to which you perhaps strive to devote yourself, you neglect the discipline of the exceedingly numerous people entrusted to you, and, for the sake of your own benefit, abandon the common welfare of the populace that awaits justice from you. For it is written: “He who keeps the law multiplies prayer; and to attend to the commandments is a saving sacrifice.” What else, then, is doing justice than praying? Elsewhere too it is written: “Justice exalts nations [gentes; printed gratias]” (Ecclesiasticus XXXV; Proverbs XIV). And the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Psalm CV).

I clearly remember that the most excellent leader Gothifred told me what I am writing. “My maternal uncle,” he said, “also named Gothifred, a man of very great power, was exceedingly devoted to doing justice, and maintained the discipline and force of legal sanctions over the peoples subject to him. Once, when an innumerable multitude of the populace had been gathered before him, the exalted leader himself cried out in a loud voice: ‘Let whoever wishes to obtain judgment bring his case forward.’

“When he had performed this herald’s office and repeated the call a third time, and no one from so great a people answered, he understood that everyone had been satisfied, with every dispute over their cases completely settled and brought to rest. Then he joyfully mounted his horse and left the people rejoicing—not in quarrels, but in mutual peace.

“After his death, a certain man, carried away in spirit during sleep, was led to hell and saw various tortures of punishment. Among them he saw Richard, abbot of Verdun, raising up lofty structures and anxiously and carefully building what looked like fortified ramparts of a camp. While he lived, that abbot had suffered from this failing: he spent nearly all the care of his diligence on the vain construction of buildings and squandered many resources of the Church on such frivolous nonsense. What he had done in life, he endured in punishment.

“Now the man who saw these things in sleep, while he looked curiously this way and that at many things, seemed to see my uncle, mentioned above, seated on a golden bench. Two angels appeared to be standing beside him; waving whips in their hands, they tried, as servants do, to temper the heat upon his face. When the man who saw these things asked who he was, he received the answer: ‘Justice.’ Indeed, because he had practiced justice while alive, after death he also merited the name of justice.”

You too, most beloved, diligently perform the office of administration entrusted to you, so that you may regard yourself as a laborer in a vineyard entrusted to you, and do not grow sluggish in the exercise of your labor if you expect the coin of worthy recompense. Let the severity of legal sanctions restrain those whom the shame of honesty does not check from the excesses [Col. 0466A] of injustice; let those who are convicted by the violence of wickedness of violating the boundary of uprightness feel the force of the law. Thus, while each person subject to you is preserved in his own rights, may a worthy reward for your ministry also be preserved for you with God.

## LETTER III. TO ALBERT, A MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

**Summary.**—In this letter he exhorts a certain Albert, a man distinguished in those times by power and nobility, to show the reverence owed to his parents, because he had heard that Albert did not hold his mother in the honor due to her, owing to his love for his wife. He emphasizes this as a grave crime.

To ALBERT, a most illustrious man, Peter, sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0466B] Without doubt, he despises the commands of the divine law who considers it of little importance to show respect to his parents; he who does not obey his own parents does not accept the thread of his lot in the land of the living. On the contrary, through Moses the divine voice commands: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the earth” (Exodus XXVI). The Wise Man also says: “He who honors his father will live a longer life, and he who obeys his father will refresh his mother” (Ecclesiasticus III). And immediately he adds: “He who fears the Lord honors his parents, and will serve those who gave him birth as though they were his masters, both in deed and in speech and in all patience” (ibid.).

It commonly happens by the just judgment of God that whoever humbly submits to his parents, once he himself has become a parent, takes pleasure in the obedience of his own offspring. Hence it is written: “He who honors his father will rejoice in his children, and on the day of his prayer he will be heard” (ibid.). For he is rightly heard by God in his prayers who, hearing God’s command, submits to the laws of his parents.

Moreover, just as one who curses his parents is worthy of being struck by the punishment of death, so one who obeys them reverently deserves to be blessed by God. For it is written in the law: “He who curses his father or mother shall be put to death” (Leviticus XX; Ecclesiasticus III). Elsewhere too it is written: “Honor your father, so that blessing may come upon you from the Lord, and his blessing may remain at the end” (ibid.). Immediately afterward it follows: “The blessing of a father strengthens the houses of his children, but the curse of a mother uproots their foundations” (ibid.).

If, therefore, the house of children is destroyed by the curse of their parents and established by their blessings, great care must be taken lest, if we offend our parents, we destroy the offspring that will come after us.

It has been reported to me, most noble man, that you despise and scorn your holy mother out of love for your wife, and grant her no right of authority in the household’s administration of property. In this action, what else do you appear to imitate than the nature of fire? Although fire comes forth from wood, it consumes the wood and turns it to ashes, while it burns stones and makes them white. The wood from which it comes forth it consumes as though it were its mother by birth; but the stones by which it is extinguished it makes white, producing the whiteness of lime.

Thus, although fire burns in wood and bakes stones, it has contrary effects upon things that are not contrary. For although stones and wood are different, they are not contraries, as white and black are; one of these the fire produces in stones, and the other in wood. It brightens those by making them bright, while darkening these, although it would entirely fail to exist in those if it did not live in these.

Hence the Wise Man rightly says: “Honor your father, and do not forget the groaning of your mother; remember that unless you had been born through them, you would not exist, and repay them as they repaid you” (Ecclesiasticus VII). Consider, therefore, how great a cruelty it is to despise and scorn those through whom you have even your existence, and how greatly you ought to submit yourself in humility to your parents, to whom you owe both the substance of your natural being and what you do not deny that you received from them in childhood. Consider how greatly you ought now to repay the elderly in grateful return.

Hence it is written: “Son, receive your father’s old age, and do not grieve him in his life; and if his mind should fail, grant pardon, and do not despise him in your strength” (Ecclesiasticus III).

But perhaps you will say: “My mother often exasperates me; by harsh words she disturbs both my heart and my wife’s. We cannot endure so many insults, nor are we able to tolerate the annoyances of her severity and stern correction.” Yet by this you acquire a more abundant reward, if, while you receive insult, you return kindness, and while you are sprinkled with the salt of reproaches, you respond with humility.

Hence it is written: “The almsgiving of a father will not be forgotten, for it will be restored to you as a recompense for the sin of your mother” (ibid.). If, then, good is restored for the sin of a mother, why should one not bear patiently when she rages or acts unjustly? The Scripture certainly says something terrifying: “How evil in reputation is he who abandons his father, and accursed by God is he who exasperates his mother” (ibid.).

Moreover, since the one who dishonors his parents is rejected by God, is he not also brought to shame in this life? But hear the Scripture: “The glory of a man comes from the honor of his father, and a father without honor is the disgrace of his son” (ibid.).

But while we gather together the testimonies of the ancient Scriptures, let us not hesitate to add a recent example, so that, at least when the vengeance of divine justice has been displayed, it may not pass by those whom the bonds of heavenly commandments do not restrain.

On the evening before yesterday, I happened to hear from the mouth of that venerable pope Alexander himself what I am about to report. “A certain Ardericus,” he said, “a native of the city of Milan, was celebrating a wedding feast after taking a wife. The caterer complained that the seasoning sprinkled over the food had run out. When the bridegroom, not without a certain swelling of quarrelsome anger, turned the accusation in this matter against his mother, angrily and arrogantly asking why she had allowed such a shortage, the mother replied in turn that she had provided the seasoning adequately for the servants. Finally, driven by the gall of anger, he did not fear to lay hands upon her; acting insolently and in a frenzy, he struck her irreverently across the face.

“But, O divine justice, avenging our anger yet not angry; raging against the madness of a furious spirit yet remaining calm; taking vengeance on the insanity of an unquiet mind yet tranquil! Hence Solomon says: ‘But you, Master of power, judge with calmness and govern us with great reverence’ (Wisdom XII).

“Suddenly sickness seized the same cheek of the striker—namely, the left—and began to torment him with excessive pains. As the illness grew more dangerous day by day and wearied the man intolerably with the sharp goads of pain, forcing him to howl with groans and shrieks, the mother, who had perceived a stepson in the blow, recognized her son by nature. She did not show the harshness of a stepmother, as he had deserved, but rather the compassion of a mother’s heart.

“By then the flesh of the swelling jaw had putrefied horribly; pus and corruption were dripping through the hollow channel of the wound. As the man was miserably tormented from side to side, the corruption issuing from him and the inward force of the pain caused him to regret the marriage he had contracted. He already feared that his wife might have another husband, and he regarded her, whom he had seen newly married, as in a certain sense already twice married.

“The mother, therefore, not repaying her suffering son with the justice of retaliation, but rather sympathizing with him through devout compassion, hurried to the church of the blessed martyr Nazarius. She multiplied her vows, offered gifts, prostrated herself on the pavement, prayed, pleaded, and entreated; and with tears she begged forgiveness for her guilty son.

“Divine mercy was present to the mother’s prayers. The one who had inspired her to seek forgiveness for the offender also heard her prayer and, in his favor, raised up the sick man. Shortly afterward, when the flesh had everywhere dissolved and putrefied, the bone fell from the jaw; immediately all pain fled, the scar became hardened, and divine mercy restored the man, already despaired of, to his former health.

“Thus, in the face of one man, both the mark of divine mercy is expressed and the sign of human guilt remains: while the face bereft of bone is seen, it visibly appears as healed and as bearing witness to what the impiety of a raging son deserved and what maternal devotion obtained for him at the ears of divine clemency.”

May this divine power admonish you, most illustrious man; may this wound inflicted upon a mother terrify you; and may it restrain not only you but also your most serene wife from every offense against your mother-in-law. Thus, while you honor your parent—which is the first commandment with a promise (Exodus XX; Deuteronomy V; Matthew XV)—may you one day pass through the wilderness and, with those who are true Israelites, deserve to enter the land of the living.

## LETTER IV. TO ALBERICUS THE SENATOR AND HIS WIFE ERMILINA

**Summary.**—He strives to console Albericus and his wife, whose infant son had recently died, showing that his death should be received with joy rather than grief, since he had been transferred from this valley of misery to everlasting happiness without any labor or struggle.

To the lord ALBERICUS, a man of senatorial rank, and to ERMILINA, his wife, Peter, sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0469A] Know, most beloved, that when we learned that the son you both held in common had passed from this world into the rule of almighty God, we were struck by the anguish of sudden grief, and the sharpness of no slight sadness pierced our hearts with compassionate affection. But when we began, after taking counsel, carefully to examine the matter, we judged ourselves blameworthy and humbly urged, with submissive prayers, the prudence of your high rank to lay aside its grief.

For what good could your devotion have done in the sight of almighty God by which he would rightly have bestowed upon you the benefit of so great a gift? Namely, that from your seed he should transfer offspring to the heavenly kingdoms, establish him among the angels, clothe him in the robe of immortality, and crown him with the diadem of everlasting glory; that he should also clasp him in his own arms, imprint kisses upon him like a loving father, and happily place him, as a child of his own womb, in that bridal chamber of eternal rest.

Behold us unhappy and wretched—I speak of myself and those like me, fellow sinners—who, fasting and continually struggling without truce against evil spirits, can scarcely hope for what he obtained without any exertion or labor. Freely he obtained it and reached that nuptial banquet of the blessed citizens without any labor of conflict or weariness.

Furthermore, he who took your son from your hands and, loving him more than you, received him into the fellowship of his adoption, is able to give you one much better in his place and to multiply offspring from you in return for one.

Anna, the wife of Elkanah, established her only son to remain continually in the tabernacle, observing the rites of the divine law; and, as Scripture testifies, “lent him to the Lord as at interest” (1 Samuel I). Hence that holy woman says to the priest Eli: “I prayed, and the Lord granted me my petition, which I asked of him; therefore I too have lent him to the Lord for all the days during which he is lent to the Lord.” To her the priest Eli also said: “May the Lord give you offspring from this woman in return for what you lent to the Lord” (1 Samuel II).

Now what is lent at interest is received not as a simple amount but multiplied. Hence it immediately follows there: “And the Lord visited Anna, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters” (ibid.).

He, therefore, who in return for one son gave so abundant an offspring, how much more could he make you rejoice in the propagation of your seed through the love of your holy marriage, since he did not command your son to serve in an earthly tabernacle but rather established him to reign forever in that heavenly Jerusalem before the sight of his majesty?

Let your tears, therefore, most beloved, cease from your eyes; let groans and sighs be restrained; let every kind of mourning vanish from your faces; and, with all grief entirely laid aside, let festive serenity shine forth.

Let your holy prudence say together with King David: “For the child, while he was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said: Who knows whether the Lord might perhaps give him to me, so that the child might live? But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him; he will not return to me” (1 Samuel XII).

Therefore, most beloved, lay aside every lament of pain and sadness; restore to your household the customary joys of spiritual gladness; lift your minds to the hope of heavenly consolation; and endure the blows of divine chastisement not only patiently and calmly, but also cheerfully.

May almighty God, who in paternal compassion deemed it worthy to take your son from your hands and transfer him into the embraces of his own love, grant you abundant offspring in place of the one child and, in addition, allow you to produce a never-dying offspring of good works.

## LETTER V. TO PETER, SENATOR OF THE CITY

[Col. 0470B] **Summary.**—He exhorts Peter, a man of senatorial rank who had undertaken to build a church but, for some unknown reason, had immediately abandoned the undertaking, to complete the work begun. He shows that what certain people chattered is not true: that God grants no reward to those who build churches. For this purpose he brings forward the examples of Solomon and others.

To the lord PETER, a man of senatorial rank, Peter, sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

It is common to the elect and the reprobate alike to begin various good works without distinction, but it is especially characteristic of the elect to bring to completion what they have begun well. The former persevere immovably in what they begin; the latter, always changing through inconstancy, quickly alter their purpose. Hence it is written: “A fool is changed like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII).

You certainly began, most beloved, to build a monastery, but before the masonry had raised itself to almost the height of six feet, you gave up. Thus, according to the evangelical saying, one might rightly mock you: “This man began to build, and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV). Or one might apply what Tobiah the Ammonite said in the Book of Nehemiah, mocking Jerusalem while it was being rebuilt: “Let them build; if a fox climbs up, it will leap over their stone wall” (2 Esdras IV).

For while the walls hang half-ruined and shamefully interrupted, they deserve rather to be called ruins than to be named a church.

Do you think, as some people babble in their madness, that there is no fruit of reward or recompense for the construction of church walls? Do you not know that, after the Temple had been completed, the Lord appeared in a dream to King Solomon and bestowed upon him not only wisdom beyond the measure of human capacity but also an incomparable abundance of every kind of wealth? “Wisdom and knowledge have been given to you,” he said, “but I will give you riches, possessions, and glory, so that no one among the kings before or after you will be like you” (1 Kings III).

Indeed, if almighty God despises the labors of those who build his churches, why did he command with such care that a tabernacle be constructed for him in the desert? (Exodus XXV.) Did he speak to Moses with contempt or negligence when he said: “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, from the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every kind of work, to devise whatever can be fashioned from gold, silver, bronze, marble, gems, and various kinds of wood. I have also given him as a companion Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan, and in the heart of every skilled craftsman I have placed wisdom, so that they may make all that I have commanded you” (Exodus XXXI)?

Moreover, he who commanded that a tabernacle be made with such skill, although he knew that it would soon be abolished, how much more does he wish a church to be built for him, one that remains immovably for the salvation of all nations until the end of the world?

The tabernacle erected in the desert and the Temple constructed under Solomon’s rule were shadows and figures of this Church, which now shines forth among the Christian people. Hence it was said to Moses: “Make everything as it was shown to you on the mountain” (Exodus XXV).

Christ is the author and builder of this Church; he is the true king and priest. When that Temple was rebuilt after its destruction had been completed, its restoration was led by Zerubbabel, who was of the royal tribe of Judah, and by Jesus son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Hence the prophet Haggai says: “The Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Jesus son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they entered and worked on the house of the Lord of hosts, their God” (Haggai I).

Concerning this restoration Isaiah says: “They shall build the ancient ruins, raise up the former devastations, and restore the deserted and scattered cities” (Isaiah LXI). Again it is said: “Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob and have mercy on his dwellings; the city shall be built upon its height, and the Temple shall be founded according to its order” (Jeremiah XXX).

Whoever strives to build even an external basilica for the honor of almighty God undoubtedly belongs to the building of this spiritual temple.

Moreover, so that not words of exhortation alone but also a sign of divine power that has been displayed may urge you to complete what you have begun well, Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, a truthful and prudent man, claims that he learned in the city of Constantinople what he reported.

“It happened,” he said, “that an emperor—though he did not remember his name—was once afflicted with blindness, and no remedy of medical skill could help him. Since he was entirely unable to escape this danger by human means, he undertook to obtain it from God through prayers poured forth.

“He then heard in a dream that if he went to the church of the blessed martyr Lawrence, he would receive from God the light of restored sight. He therefore made a vow to go to Rome, ordered a ship to be prepared at once, and firmly resolved to set out immediately.

“But his wife, fearing that she might lose the empire while her children were still young, fearing the danger to her husband as royal dignity declined and the perils of the sea, devised a pious deception. She therefore gave the rowers this order: they were not at all to make directly for Rome, but, stopping at various harbors and coastal stations and slowing the ship’s progress, they were merely to pretend to be making the journey.

“While the sailors, as they had been instructed, deceived the king by changing the names of various places—now proceeding forward, now through winding turns and reversals slipping back to the very places from which they had departed—the queen, employing a multitude of stonecutters and builders, constructed a most august and exceedingly magnificent church in honor of the blessed Lawrence, precisely according to the dimensions of the basilica that the aforesaid martyr has in the very suburb of Rome.

“She said: ‘If it has been granted that through the blessed Lawrence my husband should return to health, then whatever God can do in Rome, he can also do here.’

“While the emperor was being led from place to place through various bends and coastal stations, the basilica was being built there by a great number of craftsmen. At the same time, the building was completed and magnificently decorated, and a year passed.

“When all this had been accomplished, the aforementioned ruler was brought back to the walls of Constantinople, though, because his companions said so, he believed that he was in Rome. Care was therefore taken, and arrangements were made with great diligence, that no one should attend him except Latin speakers, who, when he asked, would assure him that he was in Rome and that the basilica of the martyr Lawrence was present.

“Then, led by the hand, the emperor entered the church; and immediately, having received back his sight, he marveled to see his wife, his attendants, and his household servants standing around him.”

On the report of the venerable Desiderius [Note: [Col. 0471D] He is Blessed Victor, Pope III.], abbot of the monastery of Cassino, I learned what I have taken care to record in these pages.

“A religious woman,” he said, “named Bella, lived in the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter, situated within the walls of the city of Benevento. Throughout her life she did not abandon the path of religious observance. Although she had been betrothed, according to her station, to a man of distinguished lineage, she despised carnal marriage in order to receive a heavenly bridegroom. Thus she broke the bond of the marriage contract and, intending to assume the monastic veil, hastened toward the author of perpetual virginity and the bridal chamber of undefiled chastity.

“From these beginnings of her holy conversion she bound herself by the rule of a stricter life. Trampling underfoot, with the step of a lofty purpose, every softness of carnal allure, she subdued her body, which had been brought up in a very different manner, by the judgment of rigorous severity. Indeed, she would often throw her limbs, weakened by fasting, against the bare floor, and provided herself with no bed except the earth itself.

“But, leaving aside for the moment her life, I shall briefly relate what she reported concerning her teacher, a woman named Offa, who had brought her into the religious life of the order of nuns and had nobly educated her. She said that when, as was customary, Offa rose early during the silence of night, and, devoting herself to frequent prayers, went around the most holy altars with the scent of burning incense, one night she took up the censer as usual and approached the place where the incense was kept. But, whether it had fallen or had been removed, she did not find the substance there as she had expected. At the same time, the force of the winds, which had then blown with unusual violence, extinguished the light of the shining lamp.
