“As the devout woman ran anxiously here and there, unable to find any fragrance to place upon the censer, suddenly someone came through the darkness and put into her hand the incense she was seeking. I may reasonably suppose that this was done through an angel.

“She also said that while her aforementioned mother was lying weakened by the illness from which she shortly afterward died, and while all those standing near the bed were watching, wonderful to behold! she was suddenly lifted bodily into the air and remained suspended there for a long time, until she had fulfilled the vows of the prayer she had begun.

“After she had happily died, her holy body was buried inside the church. A peasant placed a sack full of grain upon her tomb; immediately, driven away by a most violent whirlwind, the sack was cast off by divine power. Thus the uneducated and inexperienced peasant was forced to gather his grain from the dust, because he had refused to show fitting reverence to the shrine of the holy body.

“When …” [Note: [Col. 0473D] The remainder is missing in the manuscripts.]

280

EPISTLE VI. TO G., A MOST NOBLE MAN

[Col. 0473C]

ARGUMENT.—In this epistle Blessed Peter Damian consoles a sick man. The chief point of the consolation is that tribulations are signs of divine predestination for God’s chosen servants; he proves this by many authorities, especially that of Saint James. He then warns him to guard diligently against despair. Finally, showing from the testimonies of Saint Paul that we ought to rejoice in afflictions, he urges him to endure suffering.

To my lord G., a most noble man, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of brotherly charity.

You asked me, dearest friend, to send you words of consolation in letters and to sweeten your bitter spirit, amid all the blows you suffer, with gentle admonitions. But if the judgment of your prudence is not asleep, consolation is already at hand, since the very words unmistakably show that you are being divinely instructed, as a son, to receive an inheritance. For what is clearer than the saying: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation”? (Ecclus. II.) For where there is fear and justice, the trial of any adversity is not servile torture but rather paternal discipline.

Hence blessed Job, amid the very blows of his scourging, said: “May he who began himself crush me; may he loosen his hand and cut me off”; and immediately he added: “And this would be my consolation, that, afflicting me with sorrow, he would not spare” (Job VI). The very striking of God is indeed a great consolation to the elect, because through the momentary scourges they endure, they grow strong with the steps of firm hope so as to attain the glory of heavenly blessedness.

For, as Scripture testifies: “The Lord does not judge twice for the same thing” (Nahum I). Yet the wicked, who do not correct themselves amid their scourges, are not judged twice, even though after the adversities of this life they are handed over to avenging flames; for their twofold crushing is so joined together by God’s just judgment that what begins here is completed there, and more unhappily. Just as scourges are merely the first beginnings of hellish torments for the hard and obstinate, so those same scourges are truly the source of heavenly rewards for the good and upright in heart.

The hammer strikes gold so that the craftsman may remove the dross; the file repeatedly scrapes it so that the shining vein of metal may gleam more brilliantly. “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation by tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII). Hence it is said through blessed James: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations” (James I).

Those have good reason to rejoice who are afflicted here temporarily for their sins and for whom eternal rewards are preserved in heaven for the good they have done. It is a blessed exchange: to be worn down here by temporal pressures and afterward to rejoice in the beauty of perpetual light; now to be subjected to bodily troubles and afterward to be transferred to the glory of angelic dignity. There no illness weighs anyone down, no trembling old age bends anyone, no loss of what has been possessed torments anyone, and no feverish eagerness for what is to be acquired inflames anyone. Rather, the flower of perpetual youth flourishes unharmed, and the beautiful appearance of those who live blessedly remains incorruptibly fresh, so that the living grace of beauty continually endures in its verdure. When everything flows in accordance with desire at a nod, anxiety about losing anything causes no disturbance, since the security of enjoyment without end endures.

Therefore, dearest and sweetest brother, while you are surrounded by scourges, while you are chastised by the blows of heavenly discipline, do not let despair weigh down your mind, let no complaint of murmuring burst forth, let no sorrowful grief overwhelm you, and let no faintheartedness make you impatient. Instead, let serenity always shine in your face, cheerfulness in your mind, and thanksgiving resound from your mouth.

God’s dispensation is worthy of praise: he scourges his own temporarily so that he may hide them from perpetual scourges; he presses them so that he may raise them up; he cuts them so that he may heal them; he casts them down so that he may exalt them. Whoever does good and suffers evil receives in heaven many times over whatever is withheld from him on earth as a just recompense.

Physicians of the body allow those whom they despair of recovering to take freely whatever foods they ask for; but those whom they judge capable of being restored, they sternly forbid every harmful delicacy. They also administer antidotes and bitter medicines, so that by drinking bitterness they may recover the sweetness of health.

What wonder, then, if God almighty, the physician of souls, allows those whom he sees subject to everlasting death to live agreeably, while he binds those whom he chooses for life under the strict law of his severity? We also treat animals that we intend soon to slaughter more indulgently and provide them with more abundant food; but we pay little attention to the scantiness and thinness of those we reserve for breeding and the propagation of offspring. Vines and all fruitful trees lie under pruning; sterile trees, however, and those destined for the fire spread out their branches and, the freer they are, the more widely they extend.

Do not therefore envy wicked people the happiness of this life; rather, share their sorrow—or, since they themselves do not grieve, groan over them instead. They hasten toward the slaughterhouse by eating like brute animals; by their wantonness they hurry toward the sword.

But rejoice in your pressures and troubles, and rejoice in the Lord with all your heart, because you who are now, so to speak, weighed down by the lightness of empty punishments will afterward carry away, as one to be rewarded, the weight of precious gold. Paul promises this when he says: “For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory” (II Cor. IV).

Examine the apostolic words simply and consider them carefully. Whatever you suffer is momentary and light, so that you may bear equably what is called light and trust that what is momentary will swiftly pass away. Do not overlook how fittingly and precisely the divine words correspond to one another: after promising that our tribulation is momentary and light, he immediately adds the eternal weight of glory.

Weigh and compare tribulation with glory, the momentary with the eternal, the light with the weight. Rejoice, then, and exult, because what you endure of tribulation is momentary, while what you await of glory is eternal. Everything you endure is light; what you await is weighty. Rejoice, I say, because in place of tribulation you will receive glory, in place of lightness weight, and in place of the momentary the eternal.

Amid pressures and hardships, always lift your eyes to him who is ready, after the scourges, to cherish you in the embrace of his sweetness; who will establish you, after storms and tempests, in the beauty of heavenly rest, and wipe the tears from your eyes with the cloth of perpetual consolation. “For God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints” (Rev. VII and XXI).

Turn over constantly in meditation that other apostolic saying, and while placed amid scourges rejoice in the Lord with all your heart: “Not only this,” he says, “but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience testing, and testing hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

Strengthen your mind, dearest friend, for patience by these and other testimonies of divine Scripture, and joyfully await happiness after sorrow. Let hope raise you up toward that joy, and let charity kindle your fervor, so that the mind, well intoxicated with good things, may forget what it suffers outwardly and may long and strive toward what it contemplates inwardly.

EPISTLE VII. TO ATTO, A DOCTOR OF LAWS

(It is found in volume III, in treatise 42.)

EPISTLE VIII. TO BONOHOMINUS, AN EXPERT IN LAW, OF CESENA

ARGUMENT.—He urges him, while enjoying prosperity, to weigh constantly in thought not the fleeting and passing goods of the present life but those that will be eternal after death. Above all, he should set before his eyes the day of the final judgment, and meditate again and again upon the destruction of the whole fabric of this world, the inexorable severity of the judge, the punishments prepared for human wickedness, and the late and useless repentance of human beings. He develops this at length with many authorities from the prophets and the holy Fathers. Finally, he concludes by urging him once more to meditate daily upon the passages he has drawn from the books of the prophets and Fathers, considering them an exceedingly effective remedy for healing wounds and injuries of the soul.

283

To my lord Bonohominus, a most prudent judge, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the bond of brotherly charity.

I am not unaware that when my letter is handed over to the grammarians of this world, they immediately attend to whether it possesses the charm of elaborate style, seek out the color of rhetorical beauty, and with curious minds probe the deceptive circles of syllogisms and enthymemes. They hunt for the knowledge that puffs up, but do not admire the charity that builds up (I Cor. VIII). Yet, according to Solomon: “The words of the servants of God should be like goads and like nails driven firmly into the heights” (Eccles. XII).

These words are compared to nails and goads because they are accustomed to prick the life of carnal people with sharp rebukes, rather than caress it with the smooth, flattering oil of harmful approval. My grammar, therefore, is Christ, who was made man for human beings; and whatever can contribute to the edification of my brothers, that alone my letter knows how to exude.

[Note: [Col. 0475] The same material concerning the day of judgment is found above in Epistle 5 of Book IV, expressed in almost the same sentences and words.]

Therefore, dearest brother, while the world smiles upon you, while bodily health is vigorous, while earthly prosperity delights you, consider what will follow these things. Consider what is at hand as though it had already passed, and let your prudence carefully examine what future things will succeed present things.

Whatever is transitory, therefore, decide already that it has passed away, and assign it to the category of a dream of deceptive illusion. Let your mind return there; let the anxious eyes of its intelligence direct themselves there—to that which, once it has occurred, knows no passing away.

Set the terrible day of the final judgment already before your eyes, and with your innermost being trembling, contemplate the sudden coming of such majesty. Do not think that day distant which the prophet, so many ages before us, proclaimed as near, as though it were already at the threshold, saying:

“The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and comes very swiftly. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the mighty man will be afflicted. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and battle cry” (Zeph. I).

Consider, dearest friend, with what severity the prophet saw the final day of judgment grow bitter over the hearts of the reprobate—he who could not explain it adequately even with so many names. Indeed, to say nothing now of those punishments of eternal damnation that never end, if only the terror and horror of that final day are carefully examined as they deserve, the whole deceptive and false happiness of this world is judged as though it were mud or barren seaweed on the shore.

Whom will that voice not terrify? Who will not tremble to the marrow when he hears the Lord himself saying in the Gospel: “For as lightning comes out of the east and appears in the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. XXIV)? Who, I ask, will not be afraid when the same Truth says: “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken” (ibid.)?

Peter also says concerning this: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on that day the heavens will pass away with great violence, and the elements will be dissolved by heat” (II Pet. III). And again he says: “But the heavens and the earth that now exist have been preserved by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and of the destruction of ungodly people” (ibid.).

Hence the apostle Jude also says: “Behold, the Lord will come with his holy thousands, to execute judgment against all, to convict all the ungodly of all the works of their ungodliness by which they acted wickedly, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him” (Jude I).

O, if only our heart’s palate could taste how bitter is what is said through John: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Rev. I).

Then the loins of those who now do not fear will be dissolved by terror; then the inward parts of those who now lie softly in the pleasures of carnal allurements will be filled with bitterness. Then, shedding bloody tears, they will begin to say to the mountains: “Fall upon us,” and to the hills: “Cover us” (Rev. VI; Luke XXIII).

Then there will be nowhere to flee, no hiding place where anyone can conceal himself, since the gates of hell will be opened, hostile death will be destroyed, and the dust that had decayed—that is, human flesh—will hear the voice of the trumpet and be brought to life. Then the earth will return, as though a deposit entrusted to it, those whom it had received into its bosom; the waters will return those whom they had swallowed; and the devouring flame those whom it had consumed. All will restore them to life without any diminution.

Then the earth will be shaken, the air disturbed by a sudden storm, the thunder will roar, and flashes and lightning will confuse human hearts with terror. “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him; he will summon heaven above and earth, to judge his people” (Ps. XLIX).

On that dreadful day he will appear with angels and archangels, with Thrones and Dominations, with Principalities and Powers; the heavens will flash, the earth will burn, and all the elements will be shaken in terror to serve him.

That distinguished prophet Isaiah rightly announces this day, saying: “Behold, the day of the Lord will come, incurable, a day of fury and wrath” (Isa. XIII), to make the earth desolate and destroy sinners from it. “For the stars of heaven will not give their light; the sun will be darkened at its rising; the moon will not give its light. I will command evils against the whole world and against the ungodly for their sins. I will destroy the insult of the wicked and humble the arrogance of the proud. Those who are left will be more precious than gold tested by fire, and a human being will be more precious than sapphire. For heaven will be shaken, and the earth will be moved from its foundations because of the fury of the wrath of the Lord of hosts, on the day when his anger comes upon it.”

The prophet Malachi also speaks in harmony with this, saying: “Behold, the almighty Lord will come, and who will endure the day of his coming, or who will withstand his sight?” (Mal. III.) For he will enter the refiner’s fire and, like the one who winnows straw, will sit steadfastly and purify, as gold and silver.

And again he says: “Behold, the day of the Lord will come burning like a furnace, to burn [probably, ‘and he will burn’] them; and all the foreigners, and all who commit iniquity, will be like straw. The day that is to come will set them on fire, says the almighty Lord, and it will leave them neither root nor branch” (Mal. IV).

But another, the man of desires, says this: “And behold, I saw, and thrones were set up, and the Ancient of Days sat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool. His throne was a burning fire, and a river of fire flowed before him; judgment was set, and the books were opened.”

And shortly afterward: “I saw in a vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven. He came even to the Ancient of Days, and was presented before him. To him were given dominion, honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages would serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed. My spirit shuddered; I, Daniel, was overcome, and the visions of my head troubled me” (Dan. VII).

When these things begin to take place, the gates of heaven will undoubtedly be opened—or rather, heaven itself will be removed from the midst, as though the curtains of a tabernacle were being gathered up, so that it may be restored and transformed into something better.

Then everything will be filled with fear, and terror and trembling will fill the universe, when he judges who needs no witness, seeks no arguments, and requires no advocate for his case. With all these things removed far away, he himself will judge deeds, words, and thoughts, set them out in the open, and display them as though painted on tablets before the eyes of those who committed them and of all who appear to be standing by.

How, then, will every creature be shaken and terrified at that time? Hence Isaiah says: “The day of the vengeance of the Lord, the year of the recompense of the judgment of Zion; and its streams will be turned into burning pitch; by day and by night they will not be extinguished forever” (Isa. XXXIV).

Blessed Job also describes this, saying: “A land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death dwells, and there is no order, but everlasting horror” (Job X).

Hence the prophet also says: “They will go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me; their worms will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI).

For what more horrible thing can be said or imagined than to receive the wounds of damnation and never bring the pains of those wounds to an end? Hence it is said through the prophet: “They descended into hell with their weapons” (Ezek. XXXII).

The weapons of sinners are the members of their bodies by which they carry out the perverse desires they conceive. To descend into hell with their weapons, therefore, is to endure the torments of eternal fire with those very members by which they fulfilled their desires for pleasure.

Paul also says: “At the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ from heaven with the angels of his power, in a flame of fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They will suffer eternal destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power” (II Thess. I). And again: “There remains a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries” (Heb. X).

Come, then: when we have arrived at that final judgment, we shall be judged by the Judge who cannot be deceived by the concealment of crimes and cannot be corrupted by the offering of any gift to obtain impunity. When all secrets begin to be revealed, and not only deeds and words but even thoughts themselves are displayed, what shall we do beneath the majesty of so great a Judge? What excuse will we be able to offer? By what skill of defense will we clear ourselves? What repentance will then come to our aid, which we despised in this flesh? What good works will defend us, which we did not perform in this life? To which apostles, or to which other saints, shall we flee, whose examples and words we alike scorned?

Or perhaps some weakness of the body will excuse us? But all the examples of the saints will cry out against their excuse. By conquering the weakness of the flesh in the flesh, they taught us that what they did we too could do—especially since they themselves resisted sin not by their own power but with the help of the merciful Lord, who reveals himself even to those who do not seek him, so that he may be sought and believed in, and who protects those who believe in him with unconquerable protection, so that they are not overcome by sin.

What, then, will they answer if the Lord says to them: “If you were able, why did you not resist sinful desires? If you were not able, why did you not seek my help against sin? Or, when you were wounded, why did you not apply the remedy of repentance to your wound?”

Will they not fall silent before these questions? What excuse can those who have none give when he says: “Bind them hand and foot, and cast them into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII)? It follows that those teeth will gnash there who here rejoiced in gluttony.

We must therefore consider and ponder with the greatest care what terror there will be on that day, when punishment will leave no remedy. What shame will come upon the one who, as his guilt demands, must blush in the assembly of all human beings and angels? What fear will seize the one whom the human mind cannot grasp even when he is tranquil, when it sees him angry?

Isaiah rightly speaks of him: “The Lord alone will be exalted on that day, for the day of the Lord of hosts will be against every proud and lofty person, against every arrogant person, and he will be humbled; against all the tall and upright cedars of Lebanon, against all the oaks of Bashan, against all the high mountains and all the elevated hills, against every lofty tower and every fortified wall, against all the ships of Tarshish, and against everything beautiful to behold. The loftiness of human beings will be bowed down, and the height of men will be humbled; the Lord alone will be exalted on that day, and the idols will be utterly crushed. They will enter the caves of the rocks and the hollows of the earth, away from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth” (Isa. II).

Now he sees the sins of those who offend and remains silent; “then he will speak to them in his anger and trouble them in his fury” (Ps. II), as he himself says through the prophet: “I have been silent; I have always kept still; I have been patient. Like a woman in labor, I will speak” (Isa. XLII).

Whoever now longs greedily for earthly advantages, whoever feeds upon the pleasures of wanton flesh, will then be consumed by the fire of eternal burning and devoured by the sword of divine fury. For as the prophet says: “The whole earth will be devoured in the fire of God’s zeal, and all flesh by his sword” (Zeph. I).

There the person who here refused to hear what the Lord commanded will no longer be able to obtain from the Lord what he asks. Those who despise the divine voice in this life will come then with their false humility and prayers before the door, but they will not be heard. Instead, it will be said to them: “I do not know you. Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

And again the Lord says through Solomon: “I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked. You despised all counsel and neglected my rebukes. I also will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you, when sudden calamity falls upon you and destruction rushes upon you like a storm, when tribulation and distress come upon you. Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and they will not find me” (Prov. I).

In what, then, do we place our confidence? Where do we have hope of attaining salvation? In the treasures of money that we store in a chest? In the abundance of riches that, empty within, we wrongly possess outwardly?

But hear the apostle James, and how highly he values human riches and what merit he assigns to possession of earthly wealth: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days.”

And shortly afterward: “You have feasted upon the earth, and you have nourished your hearts in luxury” (James V).

Let the unhappy man now go and yield feebly to the flow of carnal allurements, only to be pestilently swallowed afterward by the abyss of hellfire. Let it now arrogantly raise itself upon the horns of pride, so that then, bound in eternal death, it may live forever.

What benefit is it if someone belches today, full from a banquet, and tomorrow lies rotting and foul in a tomb? What help is it if today he dresses himself in purple garments and tomorrow descends poor and naked to the underworld?

Alas, alas! What will those wretched people say then, when they see that they have irrecoverably lost temporal goods and that perpetual evils inevitably threaten them? What will their minds be like when they see that the acceptable time and the day of salvation (II Cor. VI) have completely passed away, and that the time has arrived in which they can do no good and find no remedy for their destruction?

How bitter will their conscience be; how mournful their complaint! “Then,” as Solomon acknowledges, “weeping and groaning in anguish of spirit, they will say:

‘We have strayed from the way of truth; the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us. We grew weary on the way of iniquity and destruction, and we traveled difficult paths, but we did not know the way of the Lord.

‘What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow, and like a messenger running ahead; like a ship that crosses the tossing water, whose trace cannot be found once it has passed, nor the path of its keel in the waves; or like a bird that flies through the air, leaving no sign of its journey, only the sound of its wings beating the light wind and cleaving the air along the path of its journey. It flew across with beating wings, and afterward no trace of its journey was found; or like an arrow shot at a designated target: the air, divided, immediately closed again upon itself, and its passage is unknown.

‘So we too were born and immediately ceased to be, and we were unable to display any sign of virtue; rather, we were consumed in our wickedness’” (Wis. V).

Such things were said in hell by those who sinned, because the hope of the ungodly is like down carried off by the wind, like fine foam scattered by a storm, like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the memory of a passing guest who stays for one day.

For this reason, dearest friend, I set before you not so much my own words as examples from sacred speech, so that even if your prudence might rightly despise me as speaking in an unpolished manner, it may not disdain to hear the testimonies of the saints, inspired by God.

Gather these and many other sayings of sacred Scripture into the storehouse of your mind. They can generate within you a salutary fear amid the false riches of the world. For as Solomon says: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful, but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. XXVIII).

We read, moreover, that no one can correct a person whom God has despised (Eccles. VII). A human being speaks emptily to another human being unless God speaks inwardly through himself.

You, dearest brother, according to the understanding of your prudence, which has been divinely given to you, examine your life carefully; always set your deeds before your eyes; fear God’s judgment. Watch over yourself on every side with attentive foresight, so that when the Judge comes he may find you not sleeping but watchful, not among the foolish but among the prudent virgins. Thus, while you now become your own judge, you will not afterward be judged; and then you will fear nothing at all, because now you never cease to fear.

But since I perhaps accomplish more with you by praying to God than by preaching to you, may almighty God, dearest brother, mercifully direct you now into the way of justice and grant you a share, with the elect placed at his right hand, in his dread judgment.

EPISTLE IX. TO BONIFACE, AN ADVOCATE

(It is found in volume III and is treatise 58.)

EPISTLE X. TO MORICUS, A DOCTOR OF LAWS

ARGUMENT.—He urges him to beware of perjury. To enable him to do so, he advises him to abstain entirely from swearing oaths and simply, in accordance with evangelical teaching, either affirm or deny the matter itself. He then attempts to inflame him to the practice of almsgiving by enumerating the benefits that it brings to those who love it.

[Col. 0482C]

289

To my lord Moricus, a most prudent judge, Peter, a sinful monk, greetings in the Lord.

Since I see that you are weak, dearest brother, and that the inner man’s tender sinews are present in your inmost being, I pass over very many precepts of Scripture and, content with a very small sickle, do not place a heavy burden upon your shoulders. And, so that brevity of expression may correspond to the matters themselves, I likewise touch upon these few things that I command in concise language, so that, since I fear burdening you with the weight of these matters, I may also take account of your weakness by using brevity of speech.

I therefore exhort you, dearest brother, and reverently admonish your affection, that you abstain both from the oaths which your fellow countrymen frequently employ in a sacrilegious manner, and that you not fail to provide relief to the needy, insofar as your means permit. From the one of these I restrain you as from being plunged into a gaping abyss; toward the other I urge you as toward the citadel and summit of a saving defense. For “almsgiving,” as Tobias says, “delivers from every sin and from death, and will not allow the soul to go into darkness” (Tob. IV).

But, to speak first and briefly about oaths, as I have already indicated: whoever violates an oath by perjuring himself separates himself from the body of Christ, as though through a kind of rupture by amputation, and estranges himself from the mysteries of human redemption. For when the one who swears customarily says, “I shall do this,” or certainly, “I shall not do it—so may God help me,” he makes a compact with God, introducing this condition according to the Gospel: that if he does not fulfill what he has promised, he will no longer receive help from God or from the holy Gospel.

And just as, when he was initiated into Christ, through the catechism of priestly office he had renounced the devil and his pomps, so, like one turning backward and deserting, he renounces God and his Gospel, so that he no longer trusts in him, as though by the bond of an agreement of his own making, according to the terms of the covenant. And just as Laban placed a heap of stones between himself and Jacob and blocked the passage between them as a precaution (Gen. XXXI), so this man in a certain sense places perjury, uttered in falsehood, between himself and God.

He seals the book of the Gospel against himself, so that he cannot open it, while he blocks every avenue of salvation between himself and that book. Concerning this book Isaiah says:

> “And the vision of all this shall be to you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say, ‘Read this’; and he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed’” (Isa. XXIX).

For what is that sealed book except the holy Gospel, wrapped in the mystical meanings of figures and removed from human understanding by a certain secret profundity? This indeed is the book of which John says:

> “I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals” (Apoc. V).

What are the seals, however, by which the Gospel book is said to be sealed, except those seven mysteries by which the entire order of the Lord’s dispensation is fulfilled: namely, the Lord’s incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, then judgment, and finally kingdom?

With these seals, therefore, the Gospel book has been so sealed that, unless Christ had opened it, it could not be accessible to anyone at all. Hence what follows:

> “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and loose its seven seals” (ibid.).

Therefore whoever commits perjury should carefully consider that, unless he has made canonical satisfaction in repentance, he so closes against himself the seven seals of the Gospel narrative that neither the Lord’s incarnation, nor birth, nor passion, nor resurrection, nor ascension, nor judgment, nor kingdom can in any way profit him. He casts all these things far from himself and, so far as he is concerned, reduces them to nothing: for while violating an oath with the Gospel’s assistance invoked, he nevertheless renounces God’s help as well.

We do not believe it pointless to append what Richard, the prior of our monastery, a man of honorable life, reported to us yesterday. He said:

A man in the territory of Perugia, recently approaching death, bequeathed his patrimony proportionately to his two sons and as many daughters, leaving two-thirds to the males in the division of the inheritance, while the female sex was to succeed to one-third. After his death, one of his sons also died. His surviving brother, thinking it insufficient that he had not divided the dead brother’s property with his sisters, added to the dispute in order to stir up a contentious claim concerning their share as well. The greater the possession became, the more fiercely the possessor’s desire was inflamed.

What more need be said? A court proceeding was initiated; advocates for the opposing parties appeared; lawyers clamored; the issue was raised; the litigation’s accusation was intensified; and the claim was withdrawn by those who resisted it. At length, after deliberation on both sides, the parties agreed that a certain priest—who was a supporter of the man against the women and claimed that he had been present at the judgment of the deceased father—should give an oath, and that the case should thereby receive a decisive judgment and the testimony of one man should silence the entire controversy.

When the priest approached to swear on behalf of the man against the women, and was already laying his hand upon the book that had been placed before him, suddenly a terrifying serpent fell from the tree that towered above, and, embracing the book, coiled its scaly body around it.

Everyone was astonished and stunned as though by some portent; the priest himself especially froze in terror and renounced the oath that he had devoted not to truth but to human favor. Thus the ancient enemy, who had poured the venom of his malice into the priest’s heart so that he might swear against the truth, visibly demonstrated through the beast familiar to him that he was present at this oath.

Their uncle also, who knew the matter but suppressed his testimony to the truth out of favor toward the man, as soon as he withdrew from the court, fell into a precipice together with the horse on which he was riding. The beast beneath him battered him violently with its whole body almost to death, so that divine providence might plainly show that he who had refused to stand firm in spirit for the truth had also, not undeservedly, fallen in body.

You, therefore, dearest brother, must not suppress the truth, but defend it in every matter and controversy to the best of your ability. For the one who resists the truth out of human favor is proved to deny Christ, who is the truth (I John V).

Beware of perjuries; indeed, if possible, restrain yourself from every oath. For just as one who does not swear cannot incur perjury, so—[the Latin here is textually disordered: “as, not speaking, never lies...”]. Truth itself says:

> “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no’; whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matt. V).

Beware, therefore, of perjury, lest you be compelled to discover the book of human redemption sealed against you.

And lest what we proposed together should also slip from your mind, redeem your soul with almsgiving and devote yourself to works of mercy. The Lord says:

> “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI).

And again it is written:

> “He who gives to the poor lends to God” (Prov. XIX).

Support the poor man, therefore, so that you may make God your debtor, as though you yourself were the creditor. For almighty God does not urge you to almsgiving as though he lacked the means to provide nourishment for his poor; rather, he displays them as needy for this reason: that he may supply you with the means of redeeming yourself. For it is written:

> “A man’s riches are his redemption” (Prov. XIII).

Moreover, our venerable brother Richard—the same man who reported what was said above—also faithfully related what I am about to recount, as he had learned it by report. He said:

Eight poor men, recently traveling on the road to Jerusalem, had absolutely nothing to eat and had spent an entire week without receiving any nourishment of food. When they were already being worn down by prolonged hunger, exhausted in strength, and wasting away from the hardship of the long journey, so that their faltering footsteps scarcely supported them, behold, a dog came toward them, dragging in its teeth a cloth in which bread was wrapped as though in a sack.

They immediately seized the bread and, giving thanks, cheerfully restored their strength. With the power supplied by that food, they completed an uninterrupted journey of eight days.

Again, when they were later suffering intolerable hunger, three Agarenians became their companions on the road, each carrying loaves for his own individual sustenance. When the hour of refreshment arrived and they reclined to eat, two of them consumed their own loaves in such a way that they gave nothing at all to the hungry Christians. But the third divided the single morsel that he himself carried into nine pieces and, contenting himself with only one, distributed equal portions to each of the Christians who were with him.

Afterward, while they were traveling together, behold, lions attacked them ferociously. They especially and conspicuously assaulted those who alone had consumed their loaves. They immediately tore those men violently to pieces and, while the others escaped, devoured only them with savage brutality.

Thus, indeed, those who had eaten alone were eaten alone; and those who had consumed food without charity, in a beastlike manner, were consumed by the savagery of roaring beasts.

Later, as they were walking over the gravel of the seashore, they found a fish of enormous size, which they immediately concealed in the sand because they saw horsemen approaching from a distance. When the horsemen drew nearer and saw the fresh mound of gravel piled above it, they thought—correctly—that the concealment of some buried object must have a hidden significance. They therefore began carefully to investigate and at length, by divine prompting, suspected that it was the burial of a dead man.

Thus, when the horsemen abandoned what they had begun and departed, the others dug it up and immediately turned the blessing of the divine gift into food for themselves. [lacuna]

[Note: The end of this letter is missing in the manuscript.]

## LETTER XI. TO THE CITIZENS OF FLORENCE

(This letter is found in volume III and is treatise 30.)

## LETTER XII. TO HERMISINDA, A RELIGIOUS WOMAN

### Argument

In the fragments of this letter, writing to Hermisinda, he inveighs against the proud and shows through various testimonies of sacred Scripture that those who rely upon the foundations of pride quickly collapse.

To Hermisinda, a religious woman, … Peter, a sinful monk, …

> “When they departed from the East, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and dwelt there. And one said to his neighbor, ‘Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire’; and they had bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar” (Gen. XI).

Now, since Christ is truly the East, as the prophet testifies when he says, “Behold, a man whose name is East” (Zech. VI), those come from the East who withdraw from fellowship with Christ by living wickedly or by wounding their neighbors.

Shinar, however, is interpreted as “the shaking off of teeth,” or “their stench.” In the plain of Shinar, therefore, dwelt those who were established not upon the citadel of virtues but rather in the valley of vices. They shake off their teeth so as to gnaw their neighbors, as it were, with biting accusations, and they emit foul odors while rotting amid the filth of a muddy way of life.

But almighty God shakes out their teeth when he confounds both the deeds and the words of all the wicked. Hence it is said there:

> “Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused, and from there the Lord scattered them over the face of all the regions” (Gen. XI).

It is rightly said, therefore, that those proud men, those seekers of empty glory—who say to one another, “Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven, and let us celebrate our name before we are divided throughout all the lands” (ibid.)—dwelt in the land of Shinar, which, as has been said, signifies for us “the shaking off of teeth” or “their stench.”

For all the wicked, while they grow proud against the commandments of divine law, while they arrogantly raise the neck of their heart against God, and sometimes damnably disparage their neighbors, are themselves more readily rolled about in the dungheap of an obscene life.

Of the shaking off of teeth David says:

> “You have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners” (Ps. III).

And elsewhere:

> “God will break their teeth in their mouth; the Lord will shatter the molars of lions” (Ps. LVII).

Another prophet also speaks of their stench:

> “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I).

And Isaiah says:

> “There will be stench instead of sweet fragrance” (Isa. III).

Indeed, whoever wishes to construct a building that will not easily be exposed to collapse must not use bricks and bitumen, which suddenly split apart, but rather stones and rocks to raise the walls, and mortar of lime and sand to bind those walls together with an unbroken joining of stones.

The fact, therefore, that the Babylonians mentioned above had bricks instead of stones and bitumen instead of mortar signifies a building of carnal life, soon to be overwhelmed by the force of winds or the violence of floods.

Those cities of tents that Pharaoh built with mud and straw—mud, which defiles, and straw, which is destined for flames—were named Pithom and Raamses not without mystery (Exod. I).

Pithom is interpreted as “mouth of the abyss,” or “suddenly.” For whoever, according to Paul’s statement, now builds upon the foundation that is Christ Jesus with wood, hay, or straw, “the fire will test what sort of work each one has” (I Cor. III). And the higher this structure of carnal life is raised, the more readily it is plunged, as it were, into the gulf of the abyss and suddenly destroyed. Hence it is written:

> “They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI).

It is rightly called both “mouth of the abyss” and “suddenly,” because from the summit of carnal life, which it signifies, one falls not slowly but quickly. And that is the mouth of the abyss which had seemed to be the summit of ascent, as the Prophet testifies:

> “You cast them down while they were being exalted” (Ps. LXXII).

Raamses, however, is said to mean “fodder” or “line.” All the reprobate are fodder for the devil, for he feeds upon them as a wolf feeds upon sheep and fattens himself, as upon a banquet, on their destruction. Of them David also says:

> “Like sheep they have been placed in the underworld; death will feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII).

The Lord said to Moses (Exod. IV):

> “Throw the staff that you carry in your hand onto the ground”; and he threw it, and it became a serpent. Moses was immediately afraid and fled. And the Lord said to him, “Take hold of its tail”; and he seized it, and it became a staff again (Gen. III).

We all clearly know that the serpent persuaded the human being to death; therefore death came from the serpent. But what is the staff except Christ, of whom the prophet says:

> “For a staff shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI)?

The staff, therefore, became a serpent; Christ became death.

Moses was afraid and fled because, when the Lord was hanging upon the cross or dying, the whole number of the apostles trembled in fear and withdrew from the solidity of certain hope and firm faith.

Since the tail is the final part of the body, what does it signify except the end of the Lord’s passion? Moses therefore seized the tail, and nothing of the serpent remained visible to him in the staff, because, once the mystery of the Lord’s passion and cross had been completed, every faithful person returned to the faith, and Christ, having destroyed death, restored in himself through the glory of the resurrection what he had been.

Aaron took a censer and ran through the middle of the multitude that the burning plague was devastating. Standing between the dead and the living, he offered incense, and thus the raging plague ceased (Num. XVI).

Whom did Aaron signify except our Redeemer? For, since he exulted to run his course like a giant (Ps. VIII), he seized the censer of his passion, ran between the dead and the living, and by the opposition of his cross—on which the incense of his sacred body was burned, and that heavenly Lamb was roasted—separated the living from the dead.

The fire’s destruction he excluded from them like an intervening wall, so that the devouring flame might consume the unbelievers, concerning whom it is written:

> “Now fire consumes the adversaries, while the just, who live by faith, escape the fire of condemnation” (Heb. X).

The two thieves are also known to have been the first of those dead and living, between whom the Lord was crucified: one was chosen, while the other was rejected because of his unbelief.

This incense, therefore, the sacrifice of salvation, unique and saving, which was offered to God the Father upon the altar of the cross, was carried by that mountain of strength among the dead and the living, when it spread the fragrance of its knowledge among believers and unbelievers. Hence the words in the Song of Songs:

> “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song I).

And the Apostle says:

> “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge, because we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the latter, a fragrance of death unto death; to the former, a fragrance of life unto life” (II Cor. II).

Saul had promised to give his elder daughter Merab to David as a wife; but when the time came when she ought to have been given to him, she was not given to him, but was joined to another man. Michal, Saul’s other daughter, loved David, and he took her as his wife (I Sam. XVIII).

Merab is interpreted as “from the multitude,” while Michal means “water” or “from all.” What, then, is signified by Merab except that multitude of unbelievers which is from the multitude that is rejected?

> “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX).

What, however, is signified by Michal except the holy Church, from whom all the elect arise, or which consists of all the elect? Although she did not bear a son, this barrenness does not obstruct the meaning here.

One mystery is involved in the fact that she was joined in marriage to King David; another, that she remained childless; another, that she entered into the marriage of Christ the Lord; and another, that she did not receive the gift of fertility but endured the reproach of barrenness in Israel.

David, the proud king Saul’s daughter, joined her to himself when Jesus—mighty in hand and desirable in merit—removed her from the service of this proud ruler of the world and united her to himself by the intimate bond of alliance.

That Michal, who is the holy Church of the elect, cannot be taken away by that proud Saul—that is, the evil spirit—together with Merab, because the faithful guardian has irrevocably enclosed her in the embraces of his love. He cries out in the Gospel:

> “My sheep hear my voice, and they will not perish forever, and no one snatches them from my hand” (John X).

Those who, rejecting the structure of earthly conduct and desire, construct the fabric of a spiritual building—these turn bricks into stone, as it were. They establish courts that will never fall, not upon the sand of worldly hope but upon the rock of faith, which is Christ (I Cor. X).

Hence Isaiah says:

> “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we shall replace them with cedars” (Isa. IX).

Whoever disciplines the wantonness of vices and pleasures with the rigor of a stricter life builds with glowing bricks and squared stones; whoever overcomes the law of the flesh by the law of the spirit; whoever changes bodily strength into the virtue of the soul.

Hence Isaiah says again:

> “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength” (Isa. XL).

For by saying not “they take up” but “they will change,” he plainly made it known that one kind of strength is laid aside and another is newly begun.

Hence the Psalmist says to the elect:

> “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. XXX).

Hence Solomon says:

> “Behold, sixty mighty men, among the strongest of Israel, surround Solomon’s bed” (Song III).

> “He has made me drunk with wormwood” (Lam. III).

A drunk man does not know what he endures, as though almost possessed or deranged in mind. Thus any wicked person, while frenziedly desiring the profits of the world, does not feel the evils by which he is oppressed through so many labors, because he is led with pleasure into all the things in which he is punished by exhaustion.

> “Like sheep they have been placed in the underworld, and death will feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII).

Christ has sheep whom he may lead into pleasant green pastures and heavenly sheepfolds. That other one, too, has sheep whom he may swallow with his insatiable, bloodthirsty mouth.

He is rightly called Death, because, although he is the author of death, he rages cruelly to inflict destruction upon us. Hence John says:

> “And behold, a pale horse, and he who sat upon it was named Death” (Apoc. VI).

## LETTER XIII. TO HIS SISTER

### Argument

At his sister’s request, he discusses the end of the world, the coming of Antichrist, and the last judgment, whose day, he says, must always be kept before one’s eyes.

To his sweetest sister, Peter, a sinful monk, humble service in the Lord.

What you ask me, dearest sister, to make known to you—what existed before the creation of the world, etc. This is the same letter as that in Book VI of this volume.

## LETTER XIV. TO HIS SISTERS RODELINDA AND SUFFICIA

### Argument

He exhorts Rodelinda and Sufficia, both widowed, to preserve a purity untouched by every stain, not only of body but also of mind, and to avoid impure thoughts with every effort. So that they may do this more easily, he declares that patience in tribulations, unceasing prayer, frequent and sincere confession, gentleness toward enemies and those who revile them, mercy toward the poor, and finally the dismissal of worldly cares will be of the greatest help to them.

To his dearest sisters in Christ, Rodelinda and Sufficia, Peter, a sinful monk, the affection of intimate spiritual kinship.

I render abundant thanks to the divine dispensation when, by report spreading abroad, I learn that you are unanimously fervent in the pursuit of spiritual virtues and yet are subject to diverse pressures of the world. For that established rule of heavenly justice is well known, by which the invisible Judge disciplines in this life with the scourges of temporal affliction those to whom he intends to grant the rights of an everlasting inheritance; and he afflicts with harsh blows, as servants, those whom he has already, by the decree of hidden provision, adopted as true sons for the inheritance of their own possession.

For whoever, while doing what is right, abounds in success ought certainly to have his heart shaken by fear, lest, since he sees temporal things repaid to him for his merits, eternal things, perhaps lesser or none at all, be rendered to him. But one who does good and is worn down by scourges, now deservedly certain of the good to be repaid to him, rejoices in the heaped and pressed-down measure of his labors, because he finds that the amount of interest due has increased afterward by as much as he had previously received not even the wages of momentary prosperity on the way. Hence blessed James says: “Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into diverse temptations” (Jas. I). And Solomon says: “Whom the Lord loves, he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. III). Therefore one who is set on the path of holy conduct rightly rejoices when he sees himself surrounded by punishing scourges, not doubting that he is being adopted into the lot of God’s sons.

Only this must be guarded against with anxious consideration: that amid the very works of righteousness for which a reward is certainly due, we also mix in some wrongful acts, however small, for which at least a temporal punishment is imposed. Hence Peter says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, or reviler, or coveter of another’s goods” (I Pet. IV). Therefore whoever either covetously desires another’s property or exceeds in reviling words against someone does not suffer deservedly and does not obtain the reward of his suffering.

But you, dearest sisters, because, having dissolved the bond of marriage and professing widowly continence, you have not only passed over to union with the immortal Bridegroom, but have also resolved, with the urgency of admirable fervor, to restrain—indeed, to crucify—all the incitements of carnal allure, both restrain yourselves altogether from inflicting injury and endure injuries inflicted by others with equanimity. Thus, because the Redeemer both did no evil and bore the cross, the pledged token of covenant with that same supreme Bridegroom may now appear in you, while your life agrees with his way. Although you cannot follow the Lamb wherever he goes as virgins do (Apoc. XIV), let it suffice you to imitate him by the way of patience, since he indeed passed through death into the resurrection of life.

And lest perhaps prolonged hardship bring you weariness, let that evangelical Anna be set before your widowhood as an example. According to Scripture’s testimony, after enjoying seven years of marriage she had already advanced in widowhood to eighty-four years of age (Luke II). Yet, having received so lengthy and aged a span of life, did she relieve the discomforts of bent old age by idle tales or luxurious living? Rather, after mentioning the duration of her continence, the Evangelist immediately adds: “For she did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day” (ibid.). What, I ask, would this woman have done had she read the apostolic exhortation, “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V), especially if she had heard the Lord himself summoning us to the practice of continual prayer? Yet, before she could learn the Gospel, she fulfilled it by knowing the Lord through prophetic inspiration; and, if I may say so, by her deeds she deserved that the Evangelist should proclaim his presence. As it is written: “And coming in at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel” (ibid.). Impress this outstanding widow diligently upon yourselves as a kind of seal, that you may deserve to carry away the reward of true widowhood, keeping in continual remembrance that apostolic saying: “But she who is truly a widow and desolate has hoped in the Lord and has continued in prayer night and day” (I Tim. V). You need not hear what follows, since by God’s grace you take care to guard against it with watchful provision: “But she who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (ibid.).

Indeed, if wives strive with the utmost desire to please mortal men (I Cor. VII), how much more vigilantly and carefully ought holy widows to adorn the appearance of the inner person, so that they may appear beautiful to the gaze of their invisible Bridegroom? For, as the same Apostle says: “She who is unmarried is concerned for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit; but she who is married is concerned for the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (ibid.). A married woman is concerned lest she displease a husband who will soon die; how much more diligently must a widow endeavor to please the heavenly Bridegroom who will reign through the ages? The married woman strives to delight her husband with the appearance of painted adornment; how much more must the widow strive to shine in God’s sight, adorned with holy virtues as with gleaming pearls? The former strives to appear lovely of face, so that no blemish of ugliness may mar her beauty; how much more cautiously must the holy widow labor lest her mind be defiled by the filth of implacable hatred or shameful desire? Finally, impress more firmly upon your minds and turn over in diligent meditation that saying: “that she may be holy in body and spirit.” For what good is bodily chastity, discipline, or affliction of the flesh, if purity and cleanness of heart are lacking? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Hence to the soul that thinks harmfully, under the figure of Jerusalem, Jeremiah says: “Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be saved. How long shall harmful thoughts remain in you?” (Jer. IV).

I know well, and have experienced more than enough, that the farther you withdraw from worldly business and secular intercourse, the more grievously you labor under the importunate tumult of intrusive thoughts—especially since there is evidently fulfilled in you what is said prophetically through mystery: “An unrighteous brother has supplanted me, and every friend has deceitfully sat in wait against me” (Jer. II).

Therefore, if among the abundant harvests of good works which you do not cease to cultivate there arise some thorns of piercing thoughts, perhaps from that root of afflictions, immediately take up the hoe of saving confession and self-correction, and uproot the poisonous shoot from the field of your hearts. On this matter the divine voice fittingly commands through the prophet: “Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns” (Jer. IV). And what it had previously said, it immediately explains by adding: “Be circumcised to the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem.” They therefore break up fallow ground who furrow the field of the heart, though it has already been ploughed, with the frequent ploughshares of devout confession, and who continually cut back with the sharp hoe of self-correction and repentance the luxuriant but evil shoots of carnal passions, because, once cut down, they do not cease to grow again and put forth shoots. Thus, if fallow ground is broken up, it is not sown among thorns, because, furrowed by the frequent ploughshares of confessions and corrections, we cut down the bristling thickets of thoughts so that we may scatter the seeds of devout conduct upon the clean level ground of the heart.

This is especially commanded to the men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that those may particularly be warned to fight against the wars of inward impulses who, despising the world’s turmoil, are steadfastly fixed in the confession of truth and vigilantly intent upon the vision of supreme peace. This also agrees most aptly with you, who, burning to the core toward God with the desire of your minds enkindled, endure the evils of a raging world because you have not loved its enticing allurements. And because the crafty artificer cannot inflame you to repay the insults inflicted by others, you must most carefully beware lest he be able secretly to stir you to hatred of them. And because, having fought with you for a long time, with God standing for you, he has been compelled to lose on the field of action, care must be taken lest through the sloth of relaxed security he may prevail in the very house of thought, so that, though your hands are outwardly clean through innocence, he may contrive to present your heart bloody in God’s sight through anger. For the Lord says through the prophet to those who perform the legal ceremonies: “Who has required these things from your hands? Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I). He said this, of course, to those whose hearts he saw to be full of malice.

Therefore, dearest sisters, since your life is perceived to be so holy, honorable, and strict that, with respect to your works, it seems in no way to need our exhortation, yet so that some place may be open to our pen in your edification, we turn to the hidden places of the mind. For there it is necessary that the higher one has been in virtues, the more subtle one should be in guarding against temptation. For the cunning enemy often turns into matter for battle the very thing that was made a cause of victory. Moreover, almighty God himself dwells in the minds of the elect. For although he is to be believed to dwell also in chaste bodies, as the Apostle says, “Your body is the temple in you of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God” (I Cor. VI), a special seat of his is assigned to the mind, which rules the body placed beneath it by a certain authority of governance. As the same Apostle says, “[that] the Holy Spirit may dwell in our hearts through faith” (Eph. III), so that, just as the soul gives life to the members of the body, it may itself likewise subsist as given life by God. If, therefore, you wish to build in your minds a dwelling worthy of God, strive diligently to cleanse those minds from every fuel of discord and hatred, and indeed from every stain of malice.

Who, I ask, would not receive a king as a guest? Yet what benefit is it if the entire house furnishes its halls with varied reliefs, if it hangs linen curtains throughout the ceilings, if it displays everything clean and polished to the eyes of the visitor, but then he enters the one bedroom where he is to rest and recoils on finding it filthy?

Since, therefore, through the persistence of constant prayer, through almost daily fasts, and through the brightness of matronly chastity you keep your bodies in holy purity, show the same strict vigilance toward your thoughts, so that, since you are building a bridal chamber for the heavenly Bridegroom in your minds, you permit nothing foul or disorderly there that could offend his eyes. For true light does not dwell amid the darkness of hatred, and the Prince of Peace does not seek the lodging of a troubled mind.

Indeed, you know that certain women who live according to the flesh grind between their teeth various kinds of spices and perfumes, so that they may please their husbands more agreeably by the radiance of fragrant scents. Let your tongue and lips likewise never be idle from divine praises; but continually turn over psalms and prayers, grinding them like spices, so that you may rightly offer before God the fragrance of sweetness.

You also know that when girls in their parents’ house grow into young womanhood and begin to approach the age suitable for marriage, they understand that their father’s property is reserved chiefly for heirs of the male sex. They therefore acquire little chests and various receptacles for purses, so that whatever they can scrape together here and there they may carefully stuff into them, in order that, when they pass into bridal chambers, they may be the less compelled to blush before strangers, insofar as they are accompanied by the richer abundance of wealth gathered from their father’s house.

You, therefore, who hasten toward the heavenly marriage on the steps of firm hope, deposit no small portion of your substance in a safe place, so that you may pass to the immortal Bridegroom without any shame. The purse in which these things may be most safely stored is the bosom of the poor, the support of the wretched. This is a faithful depository, which will return without any loss whatever it has received.

Do not therefore leave everything to those who remain here in such a way that you neglect to provide also for yourselves, who will shortly depart from this place. But if you lack the means, if poverty constrains your household resources, he who preferred the widow’s small gift to the offerings of the rich (Luke 21) also receives your little gifts, however tiny, without displeasure, into the treasury of his hearing. But if even these things—which we do not believe—are entirely lacking, let it be enough for you to offer devout tears, deep groans, and profound sighs. Indeed, place upon the altar of your devotion whatever you understand, whatever you can, whatever you live, whatever it is that you breathe; and thus sacrifice and burn yourselves as an offering to God, which is greater than all burnt offerings.

Shun, therefore, conversations with worldly people; avoid the gaze of the carnal; and, finally, let your door not be open to everyone. Until the reason for someone’s visit is known, let access be denied to some.

Let that holy woman Judith also be a model of life and a discipline of widowly continence for you. Sacred Scripture testifies concerning her in these words:

> “For in the upper part of her house she made herself a private chamber, in which she remained shut in with her maidservants; and, wearing sackcloth around her loins, she fasted all the days of her life, except Sabbaths, new moons, and the festivals of the house of Israel” (Judith 2).

Clearly one must consider how worthy of praise this widow was, since she burned with so great a fire of divine love. Moreover, not content with the limits of widowly duty, she had advanced so far in holy religion that she became a hermit not alone but together with her maidservants. She made a retreat out of a common house, and in a populous city love, the artificer, discovered solitude.

With how many endowments of worldly prosperity did she abound—endowments that could have enticed her into a second marriage, with its flattering seductions! For, as the sacred history relates:

> “She was exceedingly beautiful in appearance; her husband had left her many riches, an extensive household, and possessions full of herds of oxen and flocks of sheep” (ibid.).

And, far more excellent than all these things, it is also said:

> “She was renowned above all, because she feared God greatly, and there was no one who spoke an evil word about her” (ibid.).

But when would she have admitted suitors, when not even conversation with her maidservants was readily open to anyone? How would she have pursued the adornment of clothing, when she constantly wore sackcloth against her limbs? Or perhaps would she have devoted herself to more sumptuous meals, when she daily weakened herself by fasting?

But perhaps you object that she could easily exercise the virtues because prosperity flowed to her from every side; whereas for those who scarcely have enough to live on, how can they lead a virtuous life as they wish? Certainly, we readily abstain from things that are offered to us, while we are generally more eager to long for what has been taken away. I freely admit that voluntary offering gladdens the giver, whereas forced necessity clouds the will of one who wastes away.

But suppose that you complain that Judith’s wealth deprives you of the opportunity to imitate her. Do you not know the exile of that poor Moabite woman, Ruth—her misfortunes, hunger, thirst, and endurance of unbearable labors (Ruth 1)? Do you not know that, for the sake of preserving for a time the honor of her most chaste widowhood [Note: [Col. 0493D] The passage is mutilated; lacuna], she came to such poverty that she gathered the leftover ears behind the reapers and, [probably *virga caedens*, “threshing with a rod”], entirely deprived not merely of male help but of all human assistance, herself threshed what she had gathered? From her, indeed, the offspring of so many kings was destined to proceed; yet she appeared to have been assigned, like a worthless slave, to servile labor.

Pressed and hemmed in by so many hardships and straits, she did not abandon the virtues of her spirit. She bore with equanimity the burden of a poor life by which she was weighed down; yet she considered it unworthy, as one worthy to become David’s ancestress, to descend from the summit of her inward nobility. She showed due reverence to her mother-in-law, preserved matronly chastity, remained faithful to her deceased husband, abandoned her homeland and parents devoted to idols, and, without any teacher’s instruction, passed over as a noble convert to the worship of the true God (Ruth 2).

Behold, then: Judith cast away the prosperity by which she was supported in life, while Ruth embraced the adversity by which she was oppressed. Each, with one and the same mind though with different fortunes, rightly pleased the one God. For the one neither succumbed to adversity, nor did the other, forgetting herself amid prosperity, cast herself down. The one endured what she possessed; the other enjoyed what she suffered.

Both, indeed, affirming the alternation of worldly instability, said:

> “As is his darkness, so also is his light” (Psalm 138).

And although one was content with her first marriage while the other entered a second, Ruth did not depart from the practice of chastity, because widowly continence was changed into conjugal chastity not by the lust of carnal attraction but rather by divine arrangement.

What, moreover, should I say about the most blessed Mother of God, who possessed no abundance of earthly riches and endured the bitterness of immense sorrow? To her, indeed, it was truly foretold:

> “And your own soul a sword shall pierce” (Luke 2).

For if almighty God had valued the prosperity of this life highly, he would never have permitted the unique and perpetual Virgin, from whom he deigned to become incarnate, to be afflicted with sorrows.

Therefore, arm yourselves with the same thought, according to blessed Peter’s instruction (1 Peter 4), and conquer the evils of the world through patience. You know, surely, that all the elect have endured them from the very beginning of the human race. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14).

Indeed, it is not unbelievable that, if this life softened and charmed you with its flatteries, it would hold you back to some extent from the course of heavenly desire, and that your mind would grow cold toward God to the degree that it found rest amid the heat of temporal affairs. Therefore divine providence permits you to toss upon the sea of this life amid storms raging on every side and, as it were, the violent blasts of furious winds, so that your mind may pass more eagerly to heavenly desires, since it finds no place amid earthly things where it can rest with delight.

Hagar, supported by prosperity, grew insolent against her mistress; later, afflicted and wandering in exile through the wilderness, she received the address of an angel promising her joy (Genesis 16). Rachel, as long as she suffered the misfortune of barrenness, offered due reverence to the true God; but after she had obtained the gift of fertility by giving birth to Joseph, she stole her father Laban’s idol (Genesis 31).

If prosperity should raise you up, as you desire, upon a swelling wave, it might swallow you in the shipwreck of some sin you had committed, or at least fleeting joy might carry your minds far away from the shore of inward peace.

Therefore I exhort and diligently admonish you: do not, God forbid, allow yourselves to be found ungrateful for divine benefits. Rather, always give worthy thanks to God your governor, who, by taking away from you the occasion of sinning, restrains you from harmful food, as it were, so that he may advance you toward the strength of eternal safety. He encircles you with harsher scourges and teaches you through blows, so that he may now file and polish his pearl, which later he will place in the building of the heavenly temple without the ringing of an axe, the sound of a hammer, or the noise of any iron tool (1 Kings 6).

Therefore, beloved, when a more violent storm surges upon you from the whirlwinds of this world, when an insult inflicted by your adversaries strikes you with abuse, immediately seek the hiding place of prayer. Run to weeping and lamentation, and hasten at once from the heat of your persecutors to the coolness of tears, so that, when your mind finds no secure place outside where it can rest, it may gather itself inwardly and strive to lull itself to sleep, free from every disturbance of worldly noise.

Nor should the dryness of weeping break your devotion to prayer, so that you give up as soon as you try and tears do not burst forth. For the nature of the fast to which you adhere so strictly is known to be such that, although it accumulates many fruits of advancement, it sometimes also kindles anger and diminishes tears.

That fasting increases anger is made clear by Isaiah’s statement:

> “Behold,” he says, “you fast for quarrels and contentions, and you strike with the fist wickedly” (Isaiah 58).

That prolonged fasting removes tears is testified by Josephus (*The Jewish War*). When he was recounting the vengeance inflicted upon Jerusalem and upon the Lord’s persecutors by the rulers Vespasian and Titus, he added this among the various kinds of punitive retribution:

> “Nor was lamentation customarily offered for the dead, nor mourning; for hunger had claimed all of this for itself, and the dryness of starvation had left no one any moisture for tears.”

Therefore, when you cannot draw visible tears from the eyes of the flesh, let it be enough for you to mourn your own excesses within the secrets of a contrite heart. Look there upon the darkness of the guilt you have committed; and, because what you suffer is deserved, judge yourselves also by the verdict of a just examination. For light grows strong amid darkness, and Lucifer, who flees the eyes during the day, spreads the rays of his own splendor at night.

If, then, we wish true light to rise in our hearts, let us not pretend that we are light, but let us truthfully acknowledge the darkness of our guilt. Then everything we suffer will seem light to us, because we perceive that what we deserve is far heavier.

It should also be noted that, just as those who cannot see hear more sharply, so that the vitality of sensation withdrawn from one member may be transferred more abundantly to another, so some people, after trampling down lust, burn more fiercely with avarice. When human desire is restrained from the will to lust, it extends itself with greater force toward the appetite for acquiring wealth.

In you, however, let the love of riches grow cold together with the desire for marriage, so that your generosity may burn piously toward assisting the needy, not blaze insatiably toward enriching the avaricious. Far be it that money should take the place of a man in your heart’s love. Rather, in place of carnal delights, let spiritual feasts pleasantly nourish your minds: namely, constant meditation on divine words, the psalm, good thought, frequent performance of pious works, expectation of death, hope of the future age, and other things like these. By them the mind is healthfully nourished, and the soul is truly fattened on heavenly banquets.

But while I prolong my address to your charity, exceeding the limits of an abbreviated letter—or, so to speak, writing a short letter at excessive length—I do not observe the rule of brevity in speaking. Indeed, because I desire to care not for my own elegance but rather for your edification, I speak at greater length.

Finally, you also confer no small benefit upon me if you strive to be perfected in the fullness of holy virtues. For I do not doubt that the one who raised Lazarus through the prayers of his faithful sisters (John 12) will also, through your merits, if they prove worthy according to faith, restore me from sins to innocence.

May the merciful and almighty Lover of souls direct me through your prayers toward righteousness, and lead you through my exhortations to higher things. Blessed be the name of the Lord.

## LETTER XV. TO A CERTAIN SICK MAN

### Argument

He commends to God the soul of a certain sick man who is already at the point of death, so that, when the course of mortal life has been completed, he may deserve to receive the palm of heavenly victory.

I commend you to almighty God, dearest brother N., and I entrust you to him whose creature you are, so that, when you have paid the debt of humanity through the intervention of death, you may return to your Creator, who formed you from dust (Genesis 2).
