For it is written that one day, while he was occupied with the craft of wool-working, he said to his wife: “I will go and see a marvelous vision—namely, how a dove comes from heaven and, according to its customary manner, settles upon the head of the chosen one.”

His wife, however, began to mock and rebuke him, saying: “Stay here and work; do not stand idle. Whether you go or do not go, the people will not ordain you bishop.”

And he said: “Let me go.”

Then she, thinking that he was lying, but unknowingly announcing the truth, said: “Go, because at the hour when you go, you will immediately be ordained bishop.”

A little later the account adds that, because of the shabby appearance of the filthy garment he was wearing, he hid himself behind the door of the very place where everyone was praying; and when the prayer had ended, the dove immediately came and rested upon his head while he was hiding behind the door [Col. 0523D].

You have heard, dearest brothers, of a man poor in worldly goods but rich in the wealth of virtues. You have heard of a man placed in a low position among human beings but established by God upon the summit of lofty greatness. You have heard of a man foul in ragged clothing but conspicuous for the splendid integrity of his conduct.

Where are those who say: “We cannot keep God’s commandments because we do not possess earthly resources for our necessary needs”? Where, I ask, are those who, while trying to excuse themselves before human beings, make themselves far more inexcusable before God?

Let them come and learn from the teaching of blessed Severus to abound in true riches, lest, while they are empty of possessions, they be full of vices; and lest the furnace of poverty, if it does not purge the rust of vices, turn the corrupt metal into the soot of empty dross.

For behold, this most blessed man, placed beneath the burden of his poverty, fulfilled the precepts of the divine Law sufficiently. And because he had nothing else, he offered himself upon the altar of holy simplicity, like some great dove, as a most abundant sacrifice to God; and because he was a dove in his conduct, he deserved to receive the gift of a dove.

Pressed by the hardship of poverty, he did not enter the house of some powerful person to serve him; he did not strive to flatter the rich, as is the custom of the poor; he did not pant to increase his money through ambitious commerce; he did not desire the pay of the perilous military life, which cannot be borne without sin. Instead, content with a woman’s occupation, he sought simple food by hand and craft, and, in the words of the Psalmist, innocently ate the labor of his hands (Ps. CXXVII).

It is not without reason that he is believed to have chosen this particular craft above others: so that between wife and husband there might be a greater opportunity for mutual charity. For if there had been an inequality of occupations between them, a difference of affections might at some time have crept in, and a division might perhaps have arisen in the peace of the household from the difference in their crafts. But while the industry of both was devoted to one occupation, there truly existed in both what is said of the primitive Church: “One heart and one soul” (Acts IV) [Col. 0524C].

This is also why, when she rebuked the most blessed man, mocked him, and attacked him with biting words, he, gentle and calm, did not burst into anger, did not answer with insulting words, and did not exercise against his wife the authority properly belonging to him in order to avenge himself. He observed the Apostle’s instruction: “Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them” (Col. III).

And because the same Apostle says: “The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (I Cor. VII), he did not presume to go of his own accord to the miracle until he had obtained permission from her [Col. 0524D].

Consider, my brothers: when could this man have been defiant toward anyone, when he obeyed the woman subject to him with such humility? When could he have returned evil for evil to hostile enemies, when he bore his wife’s insults with such equanimity? Or when could this man have presumed to inflict insults upon his neighbor, when he refused to avenge the insult inflicted upon himself, although he certainly could have done so?

“Blessed is the man who could have transgressed but did not, who could have done evil but did not; therefore his good deeds have been established in the Lord” (Ecclus. XXXI) [Col. 0525A].

But what is this, my brothers: why does almighty God afflict so severely, as though despising them, those whom he foresees will be so dear to him forever? Why does he surround with blows of adversity in this world those whom, before the ages, he chose for the ineffable joy of heavenly blessedness? Is it not because this is evident to the piety of the faithful: he presses them so hard in the depths because he sees how he will reward them in the heights? And he casts them outwardly down even to contempt because inwardly he leads them even to what cannot be comprehended. From this, then—from this let each person infer what those whom he rejects will suffer, if here he chastises with such severity those whom he loves.

For behold, blessed Severus is deprived of the necessities of life, befouled by the squalor of misshapen clothing, worn out by the labor of coarse wool-working, [Col. 0525B] and—what is more intolerable to everyone—he is tormented by the mockery of a jeering wife. For the ancient enemy, who could not provoke him to impatience through poverty’s lack, the affliction of continual labor, or the ugliness of dishonorable clothing, inflamed his wife’s mind to inflict verbal insult and sharpened her tongue for the injury of biting rebuke. He stirs the woman’s heart with the familiar goads of his own suggestion and loosens her tongue into the boldness of shameless presumption, so that the manly spirit, which is not bent to impatience by the world’s adversity, might at least be provoked to anger by the wife’s insult; and so that the most strongly fortified rampart of Christ, which the surrounding multitude of enemies cannot penetrate, might be opened by an internal civic rebellion; what the battering rams of a besieging army cannot demolish might be captured when domestic division provides an entrance.

For the holy man had fixed the edifice of his mind on high, and therefore hostile assaults could not break in there. The adversary therefore asks how he may ascend to it, since this lofty fortification appears impregnable. But a woman is near to the man and subject to him. Thus he seized the woman’s heart and found, as it were, a ladder by which he might climb to the man’s heart. The wife’s mind became the husband’s ladder; but he gained nothing by this device, because the strong man opposed the shield of patience to the missiles of words. Treating them as nothing, he “heard without hearing.” It was indeed fitting that a manly spirit should not admit the woman’s words, since from the very first fall of the human race he had learned that a woman did not know how to teach what was right. Hence it is also rightly said through Paul: “I do not permit a woman to teach” (I Tim. I). For when she once taught, she strayed from the path of wisdom.

Thus the ancient enemy was defeated by Adam in the workshop of wool-working—the Adam whom he had overcome in paradise (Gen. III); and, while he ascended through his female accomplice to the insult of bitter correction, he unknowingly assigned her instead as an example from which patience should be learned. While he perversely taught her what she should teach, he sent her to the school of uprightness; and she who had been aroused in order to destroy him was instructed so that she would not perish. Thus, thus is the enemy struck down by our strong men, so that his own weapons are snatched from him. [Col. 0526A] From the very thing by which he thinks he magnifies the pain of their wounds, he supplies them with weapons of virtue against himself.

From the words of the wife who rebuked him wrongly, dearest brothers, we should carefully observe that the ancient adversary seeks to bend the state of our mind not only through himself but also through those who are attached to us. When the slippery serpent cannot overthrow our heart by his persuasion, he creeps toward it through the tongues of those who are close to us. Hence it is written: “Beware of your sons, and pay attention to your household” (Ecclus. XXXII). Hence it is said through the prophet: “Let each one guard himself from his neighbor, and let him place no trust in any brother” (Jer. IX). Again it is written: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. VII; Matt. X).

For when the wicked adversary sees himself driven back from the hearts of the good, he seeks out those who are loved by them with greater intimacy, and often stirs them up to inflict injury, so that holy men are wounded by the perversity of those from whom they ought especially to have received honor, and their minds are more readily provoked to anger.

But behold, the wicked enemy is broken everywhere and overcome everywhere. For he has already succumbed to Christ’s warriors through every stratagem of temptation, having lost even that familiar consolation of his when he was frustrated by a woman. Thus blessed Job, after the enemy had taken away all that he possessed and then wounded his very body with a grievous ulcer, because he could not reach the wound of his mind through the wounds of his flesh, also sought the tongue of his wife who was near him; and because he grieved at being overcome in open combat, he hurled a dart from his wife’s mouth as though from an ambush. For she said: “Do you still persist in your simplicity? Bless God and die” (Job II).

In the same way, after blessed Tobias had, by God’s providence, fallen into the misery of extreme poverty and had lost the light of his eyes, the evil spirit saw that he was blind to corporeal light but inwardly shining with divine splendor, outwardly empty of possessions but inwardly full of God; so he ran to his customary weapons and incited Tobias’s wife to utter the reproach of vehement rebuke. She said: “Truly your hope has proved vain; now your almsgiving has become evident” (Tob. II). And just as he said nothing in reply to this wicked wife but, after the devil’s suggested dart had been cast at him, immediately hastened, as Scripture testifies, to the weapons of prayer (Tob. IV), so blessed Severus disdained to answer his wife’s words; instead, prompted by the same Spirit, he unknowingly hastened to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

But if we weigh the order of divine justice through careful meditation, we find that holy men are not afflicted without cause by the troubles brought by their wives. Since the man, by consenting wrongly to the woman, had despised the commands of his Creator, it is now fitting that the woman, by dissenting from the man, should afflict him severely with harsh blows of insult. In the very matter in which he obeyed the woman wrongly, he was disobedient to his Creator. For it is written: “The woman took from the fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband, who ate; and the eyes of both were opened” (Gen. III). From that one, therefore, whom in his error he had placed before the Creator, he was to be struck by the Creator, so that from the source where, in his pride, man had not feared to commit his fault, he might find his corrective punishment. And all the sooner would he turn back to the one whom he had despised in pride, when he saw that the woman whom he had obeyed with delight was full of bitterness.

Nevertheless, we do not say these things in order to assert that the blessed man’s wife perished with the reprobate women. For if he had known that she was excluded from the company of the elect, a man filled with the Holy Spirit would never have wished to share one tomb with her. Their common burial therefore indicates that the variety of their merits did not separate the souls of the blessed spouses; and since the man willingly associates himself with his wife in death, it is clear that in the other life the merits of the two were not far apart from one another. It may reasonably be believed that after the woman saw the most blessed man, divinely chosen, raised to the episcopal dignity contrary to her expectation, she immediately recognized the stain of her guilt, was confounded and ashamed, did penance, and thereafter applied herself more diligently to the virtues of holy conduct. Hence it is also written of her that, after the most blessed man became bishop, she rejoiced and congratulated him in admiration.

But you, my dearest brothers, who, inspired by God, listen attentively to the praises of so great a man: you praise patience, you exalt humility—take the insignia of such great virtues for your own use, and earnestly strive, by God’s grace, to become what you gladly hear that he was. For you will be what he is, if you strive also to be what he was. On the journey of this pilgrimage, therefore, let no persuasion of prosperity deceive you; let no adversity that rushes upon you break you; let poverty’s lack not depress your mind; let no hope of temporal abundance [page 22] exalt it; let no insult uttered by your neighbor provoke you to anger; let no freedom to exercise permitted power against anyone incite you to take revenge. Thus, while you now follow in life the footsteps of blessed Severus, may you afterward rejoice with him in the reward of eternal blessedness in our homeland, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and is glorified [reigns] with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. II. ON SAINT SEVERUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA AND CONFESSOR. (1 FEBRUARY)

[Col. 0527D]

You heard, dearest brothers, from the history of blessed Severus, when it was read, how God raised him from the wool-working workshop, and how wonderfully he chose him—not only contrary to the opinion of all the citizens but even contrary to his own—to the citadel of the episcopate. You heard how a poor little man was taken by God away from the rich of this world. You heard how one cast down [abject] and humble was gloriously raised above the power of nobles. You heard the Holy Spirit passing over the wise men of the age and choosing a simple man, passing over those adorned in clothing and descending upon one dressed in rags and squalor, as upon a familiar friend and one long known to him.

[Col. 0528A] It is pleasing, dearest ones, to spread out carefully all the rays of our inward light upon that beautiful spectacle and, insofar as I am able, diligently to consider how almighty God judges in a manner different from human beings. All the citizens gather at the oratory; the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove upon the assembled people. Below are many hearts; above is one observer. They await the election of some great man from among the rich; he considers who among them all might be found richest in virtues. They prefer an educated tongue and eloquent speech; he chooses a simple mind and purity of heart.

Here the people pass over those of common appearance and look toward the leading men to see which of them will be chosen; but there, “the exalted Lord looks upon the humble, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. CXXXVII). Here many desire for themselves the summit of sacred dignity and cry out silently within their consciences, with chattering silence: “If only the dove would come upon me! If only God would choose me! Do you think I shall be chosen? Do you think the episcopate will be given to me?” But there is the one who searches the kidneys and hearts (I Chron. XXVIII; Ps. VII), “who fashioned their hearts one by one and understands all their works” (Ps. XXXII).

Indeed, many were present there, as was fitting in a distinguished city: some accustomed to walking with the clustered steps of snorting horses; some marked by illustrious titles of birth; some conspicuous for the splendor of expensive clothing; some surrounded by frequent bands of attendant soldiers; some richly endowed with all these gifts of the world; others furnished according to their own ability with certain of them. But almighty God, who was attentively examining the hearts of all, repeated without any sound of a voice what he had once said through the prophet: “Upon whom,” he says, “will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

The people saw the dove waiting in an open place for the heavenly sign. The dove saw the poor little Severus hiding behind the door. He who hid himself from human beings could not evade the gaze of divine majesty. What is this, holy Severus? So poor, yet so rich? So humble, yet so exalted? So ragged, yet so glorious? Cast down in human judgments, yet invisibly exalted by divine providence? Why do you try to hide yourself, when you are being raised up so that you may be set before the eyes of all as an example of virtue? Why do you blush before human faces, when you have pleased the sight of divine majesty above all others? Clearly, you have hidden yourself for this reason: that you might see and not be seen; that you might see the dove as a wonder, but not be seen because of the foulness of your clothing.

Come now, reveal yourself in public; come forward into the midst and undertake the stewardship of the Christian household. Let the pearl come forth from the dung heap, so that it may shine in the adornment of the highest King. Let the lamp no longer remain hidden beneath a bushel, but, placed upon a lampstand, let it pour the light of its brilliance upon all who are in the house (Matt. V). Feed, then, the Lord’s flock, and exercise pastoral care over Christ’s fold. Christ has already determined to entrust his Church to you, [Col. 0529A] the Church he purchased at the immeasurable price of his blood. Take up the office of distinguished administration, so that you may return an increased profit from the interest on the talent entrusted to you.

Do not be terrified by your ignorance of letters; do not doubt because of the disorder and crudeness of your speech. For the one who promotes you will instruct you without the labor of reading; the one who entrusts you with the office of teaching will also provide the increase of instruction. For the supreme Word presents you with the ministry of sowing the word. This Word says through itself to you and to those like you: “When you stand before kings, do not consider how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak” (Matt. X). And again: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (ibid.).

[Col. 0529B] What more is there to say? At last the dove came, and, while all marvelled, visited the head beloved by it. Certainly it had already been invisibly present in his breast, upon whose crown it was now descending bodily. But what could God’s fugitive do now? Where could he turn? What safer hiding place could he find? He fled from everyone’s sight, barred the doors, and left himself only the narrow cracks of the doorway through which to look. But he who could turn away human eyes did not escape the sharpness of the dove’s gaze. He saw that he had been discovered and complained inwardly that his refuge had done him no good. Nevertheless, he still suspected that the dove had been deceived and was wandering, unable amid so great a crowd to identify the right person to choose. Therefore, when it flew toward him for the third time, he drove it back with waving hands, and so, in the name of the most holy Trinity, [Col. 0529C] he received the blessing of his consecration.

O new and unheard-of order of promotion! O admirable dignity of this distinguished pontiff! For what else did the dove’s descending upon the head of the most blessed man for the third time signify except that it openly consecrated him in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? And what else did it signify that, when he drove the same dove away, he touched it with his hands, except that, according to the order of ecclesiastical institution, he received the oil of holy anointing in those very hands? For when the dove descended and slipped upon the head of the most holy man, it fulfilled the office of the laying on of hands. But by allowing itself to be touched by those sacred hands, it marked those hands with the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

And now, how great was the grace and excellence of receiving the Holy Spirit in that form in which he is known to have descended upon the Lord himself, namely, the Mediator between God and human beings? (Matt. III.) Certainly, however anyone receives the Holy Spirit, it is a sign of very great merit; but to receive him in the form in which the only-begotten Son of the Father himself received the Holy Spirit is an indication of the highest holiness. For the Holy Spirit appeared above the apostles in tongues of fire (Acts II); but above blessed Severus he appeared not in the image of fire, nor in a diversity of tongues, but, as above the baptized Lord, in the form of a dove (Matt. III). He thereby plainly showed that, just as a dove is a simple animal and free from the bitterness of gall, so the most blessed man was free from every bitterness of envy and lived in the holy purity of a simple heart.

Behold, it is clearly manifested what is said through the prince of the apostles: “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X). Divine providence also preserved in the election of this most blessed man what it once admonished us to observe through blessed James. For he says, among other things: “My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glory, with partiality” (Jas. II). Then he adds: “For if a man wearing a gold ring and splendid clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also enters, and you look upon the one dressed in splendid clothing and say to him, ‘You sit here in a good place,’ but say to the poor man, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit beneath my footstool,’ are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts?” (ibid.)

For if the blessed apostle speaks here of ordinary gatherings, who does not very often fall into the guilt of partiality, unless perhaps he judges within himself in such a way that the person to whom he gives honor seems better to him precisely because he is richer? But this apostolic judgment is understood more correctly if the difference between sitting and standing is referred to ecclesiastical honors. It should not be considered a minor crime for any rich person to be raised to the summit of ecclesiastical government while a poorer person, though holier and more learned, is excluded from the dignity of receiving that honor.

Thus almighty God did wonderfully among his saints (Ps. LXVII) what he taught through his apostle ought to be done, when, passing over the rich, he wonderfully raised this great poor man, dressed in squalid clothing, to the episcopal chair. After undertaking the office of the episcopate, he ascended not only through the order of ecclesiastical dignity but also grew into the citadel of the highest holiness.

For when some people undertake the responsibility of government, they immediately burn to tear apart their subjects; they display the terror of power and harm those whom they ought to benefit. Because they do not have the inward organs of charity for their children, they desire to appear lords and do not acknowledge themselves to be fathers. They change the place of humility into the arrogance of domination, raise themselves like tyrants upon the horns of pride, and, even when they flatter outwardly, rage inwardly. Of them the Truth says through himself: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII). They come in sheep’s clothing because they display the fleece of innocence on the surface, but they are ravenous wolves because they sharpen the bite of malice in the secrecy of their hearts, not attending to what the Lord says to his disciples: “Behold,” he says, “I send you as lambs among wolves” (Luke X).

For whoever undertakes the place of preaching ought not to inflict harm but to endure it, so that by his own gentleness he may calm the anger of those who rage and heal the wounds of sinners in others while himself wounded by afflictions. And when zeal for righteousness requires him to be severe toward his subjects, his anger itself should arise from love, not cruelty, so that he may both exercise the rights of discipline and inwardly love with paternal affection those whom outwardly he chastises as though pursuing them [or: by severity].

But evil shepherds are not like lambs among wolves; rather, they are like wolves among lambs. For while they generally suffer no bite of injury from their subjects, they themselves cruelly sink the teeth of their rapacity into them.

Others, however, before they reach the summit of priestly office, display themselves as gentle and humble in all things; they strive to grow in virtues, are distinguished by good morals, and exercise themselves in every form of honorable holy conduct. They never inflict harm on anyone, patiently endure what is inflicted upon them, tame their flesh continually with fasts [Col. 0531B] and prayers, and restrain every movement of vice within themselves through the discipline of strict severity.

But when they undertake the rights of pastoral guardianship, they lose whatever holiness they had possessed—in the words I must use with grief, as though in an exchange through a wretched bargain. They forget everything in which they had lived devoutly, and, like flowing rivers, they roll down toward the depths without any obstacle of restraint. Like bad rowers, when they reach the open sea under the force of the wind—when greater exertion is required—they abandon themselves to sleep in a deadly security. Or rather, when they take hold of the helm of a ship, those who had previously sailed vigorously with the others, once placed in command, cast themselves down into the torpor of negligence; they not only fail to guard others but also disastrously destroy themselves.

[Col. 0531C] But why do we speak of these things concerning reprobate shepherds, when even men of the highest holiness, after undertaking the office of pastoral care, although—God forbid—they do not at all rush into evil, nevertheless are often diminished somewhat by the very perfection of goodness, necessity compelling it? Hence blessed Pope Gregory boasts that in the conduct of his earlier life he had transcended all visible things, but afterward complains with devout lamentation that he was entangled in external cares (Gregory, *Dialogue*, Preface to Book I). Hence it is also read concerning blessed Martin, bishop of Tours, that his virtue had been greater before his episcopate than after his episcopate (Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, Book II, chapter 5). Nevertheless, there is no doubt that whatever is withdrawn from the personal perfection of holy preachers for the guardianship of others is increased much more generously and abundantly in gaining the spiritual profit of their subjects.

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, how remarkable blessed Severus was: the merit of holiness added to him through the responsibility of government what it ordinarily diminishes even in other men of outstanding excellence. For what is often the cause of descent in others proved in him to be the material of advancement; and from the very source from which the perfection of the most perfect men is often undeniably diminished, the summit of his perfection was increased.

Behold, before he received the office of prelate, he is known to have led a life of virtue, but he is not at all reported to have performed signs of virtue. After his ordination, however, the signs of miracles performed through him [Col. 0532A] cry out in clear voices how greatly his later merits surpassed his former life.

For how splendid, dearest brothers, how astonishing was that remarkable miracle in which, during the very solemnities of the Mass, he was suddenly carried into ecstasy and, in spirit, journeyed to the town of Modena; commended the soul of his deceased brother and fellow bishop to God; placed the body in the tomb; and celebrated, in due order, the entire office of the funeral rites!

O what a new spectacle, and one worthy of how great an admiration, if mortal sight could have grasped the whole of it at once! He was present, though absent from the faithful gathered there; yet he was absent, though present. Indeed, being far removed from himself, he was here rendering the debt owed to the living children entrusted to his pastoral care, while there he was rendering the duty of pious humanity to his dead brother.

And how light, how swift a vehicle did our bishop have, who crossed so great a distance of land not, I will not say, in a point or a moment, but in the briefest instant of time? That vehicle surely knows nothing of being checked by the roughness of roads; it knows nothing of being delayed by the brake of resistance. Yet this so great a miracle, which is more rarely heard to have been displayed by any of the saints, is perhaps more difficult for those who do not believe that all things are possible to one who believes.

For what is rarer, what more worthy of admiration, than for a pure spirit to bury a bodily body? And, so to speak, for a soul visibly to commend a soul? But we quickly incline our minds to believe this if we carefully consider other works of divine power as well. It is clear that spirit is of a more mobile nature than body; and certainly, as Scripture testifies, we know that the prophet Habakkuk, lifted up from Judea, was suddenly carried to Chaldea with a meal. There he refreshed the prophet Daniel, and then found himself again in Judea (Dan. XIV). If Habakkuk could thus go bodily so far in a moment and carry food, what is surprising if blessed Severus obtained the power to go in spirit and perform the funeral office for his dead brother? Just as the former went bodily to carry bodily food to the prophet, so the latter went spiritually to commend the spirit of a most blessed man to God.

And now, how great was the virtue and power shown when the dry ashes of a corpse long since dead obeyed him, and, at his command, the lifeless flesh of his wife contracted itself into the narrow corner of a grave so as to yield its place to his daughter? [page 27] By the just judgment of God, the woman who had once despised him in this life by mocking him now, with her judgment changed, humbly observed his commands. No doubt she saw with eyes that could not be deceived how great he already was in the court of the heavenly King—the poor little man whom she had known spinning threads in a humble workshop.

But perhaps someone judges it incredible that, although he was a venerable and most holy man, he was still dwelling in this corruptible flesh and could subject insensible dust to his laws, when it is clear that his soul had already passed over to that invisible judgment. Yet this too is easily believed if the divine grace bestowed upon human beings is carefully examined.

Was Peter not still in this flesh when he heard from the mouth of the Truth: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven”? (Matt. XVI.) All who hold the place of holy government in faith and conduct now possess Peter’s role in binding and loosing. But in order that a human being might exercise such power over the earth, the Creator of heaven and earth came from heaven into the earth; and in order that flesh might be able to judge not only concerning flesh but also concerning spirits, God, having become flesh for human beings, graciously bestowed this power upon it. For our weakness rose above itself from the place where the strength of God was weakened beneath it.

[Col. 0533B] But why do we speak of the ancient miracles of blessed Severus, when today we frequently hear that no small number of miraculous signs occur in the basilica of his venerable burial? To say nothing of the others, how worthy of what praises and of what joy is that one miracle which should be reported to the glory of divine omnipotence: that beneath the very altar of his most sacred body most clear water gradually flows forth, destined to benefit the various ailments of the sick? For if the faith of those who drink requires it, as soon as sick breasts receive it, they immediately recover from illness to their former health.

And, to hear of a marvelous thing happening marvelously: you should know that it does not spring forth during the harshness of spring weather, nor in the rains of autumnal flooding, nor amid the cold rains of winter, when water usually seeps thinly from various masses of stone, but in the very heat of burning summer you should know it to bubble forth from dry lime and hard stones. Thus, precisely when the greater necessity of illnesses presses upon us, divine mercy most especially provides a remedy; and, like a physician, it applies the power of healing through the contrary element to human weakness, which is then produced by the fault of fiery heat.

To this may reasonably be compared the miracle that likewise occurs in the river Nile of Egypt: it does not rise into a mass at any other time than summer, but then irrigates all the surrounding plains and makes the veins of the earth fertile with the abundant moisture of its flood. Thus, so that human foolishness may not attribute the works of divine power to the forces of nature, let it at least learn from the very time in which they occur to whom they rightly belong; and let it rise all the more eagerly to give thanks to its Creator, the more it recognizes that even the changes of nature have been altered for its benefit.

Behold, almighty God repeats the ancient miracles of his working; behold, once again, through another Moses he brings water from a rock (Exod. XVII). He renews for us the age of Israel, so that through outward benefits, as true Israel, he may kindle us to love the vision of himself. Behold, from the Church of his most blessed confessor he restores to us, in a manner, another paradise, whose most health-giving fountain gently waters the soil of our frailty.

Let us therefore, dearest ones, give thanks to our Creator, who for this reason still brings water from the rock of a crag, so that through it we too may draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior (Isa. XII). This is the water of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV). And again he cries out, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and from his belly will flow living waters” (John VII).

How many are there today who, if they could have seen that rock from which water was brought forth in the time of Moses, would have considered it no small gain? Let such people now enter the church of blessed Severus and see, in many stones together, what they exult with the joy of pious devotion to have seen happen in one. With this further difference: that water removed thirst alone from those who drank it, whereas this also heals various illnesses of the sick. When the former was drunk, it gave evidence of itself as ordinary water; when the latter heals, it performs the function of various spices and medicinal substances.

Turn, therefore, all these many and splendid miracles, dearest brothers, toward the gain of true usefulness, and through the outward benefits of the divine gift, yearn from the depths also for inward things. For what benefit is there in receiving these perishable and transitory goods temporally through divine kindness, if it does not happen that we reach the rewards of receiving eternal good as well? Remember what the Truth said to the Jews concerning their ancient fathers: “Your fathers,” he says, “ate manna in the desert, and they died” (John VI).

Consider also how great is the glory of the saints in heaven, for whom the elements themselves, contrary to their natural order, serve and obey here on earth. For what can the souls of the saints not do, whether in heaven, on earth, or even in the abyss, since they are one with the one who presides over all? Strive, therefore, dearest ones, with all your strength toward the dignity of so great a glory; hasten daily toward it by the steps of holy virtues and devout conduct.

You must despise everything you see if you wish to reach what you hope for. For, as blessed Paul attests, we cannot rejoice here in the world and reign there with God (Rom. XII). He says again: “We do not contemplate what is seen but what is unseen. For what is seen is temporal, but what is unseen is eternal” (II Cor. IV).

Despise, therefore, the fleeting and deceptive blandishments of this unclean world; overcome its threats with courage; restrain the rising incentives [fires] of the flesh; enlarge your minds in virtues with God’s help; drive the cold of torpor and negligence from your hearts; and continually sigh with a burning desire of mind for that ineffable joy of heavenly blessedness. For Jesus Christ our Lord, that watcher [spectator] who lovingly looks upon your hearts directed toward himself, also gladly opens to you the door of his fellowship. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON SAINT ELEUCHADIUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA AND CONFESSOR. (14 FEBRUARY)

Today’s festival, dearest brothers, heaps a twofold joy upon your—indeed, our—holy devotion, because while we celebrate the solemn rites of the venerable confessor Eleuchadius, we must immediately also recall the splendid deeds of blessed Apollinaris, Christ’s triumphant martyr. For since, as Solomon says, “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. X and XV), the one depends upon the other, so that whoever has worthily recounted the praises of one cannot remain silent about the other’s distinguished praise.

And because the Truth says, “The Son cannot do anything except what he has seen the Father doing” (John V), this blessed disciple followed his father’s footsteps. By preaching, he held firmly to the straight line of the true faith; by living religiously, he displayed conduct consonant with his holy teacher; and thus he deservedly succeeded to the government of the one whose holiness he had imitated.

For just as blessed Peter, prince of the apostolic senate, is known to have had three more eminent disciples among the others, who afterward succeeded him in order in the citadel of the episcopate—first Linus, then Cletus, and third Clement—so likewise blessed Apollinaris had four distinguished disciples who succeeded him in ecclesiastical government after the blessed glory of his martyrdom: namely, Aderitus; this blessed man, Eleuchadius, to whom the present sermon will render service; then Marcian; and finally Calocerus.

Eleuchadius was a philosopher, as the history of the blessed master himself relates. Thus the wisdom of Plato was overcome by the disciple of a fisherman. He cast the net of the word into the deep brine of the Ravenna [Col. 0535C] sea and drew a golden bream to the shore of faith. Indeed, the one whose master had once learned to steer a little boat through all the pools taught his disciple to dispute with the clever subtlety of dialecticians; he taught, I say, a disciple of keen intellect and sharp eloquence to confute men by simple speech—he who had been accustomed to tie together cheap nets for enclosing fish in the depths of the sea.

Clearly, after the sailor of the sea had been appointed the key-bearer of heaven, the disciples of fishermen became teachers of orators; and the wisdom of the world was conquered by the simplicity of Christ. For, as the Apostle says, “the world through wisdom did not know God; it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (I Cor. I). By this simplicity Paul, who judged that among the Corinthians he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (I Cor. II), overcame Dionysius the Areopagite at Athens. By this simplicity the blessed Apollinaris overcame the philosopher Eleuchadius in the city of Ravenna. When consulted about the skill of healing, Eleuchadius himself replied that he knew nothing apart from the name of Jesus.

Nevertheless, blessed Peter bears witness to the wisdom of both these wisely simple men. For concerning Paul he says: “Our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you” (II Pet. III). To Apollinaris, however, he says: “Behold, you have been instructed in all the things that Jesus did.”

Yet those who were wise with God presented themselves to the world as fools. For God chose the foolish things of the world [Col. 0536A] to confound the wise (I Cor. I). And, to make you wonder even more, he cast those supposedly wise men down from the empty swelling of their proud wisdom, and afterward raised them to the authority of free preaching, so that subsequently they might steadfastly assert the very thing which they had previously struggled anxiously and cruelly to oppose.

Moses mystically prefigured this when, taking the golden calf, he burned it with fire, ground it to powder, and, sprinkling it upon the waters, gave the Israelite people to drink of it (Exod. XXXII). For what is that molten calf, figuratively speaking, except the body of the devil? It is, namely, humanity deceived in every kind of faithlessness and likewise in the error of idolatry, joined together under its own pestilential head like different members by a sacrilegious conspiracy. Over these that spirit of wickedness, as their author, insolently raises itself while presiding, and like a head tyrannically rules its own body.

The calf is described as golden because the practice of idolatry appears to have been established as though by wise men. For wisdom is signified by gold, as it is said through Solomon: “A desirable treasure is in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. II). The calf, therefore, was golden because the wise men of the world are shown to have been the authors of demonic worship before the grace of the new faith. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness [Col. 0536C] of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed creatures, and serpents” (Rom. I). Through this vanity of mad wisdom, poets, philosophers, magicians, investigators of the stars, and those trained in every liberal discipline used to worship the monstrous fabrications of demons.

In the calf, therefore, the whole body was signified—that is, the entire society of the Gentiles devoted to idolatry. Moses burned the calf with fire because our Redeemer, whom Moses prefigured, kindled the wickedly conspiring hearts of the Gentiles with the flame of his love. Hence he himself says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII). And the Prophet says: “There is no one who can hide himself from its heat” (Ps. XVIII). Thus divine fire is suddenly kindled in the minds of the Gentiles, so that the irrational, bestial form of idolatry may be dissolved in them.

Then the entire body of this calf is ground to powder, because that Gentile society, forged into one by the art of diabolical conspiracy, was, at Christ’s coming, as if struck by the hammer of saving correction and crushed, away from the hardness of its rigidity, by the power of the divine word. Indeed, what had seemed, in the form of its pride, to stand senselessly intact is healthfully ground to powder by the word of truth. Then it is scattered into water, so that the Israelite people may drink of it.

Finally, the crushed calf is cast into the water because the humbled Gentile people must be washed in the bath [Col. 0537A] of the saving font. The Israelites immediately drink it, because the holy preachers of the Gospel, who are truly Israelites, transfer those whom they bring to the Lord’s body, which is the Church, into their own members, receiving and transforming them as if by drinking. To these Israelites it was first said: “Kill and eat” (Acts X), which is equivalent to saying: “Grind and drink.” Thus, thus, that calf was absorbed through the fire of zeal, the edge of the word, and the water of baptism by those whom it had attempted to absorb; it was poured into those whom it had tried to transfer into its own—that is, the devil’s—members.

Nevertheless, because Moses did not set the limit of vengeance at merely breaking the idol, but further added that he should slaughter twenty-three thousand men, he mystically taught that it is by no means sufficient for someone to turn away from the worship of idolatry or from a wicked way of life unless he also strives to put his own vices to death with the sword of the Spirit. Hence the outstanding preacher says: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. III).

And it must be noted that just as vices here are called our members, so there those who were killed were joined to their killers by the bond of kinship, as was said through Moses: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh; go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let each one kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor” (Exod. XXXII). If, then, anyone delights in rising to arms, whoever longs to fight against the enemy’s ranks, let him turn his hands against himself. There he will find more adversaries to cut down, so that after victory he may not incur the disgraceful name of murderer but rather appear as a glorious victor; so that he may not deserve to be excluded from the thresholds of the sanctuary, but, consecrating himself to the Lord, may be increased by the blessings of divine grace, just as it was said to those men: “You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, each one in his son and brother, so that a blessing may be given to you” (ibid.).

The report that those who were slain numbered twenty-three thousand indicates, through the number three thousand killed, a threefold form of sins [Col. 0537D]. For we commit every sin either by deed, by word, or by thought. But since the number ten is also doubled there, it is made known that, just as we have scorned to keep the Decalogue of commandments through the fault both of flesh and of soul, so we must also crush and put to death the vices of both by the weapons of the virtues.

Blessed Eleuchadius, then, once a great philosopher, was crushed like a golden calf by the hammer of preaching and poured into the members of Christ’s body. Once a teacher of earthly wisdom, he now became a master of ecclesiastical discipline. Once he investigated the hidden causes of nature; now he clearly contemplates the author himself of all natures [Col. 0538A]. And he who perhaps once marked the stars with a pointer now gladly observes the mechanism of heaven revolving with its stars.

Thus the man who had previously been a philosopher of truth, converted to the Lord, became a preacher of truth: third, namely, in the order of discipleship from blessed Peter the Apostle, and likewise third in the dignity of the episcopate from blessed Apollinaris. The order of persons was extended, but the same purity of faith, which had proceeded from the highest and original source, flowed onward through the descending course of its channel. For from Christ to Peter, from Peter to Apollinaris, and from Apollinaris to Eleuchadius, the river of heavenly speech poured forth, so that the proclamation of the Psalmist might be fulfilled: “He sends forth his word to the earth; swiftly his speech runs” (Ps. CXLVII).

Blessed Apollinaris and Eleuchadius, worshipers and helpers of Christ—the one a father, the other a son; the one a master, the other a disciple—undertook the ministry of one work, or, so to speak, the cultivation of one field and the husbandry of one vineyard. The former was to cut down the dense thickets of the forests; the latter to uproot from the roots the remaining trunks of trees and the thickets of bristling briars. The former was to cleave with the sharp plowshare of the word the hard, barren fields of the desolate wasteland; the latter, following him, was likewise to break up the clods swollen with vices with the hoe of holy preaching and carefully clothe the newly cultivated ground with the fruits of good works. The former was to plant with Paul; the latter to water with Apollos (I Cor. III).

And, to go back further, the former with Moses led the Lord’s people through the divided Red Sea into the wilderness [Col. 0538C] (Exod. XIV); the latter, succeeding his master with Joshua, was the first to introduce that same people into the promised land (Josh. IV). The former taught how Israel, dwelling in Egypt, should reject Egypt; the latter how it should possess the land flowing with milk and honey after the lots had been distributed among them. The one taught them to shake their necks free from Pharaoh’s iron yoke; the other admonished them to trample with victorious feet upon the conquered necks of their enemies. The one instructed them how quickly to flee the disgrace of servitude; the other how most carefully to guard the very titles of freedom.

Nor should it be believed, my brothers, that blessed Eleuchadius, while he still lived, lacked the labors of martyrdom, although he was not consummated by martyrdom. He saw that some remnants of the recently extinguished paganism still survived [Col. 0538D]; he grieved that even the final traces of superstitious worship remained among the people entrusted to him. Therefore, although the hands of persecutors did not draw swords, his holy soul was tormented, consumed by the fire of pious zeal and paternal compassion.

For what does it profit if someone believes in a Catholic manner but lives like a pagan? Or how does correct belief agree with a heretical life? What benefit is there if apostolic faith is present where one’s conduct is Arian? Concerning those who believe as Catholics but live as heretics, the blessed Apostle complains, saying: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I). For whether by believing or by living, to deny God is without doubt nothing other than to perish.

Therefore blessed Bishop Eleuchadius endured a martyrdom not to be despised in the very peace of the Church. For although he is shown to have had an irreconcilable conflict not with those who believed perversely but with those who lived perversely, we nevertheless rightly infer that he also labored strenuously in the teaching of the faith, since we recognize that the cities and towns of nearly all the dioceses adjoining the metropolitan see of Ravenna [Col. 0539A] scarcely contained any martyrs.

From this we cannot adequately marvel at the glory and excellence of blessed Apollinaris, whose martyrdom, prolonged for twenty-nine years through innumerable torments, accomplished so much by itself that no one else was found in almost all those regions who could die for the testimony of the faith [Col. 0539B]. If anything nevertheless remained incomplete, the revered succession of his disciples supplied it. Among them blessed Eleuchadius shone like a golden star and, in accordance with the etymology of his name, truly carried away the marks of his father’s whiteness and splendor as a son. For *Eleuchadius* in Greek is understood in Latin to mean “white.”

And not without reason. He belonged to the number of those of whom it is said: “Her Nazarites were made whiter; they gave splendor to God, and they were congealed like milk” (Lam. IV). And Jacob says of Christ to his son: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX).

The eyes of Christ are the apostles and evangelists, who furnished the light of wisdom to the whole body of the holy Church. Their teaching, while softening the rigidity and harshness of the ancient law, in a certain way surpasses the austerity of old wine by its beauty; for the precepts of the Gospel are far clearer than the commandments of the Old Testament.

The teeth are the holy preachers, who cut converted people away from the company of the wicked and transfer them into Christ’s body, as was said above, as if by chewing them. By the name “milk,” moreover, the teaching of the Law is indicated, which seemed to nourish the carnal people with a drink of milk as though they were little children. The teachers of the Church are whiter than that milk because they themselves eat solid and substantial food of the word and hand it on to others. Concerning them the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Solid food belongs to the mature” (Hebr. V).

And the teachers of the Church are rightly said to be white because they are both free from the stain of wickedness and bright in the conspicuous works of their conduct. Therefore, my brothers, we must take care that no blackness of vices disfigure us, since we have white leaders in Christ’s army. The appearance of affairs is dangerous when the insignia of the army that follows do not agree with those of its leaders.

Our blessed fathers readily displayed themselves as ready to endure punishments; let us at least, when injured by our neighbor, restrain our spirits from revenge. Moses, descending from the mountain as a sign of vengeance, appeared with horns (Exod. XXXIV); but upon the Lord the dove descended in the Spirit of gentleness (Matt. III). They resolved to despise everything of their own for Christ; let us at least learn not to covet what belongs to others. Let concern for the present necessity suffice for the present, and let the bitterness of anxiety not anticipate the day of tomorrow.

Indeed, as sacred history testifies, when the Israelite people gathered manna, it boiled with worms and rotted if anyone, acting faithlessly, kept some of it for the following day (Exod. XVI). So whoever, inflamed by the heat of greed, stores up earthly substance for himself as though providing food for his own body, causes that worm to boil within him which gnaws at his conscience and eats away at the secrets of his heart.

Indeed, these worms of anxiety [34], which greed produces, prepare those other worms of which it is written: “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worm shall not die” (Isa. LXVI), so that fire may kindle the fire of greed and worm proceed from worm.

Yet this may also suitably be understood in another way: just as Christ himself, who says, “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI), becomes for some the source of resurrection, so likewise his word becomes manna and the sweetness of honey for the faithful, but for the faithless and those who live wickedly it becomes a worm—not one that nourishes by restoring the soul, but one that bites the conscience by terrifying and threatening it.

On the sixth day a double measure was commanded to be gathered, so that half of it might be kept for the Sabbath. The sixth day, moreover, signifies the sixth age of the world, in which we now are. Therefore, on this day, the person gathers a double portion for the coming Sabbath, where perpetual Sabbath and true rest exist, who both hears and does the word of God with a view to heavenly glory.

On this day he stores up a double portion who both lives well and shows others an example of salvation; or, in the more direct sense, he gathers a double measure who labors so diligently in good works that his soul pleases its Creator here and afterward lives eternally with him. What was stored up for the Sabbath could not decay, because good works performed out of desire for heavenly rest will endure forever.

We must not therefore accumulate those riches which rust destroys, moths consume, and the outpouring of worms causes to rot (Luke XII). Concerning such riches blessed James rebukes their possessors, saying: “Your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths, your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will devour your flesh like fire” (James V).

Let us therefore, brothers, desire those riches which can adorn us with gems and pearls of virtues and raise us to the heavenly titles of dignity. The Prophet intimates these riches when he says: “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is his treasure” (Isa. XXXIII).

Blessed Eleuchadius desired these riches when he stepped down from the chair of philosophical teaching, when he cast aside the instructor’s rod, and when he humbly submitted himself from the authority of the teaching office to discipleship under Christ. Whatever superfluous material he had previously learned there, he cut away in the far nobler studies of this school; whatever falsehood or superstition he had been taught there, he corrected within the discipline of ecclesiastical purity.

Hence the Law decrees through Moses that a woman captured in war and chosen for marriage by the victor should have the superfluity of her body removed: “She shall shave her hair, cut her nails, and remove the garment in which she was captured; she shall sit in your house and mourn her father and mother for one month. Afterward you shall go in to her and sleep with her, and she shall be your wife” (Deut. XXI).

We shave the woman’s hair when we cut away the superfluous notions of rational discipline. We also cut her nails when we sever from it all works of dead superstition. She is likewise commanded to remove the garment in which she was captured, so that she may strip off the surface overlay of stories and every kind of fabrication and present the solid truth of true reason [Col. 0541B].

She mourns her father and mother because she counts the authors of the liberal arts among the dead and compassionately laments that they perished in error. It is customary for women to cleanse themselves each month through the shedding of their blood. After one month, therefore, we are commanded to enter this woman, so that, purified from every contagion of superstition, we may take the art of any discipline as though in marriage, so that, having become Israelite, it may consequently pass into the marriage of an Israelite and produce a fruitful offspring of spiritual works.

Something similar is also found in the fact that Moses commanded the Israelite people to borrow gold and silver, together with garments, from the Egyptians. To say nothing of lingering over this, mystically we ask gold and silver, together with garments, from the Egyptians in order to build a tabernacle for the Lord when we read worldly poets and philosophers, so that we may advance more brilliantly in the divine utterances.

Or, in the clearer interpretation, the gold and silver are precious souls, who, together with their garments—that is, their bodies—join themselves to the people of God, so that they may leave this dark world, as though it were Egypt, and acquire the promised land of everlasting blessedness.

Thus what blessed Eleuchadius borrowed from the Egyptians benefited the Israelites, and the treasure which he seized from paganism the holy steward of the Church faithfully distributed. His deeds are not found recorded in written documents; but antiquity did not, without reason, either build a basilica in his honor or dedicate his death to the honors of an annual solemnity. He is also said to have written several volumes on the Old and New Testaments, and likewise on the Lord’s incarnation and passion, although we believe these works to have been destroyed through the forgetfulness of writers.

Nor does it seem unreasonably to belong to the accumulation of his merits that he consented to become bishop at a time when poverty oppressed the Church, when the labor of a faith still immature and newly planted was more difficult, and when the task of uprooting from the roots the shoots sprouting from the former rites lay heavily upon him, while both a grave burden and the benefit of temporal assistance were lacking. For although the Church had already been founded in faith, Christian religion had not yet been refined in the practices of life.

Let us, therefore, dearest brothers, imitate the example of this holy fervor. Let us never fear to undertake steadfastly and confidently that labor in which we expect to be wearied by pressures and adversities, whether for divine service or for the salvation of our brothers. Let honor, glory, riches, and every temporal dignity be shunned. Let the labor of obedience, the narrowness of poverty, and the unrest of charity by which we are exercised be desired.

When the Jewish people had been satisfied with bread, they wished to make our Redeemer king; but, as John testifies, lest he be found, he fled to the mountain (John VI). When he was sought for the cross, however, he offered himself willingly to those who did not recognize him, saying: “Whom do you seek?” When they replied that they were seeking “Jesus the Nazarene,” he immediately answered: “I am he” (John XVIII).

For what does it mean that the Mediator between God and humanity, when he was to be advanced to kingship, escaped, but, when sought for death, thrust himself forward voluntarily, except that he wished to admonish us to avoid the glory of this world and to seek gladly, for God’s sake, tribulations and the pressures of labors and sorrows?

When Paul was at Miletus and saw all those who served him and loved him most affectionately—so much so that Luke testifies in the book of the Acts of the Apostles that, when Paul departed, great weeping arose among them all, and they fell upon his neck and kissed him—he nevertheless hurried most eagerly to Jerusalem to suffer, as though going to a feast, saying: “Behold, bound in spirit I go to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that chains and tribulations await me. But I fear none of these things, nor do I consider my life more precious than myself, provided that I complete my course and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Gospel of the grace of God” (Acts XX).

Behold, surrounded by a crowd of weeping people, he is not at all turned aside; soothed by kisses and flattered by their services, he is not moved to pity himself, but joyfully hastens to chains and torments as though he were approaching a wedding banquet.

We also, beloved, following the examples of the imitators of Christ, must flee the flatteries of the world, and bravely gird the loins of our minds to endure every adversity for God. As we strive toward the inheritance of the children, which is in our homeland, let us, placed in exile, bear patiently the injuries of our fellow servants, so that our heavenly observer and judge, seeing that we do not resist the command of his will, may afterward reward us with greater happiness in glory in proportion as he now sees us more oppressed in punishment—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## MARCH

[Col. 0543A]

XX. Homily on Palm Sunday. XX. Sermon on the vigil of Saint Benedict, abbot and confessor. XXI. Homily on the same Saint Benedict, abbot and confessor. XXIV. Sermon on Holy Thursday. XXV. Sermon on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. XXVII. Sermon on the Resurrection of the Lord.

## VII. HOMILY ON PALM SUNDAY (XX MARCH)

“When Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then he sent two of his disciples, saying to them: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you,’ etc.” (Matt. XXI.)

The Lord, about to suffer willingly for the salvation of humanity, approaches the place of his passion willingly. For this he came into the world; for this he was born: to free us through his passion. Knowingly he came to Jerusalem; knowingly, accompanied by a great crowd of peoples, he entered the city in solemn procession, the city in which he was to be handed over and crucified.

This is the Jerusalem that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it (Matt. XXIII). O unhappy city! How glorious the things that would have been said about you if you had recognized the Lord when he came, and if, having recognized him, you had shown him the reverence due to him. O wretched city, blinded by the error of wickedness! Your Savior came to you, and you neither can nor wish to recognize him. He came to save; by withdrawing, you approach to destroy him. He prepares salvation for you as for a sick person, while you prepare a cross for him as for a thief.

Why has so great a cloud of darkness covered you? Why do you not recall what was said through the prophet Zechariah: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes to you, gentle, sitting upon the foal of a beast of burden”? (Zech. IX.) Behold, you are so desperately foolish in your counsel that you fear to receive your king lest you lose your earthly kingdom. But while you do not receive him, you lose the kingdom and the nation. “It is better,” you say, “that one man should die, lest the whole nation perish” (John XI). Yet while you kill one, all your own perish.

Therefore it is rightly said concerning you: “Woe to the sinful nation, a people heavy with iniquity, an evil seed, wicked children. You are the offspring of vipers, which are born only after tearing open their mother’s sides” (Isa. I; Matt. III, XXIII; Luke III). Thus you do not think you can escape except by staining with blood the side of your Father who made you. It is a cruel birth, and the one who kills the mother who gives birth must be put to death.

But what does the blindness of the Jews contribute to the present subject? They were blind, leaders of the blind (Matt. XV), and therefore both—that is, their leaders and their younger men—fell into the pit.

Concerning you, Lord Jesus, wonder and compassion increase. Why do you go to the Jews, who plot against your life? They are traitors and murderers. Do not trust them, for they do not love you and will not pity you; they will condemn you to a cruel and most shameful death. Why do you hasten to endure so many mockeries, so many scourges, so many insults—to be crowned with thorns, spat upon, given vinegar to drink, pierced with a lance, to die and be placed in a tomb?

In this your deliberation, in this your plan, my spirit fails. I pity you, Lord Jesus, in the anguish of your passion. The advice of your friend Peter seems to me sound, when he says: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen” (Matt. XVI). It is not fitting for the Son of God to taste death. Yet this advice differs from yours, since you have resolved to undergo death.

What, then? Is the counsel of Peter or of Jesus to be followed? Of the servant or of the master? Of the disciple or of the teacher? But “the servant is not greater than his master, nor the disciple more learned than his teacher” (John XIII; Matt. X; Luke VI). We must therefore consent to the counsel of the Lord and teacher, who needs no counsel, lest it be said to me, as to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you do not understand the things of God” (Matt. XVI).

For Peter did not know that Christ had determined from the beginning [Col. 0544B] to destroy our death by dying and restore life by rising again.

What divine Wisdom had therefore ordained, he wisely wished to fulfill. In accordance with the prophetic words, he wished to sit humbly and poor upon a donkey and come to Jerusalem (Zech. IX), as the Evangelist relates, saying: “When Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then he sent two of his disciples, saying to them: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a foal with it. Untie them and bring them to me’” (Matt. XXI).

This village is the world, which was opposed to the Lord and his disciples, not only persecuting them with insults and scourges but also inflicting the most cruel death. Hence the Lord says: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV).

By the donkey and the foal, which were tied in the village, the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles are signified, both of whom were subject to the bonds of sins. The donkey under the yoke signifies the Jewish people subjected to the yoke of the Law. The playful and unbridled foal signifies the Gentile people walking according to the desires of the flesh.

The two disciples sent into the village are the preachers of the two Testaments, endowed with the double love of God and neighbor—or Peter and Paul, one of whom was the apostle of the Gentiles, the other the apostle of the Jews. Hence Paul himself says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship, worked also through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. II).

They released both peoples from the error of unbelief and led them to faith in Jesus Christ by the word of preaching. The Lord sat upon them because he justified them by their faith, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of Wisdom.” Concerning the justification of both the Apostle said: “Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of Gentiles? Indeed, of Gentiles also, since there is one God, who justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith” (Rom. III).

These things may also be understood morally. Bethphage is interpreted as “house of the mouth,” and it is the understanding of priests [Col. 0545A], by which confession is signified. The Lord came to it because he kindles hearts to confess.

The village that is opposed to the Lord and his disciples is the obstinate mind, devoted to its own will. Two disciples were sent to it: hope and fear. The tied donkey and foal are humility and simplicity. Such a mind sometimes knows what humility and simplicity are and that one must live simply and humbly; but it ties and stores them away, as it were, when it does not wish to exercise them in practice.

Fear terrifies this mind when it has turned away from evil, threatening it with punishments. Hope strengthens it if it repents, promising rewards. The mind is pierced by these two. The donkey and foal are untied when, going to meet the Lord at Bethphage, it confesses that it has sinned and promises henceforth to live humbly and simply.

Thus the one who was previously the village of the devil becomes Zion, the city of our strength; the Savior is placed in it as a wall and a bulwark (Isa. XXVI). The wall is humility; the bulwark is patience.

Let us therefore, dearest ones, go out to meet the Lord at Bethphage, pierced by fear of punishment and strengthened by hope of heavenly life, confessing our sins humbly and walking simply, laying down the garments of our carnality, so that the Lord may deign to sit in us and lead us with himself into the heavenly Jerusalem. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT BENEDICT, ABBOT AND CONFESSOR (XX MARCH)

Dearest brothers, today we celebrate the vigil of the outstanding confessor, namely blessed Benedict. We must therefore prepare eager hearts to celebrate the marks of his solemnity. Let the devout mind now conceive the splendor of so great a solemnity, gird itself for the watches of pious service, and grow hotter than usual with the flame of divine love.

As the Church is cleansed with brooms according to custom, so let the conscience also be purified through sincere confession from the dust of evil thoughts. Lamps are prepared and various kinds of ornaments are hung up; likewise, by the mercy of God’s generosity, let various ornaments of virtues be arranged within our breasts. Thus let the light of the inner temple be kindled by as many pious endeavors as by shining lamps.

Today we ought to compassionate the blessed man, as though he were sick, with loving inward feeling, so that tomorrow we may rightly rejoice with him over his assumption. As the Apostle says concerning our Redeemer: “If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II). Again he says: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection” (Rom. VI).

What, therefore, we owe to Christ, the head of all the elect, we owe also to his venerable servant Benedict: namely, to share the suffering of one who is afflicted and to rejoice with one who happily ascends to heaven. First, by temporal death, he paid the debt owed by nature; then, accompanied by choirs of angelic singers, he migrated to the heavenly kingdoms.

On this day he endured the hardships of bodily weakness [Col. 0546A]; he entered the homeland of eternal happiness, to reign there forever. On this day he succumbed to a momentary fever while his disciples mourned; but in that other realm he was carried into the brightness of heavenly glory while the powers of heaven rejoiced with him. He laid down the burden of his body and immediately put on the garment of immortality (Gregory, *Dialogues* II, chap. 37).

Lying upon a cheap haircloth, he gave up his spirit among the hands of a few disciples; but immediately, along a road spread with cloths and shining with lamps, he flew to the joyful fellowship of countless angels.

But what wonder is it if the renowned senator of the heavenly court, after his blessed death, sought the company of angels, when, while still established in corruptible flesh, he so often merited their familiar conversation? For, to say nothing of the rest, I do not think I should conceal from your charity one matter which escaped a sacred and truthful passage of the Gregorian style.

Clearly, when the man of God Benedict was living as a solitary at the place called Subiaco, with monasteries built all around him, he was divinely warned to leave the place and hasten to the fortress called Cassino. Immediately the holy man, without the assistance of any companion, set out alone, as he was, and after walking nearly fifty thousand paces, visited the place to which he had been directed. But while he was travelling alone through unknown regions, whenever a fork in the road appeared, two young men immediately seemed to stand there and indicate to him in which direction he ought to turn. Who, indeed, should those two young men be thought to have been, if not angelic spirits assigned to guard the holy man? And what wonder if angels—lovers, that is, of holy men—showed him the way, so that the holy man would not go astray, when even brute animals followed his footsteps lest he travel alone? For three ravens were his inseparable companions along the whole journey, constantly following his tracks. Even today, in the forest adjoining the venerable monastery of Mount Cassino, two—or, as they say, three—ravens always build their nests each year; some assert that they descend by a succession of offspring from those ravens of ancient times. Indeed, every day they fly to the monastery doors, and, croaking and spreading their wings and beaks, demand their customary food, as though it were a tribute owed them by right of their ancient possession.

And, so that it may become clearer how vigilantly divine grace shone over the blessed [Col. 0546D] man, a certain holy man was then living in the fortress of the aforesaid Mount Cassino. He was commanded by a divine voice to depart and make room for another who would come as the new inhabitant. We have already culled this account from the graceful poem of Mark, likewise a disciple of the blessed Benedict, because we found it nowhere in the venerable sequence of Gregory’s history.

Recently also, near the monastery of Mount Cassino mentioned above, a sufficiently remarkable miracle occurred, which we believe did not happen without purpose if we refer it to the glory of him who is wonderful in his saints (Psalm 67). From nearly the beginning of May until the fifth day before the Kalends of August, scarcely at any time had even the lightest rain moistened the parched fields. And when the whole earth was drying out, and the world was suffering more fiercely than usual from the fiery heat of the dog-star, on the day we have mentioned a certain farmer, in order to provide abundant crops for his newly cleared fields, set fire to the stubble remaining after he had harvested the grain. Suddenly, however, the raging flame seized the fields on every side, and, not content with the straw and stalks, consumed forests, groves, and everything in its path in furious masses of fire. When matters had reached the point that the flames were already almost licking every place adjoining the monastery, and destruction was plainly threatening the holy site, a very small and thin cloud suddenly appeared in the vast expanse of the sky. Then, gradually extending itself into greater dimensions, it spread over the entire circuit of the monastery on every side. [Col. 0547B]

Why prolong the account? O indescribable power of heavenly strength! O divine protection over his elect, which never fails! At once the cloud dissolved into streams of the most abundant rainfall, so that it not only extinguished the flames of the devouring fire, but also drenched the entire circuit of the holy place with the copious floods of the pouring storm. And so that no one might doubt that the cloud had been produced through the merits of blessed Benedict and had come forth solely to protect his holy place, while the whole sphere of heaven shone everywhere with uninterrupted serenity, the cloud restrained itself to the measure of the monastery. It thoroughly drenched everything adjacent to the sacred buildings, but not a drop fell upon any of the neighboring and adjoining places. Indeed, those who had flocked from the surrounding areas to protect the monastery everywhere were astonished to find themselves suddenly soaked, although up to that moment they had been weakened not by water but by sweat. [Col. 0547C]

What firm confidence, then, my brothers, can we have in so active and vigilant a patron! For if he prevented the flames of the raging fire from consuming worthless wood or stones, how powerful an aid may we think he will provide in defending our souls, made in the image of God, from the heat of burning vices! He moved the cloud, drew out the rains, extinguished the flames, and rescued the building.

You too, if the incitements of lust are burning in your inward parts; if they hasten to invade the temple of your breast by tickling it, as though by licking it; and if perhaps your soul, withering from dryness and growing sluggish, does not recoil from them, ask for the rain of tears. Beg for the saving compunction of a contrite heart, which will soften the hardness of your stony heart. Thus may your dry mind revive to produce the harvest of good works, so that what the Lord says through the prophet may come to pass for you: “Your soul shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring whose waters do not fail” (Isaiah 58).
