Scripture also says elsewhere: “When you think yourself consumed, you shall rise like the morning star” (Job 11). Thus, then, my most beloved brothers, let us strive to celebrate the vigils of the saints, so that for that supreme and continual solemnity celebrated in heaven we may make, so to speak, one continual vigil out of our entire life.

[Col. 0548A]

For during a vigil the one who celebrates ought to be afflicted, so that at the solemnity he may be able to rejoice. Therefore we now celebrate the vigils of that final resurrection, namely, the true Passover, if we break our own wills, restrain the impulse of the flesh, drive wicked thoughts from our hearts, and, by afflicting ourselves, carry the cross after Jesus in our hearts; if, finally, we strive to pardon those who offend us, assist those in need, speak the truth with our mouths, and preserve sincere charity in our hearts; if we do not give ourselves over to gossip, do not attend to idle words, do not desire any earthly thing, and do not entangle ourselves in worldly affairs; if we strive to offer God pure prayers, cleansed each day; and if we continually delight to hear the word of God with the whole affection of our hearts, so that Christ may be heard on the tongue, Christ may be seen in the life, Christ may be in the heart, and Christ may be in the voice. Indeed, whoever carefully observes these things truly celebrates the vigils of the eternal festival. And whoever now mortifies himself with Christ through humility must necessarily rise together with him, when all corruption has been utterly consumed.

Let us therefore always celebrate these vigils, dearest brothers; let the whole attention of our spirit be directed toward attaining the glory of that eternal happiness, so that by performing vigils of this kind we may always behold Jesus hanging on the cross, and afterward deserve to contemplate him amid the very solemnities, reigning in the majesty of the Father’s glory. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## IX. HOMILY FOR THE HONOR AND PRAISE OF SAINT BENEDICT, ABBOT AND CONFESSOR. (21 MARCH)

[Col. 0548C]

Simon Peter said to Jesus: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you,” etc. (Matthew 19).

At the principal solemnity of this our father, we ought to devote all our strength to the task, were it not that Gregory’s noble tongue had gathered his entire journey into magnificent speech (Book I of the Dialogues, throughout). For he portrayed his deeds and life with such radiant eloquence that the style sparkles with the majesty of his thoughts, while the thoughts shine with an even brighter style. It is therefore superfluous to add anything after the words of so great a man, in comparison with whom we know ourselves to be not merely inarticulate but mute. Yet let it suffice to say this alone: he alone will present a military host to the exalted Prince more abundantly than the others, and will fill the palaces of heaven with companies of monks living after the manner of angels. How radiant and splendid, then, will that soldier stand before the imperial tribunal, filled with innumerable virtues, accompanied by countless ranks, counsellor of the King, friend of the Judge, and the unique enemy of the ancient foe!

Concerning him, and concerning those who follow him, Simon Peter said to Jesus: “Behold, we have left everything” (Matthew 19). This is truly a friendly conversation of Simon with Jesus, and a speech more beautiful than every flower of rhetoric; and Simon was worthy to speak more fully with the Savior: Simon means obedient, Jesus means Savior. [Col. 0549A] Obedience therefore speaks with salvation, because eternal salvation is owed by hereditary right to the obedient alone—provided that Peter is present there, that is, provided obedience does not waver or stumble but is founded upon the firm rock.

And what does he say? “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” A solemn word, a great promise, a holy work worthy of blessing: to leave everything and follow Christ. These are the words of voluntary poverty’s persuasive power, which gave birth to monasteries, filled cloisters with monks, and more abundantly filled the forests with anchorites. For these are the words of which the Church sings: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways” (Psalm 16)—about to receive rest for labor, riches for poverty, and reward for tribulation. Truly, it is a great thing to leave everything, but greater still to follow Christ, since we read that many left everything but did not follow Christ. This is the work, this is the labor; here the whole of human salvation consists. Nor can we follow Christ unless we leave everything, because he rejoices like a giant to run his course (Psalm 18), and one burdened cannot follow him. “No one swims with baggage,” said that orator of secular learning whom nobility of language and depth of understanding made a friend of poverty. Rightly does one leave everything who follows him who is above everything, since our sufficiency is from him (2 Corinthians 3), and God will be all in all (Colossians 3).

“Behold,” he says, “we have left everything”—not only the world’s possessions, but also the desires of the soul. [Col. 0549C] For he has not left everything who has retained even himself; indeed, it profits nothing to have left all else without oneself, since no burden is heavier for a human being than the human being himself. What tyrant is more cruel, what power more savage toward a person, than that person’s own will? It never permits one to rest under it, never allows one to sit down; and the more it knows that you are wearied in obeying it, the more it presses, goads, and burdens you, forgetful of piety and ignorant of mercy. For this is what self-will has as its special characteristic: the more obediently a person obeys it, the more it binds him in cruel chains. It alone is loved, although it alone deserves hatred; it is the beginning of wickedness, the infusion of death, and the great destruction of virtues.

“Come, therefore, you who labor and are burdened,” to the lifter of burdens, and answer him in word and deed: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 11). Consider that formerly, before the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1), the fathers of ancient times followed God, clinging to the spirit by spirit alone. But now he must also be followed in the body, so that, although those earlier fathers are read to have abounded in earthly riches, henceforth no one can be his disciple unless he renounces all that he possesses (Luke 14)—he who, though rich, became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8). Possessions and one’s own will must therefore be abandoned if we wish to follow him who had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9), and who did not come to do his own will but the will of him who sent him (John 6).

It follows: “What, then, will there be for us?” Peter has now left everything; he not only follows, but has followed for a long time; and now for the first time he asks what he will receive. What is this, Peter? Did you not promise obedience in the hearing of the ears, not in a contractual agreement? But now hear what the Lord God says, and attend to the hope in which we ought to hope while the world is tossed about: “Amen, I say to you, you who have left everything and followed me: in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit, judging” (Matthew 19). [Col. 0550B]

The sweetness of the Lord’s mercies toward his poor is utterly boundless; nor does he abandon those in death for whom he exposed himself to death and torments. “You,” he says, “who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit, judging.” What else does this mean than that you shall attain the one whom you follow—provided that you pursue him, as it is written: “Seek peace, and pursue it” (Psalm 33)? Run, therefore, so that you may obtain it (1 Corinthians 9), and do not wish to sit down before you grasp the one who is sitting and deserve to sit with him.

He rejoiced like a giant to run his course (Psalm 18) throughout the whole time in which he was seen on earth and lived among human beings (Baruch 3); nor did he sit down until he reached the one whom he himself appointed as the end of labor and sorrow: “My soul,” he said, “is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26). Therefore, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of majesty—he who first stood in the most shameful punishment of the cross, questioned amid insult and torment—you also shall sit, judging. You, from whom judgment now begins, grant yourselves no rest—because he too came not to judge but to be judged, and not to be served but to serve (Matthew 20). There indeed “thrones shall sit in judgment” (Psalm 121).

For the Son of God, the Savior, by the indivisible unity of the natures, sits at the right hand of God insofar as he is God (Psalm 109); insofar as he is human, he now stands before the face of God for us (Hebrews 9). Nor will his triumphant session take place until God is all in all—that is, until the body is joined to the head in such peace that we are like him, though not equal to him. For he is still denied by the Jews, mocked by the nations, torn apart by heretics, and fiercely attacked by false Christians. Do you think that he sits quietly and pays no attention to the eyes of the proud, the assaults of the wicked, or the wills of those who resist? But in the regeneration he will sit with those who sit, when we are purified to the most genuine brightness in both substances, and he himself, having conquered his enemies, will enter glory with his friends, joining angels to human beings in everlasting unity and repairing the losses of the blessed city. All this will occur in the regeneration. Blessed is that regeneration, which will renew earth and heaven, unite earthly beings with heavenly ones, and pour forth the fountain of perpetual peace in an indefatigable flow.

It must be noted, however, that there is one generation and two regenerations. In the generation that we derive from a corrupted root, the body is filled with mortality and the soul with iniquity. In the regeneration of baptism, where we must be born again (John 3), the iniquity of the soul is cleansed, but the body’s mortality is not removed. Another regeneration, therefore, or resurrection, is necessary, in which bodies too will be found conformed to the body of Christ’s glory (Philippians 3)—provided that hearts have first been reformed according to the gentleness and humility of Christ’s own heart. Hence blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection (Revelation 20), precisely because he will also become a participant in the second. In this regeneration, therefore, when the Son of Man sits, etc.

This is what Scripture says elsewhere: “For double shame and disgrace, they shall praise their portion” (Isaiah 61). The poverty of those who follow the Lord has two aspects: affliction, namely, and lowliness. Hence the Prophet says: “See my humility and my labor” (Psalm 24). Therefore they shall possess double in their land (Isaiah 61), so that honor of judicial power may correspond to lowliness, and the refreshment of a most peaceful session to affliction.

When, then, shall we sit, we whose body and soul do not now sit, in whom nothing has settled, nothing is at rest, and nothing remains in the same condition? When shall we be freed from the restless movement of this present life? Our body is not permitted to sit, since it is hindered by the pain of present sensation and the future anxiety of death, being subject to suffering and mortality. [Col. 0551C] The spirit itself also has no rest because of the expectation of hope and the anxiety of fear. But there will be a time when the soul will rest, established in hope alone (Psalm 4), free indeed from anxiety but not from expectation.

This will happen after the death of the flesh but before the day of judgment. On that day, when the Son of Man sits, we too shall sit perfectly and completely, because the body will not be disturbed by the sensation of pain or troubled by fear of death; glorified with the double robe of impassibility and immortality, we shall be free—and as far as the soul is concerned—from all expectation and anxiety, lacking nothing and thereafter fearing no danger, in perfect security and most secure perfection. “You shall sit,” says the Lord; the Truth says it. A solemn session, welcome rest, complete sufficiency.

“Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4.) You seek the glory that comes from one another, plainly vain and false, since the sons of men are vain and the sons of men are false (Psalm 61); yet you do not desire the glory that comes from God alone, glory unquestionably abiding and true. Wretched and pitiable are those who, for brief pleasure, lose the torrent of delight and interrupt divine mercy for themselves, so that they may never be satisfied from the breasts of his consolation (Psalm 35).

But lest patient waiting should torment us through the sweetness of so great a promise, he moderates the restlessness of our mind with gentler speech. For he himself knows our formation (Psalm 102), since our faintheartedness cannot endure the delays of postponement. Therefore, in his kindness, he also meets this thought and comes to meet us in this respect, saying: “Everyone who has left house, or father, or mother, or brother, or wife, or fields, or children for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19).

“Certainly the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped” (Psalm 62). Now let all who act wickedly be put to shame without cause (Psalm 24). For we have the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come (1 Timothy 4), and it is evident that the promise of a hundredfold belongs to the present time, from what follows: “And he shall possess eternal life.” But lest anyone retain a pretext for obstinate evasion, I turn to the Gospel according to Mark, where it is openly declared that the promise of a hundredfold belongs to this present time. For the Lord says: “There is no one who has left father, or mother, or children, or fields for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who shall not receive a hundred times as much—now in this time, houses and brothers,” etc. (Mark 10).

And, so that you may marvel still more, do not suppose that this promise, although it belongs to the present time, is fulfilled through temporal things; “with persecutions” has been added. For what earthly substance did the holy martyrs receive while they were in persecution, when even the earth itself was given over to the hands of wicked men together with the bodies of the blessed? That he means “a hundred times as much in houses, or brothers,” etc., not according to the flesh, is also evident from the fact that no one receives a hundred mothers. Now, if we wish to understand this promise in terms of the sharing of possessions and the affection of souls that exists among the elect, it may apply to some, but not to all. For we know that some saints lacked this earthly and human consolation.

You must therefore seek this hundredfold in the heart and in the inner person, so that now you may have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end—eternal life. Those who have not yet received the hundredfold should examine their hearts and carefully investigate all the works of their hands. They will doubtless find a corner and a lodging that the Savior does not know. Yet “foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have nests” (Luke 9). They should rather leave everything more perfectly; they should not seek what belongs to them, and should retain nothing for themselves or for others.

For many, although they sufficiently despise their own exaltation and pleasure, nevertheless in some way retain for their relatives what they ought to have left behind, laboring on their behalf with an inappropriate solicitude contrary to religion. How many monks, while caring for their parents more than was right, have lost their own souls? Let them therefore leave everything, follow Christ alone, strive to please Christ alone, and cling with vigilant concern to his good pleasure. Without doubt they will immediately experience what the Truth promises to those who leave everything and follow him: “He shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19).

The one is received along the way for consolation; the other will be possessed eternally in the homeland for blessedness. But what is this hundredfold except consolations, visitations, and the first fruits of the Spirit, who is sweeter than honey; except the testimony of our conscience; except the joyful and most delightful expectation of the righteous; except the remembrance of the abundance of God’s sweetness and the great multitude of his delight, which no one can express in words either to those who have experienced it or to those who have not? It is not father, mother, house, field, food, or clothing; indeed, it is not anything earthly or bodily, but is plainly more delightful than all these things, sweeter and more pleasing than them all.

[Col. 0553B]

To whom, indeed, can the whole course of the Gospel reading be assigned so particularly as to our father and teacher, blessed Benedict? From childhood he left the world while still in the flower of youth, and followed Christ, who was running, with the swiftest course; nor did he stop until he overtook him. Who will judge more sublimely among those who judge? Who received the hundredfold in this life in such a manner? Who will possess eternal life more gloriously? Therefore may he, who came so that we might have life and have it more abundantly (John 10), Jesus Christ our Lord, who is blessed for ever, deign through Benedict’s intercession to administer to us the abundance of his grace for the consolation of the present life and the possession of eternal life. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER. (24 MARCH)

[Col. 0553C]

Today, dearest brothers, while we celebrate the solemnity of the Lord’s Supper, we recall many mysteries of the heavenly virtues. Today our Savior, who is the head of the angels, while washing the feet of his disciples, clearly set before us an example of true humility, so that what the Lord bestowed upon servants, servants would not disdain to bestow upon fellow servants, and dust would not deny dust what seemed fitting to so great a majesty.

When Peter refused to receive the service of the highest [or: so great a] Teacher, and the Lord threatened to reject him unless he allowed himself to be washed, Peter, finally shaken with fear and immediately yielding to the command that pressed upon him, said: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” (John 13). In these words the blessed Apostle indicated that our works and our thoughts alike need to be purified and cleansed by the Lord. For the hands perform works, while thoughts proceed from the mind, which is the head of the inner person. True and perfect purification therefore occurs when almighty God not only keeps our works clean and undefiled but also drives wicked thoughts from our hearts by the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Today the Savior changed the appearance of earthly bread and wine into the sacraments of his body and blood, and bestowed upon his disciples the nourishment of life-giving food. For that forbidden food, which the first human being consumed as pride swelled and greed for food pricked him, spread through all his inward parts the poisons of every vice and mortal corruption. [Col. 0554A] Against this deadly virus, therefore, the Christian people receive an antidote, by which the pestilence of spiritual disease may be healthfully vomited out. Through the power of this new sacrament we expel that leaven of condemned antiquity [variant: immediately], so that we may pass from slavery into the freedom of the spirit and into the unleavened bread of the new regeneration.

Today the sacred chrism is prepared, by which the sanctification of all heavenly gifts is confirmed [or: designated] in us. This is recognized as that most holy chrism which in the Old Testament anointed not only priests, kings, and prophets, but also sanctified the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors in the New. Today [in this] we too are anointed with the oil of divine power, so that, wrestling in the contest of the spiritual arena, we may triumph over enemies whom we have subdued and defeated.

Concerning this oil the prophet says: “The yoke shall rot before the face of the oil” (Isaiah 10). For when, through the sacrament of this divine chrism, the freedom of the spirit is restored to us, the yoke of ancient slavery must be reduced to decay. The prophet David undoubtedly recognized this mystery of the chrism when he sang that our face should be made joyful with oil (Psalm 103).

Indeed, when the crimes of the world were once cleansed by the outpoured flood (Genesis 7), the dove presented the likeness of the future gift when it announced that peace had been restored to the earth with an olive branch. Scripture says: “After waiting another seven days, he again sent the dove out of the ark. And it came to him in the evening, carrying in its mouth a branch of an olive tree with green leaves” (Genesis 8). In the sending out and return of the dove, the number seven is placed because there are unquestionably seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The dove returns to the ark in the evening because the Holy Spirit, who in the beginning of the world was borne over the waters (Genesis 1), filled the holy Church as the age was already growing old.

The sacrament of the divine chrism also pertains to the command that almighty God gave to his servant Moses: first to wash his brother Aaron with water, and then, by the pouring on of this ointment, to appoint him priest: “You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and you shall consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. You shall also say to the children of Israel: This shall be holy oil of anointing for me throughout your generations” (Exodus 30). Just as, after the world had been washed by the flood, the dove returned to the ark with an olive branch, so Aaron too was first washed with water and then anointed with chrism so that he might be promoted to the priesthood.

So now, whoever comes to the grace of regeneration is first immersed in the waters of sacred baptism, so that afterward he may be signed with the mystery of the divine chrism. The oil that consecrated the tabernacle of the covenant and all its implements also clearly prefigured this sacrament of the divine chrism. For the Lord said to Moses: “You shall take oil of olives, measured by the hin, and make holy anointing oil, a compounded ointment prepared by the work of the perfumer; and with it you shall anoint the tabernacle of the testimony, and the ark of the covenant, and the table with its bases, and the lampstand and its vessels, the altars of incense and of burnt offering, and all the equipment belonging to their worship. You shall consecrate them all, and they shall be most holy; whoever touches them shall be sanctified” (Exodus 30).

The mystical chrism, then, which at that time consecrated the tabernacle in the desert, now sanctifies the Church in the New Testament. This sacrament also appears to have been fulfilled more fully and abundantly when our Redeemer emerged baptized from the waters of the Jordan, and when the heavens were immediately opened and the Holy Spirit descended visibly upon him in the form of a dove. Then the voice of the Father thundered: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3). It plainly confirmed him as the one to whom David, once taught by the same Spirit, had said: “The Lord your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

From that very Spirit, which now also consecrates our chrism, the nature of all waters received such power that in whatever waters a person is immersed to be washed under the profession of the divine Trinity, the full and perfect mystery of the new regeneration is divinely accomplished.

Our chrism also typologically signified that oil with which the Lord commanded seven lamps in the tabernacle to be filled and kept continually burning. “Command the children of Israel,” he says, “to bring you pure oil of olives, clear, for preparing the lamps, so that they may burn continually outside the veil of the testimony in the tabernacle of the covenant. Aaron shall set them from evening until morning before the Lord, by a perpetual observance throughout your generations; they shall always be set upon the purest lampstand in the sight of the Lord” (Leviticus 24).

What, then, are signified by the seven lamps in the tabernacle except the seven churches in the one Christian people? In them the oil is commanded to burn without ceasing because in them sincere charity, which is given through the Holy Spirit, ought to grow fervent with the fire of a twofold love and always shine forth in clear and conspicuous works.

But since the Catholic, universal Church is unquestionably one, as Solomon says: “My dove, my perfect one, is one, the only one of her mother” (Song of Songs 6), what does it mean that the sacred writings report seven churches, except that the one Church is one through the unity of faith but sevenfold through the corresponding seven gifts of the Holy Spirit? These are the seven women who, according to the prophet’s prediction, took hold of one man (Isaiah 4). The man is Christ, the Church’s husband.

All the nourishment of the sacred Scriptures is seasoned with this oil of the Holy Spirit, so that the inward parts of our souls may be nourished. This oil, infused into the life-giving feasts of heavenly speech, has a flavor in the throat of the soul; it refreshes its stomach and sweetens the taste of the one who receives it. For it is written: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3). Hence it must be understood that all the pages of the sacred volumes are seasoned with the oil of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0556A]

For this reason we also read in the Book of Numbers: “The people went around, gathering manna and grinding it in millstones, or pounding it in a mortar, cooking it in a pot, and making from it cakes of a flavor like the taste of bread seasoned with oil” (Numbers 11).

We have, as it were, passed through many jars in the Lord’s storeroom in order to reach the one oil-seasoned vessel, like a little container of oil. The manna, by which the Israelite people lived, signified the sacred word, by which Christian religion is nourished and grows. It is truly seasoned with oil because it has been sprinkled with the mystical anointing of the Holy Spirit.

It should be noted, however, that the same manna which the Book of Numbers calls oil-seasoned is said in Exodus to have had not the taste of oil but rather that of honey: “Its taste was like flour mixed with honey” (Exodus 16). What does it mean that this angelic food is first said to have displayed the sweetness of honey and afterward to have offered not the sweetness of honey but that of oil, except that our Redeemer, the author and creator of all the sacred Scriptures, whom that manna principally prefigured, displayed the sweetness of miracles before his Passion, like honey, and after his ascension poured out the Holy Spirit upon his disciples, like oil? (Acts 1 and 2.) He seemed to offer the sweetness of honey while he shone forth in signs and wonders; but he gave the sweetness of oil when he poured the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, upon his apostles.

Moses fittingly maintained this sequence when he sang symbolically in Deuteronomy about the rock, which nonetheless was manna: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest rock” (Deuteronomy 32). Concerning this oil of mystical anointing, the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song of Songs 1). The bridegroom’s name is called poured-out ointment because, just as Christ is named from chrism, so a Christian is consequently named from Christ.

Since, therefore, dearest brothers, through the grace of our Savior we have already received the sacrament of this chrism, and since we already bear upon our foreheads the expressed sign of royal dignity, let us strive to live nobly, so that our conduct may be worthy of agreement with mysteries so divine and magnificent. For we are the ones to whom the chief of the apostles says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2).

Certainly it is most ignoble to live in slavery to carnal vices when, by God’s adoption, we possess the dignity of royal lineage. It is exceedingly shameful for us to be devoted to earthly desire when we are called children of God and, through Christ’s grace, are deemed worthy to be enrolled for the inheritance of heaven.

Clearly, since we are disciples of the crucified Teacher, it is fitting that we too should present ourselves as dead to this wicked age. Therefore, in bearing the cross after our Master and Lord, let no concern for temporal business impede us, and let no love of earthly substance or attraction of the flesh turn us aside. Let us direct the eyes of our faith and devotion along the road of the cross, already laid out and appointed for us, so that, walking along it with unhindered steps, we may deserve to reach him who is the author and the one who summons us to the glory of the resurrection. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

* SERMON XI. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. (25 MARCH)

Exult, brothers, in the Lord, because the discourse now turns to that Lady who claims a singular primacy in our hearts. She is the one at whose name you humbly bow your bodies, at whose hours you reverently attend, whose memory you continually frequent. She is the one who becomes sweetly delightful to your affections, because great is the abundance of her sweetness. Her spirit is sweeter than honey; in her the Lord came, with all his sweetness.

For when God had made all his works “very good” (Gen. I), he made this one better, consecrating for himself in her a golden resting place, in which alone, after the tumult of angels and human beings, he might recline and find rest. This is what nature marvels at, the angel reveres, the human being fears, heaven is astonished by, earth trembles at, and hell dreads. In her womb the majesty of the Most High was wonderfully melted down; like fat and richness, it filled the earth, flooded the heavens, and sprinkled the underworld. Here the exalted and immeasurable one “emptied himself” (Phil. II), sending “a good measure, pressed down and shaken together” into our bosom (Luke VI). Here he was anointed by divine hands with the oil of gladness, and consecrated as though from the altar to the dignity of high priest. From this altar, ascending to the altar of the cross and drenched in his own blood as though in another kind of oil, he was no longer merely consecrated but also consecrating, and joined the whole body of the world’s structure together with a more generous bond.

Let grief therefore depart, let sadness flee, let pain be driven out, let resentment withdraw, so that we may have leisure to behold with Moses this great vision (Exod. III): how God is conceived in this womb, the devil is deceived, what was lost is received again, and what was not owed is accepted. My whole being is carried away by affection, but prayer fails, and rich thought is confounded by the poverty of speech. My inner parts burn and boil up into a billowing height, but the coldness of my tongue cools the heaps that overflow.

What is this, most blessed Lady? Shall I gradually fall silently asleep, so that I am mute there where every creature speaks? Nevertheless, I shall not be silent, and I shall not rest until your countenance goes forth like splendor, and the word conceived concerning you is kindled, if not as a lamp, at least as a spark (Isa. LXII).

I confess that I am moved by the fact that, with God permitting it, rational creatures sin, and that for many thousands of years both heavenly and earthly things seem to stand uselessly—these destined to serve, those laid waste. That great city stands deprived of the multitude of its citizens, and a manifold population of inhabitants is driven from the starry palaces; the fires of the stars are darkened—by the sun I mean, the moon, and the stars—and, deprived of much of their brightness, they are punished; the earth is cursed; the succession of humankind is condemned; “and every creature,” according to the Apostle, “groans and labors in childbirth” (Rom. III). Almighty God is silent, and his omnipotence, ordering all things, feigns not to notice so great a confusion.

At last Mary is born, and when she comes forth into marriageable years she assumes a beautiful appearance that might allure God himself and turn the eyes of divinity toward her. See what that not insignificant explorer of God’s secrets says about this:

“Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. And the king desired your beauty, because he himself is the Lord your God” (Ps. XLIV).

Thus the branch of Jesse sprouts from the twisted root of the human race, and, bursting upward and straight from the tree of the patriarchs, knows no tangled growth, knows nothing of the darkness of leaves [editorial correction: *filiorum* (“of sons”) should perhaps read *foliorum* (“of leaves”)], and bears none of the fruitless things [editorial correction: *fructuosa* (“fruitful”) should perhaps read *infructuosa* (“fruitless”)]. That ardent lover sees and burns, and sings the whole wedding song in her praises. There the bridegroom is plainly introduced, breathing the purest love and no longer able to conceal what he suffers.

That heavenly assembly is immediately summoned, and, according to the prophet, God takes counsel and convenes a council (Isa. XVI). He speaks with the angels about their restoration, the redemption of human beings, and the renewal of the elements, and, while they are stunned and amazed with joy, about the manner of redemption. At once the name of Mary is drawn from the treasury of divinity, and it is decreed that all this should be accomplished through her, in her, from her, and with her, so that, just as nothing was made without him, so nothing might be restored without her.

The letter is entrusted to Gabriel. In it are contained the Virgin’s greeting, the Redeemer’s incarnation, the manner of redemption, the fullness of grace, the greatness of glory, and the abundance of joy.

Therefore the angel Gabriel was sent by God to the Virgin. After he had spoken to her, she perceived God having entered her inward parts and his majesty enclosed within the narrow space of her virginal womb (Luke I). O womb more expansive than the heavens, broader than the earth, more capacious than the elements, which encloses the one who encloses all things, in which the God of glory reclines!

Finally, the archangel says: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (ibid.), because the Holy Spirit was about to take her wholly for himself—she having been chosen and prechosen by God—and to mark her with heavenly ornaments. She was now to be consecrated as the place of delight, from which that fountain was to rise that would irrigate the entire surface of the earth (Gen. II).

Thus far we have scattered words and sown various things in fleeting speech. Now let us remain here, if perhaps we may draw forth something worthy. “A river,” Scripture says, “went forth from the place of delight to irrigate the entire surface of the earth; from there it divides into four heads” (ibid.).

This river is my God Jesus, who goes forth from two places of delight: from the Father’s womb and from the Virgin’s womb. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river, leaping forth upon thirsty land” (Isa. LIX).

Yet by ineffable distinctions he proceeds very differently from the Father than from the mother. For although his temporal birth is glorious, his eternal birth is much more glorious. Since you ask concerning both generations, I wish to disclose what I perceive—not that I presume to explain anything, since this lies beyond everyone’s strength, and all the more beyond mine. Indeed, it would be the height of madness to wish to speak ineffable things, especially for an uninstructed man.

For I have not forgotten Solomon’s saying: “As one who eats too much honey vomits it up, so one who is an investigator of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. XXV). Concerning both generations, I think it is said through the prophet: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. V). The generation from the Father is truly ineffable and inaccessible, open to no creature. I believe the Apostle had this sense when he said of God: “Who alone dwells in inaccessible light” (I Tim. I), since even purer natures are dazzled by such a vision and cannot break into the abyss of so great a brightness.

The Son himself also declares: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI)—not as he is in himself, but as the one to whom such condescension is revealed is able to grasp him. Hence that sublime soul which had been caught up into the riches of glory as far as the third heaven (II Cor. XII) says: “I do not consider that I have comprehended” (Phil. III).

The truest definition, therefore, is that no intellect at all penetrates the generation of the one who begets and of the one begotten. I also consider the generation from the mother inextricable for every human creature. I do not know whether it can be comprehended even by that more excellent nature. For who can comprehend the joining of flesh and the Word? How do God and man come together in one person while the properties of the natures remain safe and undisturbed? Let each person abound in his own judgment; I believe this surpasses every judgment, following the footsteps of the ancient men who left sound and unshaken opinions concerning it.

Returning, then, to the paternal generation, we consider the Father to be the place of delight, since God is not located in space; but we cannot explain the effects of things except through familiar expressions. The one who reads the Apostle understands that all delight is in him when he says: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI). Another, uttering a similar statement from that twelve-pointed summit, says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights” (James I).

The Son himself also says: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God” (John XVII). Knowledge of the Father, then, is eternal life; and where eternal life is, there is everlasting delight, because God is begotten from the Father’s womb: God from God, light from light, Lord from Lord.

He proceeds in identity, because he is the same as the Father. I say “the same” according to substance, not according to person. He proceeds in equality, because with equal omnipotence he regards the Begetter, since whatever the Father can do, the Son can also do, as he himself testifies: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does; nor can the Son do anything except what he sees the Father doing” (John V).

He proceeds in eternity, because although he is begotten, he is not later than the Begetter; both are of one antiquity, if only one does not object to the novelty of the term. Although this signifies what is being said in some fashion, it is nevertheless far from the majesty of the meaning.

He proceeds in likeness, because he is like the Father, the Father’s image, “the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his substance” (Heb. I). He proceeds in otherness, because he is another than the Father—another, I say, not another thing: “I and the Father are one” (John X). He said “one,” not “one person”: “one” signifies unity of substance, while “we are” signifies the distinctness of the persons.

Thus, in a manner far more excellent, the Son proceeding from the Father floods the angelic stations, because, according to Solomon, “the fountain of wisdom, the Word of God, is on high” (Ecclus. I). The boy harpist had drunk deeply from this full fountain when he said: “With you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV), because not only are you life, but your Son also is the fountain of life. And, to show plainly what he meant, he added: “In your light we shall see light” (ibid.).

“To irrigate the entire surface of the earth” (Gen. II). What earth is situated at that summit of the heavens which the glorious river does not pass over and irrigate? The kingdom of heaven is the land of the living, of which the holy man says: “The Lord is my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. XIV); and: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI); and: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV).

This irrigation is indescribable. The angels are indeed drunk from the abundance of God’s house and drink from the torrent of his delight. What can I say here? I do not know, because overwhelming astonishment oppresses both sense and mind. Where are the rhetorical speeches which that whole chorus of philosophers forged in the furnace of rhetoric? Where are the giants celebrated by the ages, who were of great stature from the beginning, skilled in war, and languishing over battles of words?

Was that greatest giant—Plato is the one I mean—not driven back from understanding such pure truth? Did he not, touching the divinity of God with the sharpest power of mind but not reaching it, say: “I have found one thing that accomplishes everything, and another through which everything is accomplished; but I could not find a third”?

Rightly was he ignorant of the Holy Spirit, who had not been infused into him, who is the teacher of holy revelations, who reveals to Paul what eye has not seen, as the same Apostle boasts: “God has revealed it to us” (I Cor. II). Through what, Apostle? “Through his Spirit” (ibid.), not through our spirit, which the philosophers followed and by which they were both deceived and deceived others.

Let us hear what our philosopher—he who understood more than the elders and more than all who taught him (Ps. CXVIII)—thought about this: “Watering the mountains from his upper places” (Ps. CIII). For he teaches about the higher angels, who behold the very substance of God with tireless eyes, not through a mirror in an enigma but face to face (I Cor. XIII).

It follows: “From there it divides into four heads.” Let us speak briefly about these four heads, because a great road remains before us.

The first is wonder, by which that whole more excellent creation is struck with amazement at the Creator’s glory and at the manner of his glory.

The second is purity, because they do not drink from the torrent of delight in an earthen vessel or through the fragility of human constitution; rather, with the veil removed, they draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior (Isa. XII).

The third is satiety. Although they desire to gaze upon him, desire does not introduce necessity, nor necessity misery. Rather, in a more marvelous manner, they always desire so that they may always be satisfied, and they are always satisfied so that they may always desire.

The fourth is security, because certain of their own stability, they immerse themselves in everlasting joys, awaiting “the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God” (Tit. II), when there will be “one flock and one shepherd” (John X), and that heavenly Jerusalem will be perfected in unity.

Thus this river flows through the angelic workshops. But faith grasps all these things; reason does not know them, and the human intellect does not understand them. Perhaps these are the four things which the vessel of election divides in a blessed fourfold arrangement in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying: “You have not approached a smoking mountain, but Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, the gathering of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven.”

Now let us gird ourselves to see how he proceeds from the Virgin, because this proceeding is sweeter and more moving to human misery. It shakes the breasts of those who behold it, moistens their eyes, and pours blessed fountains over the faces of lovers.

Here I understand Mary’s womb as the place of delight, in which the Lord heaped up all the delights of delights. Concerning these delights the Holy Spirit, in admiring speech, pours forth this in the Song of Love: “Who is she who rises from the wilderness, overflowing with delights?” (Song VI).

Does the Most High have delight in the angels, in whom he himself found perversity? In the constellation or glittering of the stars, some of which are turned into blood, some fall from heaven, and others are darkened into shadows? In air, fire, or winds? Not at all, because “the Lord was not in the fire, the Lord was not in the disturbance, the Lord was not in the spirit” (III Kings XIX), if the one who was taken up into heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses is truthful (IV Kings II).

In the waters, where the raging and twisted Leviathan dwells? Or in the earth, which under Adam’s curse sends forth thorns and thistles? There is no place of delight except the Virgin’s womb.

From this place he proceeds with humanity, because clothed in the sackcloth of our mortality he appeared visibly to human eyes. From the Virgin he made a branch, and from the book of generation a line, attaching the hook of divinity, which he covered with virginal flesh, so that the great dragon, lured toward the flesh, might feel the iron of divine power beneath it.

He proceeds also with newness, because no human being was ever born as he was. The first man was formed first from earth; second, the woman was fashioned from his side; third, Cain was begotten by both according to the customary order of birth. This one alone was born from a virgin alone, and divinity made human sealed the Virgin’s womb with a new and singular birth.

Where now is the eloquent but barren loquacity of Aristotelian subtlety? If she gave birth, did she have intercourse with a man? Whether it wishes to or not, privation is turned into habit; the one who terminates all things is not confined by dialectical terms. At his command nature gives birth, and custom ceases to be customary.

He also proceeds with brightness. At his birth all that luminous serenity of the starry lights is buried, and a star, white and flashing with brighter rays, seizes for itself the whole position of the heavens. “Kings walk in the brightness of his rising” (Isa. LX), for behold, kings have gathered and come together as one. Seeing God and man born in this way, the mother giving birth while remaining a virgin, they marveled, were troubled, were shaken, and trembling seized them (Ps. XLVII) amid the light of such great miracles.

He proceeds also with poverty, because wrapped in the cheapest rags and laid in a very hard manger (Luke II), he already then prefigured the law of martyrdom for his most holy limbs.

He proceeds secretly, because that most subtle investigator of frauds is excluded from the height of such condescension. Hence, wearied by ambiguous disputes, he now tempts him, now calls the tempted one the Son of the Most High, now prepares the cross, now destroys it, through a woman—his customary instrument—delivering the command: “Nothing to you and to that just man” (Matt. XXVII).

It follows: “To irrigate the entire surface of the earth.” This means to cleanse the earthly misery that the first sinner left to us as an inheritance. I want the Apostle to distribute him here into four heads, as above, because I receive his exposition more securely: “He was made for us,” he says, “wisdom, justice, sanctification, and redemption” (I Cor. I).

Coming to us who were in prison, he first drove away the darkness of our ignorance with the light of his wisdom. Then, through the justice that comes from faith (Rom. X), he loosed the cords of our sins, sanctifying us in his body and redeeming us through the suffering of his body.

“For the Lord looses those in chains; the Lord enlightens the blind” (Ps. CXLV); “he sanctifies his tabernacle” (Ps. XLV); “he redeemed us from the hand of the enemy” (Ps. CV).

He is divided also into patience, by which he endures sinners; mercy, by which he cherishes the penitent; generosity, by which he raises up those who are making progress; and strength, by which he preserves those who have been raised up.

I have spoken to your brotherhood throughout this Advent about this second fourfold division, interweaving moral matters with mystical ones through the course of the rivers and the interpretation of the names. Whether I have done anything worthily, you shall judge. Yet we cannot compress everything into the present sermon, since we wish to avoid weariness.

I have four heads sweeter than the earlier ones, which perhaps will please your hearts more pleasantly. For our Lord, lifted upon the cross, poured out the most abundant waves of blood from four parts of his body. When piercing thorns bent back his most holy head upon his snow-white neck, and nails pierced his feet and hands, and a spear transfixed his side, precious blood flashed forth. By its sprinkling, the judge passed over into the Father, wrath into gentleness, the rod into mercy, and captivity into a crown.

Christ, therefore, is a hidden fountain concealed in the heavens and an open fountain revealed on earth. There he proceeds from the Father’s womb; here he proceeds from the Virgin’s womb. There, living, he irrigates the land of the living; here, dying, he irrigates the land of the dying. There he is divided into a marvelous fourfold division; here into a sweet one.

The Lord is sweet, and the Lady is sweet, because he is my God, my mercy, and she is my Lady, the gate of mercy. May the mother lead us to the Son, the daughter to the Father, the bride to the bridegroom, who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD  
*(27 March)*

On the verse of Psalm II: “I asked my Father; he gave me the nations.” Alleluia.

[Col. 0563B]

If we consult the assistance [editorial correction: perhaps *auditorium*, “audience,” rather than *adjutorium*, “assistance”] of the legal experts, the first word of the proposed chapter is defined as follows: to petition is to set forth one’s own desire, or that of one’s friend, before the one presiding over jurisdiction in court, or to oppose another’s desire. This act is public, and it is the office of advocates, who, trusting in the protection of their glorious voice, raise up what has fallen and restore what is weary; nor do they provide less for the human race than if they defended their country and themselves with shields and breastplates.

In carrying out this act, we must consider who petitions, whom he petitions, where, and what he petitions. An advocate petitions a judge in court concerning his case, or petitions on his own behalf after bringing an action. In the present case the advocate is Christ; the judge is God the Father; the place of jurisdiction is the gallows of the cross; the thing petitioned for is the Church from the nations; and the name of the action is a claim to inheritance.

We rightly call Jesus Christ an advocate. Hence John says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ; he is the expiation for our sins” (I John II). This advocate set forth his desire before the Father when he was offered for the salvation of the human race, because he himself willed it (Isa. LIII). His desire is our salvation, for which, thirsting on the cross, he is read to have loved his own to the end (John XIII).

But this was also the desire of his friends, to whom he said: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends, because a servant does not know what his master does. But I have called you friends, because everything I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV). Again: “No one has greater love than that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (ibid.).

It is fitting that he petition the Father, since he has always been heard. For it is commonly and proverbially said: “He goes confidently to court who has a father as judge.” The Father said of him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III and XVII). Since the Son is of the same substance as the Father, in the human nature which he personally united to himself he petitions for us, or pleads before the favorable judge, and brings back to us the fruit of his desired purpose.

Nor is it inappropriate to call him Father, since the Prophet says in the person of the Son: “Judge, Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me” (Ps. XXXIV). The Son himself says: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges” (John VIII).

In many places of Sacred Scripture a certain order of judgments appears to have been instituted and maintained by God himself.

A certain simple and upright man who feared God, after completing his morning office and leaving the church, was asked by his disciples: “What did you hear in church, father?” He replied: “I heard four things; I noted six.” It was plainly a subtle and faithful response. He had heard four verses of the eighteenth Psalm, namely: “The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls” (Ps. CXVIII), and three others that follow, in which six things are noted: law, testimony, justice, commandment, fear, and judgments.

In these, some of the persons necessary in court and some of their acts are expressed. The Lord, who is judge, is indicated, as is the law according to which judgment is made. The office of witnesses is represented by the word “testimony”; the merits of the plaintiff and defendant by the word “justice,” since the merits of cases are disclosed by the assertions of the parties. The judge’s sentence is represented by the word “commandment”; the offices of the accuser and executor are indicated by the final two words, “fear” and “judgments.”

The first five rest upon two attributes each, while the sixth rests upon four:

“The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls.  
The testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to the little ones.  
The justices of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts.  
The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes.  
The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever.  
The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.  
They are more desirable than gold and a very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (ibid.).

These things are expressly said to belong to the Lord. For there is a law that is not the Lord’s, namely the law of sin, about which the Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. VII).

There are also human justices, of which it is said: “All our justices are like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. LXIV). There are human commandments, which Peter says must not be obeyed: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V). Human fear too is rejected by the Lord. Hence he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X).

[Col. 0564D]

In the verses under discussion, everything is said to belong to God. The first, namely law, has two attributes: “immaculate” and “converting souls,” whether you understand this as the natural law, the written law, or the law of grace. These two qualities belong to each of these three laws—natural, written, and the law of grace—for each ought to be immaculate and converting souls.

The natural law had these two commandments: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another; and what you wish to be done to you, do for another” (Tob. IV). These are not harming and benefiting. The first concerns “immaculate”; the second, “converting souls.” In the first it is non-harmful; in the second beneficial; in the first without the stain of wickedness; in the second converting souls to the gentleness of goodwill.

Since three natural powers exist in the soul—anger, reason, and desire—desire was given so that you might be moved to seek what is permitted to you, and likewise to become indignant against what is forbidden. Reason was given as an intermediary, restraining and directing both, so that anger might not be moved beyond its limits and desire might not seek what is forbidden. Thus the natural law, insofar as it is considered in itself, is immaculate.

The written law too is immaculate and converts souls: immaculate, that is, without the filth of idolatry; converting souls to serve God, which only the children of Israel did.

The law of grace is truly immaculate and converts souls. The Church is guided by this law, for it is said to be “without stain or wrinkle” (Eph. V): without the stain of crime and without the wrinkle of pretense. The evangelical law too is without the error of heresy, converting souls simply and directly, without the fabrication of hypocrisy.

Observe these degrees: the first law is immaculate, the second more so, and the third most of all; likewise with “converting souls.”

The testimony of the Lord has two attributes: it is faithful and grants wisdom to the little ones. The testimony of the Lord is whatever the Lord testifies in the sacred writings, whether promising or commanding. Testimonies are therefore contained in promises and commandments, because what he promises he fulfills, granting rewards to the just and punishments to the unjust.

It grants wisdom to the little ones insofar as it commands, because those who are little in knowledge are made wise through the Lord’s commandments, as is shown there: “From your commandments I gained understanding.” The testimony of the Lord is therefore faithful in the explanation of his commandments.

In the first attribute understand promises and threats; in the second, prohibitions. It is faithful in promising and threatening; it grants wisdom to the little ones in forbidding and commanding.

The justices of the Lord are characterized by two attributes: they are right and gladden hearts. The justices of the Lord are the works of the just; hence the just themselves are called by that name. They are said to belong to the Lord because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I). For what do you have, O human being, that you did not receive? (I Cor. IV). Again: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV).

Those works may be called works of justice which are born from faith and brought to perfection by love. For just as without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. II), so faith without works is dead (James II). Faith that works through love both makes progress and suffices for salvation. These are the justices of the Lord, right and gladdening hearts through a serene conscience.

The commandment rejoices in two attributes. It is lucid, enlightening the eyes through its teaching. Some things are indeed lucid but do not give light; for example, a coal without flame is bright but does not illuminate. A flame without coal both shines and illuminates.

The commandment of the Lord is lucid, without confusion of meanings; it enlightens the eyes through the infusion of grace. Hence: “Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Ps. CXVIII). Blessed Peter likewise says: “You do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (II Peter I).

The commandment is singularly expressed, although the commandments are many, because, as Gregory says (Homily 27 on the Gospels), “the commandment of the Lord is both one and many: many because of the diversity of works, one in the root of love.”

“The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. CX). Once human fear has been excluded, filial or chaste fear is signified here. In the phrase “the fear of the Lord is holy,” chaste fear is understood; and “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” But the phrase “enduring forever and ever” designates filial fear.

[Col. 0566B]

The judgments of the Lord are borne by their fourfold arrangement. They are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and a very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

The judgments of the Lord are the retributions by which he either punishes the rejected or rewards the just. Although they are often hidden, they are always true and just, following the truth of the just judge. They are justified in themselves, unlike human judgments, which are formed from outside sources, such as the allegations of advocates, the depositions of witnesses, and the reading of documents.

Hence judges are often deceived by these things. Although judicial procedure is observed, an innocent person is sometimes condemned and the guilty acquitted. The judgments of God, however, receive their justification from themselves, as is said through the prophet: “He will not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears; but he will judge the poor in justice and reprove the meek of the earth with equity” (Isa. XI).

They are desirable—that is, supremely worthy of being desired—more than riches and delights. Understand riches by gold and precious stone; delights by honey and the honeycomb. Riches are chiefly understood as money and power. By the precious stone, which the powerful and noble use, understand the glory of power.

Some riches are acquired with difficulty, others without difficulty. In honey, which is liquid, understand delights and pleasures without labor; in the honeycomb, which contains honey and wax together, pleasures accompanied by difficulty.

[Col. 0566D]

Here a certain judicial allegory presents itself to us in Scripture, representing God the Father. The place of jurisdiction in which our Advocate petitions was the gallows of the cross. Although advocates, by the nature of their office, are required to stand, he did not stand; rather, with his whole body extended upon the wood of the cross, he pleaded before the Father for us, setting forth his own desire and that of his friends, and opposing the desire of his adversary, even to the shedding of his own blood.

He petitions for his case—that is, the human race, which he himself created and over which he held true dominion. He petitioned for the Church from the nations to be converted, as the true heir presenting a claim to the inheritance and desiring to be legally placed in possession.

A claim to inheritance is brought according to orderly and regular law against the one who possesses as heir or as possessor. One possesses as heir who says he is an heir when he is not. One possesses as possessor when he can defend his possession by no title; if asked why he possesses, he alleges no other reason than: “I possess in this way.”

Our Lord rightly brought his claim against the devil, who, as a malicious plunderer, possessed the Lord’s inheritance as a mere possessor. Concerning him the prophet says: “Woe to you who plunder; will you not yourself be plundered?” (Isa. XXXIII).

The Church especially rejoices in this advocacy or petition of our Advocate on the day of the Lord’s resurrection: the Advocate petitioned; what was petitioned for he obtained; what he obtained he took and possessed.

Hence she adds praise three times. Introducing the Son speaking to the Father and saying, “I asked my Father,” the Church responds: “Alleluia”—that is, praise to God, because you asked. Again: “He gave me the nations.” The Church responds: “Alleluia”—that is, praise to God, because you obtained it. Again: “As an inheritance for me” (Ps. II). She responds: “Alleluia,” because you obtained and possessed it.

Let us therefore join ourselves to this praise of the universal Church, so that, destined to enter into the Lord’s inheritance with the elect, we may be able to reach the Lord’s resurrection and rejoice forever. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## APRIL

[Col. 0567C]

23. Sermon on Saint George the Martyr.  
25. Sermon I on Saint Mark the Evangelist. Sermon II on the same. Sermon III on the same.  
28. Sermon I on Saint Vitalis the Martyr. Sermon II on the same.

## SERMON XIII. ON SAINT GEORGE THE MARTYR  
*(23 April)*

Today’s festival, dearly beloved, doubles the joy of Easter glory and, like a precious gem, illuminates the gold into which it is set with the beauty of its own radiance. It is entirely fitting that blessed George should be granted his triumph at this particular season, when, after the severity of the winter storm has passed and the warmth of the south wind has been released, the joyful earth eagerly gives birth, and, with the various flowers of herbs and trees bursting forth, grows youthful and comes into maturity, so to speak.

For George, which in Greek sounds in Latin speech as “cultivator of the earth,” in keeping with the omen of his name, not only cultivated the field of his own mind through the disciplines of spiritual practice, but also furrowed the earthly hearts of many with the plowshare of holy exhortation and devout correction. Having uprooted the brambles of vices, he planted within them fruitful orchards of virtues.

Rightly, then, today the soul of this blessed martyr, after the bloody fury of the raging prince, after the savagery of executioners ferociously assaulting him, after the elaborate tortures inflicted upon his mangled body, after the unjust torments of fire, iron, pitch, and sulfur, and finally after the blows of scourging, after the darkness of prisons, [Col. 0568A] as though after the winter storms of raging winds and snows, was deemed worthy to hear this oracle of divine calling: “Come,” he says, “my dove, my bride, my beautiful one; for winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come” (Song 2). He was plainly transferred from one military service to another, because he exchanged the office of the earthly tribunate which he held for the profession of Christian soldiery. And, as a truly strenuous soldier, first giving all his possessions to the poor, he cast off the burden of earthly wealth; thus free, unencumbered, and girded with the breastplate of faith, he ardently plunged himself into the very front line of the dense battle as a soldier of Christ—observing, of course, this order: that he should lay down the weight of his possessions beforehand, and then advance undaunted [Col. 0568B] into the field of combat.

Hence it is that the Law commands that a fearful man, one fainthearted, should not go forth to war, but should go, it says, and return to his land, lest he make the hearts of his brothers afraid, as he himself is terrified (Deut. 20). By these words we are clearly taught that those who still fear to strip themselves of earthly wealth cannot fight bravely and effectively in defense of the faith; and that it is more tolerable for them to live ignobly and unwar­like, as it were returning home, than by examples of degenerate fear to turn themselves and others away from the glory of victory. But blessed George, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit and made unconquerably secure by the banner of the cross, engaged the wicked king in such a way that he both defeated the prince of all the wicked [Col. 0568C] in the person of his henchman and stirred the hearts of Christ’s soldiers to act bravely.

At that time, indeed, the emperor Diocletian—as is found in the written account of his passion—whose mouth, according to the Psalmist, was full of cursing and bitterness <sup>61</sup>, and under whose tongue sat toil and sorrow, who sat with the rich in secret in order to kill the innocent, lying in wait like a lion in his lair (Ps. 5), first craftily assumed the appearance of a sheep and attempted to persuade him by a certain art of cunning and by the painted colors of flattering words. But when Christ’s renowned athlete scorned the foaming poisons from the mouth of the ancient serpent, and showed that within him there now lived not the origin of the first parent but rather the marks of the second, [Col. 0568D] the emperor immediately, like an arrow emerging from Satan’s quiver, revealed the savage wolf that had been concealed, and, like a bloodthirsty beast, ferociously boiled over with a desire to inflict various punishments.

The executioners were therefore gathered, and the blessed martyr was stretched out, beaten with blows, and torn by harsh strikes. Then a wheel armed with swords was brought into the midst, so that the martyr’s bound body might be pierced, the more cruelly because the weapons were more numerous. The contriver’s savagery [artificis, “of the contriver”] found new and elaborate devices of punishment and, to satisfy the fury of his rage, philosophized on surpassing the measure of human cruelty—ignorant, naturally, that the precious pearl of conspicuous brilliance, destined to be set among the living stones of the heavenly Jerusalem, is rendered more splendid the more it is polished by the roughness of a harsher file or by the blows of a hammer. [Col. 0569A] The transcendent and invisible Arbiter was plainly present, permitting the hands of the wicked to rage on one side according to the decision of his providential dispensation, while on the other preserving his jewel in the unimpaired integrity of its own solidity. Although he handed the limbs of his martyr over to the executioners’ hands, he guarded his soul, supported by the impregnable fortress of faith, with the unwearied protection of his defense. He did not allow them to touch what lay hidden; he exposed to them only what appeared outwardly. It was as with the waters of the Flood: they could indeed flow all around the ark, but they could not penetrate its interior (Gen. 7).

Let blessed George, then, speak—let him speak: [Col. 0569B] “If the Lord had not been with us when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive; when their fury raged against us, perhaps it would have engulfed us like water” (Ps. 123). These are plainly the waters of which the Savior says through the Psalmist: “Save me, O Lord, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. 11). And through Jonah: “You cast me,” he says, “into the deep, in the heart of the sea, and the flood surrounded me; all your whirlpools and your waves passed over me” (Jon. 2). But over these waters and the sea, according to Scripture, the Lord placed a boundary (Ps. 103), because he permits the reprobate to rage against his elect according to the measure of his providential dispensation, not according to human perversity’s desire.

This is why, at the beginning of the world’s creation, [Col. 0569C] God divided the sea from the dry land (Gen. 1). For what does the sea signify mystically except reprobate and unbelieving people? They are cunning through a certain saltiness of carnal understanding, yet they are always found bitter toward one another through hatreds and conflicts, and, like the sea, they swell under the various blasts of temptations and are shaken by the storms and tempests of carnal desires. What, on the other hand, does the dry land signify except the soul thirsting for the fountain of faith, or panting toward its Creator with ardent desire <sup>62</sup>, as with a thirsty mouth? Thus a certain soul, happily made dry by this thirst, cried out in its burning: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 31).

The sea, then, is divided from the dry land when almighty God restrains from himself the assaults of the thirsty reprobate [Col. 0569D] and, as it were, opposes a shore to the waves of the sea, setting the boundary of his restraint against the efforts of raging madness. This is certainly proved by that word of God in which he says: “Who shut up the sea with doors when it burst forth, proceeding as though from the womb?” (Job 38). And shortly afterward: “I surrounded it with my boundaries, and I set its bar and doors, and I said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall go no farther, and here you shall break your swelling waves’” (ibid.).

Indeed, the heart of an evil person is rightly signified by the sea: turbid with fury, bitter with quarrels, swollen with the pride of arrogance, and darkened by the gloom of malicious deceit. God therefore separated the sea at that time and restrained its threatening waves from flooding the land, so that the land might bring forth green [Col. 0570A] plants and fruit-bearing trees, and afterward yield the fruits of crops. Even now he separates from his elect the storms of persecuting reprobates and restrains, as though in fury, the assaults of tempests. Although he permits them to rage as far as inflicting tortures upon bodies, he nevertheless guards them from harming souls by the invincible and ever-watchful protection of his arm, saying, as it were, to the sea: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall go no farther, and here you shall break your swelling waves.” It is as though he openly said: “I release you to inflict tortures upon bodies; but lest you overflow as far as the soul with mounting heaps of waves, I set against you the shore of my law, so that, while a shore is opposed to the fury of your waves, the land of the heart may remain free to bring forth the shoots of fruits.”

[Col. 0570B] And because, as we said above, Georgius is interpreted as “cultivator of the earth,” this mystery of allegorical imagery is rightly adapted to that most blessed martyr. Although the waves of persecution boiled up as far as the shore of his flesh, the storm of the tempestuous whirlwind did not engulf the most solid land of his soul; nor did the abyss of the raging sea swallow him, because he fixed the anchor of his hope not in the crumbling [or: cut-away] remnant of rotten sand but in the solidity of the rock, which is Christ (1 Cor. 10).

Hence, indeed, Truth says: “Whoever hears my words and does them, I will compare him to a prudent man who built his house upon a rock. The blasts came, the winds blew and struck that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon a rock” (Matt. 7; Luke 6). [Col. 0570C] Truly this distinguished soldier of Christ established the foundations of his faith upon the rock: in view of the heavenly reward he despised the threats of princes, mocked the promises of those who offered evil flattery, scorned the tortures of executioners, and trampled iron, fires, swords, and various kinds of punishment beneath the majesty of unconquered endurance.

Let us not merely admire this warrior of the heavenly army, dearest brothers, but also imitate him. Let our spirit already be lifted toward that reward of heavenly glory, so that, while we fix our hearts upon its contemplation, we may not be moved whether the world smiles upon us as a seducer or, threatening adversity, roars against us, saying with the Psalmist: “As its darkness <sup>63</sup> is, so also is its light” [Col. 0570D] (Ps. 139). Let us therefore cleanse ourselves, according to Paul’s instruction, from every defilement of flesh and spirit (2 Cor. 7), so that we may one day deserve to enter that temple of blessedness toward which we now direct the gaze of our mind.

This is why Aaron is first washed with water, and only afterward enters the tabernacle to offer sacrifice (Exod. 30). Concerning him, a divine voice rightly commands Moses: “He shall clothe himself with a tunic; he shall cover his nakedness with linen undergarments; he shall gird himself with a linen belt; he shall place a linen turban upon his head. For these are holy garments, with which, after he has been washed, he shall be clothed” (Lev. 16). Whoever strives to sacrifice himself to God in the tabernacle of Christ, which is the Church, must, after being washed in the bath of the sacred font, also be clothed in various [Col. 0571A] garments of virtue, as it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131). Thus the person who is reborn in Christ through baptism as a new human being must no longer wear the tunics of skin, signs of mortality, but, having put off the old person, must put on the new and live renewed in him through devotion to a pure way of life.

It should also be noted that all those garments are described as linen. Linen is brought to whiteness through labor, and the life of virtue is not acquired in the torpor of laziness but rather through the practice of arduous discipline.

Having therefore been purified, beloved, through the sacrament of the new baptism, let us put on the linen tunic, so that the whiteness of holy conduct may adorn us. Let the undergarments [Col. 0571B] cover our nakedness, so that, when the covering of an honorable life has been assumed, the shamefulness of past crimes may be hidden from God’s eyes. Hence David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 32). Let us also be bound with a linen belt, and let a turban be placed upon our head, so that, with the loins of our mind girded in truth, we may be protected by the helmet of the hope of salvation.

Thus, thus indeed—purged from the squalor of former sin and distinguished by the brightness of a new way of life—we worthily celebrate the paschal mystery and truly imitate the example of the blessed martyrs. And do not despair, my brothers: though you are still weak, though perhaps you are still entangled in outward actions, do not despair of belonging to the company of the martyrs, since you recognize that you love the victories of the martyrs from [Col. 0571C] your heart.

The five daughters of Zelophehad are known to have received an inheritance among their brothers, when Moses so decreed (Num. 27 and 36). Five women, certainly, so that by the number five outward occupation might be signified, and by the female sex weakness. Jonathan too, placed at a kind of midpoint between the two, neither remained with Saul in evil nor could he altogether be equated with David in goodness (1 Sam. 18–20). But because he was a friend of God’s beloved Prophet and rejoiced with brotherly kindness in his future success, he is piously believed not now to be separated in spirit from his fellowship—he who, while he lived in the flesh, was united with him in unanimous love.

But we, beloved, who, with God’s help, have left the evil spirit that persecuted Saul behind us (1 Sam. 16)—indeed, who have escaped through the power of the paschal sacrament after Pharaoh’s army was drowned in the Red Sea (Exod. 18)—still remain in the wilderness because of the weakness of the flesh <sup>64</sup>. Let us pass on to the perfection of life, that is, to the land flowing with milk and honey.
