Having gone out from Sodom, let us not linger longer in Zoar, but, once delivered, let us swiftly ascend the summit of the mountain with Lot (Gen. 19), so that we who, already amid the very beginnings of our apprenticeship, have begun to rejoice in the triumphs of the blessed martyrs may one day also be advanced to the point of learning to triumph with the saints.

And may he himself be our strength as he protects us—he who became the price when he [Col. 0572A] redeemed us—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. I. ON SAINT MARK THE EVANGELIST (25 APRIL)

Today, beloved, a precious and conspicuous beryl is set before our eyes, gleaming like radiant gold, while the solemnity of blessed Mark the evangelist dawns and our paschal joy is doubled. And appropriately enough, while holy Church is still persevering in the paschal celebrations, this blessed man passed from this life happily: for through the palm of martyrdom he left this sorrowful age, and, crowned with victory, carried the tokens of triumph into the hymn-singing choirs of the angels.

Moreover, just as four rivers proceed from one fountain of paradise [Col. 0572B] and flow into the regions of the whole world, so the four blessed evangelists flow forth from Christ, who is the fountain of life and the source of wisdom, like an equal number of streams, and water the parched fields of human hearts with the streams of their teaching.

Hence the Wise Man, after saying: “He appointed David to raise up from his own people a king, the strongest of all, seated upon a throne of honor forever,” immediately adds: “He fills, like the Pishon, with wisdom; and like the Tigris in the days of new growth, he fills with understanding; he multiplies, like the Jordan in the time of harvest; he sends forth discipline like light, and, standing forth like the Gihon in the days of the vintage” (Sirach 24). A little later he also says: “I, Wisdom, poured out rivers; I, like a channel of immense water [Col. 0572C] from a river; I, like the river Dorix [Diorix], and like an aqueduct, came forth from paradise. I said: ‘I will water my garden of plantations and will drench the fruit of my father’” (ibid.).

Christ, therefore, the Wisdom of the Father, who came forth from paradise through the mystery of the humanity he assumed, watered his garden—that is, holy Church—through the four evangelists, as through an equal number of rivers of heavenly teaching. Among them blessed Mark, clear and pure like the Gihon, pours forth and makes human minds fruitful by flooding them with life-giving moisture. According to the sequence of Scripture, he circles the whole land of Ethiopia (Gen. 2), that is, he embraces the universal Church, darkened by preceding sins.

Concerning the people of this Ethiopia the Lord says through the prophet: “From beyond the rivers [Col. 0572D] of Ethiopia, there shall come my suppliants” (Zeph. 3). Though oppressed by persecutions, she says in the Song of Songs: “I am black, but beautiful.” And shortly afterward: “Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me” (Song 1).

But these same holy evangelists, whom Moses narrates under the figure of rivers in the sequence of typological history, the prophet Ezekiel declares that he saw under the form of various living creatures: “The likeness of their faces was the face of a man; and the face of a lion was on the right side of all four, and the face of an ox was on the left side of all four, and the face of an eagle was above all four” (Ezek. 1). Among these creatures blessed Mark is found placed second <sup>65</sup>, because he is described as having the face of a lion.

For [Col. 0573A] because he begins his Gospel with the cry of a voice in the wilderness, he rightly received the form of a lion. But if the very beginning of his Gospel is carefully considered, the most orderly dispensation of the Holy Spirit is found in it. He begins with this declaration: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark 1). As it is written in the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who has prepared your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”

Matthew, however, says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matt. 1). What, then, is the meaning of the one’s saying “Son of God” and the other’s “son of David,” except that through his instruments the Holy Spirit distinguished the mysteries of the mediator between God and human beings, so that through one [Col. 0573B] he might show him to be the Son of God and through the other the son of a human being? It is as though, through the two breaths of a single flute—or rather through the two nostrils of the Church—one spirit flows forth, while one describes the divinity and the other the human generation of the incarnate Word.

It may be asked, however, why blessed Mark the evangelist, after promising that he would set down the words of Isaiah, immediately introduced not Isaiah’s words but rather those of Malachi, and only afterward came to Isaiah’s words. For what is said first—“Behold, I send my angel” (Mal. 3)—was spoken by Malachi, who is the last of the Twelve Prophets. What follows—“The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isa. 40)—is unquestionably Isaiah’s oracle.

Why, then, did the one who promised Isaiah not immediately give Isaiah, but first bring Malachi forward as a [Col. 0573C] witness? Could a man full of the Spirit of God, especially at the very beginning of his narrative, either have erred or lied, so that he would dedicate his book to falsehood while describing the deeds of Truth? But this was done as a lesson in instruction: at the very beginning of his Gospel the Holy Spirit, whose author he was, showed that he had spoken as one and the same through the mouths of all the prophets, so that what is said specifically by one might be uttered commonly by all.

Whatever Malachi says, therefore, Isaiah also says no less; and the words of each have been uttered by all through the unity of the Spirit. In this the blessed evangelist also teaches that if he says something that appears different from the other evangelists, [Col. 0573D] nevertheless all are understood to utter one discourse through the unity of the Holy Spirit, who speaks in them all. Thus, among the evangelists as among the prophets, what has been uttered by the authority of one Spirit who dictates should in no way be considered different because of the ministry of the human writer.

Indeed, whoever considers the Gospel of blessed Mark with subtle meditation and examines it with the profound investigation it deserves will find it written in simple and unpolished words, yet overflowing with the richest mysteries of heavenly understanding. It is compressed by the brevity of its style, but extended by the deep abundance of spiritual mystery <sup>66</sup>. For when we scrutinize almost all the pages of Scripture, we can scarcely find the spirit of truth [Col. 0574A] speaking through anyone else with greater caution or circumspection than through the mouth of blessed Mark, to such a degree that the very sequence of the narrative and order of the words contain a great mystery. To make this more readily apparent, let us briefly point it out in the very beginning of his book.

The first miracle he records is that in which the Lord commanded a demon crying out through a man’s mouth to be silent and immediately drove it out: “Be silent,” he said, “and come out of the man” (Mark 1). The second miracle is that in which he healed Peter’s mother-in-law, who was feverish, by driving away the heat of the disease (ibid.). The third is that in which he touched and cleansed a leper (ibid.). The fourth is that in which he commanded a paralytic to rise, take up his bed, and depart (Mark 2).

This sequence, if carefully considered, [Col. 0574B] clearly teaches how great was the art of instruction with which the Holy Spirit held the writer’s pen and arranged everything, as along a certain line, to disclose the mystery of human redemption. At the beginning of the first human being’s downfall, the devil spoke and persuaded him to eat the forbidden fruit; then the woman, because she fell into the desire of pleasure, contracted, as it were, the burning fever of one in a state of heat. Adam, after he wickedly consented and tasted the fruit of the tree (Gen. 3), was immediately covered with the leprosy of all vices; finally, like a paralytic, he was bound by the sickness of the inner person and deprived of every good work.

Since, therefore, the Son of God came, as the apostle John says, to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3), he pursued death along the same path by which it had entered the world. [Col. 0574C] Where the poison of our destruction had been poured out, the physician of souls placed the antidote of salvation; and by the same route through which the cunning enemy introduced death, our Redeemer restored the beginnings of returning life, so that he might compel the devil, who had spoken for our ruin, to be silent at once; free Eve from the fevers of burning desire; cleanse the man not only from the leprosy of vices and crimes, but also release him, who had been a paralytic until then, strong and free to perform works of piety. Thus, just as the whole human race perished in those first human beings, so in these people healed by the Savior it was restored to its former salvation under the mystery of the figure.

[Col. 0574D] In the opening of this Gospel book, therefore, let the diligent reader learn how profound and mystical are the sacraments of grace contained in the sequence of the writing that follows. Nor is this surprising, since that book is said to belong no more to Mark than to the apostle Peter. For whatever Mark wrote, he heard from the mouth of his blessed master, having, so to speak, carefully drawn it out.

According to the reliable antiquity of historical accounts, he was a Levite by bodily descent and a priest in Israel according to the dignity of his order. Converted to the faith, he became the son of blessed Peter in baptism and a disciple in divine discourse. Without his teacher’s knowledge, he wrote the Gospel in Italy; once written, he reverently presented it for his judgment. When Peter discovered that this pious and religious theft had preserved his interpreter’s purest fidelity and most sincere truth, he bestowed upon it the strength of his authority <sup>67</sup> [Col. 0575A] and entrusted it to the holy universal Church to be read.

Later, the apostolic man crossed over to Egypt and sowed the seed of the faith in Libya, Marmarica, and Ammoniaca; he also preached Christ’s Gospel to the Gentile peoples of the Pentapolis. It is further read that he cut off his thumb so that he might be deemed unfit for the priesthood. But the predestined election of heavenly providence had such power in him that even then he did not lose, in the faith of new grace, what he had first possessed by birth.

For, having become a bishop, he founded the Church of Alexandria and, after raising it as a distinguished architect upon the rock that is Christ, faithfully dedicated it to the glorious name of his master. [Col. 0575B] Hence it came about that this Church is called an apostolic see not so much from Mark as from the name of blessed Peter, as though Peter himself had personally held the episcopal chair there. For this reason, marked with the title of the heavenly keeper of the keys, that Church holds the second throne in the whole world after Rome.

And although at Antioch, where the name of the Christian religion first arose, Peter himself personally introduced the first fruits of the faith, the see of Alexandria nevertheless obtained the higher place, so that among the more eminent catalog of sees the Roman Church holds the first rank, the Alexandrian the second, and the Antiochene the third.

And rightly: where Mark is, there is Peter, because with the stream of the Gospel that flowed from Peter’s mouth as from an overflowing fountain, Mark, like a most abundant and clear river of paradise, [Col. 0575C] flooded the fields of the whole Church more copiously.

But it may be asked why blessed Mark, who is recognized as having possessed such great faith and such great love for his master that the two seem to have been one heart and, certainly, one soul in two persons, remained entirely silent about his master’s praises and commendations. For while the other evangelists frequently enumerate the exalted merits and principal glory of blessed Peter’s eminence, this one alone, if the whole tenor of his Gospel is examined, is scarcely found to have reported anything about his master that contributes to his praise.

Indeed, if the matter is carefully considered, he increases and heaps up in his words whatever is blameworthy in Peter; but he suppresses, smooths over as though deliberately, or often passes over in silence whatever is praiseworthy. [Col. 0575D] We shall show this more clearly if we briefly set forth a few testimonies from the same Gospel.

It is certainly proclaimed throughout all the Churches in daily and celebrated reading that blessed Peter is described as walking upon the waters. Matthew declares this so openly that, when the Lord was walking upon the sea, he reports Peter as crying out: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” And when he had said, “Come,” he immediately adds: “And Peter, descending from the boat, walked upon the water to come to Jesus” (Matt. 14).

But when Mark reaches this passage, he describes everything fully and in order (Mark 6), except that he makes no mention whatsoever of Peter.

[Col. 0576A] Who, moreover, would not marvel at Peter’s glory and at the excellence of such extraordinary eminence? When the Savior asked whom people said he was, and after the various opinions had been set forth asked what the Apostles thought, Peter was the first in the confession of true faith, just as he was first in apostolic dignity <sup>68</sup>.

For Peter says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). And the Lord says: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in [Col. 0576B] heaven” (ibid.).

Could the ears of blessed Mark have missed this thunder of singular privilege, which filled the breadth of the whole world and the mouths of all the faithful everywhere? What Matthew said about Peter, did Peter fail to know so that he might tell it to this disciple of his? Yet Mark passes over this passage of the history as though neglecting it:

“Peter answered and said: ‘You are the Christ.’ And he charged them not to tell anyone about him” (Mark 2). He not only fails to report that Peter was raised by the Lord to the glory of a privilege singular among the others; rather, he tells of Peter being rebuked with severe correction. For shortly afterward, when Peter dissuaded him from allowing himself to be crucified, Mark testifies that the Lord, moved as though by zeal, said to him: “Get behind me, Satan, [Col. 0576C] because you do not understand the things that are of God, but those that are of human beings” (ibid.).

What, then, is the meaning of blessed Mark’s consigning to oblivion whatever pertains to his master’s glory, while committing whatever pertains to his reproach to such tenacious memory? Why did he pass over, as though in ignorance, whatever would make his teacher praiseworthy, while setting out with sharp and clear narration whatever would mark him—especially when he intended to present everything he secretly wrote to Peter’s eyes and reserve it for his judgment?

Now, to pass over many matters for the sake of brevity, let us come to the Lord’s Passion.

It is well known that, when the attendants were arresting the Lord, Peter, truly a faithful servant and fervent in spirit, rose up in a retaliatory sword-stroke and cut off the right ear of the servant accompanying Judas, the impious betrayer. [Col. 0576D] Hence John says: “Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear” (John 18).

But where John wrote “Simon Peter,” Mark wrote “one of those standing by” (Mark 14), so that he might weave the history of the truth in such a way as nevertheless to pass over his master’s glory in silence. Thus he fulfilled the duty of a truthful writer without incurring the blemish of a flatterer by favoring any particular person through deliberate ignorance.

Serving pure truth, he knew no hope of advantage in anything he wrote, disregarded the obligations of friendship, and utterly ignored human favor. Finally, when he comes to Peter’s denial, [Col. 0577A] while the other evangelists soften what Peter said with gentler words, he alone speaks more harshly and, as though exaggerating the crime, testifies that his master rashly poured forth words lacking caution:

“He began,” he says, “to curse and swear: ‘I do not know the man whom you mention’” (ibid.).

Why, blessed Mark, do you spare your pen so little for such an excellent and distinguished teacher, whom you love with unique devotion of heart? Why do you pass over what should be exalted in praise and describe what appears suitable for reproach? <sup>69</sup> Why do you not rather insert into your book the account of Peter’s catching a fish at the Lord’s command, at the very first casting of the hook, and finding in its mouth a stater, which he paid for himself and for the Lord as well, the tribute owed to Caesar, as though he were compared with the Lord? [Col. 0577B] (Matt. 17).

Did you also fail to remember that, after the Savior had granted him the privilege of closing or opening the kingdom of heaven, after he had subjected to him all the kingdoms of the earth (Matt. 16), and finally after he had declared that he had prayed lest his faith, as the foundation of the whole Church, should ever fail (Luke 22), he immediately entrusted him, in his own place, with the guardianship of the entire flock of his sheep?

“Peter,” he says, “do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21).

Why, then, do you restrain your pen from so many praises of your master and commit only what belongs to weakness to the memory of posterity?

But we must believe absolutely, my brothers, that since one and the same spirit filled both and one and the same spirit possessed both their hearts, the one did not disagree with the other—one in the work of teaching, the other in the work of writing. [Col. 0577C] For just as Peter restrained himself from his own praise, so his truthful interpreter restrained the course of his writing from the praise he had not learned from his master.

This was done as a great example for our edification: one should speak about himself not what is to be exalted but what is to be censured, while the other should walk so straight along the line of truth that he would not bend even slightly toward favoring his teacher. For when the apostle Paul says, “If I wished to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1), and elsewhere Scripture forbids us: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4), the blessed evangelist did not wish to offer his teacher what he would not wish another to offer him.

If he had preferred him with praise, he would have offended him more than he would have honored him. Those who seek praise from flatterers are plainly the ones who willingly exalt others with praise. But whoever refuses to accept it disdains to offer it.

Indeed, from Matthew’s book, which had already been published [Col. 0577D], Mark could have learned the praises of blessed Peter that he had not heard in his master’s accounts. But he showed deference to his teacher and, since he took no pleasure in his own praises, abstained from praise of another.

Moreover, some passages are found to have been arranged by blessed Mark in such a way that they appear contrary to the other evangelists. Yet if they are examined more keenly, they are found both consonant with the others and grounded in the truth of the most sincere faith.

Such is the case where the others say that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour (Matt. 27; Luke 23; John 19), while Mark asserts [Col. 0578A] that it occurred at the third hour (Mark 15). This difference is resolved as follows: because at the third hour the Jews cried out, “Crucify, crucify,” they crucified the Lord with their tongues at that hour, whom the Gentiles physically fastened with nails at the sixth hour. Thus the others speak according to the bodily—or, so to speak, historical—account of what happened; Mark, however, pronounced a spiritual judgment concerning the furious cruelty of the Jews.

Furthermore, the other evangelists report that Peter denied the Lord three times before the cock crowed (Matt. 26; Luke 22), whereas Mark, who heard this from the mouth of the denier himself, wrote that the denial occurred not before the cock crowed but before it crowed twice (Mark 14). It is unquestionably recognized that this happened truthfully, according to the actual event, just as Mark asserts. [Col. 0578B]

What the other evangelists say must be understood <sup>70</sup> in this way: that triple denial was begun entirely before the cock crowed, but was completed after it had crowed once. Since Scripture commonly places a part for the whole, what Matthew says—“Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times”—is to be understood as though he were saying: “Before the cock crows, you will begin to deny me three times; but you will complete that same denial after it has crowed once, before it adds a second crow.”

Thus both what Mark says, “Before the cock crows twice,” and what the others say, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times,” although they appear outwardly discordant in their wording, are found to agree most harmoniously in their intention.

[Col. 0578C] For it is not without reason, my brothers, that this blessed Mark holds the second place among the holy evangelists, whether under the figure of the rivers in Moses (Gen. II), or through the faces of the living creatures in Ezekiel (Ezek. I), as was said above. But he preserves in evangelical truth the honor he received in the order predestined for him. For in the Apocalypse of John, when the order of the holy living creatures is described, this one is found not now second but first in their catalogue. “In the midst of the throne,” he says, “and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind”; and immediately he adds: “And the first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like a calf, the third living creature having a face like a man, and the fourth living creature like a flying eagle” (Apoc. IV).

[Col. 0578D] This, surely, is that chariot of the Lord, and the true Cherubim, leaning upon which he travels around all things and runs everywhere. Innumerable watchful eyes shine on every side; sparks flash frequently, and terrifying lightning gleams. Their feet are upright and reaching upward; their backs are winged and flying everywhere. They hold one another and are intertwined with one another. And like a wheel within a wheel, they continually proceed wherever the power of the Holy Spirit drives them. This, I say, is the chariot of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Cant. VI).

It is the voice of the Synagogue, which, seeing that so great a grace has been bestowed upon the holy Church, grieves that it received the faith so late, because it did not recognize the truth of the Gospel. Aminadab [Col. 0579A] is known to have been the grandson of Judah, and he is counted among the forefathers in the genealogy of the Lord. Aminadab is interpreted as “spontaneous of my people,” and therefore it not incongruously signifies Christ, who was spontaneous on behalf of his people, because, although he was God, he freely became man. For he who created us not from necessity but solely from goodness nevertheless redeemed us by his own will. Hence James also says: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth” (Jas. I).

He therefore became the freely acting one for his people, because the one whom human perversity had driven away was restored solely by the will of divine grace. The chariot of Aminadab, moreover, is the Gospel, compacted from the most harmonious diversity of the four evangelists. Christ the charioteer directs this chariot, and with the swiftest [Col. 0579B] speed of preaching travels through the fourfold structure of the world, as it is said through the Psalmist: “He sends forth his word to the earth; swiftly his word runs” (Ps. CXLVII).

When the Synagogue therefore saw the grace of evangelical preaching suddenly bursting forth and swiftly flying throughout all the provinces of the world, it was suddenly troubled and complained that, while the nations were converted to the faith, it alone was being abandoned in its unbelief: “I did not know,” it said; “my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.”

The Lord prefigured this grace of fourfold preaching when he commanded Moses concerning the ark to be carried by the priests: “You shall make,” he says, “four rings of gold, which you shall place at the four corners of the ark; and you shall make poles of acacia wood, cover them with gold, and put them through the rings that are on the sides of the ark, so that it may be carried on them. They shall always be in the rings and shall never be removed from them” (Exod. XXV).

[Col. 0579C] What is signified by the ark except the holy Church? Four golden rings are commanded to be attached to its four corners, because, as it is extended and spread through the four parts of the world, it is undoubtedly girded with the four books of the holy Gospel in its preaching. The poles are made of acacia wood and inserted into those same rings for carrying it, because strong and steadfast teachers are to be sought as though they were imperishable wood. Always adhering to the instruction of the sacred books, they proclaim the unity of the holy Church and, as though inserted into the rings, carry the ark.

To carry the ark with poles is for good teachers, by preaching, to lead the unformed minds of the faithful to the holy Church. They are also commanded to be covered with gold, so that, when they sound forth their words to others, they may themselves also shine with the splendor of their life. Concerning them it is aptly added: “They shall always be in the rings and shall never be removed from them.” For it is surely necessary that those who keep watch over the office of preaching should not withdraw from the study of sacred reading.

[Col. 0579D] For this reason the poles are commanded always to remain in the rings: so that, whenever the need to carry the ark arises, no delay in carrying it may be caused by having to insert the poles. For when something spiritual is sought from those subject to him, it is very disgraceful if a pastor then seeks to learn what he ought to explain. Rather, let the poles remain attached to the rings, so that teachers, always meditating on the sacred words in their hearts, may raise the ark of the covenant without delay and immediately teach whatever is necessary.

[Col. 0580A] Hence the first pastor of the Church rightly admonishes the other pastors, saying: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Pet. III). As if he openly said: so that no delay may impede the carrying of the ark, let the poles never at any time withdraw from the rings.

Beloved, let us also be inserted into these golden rings as poles of acacia wood, so that, rejecting the rottenness of this world, we may continually dwell in the pages of the holy evangelists. Among other things, not only the holy teaching but also the distinguished life of this blessed Mark summons us to imitate him. To him the prophetic saying may not inappropriately be applied: “The first says to Zion: Behold, I am present; and I shall give an evangelist to Jerusalem” (Isa. XLI).

He was truly a golden ring, because, while he taught holy things through the office of preaching, he also radiated through the conduct of a shining life. And, like a pole of acacia wood, he despised all earthly things that decay and sought heavenly things that do not wither. By cutting off a limb he disfigured the appearance of his body, lest he ascend to ecclesiastical dignity contrary to the rule of the Church. But what he thought would be a protection for flight became a title of glory. For by that which made him deem himself unworthy, he became more worthy; and what he was fleeing, he was compelled to undertake.

[Col. 0580C] Blessed are you, Alexandria, made purple by the triumphant blood of an apostolic martyr. And blessed are you, Italy, both once the foster-mother of him who wrote the Gospel and now enriched by the precious treasure of his most sacred body. Thus the East is adorned through Egypt, and the West through the Roman Empire. Glory be to him who is wondrous in his saints (Ps. LXVII) and makes them wondrous for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XV. II. ON SAINT MARK THE EVANGELIST (25 APRIL)

Behold, beloved, I see that, while reclining at the table of the Church and receiving the nourishment of spiritual delights, you are not satisfied with one discourse but hunger even more eagerly for another. Therefore we too do not cease to serve the dish of your refreshment, so that we may at least temper the holy hunger of your devotion with some slight food, saying with the Apostle: “To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, but is necessary for you” (Phil. III).

Among all the teachers of the Church, we judge this blessed Mark, whose triumphant deeds we commemorate today, to be especially distinguished and conspicuous. He was both the son in baptism and the disciple in teaching of the blessed chief of the apostles. Just as he heard him recount the deeds of the Savior, so, when asked by the brethren at Rome, he wrote the Gospel through the unerring line of a faithful report, as Clement of Alexandria and Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, also testify.

Having immediately taken up the Gospel that he himself had composed, he tirelessly went to Egypt and, being the first to announce Christ at Alexandria, laid the foundation of the new faith [law]. And while he was both the writer and preacher of the Gospel, he was, in a certain sense, both craftsman and farmer: he forged for himself a plowshare with which he furrowed the fields of the human heart for sowing the seeds of the sacred faith.

In this way he founded the Alexandrian Church and entitled it not with his own name but with that of his teacher, so that the apostolic see might be called the see of blessed Peter, although Peter is not recorded as having visited it. Thus teacher and disciple were joined by such unanimity and fashioned by such harmonious inspiration of the Holy Spirit that Peter revealed the Gospel to Mark, and Mark built the Church for Peter. In this way, while each transferred to the other what belonged to him, what was proper to each became common to both, and each possessed wholly whatever belonged properly to the other.

Hence blessed Peter calls him his special and harmonious son above the others, when, referring uniquely to Rome under the name of Babylon, he says: “The Church that is gathered in Babylon greets you, and so does Mark, my son” (1 Pet. V).

Nor is it surprising that blessed Mark was pre-eminent with his teacher and obtained a privilege of apostolic affection above the others. Almighty God bestowed upon him such power of the word and granted him such effectiveness in preaching that all who then flocked to the beginnings of the faith soon hastened, through continence and the devotion of an entirely holy way of life, as though toward the summit of monastic perfection.

Hence Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, when he writes about the primacy of blessed Mark in the Alexandrian Church, praises the Christians and calls their dwellings monasteries. He testifies that not only throughout the territories of Alexandria but also in many other provinces, while Mark was administering that Church, there were Christians such as Luke also records the disciples of the apostles to have been: their heart was one and their soul one; none of them called anything his own, but they all possessed everything in common, and among them there was an inseparable unity of spirits, among whom no diversity of possessions could arise (Acts IV).

Such, therefore, was the Alexandrian Church under Mark as Jerusalem is read to have been under apostolic discipline: no one was oppressed by want, none of them abounded in riches, but, as each received the necessities that were required, there was no room among them for complaint or murmuring [printed: *murmuro*].

The aforesaid Philo thus indicates that, amid the new cradles of the newly born faith and the tender infancy—so to speak—of the nursing Church, those who were placed under the rule of blessed Mark were devoted alike to sobriety and chastity and intensely committed to prayers and fasts. The blessed evangelist instructed them not only by the marvels of very many miracles and not only by the words of holy preaching, but also urged them toward the uprightness of spiritual life by the outstanding examples of his own continence and piety. Thus almost all, kindled by the fervor of their steaming faith, seemed to pant after the purpose of a new way of life as though they were undertaking the arduous discipline of monastic perfection.

When blessed Mark, like a chosen trumpet of the heavenly army, thunders with the most powerful blasts and dispenses God’s commandments with such skill in preaching that he immediately raises his hearers to the heights of supreme perfection, what else does he do than persevere in the etymology of his name? For Mark is interpreted as “exalted by command.” And truly this blessed man was not exalted in spirit but by command, because, while he carried a humble mind, he strove to possess a lofty life; and he who had humbled himself beneath all others walked sublimely along the way of the heavenly commandments.

[Col. 0582B] I will not allow you, beloved, to remain ignorant of this also: in the eighth year of Nero’s reign, blessed Mark obtained the triumphant palm of martyrdom. Anianus soon succeeded him in the dignity of the Alexandrian see, and the blessed apostle Peter survived at Rome for seven years.

Thus, by the ordering of heavenly mercy, it came about that, after he had first illumined Alexandria both with the splendors of evangelical preaching and with the outpouring of his most sacred blood, he afterward returned to Italy in a kind of restoration, so that the very land in which he had been granted to write the Gospel might deservedly possess his sacred relics; and where he had been permitted to pour forth the radiance of his evangelical writing, there, through the presence of his glorious remains, he might shine with many rays of virtues and signs.

[Col. 0582C] Moreover, if we carefully pass through the places where all the evangelists died, we find that none of them continued in the tomb he received. At the burial of John, after his death, not his body but manna was found. The body of blessed Matthew does not adorn Ethiopia, where he is known to have been killed, but rather the city of Salerno. Saint Luke, although he died in the regions of Bithynia, as history testifies, was transferred from Achaia to Constantinople in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantius, together with the most sacred relics of the blessed apostle Andrew.

But this holy evangelist Mark, with whom we are now concerned, was transported from Alexandria to Venice, by the merciful ordering of God, so that he who had then illumined the whole East like a golden morning star might now shine through the regions of the western world by the rays of his presence. Through Egypt he claimed his rising; through Venice he holds his setting. There he received the soil of the Alexandrian Church; here he established the new primacy of the reborn Aquileia. He is therefore like a golden star, renowned throughout the whole world and conspicuous in the celebrated veneration of the entire Church.

Let us therefore, beloved, keep this star continually before our eyes and imitate its example, if we wish to avoid shipwreck amid the foaming waves of the world’s abyss. Let the swollen sea rage on one side and raging winds strike from the other; if we do not turn the eye of our mind away from this star, we need not fear the assaults of the surging storms. Let the sure course of our mind’s net be directed toward this star; toward it let all the rowing of our labor be aimed, so that—God forbid—the abyss of Scylla’s depth may not swallow us, nor the reefs of error or the treacherous shoals [printed: *invadosae syrtes*] overwhelm the unwary. May the heavenly helmsman, Jesus Christ our Lord, drive us into the harbor of safe repose and the haven of our desired tranquility—he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. III. ON SAINT MARK THE EVANGELIST (25 APRIL)

You know, beloved, that we have already completed two sermons on the merits and glorious virtues of blessed Mark, yet our conscience, urging us onward, does not allow us to rest from praising him. For while we consider this deed and that deed of his virtues and turn over in our minds the merit of so lofty a grace, we cannot keep the pen of our outward discourse idle either.

Among all the distinctions of such conspicuous splendor, one thing seems to me singular and pre-eminent: through Mark, Alexandria has been called by the holy Fathers the second see of Peter and therefore an apostolic see. For no authentic writing testifies that the blessed apostle Peter held a chair in Alexandria or even displayed his presence there. But when he appointed Mark, that outstanding disciple, to preside over it, he dedicated it to himself as though through the presence of his own visitation.

Similarly, the Gospel of Mark is called Peter’s Gospel, because this faithful interpreter wrote simply and unalterably what he heard from the mouth of his teacher as he truthfully recounted it. Moreover, since this key-bearer of heaven sent disciples throughout so many kingdoms of the earth and entrusted them with the governance of Churches in various provinces of the world, why is none of them, except Alexandria alone, called either Peter’s see or an apostolic Church?

Antioch itself is plainly called Peter’s see, because he is said to have held his chair there personally. But Peter himself did not preside personally over Alexandria; rather, through blessed Mark, whom he had both as a disciple in teaching and as a son in baptism, he adorned it with the title of his own name.

And what is more marvelous, just as the Roman see surpasses Alexandria by the height of its singular excellence, so Alexandria rises above Antioch by a certain dignity of privilege, so that the see over which Mark presided in Peter’s place is superior to that over which Peter himself presided in his own chair. Why did the Holy Spirit inspire the minds of the blessed pontiffs to establish this, unless he recognized Peter and Mark in mind and spirit, in faith and will, as not somehow two but rather one? The same Spirit had bound them to one another with such great love and fused them with such unanimity of mind that the two had one heart and one mind. Hence it came about that the see which belonged to Mark became, without distinction, Peter’s also.

[Col. 0584A] We know plainly that blessed Andrew was the blood brother of the same holy Peter. Scripture also testifies that a certain Martial, a bishop of glorious sanctity, was his nephew. Yet neither Achaia, which he illumined with the triumphant standard of the cross, nor even the province of Lemovica, in which this man shines with the great brilliance of miracles and signs, is called Peter’s see; rather, each is designated only by the name of the one who presides over it.

Alexandria alone especially merited that, through the chair of blessed Mark, it should be called the see of the apostle Peter. Nor, as we believe, was this name impressed upon that city without divine prompting. Alexandria was named after Alexander. Alexander is interpreted as “one who relieves the distresses of darkness”; and Egypt, in which Alexandria is situated, is also called “darkness.”

What else was the whole world before the coming of the Redeemer except dense darkness and confusion? Hence Isaiah says: “Upon those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has risen” (Isa. IX). The world was dark because it had not yet been illumined by the splendor of heavenly grace. The people of this world were darkness because they had not yet been turned from the blindness of their perversity to the true light. To those who have now been led out of the darkness of unbelief and shine with the light of true faith, the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

Who, then, relieved the distresses of this darkness except the sun of justice, our Redeemer, who dispelled the gloom of sins? Who, I ask, relieves the distresses of darkness except he of whom the apostle Peter says: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood” (1 Pet. II), and of whom Isaiah says: “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he carried our pains” (Isa. LIII)?

For if darkness is sins, the distresses of darkness are undoubtedly the retributions and punishments of sinful people. And who relieved these distresses of darkness—or rather, who endured the deserved penalties of wrongdoers—except he of whom the same prophet says: “He was wounded because of our iniquities; he was crushed because of our crimes” (ibid.)?

Just as Alexander built the city of Alexandria in Egypt, so our Redeemer built the holy Church amid the darkness of this world. He truly relieved the distresses of darkness when he endured the punishments of our crimes and flooded this Egypt of the world with the new splendor of true faith. Christ did this in Egypt through Mark, and through the other senators of the heavenly court he did it throughout the entire world.

But why, brothers, do we ascribe Egypt to blessed Mark and confine the immense glory of so excellent a man within the narrow corner of a single land? This man, the powerful trumpet of the heavenly thunder, thunders terribly and, like one of the rivers of paradise rushing forth, floods the whole breadth of the world with the overflowing streams of the holy Gospel.

Happy indeed is Alexandria, which this unconquered warrior of Christ dyed purple with the blood of his triumphant martyrdom; but especially happy and exceedingly blessed are you, Venice, whom he chose in order to entrust to you the precious treasure of his body. A great abundance of riches certainly flows into you from various parts of the world, but this heavenly jewel, placed in your midst, raises you aloft in the conspicuous glory of dignity.

For this incomparable treasure surpasses every kind of glittering metal and exceeds all the ornaments of sparkling gems. As blessed Job says of wisdom: “Gold and glass shall not be equal to it; vessels of great price and eminence shall not be exchanged for it; gold from Ethiopia shall not be compared with it, nor shall the purest dye be joined with it” (Job XXVIII). And, so to speak, this is a distinguished kind of aromatic substance which, by its honey-sweet power, surpasses cinnamon and balsam and exceeds the fragrance of every spice.

[Col. 0585B] Moreover, if Alexandria possesses such great dignity through him, because he drenched it with the glorious blood of his martyrdom, that it is called an apostolic see, of how great an excellence do we think that blessed province is in which the precious remains of his body are now buried? Is it not to be believed to possess the same grace and dignity, even if not by the commonly used name, then in reality itself and through the hidden sacred truth of the mystery?

He entered those regions while he still existed as a mortal in corruptible flesh; but he chose these when he was already reigning eternally in the court of the heavenly kingdom. He visited the former in order to lead them out of the darkness of unbelief to that light of true faith which he had already conceived in his mind; but he wished to be transferred to the latter in order to recall them to the guide of light, with whom he now is.

Rejoice, therefore, and exulting in the Lord, applaud, Venice, because through the talent of that precious treasure which is known to be stored up in you, you have become the treasury of the heavenly King; and, because you received in your bosom a man of apostolic grace, you too have in a certain way deserved to become an apostolic see.

Therefore, just as Rome, the mother of cities, is exalted above all the kingdoms of the earth in Peter, so you, like his distinguished daughter, glory in Christ through Mark. We humbly implore him that, just as he called blessed Peter from the sea and the boat (Matt. IV; Mark I), and afterward held him up when he was about to fall and be overwhelmed in the deep, so he may guard your rowing amid the dangers of the sea and bring you with your children to the harbor of eternal rest—he who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. I. ON SAINT VITALE THE MARTYR (28 APRIL)

Let us offer immense praise and thanks to God, beloved brothers, because, while the Paschal feast shines throughout the whole world, the triumphant day of blessed Vitale also illumines the borders of our homeland.

Today the glorious soldier of Christ fell for the faith of his emperor, destined to live for ever. Today, having conquered the enemy of the human race, he entered the starry kingdoms in triumph and glory. Today, having completed the course of his service, he emerged victorious from the prison of the flesh. Today, amid the alternating choirs of hymn-singing angels on every side, he entered the palace of the eternal King, purple-clad; there he shines indescribably among the fiery companies of the blessed spirits, rejoices with the senators of the heavenly court in their robes, is enthroned sublimely with the patriarchs upon a golden throne, wondrously crowned with the laureled martyrs, and, clothed with all of them in a robe of glory, dances in ineffable exultation and sings the melodious Alleluia with most joyful sweetness in the sight of the eternal King.

O how blessedly he dies who, by dying, is born! How happily he ends temporal life who begins to live eternally! Hence the holy Church has become accustomed to call the day of the saints’ departure their “birthdays,” because they are immediately born in heaven when they visibly die on earth; and they truly begin to live when they seem to end their mortal life.

Consider, my brothers, how strong and robust a breast this invincible soldier of Christ possessed. Entirely secure concerning his own danger but concerned for another’s, with a single weapon of the word he struck down the enemy and urged his already wounded and limping companion to act bravely. His trained hand, while brandishing the spear for battle, touched his companion so that he might rise and inflicted a mortal wound upon the adversary who was already winning.

For, as the most truthful account of his deeds relates, when Ursicinus, after excessive tortures, wished to escape the death sentence, blessed Vitale cried out, saying: “Do not, do not, Ursicinus the physician, who have been accustomed to heal others, wound yourself with the dart of eternal death.”

It is the custom of holy men, my brothers, when caught in the battle of tribulations, to see enemies pursuing from one side and their own people fleeing from the other: against the former they raise the shield of patience; against the latter they hurl the darts of instruction. They rise to both modes of combat through a remarkable art of virtue, so that the weak within may rise bravely and they may manfully despise adversities without; they correct the weak by teaching and press their hostile opponents by enduring them.

They despise the attacking enemies by enduring them, but restore their weakening fellow citizens to salvation by compassion. They resist the former lest they carry others away with them; they fear for the latter lest, by fearing death, they utterly lose life. On one side they strike hostile breasts with darts; on the other, holding the shield behind them, they protect the weak. Thus on both sides they keep watch with the speed of vigilance, so that they may stab the bold before them and defend the fearful behind them from injury.

But whoever wishes to act bravely on the field of battle must take care to preserve himself in domestic peace; let him exercise himself frequently in leisure, lest, ignorant of fighting, he rush carelessly into war; lest, if inexperienced and unskilled, he engages a more practiced opponent and, while trying to clash weapons with weapons beyond his custom, he be thrown down by an unforeseen wound and perish defeated, having strained with all his efforts to become victorious.

Nor should we believe that blessed Vitale began to live religiously and serve God above all only when the cruelty of the persecutor provoked him to the contest of martyrdom. This holy man was already supported by the greatest strength when, without any trouble from persecution, he rested in the tranquility of his peace. Known only to himself and God, he could not have been recognized by us at all unless he had been compelled to advance onto the field of battle.

For virtue exercised itself even in a time of rest, but, pounded by the blows of the wicked in the mortar of adversity, gave forth its fragrance. He who, when quiet, contained within himself what he was, when stirred, scattered the fragrance of his fortitude for all to know.

For just as perfumes do not spread their scent more widely unless they are shaken, and just as spices do not expand their fragrance until they are burned, so holy men become known in tribulations for everything with which they are fragrant through their virtues. Hence it is rightly said in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Matt. XVII).

For the power of the mustard seed is not recognized unless it is crushed. When uncrushed, it is mild; but when it is crushed, it grows hot and reveals whatever sharpness had lain hidden within it. So, indeed, every holy man, when he is not struck, appears contemptible and mild; but if the grinding of persecution presses upon him, he immediately displays whatever tastes hot, and whatever previously seemed contemptible and weak in him is turned into the heat of virtue. What he willingly concealed within himself during times of tranquility, when shaken by tribulations, he is compelled to make known.

Hence the Prophet rightly says: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Ps. XLI). The Lord’s mercy is commanded by day because the virtue granted by God is perceived in tranquil times; but it is declared by night because the gift received in tranquility is revealed through tribulations.

[Col. 0587C] If it is asked what virtue blessed Vitale possessed before the contest, with what discipline the good head of the household governed his home, and with what religious and holy order of life he instructed his children, let his blessed wife Valeria, together with her two sons, answer when questioned, “so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII).

For when she heard of the death of her most blessed husband Vitale, she did not fear greedy usurpers of her possessions, did not seek the protection of any more powerful person, and did not, as widows commonly do, try to gather her scattered belongings from everywhere into a safe place. Rather, preserving the faith of her chaste marriage, she came with remarkable ardor from the city of Milan all the way to Ravenna to perform the service owed at his burial.

The difficulty of so long a journey did not deter her; fear of losing her property could not hold her back; affection for relatives or fellow citizens in the city of Milan did not bind her there; and the savage fury of the consul did not drive her from the borders of Ravenna. Her spirit, raised upright, was fixed with all its inmost strength upon that place where she knew the most blessed man had gone before her, having already trampled death beneath his feet.

For where her treasure was, there also was her heart (Matt. XVI). She rejoiced that he was already dwelling in his home, and grieved that she still remained in exile. With all her heart she longed, while still on the way, for that which he was already delightfully enjoying in his homeland. She rejoiced to be called by people the wife of a martyr, but she burned far more ineffably to be crowned with the same glory of martyrdom.

Hence there is no doubt that she daily entreated her most blessed husband with a special familiarity of devotion, so that through his sacred prayers she might deserve to attain the palm of martyrdom. Thus those whom the marriage-bond of mutual love had joined here in purity might be joined by a similar triumph in the glory of heavenly blessedness; and, because they had been two in one flesh, they might also become united in one crown.

Therefore, when the Christians who were then at Ravenna forbade her to take away the holy body, and, having abandoned this intention, she was returning home, she encountered men sacrificing to Silvanus. Taking her down from the pack animal, they urged her to feast with them on what had been sacrificed to Silvanus.

[Col. 0588B] But what will you do, blessed Valeria? Will you be able to abandon your husband’s footsteps and incline a mind already raised to the heavens toward diabolical suggestions? Will you, brought up in the Catholic faith, be able to set aside through fear of executioners what you learned in tranquility and violate, through any storm of trembling, the foundation placed upon the firm rock of faith?

Act, act, blessed Valeria! Come, noble matron! Now recall manfully the teachings of your husband and declare what the instruction of so great a teacher has given you. She said: “I am a Christian, and it is not permitted for me to eat from the sacrifices of your Silvanus.”

But when they heard this, they slaughtered her with such a beating that her own people could scarcely bring her, half-dead, to the city of Milan; and within three days blessed Valeria departed to the Lord.

[Col. 0588C] O how ineffably the order of divine providence is arranged! How mercifully the course of human condition is transformed! A woman drove a man out of paradise (Gen. III); a man recalled a woman to the homeland of paradise. The former became an instrument of the devil so that the man might be deceived; the latter offered an example of virtue to be imitated so that the woman might be crowned.

The ancient woman, eating the forbidden fruit, condemned herself to the misery of hunger through fasting; but the new woman, abstaining from food sacrificed to idols, prepared for herself a banquet of eternal satiety. The former, delighted by the fruit of the tree, by going out barred against herself the door of blessed delight with the bolts of desire; the latter, rejecting the eating of meat, opened for herself, by the keys of continence, the pastures of everlasting greenness.

Behold, it is plainly evident how conspicuously the holy man shone in the honesty of his conduct during tranquility, since he led his most blessed wife to the summit of such perfection. If she had learned from him to practice greed, she would certainly not have despised all her possessions merely in order to carry out the corpse for burial [printed variant: *venerandi*, “of honoring”]. If she had indulged in luxurious banquets with him, she would surely, exhausted by the journey, have more readily consented to refreshment than to be mangled by blows almost to the boundary of death.

And, to conclude everything briefly, unless in time of peace she had learned in every respect to live for Christ, she could never, at the moment of persecution, have died for Christ.

But since Valeria, when asked what excellence of virtue her most outstanding husband had possessed before the contest, briefly offered the testimony of her assertion, let other witnesses now come forward. To prove how honorably the parents lived, let the heirs be summoned to testify. For it is plausible that whatever virtue is seen in the children of saints should be believed to have been handed down entirely by those parents.

Therefore the most blessed Gervasius and Protasius, deprived—not, I should say, of both parents, but rather happily illumined by their parents’ most glorious death, as their sacred history relates—coveting nothing earthly and nothing carnal, but confining themselves in a single upper room, devoted ten years to reading and prayer.

Consider, dearest brothers, the immeasurable praise of their paternal upbringing; weigh the remarkable legacy of strict discipline; observe the example of a new way of life left to orphans; recognize the clearest indication of their father’s severity. Among brothers, common property often becomes a cause of division and discord. Yet among these two, although an inheritance awaited division, one charity filled both hearts. [Col. 0589B] They turned a populous city into a desert and transformed their dwelling-place into an oratory.

Young men who have lost their parents commonly dissipate themselves luxuriously through the freedom of their own judgment, and, as though already their own masters, freely loosen the reins of their pleasures. Indeed, all those exceed the bounds of uprightness in what is permitted who suppose that anything whatsoever is permissible. But these boys, angelic in character, neither anxious about the life yet to come nor making provision for themselves of the expense of earthly goods or wealth, nor entered into any marriage of carnal union not to be dissolved by death, nor took delight in neighing horses, nor relaxed into the wantonness of pleasures, [Col. 0589C] nor vainly desired to be adorned in costly garments.

They fled the business of worldly commotion, rejected the riches of earthly things, spurned the heights of transitory dignity, and despised the allurements of the flesh. They not only sought none of what belonged to others, but also scattered all their own possessions in lavish generosity toward mercy. From the whole breadth of the world they chose for themselves a plot of the narrowest prison, where, gathering their senses from every side away from the world’s vanity, they contemplated deep within their souls the sole vision of their Creator. To him, already passing beyond the confines of the flesh, they directed their spirit through the practice of constant meditation; toward him, kindled by the flames of an immense love, they burned with all their inward being.

The mind of each was anxious in heavenly desire and estranged from earthly cravings; for the true love that had filled them [Col. 0589D] tormented them with tears. Yet while they were tormented by such ardor, they were nourished by those very torments, and they persisted for so long in the fervor of this admirable way of life that, following the glorious footsteps of their parents, they were crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ. 81

Indeed, those whose examples they imitated in living, and from whom they had been carnally born on earth, became their companions in the fellowship of heavenly blessedness. Those whom carnal generation had joined, inequality of merit did not divide; and in the order in which nature brought them into the world, divine grace also raised them to the heavenly realm. Those who gave birth, namely, go before; those who were born follow them in due order.

O blessed family, which, leaving Egypt, crossed the Red Sea so bravely and, formed into a marching host, reached the promised land in triumph! [Col. 0590A] O noble offspring, which, though born from the earth, deserved through life-giving death to pass into heavenly dignity, a nobility of character having translated it into the nobility of angels!

How exalted was that household which deserved to send so many illustrious citizens to the heavenly Jerusalem! What city, however lofty its towered walls, could surpass the dignity of this little house, which, worthy to be called heaven, contained within its happy dwelling a numerous throng of martyrs? Those whom the whole world was not worthy to contain, that house enclosed beneath a single roof. For when the Apostle spoke of the holy martyrs, he immediately added, saying: “The world was not worthy of them” (Hebrews 11). [Col. 0590B]

Rejoice, therefore, Ravenna, most illustrious city, purpled with the precious blood of so many martyrs. Although of these four you physically possess only the most sacred body of blessed Vitalis, you are nevertheless by no means deprived of the other three through the mystery of hidden power. For if blessed Valeria was, according to the testimony of Scripture, one flesh with her husband (Genesis 2), it necessarily follows that there should be one burial-place for one flesh.

And when we read, “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19), let us also rejoice and say that what God, who is eternal life, joined, intervening temporal death did not divide. What else, moreover, should be said about the sons except that those who were joined to their most blessed father by nature’s unbreakable bonds could in no way be separated from him by spatial distance? [Col. 0590C]

It is written that Adam, when he first saw his wife, immediately said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2). If Eve, then, because she was formed from her husband’s side, is called bone from his bones and flesh from his flesh, why should the sons also, who came forth from their father’s loins, not be said to have the same bones and flesh with their father? Though they appear separated by intervals of place, they are nevertheless joined through the hidden sacrament of mystical power.

Rejoice, therefore, noble city of Ravenna, and delight in the Lord with all your inward being. Although you are lofty in the height of your mural structure, you are much higher still in the dignity of blessed martyrs: enclosed by stone defenses that cannot be conquered, yet surrounded by the still more unconquerable protection of Christ’s mighty soldiers. [Col. 0590D]

In a certain sense, you rival the Roman citadels in friendly competition. Through two outstanding martyrs, namely Vitalis and Apollinaris, you have deserved to become both mother and mistress of whatever cities surround you. As Rome, through the two supreme apostles, Peter and Paul, claims for itself the primacy of the whole world, having become like a head to the other cities, so you shine with the splendor of two saints, like a human face with the paired lights of its eyes. 82

Rejoice, therefore, and exult, because although you were formerly a shrine of demons, now, through the regard of divine grace, you have become a capitol of heavenly senators. Though formerly evil in fertility, producing countless stalks for hell among your children, [Col. 0591A] now, through the merits of blessed martyrs, you give birth to many citizens for heaven.

For though in the shamefulness of your men you were once an ancient Babylon, through the newness of your virtues you have become a new Jerusalem, adorned with living stones, so that it may now rightly be said to your people through Paul: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Ephesians 2); and through Peter: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Peter 2). Nor is the sign of divine love bestowed upon you a small one in that blessed Vitalis wished to have his tomb in you even after his blessed departure. [Col. 0591B] He did not allow his body to be taken away from you, because he did not wish to leave you deprived of the protection of his patronage. In this matter he certainly favored you more than his most blessed wife, since, while he cared for your welfare, he did not comply with her holy wish.

For it is written that when holy Valeria wished to take away the body of blessed Vitalis, she was prevented by Christians and was often warned by him in visions not to violate the holy body, which had been properly placed there by an evil man.

Certainly, my brothers, I cannot express how joyfully and delightfully I contemplate the contest of this struggle, how eagerly I extend all the rays of my inward vision toward the spectacle of this holy contention. I consider the differing sides of the litigants: here I see a city, there a single woman; in the middle, the body of Saint Vitalis is the object and cause of the dispute. [Col. 0591C]

Each side employs its own arguments and defends its case by a different legal principle. The one claims the right of ancient possession; the other invokes the title of divine grant. The one complains that the body was violently taken from her; the other, on the contrary, asserts that it was bestowed upon her by divine kindness.

The one says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exodus 20). The other replies: “Do not demand back what is not yours” (Luke 6). The one says: “But,” she declares, “he is joined to me by the law of a marriage endowed with a dowry.” The other replies: “He is also joined to me by the precious blood of martyrdom. You had your husband while it was permitted; let me also have my martyr without disturbance. He is joined to you by the bond of carnal union; in me he is crowned with the glory of triumphant martyrdom.”

Hear the Apostle saying: “A wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but when her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband” (1 Corinthians 7). [Col. 0591D] If, then, you are released from your husband’s law while you still live in the flesh, how do you seek to bind with a bond him who has already passed to the heavenly kingdoms?

But to settle this dispute in the holy litigation, blessed Vitalis himself came forward and set a limit to the complaint of his venerable wife. He who until then had been the object of contention became an agent and mediator of peace.

Yet while we say these things to you, dearest brothers, there also comes to mind what sacred Scripture testifies that the patriarch Jacob did. 83 For it is written that, when he saw the day of his death approaching, he called his son Joseph and said to him: “If I have found favor in your sight, put your hand beneath my thigh, and show me mercy and truth: do not bury me in Egypt, but let me sleep with my fathers; take me from this land and bury me in the tomb of my ancestors.” [Col. 0592A]

Joseph replied: “I will do what you have commanded.” And he said: “Swear it to me, then” (Genesis 47). When Joseph had sworn, Israel worshiped God.

What does this mean, my brothers? What is meant by such anxious concern over the burial of his body on the part of so great a man? If we measure this according to human custom, we certainly find nothing worthy of such excellence of prophetic mind. Wherever a human body is buried, it is surely not for that reason believed that its resurrection will be either less perfect or less glorious.

But if the depth of the mystical sacrament is sought amid the darkness of this question, clear light of understanding will arise for the one who discovers it. [Col. 0592B] The corpses of the dead signify the sins of those who live unjustly. For just as the law commands people to be purified after contact with dead bodies (Numbers 19), so after committing offenses we are commanded to be cleansed through repentance.

Hence that saying was uttered: “One who is baptized from contact with a dead person and again touches him, what benefit is his washing?” (Ecclesiasticus 34). He is baptized from a dead person who is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead person who, after shedding tears, returns to his fault.

The burial of the dead signifies, therefore, the remission of sins. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31). Where, then, were the corpses of the patriarchs to be buried except in that land where he was to be crucified by whose blood remission of sins was accomplished? [Col. 0592C]

The reason, therefore, why the patriarch Jacob was buried in the land of the Canaanites was the same reason why blessed Vitalis specifically chose a tomb for himself in the city of Ravenna. For just as Jacob signified through the burial of his body that remission of sins would come to those regions of the world because the Lord was to be crucified there, so Vitalis recognized by divine revelation that this most fortunate city was to be called to the grace of baptism and to the faith of Christ.

Therefore I entreat and exhort you, beloved brothers: recall continually through meditation the great dignity you have received by God’s freely given gift, and take care to offer thanks worthy of such benefits—not only with mouth or heart, but also through worthy deeds—always saying with the Prophet: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115). [Col. 0592D]

Let the one who desires to reach the sweetness of perpetual safety not shrink from drinking the bitterness of a momentary draught. Whoever wishes now to be enrolled among Christ’s soldiers, let him gird himself manfully for battle, so that after victory has been achieved he may receive, as a veteran, the citizenship of blessed rest. Let him now prepare to engage, so that he may deservedly be crowned after victory. “For no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy 2).

For that soldier is delicate who wishes to win before he begins to fight, who wants victory without battle, or who longs for the palm without victory. 84 [Col. 0593A] No, brothers, no one can reach great rewards except through great labors. As it is said through the Apostle: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). Hence Truth itself says: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).

Despise, then, my brothers, the passing allurements of this age; yearn from the depths of your being for the joys of the heavenly homeland; restrain the incitements of the flesh; fulfill in your works the commandments of God that you have previously received. Let no prosperity of the world draw you back from the love of God; let no adversity break you; let luxury not defile your body; let the flame of envy not consume you; let pride not inflate you; let desire for earthly things not weigh you down; let anger not divide you from love of your neighbor; let disordered affection not join you to the vices of the wicked. [Col. 0593B]

Wipe away past evils with the tears of worthy repentance; avoid impending evils through prudent foresight; place the terrible Judge who is to come before the eyes of your mind; tremble and fear the sentence of his strict judgment. Thus may you, fearing now that he will come and striving to carry the cross of his humanity, afterward behold Jesus Christ our Lord—when he comes in the glory of his majesty—with confidence and joy. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVII bis. II. ON SAINT VITALIS THE MARTYR (28 APRIL)

We have gathered, dearest brothers, for a spectacle exceedingly beautiful and delightful to behold on today’s feast, and we have contemplated with the eyes of faith the admirable victory of a triumphant battle. [Col. 0593C]

For we saw the ancient dragon contending with a human being; we saw venomous guile overcome by the cunning of the better serpent; we saw him who was accustomed to conquer yield feebly; we saw him who had lain prostrate carry away victory, his spoils seized from the defeated enemy.

From one side we perceived the roaring lion savagely raging against Christ’s flock; from the other, the new David rescuing a stolen sheep from the bloodstained teeth of the most voracious predator. That one, gaping with parched jaws, thirsted for human blood and, with the throat of his wickedness opened, had already begun to swallow Christ’s sheep. But this one, piercing his mouth with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6), violently snatched away the captured prey and, through the opening he had made in Leviathan’s jaw, recalled it from almost the abyss of death to the pastures of life. [Col. 0593D]

Thus the Lord rightly says to blessed Job in a divine utterance: “Can you pierce Leviathan’s jaw with a bracelet?” (Job 40). By Leviathan, whose name is said to mean “their addition,” is signified that crafty devourer of the human race who, when he promised to add divinity to the human being, took away immortality; who, while multiplying through his worst persuasion the guilt of transgression that he offered to the first human being, heaps punishments upon those who follow him without cessation.

The Lord therefore pierces Leviathan’s jaw with a bracelet through his chosen ones, because by the power of his ineffable mercy he confronts the wickedness of the ancient enemy, so that eventually he may lose even those whom he has already captured, and those may fall, as it were, from his mouth who return to innocence after committing their sins. 85 [Col. 0594A]

For who, once captured by his mouth, could escape his jaw if it had not been pierced? Did he not bite blessed Ursicinus when, after immense torments, he feared the executioner’s sword? Did he not hold him fully in his mouth when Ursicinus consented to sacrifice to idols? But when, through the exhortation of the glorious martyr Vitalis, he returned to life, this Leviathan in some way lost him through the opening in his jaw.

For, as the sacred history of his deeds relates, when Ursicinus had come to the palm of martyrdom after immense torments and was about to be beheaded, he became afraid and tried to escape. Vitalis cried out, saying: “Do not, do not, physician Ursicinus, who are accustomed to heal others, wound yourself with the dart of eternal death; and you who have come to the palm through immense sufferings, do not lose the crown prepared for you by the Lord.” [Col. 0594B]

O remarkable soldier of Christ, who, while still girded with the weapons of earthly military service, was suddenly, through the divine Spirit’s kindling, fervently stirred to spiritual battle! O new and incomparable recruit, who, at the very beginning of his service, breaking fearlessly into the midst of the hostile ranks as they roared, rushed upon the tyrant himself and rescued his fellow soldier from beneath the very swords of his executioners!

A learned and most fervent soldier of Christ, making an assault upon the enemy, drove back the captive, drew his comrade to himself, and repaired the loss to his army by restoring a soldier.

It is pleasing to consider, dearest brothers, with what ardor of charity the mind of blessed Vitalis had been kindled. To care for his brother’s salvation, he did not fear danger for himself. Girded with a military belt, distinguished by the proud titles of military service, enrolled in the cavalry, and adorned with a warrior’s cloak, he was entirely secure regarding himself. [Col. 0594C]

But when he saw his comrade in the interior army caught in the battle of temptations, already failing beneath the approaching hail of weapons, having lost the shield of patience and exposed to hostile swords, he immediately sprang forward and placed himself in mortal danger. He imitated his commander, namely the Redeemer of the human race, who endured death so that we might live and allowed himself to be crucified by the members of the devil so that he might rescue us from the yoke of the devil’s power.

In body he was present in the service of the consul, but in mind he had already passed over to the service of the Creator. From the former he received the pay of the present life; from the latter he awaited the perpetual citizenship of future blessedness. From the former he received a gift that he could see temporarily; from the latter he hoped for the prize that he could not yet see before completing the course, saying with the Apostle: “While we do not contemplate the things that are seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4). [Col. 0594D]

He rendered military service to the former; he preserved for the latter the immovable foundation of perfect faith, already keeping that Gospel saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke 20).

O how effective and living was the voice that then came forth from his mouth! How fervently the flame of charity boiled from his steaming breast! 86 [Col. 0595A] “Do not, do not,” he said, “physician Ursicinus, who are accustomed to heal others, wound yourself with the dart of eternal death.” Nor could that voice descend coldly into the hearer’s heart, for it had proceeded in words of exhortation from the very fire of the Holy Spirit.

When Ursicinus heard this, he knelt and urged the executioner to strike, repenting that he had been afraid of Christ’s martyrdom.

But when the fall of blessed Ursicinus is heard, someone’s mind may perhaps ask why almighty God permits those whom he has chosen eternally, whom through more abundant grace he even raises to the summit of martyrdom, to fall into the abyss of dangerous fear because of the weakness of the flesh. Since we believe that an answer will quickly satisfy the question, we shall reply briefly. [Col. 0595B]

For holy men who are raised to the summit of perfection by the grace of the divine gift are restrained by certain temptations as long as they remain in this life, lest they become proud through some form of exaltation, so that they are in no way able to advance as far as they wish. Thus, lest they be lifted up by the vice of pride, a certain measure of virtues is established in them.

Hence Elijah, although he had advanced to a great height through so many virtues, was held back by a certain measure when he fled Jezebel, though she was a queen, since she was nevertheless only a little woman (1 Kings 19). I consider this man of extraordinary virtue drawing fire from heaven and, on a second occasion, consuming fifty men with their followers (2 Kings 1); opening the heavens to rain by his word; raising the dead; [Col. 0595C] and foreseeing future events through the spirit of prophecy.
