But then it comes back to mind that, after performing all these things wondrously, he fled before a single woman, terrified by a woman’s fear. I consider a man struck by fear asking death from the hand of the Lord and not receiving it, while fleeing death from the hand of a woman and thus avoiding it.

For he sought death while fleeing, saying: “It is enough, Lord; take my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (1 Kings 19). How, then, was he so powerful as to perform all those virtues? How was he so dear to God as even to restore life to the dead, unless, by the profound counsel of divine dispensation, measures of a hidden balance are weighed out, so that these men of the highest devotion may accomplish much through divine power and yet be moderated by a certain measure through their own weakness? [Col. 0595D]

In those virtues Elijah recognized what he had received from the Lord; in these weaknesses he recognized what he was in himself. That power was a virtue; this weakness was the guardian of virtue. In those virtues he displayed what he had received; in these weaknesses he preserved what he had received. In miracles Elijah was revealed; in weaknesses he was preserved.

For it is written that Jezebel said: “May the gods do this to me, and may they add this, unless by this hour tomorrow I make your life like the life of one of them.” And Elijah heard, feared, and fled, going wherever his will carried him (ibid.). [Col. 0596A]

O force of the word! O magnitude of fear! At the word of a woman Elijah fled; and he fled not for one, two, or three days, but rather for forty days and forty nights! For the woman’s speech had entered his heart like a sword, and, having lost the guidance of reason, he did not know what to do. 87

Driven and tossed by fear through the length of so great a journey, like a whirlwind that catches from the opposite side the mast of a ship driven by favorable winds and turns back its momentum, so the woman’s speech struck the prophet’s mind as it sailed under the sail of virtue and tossed his entire ship through all the waves of fear, its helmsman thrown into confusion.

What, then, are you doing, Elijah? You are the one who by your word had shut heaven and withheld the rains; who had commanded the air and brought forth divine fires; who had salutarily ordered the false priests to be killed; who had boldly reproached the king to his face because he and his house had overthrown Israel’s people; who had said: “As the Lord lives, there shall be neither rain nor dew except at the word of my mouth” (1 Kings 17); who had made the widow’s house a threshing-floor of grain and a winepress of oil; who had commanded all the elements. And now you fear the speech of a prostitute? [Col. 0596B]

What wonder is it, then, my brothers, if blessed Ursicinus feared the consul’s sword after immense torments, when the outstanding prophet Elijah himself, scarcely inferior to any of the saints, fled for so many days like a stag struck by an arrow of fear—not from a man but from a woman, not at the sight of a sword but at the sound of a threatening word?

How great Elijah’s merit was can quickly be gathered if evangelical authority is brought forward as testimony concerning him. To Zechariah, concerning the promise of John, the angel says: “He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1). Concerning this same John the Lord also testifies, saying: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11). If, then, no one greater than John arose among human beings, who was greater than Elijah, who possessed one virtue and one spirit with John? [Col. 0596C]

But while we strive to defend fearful Ursicinus by means of fearful Elijah, the weakness of the Church’s supreme shepherd is also recalled to mind. Struck by the voice of a single woman, he feared death and denied life. At that time Peter did not dare to give testimony about the Lord on earth (Matthew 27), while the thief did not fear confessing him on the cross (Luke 23).

In this matter we must consider why almighty God permitted the man whom he had determined to set over the whole Church to fear a servant girl’s voice and deny him. We understand that this was done through a dispensation of great mercy, so that he who was to become the Church’s shepherd might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others. [Col. 0596D]

He first showed Peter to himself and then set him over the others, so that from his own weakness he might learn how to bear with the weaknesses of others. For this reason sacred Scripture also indicates the falls of such men, namely Elijah and Peter, so that the downfall of the great may be a safeguard for the small. For this reason it also reveals the repentance and forgiveness of the saints, so that there may be hope for those who are perishing and recovery for the lost.

Therefore, let no one grow proud because Peter fell from his position; and let no one despair because Peter rose after his fall.

By contrast, consider how wondrously divine Scripture subdues the proud and raises the humble. It reported one event, yet in different ways it recalled the proud to fear of humility and the humble to confidence in hope. For immeasurable is this new kind of medicine, which, set forth in one and the same arrangement, both dries up what is swollen by pressing it down and pours moisture into what is parched by lifting it up. [Col. 0597A] 88

It terrified us through the fall of the great, but strengthened us through their restoration. Thus, always thus, the mercy of divine dispensation both restrains us when we are proud and supports us lest we fall into despair.

It is pleasing to consider within the protected bosom of grace how great a favor of mercy God uses to preserve us. Behold: the one who exalts himself over his virtues returns through vice to humility. The one who is lifted up by the grace of a virtue received is wounded not by a sword but, so to speak, by a medicine.

For what is virtue except medicine? And what is vice except a wound? Because we turn medicine into a wound, God turns a wound into medicine, so that those struck by virtue may be healed by vice. We turn the gifts of virtues toward the use of vices; he takes up the evils of vices in the art of virtues, so that, fleeing the humility of the healer, we may cling inseparably to the one who grants salvation.

Yet amid these things we must know that many people are bound more tightly by the very things in which they repeatedly fall. When the ancient enemy strikes them through one vice so that they collapse, he also binds them through another so that they cannot rise. [Col. 0597B]

Let a person therefore consider what sort of adversary he is fighting; and if he recognizes that he has already sinned in some respect, let him at least fear after his fault, so that he may diligently avoid the wounds by which he is frequently killed. It is exceedingly rare for our enemy to heal the sickness of the elect even through wounds.

For the Lord often subjects his chosen ones to the tempter in order to educate them. Thus, after the gates of paradise and after the secrets of the third heaven, so that the Apostle Paul might not become proud because of the greatness of his revelations, an angel of Satan was given to him.

Behold: the one who had first contemplated the secrets of paradise, returning to himself, struggles against the battle of the flesh and bears another law in his members, whose rebellion wearies the law of the spirit. [Col. 0597C] After granting a gift, therefore, God tests a person, because through the gift bestowed he raises him up, and, withdrawing it for a little while, shows the person to himself.

Without doubt, we suffer this only to the extent that, once the stain of sin has been thoroughly wiped away, we may be restored to the substance of the promised incorruption. Yet this very temptation is arranged so that those who might have perished through being exalted may be saved from destruction through being humbled.

Thus, by the secret order of divine dispensation, from the place where the devil’s wickedness is permitted to rage, God’s kindness is lovingly brought to perfection. Our adversary obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely from the place where he exercises the anger of his most wicked will. [Col. 0597D]

For when blessed Ursicinus endured so many torments for the love of Christ and remained unmoved amid the hands of his executioners as they tore him apart, pride might perhaps have stolen upon him from the steadfastness of his courage and plunged him much more deeply, had he not been struck by the lighter breeze of temptation.

After the Lord strengthens our minds toward perfection, he immediately tests them by visiting them with the barbs of temptations. By approaching, he advances our hearts toward virtues; by withdrawing, he permits them to be shaken by temptation. For if no breeze of temptation shook us after gifts of virtue, the mind would boast that it possessed this strength from itself.

Therefore, so that it may both possess the gifts of firmness profitably and humbly recognize its own weakness, it is lifted toward other things through the approach of grace and healthfully learns what it is of itself through grace’s withdrawal. 89 [Col. 0598A]

This is also well suggested to us by the history of sacred reading, in which Solomon is said both to have received wisdom divinely and, nevertheless, after receiving that same wisdom, to have immediately been challenged by the question of prostitutes (1 Kings 3). As soon as he received the grace of so great a revelation, he endured a contest involving disgraceful women, because often, when the visitation of inward brightness illuminates our minds through the virtues granted to us, slippery thoughts also disturb them, so that the mind which exaltation through an abundant gift of perfection raises up may discover through being struck by temptation what it is. [Col. 0598B]

Blessed martyr Ursicinus saw everyone around him raging cruelly, irrationally raging to destroy the name of Christ, all rushing headlong through the precipices of error, and everyone ignorant of the way of truth because they had lost the eyes of their hearts. For this reason, in so deep a thought, he might perhaps have supposed that no one remained who could equal him in merit. [Col. 0598C]

Therefore divine mercy wished him to fall for a moment and immediately raised up, by divine providence, a man from the earthly army who would lift him up. Thus, when he saw a man from the secular order much stronger and more stalwart than himself, he humbly inclined the neck of his heart toward recognizing his own weakness.

Hence it is that Elijah, of whom we spoke above, when he fled terrified by Jezebel and supposed that he alone of all had remained alive for God, saying, “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life” (1 Kings 19), received from the Lord this response to restrain the pride of his mind: “I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent their knees before Baal” (ibid.). [Col. 0598D]

It is certain that the one who neglects to consider the merits of his neighbors, even when acting rightly, extinguishes the eyes of his heart. By contrast, the one who carefully weighs the good deeds of others illuminates himself with a great ray of humility. For when he sees outwardly, accomplished by others, what he himself has done, he suppresses the swelling of pride that seeks to break forth within him from his supposed uniqueness.

“I have left,” he says, “seven thousand men for myself who have not bent their knees before Baal,” so that, when Elijah recognized that he was not the only one remaining, he might bow down the glory of exaltation that had arisen in him from his supposed uniqueness.

He was indeed a prophet and had often known heavenly mysteries. What, then, was difficult about recognizing that faithful servants of God and others still remained in the world? But here we must carefully observe how wickedly pride closes the eye of the heart: the humble man knew the hidden things of God, while the proud man did not know what was openly evident. [Col. 0599A]

Therefore, for blessed Ursicinus to escape the abyss of pride, it was fitting that through falling he should learn that he had stood not by his own virtue but by another’s. Divine clemency permitted the lofty cedar of paradise to be lightly shaken, lest, when a stronger whirlwind rushed upon it, it should be uprooted from its foundations.

It permitted its soldier to yield to hostile swords even for a moment, so that, repenting of his flight, he might more fervently restore his courageous heart to renewed battles, and so that it might immediately make the pursuer from the fugitive and, in turn, the victor from the defeated.

By loving his flesh, Ursicinus wished to abandon Christ; but then, by fearing Christ, he willingly handed that flesh over to the executioners to be struck. From the very place where he sinned, he immediately hastened to make amends. From the source of his guilt, he endured repentance. 90 [Col. 0599B]

Comforted, Ursicinus knelt upon the ground and urged the executioner to strike, repenting that he had feared Christ’s martyrdom.

Learn, brothers, learn to perform perfect repentance; learn to cleanse the stains of your guilt with the tears of complete remorse—namely, so that consummated sins may be washed away by perfect lamentation, lest you become more deeply bound by the debt of the deed committed while paying less in the tears of satisfaction. For it is written: “You gave us drink in tears, by measure” (Ps. 79), so that each person’s soul may drink, in repentance, as many tears of remorse as it remembers having been dried up by its sins before God.

For, fearing death, [Col. 0599C] Blessed Ursicinus was already abandoning the author of life; but when he received the life-giving words of exhortation, he immediately rose up against his own flesh and willingly handed it over to death—the flesh for whose life’s love he had sinned. He did not resist; he did not raise himself in presumptuous words of self-defense; he did not postpone his repentance; rather, he humbly obeyed at once the life-giving command of the one correcting him. There are indeed some who, when they hear words of correction from the mouth of their neighbors, immediately burst into anger, swell with the vice of puffed-up pride, and burn with the torches of deadly hatred. These people make the medicine of salvation into material for their sickness, and the cautery intended for healing into an instrument for wounding. By the audacity of their self-defense they provoke God to anger far more grievously than when they were sinning in the common weakness of the flesh [Col. 0599D]. For a person sins more by defending sin than by committing sin. To sin is human; to defend sin, however, is devilish.

Thus the Psalmist also humbly implores divine assistance, saying: “Let not the abyss swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68). The person who falls into the precipice of grave sin is swallowed up by the abyss. But then the pit closes its mouth over him, so that he cannot escape, when the sinner, advancing into the audacity of self-defense, plunges himself ever more deeply. Thus the first man also fell, as it were, into the abyss when he ate the forbidden fruit through disobedience. Then the pit closed its mouth over him, when he boldly presumed to defend his guilt. [Col. 0600A] For he said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion—she gave me some of the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3). He had fled in fear, intending to hide himself; yet, when questioned, he revealed how greatly he was swollen with pride even while afraid. For when present punishment is feared because of sin, and the lost face of God is not loved, fear arises from swelling pride, not from humility. The person who does not abandon sin, if he may escape punishment, but rather presumptuously undertakes to defend it with swollen pride, is indeed proud.

Let us therefore now, most beloved, strive to imitate the virtues of the blessed martyrs, so that afterward we may deserve to be crowned with them by the Emperor of the martyrs. Let us hold to the footsteps, along the way, of those whose company we desire to have in our homeland. Certainly, we shall be there [Col. 0600B] what they are, if here we have been what they were. For “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Tim. 2). Let us not, then, be divided on the journey if we wish to be joined together upon arrival.

Let Blessed Vitalis teach us to possess zeal for righteousness; let Blessed Ursicinus teach us to maintain the pattern of humility; let both of them teach us to preserve the bond of twofold charity. The former, inflamed by the ardor of twofold charity so that he might free his neighbor who was perishing and restore God’s pure image in him, utterly despised himself and did not fear the sentence of the most cruel persecutor. The latter humbly obeyed the neighbor who corrected him and hastened, by the sword, to proceed as quickly as possible into the presence of his Creator.

But since we proposed to compose this sermon on the triumph of Saint [Col. 0600C] Vitalis, although the subject matter that arose led us to speak at greater length about Ursicinus, let no one suppose that we have deviated from the path of our intended purpose. For when the triumph of Saint Ursicinus is exalted, the praise of Blessed Vitalis is not left unspoken. The salvation of a sick man is the physician’s praise, and the skill of a disciple is the glory of his teacher. Great indeed is the man who learned to die for life; but far greater is the one who taught him to despise temporal life for the sake of eternal life. Strong is the man who was able to drink the bitter cup of salvation; but much stronger is the one who powerfully led him out of the very jaws of everlasting death. Therefore, when the virtue of triumphant Ursicinus is exalted, the honor of glorious Blessed Vitalis is also increased. Indeed, whatever is said to be great about either of them belongs wholly to the glory of the Creator [Col. 0600D] of both. “Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3).

Amid all this, dearest brothers, return to yourselves; examine your actions with careful scrutiny; and since you gladly hear the praises of the martyrs, take care also to possess a praiseworthy life. “Praise is not becoming in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). Those who extol the saints worthily with praise are the ones who live praiseworthy lives; and those who hear the virtues of the strong to good effect are those whom the praise they hear kindles to the love of imitation. “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15).

Whoever, therefore, rejoices that the martyrs of Christ fought bravely, let him also seize weapons [Col. 0601A] among Christ’s soldiers. If enemies are lacking outside, turn your hands against yourself, and you will find many rebellious citizens within. Subdue pride, behead anger, extinguish lust, restrain greed, kill envy; and, to embrace everything briefly with the Apostle, “crucify your flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5). This is to act bravely; this is to fight manfully.

For what does it avail if armies of persecutors do not besiege you around the rampart, while barbarism of vices rages within the walls of the city? Indeed, what does it profit if the members of the devil do not fight you externally, while the devil himself possesses you inwardly by an undisturbed right? For all who are subject to his will are possessed by him, as it were, by an unchallenged right, and their proud king enjoys a certain security while he rules their hearts with unshaken [Col. 0601B] power.

But when each person’s spirit grows warm with desire for the Creator, when it abandons the torpor of negligence and kindles the coldness of its former insensibility with the fire of holy love, when it remembers its inborn freedom and is ashamed to remain a slave held by the enemy—because the enemy sees himself despised, because he sees God’s ways being embraced—he is grieved to find resistance raised against him. At once he is kindled by zeal; at once he is moved to battle; at once he rouses himself against the rebellious mind and incites it by every art of torment, so that, hurling the darts of temptation, he may pierce the heart that he had previously possessed by an undisturbed right.

He was, as it were, asleep while he rested, lulled in an evil heart; but he is awakened to the provocation of battle when he has admitted the right of perverse domination. For it is written: [Col. 0601C] “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). Whoever hastens to gird himself for divine service is preparing himself for what other thing than battle against the ancient adversary, so that, free in combat, he may receive blows who had served in captivity, peacefully subjected to tyranny?

In this battle, dearest brothers, let our spirit always exercise itself; toward victory in this struggle, let our mind burn with all its inmost being. “He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2), so that we who now strive to contend lawfully by imitating the blessed martyrs may, once we have received the crown of victory, rejoice ineffably forever with that very King of the martyrs. He, the triune and one God, lives and is glorified [reigns] through infinite ages [Col. 0601D] of ages. Amen.

## May

III. Sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross. XI. Sermon on Saint Anthimus the Martyr. XIV. Sermon on Saint Boniface the Martyr. XV. Sermon on the Holy Spirit and His Grace.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE FINDING OF THE HOLY CROSS  
### (3 May)

Today, dearest brothers, because we celebrate the Finding of the Cross, we ought to rejoice together in Christ as though a common treasure of the whole world had been discovered; and just as the man who found the lost sheep or drachma summoned his friends and neighbors and congratulated them [Col. 0602A] (Luke 15), so it is right for us to glory in that which we have found: not that which he himself had lost, but that by which he had acquired us when we were lost—especially since the Apostle says: “But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). We should conceive spiritual joy in an eager mind all the more earnestly because we know that the enemy of human salvation himself groans more bitterly.

The devil rejoiced that he was escaping the disgrace of his shameful confusion: the victorious standard beneath which he had lost, beneath which he had been overthrown and taken captive, had remained hidden until then. By concealing the sign of victory, he compensated for the disgrace of his downfall, which he had endured by being overcome. But when it was found, when he perceived that it had become visible with such great glory [Col. 0602B] to Christian devotion and piety, he was ashamed to see himself now prostrate everywhere, because everywhere he saw the title of divine victory erected. For wherever the sign of the cross is raised, there, without doubt, the victory of Christ and the captivity of the devil are also signified.

Moreover, the ancient enemy had conquered the first man through wood, and for almost five thousand years had oppressed all his descendants like slaves under the yoke of his tyranny. But the Son came “like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18), to overthrow the aerial powers, and he set wood against wood, expelling through the bitterness of the cross the poisonous pleasure of that forbidden fruit.

The first man, when at the devil’s prompting he extended his hand toward the tree, inscribed upon a wooden [Col. 0602C] tablet the bond of servile captivity. The second man, when he stretched out his hands upon the cross, erased that document of the deadly pact [passion], so that it might be obliterated. Through wood, therefore, we were made slaves; through wood, we were restored to our former freedom. Through wood, we had been expelled from paradise; through wood, we were called back to our homeland. And we who had been reckoned enemies through wood were, through the mystery of the cross, reconciled to God’s friendship and to harmony with the angels. The Apostle testifies to this when, speaking of Christ to the Ephesians, he says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one and, by dissolving the middle wall of the dividing barrier, the enmity in his flesh, having annulled the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and might [Col. 0602D] reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself” (Eph. 2).

This standard of human salvation was not only prefigured by the Law through certain typical interpretations and riddles; the utterances of all the prophets and the entire authority of the Old Testament also venerate it. For what page of sacred speech is there that does not breathe the mystery of the cross and direct its attention toward it as toward the head and beginning of all human salvation? From these sources, therefore, we believe it useful to bring forward here some testimonies that hint at the mystery of the cross, so that through what we touch upon here in a brief discourse we may open an easier path of understanding toward those things that remain unspoken.

Let Abraham, then, first [Col. 0603A] come forward. When he wished to sacrifice his son to God, he signified almost all the mysteries of the Lord’s passion in their proper order. For just as Abraham—whose name means “exalted father”—did not hesitate to offer his only and beloved son to God, so the supreme Father handed over his only-begotten and beloved Son for us all. And just as Isaac himself carried the wood on which he was to be placed, so Christ also carried upon his shoulders the wood of his cross, on which he was to suffer for our salvation.

The two servants dismissed some distance away signify the Jews, who, while living servilely and understanding according to the flesh, did not comprehend Christ’s supreme humility [poverty], and therefore did not ascend the mountain, that is, the place of sacrifice. Why two servants, unless because, when Solomon sinned, [Col. 0603B] one Israelite people became two peoples? To them the prophet often says: “Israel the adversary, and Judah the transgressor” (Jer. 3).

The ass that Abraham was then using was the senseless folly of the Jews. That brute folly carried all the mysteries, yet, like an irrational animal, did not know what it carried. But what does it mean that he said to them: “Wait here with the ass; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you” (Gen. 22)? Hear the Apostle: “A blindness in part has happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved” (Rom. 11).

What does “a blindness in part has happened to Israel” mean? It means, plainly, “Wait here with the ass.” “So that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter”—that is, “after we have worshiped,” when [Col. 0603C] the sacrifice of the Lord’s cross has been fulfilled and proclaimed among all the nations. What follows, “and thus all Israel will be saved,” means: “We shall return to you.”

But what does it mean that a ram is found caught by its horns among the thorns and is offered in sacrifice in place of Isaac? The cross, certainly, has horns: two pieces of wood are joined together, and thus produce the form of a cross. Hence it is written concerning Christ: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. 3). The ram caught by its horns is therefore Christ crucified amid the sharp and wounding iniquities of the Jews, just as he himself complains through Jeremiah, saying: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins [Col. 0603D]” (Jer. 30).

After the sacrifice had been completed, it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). And after the Lord says, “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21), he adds shortly afterward in the same Psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, because the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (ibid.).

Thus, after Abraham had offered his son and the ram had been sacrificed in his place, he called the name of that place “The Lord sees,” because our Redeemer, after being offered upon the altar of the cross and paying the debt of our death, thereafter presented himself to the sight of his faithful, so that all the redeemed might now see through faith the one whom until then they had lacked the eyes of faith to see [Col. 0604A].

But while we pursue Abraham the sacrificer at somewhat greater length, we are delayed too long from the other matters that must be said. Jacob too expressed this mystery of the cross figuratively when, among the other words of his blessing concerning Christ, he said: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49).

Christ’s robe and cloak are the multitude of the Gentiles, whom the Lord then clothed when he joined them to himself through the grace of redemption, as he promises through the prophet, saying: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as a garment” (Isa. 69). The Lord washed his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood [Col. 0604B] of the grape when he hung upon the wood of the cross like a cluster of grapes. Then blood and water flowed from his side. The water washed us, and the blood redeemed us, so that he might present to himself a bride “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5).

Jacob also plainly displayed the mystery of the cross when, preferring the younger Ephraim to the firstborn Manasseh, he crossed his arms over them in the form of a cross (Gen. 48). Through the cross it came about that the people of the Gentiles, as though having seized the right of the firstborn, preceded the people of the Jews.

That passage also which is read in Exodus undoubtedly refers to the mystery of the Lord’s cross. For the Lord said to Moses: “Throw upon the ground the staff that you hold in your hand.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent. “Moses was immediately terrified and fled. [Col. 0604C] And the Lord said to him: ‘Take hold of its tail.’ He seized it, and it became a staff again” (Exod. 4).

We all clearly know that the serpent persuaded man to death (Gen. 3). Death, therefore, came from the serpent. But what is the staff except Christ, of whom the prophet says: “A staff shall go forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11)? Thus the staff became a serpent, and Christ became death.

Moses was terrified and fled because, when the Lord was suspended on the cross or dying, the whole company of the apostles trembled in fear and withdrew from the firmness of certain hope and steadfast faith. Since the tail is the final part of the body, what does it signify except the end of the Lord’s passion? Moses therefore seized the tail, and thereafter no form of the serpent appeared in the staff, because, when the mystery of the Lord’s [Col. 0604D] passion and cross had been completed, every faithful person returned to faith, and Christ, having consumed death, restored in himself through the glory of the resurrection that same nature which he had been.

What else does it mean that the Israelite people were commanded to put the blood of the lamb on the doorposts of their houses (Exod. 12), except that it prefigured us carrying the cross of Christ, who is the true Lamb, on our forehead? The lamb was sacrificed in the evening, and Christ suffered in the evening of the world. The doorposts were smeared so that the destroying angel would not dare to inflict harm; and we carry the standard of the cross in our heart and on our forehead, so that the sudden attack of the enemy may not be able to take away our salvation. Hence we confidently sing: “The light of your countenance [Col. 0605A], O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4).

We sing this, however, more confidently and more worthily if, having now crossed the Red Sea and drowned the enemy, we carry the tambourine with Mary, the sister of Moses (Exod. 15). But what does it mean to carry a tambourine? Hear the Lord saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9). Whoever crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5), whoever mortifies by abstinence his members that are upon the earth (Col. 3), truly carries the tambourine with Mary, because he keeps himself dry and free from the harmful fluids of earthly pleasure. In accordance, therefore, with the logic of what follows, the tambourine here too clearly signifies the mystery of the cross.

[Col. 0605B] Moreover, it is not unfitting to recall that the Israelite people murmured against Moses at Marah, crying out that they could not find anything to drink. Then the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood, and when he put it into the exceedingly bitter waters, they were immediately turned into sweetness (Exod. 15). What were those bitter waters except a figure of the letter that kills and of the harsh and tasteless Law? For it is written: “The Lord established a law and judgments for his people, and tested him” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live” (Ezek. 20).

Yet when confession of the cross and the mystery of the Lord’s passion are joined to that Law, what had been bitter is immediately turned into the sweetness of spiritual understanding [Col. 0605C].

It should be noted, in accordance with the truth of the historical account, that after the water had been turned into sweetness, the people came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. What are the twelve springs except the twelve apostles, whom the Lord appointed for this purpose: to irrigate the dry and barren hearts of the human race with the floods of their preaching? And what are the seventy palm trees except the same number of disciples whom he sent before his face (Luke 10), so that through them the world might recognize the palms of his victory?

Certainly, the order of the events that follow seems to have been arranged very suitably: first the people were led to the letter of the Law [Col. 0605D], from which, while it was bitter, they could not pass. But after it had been made sweet through the wood of life and began to be understood spiritually, the people of God immediately passed from the Old Testament to the apostolic springs and palm trees—that is, to the grace of the Gospel.

And rightly, after the Decalogue had been received, a sevenfold number of preachers is established, because every commandment of the divine Law is fulfilled through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Nor is it without reason that the preachers of the cross appear to be represented by the name of palm trees, since the cross itself ought rightly to be called a palm: in it, victory was achieved over the fallen enemy of the world. Thus the bridegroom says concerning the cross to the bride: “I said, I shall ascend the palm tree and take hold of its fruits; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and your fragrance like apples, your throat like the finest wine [Col. 0606A]” (Song 7). The fruits of the cross are, of course, all the elect.

The Lord therefore ascended the palm tree and took hold of its fruits, because as soon as he hung upon the cross for our salvation, he drew all the elect to himself through the desire of love. Then holy Church, through the breasts of the two Testaments, began to pour forth the wines of spiritual joy and to breathe the fragrance of heavenly desire into the nostrils of human minds, so that our mind, stirred to obedience and rejoicing in itself, might say: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

The stone of Horeb at Rephidim [Col. 0606B] also announces this very clearly. At the Lord’s command Moses struck it with his staff, and it brought forth water (Exod. 17). The Apostle likewise testifies that this stone bore the figure of Christ when he says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). The wood of the cross approached this rock, and immediately, like a flood of flowing water, it poured forth the abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit. The Lord himself invites all who thirst to draw these waters when he says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). The evangelist adds: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid.).

But why linger longer over the remaining matters, when it is clear that even the tablets written by the finger of God prefigured the mystery of the Lord’s cross? Ten commandments were written on them [Col. 0606C], and the number ten is represented by the letter X, which expresses the form of the cross. In this letter, which contains the number ten, one stroke is drawn obliquely from top to bottom, so that another similar stroke is joined to it across the middle, with arms extending on either side. Thus the joining of the two strokes not only presents the outward image of the cross but also seems to indicate a certain mystical power belonging to it.

For the Lord says: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). Through the mystery of the cross, therefore, he joined the commandments of the Old Testament to evangelical grace and, so to speak, made the two Testaments into the body of a single teaching.

The tablets were indeed given first, but immediately, when the people transgressed, they were broken (Exod. 32). The tablets are given a second time [Col. 0606D], but they are to remain forever. Clearly, the first tablets bore the figure of the ancient Law, which was later to cease [fail] in the observance of its worship. The tablets are given afterward, but they are not broken, because the grace of the New Testament, which has been made firm through the mystery of the cross, knows no failure.

Moreover, the ark of the Old Testament should not be thought to have lacked the treasures of the blessed cross. It concealed the incomparable riches of the cross, because even then it served the cross through all the mysteries of its figures and riddles. It was already its minister, the image of the truth and the beginning of fullness.

The ark signified the holy Church [Col. 0607A]. Three things were contained in the ark. First were the two stone tablets, which clearly indicate the perpetual firmness of the two Testaments; we have already shown that they contain within themselves the mystery of the cross. There was also a golden urn containing manna. This clearly expresses the pure and undefiled flesh of the Redeemer, which undoubtedly contains the sweetness of eternal divinity. That sweetness began to be tasted on the palate of our minds when the soldier opened the side of the Lord hanging upon the cross (John 19), when the cluster of grapes was pressed—he who, while being trodden, alone trod the winepress.

Third, the rod of Aaron was in the ark, and after being dry it blossomed (Num. 17). What else does this signify except that saving standard of our supreme and true [Col. 0607B] high priest, ever blossoming with the evergreen of immortal memory and fruitful with the abundance of flourishing fruits? The cross is ever green in hope, blossoms in faith, and bears fruit in charity. After it was cut off from the earthly ground, it puts forth leaves, because whoever, through love of the cross, cuts himself away at the very root of his mind from earthly desires grows strong to obtain an unfading inheritance and the ever-green pastures of eternal life.

But why should I say more about the praise of the blessed cross, when all those sacrifices commanded to be offered according to the rite of the legal ceremonies refer to that one, singular, true sacrifice offered upon the altar of the cross?

Through the calf [Col. 0607C] that is commanded to be offered from the herd (Exod. 29), our Redeemer is prefigured, since he descended from the offspring of the patriarchs. By the plow of his cross he subdued the soil of our flesh and enriched us with the fruit of virtues from the seed of the Holy Spirit. This unblemished calf was offered by the sons of Aaron not in the tabernacle but before its entrance (Exod. 29), because the Lord, who is without sin (Isa. 53), was crucified outside the gate under Annas and Caiaphas (Luke 3). He is the Lamb who wiped away the sins of the world (John 1). He is the kid who slaughtered the author of sin, the devil, with the sword of the cross. He is the dove, in whose form the Holy Spirit descended upon him at the waters of the Jordan (Matt. 3). He is also the turtledove, because he is the author of perpetual chastity, as the bride says to him: “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove [Col. 0607D]” (Song 1).

The red heifer too signified the same victim of the life-giving cross, since it was commanded to be sound in age but unfamiliar with the yoke (Num. 19). The red heifer is the flesh of the Savior, rosy with the blood of his passion. The Lord came to his passion at the fullness of his age, but the yoke of any sin did not wear down his neck. Those who offer the heifer are unclean; and those who crucify Christ—through whom the world is washed—are themselves damnably defiled. But the person who gathers the ashes and casts them outside the camp is clean, because all who proclaim the mystery of the Lord’s cross and passion throughout the breadth of the world cleanse themselves from the contagion of sins [Col. 0608A] through the ministry of edifying their brothers.

Perhaps some people will be displeased that we have gathered so many examples from sacred speech in praise of the cross and have shown, as though drawing up the battle line of the Old Testament, that its entire array is directed toward this royal standard. What else should be said to them except what the Apostle declares: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1)? Whatever we say about the praise of the cross undoubtedly redounds to the praise of the one who made the standard of the cross glorious by his own death.

From what has been said, therefore, my brothers, we can clearly gather that this sign of heavenly victory [Col. 0608B], through which the world was to be freed from the bonds of its ancient captivity, has been worshiped by the Fathers from the very beginning of the world, foretold by the Prophets, and prefigured by every page of the sacred [holy] Scriptures. What we worship as a gift, they already revered in faith. What among them had been represented through certain riddles, we now see fulfilled through the grace of the Mediator, so that what was foretold to them by the Spirit we now behold and embrace with bodily sight.

O admirable and merciful kindness of our Creator! O singular humility of our Redeemer, worthy of proclamation! He deigned to undergo the punishment of the most atrocious death in order to raise us to the crown. Of his own will he chose the most shameful punishment of the cross [Col. 0608C] in order to exalt us from the yoke of slavery to the kingdom. He did not refuse the curse, in order to release us from the curse of the Law. He endured a disgraceful death in order to free us from the disgrace of eternal death.

Hence the Apostle says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree,’ so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith” (Gal. 3).

Therefore, my brothers, since we have been released from the yoke of slavery and have already obtained the blessing of Abraham in Christ, what remains except that we preserve, by the merit of our life, the gifts we have received through prevenient grace? Otherwise, although we are reborn in Christ through baptism, by living once more according to the old man [Col. 0608D] we may be recalled to his sentence of condemnation.

For today also in the church we sing that word of David: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments” (Ps. 118). The sentence must certainly be considered carefully, because it does not say, “Cursed are those who are not reborn in your sacraments,” but “those who turn aside from your commandments.” For not only are those subject to the bonds of the curse whom the water of baptism does not regenerate in Christ; those also are subject to it whose perversity turns aside from the straight path of God’s commandments along the abrupt paths of vice.

What, then, does it profit anyone to be released from the bonds of the ancient curse if, through a reprobate life, he is thrust back into those same bonds? For the Apostle also says: “If anyone does not love our Lord [Col. 0609A] Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: Maranatha [‘Our Lord, come’]” (1 Cor. 16). Here too it must be noted that he does not say, “If anyone is not reborn in our Lord Jesus Christ,” but “if anyone does not love him.” Thus, even if someone is shown to have been reborn in Christ through baptism, if he has not also died with him in conduct of life, he is by no means entirely released from the bonds of the curse: “For if,” according to the Apostle, “we have been grafted into the likeness of his death, we shall also be of his resurrection” (Rom. 6). And again: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Tim. 2).

But who is the person who does not love Christ? Which one of us, if asked about the love of Christ, would not immediately, indeed most readily, confess firmly that he loves Christ? Yet the person who does not love the cross of Christ does not love Christ.

And who are those who do not love Christ’s cross? Hear Paul identifying them in a clear voice: “Many walk,” he says, “of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears, who are enemies of the cross of Christ [Col. 0609B]. Their end is destruction; their god is their belly; and their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. 3).

Let James also speak: “Whoever is a friend of this world,” he says, “is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4).

Whoever, therefore, desires to be freed from every bond of the curse and to attain the full blessing of the new grace should love the cross, from which, plainly, the whole fullness of blessing flows. Through the cross let him bind himself to God’s commandments. Through the cross let him restrain the impulses of unbridled flesh. For just as by consenting to the flesh [Col. 0609C] we incur the sentence of the curse, so by disciplining the flesh we merit the grace of blessing.

From the winepress [indeed] of the cross there flowed an exceedingly abundant stream of blessing, which washed away all the poison of the ancient curse. From it, certainly, drops of heavenly charisms burst forth; these healthfully irrigate the aridity of human minds and make them fruitful with the happy harvest of every virtue. For this is that cloud which appeared to Elijah, during a time of drought, under the form of a man’s footprint, and soon afterward poured forth abundantly in a flood of rain. Thus Scripture records: “Behold,” he said, “a little cloud was rising from the sea like a man’s footprint (III Kings XVIII).”

Since it is said to have risen not like a man but like a man’s footprint, the cross—which was fitted to the Lord’s limbs—is rightly signified by this [Col. 0609D]. And the cross is aptly called a man’s footprint, because through it God, having become man, made His passage when He returned to the Father, as it is said through John: “Jesus, knowing that His hour had come, so that He might pass from this world to the Father (John XIII).” For Passover is called a passing-over. This passing-over was accomplished through the cross, as the Apostle says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed (I Corinthians V).” Therefore, just as through the Virgin He descended to what is ours, so through the cross He returned to what was His own.

This was fittingly expressed by that miracle performed under Elisha. For when wood was being cut beside the Jordan, suddenly the iron of a certain axe, as it cut through the material, fell into the water. Then the prophet threw a piece of wood [Col. 0610A] into the water, and at once the iron floated and returned to its handle (IV Kings VI). What, then, is the axe except the wisdom of God working through the body? What is the iron except divinity? What is the wood except humanity? And Christ’s body is rightly called wood, because it hung upon wood.

The axe, therefore, was cutting down trees beside the Jordan, because the wisdom of God, beside the flowing course of our mortality, deigned by the severity of its preaching to rebuke the impious Jews and, like fruitless trees, to cut them away from their position of rigid pride. Hence John also says: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew III; Luke III).”

Thus, while the wood was being cut, the iron fell from its handle into the water, because [Col. 0610B], while Truth was rebuking the savage minds of the Jews, divinity, abandoning the flesh, descended into the depths of hell. But the wood is thrown into the water and the iron returns, because the Lord’s body, which had hung upon the wood, is placed in the tomb; then, with the spirit returning, He rose from the depths of hell.

Therefore, my brothers, we must note and consider most carefully that our Redeemer Himself first passed through the cross, and thus raised His humanity to the glory of the Father’s right hand. He gave us an example, so that where the Head is known to have gone before, the members following might also walk by the same way.

We carry the cross upon our forehead; but let us store that same cross far more profitably in our heart. [Col. 0610C] Let the destroying angel see the blood on both doorposts (Exodus XII), so that he may pass by and depart excluded, rather than enter to destroy. Let no one applaud himself merely because of the sign of the cross, if he does not display the truth of the cross in his works. He had distinctly expressed the cross in his conduct who said: “For I bear the marks of Jesus in my body (Galatians VI).”

Let us therefore cleanse ourselves, dearly beloved, from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Let us gird ourselves to break the attacks of hostile vices, to resist the passions of carnal enticement, to yield graciously to the needs of our neighbors, and to endure, while preserving charity, even the insults inflicted upon us. Let our mind be free from every burden of earthly desire, so that, balanced on the wings of holy longing, it may already leave the lowest things behind [Col. 0610D] and, returning to its Author, rest sweetly in His love.

Let all that we see be loathsome to us. Let us hasten with unremitting labor toward those things that we believe. This, in truth, is the cross that we ought to impress upon our conduct and actions. This is the cross which we are commanded daily to carry after the Lord. Whoever bears it truly shares in the passion of his Redeemer. This sign separates the sheep from the goats at the final judgment (Matthew XXV). And the Judge, who does not recognize the reprobate as His own, recognizes this character in His own people. When He sees in them the mark of their own death impressed upon them, He immediately, as a gracious rewarder, invites them to the prizes of eternal life: “Come,” He says, “blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom (ibid.) [Col. 0611A],” with whom He Himself lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## 101 SERMON XIX. ON SAINT ANTHIMUS THE MARTYR (11 MAY)

When we recall, dearest brothers, the triumphant deeds of blessed Anthimus, we celebrate Christ’s victories in the one who triumphed. For it was He who fought in him; it was He who conquered—He who supplied the steadfastness of faith to his spirit, so that he would not yield to punishments, and suggested words of life to his lips, so that he might recall unbelievers and the lost from the error of their ancient faithlessness. “For,” He says, “it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matthew X).”

His body was bound with the straps of fetters, but the word of God was not bound (II Timothy II). The narrow prison shuddered with darkness, but his mind, inhabiting the halls of heavenly brightness, enjoyed blessed light [Col. 0611B], saying with Paul: “He raised us up and made us sit with Him in the heavenly places (Ephesians II).” His limbs were livid from the wounds of blows, but he said: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (II Corinthians IV).”

With such armed men our Jesus ascended into battle, Moses having died and the Jordan having been crossed—that is, with the observance of the old law brought to an end and the sacrament of baptism received. “For the law and the prophets were until John (Luke XVI),” so that the end of the Old Testament law might occur precisely where the bath of the new grace found its origin for flowing forth unto human salvation.

That Jesus, therefore, the leader of the Israelite people, both prefigured our true Jesus, the Savior of the human race, by his name and represented Him by his deed. [Col. 0611C] He was sent to destroy the nations of the Gentiles; this One came to overthrow the aerial powers. He sent two spies to Jericho (Joshua II); this One, under the sacramental significance of the same number, sent His preachers into this world. “For,” as the Evangelist testifies, “He sent them two by two before His face into every city and place where He Himself was about to come (Luke X).”

Those men were sent to investigate the situation of the places with careful curiosity; these were sent to prepare, by faith in human hearts, the way for the coming Jesus. They were received in the lodging of Rahab the prostitute (Joshua II); these rest within the Church of the Gentiles, which had fornicated with idols. Moreover, Rahab hung a scarlet cord, that is, one of blood-red color, in the window of her own house; [Col. 0611D] and the holy Church places, in a manner of speaking, the redness of blood in the window of her house, when she publicly confesses Christ’s passion with her voice and openly carries the sign of the cross upon her forehead.

Hence the bridegroom rightly says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet (Song IV).” For what are the lips of the bride understood to be except the teachers of the Church? Scarlet has the redness of blood, or the appearance of fire, which signifies charity. The lips of the Church, therefore—that is, the holy preachers—are like scarlet ribbons, because they proclaim Christ’s death and steadfastly affirm that He endured the cross’s punishment out of love for the human race.

And the order of preachers is rightly signified by a scarlet ribbon. For a ribbon binds the hair [Col. 0612A] and gathers it together, and the holy teachers, through their preaching, gather the multitude of the faithful into unity of faith and bring them together under the bond of mutual charity. Finally, whoever was found outside that house did not escape the swords; likewise, whoever is outside the boundary of the Church, which is faith, undoubtedly incurs the danger of death.

Outside this house that sacrilegious man Ceremon was found. Having received letters from imperial tyranny, he raged with insane fury against the Christians and hungered for their death with bloodstained teeth. He was suddenly seized by a demon, fell from his vehicle, and, after being tormented for a long time, died while invoking the saints whom he himself had cruelly torn apart.

To this house Pinianus [Col. 0612B] fled for refuge. As soon as he heard the word of salvation through blessed Anthimus, he believed in Christ and escaped all the affliction of the desperate illness from which he suffered. And rightly, having become a deserter from the enemy, when he joined the camp of the victorious Jesus he passed from stranger to member of the household; as a foreigner, he entered into the Israelite inheritance.

For from the mouth [work] of blessed martyr Anthimus, as though from the window of the scarlet house, a cord hung down in a certain sense, because he never ceased to make Christ’s trophy of the cross known to everyone [make it known]. Let it not seem surprising that we have described blessed Anthimus above as having come armed with the leader Jesus, and now say that he represents the house of Rahab. For, as is evident, preachers and hearers, sheep and rams alike, are gathered within one [Col. 0612C] sheepfold, just as they are known to have one Shepherd.

Moreover, blessed Anthimus, whose victories the earth had already witnessed through many contests, was plunged into the waters of the Tiber, so that his noble palm might shine forth also in another element. And, so that the fury of the executioners, bearing hearts of stone, might leave [release] nothing unattempted, they tied the weight of a stone to him, placing little trust in the heaviness of his body. But the stone mass weighs down in vain the one whom the wing of his merits lifts up. Perverse human wickedness uselessly crushes the one whom the virtue of his own holiness, reaching toward the heights [seeking lofty things], raises up.

Blessed is that fettered man who, while deprived of human assistance, is visited by an angel so that he may not become fainthearted. Blessed, I say, is that shipwrecked man who, in order to be carried from the abyss of the sea [Col. 0612D] to the safety of the shore, enjoys not the service of an earthly oarsman but is borne by the vehicle of a heavenly messenger. For an angel of the Lord came, as the account of his passion itself relates, both loosed the bond of his chains and brought the blessed martyr back to his little cell of prayer [his oratory].

Let us imitate this outstanding man, beloved, by living holily, restraining the impulses of the flesh, and despising the glory of the world. Let the martyrs go before us in their deeds, so that the holy angels may come to our aid in tribulation. For a delicate soldier is one who wishes to triumph before joining battle, and to thresh before plowing the fields.

When the order of the Scriptures is properly considered, the sequence of our actions is rightly discerned [Col. 0613A]. First comes the law, then judgment, and finally the history of the kings. Now it is necessary for us to keep the commandments of the divine law imposed upon us; afterward we are compelled to give an account of our deeds before the tribunal of the fearsome Judge; finally, we shall be granted the opportunity to reign without end in the glory of heavenly brightness.

Let him keep the order who wishes to avoid Babylon. He confuses the order of his life by living it who wishes to laugh before weeping, although Solomon says: “A time for weeping, and a time for laughing (Ecclesiastes III).” He likewise abandons the line of right order who places the Creator of all things after created things in his love. Thus the divine voice says to the perverse man: “You placed me after your body (III Kings XIV).” He places God after his body [Col. 0613B] who is more eager to provide for the usefulness or pleasure of his flesh than to keep God’s commandments.

Hence the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered charity in me (Song II).” She does not say, “He gave it,” since He did not find it; she says, “He ordered it,” because He found it disordered. For some people place wives, children, estates, or honors in the chief place of their heart; they place God, in a sense, second, by loving Him less. Such people appear indeed to have charity, but disordered charity; nor do they preserve the order of charity that Truth itself established when it says: “To love God with the whole heart is the greatest and first commandment; and the second is like it, that one should love one’s neighbor (Matthew XXII).”

Therefore [Col. 0613C], let no one boast that he has charity if it is not ordered, just as he should not boast of faith if it is without works and consequently idle (James II).

For it is written that Solomon had seven hundred wives who were queens and three hundred concubines (III Kings XI). But what have I to do with Solomon’s women’s quarters? When the chaff of the words is shaken away, a mystery is found in the marrow. For what are represented by the seven hundred who are mentioned both as wives and queens except those souls who possess the Spirit of the sevenfold grace and exercise, as it were, royal sovereignty over the movements of vices that rise up against them?

And what are represented by the three hundred concubines, who are likewise concubines, except those souls who, through faith alone in the holy Trinity, have entered the king’s chamber [Col. 0613D] but, lacking the purity of chaste conduct and, in a certain sense, matronly modesty, do not deserve the marriage documents belonging to wives? These too are joined to Solomon through carnal intercourse, because they receive the mysteries of our Savior, the true peacemaker, and yet, through the degenerate torpor of a pandering life, lacking the affection of chastity toward one husband, they do not rise to the marriage covenant’s dowry.

Those souls are worthy of the name of wife and queen who rest in the desire of the heavenly Bridegroom alone and fight without truce against the assaults of wicked spirits. As Scripture testifies concerning this same Solomon: “He made all the foreigners tributaries; but from the children of Israel he appointed no one to serve as king, for they were men of war, and his ministers, princes, commanders, and overseers of chariots and horses (III Kings IX). [Col. 0614A]”

Here it is plainly shown what difference there is between concubines and queens: what difference exists between those who pay the tribute of sin’s harsh exaction as slaves and those who, through wars brought to calm, obtain the insignia of command in battle.

Among these princes and warriors of the heavenly army, blessed Anthimus shone conspicuously. He neither yielded to the bloodstained hands of the impious in persecution, nor, when placed in peace, failed to cut down the monstrous vices that rose against him with the spiritual sword of virtues. He exposed the members of his flesh to tortures and preserved the entrails of the inner man unharmed. He did not fear to submit his head to the striking sword, so that he might deserve to cling inseparably to Christ the Head.

For faith was in him [Col. 0614B]—not faith that was dead in itself, but faith that worked through love. The faith of some is plainly vain and slack, displaying on the surface a likeness but not possessing the truth within.

Those people were prefigured by those who once came from the people of Ephraim to the fords of the Jordan. Unable to pronounce *sebboleth* (Judges XII), they instead uttered *jebboleth* as though with a foreign tongue, and were struck down by the swords of the Gileadites [*scibbolet*, *sibbolet*].

For what is signified by the Jordan, in which our Savior deigned to be baptized, except baptism? And what is to be understood by *sebboleth*, which is interpreted as “ear of grain,” except faith? For just as an ear of grain provides food for human beings, so it is said of faith: “The righteous [Col. 0614C] lives by faith (Habakkuk II; Romans I).” And just as an ear of grain conceals many grains in its awns, so the symbol of our confession gathers within itself many seeds of faith.

When the Ephraimites came to the Jordan, therefore, the Gileadites asked them how they pronounced “ear of grain”; and when catechumens come to the bath of baptism, the priests inquire how they believe. And since Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” the priests of the Church are rightly understood through the Gileadites, for by their preaching they bear witness to divine works.

Through Ephraim, however, whose name signifies “fruitfulness,” those are designated who come to the ear of faith for this reason: that they may bring forth the yield of fruitfulness through the harvest of good works. Therefore, just as those who come to the Jordan understand the ear of grain but [Col. 0614D] die because they do not know how to pronounce it, so those who seek the fountain of baptism fall utterly from life unless they also strive to utter by the proclamation of good works the faith itself that they have been taught to believe.

Thus one depends upon the other, so that the seed of faith must rise into the ear of works. Our Savior also clearly demonstrated this. For when He commanded His disciples, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” He immediately added: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you (Matthew XXVIII).”

It is as though He plainly said: “Sow the seed of faith in human hearts, and then teach them how, with the tongue of action, they ought to express the ear of the commandments that are germinating [Col. 0615A], lest they commit a solecism in the ear of their works who testify that they are from Mount Ephraim—that is, from the height of ecclesial fruitfulness”.

Therefore, beloved, let us beware lest our faith deceive us by covering us with the mere color of profession and, like an empty ear of grain with hollow stalks, swell without the marrow of love. Let us imitate the faith of the martyrs, through which they conquered earthly kingdoms and obtained the promised rewards of heaven (Hebrews XI). Let our faith therefore be solid, true, and strong, so that now, proceeding by faith, we may arrive at sight, seeing through the mirror of an enigma (I Corinthians XIII), and may one day be brought to the vision of supreme Truth itself.

There blessed martyr Anthimus, having laid down the burden of corruptible flesh, has obtained the robe of angelic brightness [Col. 0615B]. For behold, he flashes among the fiery stones of heavenly Jerusalem; behold, victorious and crowned, he rejoices among the purple-clad ranks of martyrs. Having completed the course of his glorious contest, he received as the reward of blessed recompense that very One who became both the price and the redeemer: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XX. ON SAINT BONIFACE THE MARTYR (14 MAY)

The glorious feast of blessed Boniface, my brothers, while it becomes a common joy for all Christ’s faithful [Col. 0615C], nevertheless grants sinners in particular an increase of certain hope for obtaining pardon. For when we review the deeds of his life and blessed completion, what else do we find except that straw of Tartarus became a cedar of paradise? Or, to put it so, that a coal of hell became a splendid star of heaven.

He came forth from a brothel to fight in the arena; from the arena he was suspended for torture; from torture he was led to the sword; from the sword he was lifted as victor and crowned into heaven. For this sinner returned to life by certain steps, because He who is without sin (I Peter II) likewise descended by certain steps to the depths of our mortality.

Hence, in the person of the holy Church, Solomon says: “Behold, this one comes leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills (Song II).” For our Savior displayed certain leaps [Col. 0615D] when He came to redeem the human race. He came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb; from the womb He came to the manger; from the manger He passed to circumcision; from circumcision to the temple; from the temple to baptism; from baptism to the cross; from the cross to death; from death to the tomb; finally, He also descended into hell, so that from there He might rescue His saints and, having trampled down the dominion of death, call them back to heavenly glory.

Plainly, so that He might make us run after Him, Truth made manifest in the flesh arranged these steps for us by descending to us; and, in a certain manner, Christ, the sun of justice, distinguished these moments by inclining Himself toward us like a certain mystical sundial. He rejoiced like a giant to run His course (Psalm XVIII) [Col. 0616A], so that we might say to Him from our heart: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments (Song I).”

And perhaps these are the steps of that sundial on which King Hezekiah asked that the shadow return ten lines. The prophet Isaiah, invoking the Lord as a sign of his recovery, immediately obtained this (Isaiah XXXVIII). The sun had descended after traversing the ten steps of the sundial, but it returned again by those same steps. This was to be a sign by which King Hezekiah might trust that he would be restored to his former health.

In truth, the human race did not recover from the sickness of its weakness into the safety it had lost until Christ, the true light, humbled Himself toward sunset and traversed those ten steps of the mystical sundial that we have enumerated. [Col. 0616B] Yet through the shadow of the ten steps we can also understand another mystery of the heavenly dispensation. For the distinctions of the ages are, as it were, divisions of lines on a sundial.

For Christ, the sun of justice, the first step of descent toward us was from God into an angel. Hence He is also called through Isaiah “the Angel of great counsel” (Isaiah IX). And the God who spoke with Jacob is called an angel. Hence Jacob himself says: “The angel of the Lord said to me in a dream: I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the stone and made a vow to me (Genesis XXXI).” This was clearly so that the very one who speaks might be shown to be both God and angel at once.

The second step of descent was in the patriarchs, through whom the Lord Himself established the worship of the one God and the foundations of true faith [Col. 0616C]. The third was in the promulgation of the law, which He first delivered while the people listened and afterward wrote on stone tablets by engraving them with His own finger.

The fourth was in Joshua son of Nun, in whom, just as He dwelt in the name, so also in the deed, He brought the people into the promised land. The fifth step was in the judges, through whom He Himself ruled the Israelite people. The sixth was in the kings of the Jews, because He Himself principally reigned in them.

The seventh was in the prophets, because through them He was both announced and spoke. The eighth was in the high priests, in whom He, who is the supreme High Priest, prefigured the mystery of His true and eternal priesthood. The ninth step was designated in man. The tenth was in the passion.

Through these ten steps, therefore, as through the shadow of the Old Testament, Christ [Col. 0616D], the sun of justice, descended into the sunset of our mortality. Through them, after His resurrection, He again ascended victoriously into heaven and illumined all that shadow of the ancient law with the rays of His truth and new grace—revealing what was obscure, opening what was closed, and uncovering everything hidden beneath the veil of the letter.

And just as at that time the sun had proceeded line by line and slowly, but suddenly returned to the origin of its rising, so our Redeemer suddenly disclosed, in the single glory of His resurrection and ascension, those things that He had signified concerning the mystery of His incarnation over long intervals of time.

It is not surprising, then, if blessed Boniface deserved to reach the crown by certain steps [Col. 0617A], since the Author of human salvation, out of love for us, descended to punishment as though by certain lines of His dispensation. He descended to sunset so that Boniface might return to sunrise. The Lord endured the evening of our temporality so that He might lead us back to the light of His eternity, which knows no setting.

But we must consider, my brothers, how, amid the very darkness of Boniface’s blameworthy life, the spark of holiness did not abandon him; rather, it fostered him in small things until it brought him to great ones. For, as the account of his deeds contains, he was a drunkard and an adulterer, and a friend of every vice that God hates.

We have heard the darkest shadows of depravity; let us also see a faint little spark of uprightness shining beneath them. He had, it says, hospitality, generosity [Col. 0617B], and mercy; yet these three are one and are members of one charity.

The account continues and explains what it briefly stated above: “If at any time,” it says, “he saw a stranger or someone coming from a journey, with all haste and eagerness he urged him to enter his lodging and served him. At night he went around the streets and lanes of the city, giving people what they needed.”

Behold, amid the densest thickets of bristling thorns, lilies and flowers of virtue were found, though rare. There are many wounds that weigh down the Lord’s bird upon the ground, but few feathers that lift it up. Yet it is easy for God, the physician of souls, to mend open wounds with a slight remedy and, where He finds something healthy, to restore the other things that are rotten all around to their former [Col. 0617C] health.

Moreover, just as the sea can wash the body of one person, so it is exceedingly easy for God to cleanse the soul of even the most fallen and sinful person from every filth of guilt. But just as someone remains unwashed by the waves of the sea as long as he stands on a mountain, so a sinner, as long as he persists in the swelling of pride, is not cleansed by the abundance of divine mercy, however great it may be.

Let him therefore who desires to be washed from the contagions of sin approach the fountain of mercy through repentance. And whoever asks God to show him mercy should himself also mercifully bestow the entrails of mercy upon his needy neighbors.

You see, dearest brothers, that only the work of mercy [Col. 0617D] freed this blessed Boniface from the many crimes he committed, so that he not only escaped the bonds of sins but also reached the blessed glory of martyrdom with the distinguished titles of victory.

Indeed, he was not worthy to be received by God; but by giving what was his, he deserved to give himself as a sacrifice to God. He who had until then lived carnally offered himself as a spiritual victim, as a pleasing fragrance.

Some first offer themselves and afterward what belongs to them. Thus it is written concerning the son of our first parent: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts [or: from Abel to his gifts] (Genesis IV).” For just as Abel had first offered himself to God and afterward offered his gifts, so the Lord is said to have looked first upon him and then upon his gifts.

Others first offer what belongs to them and afterward, with the aid of their merits, add themselves. [Col. 0618A] Such was Cornelius the centurion, who, while still a Gentile, persisted in almsgiving and prayers. With these things assisting him, he afterward reached the sacrament of baptism.

To him the angel, before he had received the grace of regeneration, said: “Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial in the sight of the Lord; and now send men to Joppa and summon Simon Peter. He will tell you what you must do (Acts X).”

It was as though he said plainly: “You have already offered to God what belongs to you. From now on nothing remains except that you yourself should be added as a gift far more excellent than your gifts, and that you, as the possessor, should offer yourself together with your resources, so that from all these there may now be made not a sacrifice but rather a whole burnt offering.”

Following the example of this centurion, blessed Boniface [Col. 0618B] first gave what belonged to him and afterward gave himself. For, in accordance with the precept of the law (Exodus XII), since he could not find a lamb of innocence in his own flocks, he took care to offer himself as the goat of repentance.

The innocent offer a lamb; sinners offer a goat. Nor is it surprising if any saint converted after sins is called a goat, since even He who came from heaven for sinners deigned to be prefigured by a goat.

Hence in Leviticus the high priest is commanded to offer a living goat in this manner: placing both hands upon its head, he is to confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their offenses and sins; then, invoking them upon its head, he is to send it into the desert (Leviticus XXVI).

What does it mean for the goat to be placed under both hands of the high priest except that the Son of Man, coming in the likeness of sinful flesh [Col. 0618C] (Romans VIII), was burdened by the persecution of both peoples—the Jewish and the Gentile—through the will of God? He plainly wished to be subjected to the hands of both, since He had come to free both peoples from the yoke of the devil.

And what does it mean that, after the confession and invocation of all the iniquities of the children of Israel upon its head, the goat is sent into the desert except that He who bore our sins and endured the curses of the law immediately went into the desert, where He had left the ninety-nine, and brought back the hundredth sheep? (Matthew XVIII.) Hence the Apostle also says: “To free us from the curse, He Himself became a curse (Galatians III).”

Through the goat, therefore, the Lord was prefigured, since He came for sinners. Boniface offered a kid, because after his sins he turned himself [Col. 0618D] to bearing Christ’s cross.

And because the law commands that whoever could not celebrate Passover in the first month should celebrate it in the second, while the first month is the first grace, this blessed martyr, because he had not offered the paschal lamb in the first month of an innocent life, offered a kid in the second—that is, in fruitful repentance.

While seeking to honor martyrs, he became a martyr, just as Obadiah, who was not unlike him in hospitality, while feeding the prophets in caves, himself also deserved the grace of prophecy (III Kings XVII).

You see, dearest brothers, how great is the power of almsgiving before God; consider how great is the majesty of mercy, the empress. Does it not appear like a mighty queen to stand out [Col. 0619A] among the other virtues, since from the common people it advances one man to the grace of prophecy and gives another the crown of martyrdom?

To one it grants the ability to feed the Church of Christ with the nourishment of a heavenly oracle; to another it provides the means to approach, after the palm of victory, the nuptial banquet of heavenly glory and feast there happily.

Let us therefore have mercy, brothers, so that we too may obtain mercy. Let us devote ourselves, insofar as our means permit, to almsgiving and works of piety.
