Let us delight in serving the practice of hospitality and fraternal welcome, so that, when we see the senators of the heavenly court have merited the glory of such dignity through works of piety, we may at least confidently hope to attain the forgiveness of our sins, as Truth promises, saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for [Col. 0619B] God will grant them mercy (Matthew V),” He who alone and truly lives and reigns in perfect Trinity forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT AND HIS GRACE (15 MAY)

We rejoice in your most honorable request, dearest brothers, and we count your plaintive complaints of persistence as an occasion for joy. For in these days, since we have set upon the body not only the barrier of more secluded custody but also the reins of a bold tongue, so that we might lament our own sins more familiarly, you knock, you ask, and, so that we may not shrink from bringing forth words of edification for you, you implore us with the greatest insistence.

This is especially so because recently the octave of holy Pentecost passed by, with me officiating, and therefore [Col. 0619C] you consider that you have suffered no small loss to your own salvation because you were unable, as is your usual custom, to have frequent conversation with me about the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Hence we rightly rejoice in the Lord when we see you eager and yearning for those banquets at which, because your minds’ stomachs are languishing as though badly diseased, we judge you sober and fastidious—indeed, close to death. And although true charity does not permit different sentiments among brothers, I confess nevertheless that at this moment your sorrow gladdens my heart and, so to speak, the bitterness of your sadness sweetens my breast, because the thing by which your pious mind wastes away in sorrow advances it into the joy of true salvation.

The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “Godly sorrow produces enduring salvation (II Corinthians VII).”

But you who read the homilies of the holy Fathers [Col. 0619D] and do not cease daily to devote yourselves to meditations on sacred eloquence—in what manner do you deign, amid the very depths filled by a surrounding torrent, to thirst for the contemptible water of such an arid and impoverished man, unless you are driven to this not by the love of knowledge, which puffs up (I Corinthians VIII), but rather drawn by charity, which builds up (ibid.)?

For if I were to speak to you, as you request, through the service of a flowing tongue, what else would I do except repeat in common words the very things you read? Yet because you request this so earnestly, henceforth, whenever you gather for the sacred solemnities and come from your cells, presenting yourselves to one another for the joy of the resurrection like people brought out of tombs, I wish—if you command it—to write something for you, as divine grace may dictate [Col. 0620A], according to the rudiments of my rusticity.

Thus I shall not seem entirely absent from your holy assembly; besides the things you read, I shall at least contribute something small, like wild herbs added to richly furnished dishes. In this way your desires will be satisfied, since, because I lack an artistic abundance of letters, the things I attempt to write may appear to differ only slightly from living speech.

Where, then, can we begin these matters more fittingly than with the Holy Spirit, concerning whom we see that you sigh gravely because, although you most recently celebrated His solemn feast, you did not hear a sermon from the ministry of our office?

We undertake this not timidly but confidently, because, concerning the One of whom we are about to speak, we conceive from Him the ability to speak worthily.

First, then, my brothers, we must note and [Col. 0620B] commit firmly to memory that, unless someone deserves to be inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, however much he may strive, however much he may appear for a time to exert himself, he can never rise fully to accomplish good things, nor can he bring forth the fruit of a work pleasing to God. For a tree, fixed firmly by its roots in the soil, draws juices from the moisture, and when these have spread through its interior, it both strengthens itself for growth and sends forth a shoot. We, too, are faithful trees, planted by the ordering of that supreme Cultivator within the sacred grove of the Church. Paul indicated this planting to the Ephesians when he said: “That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and founded in charity” (Eph. [Col. 0620C] 3).

Now our soil, on which the root of our hope rests, is surely that of which the Psalmist says: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. 141); or else it is the humanity of Christ, of which the same prophet elsewhere testifies, saying: “For he established the world, which shall not be moved” (Ps. 92). If, therefore, we do not wish to wither like fruitless trees, if we fear being uselessly cut down with axes and assigned to the flames, let the root of our hope remain always attached by the bond of charity in that homeland of the citizens above—in the humanity of our Redeemer—so that, for bringing forth the fruits of good works, it may grow firmly strong in the strength of fortitude.

But just as a tree immediately dries up if it is deprived of the moisture of its life-giving sap, so our soul, unless it is watered with the dew of the grace of the Holy [Col. 0620D] Spirit, will be utterly dried up and unable to bear the shoot of any holy work. For he brings light to minds, awakens desire, and pours in strength. He enlightens us so that we may see; he urges us so that we may will; he strengthens us so that we may be able to fulfill the good things we will. From that fecundity come our tears, from it the compunctions of our minds, from it the confession of sins. For just as the soul is the life of the body, so the Holy Spirit is the life of our soul. And just as our body collapses when the soul departs, so that same soul must die if the life-giving Spirit withdraws. Without his gift, indeed, we can neither reach knowledge of God by any means nor penetrate in any measure the things that are God’s, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The Holy Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2). Immediately he adds correspondingly to this statement: “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in him?” (Ibid.) So also no one has known the things that are God’s except the Spirit of God.

But perhaps you wish to ask, dearest brothers, how we can know whether we have the Spirit of God. It is established, surely, that you have the Spirit of God if you truly know God. For if, according to the apostolic words, “no one knows the things that are God’s except the Spirit of God” (Ibid.), who could know God himself unless he deserved to have his Spirit? But perhaps you still doubt whether you know God. Hear, then, the Apostle John saying: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2). He, therefore, truly knows God who keeps his commandments. Hence that perfect keeper of God’s commandments confidently said: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit of God, who is from God” (1 Cor. 2).

What, then, is the spirit of the world? Surely it is the one that persuades people to despise divine commandments, to toil eagerly at earthly affairs, to seek the summit of worldly domination, to submit shamefully to the passions of carnal enticement, to extend the boundaries of transient possessions, and, with the swollen arrogance of pride, to pursue rights of power over their neighbors. By contrast, the Spirit who is from God fills minds, urges them toward heavenly things, and, banishing the coldness of the body and negligence, sets them aflame with divine love; he restrains the desires of fleshly wantonness and suspends the free heart from every earthly delight. He makes a person stern in despising prosperity and strong in overcoming adversity; he displays him as humbly submissive to those who live well; he sets him upright, with the rights of free authority, against those who act wickedly; and, when he fills someone wisely, he makes him wisely drunk and knowingly alienates him from the perspective of the present life.

Were those not truly drunk with divine sobriety of whom the violently insane said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2)? Is it not a kind of divine drunkenness to despise all present things placed before our eyes and to yearn from the depths of the mind, with total desire, for those that are not seen; to disdain everything soft and pleasant, but willingly endure what is hard and harsh for the love of God? We must seek this drunkenness, my brothers, through the constant urgency of prayer; like people whose minds are parched, we must thirst for it with our whole attention.

Let our soul, then, seek this Spirit continually: by whose vivifying it may live, by whose enlightening it may see, by whose teaching it may be wise, and under whose guidance it may move toward the homeland along the unhindered course of love. Let us therefore ask our God for what the poor of this world ask from the rich of this world—not money, not digestible food, not clothing for a naked body. For he who forbids us to be anxious about these things knows that we need them all. Let us ask for what is most necessary for us above all else and what he takes greater pleasure in giving to those who ask. Let us ask him without ceasing, I say, for that which he himself both urges us to seek and confirms us in hoping for through a sure promise, saying: “If we ask, if we knock, it will be opened to us; and our Father from heaven will give the good Spirit to those who ask him” (Matt. 7; Luke 11).

But since we seek alms from our rich Lord, so that the opportunity of obtaining may be granted, let us borrow the manner of seeking from the poor of this world as well. For when the poor desire to receive something from those who live above them, they immediately open the mouths of their purses and, thus prepared to receive, cry out with whatever voices they can, so that, when someone is seen prepared in this way through the window of a house, he may easily obtain mercy.

Our purse, then, is our heart. If we wish to receive new gifts of heavenly grace into it, we must empty it of every earthly desire—that is, of the old leaven. We unquestionably spread open the lap of this purse if we long for heavenly gifts with the fire of perfect love. Paul had opened the mouth of this purse well when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6). He urged them also to open it when he added: “You are not restricted by us.” And shortly afterward: “As I speak to children, be enlarged also yourselves” (Ibid.).

Let us also consider how that poor man had prepared himself to receive gifts from above when he cried out, shouted, prayed, and repeated the voices of his inner instrument, saying: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56, 107). As if he openly said: “Lord, I prepare my heart to receive the gifts of your generosity; I cleanse it from every foulness of wicked thought, and nothing is left in it that would prevent your gift of grace, coming from above, from being poured into it. I have taken care to cast out the things that were badly kept within; hasten, in your graciousness, to fill it from the house of your mercy. I keep my heart emptied and prepared for you, because, having dug out from it the rubble of vices, [112] I sigh with the whole intention of my mind to embrace the grace of your Spirit.”

Behold, you hold the heart of God’s poor person ready, since you keep it clean from wicked thoughts. But unless someone who is about to extend alms to the one crying and shouting hears him from the inner rooms of a loftier upper chamber, let no one approach. After saying, therefore, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready,” he immediately added: “I will sing and make melody to the Lord” (Ibid.). It was as if he said: “I prepare my heart and send forth the voices of insistent petition, so that the voice, when heard, may move him to mercy, and so that the ready heart may not spill what is sent forth from the generosity of the merciful one.”

These two things, my brothers, are especially necessary for you who inhabit the more remote parts of the desert in pursuit of solitude, and who labor in the contemplation of the contemplative life. It is beneficial for you to devote yourselves constantly and vigilantly to the chanting of psalms and to frequent prayers, and to fight with every effort of virtue against the assaults of invading thoughts. Let us therefore eliminate every impurity from the lodging of our heart and sprinkle it, as best we can, with the various flowers of virtues. May God delight to enter the shining tabernacle of our breast and feast there upon the sweet delights of good works. And when the inner house has thus been prepared and arranged with the beautiful ornament of its decoration, let us sing psalms, pray, and invite him with supplications from our loudly crying mind, in whatever ways we can. Thus the prophetic voice will be fulfilled in us: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord.”

Let us therefore continually beseech our Redeemer and implore him with all our inmost being to deign mercifully to visit our heart and, removing every darkness of vices, to illuminate it with the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that, as that Spirit regenerates us, we may believe in him and, as he inspires us, may be able to reach him by the straight path. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the same Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## JUNE

III. Sermon on the holy martyrs Laurentinus and Pergentinus, brothers. XXIV. Sermon on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. Second sermon on the same. Third sermon on the same. XXIX. Sermon on Saint Peter the Apostle. Sermon on the holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE HOLY MARTYRS LAURENTINUS AND PERGENTINUS (3 JUNE)

[Col. 0623C]

Today’s feast, beloved, as you know, is reverently celebrated in honor of the blessed martyrs Laurentinus and Pergentinus, and their natal day is illumined as though by two golden stars. If we attend carefully to this twin star, we cannot go astray as we sail across the sea of this life; rather, after passing through the dangers of waves and storms, we shall arrive joyfully at the quiet harbor’s haven. Hence, not without some foreknowledge of heavenly arrangement, they received such names, so that they should be called Pergentinus and Laurentinus. For both go together toward the laurel, and, if we do not neglect to follow them, they who go before us summon us to the crown.

All who, not sluggish but fervent and active, hasten toward the homeland do not plant their steps in the journey; rather, by continually proceeding from virtues to virtues and striving from good things toward better things, they advance. Nor do they show themselves as citizens or inhabitants on the road of this pilgrimage, but pass through it always as guests and exiles. Hence Peter says: “I beseech you, as newcomers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires that wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2). And Paul says: “We do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one to come” (Heb. 12).

For this reason that Paul who, proceeding from Egypt, entered the promised land as a Hebrew was called “one who passes over.” And whoever enters from the Egypt of carnal life into the land flowing with milk and honey is commanded not to plant his footsteps but to pass continually, so that, according to John, “the one who is righteous may be justified still, and the one who is holy may be sanctified still” (Rev. 22). Milk flows from the flesh; honey descends from higher things into lower ones. And what is that land watered with milk and honey, to which we are summoned so earnestly, except the one person who is the Mediator of God and human beings? In him, certainly, there is both the manifest flesh that came forth from the Virgin and the inward sweetness of divinity that proceeded from the Father’s substance.

Only a Hebrew is admitted to that land—or, to put it so, no one except a Pergentinus and a Laurentinus—for whoever labors to reach Christ must by no means plant the footprint of his mind in this world as though in a dwelling place. Rather, always showing himself to be a Hebrew, let him proceed with Pergentinus along the way of justice, and with Laurentinus let him together desire from his labors not the advantages of this life but only the crown of glory.

Concerning the inhabitants of this world, as it is said in the Apocalypse, the blessed martyrs cry out: “How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. 6). But concerning those who do not dwell here, but continually pass through by proceeding onward, Isaiah first says: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; the calf, the lion, and the sheep shall remain together”; then he immediately adds: “and a little child shall lead them” [Col. 0624C] (Isa. 11).

Who is this little child except the one of whom the same prophet says: “A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us” (Isa. 9)? He leads them while they dwell together because, lest our hearts cling to earthly things, he continually inflames them with the desire for heavenly things. And this very act of leading consists in kindling us with the flame of continual charity toward his love, lest, while we love one another with reciprocal affection, we forget the one to whom we ought to return and remain in this exile in mind.

The little child, therefore, leads the troops of various animals because our Redeemer, who inseparably fuses the many kinds of human minds into fraternal unity, does not permit them to plant a foot in this world, as he sets them aflame with love for the heavenly homeland. We do not go to God on the footsteps of our feet, but by the steps of good works; nor can anyone ascend to him by an avenue of bodily effort, but through the continual growth of holy action.

Let us therefore see also how these blessed martyrs could not rest, aflame with the divine fire, but always labored to hasten from good things toward the best. Although, even before the moment of persecution, they were already of such holiness that God displayed signs and miracles through them, they were not content with this. They were dragged before the judge, and in battle they demonstrated how much virtue they had possessed in peace.

At first, the craftsman of the ancient enemy and his crafty wickedness began to deal with them, through its vessel, as though more gently; then, unable to endure their unshakable constancy, it proceeded to rage cruelly against them. With executioners raging on every side, each martyr, as though they were one mind and the same flesh, is beaten with blows, slaughtered under a mass of wounds, then handed over to prison custody and tortured by hunger.

But did divine protection fail its warriors? Did God himself not show by an unmistakable sign that he was fighting in them? For while the executioners wear them down with blows, their arms, which were raging in their strikes, wither, so that those stony breasts, alien to the bowels of compassion, might at least through the stiffness of dried-up flesh learn to possess tenderness of heart, and might understand from the bonds of their own limbs how fearful is the power against which they had fought so furiously and so savagely.

[Col. 0625B] Moreover, what a lofty merit of grace, what an indication of intimacy with God, is recognized in the fact that, while they were in prison and weakened together by a three-day fast, they were visited by an angel and received the nourishment of a heavenly table. In them Christ was hungry; in them he endured punishments; with them he was shut up in prison; with them he was in chains; with them he was their inseparable companion in torments. And he who long ago was seen as the fourth among the youths walking about in the Chaldean furnace was undoubtedly made the third with these most invincible warriors of his.

“Behold,” said the king, “I see four men unbound walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3).

Hence that persecutor Tiburtius, driven by the gall of raging anger, vomited forth flames from the furnace of his furious breast and ordered the blessed martyrs to stand barefoot upon burning coals. But immediately the coals were extinguished, and the glorious feet of the martyrs delighted in a gentle step as though upon glowing lilies or saffron-colored roses.

Nor does the fierce spirit of wickedness cease even now. It leaves nothing unattempted, but runs through every device of crafty fraud and every weapon of raging fury. Yet the more darts it hurls against Christ’s soldiers, the more brightly blind cruelty makes them shine. The more furiously the savagery of battle attacks them, the more abundant the opportunity it provides for triumph.

Thus an idol is set up, and the judge’s insane rage orders it to be worshiped. But when the almighty God, not the idol, is worshiped, the ghostly image collapses, reduced to dust. Finally, those who had disdained to bow their necks to idols gladly submit their blessed necks to the sword, and thus, dyed purple with glorious blood, return to their Emperor after victory has been accomplished.

O blessed brotherhood, which could neither be divided in conception, distinguished in birth, nor separated in the manner of its precious death—equals in punishment, coequal in glory! Together they pour forth from their mother’s womb into the world; together, when their contest in the arena is complete, they arise into heaven.

In a certain sense this birth must be called happier than Rebecca’s. For, according to the testimony of Scripture, the children struggled with one another in her womb because they were destined to live under different conditions of character and subsequent fortune. Hence it was divinely said to her: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your womb; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25).

But in these brothers there is no difference. A life that is not divided unites them, and the unanimity of indivisible charity fuses them together. This birth is also happier than that of Tamar, from whom Pharez and Zerah arose (Gen. 38). One of their names is interpreted as “division,” the other as “rising.” And just as the interpretation of their names differs from one another, so there is a certain difference in the works of each; nor do they possess the same mystery in the figure.

But these blessed martyrs do not differ in the interpretation of their names, because what they signify is, in a certain sense, one, and the name of either agrees with both. For Pergentinus and Laurentinus both proceed toward the laurel; and since their way is one, their desire is one. Proceeding together, they arrive at the crown.

Nevertheless, as their history testifies, a certain difference is found even between these two. When violence dragged them before the tyrant, Pergentinus entrusted the duty of answering to his brother because he judged him more eloquent, so that he might speak like Aaron to Pharaoh while they stood before the governor.

The difference between these twins of blessed brotherhood is therefore like that which Scripture records between Moses and Aaron. One of them complains about himself, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither from yesterday nor the day before, nor from the time when you spoke to your servant; I am slow and hesitant of tongue” (Exod. [Col. 0626C] 4). Of the other it is said: “Aaron your brother, the Levite—I know that he is eloquent; he shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth” (Ibid.).

Thus the blessed martyrs, insofar as they are found to have been unlike each other in this respect, appear in a certain way to have been equals to Moses and Aaron. And perhaps not inappropriately. For just as through those men the Law was once given to the Israelite people, so through these men the Christian faith and the Gospel shone upon the citizens of Arezzo.

When pagan ritual still bristled with deadly force and the fury of persecution against the Christian name was boiling savagely—at the time when the blessed Donatus reddened the Church of Arezzo with his precious blood—Julian was the twentieth emperor, under whom the blessed Donatus, a distinguished martyr, shone forth, while it was under the emperor Decius that the persecution crowned these glorious martyrs.

And if you carefully run through the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, you will find that from the blessed Sixtus, whom the rage of Decius was compelled to serve while it raged, down to Pope Liberius, who presided in the time of Julian, twelve pontiffs preceded him in the apostolic see.

Since, then, these glorious martyrs are known to have preceded the blessed Donatus by so long a time, they are rightly called, in the regions where they suffered, leaders of believers, princes of the faithful, and, so to speak, founders of the entire Church of Arezzo. They are now gleaming gems and shining pearls, radiant with splendid brilliance in the diadem of the eternal Emperor and flashing with undying splendor among the fiery stones of heavenly Jerusalem.

Moreover, just as the twin lights of the eyes, set in the head, adorn the body’s limbs beneath them, so the blessed Donatus, with these two stars of heaven, as the head of holiness and the beginning of faith, surpasses all the neighboring places and, so to speak, suffuses the whole body of Tuscany with the brightness of exceptional splendor. They are now conspicuous with the brilliance of such eminent glory precisely because they had been pressed down by the more grievous savagery of the raging persecutor. Thus they were transferred from punishments to glory and from combat to the crown.

Jesus Christ our Lord himself became their reward when he received them—the one who had offered himself as their price when he redeemed them; he lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. I. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST (24 JUNE)

[Col. 0627B]

Today, beloved, a distinguished day has dawned, holier than the other days to the extent that it brought forth upon the earth a holier man. On this day was born that radiance of the saints, the glory of the righteous, the joy of the angels, the most excellent of human beings, Christ’s kinsman, the Bridegroom’s friend, and the preparer of the Bride.

He is unique and has no equal; interwoven with the angelic choirs, he surpasses the ascent of the whole human race by the titles of a higher crown. Finally, “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11).

Happy is the man who, traversing the workshops of heaven in happiness, follows the Redeemer at swiftest speed and is blocked by no pinnacle of dignity—he whom the immensity of supreme happiness has watered so abundantly! The angels rejoice, and the multitude of both natures marvels at a human being who entered the abyss of light and was so absorbed into the sea of eternal divinity that he even reflects the source of angelic purity.

Let all be exalted and rejoice before the tribunal of majesty in the prerogatives of their merits; nevertheless, no one will dare aspire to the privilege of John the Baptist. Come, then, let us approach the marks of virtue that the God of majesty has gloriously heaped upon his friend and stamped upon him. For he lived among human beings from the rising of life to its setting in such a way that the pattern of life may be regarded as an instruction in conduct.

And although the beauty of golden speech does not glitter here, we shall nevertheless attempt to touch upon the truth of events with whatever sort of style we possess, mindful of the saying of the Wise One: “Prudent men do not delight in ornamented things, but in strong ones” (Eccl. 9).

[117] His first honor is glory in the annunciation. We must not pass over in concealed silence how solemnly the entrance of this child into the world was announced. The angel Gabriel is present, and the strength of the Lord, descending from the upper hinge of heaven, stands at the right side of the altar of incense (Luke 1)—not any angel, but that higher one who brought the singular message to the blessed Virgin and was chosen to announce the soldier who was to announce the King (Ibid.).

The priest stands there clothed in priestly garments and in the varied richness of his vestments, prefiguring the image of heavenly mysteries; he foreshadows the purification of sins through the sprinkling of mystical blood. He stands before the ark of the covenant and before the tablets of the testimony, the golden urn holding manna, Aaron’s rod, the cherubim, and the mercy seat. Solemnly adorned with the priestly headdress, he celebrates vows before the face of God, the glory of majesty, the Lord of all things.

The solemn day arrives, more celebrated than other days among the multitude of the Jews, exalted by the testimony of the Lord’s command—plainly splendid and festive—the day on which alone the high priest was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies and, by manifold sprinkling, cool the wrath of the supreme divinity.

People gather from every side in the holy city, and the more numerous crowd of peoples increases the material for joy. Amid these sacred rites the archangel says: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah” (Ibid.), because a son will be born to you: the joy of his parents, the nobility of his race, the example of the world, the end of the Law, the beginning of the Gospel, the expulsion of death, the gate of life, the adornment of human beings, the splendor of conduct, and the principate of all justice.

And lest we confuse the excellence of events through a more extended treatment, the integrity of his birth and conduct is set forth more fully in the Gospel books.

Consider the sublimity of the messenger, the dignity of the place, the reverence of the day, and then you will be able to understand with what surpassing glory the birth of John the Baptist is proclaimed. Let the reverence due to the Redeemer be preserved: we do not dishonor the King if we honor the King’s soldier, since the one is Lord and the other servant; the one Creator, the other creature. John is announced with a more dignified foretelling than Christ.

Perhaps Christ was announced in a bridal chamber, John in the temple—and not merely in the temple, but before the Holy of Holies on their distinguished solemn day. John is proclaimed by the same archangel, in a more dignified place, at a more sacred time, and with a more evident miracle.

Recall Isaac, announced by angels (Gen. 18), and Samson, proclaimed through an angel (Judg. 13); survey the whole sect of the Nazirite, and you will find the Baptist alone more distinguished both in this respect and in others.

The second honor is sanctification in his mother’s womb. All of us who enter the world from the sinful mass drag with us the long chain of original sin. Only the one who committed no sin (1 Pet. 2) is excepted: the one whom the Virgin’s bridal chamber brought forth to the earth without the intervention of a man. He was conceived in a wholly different and dissimilar manner, with the Holy Spirit in all his majesty flooding and cleansing the Virgin, surpassing the use of the flesh, the order of nature, and the union of a man.

For it was fitting that the one who took away sins should not know sin, that he should assume the likeness of sinful flesh but not sinful flesh. Since, therefore, all are conceived in iniquities (Ps. 50), we read of no mortal ever sanctified within his mother’s womb except Jeremiah and John the Baptist. There is, of course, no ambiguity concerning the unique Virgin: enclosed within her mother’s womb, she was herself cleansed by a higher kind of sanctification, since she was that sanctuary in which God, the Son of God, was to assume flesh.

But Jeremiah’s sanctification was far less than John’s. Jeremiah was sanctified in his mother’s womb; John is known to have been filled with the Holy Spirit. For it is much more excellent to be filled with the Holy Spirit than to be sanctified. In the former case, sanctification signifies cleansing; in the latter, fullness signifies an overflowing.

Finally, even the apostles, who handled with their hands the Word of life (1 John 1), after receiving the Holy Spirit through the breath of the Savior (John 20), could scarcely reach that degree by the fiftieth day after the resurrection that it might be said of them: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2). And although the Holy Spirit then filled the hearts of believers with a more abundant gift, John is read to have attained in the womb what the apostolic height eventually deserved to obtain through a more abundant promise.

Attend carefully, I beg you, to the ordered arrangement by which that manifold Spirit sanctifies Jeremiah, fills John, and comes upon Mary. Jeremiah’s sanctification is indeed marvelous: although he was conceived in sin, he was nevertheless born without sin. For he was sanctified before he came forth from the womb, and he could not be born unsanctified who had been sanctified in his mother’s womb. It is a wondrous thing, unheard of in the centuries past: that a human being conceived in sins should be born without sin.

But John was filled by a far more glorious power. He was sanctified from sin and so suffused by the ruling Spirit that he came forth both cleansed and filled. Truly great before the Lord is he whom the angel announces, whom God sanctifies, whom the Holy Spirit fills, and whom his life commends.

In a still more ineffable manner the Spirit comes upon the Virgin, whom the whole fullness of divinity poured over without measure, so that she might contain the one who made all things; so that she might be believed not only to have been washed from sins and filled with the Spirit, but also to have conceived from the Holy Spirit, because “what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1).

Hence, by a unique prerogative, the catholic faith confesses that the Son of God was born from the Virgin and conceived from the Spirit, so that the indivisibly united connection of divinity and humanity might be indicated by the indistinction of the terms. You see, therefore, by what more remote privilege the one who is “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44) was distinguished from the sons of men in his conception. They were conceived from sins and in sins; he was conceived in the Spirit and from the Holy Spirit.

These things have been said about John’s conception, prejudging nothing against what a sounder judgment may hold. But even if they appear in some respect to conflict with the authorities of the saints, we wish them to be overthrown without the support of any excuses or defenses.

The third is excellence in exultation. From the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone exulted in his mother’s womb, whereas this child is read to have exulted in joy. Utterly astonishing is the condescension: that a child scarcely conceived should burst into a movement of exultation and gratefully meet, with sweeter service, the one whom he perceived to have been infused into virginal substance.

Blessed is the soul that did not stand in the way of sinners, but, emerging by a more secret path from the workshops of heaven, received the sweetness of unheard-of rejoicing. Happy is Elizabeth, to whom the mother of the Redeemer hastens, whom the Queen of heaven addresses with a greeting of salvation.

But far happier is the child who, recognizing the majesty of the one who greets him, rejoices within the dark folds of the womb because he perceives the power of so blessed a greeting. “And it happened,” he says, “that when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the infant leaped for joy in her womb” (Luke 1).

The Virgin hastens into Zechariah’s house to greet Elizabeth, carrying in her womb the Son of God, the King of glory, the Lord of majesty. Elizabeth comes to meet her, freed from the reproach of her former sterility, carrying in her most fortunate womb the Bridegroom’s friend and the herald of the Word.

Embraces join them, they come to kisses, their blessed wombs are united, and only two most tender walls separate the King and his soldier. What wonder if the child marvels and exults when touched by such nearby divinity? Could anyone be free from some miracle when the presence of the King, the Mother of the Ruler, and the Redeemer of the world were present?

Moreover, the union of such holy embraces was celebrated not only once. “Mary remained with her for about three months,” says the evangelist (Ibid.). For so long the virginal integrity remains with Elizabeth, now consecrating and marking the infant John with sweeter conversation, now with a happier embrace.

And perhaps the glorious Virgin stayed with her kinswoman until the day of his birth, until she might warm the newborn child in her most blessed lap and, with one wall removed, bring him closer to the presence of the Creator. It is easy to infer this from the Gospel, because six months had already passed from John’s conception when the archangel was sent to the Virgin, carrying to virginal modesty, through a new greeting, the renewal of the world.

From that point the Virgin hastens to Elizabeth and, for three months, deigns to provide her kinswoman with the hospitality of her presence, until, when the end of the ninth month has been completed, the patriarch’s birth draws near.

Others who have examined the Book of the Just with more attentive eyes testify that they saw there that the Mother of God herself first lifted the blessed child from the ground and attended the birth of her kinswoman with every service. However the truth of this matter may be determined, this at least is entirely certain: that such a happy and prolonged hospitality of the undefiled Mother contributed greatly to the child who was about to be born.

### Fourth: joy in the nativity

“Blush, Lucifer, who were rising at dawn” (Isa. 14), and at last understand, with the impulses of your attempts shattered, that in the last days you will remain like the most foolish partridge. Through your machinations it came about that the whole human race was conceived in sins and born in sorrow (Gen. 3). But behold: this man is sanctified in the womb, rises in joy, and by his birth pours gladness back upon the world. Behold the kind of weaponry you had prepared for victory: for John it is born for a crown. Take up arms and shield, and rage with all the spirit of your malice; nevertheless, you will not be able to break through John’s privilege, which the kindly hand of the writer has attested in its own script. You have been greatly deceived, greatly deluded. Do you not know that a warrior rises against you from his youth, and even from his mother’s womb [Col. 0631A]? Do you not know that from the days of this man “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11)? Have you forgotten that he is sent to prepare for the Lord a perfect people (Luke 1)? Consider the order of events, and from the very beginnings of his conception you will find that he broke through your strength with a more powerful assault.

You caused Cain, the fratricide who was born first (Gen. 4), to emerge polluted and wrapped in corruption, sprinkled with the disgrace of original sin. A terrified world received him, and the birth that followed for the human race passed over into an accumulation of infinite sorrow. But the birth of this man is in joy and in splendid solemnity. The world rejoices, and the four regions of the earth resound with the approach of glorious festivity; even the heavens celebrate it with renown and fame. “What, do you suppose, will this child be?” The Bridegroom’s friend, your enemy, more powerful than you are in your own power.

One must consider with what dignity the devout celebration of this birth excels, and how great a grace it was able to find in the eyes of the Church. The Church has admitted the nativity of no human being into the citadel of authority, except that of God and of his mother, while preserving this man as an exception. For it knows that “the day of death is better than the day of birth” (Eccl. 7), and that the birth of human beings is accompanied by sorrow. Hence the Church solemnizes the deaths, not the births, of the martyrs, calling their deaths “nativities,” since through death a birth was made for them. They began then to be born into life, when they laid down their lives for Life. But the bride of Christ received this man’s nativity with benevolent devotion all the more securely because the unassailable authority of evangelical truth commends it in a uniquely singular manner [Col. 0631C].

### Fifth: singularity in conversion and conduct during the years of childhood

For this blessed child John was led into the desert, under the guidance of the Spirit; nor did the weakness of age stand in his way, since the majesty of the Lord made it fruitful. The Holy Spirit does not consider differences of sex, the frailty of bodies, or the length of years; rather, whomever and however he wills, he fills with his most gracious kindness.

John leaves the world, flees human beings, knows no homeland, spurns his parents, and fixes his gaze in blessed contemplation upon the summit of divinity alone. What a marvelous reversal of affairs: for a man scarcely entered into the world to flee the world’s glory, and not only to forget the desires of the age but not even to know them, and to establish a perpetual fellowship with divinity. The mountain retreats, the winding recesses of the forests, and the waste lying beneath the valleys provided dwellings for the child-patriarch.

Let no one set Jeremiah against me, nor let the virtue of the preaching child dare to oppose this claim: if Jeremiah was consecrated as a prophet (Jer. 1), John was consecrated as more than a prophet (Matt. 11). And although Jeremiah proclaims the future to the people, he does not withdraw from the sight of human society. Thus, yes, thus John, having passed beyond the infancy of his age and forgotten the nobility of his noble lineage, gives himself wholly to divinity: the pattern of the monastic life, the beginning of the anchorites, the affirmation of the whole religious life. This is enough concerning his conversion [Col. 0632A].

But how sublime his conduct was must not be discussed with the pleasures of a hurried tongue; it must be demonstrated by the eloquence of evangelical dignity. “John,” it says, “had a garment of camel’s hair, and a leather belt around his waist; his food was locusts and wild honey” (Matt. 3). “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11). Rigid clothing, woven throughout with the harshest roughness, afflicts the patriarch’s body with abrasive severity and constrains his tender flesh with the untimely ferocity of discipline; the long duration of uninterrupted martyrdom shakes his tender limbs, which had been suffused with a more sacred spirit.

And what was his food like? No pheasant birds are sought, nor does anyone travel through the whole region in order to fill the patriarch’s stomach. “His food,” it says, “was locusts and wild honey.” He is nourished by the dew of heaven and satisfied with the food of a most insignificant animal; the austerity of his fasting accepts nothing cooked. His stomach, chastened and distended by prolonged mortification, knew no variety of dishes; nothing entered his mouth that might entice the palate, suffice for the belly, or flatter the stomach. Elijah ate meat (3 Kgs. 17), and whatever else was set before him he received with thanksgiving; nor, unless I am mistaken, do we read that anyone in the old workshop of the law aspired to the summit of this observance. Rough clothing, scant food, and a devout mind consecrate the perfect patriarch [Col. 0632B].

### Sixth: novelty in preaching

Here I want your attention to be especially attentive, because the magnitude of the subject requires that its treatment begin somewhat more subtly. After Adam’s sin and the solemn devastation of that flood, an innumerable multitude of righteous men was chosen, with whom God is known to have spoken face to face. Enoch is translated (Gen. 5), Noah is chosen (Gen. 6), Abraham is called (Gen. 12), Isaac is loved (Gen. 17), Jacob contemplates God face to face (Gen. 33), and Joseph is called the Savior of the world (Gen. 41). Yet no mention is made, either by God to them or by them to human beings, of an everlasting dwelling in the kingdom of heaven.

Moses is taken up as leader of the Jewish people (Exod. 3) and is appointed as a god to Pharaoh. God performs great deeds in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and terrors in the Red Sea (Exod. 7–8, etc.). Moses ascends into the darkness in which God was. On the mountain he is given the authoritative multiplicity of the commandments. He speaks with God as a man speaks with his neighbor. Nothing that the Lord does in secret is hidden from Moses, and the glorious name Adonai, which had been veiled from everyone, is revealed (Exod. 4, etc.). But amid all these things the kingdom of heaven is neither named nor heard of.

Aaron, the high priest, bearer of the mighty staff, anointed and drenched with the anointing of heavenly mysteries, stands before them. Joshua succeeds him, together with that whole multitude of judges, yet there is not even the slightest mention of the kingdom of heaven (Joshua, book). The Lord finds David, a man after his own heart (Ps. 88), and fills his son Solomon with singular wisdom (3 Kgs. 3); and the Holy Spirit orders and pours himself into the whole prophetic choir, yet nothing is prophesied concerning the glory of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0633A]. Elijah shuts the heavens for three years and six months (3 Kgs. 17); Elisha, though dead, restores a dead man to life (4 Kgs. 4); yet from these men not even a spark of the blessed dwelling shines forth.

Why say more? From the beginning of the world up to John, review the whole election of the human race, and you will not be able to find in the speech or deeds of that sanctuary any sweetness concerning this matter. Come, then, to John, and hear the voice of exultation, the voice of novelty, the voice of joy, the word of mercy, the speech of glory, the abundance of grace—what God had concealed, the angel had kept silent about, the patriarchs had not known, and the prophets had been ignorant of: “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. 3).

The word of repentance is sweet, and the glorious word of the kingdom of heaven is joyful and worthy of adoration, fitting only for that chief man who first laid the foundations of the New Testament. This is that voice of which the great contemplator of heavenly visions continues in these words: “And the voice that I first heard was like that of harpists playing their harps” (Rev. 14).

From the days of Adam until John, our instrument had been turned into the voice of mourners, because there, amid the multitude of sins, there was no place for repentance, and the material for lamentation was doubled. Do you kill? You are ordered to be killed. Do you gather wood on the Sabbath? You are ordered to be stoned (Num. 15); and he whose proper nature is always to show mercy and spare knew nothing except striking. The betrayer of commandments had given them commandments that were not good, and statutes by which they could not live (Ezek. 20). This is what the righteous man wonders at when he says: “Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?” (Ps. 88).

John, once born, showed the medicine for the wound: repentance for sin, pardon for iniquity. This is the first voice that the voice of one crying in the wilderness (Matt. 3) proclaimed: “And the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2). From that time he put into our mouth a new song, a hymn to our God (Ps. 39), and thanksgiving and the voice of praise resound in our mouths. Mercy is exalted above judgment; sinners are spared; compassion reigns; justice is passed over; and the merciful and compassionate Lord seeks an opportunity to show mercy rather than to strike.

Those “play their harps on their harps” who beat back the outpouring of pleasures with the rigor of repentance. Breathing again from the deep abyss of sins, with Pharaoh drowned, they sing in the ways of the Lord, “for great is the glory of the Lord” (Ps. 137) [Col. 0633D].

### Seventh: dignity in baptism

Utterly singular was the humility by which the Word made flesh, emerging as a fully grown man, left the whole human race behind and sought John, desired John, and went to John. God is “terrible in his counsels over the sons of men” (Ps. 65), and, bearing all things by the word of his power and making purification for sins (Heb. 1), he came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.

John is astonished and shaken with fear, and infinite dread overwhelms the whole patriarch. “I,” he says, “ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matt. 3). The Savior replies: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid.). Both yield to these saving instructions, and John girds himself to baptize and to receive the Lord of angels.

The King of glory, the radiance of light, the form of God’s substance, removes his garments and is handled by John’s hands. That flesh taken from the Virgin, derived from a purer substance, is stripped bare in the river, to be poured over by the blessed hands of the Baptist. The angels descend, and all the hosts of heaven run with complete reverence toward the Creator; the ruling powers surround him, both baptizing and baptized. A nobler creature pours water over the Creator’s head, and a mortal hand touches and handles the crown of God. Heaven trembles, earth is astonished, the Jordan smiles, and the archangels marvel that the Lord Sabaoth is enclosed within the hands of the baptizer [Col. 0634B].

What is this, John? The cherubim and seraphim scarcely dare to look upon him, yet you presume to hold him naked! This is the one into whom angels long to look (1 Pet. 1); to whom the assembly of the blessed city repeats “Holy, holy, holy” with the exalted music of its melodies (Isa. 6; Rev. 4); who alone dwells in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6), Lord of hosts, God of knowledge, Father of mercies—and you are not afraid! To you has been given what has been denied to all others: to baptize the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire, and with virginal hands to sprinkle the Virgin’s Son.

I am wholly astonished at the baptizer; I revere the human teacher of God; I admire the one who deigns to do this; I venerate his condescension; and I see a human being inflicting violence upon heaven itself [Col. 0634C].

Moreover, what is the significance of the fact that in this baptism the law comes to an end, prophecy reaches its conclusion, and that whole multitude of sacrifices is thrust aside and driven away? Here begins and is established the purification of the new birth, which is to endure; and the expenditures of the legal figures pass over into one form of baptism. At the washing with water and invocation of the Holy Spirit, the bloodstained mass of goats and calves is buried, and we leave the cattle to the cattle-loving Jews, attending to David’s words: “You did not desire burnt offering or sin offering” (Ps. 39).

### Eighth: the first revelation concerning the Trinity

From the creation of heaven and earth until this moment, the Trinity had never appeared openly to human beings; rather, the eternity of such immense clarity had been wrapped in the coverings of things and words. Finally, when the Creator of all things commends the creation of humanity with the highest dignity, he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Truly a privilege worthy of reverence, and one granted to no other creature.

The exalted multitude of angels is created, and the varied interconnection of all the elements is ordered; yet the presence of the Almighty merely observes this work in profound silence. But when he comes to humanity, and the noble creature is destined to be created, the Trinity girds itself to create, and Wisdom takes counsel, so that the dignity of the creature may be shown to be bright with the Creator’s privilege.

Even there, however, the names of the divine majesty did not shine forth clearly enough, since some refer the oracle of the divine speech to the attending angels; or, if this is not sufficiently well guarded, they proclaim a marked plurality without distinction of names. Abraham saw three and worshiped one (Gen. 18). But there too the reverence of sacred Scripture closes its discourse, now collectively and now separately, so that it is pleased at one moment to call them “the Lord” and at another “men.”

The Jews, however, weave here a lengthy tale of criticism, asserting that three angels were sent by the Lord: one to announce the birth of Isaac and two to overthrow Sodom. They dream that the one with whom the righteous man spoke, saying, “Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes” (ibid.), was recognized by him in a prophetic spirit as the herald who had come to announce Isaac’s birth. He worships him, just as Bathsheba did King David, and out of reverence for him remains tirelessly present with his companions (2 Sam. 3). Hence only two are counted in the overthrow of the unhappy cities, the one who had already returned above after faithfully accomplishing the announcement of Isaac’s birth.

Three men command Sarah to be called, but one of them reveals the mystery of the unexpected promise. Such are the Jews, and those who have preferred to Judaize rather than believe.

But, to conclude briefly, that whole united company of patriarchs and prophets is found to have made no open mention, either in words or in deeds, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Come, then, and behold the son of Zechariah holding God and man in his own hands. See that the heavens are opened there, and that the Holy Spirit descends in bodily form like a dove upon Christ; and hear the Father’s voice: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3) [Col. 0635C].

Do you see that the palaces of heaven are opened at the novelty of these most sacred names? The Father is heard in the voice, the Son is baptized in the river, and the Holy Spirit is shown in the form of a dove. John stands in the midst of the whole Trinity, and the personified names of the undivided substance sanctify the glorious Baptist. The name of the Trinity, veiled in earlier ages, shines forth without the shadow of any covering.

“Lord, who is this, that you have made yourself known to him?”

### Ninth: testimony of wisdom

When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent his disciples to him, and they received the answer: “The blind see,” and so forth (Matt. 11), as the abundant narrative of evangelical truth continues. After the messengers had departed, lest he seem to be uttering flattery in their presence, Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (ibid.).

O marvelous testimony of the Redeemer! Who has entered the world and not known the world in some respect? Who is not bent by fickle prosperity, troubled adversity, or even the slightest breath of any sin? Finally, it is added that he surpasses the earth, passes beyond heaven, and reaches the very summit of angelic dignity: “Among those born of women, no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (ibid.).

What more do you want? Augustine says that nothing said of anyone else could be said as it was said of John. Do not set against me the evangelist who was more beloved than the other apostles; nor the chief of the apostles, placed before all the apostles; nor the Chosen Vessel, translated into the secrets of the third heaven. Nor should apostolic splendor dare to confront the Forerunner, since all those men had already passed beyond the limits of youth when Truth declared: “Among those born of women, no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” [Col. 0636A].

Consider the dwelling places of the kingdom and walk through the whole order of human generation; you will see that John alone has been set above both the new and the old.

### Tenth: the affirmation of Mother Church

The fringe of the cloak is woven, and ointment poured out upon the head flows down abundantly even to the edge of the garment. For that mother and teacher of all the churches, the Roman Church, to which it was said, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22), has been consecrated and marked in honor of John the Baptist, after the name of the Savior.

It was fitting that the authority of the bride should follow the judgment of the Bridegroom and advance his singular friend to the place where she herself has ascended to primacy. Beyond doubt, it was a singular election that in that very city John should claim primacy in the Church—the John whom two lights of heaven consecrated by their most glorious deaths. Peter is crucified; Paul is beheaded; the dignity remains with the Forerunner. Rome is made purple by its multitude of martyrs, and its entire sublimity is poured back upon the blessed patriarch.

John is everywhere greater, singular in all things, marvelous above all. Who was announced in such glory? Who, as we read, was so specially filled with the Holy Spirit in his mother’s womb [Col. 0636C]? Whom have you read of leaping in his mother’s womb? (Luke 1.) Whose nativity have you seen the Church of God celebrate? Who desired the desert as a child? Who is recorded to have conducted himself so sublimely? Who first displayed repentance and the kingdom of heaven? Who baptized the King of glory? To whom did the Trinity first reveal itself? To whom did God give such testimony? Whom did the Church honor in this way? See whether all these things are not so singularly singular in him that no mortal dares aspire to the dignities mentioned above.

Perhaps you are preparing to object to me that these qualities are so proper to John that he does not touch upon the other attributes common to the saints. Hear, then: John is a patriarch—indeed, the end and head of the patriarchs. John is a prophet—indeed, more than a prophet, because he points out with his finger the one whose coming he announces [Col. 0636D]. John is an angel, and even the chosen among angels, as the Savior testifies when he says: “Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare my way before my face” (Matt. 11). John is an apostle, and even the first and chief of the apostles, because “there was a man sent from God” (John 1). John is an evangelist, and even the first reaper of the Gospel, proclaiming the Gospel of the kingdom. John is a virgin—indeed, the mark of virginity, the title of chastity, the example of purity. John is a martyr, and even the light of martyrs, a most steadfast model of martyrdom between the birth and death of Christ.

I pass over the fact that he is “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isa. 40), because he is the herald of the Word and the Forerunner of the Judge. I also leave aside the fact that the law and the prophets lasted until John, that John himself is Elijah, that he is a burning and shining lamp, and that he is the Bridegroom’s friend and the preparer of the Bride. I pass over in silence the fact that he has been inserted into the nine orders of angels in such a way that he is even transferred to the summit of the seraphim.

But this belongs to a laborious work, and the poverty of our understanding is insufficient for it. For the present, let these things suffice—things said about John’s praise for the glory of the Redeemer, who is God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON XXIV. II. ON THE NATIVITY OF ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST (24 JUNE)

Today’s feast, beloved, conspicuous throughout the whole world, illumines our minds with the brighter splendor of a new light, since it also invites us to recall the beginning of our redemption and the rising of the true light. For when someone meditates upon John’s nativity, whose birth does not immediately come to mind—especially since there was no other reason why John should be born of an aged father and a barren mother except that, born wondrously, he might go before the one who was to be born uniquely?

The friend should go before the Bridegroom, the servant before the Lord, the voice before the Word, the lamp before the Sun, the herald before the Judge, the saved man before the Savior. John himself bears witness that this was the reason for his coming: he did not come simply to appear, but to precede the Lord as a sign of his manifestation. “After me,” he says, “comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me; and I did not know him. But so that he might be manifested in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water” (John 1).

He preceded him by being born, by preaching, by baptizing, by dying, and finally also by descending into the underworld. Thus he preceded the Lord, and he preceded himself.

Before he was conceived in the womb, disbelief closed his father’s mouth; but before he himself could speak, he wonderfully opened it by the expression of his name. Indeed, although he was not yet able to utter words to human beings, by leaping he was able to announce the King of heaven, hidden in the Virgin’s womb, through his mother’s womb. For the Holy Spirit, who animated him before he drew the breath of life, also filled the dwelling of his mother’s modesty in which he lived. Hence Elizabeth says: “Behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke 1) [Col. 0637D].

Here one must ask how it could happen that the Holy Spirit poured out his gifts upon John, since, according to the custom of human condition, he still existed conceived in iniquities and had not yet loosened the bond of original sin by receiving the circumcision required by the law, when the divine voice says through Moses: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall perish from my people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. 17).

But it must be noted that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not bound by the law or held by the bond of necessity. Rather, just as he breathes where he wills, so he freely distributes his gifts to whomever he wills. For he inspired the centurion Cornelius before he received the washing of baptism (Acts 10); and upon some who were still Gentiles, while Peter was speaking, he not only fell, as Scripture testifies, but also instructed them so that they might speak in tongues (ibid.).

What wonder, then, if the Holy Spirit filled [replevit, ‘filled’] blessed John before any remedy of the legal commandment, when divine providence appointed him as a certain boundary—and, so to speak, an impassable limit—of the law itself, of the prophets, and of the whole Old Testament? For, as Truth says, “the law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. 11).

This John indeed received circumcision in his own flesh together with the Lord, but by receiving it he brought it to an end. And therefore, since he shone forth as the herald and magnificent announcer of the new grace, he did not need circumcision in order to escape original sin; rather, divine election raised him above the law and above the order of human condition. To him was also granted the glory of such great honor that the very Mother of God was present at his nativity, and the Creator of the world dedicated its beginning, hidden in the womb, by his presence.

The evangelist Luke bears witness to this when he says: “Mary remained with her”—namely, Elizabeth—“about three months, and returned to her own house” (Luke 1). From the conception of the Lord until the nativity of blessed John there are three months. Mary therefore did not wish to depart until she had diligently provided service to the aged woman and mother in childbirth, and until she had seen the herald go before the one whom she carried as King in the palace of her body. Blessed is the birth received by that light which illumines every person coming into this world (John 1)!

But as we speak of these things, a question suddenly arises that seems, not without reason, to introduce doubt. For the Lord testifies that “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11). He excluded one who was greater, but did not deny one who was equal. Hence the angel says to Zechariah: “He himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1). John therefore seems equal to Elijah, in whose spirit and power he is asserted to come—especially since Truth itself says elsewhere: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished” (Matt. 17:12); and, if you wish to know, John himself is Elijah.

But, on the other hand, there is the fact that Elisha received Elijah’s spirit doubled, in accordance with the manner of his request: “I beg you, Lord, let your spirit be doubled in me” (2 Kgs. 2). If Elisha surpasses Elijah twofold, how can he not surpass John, who is said to be equal to Elijah, when no one greater than John has arisen among those born of women?

Nevertheless, in order to resolve the question, the meaning must be weighed, so that a sober judgment may understand that what sounds harsh in the outward words proceeds from a devout intention. It sounded harsh that Elisha asked for a double portion of his master’s spirit, since “the disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10). But this request proceeded from a pure mind, because he asked not for something earthly but for spiritual grace.

Hence Elijah, as though somewhat indignant, rebuked the words of his disciple when he said: “You have asked for a difficult thing” (2 Kgs. 2). Yet, looking upon the simplicity of his devout intention, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, it will be granted to you as you asked” (ibid.). It was not a doubling produced by the careless wording, but the gift of the Spirit that he sought with humble and sincere intention of mind.

In this way, then, Elisha in no way surpasses John, just as he is not greater than Elijah. Nevertheless, if we examine carefully the course of sacred history, we find Elisha more abundant, or more illustrious, than Elijah in the power of miracles. Elijah, while still alive, restored a dead child to life (3 Kgs. 17); Elisha, already dead, raised a dead man (4 Kgs. 13). While Elijah was prophesying, the jar of flour and the jug of oil did not fail (3 Kgs. 17); Elisha immediately supplied a besieged and afflicted city with incredible abundance from the enemy camp for the following day (4 Kgs. 6).

And, to conclude everything briefly, Elijah shone forth in twelve miraculous signs, while Elisha, as the truth of Scripture relates, shone forth in twenty-four. Since we wish to avoid tediousness, we postpone enumerating them here [Col. 0639B].

How, then, shall I escape from the knot of this question, so that, once John’s greatness has been proclaimed, the judgment of Truth may not waver—the judgment that says that among those born of women there is no one greater than John the Baptist? For if Elisha is greater than Elijah, then he is also greater than John. But this is impossible.

It must be noted, however, that doing something great through miraculous signs is one thing, while being great in excellence of merit is another. If miracles are under discussion, John is found in the pages of Scripture to have performed no miracle. But will he therefore be the least of all the saints, because he is not recorded to have performed signs of power? Elisha, then, is greater than Elijah in the display of signs, yet he does not surpass him in the accumulation of merits.

So also John is indeed equal to Elijah: just as Elijah is to be the herald of the Judge who will come, so John became the Forerunner of the Redeemer. But he is greater than Elijah, because he not only pointed out the one whom Elijah announced; he also baptized him.

In that sacrament of baptism, finally, the water of the Jordan was washed more than it washed, and from it, moreover, every water throughout the world received the power of sanctification. There blessed John heard the Father’s voice, saw the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove, and dipped into the waters, with his own hands, the Son of God, awesome to the angels [Col. 0639D].

That event showed in deed the foundation and origin of baptism, which Truth later taught the disciples to enact in words full of power: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). There the reality was manifest and there were no words; here there are words and a true, though hidden, reality.

John, therefore, is the boundary of human merits. However greatly the authority of the apostolic senate excels, however greatly the faith of the patriarchs advances in knowledge of God, however strongly the oracles of the prophets grow in recounting hidden mysteries, however much the glory of the triumphant martyrs is increased, however luxuriantly the fresh purity of virgins blooms, or however diligently the tongue of teachers exercises itself in the words of life—all these things are restrained short of John’s boundary. Nothing of human virtue, nothing of religion, nothing of perfection advances beyond it [Col. 0640A].

The sequence of his incomparable life was not woven by some historian after his death; rather, that chief archangel narrated his wondrous deeds before he was conceived in the womb, just as he had narrated those of the Lord. We learned the praise of this man not from the testimony of any truthful human being, but from the mouth of Truth itself. And that Truth is his advocate and praiser—the one praised and blessed by all heavenly and earthly creatures.

From that Word, finally, by whom the dry land was founded, the stars are moved, and the elements were created, John’s praises were drawn. Indeed, how great is the magnificence of earning glory and praise from the one with whom the highest happiness is to obtain the pardon of mercy, and of being preferred by him to human beings by whom it is glorious to be approved in any manner! He says: “What did you go out to see? A prophet? I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matt. 11).

But since a prophet is outstanding and distinguished among human beings, having no equal in the common human race, and is even set above the prophets, it remains that he should now be called not a man but an angel. Hence he added: “For this is the one about whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare your way before your face” (ibid.).

John is also shown more clearly in what follows to be preferred to the other human beings, when the Lord says of him: “But the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (ibid.). For our Redeemer, who is less than John on earth through the succession of his advancing age, is greater in heaven through the privilege of eternal majesty [Col. 0640D].

O blessed abasement, when a human being is placed beneath God, when the creature is preceded by the Creator, when the small is surpassed by the glory of immensity! Christ is said to be greater than John in heaven, where he is adored by all the powers of angelic dignity; before him the cherubim and seraphim humbly fall; at his command the Principalities and Powers tremble; and his face the angels desire to see (1 Pet. 1). He declares himself superior to John in heavenly dignity, he before whose sight all nations are counted like a drop from a bucket and, according to the prophet’s oracle, as nothing and emptiness (Isa. 40). He does not disdain to place himself before the blessed man in comparison, so that a human being may be found to possess, before God, a place of comparison in excellence of merits.

For the one who is the author of exaltation himself became for us the teacher of humility. To him be glory and dominion, now and henceforth, for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON XXV. III. ON THE NATIVITY OF ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST (24 JULY)

Beloved, we know that many things have been composed in praise of blessed John by our fathers, polished by a refined style and expressed with brilliance. Therefore we are ashamed to thrust our roughness among the learned and to stammer among eloquent men.

But who would remain silent at the nativity of the voice? Who would fall silent in praising the herald, unless perhaps he distrusts what he hears from an angel? When Zechariah did not believe the oracle of the speaking angel, he was immediately deprived of the ability to speak; and at the arrival of the voice he lost the power of speech (Luke 1). But when the offspring had been born, adorning the ancestry of his father’s line with a new title of glory, and when Zechariah no longer doubted but rejoiced instead to impose the name, not only was the organ of speech restored to him, but he was also filled with the grace of the prophetic spirit. The man who until then had lost the ability to utter any speech whatsoever, now endowed with the oracle of prophetic prediction, revealed the mysteries of saving revelation.

John truly was the voice; he went before the Word, and he announced the Word [Col. 0641B]. Isaiah, the outstanding herald among the prophets, had also become the herald of this voice—or of this preacher—when he cried: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isa. 40). Through Malachi also the divine voice says: “Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare your way before you.”

Let us consider, dearest brothers, how greatly this man stands out by the privilege of his exalted dignity, how he excels among the choirs of the saints by the incomparable loftiness of his merits: like the Savior, he was foretold beforehand by the prophets, announced by the same angel who announced the Lord, and, moreover, glorified by immense proclamations of praise through the testimony of Truth itself. Such a man was fitting for the heavenly Bridegroom to have as his friend; such a man ought to have been the mediator of the heavenly wedding. “He who has the bride,” he says, “is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3).

Now, so that holy Church might be cleansed from every defilement of contamination and, having neither stain nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5), might deserve to enter the chambers of the heavenly Bridegroom, this was accomplished through the mystery of this blessed friend of the bridegroom. He immersed in the Jordan’s waves the very author of baptism and of all purity, who was cleansing those same waters.

That wedding was certainly prefigured by Judah, who went down to Thamnas to shear the sheep with Hira, the shepherd of his own flock (Genesis 38). Thamnas is interpreted as “failing”; through it the Synagogue is indicated, in which kings and prophets had failed, and likewise the anointing, until he should come for whom it had been reserved. Hence it is also said through the prophet: “When the Holy of Holies comes, the anointing will cease” (Daniel 9).

What, then, is signified by Judah, who came to Thamnas to shear the sheep, except our Redeemer, who is understood to have come to the Synagogue in order to relieve from sins the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel (Luke 15)? Hence the Bridegroom says to the bride in the Song: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song of Songs 4). The teeth of the Church are understood to be her holy teachers, to the first of whom it was said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). It was as though he said: “Kill them with the sword of the Spirit, that is, with the word of preaching, in respect of what they are, and transfer them into the body of the Church.”

The bride’s teeth, therefore, are the holy teachers, who, because they are simple through innocence and, leaving everything behind, have been stripped of the fleeces of their possessions and purified by the water of sacred baptism, are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.

Judah therefore came to shear the sheep, not alone, but with his Odollamite shepherd, whose name was Hiras. Whom do we understand by the Odollamite except John? “Odollamite” is interpreted as “testimony in water.” With this testimony the Lord plainly came to the water of baptism. He had, indeed, a testimony greater than John’s, but for the sake of the weak sheep he deigned to use this testimony in the water. Thus, when John saw him approaching the banks of the Jordan, he immediately cried out: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

And the Evangelist says: “John bore witness, saying: ‘Because I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him; and I did not know him. But he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit”’” (ibid.).

The name of that shepherd also most aptly corresponds to this vision. For Hiras is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” The Lord was John’s brother, not only according to the seed of Abraham, but also according to the kinship of Mary and Elizabeth.

John therefore saw his brother while he was still enclosed in the womb; he saw him at the baptism; he saw with the eyes of the flesh a human being; he saw in the spirit his majesty. Thus the same John included the interpretation of both these names—Hiras, which means “the vision of my brother,” and Odollamite, which signifies “testimony in water”—in the verse of a single statement, saying: “And I saw, and bore witness, that this is the Son of God” (ibid.).

When Judah came to shear the sheep, Tamar changed her clothing, because she changed her spiritual name. For Tamar is interpreted as “changing.” Thus the Synagogue becomes the Church. Yet, according to the literal meaning, the same name of bitterness remains—not the bitterness in which a soldier offered the Lord gall to drink, but rather that in which Peter wept bitterly after his fall (Matthew 27).

Judah (Matthew 26) is called “confession.” Tamar, therefore, sleeping with Judah, immediately conceives, because when bitterness is joined to confession, holy Church is at once made fruitful in producing the fruits of repentance. Hence John also says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3). These fruits of repentance first burst forth in Jerusalem and afterward spread throughout the whole breadth of the world. Therefore Truth says: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24).
