Indeed, the harlot’s clothing itself signifies confession of sins; or else because Tamar is composed of two corrupted words: Thamna, which is said to mean “failing,” and Mara, which means “bitterness.” In her, bitterness rightly failed when, made fruitful from barrenness, she produced the sweet offspring of a new growth.

Tamar therefore is made pregnant by one who does not know her, because holy Church, insofar as she is among the Gentiles, is not recognized at the beginning, while she conceives the seed of the new faith. Hence it is sung: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Psalm 17). And Isaiah says: “Behold, you will call a nation that you did not know, and nations that did not know you will run to you” (Isaiah 55).

Moreover, what is signified by the fact that a young goat is sent to her through that same Odollamite, except the reproach of sins made through John? It was as though the bearer were bringing a young goat to the harlot when he said to the crowds hastening to the bath of baptism by way of rebuke: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3).

Hiras the Odollamite asked Tamar for a ring, a bracelet, and a staff. The ring signifies the seal of faith; the bracelet, the labor of works; and the staff, the rest of hope.

He was, as it were, asking for the ring of faith when he said: “He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward Christ the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3). Did the ring not also belong to his saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom”? (ibid.)

He displayed the bracelet of labor when he said: “Repent” (Matthew 3). He also displayed the rest of the staff when he immediately added: “For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.). It was as though he were speaking plainly: “Do not grow weary under the labor of the repentance imposed upon you; rather, strengthen your spirit with firm hope in the nearness of the heavenly kingdom.”

Judah sought her at the crossroads but could not find her, because she who, according to the prophet, had been prostituted in public and under every leafy tree (Jeremiah 1–2), had now restrained herself within her father’s house, that is, under the discipline of Christ. The reproach of sin did not find her, for bitterness had changed her into confession.

She put on the garments of widowhood, because apart from the heavenly Bridegroom, who died for her, she admits no other. The fact that twins appeared in the womb signifies the two peoples generated within the bosom of the Church through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

In the very act of the children being born, one extended his hand, and, after the scarlet thread had been tied, immediately withdrew it; thus he opened the way for the other to be born before him. This signifies that the Jewish people, which first began to be born into the light of the Spirit, displayed the works of its preceding prophets, stained by the blood of the Lord himself.

Hence Zara is interpreted as “rising,” because that Hebrew people arose first according to the letter of the law, but became later in receiving the grace of the Gospel. In this way the people of the Jews, which had already begun to be born through the Spirit, withdrew its hand; and immediately the people of the Gentiles burst forth and became the firstborn people. Thus, according to the judgment of Truth, those who were first would become last, and those who were last would become first (Matthew 20).

Pharez therefore rightly received the name of “division.” Hence, when he was being born, the midwife cried out: “Why has the wall been divided because of you?” The entire human race had made itself like a wall—like twisted branches of the forest—against the Lord coming in the flesh, and unanimously resisted him so that he would not enter to accomplish the mystery of redemption. Hence Paul says: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block; but to the Gentiles, foolishness” (1 Corinthians 1).

But the Gentile people divided this wall, as though by being born, when, through the centurion Cornelius and others who were the first fruits of faith, they received the washing of baptism and hastened together under the name of Christ (Acts 10).

Blessed John was considering this alternation in birth when, as crowds of Jews flocked to him from every side, he said: “Do not begin to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3). It was as though he openly said: “The Gentile peoples, who are stones because they worship stones, will become firstborn for you in the sacrament of regeneration and of the new grace, although through the legal ceremonies you appeared to reject their primacy.”

These matters, dearest brothers, we have briefly passed over—not explaining them, but touching upon them in some fashion—in order to demonstrate from the ancient pages of sacred Scripture that blessed John was the minister of the new grace and the friend of the bridegroom at the spiritual wedding.

For the Savior enlisted this distinguished and excellent man of the whole human race as his companion for running, like a giant, the course of our mortality; and, in carrying out the business of our redemption, chose him in a certain way to be a participant and fellow worker.

Therefore, when the Lord approached him to be baptized, and the exalted yet humble servant, trembling, excused himself from the ministry entrusted to him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (ibid.), he replied: “Let it be so for now. For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”

O Lord, you said: “Let there be light, and there was light” (Genesis 1). Let the stars of heaven, the beasts of the field, the birds of the air, and the fish of the waters come into being. All these were created solely by the command of your word; all are ordered at a single sign of your will. Nor did you summon the aid of any angelic power to accomplish these things. How then do you now say, as though making yourself equal to a human being of earthly condition and adapting yourself to our weakness, “Let it be so for now; thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness”?

Behold, let the one whom you raise to share in your cooperation, whom you in a certain way lift to the summit of your likeness, say what comparison can be made between you and him. He says: “God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3). The Father loves the Son and has given everything into his hand. But because he declares that you have no measure of the Spirit, let him say what he thinks of himself: “We,” he says, “have all received from his fullness” (John 1). It is as though he said: “We are vessels; he is the fountain. In us he distributes according to the measure of his governance that from which the fullness of his immensity flows over beyond comparison.”

And what comparison exists between you and him, he again makes clear when he says: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3).

How great, then, was the service of submission that he owed you! He cries out publicly before the whole people: “One mightier than I is coming, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (Luke 3).

O lofty majesty of blessed humility! While, by its own judgment, it is lowered to the depths, it is raised to heavenly things by divine mercy; and while it humbly submits itself to God, it rises gloriously into fellowship with God.

John declares himself, together with the other human beings, to be earth and to speak earthly things; but the Lord testifies that no one born of women has arisen greater than he (Matthew 11). John cries out that he is unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal, yet the Lord places his whole body in John’s hands when he approaches to undergo the washing of baptism. John humbly denies that he is a prophet, yet the Savior affirms that he is more than a prophet and, moreover, an angel; concerning him he later says: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5).

Consider, my brothers, how admirable—indeed, how angelic—the life of blessed John was, and how greatly it had shone in the opinion of all. Although he displayed no sign of power, the whole people nevertheless believed that he was the Christ, as Luke testifies when he says: “As the people were in expectation, and all were reasoning in their hearts about John, whether perhaps he might be the Christ” (Luke 3).

What religion, what perfection, what virtue, what kind of holiness is found in any of the saints that does not hold the chief place in John, as though by a certain prerogative?

There are holy hermits and anchorites, but who established for himself a rule of life in wild honey and the inedible food of locusts? To whom would goat-hair cloaks not suffice for the harshness of clothing? Yet this man, girded with a leather belt, is clothed in camel’s hair.

There are also holy renunciants who leave the world. But this man, while still of childish character, before he had learned to live among civilized people, penetrated the deserts and resolved to dwell alone. Nor did he deem it worthy to succeed his father in priestly dignity, so that he might proclaim with a free voice the true and supreme Priest of all.

The prophets foretell the future coming of the Savior; the apostles and the other teachers testify that it has been fulfilled. But John shows him present, the one for whom the preaching of the whole world—both the ancient and the present—has labored.

In this also he surpasses all the prophets: they receive the Holy Spirit as their ages advance, but he, still enclosed in his mother’s womb, conceived the power of the Spirit through preceding grace. As the Author of all joy drew near, he rejoiced by the movements of his scarcely formed body.

Others, keeping their garments undefiled, remained virgins. But this man, so that he might cut away from himself every enticement of the flesh from its very root, and preserve not only his generative members but also his ears and eyes in the unfailing greenness of a fresh and flowering virginity, rejected the companionship of human dwelling and, through the fervor of the spirit, immersed himself in the dens of wild beasts.

Among the purple-clad choirs of the martyrs, blessed John presides in the chair of teaching, because he fell as a vigorous champion for the testimony of truth. Having become the leader of all who fight for Christ, he first carried the triumphant banner of martyrdom into heaven.

Blessed John therefore became a participant in the choirs of all the saints, because no virtue of holiness was lacking in him. Indeed, he shines among all the orders of the saints all the more distinguished, the more sublimely he approaches the Author of all through incomparable merit.

He lives and reigns, one true God in the perfect Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon XXVI: On Saint Peter the Apostle  
### 29 June

On the words of Solomon’s Song: “The young women loved you greatly.”

[Col. 0646B]

The apostle Peter, prince of the apostles and first among princes, has made this day brighter for us. Truly it is a sacred day, because it has been consecrated to a most sacred man and assigned to his praises—a man whom the angelic assembly reveres in no ordinary way.

He alone is distinguished by the insignia of singular primacy: the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, the tongue, the foundation of faith. Honor and glorious dignity are consummated when a man placed on earth commands the heavens and exercises judicial power among the choirs of angels.

The Lord and Ruler sits among ranks shining with brighter light, and, flying from the Thrones to the Cherubim, changes the places of his sitting. Therefore the change of seats is truly astonishing and far beyond the sight of human reason, since he is read to have sat now upon the Thrones, now upon the Cherubim.

Although angels stand by, awaiting the command of the one who presides, and ministering spirits receive their assigned ministries, none of them possesses the power of binding and loosing.

Peter is present, and at his discretion the whole world is loosed and bound. Peter’s sentence precedes the Redeemer’s sentence, because Peter does not bind what Christ binds; rather, Christ binds what Peter binds. He himself bears witness to this: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

O how powerful a dignity, how dignified a power! Peter judges, and the Omnipotent confirms Peter’s judgments; the hand of the Most High is in Peter’s hand. Only he becomes Christ’s intimate who has enjoyed Peter’s intimacy.

What is this, that, with the ranks of angels and human beings excluded, Peter alone sits in fellowship with the divine majesty and with the Lord who presides? It is a sweet conversation, a holy companionship, a special council of Peter and God, in which the sharing of secrets joins and unites a mortal man to God.

It is therefore no wonder if the apostle Peter loves the Savior with more ardent affection, since a singular love has been poured into him, so that he both loves singularly and is loved specially. His soul is one of the young women who loved him greatly.

Childhood is not yet suited to love; old age has ceased from love. A child is one who has not yet begun to pursue eternal things; an old man is one who began but abandoned them. The supreme lover therefore excludes both and drives them away from the majesty of his love.

Only youth, glowing with the most ardent fires, does not receive a love that is eclipsed but claims for itself an abundant ardor. Among the young women, that is, the souls of the elect who have promised love and fidelity to the heavenly Bridegroom, this soul alone loved more ardently and, unable to endure the intensity of love, said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matthew 14).

She did not fear the singular danger of the element, and the swelling waves of the raging sea could not restrain the Apostle’s affection. But what does “greatly” mean, since the one whom we are commanded to love with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength cannot be loved too greatly?

[Col. 0647B]

There are three degrees in the love of God, and without one another, ascending to either of the others is of little or no value. The Apostle ran with a swifter foot until, established at the summit of the third, he flew up to the heavenly palace.

God must be loved sweetly, wisely, and courageously. But let us now see what it means to love God sweetly.

He is sweet, and he should be loved sweetly, because he never ceases to bestow the abundance of his sweetness upon those who love or fear him. He is loved in sweetness when he is loved in the flesh; when we know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified; when the whole reality of his flesh is held in frequent remembrance; and when such great condescension of mercy shakes our bones to the marrow.

For when we remember the King of glory enduring the sufferings of a little crying child, being brought down into the lowliness of wretched rags, sitting down wearied from his journey, enduring with the most patient ear the insults of the Pharisees and the abuse of the Jews, should we not be moved at the sight of such great compassion?

Consider the Son of the Virgin smeared with spittle, bruised by wounds, fastened with nails. See the ruler of heaven standing upon the cross, pale in death and disfigured in the flesh. Do not pass by the Lord of angels, made the reproach of human beings, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity, a man struck and humbled by God, a leprous man exposed to every kind of harm.

This remembrance kindles the heart, burns the breast, and consumes the inward parts. Such memory draws out tears, fills the eyes, and moistens the face.

Nearly all the efforts of religious people are wrapped around this degree, and rare indeed is the bird on earth that can pass beyond this progress. For either an image of the newborn God or of him hanging on the cross stands before those who pray, and a warming affection holds the mind’s devotion, scarcely allowing it to run farther.

At this degree Peter remained fixed when, loving the flesh and manner of life of Jesus Christ most tenderly, he even tried to draw the Savior back from the salvation of the human race, saying: “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matthew 16). To him the Lord said: “Go behind me, Satan, because you do not understand the things of God,” blaming the counsel, not the affection.

For Peter loved sweetly, but not wisely. How could he have loved wisely when he was trying to exclude the redemption of the world and the providence of God? But a sweeter familiarity had kindled his heart, and the kindness of the one who loved could not endure a word about the Redeemer’s absence.

God is loved with the whole heart when affection and sweetness dwell in a person’s heart, and when the heart alone preserves the sweetness of the love of his name with steadfast perseverance. Hence common usage has established that when we see someone being intensely loved by another, we say: “He loves him from the heart”—that is, he loves and follows him.

The second degree is to love wisely. This degree is of great height and promises a very difficult ascent. No mind reaches its summit except one that is purer and that surpasses the wisdom of this world with the wisdom of the angels.

Here devotion is not concentrated upon the God who is being born or traveling, but upon the Word who was in the beginning with God (John 1). Recall the Son of God making all things with the Father, creating the angels, joining the elements, ordering the world, governing everything; and recognize how much loftier this knowledge is than the former.

Contemplate his ineffable generation, and the one begotten unlike in no way to the one who begets; nor is the Father earlier than the Son. Then you will understand how great a difference separates the two births: it is one thing to be born in glory, another in misery; one thing to be equal to God, another to be lower than the angels.

This is singular wisdom: to rise above the obstacles of the body and bodies and to leap into the splendor of that light in which light is seen in light, and God is shown not serving but commanding.

Blessed is the soul that, having overcome the filthy substance of the flesh, rests in the light of this wisdom!

Would you like to see how Paul ascended from the first degree to the second? After saying, “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6), he wrote elsewhere: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Corinthians 5).

Here the affection of wisdom sits in the soul, which alone is capable of reason, and through tireless meditation gazes upon the incorporeal and uncircumscribed Spirit. Here God is loved with the whole soul, that is, with the whole of wisdom, whereas previously he was loved with the whole heart, that is, with sweetness.

The third degree is to love courageously, that is, with all one’s strength. He loves courageously who, when necessary, exposes body and soul to torments for faith in the Savior. This is the fruit of action, the completion of labor, the proof of love.

The apostle Peter had ascended from the degree of sweetness to the degree of wisdom when he said: “I lay down my life for you” (Matthew 26). Nothing is wiser or braver than “I lay down my life for you”; nothing is more foolish or weaker than “I do not know or understand what you are saying” (John 18).

Certainly he already loved sweetly and wisely, but he lost both when he did not love courageously, when at the voice of a servant girl he swiftly denied his Lord and Master.

But when he resolved to die for Christ, he loved greatly, because “no one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (ibid.). Fastened to the cross, he could not be separated from faith.

You see, then, how these three degrees correspond to the threefold commandment of love in the Law. Let us therefore love sweetly, wisely, and courageously, so that through Peter’s intercession we may be able to reach the Master, who is blessed forever. Amen.

## Sermon XXVII: On the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul  
### 29 June

Today, beloved, is bright and solemn, and sanctifies and suffuses the whole creation with its light. It is not an unknown festival or one darkened by the shadows of obscurity; rather, it is known throughout the world from the rising of the sun to its setting, and it shines with a clear light even in the heavens themselves.

For on this day two princes of the apostles, lights of the Church, supreme martyrs, teachers of the law, friends of the bridegroom, eyes of the bride, shepherds of the flock, and guardians of the world ascended to the heavenly kingdoms through a blessed martyrdom.

One was prince of the kingdom of heaven; the other was caught up to the third heaven. One was appointed over the Jews; the other was given to the Gentiles. Companions in life, partners in death, equal in their crown, equal in glory, judges of the world, confessors of the Lord.

The ordering of the Redeemer is truly astonishing, and the judgments of God are a great abyss (Psalm 35), since he placed over his Church those who had fallen so criminally that they were swallowed up in the waves of sins.

When I look upon Peter, whom the very hand of the Omnipotent invests with the keys of the heavenly kingdom; to whom the Father reveals the majesty of the Son; upon whom the Church is founded; to whom the power of binding and loosing is granted (Matthew 16); who closes and opens the heavens, something that the cherubim and seraphim are not read to possess, I am profoundly amazed.

Then, when I turn my eyes back and see that same Peter following the Savior from a distance, denying him and swearing at the voice of a single servant girl, “I do not know the man,” and abandoning in trembling flight the one whom he had confessed to be the Son of God (Matthew 26; Luke 22), I am shaken with fear and say to myself: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11).

When I look upon Paul breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, leading them away bound, condemning them to death (Acts 9), and raging with complete fury against the body of the Church, I tremble within myself and say: “A human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Ecclesiastes 9).

When I look from above and see the chosen vessel carrying the name of Christ before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel; being caught up to the secrets of the third heaven; hearing secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Corinthians 11–12); and fixing clearer eyes upon that very Trinity, I rejoice and say: “This is the man who was not abandoned by the Lord” (Wisdom 10).

What is the meaning of their falling so greatly, when they were placed over the Church? Wisdom, gently ordering all things, did this so that these princes might learn in themselves how they ought to show mercy to others.

The present passage attempts to demonstrate the power of this mercy. “These,” it says, “are the two olive trees” (Revelation 11). The comparison of the olive tree to the apostles is entirely worthy, and no other is more worthy.

This tree is always green and pours forth that most excellent liquid, oil, without which neither royal nor priestly authority can stand. Oil has four properties: it floats above all liquids, gives light, nourishes, and anoints.

For whatever liquid you place oil upon, it immediately claims the power of the higher position. So also the mercy of God is placed above all his works, as the Psalmist bears witness when he says: “His mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144).

The Lord is proclaimed merciful and compassionate, patient, mild of heart, and sweet to all (Psalms 85, 114). He is also just (Psalm 10), but Scripture never speaks of him as “very just” as it speaks of him as “very merciful.”

Would you like to see how the disciples follow their Lord and Master? Observe how great an affection of compassion poured itself into the prince of the apostles when all the widows surrounded him, weeping and showing the tunics and garments that Dorcas had made for them (Acts 9).

The prince of the apostles is surrounded by a multitude of the poor and shaken by the tearful voices of the widows; an abundance of clemency breaks into the apostolic breast. The Apostle prays before the face of glory, before the Lord of majesty; the woman is raised again and restored to the poor as a source of mercy.

This mercy makes Peter run from Jerusalem to Antioch (Acts 10), come from Antioch to Rome, preach the word of God, aid sinners, spare sins, and cause mercy to triumph over judgment.

Look also upon Paul, and understand how the abundant kindness of a sweeter mercy had kindled the whole apostle’s mind with true compassion. “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? I grieve and mourn,” he says, “over those who have sinned and have not repented” (2 Corinthians 11).

Blessed is the soul that had made everyone’s sufferings its own, so that it might win everyone. With this affection he sails the sea, runs to Jerusalem, is stoned, beaten, and afflicted. From there he runs to the Ephesians, seeks the Corinthians, travels around to the Colossians, visits the Philippians, returns to the Romans, scatters mercy, spreads compassion everywhere, and sows the seeds of heavenly joys.

You see, then, that just as oil surpasses all liquids, so apostolic compassion is placed above all their virtues.

Oil gives light; the apostles also give light. Recall the Acts of the Apostles and see with how great a light the apostle Peter shines. “In the streets,” Scripture says, “they placed the sick on beds, so that when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some of them, and they might be freed from their illnesses” (Acts 5).

What an immeasurable and astonishing light of oil, brighter than every sun, so that at the shadow of the apostolic body diseases fled, infirmities departed, and every force of illness was driven away with unheard-of speed!

Did not an immense abundance of light leap forth more generously from Peter’s mouth when he said to the lame man: “In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk”? (Acts 3.)

Look upon Paul traversing the whole of Illyricum, raising the dead, overthrowing the temples of the gods, and illuminating the circuit of the whole world with the splendor of this light (Romans 15). Paul runs, and by the powerful force of his words gives light to what is in darkness; bright in speech, brighter in action, brightest in the flashing of miracles.

“Have,” he says, “the pattern of our life, and attend not only to what you have heard, but also to what you have seen in me” (Philippians 3). He is a good and perfect teacher, who gives his words credibility by better deeds.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Something is missing here.]

[Lacuna.] In the brightest serenity of this light, your flashes have shone, O God, upon the whole world (Psalm 76). The earth was shaken and trembled at the voice of the apostles, when their sound went out into all the earth (Psalm 18).

Oil nourishes; the apostles also nourish. Do the letters of Peter and that sublime teaching of his words not nourish the Church of God wonderfully?

Hear what the Savior says to him concerning this very nourishment: “Feed,” he says a third time, “my sheep” (John 21). Feed by the word; feed by example; feed by prayer.

Feed by the word, so that you may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict. Feed by example, so that you may fulfill in action what you preach with your voice. Feed by prayer, so that you may intercede for those whose souls have been entrusted to you.

See how the apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, feeds the people of God with a variety of dishes: “I gave you milk to drink,” he says, “not food” (1 Corinthians 3); but the solid food of the mature is for those who through practice have their faculties trained. And elsewhere: “You have become people who need milk, not solid food” (Hebrews 5). And again: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (1 Corinthians 2).

You see how he adapts and conforms himself, instructing some with sublime doctrine and others with tender teaching.

Oil anoints; the apostles also anoint. Does not the apostle Peter anoint everyone when he says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light”? (1 Peter 2.)

Does not Paul himself also command, saying: “If someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness”? (Galatians 6.)

The olive tree is always green and is not struck down by the immensity of the cold; and the faith of the apostles endures unshaken and could never be overcome by tyrannical fury.

And although Peter was driven to fall, he did not remain fallen, because the Lord upheld him. The apostle was indeed stunned and hesitated for a moment, but immediately returned in the power of faith; when the Lord looked upon him, he wept bitterly (Luke 22).

And although he was shaken for a time, he could not be cast down, because the sentence of Truth could not be annulled: “I have prayed for you,” Peter, “that your faith may not fail” (ibid.).

For on this day Peter is crucified, Paul is struck by the sword, and they lay down their lives for the faith of Christ, so that the faith of Christ may not fail.

These, then, are the two men who are olive trees: men possessing faith, enlightening their homeland, feeding the Church, and anointing sinners.

What Scripture says here—“These are the two olive trees” (Revelation 11)—it explains more plainly elsewhere, saying: “These are men of mercy” (Isaiah 57).

It continues: “And the two shining lampstands before the Lord.” A lampstand rests upon three feet and, rising upward, carries a candle, so that those who enter may see the light (Luke XI). So also the apostles, resting upon three virtues—action, preaching, and the radiance of miracles—showed the true light, the Lord Jesus Christ, in all his brightness to those entering into the faith. And one must note that he says, “before the Lord.” Hypocrites shine, indeed, not before the Lord but before the world, so that they may be seen by human beings. The apostles, however, shone before the Lord but not before the world; for, having experienced mockery and blows, they strove only to please the divine majesty. [Col. 0652B]

That they are the two olive trees and the two shining lampstands, and that they are before the Lord, the prophet Zechariah clearly indicates in these words: “These are the two sons of the oil of splendor, who stand beside the Ruler of the whole earth” (Zech. IV). They are sons of oil because they are men of mercy; they are also sons of splendor because they are shining lampstands. They shine before the Lord because they stand beside the Ruler of the whole earth.

It continues: “They have power to shut the heavens with clouds.” The clarity of the sky is obstructed by clouds, so that it cannot be seen; the contemplation of divinity is closed by our sins, so that God may not be seen, as the prophet testifies when he says: “You have set up a cloud, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. III). A cloud is set up so that prayer may not pass through when our sins separate us from God. They have [Col. 0652C] power to shut heaven with clouds—that is, with sinners—and to open its gates to the faithful. A wondrous thing, and worthy of every astonishment: that the palaces of the heavenly dwellings should be closed and opened at the word of human beings. [Note: [Col. 0652D] Some material seems to be missing.] Amen.

[p. 140] JULY.

Third Sermon on the same. XX. Sermon on Saint Christopher the Martyr. XXIX. First Sermon on Saints Flora and Lucilla, virgins and martyrs. [Col. 0652D] Second Sermon on the same. XXX. SERMON XXVIII. ON SAINT ALEXIUS THE CONFESSOR. (17 JULY)

Today’s festival, beloved, urges us not only to celebrate joyfully the triumph of blessed Alexius, who is its particular subject; it also sets before us his parents themselves as an example for our edification and salvation. For although they are reported to have abounded in such great riches and such incomparable wealth that three thousand boys reverently attended upon them—boys who were adorned with silk garments and girded themselves with golden belts—[Col. 0653A] yet every day they did not cease to prepare costly tables of food for widows, orphans, and all who were in need, while they themselves were usually content with bread and water only once a day. Adorned, therefore, with these and other flowers of spiritual virtues, and distinguished by the honorable character of a devout life, they were such that what the Gospel history relates about the parents of blessed John the Baptist rightly applies to them as well: namely, that “they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke I). It was therefore fitting that from so chaste, so holy, and finally so immaculate a bridal chamber of conjugal purity such a distinguished offspring should be born. As it is said through the Prophet: “The generation of the upright shall be [Col. 0653B] blessed” (Ps. CXXI). “For this is the generation of those who seek the Lord” (Ps. XXIII).

Therefore, my brothers—I address you especially now, you who have not yet undertaken the summit of the spiritual life, who are still devoted to worldly pursuits and bound by the ties of the marital union—apply yourselves diligently to works of piety and mercy; provide the necessary assistance to brothers suffering want; and strive, insofar as your state requires, to display a chaste, temperate, and honorable life, so that, for the preservation of the lineage of your descendants, you may be able to beget offspring worthy of God. For although that saying of the prophet is true, in which it is said: “The soul that sins shall itself die. The son shall not bear the iniquity [p. 141] of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. XVIII), [Col. 0653C] nevertheless, according to the conduct of parents, the merits of children often arise, so that honorable offspring correspond to honorable parents, while the wicked join with the wicked in depravity. Hence these people say: “We are children of saints, and we await that life which God will give to those who never change their faith in him” (Tob. II). To the others, by contrast, it is said: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III.) Indeed, if you live religiously, conduct yourselves with discipline, and keep God’s commandments, you benefit both your children and yourselves; but if you do the opposite, you harm both them and yourselves. On account of the merit of holy David, although his descendants [Col. 0653D] were subject to downfall because of idolatry, they retained the royal power for a long time. Jonathan, on the other hand, although devout toward God and a friend of the holy Prophet, nevertheless, because of his father’s arrogant pride, fell beneath the sword of the wicked (III Kings XVIII, XIX, XX, XXXI).

To return, then, to blessed Alexius: his parents deserved to beget such an offspring, so that from a holy root a holy shoot might burst forth, and the branch of a good tree, growing through the increase of heavenly grace received, might offer fruits of good works worthy of its kind. Merit is not suddenly granted to any holy man who has not yet reached perfection; rather, he arrives at it gradually through the growth of devout dedication and special discipline. While the mind, having received the fire of divine love [Col. 0654A], is lifted on high through heavenly desire, it is advanced toward the summit of inner perfection, as though by certain steps of ascent. Hence that holy man said: “I shall declare him by my successive steps” (Job XXXI). Of these steps of merit it is said: “They shall go from virtue to virtue” (Ps. LXXXIII). The same Prophet, contemplating the holy Church, says: “God shall be recognized in her steps, when he receives her” (Ps. XLVII). For, as has been said, one does not reach the heights suddenly; rather, through the vow of devout dedication and the exercise of holy labor, the human mind is gradually raised to the heights of spiritual virtues. Hence it is said through the same Prophet: “I have been exercised, and my spirit failed little by little” [Col. 0654B] (Ps. LXVI). What does he mean by saying “my spirit,” except the spirit of pride? The spirit of the flesh? And because, through hidden grace, the mind advances by a measure tempered from above toward the love of God, the more the divine Spirit grows in us each day, the more our own spirit—that is, the spirit of carnal desire—fails. Since this harmful and detestable spirit is not suddenly cut away from us completely, nor immediately severed as soon as we strive to do so, it is rightly said to have failed little by little, that is, gradually. We then advance fully toward God when we truly perceive that we ourselves have failed away from ourselves. This growth of increasing virtues, gradually and slowly attained through the accumulation of daily progress, reaches the increase of perfected holiness. Each chosen person begins from the tender weakness of his first beginnings [Col. 0654C] and thereafter grows strong toward what is firm and powerful. Truth clearly indicates this when it says in the Gospel: “The [p. 142] kingdom of God is as if a man should cast seed upon the earth, and sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should germinate and grow while he does not know it” (Mark IV). Announcing the growth of this seed, he added: “For the earth bears fruit of itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear”; and immediately he continues: “And when the fruit has appeared, he at once sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” Behold: by the voice of Truth, the increases of merits are distinguished according to the different stages of the crop. He says: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. Let us therefore see how the example of this saying of the Lord applies, word by word and with the greatest clarity, to blessed Alexius. [Col. 0654D]

It is evident that this remarkable man, as his illustrious history testifies, during the very festive solemnities of his wedding celebrations, dismissed his wife while preserving the virginity of both, abandoned his parents, and exchanged residence in the city of Rome for exile in Edessa, a very small town. He set aside, for love of Christ, a spouse of royal lineage and, following Christ’s poverty, despised the ample resources of princely wealth. Therefore, just as four stages are mentioned in that Gospel saying of the Lord, so four remarkable things are likewise found in the servant. There it says: first the blade, then the ear, afterward [Col. 0655A] the full grain in the ear; and in the fourth place the sickle is sent, and what is ripe is cut down. There are, then, as has been said, four things that correspond most suitably to what is found in blessed Alexius. The first is that he despised the world and everything worldly; the second, that as an exile, stripped of every resource, he endured every kind of poverty for seventeen years in the Mesopotamian city of Edessa; the third, that, returning to his own home by a fortunate restoration and undertaking a hard struggle, he deceived the sight of everyone—his wife, both parents, the household servants, and the various members of the family—in order to become truly known to God alone. Finally, the fourth is that there, after the slaps and beatings inflicted by the servants, after the mockery and insults [Col. 0655B] of those who ridiculed him, after the blows of those who laughed and raged, and finally after the intolerable injuries of calamity endured with the greatest patience, he at last died happily and completed the immense struggles of so great a labor with a blessed end.

When this distinguished man abandoned the world, was he not then, in a certain sense, the blade? He was still weak through the beginnings of his recent conversion, but already burning with the desire for heavenly hope that he had conceived in his mind. For unless the world had withered in the field of his merits, he would not have rejected it; and unless the green growth of heavenly hope had been within him, he would not have hastened so eagerly toward God after abandoning everything. He had fixed his root in that inheritance which blessed Peter calls “undefiled, unfading, kept in heaven” (I Pet. I), and which the Lord calls pasture (John X). This blade had taken root [Col. 0655C] there, and therefore flourished with the greenness of heavenly grace. But when he had remained for a long period in exile in an unknown land and [p. 143] had strengthened himself to endure the continual hardships of such poverty and sorrowful distress, what else did he do, so to speak, than rise from tender grass into an ear? Later, when, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, he had conceived the strength of inner fortitude and entered his father’s house prepared to endure the fiercest and, beyond human strength, grievous struggles, what else did this rich ear become than full grain? This ear had already grown into such a state of strength that the shameful blasts of insult flowing from the mouths of the servants could not overwhelm it; the waves of temptation striking it daily through the sight of his wife and parents could not overthrow it. [Col. 0655D] For the house had been founded upon a firm rock (Matt. VII). And although outward poverty made him destitute, and his ragged clothing and unkempt hair made him deformed, so that he seemed like worthless stalks and barren ears among straw, nevertheless a full grain lay hidden within the treasury of his conscience. That grain of which he said concerning himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John XII). Finally, in the fourth place, the sickle was sent, so that the ear which had reached the fullness of maturity might be reaped, when, by the decree of divine providence, God cut off his chosen one from this life and, casting away all the straw of his calamities, stored him—pure and completely cleansed—in that storehouse of the heavenly granary, bringing him to a blessed consummation. [Col. 0656A] Thus, by the measure ordained by the heavenly farmer, the seed rose into the blade, the blade grew into the ear, the ear produced the grain, and the grain reached the granary. The fullness of virtues, as has been said, is not granted all at once but through successive growth, so that one ascends to it through the progress of long advancement, as though by certain steps of great discipline.

This fourfold ordering of our progress, which the Lord himself describes under the figure of seed, is represented by the prophet Ezekiel under the term “water.” Concerning the man whom he had seen upon a high mountain, he narrates the following in order: “He measured,” he says, “a thousand cubits, and led me through the water up to the ankles; again he measured [Col. 0656B] a thousand, and led me through the water up to the knees; and he measured a thousand, and led me through the water up to the loins; and he measured a thousand, a torrent which I could not cross, because the deep waters of the torrent had swollen and could not be forded” (Ezek. XLVII). What is signified by the number one thousand, if not the fullness of the gift bestowed? What is this water, if not heavenly wisdom? Hence Solomon says: “By the wisdom of God the abysses burst forth, and the clouds gather dew” (Prov. III). The man who appeared measures a thousand cubits, and the prophet is led through the water up to his ankles, because when our Redeemer grants us, who have turned toward him, the fullness of a spiritual beginning, he pours into us, through the gift of heavenly wisdom, as it were the first traces of our action. The water reaches, as it were, to the ankles when, through the wisdom we have received, we plant the first steps of our desired uprightness. [Col. 0656C] Again he measures a thousand cubits, and the prophet is led through the water up to the knees, because the strength of our wisdom is then increased so that it does not bend toward the performance of wicked deeds. Hence Paul says: “Raise your drooping hands and your weakened knees, and make straight [p. 144] paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray but rather be healed” (Heb. XII). The water reaches the knees when the wisdom we have received binds us completely to uprightness in good works, so that our spirit no longer wavers or stumbles but firmly fixes its steps in the good it has begun.

The aforementioned man again measures a thousand, and the prophet is led through the water up to the loins, because the fullness of holy action then grows within us when [Col. 0656D] the wisdom we have received extinguishes, as far as possible, every delight of the flesh. For unless delight of the flesh existed in the loins, the Psalmist would not say to God: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. XXV). The water therefore reaches the loins when the wisdom poured into us extinguishes wanton allurements and incentives of the flesh. The man then measures a thousand once more: a torrent which, as it is said, the prophet could not cross, because the deep waters of the torrent had swollen and could not be forded. What else is indicated to us by this, except that, after our feet have been established in the path of good works, after the knees of our heart no longer waver doubtfully but have been firmly strengthened for walking along the path of righteousness, [Col. 0657A] and after the pleasures of the loins and the burning incentives of the flesh have been extinguished, every perfect person is raised to such fullness of contemplation that, since the mind cannot fully comprehend so extraordinary a depth, it is unable to cross the ford of the swelling waters.

All these things seem most fittingly applicable to the deeds of blessed Alexius. When, withdrawing from his ancestral home and from the vanity of this world, he sought exile, then the water of this torrent reached him, in a certain sense, up to the ankles. This water rose to the ankles of Moses and Joshua when the divine voice commanded them to remove their sandals from their feet (Exod. III; Josh. V). It later flowed up to the feet of the apostles [Col. 0657B] when they were told: “Do not carry a purse, or a bag, or sandals” (Luke X). It was necessary that the announcers of the Old Testament and preachers of the evangelical faith should walk along the road of true humility and not protect their footsteps with a covering of death, since they were announcing life to the people; rather, they were to display within themselves that spiritual covering of which the Apostle says: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). Hence Isaiah says: “Blessed are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Isa. LII).

But when Saint Alexius had steadfastly and most patiently endured for the longest periods of time such poverty in unknown regions, then the water of the torrent rose to his knees, because, with all hope in the world utterly extinguished, [Col. 0657C] he had now strengthened the steps of his mind firmly and unconquerably in the way of the Lord. Later, when he lived within the halls of his father’s house, when he saw carnal affections on every side, when he could not avoid the presence of his parents and, certainly the more difficult and intolerable matter, the beautiful appearance of his bride in their daily and mutual encounters, then the water of the torrent rose, as it were, to his loins; for heavenly wisdom so subdued and extinguished the incentives of his flesh, and the ardor of the Holy Spirit so scorched his loins, that, while he filled his vessel with the daily [p. 145] streams of heavenly grace, the substance of his extinguished flesh supplied no fuel to tickling lust. The water therefore reached the loins of the blessed man because the Holy Spirit, boiling within him, [Col. 0657D] drenched the fire of youthful age and the alluring movements of tantalizing passions with the hidden moisture of his dew; and thus it consumed every fuel of lust that could naturally burn in his marrow and inward parts.

To apply the whole oracle of this prophecy appropriately to this blessed man, it is also not inconsistent that the prophet mentioned above was finally unable to cross the torrent, of which it is said: “Because the deep waters of the torrent had swollen and could not be forded” (Ezek. XLVII). From small and shallow waters one reaches the unfordable fullness of a deep torrent; for from a small contemplation—fleeting and seen only in passing—which any holy man enjoys while still in this corruptible [Col. 0658A] flesh, he is raised, as soon as he dies, to the fullness of deep and perfect contemplation, so that he is advanced to behold the very appearance of supreme truth (I Cor. XIII). The torrent therefore cannot be forded, because the eternal sweetness of honeyed contemplation can no longer be enclosed by any limit or ended by any length of time. That torrent, then, is eternal contemplation, which is not sought through faith at that time but already possessed through sight. Since it does not pass away, it cannot be crossed; and since it cannot be expressed in human words, it cannot, as is said, be traversed by a human being.

That torrent was thirsted for by the one who, already rejoicing in certain hope, said: “But I shall appear in your sight with righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” [Col. 0658B] (Ps. XVI). Again he says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV). To the deep streams of this immense torrent blessed Alexius came when, after the triumph of his glorious victory, he died happily in his father’s house: a triumph, I say, because the life of this holy man is truly an astonishing triumph and an almost new and unheard-of victory. And since, according to the prophetic word, God is wondrous in his saints (Ps. LXVII), he appeared all the more wondrous in the testing of this unconquered soldier of his, insofar as through him he fought against the allurements of the flesh and the temptations of the devil’s deceit by a new and unusual kind of martyrdom.

An ancient history records (Eutropius, Roman History, [Col. 0658C] book II, at the end) that when the Romans engaged the Carthaginians in a naval battle, they won the victory; and, as it is read there, no triumph could ever have been more pleasing to the Romans, since those who until then had been terrifying to their enemies in earthly combat were now victorious amid the waters of the sea. That victory was therefore dearer because it was rare, and more glorious because it was new. Thus, just as that naval triumph was more welcome at Rome because it was new, so certainly the virtue of blessed Alexius pleases the Church more because of its unusual novelty.

David, when he pretended before Achish, king of Gath, to be insane and demented, wisely escaped his sword (I Kings XII). Our Savior descended into hell, not to inhabit it as though he were its resident [p. 146] [Col. 0658D], but rather to destroy it and, as its overthrower, disperse the hiding places of diabolical wickedness. So also blessed Alexius, when he entered his father’s house as though he were renouncing his former course and turning backward, deceived the prince of this world and eluded the author of every deceit and wickedness.

Hence he offers a new kind of martyrdom and a new spectacle for admiration. For to the martyrs, prison was punishment and chains were oppression; but for this man, his own house, decorated with gilded dining rooms, was the material of temptation. The armed hand of executioners tortured them; the daily sight of his parents’ affection punished him more severely. Horrible rage on the part of the judge raged against every other martyr; against this man, the gentle, mild, and lovely face of his wife contended. Punishment was inflicted upon the martyrs in the halls of princes; [Col. 0659A] but he was invisibly tortured in his own house, as though in the arena of a tribunal. For them, torment was punishment; for him, by contrast, caresses were torment.

Lazarus, who lay at the rich man’s gate, unwillingly suffered hunger and longed for the crumbs falling from the table, although they were not given to him (Luke XVI); [Col. 0659B] therefore, without doubt, this poor man was of greater merit than Lazarus. The former desired not merely to receive a little but, as Truth testifies, to be satisfied, yet no one mercifully granted him food. This man, however, although the costly abundance of all riches was freely available to him, although all the glory of this world deigned to offer itself to him without charge—indeed, even forced itself upon him against his will—rejected everything, despised all things, and irrevocably turned them away and cast them aside. O vigorous soldier of Christ! O wholly unconquered and most distinguished warrior of the heavenly army!

It is certainly recorded in the Annals of the Romans (Eutropius, Roman History, book III, at the beginning) that when the consul Marcellus, having imprudently fallen into the hands of the enemy, found no way by which he could escape because the Gauls surrounded him in a circle, he suddenly plunged, as a most ardent warrior, into the midst of the enemy; and, while all were struck by his unexpected boldness, he killed their king, named Virdumarus [Vitromarus]. Where a great victory would already have seemed to have been achieved if he had merely escaped unharmed, he then brought back spoils of exceptional value beyond all hope. So too this Marcellus of ours—no longer a defender of Rome but [Col. 0659C] a soldier of the holy Church—when it was undoubtedly considered a great victory if he fled naked from such ample and splendid riches, did not think it sufficient unless, on returning home, he also voluntarily provoked intolerable struggles against himself.

Yet we are commanded by the Lord himself, who is the author of virtues and leader of spiritual warriors, to abandon everything; we are not commanded to fight against those things daily at close quarters, as though engaging hand to hand. The Israelite people were commanded to depart from Egypt (Exod. III), not ordered to return. Abraham went out from his land at the command of the Lord who ordered him (Gen. XII), but afterward he never returned to renewed struggles with the Chaldeans. Peter, roused by an angel, left Herod’s prison [Col. 0659D] (Acts XII), but did not return again to Herod. It is therefore enough if we leave behind what we have possessed; there is no need to return again to endure their struggles.

[p. 147] Blessed Alexius, therefore, when he abandoned all earthly things and cast away all the wealth and riches belonging to his father, fulfilled the commands of the heavenly injunction (Luke XVIII). But when he returned to his own home, that outstanding renouncer undoubtedly surpassed the limit of the divine law. And because the chosen receive “a good measure, pressed down and shaken together” into their bosom, and each receives his own reward according to his labor (I Cor. III), he possesses immeasurable glory who did not keep within measure in his labor. He who exceeded the evangelical rule in the contest of his struggle [Col. 0660A] received an exceeding reward from the hand of the just Rewarder. For he himself became the reward of recompense who had been the cause of his struggle; and he who had been the author of the battle became the crown of victory: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

*SERMON XXIX. ON SAINT MARY MAGDALENE. (22 JULY)*

Today mercy and truth have met one another, and the multitude of the Lord’s mercies has been poured out upon a sinful woman (Luke VII). For the Son of the Virgin is touched by the hands of a sinful, menstruating woman; God, and the Son of God, is touched by a woman weakened by illness. The unclean woman touches the feet of the pure one and the purifier, [Col. 0660B] and the guilty woman falls at the feet of the Creator. The transgressor passes into heartfelt affection and returns to her heart; the multitude of tears condemns the enormity of her crimes. Mercy overlooks the service of the woman who touches him, and that recompensing eye of majesty, in blessed disregard, does not regard the urgency of her acts of homage. Mary kisses Christ’s feet with repeated kisses, floods the Redeemer’s feet with her streaming eyes, wipes them with her hair, anoints them with fragrant ointments, and drenches them with perfumes. He who loves singularity sees and is envious, and the Pharisee’s arrogance rebukes both: him for ignorance, her for presumption. But deliberate providence suspends judgment while she seeks to perform her service, and holds back its prepared rebuke until Mary’s sacrifice passes into a burnt offering. The angels rejoice over the sinful woman who is doing penance [Col. 0660C] (Luke XV), and that heavenly assembly is sprinkled with the fragrance of the perfume; the sweetness of mercy surrounds both the one who saves and the one being saved. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V); and mercy, outweighing the multitude of crimes, shuts that multitude out.

How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord (Ps. XXX), in the confession of the sinful woman! How just the rebuke of the Pharisee’s pride and abuse! The service of the woman who attends upon him is enumerated, while the wickedness of the indignant man is touched upon indirectly, the entire literal coherence of the passage attacking Simon’s envy. And because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III), her sins are forgiven because she loves much; indeed, they are imposed upon him who neglects much. He had not been satisfied from the breasts of the bride [Col. 0660D], nor had he put on the feeling of compassion while rereading the law, which knows no mercy but knows justice.

The law is harsh toward the harsh, promulgated on stone, ready to strike, ignorant of mercy. [p. 148] The law excludes the place of repentance, denies pardon, and knows nothing of amendment. The law is hard and sour wine, strained from the most bitter grapes, consecrated to savagery, passed on to Israel, and offered to the Savior. It is the wine whose drinkers’ teeth are set on edge, not that produced from the vine’s offspring which the Savior drank new in his Father’s kingdom (Luke XXII). Truly, “the breasts of the bride are better than this wine” (Song I).

But what are those breasts? Let the apostle Paul come forward and identify for us the breasts flowing with blessed milk. “Rejoice,” he says, [Col. 0661A] “with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII). O how, in a very brief saying, he depicted the mark of the whole of religion! In so elegant a phrase he set forth piety, established equity, and removed envy. With these breasts Mother Church gives milk to those making progress and nourishes the perfect. “Rejoice,” he says, “with those who rejoice.”

Let the madness of worldly applause depart from here, and let worldly merriment withdraw; for “there is no rejoicing for the wicked,” says the Lord (Ps. XLVIII). Do you suppose that the mouths of those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things are filled with joy? (Prov. II.) Or have those who are carried away by the praises of flatterers recognized the joy of divine rejoicing? Will those who are clothed in purple and fine linen and feast splendidly every day (Luke XVI) obtain joy and gladness? [Col. 0661B] Far be it from us to think that in the land of those who live softly there is found material for joy, when the face of the world is changed by so many alternations, so that what is lifted up is dashed down, and what has been dashed down takes breath.

But there is a joy made most firm by its continual delight, which the perfect soul promises itself from a secure conscience. For the mind, purely and closely wiped clean of the dust of this world, fixing the whole affection of its desire upon the sharp point of divine contemplation, rejoices—yes, rejoices—in the Lord, and its soul exults in its God (Isa. LXI). Such a soul despises threats, knows no fear, mocks false hope, and, immune from every scandal, sleeps in peace in the same place and rests (Ps. IV). “Great peace have those who love your law,” says the righteous man, “and there is no scandal for them” (Ps. CXVIII). For he knew that executioners do not persecute martyrs but crown them. [Col. 0661C]

With those who rejoice in this way the Apostle rejoices (Rom. XII), and, so that they may rejoice more abundantly, he promises it with complete confidence. This joy is full and certain, and it is all the more certain insofar as it is impressed more closely around steadfast identity. This is the breast of shared joy, from which the milk of exhortation is poured out; by it the perfect are nourished (Isa. LXVI), so that, when they have been weaned from this milk, they may feast at the entrance into God’s glory.

The second breast is: “weep with those who weep.” Does the Apostle command us to weep over the loss of possessions, the cessation of pleasures, the deaths of children, the onset of illness, the severity of poverty, or the power of one stronger than ourselves? Far from it. Those who weep in such matters are the ones to be mourned. Religious sorrow either grieves over another’s sin or over one’s own. [Col. 0661D] Blessed are those whose mourning is directed toward this purpose, because they may await the sweetness of consolation.

With how gentle and sweetest a spirit was the spirit of the one who knew how to instruct sinners in a spirit of gentleness, suspend vengeance, and embrace the sinner within himself through affectionate services until the sinner was restored to life. From this breast of compassion the milk of consolation is poured out, [p. 149] and with this milk the Apostle feeds those who cannot yet partake of solid food (I Cor. III). The lover of innocence, the friend of peace, compassionate toward those who suffer and rejoicing with those who rejoice, reaches the goal of perfection when his course has been completed. These are words sprinkled with milky fluids, better than wine, sweeter than honey, sounding of mercy and redolent of piety. “Fragrant,” [Col. 0662A] he says, “with the finest ointments” (Song I). Truly worthy are the breasts from which an infinity of ointments is strained, spreading their scented flow all around the city of the living God. These are the ointments which the queen of Sheba brought to Jerusalem, concerning which Scripture says: “No such spices were brought again, as those which the queen of Sheba gave to Solomon” (III Kings X).

How excellently that subtle Spirit has added “best,” a word which claims for itself possession of this entire book! There is a good ointment, which Mary poured upon the Savior’s feet (Luke VII). There is also a better one, which the same woman—if indeed she is the same—poured upon the head of the one reclining (John XII). And there is the best, which she herself prepared for the whole body of Christ (Mark XVI).

The first [Col. 0662B] ointment is that of contrition, descending from the remembrance of sins and from a contrite and humbled spirit. With this the feet of the one who walks upon the wings of the winds are anointed (Ps. XVII). Here Mary adores him at the place where his feet stood. They stood, I say, because with the very strong hand of love she held both feet until she had anointed both and heard the remission of her crimes, her dismissal in peace: “Your sins are forgiven,” he says, “go in peace” (Luke VII). Great misery is truly washed away and wiped clean by great mercy; and this happens swiftly, because the sinful woman’s tears and the Savior’s forgiveness are joined together without any interval. Her sins are forgiven, and she is dismissed in peace, so that she need not be anxious about the past and may be secure about the future.

[Col. 0662C] These feet are mercy and judgment; to kiss one without the other is either reckless presumption or a despair that must be fled. For who, constantly attending to God’s mercy, would not immediately desire the repose of a more tepid life? When he considers the Lord of the universe assuming the form of a servant for servants, laboring for thirty-three years for our salvation in the midst of this earth, being seized, bound, pierced with a lance, crucified, and suffering all this for the sons of men, he immediately flatters and beguiles himself with deceptive hope. He rejoices to encounter mercy and mercies; he knows nothing of judgment, is ignorant of justice, and considers punishable things not to be punished. He is deceived who kisses the foot of mercy in such a way that he does not attend to the foot of judgment, who presumes entirely upon the compassion of mercy, [Col. 0662D] believing that this alone is sufficient for salvation: that he believes.

But again, when he withdraws his mouth and touches the foot of judgment with more frequent kisses, the substance of flesh and soul is shaken, and a more violent blast strikes the condition of both men. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10), to offend the Creator, not to know the Lord, to kick against the command of the Ruler, who has authority to cast body and soul into Gehenna (Matt. 10). Truly, as the Apostle says, there is a terrifying expectation of judgment (Heb. 10), when fire will blaze before him (Ps. 49), and the powers of heaven will be shaken (Luke 21), and the strongest fire will consume the breadth of the world while consciences waver.

150 [Col. 0663A] Nothing is more terrifying than to see a robber’s workshop full of blood, piled high with insults, and surging with torments. Who, thinking upon these things for long, would not immediately tremble and be rolled into the abyss of despair? One must not therefore linger too long upon this foot, lest the fierceness of the Judge close off the gaze of mercy. Let the affection of the penitent soul therefore anoint both feet: now embracing mercy, now kissing judgment; and let the contrite spirit offer a holocaust.

See Mary firmly attending to the foot of judgment, while the noble and wanton woman does not regard the faces of the guests but throws herself forward, stretched out at the feet of Majesty, full of sorrow, unable to endure fear, wounded by the dart of compunction. Yet she also kisses the foot of mercy with lips pressed more fervently, and clings firmly in hope to the footprints of the one reclining, until she hears: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 7).

Truly, it is a precious ointment by which not only an earthly house but also the heavenly one is sprinkled. Yet the substances from which it is compounded are of the lowest kind, and their great abundance can be found within our little gardens. Our sins, therefore, planted in our consciences—so numerous that they cannot be counted because of their multitude—are its ingredients. Crushed in the mortar of penitence with the pestle of mortification, sprinkled with the oil of discernment, with the fire of sorrow placed beneath, and cooked in the cauldron of discipline, they produce a precious ointment, acceptable to the Savior’s feet. We have prepared it briefly, leaving to the wise ample opportunity to develop the matter fully. And although the material may seem rather unworthy, this ointment is nevertheless good: it fills the house, penetrates the heavens, gladdens the angels, and pours joy and gladness back into the blessed city. This is the sacrifice of justice, because “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50).

The second ointment is that of devotion, made from remembrance of God’s benefits. The composition of this ointment is altogether most worthy, and in comparison with it the earlier mixture deserves to be despised. Its ingredients have been brought from the heavenly paradise and cannot be found in the land of the sons of men. For divinely bestowed virtues, ground in the mortar of thought with the pestle of the most diligent meditation, poured over with the oil of exultation, infused with the fire of justice, and boiled in the cauldron of humility, produce an ointment marvelous both in fragrance and in power. It alone can be poured and offered upon the head of the reclining Lord as a sign of reverence for his Majesty. We have also gathered this together briefly, reserving a multitude of words for those who know how to extract much from little. Yet the difference between the two must be noted, and the superiority of the second must be considered: the former is “a contrite spirit” offered as a sacrifice to God (Ps. 50), whereas the latter is “a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49), which honors God. We therefore anoint the Redeemer’s feet when we are pierced with compunction over our sins; we anoint his head when, for the virtues bestowed upon us, we heap thanks upon the giver of virtues.

Yet there must be an interval of lingering between the feet and the head, because it is certainly a very difficult and presumptuous leap to fly from the Lord’s footprints to his crown. For she who anointed his feet did not also anoint his head: that prostitute is read to have done the former, this woman none of those things, according to the saying: “Overturn the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. 12). Mary therefore anointed the holy head of God, surely by then beloved, by then become intimate, and far removed from the contaminations of that sinful woman, whom that wretched sevenfold [spirit] tormented.

Furthermore, if the two ointments already mentioned are of such dignity that one pleases the Lord upon his feet and the other upon his head, where will we find the third, which is the best and surpasses all others? But far be it from the Bride of Truth to disagree with the truth, and to boast that she possesses something which she cannot possess. There is therefore a third ointment, the ointment of compassion, which is above all spices, salutary for every sickness and danger, and never found ineffective against any plague. For concerning it we read: “Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices so that, coming, they might anoint Jesus” (Mark 16).

Do you see what is set forth at the very beginning of the chapter: that not one or two, but three women scarcely suffice to buy an ointment of such composition? Do you understand that this preparation claims for itself not the feet or the head, but the entire body of the crucified one? Surely it is a precious preparation, sufficient for the whole body of the Creator. And observe that the ointment poured upon his feet was received with such worthy gentleness that it convicted the murmuring Pharisee through an extended parable and reproached him with a pointed example (Luke 7). Likewise, by the ointment poured over his head he refuted the indignant disciples, declaring the woman’s deed good and restraining their swollen arrogance with measured words.

But this ointment, so salutary and so wondrous, he willed to be expended upon his dead body, though he had of course reserved it while he was alive. For Christ has two bodies: one which he assumed from the Virgin, and the other, the Church, which the kindness of the Redeemer holds more dear. Indeed, he exposed the former to death for the sake of the latter, handing himself over to torments, bound to the cross with criminals, and condemned to the most shameful death. Can we prepare so salutary a composition? The miseries of all the wretched, both of souls and of bodies, when examined with the eye of compassion, are its ingredients. Crushed in the mortar of generosity with the pestle of sweetness, smeared with the oil of love, kindled by the fire of compassion, and skimmed in the cauldron of perseverance, they produce an ointment marvelous even to the angels.

There are men rich in virtues in the house of the Lord; let us investigate whether such ointments are found among them. Paul is the first to come to my mind, as he usually does, wholly anointed with the ointment in question. “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11.) Happy soul, which made itself like a lost vessel, so that it might gather all the miseries of others into its own conscience. He had given himself wholly to the whole body of Christ, becoming all things to all people, so that he might win them all (2 Cor. 9).

But consider also that simple and upright man, one who feared God: see how he walked not according to man—or rather, according to man; and what is truer, above man: “I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor” (Job 1, 29), and so forth. These things had so anointed him with this ointment that he emerged more abundantly watered from the chamber of mercy.

I recall Samuel, who mourned over Saul not once but throughout all the days of his life. Although he knew that Saul had been removed far from the eyes of the Godhead, the compassion that had entered the soul of the one who grieved did not cease, pouring out tears—perhaps not useful, but nevertheless pious ones (1 Sam. 15). David mourned his parricidal son with continual lamentation (2 Sam. 18), grieving in him not a bond of flesh but the destruction of faith.

See how Joseph was wholly smeared with this honey (Gen. 43). His brothers come, no longer standing before a brother but before a lord: conscious of betrayal, guilty of murder, burning with fraternal bloodshed. When Joseph sees them, forgetful of every injury, he is flooded with the sweetest tears, and the fat of compassion hidden within flows outward through his eyes. Hatred flees; he knows no anger; he does not store up time for wrath. He returns good for evil and sweetness in return for trust.

I almost forgot Moses, so drenched with the dew of this sacred liquid that he was wholly overflowed and drenched by it. Israel sins, and Moses strives to reconcile the sinner to the Creator; but the Lord pretends not to hear the one who pleads. The Creator of all promises Moses many things and seeks permission from Moses—the Moses whom he himself made—to strike them. “Let me be,” he says, “so that my anger may burn against them, and I may make you into a great nation.” Moses replied: “If you forgive, Lord, forgive; but if not, erase me from the book which you have written” (Exod. 32). Astonishing sweetness indeed: he rejects the leadership of another nation and desires to be erased from the book of the living unless the offense of the sinners is forgiven.

These are the ointments of offering and mercy, drawn from the breasts of the bride, driving away all weaknesses and dispelling [or, perhaps, “defeating”] passions.

Happy is Mary, who anointed Jesus’ feet; happier is that same woman, who anointed the head of the Author; happiest is she who prepared the fragrant ointment for the whole body of Christ. Consider with what most vehement affection of love this blessed woman loved Christ the King. “Lord,” she says, “if you have taken him away, tell me, and I will take him away” (John 20).

Whom do you mean by “him,” Mary, when you have mentioned no one to whom your reference could be made? Do you think that the memory of your beloved is present in everyone’s heart in the same way as it is in the chamber of your heart? “And I,” she says, “will take him away.” What a wondrous thing! Will a tender woman carry and take away a man of mature age, whose body scarcely requires a hundred pounds of ointments? It is an ardent and impassioned utterance, poured forth from the love of purity, promising what she cannot accomplish. For nothing seems difficult to one who loves.

Who ought to despair, when such a great sinner obtained not only forgiveness but glory? May she herself intercede today for our sins and render our Judge, her bridegroom—the blessed God throughout the ages of ages—merciful toward us. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. I. ON SAINT APOLLINARIS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA AND MARTYR. (23 JULY)

On this day, dearest brothers, we have come to a most joyful and sufficiently delightful spectacle, and with the eyes of faith we have contemplated the contest of a glorious arena. For we have seen one citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem bravely go forth to battle for his king, while the innumerable populace of Babylon fiercely fights in unanimous conspiracy against a single head. We have seen this soldier of Christ carry forward the triumphant banner of the cross against the world; and, on the other side, we have seen the lovers of the world confront their beloved one in compact ranks.

They, finally, surround him on every side, hurl various weapons, discharge arrows, raise engines, and, so that they may break through Christ’s rampart, assemble every device of warfare. But he, girded with the sword of the spiritual word, clothed in the breastplate of faith, protected by the helmet of hope (Eph. 6), gathers himself beneath the shield of his patience and keeps it moving with watchful eye against every blow of the storm of battle.

They apply fire; but he, kindled by the immense ardor of charity, does not feel the flames of the outward fire. They pour boiling water over his mangled limbs; but he is divinely refreshed by the abundant shower of the Holy Spirit, singing with the Prophet: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65). They beat him with rods, break him with clubs, suspend him on the rack, cast him into prison, and finally send him away in chains into exile. But he, established in the citadel of his mind, watches from a distance, as though he were someone else, whatever is done against him and beneath him, saying with Paul: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). And again: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing in us, beyond all measure in the height, an eternal weight of glory” (ibid.).

Thus all the darts of the enemies became for Blessed Apollinaris material for glorious victory. From the very place where their cruelty tries to cast him down, his patience is strengthened to stand more firmly. For when the holy man is caught amid the battles of persecution, the more harshly he sees the hailstorm of weapons raging, the more carefully he presents his shield of steadfastness on every side. The more violently he sees the assault of battle advancing, the more he strives to gather his strength within himself and to stir himself to courageous action. He stands ready everywhere, watches attentively everywhere, and meets the swords coming from every side without disturbance.
