Since, then, my brothers, we have above called Blessed Apollinaris’s struggle an arena, let us inquire a little more subtly, if you please, whether this comparison has been appropriately made. The wrestler in the arena fights naked, and Blessed Apollinaris is known to have been naked of the garment of worldly possessions. Such a contest is presented in the spectacle of the citizens, as Blessed Paul fittingly testifies concerning himself and the other soldiers of Christ, saying: “We have been made a spectacle to angels and to men” (2 Cor. 4).

It is customary for trainers to give boys the oil which they call *ceroma*, so that all the members of their bodies may be anointed with it. But the holy apostle Peter, the blessed Apollinaris’s trainer—or rather, not merely trainer but leader—poured over him the anointing of the Holy Spirit when he sent him to the contests of persecution. For, as the sacred history of his deeds relates, Blessed Peter the Apostle said to his disciple Apollinaris: “Why are you sitting with us? Behold, you have been instructed in everything that Jesus did. Rise, receive the Holy Spirit and likewise the episcopate, and go to the city called Ravenna.”

What he says—“Receive the Holy Spirit and go”—is as though he were saying: “Anoint your limbs with oil and engage courageously in battle.” For concerning this oil of the Holy Spirit it is said through the prophet: “The yoke will rot from the face of the oil” (Isa. 10). Concerning it the Psalmist also sings: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him” (Ps. 88).

It is customary for trainers to examine beforehand the limbs of the disciples who are about to fight: how broad and strong the chest is, how healthy and full the muscles swell, how the abdomen lies beneath, neither weighing the body down by its bulk nor weakening it through excessive thinness. If they see that everything is suited to military use, they immediately rebuke his sluggishness with stern severity and kindle his still-reluctant spirit to love of glory; they encourage and urge him on, and, so that he may not be afraid, they praise their own strength before him.

So indeed, so indeed, the blessed Apostle examines the limbs of his pupil as though before the very entrance to the arena, and inflames him to prepare for confrontation with words of persuasive exhortation. What does it mean to say, “Why are you sitting with us?” except: “Now lay aside your sluggishness, so that after completing the victory you may reach the crown”? And what does it mean to say, “Behold, you have been instructed in everything that Jesus did,” except: “All the joints of your body are now vigorous with perfected strength, and nothing remains for you except, setting fear aside, to begin the fight”?

Hence he aptly adds: “Preach to them in the name of Jesus, and do not be afraid,” as though he were saying: “By the authority of my command, engage in combat; join battle, so that you may carry away the common victory of both kings from your defeated enemies. Run eagerly through the stadium, so that you may deserve to reach the prize appointed for victors. Do not hesitate to take up the fight from which, with God as its author, you will bring back the noble palm of victory.

“I—I myself—command you, because I possess the power of binding not only on earth but also in heaven. I send you to feed the Lord’s sheep, I who guard the fold of the whole holy Church under the care entrusted to me.” Let the prerogative of the teacher therefore be the disciple’s confidence to presume, and let the authority of the one who sends be the confidence of the one sent.

O blessed Apostle, how gladly and cheerfully I contemplate the shifting contrast in you! With a beautiful variety I behold you now weak, now most strong: weak, I say, when denying your teacher, but most strong when sending a disciple forth for the confession of that same teacher. You do not fear assigning Ravenna, mistress of many cities, to your disciple, although you yourself had trembled before the maidservant of a single priest. You do not fear sending him alone into the stormy waves of a most turbulent city, although you had been afraid to walk upon the sea’s waves with the Creator of the seas himself.

For it was said to him: “You created the north and the sea” (Ps. 88). Although you said, “Lord, command me to come to you” (Matt. 14), nevertheless, unless you had been afraid, you would not have begun to sink; unless you had endured some wave of shipwreck in the boat of faith, you would never have heard from the mouth of Truth: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (ibid.)

Nor is it surprising that you then feared the danger of the sea, since, through the same weakness of mind, you were unwilling to undergo the cross for your teacher and Lord. For when he told you that he would be crucified for the redemption of the human race, you immediately replied: “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be gracious to you, Lord; this shall not happen” (Matt. 16).

What is this, blessed Apostle? Do you wish to close the place from which the price of our redemption will emerge? Do you wish to restrict the spring that descends to cleanse the stains of our wickedness? Behold, you already know beyond doubt that he is God, yet you dissuade him from undergoing death. For if you did not believe him to be God, you would not have said, “May God be gracious to you, Lord.”

Finally, the disciple’s faith agrees with the Teacher’s assertion: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10). But you who stand firm through faith lie prostrate through weakness; the one whom faith raises up, fear lays low. Thus, although you had feared death for the Teacher on the cross and the depth of the sea for yourself, you then do not hesitate to send your beloved disciple amid the fury of raging persecutors.

Why is this, unless what is said through your fellow apostle has been fulfilled in you: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4)? For you had now heard the Lord say again: “Simon, do you love me?” (John 21). And when you answered, “Lord, you know that I love you,” you immediately heard: “Feed my sheep.” Again the Lord had said: “As the Father has loved me, so I love you” (John 15). Therefore, just as the Lord loved you when he sent you among the dangers of persecutors to feed his sheep, so you love your disciple when you send him to martyrdom for those same sheep.

But, my brothers, let us examine these apostolic words by subtle investigation and observe how the authority of the canonical rule of the Church everywhere maintains one principle in choosing superiors. For Blessed Apollinaris is told: “Why are you sitting with us? Behold, you have been instructed in everything that Jesus did.”

Again, when the same prince of the Apostles wished to appoint another apostle in the place of Judas, so as to restrain the perversity of the newly converted, he said: “Therefore it is necessary that one of these men who have gathered with us throughout all the time in which the Lord Jesus entered and went out among us should become with us a witness of his resurrection” (Acts 1).

Hence, while preaching Christ to the gentiles, that same man said: “God raised him up on the third day and granted that he should become manifest, not to all the people, but to witnesses appointed beforehand by God—to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10).

Hence the Lord himself, speaking in the Gospel about sending the Holy Spirit to the Apostles, said: “He will bear witness concerning me, and you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning” (John 16), as though he were saying: “For this reason you will bear suitable witness concerning me: whatever you teach others, you yourselves first learned through long and continuous association.”

Let the newly converted hear; let the arrogant hear—those who, like bellows inflated by the wind of arrogance and the fire of desire, wish to teach before they know, and in Christ’s school long to preside in the chair before they have felt the rod. When, in disorderly fashion, they burst into the rights of governance not through the door but from elsewhere, they plainly show themselves to be not shepherds but thieves and hirelings, who care nothing about benefiting others but burn with the most destructive flame of ambition to preside.

These men are not placed above others to guard Christ’s fold, nor to feed the Lord’s flock, but to nourish their wretched flesh softly in lusts and pleasures. When they see themselves set over their neighbors, they raise their blind minds upon the horns of pride.

Let those who are such hear, therefore, and either take care to restrain themselves from this presumption or know that they already lie severed from the body of the holy Church—perhaps not openly, but truly and by the roots. Behold, the blessed Apostles, upon whom the holy Church is founded as upon the most solid foundations, appoint not a novice or an unlearned man, but one whom they have observed to be mature in teaching and in devotion to holy conduct.

This is what Peter seeks in Matthias when he chooses him for the apostleship; this is what he seeks in Apollinaris when he promotes him to the episcopate. What the Lord had provided in the Apostles, the Apostles consider in apostolic men.

[Col. 0669D] Nor should this be passed over: the blessed Apostle kissed his disciple and sent him away from himself. Here the custom of the ancient Fathers is recalled, and in the new age the antiquity of the ancient patriarchs is restored. Behold, Isaac again kisses his son. Behold, Jacob is again blessed, and patriarch is consecrated by patriarch according to the authoritative order of tradition.

To the former it was said: “Come near to me, my son, so that my soul may bless you” (Gen. 27). To this one it was said: “Rise, receive the Holy Spirit.” To the former it was said: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth an abundance of grain, wine, and oil” (ibid.); to the latter it is said: “May our Lord Jesus Christ send his angel, who will prepare your way, and may he grant you what you ask.”

Thus Jacob himself also gave a kiss to Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh when, placing them among the other patriarchs, he blessed them (Gen. 48). From this too the ecclesiastical custom arose that bishops give a kiss to those whom they consecrate.

From this, brothers—from this, I ask you—understand how great is the exaltation of Blessed Apollinaris: he is chosen as an apostle for the citadel of the episcopate and solemnly ordained as a patriarch. He is advanced by the one, and in no different manner, by whom the Apostles are also promoted.

In him, therefore, there appears both apostolic dignity and patriarchal sublimity, because he is advanced by an apostolic mouth and consecrated with patriarchal solemnity. Hence it follows that while the others who have suffered punishments for the testimony of the truth are called martyrs, he, who not only suffered but was also so nobly chosen by an Apostle for martyrdom, is rightly called an apostolic martyr.

Amid these things, dearest brothers, return to yourselves and examine your deeds with anxious scrutiny. You who gladly hear the praises of a martyr, take care to lead a praiseworthy life. For “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15). Those who live praiseworthy lives rightly exalt the saints with praises. And those who hear the virtues of the strong hear them profitably when the praises they hear kindle them to love imitation.

Otherwise, what benefit is it if you see others established in the heights while you yourself descend headlong to the depths? What benefit is it to extol the triumphs of strong warriors if you yourself are not ashamed daily to turn your back on the enemies? Whoever, therefore, rejoices that the martyrs of Christ have acted bravely, let him also take up arms among Christ’s soldiers.

Are there no enemies outside? Turn your hands against yourself, and you will find many rebellious citizens within. Subdue pride, slaughter anger, extinguish lust, restrain avarice, kill envy; and, to embrace everything briefly with the Apostle: “Crucify your flesh with its vices” (Gal. 5). This is to act bravely; this is to fight like a man.

For what good is it if the ranks of persecutors do not besiege you around the rampart, while barbarism of the vices rages within the city walls? Do you wish to learn still more clearly how you may find martyrdom in the peace of the holy Church? Listen attentively; understand carefully. Let the heart keep watch; let the eye not sleep.

For what I say is very brief. Ascend, therefore, the tribunal of the mind and drag yourself before the court of inquiry. Let thought accuse; let the spirit judge; let the penitent conscience strike like an executioner; let a stream of tears burst forth like a wound. Thus, through the likeness of martyrdom, you will reach the true dignity of martyrs, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. II. ON SAINT APOLLINARIS, BISHOP AND MARTYR. (23 JULY)

The glorious solemnity of the apostolic martyr, dearest brothers, has caused your assembly to be present with joyful devotion. It is therefore fitting that we should rejoice together with you in shared gladness and spend this entire day in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

Today the whole world everywhere rightly rejoices with overflowing happiness. Rightly the holy Church, arranging the choirs of the faithful, alternates sweet-sounding voices of melody. Let Antioch rejoice, which deserved to give birth to such a son; let Rome exult, which was able to have such a disciple; but above all let the city of Ravenna rejoice, which deserved to receive so great a patron.

For what was previously a shrine of demons has through him become a capitol of heavenly senators. There the bodies of martyrs now rest; there the patronage of many saints is treasured. What was formerly fruitful in evil offspring, producing much chaff for hell, now, by God’s grace, gives birth to many citizens for heaven, so that it may now be said, not undeservedly, to its people: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household!” (Eph. 2.) And through Peter: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition” (1 Pet. 2).

We are kings because we carry the banner of the cross upon our foreheads. We are rightly called priests because we are marked with the anointing of chrism.

Rightly, therefore, that distinguished metropolis rejoices especially in the feast of Blessed Apollinaris, through whom it, once profane and rustic, has now become priestly and royal. Its dignity is so shared with the Roman citadel that the one may appropriately be called the mother and the other the daughter. What the mother possesses in the heavenly keeper of the keys, the daughter possesses wholly in his disciple; and what the Apostle confers upon her, the apostolic martyr adds to it.

For if the city of Constantinople, because it transferred Roman citizens into itself, was called a second Rome, how much more should this city, which received so great a prince from Rome, be called a second Rome! Is it more glorious to receive Quirites from the Roman senate than to possess a martyr from the Roman Church?

From that aspect by which Rome is carnal, it produced carnal sons; but from that by which it is spiritual, it brought forth from itself a spiritual son. “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John 3). But whatever honor we attribute to that city by saying that it resembles Rome, we refer it to the praise of God; we do not seek the favor of men. For the adornment of a dwelling is the honor of its inhabitant, and the honor of a soldier is the glory of the emperor.

But, beloved, let us carefully consider the beautiful order of divine providence and investigate how wonderfully almighty God determined to illuminate the darkness of that region. For just as the morning star rises at its appearance and precedes the sun, so the most blessed martyr, proceeding from the eastern region, first introduced within the borders of Ravenna the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is truly the sun of Justice.

And how well the name “Morning Star” suited him, since he made the first miracle of his coming a miracle of light! For as soon as he was received as a guest in a suburban dwelling, he restored sight to the blind son of the soldier Irenaeus. Thus he drove away the darkness of unbelief from the hearts of the parents; and while he restored the eyes of the forehead to the one, he opened the light of the heart to the others much more happily.

Rightly, therefore, it is said that just as the Morning Star is carried throughout the world, so the most blessed man was carried into his city. But how many punishments he endured there, how many torments of death he underwent, he was indeed able wonderfully to endure, but we cannot recount, with however great eloquence of tongue, what he suffered.

He is beaten, burned, wounded, tortured on the rack, and torn through all his limbs. But the more the flesh is shaken by torments, the more firmly the mind fixed upon God is strengthened. Like wood kindled by fire, the more it is driven by the winds of adversity, the more ardently it blazes with love of God.

For while the holy man outwardly endures the tempest of persecution, inwardly he returns to the citadel of the mind; and from there he looks down upon all things as passing beneath him, seeing even himself pass bodily among them. He does not fear threats; by enduring torments cheerfully, he despises them. Hence Solomon says: “The righteous is confident like a lion and will be without terror” (Prov. 28). Again it is written by him: “Whatever happens will not grieve the righteous” (Prov. 12).

For now the Spirit, lifted up to the heights, rejoices ineffably in this: that it sees joys being heaped upon it through torments. It is nourished by punishments, refreshed by burning, restored by hunger, enlarged by want; and it counts it the greatest gain if it carries the heavy burden of the Lord’s passion. It fears losing as much of its reward as it sees being taken away from its torment.

What more? Again he is beaten; again he is tortured; finally he is compelled to stand barefoot upon burning coals. But while both feet are burned by the fire placed beneath them, his tongue is released more freely in confessing Christ.

For the fire that burned outwardly was slower than the one that inflamed inwardly: as though one were being cooked and the other speaking; one producing words and the other enduring blows. And in truth, one did this in accordance with the testimony of Truth, which says: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10).

And so, in the triumph of the most blessed martyr, let the opposing elements themselves serve together in harmony: while fire is despised by a more powerful fire, the flesh that had been burned is boiled in bubbling water. Thus, in the fragrance of sweetness offered to the Lord, two sacrifices are made from a single victim.

[Col. 0672D] Come, come, answer me, frenzied crowd, rightly deserving to be mocked even by the mad. Why do you rage? Why do you act savagely? Why do you rave with bloodied teeth and wolfish fury? Do you hope that Christ’s soldier will yield to punishments and that his mind can be changed from its holy purpose?

A mind fixed upon God is not of this kind; it does not know how to lose the Christian soldiery in battle. Our warrior does not know how to grow soft through severity; he does not know how to fear swords. Rather, the more he is attacked, the stronger he is found.

Come, strike, burn, cook, turn, turn again, tear flesh from flesh, inflict wounds upon wounds. When our Apollinaris is examined, he is found to be the very same person he had been. His tongue can no longer deny Christ in speaking, whom the rest of his members have confessed by suffering.

For if, while the little earthen vessel of his body was still sound, he allowed it to be torn apart in order to preserve the treasure of faith, how much more will he then fear losing so precious a treasure after the vessel has already been shattered and broken?

You, then—you miserable crowd—while you attempt to cast down Christ’s combatant, exalt him; while you strive to overcome him, you make him unconquerable. You cause him to despise his body and to strive with all the eagerness of his soul to depart from it. While you torture him wonderfully with new and elaborate punishments in order to make him a wondrous martyr, you labor toward that very end.

Your foolish wisdom has caused the name of Blessed Apollinaris to run so brightly and famously through the mouths of the faithful today. You served him while you raged, and you increased his palm while you magnified his punishment. For what did your foolish ingenuity fail to devise for the victor’s glory, when even the instruments of punishment themselves passed into honor as trophies of triumph?

But examine the torn body still more carefully; examine again those very limbs that have been pierced, and burn them, tear them apart, strike, beat, scourge, and smite them. Now, from the entire body of the unconquerable martyr, what else will you be able to wound except wounds? Let gold boil: it is not diminished. Let adamant be struck: it is not severed. At last he already yearns toward the summit of heaven; already in his mind he dwells in the heights. He feels and fears nothing except, O persecutors, your mercy alone—which, if it is shown to him, he counts as the most savage impiety. And if you wish your weapons to reach his inmost being, strike him with mercy alone. For then you are gravely indignant, if you show pity; then you tear him savagely, if you spare him; and, so to speak, then you punish him, if you do not punish him.

160 O most steadfast breast, which no weapons can pierce through, no darts penetrate! O most strongly fortified rampart of Christ, which neither battering rams striking against it destroy nor any engines of war tear down! With how great a glory of recompense he now exalts to the heights him whom so great an adversity of tribulation pressed into the depths! On the contrary, now he shines forth amid the fiery companies of the blessed spirits; now he rejoices with the senators in robes of office of the heavenly court; now he is enthroned with the patriarchs upon a golden and exalted throne; now he is wondrously crowned with the martyrs clad in purple. Clothed with a robe of glory, he shines ineffably with all these, and continually cries out a melodious Alleluia before his King.

[Col. 0673D] Wherefore we beseech you, most blessed martyr, that the hand of your prayer may raise us, whom the burden of our guilt weighs down below, so that we who here rejoice to recount the praises of your virtue may there experience some share of your blessedness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. III. ON SAINT APOLLINARIS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA AND MARTYR. (23 JULY)

Today, dearest brothers, we have heard of the unconquerable courage of Christ’s soldier; we have heard of the apostolic martyr’s triumphant passion. Wondrous was the battle among the persecutors; wondrous was the victory of the persecuted. For in order to overcome the brave warrior of the Christian army, they seize not only iron weapons, but make fire, water, wood, stones, and all the elements plainly into the material of weapons and turn them into instruments of battle.

But the more fiercely this man is attacked, the stronger he is found; and the more his body is stretched by torments, the more his faith is increased. He is, in short, an unconquerable soldier, whose strength grows from wounds and whose courage rises from the terrors of threats. It is a new and unheard-of battle, in which a stranger attacks a city, a resident attacks a state, one man attacks a people, an unarmed man a column of soldiers, a weaponless man an army, and one person casts down a legion. It is a wondrous and astonishing victory, in which he who is killed lives; he who is cast down rises; he who is overcome conquers; and after he has died, he turns the entire battle-line of the opposing side toward the standards of its own commander.

[Col. 0674B] Here death is escaped by undergoing it; life begins when it ends. It is a new kind of litigation, in which the people preside over the judgment and one man is led forward to be judged; in which one innocent man is accused, while the sentence of many guilty men is pronounced; in which the just man is beaten and the guilty man condemns.

But among all the blessed Apollinaris’s judges—or rather executioners, not governors but torturers—your cruelty, Messalinus, surpasses the rage of wolves and exceeds the savagery of lions. For after the slaughter of bloody beatings, after the multitude of gaping wounds, after his suspension upon the rack, after the burning of boiling water, you order his mouth to be crushed with a stone and punish words with blows in a new kind of torment.

Behold: the contrivance of your cruelty, through the outpoured bitterness of gall, has made me know you as the author of a new punishment. And the eye of your mind, blinded by anger, foresees by devising this new torment what, with sound judgment, it could scarcely have discerned. And indeed, what had his other limbs done to you, when you tore, tortured, tormented, and savagely devoured everything with wolf-like bites? He had offended you with his mouth; with his mouth he had rebuked you; with his mouth he had exposed the shamelessness of your face. The mute limbs had done nothing.

Why, then, does what committed no offense endure punishment? Why is what did not harm you harmed? Why is what did not sin punished? If, then, you wish to exercise the full force of your strict sentence against the accused, let the word be examined, let the word be judged, let the word be tortured with blows. And what more shall I say? Let the soul of the tongue that sinned die by itself.

[Col. 0674D] But what does it profit if you exercise vengeance against him in whom you cannot suppress the cause of vengeance? For if you crush the fleshly mouth, there is one within who fashions another mouth—which indeed you may hear, but which you cannot punish by any act of correction: namely, the one who says to his disciples, “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21). He, I say, who says, “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10).

But again he is shut up in a dreadful prison, hindered by the heavy weight of chains, stretched upon wood, and deprived of every means of nourishment. A prison alone would have been entirely sufficient to confine him, even without chains; and the punishment of fire would have been sufficient to punish him, even if the deprivation of hunger had ceased. But he from whom earthly food is withdrawn is fed with heavenly banquets. What the impiety of the judge denies, the generosity of God supplies. What the jailer does not provide, an angel, made the servant of man, supplies.

[Col. 0675A] For an angel of the Lord came to him by night and, while the guards watched, fed and strengthened him. How delightfully is he afflicted by hunger who is filled with the provisions of the heavenly storehouse; for whom heaven becomes a storeroom and the heavenly steward provides his service! How blessedly wretched is he who, while lacking earthly provisions, is supported by angelic service; to whom a heavenly gift is sent and an angelic ministry is supplied!

But O, what a beautiful spectacle, and how worthy of the admiration of all who behold it, when the general so bravely follows the Emperor and the martyr imitates the King! Who could depart satisfied from the sight of that spectacle, if he were able to possess a clear eye of the mind with which to see what was not visible—when he saw Christ’s unconquerable warrior confined in the horror of a prison, while the most splendid court of the heavenly kingdom awaited him so eagerly? When he saw heaven’s citizen recalled with such triumph from exile to his homeland? When he saw Christ’s soldier, after so powerfully conquering the world, entering the starry kingdoms?

[Col. 0675C] Yet the delay continues; he is still retained in exile, so that his desire to return to his homeland may increase more and more. For the devil still does not cease to rage savagely through his vessel; the bloody beast still does not cease to rage against Christ’s martyr with all the powers of his malice. For behold, again he is chained; he is dragged from the prison, placed upon a ship, and sent into exile. Then a storm arises, the ship is wrecked, and all the sailors die in the shipwreck; but the blessed martyr is saved with his three clerics and two soldiers.

What is this, Messalinus? Why are you raging again? Why are you acting foolishly again? Having lost the counsel of reason, do you not attend to what you are irrationally doing? Come, I beg you, tell me: who can send an exile into exile? Who can send a stranger away into foreign lands? Can an Antiochene be sent from Ravenna into exile? Can an easterner be deported from western territories?

[Col. 0675D] Yet while you make him an exile, you demonstrate that he is a citizen. And when he returns by the right of restoration, he will return under the laws to the titles of civic status from which he had been deported. Certainly, if the holy man had feared exile, he would not have come from Antioch all the way to Ravenna. Finally, why do you compel him to go farther without releasing him from the bonds of his chains? If you wish to hold him, why is he sent away? If you wish to send him away, why is he bound? Especially since your chains bind him no more by their links than they burden him by their weight.

On the contrary, where the sea subsides, you swell up; where the wind moderates its force, you blow; where the east wind ceases, you puff; the storm fears to drown the man, yet you do not hesitate to lift him upon the rack; the cold wave scarcely dares to wash over him, yet you do not fear to boil him in hot water. Your fury exceeds the savagery of all beasts. Your stupidity surpasses the very ignorance of insensible things. Ask your sailors; learn your own madness.

[Col. 0676A] Behold: while they themselves finally perish after laboring to free their arms, our men, lying bound and without any exertion on their part, escape. As for the soldiers, even if they do not perish, they are nevertheless utterly lost to you. They rightly deserve to be called faithful deserters: coming to the faith, having renounced the governor’s arms, they follow the military service of the exile.

For the soldiers say to him, “Lord Father, where shall we go? What shall we do?” He says to them, “Be baptized in the name of Jesus, and you will live.” Immediately renouncing the idols, they were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

But we, most beloved brothers, who by God’s favor have again come to know the truth; who have before our eyes so many insignia of virtue as examples for imitation—let us strive with every desire toward that blessedness in which we now know the world’s conquerors rejoice in the reward for their labors. Let us follow on the way the footsteps of those whose fellowship we desire to have in our homeland. Surely, there we shall be what they are, if here we shall have been what they were. For “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we abide with him, we shall also feast with him” (2 Timothy 2). “And if we have been planted together in the likeness of the Lord’s death, we shall also share in his resurrection” (Romans 6).

[Col. 0676C] Let us not, then, be separated on the journey if we wish to be joined at its end. Let him who desires to reach the sweetness of perpetual well-being not shrink from drinking the bitterness of a momentary draught. Whoever wishes to be enrolled among Christ’s soldiers must now gird himself manfully for battle, so that after completing his military service he may receive the citizenship of blessed rest; he must now prepare himself to engage in combat, so that after victory he may rightly be crowned: “For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy 2).

For that soldier is delicate who wishes to conquer before he begins to fight; who desires victory without battle, or pants for the palm without victory. That farmer is foolish who wishes to pluck the swelling clusters of grapes gently from the vine but neglects laboriously to plant the shoots of the vine; who longs to fill his granary with crops but does not care to cultivate the field bristling with thorns.

[Col. 0676D] So, my most beloved brothers, it is necessary for us in this world to travel with the saints along the narrow and difficult road of arduous labor, if afterward we wish to reach the breadth of their joy. For “whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (John 2). Without doubt, he strays from Christ’s footsteps who, fleeing the narrow road, treads the road of breadth: “For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14).

Behold, the blessed Apollinaris, whose festive day has dawned upon us today, did not desire earthly honors; he did not gather deceptive riches; he did not seek the glory of the world; he did not enlarge the estates of transitory possession. He despised his relatives, left his homeland, and completely denied even himself. Finally, through iron, swords, weapons, fires, and prolonged and countless deaths, he entered the starry kingdoms.

[Col. 0677A] Thus, in the saints, it is manifested more clearly than light what is said by the Truth in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).

Nor do we say this so that only those who are struck down by the swords of persecutors may be considered worthy of heavenly rewards. Often many men of perfect and praiseworthy life have desired with all the longing of their minds to attain the summit of martyrdom; but because divine providence judged otherwise, they were compelled to remain in their own rank. Although they were not brought to perfection through martyrdom, they are by no means strangers to the glory of martyrdom.

Thus, the holy disciples of the blessed Apollinaris—Adheritus and Calocerus, Marcianus and Eleuchadius—although they were not struck by the executioner’s sword, are nevertheless believed in no way to have been foreign to the desire for martyrdom. Rather, almighty God, who mercifully chose them before the ages, established them in the order he willed through the profound administration of his counsel. Although this is hidden from us, it must in no way be believed unjust; although it is incomprehensible, it must in no way be judged blameworthy.

[Col. 0677B] Thus, when an architect builds a house wall, he constructs some stones evenly in the foundations and places others at the top with artistic elevation. While the latter project above and the former lie below, together, in harmonious diversity, they complete a single wall. Thus, when a skilled craftsman fashions golden or silver vessels, he impresses various carvings and images upon some, while deliberately leaving others merely polished. In the latter—the simple vessels—the natural color shines more brightly; in the former—the embossed vessels—the painstaking art of the embossing craftsman is displayed, so that the beautiful variety of the objects draws the eyes of those who look upon them.

Likewise, among royal garments, some appear dyed with the blood-red color of purple or murices, while others gleam with the brilliance of a snowy hue.

[Col. 0677D] Although they differ greatly from one another in their particular qualities, they nevertheless derive one dignity from the body of the king, which they commonly cover. So, indeed, so does almighty God, when he raises his elect to the rank of a single blessedness, distinguish the body of his Church through the varied outlines of its members. Hence it is said through the Apostle: “He himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4).

Although there is a varied diversity among those who pass onward, there is nevertheless one road by which the passage is made: namely, the road that the Truth laid out for those who followed him when he said, “Narrow is the road that leads to life, and few there are who enter by it” (Matthew 7). The Lord himself followed this road; by this road he commanded everyone who wished to follow him to walk. The holy martyrs followed this road with complete devotion before they were found worthy to attain martyrdom.

To follow the narrow road perfectly is to break one’s own wills in everything and humbly obey the command of a superior. Whoever flows away through the breadth of his own will has turned the foot of his mind aside from the path of the narrow road. He directs his journey along it more fully in proportion as he crucifies himself more tightly upon the wood of his heart with the nails of obedience.

[Col. 0678A] But because, beloved, we wish to set before you an example of this especially important virtue for our instruction, and because no example comes to mind more readily, let us bring forward the blessed Apollinaris, whose case is under discussion.

As you have already heard, the beginning of his deeds is narrated in this way: the blessed apostle Peter said to his disciple Apollinaris, “Why are you sitting here with us? Behold, you have been instructed in all that Jesus did. Rise, receive the Holy Spirit and, together with it, the office of bishop, and go to the city called Ravenna. A multitude of people dwells there; preach to them about the name of Jesus, and do not be afraid.” A little later it adds: “And he kissed him and sent him away.”

Consider, my brothers, how free was the authority of the master in giving orders, and how devoted was the humility of the disciple in obeying: how ready the one was to impose the yoke of command, and how prepared the other was to submit his neck to obedience. The former does not temper the severity of his command by flattering words; the latter does not refuse to undertake the burden of so great a labor.

Those trained in worldly eloquence usually arrange their speech with the sweetness of rhetorical color and, whenever they wish, make difficult things seem easy through pleasing and elaborate words, so that whenever they command something burdensome, they may turn the listener toward their wishes. But the blessed apostle did not compose flattering words, nor promise a favorable outcome; he simply commanded a difficult task.

[Col. 0678C] Here too there comes to mind what the Lord commanded Abraham in a similar, though not identical, manner: “Take,” he said, “your son, whom you love, Isaac, and offer him to me as a burnt offering” (Genesis 21). It would have been enough for the Lord to say, “Take your son”; but he added, “whom you love, Isaac,” so that, by bringing the love of his son back to the father’s ears, it might be proved how great the love of God was alive in his heart. Thus, when he heard the son described as beloved, the father’s breast would be inflamed; but then, when the flame of divine love overcame it, he would slay himself with the sword of obedience and offer himself more truly upon the altar of his heart.

In the same way, when the blessed apostle said to his disciple, “Go to Ravenna,” as though he wished to instill terror in him, he immediately added, “For a multitude of people dwells there.”

The blessed Apollinaris could have answered his master with words of this kind: “You speak of a multitude of people, yet you send one man against a multitude. You yourself do not deny that the enemy hosts are many; and you do not fear to send one unarmed man against them? How will the naked tongue of one man fight against the armed hands of a hostile multitude? What can the person of an unarmed stranger accomplish against so many ranks of roaring citizens? The battle is not evenly matched when words are hurled from one tongue and blows are inflicted by countless hands; when speeches are sent from one side and clubs fly from the other.

[Col. 0679A] “At least you might give me one companion, provide me consolation for so difficult a journey, or even furnish me an assistant for the preaching itself. Your own master, the Lord Jesus Christ, whenever he sent you to preach, always provided you with consolation as the need required. The Evangelist, too, who relates that he sent seventy-two to preach, declares that he sent them not singly but two by two before his face” (Luke 10).

The blessed martyr could have advanced these and many similar words of excuse if, with an unyielding neck of mind, he had wished to evade the yoke of obedience. Yet he did not resist or contradict. As soon as he received the command of the one ordering him, he fully believed that what he recognized as commanded to him by the Lord himself through the mouth of his master was necessary.

And so that the blessed Apollinaris might appear in every respect like Abraham in the virtue of obedience, just as God commanded Abraham, saying, “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12), and Abraham obeyed without hesitation, so this man, as soon as he received the words of the apostolic command, immediately strengthened his mind with certain hope for obedience. What he was going to teach by word, he demonstrated beforehand by his deed.

[Col. 0679C] Finally, he took care humbly to display to his subjects what he himself, as their superior, was rightly going to require. And, as it is read of the Lord, “he first began to do and afterward to teach” (Acts 1), so that by experiencing it in himself he might learn how, after receiving the authority of power, he should command others.

But how beautiful is the order of divine providence, if the dignity of this matter is carefully weighed according to its merit! For we, who learned from Adam, badly instructed, the first vice of disobedience, have been taught the first virtue of obedience by this most blessed martyr. And just as Adam, among the other seeds of vice, taught his carnal offspring the first disobedience not by speaking but by transgressing, so this man, among his other lessons of virtue, instructed his spiritual children in obedience above all, not by speaking but by acting.

Thus, we who fell from the height of our heavenly homeland through disobedience return to it by obedience, retracing our steps from the degradation of exile. Hence the Truth says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6). For those who come to the first Adam learn through disobedience to go out from the inner places. But the second Adam, “becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2), does not expel those who come to him from the joys of paradise, because he gives them the example of obedience.

[Col. 0680A] Let us hasten, beloved, to return to these joys—not by the steps of our feet but by progress in good works. Perhaps we have not yet left the world; perhaps, after the manner of those who renounce it, we have not yet chosen one above all others whom we must obey. Nevertheless, with God’s help we can possess this virtue by which one especially returns to heaven—I mean obedience.

For Saul was not one of those who had renounced the world, when he heard from Samuel, angry with him: “Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that his voice should be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Samuel 15).

Whoever, then, wishes to possess this virtue perfectly, let him be obedient to God, but let him not be disobedient to his neighbor. Do you wish to hear how you should obey God? Beware what he forbids; fulfill what he commands. For neither one without the other can be perfect.

Do you also wish to hear how you should obey your neighbor? When your brother sees you falling into some vice, rebukes you for being lukewarm in good work, and kindles you to fervor by words of charitable exhortation—if you do not resist, if you do not contradict, but humbly listen and gird yourself for what you are called to do, then through the virtue of obedience you will immediately restore your return to the homeland from which you had been cast down through disobedience.

[Col. 0680B] In this way, even if you are unable to undergo death for God, you can nevertheless lead a life pleasing to God. It is a great thing to die for Christ, but it is not inferior to live for Christ. Paul weighed both on an equal scale when he said: “Whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Romans 14).

You say to me, “I cannot find martyrdom.” Make yourself worthy of martyrdom, and without doubt you will obtain the reward of martyrdom. You cannot shed blood, but you can strike yourself with the weapon of repentance and slay yourself in the contrition of your heart. Let the throat be prepared to be struck; the rewarder will not be absent, even if the sword is absent. The executioner who strikes the neck outwardly is lacking; the Judge who rewards good will is present.

“For glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. ON SAINT CHRISTOPHORUS THE MARTYR. (25 JULY)

As we desire, beloved, to discuss the triumphal victory of the blessed martyr Christophorus, his name first comes before us. If we examine it with the careful investigation it deserves, we find that it was not then imposed upon him at the end by a divine dispensation of foreknowledge. Christophorus is plainly derived from Christ. Hence the bride says to her beloved in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song of Songs 1)—namely, chrism, from which Christ is called “the Anointed.” Through oil, the Holy Spirit is mystically signified.

Our Savior was principally anointed with this oil when he received the sacrament of baptism, and immediately afterward the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove (Matthew 3). Hence the prophet says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 44).

[Col. 0681A] This oil was poured out when the grace of the Holy Spirit, which Christ received in a unique manner, was granted to all the elect through his distributive participation. Therefore the Apostle says: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4). Hence we are called Christians from Christ, because, by his gift, we have been anointed with the same oil.

David also promised this ointment when he said: “Like ointment upon the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descended to the hem of his garment” (Psalm 132). The ointment upon the head is, of course, the Holy Spirit in the Savior, who is mystically signified by Aaron, whose name is interpreted as “mountain of strength.” Since Aaron is the mountain of strength, the beard is also a sign of manly vigor.

[Col. 0681B] Therefore the apostles are the beard of this Aaron. By the strength of their manliness, which they had conceived from the anointing of the Holy Spirit, they conquered every battle of the raging persecutors and triumphed with glory over the prince of the world, who roared savagely like a lion against Christ’s sheep. Hence Peter says: “Resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5). Paul also says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of fortifications, destroying the counsels of the flesh and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ” (2 Corinthians 10).

From this beard of the supreme priest Aaron, then, the ointment trickles down to the hem of his garment, because after the blessed apostles it irrigates, in succession, the holy martyrs and thereafter the whole Church together with the flow of the Holy Spirit. Upon this hem, namely, of the mystical and priestly garment, the blessed Christophorus—“the bearer of Christ”—was deemed worthy to be named.

He bore Christ in his heart; he proclaimed Christ with his voice. Anointed with the oil of heavenly grace and stripped of the burdensome garment of earthly desire, he leaps forth like a remarkable athlete into the arena and seizes the struggle of combat. Still a new soldier, he takes up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6), immediately enters battle, and wrestles in an irreconcilable struggle against the enemy of the human race.

[Col. 0681D] He brandishes the two-edged sword that proceeds from the Savior’s mouth, and as a fervent warrior he engages the enemy. With weapons locked, he fights at close quarters, and his mind cuts down every hostile neck that confronts it. Armed with the breastplate of faith and supported upon the lofty citadel not of a mountain but of the mind, although the ranks of the enemy roar and gnash their teeth on every side, the strongest athlete does not know how to fear the onset of battle. He exposes his body to outward punishments, but the inner man who lies hidden does not admit the dart of the persecution inflicted upon him.

He hastens to enter the promised land, but there the phalanxes of the aged enemy confront him amid the fury of the persecutors. Yet while they try to impede his journey, they free it. For while they prepare to overwhelm him, they fall; while they attempt to kill him, they perish; while they hurl darts, they are pierced by sharper darts.

The Israelite people represented the figure of this spiritual battle. When it asked and humbly sought passage, Sihon, king of the Amorites, did not permit Israel to pass through his territory. For, as Scripture testifies: “Israel sent messengers to Sihon, saying: I beg you, let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into the fields or vineyards; we will not drink water from the wells; we will travel along the royal road until we have passed beyond your borders” (Numbers 21).

[Col. 0682A] He refused to grant Israel passage through his territory. Rather, as the same sacred history testifies, “Sihon went out to meet him in the wilderness with his army gathered, and he came to Jahaz [Isaar], fought against Israel, and was struck down by him at the edge of the sword; and his land was possessed by Israel.”

But what was then accomplished historically under Moses is accomplished daily under Christ through the mystery of spiritual warfare. For that battle was prefigured by the people who then fought, and it is now continually fought by the holy Church against the devil.

Sihon has a twofold interpretation. He is said to mean “a fruitless tree,” and he is also said to mean “the exalted one.” For who is this exalted one, who is this proud one, except that reprobate spirit who says: “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High”? (Isaiah 14.) Who, I ask, is this exalted one except the one of whom Scripture says that he is king over all the sons of pride? (Job 41.) So much so that, according to the Apostle, he will at some time sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God (2 Thessalonians 2).

[Col. 0682B] That he is also a fruitless tree requires no explanation, since, like a dry tree, he has been assigned to eternal fires.

This Sihon, then, is king of the Amorites, who themselves are interpreted as “speakers” or “those who bring into bitterness.” For all who are subject to the evil spirit through a reprobate life and obey the laws of his dominion are indeed speakers, but not wise. Many lovers of the world, being empty of earthly wisdom, are eloquent through the cleverness of their outward speech. Of them Solomon says: “All the labor of man is in his mouth, but his soul will not be filled” (Ecclesiastes 6). The kingdom of the saints, however, is not in speech but in power.

But those who are speakers are the same as those who bring into bitterness. For just as the saints distill the honey of heavenly eloquence, so every reprobate pours out to his hearers the poison and bitterness of earthly cunning. To the former, in the person of the holy Church, it is said: “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb” (Song of Songs 6). They also sing in the figure of that same Church: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118).

[Col. 0682D] Of their teacher, too, the bride says in the Song of Songs: “His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable” (Song of Songs 5). But of the others, by contrast, it is said: “They dealt deceitfully with their tongues; the venom of asps is under their lips” (Psalm 13). Immediately afterward it follows: “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (Isaiah 5).

Thus, through the prophet, the Lord complains that the vineyard which had received from him the land of milk and honey had been turned into bitterness and afterward offered him the bitterness of vinegar together with gall (Jeremiah 2; Deuteronomy 11; Matthew 27).

[Col. 0683A] Sihon, then, is king of these speakers or those who bring into bitterness. He is called “the exalted one” because the devil, the author of pride, rules over the vain-speaking and bitter lovers of this world. Hence he is also called the prince of the world—of that world of which John says: “The world is placed in the Evil One” (John 12, 14). And the Lord promises the disciples that the Spirit will be sent, the Spirit whom this world cannot receive (1 John 5; John 14).

Israel says to Sihon: “Let us pass through your land; we will not turn aside into fields or vineyards” (Numbers 21). We, plainly, we are the ones who desire to pass through this world into the land of the living. We, I say, desire to walk humbly through the borders of the proud king toward the homeland of divine promise.

And since “Hebrew” is interpreted as “one who passes over,” we who are disciples of the one who did not dwell here but passed through doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil (Acts 10), because God was with him, promise that we will never dwell with King Sihon, but that we will proceed only along the royal road.

[Col. 0683B] But when did we make these promises to King Sihon? When we rejected cohabitation with him; when we made a covenant with him of eternal separation.

Let us therefore recall the day of holy baptism; let us bring back to memory the very beginning of the new birth. There, without doubt, we shall find that we renounced the devil and all his pomps and works. Let each of the faithful remember when he first approached the font of saving washing, when he first received the seals of faith.

Did he not, through the priestly office of catechesis, use words by which he signified that he was rejecting the deadly desires of this world and professed that he was completely renouncing fellowship with the devil? This is what is represented in the words of the history: Israel would turn aside neither into the field nor into the vineyard of King Sihon, nor would it promise in any way to drink from his reservoir.

By the field is understood the exercise of works; by the vineyard and the reservoir, the draught of empty arts—astrology, magic, necromancy, and whatever teaches anything vain or sacrilegious against the devotion of the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0683D] Concerning these pestilential drinks, the Lord complains through Jeremiah against the perverse people, saying: “My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2). Of these Solomon also says: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Proverbs 8).

But Israel has its own fountains. “In the churches,” he says, “bless God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel” (Psalm 67). Let Israel, therefore, reject the waters of the proud king Sihon; let it despise the streams of heretical doctrines; and let it draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior (Isaiah 12).

For he who broke open the fountains and torrents (Psalm 73) says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7).

Let him also walk along the royal road, as he promised. “We will walk,” he said, “along the royal road.” And what is the royal road except the one who says, “I am the way” (John 14)? He also proves himself a king at the very moment of his passion when he says, “You say that I am a king” (John 18).

[Col. 0684A] We therefore promised the proud king Sihon that we would not drink his streams, that we would not turn aside into his fields or vineyards, and that we would walk along the royal road—that is, hastening to Christ through Christ himself, we would abstain from all the pomps and works of the devil.

But that exalted Sihon gathers an army and does not permit Israel to pass through his territory.

Source/review notes: The draft reversed the agent and recipient in the miracle involving Elisha’s corpse.; It rendered mortificatio Jesu as “death of Jesus” and introduced an unwarranted possessive in the myrrh-bundle explanation.; Several smaller corrections restore the source’s citation, title, image of the lamb, duration, and Christopher-name wordplay.

Who, then, is that people whom Sihon gathers against Israel, if not all the reprobate who persecute the Church? Among these are the tyrants, leaders, and princes of this world, who either oppose Catholic men with the obstacles of contradiction through heretical perversity, or endeavor to inflict torments upon the holy martyrs. But what does Israel do in response? Let us consult the history. “He came,” it says, “to Jasa and fought against him. Sihon was struck by the edge of the sword, and his land was possessed from the Arnon to the Jabbok” (Num. 21). Behold the proud man; behold the haughty one: he engaged in battle, but was crushed, defeated, and destroyed. He rushed into arms and fell. He who refused to grant a road lost his life; and while he scorned to allow passage along the public way, he lost the dominion of his own royal glory. Israel, however, who did not obtain passage, reached the rights of hereditary possession; and he to whom passage was denied made a homeland for himself from the road.

[Col. 0684C] But where, I ask, my brothers, where was this victory accomplished? Surely it was a blessed place that deserved to witness so great a triumph! Where, I say, did Israel overcome the proud king? At Jasa. Now Jasa is interpreted as “the fulfillment of the command.” And if, with God as our guide, we reach this place, we undoubtedly overcome the devil, who is the head and origin of pride. For we conquer the devil when we fulfill the commands of our Redeemer. Indeed, conquering the devil is itself the fulfillment of the divine commands. For when we break the enticements of the flesh; when we resist the wicked passions of our inward parts; when we submit to the authority of the divine command and keep not our own desires but his orders—then without doubt we defeat the prince of this world and the author of every form of wickedness.

[Col. 0684D] Then that apostolic prayer is fulfilled in us, in which it is said: “The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet” (Rom. 16). And the Lord grants us what he promised: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you” (Luke 10).

But since Sihon signifies the ancient enemy, and his people all the reprobate—that is, the persecutors of the Church—who have been overthrown by the arms of Israel, that is, by the holy preachers, with what blade were they pierced, and by what sword were they finally slain? Hear the Apostle, surely the commander of spiritual warfare and the vigorous champion of the inward battle: “The word of God,” he says, “is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. 4).

[Col. 0685A] That sword of division was unsheathed by the leader and author of those battles, the Lord of warriors, when he said: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10).

You have heard of the sword that divides; hear next of the division itself: “I have come,” he says, “to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (ibid.). By this sword, therefore, Sihon was slain, and his entire army was thrown down in a common slaughter. For by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6), the devil fell, and the people subjected to him abandoned the life of their unbelief.

Since Scripture declares that those men were slain by the edge of the sword, it may appropriately be said of these that they were killed by the sword of the mouth. And when the Lord says, “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12), as soon as Sihon is cast out, Israel—that is, the holy Church—immediately spreads throughout the breadth of the world. For as soon as unbelief, together with its prince, is extinguished and collapses, the faith of the triumphant Church is extended. Those who had until then been exiles become possessors after the victory. Hence the same Church is told through Isaiah: “Your people—all of them righteous—will possess the land forever” (Isa. 65). Concerning this people he later also says: “They will dwell there, plant vineyards, and eat their fruits” (ibid.).

Again, the same prophet clearly announces that the holy Church must be extended through the territories of the nations: “Enlarge,” he says, “the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your dwellings; do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your tent-pegs” (Isa. 54). He explains why she must do this when he adds: “For you will spread out to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations” (ibid.). Thus the whole land of Sihon fell into Israel’s inheritance, because, while the prince of this world is pierced and driven out by the sword of the divine word, the holy universal Church is extended throughout the boundaries of that same world.

[Col. 0685D] Nor, I think, should we pass over what is said: “His land was possessed from the Arnon to the Jabbok.” Arnon, which is the beginning of Sihon’s kingdom, is interpreted as “their curses.” For the whole world, which before the Savior’s coming was oppressed under the devil’s dominion, had its origin in a curse, because it did not know the author of blessing. Concerning him the Prophet says: “He will give blessing, the one who gave the law” (Ps. 83). Hence the Apostle also says: “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse” (Gal. 3). Did we not have a beginning in a curse, of whom it is said: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2)?

The end of that kingdom is the Jabbok, [Col. 0686A] which is interpreted as “struggle.” For all who wish to leave the devil’s kingdom and escape his territories must endure the conflicts of mounting temptations. But if someone fights lawfully, wrestles bravely, and prevails, Jabbok will no longer be a city of Sihon but a city of Israel—not, to be sure, of Israel according to the flesh, nor a Jew outwardly, but one who is Israel in Christ, circumcised in heart and not in flesh.

I have said these things to you, dearest brothers, as a kind of digression, so that through the mystery of sacred history I might also teach about the spiritual struggle in which blessed Christopher shone forth as a distinguished victor. Nor should it seem strange that we describe the order of a sacred battle when we wish to praise a vigorous combatant.

[Col. 0686B] He, surely, as a true and valiant Israelite, scorned Egypt and the laws of iron slavery; and through battles, fires, iron, arrows, and swords he entered the promised land. Indeed, like a purple rose, he blossomed from the thorns of the Canaanites, and, like a luxuriant olive tree, he sprang from the wild oleasters. He sought the initiation into Christian warfare, and, receiving the beginnings of the new faith, fervently plunged himself as a warrior into the midst of the heat of battle.

When the tyrant saw him girded as God’s soldier, he raged and attempted to attack him with various kinds of weapons and many engines of war. At one time he sought to bend God’s soldier through the seductive blandishments of prostitutes; at another he prepared to terrify him with the harshness of thunderous threats; at another he set out to stitch him through with arrows; at another to dissolve him in streams of boiling oil. But Christ’s most invincible soldier and undaunted warrior could neither be seduced by blandishments, nor broken by carefully devised punishments, nor recalled from his holy purpose by the raging fury of executioners.

[Col. 0686C] The tyrant heaps various kinds of tortures upon Christ’s soldier, but the foundation of his unconquered faith remains immovable. Swollen rivers roar around him; foaming masses of storms rush headlong upon him; raging winds strike him from every side. Yet the structure of the lofty house, rising upon the solidity of firm rock, does not know how to tremble at any violent assault. God’s pillar stood immovable amid the storms of persecutors raging everywhere; he endured amid the tempests of hail descending with monstrous force.

[Col. 0686D] For Christ’s soldier, caught among hostile ranks, not only could not be bent by being beaten, but also hurled the darts of holy preaching with vigor; and, like a trained warrior, turned the weapons of others to his own use. The persecutor served by raging, and, while wishing to inflict harm, unwittingly became an instrument; for the more calmly he found him enduring the madness of his fury, the more brightly he made him shine, like the appearance of refined gold.

Let us therefore, my brothers, imitate the example of so outstanding a warrior; let us hold fast to his pattern and preserve his watchfulness in our own temptation. The tyrant stirred almost all the elements against him, and [Col. 0687A] could not overcome him. Let us at least resist the enticements of our flesh, restrain anger, strive to tame pride, and trample underfoot, by the power of faith, the monsters of every vice. Since we know that this glorious man did not yield to the tortures of his executioners, let us at least refuse to submit to the allurements of enticing pleasures.

Even if we are not yet able perfectly to love God after the example of this blessed martyr, let us meanwhile strive to fear him by loving him, to persevere in his commands by fearing him, and thus gradually to ascend to the summit of his love. For if we attend carefully, we find this order of formation also in the Lord’s own words. In Deuteronomy it is written: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, and love him?” (Deut. 10). The human mind is thus to begin by fearing its Creator, then to exercise itself in his commands, and finally to grow strong enough to conceive the sweetness of divine love.

This order of inward love the bride seeks in the Song of Songs: “Set love in order within me” (Song 2). Therefore, beloved, let the ardor of our minds be kindled toward love, through which it may reject the devices of hostile cunning and scorn the slippery pleasures of this world. Let us renounce the world and offer God a dwelling within our inward parts, so that, in accordance with the name of the blessed martyr, if we now bear Christ in our breast, we may later be borne to him by angelic conveyance.

[Col. 0687C] For he is the one who grants glory to holy martyrs and forgives converted sinners. He is the one who overcomes in the victory of those who strive and triumphs in the conversion of the penitent: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. I. ON SAINTS FLORA AND LUCILLA, VIRGINS AND MARTYRS (29 JULY)

We rejoice, dearest brothers, to celebrate the triumph of virgins, since we do not doubt that the virginal birth was the beginning of our redemption. The author of virginity, who through a virgin deigned to enter the arena of this world in order to fight, also wished to restore the insignia of his victory through many virgins.

[Col. 0687D] Among these, these virgins shone forth like twin lamps: in accordance with the prophetic significance of their two names, one suggests a flower, while the other flashes with light. Thus, as the history of ancient deeds relates, they were captured by a certain barbarian king and held under honorable custody through two successive periods of ten years. The king at first burned fiercely with the fire of lust; but, thoroughly broken by their constancy, he finally submitted with good sense to the counsel of chastity.

At last, he who had taken them captive became their fellow captive, laid down his royal scepters, and together with them exchanged an earthly kingdom for the glory of heavenly rule through the palm of martyrdom. He laid aside his fleeting purple and attained the robe of immortality. In place of the dining halls of a ruined palace, he merited a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens. And what a beautiful transformation: he who had previously been like a roaring lion among the lairs of wild beasts now, within the folds of the Church, became a gentle little lamb and suckled at the breasts of the sheep.

We therefore recognize that what the bridegroom mystically promises the bride in the Song of Songs was plainly granted to these two holy virgins: “You will be crowned from the summit of Senir, from the head of Amana and Hermon, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards” (Song 4).

Amana is said to be a mountain of Cilicia, which many also call Taurus. Senir and Hermon, however, are mountains of the Jewish land, where lions and leopards are believed to dwell. By these mountains, therefore, we are to understand kings and princes and the various powers of this world, which raise themselves like mountains to the summit of pride and provide a dwelling for evil spirits as though for leopards and lions.

Wicked spirits are called lions because of their cruelty; they are called leopards because, since this animal is of varied color, they represent the manifold variety of deception and fraud.

[Col. 0688B] From these mountains, therefore, every faithful soul or the holy Church is crowned when it converts the princes of the world to the faith or directs them toward the uprightness of a holy way of life. It is crowned either because Christ rewards it for the gain brought in through them, or because it is honored in this world by those by whom it was formerly oppressed.

It is crowned, I say, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards when it turns the proud and deceitful away from their perversity and receives eternal rewards for their reformed conduct. This is proved to have happened to these holy virgins, if faith is to be given to the account that is told: they obtained both the palm of victory over the previously wicked king and the glory that followed his conversion and happy completion.

Let the blessed virgins therefore say to the heavenly Bridegroom what is said in the same Song: “We will exult and rejoice in you” (Song 1). Not in ourselves, but in you; because you once brought us from the darkness into the light of your truth, and through us you also summoned others from the darkness of ignorance to the knowledge of your name, so that what is said might be fulfilled: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1).

Now, according to what the written history relates, the Lord spoke to them in the silence of night and urged them to return to Rome to complete their martyrdom. Does this not plainly correspond to what is woven through the sacramental, typological conversation between the bridegroom and the bride?

“I sleep, but my heart is awake. The voice of my beloved knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights’” (Song 5).

[Col. 0688D] Thus each blessed virgin speaks, since they had one heart and one soul: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” For the holy mind, the more it restrains itself from the clamor of temporal desire, the more truly perceives inward things; and the more vigilantly it watches over the inner life, the more carefully it conceals itself from outward disturbance.

[Col. 0689A] These holy virgins slept, then, with respect to the affairs and desires of the world, but they kept their eyes open and watchful in the heat of the love of God. But since this is not a time of complete rest, but rather of labor and struggle, suddenly the beloved knocks at the door and awakens them by his exhortations to take up the battle array: “The voice,” he says, “of my beloved knocking” (ibid.).

The beloved knocks when Christ urges his faithful either to increase their virtues or, certainly, to win the souls of their neighbors. “Open to me, my sister”—a sister, to be sure, because you have become my co-heir in the kingdom and have been adopted into the bond of fraternal kinship with me. “My friend,” because, freed from the yoke of slavery, you have come to know the secrets of my truth. “My dove,” because you are free from the bitterness of gall and have been enriched by the gift of my Spirit, who descended in the form of a dove. “My undefiled one,” because by the outpouring of my blood you have been cleansed from every stain of your sins.

Open to me, then—that is, leave the rest and leisure of the contemplation you love, and devote yourself with the utmost fervor and constancy to bearing witness to my truth: “For my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights” (1 Cor. 11).

[Col. 0689B] God is the head of Christ, as the Apostle says. The locks, however, are the innermost thoughts of the saints, which do not flow loosely and dissolutely but are bound together by the bond of the fear and love of God. What else, indeed, should we understand by the dew and drops of the nights except the dark and cold minds of certain reprobates?

The bridegroom’s head is therefore full of dew among reprobates [Col. 0689C] when worldly people grow numb toward the love of God and flow away into the wantonness of their pleasures, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24). When such people persecute and hate God’s holy ones, the bridegroom’s locks within their hearts are, as it were, full of the drops of the nights.

When such people multiply and burden the Church with persecutions, the bridegroom exhorts the bride to rise and devote herself courageously to the work of preaching. Hence it is that the most blessed virgins Flora and Lucilla are divinely admonished during the night to return to Rome and not to fear approaching the struggle of martyrdom. For wherever almighty God saw the heat of persecution boiling most fiercely, there he determined to triumph more gloriously through the fragile sex.

But to return to the Song: each of these venerable virgins, as though with a single and unified utterance, expresses the following words: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5). As though she were saying: I have stripped myself of the cares and occupations of the world and have confined myself wholly to the love of contemplating you. How, then, shall I now undertake the journey of wandering about? How shall I endure the clamor and struggle of those who insult me?

That tunics signify cares, anxieties, and concerns, the Lord shows when he says: “Let the one who is on the roof not come down to take up his tunic” (Matt. 24). This is plainly to say: Let the one who stands upon the lofty height of contemplation not descend, lest he again become entangled in the occupations of worldly business.

[Col. 0690A] “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song 5)—that is, I have washed the steps of my conduct from the sprinkling of earthly dust with fitting tears of repentance; how now will I be able, unless I meditate on heavenly things, to which I am accustomed?

Nevertheless, these blessed virgins, Flora and Lucilla, set aside the repose of contemplation, with which they had until then lived in the palace of the kingdom as in a desert. Proceeding at the Savior’s command, they recompensed the loss of their rest with the glory of undergoing martyrdom. He who gave them words outwardly also kindled their minds inwardly with the fervor of obedience.

Hence both most blessed virgins, as though with one voice, say: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch” (ibid.). The beloved puts his hand through the opening and touches the inward parts when, by a hidden inspiration, the Creator visits the heart and inflames it for the struggle of combat and holy labor.

That “inward parts” signifies the heart the Prophet shows when he says: “I am in pain in my inward parts.” He explains what this means when he adds: “The senses of my heart are scattered” (Jer. 4).

[Col. 0690B] The inward parts of the blessed virgins, Flora and Lucilla, therefore trembled when the beloved put in his hand and touched them. For immediately their heart conceived the commands of the divine order; renouncing themselves, they thereafter reserved nothing to their own will.

Hence each still says, as though individually: “I arose to open to my beloved” (Song 5). The holy virgins arose to open immediately to their beloved, because they resolved with the readiest spirit to obey humbly. They opened to their beloved when, bowing the neck of their hearts to his command, they trampled down their own will and fulfilled the divine will with all their strength.

[Page 176] Perhaps someone may accuse us of this: why, abandoning the open fields of Scripture, do we pluck the fragrances of flowers from the single corner of the Song of Songs in order to weave a garland of glory for the holy virgins? I confess, my brothers, that we do this deliberately, because we think that no nuptial song is more fitting for these holy virgins than this one. Through the outstanding victory of martyrdom they ascended to the bridal chambers of the heavenly Bridegroom; they now rest in the embrace of that bridegroom for whose love they labored beneath the harsh burden of toil and affliction; and in his nuptial covenant corruption found no place, but virginal integrity increased.
