Let us therefore follow, beloved, these most holy virgins along the road of labor and struggle, so that at least as the last and least among them we may deserve to be joined to them in the rewards of merit. Let men be ashamed to serve carnal enticements when we see the fragile sex penetrate the heavenly kingdoms through various tortures, through iron and swords. Let a man blush to grow numb beneath the shadow of degenerate leisure when he sees young women battle manfully in the arena of combat amid the heat of persecution.

Thus let us now imitate, insofar as we can, the example of the holy virgins, so that one day with them we may be brought to the author of virginity, the Son of the Virgin, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXV. II. ON THE HOLY VIRGINS AND MARTYRS FLORA AND LUCILLA (31 JULY)

Still the virginal offspring blossoms; still that virginal fecundity gathers the fruits of heavenly harvests, when womanly weakness not only surpasses her sex but also triumphs over the prince of this world with unconquerable greatness of mind. For this reason the Son of God was conceived in the flower of a flourishing womb: to change the old leaven into unleavened bread and, through the flesh that had been defeated, to bring victory to the human race.

He fashioned a breastplate for himself from our weakness; in it, rejoicing like a giant (Ps. 18), powerful and strong in battle, he defeated the aerial powers.

Thus from weakness constancy was produced, from captivity victory, and from ruin ascent. Hence it came about that the ancient enemy, who applauded himself for having gained victory through the folly of one woman, is now ashamed to find himself defeated and confounded by many women.

[Col. 0691B] This is also why the matter now before us has occurred: these most holy virgins, Flora and Lucilla, first scorned the allurements of pleasure and afterward the swords of their torturers. Each had long been a martyr in secret, and afterward shone forth publicly as a victor.

To them most aptly applies what the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts” (Song 1). Myrrh is an aromatic substance of great bitterness, with which the bodies of the dead are embalmed so that they may not quickly decay. Hence the body of the bridegroom himself, taken down from the cross by Nicodemus and Joseph, was embalmed with myrrh and aloes, wrapped in linen cloths, and committed to burial (John 19).

[Page 177] What, then, is signified by a bundle of myrrh except manifold mortification? For she does not say “a sprig of myrrh” or “a little branch of myrrh,” but “my beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me.” As though she were saying: I mortify myself in every aspect of my manner of life, and now live by none of the works of my own will; my beloved has not become for me a simple branch but a bundle of myrrh.

Hence the outstanding preacher says: “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. 6). He exhorts us along with him to this manifold mortification when he says: “Always carrying in our body the mortification of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh” (2 Cor. 4).

From the fact that we carry it in our body, we leave no part of the body empty. He, therefore, carries the death of Jesus in his body who leaves nothing of himself for himself; who lives in everything not for himself but for Christ; who crucifies himself everywhere to his own desires. Thus this beloved one becomes a bundle of myrrh, because by presenting himself as though extinguished in all his actions, he gathers, in a certain sense, a manifold sheaf of Christ’s mortification.

Let the most blessed virgins sing together, for, having one bridegroom, they knew no jealousy; and just as through the glue of charity they fuse two souls into one, so let them say with one mouth, individually: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me.” Appropriately, the text adds: “He will dwell between my breasts.” No one doubts that the place of the heart is between the breasts of the chest.

The beloved therefore dwells between the breasts of both virgins because the unceasing love and desire for him are not erased from their memory. “He will dwell between my breasts,” as though she were saying: He who became a bundle of myrrh to me through the bitterness of his passion dwells continually between my breasts through the sweetness of my heart; and he who outwardly sharpens me through the example of the death he endured makes me inwardly sweet through the grace infused into me.

Thus the bride says of the same bridegroom: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5). White, plainly, from the glory of his divinity; ruddy through the blood of his passion. He is called chosen from among thousands because, from the entire multitude of the saints, he alone was worthy to hear: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3; 17).

[Col. 0692C] Unless these venerable virgins had continually gazed with the eyes of faith upon this beauty of their beloved, they would never have endured so many hardships and afflictions, like a bitter and manifold bundle of myrrh. Unless they had been inflamed by the embrace of that supreme beauty, they would never have made a desert of the king’s palace and, among carnal and licentious men, cut away every enticement of the flesh with the sword of perpetual continence for nearly three weeks of years—that is, nearly twenty-one years.

For they had what is said: “The bridegroom’s throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable” (Song 5). The bridegroom’s most sweet throat is the inward sweetness of his words. In Christ’s words many easily understand the surface, but to few is it given to penetrate the inner sweetness, of which the Prophet says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33).

But he who is sweet in the throat tastes bitter in the mouth. Hence it is written: “His lips are dripping with myrrh, with first myrrh” (Song 5). Through the lips, food is conveyed into the throat. The lips of the bridegroom, therefore, are the words of the Redeemer. They drip myrrh because they teach that one must reach the sweetness of inward delight through the mortification and bitterness of the flesh.

By this path of bitterness, dearest brothers, let us now strive to walk with the blessed virgins, so that afterward with them we may deserve to enter, with the blessing of sweetness, the royal wedding of the eternal Bridegroom.

Let the false sweetness of the flesh not caress us away from the desire for this eternal banquet; let the harshness of approaching labors not break us; let the burden of temporal possessions not weigh us down; let affection for children or the ties of any loved ones not hold us back; let implacable anger toward our neighbor not impede us; let anxiety over acquiring or preserving possessions not restrain us.

Let us cut away from ourselves all the thorns of vices growing evilly; let us drive from the eyes of our heart the darkness of earthly desire, so that with the blessed virgins, Flora and Lucilla, we may strive to flourish in virtues and live in the light of good works. Then, walking in their footsteps, while we do not cling to transitory things, we may be carried into eternal ones; and while we scorn the world, we may reach Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI. ON SAINT RUFFINUS THE MARTYR (30 JUNE)

[Col. 0693B] You know, dearest brothers, as you have learned from the instruction of the Catholic faith, that at the examination of the final judgment all—sinners and righteous together—must be presented before the tribunal of the eternal Judge with their bodies, as the Apostle testifies: “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5).

The reprobate will appear for this reason: because here, together with flesh and soul, they trampled upon the commands of their Creator, they may there receive the sentence of just condemnation in both substances together and thereafter feel the bitterness of punishment in both, having served their wicked pleasures through both while they lived.

The elect, however, will appear because they do not cease now to crucify their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5), so that with those same bodies—bodies which they have used like tents in the service of God—they may be raised to the glory of heavenly splendor. Then, when the belt of service has been removed, the inner and outer person together will receive the commonwealth of perpetual rest: those who reached unity through shared battles. Those whose struggle was one will likewise have one crown.

That will truly be our Sabbath, the seventh year of the law, the genuine Jubilee (Deut. 15; Lev. 25). The Sabbath is commanded to be a day of rest so that eternal repose might be prefigured through it. Under the same mystery of signifying eternal rest and resurrection, freedom is restored in the seventh year. In the Jubilee, trumpets are sounded so that each person may return to his own possession. “For the trumpet will sound,” as the Apostle says, “and the dead who are in Christ will rise” (1 Cor. 15).

[Col. 0693D] Then all return to their own possessions, because on that day of the final resurrection each person receives his own body, in which he lived while leading his present life. Then Adam, then Noah, then all the ancient Fathers—in fact, all the souls of mortals—return to the land of their lost flesh. Having received their bodies, they will possess them forever; brought into the freedom of the children of God, they will now rejoice securely, all released from the servile bond of human corruption.

Since the bodies of the saints are destined to possess such dignity that together with their souls they will receive both the crown of perpetual life and the robe of immortality, what wonder is it if almighty God now provides suitable places for them and arranges their tombs not randomly or by chance but by the choice of his own will?

Indeed, people often rightly ask why Abraham, who confessed that he was dust and ashes as to the bodily part of himself (Gen. 18), took such ambitious care in arranging his burial that, from the whole extent of his wandering, he chose only Hebron, in the region of Canaan, and there purchased for himself a double cave at no small price (Gen. 23). Jacob likewise adjured his sons, and Joseph his brothers, making them swear that after death they would transfer their bones to the same cave (Gen. 49).

What, then, is the reason that holy men, who had looked down from the lofty height of their minds upon both the present life and all the glory of the world, contended so eagerly, anxiously, and earnestly over the place where their ashes would be buried? It was because, through the prophetic Spirit, they knew that the Savior of the world would one day be born there from their offspring, and that the blood which would cleanse the sins of the world would be shed specifically in that region.

As the Psalmist says: “Our God worked salvation in the midst of the earth before the ages” (Ps. 73). This may certainly be understood especially of the Lord’s own body; yet it also seems appropriately applicable to that region where he deigned to suffer, which is indeed the center of the world.

[Col. 0694C] In the land of Canaan, therefore, our holy Fathers chose their tombs, so that they might one day deserve to rise from the place where the author of resurrection himself—the Firstborn of the living and the dead—deigned to reveal the glory of resurrection in his own person.

And what more can I say about the honor that God, the rewarder of the good, displays toward the bodies of his saints? Almighty God himself deigned to bury the body of Moses (Deut. 34), and the corpse of Elisha is recorded as having raised a dead man (2 Kings 13). Indeed, to speak truly, what divine providence often did not grant to the saints while they lived in the flesh, it frequently bestowed upon them after death.

This is clearly seen in the case of Abdo, the man of God: while he was alive, a lion was able to attack him in order to kill him, but it was not permitted in any way to violate his corpse (1 Kings 13). “Precious indeed in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115).

It is therefore no wonder if divine providence assigns fitting places to the bodies of the saints and now entrusts them to the earth as a kind of deposit, to restore them later for transfer to the heavenly kingdoms. But now, since this is why we have prefaced these remarks, let us briefly touch upon some of the miracles of blessed Ruffinus.

### 180

The body of this blessed martyr was therefore transferred at a later time from the suburb of the town of Assisi, where it had formerly been placed, within the walls, out of fear of a pagan incursion. The stone sarcophagus in which the aforesaid body had previously rested had been left abandoned outside the walls for a long period. Over it, a serious dispute arose between the people and Ugo, then bishop of that see. The bishop maintained that it ought to be carried to the church of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, which was the principal church of that place, intending that what the mother church lacked in possessing the martyr’s body should at least be compensated by the consolation of an empty tomb. The people, on the other hand, asserted that a division ought not to be made between the sacred relics and their proper tomb, nor should human inventions now alter what appeared to have been divinely established from the moment of the glorious martyr’s completed triumph. Thus, while they contended on both sides, the sarcophagus was brought to the city walls, and both parties together reached the crossroads of a certain fork in the road.

There, while the bishop’s supporters attempted to drag the sacred vessel to Saint Mary, and the remaining part of the people sought to pull it toward the basilica of Blessed Ruffinus, each side straining in the opposite direction, the quarrel increased until the enraged parties seized weapons and, having lost control of their minds, exchanged blows with one another. Swords were brandished, and they rushed together at close quarters on both sides; burning with anger, they raged fiercely to inflict wounds upon one another. But O divine mercy worthy of praise, which takes pity on human errors and often confronts our perverse desires, so that it may bring even badly begun undertakings to good outcomes! Why delay with many words? No one there was wounded; indeed, not even a tiny drop of blood was shed. And, so that marvels might be followed by still greater marvels, about sixty men on the bishop’s side attempted to drag the aforesaid vessel to the church of Blessed Mary, but despite all their efforts they could not move it from its fixed position. When they were now completely exhausted by weariness and had utterly abandoned hope of transporting the stone, scarcely seven men from the other side seized the urn and were permitted to carry it to the basilica of Saint Ruffinus with such speed that they seemed to be carrying not a stone but rather a bundle of straw.

At once the cry of the rejoicing people rose up, joyful thanksgiving was offered unanimously to God their helper, and everyone eagerly proclaimed that the merciful God had shared the people’s judgment. Then it was proved true that saying: “The voice of the people is the voice of God.”

For further confirmation of the matter, there was also a certain priest, sent by Blessed Ruffinus himself to the bishop. When the aforesaid bishop had been considerably angered against those who had resisted him, and they were preparing to make fitting satisfaction and appease him with devoted humility, the blessed martyr appeared in a vision to the priest whom we have mentioned and said to him:

“Go and tell the bishop that, if he does not wish to offend me, he must not accept any satisfaction from the people, but should freely return to them the pure grace of his love and blessing. This deed was done by my will, so that that vessel might be carried to my church, in order that my little body might be placed in it again. Let him also know that, unless I had been present among those who were making the disturbance and had opposed myself to their weapons, a great slaughter of men would have lain strewn there.”

But while the bishop was still hesitating and was not prepared to put his faith even in the priest’s words, behold, a certain man who had been crippled declared that on that same day he had been raised up by Blessed Ruffinus and was rejoicing and exulting. He also stated that the blessed martyr had charged him to report to the bishop all these things in the same order in which the priest had related them. At last, with every scruple of doubt removed, the bishop unhesitatingly carried out what had been commanded him; he forgave the offenses and was reconciled with his people.

But, lest anyone perhaps find fault with the bishop, on the grounds that, for a time disagreeing with his own church, he had judged contrary to God’s decision, Isaac should be recalled to mind: he blessed not Esau, whom he himself had chosen, but Jacob, who had been substituted by his wife (Gen. XXVII). Thus, in the one case a carnal wife, and in the other a spiritual bride, prevailed over her husband in opposition to his own judgment, because God, who chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong (I Cor. I), consented to both.

The prophet David, too, wished to build a temple (II Reg. VII), but heavenly providence did not permit him to do so. We also read that a certain disagreement arose between Paul and Barnabas over John (Acts XV); yet, on that account, not only was the merit of either apostle not diminished, but the disciple himself did not depart from the path of apostolic discipline. It is therefore not surprising if a human being sometimes unknowingly dissents from the truth, since the authority of Scripture proves that something of human weakness affected even the apostles and prophets. But enough of this elsewhere; let us now return to the subject before us.

On the same day, moreover, two blind men were given sight at the altar of the blessed martyr. Another man, whose limbs were weakened and whose back was hunched, was also raised upright and restored to health in every respect. Of these miracles, it is enough for us merely to report what happened; for if we attempted to relate how each one was accomplished in the order of the events, we might perhaps burden our hearers—God forbid!—with the excessive length of a ragged style. In enumerating the miracles themselves, we likewise omit pursuing them all; rather, as though drawing a cupful from some great river, we draw out what we may beneficially serve to those feasting at Christ’s table, lest the stomach of the mind be weighed down by overfilling, but that thirst may be removed by moderate drinking alone. Let us therefore proceed to recount further miracles that were divinely displayed through the same most blessed martyr.

At about the same time, a certain cruel and harsh man, possessed by an intolerable madness, had made a deed concerning a poor woman’s land, which was under his jurisdiction; then, driven by a great frenzy, he insistently demanded it. He had also violently taken from her an ox and an axe—the strength, namely, of her household resources and the hope of managing her family. Unable to endure this from grief, she hurried into the church of Blessed Ruffinus with a spirit embittered by anguish, prostrated herself before the altar, and tearfully begged him to help her in such a moment of great calamity.

Why say more? At last divine mercy was present, and as soon as she rose from prayer, she saw, to her astonishment, her axe lying on the pavement before her feet. Immediately her sorrow was turned into joy, and all who were present unanimously offered worthy thanksgiving to God. But behold, the robber continued to carry out his wicked purpose and threatened the aforesaid woman with punishment unless she returned the document [chartula]. Yet as soon as he learned that the axe had been restored so miraculously, he was confounded and astonished, became afraid, returned the ox, repented, and, his anger having been calmed, put to rest every grievance he had previously held against her.

Furthermore, twelve thieves, conspiring together, violently burst into the house of a certain peasant. They first bound him, then immediately departed after driving off his oxen and the other animals of the household. Meanwhile the peasant cried out tearfully and lamented:

“Alas, Saint Ruffinus, look upon me in my misery; raise up one crushed by calamity. May it not please you that robbers and utterly wicked men should enrich themselves through the poverty of my meager possessions.”

At these words, a marvelous thing occurred. When the robbers had already gone far away, having traveled nearly twelve miles while driving the animals before them, behold, all those that had been carried off—flocks bleating and cattle lowing—came running back and returned to their pens in the customary manner. Thus it happened that those who had seemed to have the animals in their hands suddenly mourned their loss, while the man who had lamented, receiving back what he had lost, rejoiced as the fortunes of both sides were reversed.

When he had witnessed so many acts of power and such unmistakable signs of miracles, the venerable Ugo, bishop of that see, built a large church in place of the small basilica in which the holy body had previously been received, and decorated it handsomely, according to the resources available. Then he placed the body of the blessed martyr in the sarcophagus that had been the cause of the dispute, and consecrated an altar over it in the presence of a great gathering of the entire diocesan people. But how many blind people were subsequently given sight there, how many were freed from demons, and how many were delivered from various illnesses—it would take too long either to record in writing or to relate in speech.

After these events had taken place, considerable investigation began into the day on which the martyrdom of Ruffinus, the unconquered champion of Christ, ought to be celebrated. Since no historical records existed among them, they had until then been content solely with the annual solemnity of the church’s dedication. At last, by God’s providence, an account of the passion was found, and the venerable bishop decreed, in accordance with the testimony of the written record, that the feast of the same glorious martyr should be celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of August.

But certain men, inflamed against the bishop by the torches of envy and violently driven by a spirit of madness, raised a tumult. They said that it was burdensome for the people to keep holiday through two solemnities of one saint, and superstitious to introduce festivals newly invented through private initiative; in short, they claimed that this had not been constructed out of religious devotion but out of greed for money.

Above all, certain insolent men, called Insulani from the name of the place where they lived, irreverently abusing the day of the celebrated festival, began not only boldly to devote themselves to weaving with their women but also to labor more freely at rural tasks. But the sentence of divine vengeance immediately punished them, and those who had refused to have a heart in prosperity came to their senses after being instructed by blows. What is said through the prophet seems most fittingly to apply to them: “Return to your heart, transgressors” (Isa. XLVI). And also: “Now fire consumes the adversaries.”

For flames suddenly seized their huts, and everything—not only whatever was in their homes but also whatever was in the fields—was consumed in unquenchable conflagration. The wretched people, already placed in extreme danger, streamed from every side to the river and threw whatever was burning into the channel of the current. But, so that it might clearly be proved that this was not an accident but a sign of divine wrath, nothing that was submerged could be extinguished.

In a marvelous way, therefore, that element both retained and partly lost the powers proper to it. The water was liquid, so that it received whatever was immersed in it as the waves opened; yet, in a certain sense, it was not wet, so that it could extinguish burning objects. But why linger over minor matters, when the flames leapt upon the very bodies of the people, and wherever they turned they could not find a means of extinguishing them? At last, scorched, blackened by smoke, and burned like a charred log, they fled amid loud cries and shrieks to the altar of Blessed Ruffinus, begged forgiveness, and promised that thereafter they would amend the offense they had committed through repentance.

Freed from the pains of the fire through the prayers of the most blessed martyr, they returned unharmed to their homes. From that time onward, without any obstacle of hesitation, the martyrdom of Blessed Ruffinus has been celebrated, and on the day we have mentioned the people gather from every direction to his church with great devotion and eagerness.

I also do not think that the following should be passed over. Certain men were attempting to carry to the church of Blessed Ruffinus a beam laboriously smoothed through hard work in the forest. Some men from Perugia, however, using force, violently seized the timber from them. But when the robbers dragged the tree with the utmost effort and anxiety, and were already approaching within scarcely one mile of the walls of Perugia, suddenly the vehicle stuck fast and could not be pushed any farther by any exertion of strength.

Meanwhile all the people in the vicinity gathered to help; quite a few teams of oxen were also added. They carefully arranged the apparatus, encouraged one another, gathered their strength, set their shoulders against it, and pushed with loud shouts. Yet the timber remained immobile, as though held fast by its roots. Finally, necessity—the teacher—showed them what their blind wickedness had failed to understand. Their minds, conscious of the crime they had committed, recognized clearly, though late, that divine power was rightly obstructing those who had stolen property belonging to the blessed martyr.

They therefore suddenly changed their plan, immediately turned the vehicle toward Assisi, and, having found it possible to move it swiftly, humbly returned to the most blessed martyr what they had arrogantly stolen.

Let us therefore give thanks to Christ our Savior and offer worthy proclamations of praise to him. While, through the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, he grants us such benefits, he invites us, as though by small crumbs and delicate morsels, to the full banquet of the heavenly table. While he abundantly satisfies those who now rest after their labor in their homeland, he also somehow sustains us on the journey of this pilgrimage with something like fragments of food. Indeed, while he refreshes them with the solid food of his vision, he nourishes us as little ones with a kind of milk of his signs, until we all attain maturity, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Eph. IV), who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## AUGUST

II. Sermon on Saint Stephen, pope and martyr. VI. Sermon on Saints Donatus and Hilarianus, martyrs. XIII. Sermon on Saint Cassianus, martyr. XV. Sermon on the Assumption of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary. XIV. Sermon I on Saint Bartholomew the apostle. Sermon II on the same.

## SERMON XXXVII. ON SAINT STEPHEN, POPE AND MARTYR  
### 2 August

You have heard today, dearest brothers, of Christ’s soldier fighting manfully against the members of the devil; you have heard the distinguished commander of the Christian people constantly and confidently exhorting his fellow soldiers to prepare themselves for glorious combat.

For at that time a decree had been issued under tyrannical law that whoever informed against any hidden Christian would not only receive all his property but would also be elevated, as a reward for his sacrilege, to whatever military honor he chose. Then Blessed Stephen, as the commander of the first rank of the Christian army and standard-bearer of the eternal emperor, gathered companies of warriors and undertook to arm them with weapons, exhorting and persuading them both to despise the perishable gains of earthly possessions and not to fear the boundless fury of their persecutors.

He drove fear from the minds of the timid and inflamed the inexperienced spirits of the recruits for the contest of divine warfare. This too was commanded through Moses in the Law:

“When the battle is already approaching,” he says, “the priest shall stand before the battle line and speak to the people thus: ‘Hear, O Israel: today you are about to engage in battle against your enemies. Let not your heart be afraid; do not fear, do not retreat, and do not dread them, for the Lord your God is in your midst and will fight for you against your adversaries, to rescue you from danger’” (Deut. XX).

It should be noted that the priest who preaches when war is already imminent is commanded to stand not elsewhere but before the battle line, so that he himself may lead the way before those whom he urges to fight, lest, while attempting to drive others into battle, he himself be weakened by negligent bodily idleness and degenerate into inactivity.

Concerning certain men who preached great things but lived sluggishly, the prophet says: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. LXXVII). Those who summon others to combat against the temptations of vice but themselves refuse to fight beneath the ignoble weakness of indolence certainly aim their arrows, but, turning their backs, do not deserve the honors of completed victory. Nor does it help them that they made a good beginning, because they do not persevere courageously to the end.

Hence what follows immediately concerning them is: “They did not keep the covenant of God, and they refused to walk in his law” (ibid.). It is as though he were saying: “They accepted the covenant, but did not keep it; they set their foot upon the law at the beginning, but did not maintain the step of perseverance.”

Whoever, therefore, summons others to spiritual combat, whoever stirs the minds of his neighbors to act bravely, must certainly make his life agree with his speech, lest, while presenting lofty things to others, he himself be weighed down in the depths by inertia.

For this reason the Law commands: “You shall not have in your bag differing weights, a greater and a lesser, nor shall there be in your house a larger measure and a smaller. You shall have a just weight, and your measure shall be equal and true for you” (Deut. XXV).

We do not have differing weights in our bag when, within the secret place of our conscience, we do not judge ourselves one way and others another, but embrace the same measures of the legal precepts—namely, when we do not impose upon others the rule of strict severity while striving to treat ourselves according to a law of more relaxed indulgence.

Concerning this deceit Solomon also says: “A double weight and a deceitful balance are an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. XX). It is therefore necessary to measure the fruits of the word not with different weights but with the same ones, so that what we command others to do, we ourselves may also effectively fulfill through living deeds.

Blessed martyr Stephen certainly did this commendably. While exhorting others to battle, he first seized his own weapons and, protected by the breastplate of faith, plunged into the very battle line of the massed legion. While providing others with an example of combat, he himself received triumph over the conquered enemy; and, so to speak, while laying down the road to battle for those who followed him, he was soon led, after victory had been accomplished, to the crown.

Since Stephen is understood to mean “crowned,” while a pontiff is as though one who makes a bridge, and is said to be a way for those who follow, he fittingly displayed both the etymology of his name and the office of his pontificate. While he opened the way for those who followed to the arena of the holy contest, the blessed triumphant victor received from God, the just rewarder, the crown of glory.

Nevertheless, we do not think it superfluous briefly to explain to your charity who this Blessed Stephen was by birth and which in succession, or how many years after year, he was in the apostolic government, according to what is found in the Catalogue of the Supreme Pontiffs.

This Blessed Stephen, a Roman by nation, son of Jobius [Julius], succeeded the blessed prince of the apostles Peter as the twenty-fourth in the dignity of the Roman see. He sat for seven years, five months, and two days. He decreed that priests and Levites should not use the sacred vestments in daily practice, but only in church. He ordained three bishops, six priests, and five deacons. Blessed Sixtus succeeded him in the pontificate and was later likewise to be crowned with the glory of a blessed martyrdom.

O blessed mother Church, for whom death serves life, and the cruelty of persecutors unknowingly ministers! For you, painful oppression gives birth to those who will reign forever; death gives birth to those who will live in eternity.

Blessed, I say, and truly happy is the Church for whom the confusion of disgrace produces glory, torments produce victory, and bonds or prisons produce everlasting freedom!

This is truly that field of the Lord in which grains of wheat fall, destined indeed to die, but afterward rise again through multiplied harvests (John XII). This is that threshing floor of Araunah [Ornan] the Jebusite, on which David offered peaceful sacrifices and appeased the Lord’s wrath when the destructive sword of the avenger was restrained from Israel (II Sam. XXIV).

On this threshing floor, or in this winepress, Gideon was cleaning grain by threshing it when he was permitted to see an angel and learned from the angel’s message that he himself would deliver Israel from the hand of Midian (Judg. VI).

On this threshing floor Abel offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. Divine grace graciously received these offerings and immediately, as the old edition testifies, set them ablaze from heaven (Gen. IV). On this same threshing floor Cain offered gifts from the fruits of the earth, which the Lord despised and therefore did not regard (ibid.).

On this threshing floor, just as there are certain things from the threshing that are destined for the fire, so there are also some of the threshers themselves who are heading together toward the fire. Whether we are speaking of the just or of sinners, John’s statement is true: “Their works follow them” (Rev. XIV).

Attend, my dearest brothers; consider and weigh carefully that the entire universal Church, spread throughout the whole world, is one threshing floor, filled with good and bad, just and wicked, like wheat and weeds, like straw and grain.

But until the cultivator of the earth begins to thresh, the threshing floor holds everything indiscriminately: both what is to be stored in barns and what is to be handed over to the flames.

What in the threshing floor is liable to the flames, and what is to be kept in the barns, except what John the Baptist plainly distinguishes in the Gospel when he speaks of the Lord and says:

“His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his barn, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. III).

But how do we discern whether we are chaff or wheat? Certainly by the steadiness or instability of our conduct, by its weight or lightness. Whoever is carried away by the breeze of pleasures, whoever is driven by the whirlwind of anger, whom at one moment the spirit of pride lifts emptily and at another grief or an inflicted injury casts down—such a person must certainly be called chaff or reed.

John, however, is denied to be such when Truth says of him: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. XI). In contrast, it is written of the wicked: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust which the wind casts away from our face” (Ps. I).

Let us not be chaff, my brothers; let us not be chaff or weeds, which the winnowing fork of the final judgment will shake out and which the fire of eternal burning will immediately consume.

Let us always fear that sentence of evangelical warning in which it is said:

“Let both grow until the harvest, and at the time of harvest say to the reapers: ‘Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn, but gather the wheat into my barn’” (Matt. XIII).

Consider carefully the words of Truth; consider with fear what is said: “Bind them into bundles to burn.” Weeds are bound into bundles because, in that fire of eternal condemnation, murderers are bound with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, perjurers with perjurers, and the incestuous with the incestuous, constrained by no different kind of punitive torment.

There the open abyss of limitless punishment, Gehenna, devours them—those who here arrogantly raised themselves upon the horns of pride. There crackling flame will consume their flesh and marrow, rich with fat—those who here burned with delights and satisfied the enticements of heated pleasure.

They are rightly said to be bound into bundles because the diversity of punishment will not separate them then, whereas similarity in wickedness had joined them here. Those who are now subject to the same crimes will afterward be held bound under the judgment of the same punishment.

Concerning all of them it is said elsewhere under the figure of a single person: “Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII). There the limbs are bound for punishment, though here they moved loose and free toward guilt. Or, what is now badly bound so as to prevent works of piety must then rightly be bound in punishments.

There the souls of the reprobate will be tortured together with their bodies in an unquenchable fire, just as here they were joined together in the execution of wicked deeds. Hence the prophet says: “They descended into hell with their weapons” (Ezek. XXXII).

The weapons of sinners are the members of the body, with which wicked people serve the devil and, by living perversely, minister to his command. Thus both bodies and souls are condemned together to eternal death—those that lived together in the perpetration of wicked deeds.

Concerning them the prophet says: “There is Asshur, and his graves” (ibid.). For what is understood by Asshur, the proud king, except the devil, of whom it is written: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI)?

What are graves except dwelling places of the dead? The devil fell into death when, through pride, he withdrew from the author of life. Whoever therefore permits the spirit of wickedness—which is truly dead—to dwell in the lodging of his heart through perverse will undoubtedly makes a grave of himself. He must therefore suffer the punishments of torment there together with that spirit for which, through the wickedness of his perverse deeds, he here offered himself as a dwelling place.

Since, then, weeds and wheat are held together in the threshing floor, let us see, brothers, whether we are wheat; let us see whether we are being reserved for the Lord’s barn.

But since the Apostle says: “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. VI), let us carefully consider what we sow each day, and thus we can already infer what we must necessarily reap afterward.

To make what we are saying clearer through an accessible example: surely, my brothers, does the man who sowed oats or darnel this year expect now to fill his granary with wheat? Surely the man who chose to plant a barren vine will be able to make it overflow with a crop of vegetables?

These weeds we have mentioned, moreover, falsely imitate, in a certain sense, edible plants. They possess at least some resemblance to nourishing harvests. Thus there are certain people who outwardly pretend to the appearance of religion while, by the way they live, refusing to possess true religion within.

Such people display the form of grain in stalks and leaves, but conceal weeds in the dryness of their pith.

It is therefore necessary, brothers, to sow now the true shoots of the virtues, from which afterward we may be able to gather the eternal joys of heavenly harvests.

Let us consider what the Apostle says: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (II Cor. IX). He sows sparingly who does little good, who thinks little of abounding in virtues, who neglects to advance in the practice of distributing mercy and kindness, and who does not extend himself in performing the duties of fraternal charity.

But he sows not sparingly but abundantly who observes the teaching of that excellent preacher: “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap, if we do not fail” (Gal. VI).

He does not sow sparingly who strives to fulfill what the same apostle says elsewhere: “Whatever you do, brothers, whether in word or in deed, do everything for the glory of the Lord” (I Cor. X).

Clearly, whoever receives eternal life reaps not sparingly but abundantly. What, then, does “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” mean, unless it openly declares that whoever is content to sow sparingly in good works will in no way deserve to receive the reward of eternal life?

Just as, my brothers, whoever wishes to live appropriately according to the order of this passing life is not content with one kind of harvest but strives to abound in various kinds of crops, so certainly whoever hastens toward the land of the living, whoever hastens toward that heavenly storehouse, must exercise himself through many labors of good works and strive to gather the shoots of every virtue into the granary of his conscience.

Therefore strive, brothers, to possess true humility, unfeigned charity, patient endurance, purity of flesh and heart, true obedience, compassionate affections, sincere mercy, and the other gifts of the virtues, insofar as God’s generosity makes this possible for you. Thus store up, as it were, an abundant and varied supply of spiritual harvests in the storehouse of your hearts.

Do not think that a single virtue is sufficient for anyone’s perfect salvation if the others happen to be lacking. No virtue exists as such if it is not joined to the other virtues.

Let the breastplate of patience always protect your breast and make you unconquerable against every arrow of adversity, against the scourges of tribulation, and against injuries inflicted upon you. For wheat is first threshed, trodden, and crushed on the threshing floor so that, after the chaff has been removed, it may be stored clean in the granary.

Thus it is necessary that our souls endure many blows and lashes of beatings, so that, once the stalks of iniquity have been laid aside, they may reach the heavenly barn purified.

This is why Blessed James says: “Be patient until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patiently enduring until he receives the early and the late rain” (James V).

Do not place your hope in the success of temporal things. And, to speak with the prophet: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI).

In such prosperity, then, let the man who said this return to your minds: “I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather all that has been produced for me and my goods. And I will say to my soul: ‘Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast’” (Luke XII).

But immediately a divine voice answered him: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (ibid.).

O how many people today, threshing the fruits of their fields, gather them into storehouses, yet will not see the harvests of another year in this world! The world now smiles upon them, but nearby death lies in ambush. If they recognized how near the end of their calling was, they would transfer their desire from earthly possessions to another place.

Therefore, my brothers, the more uncertain you are about the end of your life, the more fearfully you must always remain on guard.

Do not retain the tithes of your possessions for yourselves, lest the terrifying Judge demand them from you there through an accounting, where no one will be able to possess anything with which to repay.

Consider what the Lord says through Malachi. When the divine voice was speaking of Israel’s return, it immediately added:

“And you have said: ‘In what way have we robbed you?’ In tithes and firstfruits. You are cursed with want, and you rob me—you, the whole nation—by bringing the entire tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in my house” (Mal. III).

The Apostle says: “Render to all their dues.” And shortly afterward: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. XIII).

If, then, we are forbidden to retain human debts, consider how dangerous it is not to return to God what belongs to God (Luke XX).

Show reverence to priests and humbly obey their commands. “Obey your leaders,” the Apostle says, “and submit to them; for they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would not be profitable for you” (Heb. XIII).

For if our Redeemer, because of the merit of the Canaanite woman, drove a demon out of her daughter (Matt. XV); if, because of the faith of those who brought him, he commanded a paralytic to carry his bed (Mark II); if, in response to the centurion’s prayers, he restored to health the servant who was being grievously tormented (Matt. VIII)—how greatly, and how necessarily, do we need the prayers of priests, who offer us to God when we are sick with various illnesses of vice and persist without ceasing in daily prayers before divine mercy on our behalf?

Without doubt we are raised up by their merits, even when we are still weighed down by the weakness of our negligence.

Meanwhile, what happened to this blessed martyr Stephen, whom the present sermon has served, also returns to mind. For, as it is related in the authentic account of his passion, as soon as he baptized Nemesius, who had begged him on account of his daughter’s blindness, that same daughter Lucilla—although she had not yet been washed in the bath of the sacred font—received her sight.

“And when Nemesius,” the account says, “was being lifted from the water, his daughter began to cry out, saying: ‘Behold, I see the man who touched my eyes, and a brilliant light around him.’” Then it immediately adds: “At that point he baptized his daughter.”

O virtue of God worthy of praise! O mercy of our redemption worthy of proclamation! One person is baptized into light, and light is restored to another. The father received the light of the heart, and the daughter immediately opened the eyes of her face. Yet both reached one true light, when they rejected all the blindness of their former error.

Thus Blessed Stephen, who, according to the word of Truth, was the light of this world (John I), poured light into hearts and offered the sacrifice of souls before the divine gaze.

Let us too, my brothers, always strive, according to our ability, to offer this sacrifice to God together with Blessed Stephen, so that we may be concerned not only for our own salvation but also diligently intent upon winning the souls of our neighbors. Thus, while the sacrifice of charity is consumed upon the altar of our hearts, may it deserve to be received as a fragrant offering by him who, for our salvation, was willing to be sacrificed upon the altar of the cross: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVIII. ON SAINTS DONATUS AND HILARIANUS, MARTYRS  
### 7 August

[Col. 0705D]

The splendid solemnity of the blessed martyrs Donatus and Hilarianus is here, beloved brethren. Since it gathers the devotion of your attendance from various regions into one place, it also invites us not to keep silent, according to our modest ability, about their distinguished praise. For this is the day on which, leaving this sorrowful world, they laid down the burden of the flesh and obtained the robe of angelic glory. Today, having triumphed over the devil, they carried the palm of their glorious struggle back to the commander of the heavenly army. Today, clad in the purple of their own blood, amid the angelic choirs resounding hymns on every side, they brought the banner of their accomplished victory into the heavenly kingdoms. Advancing step by step, [Col. 0706A] they proceeded through battle to the palm, and from the palm they were elevated to the crown. Although they plainly seemed to fight against a visible enemy, they deserved to overcome in him an invisible adversary. They exposed their bodies as a barrier against hostile arrows, but their faith, fortified and supported by the stronghold of the mind, stood forth unconquerable.

Yet when we review the common deeds of both martyrs, we find that there was some difference in their manner of life. Someone might reasonably conjecture that Hilarianus was that Hilarion whose life was described by blessed Jerome, were it not that the different manner of their deaths prevented this conclusion. For anyone who attentively examines the sequence of their lives, the miracles with which they shone forth, and likewise the places that they illuminated by their dwellings, [Col. 0706B] as the records make clear, will discover no small similarity when the matters themselves are compared. But since one attained the palm of martyrdom while the other rested in peace after this life, there is no doubt that they were different persons, whom we know to have been brought to completion by different kinds of departure. Although they agree in the earlier parts, in keeping with the likeness of their names, they differ at the end.

Blessed Donatus, whom this sermon is especially about to serve, as his truthful history testifies, was not only Julian Caesar’s companion in the study of the liberal arts, but also undertook with him the first rudiments of the ecclesiastical rank. Here one should note and ponder with even greater fear how deep are the divine judgments (Ps. 35), and how terrible God is in his counsels concerning the sons of men (Ps. 65). For behold, two shoots grow up together in the field of the Lord: one, through hidden grace, is a cedar of paradise; the other is prepared as fuel for fires that will never end. The former was driven from the schools to the kingdom, and from the kingdom was thrust naked into Tartarus; the latter, having become a priest, was snatched from the chair to punishment, and from punishment, robed in purple and crowned, was raised to heaven. The world smiled upon the former, but the heavenly court did not open to him; the latter, after suffering shipwreck in the storm of the world, reached the harbor of eternal rest in blessed security. In these men that true evangelical saying is confirmed: “There will be two in the field; one will be taken, and the other will be left behind” [Col. 0706D] (Luke 17). Yet both served God, like the angel and the devil, with a different intention: the one under compulsion, the other unquestionably of his own will. For is not Julian the Apostate also shown to have obeyed the divine decrees, when his bloody rage boiled against Christ’s martyrs and, with the sickle of his persecution, brought into the Lord’s granary so many harvests of the elect, as though they were ripe crops? For this reason tyrannical power was applied to a wicked will, and the horns of a fattened bull were divinely raised up, so that it might thresh the threshing floor of the supreme master of the household and separate the clean grain from the chaff destined for the fires. Hence the Histories relate that, when this Julian was stationed inside a certain basilica of Gaul, a crown hanging above him suddenly fell upon his head, and thus seemed to foretell, in the opinion of the people, that he would become emperor. But we shall leave the burning log in its own fire and pluck the sweetly fragrant fruits of the flourishing tree.

Blessed Donatus, whom the Holy Spirit claimed for himself from the very auspices of his earliest age, rejected the broad ease of a softer life. By the rigor of abstinence he trampled down the enticing provocations of the flesh; and before his tongue, through the dignity of priestly office, proclaimed him, his life was already preaching effectively through honorable and disciplined conduct. He followed the example of the one who first began to do and afterward to teach (Acts 1): by living, he conceived streams of doctrine, [Col. 0707B] which later he offered others to drink from the cup of his mouth. Moreover, while he chastised himself with a strict rule of life, he was already shaping his body for martyrdom through laborious repose; and, so that he might finally deserve to die for Christ, he put himself to death daily through mortification. In the end, he furrowed his own soil with the plow of discipline, so that an abundant crop might spring forth and, when the ray of heavenly grace shone upon it, germinate more fruitfully. Hence, at the beginning of the world, the earth is commanded to germinate on the third day, while on the fourth it is illumined by the sun, moon, and other stars (Gen. 1); for once we have received the mystery of the divine Trinity, the shoots of good works must immediately be brought forth by us, so that afterward the light of heavenly grace may burst upon us. Accordingly, the outstanding martyr first bore abundant fruits of holy action, as though in the cultivated and furrowed new fields [Col. 0707C] of his flesh; then, like a flashing ray of heavenly grace, he was illumined by the splendor of miracles and signs. Hence it was divinely arranged that he should begin to perform works through light. His first miracle was that by which he opened the light of both forehead and heart to the widow Sirena, so that, converted from the blind superstition of idols and restored to her former light, she might worship God, who is truly light, and henceforth no longer bear the darkness of her eyes.

Clearly, although we see many astonishing miracles performed by him recorded in written accounts, we cannot keep silent about one that we see daily with our eyes and touch with our hands, and that is always presented anew before our gaze, as though it had not happened long ago but were happening just now. A secret enemy, by a crafty stratagem, stole a fragment from a chalice that had fallen from the hands of a Levite and has cunningly hidden it to this day in the treasure-house of his malice, for the greater glory of the Lord. Although that small particle appears to be missing from the bottom of the chalice, by the ever-present resistance of divine power not even a thin drop of any liquid can pass through it. As soon as any liquid flows into the sacred vessel, it is liquid, so that it may offer itself as drinkable to those who drink, and in a certain sense it is not liquid, so that it may not burst forth through the vacant opening. Since this certainly happened at that time, it is a miracle; but because it has continued for so long, it may, so to speak, be called a miracle of miracles [Col. 0708A]. For most heavenly signs of divine power occur for a time, but after they have displayed and revealed themselves, they cease. For the entry of the Israelite people, both the sea is divided and the riverbed is dried up; but once the command of divine power has been fulfilled, as Scripture testifies, each of the sea’s waters immediately flows back to its former place, and the river’s customary freedom of course is restored (Exod. 14).

Elisha crossed the Jordan with Elijah on dry ground and returned a little later; but again, so that he might deserve to enter alone without hindrance, he obtained this by his prayers (2 Kings 2). The people traveling through the desert used heavenly food for nearly forty years; but after they reached the borders of the Canaanites and tasted the produce of the land, the manna immediately ceased. But this sign of divine power about which we are now speaking, so that it is not a matter of faith but of manifest sight, continues without failing, just as it began once to proclaim the merit of the precious martyr. “Faith is,” as the distinguished preacher says, “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11). Indeed, just as the author of human salvation wished the marks of the nails to remain in his body, so he also chose to preserve in this sacred vessel a rare little wound without any compensation. In the former case, so that it might give faith to those who doubt; in the latter, so that it might kindle the minds of the faithful to proclaim his praise. In the former, so that the almighty Father might always produce the signs of human redemption; in the latter, so that every devotee of God might recognize how exalted he makes his servants even in this life.

[Col. 0708C] But lest anyone accuse us of comparing great things with small, we are not unaware that the same life-giving blood becomes present in the chalice which flowed from the Lord’s body through various wounds. The one who created the exceedingly tiny worm also created the enormous elephant. Truly, God is wondrous not only in himself but also in his saints (Ps. 67). He who deigned to drink the chalice of suffering for our salvation is also the one who does not permit his blood to flow from the broken chalice. Consider, dearest brethren: if this man had such power with God that what he once obtained in a worthless vessel cannot be changed, how much power will he have on behalf of the redeemed, if only we follow the footsteps of the Redeemer? Let us therefore hold fast to the rule of this blessed martyr if we desire to reach the crown. This man is known to have been conspicuous for such a distinguished brilliance of religion and uprightness, and adorned with so many flowers of virtue, that, being a suitable guide for both kinds of human beings, he suffices as an example for martyrs and teaches a way of life to those living in peace. Through a strict rule of life he deserved to attain the palm of martyrdom; and for that reason he did not succumb in the ordeal to the armed hands of the executioners, because earlier he had not weakly overcome the devices of the hidden enemy. He triumphed in the arena because he had already despised the ambushes of the hidden enemy in secret.

For this reason the seed of his word grew strong in another person’s field of heart, because it had first reached maturity through the work of the same sower. The distinguished Preacher, [Col. 0709A] since, in accordance with the word of Truth, he was the light of this world (John 1), poured light into hearts, placed the fire of the word into the minds of his hearers, and fused people of different hearts into one body in the unity of faith. Moses clearly signifies this mystery when he says: “The priest shall take a handful of fine flour mingled with oil, and all the frankincense placed upon the fine flour; and he shall burn it on the altar as a memorial, a most sweet-smelling offering to the Lord” (Lev. 6). What is signified by the fine flour, if not the holy Church of the elect? As it is gathered from the mutually joined members of believers, it is like fine flour mixed from many grains of wheat. And just as fine flour is crushed between the two millstones so that the bran may be separated from the flour’s finest meal, so [Col. 0709B] the holy Church is pressed, as it were, between the two millstones of the Law and the Gospel, so that the surface of the letter may be distinguished from the marrow of the spirit. This Church, as truly spiritual fine flour, is united through the water of baptism, mixed with the oil of chrism, and solidified by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it may be, in the Apostle’s words, “a sacrifice pleasing to God, and perfect” (Rom. 12). The frankincense said to be placed upon the fine flour signifies the prayer of that same Church. This is shown in John’s Apocalypse, where he says: “For the bowls full of perfumes are the prayers of the saints” (Rev. 5).

Blessed Donatus, priest and martyr, offered this fine flour to God and burned it as a memorial of the sweetest fragrance when he converted the pagan people to the sacraments of the faith in the unity [Col. 0709C] of the Spirit. The fruit of souls indeed smells more sweetly in the sight of God than any pleasantness of sacrifices. Let us also, my brethren, strive always to offer this sacrifice to God together with blessed Donatus, according to our modest ability, so that we may be concerned not only for our own salvation but also diligently intent on winning the souls of our neighbors; so that, while the sacrifice of charity is burned upon the altar of our breast, he may deem our sacrifice worthy of acceptance as a sweet fragrance—he who deigned to be sacrificed upon the altar of the cross for our salvation.

Moreover, the holy man burned with such zeal for the faith even toward his own people that his still-pagan parents rejected him and entirely cast away the beloved pledge of their affection; but afterward he led them both to the sacraments of the Christian faith and, in an appropriate ordering, sent them ahead to martyrdom. Thus he must rightly be counted illustrious among the blessed martyrs, for he is both a son and a father of martyrs: a son by nature, a father through the grace of the faith he bestowed. In a blessed exchange he begot them for God, from whom he had been begotten for the world. Blessed are those parents who, in their earthly inheritance, begot such a man, through whom they become fellow heirs with the citizens above in the land of the living. Rejoice, too, fortunate Arretium, because by divine generosity you have deserved such a patron. Rejoice, I say, and rejoice in the Lord with all your heart; for while you cherish in your bosom the soil containing his sacred body, you possess the pearl that is solemnly to be set into the diadem of the heavenly king [Col. 0710A]. You guard a treasure with which no gold can worthily be compared and to which no sum of any riches can be equal. Therefore you should no longer be called Arretium in the customary way, a name evidently imposed on you from the aridity of the land; rather, you should be called Auritium, from the most precious gold of the sacred corpse, which is shown to be hidden in your entrails.

Blessed, therefore, and rich is the vein of earth which, made as it were the heavenly king’s depositary, conceals within its boundaries the talent entrusted to it, destined on the day of restoration to be brought into the heavenly treasuries, where living stones shine perpetually, glowing like fire, and where flourishing pearls splendidly adorn dining halls radiant with gold. This will unquestionably be fulfilled when our jubilee arrives, when that final trumpet [Col. 0710B], no longer legal but judicial, begins to sound. For just as the seventh day is commanded to be a day of rest, so too the jubilee year, by which the rest of eternal life is signified, is commanded to be kept as a holiday.

When the Jubilee arrives, therefore, the trumpet sounds, and each person immediately returns to his ancient possession; for as judgment approaches, “at the voice of the archangel, at the last trumpet” (1 Thess. 5), the possession of their bodies is restored to all mortals. As Paul testifies: “The trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. 15). Blessed are those souls, my brethren, who at that time, while clothing themselves again with their bodies, receive a share in the company of the holy martyrs. Blessed are those who now keep vigil at the memorials of the saints in such a way that they always set their examples before themselves for imitation; [Col. 0710C] who attend their solemnities with praise in such a way that, nevertheless, by their manner of life they do not depart from their path. We follow the holy martyrs if, while they despised the sufferings of their bodies, we too strive to break the desires of our flesh.

Let us therefore venerate, brethren, and honor with prayers and worthy acts of devotion these blessed martyrs, Donatus and Hilarianus, through whom almighty God wished to illumine the whole body of Tuscany as through twin eyes of heavenly light. Thus, while we now pursue the glorious martyrs with love and imitation, may we deserve, through their intercession, to reach the emperor of the martyrs, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIX. ON SAINT CASSIANUS THE MARTYR (13 AUGUST)

[Col. 0710D]

The admirable and glorious providence of our Creator, dearest brethren, has so ordered the course of our mortal life that, through the successive alternation of times, the various festivals of Christ’s victorious soldiers come before us, kindling our souls to love that supreme and unceasing solemnity. Clearly, when almighty God varies the circle of the whole year with the titles now of martyrs and now of confessors, what else does he construct but something like a wreath of glory, painted with the beautiful variety of lilies and roses? Among these solemnities, today’s is by no means insignificant: that of the martyrs Hippolytus [Col. 0711A] and Cassianus, which shines like the twin light of two stars. These most valiant warriors of the eternal king suffered punishments in different places, but the cause of their struggle was one and the same, because both were animated by the same profession of truth. Indeed Cassianus, whom this sermon is especially about to serve, remained hidden for a long time; but when the time of combat arrived, he revealed how much sharpness, savor, and strength the mustard seed concealed. Or rather, in accordance with the omen contained in his name, when he began to be beaten and crushed in the mortar of his passion by the hands of his persecutors, he immediately scattered the fragrant sweetness hidden within him. For cassia is an aromatic substance which, while whole, seems to have no scent, but when crushed releases the power of its natural sweetness.

Accordingly, blessed Cassianus, as the history of his deeds testifies, was brought to trial for the faith of Christ while he was a teacher in the schools and was instructing boys by teaching them to grasp words in brief written signs. When, inflamed with zeal for the faith, he despised the judges’ decrees and trampled upon profane sacrifices, he was handed over to the hands of his pupils for torture, so that he might in turn pay the penalty to those whom he had once terrified under the rod of discipline. Thus, stripped of his clothing and bound with his hands behind his back, he was surrounded by a raging crowd of boys armed with their writing-styles and tablets. Pierced and torn on every side, he was lacerated throughout his body. This entirely new and unusual kind of martyrdom consecrated him as a distinguished martyr to God. Yet this form of martyrdom seems, by way of comparison, to correspond to no one better than to the very king of martyrs, the Lord and Savior. For he too was killed by his own faithful people, namely the Jews, [Col. 0711C] to whom he had handed over the precepts of the Decalogue written with his own finger, whom he had instructed in their ceremonies and sacrificial rites, and whom he had formed for every uprightness of life like tender children under discipline. As he himself says through Isaiah: “I nourished and exalted sons, but they despised me” (Isa. 11). Those carnal Israelites were also rightly called children, for they did not weigh the commandments of the Law and the mysteries of the prophets with the gravity of mature understanding, but understood everything superficially and childishly. Although this can be confirmed by various authorities of Scripture, it is enough to insert here only what is recorded to have happened to the prophet Elisha. As he was going up by the road leading to Bethel, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” When he turned and saw them, he cursed them in the name of the Lord. Scripture immediately adds: “And two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys” (2 Kings 2). Clearly, what should be understood by Elisha if not the Mediator between God and human beings? What, moreover, is signified by Bethel, which is interpreted as “house of God,” if not heavenly blessedness? Therefore our Redeemer was going up by the road leading to Bethel when he was approaching his Passion, [Col. 0712A] just as he says to his disciples at the sacred and mystical supper itself: “I am going to him who sent me” (John 6). But as he goes up to Bethel—that is, as through the mystery of his most sacred Passion he strives to return to the Father—little boys come out of the city and mock him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” For the Jews, empty of every weight of gravity and wisdom, in that childish immaturity of which it is said, “The child of a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. 65), drag him to the place called Calvary and rage against him with the viperous fury of mockery and insults. That place was called Calvary from the shaved heads of those condemned who were accustomed to be beheaded there.

It should also be noted that the boys are said to have come out of the city, [Col. 0712B] because, as the Apostle says: “To sanctify the people through his own blood, the Lord suffered outside the gate” (Heb. 13). Moreover, in what follows—“two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys”—the number of the boys signifies a number of years. For in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion, as the histories relate, Titus and Vespasian, two kings from the forests of the nations, like two fierce bears, came out of the wild forest and tore the boys apart, because, coming for the destruction of Jerusalem, they conquered the Jews in fury. The boys therefore signify those who crucified the Lord; the boys also signify those who killed blessed Cassianus the martyr. In neither case was it innocent childhood, but crafty and poisonous malice. Christ was killed for Cassianus, and Cassianus was killed for Christ: the Lord for the servant, and the servant for the Lord. For he said: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115). He was willing to die so that he might lead this man out from under the yoke of savage slavery; the latter was granted death so that he might reach with glory the inheritance of the children, to which he had been enrolled. [Page 197] The former accepted death in order to destroy death in his flesh; the latter did not fear to die in order to carry the victorious insignia of his triumph back to the author of life. The former had as persecutors those whom he had created; the latter endured as executioners those whom he had taught. But Christ was fighting in his martyr, supplying him with the strength to fight; Christ alone was conquering in the one whom he strengthened amid the struggle. For the whole universal Church, girded with the weapons of virtue, fights against the devil throughout the entire course of this mortal life in Christ; in Christ it always triumphs, not by its own power but by his. This victory over the ancient enemy, because the Synagogue was unwilling to receive it, the Church received.

We shall show this to you more clearly, dearest brethren, if we recall the victory of the Old Testament that was accomplished through a woman. To summarize the sacred history in a few words: at that time Deborah the prophetess, wife of Lapidoth, judged the people and sat beneath a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, [Col. 0713A] on Mount Ephraim, and the sons of Israel went up to her for every judgment (Judg. 4). But one reaches the conclusion more quickly if, while the history is being woven together, it is explained piece by piece along the way. Deborah, which is interpreted as “speech” or “bee,” suitably signifies prophecy. A bee makes honey, and of prophecy the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118.) Meanwhile, beloved, I do not want you to be unaware that this history, which we have undertaken to treat on this occasion, requires many words, since it is filled with many mysteries; but for that reason we condense it briefly, so that we do not burden your charity with the weariness of excessive length. Let us therefore consider where prophecy is described as having its seat, namely beneath a palm tree, because those whom prophetic teaching instructs through its lessons it leads to the palm of the heavenly calling, and while through it people learn the order of life, they become victors over rebellious vices. Nor should it be passed over that she is said to have sat between Ramah and Bethel. Ramah is interpreted as “exalted,” and Bethel as “house of God,” as we have already said. Prophecy is therefore rightly described as dwelling between Ramah and Bethel, because whoever diligently attends to prophetic teachings, whoever sincerely devotes himself to the words of the sacred Scriptures, dwells in the house of God through the desire of his mind in such a way that he always seeks not weak and fleeting things, but rather those that are exalted and heavenly.

She summoned Barak to herself. Barak, moreover, is interpreted as “flash of lightning.” A flash of lightning has light, but it does not last long. As soon as it begins to shine, it immediately fades. This Barak, therefore, represents the Israelite people, who, instructed before all others by prophetic oracles, shone for a little while in the Law they had received, but flashed only briefly. In the Law, of which it is said, “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Ps. 118), that ancient people began to shine but ceased. It produced a flash like a clear life, but did not remain in luminous works. For when they said, “All that the Lord commands us, we shall both hear and do,” behold, a light like a flash had arisen; but when they suddenly bent their knees before Baal, behold, the flash appeared extinguished. Deborah therefore said to Barak: [Col. 0713D] “The Lord God of Israel commands you: Take with you ten thousand fighting men and go up to Mount Tabor. I, however, will bring Sisera, the commander of Jabin’s army, to you at the torrent of Kishon, together with his chariots and his entire multitude, and I will deliver them into your hand” (Judg. 4). It is as though almighty God were saying through prophetic teaching to the former people: Take up the ten commandments of the Law, ascend the summit of virtue, and with me supplying you with strength, overthrow the prince of the wicked and the author of all iniquity.

Nor should it be passed over that the military commander Sisera, who was liable to near destruction, was previously promised to be led to the torrent of Kishon. For what should be understood by the torrent of Kishon if not baptism? When a catechumen is plunged into the washing of the sacred font, the most wicked spirit, together with all the vices that serve him, must necessarily be destroyed just as Sisera was destroyed with his army. Barak answered Deborah: “If you come with me, I will go; if you do not wish to come, I will not proceed.” It is as though that carnal Israel were answering prophecy: Unless I always have you with me according to the letter, and as though according to a woman’s understanding, I do not dare to undertake the spiritual struggle. Deborah said to him: “I will certainly go with you, but the victory will not be credited to you, because Sisera will be delivered into the hand of a woman.” It is as though the ancient people heard: Prophecy will indeed be with you externally, as you request; but the spiritual triumph over the ancient enemy will be won not by you, but rather by the holy Church. The victory will rightly belong to that Church [Col. 0714B] which, while seeking the marrow of spiritual understanding in the mysteries of Scripture, pays little heed to the chaff of the killing letter.

When the battle had therefore begun, Sisera finally fled into the house of Jael, a foreign woman. She opened a skin of milk for him, thirsty as he was, and gave him a drink; then she drove a tent peg through both sides of his head at the same time and thus, in the form of a man, killed the devil, the head of all the wicked. For what does Jael, which is interpreted as “ascent,” signify if not the holy Church, through which alone heavenly blessedness is revealed? Hence the Synagogue says of this same Church in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8.) This woman was foreign, [Col. 0714C] because the holy Church came forth from the nations. She first gave the enemy of the Israelites milk to drink, and afterward drove the peg into his head; for the holy Church first nourished the enemy of the human race with a carnal way of life, but afterward, by living spiritually, destroyed him with a certain sharpness and with the power of the cross. Unless the insatiable murderer thirsted with utterly unappeasable greed for the destruction of the human race, Scripture certainly would not say of him: “He will swallow the river and not be amazed, and he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40). Milk is the fruit of the flesh and signifies the allurements of carnal pleasure.

As long, therefore, as the pagan people lived voluptuously according to the law of the flesh, they offered the softness of their life to the devil, thirsty for our death, like milk. [Col. 0714D] But after they had bound themselves under the discipline of the spirit, they immediately seized the weapons of the unconquered cross and pierced with the wood the enemy of human salvation, whom they had formerly given milk of pleasure to drink, now fortified by the protection of repentance. Thus the foreign woman—the Church of the nations—overthrew by the wood of the cross alone the one whom the Israelite people could not overcome.

Hence this unconquerable soldier of Christ, blessed Cassianus, likewise could not be overcome amid the most grievous torments of his punishments, because neither did an iron cuirass surround him nor a crested helmet protect him; only the wood of the cross armed him. For whoever is fortified by the banner of this wood safely undertakes the battle against spiritual wickedness. The sacrilegious Philistine did not know this sign when he went forth against David for battle, and therefore, struck immediately on the forehead, he perished (1 Sam. 17), in the place where he had not impressed upon himself the sign of life.
