This sign of salvation is depicted on the forehead, where the high priest was commanded in the Law to place a golden plate for glory and beauty (Exod. 28); on that plate the glorious and ineffable name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, was visibly engraved. What else, surely, did this seem to express but the cross of the Savior? For just as the cross has four arms, so that name consists of four letters.

The cross, therefore, the adornment and glory of the priestly office, is placed upon the forehead, so that, when the lintel of the house has been stained with the blood of the lamb, one may escape the sword of the passing angel (Exod. [Col. 0715B] 12). Conversely, on this part of the body King Uzziah was struck with leprosy (2 Chron. 26), in accordance with the prophet’s words: “Fill their faces with shame” (Ps. 82), because, when he arrogantly swelled with royal pride, he usurped for himself the right to sacrifice, which was owed only to priests.

Foreseeing this sign in the spirit, David joyfully said: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us”; and therefore he adds: “You have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4). How precious and wondrous is the sign of the cross, my brethren, which both destroyed every proud person together with the author of pride and raised those who fight for Christ to the advancement of triumphal glory! “Behold,” says Simeon, “this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” [Col. 0715C] (Luke 2). Precious, I say, is the sign of the cross; but, since we bear it on our foreheads, would that we might also carry it in our hearts. For that person truly has the sign of the cross impressed upon his heart who loves Christ, who was hung upon the cross; who embraces him with the whole love of his heart; who certainly delights in him with all his inward being; who rejects whatever he has forbidden and lovingly keeps whatever he has commanded. For there are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose “end is destruction, and whose glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things,” as the Apostle says (Phil. 3). There are also friends of the cross of Christ, whose citizenship is in heaven. At the dreadful judgment, whoever does not bear the mark of this life-giving sign will be found among the left-hand side. Nor will the one who was crucified, the judge, give a reward to anyone who cannot show that the emblem of the cross has been impressed upon him. For in the Book of Ezekiel the Lord commands this sign to be impressed upon the foreheads of those who groan and mourn; then he commands all the others who are found without this sign to be killed (Ezek. 9). For if we examine carefully, we also perceive that the commandments themselves of the Old Testament breathe the mystery of the cross. When the divinely given Law is delivered under the number ten, which is represented by the letter X, what else is expressed in this but a figure of the cross? This letter has the appearance of a cross, and, since it contains the number ten within itself, it clearly shows that all the commandments of the Law belong to the cross.

Let us therefore love Christ, beloved, let us love the cross, and let each one of us diligently watch to restrain the perverse will within himself. Let us not merely express this sign of life upon the forehead of the flesh, but also hide it in the innermost depths of a chaste and sober will, fulfilling what the bridegroom commands his bride in the Song of Songs: “Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8). It is clear that what the heart thinks, the arm performs. That person therefore places Christ upon his heart like a seal who loves him from the depths, who ardently longs for him, who anxiously calls upon him, who continually perseveres in his desire for him. But he places Christ upon his arm who also outwardly devotes himself to his commandments and demonstrates in action the one whom he conceals in the depths of his heart. We too place a sign upon any limb of our body so that we may not lose the memory of something dear to us. Let Christ therefore be held in the heart, and let him also be held as a seal in action, so that his living memory may always restrain the wickedness of creeping thoughts within us and clearly display the mark of the Crucified in the things we do outwardly. Indeed, if Christ is our seal, he too places us as a seal upon himself in a gracious exchange. As he promises Zerubbabel, the leader of Judea, saying: “On that day I will take you, Zerubbabel my servant, and I will place you like a seal in my presence” (Hag. 2). The righteous person is placed as a seal in the presence of God because, through the grace of continual love, he is always held in God’s memory. But concerning the wicked king Jeconiah, who, because he was forgetful of almighty God, did not deserve himself to be held in God’s memory, Scripture says: “Even if Jeconiah were a signet ring on my right hand, I would tear him away from there” (Jer. 22).

How inviolable and firm a seal Christ was, whom blessed martyr Cassian had placed upon his breast, for he remained immovable in such steadfastness of faith! Blows of scourges rain down; wounds from piercings are inflicted; the darts of mockery are hurled; bonds are fastened around his hands. There is also the nakedness of his body, and the spectacle of mockers barking at him from every side. Amid these storms of raging tempests, amid, finally, these repeated hailstorms, the wholly immovable column of God stands firm. It is not shaken, it is not shattered; but it constantly and steadfastly leans upright and firm upon the stone on which it has been founded. For he was saying: “Who will separate me from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?” (Rom. VIII). They were gnashing their teeth; he, gentle, was contemplating the patience of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. 201 The executioners, by inflicting punishments, were satisfying the bloody fury of their hearts; he, already secure, was turning over in his mind the dignity of heavenly glory. And, so to speak, this cautious and prudent merchant, my brothers, what happy commerce he was conducting with Christ, the rewarder of those who contend! For he was laying down the burden of the flesh and hastening toward the robe of angelic brightness. He was enduring the rod of cruel boys, so that he might become the companion of the holy angels. He was setting aside the office of teaching letters and was eagerly hastening toward that one Word to whom all the volumes of literature throughout the world serve as soldiers: Christ our Lord, who with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

*SERMON XL. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. (15 AUG.)*

Here let all the resources of eloquence run their course, and let golden speech shine forth in its full majesty. May the Mother of God, mistress of the world, queen of heaven, make the willing offerings of our mouth pleasing to herself (Ps. CXVIII). May she sharpen the mind, direct the style, and sprinkle the tongue of the poor man with more graceful speech. May she illumine this light with a brighter radiance, and deign to grant her presence to her assembly. This is the sublime day, resplendent with a more brilliant sun, on which the royal Virgin is raised to the throne of God the Father and, placed upon the seat of that very Trinity, summons even the angelic nature to behold her. The entire multitude of angels gathers to see the queen seated at the right hand of the Lord of hosts, in a garment of gold (Ps. XLIV), in a body forever immaculate, surrounded by variety, distinguished by a multiplicity of virtues.

This is that day which filled the workshops of heaven with more exalted joy: annual for the world, perpetual for the angels; joining human beings to angels and angels to human beings in a blessed alliance. Look with the eyes of the mind upon the Son ascending and the Mother assumed, and you will see something more excellent displayed in the Son’s Ascension and something more glorious manifested in the Virgin’s Assumption. For the Savior ascended into heaven by the command of his authoritative power, as Lord and Creator, accompanied by the service of angels, supported not by their aid. Mary was assumed into heaven, but by the judgment of uplifting grace, with the angels accompanying and assisting her; grace, not nature, was lifting her up. Therefore this day is called the Assumption, whereas that is called the Ascension; for power is one thing and mercy another, and it belongs solely to the Creator as a privilege to surpass the nature of things by his own power. This is that excellence which the Creator claims over the creature, where even abundant and singular grace would not dare aspire.

[Col. 0717D] But if we attend carefully to the Son’s Ascension and the Mother’s Assumption, we shall certainly find something that we will rejoice to have discovered. When the Lord was ascending, that entire glorious company of blessed spirits went out to meet him, when he placed the lower nature above the higher and enclosed the man he had assumed, by an unchangeable sacrament, within the very identity of the Godhead. When the angels met him, he joined to them the souls of the elect whom he was leading out with himself; and thus, escorted by the triumphal procession of both, he was led to the Father and sits at the right hand of Majesty. Now raise your eyes to the Virgin’s Assumption, and—without diminishing the majesty of the Son—you will find the encounter of this procession appreciably more worthy. The angels alone were able to meet the Redeemer; but when the Mother of heaven was entering the palaces of heaven, the Son himself, solemnly coming to meet her with the entire court of both angels and the righteous, lifted her to the council-chamber of blessed session and said: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV). Wholly beautiful, because wholly divinized; there is no blemish in you, because the Holy Spirit came upon you, and he cleansed you. And the Virgin, heaped with gracious gifts, responds in David’s words with such kindness, marveling at the splendor of the highest condescension: “You have taken hold of my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. LXXII). Observe the arrangement of the words, marked by a distinction of degrees. “You have taken hold,” she says, “of my right hand,” because, although your left hand is beneath my head, your right hand already embraces me. “And in your will you have led me,” not in my sublimity, because the whole work is of grace, not of nature. “And with glory you have received me”—glory, certainly, that is glorious, which no one knows except the one who gave it and the one to whom he has deigned to give it.

Now consider the diligence and sequence of the Scriptures. For the Holy Spirit, by whose workmanship the composition of both the Old and the New Testament was fashioned, proceeding in a similar style through the Son’s Ascension and the Mother’s Assumption, asks three times: “Who is this?” (Ps. XXIII). And a third time he repeats: “Who is she?” (Song III). Let us look first at the Son, then at the Mother. Descending to the underworld in the spirit of strength, the Savior crushed the bronze gates and broke the iron bars; and, with the fragments of the infernal cauldron scattered, he shook that entire unhappy dwelling with a ruinous convulsion, while the angels cried aloud: “Lift up your gates, you princes” (Ps. XXIII). Those who had fallen in an irremediable fall through pride answered with disdainful ignorance: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ibid.). This is that fool who said in his heart: “There is no God” (Ps. XIII). And: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. V). The angels of peace confidently repeat: “The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII)—strong to weaken your strength; mighty to empty your might; mighty in that saving battle in which he alone defeated the powers of the air. Rising from the underworld and bringing back the standards of solemn victory, he raised up the man united to himself, whom he had never abandoned, and, borne into heaven with the palm of triumph, presenting to the Father the hundredth sheep that he had lost (Luke XV), he hears from the angels: “Who is this King of glory?” But when the same angels cry out: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII), the words resounded through the palace of heaven, and the whole heavenly household overflowed with more abundant joys. Truly the Lord of hosts, in the Resurrection, performed a mighty deed that he had not previously performed: redeeming the servant and making him a son in place of a servant. On the most glorious day of the Ascension, when he was lifted up into heaven before the eyes of the disciples (Mark XVI), that supreme and revered company came to meet the Redeemer; and the entire authority of the angels, both those standing by and those ministering, ran to the Son and, marveling at him as he ascended, said: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. LXIII). Seeing him drenched in a flood of blood-red color, they marvel at his patience and at the savagery of the Jews, who were not afraid to condemn the Son of God to the disgrace of the cross. “He walks,” they say, “in the multitude of his strength” (Ibid.): not merely in strength, but in the multitude of strength, because no strength was stronger than redeeming a servant and placing him forever at the right hand of the Godhead.

These are the voices that accompany him who descended to the underworld, rose from the underworld, and ascended to the heavens, with manifold proclamation. But now the style must be turned toward the holy of holies, and the particular meaning of those words that have been specially dedicated to the Virgin Mother must be unfolded. But, to set a threshold inscription at the front of the building that is about to arise, let us say briefly that the first question applies to her Nativity, the second to her conduct of life, and the third to her Assumption. “Who is she?” says the Holy Spirit concerning her Nativity, “who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array?” (Song VI). This is she “who knew not a marriage-bed in sin” (Wis. III). A virgin uniquely consecrated to the Son of God, specially joined in marriage to the Holy Spirit. “Who comes forth,” he says, “like the rising dawn.” What an elegant and brilliant comparison, descending from the teaching of him who abundantly enclosed the supreme fountain of wisdom in the Song of Songs!

[Col. 0719C] In the light of midday that first parent was created, made in the image and likeness of the Creator. For what could be clearer than that the created should not be unlike its Creator? “Let us make,” he says, “man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). He gave him the image in eternity and likeness in conduct, so that he might be like the Creator, if not in identity, nevertheless in likeness. But that man, rejecting the dignity of so great a privilege, was seduced by the false promise of the apostate spirit, clung to it, and consigned himself and his descendants to perpetual death and darkness. From that hour darkness came over the whole earth until the Virgin; nor was anyone found who either emerged from the darkness or dispersed it. Rather, as the world grew, the dark abyss grew with it, until, gathered into the thickest blackness, it buried the human race in a terrible night. This is that solitary night, unworthy of praise, of which it is written: “You appointed darkness, and it became night” (Ps. CIII). In it all the beasts of the forest had remained, because cruel and untamed spirits, once the barriers had been removed, crushed the human race with all their strength. But when the Virgin was born, dawn rose, because Mary, the forerunner of the true light, made the clearest morning serene by her birth. She is the morning star in the midst of mist, flashing with the greatest brilliance at the highest hinge of heaven and coloring the world beneath with brighter rays. She is the dawn that is followed by—or rather from which is born—the Sun of justice, yielding only to his radiance. She is the dawn whom he did not see who saw all that is sublime; and blessed Job prays that it may be shut away from him by deep concealment, saying: “Let him not see the rising of the coming dawn” (Job III). Yours is the day, Lord, in which Adam was created; yours is the night in which Adam was expelled from the day; you fashioned the dawn, that is, the Virgin Mother, and the sun, namely the Sun of justice, who arose from the virginal bridal chamber. For just as dawn testifies that the limit of night and the beginning of day are present, so the Virgin drove out everlasting night and poured upon the earth the day that arose from the day, from the soil of her virginity.

“Comes forth,” he says, as though she were coming out from far away, because from far away, and from the furthest ends, comes her price (Prov. XXXI). Dawn, because she is the end of night and the beginning of light; rising, because she rises above matter that is falling. [Col. 0720B] Beautiful as the moon. What is more beautiful than the moon, when, with its flashing stars along the sign-bearing path, it surpasses the brightness of the remaining heavenly bodies? Consider how the serene trembling of the stars and the luminous brilliance pour over the circular orb of so great a heavenly body, so that they substantially dim the brightness of the other lights. So too the Virgin, rising above and elevated among the souls of the saints and the choirs of angels, surpasses the merits of each and the honors of all. However brightly the other stars may shine, the moon nevertheless excels them both in size and in splendor. Thus the singular Virgin surpasses both natures by the immensity of grace and the radiance of virtues. Chosen as the sun. Consider this comparison, than which none can be more exalted among worldly things. For the Spirit had nothing more excellent among visible creatures with which to compare the Virgin’s excellence. The sun’s brightness is much higher than the moon’s; for although the moon obscures the smaller stars, it does not entirely conceal them. The sun, however, burning with greater brilliance, so takes away the position of the stars and the moon for itself that they seem almost not to exist and cannot be seen.

Likewise the shoot of Jesse, the forerunner of the true light, shining through that inaccessible light, so dulls the dignity of both kinds of spirits that, in comparison with the Virgin, they neither can nor ought to appear. Do you think that the whole rational creation does not tremble at the contemplation of such dignity? Consider what has been refashioned in the Virgin both in heaven and on earth: God, who measures heaven with his palm, enclosed within the smallness of a virginal womb; the redemption of human beings; the restoration of angels; finally, whatever is, was, and will be, renewed through the Virgin’s womb. Then your thought will suggest to you what speech cannot demonstrate. “Chosen,” he says, “and also prechosen.” As the sun, because just as the sun alone illuminates the world, so she alone illumines angels and human beings with a more solid light. Terrible as an army set in battle array: terrible to demons, ordered in virtues, the singular dread of evil spirits, the special love of the blessed citizens.

The passage concerning her conduct follows: “Who is she who comes up through the wilderness like a little column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” “She is beautiful among the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song III). The wilderness is the desolation of this world, in which the beasts of the field play most frequently, where that most wicked prince rules with all his strength. It is called a wilderness as though abandoned by the administration of the virtues, since their assembly, with iniquity abounding, has flown back to its own origins. “Who comes up,” he says. In the vanities of this age everyone is known either to descend or to fall, and rare is the person who does not descend or fall into the ocean of this most turbulent depth. That mother and daughter of the Creator alone neither descended nor fell, but, ascending from virtue to virtue, was clothed in the perfection of virtues. How did she ascend? “Like a little column,” he says, “of smoke.” But gather also what work is signified by so meaningful a comparison. A little column of smoke is upright, slender, fragrant, and the farther it extends into the air, the more widely it spreads. So too the queen of angels is upright in the sublimity of her conduct, because she is the rod of direction, the rod of the Lord’s reign (Ps. XLIV). She is slender in contemplation of the Godhead, because she is the one who kept all these words, pondering them in her heart (Luke II). She is fragrant in the reputation of her virtues, because “we run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I). She is narrow in temporal matters, because there was no room for her in the lodging-place (Luke II). In spiritual matters she is enlarged, because “the queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. XLIV). She is that rod by which the assaults of opposing demons are beaten back: the rod of Aaron, through which signs and wonders are performed. Understand the staff of the cross, by which not only was he struck, but that incurable [or: insatiable] homicide, who feeds and nourishes himself on the deaths of human beings, was also killed. In the Virgin, the rod and staff of the cross contain the hope and consolation of the wretched. As the sublime Prophet declares in a clear voice: “Your rod,” he says, “and your staff—they themselves have comforted me” (Ps. XXII).

The passage continues: “From the spices of myrrh and frankincense.” The ingredients from which the aromatic little column is raised are named: myrrh and frankincense. Myrrh consolidates bodies that have been dissolved and claims the lifeless corpse for itself, so that it may not decay. Frankincense, however, is burned to God in prayer, as we are taught by many testimonies of Scripture. Understand continence in myrrh and devotion in frankincense. For the Virgin’s flesh, taken from Adam, did not admit Adam’s stains; rather, the purity of singular continence was transformed into the brightness of eternal light. Moreover, who could equal her devotion with votive praises, when he recalls the archangel sent, the Spirit coming upon her, the Son conceived, God born, the new star, the glory of the magi, the grace of their gifts, and above all these things the testimony of her own conscience? These are the two qualities that surrounded the virginal substance with their whole power: continence and devotion. One possessed the flesh, the other the mind, so that the most pure flesh and the purest mind might consecrate the Mother of the Lord in a uniquely exalted way.

But lest you suppose that the mistress of the world and queen of heaven was distinguished by these two virtues alone, the authority of Scripture continues: “And every powder of the perfumer.” Here everything that could be expressed has been expressed. Whole spices do indeed give off fragrance, but not as much as crushed ones. Ground down by frequent pounding, they spread their fragrant sprinkling even into a more distant place. So too virtues breathe forth a strong fragrance in peace, but a stronger one in tribulation, because virtue is acquired in peace, tested in persecution, and approved in victory. Therefore every powder of the perfumer was cast into the Virgin, because the assembly of virtues consecrated a revered bridal chamber for itself in her. And although the Spirit flows to others in portions, the whole fullness of grace came upon Mary. Nor were the spices whole in her, but crushed into the finest powder, because she is the one who, having overcome the stronger hammers of tribulations, saw her own Son and God’s Son fastened to the cross, wounded by a soldier’s lance, and placed between two thieves as he expired (John XIX).

[Col. 0722B] The passage concerning her Assumption follows: “Who is she who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?” She is that queen whom the daughters of Zion, when they saw her, “declared most blessed, and queens praised her” (Song VI). Today she comes up from the wilderness—that is, from the world—raised to the height of the royal throne. “Overflowing,” he says, “with delights.” Truly overflowing, because “many daughters have gathered riches; she has surpassed them all” (Prov. XXIX). Her delights, moreover, have no number, because, when she receives the Holy Spirit, conceives the Son of God, gives birth to the King of glory, enters the heavens, and, heaped with riches and overflowing with delights, flies away to her everlasting kingdom. “Leaning upon her beloved.” The Father is the King of hosts of the Beloved, in whom he was well pleased (Matt. III, XVII). [Col. 0722C] Upon him that happier Mother leans; reclining upon the golden couch of divine majesty, she rests within the arms of her spouse—or rather, of her Son.

O what dignity, what singular power: to lean upon him whom the angelic powers revere to behold!

These, then, are the things that graciously allude to the present feast beneath shadows and images, and, veiled under a more sacred covering, shine more graciously when they are able to be revealed. Amen.

SERMON XLI. I. ON ST. BARTHOLOMEW THE APOSTLE. (24 AUG.)

Beloved, today’s feast, on which we recall the triumphant deeds of blessed Bartholomew, does not belong to any one city or homeland, but is common to the entire Catholic Church. Nor is it without reason that he is honored and venerated by all: as a noble architect, together with his blessed fellow apostles, he laid the foundation of faith upon which the structure of the nascent Church arose. Moreover, since the apostolic senate claims for itself the throne of judgment and holds the primacy of eminent dignity among all the ranks of the blessed, he occupies the sixth place in their catalogue, distinguished and conspicuous to no small degree. For the evangelist Matthew says: “Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: first Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananaean and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him” (Matt. X). When these had been summoned, as the evangelist relates above, the Lord gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every infirmity (Ibid.). Mark likewise places him sixth (Mark III). From this we can gather how great was the distinction of merits that shone in blessed Bartholomew, who surpasses in apostolic dignity men of such sublimity and glory. For he is placed before Matthew, who holds the principal place in the mystical chariot of the evangelists and, like the Pishon among the other rivers, first gushes forth from the fountain of paradise (Gen. II), flooding the whole breadth of the world with the streams of evangelical teaching. He is likewise placed before blessed Thomas, whose finger became the teacher of the world and who, by a certain principal dignity, may truly be called the indicator, because he pointed out the truth of the Lord’s flesh to those who were ignorant of it. For this blessed apostle provided us certainty through his doubt; and, while examining the Savior’s wounds, he overturned the errors and deceits of heretical depravity. He touches the truth of the flesh and understands the omnipotence of the Godhead. “My Lord,” he says, “and my God” (John XX).

Although nothing proper or distinctive is read about blessed Bartholomew in the authoritative books beyond the common history, nevertheless whatever is found arranged in the style of Scripture concerning those whom he precedes is also, without doubt, a praise accruing to him, even though all the holy apostles are shown to possess the dignity of one privilege, the height of one eminence, and the power of heavenly grace without difference. For when the Lord wished to entrust the keys of the kingdom of heaven to blessed Peter by a certain special grant (Matt. XVIII), this was done so that he might commend the unity of the Church. Otherwise, whatever he gave specially to one, he bestowed upon all in common. For he says to all: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX). And Luke says that, when he had summoned the twelve apostles, he gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases (Luke X). Hence the Lord himself says: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you” (Ibid.). And a little earlier: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Ibid.). He also said to all: “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and he will do greater than these, because I am going to the Father” (John XIV).

Furthermore, the reason why our Savior wished to choose a number of twelve in order to complete the apostolic order is this: since three times four makes twelve, the order of reason required that twelve apostles be chosen to spread the faith of the Holy Trinity through the four quarters of the world. This mystical number is plainly recognized as fitting the holy apostles when the Israelite people are said to have camped at Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees (Exod. XV). For what are signified by the twelve springs except the holy apostles, who never cease to water the dryness of the human heart with the streams of holy preaching? And what by the seventy palm trees except priests of a lower rank, who have been established throughout the world to proclaim Christ’s victories? For a palm tree customarily honors a victorious hand. The very name Elim also seems most aptly to correspond to the apostles. For Elim is translated as “rams.” They are surely the leaders of the flock, shepherds of sheep, teachers of the nations, rulers of peoples. Supported by the authority of the two Testaments, as though fortified with twin horns, they drive back the wolfish fury of heretics and those who resist God, so that they may lead the following flocks of sheep without harm to the pastures of eternal verdure.

And it should be noted that, just as blessed Bartholomew is sixth within the apostolic order, so Elim also occupies the sixth place among the encampments of the Israelite people, so that the name of spiritual “ram” may fit him most aptly; and the place itself, which possesses apostolic springs, does not disagree with him through the mystery of its name and order. Issachar likewise held the sixth place among his brothers when the patriarch Jacob blessed him together with his other brothers. His blessing also clearly corresponds to blessed Bartholomew, who received India—a gentile people—as his portion for preaching. For when the blessings had been distributed among the five sons and the blessing of Issachar had been reached, Jacob said: “Issachar, a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries, saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he placed his shoulder beneath the burden” (Gen. XLIX). To lie down between the boundaries means to rest while awaiting the end of the world, to seek nothing of the things now present among us, but to desire the final things. The strong ass saw the best rest, when simple gentile faith raises itself to the strength of good works for this reason: that it is journeying toward the homeland of eternal life. It also places its shoulder beneath the burden, because, having seen the heavenly rest, it submits itself in action even to difficult commands; and whatever faintheartedness declares intolerable, the hope of reward shows to be light and easy.

The blessing of Issachar, therefore, corresponds to blessed Bartholomew through the gentile people. By joining them to the Christian faith from the worship of demons, he in a certain sense made them his own body in the unity of the Spirit. We too are one with the holy apostles if we imitate not only the merit of their faith but also the example of their conduct, as it is said through Paul: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or gentiles, whether slaves or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink” (1 Cor. XII). Therefore we must always set their examples before us, so that those by whom we are recognized as begotten in faith may not find us separated by a discordant quality of life. Hence, after the crossing of the Jordan, the Lord says to Joshua: “Choose twelve men, one from each tribe, and command them to take from the middle of the Jordan riverbed, where the priests’ feet stood, twelve very hard stones, which you shall place in the place of the camp where you will fix your tents tonight” (Josh. IV). What, then, is signified by the crossing of the Jordan except the sacrament of baptism? Why is it said that they placed twelve very hard stones as a testimony, unless to instruct us that, as soon as we rise from the font of the sacred bath, we should set before ourselves the strongest examples of apostolic virtue, so that these stones may be a testimony to us as we strive for an increase of virtues? Thus Joshua is immediately commanded to cross with the people into Gilgal and there circumcise them with stone knives. “The rock,” as the Apostle says, “was Christ” (1 Cor. X). We are therefore circumcised with stone knives when, through Christ, we cut away from ourselves all the enticements of flesh and spirit. By this circumcision, as it is said there, we also drive away the reproach of the Egyptians, because we crush the insolence of the vices that mock us: “Today,” says the Lord to Joshua, “I have removed the reproach of Egypt from you” (Josh. V). Nor should it be passed over that Gilgal is interpreted as “revelation.” Carnal life blinds the eyes of the mind; spiritual life enlightens them. “Reveal,” he says, “my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII). For when a person is circumcised from his own vices, the sharpness of the mind is raised to contemplate the mysteries of the divine law. In that place, moreover, the Passover is celebrated by the Israelite people, and typologically that Lamb is eaten who takes away the sins of the world (John I).

[Col. 0725C] And note the order of events, and weigh the mystery of human salvation. After we come out of baptism as from the whirlpool of the Jordan, we establish for ourselves the stones of apostolic virtue and steadfastness as a testimony of example. Gazing upon them with the zeal of emulation, we are circumcised from the foreskin of our own depravity; and thus, with the fog of vices removed far away and wiped clean, we celebrate the Passover with the face of spiritual joy unveiled, in the light of virtues. There the people first ate unleavened bread from the produce of the land; and the manna by which they had until then been accustomed to nourish themselves appeared no longer. For after that living bread which descended from heaven (John VI) came forth from the field of the virginal womb; after the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, died and brought forth many fruits (John XII), immediately the manna of the figurative law ceased. The land of promise is the Virgin’s womb. Of this land Isaiah says: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. XLV). Therefore, when one arrives at this bread, the manna of the old law is no longer sought. Next, Jericho, besieged for seven days, is destroyed (Josh. VI), by which this world is signified. For just as that city was not overthrown by missiles or by the attacking wedges of warriors, but only by the sounding of priests’ trumpets, so this world was not overcome by earthly weapons, but as if by the trumpets and blasts of apostolic preaching. The priests sound the trumpets, and the walls of Jericho collapse, because, when the apostles preach, the lovers of this world humbly bend themselves away from the rigidity of their swollen pride.

And we, dearest brothers, must always humble ourselves before apostolic commands, striving to subject the stiff neck of our hearts to their teachings. Certainly they are our judges, and by them we shall be examined in the dread judgment of the supreme Judge. Behold, throughout the whole world the trumpet blasts resound; behold, their teaching still surrounds rebellious Jericho as though with the ark of the covenant. Let us be roused by the thunder of such preaching, and let the sleep of death not overwhelm us while the shadow of carnal life delights us. Let us hear Paul thundering terribly like a powerful trumpet-call: “Rise,” he says, “you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V). [Col. 0726B] But when the stones of Jericho had obeyed the priestly trumpets and that insensible material, with the city utterly destroyed and overturned, had collapsed, how will we sleep like insensible things at the command of apostolic preaching, when through Christ—who is the cornerstone—we ourselves are living stones? Let us hear what the apostle Peter says: “Coming to him,” he says, “a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves also, like living stones, are being built up into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. II). Let proud Jericho, then, the dwelling-place not of Canaanites but of vices, collapse within us; and let the new Jerusalem, built with the stones of virtues, arise, so that, according to the Apostle, “having died to sin, we may live for righteousness,” and, “having died with Christ, may also live with him” (2 Tim. II). He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

SERMON XLII. II. ON ST. BARTHOLOMEW THE APOSTLE. (24 AUG.)

We rejoice and glory in the Lord, beloved, over the holy affection of your devotion, because the more abundantly you drink the cup of the divine word, the more fervently you burn with the thirst of desire for that same word. And rightly so: for the blessedness of the entire apostolic height is joined together in such a way, and is shown to be united by so many bonds or fastenings of grace, that whenever the feast of one of them is celebrated, the undivided eminence of all the apostles is immediately presented to the inner gaze. Among them there is one excellence of judicial power, the same dignity of order, and no different authority of power in binding or loosing. For these are those precious pearls that blessed John says he saw in the Apocalypse, from which he also declares that the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem were constructed: “Each of the gates,” he says, “was made from a single pearl” (Rev. XXI). They are themselves the gates, and they are likewise the pearls, because, while sending forth through signs and wonders certain rays of the divine splendor, they open an entrance to the glory of the Jerusalem above for the nations converted to faith. And whoever is saved through them enters the way to life as through gates.

The stones that, at God’s command to Moses, were set into the breastplate of the high priest also bore their mystical figure (Exod. XXVIII). This breastplate the priest carried upon his chest when he entered the Holy of Holies. It was therefore commanded that twelve stones be placed in it, three at each of the four corners, enclosed in gold, because clearly the holy apostles proclaimed the truth of the Catholic faith concerning the Trinity, which is God, throughout the fourfold world. These stones are also said to be enclosed in gold, because the blessed apostles likewise remain inviolably strengthened in the secret treasury of heavenly wisdom.

It is therefore fitting that when the priest enters the sanctuary, he should carry twelve precious stones upon the breastpiece of the rational, so that whoever approaches the sacred altars may set before himself examples of apostolic uprightness [Col. 0727B], and, insofar as he is able, imitate the life of those whose ministry he exercises; and that, in regard to those whose office he bears, he should fix the gaze of his mind upon them in the zeal of holy emulation. And what wonder is it if we, weak and immature, are commanded to imitate the standard and hold fast the teaching of the blessed apostles, who are the foundations and pillars of the holy Church, when the apostles themselves are established by the authority of their predecessors, namely, the ancient Fathers?

Hence, too, in the construction of the tabernacle, bronze pegs were ordered to be driven all around on the outside so that the silver columns might stand within (Exod. XXXVIII), and the tabernacle might be held fast by ropes tied to them. Thus the silver columns are set within, while the bronze pegs are driven all around outside [Col. 0727C], and the ropes are fastened to them so that the tabernacle might remain fixed. For, so that the holy apostles might stand firm in the light of their preaching, and so that the whole tabernacle—that is, the holy Church—might remain established in the integrity of faith, the Fathers of the Old Testament and the prophets were fixed externally like bronze pegs around it; by the ropes of their words they bound the minds of preachers in firmness and fastened this dwelling of God with the stability of faith.

The pegs, then, are outside because they existed before the time of this holy Church. Yet they bind those who are within it, because, while they foretold the heavenly mysteries that were to come, they made all these things believable once they had been revealed. Thus, just as the pegs outside hold the ropes so that the columns inside may stand immovable, so, in order that the holy [Col. 0727D] apostles might believe the mystery of the Lord’s perfect incarnation, the preaching of those who could both see and proclaim it before it happened prevailed.

Hence the first of the apostles himself, plainly a great column of the true tabernacle, rightly says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (II Pet. I). In these words he indicates, although he has ascended to lofty heights, how it remains bound fast in faith from its lofty summit. Yet the lamp of prophetic speech already shines for those who understand, while it still remains concealed from those who do not understand beneath the obscurities of allegories. Hence the Psalmist likewise says of these same prophetic utterances: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII), because wisdom in the prophets is hidden.

Nor is it without reason that the columns were made of silver, while the pegs were made of bronze, because what the apostles now preach clearly, the prophets spoke obscurely under mystical interpretation. They were rightly represented by the metal bronze, since they were not clear in their preaching; but the holy apostles, because they possessed the light of preaching concerning the mystery of our Redeemer, were represented by silver columns.

It should also be noted that silver both rings and shines, whereas bronze rings but does not shine. The preachers of the New Testament spoke openly of things they were also able to display. But the preachers of the Old Testament, because they uttered obscure statements about the heavenly mystery beneath the shadows of allegories, gave forth a sound, as it were, without light [Col. 0728B]. Nevertheless, bronze is sometimes found to be appropriate to the holy apostles as well. Concerning them, under the figure of Asher, Moses says in Deuteronomy: “Iron and bronze shall be his footwear” (Deut. XXXIII).

Footwear in sacred Scripture signifies the protection of preaching, as it is written: “With your feet shod in the preaching of the gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). Since, therefore, strength is expressed by iron and patient endurance by bronze, iron and bronze are said to be the footwear of the apostles and also of any holy preachers. Through iron they patiently endure adversities; through bronze they preserve the good things set before them with long-suffering.

Concerning these apostles—or apostolic men, that is, holy preachers—after saying to the same Asher, “The rider of heaven is your helper,” Moses immediately added: “His magnificence makes the clouds race.” For who is the rider of heaven except our Savior, who, after destroying the dominion of death by dying, entered heaven accompanied by angels and watched by his disciples? At his command the clouds race, because by his authority holy teachers rain upon the world the shower of saving preaching.

Of these the prophet also says: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. IX.) These clouds dissolve into water when they refresh the soil of our hearts with the streams of their teaching, making it fertile for producing the shoots of godly works.

Hence Bartholomew—which is certainly a Syriac name [Col. 0728D], not a Hebrew one—is interpreted as “son of him who suspends the waters”: namely, the Son of God, who suspends the minds of his preachers so that they may contemplate heavenly things. The more freely they balance themselves on the wings of the virtues in order to understand their Creator, the more fruitfully and abundantly they can pour the rain of heavenly speech into our hearts; and, suspended from that fountain, they drink what they later pour into us by giving it to drink.

Thus Moses speaks mystically and fittingly about the holy Church: “It is not a land, into which you are entering to possess it, like the land of Egypt from which you came out, where, when seed is sown, waters are led in as in a garden”; but it is “a land awaiting rains from heaven, which its God visits continually” (Deut. XI).

For worldly prudence creeps along the ground like a serpent and turns here and there in slippery variety, whereas divine wisdom thunders from the heavenly places. The garden also has a sinister meaning. It appears to signify the wantonness of carnal knowledge. So, too, in the passage where Ahab asked for Naboth’s vineyard: “Give me your vineyard,” he said, “so that I may make it into a garden of herbs” (II Kings XXI). He tries to turn the vineyard into a garden who wishes to exchange the rigor of virtue for the pleasant beauty of carnal allurements. The Psalmist likewise compares the wicked to vegetables, saying: “They will wither quickly like grass, and like the green herb they will soon fall” (Ps. XXXVI).

The land of promise, then—that is, the holy Church—awaits rains from heaven, because it is drenched by the rain of heavenly wisdom. Its clouds, namely, its holy teachers, invisibly draw from the one heavenly fountain what they afterward pour into us by a gracious outpouring. Hence the Prophet says: “They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will exult in your righteousness” (Ps. CXLIV).

Did Paul, that great cloud, not return to that fountain when, caught up above the third heaven, he heard words that were not permitted to be spoken? (I Cor. II.) Did Peter not return to the same fountain when he was suddenly caught up in ecstasy and was commanded to kill and eat not only various kinds of animals but also creeping things? (Acts X.)

At that time this cloud was not yet fully pregnant with the water of wisdom, because it was ignorant of the calling of all the nations. But it approached the fountain and drew from it the purest and clearest understanding concerning the salvation of the nations.

Did this blessed Bartholomew likewise not receive a draught of heavenly grace from the fullness of this fountain when the Holy Spirit came upon him and all his fellow apostles in the diversity of fiery tongues? (Acts II.) But when you hear of fire, perhaps you do not understand water. Hear how the Lord called the same Holy Spirit, who came upon the apostles in fire, water: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Then he immediately added: “Whoever believes in me,” as Scripture says, “rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” “Now,” the Evangelist says, “he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive” (John VII).

Of these believers the Prophet says: “They will be intoxicated by the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV).

Philosophers say that the extent of the thickness of the air does not rise more than ten stadia above the earth; it sometimes takes away the sun’s brightness from us and pours down rain. But these clouds of heaven of which we are now speaking rise beyond the lofty heights of the heavens. They do not take away the light of the true Sun but display it.

Of these, too, Solomon speaks under the name of rivers: “All rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers go out, there they return, so that they may flow again” (Eccl. I).

Among these rivers the blessed Bartholomew is distinguished and conspicuous; by a kind of foreshadowing of future things, he is seen to be marked by the title of this mystical name. For when he is called “son of him who suspends the waters,” he is undoubtedly called a son of God—not by the origin of natural generation, but by the dignity of more abundant grace.

He was truly a temple of God, a sanctuary of heavenly grace, an ark of the covenant, a tabernacle of testimony. For just as that legal ark had been mystically fashioned from incorruptible wood of acacia and shone with the purest gold, gilded within and without (Exod. XXV), so this marvelous man, who had placed his hope in eternity, radiated outwardly with the splendor of an imitable life and shone inwardly with the brightness of divine wisdom.

In that ark there was also a golden urn in which manna was kept, as well as the tablets of the covenant and Aaron’s rod, which had blossomed. What is the golden urn except Christ’s pure, bright, sincere flesh, utterly free from every stain of guilt? It contains manna, namely, angelic bread—that is, the sweetness of eternal divinity.

The two stone tablets signify the inviolable firmness of both Testaments. What does Aaron’s rod signify except the saving standard of our supreme and true High Priest and the sacrament of the life-giving cross? In that it is said to have blossomed, it also prefigured the blessed cross, flourishing with the verdure of immortal remembrance.

These are the mysteries of the universal Church; these are also the saving instruction of every faithful Christian soul [Col. 0730C]. For what the ark presented under a shadowy image, the Church now possesses in effective and manifest truth, as does every mind of the righteous.

The blessed apostles carried these provisions of mystical nourishment; they broke them and set them before the little ones as bread. For after that Gospel saying burst forth—“he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV)—the prophetic lament ceased, in which it is said: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV).

This is that daily bread, my brothers, which Truth taught us eagerly to seek; this is the food of heavenly wisdom, for which we ought continually to hunger.

Let us therefore hear Wisdom, through the mouth of Solomon, inviting us in clear tones to the table of spiritual nourishment: “Wisdom,” he says, “has sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table; she has sent her maidservants to call at the citadel and at the walls of the city: ‘If anyone is little, let him come to me.’ ‘Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you’” (Prov. IX).

For Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father, sacrificed victims when, as an example for our imitation, he allowed the blessed martyrs to be killed. He mixed wine because he gave the Holy Spirit to believers as drink. He set the table because he prepared heavenly glory for human beings. He sent his maidservants—that is, the holy ministers of the Word, who affirm that they are weak and fragile.

What, then, remains except that, abandoning the hunger of the world, we hasten to God’s table? But we cannot find access for entering it except through the holy apostles, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted (John XX).

Hence it is written: “Wisdom preaches outside; she gives her voice in the streets; at the head of the crowds she cries out, at the entrances of the gates” (Prov. I). They themselves are the head of the crowds and the doors of the gates, because they are the princes of the peoples and, by the privilege of their lofty excellence, the doorkeepers of the heavenly Jerusalem.

They are those royal seats of which the Book of Wisdom says: “While all things were held in the midst of silence, and night was halfway through its course, your almighty Word, Lord, came from heaven, from the royal seats” (Wis. XVIII).

At the Lord’s coming, all things were held in the midst of silence, because the prophets had already ceased and the apostles had not yet come to preach the grace of the new faith. The world plainly stood at a kind of midpoint: the oracles of the prophets no longer remained, while the apostolic preaching had not yet flashed forth.

What is meant here by night except the devil, who is the author of darkness? He walks, in a certain sense, when he is not easily able to accomplish what he desires; but he runs when he fulfills the wishes of his malice without any obstacle of opposition. He occupies not the edge but the middle of the course when he sees nothing in his way capable of slowing the force of his advance.

When, therefore, the world was hushed beneath such a destructive silence of night [Col. 0731C], and this opportunity for destroying human beings provoked the devil, he not only occupied the middle of the course but ran, because whatever his wickedness had conceived in his mind he effectively accomplished.

By then the Roman Empire had already seized everything, and those who had at least preserved the law of God in some fashion had necessarily come under the laws of the pagans.

Thus, beneath the silence of the perishing world, the word of the Lord came from the royal seats, because the word of evangelical preaching burst forth from the breasts of the apostles, which are truly the seats of the eternal King. They are royal seats because God inhabits them; they are kings and Fathers of the Church, as it is said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV).

These kings, armed with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI), conquered the prince of the world. Concerning this sword of the apostles it is written: “The stern warrior leaped into the midst of the land of destruction, carrying your unfeigned command as a sharp sword; standing, he filled everything with death, and, standing on earth, he reached even to heaven” (Wis. XVIII).

Therefore, beloved, let us submit to the rule of these kings; let us be instructed by their teaching; through their protection let us strive to escape and be absolved, so that, absolved by the authority granted to the blessed apostles, we may be brought to the author of apostolic dignity himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SEPTEMBER

I. Sermon on Saint Victor the Confessor. VIII. Sermon I on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Sermon II on the same. Homily on the same. XIV. Sermon I on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. Sermon II on the same. XXI. Sermon on Saint Matthew, Apostle and Evangelist. Sermon II on the same. Homily on the same. XXIX. Sermon on Saint Michael the Archangel.

## SERMON XLIII. ON SAINT VICTOR THE CONFESSOR. (1 SEPTEMBER)

[Col. 0732B]

That great eye of Providence afflicted my flesh, which walked carnally, with a gentler scourge, and pierced it with his fear. For I, who had contemptuously and shamelessly disregarded the patience of God, the punishment of hell, and the glory of the kingdom, am now ready and am not disturbed, so that I may keep the commandments of the Lord (Ps. CXVIII).

Within me conscience was burning, wrapped in many crimes, and, cherishing detestable silence beneath an artful veil, it had preferred to die rather than speak, to perish rather than return. Thus, pressed down by the laws of its own hardness, it had determined to cast its eyes toward the ground.

But he who neither sleeps nor slumbers, remembering the soul of the poor man [Col. 0732C], undertook to conquer with scourges what he could not conquer with benefits. That severe fever, which physicians call acute, appeared, spread profusely through all the limbs, and settled upon the wretched body. The heat intensified, and furious fire burst into the very seat of the soul.

The substance of the sinner was now being consumed by avenging flames, and it experienced the beginnings of eternal torments. Understanding, therefore, that “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X), I recalled the multitude of my crimes and confessed them to him whom election had made a father, friendship a faithful companion, and intimacy a partner [Note: [Col. 0731] Here you have a sacramental confession made to a priest.].

Whether he answered in the manner in which I had cried out, I judged should be left to his discernment. My purpose is both to lament my past and to guard against the future. May he grant perseverance, who aroused negligence. His servant trusts in his mercy, not in his own justice, so that he may remember his commandments not only in order to write them but also to do them.

This, then, was the reason for the interruption of the work. This was the occasion of such great silence. Now, therefore, we shall write all the more gladly because we do so with greater security, since it is a grave danger to teach and not to act. Nor should the indulgent flourishes of a polished style be considered here, since true religion consists in having been stripped of verbal displays and in not giving off the scent of verbal glory.

The solemnity of our father Victor is at hand, at whose most sacred body—if the trustworthy tradition of antiquity is true—we sit daily. He was a man who shone gloriously in the power of the Lord through signs and wonders, comparable in the glory of miracles to the apostles and apostolic men.

How numerous and how great these miracles were, and with what sublimity they shone, is sufficiently indicated by the book written at greater length about his life and birth. The saying written in that solemn vision to the angel of the Church of Ephesus can appropriately be applied to him: “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. II).

For he, having received his name from his deed, conquered before he knew how to conquer; and he conquered not just any enemy but that enemy over whom victory is rare and never secure. The tree of life is wisdom, from whose fruit he eats here in hope and there in reality—a fruit beautiful and precious: beautiful because of its appearance, precious because of its usefulness.

This is that lofty tree whose shade covered the mountains and the groves of God’s cedars (Ps. LXXIX). It is the cedar of Lebanon, whose dense branches overshadow the angelic stations. Beneath the shadow of this tree the bride sits, and its fruit is sweet to her throat (Song II). To this tree we say: “In your shadow we shall live among the nations.”

Its shelter protects from the heat of day, for security and concealment from storm and rain (Isa. IV). This is that mustard seed which, sown in the Virgin’s womb by the hands of God the Father, was smaller than all the vegetables of the earth, but rose to such a height that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches (Matt. XIII). It is the tree planted beside streams of water (Ps. I), the tree of life in the midst of paradise (Gen. III).

And consider the great mystery. The Son of God, wholly and entire, was poured forth from the Father’s heart into Mary’s womb, and from his Mother’s womb into the lap of the Church. As great in the Father, so great in the Virgin; as great in the Virgin, so great in the unity of the Church. In the Father, ineffably; in the Mother, wondrously; uniquely in the Church.

With the Father, of the same and equal substance; with the Mother, of the same substance yet divided; with the Church, of the same substance yet hidden. Thus the heavens distilled mercy; thus the Word of God was transfused and poured forth everywhere, wholly, without which nothing is whole.

Blessed is that outpouring, which invites running maidens to the fragrance of sweetness, refreshes by sight, satisfies by taste, and yet is everywhere in the midst. For within that essence of divinity, the person who is familiar to the human race by his goodness stands in the middle between the Father and the Spirit, and is even more familiar by identity, since he alone assumed the poverty of our flesh.

Hence David, immersed in the abyss of his divinity, says: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. LXVI), declaring him to be in the midst of majesty and affirming him especially as ours, because he put on the garment of our mortality.

The Father and the Spirit indeed filled the Virgin, but by majesty, not by assuming flesh. He also entered substantially into the midst of that Virgin’s womb, who encompasses the midpoint of the human balance. For our God and King, before the ages, worked salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. LXXIII)—namely, in that earth of which it is written: “There was no one to work the earth” (Gen. II).

He is also in the midst of the Church, as the Psalmist says: “The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle; God is in the midst of it, and it shall not be moved” (Ps. XLIII).

Let us gather a few things from many, showing how the Savior is in the midst and is always seen in the midst. “Foxes have dens, and birds of the air have nests” (Luke IX); he has no nest, knows no den, and recognizes no corner. He chose the place from which he might be visible to everyone, excluding partiality toward persons.

Thus, when he was born, he was placed in the midst of two animals; when sought, he was found in the midst of the teachers (Luke II); and he stands in the midst of the Jews, who do not know him.

He also says to the disciples: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII). And: “I am in the midst of you as one who serves” (Luke XXII).

He was also crucified in the midst of two thieves; when he rose, he stood in the midst of his disciples (John XIX, XX); and John saw him in the midst of seven golden lampstands (Rev. I).

You, then, who are in the midst, follow the one who is in the midst. Do not delight in the filth of corners or the darkness of dens, but say with the righteous: “In the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. XXI).

This, then, is the tree of life planted in the midst of paradise (Gen. II), an aromatic and utterly pure tree, distilling the honey of balsams. From the substance of this tree grows a sevenfold crown of branches, at whose summit hang those fruits which that heavenly pipe, the Apostle Paul, explained in elegant words.

The first branch is the incarnation of the Son of God. It is subtle and necessary, since it restores heavenly things, renews earthly things, and vivifies both natures with its greenness. “If they do this,” he says, “in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke XXIII.)

He calls himself the green wood, sprung from virginal greenness, although it is true that in our first parent we lost both the purity of birth and the greenness of faith. This greenness was devised by Wisdom herself so wisely that it surpasses the capacity of both heart and mouth.

For the redemption of humanity required that the conquered human being should conquer the conquering devil. But how this could happen was not available to humanity. We had all been condemned in him and, through him, weighed down by the burden of original sin.

Yet God ought not to have done this by himself, since it would rather have seemed an exercise of power had he freed the servant who had departed from him and had subjugated him. What humanity could not do by itself, God ought not to do by himself. Wisdom the Craftsman therefore brought God and man together, so that from the human side he might make satisfaction on behalf of human beings, and from the divine side humble the proud one as though wounded.

This glorious union was hidden from the prince of darkness, and crafty cunning could not anticipate God’s plan. Pure seed was taken from virginal purity, and the Wisdom of God cleansed that fountain of propitiation by a more secret novelty.

The first branch, then, is his incarnation; its fruit is the Spirit of wisdom.

[Col. 0735A]

The second branch is Christ’s baptism. Observe that the Son of the Virgin was not baptized for the cleansing of his limbs, which had come forth from virginal limbs, but so that the privilege of such great purification might be consecrated in the substance of water.

Understand intellectually what you cannot see with your eyes: when someone is baptized, a son of the devil descends into the water and a son of God rises; vessels of wrath are transformed into vessels of mercy (Rom. IX); original sin is overthrown; the thief’s building is destroyed; and a dwelling place for divinity is prepared.

The Holy Spirit is present, descending from the highest citadel of heaven; he sanctifies the element, deifies the baptized person, and glorifies the dignity of the ministry. The angelic powers gather around, rejoicing in the sacramental ordinances, and the cleansing wave is crowned by heavenly creatures.

The sacrament’s transcendence requires the eyes of the heart, not of the flesh, because it is intelligible. The second branch, therefore, is Christ’s baptism; its fruit is the Spirit of understanding.

The third is the passion of the Redeemer. See the plan of God, which had been closed from eternity in the abyss of his judgments. “May your ancient and true counsel, Lord, come to pass,” said one of those admitted to the secret of divine Providence.

Did he not take counsel for you, who had no helper, when he subjected that most holy flesh to insults and exposed it to torments, and “with bowed head gave up his spirit”? (John XIX.) O what undeserved mercy, how freely given! What love thus proved, what unexpected condescension, what astonishing sweetness: that the Son of God should be so afflicted, that the King of glory should be crucified in the pit of misery!

In the end, he had nothing better with which to redeem you than to empty himself, nor did the wisdom of God, in all its wisdom, find a more excellent way. This passion is the plan of your redemption. It is a necessary and marvelous branch, whose fruit is the Spirit of counsel.

The fourth is his descent into hell. In singular strength he descended into hell, like a mighty man overcome with wine, and disturbed the man who had disturbed the earth, who had made the world a desert. He broke the hammer of the whole earth and shook that dreadful palace with a most powerful overthrow.

That one was strong, but a stronger came upon him, to plunder his vessels, take away his weapons, and bind the enemy (Luke XII). This branch is straight and subtle; its fruit is the Spirit of fortitude.

The fifth is Christ’s resurrection. Here he showed us by example what he had promised as a reward, and made us know that when his flesh rose, we too would rise—for that flesh, although of a different glory, had nevertheless been fashioned from the same nature in the Virgin’s womb.

Every offense of doubt was excluded. The apostles saw his hands, held his feet, touched his side (John XX), and beheld with blessed eyes all the marks of death.

This branch, too, is great and sublime; its fruit is the Spirit of knowledge.

The sixth is his ascension into heaven. O singular piety, special sweetness, when he brought the light of our flesh into the lofty courts and placed it in glory at the Father’s right hand [Col. 0736A]!

The hosts of the heavenly legions see and marvel, and continually stand astonished at the generosity of such great grace. The vision of such condescension surpasses every understanding and is accessible only to the Trinity itself.

This branch, too, is splendid and wondrous; its fruit is the Spirit of piety.

The seventh is the day of judgment, when he will come with great power and majesty (Luke XXI) to repay vengeance in wrath and destruction in a flame of fire. Then there will be that fearful fear, when the heavens burn, the elements contend, the earth is set ablaze, consciences are covered over, demons accuse, angels tremble, and the judge is enraged and knows no mercy. Then the inquiry will take place—may it find us ready! (II Thess. I.)

This branch is great and to be feared; its fruit is the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.

Let us therefore love the tree of life and continually eat of its fruit, because this fruit is the Son of Mary, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV. I. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. (8 SEPTEMBER)

From joys we hasten to joys, and glorious subject matter makes an already fervent style more fervent. We come from the Virgin to the Virgin, and from Mary we return to Mary. It is good for us to be here, better to linger, best of all to remain.

Happy are the angelic spirits who enjoy the presence of the blessed Virgin! Meanwhile, we pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness. They have the presence; we have the memory. If the memory is sweet, what must the presence be?

They, indeed, drenched with the more abundant dew of divinity, behold the Begotten One and the Mother in wondrous vision, enriched with the glory of King and Queen. But we, whom the hardship of our mortal prison torments, are nourished by memory and lifted up by the Scriptures; what they see, we read.

Would that the day might come which would restore us to the light, when it would be permitted not to read but to see! Meanwhile, let us console ourselves with the sweetness of memory until we are satisfied with the sweetness of presence.

Today she was born through whom we are all reborn, whose beauty the Almighty desired, and in whom God placed his throne (Ps. XLIV). She is that marvelous throne of which the history of the Kings says in these words:

“King Solomon made a great throne of ivory and covered it with exceedingly bright gold. Six steps led up to it. Its back was rounded. Twelve little lions stood upon the steps, looking toward the throne. Moreover, two hands held the seat on either side. Two lions stood beside the armrests. No such work had been made in any kingdom” (III Kings X).

But now let us bring the words before us into the light and draw water from the rock, with her herself speaking in us, concerning whom we propose to speak to you.

“Solomon the king,” Scripture says, “made a great throne of ivory.” We read that Solomon is called by three names in Scripture, and everywhere is given a royal title: namely, Solomon, Ecclesiastes, and Idida.

The King’s Son—indeed, the King himself—not only the Son of God but also God, is Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” for us in this exile. He will be Ecclesiastes, that is, “the preacher,” at the judgment; Idida, that is, “glorious,” he will be in the kingdom. In exile he is beloved; in judgment, terrifying; in the kingdom, wondrous. In exile, merciful; in judgment, just; in the kingdom, glorious.

Consider whether he is not a king everywhere: in exile, ruler of morals; in judgment, discerner of merits; in the kingdom, distributor of rewards. At the same time, consider that it is not Ecclesiastes or Jedidiah, but Solomon, who is foretold as making this glorious work.

Turn your eyes away from the pleasures of that earthly king who, although he possessed singular wisdom, exalted glory, abundant possessions, and security through peace, nevertheless could not make such a work as had not been made in all the kingdoms.

Had the sacred historian carefully surveyed all the works of the world and its glory, so that with deliberate judgment he could immediately place this work above all others, not merely above one but above every kingdom? These things are empty if we do not return to the innermost recesses of heavenly discipline, if we do not depart from the path of literal interpretation.

Our Solomon, not only wise but also the Wisdom of the Father, not only peaceful but also our peace, who made both one, made the throne—namely, the undefiled Virgin’s womb, in which that majesty sat which shakes the world at a nod.

The Father both approved and knew this sitting of the Son, as he himself says: “You have known my sitting” (Ps. CXXXVIII); and: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Ps. XLIV); and: “This throne is like the sun in your sight” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

“You sit,” Scripture says, “upon the throne, judging equity” (Ps. IX). For what is more just than to consign a vile and renegade servant, and the diligent deceiver of his fellow servant, to everlasting fires, and to restore to his origin the one whom he had deceived?

That other Son of the Virgin says: “And a voice came out from the throne, saying: ‘Give praise to our God, all his saints’” (Rev. V). From this throne the praise of angels and human beings bursts forth, because, while one is restored here and the other repaired, both owe the devotion of thanksgiving.

Do you know what the one seated on the throne says? “Behold,” he says, “I make all things new” (Rev. XXI).

Blessed is the throne upon which the ruling Lord sits; upon which, and through which, not only everyone but everything is renewed!

I spare words because I sense that some of you are flying ahead and anticipating the poverty of my running style. It is therefore rightly said that such a work was assigned not to the eloquent or glorious one but to the peaceful one, because Jesus came to restore both the things in heaven and the things on earth, and, through the Virgin, to reestablish peace and harmony between human beings and angels.

“Of ivory,” he says. Why is the glory of gold, silver, precious stones, and, finally, every more precious material passed over? Only the substance of ivory is capable of such a composition, and in it is fashioned something to be preferred above all works.

Ivory both shines with wondrous whiteness and excels in great strength, and it possesses the quality of a colder nature. What is whiter than that virginity which, by the beauty of its unique appearance, draws the heavenly court to gaze upon it? What is stronger than that strength by which the Lord’s strength plundered the vessels of the stronger one? What is colder than that substance which the power of the Most High overshadowed, and which the fullness of the Spirit who came upon her defended from the heat of sin?

From this ivory, unless I am mistaken, those ivory houses are made of which the Psalmist says: “Myrrh, and spice, and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses” (Ps. XLIV).

It follows: “Great.” What is greater than the Virgin Mary, who encloses the greatness of supreme divinity within the hidden mystery of her womb? Look upon the Seraphim, soar beyond the dignity of that higher nature, and you will see that whatever is greater is less than the Virgin; only the Maker himself surpasses this work.

[Col. 0738B] “And he clothed it with exceedingly bright gold.” Gold, more precious than all metals, signifies the divinity of God, which surpasses the whole world and governs all things. With this the Mother of the Most High was clothed—or rather, super-clothed—and that entire indivisible nature poured itself over the whole Virgin with more abundant grace. But what does he mean by “exceedingly bright”? That many-sided Spirit has left something here for us to investigate; would that I could explain what I perceive.

God is present in all creatures in four ways. First, essentially, in both the good and the evil: nothing excludes the essence of divinity, through which all things received their being. Hence he is said to exist nowhere and everywhere, since he is present to all things and is comprehended by none. The wicked, too, possess God’s presence, [Col. 0738C] but they do not rejoice in it, since even any inanimate things can glory in this privilege.

Second, he is present in the good through operation, for his operative power acts in them so that they may perform the works of God; nor were they created uselessly among creatures, as were the wicked, who chose to wither in order to furnish nourishment for everlasting fires.

Third, he is present in many of the good through illumination, ennobling them by knowledge of future things and making them participants in his secrets.

Fourth, he is present in one creature—namely, the Virgin Mary—through identity, because he is one and the same with her.

Here let every creature be silent and tremble, scarcely daring to behold the immensity of such dignity and condescension. “The Lord is with you” (Luke 1), says the archangel. God dwells in the angels, but not with the angels, because he is not of the same essence as they. [Col. 0738D] God dwells in the Virgin; he dwells with her, since with her he possesses an identity of nature. This, then, is the exceedingly bright gold with which the throne is clothed: God clothed the Virgin in such a manner, and was clothed in the Virgin, that nothing better could be imagined.

Next follows: “Six steps led up to it.” Choose to meditate on holy things, because “perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wisdom 1), and you have climbed the first step. Accustom your tongue to speak well, and you have leapt up to the second. Do what is just and right, and you have deserved to climb the third. Teach sinners the ways of the Lord and console all who mourn, and you have been carried up to the height of the fourth. Abandon the world and the things that are in the world, and you have flown to the summit of the fifth. Let perseverance hold you in your ascent; do not abandon perseverance, and you have bravely reached the sixth step. From there you may leap into heaven and aspire to that glory in which the more glorious Queen reflects back the dignity of the angels.

Next follows: “It was rounded at the back.” By the back of the Virgin understand her Assumption, in which she reached the end of mortal life, the one who restored life to the world. Observe with what profound mystery Scripture compares the Virgin’s passage to roundness. In a circle you can find neither beginning nor end; so too the glory that received her as she passed from this world knows no beginning and no end. Of it we can say nothing other than: “Glorious things are spoken of you” (Psalm 86), the glory of God.
