[Col. 0739B] Next follows: “Twelve young lions stood upon the steps.” The twelve young lions are the twelve apostles, who stand more firmly upon the appointed steps and gaze upon the Queen of heaven with the utmost wonder, saying: “Who is this who rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?” (Song of Songs 6.)

Moreover, the two hands that held the seat on either side signify the active and contemplative life. These surrounded the Virgin Mother with devoted diligence, so that action did not diminish contemplation, nor contemplation abandon action. Recall that “there was no place for her in the inn” (Luke 2), and consider how she nursed her son with her own breasts and endured all the activities of her crying infant; [Col. 0739C] then you will understand how greatly she ministered. Consider that she is the one who, lifted into the sweetness of contemplative dignity, fixed her clearer gaze upon the very substance of God. “His left hand,” she says, “is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2).

“Two lions stood beside the armrests.” The two lions are the archangel Gabriel and John the Evangelist, one appointed guardian of the Virgin’s right side and the other of her left. Gabriel guarded her mind, John her flesh, with wakeful care. They are rightly called lions because of the roar of their high-sounding voices: they announced to the world two words such as have never been spoken and never will be, and beside them all other words ought to appear mute.

“Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1), said the archangel. Do you hear in this word the incarnation of God, the redemption of humanity, and the renewal of the world? “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), said the Evangelist. Do you perceive here the divinity of the Word, the faith of the Church, the silence of heretics, the place of rest, the secret of solitude, the mystery of light, and the dwelling-place of peace? Perhaps for this reason he called James and John Boanerges—that is, “sons of thunder” (Mark 1).

“No work like this was made in all the kingdoms.” Nothing is truer, nothing more exalted, nothing sweeter to wretched mortality and mortal wretchedness. For although many great things were made among the creatures of the world, the works of God’s fingers made nothing so excellent or so magnificent. Virgin and Mother of God, whose beauty the sun and moon admire, [Col. 0740A] come to the aid of those who continually cry out to you: “Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may behold you” (Song of Songs 6). You who are blessed and more than blessed, return—first, through nature. Surely, because you have been so divinized, you have not therefore forgotten our humanity? By no means, Lady. You know in what danger you left us, where your servants lie, and how greatly they sin. For it is not fitting that such great mercy should forget such great misery. Even if glory withdraws you, nature recalls you: you are not so mindful of the justice of God alone that you lack mercy; nor are you so impassible that you are without compassion. [Col. 0740B] You possess our nature, not another nature; and it is just that we should be more abundantly drenched with the dew of such great compassion.

“Return,” secondly, through power. He who is mighty has done great things in you, and all power in heaven and on earth has been given to you. What will be denied you, to whom it was not denied to recall Theophilus from the very jaws of perdition [Note: [Col. 0739] See Surius, volume I, *On the Saints*, under 4 February]? You lifted that unhappy little soul—which, by its own signature, denied everything that had been done in you—from the mire of filth and misery. Nothing is impossible for you, to whom it is possible to raise the despairing into the hope of blessedness. For how could that power oppose your power which received its origin from your flesh? You approach that golden altar of human reconciliation, not merely asking but commanding, Lady, not as a servant. Let nature move you; let power admonish you, for the more powerful you are, the more compassionate you ought to be. It contributes to glory when one refuses to avenge injuries despite having the power to do so.

“Return,” thirdly, through love. I know, Lady, that you are most kind and that you love us with invincible love—us whom your Son and your God loved through you and in you with supreme affection. Who knows how often you cool the Judge’s anger, when the force of justice proceeds from the presence of the divinity?

“Return,” fourthly, through uniqueness. In your hands are the treasures of the Lord’s mercies, and you alone have been chosen to receive such great grace. Far be it that your hand should cease when you seek opportunities to save the wretched and pour out mercy! Your glory is not diminished but increased when penitents are received into forgiveness and the justified into glory. [Col. 0740D] Return, then, O Shulamite—that is, you who were despised, whose soul a sword pierced (Luke 2), you who were called the wife of a craftsman. Why? “That we may behold you.” After God, the highest glory is to see you, cling to you, and remain within the protection of your defense. Hear us. For the Son also honors you, refusing you nothing—he who is God, blessed forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLV. II. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. (8 SEPTEMBER)

The nativity of the most blessed and undefiled Mother of God, dearest brothers, rightly provides humanity with a special and singular joy, since it was the beginning of the salvation of the entire human race. For just as almighty God, in the contemplation of his ineffable providence, foresaw before humanity was made that humanity would perish through the devil’s contrivance, so too he held the plan of human redemption, before the ages, in the depths of his immense compassion. Not only did he establish in the profound reason of his wisdom how and by what order he would redeem humanity, but he also predetermined a definite moment in time when he would redeem it.

Therefore, just as it was impossible for the redemption of the human race to take place unless the Son of God were born of a Virgin, so it was also necessary for the Virgin from whom the Word would become flesh to be born. [Col. 0741B] For the house first had to be built in which the heavenly King, descending, would deign to find lodging. This is the house of which it is said through Solomon: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9). This virginal house was supported by seven pillars because the venerable Mother of the Lord was endowed with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom and understanding; counsel and fortitude; knowledge and piety; and the fear of God (Isaiah 11). Eternal Wisdom, which “reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8), constructed her in such a way that she would become worthy to receive him and bring him forth from the womb of her undefiled flesh. The bridal chamber also first had to be raised, so that it might receive the Bridegroom coming to the wedding of holy [Col. 0741C] Church—the Bridegroom to whom David, rejoicing in the Spirit, sings an epithalamium, saying: “Like a bridegroom the Lord comes forth from his bridal chamber” (Psalm 18).

Rightly, therefore, today the whole world everywhere rejoices with overflowing gladness; rightly, the entire holy Church, at the birth of the Mother of her Bridegroom, alternates praises—as I may say for joy—in a Fescennine song. Let us rejoice, then, dearest ones, on this day, on which, while we venerate the birth of the most blessed Virgin, we also celebrate the beginning of all the festivals of the New Testament. Let us rejoice, I say, on this pre-eminent day, and delight in the Lord with all our hearts: on it, while we commemorate the Mother of our Redeemer, we celebrate the origin of the remaining festivals.

For the one that is older in time than all solemnities ought by no means to be inferior in dignity. If Solomon, with the Israelite people, solemnly celebrated at the dedication of the temple made of stones a sacrifice so abundant and magnificent (1 Kings 8), what kind and how great a joy ought the birth of blessed Mary to bring to the Christian people? Into her womb, truly a most sacred temple, God himself descended, deigning both to assume human nature from her and visibly to dwell among human beings. Although God must also be believed to have descended into Solomon’s temple, in this rational sanctuary—that is, in the womb of the most blessed Virgin—he deigned to remain for us much more wonderfully and much more happily, [Col. 0742A] for “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

Of that ancient temple, it is written: “When the priests had gone out from the sanctuary, the cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand nearby because of the cloud. For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord” (1 Kings 8).

All these things, as the excellent preacher says, “happened to them in figure” (1 Corinthians 10). The glory of the Lord [225] is understood as Christ, whose faith has filled the world. When Moses was pleading with the Lord on behalf of that glory, asking him to spare the sinful people after they had worshiped the calf, the Lord replied: “I will be merciful to it” (Numbers 14). Nevertheless, “as I live, and as my name lives, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory” (ibid.). And the Psalmist says: “His glory shall fill the whole earth” (Psalm 71).

But the fact that the cloud filled the house of God, and the priests could not minister because of the cloud, signifies the proud Jewish high priests and teachers. While they disdain investigating the mysteries of Christ’s Incarnation, they lose the ministry owed to their faith through the cloud of error. The darkness of unbelief so filled their minds that, because of their own deserved failings, they did not recognize the worship of faith.

The Lord therefore descended into that temple in a cloud, to signify the blind darkness of Jewish unbelief; but in this temple, as it is written, “he set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 19), so that he might illuminate those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. To that temple almighty God indeed granted the glory of his coming, but he assumed nothing from it into his own nature. Into the womb of the most blessed Virgin, however, he not only deigned to descend, but also united to himself from it the perfect substance of our mortality. Therefore, the greater the dignity of our temple, the more glorious its solemnity ought to be.

But how can human weakness worthily celebrate the festival of one who merited to bring joy to the angels? How can the transitory word of mortal humanity praise her who brought forth from herself the Word that remains forever? What tongue can be found adequate to praise her who gave birth to him whom all things bless and the elements obey with trembling?

When we wish to exalt the brave deeds of any martyr, when we proclaim the marks of his virtues to the glory of our Redeemer, even if a sluggish mind impedes our ability to think or a stammering tongue fails us in speaking, the subject itself supplies an abundance of words. But when we wish to write the praises of the most blessed Mother of God, because the matters we undertake to discuss are new and unheard-of, we find no words sufficient to express them worthily. The singularity of the subject takes away the power of speech.

What tongue could suffice to explain, or what human reason not be astonished, when it begins to consider that the Creator arises from a creature and the maker becomes part of what has been made? He who is not contained by the immense expanse of the entire world is conceived in a virgin girl’s womb. The little one lies within his mother’s womb, while he who is immense governs, with the eternal Father, the laws of all things. O blessed breasts, which, while pouring thin milk into a child’s tender lips, feed angels and human beings! They express a tiny liquid and refresh the Creator of the world. He who by the command of his power calms the storms of the sea, who supplies rivers with their unfailing rush of waters, who waters the dry earth everywhere with countless springs, awaits a few drops of milk from a virgin breast. Liquid flows from the Virgin’s breasts and is turned into the flesh of the Savior.

[Col. 0743B] Here, dearest brothers, here I ask you to consider how much we are debtors to this most blessed Mother of God, and how great are the thanks we owe her, after God, for our redemption. For that body of Christ which the most blessed Virgin bore, which she cherished in her lap, which she wrapped in swaddling clothes, and which she nourished with maternal care—that body, I say, without any doubt, is what we now receive from the sacred altar, and we drink his blood as the sacrament of our redemption. This is what the Catholic faith holds; this is what the holy Church faithfully teaches.

No human speech is adequate to praise her from whom the mediator of God and humanity is known to have been incarnate. Every praise of the human tongue is unequal to her who brought forth for us, from the womb of her undefiled flesh, the food of souls—namely, the one who testifies concerning himself, saying: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6).

Through food we were cast out from the delight of paradise; through food also we were restored to the joys of paradise. Eve ate food, through which she inflicted upon us the hunger of eternal fasting; Mary gave birth to food, which opened for us the entrance to the heavenly banquet.

Here also, I beseech you, dearest brothers, carefully attend to the line of our redemption, and weigh with the ear of your heart how intently the bowels of divine compassion were directed toward us. God made humanity, so to speak, mortally immortal: that is, if humanity wished to keep the commandment of obedience, it would live forever; but if it disobeyed, it would immediately become subject to the dominion of death.

What more is there to say? Humanity sinned at the devil’s urging (Genesis 3), and the entire tree of the human race was poisoned at its root. The unhappy father fell through the throat, and all his offspring became guilty by nature, as the Apostle says: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2).

Adam therefore became leaven and corrupted the whole multitude of his children; for when he was infected by the poisonous venom of the serpent, the entire mass of the human race was corrupted in him. Hence, now that the splendor of new grace is shining, the excellent preacher says to us: “Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough” (1 Corinthians 5).

But the merciful and compassionate God did not wish his creature, whom he had formed in his image and likeness, to perish completely. From the entire multitude of nations, therefore, he chose one for himself—namely, the Israelite people—to whom he gave the law and commanded sacrifices of various animals to be offered to him.

Yet that law was by no means capable of saving humanity perfectly through itself. As it is said through Paul: “The law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7). Because that people was still uncultivated, proud, and stubborn, it could not bear the yoke of a perfect law or humble the neck of its heart. Concerning this people the Lord says to Moses: “I see that this people is stiff-necked” (Exodus 32).

A law of this kind therefore had to be given to them—one that would neither allow them to depart entirely from divine service nor frighten them by commanding the highest and most difficult things. The sacrifices that were then offered could provide some benefit for cleansing the flesh, but they could not suffice to confer salvation upon souls, as the Apostle says: “For if the blood of bulls or calves, or the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience for service to the living God?” (Hebrews 9.)

When he declares that those sacrifices benefited the cleansing of the flesh, he thereby indicates that they could by no means confer purification upon souls. For an irrational creature could not possess the power to sanctify a rational one. Nor could the priests themselves sanctify the people, since they too needed to offer sacrifices for their own guilt. Subject to sins, they could not release the bonds of sins; nor could a sinner justify sinners.

It was therefore necessary that a priest be found who, while washing away the filth of sins in others, would perceive nothing in himself that needed washing; and who, while cleansing the contagion of another’s guilt, would have no stain of leprosy in himself. But such a man could not be found among the human race, since each person truthfully sang with the Prophet this verse: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins” (Psalm 51); and, as it is said through the Apostle: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3).

I beseech you, dearest brothers, carefully attend to this history of your salvation—or rather, of our salvation—and arrange within your hearts the order of human restoration. Let hearts be vigilant; let eyes not sleep.

Since such a man could not be found within the human race, lest humanity perish in its sin, the Creator of humanity took flesh from the most blessed Virgin and became a man without sin: he was conceived without sin in the Virgin’s womb and lived in the world without sin.

Come, brothers, pay attention—pay attention, I say—and listen vigilantly to the ineffable mystery of our redemption. Behold now the priest, brothers: he himself has no sins, and therefore is worthy and powerful, by offering sacrifice, to cleanse the sins of others. He is the one to whom the Prophet says: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110).

Yet, as it is said through Paul: “It is necessary for a priest to have something to offer” (Hebrews 8). Nevertheless, as was said above, it was impossible for the flesh of brute animals to sanctify human souls, or for an irrational victim to suffice to abolish the sins of rational beings. Hence, in the person of the Son, the Psalmist says to the Father: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering; you did not ask for burnt offerings for sin. Then I said: Behold, I come” (Psalm 40).

A rational victim therefore had to be made, one that would expiate the rational creature. But just as a sinful human being was unworthy to offer sacrifice, so likewise he was unworthy to become the sacrifice himself. What, then, would our priest do? Where would he turn? What plan for our redemption would he find? From where would the mediator of God and humanity take the victim of appeasement by which he would restore peace between God and humanity? For every earthly creature, if rational, had contracted the poison of sin from the root of the first parent; if irrational, it could not justify a rational creature.

[Col. 0745B] What, then, would the mediator of peace do—and he himself is peace? For “he is our peace, who made both one and, breaking down the middle wall of hostility in his flesh, abolished the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, so that he might create the two in himself into one new man, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself; and coming, he preached peace to those who were far away and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2).

What, I ask, would he do? Consider carefully, my brothers, the ineffable depths of compassion; weigh the immense and incomparable weight of divine love. Because the price of our redemption could not be found among created things, our Redeemer offered himself to the Father for us as a victim of pleasing fragrance. Thus he himself became both priest and sacrifice, both redeemer and price.

Hence Paul rightly says: “For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those other priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for he did this once for all when he offered himself” (Hebrews 7). Our Lord Jesus Christ.

You have now heard, dearest ones, a brief account of the marvelous sacrament of our restoration; hear also the very timely counsel of our salvation. Christ gave himself over to death for us; let us also put to death, for love of him, every pleasure of earthly desire within us. By choosing to undergo the gallows of the cross, he paved for us the way by which we might return to our homeland: those who departed delighted by pleasures should return embittered by tears; those who fell by flowing into unlawful things should rise by restraining themselves even from lawful things; and those whom proud arrogance had cast down should be raised up by the abasement of a humble life.

Hence the pastor of the Church cries out, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2); and Paul says: “Be imitators of God and walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance” (Ephesians 5).

Let us therefore now taste, dearest ones, with Christ the bitterness of temporal, momentary death, so that afterward we may deserve to attain the sweetness of his eternal resurrection. For what he did for us he also desires to be done by us, as the Prophet testifies, saying: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 116).

For our redemption he did not give gold, did not weigh out silver, and did not count out money; rather, he gave himself over, poured out the precious blood of his body, and laid down his own life for us. Hence Peter says: “You were redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your fathers, not with perishable things such as gold or silver, but with the precious blood, like that of a spotless and undefiled Lamb, Christ” (1 Peter 1).

It is therefore fitting that whoever hastens to reach fellowship with his Redeemer should offer himself to his Redeemer. Let him imitate on the way the footsteps of the one with whom he longs to rejoice in his homeland. Let him make his guide on the journey the one with whom he desires to share in the arrival. “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we dwell with him, we shall also feast with him” (Romans 8). And again the same Apostle says: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection” (Romans 6).

Let no one, my brothers, deceive himself in vain; let no one cheat himself with the security of a false hope. We cannot rejoice in the world here and reign with Christ there.

Behold the undefiled and glorious Virgin Mary, whose most radiant nativity today illumines the holy Church throughout the world: prefigured in the Law, foretold in the oracles of patriarchs and prophets, and greeted by the angel with the privilege of singular honor. She is set before us as an example—the throne of God, the seat of divinity, the palace of the eternal King, the treasury of treasure, through which we were purchased from the service of the bloodthirsty robber.

This Virgin, so singular and incomparable, would never have reached the height of Christ if she had not followed the humility of Christ; if she had despised the commandments entrusted to her, she would in no way have attained the promised rewards. For when a certain woman, raising her voice from the crowd while he was preaching, said, “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you,” he replied: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11).

Elsewhere, when someone announced to him in the temple that his relatives according to the flesh were outside, saying, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you,” he replied: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hands toward his disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12).

[Col. 0747A] Observe, brothers, observe your dignity, if, by fulfilling the will of God, you break your own will. Behold, blessed and venerable Mary was indeed the mother of Christ according to the flesh; she was not his brother, nor was she his sister. Whoever stands in any one of these relationships to another according to the laws of physical kinship cannot at the same time be anything else: if someone is a mother, he or she cannot be a brother or sister; if someone is a brother or sister, he or she is not a mother.

But through the Spirit we are all these things to Christ at once, if we strive to fulfill the will of Christ, which he always shares with the Father. [Col. 0747B] “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John 3), because God is Spirit. From that aspect in which our Redeemer is God, therefore, we are his relatives in so many ways, as the blessed Virgin, from whom he deigned to be born, could not be according to the flesh.

It was proper and singular to that most blessed Virgin to conceive Christ in the womb; it is common and universal to all the elect to carry him in the devotion of their hearts. Blessed—and exceedingly blessed—is that woman who carried him in her womb for nine months; blessed are we also if we strive constantly to carry him in our minds. It was indeed more marvelous for Christ to be conceived in the womb of flesh; but it is not inferior for him to be carried in the prison of the heart.

Hence John also testifies, saying: “I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3).

[230] It should be noted that he first says that he will dine with the person and afterward, in gracious reciprocity, declares that he will give the meal. For the one whose good works now provide him nourishment will afterward feast with him on the banquet of the eternal meal.

Here also, dearest ones, consider how great our dignity is and how great is our likeness to Mary. Mary conceived Christ in the womb of flesh; we carry him in the inner chambers of the mind. Mary refreshed Christ when she expressed milk from her tender breasts; we too refresh him with the varied delights of good works.

Now, dearest ones, for our edification, let us briefly fix the rays of our mind upon the rule of divine justice and investigate how almighty God permits his elect to be humbled temporarily, when he has decreed to exalt them eternally.

To say nothing now of the others, this same most blessed Virgin, whose nativity we honor today with due devotion, was chosen and preselected before the foundation of the world in the counsel of eternal Wisdom. Although she was born from royal stock, she nevertheless did not flourish in any height of human dignity and did not abound in any riches of temporal possessions. The manger of the woman giving birth indicates that she had no inn where she could give birth (Luke 2).

People customarily make joyful promises concerning the future success of newborn children and announce prosperity to their mothers from such omens. But blessed Mary, when she brought her son to the temple and Simeon received him in his arms, heard: “And a sword will pierce your own soul” (ibid.). It was as though he were saying openly: When your son experiences the suffering of the cross in his body, the sword of compassion will also transfix you in your mind.

Let us also, dearest ones, strive to despise the blandishments of this age, avoid the abundance of earthly things, restrain the incentives of the flesh, and carry the cross of Christ constantly in our minds, so that, while our soul is now pierced by Mary’s sword, it may afterward, with her, be satisfied by the sweetness of eternal happiness. May he deign to grant this, who was begotten from the Father before the ages and deigned to be born from her at the end [Col. 0748B] of the ages. Amen.

## XLVI. HOMILY ON THE NATIVITY OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. (8 SEPTEMBER)

Beginning of the holy Gospel according to Matthew: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac, however, begot Jacob; Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.” And the rest. (Matthew 1.)

You have heard, dearest brothers, the ineffable mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation; you have heard, in the genealogy of the most blessed Mother of God, the mystery of restoration; you have heard that the Creator of the angels deigned to be descended from the stock of mortals; you have heard that the one who governs the laws of all things in heaven, the fountain and origin of all things, deigned to have forefathers on earth.

For the blessed Evangelist says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matthew 1).

But it seems necessary to ask here why the numerous succession of so many fathers is interrupted, so that our Redeemer is said to be the son only of these two—David, namely, and Abraham. Why “son of David” and immediately “son of Abraham,” and not rather “son of Jesse,” or “son of Obed,” or “son” of the others placed between them in succession?

This question is easily resolved if the divine promise made to both is recalled. For Abraham was told by the divine voice: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “He does not say, ‘in seeds,’ as though in many, but ‘in your seed,’ one, which is Christ” [Col. 0748D] (Galatians 3).

Because Abraham believed while still in uncircumcision, he deserved to become the father of the nations; because afterward he received the sign of circumcision, he deserved to become the father of the Jews; and because the one through whom blessing is restored to the formerly cursed earth came forth from his stock, all the tribes of the earth are blessed in his seed.

But David was told: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon my throne” (Psalm 132). Therefore, since he was specially promised to these two, Christ is not undeservedly said to be especially the son of both.

But it must also be investigated why David is placed before Abraham in Christ’s generation, although there is no doubt that Abraham lived many years before him.

[Col. 0749A] But if we carefully consider the manner of the promise made to each of them, we find that David was placed before Abraham not without reason. For what is read as having been promised once to Abraham was confirmed to David by frequent promises. To Abraham it was said only: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed.” But David deserved, in a certain special privilege, to be called the father of Christ, since he received several promises concerning him, as in the psalm: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set upon my throne.” And again: “Once I have sworn by my holy one: If I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever” (Ps. LXXXVIII). And in the Book of Kings, the prophet Nathan speaks to David in the Holy Spirit, saying: “When you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed, which shall go forth from your loins; and he himself shall be my son, and I shall be his father” (II Kings VII). Rightly, therefore, is David preferred to Abraham in the generation of Christ, since a more extensive and therefore wholly immovable promise was granted to him.

The following point, however, may not unreasonably trouble some people: why did the holy evangelist make a point of inserting only blameworthy women into Christ’s genealogy, while passing over the holy women, who were praiseworthy without any question, in silence?

But this was done so that, while our Redeemer is described as born from sinners, he may be believed to have descended from heaven to earth for sinners. For he descended so that he himself might bear our sins; [Col. 0749C] but he ascended so that he might make us participants in his divinity, as the Apostle says: “He died because of our sins, and rose again for our justification” (Rom. IV). This is why Matthew, descending through Solomon—whose mother David sinned by desiring—counts forty generations, while Luke, ascending through Nathan, through whose namesake prophet the Lord expiated David’s sin, describes seventy-seven generations. Through Matthew it is signified that the Son of God descended to us sinners for this reason: that he might become a participant in our mortality. Through Luke it is indicated that after the resurrection he ascended to the Father for this reason: that he might make us sharers in his divinity. As the distinguished preacher says: “But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended above all the heavens, in order to fulfill all things” (Eph. IV).

By the number which Matthew arranges, therefore, the assumption of our mortality is expressed; by that which Luke gives, the abolition of human depravity is expressed. For the number forty arises from four and ten; and the number ten itself is derived from four. One, two, three, and four, with the units always increased, grow into ten.

By the number forty, therefore, this present age is signified, because the year through which we proceed in time revolves through four seasons, and the world in which we live is bounded on every side by four regions. Moses foresaw this; Elijah understood it: for each fasted continuously for forty days (Exod. XXXIV; III Kings XIX). Our Redeemer likewise consecrated this same fast for the same number of days (Matt. IV). This is why the children of Israel, who endured the labor of so long a journey through the desert, entered the promised land after forty years (Deut. I; Josh. XI). Finally, brothers, we are the children of Israel: first we endure the labor of this sorrowful life, and only then do we enter the promised land—that is, the stability of the heavenly kingdom.

This is also why Jonah, who was sent to Nineveh by divine command, threatened that destruction would come upon it after forty days. “Yet forty days,” he said, “and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jon. III). Since this is not read as having happened historically at that time, it is still awaited for spiritual fulfillment. For by Nineveh this world is signified; by the forty days, therefore, the whole condition of the present life is indicated. After forty days, then, Nineveh shall be overthrown, because after the course of this mortal life has ended—that is, when the number of the elect has been completed—this world shall be destroyed.

By the number seventy-seven, which Luke gives, the remission of sins is expressed, as the Lord himself bears witness in the Gospel. When Peter asked, saying, “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” he answered: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII). Fittingly, the remission of sins is signified by the number seventy-seven, which arises from eleven and seven. For if eleven is multiplied seven times, it makes the number seventy-seven. The number ten is recognized as perfect, and by it the Decalogue is signified. But if ten is perfect, it necessarily follows that eleven is imperfect.

What is sin, moreover, except transgression of the law? If, then, the law is understood by ten, transgression of the law is rightly represented by eleven. [Col. 0750D] By the number seven, however, the whole totality of this age is contained, since the entire course of the present life unfolds in seven days. By eleven multiplied seven times, therefore, all our sins are brought to the number seventy-seven, in which there is truly remission of all sins.

Hence this series according to Luke appropriately begins with Christ’s baptism and ends with the person of God the Father (Luke III). In Christ’s baptism, the remission of all our sins comes to us through the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the baptized Lord in the form of a dove (Matt. III). Thus, thus redeemed through Christ and cleansed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we are reconciled to God the Father. The blessed Paul comprehends the meaning intended by both evangelists in a single sentence, saying: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and by sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. IX).

[Col. 0751A] When he says, “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he clearly declares the assumption of our sins, which Matthew shows when, descending, he counts forty generations. But when he continues, “And by sin he condemned sin in the flesh,” he indicates the expiation of all our crimes, which Luke expresses when, ascending, he describes seventy-seven generations.

We could indeed expound many things for your affection, dearest brothers, from the Gospel reading, which is pregnant with many mysteries and sacred meanings. But we pass over it briefly for this reason: so that we may not seem needlessly to repeat what our predecessors have said about it at greater length. There is, however, one point which I desire not so much to explain as to admire: the person of our Redeemer is placed at the end of this lineage as though a hook were fastened to the end of a line. He is added to the genealogy in due order, just as a hook is inserted into an extended line.

When it is said, “Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob,” and the other ancestors are counted twice, it is as though a lily were inserted into a lily, so that one line is extended lengthwise from many. But when it is added, “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (Matt. I), the hook is no longer attached directly, but as if obliquely, so that it may be fixed in the jaws of that ancient Leviathan.

Hence the Lord says to blessed Job: “Can you catch Leviathan with a hook?” (Job XL). For by Leviathan, whose name is said to mean “their addition,” that devouring monster of the human race is signified. When he promised that he would add divinity to man, he took away immortality (Gen. III); and when he multiplies the guilt of transgression, which he first offered to the first man, by his evil persuasion among those who follow him, he heaps punishments upon them without ceasing. In a hook the bait is displayed, while the barb is concealed.

The almighty Father therefore caught him with a hook, because he sent his only-begotten Son, having assumed flesh, to his death. In him flesh could be seen to be passible, while divinity could not be seen to be impassible. When that serpent bit the bait of the body in him through the hands of his persecutors, the barb of divinity pierced him. Previously he had recognized him as God through his miracles, but he fell from recognition into doubt when he saw him subject to suffering.

The hook, therefore, held the throat of the devourer, when the bait of flesh appeared in him, which the devourer desired to consume, while divinity, which would destroy him, lay hidden during the passion. He was captured by the hook of Christ’s incarnation, because, while he desired in him the bait of the body, he was pierced by the barb of divinity. There was humanity in him, to draw the devourer toward itself; there was divinity, to pierce him; there was manifest weakness, to lure him; there was hidden power, to transfix the throat of the ravager. He was therefore captured by the hook, because he perished by the very thing he bit; and the mortals whom he had held by right he lost, because in his death he presumed to desire those over whom he had no right of death.

[Col. 0752A] From this, brothers, from this, I beg you, consider with what praises the blessed and glorious virgin Mary ought to be honored. From her most chaste womb she bore for us him who rescued us from the deepest throat of the ravenous dragon. To proclaim her praises worthily, neither the eloquent fluency of rhetoricians, nor the subtle arguments of dialecticians, nor the keenest intellects of philosophers are sufficient. And what wonder if this ineffable Virgin surpasses the measure of human speech in her praises, since by the dignity of her surpassing merits she also transcends the whole nature of the human race?

The most excellent chorus of patriarchs, the discerning number of prophets, the senate of the apostles, the victorious army of martyrs, no one among the ancients, and no one among those who come after, can be compared with this most blessed Virgin. What holiness, what justice, what devotion, what perfection could be lacking in this singular Virgin, who was full of the whole gift of divine grace? For when she was greeted, she heard from the angel: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke I). What vice, I ask, could claim a place in her mind or body, who deserved to be the sanctuary of the whole fullness of divinity, like the heavens? For “in Christ,” as Paul says, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. III). Nor is it surprising that she surpasses the merits of all mortals, since she herself rises above the height of the angels.

Through this most blessed Virgin, not only is the life once lost restored to human beings, but the blessedness of angelic exaltation is also increased, because, when the human race is brought back to the heights, the number of the angels that had been diminished is restored. That multitude of angels signified this when, at the birth of our Redeemer, they cried out as the shepherds listened: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II). When it is first said that glory is to God in the highest, and then “on earth peace” is added, it is clearly shown that the ineffable birth of the undefiled Virgin generated joy not only for the earth but also, in the same way, for heaven itself.

This too was asserted by the innocence of those blessed children who, when the Lord came to his passion, sang with one voice: “Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name [Col. 0752D] of the Lord” (Matt. XXI).

O wonderfully fruitful virginity, which by a new and unheard-of miracle could be called both mother and virgin! He whom the whole world cannot contain was poured into the limbs of an unmarried girl. She felt the weight of pregnancy without losing the honor of chastity. She marveled at the signs of childbirth, though she had known no contamination from a man. There was hope in the childbirth, though there had been no pleasure in intercourse. She conceived the immeasurable, bore the eternal, and gave birth to him who had been begotten before the ages.

The conception brought her the gift of fruitfulness, while the one born did not take away the glory of her virginity. Before he was born, he created her such that he himself could worthily be born from her, of whom the prophet David had long before foretold: “Mother Zion shall say: ‘A man, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’” (Ps. LXXXVI).

[Col. 0753A] He was created from her whom he created; he was carried in the hands that he had formed; he suckled the breasts that he had filled; he was cherished in the lap of a girl whom the vast breadth of heaven cannot contain; he was wrapped in swaddling clothes who encompasses the immensity of the world in his fist; he obeyed his mother’s direction who governed the rights of all things by his authority; he whimpered in a cradle who was the joy of the angels in heaven; he was covered with humble rags who clothes his elect in the robe of immortality; the girl commanded him whom all the elements obey and serve. For it is written in the Gospel: “He came with his parents to Nazareth, and was subject to them” (Luke II).

[Col. 0753B] Rightly, therefore, blessed Mary is called the parent of the one who gives birth, the dawn of the one who dawns, the fountain of the living fountain, the origin of the Beginning, because from her, through the material of flesh, came forth he who in the essence of his divinity is the head and beginning of all things.

She is, finally, that gate of which Ezekiel testifies, saying: “He turned me toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary, which looked toward the east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate that you see shall be closed, and it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, and it shall remain closed forever’” (Ezek. XLIV). Truly forever closed, because forever undefiled: undefiled before childbirth, undefiled after childbirth, conceiving a man while knowing no man, as it is said through Jeremiah: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth, and a woman shall encompass a man” [Col. 0753C] (Jer. XXXI).

Let us therefore rejoice, dearest ones, and exult in the birth of the most blessed mother of God, Mary, who announced new joy to the world and became the beginning of the salvation of the whole human race. Let us exult, I say, and just as we are accustomed to rejoice at the birth of Christ, so let us likewise rejoice at the birth of Christ’s mother.

Today was born the queen of the world, the window of heaven, the gate of paradise, the tabernacle of God, the star of the sea, the heavenly ladder by which the heavenly King, humbled, descended to the depths, and the human being who lay prostrate was exalted and ascended to the heights. Today the star appeared to the world through which the Sun of justice shone upon the world—the star of which the prophet says: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” [Col. 0753D] (Num. XXIV).

Today was born that most splendid Virgin from whom came forth one more beautiful in form than the sons of men, like a bridegroom coming from his bridal chamber (Ps. XLIV). Today she came forth from her mother’s womb who deserved to become the temple of divinity. Today was fulfilled that prophecy which the distinguished prophet Isaiah, as though made a herald for the arrival of the queen of the world, proclaimed in a loud voice, saying: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root” (Isa. XI).

And rightly is this incomparable Virgin called a rod, since she shot upward toward the heights through the direction of her desire, and through the purity of her good works did not incur the defect of crooked knots. From this rod our Redeemer rose like a flower, and he adorned the fields of the whole world for his martyrs and confessors as though with roses and lilies.

For he himself is the singular flower of the holy Church, as he says of himself in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). This lily is born not on the mountains but in the valleys, because God resists the proud and is found in the hearts of the humble. Christ is called a lily, and the mother of Christ is also called a lily, as is added in the same Song: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (ibid.).

As a lily among thorns, so the most blessed virgin Mary shone among daughters. Born from the thorny lineage of the Jews, she gleamed with the purity of virginal chastity in her body; in her mind she burned with the ardor of the twofold love; everywhere she gave forth the fragrance of good works; and by the constant purpose of her heart she reached toward sublime things.

Some people, however, while striving to know more than they ought, inquire with excessive curiosity who the father or mother of blessed Mary was. But a reader asks something entirely useless when he asks what the evangelist judged unnecessary to relate. If he had recognized that this knowledge contained any benefit, the noble historian would certainly not have passed over a necessary matter in silence.

It should be known that this is the custom of the writers of sacred discourse: just as they always strive to keep silent about what is harmful, so they also disdain to report what it is not useful to know. Sometimes, however, something is omitted in Holy Scripture for the sake of a definite mystery, so that through the silence itself, as though it were crying out, something great may be understood.

Such is the case with Melchizedek, who is introduced in the ancient historical narrative by Moses without father, without mother, and without genealogy (Gen. XIV; Heb. VII), so that Christ, who is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX), might be signified through him—the one of whom the prophet says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII).

In Christ’s genealogy, therefore, those persons rightly had to be arranged through whom the descent would be made to Joseph, rather than turning toward Mary, who belonged to the same tribe as he. For it had been the custom of the ancients scarcely ever to place the names of women in the genealogy of men. If they wished to describe the lineage of women, they sometimes traced it through women.

The evangelist Luke bears witness to our assertion. He presents Zachariah, the father of John, through the male line, but designates Elizabeth through the female sex. “There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zachariah, of the course of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron” (Luke I). Thus, appropriately, the man appears to be descended from men, and the woman from women.

Matthew, therefore, who had proposed to describe the lineage of a man—namely, the one of whom the prophet says, “Behold, a man: his name is Rising” (Zech. VI)—wisely wished to descend through Joseph, while he judged it superfluous to list Mary’s parents.

Whoever, therefore, desires to know Mary’s parentage should understand that she descended from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Judah, and from the royal line of David. [Col. 0755A] Let him also know that she had kinship with the priestly line of Aaron. Hence the angel says to her: “And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman, she too has conceived a son in her old age” (Luke I).

Our Redeemer therefore rightly wished to assume flesh from both a priestly and a royal lineage. Existing as King before the ages, he nevertheless, as the true priest, offered himself to the Father for us as a sacrifice of sweetness. For when King David ate the bread of the Presence, which only priests were permitted to eat (II Kings XXI), he prefigured in one and the same person, Jesus Christ our Lord, the two realities that were to come—namely, kingship and priesthood.

Nor is the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ, rightly called only King and Priest; anyone who is joined to him in perfect love also merits the title of both dignities. Hence it is said through Peter: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (I Pet. II). And in the Apocalypse of John: “You are worthy, Lord God, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood from every tribe, language, people, and nation; and you made us for our God a kingdom and priests, and we shall reign upon the earth” (Rev. V).

We are kings through the grace of Christ, because we bear the standard of the cross upon our foreheads. We are rightly called priests because we are anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit and with the unction of chrism.

Among all the distinctions of this venerable solemnity, dearest brothers, it is also believed, not without a profound mystical reason, that the Mother of the Lord was born almost at the very time of the grape harvest. Now the branches of the vines, laden with an abundance of fruit, droop toward the ground; now the clusters of grapes swell with pregnant ripeness; now the hope of the farmers, which had hung suspended throughout the whole year, rejoices to gather the abundant fruits of its completed labor; now the trees give off the fragrance of their sweet-tasting fruits, so that apples which had irritated human taste by their sourness may soothe it with pleasant ripeness.

But through these things, which we see outwardly, we ought to turn our eyes toward inward realities. The vineyard was the synagogue, which had received the words of the law and the prophets like plantings for producing fruit. Hence it is said through the prophet: “The vineyard of Sabaoth is the house of Israel” [Col. 0755D] (Isa. V). And the Psalmist says: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX).

As the fruit of the vineyards is awaited throughout the whole year but gathered only in autumn, so, precisely so, our Redeemer—whom the law had prefigured, whom the prophets had foretold, whom all the holy ones from Adam through the completed fifth age had awaited with the greatest longing—came in the time of Mary alone. Then, like wine pressed from spiritual grapes, he disclosed the hidden mystical meanings of the letter [reading uncertain: *sustemphia*]. Hence it is said through the Apostle: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV).

[Col. 0756A] O how many thirsted for this vintage with parched throats of mind; how many, with indescribable longing, begged to reach the new wine of evangelical grace! Hence Truth says to the disciples: “Amen, I say to you, many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke XIX).

The bridegroom speaks of this vineyard in the Song of Songs, saying: “I went down to the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to inspect whether the vineyard had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded” (Song VI). The pomegranate is covered by a bitter rind, but a sweet pleasantness is hidden in its seeds. There are some who, while continually suffering Christ’s cross in the body through the bitterness of affliction, are refreshed in mind by the sweetness of inward contemplation through the desire of love. The bridegroom’s vineyard therefore produces pomegranates, because the holy Church never ceases to bring forth such people.

In the same vineyard, in the same Song, the bride speaks to the bridegroom, saying: “Let us rise early and go to the vineyard; let us see whether the vineyard has blossomed, whether the flowers have brought forth fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed” (Song VII).

The vintner of this vineyard was the one who, pressed in the winepress of his passion, opened for us the mystical meanings of divine speech and offered us the wine of evangelical grace. Concerning this wine, the bride again says to the bridegroom in the same Song: “Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy of being drunk by my beloved” (ibid.).

[Col. 0756C] Isaiah had long before seen this bloodstained vintner through the passion of the cross, when, filled with the prophetic spirit, he cried out in the form of a question: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bosra?” And shortly afterward: “Why, then, is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread in the winepress?” (Isa. LXIII).

The garment of Christ is nothing other than the body which he assumed from the Lady and Virgin Mary. Yet his garment is not something other than he himself. For our garment too is called flesh, but nevertheless we ourselves are the flesh with which we are clothed. Concerning this garment it is said through John: “He had written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. XIX).

For propagation through the flesh takes place through the thigh. Therefore, because he came into this world from the Virgin through the propagation of the human race, and through the mystery of his incarnation made known to all nations that he was King and Lord, he had written upon his garment and upon his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” Where he became known to the world, there he inscribed the knowledge of his majesty.

This garment appeared red to the prophet because our Redeemer poured out his own blood for our redemption. To him he himself replied: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. LXIII). For he alone trod the winepress in which he was trodden, because by his own power he conquered the passion which he endured. He who bore the scaffold of the cross even unto death rose again from death itself in glory.

[Col. 0757A] It is rightly said, “And of the nations there was no man with me,” because those for whom he had come to suffer were destined to become participants in his passion. Yet he complains in his resurrection about those whose life was being sought through his death, because they had not yet believed.

He is also called the vine, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I,” he says, “am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer” (John XV).

This most sacred vine extended its branches throughout the whole world, because, spreading everywhere and bearing fruit, it sent out as many shoots as it chose saints within the holy Church through the grace of its calling. Hence, repeating the point, he adds: “I am the vine, and you are the branches; whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit” [Col. 0757B] (ibid.).

The same Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, was signified by that cluster of grapes which the scouts carried from the promised land to the children of Israel on a carrying-pole (Num. XIII). With two bearers placed on either side—one going before and the other following—the cluster was carried in the middle [the printed text reads *botru sin medio*, apparently corrupt]. Our Redeemer is carried like a cluster on a pole because the fathers of the Old Testament proclaimed that he was to come, while the preachers of the New announced that he had already come, so that the minds of the faithful might be kindled to take possession of the land of the heavenly promise.

The carrying-pole borne on the shoulders of the bearers is the divine law imposed upon the necks of human beings. The middle cluster connected its two parts, because our Savior, who made both into one, joined the commandments of the law and the prophets to evangelical teaching.

But the one who went before could not see with his eyes what he carried on his shoulders; the one who followed always looked upon his burden. By the one who went before, therefore, the Jewish people is fittingly signified; by the one who followed, the multitude of the nations. The former carried Christ on its shoulders, as it were, through the pages of Holy Scripture; but because, through the darkness of its unbelief, it did not recognize him present in the flesh, it somehow turned its back toward him instead of its face. The latter, who follows, looks upon him, because the Gentile people clearly recognizes its Redeemer, in whom it faithfully believes.

[Col. 0757D] The promised land may also, not inappropriately, be understood as the very body of the most blessed Mother of God, from which our Redeemer wished to spring humanly like a singular cluster of grapes, in accordance with what is written: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV).

And rightly is the flesh of the most blessed Virgin called the promised land, since it was promised in many ways by the prophets long beforehand as destined to bear the Savior of the world. Truly it poured forth milk and honey, when in undefiled virginity it brought forth God and man. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. VII).

Rightly, therefore, blessed virgin Mary was born at the very time of the vintage, so that the new wine of grace might already be pressed from the various sayings of Holy Scripture, as from different grape skins. Rightly she was born in the autumnal season, so that already, as in autumn, the fruit of the spiritual trees of the whole age might be eaten. She came in the fullness of time, because she was full of grace: “Hail,” said the angel, “full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke I).

O sweet, O marvelous message, O new and unheard-of service of an angelic greeting! He calls her full of grace because he himself was descending into her, through whom grace had been bestowed upon the whole world. “The Lord,” he says, “is with you,” because he is in you who made you such that he himself might also be born from you. “Blessed are you among women.”

Through a woman the curse was infused into the earth; through a woman the blessing of the earth is restored. By the hand of the one through whom the drink of bitter death was offered, the cup of sweet life is also presented. The most abundant stream of the new blessing wiped away the contagion of the ancient curse.

But what did Mary do in response to these things? When the message was brought to her from heaven, did she break into laughter from immoderate joy? Did she raise the neck of her mind in a proud display? Did she not, before answering, weigh the very burden of the angelic greeting on the scales of a discerning mind? For the evangelist says: “When she had heard, she was troubled at his saying, and considered what sort of greeting this might be” (Luke I).

Where are those women who say, “I am a virgin, I am a virgin”—the talkative, quarrelsome, suspicious, excessive women, carefully arranged in dress but disordered in conduct? “I am a virgin; I do not know a man; I am ignorant of marriage.” O virgin, how happy you would be if you preserved in your mind and guarded in your actions what you possess in the flesh! For what benefit is there in preserving bodily integrity alone while corrupting the inner chambers of the mind through the adulteries of evil spirits? What advantage is there in being a virgin while, because of the demands of one’s deeds, failing to reach the reward of virginity? A virgin in flesh but not in spirit does not obtain the reward of virginity. It is one thing bravely to resist the enticements of temptations; it is another thing, when they creep in gently, to yield to them feebly—not in body, perhaps, but in mind.

It is not enough, therefore, for anyone to possess virgin modesty alone in order to obtain the rewards, unless it is enriched by other virtues as well. For it is said to John in the Apocalypse through the angel: “These are they who have not been defiled with women. For they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV).

Our Lamb—the one who takes away the sins of the world—possessed love, because he poured out his own blood for the salvation of human beings. The grace of humility shone forth in him, because he humbled himself even unto death, and death on a cross. He preserved patience, because when he was cursed, he did not curse; when he suffered, he did not threaten. He despised the height of worldly dignity, because, as it is said through John, when they wished to make him king, he sought the hiding place of the mountain (John VI). He loved his enemies, and for them, while hanging on the cross, he also prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

[Col. 0759A] That person follows the Lamb wherever he goes who imitates his footsteps not by virginity alone, but also, insofar as he is able, along every path of the virtues. That person follows the Lamb into the rest of arrival who has striven to imitate him amid the adversity of the journey.

But often the conduct of married people puts the life of virgins to shame, when the former take upon themselves works beyond their state, while the latter, according to their proper order, do not stir up their hearts. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. XXV). Sidon is brought to shame, as it were, by the voice of the sea when, through comparison with the life of worldly people and of those who are tossed about in this world, the life of one who appears fortified and, as it were, stable is condemned.

Often, some who return to the Lord after sins of the flesh display themselves more fervently in good works precisely because they see themselves as more blameworthy on account of their evil deeds. And often some who persevere in bodily integrity, because they consider themselves to have less for which to grieve, think that the innocence of their life is fully sufficient for them, and kindle themselves with no goads of spiritual fervor.

Thus a life burning with love after sin is often more pleasing to God than the innocence of a virgin that grows torpid in security. Hence the voice of the Judge says: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII). And again: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance” (Luke XV).

[Col. 0759C] That virginity, therefore, is perfect which is surrounded by the other virtues and founded upon true humility of mind. It not only preserves itself undefiled in the flesh but also guards purity in speech.

Hence blessed virgin Mary, after hearing the mystery of the angelic message, maintained the customary strictness of modest silence. Although she could not examine within herself what sort of greeting it was, she nevertheless judged it superfluous to inquire about it in words. But by remaining silent she soon merited hearing what she had not presumed to seek by questioning.

The angel said to her: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke I).

What the prophet had long before foretold would happen, the angel announced as present in the same words. For, as was stated earlier, Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII). There, Jesus, which is interpreted as “Savior”; here, Emmanuel, which is interpreted as “God with us.”

What joy, what exultation, my brothers, must have filled Mary’s mind when she compared these prophetic and evangelical words with one another: “For Mary,” says the Evangelist, “kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2). To what extraordinary height she saw herself exalted above the whole human race, when she heard that she was to become the mother of her Creator! Yet she who deserved to rise to such dignity before God, with how great a humbling abasement did she abase herself before herself? For she says: [Col. 0760A] “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). She was called the mother of God by the angel, yet she herself confessed that she was the Lord’s handmaid. And truly, both mother and handmaid: handmaid, indeed, through the common condition of human nature; mother, however, through the ineffable grace of the divine gift. Mother in that she gave birth; handmaid in that she was created.

The Gospel had not yet been written, and already she was observing its commandments. For the Lord commands: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Matthew 23; Sirach 3). What is greater than the Lord’s mother? What is more humble than the Lord’s handmaid? “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

Hence, in the Song of Songs, this bride and mother of the Lord is fittingly praised in the voice of her bridegroom, when it is said: “Who is she that comes up through the wilderness like a little column of smoke, from the aromatics of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song of Songs 3). Blessed Mary rises like a little column of smoke from the aromatics because, through the virtues of her life, she always strove to advance toward the rectitude of inward devotion. She did not dissipate herself and sink away through her thoughts, but bound herself within the secret recesses of her heart like a rigid rod. Because she never ceased to reconsider and review what she had done, she possessed myrrh and frankincense in her deeds, but powder in her thoughts. And she is rightly called a little column of smoke, since she is mystically prefigured also by Aaron’s rod. The latter produced almonds without any moisture from the earthly soil; the former, without any human seed, gave birth to the Son of God.

If the fruit of that rod is examined carefully, it too is found to bear some likeness to Christ. For just as an almond consists of a kernel, a shell, and a husk, so our Redeemer consists of divinity, together with soul and flesh.

Since he was to be born of the Virgin without any human seed, he himself had said long beforehand through the Prophet: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21). For just as a worm is born from wood without another’s seed, so Christ was born from the blessed Virgin without any desire of the flesh.

Hence it is said through another prophet: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud” (Isaiah 19). When the sun is covered by a cloud, it is hidden from human sight. Thus, indeed, thus our Savior clothed himself in flesh taken from the Virgin; in that flesh, with divinity concealed, he could not be seen by human eyes. This cloud is called light because the most blessed Virgin, pregnant without any seed of man, was made fruitful solely by the grace of the Holy Spirit. She obtained the dignity of Mother and did not lose virginal purity. She conceived without defilement and gave birth to her son without pain. Pain did not follow childbirth, because lust did not precede conception.

For it had been said to Eve: “In pain you shall give birth to a son” (Genesis 3). This sentence prevailed among other mothers, but in Mary it lost the force proper to it. It remained fixed among women, but could not prevail over the Virgin. For because she remained a virgin in conceiving, she could not feel pain in giving birth. He who ineffably came forth from her did not violate the enclosure of virginal purity. He entered her while she was a Virgin and, likewise, left her still a Virgin. She is indeed the enclosed garden and sealed fountain (Song of Songs 4), who brought forth the fruit of fertility without diminishing the merit of virginity.

O wondrous, O uniquely noble flesh of the most blessed Virgin, in which womanly nature is transformed and the human condition is not confined! It was indeed born through intercourse, but it did not give birth through the efficacy of intercourse. Brought forth under the common law of birth, it brought forth by the newness of singular grace.

Among the human race, that man is called noble who is distinguished by the illustrious titles of his ancestors. Blessed Mary, however, although descended from a noble line of fathers, derives the lineage of her supreme nobility from him who was begotten from her by a new manner of birth and, through that most illustrious offspring, surpasses the nobility of the entire human stock. Illustrious through the titles of her great-grandfathers, but incomparably more illustrious through the nobility of her offspring. She is the daughter of kings, but the Mother of the King of kings: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86).

Yet whatever is said of you by mortal man does not equal the merits of your exalted dignity. The excellence of grace raises you above the angels, and human frailty cannot aspire to proclaim your praises worthily. We ask you, most merciful one, mother of mercy and of compassion itself: may we who rejoice to celebrate the marks of your praise on earth deserve to receive the help of your intercession in heaven; so that, just as through you the Son of God deigned to descend to us, so through you we may be able to reach his fellowship. He lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVII. I. ON THE EXALTATION OF THE HOLY CROSS (14 SEPTEMBER)

From the rod of Jesse we have come to the rod of the cross, and we conclude the beginning of redemption with its end. From the former, Jesus Christ was wondrously begotten, the Virgin's offspring from a virginal rod; upon the latter, the martyr who is the head of martyrs and the pattern of martyrdom was disgracefully hung.

“That rod is the rod of uprightness, the rod of your kingdom” (Psalm 44), says that familiar instrument of the Holy Spirit, for nothing is more upright than the Virgin, nothing more subtle. Hear also concerning the other: “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your strength” (Psalm 109). Clearly the cross was the rod of strength, upon which the Lord of hosts fought manfully and conquered.

“I took two rods,” says the prophet; “one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord” (Zechariah 11). The rod of beauty is the Virgin’s womb: “Beautiful as the moon” (Song of Songs 6). The rod of cord is the wood of the gallows, separating the kingdom of God from that of the devil, putting a bridle on his wickedness and restraining his widespread wandering with mighty power.

On this wood the innocent side was pierced, and for a time the innocent man, pure in heart, was crucified by human hands. That terrible robber, whose hands were full of blood, was likewise pierced and slain on it. But Christ was treated one way, the robber another. Christ went to the tomb; the robber to eternity. The Apostle says that he “disarmed the powers of the air” (Colossians 2) and [Col. 0762A] fastened them to his cross. On one side our Redeemer was crucified; on the other, that supreme transgressor.

King Hai, as the history relates (Joshua 8 according to the Septuagint), was hanged on a double gallows. Thus the king of death is suspended on a double gallows, because, while he kills Christ, he himself is crucified on that very cross. Here he discovered the great sacrament of the cross, and nothing is more sacred than this sacrament.

Look at the cross standing, and see how, in its straight ascent, it rises from earth to heaven and itself proclaims the truth of the matter by its image. Does it not seem to you to join heaven and earth by its lofty continuity? This is the firmest and indissoluble bond by which rational creatures are joined together, so that from both there may arise that city “whose participation is in unity” (Psalm 129).

Observe also how, in its fourfold arrangement, it embraces the four regions of the world and draws every creature toward itself. Jesus stands in the middle, stretched out in the fourfold extension of his body, and with his hands spread wide he displays to all who come to him from every side the broad bosom of mercy. For “with the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him” (Psalm 129). Truly abundant, not narrow, because a generous stream of blood flowed from Christ’s body through its five parts. A single drop of that most precious blood would have sufficed for the redemption of the world; but abundance was given, so that the power of the one who loves might shine forth in the overflowing of the gift.

But lest it perhaps occur to you that, running throughout all the earth, you might be unable to find your Redeemer, from whatever part of the world you proceed—whether from the east, the west, the south, or the north—he is ready to receive the one who comes and to cherish him with gentle sweetness.

But consider what is expressed to you from the heart of the Most High. Do you come to a crucified man? Come crucified, or destined to be crucified. For “those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5). Thus the wood is Christ’s, but it is necessary for you.

Now ascend to the higher heights of this word and see what it is that proceeds from it. It is written in the history of Kings that the blessed mother said to Elijah: “Behold, I am gathering two pieces of wood” (1 Kings 17). The two pieces of wood are the two arms of the cross. In these two understand human and angelic nature.

The wood that rises straight upward toward the heavens signifies the higher nature, which stood upright and adhered to the will of the Ruler with most dutiful devotion. The wood that lies crosswise signifies human nature, which, being crosswise—or, more truly, overturned—lost the balance of its former state.

Consider with what great sacramental meaning they are joined. In both pieces of wood there is a division, and, through the occasion of wounds, a joining connection is formed. The heavenly spirits received no ordinary wound when God found perversity in his angels (Job 4); nor was the wound insignificant, since it must be repaired, because, if the shared number is not restored, the fallen multitude seems to have become useless.

The lower nature, however, was infected from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head by such poisonous fermentation that it does not know where it comes from or where it is going.

Thus, while the wounds of both spirits gaped widely on both sides, a joining impression was made, which Christ, by joining them, repaired so completely that nothing wounded seemed to remain. For Christ was fastened in both and for both; with the strong nails of his body he binds both together and sets his own body against the joints, lest they be able to spring apart.

The cross therefore joins heaven and earth; Christ on the cross draws all things to himself; the roaring lion is bound there; the angel and the human being are reconciled; and through it everything that the hand of the Most High made is restored.

Rise, then, for a little while above the senses of the flesh and the invading phantoms of bodily pleasures, and contemplate the goodness, sweetness, and condescension of the divine nature. Meditate upon the position of the crucified body. See whether there is anything in it that does not plead for you before the Father.

That divine head, thickly crowned with a multitude of thorns, was pierced even to the tenderness of the brain as the thorn was driven in. “With the thorns of their sins,” says the Lord through the Prophet, “this people surrounded me” (Psalm 21). Why was this done? So that your head might not ache, so that your intention might not be wounded.

His eyes grew dim unto death, and those lights that illuminate the world were extinguished for a time. When they were darkened, did darkness not come over the whole earth, and were those two great lights not removed together with those other lights? All this happened so that your eyes might be turned away from seeing vanity, and, if they saw it, might not cling to it.

Those ears that hear in heaven, “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah 6), heard on earth, “You have a demon” (John 7), and, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23). Why was this? So that your ears might not become deaf to the cry of the poor, might not receive vain speech, and might not take in the venom of detraction through ears open and receptive.

That beautiful face, more beautiful in form than the sons of men, was smeared with spittle, struck with blows, and given over to mockery. For it is written: “They began to spit in his face, strike him, and mock him, saying: ‘Prophesy, who is it that struck you?’” (Matthew 26). Why was this done?
