So that your face might be enlightened, and, once enlightened, might be strengthened, and it might be said of you: “His countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Samuel 1).

That mouth which teaches angels and instructs human beings, which spoke and it was made, was silent for a little while, so that your mouth might speak truth and judgment and confess the Lord its God.

Those hands that founded the heavens were stretched out on the cross and pierced through with the hardest nails, so that your hands might be extended to the needy and you might say: “My soul is always in my hands” (Psalm 118). What we hold in our hands we do not easily forget; so too, one who impresses his soul upon good works does not consign it to oblivion.

That breast in which are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Colossians 2) was pierced by a soldier’s spear, so that your breast might be cleansed of evil thoughts, sanctified once cleansed, and preserved in sanctification.

Those feet whose footstool we ought to adore, because it is holy (Psalm 98), were pierced through with a hard penetration, so that your feet might not hasten toward evil but might run along the way of the Lord’s commandments.

What more? “They pierced his hands and feet, and counted all his bones” (Psalm 21). For you he offered his flesh and soul, so that he might claim your body and spirit for himself. He purchased you entirely with his whole self. What more ought he to have done that he did not do? He released the captive and enlightened the blind, because “the Lord releases those in chains; the Lord enlightens the blind” (Psalm 145). He brought back the one who had gone astray and reconciled the guilty—he who carried you on his shoulders and, for you, satisfied the Father with his own blood.

Consider, then, the counsel of your God, who reigns not only with the Father but also hangs on the cross as your sweetest friend. He cannot be deceived, because he is wisdom; nor does he wish to deceive you, for whose sake he endures an ignominious punishment: “If anyone wishes to come after me,” he says, “let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9).

Hear the counsel, not a command. If it were a command, all who did not carry it out might expect eternal torments. But when he says, “If anyone wishes,” he has placed it within our will whether we hasten to run on equal terms with him. The labor is certainly great, but the reward incomparable.

“After me,” he says. We must go after him because he is the truth, lest we be deceived; through him, because he is the way, lest we go astray; to him, because he is the life, lest we die: “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

Then follows: “Let him deny himself.” That first parent, constrained by the established laws of obedience, went out into the field of evil freedom. He had received the command to place the Creator’s will before his own; but when he used—or rather abused—his own will and wished to make himself happy, he lost himself.

Driven, therefore, from that happy inheritance, he received exile instead of homeland, death instead of life, and disgrace instead of glory. If, then, you wish to return to your inheritance, deny your own will.

In this denial there are only two things against which we must fight and prevail: exaltation in the mind and pleasure in the body. Flee the king and the king’s army—pride and the offspring of pride—and, following him, you will attain the one who said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11).

Let costly clothing, sumptuous foods, and more secret pleasures be far from you, and pierce your flesh with the fear of the Lord. The denial of the will is therefore the recovery of the inheritance.

Then follows: “Let him take up his cross.” If Adam had not fallen and had remained in that dignity of his original state, he would nevertheless have had to be summoned elsewhere and promoted into the angelic order. For he had been made for a twofold purpose: both to repair the diminished number and to fill the place that would have been lacking if an angel had not fallen.

[Col. 0765A] Since, therefore, the inheritance is restored to us through renouncing our own will, so through carrying the cross that gracious fellowship of the blessed spirits is restored. There are two notable things that we ought to possess in carrying this cross: that, when injured, we do not injure others, and that we do good to those who injure us.

It is great, indeed, and beyond human strength, not only to endure harsh words and blows but also not to return them. But this is greater still and savors of something divine: “Do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6).

Our Teacher and Lord, Christ the Son of God, patiently endured those who injured him and did good to those who injured him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). Consider the benefit, when gall was applied to his mouth, nails to his hands, and a spear to his side by his enemies: his mouth, hands, and side acted on behalf of his enemies.

See, then, whether we rightly assign these things to angelic dignity. These two qualities properly belong to the angels. Every day we offend them in many ways, since they are appointed to guard us, and through negligence we add to our offense. Yet although they frequently suffer injuries from us, they endure them and show compassion toward sinners. Their guardianship of us is not lessened—indeed, their solicitude is greater—since it belongs to a good guardian to devote more care to the weak than to the healthy.

It follows: “And let him follow me.” When the inheritance is recalled through self-denial, and the dignity of the angels through taking up the cross, supreme happiness is reserved for us through imitation of Christ. This is the consummation of the virtues, the end of the course, and the beginning of rewards.

But in this imitation two things must be fulfilled: that you submit to the commands of your teachers and that you do not lose perseverance. Thus you will truly be able to follow Christ, who did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him (John 5), and who, for that same will, did not fear to lay down his life (John 12).

With what fruit, what benefit, what reward? “So that where I am,” he says, “there my servant may also be” (ibid.). What great dignity it is to be with God, to be among the blessed spirits, and to be counted forever among that heavenly assembly!

See, then, lest you crucify the Son of God again for yourself and have him as your enemy, constructing again a cross on which he may be crucified—he who, having risen from the dead, dies no more (Romans 6). Take care lest you make a deadly cross on which you cause the Son of God to perish in bitter pains.

Pride above, lust below, the prosperity of iniquity on the right, and despair in adversity on the left represent thorns, nails, and a spear to the Son of the Virgin.

When, exalting yourself and walking with your neck extended, you twist the head of the Most High with a multitude of thorns, and when you are displeased at being surpassed by those above you—or, rather, strive to surpass your superiors—you are like the one who imagined himself to be like the Most High. For it is written: “God resists the proud” (1 Peter 5), namely, those who strive to stand on equal terms with him.

When you direct your eyes so that you do not look toward heaven, and are moved and dragged along by the pleasure-seeking habits of your flesh, you pierce the feet of the Almighty with your harsher nails and inflict punishment from below, excluding the will of the Ruler for the sake of momentary pleasure.

When you prosper in iniquity and heap sin upon sin in a more fetid course of conduct, you drive a nail into the right hand of the one whom you do not cease to persecute for his own gifts.

But when you are overwhelmed by excessive sorrow and set your own wickedness above the goodness of God, you pierce his left hand and increase the anger you have conceived with the anger of your despair.

Finally, when you presume to defend what you have done, you drive the blow of a spear into the Savior’s side; you do nothing more grievous to the Crucified than to defend what he hates. Of this sin it is written: “Do not show mercy to all who work iniquity” (Psalm 58).

You now see how great a distinction lies between the two crosses. Leave, then, the cross that you have fashioned for yourself, and glory in the cross of the Lord your God (Galatians 6), who is blessed forever. Amen.

## XLVIII. II. HOMILY ON THE EXALTATION OF THE HOLY CROSS (14 SEPTEMBER)

We honor the standard of the eternal Emperor, dearest brothers, with the devotion with which we also venerate him who deigned to triumph through it. This honor, as is known from ecclesiastical practice, has been bestowed upon none of the saints. We pray to the saints, and even to the heavenly powers, but we do not adore them. When, however, we confess that we adore or venerate the cross, we are understood to be showing this reverence only to the image of the Lord’s body that was made upon the cross.

In the sign of victory we honor the victor, and by adoring the cross we adore the one who was crucified. Therefore, just as we are accustomed to rejoice with the Lord when he rises or ascends, so we rightly rejoice with his exalted cross.

This scale weighed our price: through it we are rescued from the yoke of Egyptian slavery and freed from the interest of the wicked exactor. This, plainly, paid the full sum of our inexhaustible condemnation and released us from the unpayable debt of the ancient bond.

Hence the outstanding preacher says to the Colossians: “And when you were dead in offenses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all offenses, blotting out the bond of the decree that stood against us and was contrary to us, and he took it away from our midst, nailing it to the cross; and stripping principalities and powers, he led them forth boldly, openly triumphing over them in himself” (Colossians 2).

What tongue, then, is found capable of praising the cross, which opened heaven, absolved the earth from the sentence of the ancient curse, and despoiled Tartarus? It grafted us, wild olive branches, into the olive tree and fashioned vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. It transferred us, who sat in darkness, into children of light; it made us members of the household from enemies; it adopted us, from a servile condition, as children of the kingdom.

Yet although eloquence and mastery of speech may be lacking, we must not cease praising the cross, because what is lacking in ability is supplied by an abundance of good will—especially since the Apostle says: “Not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power” (1 Corinthians 1). God appointed fishermen as preachers of the cross, not orators. Thus the cross is not upheld by polished words; on the contrary, it is emptied by them. Therefore it is not unfitting if the blessed cross is now preached in simple words, by which it is known to have been introduced to the world amid the very beginnings of the new faith.

It should be noted that, just as the cross consists of two signs, ecclesiastical tradition celebrates two solemnities of it through the annual cycle. These two pieces of wood the woman of Sarepta wished to gather so that she might prepare impoverished food for herself and her son; but the flour and oil of this widow were blessed for an increase of abundance (1 Kings 17), so that the fruit of charity and cheerfulness might already then be commended in the sacrament of the Church, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

This widow was the holy Church, of whom it is said: “Blessing I will bless her widow” (Psalm 131). She was permitted to be joined to whomever she wished after her husband’s death, because, when the law had come to an end, the Church immediately deserved to be joined to Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10).

She longed for food that would be cooked with two pieces of wood; and the holy Church hungers for the bread that comes from heaven, which is roasted on the altar of the cross. Whoever desires pleasurable and fleshly foods is handed over to the bites of serpents; whoever looks toward this bread is freed from the deadly harm of the spreading poison.

What do I mean? You are not unaware, brothers, that that carnal Israel, once murmuring against Moses in the desert, said: “There is no bread, there is no water, and our soul now loathes this most insubstantial food” (Numbers 21). Then the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When they repented and sought forgiveness, Moses, at the Lord’s command, made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. Whoever had been bitten and looked upon it was immediately healed.

Indeed, through the serpent’s counsel man fell into death; bronze, however, is found to be more durable than the other metals.

The bronze serpent therefore prefigured the Lord, who drove away the poison of the devil’s suggestion poured into us. It was fittingly a bronze serpent, so that the one made subject to death through the serpent might be signified through the serpent, and the eternal Lord through the bronze. For although he endured the punishment of the cross in his humanity, in his divinity he lives perpetual and impassible.

Moreover, the bronze serpent has the likeness of a serpent, but does not have the serpent’s poison. So our Redeemer appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, but the poison of sin could find no place in him, since he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2).

Nor should it be passed over that the place where these things happened is suitably called Salmona, which is interpreted as “little image,” because there, in the form of this bronze serpent, the image of our Savior was indeed represented.

Hence the Savior himself says: “Just as Moses exalted the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be exalted, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life” (John 3).

The bronze serpent is therefore rightly set up as a sign, and the people, looking upon it, are freed from the bite of the serpents; for all who, moved by the desire for imitation, gaze upon the Savior who was hung on the cross immediately escape every poison and deadly bite of the ancient serpent.

And it should be noted that that serpent is said to have been set up as a sign. For that just Simeon too, when the Lord had been brought to the temple, prophesied and said: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel and for a sign that will be contradicted” (Luke 2).

The Redeemer was set up as a sign of contradiction because he was to suffer on the cross for the salvation of the human race. All the wisdom of the world contradicted that cross, but in the end it was defeated and bowed before the King of glory triumphing through it.

As it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “Concerning this sect, we know that it is contradicted everywhere” (Acts 20). And Paul says: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to the Jews, but folly to the Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1).

But because what is foolish in God is wiser than men, and what is weak in God is stronger than men, our Redeemer, who came not to bring peace but a sword (Matthew 10), girded with the armor of flesh, entered the field of this world to fight. Carrying before him the standard of the cross, he trampled the necks of all who resisted him.

Thus, indeed, our Mighty One in battle eventually turned hostile ranks to his own side, and, pursuing not only death but death’s very prince all the way to the depths, destroyed him.

Moses was already then a minister of this battle when he fought against Amalek (Exodus 17). For that battle he brandished neither swords nor weapons, but carried the rod of God in his hand, which undoubtedly prefigured the wood of the Lord’s cross.

But suppose that he carried the rod so that he might trust in the sacrament of the wood, and suppose that, armed not with weapons but with wood, he had no doubt that he would defeat the enemy’s ranks. Unless, however, he expressed the form of the cross, unless he raised the triumphant standard on high, he would certainly obtain no victory over the fallen enemies.

Moses therefore had the rod in his hand, and added this as well: he stretched out his arms in the form of a cross. Thus it came about that he overcame the ranks of his adversaries by the wood and by this sign filled with the complete mystery of the cross.

The sacred history bears witness to this when it says: “While Moses raised his hands, Israel was victorious; but when he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed” (Exodus 17).

This event, my brothers, conveys to us not only the sacrament of spiritual understanding but also a most salutary example of virtue. For while we take up the cross after the Lord, while we raise our hearts to God together with our hands, the rulers of darkness immediately fall; struck down below, they are crushed with their strength broken.

But if we lower our hands, and, forgetting heavenly things, pursue earthly ones, the enemy immediately follows as victor, and, having lost the victory, we are cut down by the swords of our pursuers.

In every spiritual battle we must carry before us the standard of the cross. If we raise it while acting manfully, we are undoubtedly victorious; otherwise, if we lower it by living sluggishly, we must necessarily collapse weakly at the first attacks of our pursuers.

Hence that distinguished instructor of spiritual warfare, Paul, says: “Raise up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no one who limps may go astray” (Hebrews 12).

Gideon also figuratively carried this standard before himself and his fellow soldiers. He abandoned weapons in opposition to weapons, attacked the armed while unarmed, and, to defeat the multitude of the Midianites, came with a few after dismissing the multitude (Judges 7).

For by divine admonition he was commanded that, when he came to the river, all those whom he saw drinking water on bent knees should be removed from the battle. This was done, and only three hundred men remained—those who, standing, had drawn the water with their hands.

What does it mean that Gideon advances to battle content with three hundred soldiers, except that this number is contained in the letter tau, which expresses the form of the cross? If what projects above in the cross were added to this letter above its transverse line, it would no longer be the form of a cross but the cross itself.

Since, therefore, the letter tau contains the number three hundred and displays the figure of the cross, it is not unfitting that in those three hundred who followed Gideon all those are signified to whom it is said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9).

Those who follow the Lord truly take up the cross in proportion as they are themselves more severely afflicted and are burned with the fire of devout compassion toward their delinquent neighbors or those in need.

Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “Mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in the midst of Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 9).

Or certainly, in those three hundred who are contained in the letter tau, this is expressed: that the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.

In the same mystery of the cross, Abraham too obtained a victorious triumph when he defeated five kings with three hundred and eighteen household servants (Genesis 14). The ark of the flood also contained the mystery of the cross, for Scripture defines its length as three hundred cubits (Genesis 6).

Moreover, just as Noah and his people were saved through water and wood, so the household of Christ is saved through water and wood, being washed in the baptism of salvation and marked with the impression of the life-giving cross.

That ark, so that it might appear to correspond in the sacrament to the measure of Christ’s human body, is said to have had three hundred cubits in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height. For three hundred contains the number fifty six times and the number thirty ten times.

The length of the human body—from the crown, that is, to the feet—is six times its width, which extends from the right side to the left, and ten times its height, which extends from front to back.

Thus the ark, in the number three hundred of its length, holds the form of the cross, and in the shape of all its dimensions bears the figure of the Lord’s body.

And just as seven souls were given to Noah to be saved through wood amid the waters, so the seven Churches, filled with the sevenfold Spirit, are saved in Christ through the wood of the cross and the water of baptism.

Through wood, the prince of pride subjected us to slavery; through wood, the author of humility restored us to the rank of the free. Through wood, the tyrant banished us into perpetual exile; through wood, the gentlest King decreed us heirs in the kingdom.

Through wood, we were brought down to guard swine and to hunger for husks; through wood also we were restored to our father’s embraces, and, having received the robe and ring, were admitted again into fellowship with our former inheritance.

Wood made us registered as owing tribute to the wicked exactor; wood paid all at once the taxes of our inexhaustible debt. Through wood, moreover, we dried up from drinking the eternal fountain; through wood, we are flooded more abundantly with the dew of heavenly grace.

Moses figuratively represented this overflowing of heavenly gifts when, at Kadesh, which is in the desert of Sin, doubting the divine promise, he brought forth abundant waters by striking the rock (Numbers 10).

Because of the people’s sins, he distrusted that he himself could do again what he had already done; and therefore, when the Lord forbade it, he did not bring that same people into the promised land.

His doubt is also attested by Moses’ own words when he says: “Hear, you rebels and unbelievers: shall we be able to draw water for you from this rock?” (ibid.).

It was as if he were saying: We cannot do what exceeds human powers, because you refuse to fulfill what is human; nor can we display a sign through the power of divinity, because you never cease opposing God through the insolence of rebellion.

But that rock, according to the Apostle, was Christ (1 Corinthians 10).

[Column anchors: Col. 0770D, “seven eyes”; 0771A, “fountain of living water”; 0771B, “Jewish people”; 0771C, “concord of the Scriptures”; 0771D, “standard of righteousness”; 0772A, “the thief into heaven”; 0772B, “Today you will be”; 0772C, “waters very bad”; 0772D, “Save me, O God”; 0773A, “sixth day”; 0773B, “276 days”; 0773C, “day of his conception”; 0773D, “temple of divinity”; 0774A, “one, two, and three”; 0774B, “Friday for us”; 0774C, “forty hours”; 0774D, “head extended toward the east”; 0775A, “exalted with the Lord”; 0775B, “divine title”; 0775C, “The body of Jesus”; 0775D, “the Tau”; 0776A, “O blessed cross”; 0776B, “O truly noble tree”; 0776C, “Through you pilgrims”; 0776D, “title of glory”; 0777A, “red gold or carbuncle”; 0777B, “which blesses all things”; 0777C, “Save, I beg you”; 0777D, “joy of today’s solemnity”; 0778A, “From the tax office”; 0778B, “Hebrew style”; 0778C, “Just as Moses”; 0778D, “Let there be light”; 0779A, “Moses therefore describes”; 0779B, “David foresaw”; 0779C, “This is the law of Adam”; 0779D, “hinges of the earth”; 0780A, “supreme architect”; 0780B, “bases covered with silver”; 0780C, “Matthew therefore”; 0780D, “this chariot”; 0781A, “Certain Catholic Fathers.”]

Thus the rod approaches the rock, and water to be drawn by the peoples is brought forth; the cross is applied to Christ, and the hearts of all believers are watered by the grace of the Holy Spirit. For this is the stone of which it is said through Zechariah: “Upon the one stone,” he says, “are seven eyes” (Zech. III). Moses himself, too, is recognized as having known this mystery through the Spirit, if his words are carefully weighed: “Open,” he says, “Lord, your treasury, the fountain of living water, so that, when they are satisfied, their murmuring may cease” (Num. XX). For he would not have described in such magnificent and divine words an element flowing from the cavities of the earth and thereafter to be led away through successive channels. Was it fitting, then, to call commonplace water God’s treasury? Surely he calls that God’s treasury of which the Apostle says: “In the breast of Jesus are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II). He also declares it to be the fountain of living water of which it is said: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV). Otherwise, with what logical consistency would he say, “so that, when they are satisfied, their murmuring may cease,” when later the same people, murmuring, say: “Why did you bring us out of Egypt, so that we might die in the wilderness?” (Num. XXI). “There is no bread; there is no water,” and many other things which their monstrous madness spewed forth in tumult.

But Moses, wearied by disgust with so harsh and rebellious a multitude, anxiously longs for the coming of the Savior. So also he had asked on that earlier occasion when he said: “I beseech you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV). That he struck the rock because he did not believe, and therefore did not reach the promised land with the people, signifies the Jewish people, who, plainly not believing that Christ is the power of God, hung him upon the wood and therefore were not worthy to enter the land of the living.

But how do we attempt to gather into one collection examples of the cross contained in the divine Scriptures, when we see the whole sequence of sacred discourse serving this dreadful sign with a certain intention of the Spirit? For this is the mercy seat, which the two cherubim behold with their faces turned toward one another, because the two Testaments, namely the New and the Old, look together and without distinction toward him who was hung upon the cross. John says: “He himself is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John II). And Peter, speaking of the Fathers, says: “We believe that we are saved through the grace of Christ, just as they were” (Acts XV).

The cross, therefore, is the concord of the Scriptures, a kind of boundary and confluence of the old and the new. The cross allies heavenly and earthly things; the cross reforms human beings and angels together into the unanimity of their ancient concord. Finally, the cross is the death of vices and the source and life of all virtues. For the foolish it is a path, for those who run it is a road, and for those who arrive it is secure rest. The cross is a bounty for recruits, strength for soldiers, and a civic home for veterans. It is the power of those who act bravely, the recovery of those who fall, and the crown of the victorious. The cross inflicts momentary death and compensates with eternal life. The cross strips us of earthly things so that it may enrich us with heavenly ones; it teaches us to hunger so that it may satisfy us; it commands humility so that it may exalt us; it imposes patience so that it may crown us. The cross is the rule for those living in Christ, the clearly expressed standard of righteousness, and the discipline of every good conduct. The cross terrifies the devil, so that he flees; it invites angels to enter among us; it restrains the phantoms of our thoughts and introduces the Holy Spirit into chaste and pure hearts. Finally, the cross revives the weary, strengthens the weak, and comforts the faltering secrets of a despairing mind.

And what more shall I say? Through the cross, the King of glory both rescued us from the chain of the bloodstained plunderer and violently broke into the infernal prison. Moreover, he released all the elect from the bonds of ancient condemnation, and also raised them with himself through the glory of the resurrection. What, I ask, shall I say in praise of the blessed cross, when it itself brought the thief into heaven as truly the firstfruits of its own harvest, and through him opened the gates of paradise, which all the elect would thereafter ascend? Indeed, that cherub who had received the sword of exclusion saw in him the sign of the cross, and did not oppose him as an adversary; nor, certainly, did he see the cross that he bore, but rather the cross whose mystery he believed and in whose power he hoped, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII). And O marvelous freedom of such a condemned man! O immeasurable power of the one who justifies! The judged man judges, and the one condemned for a crime releases crime by his authority. Moreover, he makes the very cross on which he hangs, in a certain sense, the throne of his pronouncing judgment, and between one thief and the other—as already between sheep and goats—he distinguishes the rights of equity. The Lord had said: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

Of those, then, who were to be drawn, the thief was the forerunner; to him he immediately says: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). The one whom he first drew from the snare of perpetual death, he first introduced into life. Through the cross, then—or rather, through him who deigned to be hung upon the cross—all things have been restored, all things blessed, all things drenched with the dew of heavenly grace. Above all, the human mind, which had been barren, bitter, and tasteless, was made fertile and sweet at the Savior’s coming, and was moreover seasoned with the salt of divine wisdom.

The miracle of the prophet Elisha clearly prefigured this. When the men of Jericho complained to him that the water was very bad and the land barren, he said: “Bring me a new vessel, and put salt in it” (4 Kings II). Then he cast that salt into the spring of the waters, and thus healed the waters from all death and barrenness. To conclude the whole matter briefly, this signifies nothing other than that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. For what are the waters except the peoples of the world? What is the new vessel except the Lord’s body, unblackened by any stain of the ancient transgression and unworn by any abuse of the old man? And what is the salt except heavenly wisdom?

The Wisdom of the Father therefore descended into a human body, and thus transformed the minds of all the faithful into fertility and the sweetness of vital understanding. This sweetness remained hidden until the salt was cast into the water—that is, until he hung upon the cross who said: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. LXVIII). From that time human beings learned what they ought to desire and what they ought to avoid—

Meanwhile, my brothers, do not begrudge learning something subtle about the mystery of the Lord’s passion or incarnation, and committing briefly stated matters more firmly to memory. For six days the almighty God created all his works, and on the sixth day formed the human being in his own image and likeness (Gen. I–II). Likewise, in the sixth age of the world the Son of God became the Son of Man, so that he might reform us according to the image of God. Moreover, on the sixth day—the Friday—the Lord himself suffered, so that on that very day the human being might be redeemed by his death on which he had formerly been fashioned by his creative work. On that same day Eve was formed from the man’s rib, on which the Church came forth from Christ’s side through water and blood.

Let us therefore see how, through that same number six, the temple of the Lord’s body was skillfully constructed by divine providence. That temple in Jerusalem had been built over the course of forty-six years; hence the Jews say to the Lord: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you rebuild it in three days?” (John VIII). If this number is multiplied by six, it completes the entire period during which the Lord remained in his mother’s womb. For forty-six times six makes 276 days. That number of days completes nine months and six days, which are reckoned as ten months for women giving birth. This is not because all women reach the sixth day after the ninth month before giving birth, but because the perfection of the Lord’s body is found to have been brought to birth in that number of days, as the ancients have handed down and the Church preserves with firm authority.

For he is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which he also suffered. On that day he was buried in a new tomb, where no dead person had been placed either before or afterward; on that day he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb, where it is certain that no mortal seed had been sown. He is said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0773C] From the day of his conception, therefore, to the day of his Nativity, 276 days are found, containing the number six forty-six times. Thus, by the same number by which that ancient stone temple was built, the temple of the Lord’s body was also perfected through six. Only this distinction is maintained: in the construction of the temple, the number of years is given, whereas in the building of the Lord’s body the calculation is made in days.

If, therefore, the number of years of that ancient temple is multiplied by six, all the days during which the Lord remained in the Virgin’s womb are completed. When the number by which God made his works is joined to the number by which the temple was constructed, the Lord’s body comes into being, so that we may understand that through that temple of divinity constructed in the Virgin’s womb all God’s works were restored. As the Apostle says: “God set forth, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in the heavens and those on earth, in him” (Eph. I).

But this temple of the body, which divine providence willed to be made through the number six, was dismantled in three hours by Jewish impiety and rebuilt after three days, as he himself says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it.” “But,” says the Evangelist, “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John II). Nor is it surprising that what was made through six was destroyed through three and again rebuilt through three, since six itself, just as it grows from three, is likewise reduced to three. For one, two, and three make six; and conversely, half of six is three, a third part is two, and a sixth part is one. This number is called perfect because it consists of its own parts.

The Lord lay in the tomb for one whole day and two nights, because by the one death of his body he freed us from two deaths, namely those of soul and body. And rightly the Lord’s death is signified by day, through which we are led back to the light. But both our deaths are signified by night, which are owed to us because of sin. The whole of this three-day period is most clearly expended in the mystery of human salvation: he suffered on Friday, rested in the tomb on Saturday, and rose on Sunday. This entire present life is Friday for us, because we are commanded to carry the cross after the Lord. From the day of our departure until the judgment it is reckoned as Saturday, because meanwhile holy souls enjoy blessed rest. But at the resurrection of bodies there dawns for us the paschal day, which is enclosed by no end but celebrates unending joy and delight.

Therefore, if we are to reach that Sunday appropriately through Saturday, it is necessary that, now carrying the cross after Jesus, we continually celebrate Friday. Otherwise, if we now live under the law of the flesh and keep something like Sunday in an inverted order, we shall undoubtedly afterward exchange joy not for joy, but for tribulation. For this reason the Lord, just as he lived in the wilderness for forty days and was with his disciples for an equal number of days after the resurrection, also had forty hours from the very moment of his death until the dawn of the resurrection. Thus, just as the number of those days, so likewise the number of hours mentioned expresses the whole period of our life: just as he remained dead for forty hours, so we, having died with him, should live throughout our life in the constant mortification of the flesh.

To overcome the devil, therefore, our emperor displayed to us the sign of the cross; and, so that it would not seem burdensome to us, he himself bore it first. We impress this sign of our salvation not only upon sacred things or things to be consecrated, but also apply it to food and to every kind of household object, so that it may plainly appear that both human beings and everything necessary for human use have been freed by the power of this sign from the jurisdiction of demons.

For even on the gibbet of our Redeemer himself, the blessed cross was balanced by the mastery of a divine rather than human art: the Lord’s head extended toward the east, his feet toward the west, his right hand toward the north, and his left toward the south, so that it might exclude the prince of the world from every direction, occupying the regions of the fourfold world by the square form of the cross. Hence he himself says: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John XII). Thus, indeed, it was fitting that the invader of all should be cast out from all at once. Such a victim ought to be sacrificed for the salvation of the whole world—one that would encompass everything through its mystery and free everything through its power. Then the cross was humbled with the Lord; behold, it will be exalted with the Lord.

I do not want you to be unaware, my brothers, that on the day of the dreadful judgment the blessed cross will be carried by the arms of angels and placed before the faces of all mortals. It will no longer be adorned with gold or gems, but through divine power it will be more radiant than the sun or the stars. It will then be displayed for the glory of those who, loving it, embraced it out of charity, and conversely for the shame of those who refused to carry it after their Redeemer.

Apart, for the moment, from those who pierced him and from the fact that all the tribes of the earth will lament themselves, everyone in whom the figure of this life-giving sign is not then seen will, as an outsider and stranger among the rejected, be driven away at the dictate of justice. But those who are found marked with the impression of this divine title, because they have become imitators of their Redeemer in punishment, will then be made participants with the same Judge in glory.

Then what the Apostle says will take place: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every principality, every authority, and every power, the most savage death will be destroyed” (1 Cor. XV). To hand over the kingdom to the Father is surely nothing other than to lead believers in him into the secrets of divine contemplation.

Then that vision of the prophet Zechariah will be fulfilled (Zech. III): he saw Jesus, the high priest, in filthy clothing; and when the devil who stood to accuse him had been defeated and rebuked, Jesus was immediately stripped of his filthy garment and clothed in an attire of honor and glory. The body of Jesus is called the Church, which now, in the hardship of this pilgrimage, is disfigured as though by the filthy garment of tribulations and afflictions. But then, when the devil has been condemned and rejected, the holy Church, stripped of its filth, will be clothed in the robe of blessed immortality and transferred from the grief of pilgrimage to the homeland of eternal rest. As is plainly sung in the psalm of dedication: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. XXIX).

For the rejected also, what is said through Ezekiel will then be fulfilled: “Pass through the city and strike; let your eye not spare, nor show pity; kill old man and young man, virgin, little children, and women, unto destruction; but do not kill anyone upon whom you see the Tau” (Ezek. IX). When the judgment has been completed, all the just will be carried together with the cross into the kingdom, whose punishment they once endured either in peace or in persecution. In that glory of immortality they will always behold the most radiant cross, and they will rejoice ineffably to have before their eyes the sign of the victory by which they were redeemed and conquered the world. Therefore they continually alternate their praises of their Savior, and, always giving him thanks, they exult in that pleasantness of perpetual joy.

Thus we too may cry out in praise of the blessed cross:

O blessed cross, which by a new balancing of weight were worthy to suspend him whom heaven and earth cannot sustain! O cross purer than glass, more gleaming than gold, adorned with the limbs of the Savior as though with budding gems and pearls! O cross brighter than the moon and more splendid than the sun, which, by the greatness of the divine light, surpass the radiance of the stars and all the constellations of heaven! You alone among all the trees of the forests were chosen for the service of human redemption. You were worthy to sustain that weight by whose power heaven revolves, earth hangs suspended, and the entire fabric of the world is poised, never to fall. The underworld fears you, the angels venerate you, and every creature marvels at you.

O truly noble tree, which rises from earthly soil, yet spreads your blessed branches above the stars of heaven! Once your fruit was subject to Gehenna; now you produce cedars for paradise, and from you living stones come forth, from which the buildings of the heavenly Jerusalem are constructed.

O blessed cross, when the sun hid its rays lest it see the sacrilege, when the earth trembled, when the trembling elements quivered with fear, you were worthy to stand as the inseparable companion of the dying Lord, to place your devoted arms beneath him, and moreover to cherish him in your gentle embrace! O blessed cross, made conspicuous by the crucifixion of the world’s Redeemer and dyed purple by the precious blood of the immaculate Lamb! You are the salvation of the lost world, the light of those placed in darkness, the medicine of the sick, the strength of those recovering, the harbor of those in danger, and the refuge of those escaping from the jaws of death.

Through you pilgrims pass into members of the household, and those who were formerly strangers you make fellow citizens with the apostles. In you, while bloody death kills, it is itself killed; the author of death is extinguished, and the life lost by humanity is restored. You armed Jael’s hand with the nail by which she pierced Sisera through both temples of his head (Judg. IV), and in the figure of the Church slew the devil. You filled David’s sling with the stone by which he, marked on the forehead, struck the Philistine Goliath (1 Kings XVII), where that profane man did not bear your sign.

O blessed cross, you are venerated, proclaimed, and honored by the faith of the patriarchs, the prophecies of the prophets, the senate of the apostles as judge, the victorious army of the martyrs, and the hosts of all the saints! The fragrance of your scent conquers all spices; your nectar surpasses every kind of perfume and all honey. O blessed cross, title of glory, emblem of victory, sign of eternal redemption! Earthly things owe you their life; heavenly things owe you their return to the fullness of their integrity. Through you the exiled human being returns to the homeland, and the number of angels, which had been diminished, is restored. You make slaves of demons become sons of God by adoption, and those who once worshiped idols now become coheirs with Christ. O glorious cross, O wondrous cross, before which the empires of the whole world fall, to which all scepters of authority obey, and to which the laws of every kingdom are subjected!

But why do we strive to apply outward ornaments of red gold or carbuncle, when whatever is placed upon you is found to be inferior and more colorless? For no human tongue, O blessed cross, can equal your praises. On you eternal life hung; the salvation of the world drenched you with its own blood; and the Word of the highest Father adorned you by the singular companionship of his body.

Your praise, therefore, belongs only to the one who hung upon you. For by a new art you deceived the devil and made the victor a captive. You had been accustomed to offer him chosen foods and to send to his insatiable throat whatever things became subject to you. But at last, O blessed cross, you offered the gaping one, eager to devour, such food as would pierce his jaws with the hook of hidden power and empty the belly of his ancient malice of those who had already been swallowed.

O glorious cross, which blesses all things! O blessed cross, which is blessed by all! For your blessing sanctifies everything, and the blessing of all things flows abundantly back into you. O venerable cross, O adored cross, marvelous form, dreadful figure! For just as wax flows from the presence of fire, so sinners perish from your presence; nor do phantoms find a place to linger or retreat when they have seen your sign.

O lovable and beloved cross, truly sweet and beautiful! Every sound heart endowed with understanding burns with the flame of your love; once the faithful mind has been kindled by the fire of your charity, it is immediately inflamed beyond expression with love of heavenly things. Who, then, O blessed cross, can praise you with worthy praises? On you the author of life, dying, destroyed death; swallowing it up, he raised us, the dead, to the glory of his immortality.

Save, I beg you; bless and protect, O blessed figure, the suppliant people who today rejoice together in your praises. May he who willed you to become the instrument of our redemption deign through you also to transfer us into a share of his glory; and may those whom through you he rescued from the bond of slavery, through you likewise, according to his holy promise, establish as heirs in the kingdom. To him be salvation and thanksgiving, praise, honor, power, and dominion, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIX. I. ON SAINT MATTHEW THE APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST (21 SEPTEMBER)

The joy of today’s solemnity, most beloved, cuts away every thorn of despair from our minds, strengthens wavering hearts to hope in divine mercy, and invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence, as the Apostle also exhorts (Heb. IV). For who, hearing that a tax collector was not only chosen by the Lord for the fellowship of discipleship but also ascended to the eminence of the apostolic senate, would not immediately be encouraged to obtain forgiveness for his sins?

From the tax office, where money was amassed, he is transferred to the chair of the Church; and he who previously exercised the office of collecting tribute is appointed to dispense the treasures of faith and heavenly riches (Luke V; Mark II). Formerly he labored to fill his purse with the sordid profit of gain; now, throughout the breadth of the world, he spreads the mystery of heavenly eloquence.

Among all the saints who have brought titles of victory over the conquered world into heavenly glory, blessed Matthew seems to me distinguished and conspicuous, and to hold among them a certain primacy of dignity. Indeed, if I may speak boldly, after Christ there is no one to whom the holy universal Church owes more. The reason the world lives is that the evangelical light has flashed upon us.

It is established that Matthew was the first of all to write the Gospel in the Hebrew style, and thus provided the faithful who were of the circumcision with a kind of mirror of the new faith. Since he was the first to rush forward to set down the holy Gospel, he opened the way of writing to the other evangelists who followed, and, like a leader, carried the standard before them, urging them by his example to write. We therefore owe the Gospel to him who clearly introduced the beginning of the evangelical narrative; and since we know him to have been first among the others, we do not doubt that he holds among them a certain primacy of privilege.

Each of the three evangelists knew blessed Matthew’s book before beginning his own, and, as he was divinely inspired, added no superfluous cooperation of his own labor. It was their task faithfully to prepare minds for writing; it was God’s task to direct the pen wherever he willed.

Just as Moses is not improperly placed before the prophets and before all who wrote anything in the Old Testament, so blessed Matthew rightly surpasses all who are found to have written in the New. For just as Moses set forth the origin of the world at its birth, so Matthew, as the author of a certain spiritual world, describes the rising newness of the Church.

Hence, with the Holy Spirit guiding the pen, it was arranged that each should place at the beginning of his books not a different beginning but one and the same, saying: “The book of the generation” (Matt. I). But that generation produced children of wrath, whereas this generation gives birth to children of grace. The former generation received the paradise of earth, flourishing with the beauty of fertile trees and plants; but this generation merited the heavenly paradise, overflowing with incomparable abundance of delights.

From that first paradise, however, the first human being expelled his posterity from his kind through the tree; the second human being introduced us through the cross into heavenly pastures. When Moses relates that God said, “Let there be light” (Gen. I), he shows that light was created; when Matthew declares that Christ was born of the Virgin, he indicates that the Creator of light had arisen.

Moses therefore arranges the old Adam, the earthly Adam, the old world, and the Old Testament. Matthew, however, introduces new things in place of old, spiritual things in place of earthly or carnal things, and eternal things in place of temporal things. In place of Adam he describes Christ; in place of the old law, the Gospel; and in place of the world—or earth—flourishing with plants and trees, he describes the holy Church, producing various foods of spiritual fruits.

“For the first human being,” as the Apostle says, “was from the earth, earthly; the second human being from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. XV); “as was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly.” The first Adam became a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. But not first what is spiritual, but what is natural, and afterward what is spiritual.

Moses therefore describes how all visible things were originally created; Matthew, however, teaches that not only earthly but also heavenly things have been newly restored through the grace of the Mediator of God and human beings, as the same Apostle says: “To make known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in the heavens and those on earth, in him” (Eph. I).

David foresaw this renewal of the world when he was once established before the Lord in prayer. For when divine clemency promised him through the prophet Nathan that one would be born from his seed who would build a temple for the Lord’s holy name, and, plainly announcing Christ, added: “I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me” (2 Kings VII), he then described what the Church, which is Christ’s body, would be like, saying: “And your house will be faithful, and your kingdom will endure forever before my face, and your throne will be established forever.”

Giving thanks, he says among the other words of his prayer: “But even this seemed a small thing in your sight, Lord God,” because you loved me, “unless you also spoke of the house of your servant for a long time to come.” Then he added: “For this is the law of Adam, Lord God.”

As though he were plainly saying: Just as at the beginning of this earthly world you appointed Adam the father of the posterity that would follow, and decreed that the offspring of the whole human race should spring from this root, so now, when you intend to renew the world, you make me like a new Adam, since you promise that Christ will be born from my seed, he who is the author and head of the Church.

“This is the law of Adam,” he says, because just as Adam was to possess this visible world in his children, so I too become the father of a spiritual people in Christ, destined to reign forever with him who is in heaven. For just as Eve, the mother of the living, was formed from Adam’s rib (Gen. II), so from the side of Christ, who is to be born from me, the Church that will live forever will come forth.

Of this new and spiritual world it is written: “The hinges of the earth belong to the Lord, and he set the world upon them” (1 Kings II). The world is placed upon the hinges of the earth when the holy Church is solidly founded, as upon bases, on evangelical teachings. Of it another passage also says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI). What are called hinges there are called mountains here.

The arrangement of the evangelists also corresponds to the location of the world and the course of time, because there are four parts of the world and just as many divisions of the seasons. It is therefore not surprising if the spiritual world is compared with this visible one, since each is recognized to possess certain similarities with the other.

And it should be noted that the supreme architect, namely almighty God, while constructing the structure of this spiritual world—that is, of the holy universal Church—upon the four evangelists as upon four columns, arranged two more substantial and excellent ones at the outer sides, so that the entire weight of the rising structure might rest upon them; he placed the two smaller ones in the middle. Thus he distinguished the beauty of the heavenly construction by alternating variety, so that plurality might pertain to its foundation, diversity to its ornament, and the divine work might remain unshaken in strength while also being conspicuous in variety.

These, finally, are the four columns of which it is said to Moses, when the tabernacle was being erected as a type of the Church: “You shall make four columns and their bases covered with silver” (Exod. XXVII). For what else is understood by silver than the brightness of divine speech? As it is written: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth” (Ps. XI). The four columns of the tabernacle are therefore supported by bases covered with silver, because the preachers of the Church, adorned with divine speech so that they may offer themselves as an example in all things, bear the words of the four evangelists both in mouth and in deeds.

Matthew therefore holds the first place, John the last. They are established at the height of the apostolic dignity and, from what they wrote, were instructed not merely by hearing but rather directly by sight and touch. One of them says: “What we have heard, what we have seen, what we have looked upon with our eyes, what our hands have touched concerning the Word of life” (1 John I).

Mark and Luke, however, who occupy the middle of the evangelical catalog, are not indeed Apostles; nevertheless, one was taught through the reports of the chief Apostle Peter, the other through those of Paul. All the holy evangelists, however, have one authority and one faith; they differ in nothing as they weave the line of the most sincere truth, and throughout every part of their account they jointly erect an impregnable bulwark fortified against all the arrows of every kind of heresy.

For this is that chariot in which the King of glory, exulting like a giant and powerful in battle (Ps. XIV, XXIII), confronts the prince of this world, who held the human race captive; armed with the cuirass of flesh, he overcame him by his assault and distributed his vessels (Luke XI).

The prophet Ezekiel declared that he had seen this chariot, the true cherub, when he said: “The likeness of their faces was the face of a human being; and the face of a lion was on the right side of the four, while the face of an ox was on the left side of the four; and the face of an eagle was above the four” (Ezek. I).

Certain Catholic Fathers distinguished them in this order: because Matthew began with human generation, he is rightly represented by the human being; because Mark began with a cry in the wilderness, he is fittingly represented by the lion; because Luke began with sacrifice, he is suitably represented by the calf; and because John began with the divinity of the Word, he is worthily designated by the eagle.

When John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God; and the Word was God” (John I), directing his attention toward that substance of divinity, he fixed his eyes upon the sun, as an eagle does.

But those who distinguish the holy evangelists by the figures of animals under this varied arrangement seem to consider more the beginning of each Gospel than the continuous text of the ensuing narrative. For those who have investigated all the statements of the evangelical account more carefully and minutely decided that not the figure of a man but that of a lion should be assigned to blessed Matthew. For the lion, as Scripture says, is the strongest of beasts and fears no encounter (Prov. XXX). And because it is called the king of animals, the form of a lion is not unfittingly assigned to blessed Matthew, who is seen to have set forth Christ’s royal person. Hence also in the Apocalypse the Lord is commemorated as a lion together with the very royal tribe. There it is said: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V).

Matthew, therefore, is especially occupied with declaring the Lord’s royal lineage; and just as he took the beginning of his narrative from this, so he carries the entire sequence of his writing through to the end with the same intention. For weaving the line of the genealogy, he reaches David; then, passing through Solomon, he runs through the remaining kings in enumerating the succession of the family. A little later he reports that magi come from the East and diligently seek the King born among the Jews; and also that King Herod was troubled (Matt. II) when he heard that a king had been born among the Jewish people besides himself. Then he adds the parable in which the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. XXII). For as the moment of his saving Passion drew near, he also reports him saying: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, all nations will be gathered before him; and then the King will say to those who will be at his right hand: Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV). Finally, after by his death he had destroyed the dominion of death and the triumph of the blessed Resurrection had shone forth, he reports him saying to his disciples: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII).

In view of these and similar statements made clear in the evangelical account, it is evident that blessed Matthew was more tenaciously occupied than the others with pursuing the Lord’s royal lineage. For each of the holy evangelists preserves his own particular order and perseveres in guarding the intention with which he began. John, indeed, is more earnestly occupied with declaring the essence of divinity in Christ. Matthew, as has been said, displays his royal dignity. Mark, however, seems to be his follower or abridger, proceeding after him in his footsteps and agreeing with him in almost everything, whether in his words or in their meaning, so that he does not depart from the path of his predecessor. Luke likewise maintains his own manner and order while describing the Lord’s priestly lineage and person; and throughout the entire sequence of his writing he persists in this intention, so that he does not fail to concern himself with the temple or with priests until the end of the Gospel. For what else does he heap together at the very beginning of his narrative than the names of various priests? “There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was from the daughters of Aaron” (Luke I). Later he places this same Zechariah in the temple before the altar, and also brings the virgin Mary into the priest’s house. On the fortieth day after the Nativity he carries the child to the temple with offerings (Luke I), and enthrones him there at twelve years of age, listening to and questioning the teachers. Then he reports that the Lord’s parents went up every year to Jerusalem, to the temple, on the day of the Passover solemnity.

Finally, he concluded his Gospel in this way, saying: “They returned to Jerusalem worshiping, and they were continually in the temple, praising God and blessing the Lord” (Luke XXIV). The Mediator of God and human beings, being one and the same according to his human nature, willed to be both king and priest, so that through the power of royal majesty he might govern us, and through the priestly office he might make expiation. These two persons, represented under the figure of Christ, have been specially commended by the Fathers; to him above all and with singular privilege God gave the throne of David his father, so that his kingdom would have no end, and so that he would be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX).

Matthew and Luke therefore divide the dignity of these two ministries between themselves in such a way that one indicates Christ’s kingship and the other his priesthood. For the Holy Spirit distributes the rights of his own power through his instruments in such a way that, while one speaks through two, a certain diversity of wording is expressed by those who share the same meaning. Hence Matthew, who had undertaken to describe the Lord’s royal person, enumerates kings in the course of the genealogy; but Luke, ascending to David himself, does not pursue the royal line. Rather, proceeding through those who had not been kings, he reaches Nathan, the son of David, who himself was not a king. Thus it was divinely arranged that he should not have a companion following him who would continue the sequence of his writing, because the priest alone entered the Holy of Holies; and for this reason he is without a companion, because he is specially occupied with the Lord’s priesthood. Matthew, however, as has been said, had Mark as his abridger and attendant, because he described Christ’s royal dignity by enumerating kings. For it belongs to royal sublimity not to proceed without the service of companions.

Let us too follow this leader, my beloved brothers—not by abridging the Gospel, but by observing the evangelical commandments. Let us follow him as our guide on the road to life. Let us imitate his saving example: as soon as he heard the command of the Savior who was calling him (Matt. IX), he did not hesitate, did not seek delays for arranging his affairs, and did not ask for the counsel of friends to be shared. Immediately he despised his riches, renounced his attachments, broke the bonds of carnal affections, and, thus freed, hastened joyfully and eagerly after Christ’s footsteps, as though carried into harbor after a shipwreck. He sang that divine song: “You have broken my bonds, O Lord; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV). Or that which the bride sings in the Song of Songs: “When I had passed on a little beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I will not let him go” (Song III), who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON L. II. ON SAINT MATTHEW, APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST (21 SEPTEMBER)

O how sweet, how joyful, how delightful is this festival, my brothers, in which the sinner is kindled to the love of God; faith is increased; the mind that had lost confidence is raised up; and the grace of certain hope is [Col. 0783B] heaped upon it. For what we are instructed in words elsewhere, here we experience through living deeds. We read: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III). Between penance, that is, and the kingdom of heaven there is nothing in between. This glorious festival not only gives those who repent hope of the kingdom of heaven, but also tells the penitent that the dominion of heavenly excellence has been bestowed upon him.

For who does not know that blessed Matthew had been a tax collector and therefore a sinner? (Matt. IX, X; Mark I.) He himself certainly does not conceal this, since in the very catalogue of the apostles he calls himself a publican: “Thomas,” he says, “and Matthew the publican” (Luke V); but the other evangelists call him Levi instead, lest they make a companion—or rather, a prominent figure—of the evangelical work into something notorious. He himself therefore asserts that he was a publican so that he might both maintain in himself the rule of humility and kindle our minds to hope for forgiveness of sins. It is as though he were saying together with his fellow apostle: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first; but for this reason I obtained mercy, so that in me first Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. I).

He therefore now urges us by his words to hope for forgiveness, just as formerly he stirred those who were present by his example. For he himself says: “When Jesus was reclining at table in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and reclined at table with Jesus and his disciples” (Matt. IX); and Matthew was there. Unless he had been present with the Lord’s disciples, sinners would not have dared to approach the Lord so familiarly. Unless they had seen a sinner cleaving to the Savior’s companionship, those whom the enormity of their crimes accused and whose conscience tormented them would in no way have presumed to draw near.

But when they saw this man diligently engaged in the Lord’s service, and even sharing his table, having become his companion at the feast, he encouraged sinners by his example toward the fountain of mercy. How much more confidently are we now urged by him to hope for mercy, since we see him raised to so great a height of eminence? He was at once called into the apostolic order and granted angelic dignity. For who does not know that “evangelist” is derived from the angelic designation? He is therefore not only an apostle but also an evangelist. And, if I may put it so, he is not undeservedly called the evangelist of evangelists, since he is found to be their leader, predecessor, and first of all. Hence, of that heavenly chariot which either John testifies that he saw in the Apocalypse (Rev. IV) or Ezekiel beheld in prophetic vision (Ezek. X), he may fittingly be called not merely a part but also the charioteer. When he was the first to burst forth into writing the Gospel, he stretched out a kind of line by going before, and marked out the path of straightness along which the others might run. Thus, as is said of Elijah (2 Kings II), he may rightly be called both the chariot and the charioteer of that mystical sacrament.

God Almighty conferred upon no mortal the privilege that these two heights of preeminent dignity should meet together in one person—namely, that anyone should be both an apostle and an evangelist—except Matthew and John. One of these was a publican, the other a virgin. This too was done through the profound dispensation of the divine plan: so that the one might present himself as a guide to sinners toward the fountain of mercy, and the other might be an example to those who preserve chastity and innocence; so that neither the magnitude of their crime might obstruct those who have fallen, nor the open door of heavenly grace fail to invite the pure and those unburdened by any crimes.

Moreover, just as Phison is read to be the first among the rivers of paradise (Gen. II), so Matthew is found to be first among the holy evangelists. This comparison is entirely appropriate to him, for Phison is interpreted as “change of mouth.” He changed his mouth, transferring it from secular words to the preaching of the Gospel; and what had previously been his in a carnal sense he made belong to God. The Lord says through the prophet: “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you will be as my mouth” (Jer. XV).

Thus what is written came to pass in blessed Matthew: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V). For just as that statement of Scripture is true which says: “It makes no difference to divine power whether one conquers through many or through few” (1 Sam. XXV), so also it makes no difference to divine mercy whether it forgives the smallest sins or grave ones. In this outstanding man, therefore, divine grace abounded wonderfully. To him it granted the double privilege not only of preaching the Gospel with the apostles but also of writing it with the evangelists; and, to make him shine forth still more excellently, he holds the first place in the order of those who are illustrious and wondrous among the other saints.

Indeed, these are those holy animals that are reported to be full of eyes on every side (Ezek. I). In them, as truly cherubim, the fullness of knowledge overflows; their appearance represents the likeness of burning coals of fire and of shining lamps. They always move before their face, driven forward by the impulse of the spirit.

These, moreover, are those chariots that the prophet Zechariah designates when he says: “I turned and saw, and behold, four chariots were coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze” (Zech. VI). Of them it is said shortly afterward: “These are the four winds of heaven, which go forth to stand before the Lord of all the earth” (ibid.). It should be noted that the chariot of the four evangelists is not spoken of as one single chariot, but each one of them is called a chariot, because one is in four and four are in one: what is written by each through the intention of the same faith is found in all, and what is said by all is found in each.

The two mountains of bronze, from between which they are said to have come forth, are the two Testaments, which are durable and resonant like bronze. For they find no end until the end of the age, and throughout all the expanses of the world they give forth their sound. “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). They are also described as winds, because it is written of them: “Wherever there was the movement of the spirit, there they went” (Ezek. I). They also go forth to stand before the Lord of all the earth, because what the holy preachers accomplish through the fruitfulness of the faithful they do not attribute to themselves but to the author, from whom all their gains proceed. Concerning them it is said to blessed Job: “Will you send forth lightning bolts, and will they go, and returning say to you, ‘Here we are’?” (Job XXXVIII).

These are the four jars that Elijah ordered to be filled and poured three times over the burnt offering when he was about to sacrifice (1 Kings XVII). This is the fourfold course of the rivers that proceeds from Christ as from the fountain of paradise and floods the dry fields of the four-cornered world (Gen. II). Concerning it that wise man says: “Moses commanded the law in the precepts of justice, and the inheritance of the house of Jacob, and the promises to Israel” (Sir. XXXIV).

But, so that we may not dwell longer on these words, this law, which is called the inheritance of promise, is the holy Gospel. It was indeed promised to the ancient Fathers, but, when Christ came, it was conferred upon us by hereditary right. Immediately afterward it says: “He appointed David his servant to raise up from him a king, most powerful, to sit forever upon a throne of honor. He fills wisdom like Phison, and like the Tigris in the days of new growth. He fills understanding like the Euphrates, which multiplies like the Jordan in harvest time. He sends discipline like light, and, standing forth like Gehon in the day of vintage” (ibid.).

These things, then, my brothers, have been spoken so clearly and openly about Christ and the holy evangelists that they need no exposition to make them understood. But when you hear the name of vintage in these holy and mystical words, you who, because of the season, have earthly vintages before your hands, ought to turn from what surrounds you toward interior realities and consider the spiritual vintage with holy prudence. For at the end of the statement he says: “He sends discipline like light, and, standing forth like Gehon in the day of vintage.”

Who is he who sends discipline like light, except the one who, after Moses’ face had been veiled, pours the radiance of his Gospel upon the world possessed by darkness? He stands forth like Gehon, of which it is also said through the prophet: “The Lord our God is a glorious river leaping forth upon thirsty land.” And what is the vineyard to which he stands forth like Gehon and which he never ceases to irrigate with the moisture of his preaching, except that vineyard of which it is said through the prophet: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V)? The Lord transferred this vineyard from Egypt, that is, from the old law, and brought it into the land of the Gospel, which flows with milk and honey.

The first fruits of this vineyard were brought forth by that cluster of grapes which two men placed upon a pole and carried to the Israelite people (Num. XIII). The two men are the two peoples, the Jewish and the Gentile. They placed the cluster upon a pole because they hung the Savior upon the cross. But the one who went before did not look upon what he carried; the one who followed looked upon it. The Jewish people, which preceded us in time, carried the Lord in the prophets and the law, but because it always turned away the face of obedience, it could not see him. The Gentile people, however, which follows, continually contemplates him as though he had been placed before its eyes.

Gideon represented this cluster when he answered the complaining Ephraimites under the guise of an excuse: “Is not the cluster of Ephraim better than the vintages of Abiezer?” (Judg. VIII.) Since Ephraim, which signifies fruitfulness, expresses the Church, what is meant by the cluster of Ephraim except Christ? And what by the vintages of Abiezer except the multitude of Jewish priests? Or, alternatively, by the cluster may be understood the small number of the faithful of the primitive Church, and by the vintage the multitude of the Synagogue.

The cluster of Ephraim is therefore better than the vintages of Abiezer, because the primitive Church was more blessed: it is made fruitful until the end of the age by the offspring of those being reborn, whereas the Synagogue, gradually destined each day to decline, grows smaller. Hence Isaiah also says: “Sing, O barren one, who do not bear; break forth into singing and shout for joy, you who did not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband. Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your pegs, for you will spread out to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations” (Isa. LIV).

This woman whose offspring inherits the nations is certainly the Church, which daily calls the human race to the unity of faith through her children. This is she of whom it is said in the Psalms, “for her who receives the inheritance” (Ps. III, title). This is the vineyard that is commanded to sing praise, as is also found elsewhere in the same prophet: “On that day the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him; I, the Lord, am its keeper” (Isa. XXVII).

Of this vineyard blessed Matthew also recalls that the Lord said: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, leased it to farmers, and went abroad” (Matt. XXI). This vineyard came forth from that cluster which was trodden underfoot by Jews and Gentiles in the winepress of the cross. From it flowed a wave of precious blood, which healthfully intoxicated human minds, previously ill-sobered, with the wine of spiritual grace. When the apostles were speaking in various languages through the Holy Spirit concerning this wine, it was said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts II).

Woe to the one who entirely abstains from this new wine and, stuffed with the drunkenness of earthly wine with which he burns, belches it forth. “Woe to you,” says the prophet, “who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. V). Truly wretched is the one who keeps himself abstinent from the wine of the Holy Spirit while carrying lungs inflamed with the harshness of carnal wine, whose belly swells with food and drink, and who does not store the wine of spiritual grace in the cellar of his heart.

But you, my beloved, devote yourselves to gathering the produce of the earth in such a way that you also remember to collect the wine of the divine gift in the little barrels of your minds. Whoever separates himself from his neighbor through the kindling of discord is not a bird of the Lord but an earthly animal that does not know the wine of heavenly grace. Hence it is that when Abraham was sacrificing, he divided the other animals through the middle and placed the two parts opposite one another, but he did not divide the birds (Gen. XV). By this he indicated that whoever is divided from his brother by the rift of hatred walks upon the earth as an earthly creature and does not fly to heaven like a bird; but whoever raises himself on the wings of virtues knows no division.

If you fear that you will be harmed by your enemies unless you take up weapons against them, make peace with God, and without doubt, once you have been quieted, you will not be harmed by your neighbor. For he says: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. CXVII).

The patriarch Jacob also taught this when he buried the foreign gods. For, as Scripture testifies (Gen. XXXV), his household gave him all the foreign gods they had, and the earrings that were in their ears. But he buried them beneath the terebinth that is behind the city of Shechem. Immediately afterward it says: “When they had departed, the terror of the Lord fell upon all the cities round about, and they did not dare pursue those who were withdrawing” (ibid.). It is therefore clear that as soon as he had reconciled the Lord to himself, he did not fear the weapons of earthly fury.
