Once peace had been made between the house of Jacob and God, every controversy on all sides was subdued and brought to an end by divine terror.

Therefore, my beloved, drive out from the vessels of your minds every plague of discord and hatred; tame the assaults of raging beasts, that is, the allurements of the flesh; extinguish the flames of earthly desire; and prepare your thirsty souls to draw from the streams of the Holy Spirit. Let each of you say: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. LVI).

May almighty God, who through blessed Matthew invites sinners to himself, mercifully open to you the door of his mercy and pour out upon your minds the gifts of heavenly grace. He lives and reigns, one true God in perfect Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LI. ON SAINT MATTHEW, APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST (21 SEPTEMBER)

At that time: “As Jesus was passing through his own city, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew” (Matt. IX). And so forth.

The evangelical reading that has now sounded in your ears, my beloved, like a distinguished saying among the other oracles of the Lord’s instruction, revives the sorrowing conscience of sinners, raises up minds that are wasting away, drives out the chill of faintheartedness and distrust, and lifts the downcast heart on high to conceive hope of forgiveness. For who could despair because of the enormity of his crimes, however monstrous, when he hears that blessed Matthew, intent upon the profits of commercial gain, was not only suddenly called but also appointed to obtain the two chief ministries of the heavenly court? That is, to ascend the summit of the apostolic senate and to receive, among the holy evangelists, the dignity of being first.

This double office was bestowed upon no one else at all except Matthew and John. And because John is said to mean “grace of God,” Matthew is also interpreted as “given,” since each obtained the gifts of a double dignity; plainly, therefore, the grace of a heavenly gift rested upon both. But, so that the statement might be fulfilled which says, “Where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V), Matthew, because he made the beginning of writing in evangelical truth, possesses among the other evangelists the distinction of a leader and teacher.

The following statement therefore most aptly applies to him: “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first; so that in me first he might display all patience, as an instruction for those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. I). Hence it happened, as the evangelical history has now related, that while he was reclining at table in the house of this same Matthew, many publicans and sinners came and reclined at table with Jesus and his disciples (Matt. IX).

Those whom the biting conscience of their crimes could have restrained from approaching the Redeemer were encouraged to come by Matthew’s familiar companionship with the Lord. When they saw a publican drawing near to the fountain of mercy, already daring in blessed confidence, they did not doubt that they too, with the other sinners, could approach the very fountain that had been made public. Concerning this making-public of the eternal fountain the prophet says: “On that day there will be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman” (Zech. XIII).

The hidden fountain is the only-begotten Son of the invisible Father, God; the open fountain is that same God incarnate. This open fountain is rightly called the house of David, because there can be no doubt that our Redeemer came to us from the line of David.

O Pharisaic pride, you prepare to obstruct this fountain of mercy when, with haughty brow, you strive to prevent the thirsty and dry from approaching it. Through the mouth of Isaiah this draught was promised to you when he said: “For I will pour out water upon the thirsty and streams upon the dry land; I will pour out my spirit upon your offspring and my blessing upon your descendants, and they will sprout among the grasses like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. XLI). Again it was promised to you when he said elsewhere: “You will be like a watered garden and like a spring of waters whose waters do not fail” (Isa. LVIII).

But you, shamelessly raised up in the arrogance of swollen pride and deceitfully puffed up by the singularity of a false righteousness, stubbornly despise the fountain of eternal salvation freely set before you and disdain the life-giving streams of the heavenly fountain. Approaching the Lord’s disciples, swollen and arrogant Pharisee, you pour out the poisonous venom of pride that raged in your breast; and the wind of elation that you had conceived in your puffed-up mind you blow out through the breath of your envious and foully foaming mouth: “Why,” you say, “does your teacher eat with publicans and sinners?” (Matt. IX.)

He plainly eats with such people for this reason: to make the just from publicans, holy persons from sinners, and apostles from criminals. For he calls sinners so that, justifying them by his own power, he may make them innocent. Thus, elsewhere, when you, Pharisee, standing in the temple, arrogantly enumerate your good deeds, and condemn the other publican by setting yourself above him, the publican ascended from the abyss of his guilt, justified so as to obtain forgiveness, while you, from the height of your false righteousness, fell wretchedly before the eyes of almighty God.

In this way, then, while you presume upon the painted brightness of your empty righteousness, and secretly bite at others as subject to judgment because of their offenses, your righteousness is turned into sin through elation, whereas their committed wickedness is restored so as to obtain forgiveness through the grace of humility. Hence it is said through the prophet: “The desert will become Carmel, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest” (Isa. XXIX).

What is meant by the desert except those who live according to the laws of their flesh and serve the allurements of their pleasures? Since no plowshares of the divine word furrow their heart, like rational soil, they produce no crops of good works from which they might store grain in the heavenly granaries. What, however, is meant by Carmel, which is interpreted as “knowledge of true circumcision,” except those who appear to be circumcised from carnal works through the brightness of outward righteousness, and who do not cease to boast of the knowledge of that circumcision as though it were their unique possession? While they arrogate to themselves the knowledge not of just any circumcision but of true circumcision, they condemn others, in a certain sense, for the falsity of an untrue circumcision.

The desert, therefore, is turned into Carmel, and conversely Carmel is reckoned as a forest, when sinners rise by sharing in the merits of the just, while those who seemed just fall headlong into the works of a wild and fruitless growth. The Apostle says something similar: “Circumcision indeed profits, if you observe the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Rom. II).

What, then, does it profit you, Pharisee, that you boast arrogantly, that you claim for yourself knowledge of true circumcision, while an evil life most clearly proves you to be a transgressor of the law? Therefore the Lord, who examines hearts, despised you as you gloried in the uniqueness of a false righteousness and consequently endured a cataract in your eye; but he admitted this publican, whom you despise and, by despising him, scorn, into the fellowship of his own company: “Follow me,” he said; and he rose and followed him (Matt. IX).

How strong and powerful is the hand of this heavenly farmer! As soon as he shook the tree rooted deeply in the earth and clinging tenaciously to worldly desire, he uprooted it, carried it away, and transplanted it into the land of the living. There, “the just will flourish like a palm tree and multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. XCI).

By the fitting arrangement brought about through the changing of the right hand of the Most High, it was granted to him not only to receive the office of preaching but also that of writing, and thus to deserve to minister a heavenly treasure to the human race. In this way, the one who had despised the profits of earthly gain became a steward of heavenly talents and faithfully distributed the treasures of heavenly eloquence that he had received to be shared.

Just as our Redeemer had earlier said to his fishermen: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matt. IV), so he might in a certain sense say to this man: “You who gaze upon temporal profits, who certainly breathe impatiently in your desire to grow rich in gold or silver, follow me as quickly as possible, and immediately I will make you distribute the immortal riches of the heavenly kingdom throughout the breadth of the world. You seek gold that will pass away with the age, but I will give you the treasure of the Gospel, which will unquestionably endure through all ages.”

Perhaps this is why it is read concerning that river of paradise which Genesis calls Phison: “It surrounds the whole land of Evilath, where gold is born; and the gold of that land is very good” (Gen. II). For just as Phison is the first of the rivers proceeding from the fountain of paradise, so blessed Matthew holds the first place among the other evangelists. It is therefore sufficiently fitting, and in complete accord with inward reason, that just as the best gold is found in Phison, so we should understand that in this most blessed first leader of the evangelical order there is contained the incomprehensible mystery of the heavenly treasure.

To him is appropriately applied what is said through Solomon: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XIV). Here it is not a vein of metal, gold in color and flashing before carnal eyes, that gives off its radiance; rather, a mystical understanding shines with the splendor of the life-giving spirit. Nor does a buyer test this gold on wavering scales; the hearer instead carefully weighs it after storing it in the chest of his own heart.

Moses also clearly represented this gold when, speaking of himself as though of another, he said in Deuteronomy: “These are the words that he spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness of the plain, opposite the Red Sea, between Pharan and Thophel and Laban and Aseroth, where there is very much gold” (Deut. I). In the place where the divine law had been promulgated, there was said to be very much gold, because beneath the dust of the language heaped up and spread over it, many weighty treasures of heavenly wisdom lay hidden, preserved like grains of wheat beneath the stalk of the letter. Gold is fittingly appropriate to the holy teachers Moses and Matthew alike: one made a beginning of writing in the old law, the other in the Gospel, so that through these leaders of the two Testaments the spiritual riches contained in what they wrote might be revealed.

Moreover, this gold mentioned in Deuteronomy seems especially to correspond to blessed Matthew. For Deuteronomy is called the “second law,” by which the Gospel is signified. The gold, therefore, that is mentioned in Deuteronomy not undeservedly corresponds to the evangelist Matthew, who was the first of all to write the second law, that is, the Gospel.

Nor should it be overlooked that through those four places—Pharan, Thophel, Laban, and Aseroth—between which the divine law is given and where very much gold is said to be present, the number of the four evangelists is designated. Among them, as among four spiritual places, the treasure of heavenly wisdom lies in the midst, while through them the evangelical law is promulgated.

We shall briefly run through the interpretations of their names, so that we may express how each one specially corresponds to one of the evangelists. Pharan is plainly interpreted as “their wildness,” or “ferocity,” or also “fruitful.” This is undoubtedly fitting for blessed Matthew, who, when he accepted the fierce peoples of the Ethiopians in his own portion for preaching, led them as a shepherd before them to the grain of the heavenly pasture, like the gentlest sheep.

Thophel, or Thobel, is interpreted as “to offer,” or “led to mourning.” This plainly agrees with Saint Luke, who represents a victim under the form of a calf. For throughout the whole sequence of his Gospel he frequently remains concerned with the temple, and displays both the apostles’ mourning over the Lord’s Passion and the Lord and Savior himself as offered, now in the temple, now upon the wood.

Aseroth signifies vestibules, or courts, or blessedness. This is not inconsistent with blessed Mark, since for this reason, like a lion, he makes the voice of one crying resound in the desert: that he may prepare for us vestibules, or courts, or even—something greatly to be desired—blessedness in heaven.

The order should be noted: first we are led to the vestibule of Christian faith, then to the court of heavenly glory, so that we may soon enjoy eternal blessedness. Finally, Laban, which is interpreted as “whitening,” is more fitting for no one than John. Certainly, while he despised all that was obscure in the darkness of the world and fixed the rays of his heart upon the one who is the brightness of eternal light (Wis. VII), he disclosed to us the riches of an unfailing treasure.

These places are said to lie opposite the Red Sea because the entire chariot of the holy Gospel wages war against the bloodstained world.

Having heard these things that had burst forth from the frenzied mouth of the Pharisees, let us hear what heavenly Wisdom answered them: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9). The Pharisees were plainly sick, but through the excessive weakness and oppressive burden of their illness they did not know themselves to be sick; and because they thought themselves entirely healthy and not weighed down by any disorders, they did not deserve to be healed by the offered power of the heavenly physician.

Indeed, as those who have experienced it and were able to revive from that danger assert, [Col. 0792B] those struck by lightning feel nothing at all, while those who are wounded, or even afflicted more lightly, do not experience the sensation of bitterness and distress. So these men, overwhelmed by the most monstrous sleep of lethargy, did not recognize the sickness by which they were oppressed. The physician of souls considered those worthy of his healing who see themselves as weak and sick, who truly lament that they are weighed down and enfeebled by a definite calamity.

And O physician of singular and incomparable mercy, who magnifies upon himself all infirmities and illnesses so that the one who is languishing may recover through his own infirmity! For “truly he himself bore our pains; he was wounded because of our sins, and bruised because of our crimes” (Isa. 53). In order that scars might be laid over the wounds of the wounded human being, he willingly allowed grave wounds to be inflicted upon himself; indeed, he not only displayed care in healing us, but himself became our medicine.

For the heavenly remedy was ground within the mortar of the cross, and from it he produced the antidote of eternal salvation, through which the human race vomited out the venom of the ancient serpent. There are, certainly, five wounds of the Lord’s body, and through the five bodily senses, as through an equal number of windows, death had pestilentially entered humanity. Hence it is also said through the prophet: “Death entered through our windows” (Jer. 9). Those five wounds, therefore, became medicine for our five divided senses.

Concerning these wounds, under an altered name, the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Rise, my beloved, my bride, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall” (Song 2).

The bridegroom calls “beloved”—that is, loved—the soul of each believer, to whom Christ says: “Rise, my beloved, my bride, and come.” He says: “Do not, my bride, grow sluggish through idle torpor, but rise and come”; that is, outwardly offer examples of virtue to your neighbors.

But when he adds, “my dove in the clefts of the rock,” the rock, as the Apostle says, is Christ (1 Cor. 10). The clefts of the rock, therefore, are the wounds of the Redeemer. Every faithful soul dwells in these clefts, because it establishes the whole foundation of its salvation in the passion of its Savior; and, placing its hope in it, it confidently trusts in everlasting glory [Col. 0793A].

This may perhaps also be understood in the manner indicated by the Apostle: “I wish,” he says, “to speak five words in the Church with my understanding, so that I may instruct others, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue” (1 Cor. 14). That is: I judge it more useful to know in my heart and teach others the Lord’s passion, which was accomplished through five wounds, than to proclaim the ancient law, given through the Decalogue, in many words and vainly for display.

He had spoken these five words to those to whom he later said: “I judged myself to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2). Moreover, just as in paradise, from one fountain flowing out into four rivers, there are five streams that water the breadth of the whole world, so from the paradise of the Lord’s body fivefold blood shone forth, and it cleansed the defilements of the human race [Col. 0793B].

Yet by those channels of paradise, which proceed from the source of one fountain, the blessed evangelists are signified with even greater clarity: they flowed forth from Christ’s fullness. In that [paradise] all who have obtained forgiveness for their offenses have been washed. For he himself, as John says, is the propitiation for our sins; and he continues: “Not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2).

Thus, to the Pharisees who knew nothing of the inward compassion of mercy, he says: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’” (Matt. 9).

[Col. 0793C] See, dearest brothers, see the high priest of human redemption; see the author of our salvation standing for us and fighting bravely against the members of the devil. Of him the Apostle plainly says: “For he stands before the face of the Father and intercedes for us” (Rom. 8). There, through the mystery of the humanity he assumed, he intervenes for us; here, by his mercy, he closes the mouths of those who accuse and bark savagely against us.

And because, as the same John says, “we have an advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2), he contends for us as an advocate in the trial and, by his own pleadings, condemns the arguments of those who speak against us.

Therefore, after he had sent those who did not know mercy to learn mercy, saying, “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’” (Matt. 9), he immediately brought forward another argument of invincible reason in defense of justice and as an aid to our cause. For he says: “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (ibid.). It is as though he said: “I have not come to call the righteous—those who are not among us—but sinners, who are all among us together.” For “all,” as the Apostle says, “have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3).

Moreover, to give sinners firm hope, he did not choose for the summit of the apostolate those who were believed righteous among humanity and seemed distinguished by some holiness, but rather people either ignorant of righteousness or even sinners.

Thus he did not raise to the summit of apostolic dignity Zachariah, who “walked in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame” (Luke 1); nor Nathanael, in whom there was no deceit and who showed himself a true Israelite (John 1); nor Simeon, in whom the Holy Spirit was present and to whom it had been promised that he would see Christ the Lord before he died (Luke 2). He did not elevate any of these or anyone like them to apostolic dignity, but judged that simple people and sinners should rather be raised to this height, so that each of them might truthfully say: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15). Thus, since they had been advanced from a lowly state, they would attribute it not to their own merits but rather to the grace of the most merciful giver. To him be glory, honor, and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LII: ON SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL (29 SEPTEMBER)

[Col. 0794B]

We are concerned with the very heart of things and pursue the magnificence of the Lord’s works with an unpolished pen; this is not presumption but devotion, because we approach not as reckless investigators but as devout petitioners. The majesty of the Virgin and the dignity of the cross have honored our pen, and we have presumed to treat of both, having been saved by both.

Now we turn our discourse to the angels and contemplate the origin of that purer nature, and this appropriately. For at the beginning we placed those two first things that claim primacy among created things. The angels occupy the third place, both in heaven and in writing; the soul perceives what the page contains, and authority is fortified by reason.

That blessed realm of the heavenly powers, in which happy spirits fly around the Lord Sabaoth and, with the lofty clapping of their wings, sing in a clear voice through the streets of heavenly Jerusalem: “Holy, holy, holy.” “I saw,” says the prophet, “the Lord sitting upon a throne high and exalted, and the whole earth was full of his majesty, and the things beneath him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it, six wings for one and six wings for the other” (Isa. 6).

Each of these words has been weighed according to its significance, and they demand the most careful exposition. Our ignorance and lack of eloquence have made us unequal to it, but we shall nevertheless attempt to carve out something—not with such solemnity, perhaps, but truthfully.

This is not a bodily vision, nor is it wrapped in fantastic illusions, but it is spiritual and pure, seeking the holiness of a purer understanding. Do any see it except those who truly see—those who have risen above the darkness of the world and receive the splendor of divinity with a most luminous mind? To define it briefly, the Spirit of God, sweetly joined to our spirit, produces this vision when he enriches us with foreknowledge of future things.

In this way, then, that man, the glory of all prophetic eloquence, saw the Lord—and saw him sitting. The Son of God was a servant, not Lord, a minister, not teacher, lowly, not glorious, for thirty-three years. And although he said to his disciples, “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am” (John 13), and, “I am the light of the world” (John 8), few nevertheless noticed the grandeur of his words: the Pharisees were envious, the Jews did not believe, and they accused him of presumption.

But after he rose from the dead and was received upon a triumphal throne, imperial decrees were proclaimed throughout the city, and the Crucified fixed the insignia of his dominion across the whole breadth of the world. That poor and solitary man is now surrounded by majestic names; the lowliness of servile titles having been removed, he shines forth in great light as King of kings and Lord of lords.

The son of Amos therefore saw him not humble but exalted; not judged but judge; not the reproach of humanity but the glory of angels.

“Seated,” he says. We read of three sittings of the Creator: one after the creation of the world, when he rested from all the work he had done (Gen. 2); another after the Ascension, when he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God (Mark 16); and a third after the resurrection, when he will sit upon the throne of his majesty and we shall sit with him (Matt. 19).

Labor ordinarily precedes rest, and standing precedes sitting. But when did that majesty labor which is not affected by suffering and is not constrained by toil? Hear how immense a labor fell upon him when he thrust that wicked usurper down from heaven into hell, and cast the human being, seized by an almost similar sin, from the paradise of delight into a wretched exile.

How great a tumult do you suppose boiled up in the heavenly palaces when that deadly ravager created an irreparable division in the heavenly court, tore apart the angelic assembly, and dragged starry beings with him into death? Then the indignation of the Almighty raged; the enemy was struck by the whole right hand of divinity and hurled into the abyss of destruction.

This grave damage, so gravely avenged, was followed by another. For the one who had been appointed to repair this ruin, and for whose sake all subcelestial things had been established, sinned. When he sinned, much splendor was taken from the starry luminaries, and a lamentable corruption confused the entire substance of the elements.

The Lord’s fury had not yet turned away; his hand was still extended. Fragile and muddy substance provoked his right hand, wearied by a singular wound, against itself. The wretched little human being felt the remnants of the lightning’s fury, and a personal sin proscribed all humanity.

The Lord of majesty was therefore driven into repeated turmoil among rational creatures. Having taken vengeance upon his enemies, he condemned the fallen angels with despair, but chastised humanity with hope, foreseeing what great goods he would bring forth from its sin.

Perhaps for this reason the angelic sin is not found explicitly stated in Scripture, lest Scripture should be charged with what could not be amended.

God therefore rested after imposing a rational end upon such great evils. But, touched again by inward grief and burdened by the enormity of sinful humanity, he destroyed the human being he had created and caused the flood to inhabit the earth (Gen. 7). Not content with this, he rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19); he drowned the Egyptians in the waves (Exod. 14); he laid the corpses of the Israelites low in the wilderness, everywhere displaying an image of the Lord grown more turbulent.

At last he himself came, cast down in a cloud of our flesh (Luke 2), sharing in sorrows and labors, and learned obedience through the things he suffered (Heb. 5).

After the assumption of the flesh had been completed, he was raised into heaven and sits at the right hand of God (Mark 16). Yet he does not sit completely, because he still stands before the face of God for us. His third sitting will be glorious, when he has enclosed the good and the wicked in different ends and different enclosures (Matt. 25).

He will sit upon the throne of his majesty when he has drawn us to himself, “and God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15). The first sitting is that of grace, by which he freely made all things; the second is that of mercy, by which he mercifully redeemed us; the third is that of glory, when he will glorify us.

Consider, moreover, the glory of the one who sits and the excellence of his sitting, where no creature presumes to sit with him. “Seraphim,” he says, “stood” (Isa. 6); they did not sit. “I saw the Lord, and the whole army of heaven standing beside him” (ibid.), says the prophet: he says standing beside him, not sitting.

“Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7), as Daniel testifies. “All the angels stood around the throne” (Rev. 7), says the evangelist. And elsewhere: “I saw a great crowd, which no one could number, from every nation and tribe, standing before the throne” (ibid.).

The singular Virgin also stands at his right hand in a garment of gold (Ps. 44). Moses, in order to see the Lord passing by, stands upon the rock (Exod. 33); Elijah stands in the sight of the Lord; and every creature stands beside the imperial majesty.

Only that renegade spirit, the beginning of dissension, the prince of wickedness, the sum of evil, wished to sit with him. “I shall sit,” he says, “upon the mountain of the covenant” (Isa. 14). All stand, all minister—and you, enemy of peace, presume to sit? Even the Son himself, identical with the Father, does not know how to sit until the Father says to him: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109).

Thus Isaiah saw him: as Lord of the whole earth and seated upon a golden throne of his divinity, in that second sitting by which he carried our flesh into heaven.

It follows: “Upon a high throne.” Understand the high throne as the angelic nature, the first creation of the Almighty and the power endowed with primary dignity. The Son of the Virgin sits and rides above it, advancing the humanity he assumed through the ranks of angels, because, although nature is better, grace is stronger. However great the dignity, God’s will is greater—the will that the supreme philosopher establishes as higher than every bond of nature.

God’s magnificence, therefore, was raised not only above the heavens (Ps. 8), but also above the angels, because he became so much better than the angels as he inherited a name so much more excellent than theirs (Heb. 1).

“And the whole earth was full of his majesty.” “The Lord our God is in all the earth; his judgments,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 104). How, then, after this exaltation of his, does the prophet assert that the whole earth is filled with his majesty? (Ps. 71.)

When he says “full of majesty,” however, he means full of knowledge of that majesty—a knowledge that before his incarnation either no one or only a few deserved. But now, from the rising of the sun to its setting, God’s great name is proclaimed among the nations (Ps. 112), and all are taught by God (John 6), whom his anointing teaches about everything (1 John 2). For although his name was great in Israel, knowledge of his divinity has now spread not merely through one corner but throughout the whole world.

It follows: “And the things beneath him filled the temple.” Understand the temple as the city of the living God, his bride, which has neither stain nor wrinkle (Eph. 5). Beneath him are the incarnation, passion, death, and all the temporal distress of that dispensation, because, rising from the dead, he no longer dies (Rom. 6).

These are the things that fill the Church, whose remembrance produces for us annual solemnities. “The house of yours will be filled with good things” (Ps. 64). Your temple is holy; it is truly wondrous in righteousness when the Church shows no partiality toward persons, rejects gifts, chooses truth, and loves reason.

It follows: “Seraphim stood above it, six wings for one and six wings for the other.” Understand the two Seraphim as angel and human being: they are called “burning” or “ablaze,” since the one burns through presence, the other through remembrance.

Let us first consider the wings of the angels and the manner of their flight. Since that well-known interpretation explains how they veil the head and feet so that only the middle is seen—that is, what existed before the world and what will exist after it, with what is present appearing only somewhat—let us bring forward Ezekiel, who distinguishes the wings of the living creatures in this way, saying: “With two wings they flew, two wings of each were joined, and two covered their bodies” (Ezek. 1).

Their first wing is the dignity of their creation. Pass for a moment into the secret of this understanding and consider the dignity of this creature. “It is the beginning of the ways of God,” says Scripture (Job 40). What a privilege: that thought of the Most High burst forth in this first work. It was certainly fitting that what proceeded from the hands of the Ruler in the primitive creation should shine forth with singular glory.

“You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God,” says the prophet (Ezek. 28). Not merely “likeness,” but “the seal of likeness,” so that the image of God might be suggested all the more subtly, the seal preceding the likeness by so much greater a distinction.

When the fullness of wisdom, perfection of beauty, and delights of paradise are named, blessedness is joined together in its entirety. Scripture adds what surpasses and exceeds the capacity of all eloquence: “Whom has God made more precious?” Here everything that could be said has been said.

The second wing is the grace of confirmation. This wing, with a happier covering, knows no weariness; it is entirely like the preceding one and inferior in nothing. When the presumptuous fell and these remained in humility, that unbounded Spirit pursued those who remained with the greatest generosity, granting them as a gift that they could no longer be corrupted by any wavering.

Having therefore been confirmed and secure in the stability of their state, they attained the summit of a brighter grace. They serve him for whom serving is reigning, with fortunate security and secure happiness. With these two wings the angels fly in tireless flight, created worthily and strongly confirmed.

The third wing is singular love for their Creator, and it is most fortunate, interwoven with delicate feathers. They love, burn, and desire to look upon him whose love happily sets them aflame. For the nearer they are, the more fervent they become; absorbed into the light of his majesty, they burn continually and are continually satisfied in an indescribable manner.

The fourth is the constant vision of divinity, and this too is interwoven with more luxuriant feathers. What dignity it is continually to see God! Those spirits, even when they are sent forth, are not deprived of the glory of vision, because the essence of divinity—which is within, containing all things, and governs them externally—meets them everywhere.

Of these two it is written: “Two wings of each were joined” (Ezek. 1), since singular love arises from constant vision, and constant vision is produced by singular love.

The fifth is the joy of our Redemption, and it is adorned with a many-colored variety. Who could comprehend in an abundance of words how great a joy the God-man produced within the angelic powers, when, as the banner of the cross advanced, he both shattered their companion who had gone out from them but was not of them, and recalled lost humanity to the heavenly kingdoms?

Nor is this surprising, because they saw the material cleansed from which that heavenly city is rebuilt, “whose participation is in unity” (Ps. 121).

The sixth is the restoration of the heavenly city, and this too is colored with more beautiful paintings. What will it be when, after that terrible judgment has been completed, the Lord of hosts joins human beings to the angels, repairing the loss, restoring the number, and raising each order to its full numerical complement from among human beings according to their merits?

Then, just as the dwelling of all who rejoice will be in the city of God (Ps. 67), everything will be ordered according to the variety of its parts, and nothing more will remain that resists or can be moved from its appointed place.

Of these two wings it is said: “Two covered their bodies,” because the joy of our redemption and the restoration of the heavenly city cover and repair the bodies of the blessed spirits, so that such a ruinous diminution may not be perceived in that higher glory.

And one must consider how great a goodness of grace the human race accumulates through these ministering spirits: they fight for us, as in the words, “There was a great battle in heaven” (Rev. 12). They conquer for us, as is added there: “Now victory has come” (ibid.). They rejoice for us, because there is “joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15). They weep for us, as it is written: “The angels of peace wept bitterly” (Isa. 33).

These are the blessed wings on which that numerous order flies above all things, standing unshakably, flying joyfully, and continuing into eternity.

But now we must return to ourselves and turn the pen back toward our human condition, from which bodily pleasures and wicked desires divide and separate us from the fellowship of the angels. Although we have fallen into this degradation, we nevertheless bear the image of the Creator. Though it can be obscured, it cannot be destroyed.

“Every human being who lives is complete vanity” (Ps. 38), says the righteous man; yet “in the image” the human being passes away. Let us assign six wings to the human being—not such wings, perhaps, but whatever kind we can.

The first wing of a human being returning to God is bitterness of heart. “In many things we all offend” (James 3), and there is no number to our offenses. But when the grace of God approaches and kindles our heart, and we recall all our years in the bitterness of our soul, we declare the image to have been darkened and are re-formed according to our beginning.

But because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. 10), the second wing follows: confession of the mouth. “Above all, confession,” Scripture says; nothing is more pleasing to God than confessing and accusing what you have done.

All sacred Scripture is full of testimony to this great power, and the entire authority of both the Old and New Testaments serves it. These are the two virtues that conceal the manifold accumulation of our crimes from the eyes of God. Of them it is said: “Two covered their bodies.” For “blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 32).

He said “imputed,” not “committed.” For the one who did not commit sin is only one—and he is the Son of God. Whatever he has determined not to impute to us is as though it had never been.

The third wing is hope. It raises fragile souls toward heavenly things, lightens the weariness of waiting, presumes upon the mercy of the Judge, and turns toward the palace of divine compassion.

The fourth is fear. It comes to the aid of our fleshly garment, penetrating the bones and pouring itself into the very marrow. Present before the eyes of your heart the image of the Lord—the Lord who made heaven and earth, who has power to cast body and soul into Gehenna (Matt. 10), whose patience you have provoked, storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God (Rom. 2).

When you have examined these things with attentive consideration, fear and trembling will come upon you, and dread of death will more forcefully overturn the inner person (Ps. 55). Since hope presumes greatly and fear distrusts excessively, do not delay in joining the two, so that together they may accomplish what they cannot when separated. Learn to hope in such a way that you fear; fear in such a way that you hope.

Of these it is written: “Two wings of each were joined.”

The fifth is humility. “The Lord is near to those who have obtained a heart,” says Scripture. Humility is the mother of virtues; pride is the queen of vices. Humility alone is the nurse of the virtues, and it alone did the Most High regard in the Virgin Mother. Throughout the time that the Son of God lived on earth, he both practiced and taught it: “Learn from me,” he says, “because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11).

The sixth is charity. This is the beginning and the end, the completion of good things, the unique daughter of the supreme King. It is unnecessary to commend it at greater length, since the whole eloquence of both secular and divine writings accords with it.

Of these it is said: “With two wings they flew.” With these twin wings the winged ones fly upward, of whom it is said: “The net is thrown in vain before the eyes of the winged” (Prov. 1). If we fly with these and do not grow weary, then one day we too shall fly on angelic wings and see him in his beauty, who is God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## OCTOBER

[Col. 0800B]

18. Sermon on Saint Luke the Evangelist. 28. Sermon on Saint Fidelis, martyr.

## SERMON LIII: ON SAINT LUKE THE EVANGELIST (28 OCTOBER)

Because through the Gospel, dearest ones, the world has been led back from darkness to light, the Christian people rightly celebrate the glory of the evangelists. Among them, however, is blessed Luke, to whom the present sermon is devoted. By weaving together a history both evangelical and apostolic in its twofold style, he enriches the field of the Church with different crops, from which the hungry people may live and from which Christ’s flock may gather fresh nourishment for salvation.

These are plainly the crops that Joseph gave to his brothers (Gen. 42); this is the money that he commanded to be placed in the mouth of the sack (Gen. 44). This money is now set out upon the table of the Church, so that later its interest may be demanded from the merchants.

But Benjamin is also given something additional beyond the others: in his sack a cup is placed together with the money (Gen. 44). Whom does Joseph indicate through this mystery, if not our Redeemer, whom he was already prefiguring through his own mystery? For Scripture says: “He changed his name and Pharaoh called him, in the Egyptian language, ‘Savior of the world’” (Gen. 41). Whom do the brothers signify, if not the holy apostles? Whom does Benjamin signify, if not Paul, who derived his origin from the tribe of Benjamin?

All the brothers therefore receive the fruits of preaching, which they must sow throughout the world, and the money that they must set upon the table of faith for the profit of interest. To Benjamin alone, however, a cup is also added, so that through Paul, whom Benjamin signified, not a little cup of the tabernacle but a broad and open cup of the word might be offered to the nations.

Hence Paul says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us” (2 Cor. 6). It is as though he said: “Since you see the drink of the word flowing abundantly to you through a generous cup, open wide the mouths of your thirsty hearts to draw it in, so that the stream flowing forth may not run uselessly but may find capacious vessels into which it can be poured.”

Concerning this drink the Lord says through Isaiah: “The beast of the field will glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches, because I have given waters in the wilderness, rivers in the desolate place, to give drink to my people, my chosen” (Isa. 43).

What does “the beast of the field” signify, if not the Gentile world, lacking reason? What do “the dragons” signify, if not the malicious? And what are signified by “the ostriches,” which have wings but cannot fly, if not hypocrites?

These beasts therefore glorify God when Christ offers the words of the overflowing Gospel to the Gentile people, which had been deserted and desolate.

The cup of evangelical preaching was therefore given to Paul in Benjamin, so that he might cultivate the wilderness of the Gentiles in a special way and drench its aridity with the abundant rain of holy preaching. Concerning this rain it is written: “He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth” (Ps. 147).

Hence Paul himself, who testifies that he is an apostle and teacher of the Gentiles (2 Tim. 1), says to the Galatians: “When they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, just as the Gospel of the circumcision had been entrusted to Peter—for he who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcision worked through me also among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2).

Here one must note how great was blessed Paul’s dignity and how great his glory. For Christ himself, while still capable of suffering and mortal, taught blessed Peter and the other apostles; but once glorified and exalted above the angels, he instructed Paul.

Christ was the teacher of the apostles while he was subject to human insults; he did not disdain to teach Paul when he was already surrounded by the services of the heavenly powers. He lived with the other apostles while he was still enduring the weaknesses of our mortality; he made Paul his intimate when, having trampled upon and powerfully overthrown the dominion of death, he presided upon the throne of the Father’s majesty.

Hence Paul says: “I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was preached by me, because it is not according to man. For I did not receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1).

Therefore, although the holy apostles perceived all the deeds of our Savior through bodily sight, they nevertheless surpassed blessed Paul in no knowledge, since the same master who had previously dwelt bodily with them on earth instructed him from heaven.

Hence he says to the Corinthians by way of a question: “Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?” (1 Cor. 9.)

With God revealing it, he therefore reached such fullness of knowledge and was led into the whole truth of the evangelical rule in such a way that, though all the others remained, he had no need of the apostles’ instruction.

Hence he says to the Galatians: “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I immediately did not yield to flesh and blood, nor did I go to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me” (Gal. 1).

When he did go, he makes clear when he adds: “Then, after three years, I went to Jerusalem to see Peter” (ibid.)—to see, not to learn.

But someone may say: “This sermon does not speak of Luke the evangelist, as it promised, but is occupied with a discussion of the apostle Paul.” Quite so; we cannot deny it. But since blessed Luke was that apostle’s inseparable companion and learned from him everything he wrote, when we express the dignity of the teacher, we do not keep silent about the praise of the pupil.

The teacher’s praise redounds upon the disciple, since Luke, receiving from Paul’s mouth the history of evangelical truth that Paul had learned divinely, faithfully inscribed it in writing.

How great, therefore, was the dignity and excellence of blessed Luke? This becomes clear here: while Mark was taught by blessed Peter, and Matthew and John, who wrote the Gospel, learned the deeds of our Redeemer on earth, Luke alone, so to speak, deserved to write the Gospel that descended from heaven. For the Holy Spirit revealed it from heaven to Paul, and afterward Christ became known to blessed Luke through that same Paul, as through his own instrument.

Hence Paul himself says: “You seek proof of Christ who speaks in me” (2 Cor. 13).

From heaven, therefore, Christ poured the mysteries of his deeds into Paul, and through Paul transferred them into Luke, as through a golden conduit. Thus what is said through Isaiah seems not unfittingly to apply to this blessed man: “The first to Zion says, ‘Behold, here I am’; and to Jerusalem I will give an evangelist” (Isa. 41).

Therefore it happened not by chance but through the instruction of the Holy Spirit that blessed Matthew, who learned the Gospel from the Lord dwelling on earth, descends by counting forty generations (Matt. 1), while Luke describes seventy-seven generations by ascending through their degrees (Luke 3).

For the number forty expresses labor, by which Christ is wearied in his body, which is the Church, through the various periods of this life. Hence Moses (Exod. 24) and Elijah continued their fast for forty days (1 Kings 19). The Lord himself likewise abstained from food for the same number of days (Matt. 4).

Through Moses, therefore, the law is understood; through Elijah, prophecy; and through Christ, clearly, the grace of the New Testament. Through the affliction of the law, prophecy, and grace together, the labor of the universal Church is indicated, wearied throughout all the ages of this mortal life.

Hence the children of Israel, worn down by the hardships and labors of their long pilgrimage, entered the promised land after forty years (Josh. 5), because all the elect, once they have completed the course of this pilgrimage, will immediately possess the land of the living by hereditary right.

By the number, then, which Matthew arranges, the assumption of our laborious mortality is signified; by that, however, which Luke set down, the mystery of our redemption is unquestionably expressed. By the former number likewise we are taught that Christ, in accordance with the prophecy, himself bore our sins (Isa. LIII); by the latter we learn in turn that, according to the Apostle, he forgave us all our offenses (Col. II). For he himself is the Lamb who was offered, because he himself willed it (Isa. LIII); he is also the one who took away the sins of the world (John I).

The number seventy-seven, which Luke set down, signifies the remission of sins, as the Lord himself indicates when Peter asks how often his brother’s sins must be forgiven and receives the answer: “I tell you, not merely seven times, but up to seventy-seven times” (Matt. XVIII). Nor is it surprising that by this number, which is formed from eleven and ten, the abolition of human depravity is signified. For if the number eleven is multiplied seven times, the total of seventy-seven is certainly completed. But ten, which is the perfect number, signifies the Decalogue. By eleven, however, which exceeds it, what else is represented but transgression of the Law?

Since, therefore, both numbers are included in that whole sum of the Law together with transgression, what wonder is it if the remission of crimes is signified through it? The number seven, plainly, which descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, abolished the eleven of our depravity. Concerning this number of gifts Isaiah says: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him; the Spirit of counsel and fortitude; the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and he shall be filled with the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI).

Therefore blessed Luke, to show that we are cleansed from our crimes through the coming of our Savior, begins the account of Christ’s genealogy not from the beginning of the Gospel narrative, but only from his baptism. This is also clearly shown in the book of Genesis, where Lamech is reported to have said to his wives: “Vengeance shall be taken sevenfold upon Cain, but upon Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (Gen. IV). Vengeance upon Lamech is said to be taken seventy-sevenfold because seventy-seven men are said to have issued from his loins and, afterward, to have been swallowed up when the Flood devoured them.

But since Lamech is represented as both striking and being struck, whom does he signify by this except the first parent of the human race? He inflicted upon the entire race of succeeding posterity the weapon of sin by which he himself, having first been struck, perished. Vengeance was therefore taken upon this Lamech seventy-sevenfold, because the sin contracted by the first man remained active in the human race through seventy-seven generations. Original sin indeed continued until Christ, who wiped it away through the sacrament of his baptism—whence Luke begins. There it is said of him: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

Thus the two holy evangelists divide between themselves the substance of our redemption, and each takes up the portion of the narrative suitable to him: Matthew, descending through the line of generations, declares that Christ came to us sinners from heaven; Luke, ascending from the sacrament of baptism all the way to the Father, shows that he drew us with him, cleansed from the filth of sins, into heavenly glory. The former sets forth Christ mercifully descending to earth; the latter acknowledges him lifting us up to heaven.

The former shows the shepherd leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert pastures; the latter teaches that he placed upon his shoulders the sheep he had lost and brought it back to its own fold (Matt. XVIII; Luke XV). The former declares that the physician descended to the sick; the latter acknowledges that he brought us back with him, healed, to the joys of eternal wholeness. The former shows the only-begotten Son sent to us by the Father; the latter teaches that he transferred a multitude of the elect to their heavenly homeland.

The blessed Apostle comprehends the intention of both evangelists in one statement, saying: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that, because of sin, he might condemn sin in the flesh” (Rom. VIII). When he says, “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he shows the assumption of our mortality, which Matthew openly declares when, descending to Abraham, he enumerates forty generations. But when he adds, “and because of sin he condemned sin in the flesh,” he proclaims the abolition of sins, which Luke unquestionably expresses when he traces the line of seventy-seven generations.

Paul himself elsewhere embraces both statements in a single verse, saying: “Jesus Christ was handed over because of our offenses and rose because of our justification” (Rom. IV). Christ descended to rescue us from sins; he rose to present us radiant with the brightness of righteousness.

This difference between the two blessed evangelists is also clearly displayed in the fact that Matthew, descending, extends the line of the Lord’s generation through Solomon, whose mother David had fallen through adultery; Luke, however, ascends through Nathan, the prophet of that name, through whom the Lord expiated this very sin of David and, as it were, in mercy raised him after his fall. The former therefore teaches that the Son of God humbly inclined himself toward us; the latter declares that he was exalted from heaven together with us, in triumphal glory. Christ descended to those lying prostrate so that, victorious, he might raise them with himself to the stars.

Hence it is believed that it was not without divine foreknowledge that this evangelist was given such a name. For *Lucas* is translated into Latin from Hebrew as “he himself rising” or “he who raises.”

In his own name, therefore, he anticipated what he later wrote about the Savior. Our Redeemer himself rose from death and raised us, living from the dead, to heavenly things. Hence it is also said through the Apostle: “He raised us together with him and made us sit together with him in the heavenly places” (Eph. II). He is therefore principally called “rising himself” or “raising,” because he rose from death for this purpose: to raise us who had been struck down in death; and he ascended into heaven for this purpose: to lift us with himself to heavenly things.

What blessed Luke testified in writing about Christ, he indicated prophetically, as it were, by his own name. And this is certainly a great mystery: that blessed Luke begins with the Savior’s baptism and, ascending through the generations, extends the line all the way to God the Father. Through the washing of holy baptism we are cleansed from sins, and thus through the Mediator between God and humanity we are reconciled to God the Father. In baptism, therefore, lies the beginning of our ascent, and through the growth of good works one reaches God from among the living.

Nor should it be passed over that, since our Redeemer is truly both king and priest, just as blessed Matthew wove the account of his royal descent, so, conversely, Luke indicates his priestly dignity throughout the whole of his work. He is frequently occupied with the priestly office, and while he passes through various deeds of the Lord’s activity, he does not depart from matters belonging to the priesthood. At one point he narrates the office assigned to a priest, at another his descent, at another his service, at another his sacrifice; at another he names the Temple. Although he includes many things within the sequence of sacred history, he nevertheless continues according to the intention with which he began: to pursue the priesthood.

For at the very beginning of his narrative he begins in this way: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron” (Luke I). Then he places this priest himself at the altar to offer sacrifice. Later he also sends the virgin Mary to the house of that same priest. He further records three songs to be sung in the Church—something none of the other evangelists is found to have done: the first of Zechariah, the second of Mary, and the third of Simeon (Luke I and II).

On the fortieth day after he was born, he relates that the Lord was presented in the Temple with the women. Then he places him, at twelve years of age, seated among the teachers in that same Temple. He also relates that the Lord’s parents used to ascend to Jerusalem each year at the feast of Passover for the sake of prayer. Finally, he concludes his Gospel in this way: “They returned to Jerusalem with great joy, worshiping; and they were continually in the Temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke XXIV).

Hence it comes about that blessed Luke bears the appearance of a calf, just as the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. I) and the Evangelist John (Rev. IV) declare that they saw. A calf, after all, used to be offered in the Temple. And appropriately a calf, because with the plowshare of sacred speech he furrows the fields of our hearts and makes them fertile with the life-giving sowing of evangelical seed.

Or certainly blessed Luke displays the image of a calf for this reason: while describing evangelical and apostolic history, he drives away the enemies of Christ and adversaries of the true faith as though with two horns, and overcomes them so that they may not ravage the field of the Catholic Church. He is armed with these horns so that he may strike unbelieving Jews and confine heretics, who deviate here and there from the rule of the true faith.

Blessed Luke therefore wrote the labors and acts of the apostles, in which he himself also took part as a fellow worker. He also wrote the Gospel, which he received from heaven like the sealed weight of a great treasure. The prophecy of Isaiah is suitably applied to it: “The vision of all this shall be for you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say, ‘Read this’; and he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed’” (Isa. XXIX).

For what is that sealed book except the holy Gospel, wrapped in sayings expressed through mysteries and removed from human understanding by a certain secret profundity? This is certainly the book of which John says: “I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and on the outside, sealed with seven seals” (Rev. V).

What are the seals with which the evangelical book is said to be sealed except those seven mysteries by which the whole order of the Lord’s dispensation is fulfilled—namely, the Lord’s incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, then judgment, and finally kingdom? The evangelical book was sealed with these seals in such a way that it could not be opened to anyone at all unless Christ had opened it. Hence it continues: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he may open the book and loose its seven seals” (Rev. V).

But in the Acts of the Apostles, while he narrates what appears to be a bare history, he in a certain sense nurses the tender infancy of the newborn Church.

Yet if we attend carefully to the fact that the writer is a physician, we find nothing else in that history except medicine for sick souls. He stretches out before human conduct a kind of line of uprightness and guides us along it as along a path, so that, having discerned how the primitive Church lived, we too may strive to live in the measure that our ability permits. Thus the same purity that flows from the source of its origin may nevertheless run through the later declines, and what advances in its beginning may be preserved in the same condition at the end.

For he himself is one of the four rivers of paradise, who watered the whole breadth of the world with the abundant streams of his teaching. Concerning these waters Isaiah says: “Waters shall burst forth in the wilderness, and torrents in the desert; the parched land shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water” (Isa. XXXV).

Let us therefore return, beloved, to the innocence of the primitive Church, so that we may learn both to abandon what we possess and to rejoice in the simplicity of royal poverty. May the weight of earthly substance not press us down into the depths, since the heavenly King invites us to the glory of the Jerusalem above. May the lure of carnal pleasure not rashly draw us back from this goal, for through the entrance of our Redeemer, who went before us, the hallways of heaven have been opened to us.

For when the line of his generation is extended from the humility of baptism all the way to the Father, it is unquestionably clear that he promises those who follow him entrance into the heavenly homeland, and that where he entered first, he prepared the way for those who serve him. “Father,” he says, “I will that where I am, there my servant also may be” (John XII), so that the members may gather to the head and, as the same one promises, “where the body is, there the eagles will gather” (Matt. XXIV).

“Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help” (Heb. IV). For, as the same Apostle says, “we have such a high priest who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens” (Heb. VIII), a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle, which God established and not man.

Let our spirit now direct itself there; let it strive eagerly to fly there, breaking the bonds of earthly desire; and, seeing where the head rises above, let it trust that it too will follow. Of him it is said: “Jesus did not enter into a sanctuary made by human hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf” (Heb. IX).

There, therefore, we have the high priest who justifies sinners; there we also have the king who crowns those who triumph after victory. He graciously descended from the heights to our depths for this purpose: to raise us with himself from the lowest places to what belongs to him—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIV. ON SAINT FIDELIS THE MARTYR. (28 OCTOBER)

You know, dearest brothers, that for this reason we frequently assemble, according to ecclesiastical custom, to hear of the victories of Christ’s martyrs: so that, while we are instructed by their deeds, we may be inflamed more ardently with love for the heavenly homeland, which they obtained by fighting bravely. And when we hear that they despised the edicts of kings, the threats of rulers, and the tribunals of judges, and passed through so many kinds of punishment, the freeborn souls of the faithful ought to be ashamed even to fail to resist the vices of their own flesh.

For it is shameful to watch the victories of Christ’s warriors in such a way that, while we see others adorned with triumphal titles and carrying away spoils from their enemies, we ourselves, in the domestic peace of our hearts, weakly succumb to creeping vices as though to ambushing adversaries.

Moreover, the blessed martyrs flourished in various virtues even before they shed their blood in combat. Since we cannot die in defense of the faith, our victory is complete if we strive to live in the practice of holy virtues, so that from the very condition in which they merited martyrdom we may immediately be transferred to the kingdom. Through the merits of life by which they deserved to obtain the palm of their contest, we are led to the crown without any obstacle of persecution.

We must therefore venerate and admire one thing in the holy martyrs alone, and imitate another. Let us admire them as they die steadfastly and nobly; let us imitate them as they live in honorable conduct. Let us venerate in them the fact that they handed their bodies over to various punishments for the faith; let us imitate the fact that they first crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. Let us admire them dying bravely, lest they themselves deny life; and let us also imitate them by persisting in holy exhortations through the zeal of charity, so that they might draw others to life.

To conclude in a shorter statement what I desire: the memory of the martyrs is worthily recalled if, while the miracle of their death is proclaimed to us, their preceding life is also made an example.

Behold blessed Fidelis, the martyr whose feast we celebrate today. As the account of his deeds testifies, he is known to have led a life worthy of martyrdom even before the occasion of martyrdom was provided.

Although he was supported by distinguished birth and, with prosperity smiling upon him, could have entered upon the way of the world without dishonor, he rejected the patronage of any great men and, devoted in religion, preferred to attach himself to a bishop. He thus plainly showed that he did not yearn for the favor or wealth of the powerful, but rather chose the blessing of a priest.

With this bishop he did not think it proper to attend the quarrels of legal disputes, the deceptive fabrications of the stage, or theatrical spectacles worthy of no one; instead, he visited the prisons of the martyrs. And because he was devoted to the martyrs, he himself eventually deserved to become a martyr.

Thus in former times that steward of the royal household, Obadiah, because he fed a hundred prophets hidden in caves, later deservedly received prophetic grace as his reward (III Kings XVIII). He who then fed a crowd of prophets with bread and water through the ministry of devoted diligence now refreshes and nourishes the whole Church with the oracles of his prophecy, that is, with heavenly food.

Likewise Joshua, who rendered dutiful service to Moses, the leader of the Israelite people, later both governed that same people laudably and triumphed with great glory over its adversaries (Josh. I). Why should I mention Elisha, who, refusing to endure separation from Elijah even for a moment, subsequently merited a double portion of his spirit? (IV Kings II.) It was as though the Lord were already then proclaiming that Gospel saying: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X).

Indeed, blessed Fidelis not only performed the office of pious humility toward the holy martyrs, but also extended his diligence to winning those who were held by the errors of idols. And, as he himself seems to assert in his own words, while he was engaged in secular military service he obeyed the divine command more than the earthly one, so much so that he restrained certain people from the profane worship of idolatry and summoned them to knowledge of the true God through saving admonitions.

He was present in military camps, but he bore the standards of the heavenly army. He appeared to be mingling with troops of armed men, but he strove to enlist for the heavenly camp soldiers belonging to another profession. To them he promised not the belt of earthly warfare or the gift of temporal pay, but citizenship in the heavenly court.

Thus, under the cloak of earthly military service, he stood ready for the heavenly camps, so that he might make deserters from the earthly ranks and increase the number of the heavenly army. We know that David did something similar when he stayed with Achish, king of Gath, while fleeing from Saul. He frequently carried away rich spoils from the regions ruled by Achish; and, to quote the words of Scripture: “David struck the whole land and left neither man nor woman alive, taking sheep and oxen and donkeys and camels and clothing; then he returned and came to Achish.”

When Achish asked him, “Against whom did you raid today?” (I Kings XXVII), David declared that he had attacked the Negeb of Judah or the regions of Israel. David therefore had presented himself to the foreign king as devoted to him, compelled by necessity; but from his profane people he accumulated many slaughtered victims.

Blessed Fidelis, however, labored under the appearance of secular military service while standing ready for the camps of heaven. Thus he mocked the world—and, more deeply, the ruler of this world—to whom he seemed outwardly to serve, striving to draw away his followers wherever he could and join them to the companies of the higher warfare.

David cut down barbarian nations with the sword; Fidelis, with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI), killed men of carnal life, uncultivated and truly barbarous in their practices. David carried off troops of various animals; Fidelis led brutish people to the sheepfold of the Church and to the life-giving pasture of acquiring reason.

When questioned, David asserted that he had become an adversary to the people of God; Fidelis, in a certain sense, appeared even to resist the faithful party, since he seemed to carry on secular military service with unbelievers. Through his military profession he appeared outwardly to assert that he was attacking the inheritance of God, of which he himself was a part, with various customs as though with different swords.

Thus, indeed, holy deception proceeded more freely, while the man upon whom suspicion did not fall persisted in winning believers for Christ. We shall therefore see that blessed Fidelis attained the crown of martyrdom through preceding merit: before his martyrdom, he had already labored in the true zeal of charity to win souls.

Like good and fertile earth, he first brought forth the shoot of holy work, and then received the light of triumphal glory. Hence, at the beginning of the world, the earth is first commanded to bring forth vegetation, while on the following day the lights are made in heaven (Gen. I). For it is necessary first to produce the living fruits of holy action, so that afterward we may be able to reach the contemplation of the light of supreme truth.

He had built his house in peace upon a firm rock; therefore, when the winds of threats raged and various waves of punishments struck against it, he remained immovable (Matt. VII). Like the root of an excellent tree, he had first conceived strength in secret; supported by it, the mature crop afterward did not fall when driven by the winds.

In peace, therefore, through good works he earned the ability to stand unconquered and undaunted in the arena of persecution. He labored in leisure for what he overcame in battle. Within the walls of peace he sought what he obtained as victor in the field.

Among the other distinctions of his merits, how great a glory it is that, as soon as this blessed and unconquered martyr was beheaded, a violent storm and excessive lightning are said to have arisen! This was a judgment of divine equity, so that it might become clear through it that the one who received his martyr into glory rightly terrified his torturers in anger.

Lightning and storm therefore broke out to terrify the reprobate. Accompanied by these, the heavenly Judge will come to judgment, as the prophet says: “Fire shall go before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Ps. XIX; Matt. XXVII). At the Lord’s death, moreover, the elements are read to have been disturbed.

How great, then, is the dignity, and how noble the mark of triumph, that, in imitation of the Lord’s death, the elements were also shaken at the martyr’s beheading—so that, by dying, he might in some measure bear the form of the death whose teaching he had imitated in life.

Nor should this be regarded as insignificant: one of the persecutors is said to have been seized by a demon. He promised that he would consign the martyr’s body to burial with great reverence if, through the martyr’s intervention, he might deserve to be freed from the demon. As soon as he touched the martyr’s corpse, the demon departed.

Here too the example of our Redeemer is plainly visible. For from among the Lord’s own persecutors, whoever deserved to touch the mystery of his most holy body was freed from the yoke of demons, redeemed by the very blood that they had shed.

And so that in his martyrdom the servant might appear to imitate the passion of his Lord as a follower, when the executioners reported to their ruler the miracles that had been displayed through the blessed martyr, he strictly forbade anyone to report such things and, terrified, commanded that they be concealed forever.

Who, on hearing this, would not immediately recall what the chief priests said to the guards: “Say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping’; and if this comes to the governor’s attention, we will persuade him and keep you out of trouble” (Matt. XXVIII). They taught the guards to fabricate a lie; he commanded his officials to suppress the truth in silence. Both are enemies of the truth, whether they wickedly construct deceitful inventions or maliciously conceal the truth in silence.

But we, dearest brothers, who have heard of the steadfastness of so outstanding a warrior, who behold the insignia of such virtue as though placed before our eyes, should ourselves strive, with the help of almighty God, to possess virtues. Let us be ashamed to languish in the torpor of cowardice, since we see others penetrating heaven with such glory.

Let our minds grow hot for the struggle of the contest; and if we do not fear to engage the enemy boldly, let us not doubt that, with Christ as our leader, an easy victory will come to us. Our labor is indeed lighter, while the reward is nevertheless common.

For who does not know that it is incomparably more difficult to offer one’s neck to the sword than to restrain the enticements of the throat? Who would not prefer to sweat through labors or grow cold in nakedness rather than endure the burning of raging flames? Who would not consider it lighter to hunger and thirst than to be torn by claws or handed over to the bites of beasts?

Is it not more dangerous publicly to despise the glittering, thundering commands of raging kings than secretly to oppose evil thoughts in the mind? Is it not harder to hand oneself over voluntarily to death than to restrain one’s own desires and the cravings of the flesh?

Since, then, we pursue the same blessedness with less labor, why do we neglect to imitate those who fought in the arena, so that we may become companions of the victors in our homeland?

Let us fight, therefore, my brothers, and take care to cut off the enticements of the vices that assail us. For, in accordance with Paul’s saying, we cannot rejoice in the world here and reign with Christ there.

We know that the blessed martyrs fought with the members of the devil; we, however, have an unbreakable struggle with the very head of the wicked. They conquered him while he raged savagely through his members; we are commanded to overcome him while he lies hidden beneath the deceptions of ambushes.

In both ways the glorious martyr Fidelis won a triumph over him: in peace, through the grace of edification, he rescued some from the devil’s bondage; when persecution arose, he nevertheless despised him both when he flattered and when he terrified through his members.

Though conquered, he conquered; though cast down, he ascended. He submitted his own head to the sword and trampled the devil’s neck beneath the foot of perpetual victory. Now, without doubt, he shines among the fiery stones of heavenly Jerusalem and alternates the song of heavenly harmony with his comrades-in-arms, clothed in purple, before his emperor.

In a blessed exchange he stripped off the fragile tunic of the body and obtained the radiant robe of immortality. He lost his head through decapitation and now walks crowned with a precious stone. He is rewarded in eternal rest as a victor by the one who had earlier protected him while he fought amid battles: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# NOVEMBER

[Col. 0811C]

I. Homily on All Saints. XI. Sermon on Saint Martin, Bishop and Confessor. XXX. Sermon I on Saint Andrew the Apostle. Sermon II on the same.

## LV. HOMILY ON THE FEAST OF ALL THE SAINTS

“At that time: ‘Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples approached him.’” And so forth.

Today a brighter day has smiled upon us, and the sun has shone upon the earth more brilliantly than usual. For not one saint but all the saints sanctify this day and illuminate it with radiant splendors. That solemnity of heaven is a spectacle that shines not with annual but with continual joys, where light is seen in light and the substance of the Trinity is opened to blessed eyes, eye to eye.

There the eternal relation of the Begetter, the Begotten, and the One who proceeds is known—a reality that can be believed here but cannot be comprehended. There the queen of virgins, accompanied by countless virgins, traverses the dwellings of the angels and, while both natures marvel at her glory, says: “Why do you marvel at me? This mystery that you behold is divine—entirely divine, not human, and never comprehended by human reasoning.”

There the numerous army of angels shines in sacred divisions, delighted by its winged service; it does not veil but reveals the majesty of the Lord. There are the original elect of the patriarchs, the venerable fellowship of the prophets, the glorious chorus of the apostles, the purple multitude of martyrs, the flourishing congregation of confessors, the radiant troop of virgins, and the countless number of monks.

The Lord of hosts sits in their midst and intoxicates those who behold him with the outpouring of his glory: “They shall be intoxicated,” says the Prophet, “with the abundance of your house” (Ps. XXXV). There are secure peace, delightful rest, perpetual life, wisdom of mind, agility of body, and illumination of the heart. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII).

As the dwelling place of all who rejoice is in you, city of God (Ps. LXXXVI), so in your streets the voice of exultation resounds in sweeter melodies. “Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess him” (Ps. XLI, XLII). I shall confess him there: here is the arena, there the reward; here the battle, there the crown.

It is vain to rise before the light. The spirit must be hardened and drawn far away from the allurements of pleasures, and the substance of both body and soul must be cleansed, if we wish to fly back to our own origins. For the present we must love the thinness of poverty, restrain bitter speech, flee arrogance, endure labors, fight against vices, and cast out worldly riches.

This is what that poor and solitary man says in today’s reading of the holy Gospel to the poor whom he had called from the poverty of the world: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V). These are eight—indeed, seven—beatitudes, because the eighth is the same as the first. They are most blessed steps by which one goes to the Lord.
