He who ascended the mountain and opened his mouth to teach his disciples first ascended all of them in his own person.

For who was poorer than the one who had nowhere to lay his head (Luke IX)? Who was gentler than the one who is gentle and humble of heart (Matt. XI)? When he saw the city, he wept over it (Luke XIX); he wept for Lazarus (John XI). He taught righteousness and practiced righteousness; no deceit was found in his mouth (Isa. LIII). Who was more merciful than the one who freed the adulterous woman and healed the sinful woman burdened with seven demons? Who was purer than the one who committed no sin? (I Pet. II.)

He came to make peace between the things in heaven and the things on earth; he left peace to his disciples (John XIV). He suffered persecution for righteousness, was scourged in the flesh, hung upon the cross, and dishonored by death (Luke XXIII). Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked (I John II).

Sing, then, the Song of Ascents, and ascend step by step; do not skip any step by a hasty leap, because whoever stumbles over one has become guilty of all (James II).

Be poor in spirit, therefore, and do not think that this first step may be reached lightly, since it requires great care to leave the world and worldly things and to withdraw heart, body, and attention from their customary course. Whoever is poor in spirit rejoices in lowliness, embraces humility, and tramples upon earthly desires.

But because that poverty is detestable which, swelling with a kingly spirit, sows discord, serves quarrels, and delights in slanderous speech, we must fly upward to the sublimity of the second step, so that we may be gentle. Gentle is the one who returns no evil for evil. When injured, he asks forgiveness and does good to those who injure him.

Nor should anyone who has perhaps ascended this step boast of complete victory, since it must be mourned with every fountain of tears that we have served for so long in mud and clay under the power of Pharaoh; and therefore blessed are those who mourn.

The mourning of the saints, however, does not concern the loss of possessions, bodily weakness, or the ferocity of superior power. They mourn sins, whether their own or others’; the ruin of the world; the weakening of faith; contempt for justice; the abundance of iniquity; and the delay of the kingdom.

Nor should the limit of perfection be placed here, since perfect righteousness is to love one’s neighbor as oneself, and to correct that neighbor’s faults with free discernment and discerning freedom. Whoever, out of regard for the person he represents, does not resist sinners should know that he is to be condemned for his own silence.

He therefore hungers and thirsts for righteousness who destroys vices and builds virtues: sober toward himself, just toward his neighbor, devout toward God. His soul is burned by zeal for the house of God, and he sings with the righteous: “Your zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

But since, according to the orator’s saying, “the highest law is often malice,” and inconsiderate justice gives birth to ruin, it therefore follows: “Blessed are the merciful.” Mercy is a beautiful ornament of human nature; whoever lacks it degenerates badly and denies that he is human. True mercy exists when mercy triumphs over judgment, when by generosity of means, good will, instruction in the word, or the example of action, we refresh the body and soul of our neighbor.

But when we have already begun to walk from glory to glory, we must proceed from the glory of our own heart toward glorifying our neighbor’s heart; we must be cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit, and purely and thoroughly wiped free from every stain of this world, as follows: “Blessed are the pure in heart.” Who will boast that he has a pure heart? (Prov. XX.) The heart of man is crooked and inscrutable. Who can know it? (Jer. XVII.) It is difficult to cleanse it, since, lurking in its hidden places, it receives the armies of invading thoughts, even when we resist them greatly but are by no means able to withstand them.

Therefore, he has a pure heart who, after calming the movements of both persons—the outward and the inward man—not only restrains the passions but does not know them; fortified by the natural course of good works, crucified to the world, and with the world crucified to him (Gal. II). Few, however, are those into whom such a fullness of grace has poured itself. Whoever they are, they are already near the prize of the heavenly calling, if they strive to make peace among those who are at odds, with the peace by which they themselves have been restored, and to say with the Prophet: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Ps. CXIX). Therefore it is added: “Blessed are the peacemakers”—not merely those who are peaceful, but those who make peace and sow the seeds of concord.

But since we often either abandon justice or fail to defend it once abandoned, whether through flattery of the powerful or love of temporal things, the right hand must be extended toward the goal of the race, so that for justice—not only our own but also another’s—we may suffer persecution and resist even unto blood, or even unto death. This is what follows: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice.”

What follows after this? Here we cling to the Lord and become one spirit with him. Here the cloud is torn apart and prayer passes through. Here, with unveiled face, we behold the glory of the Lord. Here are the sweetness of the Spirit, the heart’s delight, and the mind’s jubilation. “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

Let us see whether, perhaps, by some continuity of reasoning, we can assign these beatitudes to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Poverty of spirit is generated by the fear of God, which pricks the soul, draws blood, and compels us to seek medicine. “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and brought forth; we produced the spirit of salvation upon the earth”—that is, the spirit of poverty, says the prophet Isaiah (Isa. XXVI), or rather, the Lord through Isaiah. This makes us either abandon worldly things or cease to desire them, “a nail driving out a nail,” and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.

Piety, however, makes people meek, when, having poured a gentler spirit over us, it introduces us into the chamber of gentleness. For those who are made fierce by pride, exalted in their own eyes, burning with envy, biting one another and consumed by one another—how can they be clothed with the garment of mitigating piety? Moreover, knowledge gives birth to mourning. We know that a distinctive form of knowledge is to recall our years in the bitterness of our soul (Isa. XXXVIII), and to bewail our own sins with many streams of tears.

From fortitude, on the other hand, hunger and thirst for justice are born, since it requires no small strength to die for the freedom of justice, let alone to speak for it; and when God is at issue, neither to be enticed by blandishments nor moved by terror. Counsel gives birth to mercy, since the highest purpose of all counsel is to advise everyone and to lift up, with the kindly hand of mercy, the weaknesses both of souls and of bodies.

Purity of heart descends from purity of understanding, which cleanses the heart’s receptacles and cuts away its hidden affections with the sharpest sickle of vigilance. Moreover, the peacemaker is born from the summit of Wisdom itself, conformed to that Wisdom which, by the price of its blood, made peace both on earth and in heaven.

[Col. 0814D] Perhaps also, if we examine the matter more carefully, we shall be able to link them once again with the seven petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer. For those embrace poverty of spirit through fear of the Lord who desire that the Lord’s name be sanctified in them, and say with the Psalmist: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. LXXXV). Who, however, are the meek except those whom piety has imbued, who frequently ask with patience and gentleness that the kingdom of God may come, desiring to be released and to be with Christ? (Phil. I.) To all of them the saint cries out: “Wait for the Lord, and keep his way, and he will exalt you, so that you may possess the land as an inheritance” (Ps. XXXVI); for the land of the living is promised to be possessed.

But who are those who mourn except those whom saving knowledge instructs, who, through the waves of devout tears, desire that God’s will be done on earth as in heaven, among human beings as among angels? Hunger and thirst for justice, moreover, are generated by strength of mind, which seeks its daily bread from the very hands of God—the bread, namely, that strengthens the human heart.

Who also are the merciful except those who, according to their means, give counsel to everyone, and with bold conscience make a covenant with God, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”? But only the most lucid understanding perceives the pure in heart. Such understanding is not led into temptation, and asks from the Father of lights not that it should not be tempted, but that it should not be led into temptation, scattering the bands of business affairs that plunder it.

Peace-making, however, descends from Wisdom itself, where we are delivered from evil and cleansed from the influx of every iniquity. These are the seven beatitudes, the seven gifts, the seven petitions, the seven lampstands, the seven lamps, the seven vessels of infusion, and the seven ears of grain, along with the other things that the authoritative tradition of Scripture has consecrated in the citadel of the number seven.

As a young man, therefore, I have dared to explain the entire sequence of this reading, requested—indeed compelled—by the prayers and command of those whom I could neither wish nor be able to resist. But, to dwell somewhat upon the present solemnity, this is a festival overflowing with favorable and honey-sweet delight, in which all his saints offer praise to God and the whole world resounds with a clear voice.

These are the advocates whom we have with the Judge. Whoever has them interceding for him need not fear a capital sentence.

Let us therefore flee to proven aids, and let the enormity of our sins not deter us, because their mercy is greater than our impiety. They are counselors of our King, and often resist his anger; nor do they abandon us in time of trouble. For they know where they have left us and to how many ambushes of enemies we are exposed.

Let us therefore sigh toward the memory of them, so that they may protect us beneath the shadow of their wings until iniquity passes, and may lead us to the Bridegroom of the Church, who is God, blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON LVI. ON SAINT MARTIN, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR (11 NOVEMBER)

[Col. 0815D] That noble confessor—the glory of priests, the jewel of bishops, the model of clerics, the light of monks—has appointed a solemn day for our entire community. This is Martin, exalted by the power of miracles, who filled the globe with the light of his knowledge. Egypt, the mother of religion and the most fertile nurse of hermits, set Martin before such sons as an example.

The fame of his name grew immensely and dared to break into the very dignity of the apostles, whose hands handled the Word of life (1 John I), who proclaimed the Son of Man among the sons of men through the ministry of a blessed voice. The memory of so great a pontiff spread throughout the whole earth, and wherever faith in Christ resounds, the life of Martin resounds.

The emperor is glorified in the soldier, and the soldier is praised in the emperor. The Church of Tours bears witness to this: it contains his bodily treasure and extends its possessions from sea to sea. Kings have enriched it, princes have adorned it, and the Roman pontiffs have provided for it the heights of supreme liberty.

The confessor’s glory is further increased by the fact that foundations of several episcopal sees were laid in his honor—something which, unless I am mistaken, is not read of another confessor. The radiance of his glory sparkles far and wide, and from distant regions of the world people hasten to the presence of his holy body.

The clemency of the Godhead has mercifully provided for both our kings and our kingdom, placing so great a light here as a remedy for sins throughout the ages. Severus, an illustrious orator, so ennobled his deeds and life by his eloquence that he presented the history with a fully truthful account and adorned it in many ways according to the laws of rhetoric.

And now what can our dry and barren tongue dare to murmur about his praises, whose praise fills the earth?

Yet lest we seem exempt from every kind of discourse amid such great joys, we must return to the Gospel reading, in which the wisdom of God the Father enclosed, within the brevity of three words, the whole sum of human perfection. For he says: “See, keep watch, and pray.”

He who sees all things exhorts us, setting aside bodily eyes, to see with the light of the mind, through those eyes of which it is said through Solomon: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. II). He therefore commands us to enter alone into the solitude of our heart and to turn over the burdens of our former sins, by which we have been polluted and entangled.

First, then, let us see within ourselves the abundance of sins. “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be gracious to my sin, for it is great” (Ps. XXIV), says that unique consecrated servant of the eternal King. We have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea, and our sins have been multiplied. Do you strive to count innumerable things and to place in a sum what exceeds every sum?

Behold, a great heap, a violent torrent; such misery cannot be scattered, because our iniquities have risen above our head (Ps. XXXVII). We walked with an outstretched neck; our eyes are full of vanity, our ears of detraction. Let us smell not the fragrance of perfumes in which the bride boasts that she runs, but the smell of death unto death; for our mouths are described as full of cursing and bitterness.

Our hands are full of blood; our feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in our ways, and the way of peace has been cast aside; there is no fear of God before our eyes (Ps. XIII).

What, then, must be done, in whom can we hope, and to where must we flee? We must stand amid this heap, not of new but of old harvests (Ezek. III), and behold the vision that must be feared. Let us set ourselves before our own eyes, lest the Judge eventually rebuke us and set us before our own face.

In this vision of God, a whirlwind appears to us, for, according to the just man, “the paths of their steps are wrapped up” (Job VI). Do not think this vision should be counted among small things, since it leads to the vision of cherubim and winged creatures, and introduces us into the very sight of the One who rules.

Having seen, then, the abundance of our sins, let us secondly see our negligence. We have dragged our sins along like a long rope; blood has touched blood, and we have pretended not to notice. There was wound, bruise, and swelling sore, and we did not look upon it (Isa. I).

The zeal of God withdrew from us, and we despised it. Thus, adding negligence to the multitude of sins, we have blocked our own path to confession. We avoid the paths of justice, not merely neglecting them but even boasting of our negligence, according to the saying of the wisest man:

“Those who do evil rejoice and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II).

Do you wish to know that from the abundance of sins the worst daughter, negligence, is born? “When the sinner has come into the depths of evil, he despises” (Prov. XVIII). On the contrary, whoever fears God neglects nothing, because “whoever despises small things will gradually fall.” The multitude of sins gives rise to negligence; negligence to contempt; contempt threatens everlasting death.

Third, see the patience and long-suffering of our God. “You have done these things, and I was silent” (Prov. XV). He sees all things and hears all things, and nothing is hidden from his eyes, of whom it is said: “The eyes of the Lord behold the good and the wicked in every place” (Ps. LXXIV).

You feared the eyes of human beings, but did not dread the eyes of the Most High? Behold, he himself knew all the latest things and the ancient things. Neither in the east nor in the west nor in the desert mountains is there a place of escape, because God is judge.

He saw your deeds, the comings and goings of your crimes, and restrained his anger. Heaven did not thunder; water did not overwhelm you; the earth did not swallow you. Although the whole earth is full of the glory of the Lord, you vomited your misery into his glory and did not revere the Lord who was present, practicing your impurities before such purity.

But what did he himself do? “I,” he says, “was as though I did not see.” Did he reveal your disgrace to any of his ministers, who are avengers of his anger and were appointed for this very purpose? Behold, he sees and is silent; he sees and does not disclose; he sees and does not judge; he sees and does not avenge; he sees and pretends not to see. He calls, and you do not hear; he promises, and you despise; he threatens, and you do not fear. You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath.

Although he is a just and powerful judge, he is very patient and does not grow angry every day (Ps. VII). Behold, he restrains his anger, represses his fury, turns away his eyes, and spares sinners; yet they gather all these things against themselves for their own judgment, guilty of everything.

Will he who has been so silent and quiet always remain silent? Or have you not read that he will come to judgment, casting aside patience, knowing no humility, and unaware of mercy?

You have watched him patiently silent; watch also him speaking impatiently: “Like a woman in labor,” he says, “I will speak” [Col. 0818A] (Isa. XLII). You have seen him overlooking; see also him counting every smallest thing. “You have counted,” he says, “the traces of my feet” (Job XIII).

What place of hope will there be when the Judge comes, he who stood beneath a judge, with trumpets sounding, angels crying aloud, and the elements burning? To whose help shall we flee when, with the winds raging across the sky, the world’s structure is torn apart, and blazing fire mingles heaven and earth in final conflagrations?

He himself will come with great power and majesty—not with sweetness and humility, because there his right hand will be full of justice, whereas here it has sown and scattered mercy. Then that merciful eye will not spare and will not pity; rather, clothed in anger, filled with fury, and full of cruelty, it will strike and kill.

But what will sinners do? Seeing, they will be shaken with terrible yet incorrigible fear, hearing that dreadful thunder: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

How great, do you think, will be the pain of being excluded from the face of God, of seeing God and losing him, when the King of glory enters the lofty city, while every hope of mercy has been sealed forever against wretched sinners?

Whoever you are, therefore, who despise the riches of God’s goodness and patience, reread the text of the Epistle to the Romans (Rom. V), and it will tell you more fully that you have not escaped God’s judgment.

Fourth, look upon his mercy, even though you have sinned, even though you have neglected and provoked God’s patience. He is nevertheless ready to show mercy whenever you wish, to return to the one who returns to him, to forget and cover your sins, and to cast them into the depths of the sea.

There will be no delay between the one who confesses and the one who forgives, between the one who groans and the one who hears his groans, because he is kind and merciful. Human beings are often quick to anger and slow to mercy; God, however, is slow to anger and quick to show mercy.

Human beings bring back the reproaches that they have forgiven; but when God has forgiven, it is as though the offense had never existed. We frequently keep watch at the thresholds of the powerful, without free access to speak with them; and if we have committed some offense, we make amends with suppliant eyes, troubled faces, and humble words.

Yet they often disdain those prostrate at their feet with haughty eyes and a disdainful shoulder, and do not even wish to look upon them.

The Lord Jesus is not like this. He speaks more willingly with me than I with him; I find him whenever I seek him; he comes out to meet me with bread when I am fleeing; he shows me a cheerful face; he embraces my repentance just as he embraces innocence—everywhere joyful, everywhere good, everywhere kind, everywhere sweet, with the great abundance of his sweetness.

He does not raise his eyebrows, avert his eyes, or twist his face; he does not utter inflated words. Rather, he comes out to meet the returning sinner and runs to embrace him, weeping upon my neck. He commands that the first robe be brought forth, that the ring of understanding be given (Luke XV), that my feet be shod in the preparation of the Gospel (Eph. VI), that I be recalled to heavenly joys amid chorus and symphony, and that the fattened calf be killed for the forgiveness of my sins.

You see, therefore, how long God’s patience is and how swift his mercy. “Long-suffering,” says the saint, “and very merciful” (Ps. CII). Gladly, therefore, I flee to you, Lord Jesus, who endure for a long time and show mercy swiftly, because you are God and not man, as the prophet says (Hos. XI), one who would preserve anger, conceal malice, and seek revenge.

In addition, we must consider this within the mercy of the merciful one: people of this world forgive once, twice, or perhaps seven or ten times; but he forgives a thousand times in a day, if that were possible, whatever we commit—and this for as long as we live, for as long as we wander away from him.

Having seen, then, the things we have enumerated, lift your eyes also to behold the Lord’s generosity, or his familiarity. If we had done something displeasing to a very powerful person, would he judge us worthy of speaking with him again, let alone of receiving anything from him, or of enjoying his familiarity?

We are burdensome to him even to look upon, and we count it a great favor if he merely refrains from harming us. Although we defend our offense with many devoted services, the memory of the injury nevertheless continually passes before his eyes, and it cannot be erased either by benefit, service, or even the passage of time.

Is my God, my mercy, like this? Far from it. For he is accustomed to honor penitents more than the innocent, those who return more than those who remain, because a fervent penitent is more devoted than a lukewarm innocent person: the former has material for fervor, the latter for lukewarmness.

Perhaps I may be accused of presumption because, contrary to the Apostle’s command, I introduce novelties of expression. But I have testimonies at hand—not few or insignificant—which themselves have become exceedingly credible and are able to satisfy anyone who murmurs.

The apostle Peter—not just any apostle, but the prince of the apostles, to whom the principate of heaven and earth was entrusted (Matt. XVI)—was he not from the company of penitents and from the lot of the gravely unjust? Was he not the one who denied God, abandoned his teacher, deserted his friend, and broke his promise? He began to detest and swear that he did not know the man (Matt. XXVI), adding perjury to denial and crime to crime.

He fell, but he was not shattered, because the Lord placed his hand beneath him. See what Scripture says: “The Lord looked upon Peter” (ibid.). Christ’s look was followed by Peter’s weeping, and the bitterness of his tears restored the sweetness of his former dignity.

Blessed are your tears, holy apostle: they wash away guilt, restore rank, cancel debts, and entrust greater things. Mercy looked upon him, and impiety withdrew; his former familiarity was restored.

Finally: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep” (John XXI)—and sayings like this: what are they except great proofs of familiarity?

And that singular instrument of the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord found according to his own heart, to whom the uncertain and hidden things of God’s wisdom were revealed—was he not marked and named as both a murderer, an adulterer, and a traitor?

But see how swiftly, by a leap of repentance, he sprang back to the citadel of innocence, and so bound up his great wounds that no trace remained—not even of the wound’s scar. Rebuked by the prophet and stung by the parable’s retort, he said: “I have sinned” (2 Sam. XII). And he immediately replied from the treasury of divine mercy: “The Lord has taken away your sin, and you shall not die” (ibid.).

The sin was transferred and removed—the sin that divided David from God. Once it had been taken away, David was again the same as before.

Let that Chosen Vessel also be added, who flew upon the wings of the winds, who labored more than all others, to whom the words of God were entrusted. Was he not said to have burned more ardently than the others against the primitive Church? (1 Cor. XV.) The Acts of the Apostles testify how many evils he inflicted upon God’s saints in Jerusalem.

Yet he who inflicted such great evils afterward suffered so much for Christ’s name and shines in the firmament of heaven; there is no jewel more precious in the crown of the eternal King.

Let that woman also approach who had been burdened with seven demons—that is, with every vice—to whom, because she loved much, much was forgiven; she was the first to see the Lord risen from the dead, the apostle of the apostles, specially beloved by the Savior (Mark XVI).

Now let the entire choir of the innocent come, and let all virginal purity assemble: who will dare aspire to the glory of these people, let alone surpass it?

Therefore I will confess to you, Lord Jesus, and give praise to your name, because with you there is forgiveness, and because of your law I have waited for you, Lord (Ps. CXXIX).

What is this law, and what is this forgiveness? It is that, although offended, you promise to be merciful; you admit repentance; you refrain from punishing. Great, therefore, is the power of true repentance, since Ambrose says: “I have found more easily those who preserved innocence than those who performed fitting repentance.”

See also, sixth, his protection, because unless he himself guards us, we keep watch in vain.

Having completed these six visions, let us pass to the Savior’s second word: “Keep watch.”

We must keep watch entirely and drive sleep from our eyes, because many robbers beset our road with poisoned missiles and must be feared; they refuse to let anyone pass without attempting an assault. For we have three chief enemies, persuaders of ruin: the flesh, the devil, and the world. Of these, the first two, even if they sometimes cease, never let us go; the third—the devil—exercises such implacable hatred against us that we can never wrest from him a truce, not even for the blink of an eye.

But, to quote that orator whose language everywhere bears the scent of Cicero: this is a daily and uncertain combat, from which innumerable wounds arise, promising no easy healing; beneath it there is frequent falling and difficult recovery; from it victory is rare and never secure; toward us it has an always wicked will and the mastery of deception.

Who can keep watch against this enemy unless that Watchman from the night comes to our aid? For we are not sufficient by ourselves; indeed, we fail if we trust in ourselves.

[Col. 0821A] Consider, moreover, how this invisible enemy enters single combat, what weapons he carries, how powerful they are, and with what whirlwind he hurls his spear. Recall the Book of Job and the history of the Kings, and consider both the armed man and his weapons, because the one who is Goliath in the Book of Kings is the devil in the kingdom of Christians.

He has the spear of pleasure, the shield of hardness, the breastplate of despair, the sword of slaughter, and pride as his arm-bearer. Pride goes before him, reproaches the armies of the living God, and the enemy says: “I will pursue and overtake them; I will divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled” (Exod. XV).

But what of you? Take up the apostolic armor: the shield of faith, the breastplate of justice, the sword of the Spirit, and the spear of vigilance. Let humility go before you, and say: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail” (Ps. VII).

O Lord Jesus, is the battle between a human being and a demon equal—between the twofold and the single, the strong and the weak? “Call upon me in the day of trouble,” says the Lord, “and I will deliver you, and you shall honor me” (Ps. XLIX).

I call upon you, Savior. Take up arms and shield (Ps. XXXIV), so that I may see the stronger armed man against the strong armed man, and that you may crush the Assyrian in your land. Once the battle has been joined, he will shatter your enemies like dust before the face of the wind and erase them like mud in the streets (Ps. LXXXII).

Against this enemy, therefore, one must keep watch in such a way that one always fears the renewed battle but does not despair of victory.

The flesh, under the guise of necessity, conceals the image of its frenzied tumult. Now filled with a variety of dishes, now changing expensive wines, it begins to revel; once the reins have been loosened, it rushes headlong toward destruction.

The passions immediately grow savage again; thoughts rebel; images appear before us, and we paint upon our hearts what cannot be erased for many days. For we are stuffed, not strengthened; filled, but not nourished; and we are stretched out in both body and heart. Thus the satirist’s saying is fulfilled:

“There is no distinction between the groin and the head.”

I will spare words, because an obscene judgment can be explained only in obscene words, and each of us knows perfectly well what we either keep silent about or wish to pass over. A meager table, harsher food, and simpler drink strengthen the body, fortify the spirit, and restore greater liveliness to the condition of both persons—the outward and the inward.

But what does the world do? It offers us whatever is beautiful to the sight, the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition, so that it may ensnare the wretched, strangle those who have been ensnared, and wrap those who have been strangled in everlasting fires.

It tempts us with manifold ambushes: above, through pride; below, through lust; on the right, through prosperity; on the left, through adversity; in front, through worldly desire; behind, through the memory of past vices; and in circular motion, through the entanglement of the senses.

It is therefore necessary to keep watch against such little thieves and against the murderous hand, and to say with Isaiah: “Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand continually by day; and upon my guard I stand throughout the nights” (Isa. XXI).

Nor is it enough merely to stand; we must stand armed with that armor of which the Apostle says: “Put on the armor of God” (Eph. VI).

Another Cicero of our times, whom I mentioned above, flowering everywhere with the blossoms of eloquence, gilded this armor with the following most brilliant passages.

If the spirits of fable and the enchanting movements of the flesh make a din around you, take confidence and say: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Ps. CXVIII).

If you feel the flesh growing hot and wishing to fly back to its follies, stand firm and say: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, O Lord” (ibid.).

If you begin to hate poverty and begin to be stirred by desire for riches, awaken and say: “Woe to you, rich, who have your consolation here” (Matt. VIII).

If a flatterer charms you and your spirit grows cheerful at the praises of the common people, take courage and say: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. CXL).

If you are prompted to postpone your resolve until a future time, rise up and say: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (2 Pet. III).

If raging gluttony recommends more elaborate dishes to you, kick back and say: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. XIV).

By such rebukes, as by certain blows, the enemies flee; the memory of pleasures slips away; the throat of the flesh grows silent; the beginnings of holy conduct grow strong; the world is despised; the ancient enemy is overcome.

Thus, seeing and keeping watch, make a threefold cord that is not easily broken, and pass on to prayers. Enter the inner sanctuary of the veil with our great High Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, who forgives all your iniquities and stands before the face of God on your behalf.

But once admitted, do not thrust yourself boldly and presumptuously before the eyes of Majesty. Rather, shaken by the deepest humility and trembling, marvel that you have been permitted to approach such great wonders at all.

Let prayer, therefore, be modest, so that we may blush for our sins and show reverence of such magnitude; pure, so that we may seek nothing from him except himself; devoted, so that we may extend it in the richness of the spirit; broad, so that we may extend it even to our enemies; continuous, so that it may not become weaker through interruption; peaceful, so that it may not be submerged by turbulent waves of thought.

I confess that I have exceeded the proper measure and have not feared burdening your ears more than usual, while my style has extended into length. But I know that you listened patiently as I discoursed on the patience of him who is God, blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON LVII. I. ON SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE (30 NOVEMBER)

Today, dearest brothers, the votive festival of blessed Andrew has shone forth for us. Amid the very darkness of icy winter, it has introduced a joyful serenity into our minds; and while the harshness of the air freezes outside, hearing the victory of so great a warrior stirs pious hearts to the battle-line of spiritual combat and inflames the distinguished spirits of Christ’s soldiers with the fire of divine love.

Among all forms of martyrdom, that one is judged nobler and, not undeservedly, foremost which is known to have been consecrated in our Redeemer himself, the head of the martyrs. Therefore, when divine providence willed Peter and Andrew to be perfected through the punishment of the cross, it made them, among the other apostles—although all share one power and dignity—in a certain way outstanding and conspicuous. For the cross, which sent the King ahead with his scepter, afterward raised both soldiers to their reward.

O blessed brotherhood! Just as one blood relationship brought them forth into the world, so the same triumphant death sent them as victors to the stars; and those whom nature produced as companions of one race in this life, the cross gave birth to as equals in that eternal blessedness.

They receive on earth the same nobility and in heaven the same elevation of lineage. For those who here are sons of John are there sons of the cross. These are the sons of Korah, who are named at the beginning of certain psalms. For the cross, which took them from this life when they died, brought them as new citizens, reborn with triumphal glory, into the heavenly Jerusalem.

Andrew is placed second in the catalogue of the apostolic senate, yet according to the Gospel he is found to have been the first to recognize the Lord. The evangelist John says:

“When John was standing there, and two of his disciples, looking upon Jesus as he walked by, he said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God.’ And the two disciples, hearing him speak, followed Jesus.”

A little later he says: “Now Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard this from John and had followed him.”

Then it follows: “He first found his brother Simon and said to him: ‘We have found the Messiah,’ which is translated ‘Christ’; and he brought him to Jesus” (John I).

Behold, Andrew bears fruit amid the very beginnings of his new apprenticeship and already becomes a preacher of the truth, although he was scarcely yet a hearer of it. Having become a new disciple, he is not content with his own salvation; he seeks fellow disciples, and brotherly love extends itself toward winning others.

He finds the treasure and rejoices in revealing it to others; he considers it theft to possess it without companions. Finally, the new recruit displays favorable and splendid signs of future character: at the very beginning of his recent conversion, he immediately teaches what he has learned and faithfully distributes what he has received.

The new and wondrous announcement visibly shows him to be proclaiming the one who was destined to be revealed, whom the oracles of so many prophets had foretold as coming.

Andrew certainly became the bearer of a great mystery to his brother. He testified that he had found the one whom, from the beginning of the world, all the saints had awaited with great desire and yet had been unable to see.

This was not granted to the patriarch Jacob, who said: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. XLIX). Nor was it granted to Abraham, to whom the divine promise was made that all the nations would inherit in his seed (Gen. XXII).

O how highly the distinguished prophet Isaiah would have valued this, if he had been permitted to aspire to such a spectacle! For he burned with the ardor of so great a desire, demanding the Mediator’s coming, and, impatient with what seemed a tedious delay, cried out in anguish:

“If only you would tear open the heavens and descend! At your presence the mountains would melt away; as things melt in the burning of fire, the waters would burn with fire, so that your name might be made known to your enemies” (Isa. LXIV).

How terrible and vehemently this trumpet-like voice resounded in Peter’s heart, and, flashing unexpectedly like a sudden bolt of lightning, struck him with astonishment: “We have found,” he said, “the Messiah, who is called Christ” (John I).

To wage war, the King of glory had come alone, and therefore he was gradually acquiring soldiers for the battle line. For he had come to overcome, by arriving upon him, the strong man fully armed, and to take away all the weapons in which he trusted (Luke XI). He had come to rescue captive humanity, oppressed beneath the yoke of the devil’s tyranny, and to restore it to the privileges of its ancient freedom. He had come to release his Israel from the bondage of the ancient Pharaoh, and, as a guide going before them with a strong and mighty hand, to bring them into a land flowing with milk and honey. Yet he did not choose as his assistants men distinguished by triumphal titles, vigorous warriors, riders of snorting horses, or, finally, philosophers and eloquent speakers, but carriers of nets and rowers of a very small boat, so that victory might be attributed solely to divine power, not to human strength.

This victory was prefigured by the ancient overthrow of the city of Jericho, when its most strongly fortified walls collapsed—not under the missiles of weapons, not under firebrands, and certainly not under any engines of war, but at the uproar of the shouting people and the blare of the trumpets (Joshua XVI). For the Lord had commanded Joshua that armed warriors should go before the ark of the covenant, while seven priests should sound seven trumpets, and that they should likewise circle the walls of Jericho for seven days. Therefore, on the seventh day, when the shouting of the people was mingled with the blaring trumpets, Jericho immediately collapsed from its foundations and was overthrown.

What is the meaning, then, of the fact that, for capturing the city, no sword is drawn, no weapons are brandished, no spear is thrown, and no military line is massed for the assault, but only the priests’ trumpets are sounded, so that victory over the conquered enemies is obtained not now by the right of war but rather by the power of the sacrament? [Col. 0824D] It would surely seem the absurdity of madness if an evident victory had not followed. But by Jericho—which means “moon”—the world is not inappropriately signified, since it ends through the fleeting moments of time, as though through monthly diminishments. The holy ark was the Church; the trumpets, however, are the apostles, or the five holy teachers of the Church. While, through their admonitions, the Church continually strives to fight against the allurements of the flesh and the ambushes of the ancient enemy, we are urged, as though to the battle line and the waging of war, by the blasts of trumpets. These trumpets are said to have been seven because the holy preachers are filled with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Through the succession of seven days, moreover, the whole period of our mortality unfolds.

[Col. 0825A] Thus the priests carrying the ark and sounding the trumpets circle the city of Jericho for seven days, and its walls fall through the presence of the ark and the sound of the trumpets. For, during the course of this mortal life, while the holy Church moves throughout the whole world and is enlarged, through the persistence of holy preaching all the pride of the exalted world is broken, and every obstacle of unbelief is overthrown.

It should also be noted that armed soldiers are ordered to go with the priests, so that those to whom the duty of producing the trumpet blast has not been assigned may in no way consider themselves removed from the battle. Thus even those who do not preach should nevertheless walk always armed and watchful against the ambushes of the hidden enemy. The leaders and princes of this warfare, therefore, are the holy [Col. 0825B] apostles, who carry the ark of the covenant around the walls of Jericho with the sound of the trumpets, because throughout the whole circuit of the world they spread the sacraments of the Church through the ministry of holy preaching. “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII). When six days have passed, on the seventh day at last the king of Jericho is consumed, together with all the people, by the devouring sword, because on the last day the devil, who is the king of pride, together with all his followers, is condemned to everlasting death by something like the sword of divine judgment. Then what the Apostle says will take place: “When he has abolished every principality and every power and virtue, last of all the enemy death will be destroyed” (I Corinthians XV).

Only the house of Rahab the prostitute [Col. 0825C] escaped; a scarlet cord distinguished it in the window. That house prefigures the one Church, which has been purified from the shame of fornication through the window of confession, in the remission of sins. It is plainly delivered from the common destruction of the perishing world, because she ties a scarlet cord in the window of her house, while she does not cease to carry in the mouth of her body the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X). The cord, moreover, was tied to the house, but it was seen outside, because faith in the Lord’s cross is retained in the heart and brought forth by confession of the mouth. While the rest were perishing, all who were found in that house [Col. 0825D] escaped the danger of death; for just as all the elect are saved within the Church, so no one can be found safe outside the Church.

But perhaps it may be asked how both the ark, which surrounded and besieged the city, and Rahab’s house, which was attached to its walls, can each signify one and the same Church, since the ark plainly besieges and attacks, whereas the house seems to be besieged. This question is easily solved if one carefully considers the diversity that exists among the members of the Church. The Church attacks the Church when preachers, teachers, rulers, and those who obey appear to proceed from one source of divine regeneration and, finally, to complete one body of the Church as different members. To this Church [Col. 0826A] the Psalmist says: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you.” These are surely the apostles, who hurled against the Jericho of human pride such powerful and mighty thunderbolts of their preaching.

The fathers and sons of one and the same Church appear, in a certain sense, to be both fathers and sons: sons, that is, of the patriarchs and prophets; fathers, however, of all the elect who came afterward. Hence Moses is commanded by the divine voice to cast silver bases and to erect gilded boards above them (Exodus XXVI). What, then, are signified by the silver bases except the order of the prophets? Since they were the first to speak about the sacrament of the Church, we regard them as certain bases rising from the foundation and supporting the weights of the structure placed upon them.

[Col. 0826B] What, then, are signified by the boards except the holy apostles, who were spread most extensively throughout the world by their preaching? The apostles’ teaching rests, as it were, upon certain bases—the prophetic preaching—and is firmly strengthened by their authority for the stability of its structure. Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board, because, while the holy prophets agree with one another in their words concerning the sacrament of the future Church and the apostles who follow build upon what they themselves have built, and while they disagree with one another in nothing, they fix the apostles more firmly upon themselves. Nor is it without reason that the bases by which the prophets are signified are commanded to be cast from silver. The brightness of silver is preserved through use, but without use it turns black. Likewise, before the apostles’ preaching made them shine, the sayings of the prophets, because they were not in use for spiritual understanding and could not be seen on account of their obscurity, remained, as it were, black. But after the hand of apostolic preaching wiped away the obscurity of the prophecies, whatever light lay hidden in them shone forth, and their mystical meanings were put to use, because the apostles clearly announced that the words had already been set forth in realities. Rightly, therefore, both silver bases and gilded boards are commanded to be made, because the apostolic precepts are far clearer than the prophetic oracles.

To return, then, to what was said above: it is not inappropriate if both the ark and the prostitute’s house, which is besieged, appear to express one and the same Church, [Col. 0826D] since, as has been said, the members of that same Church are diverse: some besieging through the sphere of holy preaching; others to be overwhelmed by the missiles of saving doctrine, because of the defenses of their unbelief or wickedness; some already belonging to the household; others still estranged through the turning away of evil conduct. Isaiah had already perceived this conflict as a testimony to spiritual warfare when, after clearly describing the Savior’s coming, he immediately added: “The heart of Egypt will waste away within it, and I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians; and a man will fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, and city against city, kingdom against kingdom; and the spirit of Egypt will be torn apart within its inward parts” (Isaiah XIX).

Since, therefore, through the siege of apostolic preaching, dearest brothers, we have been rescued from the slaughter of perishing Jericho—indeed, divinely delivered from the destruction of overturned paganism—let us not find it burdensome to follow our leaders wherever they go before us; let nothing that they command for our salvation seem burdensome.

Behold, the blessed apostles Peter and Andrew, at the single command of the Lord who ordered them, did not hesitate to leave everything they possessed, so that they might deserve to exchange earthly things for heavenly ones. They abandon what is before their eyes in order to receive invisible goods. They set aside what they possessed and attain what they hoped for; through suffering they pass to the kingdom, and through the momentary gallows of the cross they are raised to the joys of eternal life. They reserve nothing for themselves in their pilgrimage, so that when they arrive at their homeland they may find everything at once. Thus, through “the changing of the right hand of the Most High,” this was accomplished for them: those who then appeared rejected and humble are now judges of souls and senators of the heavenly court. Once possessors of worthless nets, they now hold the chief place of glory in the heavenly kingdoms. Those whom, while placed on earth, the abundance of earthly things had left destitute now possess the monarchy of the whole world and preside over judicial authority in that heavenly Jerusalem. Those who had been almost the last of human beings are now fellow citizens and companions of the angels. Indeed, they adhered to the footsteps of a good teacher and a gracious rewarder, who gave them gold in place of dung, everything in place of nothing, light in place of darkness, and reality in place of a dream. For them he himself is the reward in heaven, and on earth he also subjects to them the rights of all kingdoms.

[Col. 0827C] By this way, therefore, my brothers, the way by which they went before us, let us follow if we wish to reach the place where they are. Walking straight after them, let us leave Jericho, overwhelmed [overthrown] and destroyed by their siege, in such a way that we do not appropriate anything from its ban. For that Jesus the son of Nun forbids anyone to desire anything from Jericho’s possessions (Joshua VI). Our Jesus also forbids us—the ancient Savior, certainly—to love anything that belongs to the world. “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matthew VI), he says. And through his apostle: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (I John I). Let us not, therefore, after the example of the wretched Achan, steal anything from Jericho’s ban (Joshua VII), so that we may not insert anything from the dissolute habits of worldly conduct into ecclesiastical discipline. Let us not take the cloak, so that after the garment of faith we may in no way put on the dress of secular conduct. Let us not take the silver shekels, so that, having stored up the eternal treasure in heaven, we may not place any temporal money in a purse through ambition. Finally, let us not take the golden rod, so that we may not introduce into Christ’s Church the carefully contrived doctrines of heretics, the weighed and tested arguments of sharply disputing philosophers, or the elaborated fictions of poets. For this is that golden rod: fashioned with polished and refined speech and clothed, as it were, in the golden brilliance of splendid eloquence. Arius, Marcion, Apelles, and the other plagues of perverse [Col. 0828A] men stole it; by trying to introduce the philosophical schools into the Church, they seemed in a certain way to provoke God’s anger against the camp of Israel. But they were buried with Achan beneath a heap of stones, because they were crushed under the most monstrous weight of sins.

But we, dearest brothers, since our philosophy is Christ, and Christ crucified, and therefore our teachers are not orators but fishermen—not crafty and eloquent, but gentle and simple—let us despise the wisdom that blinds and pursue the folly that enlightens learners. “Because,” as the Apostle says, “the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the folly of preaching to save those who believe” (I Corinthians I).

Let us therefore preserve the doctrine in its purity and apply the effectiveness of works to right faith. Let us swim through the stormy wave of worldly disturbance. Let us willingly be enclosed in the nets of such great fishermen. Let our heart grow warm at the example of such ready obedience and such fervent devotion, and let us, with divine mercy assisting, strive to fulfill what we know our teachers then did. Behold, we never read that the blessed brothers Peter and Andrew, after their conversion, clung to one another with some carnal bond more familiarly than to the others, or that they were bound together by a closer affection, or that they shared the same provinces for the sake of preaching. And, to make you marvel even more, Andrew was not distressed that, though first in faith, he became second in rank and dignity; nor was he moved by jealousy because Peter, who believed later under his leadership and to whose faith he himself had gone before, nevertheless received the rights of primacy among all the apostles. This rule of mortification the heavenly teacher set before our eyes in them; this model of true humility he displayed to us, so that we might follow him by the straight path. In those first disciples, whom he also appointed teachers of the world, he distinctly expressed the pattern of every virtue, so that until the consummation of the age every believer might direct toward them the eyes of imitation and walk along their path without deviating to either side. Thus, by holding to the life-giving streams of abundance, we may reach the fountain; by following the soldiers, we may be led by the straight road to the King, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON LVIII. II. ON SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE. (30 NOVEMBER)

Both the tranquil devotion and the attentive silence, as well as the great festivity of so great a man, urge us—indeed compel us—to say something in order to display the glory of the Godhead, the glory of apostolic dignity, and the virtue of confession. Let us give him the glory of praise (Psalm LXV), whom all nations praise, who both praises his ministers and makes them worthy of praise. He is the one whom the angels attend in order to hear the voice of his words (Psalm CII); who calls the stars, and they say, “Here we are” (Baruch III); whose hand stretched out the heavens; who founded the earth upon its stability (Psalm CIII); who walks upon the waves of the sea; who alone performs wonders (Psalm LXXI); into whom the angels desire to look. He is the one who made all things and accomplished, in all that he made, whatever he willed. To serve him is to reign. He served for us under harsh and grievous necessity, and, covering the purple of his divinity with the sackcloth of our mortality, he came poor and beggarly into our region.

Does it not seem a joke to you, Jews, pagans, heretics, and all that crowd of mockers—indeed, of madmen—when we say that the Son of God endured flesh, the cross, death, nails, and the lance? It is certainly a joke, by which we are so mocked that you yourselves are made the objects of derision:

That one and only Wise Man, who was not ignorant of this mystery, anticipated this joke in elegant speech. “I was delighting,” he says, “every day, playing before him in the inhabited world” (Proverbs VIII). He played before God when, at God’s command, he assumed flesh, and in the inhabited world because, for the redemption of the inhabited world, he delighted every day, rejoicing in each of the apostles: while to one he entrusted the kingdom of heaven (Matthew XVI), and for another he made a resting place upon his breast (John XIII). “And my delights were to be with the sons of men” (Proverbs VIII).

I had thought, Lord Jesus, that your delights would be not with the sons of men but with choirs of angels, where, in the glory of divinity, you astonish the eyes of the higher natures above thrones and powers. There you dwell in inaccessible light (I Timothy VI), and with the majesty of your radiance you conceal the assembly of the most brilliant lights. But your most merciful compassion and kindness, worthy of adoration, says that its delights are with the sons of men. These are the sons of men who hoped beneath his shelter (Psalm XXXV), whom you chose from the common people, whose feet you washed, into whom you poured your Spirit, and who carried the faith of your name throughout the fourfold world on the four evangelical chariots.

Note, however, that he says not “with men” but “with the sons of men.” I think that “men” pertain to the old man, but “sons of men” to the Son of Man, according to which understanding the young harpist sings out: “What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him?” (Psalm VIII). Do you see that he confirms God to be mindful of man, but to visit the son of man? We presume and sigh that he will show us his mercy in the sight of the sons of men, if in the meantime he protects us in the hidden place of his face from the disturbance of men (Psalm XXX).

Our teacher and Lord, whose school is on earth and whose chair is in heaven, from all those whom he chose also chose and selected the apostle Andrew. We call out his solemnity with our voices and hearts: O sweet apostle and first calling of the Savior, who is marked by so great an eminence of primacy in that apostolic choir! It does not escape us that he is, in a certain sense, most tender and dear in the hearts of the faithful. His passion pours forth with such devotion of spirit that it seems to fill the minds of those who hear with richness and fatness. [Col. 0830A] Therefore it was not without reason that it was received into a singular citadel of authority: those who saw it wrote it for the world and became ministers of the word. You know his calling, life, and passion, and now what more do you expect from me? Nevertheless, the apostolic reading urges me to speak with your reverence for a little while about it. For it says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X). Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isaiah XVIII).

Three things are set forth here: believing with the heart unto righteousness; confessing with the mouth unto salvation; and believing in him, in whom whoever believes will not be put to shame. The human heart alone is capable of reason and receptive of the mysteries of God. When purified and polished, it does not comprehend the very substance of divinity, yet it apprehends it. The heart is in the breast, the soul in the heart, the mind in the soul, faith in the mind, Christ in faith. And I think this is what the Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Ephesians III).

This faith, then, has been filtered into the purest clarity when every mystery of Christian faith, through unwavering faith in the Prince, produces no doubt in you, even though you do not see the reason. This is consummate righteousness, perfect truth, and true perfection—provided that confession of the mouth follows. For faith of the heart without faith of the mouth is either nothing or little, since the Savior says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed before the angels of God” (Luke IX). And the prophet says: “Faith has perished; it has been taken away from their mouth” [Col. 0830C] (Jeremiah VII). He did not say “from the heart” but “from the mouth,” because faith of the heart is worth nothing without faith of the mouth, nor faith of the mouth without faith of the heart: the one grants righteousness, the other salvation, because salvation cannot be separated from righteousness, nor righteousness from salvation. Therefore believe and confess; nevertheless, confess and believe, because faith is directed toward righteousness and confession is made toward salvation.

But since we have come to this subject and an occasion for confession has presented itself, what we promised elsewhere must now be given, and everything we think about confession must be set forth. Be patient, then, and, if I should extend the sermon somewhat at length, attend to what is said, because it is spoken for your benefit. For it is the way without which no one comes to the Father; whoever has lost it has lost God. When, therefore, you intend to emerge from the abyss of vices, let your chief refuge be with the one to whom your soul has been entrusted, whom God has placed over your head. Do not be troubled if he is uneducated or undiscerning, because this itself is a sign of humility, which gives birth to confession. Remember that there is no authority except from God (Romans XIII). “The scribes and Pharisees,” he says, “have sat upon the chair of Moses” (Matthew XXIII). And pay attention not to the one sitting, but to the seat; to the chair, not the person. Even if his permission should allow you to flee to another, nevertheless first reveal to him the secret of your heart, because salvation is not complete if the one to whom you ought to cling and whom you ought to honor is fled from or despised. If his instruction seems insufficient for you, the way to freedom is open: pour out your heart before another who is educated and discerning, while preserving the privilege of the one to whom you entrusted your soul.

Do not flatter yourself if a lighter penance is prescribed for one who has sinned gravely, whether by someone ignorant or by someone who conceals the truth, since whatever you do less here must be completed in the purifying fires, because the Most High seeks fruits worthy of repentance. Although you have not escaped the hands of the living God, who did not fully advise you, reason nevertheless presides as your teacher and teaches you to abstain from permitted things to the extent that you remember having committed forbidden things.

From the vestibule of this most sacred virtue, therefore, we exclude all those whom fear drives to confession, because confession extorted is not confession but confusion; whom the accusation of others draws, because that is not confession but offense; whom self-excuse leads, because that is not confession but defense; whom empty boasting seizes, because that is not confession but deception; and, likewise, whatever other plagues there may be that imitate the sanctity of so great a sacrament beneath a concealing veil. Only a heart crushed and humbled in itself and from itself can rise to the purity of this purification. I will show you one of the righteous confessing most righteously. Do you ask who it is? It is the Lord’s Psalmist: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord” (Psalm XXXII).

“I said”—that is, I resolved in my heart, not compelled or forced, but voluntarily. “My injustice,” he says, not another’s; “against myself,” accusing and charging myself. Do you see that the Lord’s holy one confesses neither out of fear of another, nor to accuse another, nor to excuse himself? “For this,” you will forgive, Lord, “the iniquity of my heart,” that is, sin. “For this every holy one will pray to you at a suitable time” (ibid.). This first germinates in the heart unto righteousness; afterward it is born in the mouth unto salvation.

Its first step is recognition of sin. “The beginning of salvation,” someone has said, “is knowledge of sin.” In this knowledge, one must consider what you have done, with how many insults you have afflicted your body, walking in the passion of desire like the nations that do not know God, possessing your vessel in impurity and dishonor, not in sanctification and honor (I Thessalonians IV). One must also consider what you have deserved: namely, that fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew XXV), and all the kinds of punishments that are heaped up and grow in those places of punishment. One must also examine what you have lost: those goods, namely, which the eye has not seen.

Terrified, therefore, by consideration of all these things, pass on to repentance. Let it grieve you that, entangled in so many and such great crimes, you have lain for so long in the mud of filth and misery. Practice repentance: discipline the body, and do not allow the enraged donkey of the flesh, rushing toward the seeds of incitement, to admit again what must be repented of, lest, repeatedly adding wound to wound, you break the bones of your soul, which the Lord guards among the righteous. “Not one of these,” he says, “will be crushed” (Psalm XXXIII). It should be noted that these two things are so joined to one another that no one can recognize himself unless he repents, and no one can repent unless he recognizes himself.

Thus, having come to know yourself and repented within yourself, fly across to the third step, namely, sorrow of heart. Then righteousness will already have been planted, with that planting which your heavenly Father planted. Grieve, therefore, because you have offended the Creator, whose law heavenly and earthly things, apart from you, preserve in unwearied attendance, while in so great a commonwealth of God you alone are an exile and do not heed the decrees of imperial majesty. Let a sharper grief also arise, because you have offended your Creator and Father, that Father who supplies you with the courses of the stars, the fertility of the earth, and the abundance of fruits. Let the sharpest grief also approach and pass through your soul: that you have despised so great a benefactor, who endured the pain of the cross so that you would not continue to endure the pains of hell. Thus, as righteousness germinates in the inner person, let the shoot burst into a tree, and let the tongue speak what knowledge was speaking.

The fourth step, then, is confession of the mouth. This must be done purely: one part of sins must not be told while another is retained; light sins must not be confessed while grave ones are denied; another must not be accused while one excuses oneself. Rather, one must say with the righteous man: “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to excuse excuses in sins” (Psalm CXL). These are words of wickedness—indeed, of grave wickedness, scarcely capable of being more serious or worse. Confession must be made faithfully and humbly, so that what sounds in the mouth is the same as what is in the heart. There are some who are accustomed to recount in confession what they have done either in disputes conducted with the pen or in contests fought with the sword—alas! They introduce pride under the cloak of humility and think they can avoid the eyes of the Judge who sees all. Did not both kings, Saul and David, when reproved by the prophets Samuel and Nathan, say, “I have sinned”? Yet Saul heard: “The Lord has taken the kingdom from you and will give it to your rival” (I Kings XV); and David: “The Lord has taken your sin away from you, and you will not die” (II Kings XII). What does this mean except that what Saul had in his mouth was not in his heart, while the humility that appeared in David’s mouth also shone in his heart?

Confession must also be made faithfully, so that one may believe, in the faith of the Church, that one’s sins are forgiven. Cain and Judas confessed purely and humbly, but not faithfully: one of them, despairing, ran to the noose (Matthew XXVII), while the other spewed out that great crime: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Genesis IV). You lie, thief, because God’s mercy is greater than any iniquity, since “his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm CXLIV).

The fifth step follows: mortification of the flesh, which must be weakened by fasts and vigils, lest, with a new itching, it fly back to its pleasure-loving depravity. This must be done with permission, because whatever is done without permission will be counted as vainglory, not as reward; secretly, so that “your left hand may not know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew VI); and with discretion, because of bodily weakness and illnesses of many kinds. We have seen many who, at the beginning of their conversion, broke through the barriers of discretion so violently that they became incapable of the solemnities of praise and afterward needed to be sustained for a long time by a more luxurious regimen.

Now, thus enlightened, let him proceed to the sixth step, which is correction of conduct. Therefore restrain your tongue from evil (Psalm XXXIII), do what is good, and bridle your sensual movements with the reins of continence; then there will be peace in the land of your flesh. According to the office you hold, and while you are present, do not allow wicked men to bury justice.

Come to the seventh step, which is perseverance in goodness. In this seventh step the Lord will call you, with Moses, from the midst of darkness (Exodus XXIV), and you will fix your inner eyes upon the very substance of divinity. Perseverance is produced by expectation of rewards, remembrance of punishments, the first fruits of the Spirit, and the heavenly gift, concerning which the Apostle speaks (Hebrews VI)—things that neither the experienced person fails to know nor the inexperienced understands. For these things are foolishness to him (I Corinthians II), and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.

Hear also, briefly, what sort of person ought to be appointed to administer this ministry. He must be no less learned than religious, so that he may have zeal for God according to knowledge, since indiscreet religion is more often harmful than useful. He must be learned so that he knows what to impose, whom to spare, when he ought to spare, and what consolation to offer from the Scriptures. He must be religious so that he may raise pure hands to God and intercede confidently for sinners. Let him beware of ever mentioning anything he has received under the seal of confession, or of agreeing with anyone who speaks of it. Let him also beware of becoming contemptible in the sight of the one who has revealed his own vileness to him; let him not be suspicious, nor judge the sinner’s future life by his past.

If, by chance, a matter that he received in confession should be brought before him for judgment, let him not take a side as one privy to the facts, but, as though ignorant, allow the judicial process to run its course. Yet he should intend to show compassion and free the person, and should strive to lessen the severity, imitating the sweetness of my Lord, of whom the holy man says: “For you have carried out my judgment and my cause” (Psalm II). But, alas! In our times a pestilential disease has spread throughout the whole world, so that persons whom neither knowledge nor life commends are placed over Churches—like blind leaders, themselves cast down and leading others into a precipice.

We have heard about the one who confesses and about the one who receives confession; let us now hear what things impede confession. As far as I can gather, four in particular present themselves: shame, fear, hope, and despair. Nothing is stronger for conquering the grace of God than human fear, because, while we are ashamed to confess what we have committed, we revere God less than human beings. “This is the shame that brings sin” (Ecclesiasticus IV). Let us oppose it with rational consideration, reverence for the God who sees, and comparison with the greater shame. Reason urges us to confess; God, who sees, compels us. And if we are ashamed to say it here, what will happen in that great shame where everything will be disclosed to everyone? Fear, moreover, crushes many lest they be struck by a severe penance and be unable to endure it. Truly, “he who fears the frost will be overtaken by snow” (Job VI).

Here one must consider how grave the punishment of gehenna is, how long, and how fruitless. In contrast, the present penance is light, brief, and fruitful. Hope overwhelms many who, while desiring present goods, refuse to open their consciences, lest, if they appear to people as they are, they rise to none of the goods of the present life. It must be impressed upon them that the goods of this age are small, uncertain, and momentary, while those of the future life are greatest, most certain, and eternal. Despair kills very many who fear only that they will be unable to remain continent. For it is true that “when the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs XII). We must crush this through the power of confession, the grace of humility, and compassion for the one to whom we open our conscience.

It must be understood that one kind of confession mourns sin, while another sings praise. Confession is a good adornment of the soul: it purifies the sinner and makes the righteous person purer.

[Col. 0834C] It follows: “He who believes in him will not be put to shame.” To believe God (credere Deo) is to give credence to his words. To believe that God exists (credere Deum) is to confess everywhere that God exists. To believe in God is to direct all one’s hope toward him. Demons believe that God exists and believe God, but they do not believe in him; whoever believes in him will not be put to shame, because they do not place their hope in him.

Behold, I have spoken about the sacrament of confession as much as I could, though perhaps not as much as I wished. But since we have prolonged the sermon, let us also hear its conclusion. May he grant us to believe with the heart unto righteousness, to confess with the mouth unto salvation (Romans XX), and to believe in him, the Bridegroom of the Church, the Son of Mary, who is God, blessed throughout the ages. Amen.

DECEMBER.

[Col. 0834D]

VI. Sermon on Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor. XXIV. Sermon on the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. XXV. Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord. Another sermon on the same subject. XXVI. Sermon on Saint Stephen, the protomartyr. 313 XXVII. Sermon I on Saint John the apostle and evangelist. Sermon II on the same. [Col. 0835A] XXX. Sermon on Saint Barbatianus, priest and confessor. XXXI. Sermon on Saint Columba, virgin and martyr.

SERMON LIX. ON SAINT NICHOLAS, BISHOP OF MYRA AND CONFESSOR. (6 DECEMBER)

My Nicholas—indeed, yours also—chosen from the womb, holy from childhood, the glory of the young, the reverence of the old, the honor of priests, and the splendor of bishops, makes your assembly rejoice through his festival. This is Nicholas, whose miracles are spread throughout the whole breadth of the world, whom the world and all who dwell in it praise. So many and such great miracles have been heaped up that all the refinements of learned men scarcely suffice to write them down, much less for us to read them. And although a multitude of scholars may, upon the rhetorical anvil, under the hammers of Quintilian or Cicero, extend the thinnest sheets of eloquence, yet the glory of the confessor surpasses voice, mind, tongue, and conscience. For wonders increase daily, nor does the Spirit of God cease to continue his miracles in memory of his soldier. He is glorified at sea, praised on land, and invoked in every danger. Indeed, “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon mighty waters, themselves saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. 106). They themselves saw the works of the Lord—and Nicholas’s miracles wrought by God—in the deep.

Does not, after the memory of the Virgin, such sweet piety—or pious sweetness—arise in the hearts of the faithful that on the day of tribulation the name of Nicholas is held upon the lips and rests in the heart? If flashes blaze and vengeance comes from above amid roaring storms, Nicholas is taken as patron, and Nicholas is sweetly called upon. If a raging tempest and the cruelty of the sea threaten death to sailors, Nicholas is tearfully entreated to hear; he is humbly invoked to come; he is mercifully acclaimed to rescue them. If we are struck by misfortunes or suffer from mishaps, his holy name immediately springs to our mouths: Nicholas is repeated, and Nicholas’s patronage is sought.

Do not think, however, that I am speaking as a declaimer or piling up verbal splendor with rhetorical elegance, when the whole world experiences the confessor’s benefits and no one is hidden from his love. Testimony is provided by the pilgrimages undertaken from the ends of the earth to his holy body, so that the wonders accomplished through him may be seen. Not only among Christians, but also among pagans, the authority of his holy name has risen to such heights of reverence that they flock together to praise and glorify his holy name. Above all, so great is the devotion of the crowd of priests and clerics toward his worship that throughout the whole world, whoever they may be and from wherever they come, they present themselves to serve so great a solemnity. Children rejoice, young men give thanks, virgins adorn themselves, old men are gladdened, and every age joins in with resounding acclamation. Each has a reason for rejoicing: children praise the fasting child, young men the young man who delivers, virgins him who redeems the disgrace of virgins, and old men him who has pity on the poverty of an old man. Young men and virgins, old men together with the younger, praise the name of this Lord (Ps. 148).

But now, after his deeds have been magnificently proclaimed in the excellent languages of the Greeks, what can this poor, stammering speech dare to say? Nevertheless, lest I seem to introduce evasive excuses, I turn to the Gospel reading; and what I have received for the common benefit, I bring forth for the common benefit. For it says: “A certain nobleman went into a far country and said to his servants, ‘Trade until I come’” (Luke 19).

I shall trade confidently, at the command of my Lord; I shall not fear the Psalmist who says: “Because I did not understand commerce, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 71). For no small strength of confidence is afforded me by the fact that the supreme commander became my merchant, and conducted my business without repose for as long as he was on earth. Carrying his bundles of precious merchandise to the Father, to the very face of God, he showed what he had bought, what he had redeemed, and from where he had redeemed it. Do you therefore intend to be idle while he was engaged in business? To rest while he labored? He himself came to trade in a far country, and do you disdain to walk into neighboring regions?

Approach and enter the region of dissimilarity—namely, this world—and see how frequent its markets are, how many vanities sprout and sprout again there: truly a region of dissimilarity, since it is evident that we have lost the region of likeness, where we were made in the likeness of God. Is it not great dissimilarity—from paradise to hell, from an angel to a beast, from God to the devil? Go, then, through the tumult of the marketplaces and look around at those contending there. As far as I can gather, every desire floats upon three things: some rely on riches, others on honors, others on glory.

You run to India, circle Ethiopia, cross the seas, and open another world for yourself by sailing, so that you may gather riches. You flee your homeland, forget your children, tear yourself away from your wife, and, forgetting all your relations, seek in order to acquire, acquire in order to perish, perish in order to grieve, and hoard treasure while ignoring to whom it was said: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4.) This much concerning riches.
