Hear briefly about honors as well. They have appointed you a leader, and you have been given the opportunity to be miserable and never again to rest. The material for anxieties is heaped up, and amid troubles that gnaw at the very heart, you are compelled to put on an appearance of joy. Can anyone be in honor without sorrow, in authority without tribulation, in exaltation without vanity? Miserable people, as the philosopher says, we love the reward of miseries and detest the miseries themselves. We put on the minds of kings, and whatever does not answer your will immediately summons it; the common humanity is not considered. Yet there is a worm gnawing away, constantly torturing the conscience: fear of a superior power.

This is the most just law: live with your inferior as you wish your superior to live with you.

Hear also about glory. If you seek glory, you have offered seeds of envy to everyone. You are puffed up and filled with a spirit that will burst you apart like a bellows, and you do not consider how many follow you but how many precede you. Everyone crowds together to disparage you; they sharpen their tongues to curse you; and you are exceedingly clever if you can escape either the tongue or the hand of the envious. Behold: from wishing to be glorious, you are proved inglorious. For the multitude pursues no one more relentlessly than the person who arrogates to himself the leadership of the multitude.

Add to these three power and pleasure—things which themselves are snatched away in a thin and fleeting joy—and you will see that abundance is poor, honor lowly, favor worthless, power weak, and pleasure laborious, so that, according to the Apostle, we may bring every understanding into the service of Christ (2 Cor. 10). Read again that greatest of Latin philosophers, and in his words you will find my own judgment. Despise all these things, therefore, because all are to be despised, and make your bundle from all of them: contempt for the world.

When you have traversed this region and taken away what is more precious there, pass to the second, which is the cloistered paradise. Truly, the cloister is paradise. Here are the green meadows of the Scriptures, and the overflowing abundance of tears, which heavenly love filters from the purest affections. Here are the most upright trees, the choirs of the saints, and there is none that does not rejoice in abundant fruitfulness. This is that lofty table at which God is both the one who feeds and the food, both giver and gift, both the one who offers and the offering, both guest and banquet. Here the riches of the Almighty are piled up; here the glory of the angels is poured forth.

Do you think there are no markets here, and that those who dwell in the house with one manner of life are idle? (Ps. 67.) You may see one intent upon sacred readings, another devoted to prayers, one weeping for his transgressions, another exulting in God’s praises, one keeping watch and fasting, and another vying with the others in the office of mutual charity. At night they rise to confess God; in the evening, morning, and midday they recount and announce his praise, and all their diligence turns in a circle around the service of God. Run, then, through them all; run through each one; and from all together and from each individually make your bundle: a model of life.

[Col. 0837D]

Having abandoned the world and adopted this manner of life, pass to the third, which is the region of purification. In this region the gracious Father examines rust-covered children as silver is examined; he leads them through fire and water in order to bring them into refreshment (Ps. 65). There are three divisions of places, which souls receive according to the diversity of their merits. Those who have used the dwelling of the body as a prison and have preserved the substance of both persons purified and clean immediately fly to heaven. Conversely, those who until death have done what is worthy of death are assigned without mercy to the places of Gehenna. But those who are neither one nor the other, who stand between both—that is, who have committed mortal sins but repented near death without completing their penance—are unworthy to rejoice at once, yet not worthy to burn forever; they receive purgatorial places, where they are chastised, but not to their destruction, so that, once wrested away, they may be transferred to the kingdom.

For those who are in heaven, we should not pray, since we ought to pray to them, not for them. For those who are in hell, prayers must be suspended: for them the door of mercy is closed and every hope of salvation is shut off. We must keep watch in prayer and offer singular sacrifice only for those who are cleansed in purgatorial places, so that the gracious Father may quickly turn their penance into satisfaction and their satisfaction into glorification. Run again through these people with the gaze of compassion, and make your bundle: the affection of fellow-suffering.

[Col. 0838B]

The fourth region is the region of Gehenna—a harsh region, a region to be feared, a land of affliction, a land of oblivion, a land of miseries, a land of darkness, a land of storm and gloom, a land of curse and death, in which there is no order but everlasting horror dwells. I tremble and shudder entirely at the memory of this region, and all my bones are shaken. There is the fire that is not quenched, the worm that does not die (Isa. 66), and dreadful cold. There an intolerable stench arises; striking hammers resound without ceasing; blinded darkness grows ever denser. There are the confusion of sinners, the horrifying faces of demons, and a fertile multitude of inextricable chains. There are weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 13; Luke 13), lamentation and groaning, and alternating evils tear the wicked apart without pity.

Nothing is so effective for uprooting the roots of pleasures as the memory of these things and the recollection of the wounds of my Lord: that he stood before the judge, received slaps, was scourged, spat upon, crowned with thorns, beaten with blows, hung upon the wood, mocked as he hung, died upon the cross, was struck with a lance, was buried, rose again, ascended into heaven, and made us a kingdom and priests for God and the Father. Run through these turbulent markets, so that while alive you may descend into hell, and make your bundle: hatred of sin.

[Col. 0838D]

The fifth region is the supercelestial paradise, a blessed and glorious region, full of delight, glory, sweetness, joy, grace, and kindness. There is rest from labor, gladness from newness, and security from eternity. There is the city of the great King, whose streets are paved with the purest gold, which is enriched with sapphires, in which the battlements of jasper are green with life, and stones are laid out in order. For all its walls are precious stones (Rev. 21). There all live; no one dies. All exult with a voice of rejoicing.

David had entered his sanctuary and had passed beyond himself in God, yet he could carry away nothing else except this: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86); and this: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). I do not know what great thing is promised: to see God and to praise him. I too have said, “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121). Already we stand in the courts of Jerusalem; already, from the vestibule of the great city, we dream of its joys. Run, therefore, through this region also, and make your bundle: love of God.

“Trade, therefore, until that nobleman comes, who went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and return” (Luke 19). He will certainly return, and then with interest he will demand the money he entrusted to us. He loses nothing, forgets nothing, and leaves nothing unpunished. Let us therefore beseech the confessor that he may deign today to plead for us with our Redeemer, his friend, who is God blessed forever and ever. Amen.

# LX. HOMILY FOR THE VIGIL OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY (24 DECEMBER)

[Col. 0839B]

At last we have come from sea to harbor, from promise to reward, from labor to rest, from despair to hope, from the way to our homeland. The “pen of a scribe writing swiftly” (Ps. 44) had indeed written us frequent letters: “Wait, wait again”; but we could say what follows: “A little here, and a little there” (Isa. 28). The runners had gone ahead, rich in promise but utterly poor in performance. One said, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26); another, “If he delays, wait for him, for he will surely come” (Hab. 2). With one purpose they had gone out from God’s sanctuary, carrying back nothing with them except a multitude of promises.

Thus our harpist had already begun to nod from weariness and, in silent charges [or accusations], was plaintively directing the whole blame against God himself: “But you,” he says, “have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ” (Ps. 88). Changed also from plaintive speech to intemperate speech, driven on by impatience, the mother of shamelessness and impudence, he says: “You who sit above the cherubim, make yourself manifest” (Ps. 79). Why, seated so long upon your sovereign throne, with angels flying about and surrounding you, do you not look upon the children of men, whom iniquity—committed indeed through Adam, but permitted by you—has swallowed up and swallowed up again? Remember what my substance is, fashioned in the likeness of your substance; for although every living human being is vanity, nevertheless, passing through in your image (Ps. 38), he cannot be vanity. Did you establish all the children of men so vainly—of whom you say, “My delights are with the children of men” (Prov. 8)—that that most crafty deceiver may beat and batter them by his skill, though he could not deceive unless you permitted it? Bow down your heavens and descend; turn those merciful eyes toward miserable suppliants, and do not, at least, forget us forever.

[Col. 0840A]

He said these things, indeed; but twisted by groans and sufferings, he renounced so presumptuous a judgment. “I said,” he says, “I will guard my ways, lest I sin with my tongue” (Ps. 38). But that noble man, illustrious for the elegance of profound speech, growing fervent in emotional transports, says: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest until her righteousness goes forth as brightness” (Isa. 62). “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down!” (Isa. 64), he says, and much else which wearisome prolixity forbids us to insert. Another, too, suspended by the long delay of a slower grace and carried beyond himself by the excess of his sorrow, impatiently barks: “Behold, the nations are before him as though they were not; they are reckoned by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40). Jeremiah bursts forth into a voice of exultant praise, with an adverb indicating its manifestation: “Behold,” he says, “the Lord will make a new thing upon the earth, and a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). Yet he is taught by tears over sudden overthrow that, taking up lamentation before the advent, he should fall wholly silent. Daniel is told: “The vision concerns days and times far off” (Dan. 10). And Ezekiel is wrapped in such darkness that one can scarcely discern whence he comes or whither he goes.

In short, that entire prophetic assembly, wearied by the long delay of lingering grace, varies its prayer, now entreating, now complaining, and often mixes indignant utterances with its petitions. We too have heard them enough—more than enough—and they are reread to our weariness. Let Moses now flee (Exod. 6): he has become too impeded in speech for us. Isaiah’s lips are unclean (Isa. 6); Jeremiah does not know how to speak, because he is a child (Jer. 1); Ezekiel eats defiled bread (Ezek. 4); Hosea takes a fornicatress and adulteress as wife (Hos. 1); Daniel is grievously weakened by a vision (Dan. 8). All the prophets are tongue-tied and mute. We can no longer rejoice and exult unless he kisses us with the kiss of his mouth; you have been heard and answered. The kindness and humanity of God our Savior is present (Tit. 3), which will no longer allow the love of those who languish either to be deferred or taken away.

[Col. 0840C]

For what have you heard? “Be sanctified, children of Israel, and be ready, for tomorrow the Lord will descend.” What separates us from the face of glory, from the child who is God, from the unique childbirth, is scarcely the remainder of this day and the half-completed course of the coming night. Run, swift hours, and with more rapid step complete your courses, so that we may see the Son of God crying in the cradle and prepare whatever services we can for his saving birth. I believe that you are children of Israel, sanctified from every defilement of flesh and spirit, ready for the sacraments of tomorrow’s day, with anxious devotion and devout anxiety. For what else have you done during these holy days dedicated to his coming?

I have seen old men, forgetful of old age, standing at the sacred vigils with youthful eagerness; and young men, their youth buried, standing with the aged gravity proper to reverence for the Godhead. The benches were full of the continent; voices resounded aloft in harmonious song, so that I beheld you with happy envy rejoicing in God with a voice of exultation. Psalters were in your hands, psalms upon your lips, devotion in your hearts; cheerfulness of face, movement of body, and diligent activity showed the festival of the mind. I watched the priests, with wakeful eyes carefully seeking out the first rise of day, putting on sacramental vestments and entering the altar of God to offer the body and blood of the Redeemer. I saw the throng of attendants, in ministerial devotion now bending the knee, now kissing hands, and obeying the nod of those in command more swiftly than a nod.

[Col. 0841A]

I also observed the boys, who do not know right from left, begrudging one another their psalters and carrying them away to their beds, stealing sleep from their eyes and, upon their beds through the nights, seeking him whom their souls loved. Although this has been ventured contrary to custom, it has not been ventured contrary to devotion.

[Col. 0841B]

I confess that amid all this I thought: These are the camps of God; “this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28). Whether I wished it or not, your devotion drew me; and while you were trading, I could not be idle. I followed you, though at a distance, either straying from the road or limping along my paths, grieving and sorrowful because I could not keep pace with those who ran. He alone knows—with whom alone I began to be one in the Lord—how often I filled his ears with complaints that you were with the bridegroom at noon, while I remained in the evening chill. Come then, brothers: if any watery moisture from the river of this mortality still sprinkles your affections, wipe it away and cover it with the snowy garment of confession; put on your feet the preparation of the Gospel of peace (Eph. 6), that you may be among those of whom the saint says, “They shall pass through the river on foot” (Ps. 65). But what follows? “There we shall rejoice in him.”

Isaiah the prophet discoursed more fully in the night readings about this river—or rather, these rivers. “The Lord,” he says, “will strike the river of Egypt into seven streams, so that they may pass through it shod” (Isa. 11). I wish to speak with you briefly about the river and its streams: how and in what manner they are struck, and what it is to pass through it shod.

Those who search the divine utterances affirm that Egypt figuratively signifies this world, which is set in wickedness and filled with darkness and confusion. The river is the flow of the human race, bursting forth in an unhappy channel from our first parents; it has spread an impetuous torrent over the whole breadth of the world. Divided into seven torrents, it has overwhelmed valleys and plains with a deep whirlpool, threatening the same inundation even to mountain peaks. Hence one of the loftier spirits cries: “The torrents of iniquity troubled me” (Ps. 17); and, “The waters entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68).

[Col. 0842A]

The first stream of this river is evil thought: an overflowing stream, repelled by no barriers. It has the abundance of rains—the windows of the bodily senses—which pour into it more copious deadly showers from worldly floodgates. What the mind saw and heard, smelled and tasted, handled and touched, comes before its sight; and often what we have looked on with a simple eye the crafty perverter twists into an occasion of offense and scandal. It fashions likenesses, paints images, applies colors, and rolls everything together in the chamber of the mind, if perhaps it may draw forth consent and infect affection. It offers dreadful things concerning the Godhead, terrifying things concerning faith, astonishing things concerning the institution of faith, and brings poisonous draughts into the channel of the mind—draughts which the sinner, burdened as he is, shudders even to vomit forth in confession. It comes into the oratory, occupies the dormitory, sits in the refectory, circles the cloister, revisits the workshops; it omits no art of doing harm, but everywhere displays the subtleties of its cunning. In choir, while one prays and sings psalms, it drags the mind in different directions, entangling the purity of understanding with recollection of the past.

[Col. 0842B]

In bed it entangles us in manifold sensations of lust, lying in wait for our solitude and attacking with stronger weapons: may it prick rather than wound, assail rather than conquer! In the refectory it entices gluttony to look at what is served and loads the distended stomach with immense greed, so that greater labor is needed to expel than to take in. In the cloister it snatches books from our hands, cuts off remembrance of the Scriptures, and now transfers us from this man to that man with gestures and buffoonery. Through the multitude of workshops it makes you run about and makes itself the companion of your wandering, until it either opens or breaks down the door of silence. Why say more? The enemy of virtue uproots devotion in choir, chastity in bed, moderation in the refectory, reading in the cloister, and the virtue of silence in the workshops. Nor is it enough for it subtly to bore through the ramparts of the heart with little darts while we are awake: in sleep it exercises and re-exercises its peculiar cunning, matters which I leave to your consciences, better informed than my pen.

These spirits also follow you to the altar of the Lord of hosts, flying into the very eyes of the mind; and scarcely can they be driven away by any remembrance either of the God just born or of him hanging on the cross. That great patriarch could scarcely drive birds of this kind away from his sacrifices. What are we, who presume to drive them away? Who would deny that he is plunged or submerged in this stream? You see how muddy is the torrent, belching back slimy filth, which is scarcely, or never, brought to complete dryness. I do not think that he who shut heaven by prayer (3 Kings 17) shut his mind against thought: it is easier to bar heaven than the mind.

[Col. 0842D]

The second stream is perverse speech. “No human being can tame the tongue,” says the Apostle: an unruly, deadly member, ready for speaking and still more prone to compliance (Jas. 3). Notice that one is born from the other: an evil thought opens the gate of evil speech. One kind of word is false, concerning which it is said, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5); another is vain, of which it is written, “Each has spoken vain things to his neighbor” (Ps. 11); another is maledictory, of which the Apostle writes, “Nor shall revilers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6); another obscene, of which he likewise says, “Let no foul speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. 4); another excusatory, whence the Psalmist says, “Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses in sins” (Ps. 140); another deceitful, of which the prophet says, “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips” (Ps. 11); another idle, of which the Lord himself says, “For every idle word that people speak, they will give account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12); and whatever other kinds there are of this plague, which we cannot pass over in a brief leap.

[Col. 0843B]

The third stream is evil action. After thought and speech, one comes to deeds, when we present our members to sin as weapons of iniquity and afflict our bodies with dishonor. What could be more shameful than to stain with lustful ardors members consecrated by Christ’s blood and buried with him in baptism, without regarding the reverence due to God who is present, threatens punishment, and promises glory? Far be it that any one of you should be laid beneath this idol, receive the Son of the Virgin in Venus’s temple, or set the ark of God beside Dagon; lest one nourished amid saffron embrace dung. What has Peter to do with the magician? Christ with Antichrist? Virginity with lust? Purity with impurity? Far be it that any of you should walk in the passion of desire, as do the Gentiles who do not know God—you who either consecrate Christ’s body or minister to Christ’s body, chosen to serve the emperor so that you may sit with the emperor when he sits upon the throne of his majesty. With what face, with what eyes, could one who served among us such great obscenities see us or live with us? With what mind and conscience could a man approach the Holy of Holies to offer the Holy of Holies, if his reputation were contemptible, his life notorious, and his speech blameworthy?

[Col. 0843D]

But if perhaps—since I speak humanly, because of the weakness of our flesh—one of us has folded up something of this sort in the chamber of his conscience, let him double it by confession and repentance; and I promise him, on the mercy of the newborn child, that, if he confesses and repents, the light of the world will be born in him, so that, false darkness having been driven away, he may receive the splendor of the true light. For how can mercy be denied to the wretched on this night, on which the merciful and pitying Lord is mercifully born? God and man are present; mother and virgin; flesh and Word; light and enlightener; good and goodness; mercy and truth; fruitful virginity, virginal fruitfulness; eternal newness, new eternity; divine humanity, human divinity; humble sublimity—and in all these mercy is fashioned. Restrain pride from your eyes, talkativeness from your tongue, cruelty from your hands, pleasure from your loins, and your feet from the untrodden path; then come and convict him if on this night he does not rend the heavens, descend to you, and cast all your sins into the depths of the sea. For who is not sunk and resunk by the persistent force of this third streamlet?

[Col. 0844A]

The fourth stream is the defense of sins. Truly I tell you that nothing so provokes the anger of the Godhead as defending iniquity. For we contend with the Lord on equal terms when we defend what he hates, when what displeases him pleases us. There is indeed a great difference between the proud and the humble sinner: he despises the former and regards the latter, because “he regards the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137). When can a person be healed who spurns the physician, tramples medicine underfoot, and inflames his sick substance by receiving contraries? You call evil good, bitter sweet, darkness light; and you turn insults back upon the Creator, so that you blame what he has praised and praise what he has blamed. This must not be passed over in flattering concealment, when I have seen some among you so goaded by the stings of impatience that at the first words of correction they offer not only excuse but defense; and unless the vigor of discipline intervenes, they break out into disturbances and quarrels. This is the greatest impiety against God (Job 31), the gravest offense, which the simple and upright man, the servant of the Lord, avoids with the utmost circumspection.

The prophet introduces a most elegant comparison concerning this matter, brought from the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit: “There,” he says, “the hedgehog had its den” (Isa. 34). If a hedgehog senses that it is being seized or touched, it contracts into such densely crowded spines that it is armed everywhere with prickings and stings; but when it thinks it has attained solitude, it uncovers its head, puts forth its feet, and shows the motions of life by walking on level ground. If anyone comes upon it, its head and feet are immediately carried back with the greatest speed into its inward hiding place, so that if you wish to hold it, you see your own blood before its body. So too the sinner’s head and feet, intention and action, are watched by the pastors’ care; and, as is the fault of almost all who sin, though seen by everyone, he judges himself seen by no one. If you endeavor to cut away the vice and to seize, with correcting hands, the entries of intention together with the exits of action, Cicero’s eloquence is immediately renewed: what you allege is excused and defended; you who make the charge are accused and offended. He asks about place and time, when it happened; and the new dialectician bursts forth with ready tongue, brings relatives into the middle, seeks advocates, judges himself oppressed, declares that he will withdraw and would rather die than suffer such things, denying what you saw and retorting against you insults which he did not see. Thus you feel the thorn and lose the fault, incur hatred and make no correction; and the person whom you thought to hold wholly, you lose wholly. You see with how manifold an accumulation this stream pours itself into every person and especially into our order.

[Col. 0845A]

The fifth stream is exultation in sins. O detestable joy, to be changed into the sorrow of everlasting pain: exulting in sins as though in virtues! Do not robbers and all evildoers, when they achieve the fulfillment of their wishes, overflow with joy, even daring to mutter thanks to the Godhead itself? “When they have done evil, they rejoice and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). “Coals shall fall upon them; they shall be cast into the fire” (Ps. 139). But how this stream overwhelms miserable souls in its billowing reflux is understood better by conscience than by eloquence.

The sixth is teaching others to do evil. This teaching flows from the chair of pestilence; he who teaches a human being knowledge detests and reproves it (Ps. 93). O how vainly does he possess his soul who hunts other souls to death, who draws sins as with a long rope, who mingles blood with blood, for whom it is not enough to perish forever unless he also drags others to everlasting destruction! You know that many vices are impressed upon the tenderest ages, which later scarcely anyone can mitigate, much less uproot, in the grown body. Unhappy teachers, who have planted such shoots, to be uprooted by that heavenly planting which the heavenly Father planted! Who can boast that he has not been hemmed in by the torrents of this stream?

The seventh is perseverance in all these things. Here the sinner is submerged and swallowed up, and the pit has closed its mouth over him. For when he does not raise his eyes to heaven or remember righteous judgments, he is dead and buried in the tomb of his conscience. Then confession perishes from one dead, as though he were not (Ecclus. 17). Then “when the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). Here he is at the far end of Egypt’s rivers. Here the multitude of the Lord’s mercies is taken from his eyes. O evil river, most wicked and destroying streams! On this night the Lord passed through them shod, when in virginal substance he assumed pure flesh, immune from every aforementioned plague, shod with that shoe which he stretched out over Idumea (Ps. 59), whose strap that great Baptist could not loose (Luke 3). From on high he sent his Son and received me in the Virgin’s womb, and so at last drew me up from the many waters which we have briefly sampled for you. “Deliver me,” he says, “from those who hate me, and from the deep waters” (Ps. 68).

[Col. 0845D]

We shall strike them if we think upon our sin; if we forbid the tongue deceit; if we turn away from evil and do good; if we confess our injustice against ourselves to the Lord; if our sorrow is always before us; if we teach the wicked the Lord’s ways; and if the praise of God is always in our mouth. And, that we may stitch something from the craft of shoemaking onto our morals, let us have close-fitting shoes, finely sewn, able to exclude the waters that meet us. Let us make our flesh firm and fixed by the fear of the Lord, so that it excludes the moisture of lust and, baked by tribulations and made dense, becomes a new wineskin for preserving new wine, concerning which it is said: “For I have become like a wineskin in frost” (Ps. 118).

[The supplied source ends here, mid-discussion.]

But now let us leave our hearts and bodies prepared to receive the Son of the Virgin in peace, and let us all together embrace in innocent arms the light for the revelation of the nations, who is God, blessed forever. Amen.

## LXI. Homily on the Nativity of the Lord (December 25)

Dearest brothers, I desire to offer your charity a word for edification. But since, as you know, I have recently been promoted, by God’s providence, to the episcopal office, I fear to speak before your wisdom, while my conscience is apprehensive and my tongue, still unaccustomed, stammers. For does not a man who boards a ship ignorant of rowing fear to take up the helm? And does not a raw recruit newly entering military service hesitate to carry the commanders’ standard? But I, who distrust my own weakness, believe that by God’s mercy I must be aided by your prayers. Otherwise, how can we utterly despair of our own imperfection when we celebrate the infancy of the Savior who has been born? For he who deigned to grow through the successive stages of life can also advance us from lesser things to greater and strengthen the tender infancy of our understanding by the grace of his perfection. Indeed, he deigned to become little among us for this reason: that he might make us great in himself; he endured our weakness for this reason: that he might establish us in the fullness of his strength.

Let us not, then, fear that the passing word will fail us when we seek the glory of that Word which remains forever, concerning whom you heard just now, while the reading from the holy Gospel was being read:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

This was spoken of that birth which is from the Father, by which God existed with God before the ages and created all things from nothing by his own power. Hence it was rightly said:

> “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (ibid.).

But he who according to that birth made all things according to this birth, which is today’s, deigned himself to be made. The blessed evangelist plainly disclosed the same thing when, after several intervening statements, he added:

> “The Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Immediately it is added:

> “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (ibid.).

In both natures, therefore, the Son of God is the same: he assumes what is ours without losing what is his own. While renewing humanity in man, he remains unchangeable in himself. For God, who mercifully bent down in order to raise us up, transferred us indeed into his glory, but nevertheless himself remained in his divinity. He bestowed something on us and diminished nothing in himself. Thus he is great in the form of God and so small in the form of a servant that neither is that greatness diminished by this smallness, nor is this smallness overwhelmed by that greatness. For when he assumed human limbs, he did not abandon divine works.

When you hear, my brothers, that the Word became flesh, you must not understand at all that the divine nature was changed into flesh, but that flesh was assumed by the Word in the unity of the person. By “flesh,” however, man is understood; with him, within the Virgin’s womb made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, the Son of God was united so inseparably that he who was begotten timelessly from the Father’s essence was himself born in time from the Virgin’s womb. But what mind can comprehend, what tongue fully explain, this ineffable mystery of the Lord’s birth? For it was not without reason that the prophet said:

> “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53).

Having therefore set aside those matters concerning the most sacred birth that our Fathers have discussed at greater length, let us, dearest brothers, turn the course of our discourse for a little while toward the humility of our Redeemer and consider together what he endured for our salvation already in his very birth. Who could worthily marvel at it? Who would not be astonished that he whom the immensity of heaven cannot contain is laid in a narrow manger? He who clothes his chosen ones in the robe of immortality did not disdain to be covered with shabby rags. He who is the food of angels reclined on straw among animals. He who stills the storms of the sea, who supplies the abundance of waters to the rivers, awaited a few drops of milk from a virgin breast. Milk is expressed from the Virgin’s breasts and is changed into the flesh of the Savior. Blessed is this mother who gave birth, who rejoices so greatly in the fruitfulness of her offspring that she feels no grief at the loss of virginity; she nourished him by whom she herself was nourished; she carried in her arms him by whom the entire structure of the world is sustained. A little infant is bound by his mother in childish swaddling clothes—he who, boundless with the Father, governs the rights of all things.

What lofty palaces of the world’s kings then existed, what dining halls adorned with marvelous stones! Yet he who chose a manger as the cradle of his birth disdained them all. He did not seek beds covered with golden fabrics, or adorned with purple or figured tapestries; but he reclined in the stall of animals, he who is surrounded by countless ranks of angels. He wished to be cast down in order to raise us to the heights; he became poor in this world in order to make us sharers in his riches.

Consider this humility of our Redeemer, dearest brothers, with the whole attention of your hearts. Take care diligently to possess it; disdain the glory of the world; regard being poor with Christ as true riches. Strive to offer God the sacrifice of a good will if you wish to appear truly rich in his sight. For you heard that today, when the Lord was born, the holy angels sang:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2).

Today, indeed, peace was made between God and men—not with men of great riches, or earthly wisdom, or noble birth, but with men of good will.

Let us therefore rejoice, beloved, and delight in the Lord with all our hearts, because Christ, who is our peace and made both one (Ephesians 2), deigned to visit the world today in order to lead men of good will into fellowship with the Godhead. He made both one because he joined men with angels in shared dwelling in the heavenly Jerusalem. He made both one because he carried back on his own shoulders the sheep that had gone astray to the flock (Matthew 18), Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, blessed forever and ever. Amen.

> **Note:** Aloysius Lipomanus and several more recent writers attribute the following sermon on the Nativity of the Lord to Blessed Peter Damian. But Cardinal Baronius has very aptly observed how questionable this is at the beginning of the first volume of his *Ecclesiastical Annals*. Since the sermon mentions Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who died eighty years after Blessed Peter Damian, it plainly seems to belong to someone else. For this reason, however, we have thought it should be inserted among the sermons of the blessed man, so that at some time, through someone’s diligence, it may be restored to its author. — **Cajetan.** It is by Nicholas, a monk of Clairvaux, as we have already noted. — **Editors of the Patrology.**

## Sermon of some anonymous author on the Nativity of the Savior and the illustrious miracles performed at it (December 25)

[Col. 0848B]

What I have conceived in my mind cannot be explained in speech, for the astonishment caused by the miracles overwhelms me; and while I review everything, everything becomes entangled:

> “Who can consider the day of his coming?” (Malachi 3).

Therefore the tongue becomes speechless, memory forgetful, understanding insensible. In this extraordinary birth everything shines forth, and everything serves the Virgin’s delivery. Wonders occur in heaven above and on earth below, and all things have sworn allegiance to the service of the God who is being born. The vaults of heaven are marked by a brighter-shining star, and places blazing with abundant light are illumined. More radiant beams are spread throughout the four-part world, and a new fire dulls the multitude of the stars’ fires. The world marvels that the heavens have produced a new splendor and that their unchangeable order has been turned into signs and wonders.

The Chaldeans see in the heavens what Balaam left in writing:

> “A star shall arise,” he says, “from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel, and the whole earth shall be his possession” (Numbers 24).

A star is born in the heights, and God on earth, whose possession extends from sea to sea. The kings of Tarshish prepare themselves so that, with the novelty of their gifts, they may see the new mother; the sons behold a new birth. A spring of oil bursts forth from the earth. The temple at Rome, which was called eternal, collapsed, although it had been completed with marvelous expenditure from the resources of both the City and the world.

When the Romans had decided, in memory of their victorious antiquity, to build a temple of singular design, they asked that whole multitude of gods—or rather demons—how long the elaborate construction of so magnificent a work could last. The response was: “Until a Virgin gives birth.” Turning the oracle toward impossibility, they called that solemn structure the Eternal Temple. But on this night, when the virginal flower of Mary came forth from the virginal chamber, it fell in such a way, and that masonry-and-column structure was shattered so completely, that scarcely any traces of the ruins can be seen.

O Bethlehem, city of the most high God! In you and in your suburbs wonders have been seen today. God hangs at the breast, is placed in a manger, bound in a cradle, and wrapped in cloths; then, loosening the swaddling bands, he spreads his happy hands and holy little arms because of the narrowness of the cradle. He plays with the virgin, smiles at his mother, and turns his caressing eyes toward Mary. The Queen of heaven stands terrified before such great wonders. She gathers in her heart the archangel’s greeting, God’s conception, and the child’s birth, and marvels that he who was able to come to us in this way wished to help us in this way.

Joseph is also present; but standing apart from both, he marvels in an ecstasy of mind and cannot marvel enough at how he has been admitted to the secret of such great condescension. A multitude of the heavenly host is present, and with glorious voices “Glory to God in the highest” is heard (Luke 2). Shepherds come and find a boy and a girl. The star goes before them; kings approach, worship the Son, honor the mother, offer gifts, and present them to his majesty (Matthew 2). Herod is tormented, Jerusalem is troubled, the scribes are consulted, the place is foretold; deception is introduced, and the deceiver is brought to nothing; the schemes of fraud are exposed. The Magi return by another road; unheard-of peace reigns such as has not existed since the beginning of the age; the whole world is registered for the census; a stream of oil seeps from the earth, and sanctified liquid boils up in a rich vein.

What is this, unless it is because true peace has appeared on earth, unless it is because citizens are enrolled in the heavenly kingdom, unless it is because a fountain of mercy flows from the Virgin:

> “Your name is oil poured out” (Song of Songs 1)?

The Holy Spirit, the one and only author of this Scripture, has left beneath this heading some sweetness of his richness. But you are so exhausted by the night vigils that you can scarcely remove sleep from your eyes. Nevertheless, wake for a little while and shake off the torpor of sleep. He of whose birth we are speaking will be present to illumine our eyes, lest we fall asleep.

The entire meaning of the discourse will borrow from the ark of him whose counsel is like the counsel of God. He is that very Lord of Clairvaux, whose religious observance and discernment, wisdom and eloquence, life and reputation rightly extend throughout the Latin world. For I gladly venerate his burdens.

> **Note:** He means Saint Bernard. See his Sermon 15 on the *Song of Songs*.

But let us return to the subject.

That gracious Spirit, from whose more secret spring the river of the *Song of Songs* flows forth, left us three things to seek in these three words: namely, the bridegroom’s name, why it is compared with oil, and how it is poured out—for the text keeps the name silent, says nothing about the comparison, and says nothing about the pouring out. Let us first examine the name.

Many names of the bridegroom, I think, are scattered throughout divine Scripture, but I can encompass them all in two words. You will certainly find none that does not sound either of the power of majesty or of the grace of compassion. The Lord’s Child, of whom I make frequent mention, was brought into the king’s chamber and heard two things, as it were more exalted than the rest, from the mouth of divinity:

> “The power of God,” he said, “and to you, Lord, belongs mercy” (Isaiah 61).

The Savior himself also, bearing witness to prophetic truth, says:

> “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly. For so I am” (John 13).

“Lord” is the name of majesty; “Teacher,” of compassion. For if it is compassionate to provide food for the body, it is much more merciful to impart food to the soul—which is properly the work of teachers, who restrain undisciplined minds under the rigor of discipline.

Let us see which of these names is poured out: whether the name of power into the name of grace, or the name of compassion into the name of majesty. Far be it that mercy should be enclosed within power, since:

> “His mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144).

It is therefore certain that the power of God has today been poured out into a greater compassion, when the heavens distilled before the face of God and the Ancient of Days arose from virginal limbs. No one can hide from this heat, because a more abundant pouring of oil descends from the head into the beard, and from there generously moistens even the edge of the garment.

So great is the abundance of the one who shows mercy that it is reckoned not only as a pouring out but also as an emptying:

> “He emptied himself,” the Apostle says, “taking the form of a servant” today (Philippians 2),

and he sprang forth from the virginal chamber with the whole multitude of his mercies. For that abyss of God’s counsels had no sweeter way of redeeming us, because whatever of divinity was found in the treasury of compassion was all heaped up in the Virgin’s womb.

I cannot contain myself for joy that this majesty, emptying its own nature, should come upon the nature of my flesh and blood and enclose wretched me within the riches of its glory—not for an hour, but forever. He becomes my brother, my Lord; the affection of a brother conquers fear of the Lord.

Lord Jesus, I gladly hear you reigning in heaven; more gladly, being born on earth; most gladly of all, enduring the cross, nails, and lance. This pouring out carries away my affection, and remembrance of these things strengthens my heart, cleansed by the sharpness of a living and life-giving drink.

[Col. 0850D] This word is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and a discerner (Hebrews 4).

One of those who is either the teacher of the prophetic choir or one of its teachers prophesied marvelously and subtly about this pouring out under the sixfold division of the divine names:

> “His name shall be called,” he says, “Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9).

My Lord was indeed wonderful among the angelic orders, hearing the hymn of his glory; wonderful to that wondrous creature, performing wonders in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths. But I, wrapped in the mud of filth and misery, wretched and pitiable, had lost every hope of rising out. He was in glory, I in misery; he wonderful, I pitiable.

> “Holy and terrible is his name” (Psalm 110),

a name that even that nobler nature scarcely dares to utter. How could I, whom an angelic eye can scarcely behold, much less grasp, contain this name, closed and complete?

But observe the pouring out. He who was wonderful to the angelic hosts bends the heavens and becomes the counselor of human beings. The majestic name is poured out into the compassionate name; he who is wondrous in heaven comes to give counsel on earth. He hides purple beneath garments of misery and, bending down to the mud where I lay, is not submerged.

I dare to say that, fixed in the deep mire, he extends his right hand to the work of his own hands: he draws him out of the depths of the waters, washes the one drawn out, clothes the one washed, carries back the one clothed, and strengthens the one carried back. He extends his right hand when he is born; he draws out when he speaks; he washes when he dies; he clothes when he rises; he carries back when he ascends; he strengthens when he sends forth the Spirit from heaven.

He is truly a good counselor, who defends by his death the counsel he gave by his voice. For, says the evangelist, he was teaching as one having authority, and not like their scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 7). “God” and “Mighty” are names of power, but “God” is poured out into “Father of the age to come,” and “Mighty” into “Prince of Peace.” I shall run briefly, since I am speaking both to those who are weary and to those who know the law.

[Col. 0851C] What have you to say, muttering Lucifer, in the midst of such a pouring out? The entire itinerary of God is closed to you, and your malicious eye has grown exceedingly dim here. My Lord was Wonderful in his birth, Counselor in his preaching, God in the flashing forth of his miracles, Mighty in his passion, Father of the age to come in his resurrection, and Prince of Peace in that eternal blessedness.

Do not be terrified by the novelty of the words, for nothing new is being introduced. In former times, too, names were changed and poured out: Abram into Abraham, Sarai into Sarah (Genesis 17), and any other changes of that old workshop that you remember having read. I also recall finding, almost from the very beginnings of the world, the pouring out of the divine name in a certain hidden place in Scripture.

God speaks to Moses about Israel’s liberation. After a long conversation between God and Moses, the prophet subtly asks his name, and the Lord says:

> “I am who I am: this is my name forever. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3).

Moses, terrified by the inscrutable authority of the name, as though saying, “This surpasses my understanding; I cannot contain it unless it is poured out,” hears from the Majesty:

> “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

Do you see the pouring out? Behold, the God of angels calls himself the God of human beings.

Let us therefore run, brothers, after the fragrance of these perfumes. Let us run to the oil pressed from the beautiful olive tree in the fields, tainted by no dregs and embittered by no bitterness of substances—the oil that gladdens the human face (Psalm 103), heals wounds, removes pain, and restores sweetness.

Did not our Samaritan bring oil and wine to us, wounded by the worst robber, to cleanse us and soothe the severity of the wound? But much oil and little wine: much mercy and little justice. So it was fitting for one who showed mercy; so it was beneficial for the miserable man.

> “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord,” says the Just One, “for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142);

but crown me with mercy and compassion (Psalm 102).

Coming today, he brought five vessels of oil and only two of wine. The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel, knowledge, and piety (Isaiah 11)—does this not sound sweetness, breathe mercy, and pour forth an abundance of delight? Fortitude and fear are wine. But that mighty one drank of this wine when Christ descended to the underworld in the spirit of fortitude—not timid, but to be feared.

Let us now see why oil is compared with oil. If you have nothing better to offer, it shines, nourishes, and anoints. The name of Christ does the same and corresponds entirely to the comparison. Proclaimed, it shines; contemplated, it nourishes; invoked, it soothes and anoints.

Consider when renowned lights carried the light of this name upon the lampstand of eloquence: did not God’s flashes illumine the world, did not the earth move and tremble at the brilliance of lightning?

> “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk,” says the chief of the apostles to the lame man (Acts 3).

Did not something like lightning leap from Peter’s mouth when the name was uttered that the mouth of the Lord had named?

> “And immediately,” he says, “his legs and ankles were strengthened.”

The name Jesus, as Origen’s more noble tongue defined it, is sweet and glorious, worthy of every fragrance and adornment. It was not fitting for this name to be first proclaimed in the world by human beings, but by a certain higher and more excellent nature. All the prophets either did not know this name or kept it entirely silent; the privilege of its dignity was reserved for the archangel Gabriel, who first unfolded it with holy mouth to the most holy Virgin (Luke 1). Did not Isaiah, carried away in an ecstasy of mind, agree with the archangel’s words in almost the same syllables, even to the novelty of the holy name? (Isaiah 7.)

It truly nourishes, and there is no happier pasture in the place of pasture where the Lord has placed us (Psalm 22). What equally fattens the mind that meditates? The name Jesus is honey in the mouth, a melody in the ear, and jubilation in the heart. Every food that is not seasoned with this is tasteless. Scripture that is not steeped in the oil of such devotion is either insipid or bitter.

Once Cicero tasted sweet to me; the poets’ songs charmed me; philosophical words shone with gold; and the sirens had enchanted my understanding with sweetness almost unto destruction. The Law, the Prophets, the Gospel, the Epistles, and all the glory of the sayings of my Lord and his servants seemed either small or nothing. But now I do not know what sweeter thing the son of Jesse murmurs, who, with a varied harmony of words and meanings, renders all those whom I was accustomed to love ineloquent and mute.

It soothes and anoints, because nothing restores us so much in tribulation. Indeed, it can be proved:

> “Call upon me,” he says, “in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Psalm 49).

This is the name; this is the oil; this is the pouring out of the oil. Amen, I say to you: this pitcher of oil shall not fail, nor shall it diminish until the voluntary rain (1 Kings 17), which has been set apart for his inheritance, rains down more abundantly; until he makes a new heaven and a new earth (Psalm 67), because his mercy is from eternity and forever upon those who fear him (Psalm 102).

But now let us rise and prepare ourselves for the rejoicing of the more solemn Mass, sparing neither our hearts nor our voices, in honor of the child who has been born for us, who is God, blessed forever. Amen.

## Sermon LXII: On Saint Stephen, the Protomartyr (December 26)

We still have the Son of the Virgin in our hands, and with dutiful discernment we honor the infancy of the crying God. The Virgin leads us to the venerable cradle. She who is beautiful beyond the daughters of men leads us to him who is beautiful beyond the sons of men (Psalm 44); she who is blessed among women leads us to him who is blessed among men.

She murmurs in our ear, lest perhaps the provoking household hear and be stirred up, that the veils of the prophets have been unveiled and God’s plan fulfilled. Behold the miracle of the Lord’s mother: she was a creature, and the Creator is created. The star sparkles, the Magus worships, the sky rejoices, the earth resounds; the angels glory, the shepherds rejoice with them; the Virgin gives birth, God is born, and the lights of heaven follow the light that has arisen in the darkness with a brighter radiance.

We are occupied with these blessings.

> “Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire with them” (Psalm 126).

I know that this is sweet to you:

> “In the beginning was the Word”;

sweeter:

> “The Word became flesh” (John 1);

sweetest of all: the Word hanging on the cross. Who, unless he himself commands it, would be so mad as to dare turn his eyes away from such a birth, much less tear them away, when he says:

> “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee” (Song of Songs 6)?

Behold, while he kisses us with the kiss of his mouth (Song of Songs 1), while through such great miracles he makes us both astonished and attentive, Stephen, full of grace and fortitude, performs great wonders and signs among the people (Acts 6).

Is it right to abandon the king and turn our eyes toward the soldier? By no means—unless the emperor commands it. The king himself, the king’s Son, rises and, breaking through the ranks of those who stone him, attends the contest of triumph, not without pain of heart. He sees the first and chief officer of the purple-clad cohort being crushed, and fountains of blood boiling from the body of the protomartyr beneath the dense hail of stones. He sees that all the frenzy pours back upon himself, and that the reproaches of those who reproach accumulate against him alone.

Where is your compassion and mercy, Lord, if you do not suffer with the one who suffers? Where are your fairness and justice, if you neither judge nor avenge the people who stone him?

Let us run to the spectacle toward which he runs who rejoices “like a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18), and let us see with what weapons the standard-bearer of the martyrs descends into the field to fight. In order that the first privilege of this singular martyrdom may shine forth more clearly, let us recall the account in the apostolic Acts, in which the life and passion of the warrior soldier are contained in historical and figurative statements.

> “Stephen,” they say, “full of grace and fortitude, performed great wonders and signs among the people” (Acts 6).

A considerable mystery lies hidden here, and the Scripture’s plain statement must not be despised by the simple. Speaking to the Virgin, the archangel, using words drawn from the heavenly treasuries and fashioned by no spirit other than the Spirit of God himself, delivers a discourse in a new greeting. There is no doubt that these words surpass the height of all other words, having been drawn from the better disciplines of the Holy Spirit; by their utterance that unique mystery—the Word and man, divinity and flesh—was to be joined.

> “Hail,” he says, “full of grace” (Luke 1).

And what of Stephen?

> “Stephen, full of grace and fortitude.”

Does Luke not speak of both with almost the same letters? Although a far more excellent manner is proclaimed in the Virgin, it is nevertheless praised secondarily in the martyr. Stephen therefore possesses grace of a higher kind than the rest of the multitude of martyrs: he is full of grace, that is, filled and heaped up with it—a rarity that the subtle investigator will seldom find in the canonical Scriptures.

Fortitude is joined to grace, because when the Spirit of freedom has been infused, the kindled mind bursts forth into the light of truth and in no way allows the rigor of sorrow ever either to be lowered or to be laid aside. Thus armored with grace and fiercely wielding the spear of fortitude, he performed great wonders and signs among the people. He can perform signs and wonders in whom grace and fortitude have established a most powerful seat.

Thus Stephen goes out to murderers, adulterers of the law, crucifiers of the Son of God the Father. He speaks to a sinful nation in Egypt, to a people heavily burdened with iniquity in the wilderness, to a wicked seed in the promised land, and to criminal children at the Savior’s death (Isaiah 1):

> “Stiff-necked,” he says, “and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

> “But some men from the synagogue arose”—that is, from the synagogue of Satan.

They gather together from every side, either to refute him or to kill him. They make one wall; impiety joins scale to scale; the serpents hiss at one another and assemble together against the Lord and against his servant. Whether it wishes to or not, impiety yields to piety, error to truth, folly to wisdom, presumption to the Holy Spirit, and the vanity of the human spirit to the Spirit.

> “And they could not,” he says, “resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke.”

He did not say, “They did not wish to,” which would belong to the rational and perfect; but “they could not,” where the evil mind’s ability is taken away, not its will changed.

> “They were refuted by him,” he says, “with complete confidence.”

He acts confidently. The fearless mind neither changes nor is changed; it loves justice more than life, faith more than blood, and death more than silence about justice. They rush upon him, seize him, and bring him before the council, rejoicing that they have enclosed him within their nets.

> “For the net is spread in vain before the eyes of the winged” (Proverbs 1).

Then his voice becomes freer, and his speech is sharpened against their stones by the truth. The Spirit of God takes the whole martyr for himself and modulates through his mouth as through a more resonant instrument. One face of Scripture appears to him, and he reduces the dispersed matter of the Old Testament to concise brevity. He recounts God’s promises and benefits, the people’s murmuring and crimes, the good things bestowed and the evils returned, and finally reproaches them with the shedding of divine blood.

He calls them rebellious against the Spirit, stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart and ears, and with exalted voice names them murderers and betrayers. He does not fear the assembly gathered from bloodshed or those who, amid hands seeking his life (Psalm 15), are gathered around him. By a deliberate judgment of justice, he ascends to the summit of truth. They are cut to the heart and gnash their teeth against him; they conceive pain and are near to giving birth to iniquity (ibid.).

It is astonishing that those unaccustomed to such a miracle are not recalled by the novelty of it, since the luminous face of the protomartyr does not restrain the madmen.

> “They saw,” he says, “his face as the face of an angel standing among them.”

What is this, Jews? The glorious levite is marked by the light of God’s face, so that Stephen is brightened by flashing radiance, your eyes are dazzled, and yet the magnitude of envy closes off the majesty of the vision. Let the students of the divine books answer me: where have they found a man set upon earth wearing an angelic face? And since they find this rarely or never in either Testament, let them marvel at the glory of the triumphant man.

It follows:

> “But being full of the Holy Spirit, gazing intently into heaven, he saw the glory of God.”

Wonderful to say—and beyond the whole of creation. He gazes into heaven and now sees not heaven but the heavens opened; he sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power.

This gaze moves me: poured forth from purity of heart, it does violence to the heavens and penetrates and reaches the very court of the divinity. The heavens are opened; the glory of God is seen; Jesus is observed standing not merely at God’s right hand but at the right hand of Power.

This gaze had been produced by rejection of the world, contempt for self, purity of heart, love of God, love of neighbor, defense of truth, and longing for Christ.

All these matters would have to be brought back to the common flowers of mortality, unless the excellence of the martyr were to be commended. Blessed are the eyes, subtle the sight, glorious the vision. At the same time, gather carefully the arrangement of the words. He is full of the Spirit, and thus gazes into heaven, because the one breathed upon by the Spirit of divinity, having trampled earthly things, longs for heavenly and eternal things.

After this the heavens are opened, and no barrier or enclosure prevails that the mind, lovingly clinging to the supreme Mind, does not fly over or break through. The heavens are therefore opened—all the heavens, I think—and the vision of God’s glory follows their opening, and the Lord Jesus is seen standing at the right hand of God’s power. Lest he be thought inferior to the Father, he stands with the One who stands; with the One who fights, he fights; he is stoned in the one who is stoned.

No ordinary astonishment overwhelms me: whether the first flower of the martyrs saw these things with bodily or incorporeal eyes. It would indeed be a great miracle if he plunged into starry mysteries with mortal sight, if eyes pure in heart looked upon so solemn a vision. But if he saw with bodily eyes, it is certain that he flew ahead of the entire human race by the disparity of his glory, and that by the wings of faith and virtues he apprehended, even if he did not comprehend, incorporeal things with corporeal eyes.

I dare not rashly define or abruptly settle the matter, since I have not read any definitive rule concerning it. More safely, however, I follow the Apostle—or rather the Spirit of God in the Apostle—who, with the utmost deliberation of words, entrusts this matter to safer uncertainty rather than dangerous definition:

> “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Corinthians 11).

Immediately they cry out with a terrible shout, hold their ears, and block themselves against the truth. With one accord they rush upon him, becoming friends in his death; they throw him out of the city and stone him.

The martyr is driven outside the city of bloodshed, in which justice had formerly dwelt but which now belongs to murderers. Concerning it the holy man says:

> “For I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city” (Psalm 45).

This is the city that iniquity surrounds day and night, the city contemptuously called a fortress, fortified against the apostles and the Lord of the apostles by the hardest bars of unbelief (Matthew 21).

Outside the gate of this city the Lord suffered; outside it the servant is stoned, going out to him beyond the camp and bearing the likeness of his reproach. The martyr’s garments are laid at the feet of the persecutor, who was to be converted by touching the sacred garments and by the prayers of the one being stoned.

> “And they stoned Stephen,” he says, “calling upon him and saying: ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit’” (Acts 7).

They run toward stones, and he toward prayers. Stones strike a stone, but a softer stone, from which the oil of charity flows and the ringing sound of compassion is returned.

> “Lord Jesus,” he says, “do not hold this sin against them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

He asks that his spirit be received—the spirit, specifically, and that spirit which the Apostle distinctly commands to be preserved as a kind of third element in man:

> “May my spirit, soul, and body,” he says, “be kept blameless for the day of the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 5).

What great piety, what devotion, and what integrity of the most ardent charity! Rightly does this man claim for himself the flower of martyrdom, in whom the likeness of the Lord hanging upon the cross has been impressed in wondrous forms. For, fastened and crucified upon the wood by thorns, nails, and a lance, he conceals that singular pain and forgets his approaching death; about to introduce a new example, he opens the breadth of charity and enlarges the limits of the law that had been handed down into a wider field: no longer [Col. 0857A] merely a friend to friends, but, whether they wish it or not, equally a friend to enemies. “Father,” he says, “forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). The prayer of the dying could not be ineffective; hence the multitude of enemies passed over into the number of friends.

**334** See with what a straight course Stephen proceeds: even if he does not equal the Redeemer, he nevertheless follows him. A rain of stones flies, and the strongest hands of his envious persecutors multiply the places of his wounds; but our crowned man endures patiently, destined to be transferred from the crown of his name to the crown of rule. He knows nothing of the inclination of the flesh and is unaware of the hour of death; and see what he resolves should be done. Then, kneeling, he cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them, because they do not know what they are doing.” He cries out with a loud voice, [Col. 0857B] because his charity is certainly great; he kneels, because his simplicity is true and humble. Praying for himself, he stands and rises; for those who stone him, he bends his knees. Who has ever heard of such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? He grieves more over the sins of his persecutors than over his own wounds, over their wickedness than over his own death.

“And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord.” Blessed is sleep with rest, rest with delight, delight with satisfaction, satisfaction with security, security with eternity. “He fell asleep,” he says, “in the Lord,” absorbed into the abyss of glory and resting amid the arms of his God. The Lord Jesus, the head of martyrs, was seated at the right hand of God before the first martyr. Do you recall what that voice of the Church—Augustine, I mean—thought about this martyr, who, after his death, asserts that he [raised] seven dead men? [Col. 0857C]

Come, you who shine forth in the Levitical order: sing a new song to this man, and devote yourselves to so great a festival with festive voices. Perhaps he will be present to those who sing and will plead for us before his Lord, our judge: “Do not hold anything against them as sin, you who are God, blessed forever. Amen.”

## SERMON LXIII. ON SAINT JOHN THE APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST (27 DECEMBER)

Today, beloved, the joys of holy gladness are doubled for us, because, while the Lord’s recent birth is still fresh, the glorious solemnity of blessed John comes before us. Today the disciple whom Jesus loved is clasped in the embraces of his beloved, [Col. 0857D] enjoys his company, and contemplates with a clarity all the greater because it is more sublime what he had seen, what he had heard, and what he had touched with his hands concerning the Word of life (1 John 1). Today, that wondrous eagle—which Ezekiel once saw rise above the other four living creatures (Ezekiel 1), and which John himself, having become, so to speak, his own prophet, beheld flying in a mystical vision—has happily soared on the wings of sublime merits toward the one food of angels and human beings. For although “wherever the body is, there the eagles will necessarily be gathered” (Luke 17), he approaches the nourishment of life all the more familiarly now that he has been freed from the bonds of corruption, just as, while he was still in the flesh, he fixed the rays of his purified mind upon the orb of the eternal sun itself—[Col. 0858A] that is, upon the brightness of the divine substance.

O how wondrous above us is the dispensation of the heavenly plan! O how profound is the depth of divine wisdom! God descended to humanity in order to disclose to human beings the Deity hidden from them. He deigned to enter into the public sphere of human mortality, so that he might reveal to us the secret of his eternity. But if, as soon as he began to break forth into the words of evangelical teaching and to open the mysteries of the new grace to the still untrained hearts of the inexperienced, he had immediately disclosed the sacrament of his divinity, whose hearing, I ask, could have borne it, whose understanding could ever have grasped it? For, to say nothing now of his divinity, when the Lord said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink [Col. 0858B] his blood, you will not have life in yourselves; and whoever eats me will live because of me” (John 6), they immediately rejected the saying and shuddered, saying, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” Then Scripture adds: “From that time, many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him” (ibid.); not, clearly, people from the crowd, not merely any inexperienced persons, but even the disciples themselves were unable to grasp the word of the mystery. What, then, would those have done before the sun who were blinded by a lamp? How could they endure the sound of thunder who were unable to bear the force of a resounding trumpet—indeed, who were deafened by the faintness of a restrained and moderated human voice?

Therefore our Redeemer made the disciple whom he especially loved [Col. 0858C] by a special prerogative a kind of instrument for declaring the essence of his divinity. So that he might supply what the Lord himself had temporarily and dispensationally held back, he left him as his representative, so that, once the mystery of his passion, resurrection, and ascension had been completed, after nearly thirteen five-year periods had passed—that is, when human beings already possessed a freer vision of mind for apprehending the truth—he might disclose the sacrament of the Word, coessential and coeternal with God, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). The order of human weakness demanded that humanity should first learn the beginnings, course, and completion of Christ’s humanity, and should also learn the miracles he performed as a human being; thus, gradually strengthened by its own advances, it might aspire to comprehend the mystery of his hidden divinity. For this reason it was part of the divine plan that the other Evangelists, who occupied themselves with describing the Savior’s humanity, should precede by a long way; but John, when human beings, like infants at first, were already planting firmer footsteps on the road of truth, should advance them toward the grace of divine knowledge. [Col. 0858D]

He finally conceived this surpassing height of divine knowledge with a mind divinely enlightened, when at the sacred mystical banquet of the Supper he reclined upon the breast of the Redeemer (John 13). And because all the treasures of wisdom [Col. 0859A] and knowledge are hidden in the breast of Jesus, from that heavenly treasury he drew the highest riches, by whose generous abundance he enriched the poverty of our need. From that treasury, I say, he brought us an abundance of riches and, prodigal in the best sense, distributed it for the common salvation of the whole world; indeed, he reclined above the fountain of perennial life, so that he himself might then continually draw in the streams of divine teaching, and afterward offer those same streams to us at a fixed and appointed time.

He is, as it were, the great river of paradise, flowing forth from the principal source of its fountain and proceeding in a richer flood of heavenly gifts; it waters the barren deserts of human minds and fertilizes them with abundant fruitfulness for producing the sprouts of good works as though they were new crops. And not undeservedly was so [Col. 0859B] profound and surpassing a revelation of the Godhead owed to the virgin [John], so that he who cut away the enticements of the flesh might, in a blessed exchange, enjoy the riches of heavenly banquets instead of carnal sweetness. He advanced to so great a privilege of grace that, surpassing every created being, he reached with the vision of his mind to where no prophet, no patriarch, and, in short, no one known to have been in the flesh from the beginning of the world had aspired. Nor is it surprising that our Redeemer entrusted blessed John with his own role in declaring the mystery of his divinity, since he also appointed him in his place, as another son, to guard his venerable mother, the perpetual Virgin: “Woman,” he said, “behold your son”; and to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (John 19). [Col. 0859C] It was fitting that the one to whom he most especially entrusted heavenly things should also entrust earthly things.

And because the Mediator between God and human beings, one Emmanuel, consists of two natures, namely divine and human, it seemed entirely fitting that blessed John should be the faithful minister of both natures: that he should write down the mysteries of the divinity and offer the blessed Mother the ministry of his perpetual guardianship and devoted service. He testifies that he is, in a sense, the minister of both of these most excellent mysteries when, throughout the whole sequence of his Gospel’s text, he so regulates his manner of writing and alternates it with a certain mystical variety that at one moment he proclaims what is human, at another reveals what is divine; at one moment inserts historically what belongs to humanity, at another expresses what [Col. 0859D] belongs to divinity with a certain majesty of sublime and subtle words. With such art does he temper the force of his words and distribute them with the sobriety of a balanced moderation that he neither allows the secrets of divinity to become commonplace nor permits those things necessary to our faith to remain hidden.

Accordingly, while he weaves together the words of history, he allows the splendor of divinity to flash into human eyes as though through the finest cracks; and while the eye of our mind is struck by the very slender ray of eternal light, it is immediately opened with greater discernment to investigate that inaccessible light of supreme truth. Since blessed John, through the alternating order of his narrative, sometimes subtly thunders forth Christ’s divinity [Col. 0860A] and sometimes asserts plainly and humbly, in a certain manner, what belongs to his humanity, he maintained this same method in orderly fashion from the beginning of his Gospel to its end. For, as you know, at the head of his book he places that divine and singular beginning: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Behold, the eagle of God soars sublimely to the summit of heaven; but, for the food of the flesh, it must at some point fold its wings and descend, lowered, to the depths. Therefore hear what he adds shortly afterward: “And the Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

This distinction, then, between the humanity and divinity united to one another yet unconfused, [Col. 0860B] the bride speaks of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “His belly,” she says, “is of ivory, distinguished by sapphires” (Song 5). Among the members of the human body, scarcely anything is more fragile or tender than the belly; therefore fragility is rightly understood by the belly as referring to the humanity assumed by Christ. Ivory, however, is the bone of an elephant, an animal said to be most chaste and of an extremely cold nature. The bridegroom’s belly, therefore, is of ivory, because the humanity assumed by the Redeemer remained entirely chaste and inviolate, untouched by every contagion of sins. “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2).

A sapphire is a stone possessing the color of a clear sky; hence it is also said in the Lord’s vision: “Under his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exodus [Col. 0860C] 24). By the sapphires, therefore, the works of divinity are understood, which the Lord displayed in the flesh. The bridegroom’s belly was distinguished by sapphires because Christ’s humanity shone with divine powers. It is not said to be full of sapphires, but distinguished by them, so that the whiteness of ivory appeared among the sapphires: in this way the Lord worked human things from the aspect of the humanity he had assumed, while nevertheless at times he also displayed divine things from the aspect of his divinity. Hunger, thirst, weeping, and finally crucifixion and death were works of humanity; performing miracles, however, and raising not only others but himself from the dead, were unmistakable signs of divinity. In this manner, then, blessed John distinguishes the bridegroom’s ivory belly with sapphires, at one time disclosing the mysteries of divinity, at another [Col. 0860D] describing the weaknesses of humanity.

Because this blessed John speaks of God in a wondrous and incomparable manner beyond other mortals, it was rightly arranged that he should be called “Theologian” everywhere, not only by the Greeks but also by the Latins. Mary is Theotocos (“God-bearer”) because she truly gave birth to God; John is Theologian because he not only saw ineffably, but also described with profound sublimity, that the Word of God was with the Father before the ages and was God. Hence he can rightly say with the Prophet: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Psalm 44). Rightly, therefore, is a virgin entrusted to a Virgin’s service, and a servant is appointed in the Lord’s place as a son, so that the splendor of virginal chastity may correspond in both persons to each other, [Col. 0861A] and the flowering appearance of inward purity may recognize blooming in the other what it sees flourishing in itself.

Here, beloved brothers, let us consider before your charity the beautiful variety of the divine arrangement and compare two distinguished disciples of our Redeemer—Peter and John—to see how they correspond to one another through a certain likeness of dignity. The Lord entrusted the keys of the Church to Peter (Matthew 16), and he also wished to delegate the guardianship of Mary to blessed John (John 16). Both are certainly mothers: Mary, mother; the Church, mother. But Mary is the mother of Christ, and the Church the mother of the Christian people. From Mary Christ [Col. 0861B] received flesh; from the flesh of his side he brought forth the Church.
