From the one he was born according to the flesh; the other he brought forth when he was already dead in the flesh. From the one he willed to be born; for the other he deigned to die. From the one he was born once in his own person; from the other his members are born daily. He drew from the one that for the other he might die, so that both might be saved together.

Great, therefore, and blessed is the mother, the blessed Virgin Mary, from whose womb Christ’s flesh was taken, and from whom the Church in turn flowed forth through water and blood. In this way, then, the Church too seems to have come forth from Mary. Yet both are chaste, both pure, and both fortified by the girdle of perpetual virginity.

Of these two mothers, these two perpetual virgins, the Lord wished to entrust one to Peter and the other to John, so that, when the weight of each ministry had been carefully [Col. 0861C] considered, the dignity of their excellent merits might appear equal in the two senators of heaven. The Lord says to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16). Was the blessed Virgin not also heaven, my brothers, in whose virginal womb the fullness of divinity remained for nine months? From her chaste and pure womb the Word of God, through whom all things were made, clothed himself with immaculate flesh. He lay enclosed in a narrow womb, yet, immense, he governed the laws of the whole world. Established, I say, in the brief dwelling of a virginal womb, he governed the dominion of heaven and had not lost his sovereignty over all earthly things. Therefore the venerable Virgin Mary is not presumptuously called heaven; and for that reason the Lord in a certain manner [Col. 0861D] appointed blessed John as heaven’s key-bearer when he decreed that he should be the guardian of his blessed Mother.

Accordingly, so that John might be compared with blessed Peter in many ways, when our Redeemer asked his disciples what opinion people held about him and they immediately replied, “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets” (Matthew 16), the assertion wavered and the bond of uncertainty was not broken until Peter was reached. But when the disciples’ understanding was examined, the one who was first in apostolic dignity took the lead in confessing the truth—Peter, namely: “You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid.). Amid the winding turns of faith that was still wavering, [Col. 0862A] amid the stormy tempests of surging doubts, this fisherman fixed the anchor of truth and placed the little boat of faith in the safest harbor of tranquil refuge.

But let us see whether John also shares some likeness with blessed Peter in this work. He is accused of unwavering preaching and is therefore sent into exile by Domitian, then Caesar. Immediately the heretics Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and very many others—whom he suitably calls Antichrists—break into the folds of the ecclesiastical flock and, like fierce wolves, rage over sheepfolds deprived of the shepherd’s aid. They dogmatize that Christ did not exist before Mary, and thus corrupt the simple purity of evangelical faith with the squalor of their faithlessness. [Col. 0862B] The world is confounded, the Church is disturbed, faith totters, and, as though in a rising storm of faithlessness, very many suffer shipwreck.

Why say more? At length, after Domitian had been killed, John returned to Ephesus under the guidance of divine grace and mourned the Church’s disturbance. But whatever he found shaken by the whirlwind and storm of error, he recalled more solidly and firmly to the foundation of the original faith. For, when he was asked, as the historians relate, by the charity of almost the entire universal Church, he finally burst forth into this declaration of divine inspiration: “In the beginning,” he said, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). By this seal of truth he fixed the boundary against the evasions of the heretics and thereafter will strengthen the faith of Catholics with perpetual [Col. 0862C] certainty.

Peter, therefore, is a rock: “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). John also became a rock, upon whose foundation of faith the structure of the whole Church rises; whether the fury of heretics strikes against it or the assault of temptations rushes upon it, it does not overturn it. This rock fulfills the sling of the true David, by which he strikingly struck the Philistine Goliath in the forehead (1 Samuel 17), where the profane and impious man had no standard of the cross. This rock destroyed all adversaries of ecclesiastical teaching; this rock overthrew Jewish faithlessness together with every heretical depravity. Nor is it surprising that John, like Peter, is called a rock, since the Lord says this to Ezekiel: [Col. 0862D] “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads; I have made your face like adamant and like flint” (Ezekiel 3).

Clearly, although what each disciple brought forth concerning the mystery of the Lord’s faith is most profound and wholly divine, and although both exceed the powers of the human mind in equal measure, and although what was uttered under the dictation of the same Spirit does not appear different in the excellence of its dignity, nevertheless John’s unique place seems to claim this distinction for itself, because no one is found to have written the same thing either before him or after him. For we read that the blessed apostle Peter’s statement was also expressed by Martha, the sister of Lazarus, in nearly the same words. [Col. 0863A] When the Savior said to her, “Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die forever” (John 11), and then added, “Do you believe this?” she immediately replied, inspired by the same Spirit as Peter: “I have believed,” she said, “that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world” (ibid.).

Why, then, is it surprising if we prefer John speaking of divinity to blessed Peter, when we see that the singular beginning of his Gospel surpasses even the Lord’s own words, if one may say so? Nor is injustice done to our Redeemer if it is said that he brings forth something more sublime through his disciple than through himself, and plainly declares through the disciple’s tongue what he clearly did not wish to reveal through himself. For, so that a further comparison may also be seen [Col. 0863B] between these same blessed apostles, the Lord granted John in words what he conferred upon Peter in miracles: namely, that the one should utter higher things and the other shine forth through greater marvels of power.

For in the Acts of the Apostles we find that they brought out the sick into the streets and placed them on beds and pallets, so that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some of them and they might be freed from their illnesses (Acts 5). Yet we nowhere read that the Lord did this, namely, that he brought healing to anyone through the shadow of his body. But he displayed what he had foretold and fulfilled what he had promised. For in the Gospel of that same John he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me will also do the works that I [Col. 0863C] do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father” (John 14). Indeed, it was he himself who worked in Peter; it was he himself who spoke in John. “For,” he says, “it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10).

Rightly does blessed John, before all the earlier and after all the later writers of divine books, surpass them in the singular glory of his eloquence. Luxury did not stain him, lust did not corrupt him; rather, virginal integrity adorned him with the title of perpetual incorruption. Abandoning the bridal chamber of marital union, he transferred all the heat of carnal enticement into the delight of heavenly pleasures and joined himself most closely to the love of his Redeemer and beloved, for whose sake he renounced the bonds of the marriage bed. [Col. 0863D]

Therefore it was divinely granted to him that his heart should be filled with such a great grace of charity even toward his brothers that the sacred temple of his breast appeared like a furnace of divine fire. This is plainly recognized in all his writings, in which, throughout almost every page, he seems to pour forth the vapors of charity through certain cracks and to burn with the heat of charity. At one time he calls fathers by name and urges them to charity; at another he calls not sons but little children, as one who loves them tenderly. At another he addresses infants, young men, and adolescents by the proper terms for their ages, admonishing each group individually. At another he even sends letters to women, [Col. 0864A] inviting them to safeguard the faith and to pursue sincere love.

Thus, inflamed by an indescribable ardor of charity, turning this way and that, circling everywhere, running throughout all places, he rouses every kind of human being toward salvation. He surveys every stage of life, investigates every rank of the human condition with the attentive eye of anxious concern, and, having become like an Argus of the universal Church, embraces the whole human race in the arms of fatherly love and strives, by admonishing each person individually, to draw everyone into the fellowship of his Redeemer. The Lord’s love, by which he loved him above all mortals, bestowed on him this weight of fraternal love: namely, that he who was loved more should love more, and that he who was first [Col. 0864B] in the Redeemer’s love should become foremost in fraternal charity.

How great a place of influence with the Lord, and how special a privilege of intimate friendship John obtained, we can gather more clearly from this: the same blessed Evangelist testifies that, during that very banquet of the life-giving Supper, Jesus was troubled in spirit, bore witness, and said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” Then it follows: “The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain about whom he was speaking.” Soon he adds: “One of his disciples was reclining in the bosom of Jesus, whom Jesus loved. Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him and said to him: ‘Who is it of whom he speaks?’” And, not to dwell upon the narrative’s wording, when John [Col. 0864C] immediately asked, the Lord replied: “It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped bread” (John 13).

O wondrous and incomparable man, to be preferred above every proclamation of Christian devotion! Behold, a word is brought forward, and the whole assembly of the apostles is silent and restrained under the discipline of silence. Such, indeed, was the authority of the presiding master that the blessed company of the disciples kept itself under strict discipline. They hesitate, they are uncertain, and they look at one another, questioning each other in a certain manner by signs of the eyes; yet they do not dare to utter with their tongues what they desire to know, or to inquire by consulting the Lord.

Peter is silent, the key-bearer of heaven is silent. Silent, finally, is the tongue that, made the key of heaven, binds and looses heaven [Col. 0864D] and earth alike. Silent, I say, is he before whom the gates cannot prevail, who possesses authority to bind and loose souls (Matthew 16). Andrew is silent, he who went before his own brother to the fountain of life (John 1). Thomas does not speak, though he had professed that he did not know the way and learned from the Lord himself that he was the way, the truth, and the life (John 14). Philip does not presume to open his mouth, though, when he asked that the Father be shown to him, he heard the profound mysteries of the undivided Trinity (ibid.). All are silent, all are uncertain, and they inquire secretly—not by uttering words, but only by signs of the eyes.

But when the matter had long remained suspended in this uncertainty, and no one could untie the knot of doubt, at last [Col. 0865A] John’s advocacy is sought, and through him knowledge of the doubtful matter is reached. He approaches as an adviser, taking upon himself the person of his fellow disciples, confident in the greater privilege of intimacy and love.

Therefore, my brothers, consider with what devoted urgency we ought to seek the help of blessed John, whom the apostles themselves sought as an intercessor for them. How much will he be able to obtain from the just Judge for sinners, who intervened even for the senators of the heavenly court themselves? And if he became an advocate for the highest, how humbly should he be implored by the lowliest?

That eminence of the man, that height of sublime merits, was recognized by the angel who forbade himself to be worshiped by him. “See that you do not do this,” he said; “for I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers [Col. 0865B] who bear witness to Jesus. Worship God” (Revelation 28). He refused to receive service from one whom he knew to possess a familiar place of grace before the common Judge. He did not want a worshiper whom he judged to be his equal. He acknowledged him as a brother and regarded him as a companion; he did not accept the obedience of subjection.

Although among all the saints there is always fellowship with angelic purity and a kindred relationship with virginity, blessed John nevertheless surpasses the other virgins by as much as, through the merit of his devoted and perpetual guardianship, he approaches the blessed Virgin Mary’s virginity. He is surpassed by her alone, because the virginal fruitfulness that is in Mary cannot be compared with any merits whatsoever—not only [Col. 0865C] because she is fruitful, but because she is God-bearing. For a virgin to give birth is new and unique; but to give birth to God so surpasses every novelty of uniqueness, so goes before everything wondrous, and rises incomparably above it, that it can neither be conceived by the mind nor expressed in any way by the tongue. But just as the virginity of the venerable Mother of the Lord surpasses the virginity of blessed John, so he, because of his glorious companionship with her, surpasses all virgins from the beginning of the world.

Moreover, that reclining upon the Savior’s breast, that divine ardor which he conceived from the Savior’s secret inspiration, so burned away in his inward being the fuel of every lust that his body, truly as a temple of the Holy Spirit, blossomed [Col. 0865D] forth cleansed of all the squalor of seething luxury. The flame of lust could claim no place in him, whose temple the grace of the Holy Spirit continually overshadowed.

Therefore it was fitting that blessed John the Apostle should be associated with the archangel Gabriel in guarding the Lord’s Mother, so that the heavenly bridegroom’s attendant of old might invisibly guard the untouched Virgin, [Col. 0866A] while John outwardly offered the service of his obedience to female frailty. And it was fitting that she who bore the one who was Lord of heaven and earth alike should have the citizens of both homelands in her company, so that “every word might stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18; 2 Corinthians 13). Therefore, the more familiarly blessed John dwells with the Mother of the Word, the closer he is also found to the Word himself.

And because he was called Mary’s son not by another but by Truth itself—“Woman,” he says, “behold your son”— and confirmed the same by repeating it to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (John 19), no one rightly appears greater in merits than he who, with a special glory, is the Savior’s brother.

Let us therefore, beloved brothers, strive to keep the commandments of this man so sublime, so devoted, so chaste, and so excellent, beloved of God; let us study, with divine grace as our guide, to walk as far as we can in his footsteps. If we cannot all possess virginity in the flesh with John, because after shipwreck a second plank remains, let us strive [Col. 0866B] to flourish in virtues, and thus we shall compensate most effectively for the loss of our virginity. Let no flame of greed therefore burn within us; let no fury of anger drive us. Let no fire of lust seethe in us; let no shameful thought defile the beautiful appearance of our soul before God. Let not an abundance of earthly possessions lift us into pride; let not stinginess close the bowels of mercy against the poor. Let perpetual chastity, humility, patience, sobriety, justice with devotion, and severity with gentleness flourish in us.

Amid these things, beloved brothers, and amid the gifts of the other virtues, let charity, which is the mother of them all, always hold primacy in the sanctuary of our breast; because, as John says, “God is charity” (1 John 4). Thus, because through charity the Son of God descended [Col. 0866C] into the Virgin, may he through it raise us to the splendor of the Father’s glory—he who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity, one and true God, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXIV. ON SAINT JOHN THE APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST (26 DECEMBER)

We rejoice, beloved brothers, that a numerous gathering of your brotherhood is present, because, while the glory of blessed John summons us to today’s festival, the Holy Spirit undoubtedly inspires you to assemble with such reverence, peace, and devotion. It is fitting indeed that the one specially loved by Christ above all mortals should also be loved most greatly by those who love Christ, especially [Col. 0866D] since he himself showed such great charity toward us that, with the keys of wisdom and knowledge divinely entrusted to him, he opened all the treasures of heavenly mysteries and generously and faithfully distributed among us the riches of eternal life, which he alone had received.

What, then, do you seek of divine wisdom that you cannot find in John? What heretical perversity, what Arian faithlessness, what mad calumny of the Jews, what subtlety of pagan philosophers, or, finally, what abominable schism of schismatics has not been overcome by blessed John’s eloquence and manifestly crushed by his teaching? Whenever works raising questions are brought against us by the enemies of truth, John immediately comes forward: John meets them; John imposes silence upon the wordy. Whenever a disputed question arises concerning Christ’s true humanity and divinity—the common subject of contention for all enemies of peace—people immediately hasten to John’s Gospel, seek John’s protection in the battle, and thus all the quarrels of contentious strife are promptly stilled.

What is there in virtues or merits in which the most blessed man does not incomparably excel? He is an apostle in the Epistles, an evangelist in the Gospel, and a prophet in the Apocalypse. A prophet, I say, and not just any prophet, but a wondrous one and, in likeness to the other John, [Col. 0867B] more than a prophet. For since the office of a prophet is to foretell future things, not to demonstrate present ones, blessed John the Baptist excelled the other prophets because he pointed out with his finger the Lord whom he was prophesying (John 1).

Is this John not also more than a prophet, who, contrary to the custom of all prophets, saw himself in the spirit and, amid the many mysteries of heavenly revelations, when he saw the likeness of a flying eagle, truly recognized himself? Ezekiel, however, saw the same eagle through the revelation of the Spirit (Ezekiel 1), not flying, but rising above the other living creatures. With this prophet, blessed John, when the books of each are considered, is unquestionably in agreement in many respects. With him he ate the book that was [Col. 0867C] sweet like honey in his mouth, and he describes the places of the sanctuary (Revelation 10); and in many other matters the prophet proceeds harmoniously together with the apostle.

O how wondrous is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High! (Psalm 76). O how terrible is the Lord in his counsels concerning the sons of men! (Psalm 65). For who could worthily consider from what great humility this fisherman deserved to be raised to what summit of exaltedness? Indeed, once content with a wretched little boat and simply exploring the depths of the sea with his nets, he now penetrates the heavenly secrets by the ray of an enlightened mind, thunders forth mysteries, reveals to human beings the hidden things of the divine counsel, brings forth prophetic oracles, and [Col. 0867D] hands on apostolic teachings to humanity. Indeed, in contemplating the essence of the supreme divinity he surpasses the prophets, rises above the patriarchs, and exceeds the apostles. Finally, he transcends the understanding of all humanity and stretches the gaze of his mind to where scarcely even the angelic creature can reach.

O man full of God’s grace! “For the peace of God,” as the Apostle says, “surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4), so that he may rightly seem to say with the bride: “The king brought me into the wine cellar; we shall exult and rejoice in you” (Song of Songs 1).

Let us therefore consider, brothers, how different this man was then from the man he is now, when, with his mother intervening, he asked that he and his brother might be granted to sit, one at the right hand and the other at the left [Col. 0868A] of the Lord. For, judging by the words, he seemed to be asking that the Lord choose one of them for the right hand and reject the other to the left, among sinners. But because he asked foolishly, he immediately suffered refusal and heard, together with the sons, what he deserved: “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” When they answered, “We can,” he at once added: “You shall indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give you” (Matthew 20).

Here it is plainly shown in the Lord’s words that John was also a martyr, since it is established that he drank the Lord’s cup. And truly he was a martyr, because he endured many punishments of persecution for the Lord. He was therefore a martyr because, through the affliction of his own body and compassion for those who had gone astray, he bore the Lord’s cross for a long time in his life; and the longer he remained in the flesh than the other apostles, the harsher were the torments of his martyrdom that he endured. Hence it is piously to be believed that among those hundred and forty-four thousand virgins who have the name of the Lamb and the name of his Father written on their foreheads, who have been purchased from the earth and sing a new song before the throne of God and of the Lamb, blessed John is outstanding and distinguished; and that, together with all of them, he follows the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation 13), all the nearer to the Lamb insofar as he was dearer and more intimate to that same Lamb, and was moreover joined to his mother, who is the Virgin of virgins, by the perpetual submission of a son. For from the companionship of both—the mother, namely, and the son—John’s virginity shone forth excellently; and, as far as human merits can advance, he continually grew as though he had become the summit of virtues.

Nor should those words which our Savior spoke while hanging on the cross—“Woman,” he said, “behold your son,” and to the disciple, “Behold your mother” (John 19)—be understood so simply that they seem to have been spoken merely in the human manner. Rather, they are wholly effective, supported by divine powers and upheld by the unavoidable authority of Truth. For that one Word of the Father, substantial, consubstantial with the Father, and eternal, hung upon the cross; and therefore the words he spoke, because they are spirit and life, could not pass away without effect: “Heaven,” said the gracious Jesus himself, [Col. 0868D] “and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24; Mark 13). For just as he said to his mother, “This is your son” (John 19), so he said to the disciples, “This is my body” (Matthew 26; Luke 22). And such was the effect of those words that at once the bread he was giving became the Lord’s body. For “he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148). Therefore, by a certain similarity, if we dare say so, blessed John not only obtained the name of son, but on account of those words of the Lord deserved to receive from the blessed Virgin a certain greater sacrament of kinship.

Let us therefore consider, beloved, how great the glory of this great man must be believed to be: through a certain mystery of secret adoption he is both the Virgin’s son and the Savior’s brother. Hence almighty God raised his mind to such a summit of purity and mystical revelation that he showed him not only the condition of the present Church but also revealed what would happen thereafter, forever. Hence he also wrote that noble Apocalypse of his, which is known to overflow with such great mysteries that it seems to have as many sacraments as it has words; indeed, multiple meanings lie hidden in each individual word.

This work, certainly, is sent to the seven Churches of Asia and is addressed to the universal Church, which is governed under the sevenfold instruction of the Holy Spirit. Consequently, all the Churches spread throughout the world [Col. 0869B] do not hesitate to regard blessed John as their common teacher. To them, like an outstanding messenger of royal authority, sent from heaven by Jesus Christ—who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the living and the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth—he brought grace and peace from him “who is and who was and who is to come,” and disclosed many mysteries of heavenly secrecy.

Now, who would not be moved by the wondrous novelty of his blessed departure? Who would not be astonished at the glory of his most blessed completion? Because he lived wondrously, he died wondrously; and because he did not lead a life common to human beings, he did not pass away by the common death of human beings. For, as the histories relate, [Col. 0869C] he ordered a square grave to be made in the church, and then, descending into it, he departed with his hands extended after lengthy words of prayer had been poured forth. Immediately such a great light was sent down from heaven over him that no gaze could endure it. Later the grave was found to contain nothing except manna, which, as is said, has not ceased to gush forth even to this day.

346 Thus, indeed, thus, it was fitting that the disciple beloved by the author of life should pass from this world, so that he was as much a stranger to the pain of death as he had been free from bodily corruption. He wished to lie in the tomb in the form of a cross, because throughout his life he continually bore the cross; and just as Peter followed the Master and was crucified by persecutors, so in a certain manner John too was buried in ecclesiastical [Col. 0869D] peace.

But the Lord taught that there would be a difference between them when he said to Peter: “So I wish him to remain until I come. What is that to you? You follow me” (John 21). For he who wished Peter to triumph with him on the gallows of the cross himself decreed that John should rest in ecclesiastical peace, so that the former might provide the others who were to suffer martyrdom with an example of undergoing it, while the latter, after the Church’s structure had been raised upon the foundation of faith, might depart peacefully to heaven; the former might be a model of steadfastness for the martyrs who would follow, and the latter a discipline of conduct and spiritual virtues for those newly planted in the faith.

“So I wish him to remain until I come.” “I will come,” he says, in order to release him from the bond of the flesh. “I will come,” in order to transfer him to participation in my glory. “I will come,” in order to repay him with the reward of a fitting recompense for his labors. Finally, he gave a clear indication of the fulfillment of this promise when, at his death, he caused a radiant light to shine forth, through which it plainly became evident that the author of light himself had come from heaven. The Lord therefore was present, not forgetful of his promise: he received his soul into that rest of the heavenly Jerusalem and transferred his most sacred body into the hidden secrets of a retreat known to him. For it is also written concerning blessed Enoch that “he walked with God, and was no longer found, because God took him away” (Genesis 5).

Now who could worthily marvel at the fact that manna is found in his tomb and that in an earthly cavern the bread of heaven is born not once but daily? Concerning manna, without prejudice to the higher mystery, it is written: “You gave them bread from heaven, Lord, having every delight” (Wisdom 16). Let all the nations of the peoples therefore come and be astonished at a miracle unheard of in every age and everywhere. Let them come, I say, and look on in wonder because in a tomb—which without doubt is a house of worms—the bread of angels is born, so that with the Prophet, in admiration of so great a gift, he may proclaim that God granted manna as food to the Israelite people, saying: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77). What was then sent to them from heaven is now seen to gush forth from the tomb. For if manna were not a great miracle on earth, the Lord would never have commanded Moses to preserve it for all ages: “Fill,” he said, “an omer from it, and let it be kept for future generations, so that they may know the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 16).

Behold what virgin chastity deserves. Behold how great is the dignity of inviolate flesh. See, my brothers, consider and weigh what delights incorrupt flesh possesses in heaven, if it produces the food of heaven in a tomb. With what honors is blessed virginity exalted there, where glory alone exists, if it is so wonderfully glorious even in a place of stench and decay?

Hence, even if we do not dare to define the matter fully, it is nevertheless pious to believe that, just as it is believed concerning the blessed Mother of God, so it may also be reasonably asserted concerning blessed John that he has already risen, so that, just as they shared virginal integrity, they may likewise rightly be seen to be equal in an anticipated resurrection; nor should there be difference in the resurrection between those whose harmony of life had been so great. For if these most blessed virgins, namely John and Mary, had not risen at all, why would buried corpses not lie in their tombs, when the bodies of blessed Peter and Paul and of the other apostles and martyrs are known to have been buried, each in its own mausoleum? Now that blessed John truly died and beyond doubt paid the debt of death can be proved in no better way than by his own words. When the report arose among the brethren that “that disciple would not die,” why would he have opposed those who were speaking truly by saying: “And Jesus did not say, ‘He will not die’” (John 21)? Surely he would uselessly be spinning out the matter and multiplying words if, while they were saying what was true—“He will not die”—he had immediately opposed them by saying, “Jesus did not say, ‘He will not die,’” and thereby in some manner contradicted the truth, even if he opposed those reporting the words. But by denying that the Savior had said that he would not die, he certainly asserted that he would die.

Moreover, whether he rose or did not rise, the fact that his holy body no longer appeared in the tomb was undoubtedly an operation of divine power. It is written in Deuteronomy: “Moses, the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab at the Lord’s command, and he buried him in the valley of the land of Moab opposite Phogor; and no one has known his tomb to the present day” (Deuteronomy 34). That miracle concerning the body of Moses has therefore now been renewed in John; and he who then deigned to bury the lawgiver where no one knew, himself also wished, through a certain secret mystery, to remove the body of his evangelist from burial. Both, certainly, were lights of the world; both bearers of heavenly commandments; both revealers of the divine counsel. Nor is it unfitting that the honors bestowed upon their corpses correspond, since in the exalted merits of their lives they shone harmoniously, although at different times.

Yet if the matter is weighed with careful consideration, [Col. 0871C] so that I may speak with blessed Moses’ permission, John is found to be superior. The former was a minister of the law; the latter was a preacher of grace. The former delivered commandments by which sins would be punished; the latter bestowed the baptism of repentance, through which all crimes would be wiped away. The former is the announcer of shadow; the latter is the minister of truth. The former said to the Lord: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me your face, so that I may know you”; but immediately he heard: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live” (Exodus 33). The latter, however, not only saw and heard God incarnate but also touched him with his hands, as he himself testifies, saying: “What was from the beginning, what we have seen, what we have heard, and what our eyes have looked upon, and our hands have touched [Col. 0871D] concerning the Word of life—and we have seen and testify and proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to us” (John 1). And he not only saw with bodily eyes God made human, but also, with a mind divinely illumined, perceived the very Word that was with the Father, through whom all things were made (John 1).

And, to carry the comparison further, Moses presided over the tabernacle that the cloud covered, so that at one point even Moses himself could not enter, as it is written in Exodus: “Because the cloud covered the tabernacle of testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it” (Exodus 40); Moses could not enter the tent of the covenant because the cloud covered everything. But John became the guardian of a better tabernacle and was made the minister of blessed Mary, whom not a bodily cloud of this air covered, but whom the Holy Spirit invisibly overshadowed. And the glory of the Lord—that is, the Son of God—who filled this tabernacle, not in order soon to depart but in order to assume true flesh, did not remain beneath the atmospheric darkness of a cloud, but rather in the light of the sun, as it is said through the Prophet: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 18). Through him manna was then given to the Israelite people; behold how much more gloriously this man has manna even in his tomb. And why say more? The former veiled his face so that he would not be seen by the people (Exodus 34); the latter even reveals the essence of the divinity, so that God may be recognized by all (John 1). And to repeat the same point, the former covered the splendor of his face so that it would not be seen by that people; the latter clearly revealed the Word of God, who is “the image of the Father, the splendor of his glory and the form of his substance” (Hebrews 1), so that he might be recognized by us.

Finally, the Son of God, whom the latter held before his hands and with whom he lived for a very long time, by whom he was uniquely and specially loved: the former indeed earnestly and desirously asked for him, saying, “I beg you, Lord, send whom you are going to send” (Exodus 4), but he was unable to obtain this. Nevertheless, although both had shone with great and supreme merits before God, each was full of the same Spirit, and both burned in harmony with the same desire for the Redeemer. Nor do we presume to put one before the other if we weigh the difference according to the dignity proper to each. For among two travelers whose eyes are equally keen, the one who walks after sunrise sees whatever lies before him more clearly than the one who rises before dawn. And the one who gathers the autumnal ripeness of fruits is richer than the one who planted the orchards of spring growth.

It was therefore fittingly done that, just as with Moses, almighty God concealed John’s grave and displayed one miracle in two wondrous events.

And we should note how affectionately, how piously, how fatherly, how lovingly the Savior said: “So I wish him to remain until I come” (John 21). “I will come,” he says; “I will not send” any heavenly power, that is, nor any angelic authority, [Col. 0872D] to perform this ministry for me or carry out the effect of this obedience. I myself will come; I myself will receive his departing soul in the splendor of my glory—the soul which, while he remained in the flesh, I also illumined divinely. How greatly, then, should this blessed John be revered by human beings, 349 whom the author of life honored while he lived in the flesh and honored also as he departed from the world: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored” (Psalm 138). He honored him in life when he made him a resting place upon his most sacred breast. He honored him again in death when he deigned to come to receive a soul made blessed by its merits [Note: Note the soul made blessed by its merits.]. [Col. 0873A] It is no wonder that he heaped various honors upon the one whom he also adopted into fellowship with himself as a brother by adoption.

Blessed James was also called the Lord’s brother; but he was a brother by nature, whereas this man was a brother by grace; the former by kinship, the latter by exceptional love; the former through the line of maternal blood relationship, the latter through the bond of paternal charity: “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). And what more shall I say? He was the Lord’s brother in the flesh; this man was his spiritual brother. But how much spiritual kinship is proved to surpass carnal relationship we can find most clearly in the Lord’s own words. For he says: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

Nature in the flesh therefore made James the Lord’s brother; but John is a brother so much more nobly as the Lord of nature himself took him into spiritual adoption as his relation. Yet James too is blessed for this reason: he shares the same spiritual fellowship with the Lord. Otherwise, unless he were joined to the Lord through the Spirit, he could in no way be saved by that bond of earthly blood relationship. But John is more excellent insofar as, standing before the cross, he heard: “Behold your mother” (John 19). Rightly, therefore, in proportion to his greater love for him than for the others, he honored him more exaltedly than the others. And let us also, dearest brothers, strive according to our measure to extol him with worthy praises and always venerate him with worthy services.

It must nevertheless be noted that we never honor the blessed apostles so worthily and reverently as when we keep the apostolic commands; when we continually look to them as they go before us on the way of God; when we follow their footsteps; and when without stumbling we hold to their narrow and constricted path. Indeed, in baptism we followed the apostles’ leadership, because through them, at the very beginnings of our regeneration, we learned the faith of the Holy Trinity. Under the mystery represented by this figure, the priests of the Israelite people once went ahead while crossing the Jordan, and the people followed. But it did not seem sufficient for them merely to follow the priests’ footsteps in crossing unless they also took twelve stones from the channel of the Jordan [Col. 0873D] and set them up at Gilgal as a testimony. “Choose,” the Lord said to Joshua, “twelve men, one from each tribe, and command them to take from the middle of the channel of the Jordan, where the priests’ feet stood, twelve very hard stones, which you shall place at the site of the camp where you will pitch your tents tonight” (Joshua 4).

Now, without examining every word, although all are full of mysteries, what is suggested to us by this event except that, after we cross the mystical streams of the Jordan and rise from the font of saving baptism, we should strive to set before ourselves for imitation twelve very hard stones—that is, the most steadfast examples of the apostles? We place the stones where the priests had planted their feet at the site of the camp if, stationed for the spiritual campaign, we hold firmly and steadfastly to the apostles’ footsteps. For according to Solomon’s judgment: “The one who is slack and negligent in his work is the brother of the one who dissipates his own work” (Proverbs 18). Those who are soft and fluid in their conduct flow rapidly downward like water; but those who are constant and firm grow daily toward the citadel of virtue. This too is evidently signified by another detail of the same history: as that people crossed, the upper waters swelled up like a mountain, while the lower waters flowed down into the Dead Sea (Joshua 3). For among those who are baptized, some persevere in the sweetness of heavenly grace they have received; others do not cease to flow into the bitterness of sins by living wickedly, and fall, as it were, into the saltiness of the Dead Sea, while, by savoring earthly things, they head toward death down the slopes of an evil life.

But let us not be so, beloved, let us not be so. Rather, transferring our minds to true wisdom, let us strive, by God’s mercy, to advance in the heights of virtues in such a way that we would be ashamed to turn aside into the chasm of vices. Let us persevere always in hastening toward the things above, toward which we are striving, so that we may continually preserve the sweetness of divine love in our minds. Let us therefore labor to become participants in that wisdom by which blessed John deserved to be incomparably illumined through an abundance of greater grace. Having taken in its splendor, he pierces heaven like an eagle, so that, transcending all created things, he reaches by contemplation of mind the very summit of all things.

[Col. 0874C] You know, my brothers, that at the origin of the world’s birth the earth brought forth vegetation on the third day, the lights of heaven were made on the fourth, and flying creatures were created on the fifth (Genesis 1). Why did this order proceed in the creation of things, unless to instruct us that our mind must first bring forth the works of flourishing virtues, so that it may thereby deserve the grace of heavenly light and finally be able to fly forth to contemplate the appearance of truth? Let us therefore bring forth growth, brothers, so that we may be illumined; so that, once illumined, we may be lifted to heavenly things on the wings of virtues. Let not the false sweetness of this world charm us; let not the luxurious pleasure of carnal allurements dissolve us. Certainly, nowhere in the ceremonies of the Old Testament is a command found that honey be mixed with sacrifices. By this it is understood that God does not wish those who offer him the sacrifice of their lives to contain any carnal sweetness, or anything in them that belongs to carnal pleasure. Oil, however, is frequently added so that the offering of all our work may be presented cheerfully: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9). Salt also is commanded to be mixed into everything, so that the sacrifice of every good work may be seasoned with the salt of reason, discernment, and heavenly wisdom.

All the teaching of blessed John seems so sprinkled with the salt of divine wisdom that he may rightly be called the mouth of God, the tongue of the Holy Spirit, the cedar of paradise, the light of the Church, the glory of the world, the herald of heaven, the light of the world, the star of humanity, the image of the angels, a living stone, [Col. 0875A] the mirror of light, the logothete of divinity, the form of faith, the pillar 351 of heaven, the architect of the true tabernacle, which God fixed and not man. For he is also rightly said to be a cherub, since he is known to have received the fullness of knowledge from the very breast of the Redeemer.

Nevertheless, however much we strive to exalt him, we do not equal the merits of his sublimity; for although he deserved the praises of divine proclamation, the weakness of the human tongue cannot rise sufficiently to praise his merits. For he himself is his praise—the one who was once his price and has now become his reward.

Therefore, beloved, let us hasten through his footsteps toward our Redeemer with the full love of our hearts; let us always carry his teaching before our steps like a flashing lamp in the darkness. Let those who have begun, through the desire of hope, to hasten toward heavenly glory now be ashamed to cling to earthly things. Whoever is hurrying toward the delights of the heavenly wedding should blush to wallow in the mire of earthly pleasure; whoever hopes to be adorned in his homeland with the titles of angelic dignity should not seek a place of dignity in exile. Moreover, we heap up earthly profits in vain, since we possess immortal riches in the treasury of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore, let the abundance of external possessions not exalt the one whom the weight of earthly corruption burdens. Whoever has been appointed to fight continually with all his strength against the adversary must not be weakened by sluggishness and negligent idleness. Thus, thus, with the help of divine mercy, flourishing in virtues and rejecting vices, if here we follow him who showed us the way of the cross, we shall arrive there [Col. 0875C] at him who, having trampled down the power of death, entered heaven with triumphant glory: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXV. ON SAINT BARBATIANUS, PRIEST AND CONFESSOR (31 DECEMBER)

Recently, dearest brothers, we celebrated the ineffable birth of our Redeemer; now, with redoubled solemn joy, we honor the venerable assumption of his most blessed priest. In that festival our Savior, with the appearance of his majesty veiled, descended into the world; in this one his most glorious servant, laying aside the burden of corruptible flesh, ascended in freedom. In that festival the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our humanity for our salvation; in this one his blessed confessor reached, by a happy death, the likeness of angelic blessedness. In that solemnity our Redeemer, clothed in the trophy of flesh, entered the world to wage war against the aerial powers and overthrow them; in this one his outstanding soldier, having triumphed over the prince of the world, entered the heavenly palace as a victor. For God descended for this reason: that humanity might ascend; he deigned to humble himself for this reason: that he might exalt humanity.

At the Lord’s nativity an angelic voice sounded: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). Today a most sweet voice of divine majesty thundered to his beloved, saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25). In that festival the Lord came forth from the Virgin’s womb; in this one his venerable servant came forth from the prison of the flesh. In that festival Christ was wrapped in swaddling clothes for us; in this one his priest was clothed by him with the stole of immortality. He did not disdain to enter the narrowness of a womb so that the breadth of heaven might receive this man’s soul. He descended veiled in flesh so that this man might ascend adorned with a stole of glory.

Consider, dearest brothers, what kind of man this was, how completely the Holy Spirit inhabited him as a truly most sacred temple, and how he shone with so many miracles in the peace of the holy Church. At the beginning of the nascent Church, even those who had not been worthy to perform signs performed miracles; and many excelled in the power of signs without the virtues of conduct. Hence Truth itself says: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name? Did we not perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I will declare to them: ‘I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (Matthew 7). For, so that the holy Church might grow in faith, it had to be nourished by miracles; for when we plant young trees, we keep pouring water over them until we see that they have grown strong in the earth. But once they have fixed their roots, the irrigation ceases [Note: Gregory thinks similarly. Homily 29 on the Gospel of Mark.]. Hence Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14).

[Col. 0876C] Yet when we say this, we see that a question arises for us, not without some difficulty. For if signs are said to have been given for unbelievers, what is the meaning of the claim that our Redeemer was scarcely able to perform a few miracles in his own homeland because of the people’s unbelief? As the evangelist Mark testifies: “Many who heard him were astonished at his teaching, saying: ‘Where did this man get all these things? And what is this wisdom given to him, and such mighty works performed through his hands? Is this not the son of the carpenter and of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon? Are not his sisters here with us?’ And they took offense at him.” Hence a little later it is added: “And he could perform no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them; and he marveled because of their unbelief” (Matthew 13). What is this, brothers? Paul affirms that signs were given for unbelievers, while Mark asserts that they were withheld because of unbelievers (Mark 6). Can those who are full of one Spirit utter mutually contradictory statements?

But it must be noted that there was a certain difference among those very unbelievers. The error of all who did not believe was equal, but their merits were greatly different. It is one thing for someone to be deceived by ignorance alone; it is another for him to err with wickedness also joined to it. Paul sinned through ignorance, saying: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly” (1 Timothy 1). Judas sinned through wickedness, and therefore deserved in no way to come to forgiveness.

Signs were therefore given for those unbelievers whom divine providence had mercifully determined to save. But they were withheld because of those whom the justice of strict severity, demanded by their sins, was driving away from the lot of the elect. In Christian times, however, when almost the whole world everywhere already persisted in the Catholic faith and scarcely any savagery of persecutors disturbed the peace of the holy Church, why did the blessed confessor of Christ, Barbatianus, shine with the power of so many miracles, unless because he shone before the eyes of the divine majesty with the virtues of outstanding merits? [Col. 0877B] For he was, as is said of John, “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5): burning, namely, through the love of his heart; shining through the splendor of an exceptional way of life. But he had wished the lamp to be hidden under a bushel when, as the history of his most holy life relates, he avoided being revealed to princes while lying hidden in a little cell. He did not want to become known to the kings of the world, so that he might cling more familiarly to the King of kings; he refused to receive temporal glory from human beings, so that he might deserve to acquire eternal glory with the angels. To this belongs the fact that, when he wished to restore health to the sick, he often applied something like a poultice or frequently supplied something to eat as though it were a medicinal antidote. His purpose, as I think, was that, while the power of herbs or the efficacy of medicinal substances was believed to be responsible, the restored health might in no way be attributed to the powers of his holiness; and while medicine was received from him, he might seem more a physician than a saint.

But tell me, good physician, from where did you bring into our regions a preparation of such effective and sudden power that one did not have to wait three days, two days, or even the space of a single moment, but as soon as it was applied, every illness and every wound was immediately restored to its former health? A poultice cannot cure unless it remains applied to the swelling for as long as necessary, until either it transfers its strength through hidden passages into the body’s interior or draws the harmful moisture outward by the power of its efficacy. An antidote taken by mouth, however, must necessarily delay until its hidden force penetrates thoroughly through the veins and pores into the viscera, either strengthening what has been corrupted or cleansing what has been swollen with harmful fluids. But your wondrous medicine creates no delay, requires no dietary regimen guarded by physicians; as soon as it merely touches the surface, complete health is restored. Therefore, Father, I beg you, release, release the bond and hand on to us the knowledge of so incomparable a medicine.

Let us too see the priceless varieties of your medicinal substances and smell the delightful sweetness of fragrant aromatics. Come, brothers, listen: let the little book of his most sacred life open before all what kinds of aromatics its account—an account most health-giving—contains in his medicine, and of what substances that preparation consists. For among other things it says that the throat of the son of a certain Julian was grievously swollen. When he had been brought to the blessed man and his father tearfully pleaded for his son, the venerable man made a preparation of bread, wax, and oil, placed it upon the wounds, and, making the sign of the cross, immediately drove every disease miraculously from the boy’s throat at the very point of his mouth.

You have heard, dearest brothers, what kinds of medicinal substances our distinguished physician possessed, who healed a mortal wound with such speed. He transformed bread, wax, and oil—which served to sustain life—into instruments of medicinal treatment; and from what nourished his own life, he drove away another’s death. He used substances found in the household and thereby reduced the estimation of the price of foreign ones. Sometimes he offered a sick person a piece of citron, sometimes a dried fig; and by this kind of treatment he restored them to the strength of perfect health, removing all the distress of illness. His intention, unless I am mistaken, was that, since each of these fruits is seen to be rarer among certain people in the Roman regions, it might be believed that something medicinal had been involved; and while the restored health was attributed to medicine, the opinion of his holiness might be diminished in human estimation.

What, then, shall we wretched people say, what shall we do at the strict examination of the terrifying Judge, since we possess no virtues and yet before human eyes we pride ourselves on the excellence of our merits? We do not seek holiness before the eyes of the inner Judge with any desire, yet we rejoice deceitfully to appropriate the name of holiness for ourselves before human tribunals. How many do we see today who, if they had been able to attain even the smallest part of the virtues of this admirable man, would exalt themselves to heaven on the horns of pride; people who often do something that may perhaps be called virtuous, but by this seek not heaven but earth. Eager, surely, for human praise, they dissipate within themselves the fruit of their labors; and when they desire to display themselves to the eyes of others, they condemn before the sight of the divine Majesty everything they do. Often, too, they instruct others in the learning of sacred law and gird everything they think with testimonies, yet by this they seek not the life of their hearers but their own favor; for they wish to say nothing except what stirs the hearts of their listeners to repeat their praises, rather than what leads them to tears. [Col. 0878C]

The mind occupied with outward things does not grow warm with the fire of divine love, and therefore words spoken from a cold heart cannot inflame their hearers with desire for heavenly things. For a thing that has not itself burned cannot set anything else alight. Hence it often happens that the words of hypocrites neither instruct their hearers nor improve the very people who utter them, but instead make them worse through the praises they receive. As Paul testifies: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (I Cor. VIII). Thus, when love does not raise up the hearers by building them up, knowledge corrupts those who proclaim it by puffing them up.

Often, too, hypocrites, my brothers, afflict themselves with remarkable abstinence, wear down all the strength of their bodies, and, living bodily, extinguish the life of the flesh almost completely; [Col. 0878D] by abstinence they draw so near to death that they live as though dying almost every day. Yet they seek human eyes for this, desiring the glory of admiration. Truth itself testifies, saying: “For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting” (Matt. VI). Their faces grow pale, their bodies are shaken by weakness, their chests are pressed by interrupted sighs; but amid all this they seek from the mouths of those around them words of admiration, and think of nothing else in return for so great a labor except human esteem.

**355** Consider, my most beloved brothers, how pitiable is the folly of laboring intensely while panting for praise from the mouths of men; of serving the heavenly commandments with strenuous effort while seeking the reward of an earthly recompense. For, as blessed Gregory says, whoever desires human favor for the virtue he practices carries a thing of great merit for sale at a trivial price. From the very thing by which he could have merited the kingdom of heaven, he seeks the coin of passing approval. Therefore, my brothers, the good deeds we perform must be kept within, if we expect to receive from the inner Judge the due return for our work. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI). Hence also the Psalmist says of the Church of the elect: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV). The daughter of kings is the holy Church, begotten in good works through the preaching of spiritual leaders; and while she exercises herself in the virtues of holy conduct, because through this she strives to please God alone, she possesses glory not outwardly but within. Hence Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). The Apostle calls the testimony of his conscience his glory because, not seeking the favor of another’s mouth, he did not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

Therefore, my dearest brothers, the good deeds we perform must be hidden, lest, carrying them incautiously along the road of this life, we lose them through the attack of marauding spirits. For behold, this most blessed man Barbatianus, whose festive natal day has dawned for us today, did not seek the glory of human praise, did not court the favor of men; although he displayed so many miracles, he did not wish to appear miraculous himself, nor did he expect the reward of human recompense for the many benefits bestowed upon the sick. Indeed, he put forward the appearance of practicing medicine, so that he might have been able to obscure the brilliant splendor of his virtue. Like a great star of heaven, he took care to place a cloud before his virtues, so that, while he spread fewer rays of his light outward, he might shine more fully in the sight of the eternal Sun, gathered, as it were, into himself on every side.

It is pleasing, my beloved, carefully to consider the beautiful order of divine providence: namely, how the almighty God determines to send his stars across the face of heaven to illuminate the night of the present life, and through them to brighten the darkness of the whole world; so that, while we see the shining stars radiating through the regions of heaven, we may walk with an untroubled step along the path of our work through our night. For just as the morning star, preceding the sun, first rises from the eastern region, then climbs the heights of the southern sky, and finally bends downward toward the western axis, so indeed—so indeed—this most blessed confessor of Christ, Barbatianus, departed from the territory of Antioch, from which he had originated, and, passing through Rome, suffused it with the great light of miracles. At last, reaching Ravenna, he introduced Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness, into the minds of very many people. In Antioch he shone with the splendor of his rising; in Rome he scattered many sparks of signs; and he illuminated the city of Ravenna as though by the setting **356** of his most sacred death. Thus, through the merits of this most holy man, the whole world gleams in his three principal regions, like the radiance of a new morning star: in one part of the world his rising is seen, in another his ascent, and in the third his setting is celebrated. [Col. 0880B]

And, as we have already said in another sermon about his fellow-countryman, the most blessed Apollinaris [Note: Sermon 2, on Saint Apollinaris], how fittingly the name “morning star” suits him who, entering Rome, performed his first miracle of virtue through light. For Queen Galla Placidia, as you have heard, humbly sought his help on behalf of one of her maidservants, who was tormented by unbearable pains in her eyes. He immediately ordered her eyes to be touched with his cloak, and at once drove away from her all the distress of that deadly illness. [Col. 0880C]

Therefore, when I consider your dignity, most fortunate city of Ravenna, in subtle meditation, I recognize that you have been enriched by the most generous benefits of divine mercy. For I see that you deserved to drink the cup of perpetual salvation from the very original fountain of the Christian religion. In Antioch, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, the disciples were first called Christians (Acts XI).

From that foundation, then, of the holy Church, you received squared stones; raised upon them as upon the firmest bases, you have been founded upon the immovable solidity of faith and holiness. From there you have Apollinaris, the apostolic martyr; from there also Barbatianus, the outstanding confessor. Like two most excellent cedars of paradise, they shade you with the branches of their protection, so that, if you are willing to remain humbly beneath them, they may drive every whirlwind of the adversarial storm away from you. And so that nothing might be lacking to them that could contribute to the height of your happiness, as soon as they departed from the territory of Antioch, they dwelt in Rome, which is beyond doubt the head and principal see of the whole holy Church—surely so that they might first learn in Peter’s school what they would afterward teach you through the doctrine of truth, and abundantly drink from the purest fountain what they would pour into you, as it were by bringing it forth, through the ministry of saving doctrine. For they were, as it were, another Paul and another Apollos: the one planted those whom he established in faith, while the other watered them with the most abundant rain of miracles and preaching. But because neither the one who plants is anything in himself, nor the one who waters, let us also follow the apostolic words and say: “But God gave the growth.” [Col. 0881A]

Therefore, my dearest brothers, love these senators of the heavenly court with perfect affection of heart, and devote yourselves with complete dedication of spirit to imitating their examples. For if you wish to be what they are, you must also do what they did. Walk, then, in this world with the saints along the narrow and difficult road of labor, so that afterward you may be able to reach the breadth of their joy. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked (I John II). Without doubt, however, he strays from the footsteps of Christ who, fleeing the narrow way, treads the broad way. This most blessed man, whose solemn feast we rejoice to attend today, did not desire earthly honors, did not gather deceitful riches, did not seek the glory of the world, and did not enlarge the estates of a passing possession. He despised his relatives, abandoned his homeland, and utterly denied himself for the love of Christ. **357** [Col. 0881B]

Let no one therefore say that only those are considered worthy of heavenly rewards who are struck by the swords of persecutors for Christ’s name. God has closed every avenue of our evasion and blocked every refuge of human excuse. Behold, although we are now unable to undergo death for God with blessed Apollinaris, at least we can lead a life pleasing to God with blessed Barbatianus. It is indeed a great thing to die for Christ, but it is not less to live for Christ. Paul weighed both on an equal balance when he said: “For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. XIV). Whoever, then, loves martyrdom should make himself worthy of martyrdom, and without doubt he will obtain the reward of martyrdom. He cannot shed blood; he can strike himself with the weapon of repentance and slaughter himself in contrition of heart. Let the throat be prepared for the blow; the rewarder will not be absent, even if the sword is lacking. The executioner who strikes the neck outwardly is absent; the Judge who repays the reward of good will is present. [Col. 0881C–D]

Let us therefore strive, my beloved, with the most blessed confessor of Christ, Barbatianus, to despise the allurements of the world, avoid the abundance of temporal goods, restrain the incentives of the flesh, and carry the cross after Christ even in the peace of the Church. Thus, having now followed his imitable life, may we afterward with him be brought to the desirable glory, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXVI. ON SAINT COLUMBA, VIRGIN AND MARTYR (30 December)

While we celebrate the birth—indeed, the still-present birth—of the Virgin, my beloved, behold, a new triumph of a virgin comes before us, producing solemn joy for us and inviting us to rejoice again, as the Apostle urges us, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV). A virginal victory is joined to the Virgin’s birth, and renewed joys are restored to the still-uplifted spirits of the faithful. Recently the Lord humbly came forth from a Virgin; today, through a virgin, he has triumphed wondrously. Then the Creator of heaven descended to us while the integrity of the Virgin’s womb remained inviolate; today, through the virgin’s unshaken faith, he has borne the trophies of victory back to heaven in glory, saying to her whom he was bringing to the heavenly thrones: “Rise, hasten, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song II). Then the Mother of God guarded Christ, crying in the manger; today blessed Columba found him shining on the throne of his Father’s majesty. Then shepherds rejoiced at the Virgin’s birth; now emperors are confounded at the sight of a virgin. For there is one, as his blessed Mother said, who both “cast down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke II). For, as is found in the written history of blessed Columba, the emperor Aurelian, in an attempt to tear her away from faith in her heavenly Bridegroom, tried to bind her in marriage to his son. But the prudent virgin, utterly foreign to the folly of foolishness, firmly kept the rule of discipline. She immediately turned to the example of our Savior, which she seized as an impenetrable shield, and with the divine Word pierced **Siromaste**—the reading is uncertain—who was directing poisoned darts against her. “This,” she said, “is the argument the ancient enemy used when he showed my Lord Jesus Christ all the kingdoms of the world, saying: ‘All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me’” (Matt. III). [Col. 0882A–C]

What is this, my brothers? How could this emperor, so powerful, so exalted, and so terrifying, subject a fragile girl to his laws by no means, and, now by promising a kingdom, now by threatening punishment, utterly fail to move her from her purpose? He extends the scepter; she disdains it. He brandishes the sword; she is not frightened. Thus skilled and bloodthirsty cruelty exerts every sinew of its wickedness; thus it mingles harshness with blandishments. For the weapons of gold are sharper than those of iron, and the ambition for honor breaks the mind more powerfully than torture. He therefore employs every kind of weapon to shake the foundation of Christ’s tower; yet the pillar of God remains immovable, and the unarmed girl despises the armed king. [Col. 0882D]

She disdains becoming the emperor’s daughter-in-law and does not shrink from undergoing the tortures of a bloody executioner. What is it, I ask, that keeps the weakness of the fragile sex from being shaken by such a hailstorm of weapons? Now softened by flatteries, she is not bent; now assailed by the clamor of thundering threats, she is not moved. What is this, except that he who had assumed the weakness of our flesh supplies the strength of his power to the weak and infirm? For this reason the power of God was emptied, so that he might strengthen our weakness. For this reason the sublimity of God was bent low, so that he might raise up the fallen. For this reason Life deigned to die, so that, destroying the dominion of death, it might recall the dead to life.

This is also declared at the very beginning of the human race. For it is written: “The Lord cast a sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh, and the Lord rebuilt the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman” (Gen. II). When the Apostle spoke about this, saying: “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” he immediately added: “This is a great mystery. I am speaking, however, of Christ and the Church” (Eph. V). And truly it is a mystery signifying great power and marvelous depth. Through Adam, Christ is signified; through Eve, the Church. What does it mean that the Lord first cast Adam into sleep, then drew a rib from his side from which the woman was to be formed, except that the Redeemer first slept in death, and thus from his side flowed blood and water as the sacrament of the Church? Eve was taken from the side of the sleeping man; the Church came forth from the side of the Savior hanging on the cross. **359** [Col. 0883A–B]

But why did the almighty Creator, when he planned to propagate the woman from the man—that is, the fragile sex from the stronger—not wish to use the man’s flesh as material for making the woman, but rather bone? God could have removed flesh from the man from which the woman might be formed, and this would certainly have seemed more fitting. For he knew what the weaker sex would more appropriately derive from the weakness of flesh than from the strength of bone. And, so that you may marvel more at the sacrament of the divine work, he did not return bone for bone, but instead filled with flesh what was lacking in the man’s body. Hence, when Scripture said, “He took one of his ribs,” it immediately added, “And he filled its place with flesh” (Gen. II). He could have taken flesh from the man to fashion the woman; he could have restored the loss of bone with bone in the mutilated body. But he took bone and returned flesh, and thus formed the fragile from strength. [Col. 0883C]

Adam was therefore made weak so that Eve might become strong. Christ was weakened so that the Church might be strengthened. His weakness is our strength, and he endured our weakness for this purpose: to establish us in his strength. “What is weak in God,” says the Apostle, “is stronger than men” (I Cor. I). And elsewhere: “For even though Christ was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God. For even though we are weak in him, yet we live with him through the power of God” (II Cor. XIII).

Indeed, the men of this world who desire to become renowned through the valor of wars, who wish their victories to be celebrated by the mouths of the populace, when they are about to enter battle, place upon their bodies what is weak and soft, and put over it what is hard and difficult to penetrate. For they clothe themselves in iron breastplates and strive to protect the flesh, which easily yields to a blow, so that what is hard and strong on the outside may defend what is soft within. [Col. 0883D–0884A]

When our Redeemer enters the arena of this world to fight, when he arms himself as a strong warrior to conquer the wickedness of the air, because he had to undertake a new battle he put on a new kind of armor: namely, he placed what is weak on top and concealed what is strong. He put on the breastplate of weak flesh and concealed the unconquerable strength of his divinity. Thus, through the flesh, the devil lost to the second man what through the flesh he had once overcome in the first man; and the same thing that had been the means of victory over our first parent now became the cause of his ruin. [Col. 0884A]

That event foreshadowed this through the mystery of allegory: David, fleeing from the presence of King Saul, pretended madness in the presence of Achish, king of Gath. Scripture says: “His saliva ran down into his beard” (I Kings XXI). Since a beard is properly characteristic of a man, what does it indicate in mystical understanding except a sign of strength? What, then, is signified by saliva, which is fluid and flowing, except the weakness of the flesh? And what by the beard except the strength of divinity? The beard is therefore covered by flowing saliva, because the power of divinity is clothed with the fragile veil of flesh.

But what David performed by the skill of providential dispensation was regarded by the ignorant as madness. Hence Achish said to his servants: “You have seen a madman; why have you brought him to me? Do we lack madmen, that you have brought this man in to play the madman in my presence?” (Ibid.) Did something similar not also happen to the true David, our Redeemer, so that he was thought mad by those who were mad, and was said by demoniacs to perform miracles through demons? Hence the evangelist Mark says: “When his own people heard, they went out to seize him. For they were saying: ‘He is out of his mind’” (Mark III). He immediately added: “And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying: ‘He has Beelzebub,’ and, ‘By the prince of demons he casts out demons’” (Ibid.). [Col. 0884B–C]

Moreover, since saliva frequently runs from the mouths of infants, did not his words seem almost childish when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves”? When the disciples heard this, they said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John VI.) And, as the evangelist reports, “from that time they no longer walked with him.” But these drops of saliva covered David’s beard, because beneath those childish words divine power lay hidden. [Col. 0884C–D]

Our Redeemer therefore became weak so that he might make us strong; he appeared foolish so that he might call us back to true wisdom. Hence the Apostle says: “What is foolish in God is wisdom to men.” And shortly before: “Because the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (I Cor. I). Nor is it unworthy to speak of weakness or foolishness concerning the Lord our Savior, since he did not disdain to be mystically represented both by a leper and by a serpent.

Thus, as Scripture testifies, God said to Moses: “Put your hand into your bosom.” When he had put it into his bosom, he drew it out leprous, like snow. “Put your hand back,” he said, “into your bosom.” He put it back, and drew it out again, and it was like the rest of his flesh (Exod. IV). What is signified here by the hand of Moses except the Son of God? Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Let your hand be ready to save me” (Ps. CXVIII). It is as though he said: Let him through whom all things were made come into being, so that, while he is created, the creature may be freed from the contagion of its guilt.

This hand is in the bosom of the Father, as John the Baptist says: “The Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John I). But when this hand was brought forth from the bosom—that is, when it appeared through the mystery of the Incarnation—the people from whom he had proceeded judged him to be a sinner and, as it were, covered with the leprosy of crime. Hence Isaiah says: “And we considered him as though he were a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. LIII). But when this hand returned to the bosom, it completely lost its leprosy, because after our Redeemer returned to the Father, having trampled down the dominion of death, at the end of the world he will appear to all the Jews not as a sinful man but truly as God and man. For it is written: “Even though the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Rom. IX). [Col. 0885A–B]

He was also represented by a serpent, when the Lord said to that same Moses: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” He answered: “A staff.” He said: “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent, so that Moses fled from it. And the Lord said: “Stretch out your hand and seize its tail.” He stretched it out, seized it, and it became a staff (Exod. IV). What is signified by Moses except the Jewish people? And by the staff except the power of divinity? And by the serpent except the mortality of our Redeemer? Since death is represented by the serpent, mortality is rightly represented in the serpent. Or certainly, since it is written, “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. X), because the highest wisdom—namely, the wisdom of God—deigned to become incarnate, his mortality is rightly represented in the serpent. Hence in the Gospel he speaks of his passion, saying: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John III). **361** [Col. 0885C]

Moses therefore held the staff because, before the Redeemer’s coming, the Jewish people trusted in divine power. But he threw the staff upon the ground because that same people, through the patriarchs and prophets, announced that God would become incarnate. The staff is changed into a serpent because our Redeemer, remaining God in himself, became mortal among human beings.
