But Moses, seeing the serpent, was frightened and fled, because the Jewish people, when they saw the Redeemer of the human race as a mortal, recoiled in fear, as though terrified, rather than believing. He is commanded to seize the serpent by its tail because that faithless people, which now refuses to believe, gathers itself back to faith in the final part of the Lord’s body—that is, in the later age of the holy Church, at the end of the world. It seizes the serpent by the tail because the one whom it had previously despised as mortal it confesses, in the final period of the Church, as its Redeemer. But the serpent immediately returns to a staff because, as soon as the Jewish people believes in our Redeemer, that same Redeemer will appear for judgment in the power of his divinity. Thus the serpent becomes a staff for it, because he who was despised as a man on earth will, coming from heaven, be seen as God over the angels. [Col. 0885D–0886A]

Therefore, just as the Lord is called mystically both a leper without leprosy and a serpent without venom, so likewise he is called foolish without folly and weak without weakness. He so adapts and accommodates himself to our weakness that he both fights alongside those who fight and endures punishments together with those who suffer. [Col. 0886A–B]

What wonder, then, if blessed Columba, while standing before the tribunals of the raging persecutor, was both strong in sufferings and wise in her answers; if, while she was being tortured, another spoke through her? She moved her tongue, certainly, but another formed the words. “For,” he says, “it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X). It was hers to expose her body to punishment; it belonged to the other to supply constancy of virtue and endurance. She stood before the king’s tribunals, subjected to the hands of the executioner in torture, yet she mocked both: she was superior to the judge and stronger than the punisher. Hence the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs seems to address her directly when he says: “How beautiful and comely you are, my dearest, in delights! Your stature is like a palm tree” (Song VII). [Col. 0886B–C]

The holy mind is called “my dearest, in delights,” because while it is afflicted outwardly, worn down by persecutions, it is inwardly refreshed by the sweetness of profound joy, burning with pious desires. Its stature is said to resemble a palm tree because, just as it is not bent by the breezes of enticing vices, so it is not bowed by the terrors of any persecutions. While the rage of its persecutors strikes it as though with battering rams of threats, it remains firmly supported on the foundation of unconquered faith and truly endures, standing and towering, unconquerable. It is not at all like those of whom the prophet says concerning evil spirits: “They humbled you and said to your soul: ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over you’” (Isa. LI). Rather, it preserves what the Lord said to the children of Israel: “I am,” he says, “the Lord God, who brought you out of the prison of the Egyptians, so that you might walk upright” (Exod. VI). [Col. 0886C–D]

And because a palm commonly adorns a victorious hand, the holy and unconquerable soul is rightly said to resemble a palm tree, because throughout the course of its entire contest it contemplates the reward of victory already achieved. Therefore whoever, standing upright like a palm, firmly hopes for what he sees in the heavens, considers worthless everything he endures below. It also contributes to this that, when the Lord of heaven is recalled as having traversed the same path of suffering, she, who is dust and ashes, greatly rejoices to imitate the footsteps of her Savior. Hence the Bridegroom says to the same bride: “The hair of your head is like the purple of a king joined to channels” (Song VII). [Col. 0886D–0887A]

Just as by the head we understand the mind, so by the hair of the head we may appropriately understand thoughts. For just as hairs emerge from the crown of the head, so thoughts proceed from the mind. Since purple has the appearance of blood, what does it signify mystically except the Lord’s passion? And what do the channels signify except the minds of the saints? For just as the blood of shellfish is poured into channels so that wool may be changed into a purple color, so in the minds of the saints the blood of the Lord’s passion is recalled through meditation. In this way every devout soul is, as it were, dyed with blood, so that it may imitate the purple of the eternal King. In this way we are made conformed to our Savior, so that afterward we may also be co-heirs with him. [Col. 0887A]

The hair of the head of blessed martyr Columba was therefore like the purple of a king joined to channels, because, established in the suffering of her own body, she continually recalled the punishment of the Redeemer, so that she would not succumb in her own passion while considering that her rewarder had gone before her along the same path. The Lord’s passion is, as it were, a substitute table set before us, so that all who are invited to it and recline at it may also prepare similar things for themselves. The Bridegroom invites us to it in the Song of Songs: “Eat, my friends, and drink, and be intoxicated, my dearest” (Song V). And in the Proverbs of Solomon: “If you sit down to dine at the table of a powerful man,” he says, “understanding, consider what is placed before you; and so put out your hand, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Prov. I). [Col. 0887B–C]

What is that table of the powerful man except the table from which the body and blood of him who gave his life for us are received? And what is it to sit at it except to approach humbly and reverently? As we consider what is placed before us, we understand whether we are thinking worthily about the grace of so great a gift. And then we put out our hand in such a way that we know it is fitting for us to prepare similar things, when we wisely understand that, just as Christ deigned to die for us, so we ought, if the occasion is given, to lay down our lives for him. “For what,” says the Psalmist, “shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation” (Ps. CXV).

Hence also, after the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs had first said to his beloved, “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” he immediately added: “Place me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song VIII). It is as though he said: Because I loved you so greatly that through the death of the cross I awakened you, who were dead, you too must love me equally [*alterutrum*, corrected in the text to *alterum tantum*, ‘by another amount as great’], and place me not only in your thoughts but also in your deeds as the seal of complete and perfect love. For by the apple tree we should understand the Lord’s cross; elsewhere he compares Christ himself to this tree, saying: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forests, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song I). [Col. 0887C–D]

The apple tree is therefore Christ’s cross, through which the soul was raised to life, that is, freed from the bonds of eternal death. “Place me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song VIII). What should we understand by the heart except thoughts, and by the arm except the strength of action? We must therefore impress Christ as a seal upon our heart, so that no hostile assault may be able to violate it. We must also carve Christ into our works, so that in everything we do we may show ourselves disciples of the Crucified Teacher. The Apostle showed that this seal had also been clearly impressed upon his outward life when he said: “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. VI). And again: “Always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus” (II Cor. IV). [Col. 0888A]

Clearly, if our Savior perceives that we have been carved with this character, he too, in gracious return, sets us as a seal for himself. Just as he promised Zerubbabel, governor of Judea, through the prophet Haggai, saying: “On that day I will take you, Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, my servant, and I will place you like a seal in my sight” (Hag. II). But if, God forbid, we forget the one whose seal we bear, it is necessary that we likewise be handed over to forgetfulness by him. Thus the Lord says concerning the wicked king: “Even if Jeconiah were a ring on my right hand, I would tear him away from there” (Jer. XXII). [Col. 0888B]

Blessed Columba, the bride of Christ, had clearly impressed this seal upon herself both inwardly and outwardly: neither royal chambers could dissolve her into frivolous pleasures, nor ambition for honor entice her, nor the fury of resounding threats ensnare her, nor could any harsh or elaborate kinds of torture hold her back from the momentum of her course. No hostile force could break into the sanctuary of the eternal King, fortified by this seal; no schemes of creeping fraud could violate it. [Col. 0888C]

Thus, armed with the weapons of virtues, the glorious martyr and virgin hastened through iron, through fires, and through monstrous punishment to the kingdoms of heaven. There she now joins in a new song among the choirs of virgins, singing in harmony, and carries the palm of victory in her blessed hands. There she is held in the chaste arms of her Bridegroom, whom she loved; she is clothed in a robe of beauty and happily adorned with a crown of glory. Now, like a golden star among the fiery stones of heavenly Jerusalem, she shines, and continually gleams festively in the sight of him who, the fountain of life and source of light, illuminates all who stand before him with the rays of unfailing splendor: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0888D]

## SERMON LXVII. ON THE NATIVITY OF VIRGINS

Among all the deeds of the saints, my dearest brothers, there is nothing that can more powerfully set pious hearts aflame with love for the Creator, or more abundantly rouse them to act bravely, than the sacred victory of virgins. For who, upon hearing the name of a virgin, would not immediately recall the beginning of human salvation and remember that singular birth of the undefiled Virgin? Moreover, when it is recognized that the fragile sex has won the victory in its contest, the listener’s spirit is kindled more eagerly for the labor of striving.

[Col. 0889B] In this way, then, the virginal offspring still germinates, and that virginal fecundity still gathers the fruits of heavenly harvests, when the weakness of woman not only surpasses her sex but also triumphs over the prince of this world with an unconquerable greatness of spirit. For this purpose the Son of God was conceived in the flower of a flourishing womb, so that he might change the old leaven into unleavened bread and, through the flesh that had been conquered, restore victory to the human race. Indeed, he fashioned for himself a cuirass from our frailty, in which, exulting like a giant and powerful and strong in battle, he defeated the aerial powers. Thus steadfastness was brought forth from weakness, victory from captivity, and ascent from downfall.

Hence it came about that the ancient enemy, who applauded himself because he believed victory had come to him through the senselessness of one woman, now blushes to find himself conquered and confounded by many women. For, in the prophet’s words: “The yoke has rotted before the oil” (Isa. X). For as soon as the grace of the Holy Spirit flowed into human minds, a person was immediately released from the yoke of former servitude and adorned with the title of a new freedom. Hence the saying in the Song: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song I). *Chrisma* is Greek; in Latin it is called *unctio*, “anointing.” From *chrism* therefore comes *Christ*, and from *Christ* comes *Christian*. Oil, moreover, is ordinarily understood to signify the Holy Spirit, as the Psalmist says to our Savior: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). The oil poured out, then, is the name of [Col. 0889D] Christ, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is spread among as many as there are who truly receive the name of Christian.

But one may ask why John the Baptist declares that “God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John XIII), whereas Paul says, on the contrary: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV). How, then, is it “not by measure,” and how “according to measure”? (Col. II.) What John asserts—that the Spirit is given without measure—must doubtless be understood of our Redeemer, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. This is plainly recognized if the sequence of the Gospel text itself is considered. For after saying, “God does not give the Spirit by measure,” he immediately adds: “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand” (John I). Hence elsewhere he says: “We have received from his fullness.” John therefore agrees with the Psalmist, because the one removes measure from him whom the other declares to be anointed above his companions.

But when the Apostle speaks of measure, he wishes this to be understood of the individual faithful. For according to the measure of the Spirit, each person possesses a corresponding measure of virtue and steadfastness, so that he may either resist attacking vices in peace or, when placed in combat, pass undefeated through torments. Samson, indeed, was unconquerable as long as he had his seven locks (Judg. XVI), and whoever possesses the sevenfold Spirit of grace shows himself invincible when any storm of warfare breaks upon him.

[Col. 0890B] This is why that most sacred virgin, whose glorious triumph we recall in today’s solemnity, could more readily die than be recalled from the holy purpose she had once conceived. For she was a temple of God, the court of the eternal King, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. Manly strength shone in a woman’s breast; it could not be bent by flattering persuasion, terrified by the harshness of threats, or overcome by any kind of punishment. Her spirit was noble and unyielding, and therefore ignorant of defeat, because it burned with the ardor of faith and because it stood, as it were, on the summit of a lofty mountain. She judged that the judge seated in the chair of pestilence was subject to her; she recoiled from his flattering words and mocked him when angry. In her estimation, it made no more difference whether he gnashed threateningly and terribly, or inflicted blows and wounds of elaborate execution, than whether he offered a weight of jewels or glittering metals.

Hence the Bridegroom says in the Song: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song IV). What is signified by the north wind, which is certainly cold, if not the harshness of persecution? What by the warmth of the south wind, if not the relaxation of those who flatter wickedly? Yet amid both kinds of persecution, amid both devices of the evil spirit, the spices of the ecclesiastical garden are commanded to flow, because a strong spirit, caught amid these struggles, reveals whatever strength, whatever faith, whatever unconquered fortitude it had until then concealed. Thus, like spices flowing outward, virtues emerge into human knowledge and the fragrances of a devout reputation spread far and wide.

[Col. 0890D] This venerable virgin therefore released the spices in the field of battle that had previously been hidden in the secrets of her heart. Worn down by the press of persecution, she scattered the fragrance of her spice. David fought in her as though in the citadel of Zion against the face of Damascus—or rather, as a little and despised one in a fragile sex, he fought alone against the great Goliath with a single stone (1 Kings XVII). Of him it is also said in the Book of Kings, as a proclamation of great praise: “David, sitting in the chair, was the wisest prince among three” (2 Kings XXIII). He himself was like the most tender worm of wood, which killed eight hundred [Col. 0891A] in a single onslaught.

What is the meaning of David’s being raised up with so novel and unheard-of a proclamation of praise? Who is this person at once so humble and so exalted? Who, I ask, is this David so weak and despised that he bears the appearance of a worm, yet so strong and powerful that he kills eight hundred men in a single assault? In the chaff of the letter this would indeed seem ridiculous, if the marrow of the Spirit did not conceal a sacrament.

Who, then, is this worm, except the one who sings through that same David in the Psalm: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI)? For just as a worm is produced from the material of wood alone, so the catholic faith confesses that Christ was born without human seed from the virgin womb alone. Yet although the worm is tender and weak, while the hardness of wood is strong and solid, the worm nevertheless turns the wood into decay, makes it cavernous, and hollows it out. So our Redeemer, truly strong of hand and desirable, who emptied himself and appeared without form or beauty, weak and despised, gradually softened the human race, from which he arose, from its former rigidity and prepared for himself a great dwelling-place in his elect.

This David, then, sits in the chair, because, established in the glory of his Father’s majesty, he judges all things; to him the Father says: “Sit at my right hand.” He is the wisest, because he is himself the Wisdom of the Father.

But how is David called “prince among three,” when he held not merely a principate among certain others but rather the dominion of a royal scepter over all? (Ps. CIX.) For this praise diminishes rather than exalts; it lowers rather than raises, since he did not merely stand among three but surpassed all. Yet although this statement appears to disagree with David, there is someone to whom it most aptly applies.

That blessed and singular man, mystically called a worm, as soon as he is assumed by the Word into the unity of person, rules without inequality in the Holy Trinity. He is therefore prince among three because he is united to the Word, who is one person in the Holy Trinity.

He killed eight hundred in a single assault. The number eight pertains to resurrection, and the hundred to perfection. David therefore killed eight hundred in a single assault because our Savior, by the sword of his Spirit, killed all who either seek the perfection of faith or desire the glory of resurrection, making them dead to the love of this world through the mystery of his incarnation and [Col. 0891D] cross. He accomplished this in a single assault—that is, in the one advent of his incarnation. For he died once for our sins and no longer dies (Rom. VI).

Is his advent not rightly called an assault, of which Solomon says: “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song II)? And David says: “He exulted like a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII). Whoever runs undoubtedly makes an assault. The Word of God also comes like a stream of living waters with force and, like a torrent, overturns all the defilements of burning doctrines. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “A spring of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon” (Song IV). Hence also the Psalmist says: “The force of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV).

[Col. 0892A] Let us therefore give thanks to this King, at once so humble and so exalted, so weak yet so exceedingly strong, who deigned to become a worm in wood in order to make us citizens in heaven. For this reason he allowed the ancient enemy of the human race to rise up against him, so that afterward he might triumph over him not only through men but also through women: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXVIII. II. ON THE FEAST OF VIRGINS

Today, dearest brothers, virginal honor has shone upon us, renewing in our memory the victory of divine virtue. Now the more fragile the sex, the weaker the vessel that carries off triumph from the enemy, the greater the devil is clothed with the disgrace of confusion; the more wondrously God is recognized in his saints; and the more joyfully Christ, King of martyrs, delights in his female champions.

For this reason also, when our Savior came into the arena of this world to defeat the aerial powers, he did not choose rhetoricians and philosophers but simple people entirely ignorant of literary learning, so that in both sexes what the Apostle says might be true: “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the strong; and God chose the base and contemptible things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh might glory in his sight” (1 Cor. I). To such people almighty God often grants a more abundant grace of preaching, and through them refutes the crafty arguments of worldly wisdom.

Hence the Bridegroom says to the bride in the Song: “Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking cups” (Song VII). The navel, however, is the most fragile part of the body. What, then, is signified by the navel of the Church except the assembly of the weak and infirm? And what do we understand by the bowl except the order of preachers, who offer the wines of heavenly teaching to the minds of their hearers and intoxicate them with the cups of holy preaching?

[Col. 0892D] The navel of the Church is therefore rightly compared to a bowl, because often any weak and infirm person becomes a vessel of heavenly teaching. It “does not lack cups,” because it never ceases to be watered by the streams of heavenly eloquence. Hence this bowl is aptly called “turned,” since a person works more easily on a lathe. For those who have received the grace of preaching not through their own study but divinely often move more swiftly and without obstruction through holy preaching.

That the grace of preaching is to be granted to simple men or holy women was foreshadowed by Samson’s victory, when, seizing a heated ass’s jawbone, he killed a thousand Philistine men (Judg. XV). For what is signified by the jawbone of an ass—which is certainly a simple animal—except the mouths of unlearned simple people? Samson therefore killed a thousand men not with weapons or various kinds of missiles but with an ass’s jawbone, because our Redeemer, whom Samson prefigured, extinguished the perfect number of unbelievers from the life of their former error through unlearned and untutored people.

But is it surprising if sacred eloquence is signified by the ass’s jawbone in the case of holy preachers, when the word of preaching itself is sometimes indicated by barley, which is certainly the fodder of beasts? This is recognized not only through the five Gospel loaves but also through what is found in the Book of Judges. For when Gideon, at the Lord’s command, was sent to the camp of Midian to listen, a certain Midianite declared [manuscript reading: “confesses”] to another that he had seen a dream. “I seemed,” he said, “to see a barley loaf baked under ashes rolling and descending into the camp of Midian” (Judg. VII). When it reached the tent, it struck it, overturned it, and leveled it completely to the ground. The listener replied: “This is nothing else except the sword of Gideon son of Joash, an Israelite; for the Lord has delivered Midian and all his camp into his hand.”

Through Gideon—whose name is said to mean “not circuit” [or “not turning,” the Latin text being uncertain], but “one going around in the womb”—the one is fittingly signified who, while enclosed in a virgin’s womb, surrounded and ordered the entire structure of the world by his power. Through Midian, which is interpreted as “judgment,” the unbelieving people are understood, of whom the Lord says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III).

Until the Savior’s coming, both the precepts of the law and the prophetic oracles were hidden, like barley beneath its chaff, under the letters. But after he came, broke the barley loaves, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowds, the meaning of this deed was also explained by what the Evangelist says: “He opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV). Thus he deigned to make bread for souls from barley, which seemed suitable for brute animals.

For just as barley is crushed between the two millstones so that the chaff may be separated from the mass of flour, so the teaching of the holy Church is ground, as it were, between the two stones of the Law and the Gospel, so that the surface of the letter may be distinguished from the marrow of the Spirit. But, to dwell no longer on these words, this barley flour, mixed and kneaded after being sprinkled with the water of holy baptism and thoroughly baked in the fire of the Holy Spirit, becomes bread. It overturns the camp of Midian because it destroys all the devices of unbelievers. This bread, according to the conjecture of the true interpreter, is Gideon’s sword, because, as the Apostle says: “The sword of the Spirit is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

[Col. 0894A] With this sword of the Holy Spirit Christ, King of armies, arms his soldiers; with it he also girds and strengthens his female warriors. For he forms the ranks of his army and orders its battle lines from both sexes, admitting men and women alike to the preparation for blessed combat. And although God is wondrous in men, he triumphs even more wondrously and gloriously in women.

Judith belonged to this army. When she rejected the gilded and jewel-encrusted chambers of Holofernes, she cut off the head of the drunken and lustful prince with his own dagger (Judith XIII). Esther was a companion of this army. By soothing the fierce temper of King Ahasuerus with artful words, she rescued Mordecai from the sentence of impending death and turned upon Haman, who had been the author of this killing, the grounds for a deserved condemnation (Esther VIII).

Deborah rejoiced to carry this army. While governing the Israelite people with prophetic oracles, she also entered battle like a kind of Bellona of God, destroyed the abundant army of King Jabin, and freed the people of God from the harsh yoke of servitude (Judg. IV). Jael, the wife of Heber, served in this army: she received the fleeing Sisera kindly inside her tent, but drove a tent peg through his brain from one temple to the other (ibid.).

[Col. 0894B] Certainly that distinguished warrior, the blessed Felicitas, was a participant in this army. Having sent her seven sons ahead of her into the contest, she triumphed in martyrdom through her sevenfold offspring, while preserving for herself the reward of her own contest. This most illustrious virgin, whose votive festival is celebrated today, also carried this army with courage. She won the victory in a double struggle, conquering both the prickling incitements of the flesh and trampling underfoot the dreadful torments of punishments inflicted upon her.

With how many rewards will she be heaped in the recompense of the just! With what glory will she be enriched when Christ judges, she who was weighed down beneath so great a burden of Christ’s cross! For, in the words of the Truth, “The seed that fell into the earth produced fruit, one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold” (Matt. XIII).

Since, then, as authoritative teachers explain, a hundredfold fruit is owed to virginity, with how many gifts will this blessed virgin be enriched, with what distinguished insignia of grace will she be adorned, when, after having harvested a hundredfold fruit from virginity, she also carried away the crown of martyrdom with such glory?

When she stood in the contest, fortified with the cuirass of faith and girded with the arms of unconquered patience and twinfold charity, she was surrounded by the double ranks of different enemies. Within, she fought against rebellious citizens; outside, she battled against the lines of persecutors and those resisting the faith. One female warrior stood before two camps. On one side she defended the enclosure of chastity; on the other, with the mark of her Bridegroom impressed upon her, she defended the seal of faith. Thus her hand, trained for battle and encircled on every side by the shield of virtue, drove back sometimes the arrows of lust smeared with poison, sometimes the hail of missiles showered down by impending treachery.

[Col. 0895A] The champion of God therefore said: “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skin of Solomon” (Song I). *Kedar* is interpreted as “darkness”; these are the unbelievers who do not possess the light of faith. “I am black,” she says, because of the heat of persecution and because of the adversities that I suffer from the children of darkness.

But inwardly I am beautiful, because “the king desired my beauty, and all my glory is within.” I am beautiful, I say, like a skin—that is, like the tent of Solomon. For just as a tent is made from the skins of dead animals, so only those are a dwelling-place of God who, having died with Christ, have also been extinguished with respect to the vices and desires of the flesh. This virgin could not have died for the Lord unless she had first died to the world. “Do not consider me,” she says, “because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me” (Song I).

[Col. 0895B] O daughters of Jerusalem—that is, O faithful souls, already established through desire in that heavenly glory—do not consider me because I am dark; that is, do not despair or be excessively afraid because tribulations oppress me, persecutions afflict me, and, in this shipwreck of storms and tempests, swelling waves dash against me. For the sun has discolored me, since the heat of persecution has burned over me and obscured the grace and beauty of my loveliness. It is as though she said: Do not attend so much to the things by which I am afflicted outwardly as to contemplate the flourishing appearance of my inward beauty.

The Apostle says something similar: “Do not lose heart over my tribulations for you, which are your glory” (Eph. III); “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

Jeremiah briefly expressed this inner beauty and outward blackness when he said: “Her Nazirites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire” (Lam. IV). Behold the beauty—but hear the blackness, for he immediately continues: “Their appearance has become darker than coals, and they are not recognized in the streets. Their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood” (ibid.).

But we see the outward blackness. Let it itself disclose where the inward beauty lies: “Tell me,” she says, “you whom my soul loves, where you feed your flock, where you lie at midday” (Song I). It is as though she said: O heavenly Bridegroom, whom my soul loves indescribably, in whom it continually rests through desire, whom it embraces in the arms of deepest love, in whom it delights with all its inward being, tell me where you feed—that is, you who are the good shepherd, where you cause your sheep to feed—and also where you lie, that is, where you rest amid the heat of persecution and the fever of our temptation; where, indeed, except among those who do not know how to yield to raging madness and who do not weakly succumb to the assaults of rampant wickedness.

[Col. 0895D] This bride therefore called herself beautiful because, at the very moment of persecution, the one who makes all things bright with the serenity of his countenance was delightfully resting in her. Hence the Bridegroom says to her: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV)—wholly beautiful inwardly and outwardly: outwardly in the perfection of a clear deed, inwardly in the purity of a spotless thought.

And what does she say to the Bridegroom? “My beloved,” she says, “is white and red, and altogether desirable” (Song V). The beloved is white in virginity, red in passion. “For he washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I). He is altogether desirable because he is desirable in his singular birth, his life-giving death, his glorious resurrection, and his triumphant ascension. He is desirable when he speaks and when he performs miracles. O what a splendid and sweet exchange, in which the Bridegroom and bride, Creator and creature, praise one another in mutual proclamation!

Thus what is said through the Psalmist is fulfilled: “Let my speech be pleasing to him; but I will delight in the Lord” (Ps. CIII).

[Col. 0896B] And truly this is that part of the human race—the virginal chorus—in which almighty God takes a more generous and particular delight. Let it be that all the disciples are loved by the Lord, just as he is loved by the Father, as he himself testifies: “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you” (John XV). Let it be that Peter received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Let it be that in heaven and on earth he received the authority to bind and loose (Matt. XVI). Nevertheless, because John is a virgin, he is the disciple whom Jesus loved (John XIII).

Hence also John says in the Apocalypse: “No one could sing the song except those one hundred forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth. These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV). But so that many virgins may be able to follow this Lamb wherever he walks, he himself gives steadfastness in preserving virginity, victory in overcoming temptation, and a crown in the recompense of reward.

He says: “I am the lily of the valleys” (Song II)—plainly a lily because of the snow-white brightness of the purest chastity; a lily not of the mountains but of the valleys, because he chooses the devout minds of the humble and does not inhabit the crags of the proud.

[Col. 0896C] Beloved, let us follow this Lamb on the way that he kept while placed in this life, so that we may also deserve to follow him in the glory to which he ascended after conquering death. Let us carefully consider where his footprints are impressed, and let us not turn aside from the path of the one who walks, if we wish to be companions of the one who reigns.

The leader of our journey became a bearer of the cross and was given gall to eat. Whoever therefore desires to follow this leader’s banner must despise the honey of carnal sweetness. “For, in Paul’s words, we cannot rejoice in the world here and reign with Christ there.”

Hence, by the command of the Law, every sacrifice is sprinkled with salt, while honey or leaven is entirely forbidden to be burned in a sacrifice. Therefore the Lord says to Moses in Leviticus: “Every offering that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven, and no leaven or honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord” (Lev. II).

Whoever either appears to spend plunder on a work of piety or performs something good for the sake of empty glory is attempting to offer not the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth but the leaven of malice and wickedness (1 Cor. V). The Lord likewise does not approve the sacrifice of honey, because he condemns the pleasure of lust and every sweetness of carnal allure.

[Col. 0897A] Salt, however, is commanded to be applied to all offerings, so that whatever we offer to the Lord upon the altar of a devoted heart, we may always strive to season with the flavor of reason and understanding. For he says: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt, and you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice.”

And to impress more deeply what he was saying, lest our mind should at some time become tasteless and foolish, he repeats: “In every offering of yours you shall offer salt” (Col. IV). This is precisely the salt of which the Apostle says: “Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (ibid.).

Of this salt the Lord also says: “If the salt has become tasteless, with what will it be seasoned?” (Matt. V.) Let us therefore not be tasteless salt, lest, God forbid, that heavenly Bridegroom come and find us among the foolish virgins and close the door of the wedding banquet against us while we knock and groan. Rather, by divine grace let us strive to be the kind of salt that he wants us to be, who says to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth” (ibid.), so that, abandoning the works of darkness, we may now labor to walk as children of light and afterward, among the wise virgins with lamps lit, deserve to meet the Judge when he comes: he who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXIX. I. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0897C] After the cross, after the virgin, after the angels, what is greater on earth, what more exalted in heaven? It is surely she whom the Most High has accepted, who wounded the heart of her Bridegroom, to whom that same Bridegroom says in the Song: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, with one lock of your neck and with one of your eyes” (Song IV).

How beautiful is this bride, who with one little strand of hair and the flashing of one small eye wounds the King of heaven, the Lord of angels, the Son of God the Father. Our subject is her, although there is no speech in our tongue adequate to her. This is she who has been established as the pride of the ages, whose glory extends from sea to sea, whom kings and princes serve, around whom the multitude of heavenly legions flies, in whom the fountain of wisdom has been placed: “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.”

[Col. 0897D] A garden where bright rosebushes shine with more beautiful color and fortunate branches are laden with the glory of flowers and fruits; a garden untouched by the changing winds, where the grace of a gentler breeze frequently breathes and the ever-renewing beauty attracts those who look upon it; enclosed not by a structure of walls or by the adhesive strength of cemented stones, but surrounded by an angelic guard; a fountain from which the fountains of Israel flow, which waters the entire surface of the earth, refreshing and cleansing it; sealed with the seal of the whole Trinity, which that malicious burglar dares not, I will not say break, but even touch. In her, dead shoots sprout again and the driest signs easily become green once more.

[Col. 0898A] In her a manifold variety of mysteries is gathered, and the antiquity of the mercies of the Lord our God is concealed. And, to reveal briefly the scope of our little investigation, there are twelve sacraments in the Church, which the devotion of one faith enfolds; around their administration the authority of the Christian religion is ordered.

The first is the sacrament of baptism (see the Scholia at the end of the sermon). This is more precious than all riches, and nothing that is desired can compare with it. For who could express in the thought of the heart or the fluency of speech how many mysteries have been completed in the substance of water?

Before the world was brought forth and the diversity of manifold forms sprang forth from unformed matter, the Spirit of God was carried over the waters like a charioteer (Gen. I), and by a figurative act of service was soothing this element. The authority of the Hebrews transmits that heaven itself was formed from waters, and through waters that universal purification was accomplished. The patriarchs take wives at the waters, and through waters the terrible murmuring of the Jews is extinguished.

The entire sequence of the Old Testament, examined with care, marked a greater height of mysteries in the substance of water. The Savior himself, following the Law, began his journey with water when, in the river, he wished that sublime power to be baptized by that great man (Matt. III). He performed his first miracle from water (John II). Beside the well, he promised the Samaritan woman the fountain of water leaping up into eternal life (John IV). Finally, he who had begun with water ended in water. For when the side of the Crucified was wounded, water flowed out (John XIX), and by its cleansing bath made the whole world white.

[Col. 0898C] At the end, in a comprehensive command that imbued the apostolic choir, he said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Mark XVI). Do you not therefore clearly conclude that the sublimity of both Laws poured the power of sacramental realities into the liquid of this element? Do not be troubled by the small number of examples, since many more were at hand had speech not avoided length.

The second is the sacrament of confirmation. In baptism the Spirit is given for forgiveness; here, for battle. There we are cleansed from iniquities; here we are fortified with virtues. Is not the consecrated hand of sacred chrism impressed in the threshold of the forehead of our earthly house? Nor is just anyone recorded as the executor of so great a mystery, but the bishop alone, over whose head the oil of anointing has been poured and to whose authority the priestly multitude is subject.

The authority of the ancients handed on the grace of baptism to every person and every sex; but the distinction of confirmation the pontifical person alone claims for his dignity. Hence decretal pages and the institutions of the holy Fathers decree that the power of this sacrament is not to be postponed after baptism, lest that deceitful disturber find us unarmed, from whom no one has ever extorted a respite from doing harm.

Anointed, therefore, with the oil of both dews—healed by the one, strengthened by the other—let us descend more securely to the single combat. Let neither the weapons of Goliath frighten us nor his bodily stature move us, because the Lord our God is great with us, and great is his power (Ps. CXLVI), taking up weapons and shield to rise to our aid (Ps. XXXIV).

The third is the anointing of the sick. When we are sick and languish until death with the mortal fever of sins, the Spirit of compassion assists us and remembers that we are dust. For the blessed James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James V).

[Col. 0899B] A solemn anointing, an excellent liquid, by which health is restored, sin is forgiven, and fear of the Lord is infused. Do you see how the priestly hand raises up the sick person’s body and, by the most sacred anointing, soothes the seductive movement of the senses? Hence the holy Fathers also decreed that this anointing is a sacrament.

The fourth is the consecration of a bishop. The more exalted it is, the more worthy it is judged. When, by canonical decrees, the person who is to undertake the summit of so great a dignity is chosen, a more distinguished bishop is summoned together with the other bishops. The Church is prepared to receive a father from among her sons.

His head is anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, in the likeness of the one who, abundantly sprinkled with spiritual balm in the bridal chamber of the virgin, caused the oil of blessing to drip upon the sons of men. His hands are also smeared, so that whatever they bless may be blessed and acceptable in the sight of the divine majesty.

The Gospel page is placed upon his reclining head, so that he may perceive the word of life to surpass his own understanding and his eyes to fail in longing for the Lord’s utterance. A tiara is placed upon his consecrated head, and the glory of a golden plate is marked upon his forehead, in which the name of divinity is woven.

The ring of secrets is entrusted to his hand, so that he may say with the Prophet: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII). His feet are also shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace (Eph. VI), so that he may be one of those of whom it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Isa. LII).

He also receives a pastoral staff, so that by the very character of the rod it may be signified how he gathers the gentle and rebukes the restless. Thus, resplendent with the solemn glorification of his garments, and entering and leaving the altar of God with greater familiarity, he turns the judge’s anger into the father’s mercy by a blessed transformation.

He has the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI). He can deliver a person to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. V).

Fifth is the anointing of the king. Sublime indeed is the anointing, because it makes the power sublime. For when blood of such nobility—whether by lineage or by election—is consecrated as king, religion is summoned together with nobility by the entire strength of the kingdom. On one side stands the glorious company of primates, metropolitans, and bishops; on the other, the not-to-be-despised nobility of dukes, counts, and castellans [Col. 0900A]. The man who is to reign over men advances in their midst, surrounded by his personal retinue. Finally he is led to the altar of the Most High Prince, to receive the beginning of his reign from him through whom kings reign (Prov. VIII). Before he is clothed in imperial regalia, the consent of the clergy and the people is sought from him, and with his own hand he swears to the liberty of the Churches. Thereafter he is stripped of his garments and sprinkled with the oil of sanctification, so that, drenched with the typological dew, he may glory in the fullness of heavenly ointment. Finally he is clothed in purple, 375 the insignia of royal majesty, carrying in his hands the scepter of the kingdom for governing God’s holy people. A golden crown is also placed upon his head, marked with the sign of holiness, the glory of honor, and the aid of strength (Eccli. [Col. 0900B] XLV). A sword is also presented before his eyes, so that he may know that he is the avenger of God’s wrath, appointed for this very purpose. Initiated, therefore, into such great and such solemn mysteries, he is escorted back to the palace, from that day onward to be feared and loved alike.

Happy is he, however, if he joins the sword of the kingdom to the sword of the priesthood, so that the priest’s sword may temper the king’s sword, and the king’s sword sharpen the priest’s sword. These are the two swords of which we read in the Lord’s Passion: “Behold, here are two swords”; and the Lord replies: “It is enough” (Luke XXI). For then the kingdom is advanced, the priesthood is enlarged, and both are honored, when they are joined by the happy confederation previously ordained by the Lord.

Sixth is the sacrament of the dedication of a church. [Col. 0900C] It can scarcely be said how great is the variety of sacraments and alternation of rites in this ceremony. First, the church is whitened inside and out; twelve crosses are impressed around the interior circuit of the church, and just as many candles are lit. The church is cleansed; the bishop circles the exterior of the church with blessed water; and, striking the lintel of the door three times with his pastoral staff, he says: “Lift up your gates, and be raised up, eternal doors, and the King of glory shall enter”; those inside respond: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII). Then he blesses water sprinkled with salt, ashes, wine, and hyssop; writes the alphabet across it in a square arrangement; sprinkles the altar seven times with the same water; anoints the crosses with chrism, but the altar with a mixture of chrism and oil; burns incense at the four horns of the altar; covers the cleansed altar with new cloths; and performs many other things that the brevity of this discourse does not permit me to include. After this, laden with all the glory of his vestments, he enters the altar area to celebrate the singular sacrifice and thus bring the sanctification to its completion. Who could illuminate the darkness of this abyss with the clarity of speech? Yet we would have touched upon it, however slightly, had not someone who presides over the Church of Chartres in our own times explained everything more clearly with the most lively fire of his mind. To that fullest fountain, therefore, we send the thirsty, so that he may draw there the fullest truth. It should nevertheless be noted that the preceding sacraments are not performed without visible anointing, whereas the following ones are rightly read as containing nothing of this kind [Col. 0901A].

Seventh is the sacrament of confession. The goodness and nature of confession cannot be extolled by the praises of our small capacity, since the illustrious intellects of the Fathers have distinguished it with many teachings. This is the common way to God, a fountain open to both the just and sinners, which washes away an abundance of crimes with an even more abundant stream. It restores the first robe of innocence and brings the fugitive son back to his father’s embrace (Luke XV). From this fountain flowed the blessed apostles’ tears; in it the demons of the sinful woman were submerged (Luke VII); through it the adulterer and murderer David (II Sam. XI) is read to have been strengthened with the princely spirit (Ps. L); in it that blessed thief was washed, 376 who by the short bridge of the cross was transferred from the gallows to the kingdom, from punishment to paradise (Luke XXIII), “having been perfected in a short time, [he] fulfilled many years” (Wis. IV).

In this virtue the eyes of many are dimmed: either deprived of discernment, or led astray by flattery, they do not know what they should impose; or, if they know, they put private favor before truth. It is not our purpose here to disclose what we think about it; we reserve a fuller treatment of its nature for another discourse. Let it nevertheless not weary the reader to understand that the penitent must offer his pastor purity of heart, truthfulness of speech, and mortification of the flesh. The one to whom he confesses, for his part, must take care to administer worthy penance, continual prayer, and perpetual silence to the penitent [Col. 0901C].

Eighth is that of canons. [Note: [Col. 0901] Let these idle canons read this—those who care for nothing but their own skin.] These are raised to a high place in the Church: shining in white clothing in the episcopal seat, they promise the innocence of their hearts by the color of their garments. Living, or obliged to live, from the common fund and for the common good, they are to be chastised by perpetual penance if they sin; for their habit is shown to belong not to penance but to innocence. Let the friends of the Bridegroom themselves consider what they will answer before the face of the Bridegroom, who judges the world in equity, when he begins to demand an account of the bride. We do not wish to attack them, but let them take care of this alone: that they not be drenched with richer banquets from the patrimony of the Crucified One, or adorned with more splendid garments, lest they hear from the prophet: “They did not grieve over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos VI).

Ninth is that of monks. These are the men who, withdrawn from the turmoil of legal disputes, patiently evade the demons’ mocking enchantments. Constant in the Scriptures, eminent in obedience, fervent in charity, they contemplate from the vestibule the joys of the blessed city. Yet let them look carefully to themselves, lest they trust in the shabbiness of a larger hood or looser footwear, since “man sees what is on the face, but God sees what is in the heart.”

Tenth is that of hermits, who hide in mountain caves and the hollows of valleys; associated with angelic spirits, they are snatched by contemplative eyes into the riches of glory, and, in the flesh, forgetting the flesh, they weary their nature through tireless meditation.

Eleventh is that of holy women. These, overcoming sex and the world with more daring strength, carry away a remarkable victory from the ferocity of the ancient enemy. Glorious is the spectacle when tender limbs are broken by prolonged martyrdom, weakening the strength of him who desired the likeness of the Most High. At the sight of this struggle, that merciful gaze is quickly turned toward them and takes especial delight in such a victory.

Twelfth is the sacrament of marriage. “This is a great mystery,” says the Apostle (Eph. V); and the Lord says in the Gospel: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Mark X). For what is more one than those who have one flesh, one table, one bed, and one inheritance? “Marriage is honorable,” says the Vessel of Election, “and the marriage bed undefiled” (Heb. XIII). By this incestuous unions are destroyed, and the worthy offspring of legitimate heirs is propagated.

These are the twelve sacraments, 377 which, unless I am mistaken, signify those twelve crosses that we see impressed around the church. But now the pen must be laid aside, because both the poverty of my talent and the weakness of my flesh, which has overflowed more harshly than usual, forbid me to write anything further. If I am able to recover, I shall carry out what I have begun, to the honor of him who is blessed for ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0902C]

There are twelve sacraments in the Church. It is established that the word *sacramentum* is ambiguous and that, in its original usage, it does not signify only the sacred sign of sanctifying grace, as theologians have adapted it to signify the proper sacraments, especially those of the New Law, which are only seven; rather, by its own nature it extends more broadly to signify any hidden mystery, particularly one which, although spiritual, lies more sensibly concealed beneath the veil of signs. In this sense, therefore, the word “sacraments” is taken here. This is clear both from the learning and faith of so great a Doctor, who was not unaware that the proper sacraments of the New Law are only seven, and because shortly before he had said: “In the Church a manifold variety of sacraments is concealed.” By this expression he shows that he is not speaking only of the proper category of sacraments, but of every variety of mysteries or visible ceremonies with which the Church is adorned.

What introduces some obscurity into this enumeration is simply the question of what principle Damian observed in the matter, and especially why, out of the seven proper sacraments, he enumerated six while omitting the chief of them, which is the most holy mystery of the Eucharist; and why, from the sacraments improperly and broadly so called, he enumerated six others, when by the same reasoning he could have counted many more—for example, the blessing or consecration of sacred vessels and vestments, the institution and blessing of all the sacramentals, such as lustral water, blessed bread, and the wax from which the *Agnus Dei* is made, as well as exorcisms and similar rites. Moreover, several of those he counts do not seem distinct, such as the various states of religious life [Col. 0902D].

First, however, it must be said that the holy Doctor did not entirely pass over the sacrament of the Eucharist. For, when explaining the sacrament of the Dedication of the Church in sixth place, he adds these words: “After this, laden with all the glory of his vestments, he enters the altar area to celebrate the singular sacrifice and thus bring the sanctification to its completion.” Behold, under this sacrament he includes the august mystery of the Eucharist. And lest he seem to have touched upon the supreme sacrament casually and as though engaged in another matter, he adds: “Who could illuminate the darkness of this abyss with the clarity of speech? Yet we would have touched upon it, however slightly, had not someone who presides over the Church of Chartres in our own times explained everything more clearly with the most lively fire of his mind. To that fullest fountain, therefore, we send the thirsty, so that he may draw there the fullest truth.” By these words he appears to refer the reader to the letter written by Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, to Adeodatus. 378 The holy cardinal, therefore, did not entirely omit this divine sacrament; rather, he seems to have treated whatever Fulbert wrote about it as belonging to his own subject.

It may also be added that he could have omitted the Eucharist from the enumeration of the twelve sacraments because he was dealing only with those sacraments—or visible signs—which are ordered toward the veneration and honor of this most excellent sacrament and are represented in the dedication of a church. Thus the Eucharist is not merely a sacrament; it also contains in itself the end of all sacraments. It is not merely a sign, but also the reality to which the sacred signs refer; and therefore it is not numbered among the sacraments that are merely ceremonies or sacred signs. Hence, in Sermon 4, *On the Same Dedication of a Church*, the same author says: “By the fact that the relics of the saints are joined to the Lord’s body on the sacred altars, the body of the holy Church, united to its Redeemer, is displayed, and it is placed as a bridegroom with his bride in the holy bridal chamber of the altar.”

In the present sermon, therefore, he counts only those sacraments with which the bride is adorned; and for this reason he could rightly refrain from counting the bridegroom himself among them, while merely touching upon him as the final completion of the bride’s entire adornment. Accordingly, in the same Sermon 4 he concludes most appropriately that all those sacraments are referred to the honor of the Lord’s body and the remembrance of his death: “It is fitting, therefore,” he says, “that on the altar upon which the Lord’s body is continually sacrificed, his death should also be proclaimed through the enigmas of invisible things” [Col. 0903C].

If anyone carefully considers those words of the holy cardinal—“There are twelve sacraments in the Church, around whose observance the authority of Christian religion is ordered”—he will understand that he wished to count only those sacraments, that is, ceremonies or ecclesiastical observances, by which the members of the Church are either constituted, perfected and adorned, cleansed, or distinguished into different degrees and orders.

For this reason he places Baptism as the first profession of the Church, and as the way by which the members of the Church are constituted. To it he adds Confirmation as its perfection, and sacred anointing and confession as medicines necessary for these members, for the health of soul and body, when appropriate. He then adds the two sacraments of orders and marriage, by which the two classes of members of the Church—that is, clergy and laity—are distinguished. Among the laity, only the king or emperor seems to belong to the Church’s special authority and defense; therefore he places the anointing of the king among these sacraments.

Among ecclesiastical persons, three degrees can be distinguished: pontiffs, clerics, and religious. He therefore adds the sacrament by which pontiffs are consecrated, under which he includes the entire sacred order and the common state of clerics. Then he counts the state and profession of religious life, as especially pertaining to the authority and perfection of the Church, and distinguishes it into four orders: canons, by whom he includes regular canons and, indeed, all religious who profess the clerical state; monks living in community; hermits leading a solitary life; and nuns who likewise profess the religious life. He not unreasonably counted this religious profession among the sacraments that adorn the Church.

Thus a plausible rationale for this enumeration is established, and the question why he omitted other things is sufficiently answered: either they can readily be reduced to these, or they do not in themselves pertain to the Church’s aforesaid authority.]

# SERMON LXX. II. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

“Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX). There are three principal and perfect sacrifices that we are bound to render to the Lord: the sacrifice of pious contrition, the sacrifice of righteous action, and the sacrifice of praise or rejoicing. Of these, two are necessary in the present life; the third begins here and will be completed in the future. Of the first it is said: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. L). Of the second: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. IV); and elsewhere: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. L). Of the third: “Blessed is the people who know rejoicing” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Again: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. XLIX). The first sacrifice appeases God, the second delights him, and the third honors him. God does not care for these sacrifices unless they are rich in marrow and fattened. Hence the psalmist says: “As with marrow and fatness may my soul be filled” (Ps. LXII).

In the Law, all fat is commanded to be offered, and a fat burnt offering is praised. Lean flesh without fat gives neither flavor when eaten nor fragrance when roasted. This fat, however, must be understood not of the body but of the spirit, not of the flesh but of the mind. The virtues are the fatness of the soul. They give off a sweet fragrance; through them the Lord is pleased with God’s sacrifice, and without them no sacrifice is acceptable. With this fatness were filled those of whom it is said: “All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped” (Ps. XXI). Likewise the three boys in Daniel prayed: “As with the burnt offering of rams and bulls, and as with thousands of fat lambs, so may our sacrifice be” (Dan. III). Therefore, if these sacrifices of ours are to please God, let them be rich and marrow-filled.

[Col. 0904D] The sacrifice of pious contrition requires the butter of humility, which consists in three things: first, that a person consider how imperfect is what he possesses, in comparison with those above him; hence the saying: “That I may know what I lack” (Ps. XXXVIII). Next, that he consider that he possesses nothing of his own; hence the Apostle: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV). He should also consider that in this life he has nothing that he cannot lose, according to the saying: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do the first works” (Apoc. II). The sacrifice of righteous action requires the oil of discernment. The sacrifice of praise requires the balm of devotion.

These sacrifices have vices opposed to them, as though coming at them from the side. Opposed to the sacrifice of contrition is [Col. 0905A] the wormwood of indignation; to the sacrifice of righteous action, the vinegar of shame; and to the sacrifice of praise, the poison of flattery or detraction. Let us therefore offer the Lord, beloved brothers, pious contrition in inward bitterness and outward penance, so that “we may live soberly, righteously, and piously in this age” (Titus II): soberly toward ourselves, righteously toward our neighbor, and piously toward God. Sobriety consists in two things: avoiding pleasure and the cares of this life. Righteousness consists in two things: harming no one and striving to benefit all, according to the saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. LVI). Piety consists in two things: namely, that in the present the just person live by faith, and in the future await eternal blessedness. Hence the Apostle says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is in part will be done away” (I Cor. XIII).

Let us offer worthy praise in confession of the mouth and devotion of the heart. Pious contrition of heart arises from remembrance of sins and fear of the future judgment; righteous action from love of virtue and confidence in hope; praise and rejoicing from the affection of charity and remembrance of God’s benefits.

There are three kinds of remembrance of sin. The first afflicts and delights, and is evil; the second exasperates and pricks, and is useful; the third is glorious, and belongs to the perfect. The afflicting remembrance is that by which a person, recalling the pots of meat of Egypt, is affected by how delightfully and pleasantly he once lived (Exod. XVI), and by how difficult is the road he is about to undertake. The pricking remembrance is when he remembers how sordidly and shamefully he lived, not in order to return to his former ways, but in order worthily to lament them and set them before himself. Thus David says: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. L). The third remembrance, called glorious, occurs when a person recalls who he was and by what grace he was freed from the pit of misery and the filth of mire; he gives thanks, saying: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII). And, delivered with the Israelites from Egyptian slavery, he joyfully sings: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XV). And with Zechariah: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke I). These are the things we ought to offer to God.

[Col. 0905D] We are also bound to pay the vows we have made to him, according to the prophet’s exhortation: “Come, and pay your vows to the Lord your God.” Whoever does not pay what he vows provokes God, as it were, and mocks him. The vow must be offered whole and perfect, because otherwise it would not satisfy God, who exacts our vow as a debt belonging to him. Hence it is also said in the Law that we may voluntarily offer an ox or a sheep with its ears and tail cut off (Lev. XXII, 23). A vow, however, cannot be fulfilled from things lacking some measure of perfection.

Let each one of us, therefore, consider what he has vowed to the Lord and strive to fulfill it. We have renounced the world; we have taken upon ourselves the name and habit of monks. [Col. 0906A] We have vowed to the Lord continence, obedience, humility, patience, and a change from secular ways.

The saints specially vowed and fulfilled the three things mentioned above. Hear what the Apostle said and did: “I am not worthy,” he says, “to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Cor. XV). 381 Here is pious contrition arising from remembrance of sin. Again: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; as for the rest, the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day” (II Tim. IV). Here is righteous action arising from confidence in hope. Again: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” (II Cor. [Col. 0906B] I). Here is praise arising from God’s benefits.

David vowed a vow and fulfilled it: “I will pay my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people” (Ps. CXV). Jacob vowed a vow and fulfilled it: “If the Lord is with me and keeps me on the way by which I walk, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and I return safely to my father’s house, then the Lord shall be my God; and this stone, which I have set up as a pillar, shall be called the House of God; and of all that you give me I will offer you tithes” (Gen. XXVIII).

Jephthah the Gileadite vowed a vow and fulfilled it: “Lord,” he said, “if you deliver the sons of Ammon into my hands, whoever first comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the sons of Ammon, I will offer as a burnt offering to the Lord.” Jephthah then went against the sons of Ammon to fight them, and the Lord delivered them into his hands. When he returned to his house at Mizpah, his only daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dances; for he had no other children. When he saw her, he tore his garments and said: “Alas, my daughter! You have deceived me, and you yourself have been deceived. For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot do otherwise.” And he did with her as he had vowed (Judg. XI).

We know that the only-begotten Son of God swore and vowed to the Father, as the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI)—namely, that he would fulfill, in the suffering of his flesh, the sacrament of religion for the salvation of the human race. Let us do likewise and pay in full the vows we have made. May he himself deign to grant this, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON LXXI. III. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

“God made two great lights, the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Gen. I). Not everything, dearest brothers, that is in a harp produces sound, but everything contributes. So not everything in divine Scripture generates spiritual understanding, but everything contributes. Therefore, if in some chapter of Scripture it is permitted to glimpse the meaning of the Spirit through some little opening, we ought not to sleep during the investigation, but should search out the treasure lying in the letter with the vigor of an alert intellect. The wise man aptly foreshadowed this when he said: “Do not sleep in the bosom of a woman” (Eccli. IX).

The woman represents the letter of sacred speech, from which the faithful expositor produces fruit. When the diligence of catholic reasoning is applied to this letter, it is married to the strength of masculine understanding; but when the ingenuity of a deluded mind corrupts it, it violates the woman’s chastity as though by adulterous intercourse. Rightly, therefore, it is said: “Do not sleep in the bosom of a woman”—as though it were openly said: Do not grow sluggish in the secret meaning of the letter, but with chaste vigilance bring forth the soul’s hidden progress.

“God made,” he says, “two great lights” (Gen. I). It is true that, in creating the world, God distinguished the bright heaven with the adornment of the sun and moon, so that one might govern the succession of day and the other that of night. But if we search more deeply within, we shall find that the secret of the allegory corresponds to us. The Church bears the figure of the world, because just as the world subsists from four elements, so the Church is formed from the fourfold teaching of the Gospel.

The Church has its own day, and it has its moon in the night. The Church’s day is a time of peace; the Church’s night is the storm of persecution. The sun in the Church’s day is wisdom; the moon in the Church’s night is patience. With these lights God has painted his Church, so that in peace she may not be heedless, and in war may not be found soft and broken. Through wisdom the Church protects herself in peace from demons; through patience she guards herself in war from persecutors. The Church does not limp and is not weaponless: she wisely eludes divine arguments and patiently endures human torments.

The comparison of the sun with wisdom and of the moon with patience is entirely apt, because just as the sun surpasses the moon, so wisdom surpasses patience. Wisdom is therefore the sun because it illuminates; patience is the moon because it strengthens. With these twin arms the Church fights, overthrowing demons with one and conquering human beings with the other. Thus God made these two great lights by which the Church is adorned and with which Christ’s dove is fortified as though with two eyes.

When the clouds of allegory have been dispersed, we can also draw this stream of Scripture toward the watering of our morals. For just as God made two great lights in this world, so he also ordained two great lights in the human being. Let what we say not seem difficult: the human being is another world; hence in the Greek language he is called *μικρόκοσμος* (*mikrokosmos*), that is, “a lesser world,” because he was made in the likeness of the greater world. For just as God presides over the greater world while being wholly present everywhere, so the soul rules the body while being wholly present throughout the body.

The human being therefore has a day and a night; he has a sun in the day and a moon in the night. The human day is a life of righteousness; the human night is a life of wickedness. The sun in the life of righteousness is charity, which presides over the life of righteousness; the moon in the life of the sinner is penance. O how bright is the sun of charity, whose fifteen [Col. 0908A] rays the Apostle Paul, the son of the Sun, enumerates in his Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says: “Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up!” (I Cor. XIII). O how bright is the radiance of penance! It removes the night of sin by wiping away the cloudiness of conscience.

This moon, namely penance, has four rays: recognition of sin, sorrow for sins, confession of sin, and the fruit of almsgiving. First it is necessary to recognize sin, but that is not enough; one must grieve for sin. Confession must also be added, because the one who does not confess grieves in vain. To these must be joined the fruit of almsgiving, which is the price of sin. Hence the prophet says of the wicked: “Let him not believe, deceived in vain by error, that he must be redeemed at some price” (Job XV). The price of sin is certainly almsgiving. [Col. 0908B] But whoever constantly gives alms and constantly sins believes in vain that almsgiving benefits him.

The word *eleemosyna*, “almsgiving,” must therefore be interpreted. *El* means “God” in Hebrew; *moys* is said to mean “water” in the Egyptian language. Hence *eleemosyna*, that is, “the water of God.” Conversely, we can see that sin is the devil’s fire. Therefore the water of God should be set against the devil’s fire. Consider, Christian, your dignity and the redemption of your guilt. Do not despise it with a bestial mind. God made almsgiving for you by handing over his own body to death; make almsgiving for him by extending a morsel of bread to the poor. First be merciful toward yourself, then pour out upon your neighbor a stream of kindness, so that together with your neighbor you may be able to reach the fountain of mercy: Jesus Christ our Lord, who [Col. 0908C] with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON LXXII. IV. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 0907] The beginning of this sermon is not preserved in the manuscript.]

… is truly the mountain of strength; the saving standard, that is, the cross, is indicated, which with undying remembrance is ever green, blossoms, and bears fruit in the minds of the elect.

By the fact that the relics of the saints are joined to the Lord’s body on the sacred altars, the body of the holy Church, united to its Redeemer, is displayed, and it is placed as a bridegroom with his bride in the bridal chamber of the holy altar. And because in the Apocalypse the souls of the holy martyrs are seen beneath God’s altar (Apoc. VI), it is most fitting that here among us also their intercessions should be stored beneath the table of the visible altar.

Moreover, just as myrrh and aloe were placed in the Redeemer’s tomb (John XIX), so incense is placed here, by which the death of that same Lord is represented, as he himself says: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (I Cor. XI). It is fitting, therefore, that on the altar upon which the Lord’s body is continually sacrificed, his death should also be proclaimed through the enigmas of invisible things.

Around the walls of the basilica we likewise impress twelve signs of the cross with holy chrism and affix just as many candles, so that by these invisible signs we may display it as anointed with the unction of the Holy Spirit and divinely enlightened by the teachings of the apostles.

There are also several other things, my brothers, that we reasonably employ in the consecration of churches for a definite mystical purpose, such as wine, hyssop, salt, ashes, powders, and a fragment of red stone. We omit explaining to you one by one why all these are used, lest we burden your charity with lengthy discourses. Yet we touch upon them briefly in passing, so that we may extend at least a slender thread of understanding more abundantly.

Just as water signifies the Old Testament, so wine signifies the Gospel, which the Lord demonstrated when he changed water into wine while attending the wedding celebration (John II).

[Col. 0909B] And just as those liquids are mixed together in the consecration of the Church, so without doubt it is fitting that both laws should continually be present in our hearts. Salt is also added at the same time, to show that the tasteless flavor of the Old Law is seasoned with the salt of evangelical understanding. Hence, when the citizens of Jericho complained that the waters of their land were bitter, Elisha said: “Bring me a new vessel and put salt into it.” When they had brought it, he went out to the springs of the waters, cast salt into them, and said: “Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be in them death or barrenness.” So the waters were healed to this day, according to the word of Elisha that he spoke (IV Kings II). By this it is signified that the bitter water of the Old Law was to be changed into sweetness through the spiritual understanding of the Gospel.

Hyssop, which purifies the secrets of the breast, signifies faith, of which the Apostle says: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts XV). In ashes humility is signified, by which Abraham, speaking with God, said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII). By the appearance of the red fragment, the fervor of charity is indicated. Hence Adam is said to mean “red earth,” so that in the name of the first human being a person may learn that, because he is earth, he should live humbly; and because he is called red, he should not grow cold in the fervor of the twofold charity. All these things are visibly mixed together in the dedication of the Church so that we may learn to store their mystical meaning in our minds. And because we are indeed the Church, what sacraments of spiritual virtues ought to be within us are mystically represented for us through visible and bodily forms. For the present, let it suffice for you to know these things, so that through what we say you may also be able to infer what we leave unsaid.

You see, beloved brothers, that this basilica is composed of stones and mortar. If the structure of a wall, rising high above the ground, is piled up from stones alone and is not bound together by the glue of lime and sand, whatever has been built must collapse under any violent assault. What else is the temple of God but the people of God? What else are the stones but human beings? What else is the mortar but the tenacious bond of charity?
