Hence the Apostle says: “Have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. III). Just as a wall structure built without mortar is overturned by driving winds, so the edifice of good works quickly collapses under any assault of temptation if it is not held together by the bond of paternal charity.

Therefore, beloved brothers, so that the structure of our holy work may endure, may the Spirit of God bind you together in the framework of fraternal charity. For not all who appear to bear the name Christian deserve to reach Christ; nor do all who share in the fellowship of the Church truly belong to the unity of the ecclesiastical body. The tabernacle of the covenant, which then prefigured the Church of Christ, was constructed jointly by Bezalel son of Uri from the tribe of Judah and Oholiab son of Ahisamach from the tribe of Dan (Exod. XXXI). But we all clearly know that Christ was born from the tribe of Judah, whereas Antichrist is to be born from the tribe of Dan. Thus the universal Church now consists of members from both, but charity alone distinguishes who is believed rightly to belong to Christ and who to Antichrist.

Hence Bezalel is said to mean “in the shadow of God,” because whoever truly follows Christ is tempered by the shadow of the Holy Spirit—from whom Christ was conceived in the Virgin’s womb—against the heat of carnal desires. Oholiab is interpreted as “my father’s protection,” because Antichrist and his members protect themselves by the testimony of their fathers, that is, the ancient Jews, while they observe the legal commandments according to the letter and falsely teach that they must be observed carnally according to their tradition.

Behold, dearly beloved: now we are building God’s tabernacle through the fellowship of our common assembly [Col. 0910C], and we are adequately filling God’s temple by our bodily gathering; indeed, by the grace of new regeneration we ourselves have been made God’s temple. “The temple of God is holy,” says the Apostle, “which you are, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.” Terrible indeed is what follows immediately: “If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III).

A temple—that is, any material and earthly basilica—is at times stained by dust or by some light impurity; at times it is violated by the shedding of blood or, certainly, by the commission of some grave crime. But when excessive dust has merely accumulated, or some slight pollution has defiled the cleanliness of the floor, what has been fouled is swept with a light twig that has been brought in, and thus it is restored to its former cleanliness [Col. 0910D]. But if it is stained by the pollution of homicide or, God forbid, of some very grave crime, it must again be restored through the ministry of the high priest.

We, certainly, were made God’s temple on the day of holy baptism through the sanctification of the Spirit. If we are touched by the stain either of idle speech or of some slight offense, it is easy for us to be cleansed through the satisfaction of a light penance. But if we happen to have incurred the leprosy of grave sin, we must immediately approach Mother Church and implore the bishop, so that the temple of our soul—which is seen to have been violated and destroyed by an atrocious crime—may be restored anew through the exercise of priestly authority and the remedy of worthy satisfaction.

[Col. 0911A] There is no doubt that this restoration of the spiritual temple, which is carried out through the ministry of the visible priest, is inwardly accomplished through the effect of divine power and might. Jesus Christ, who is the true King and Priest, sees what has collapsed or been destroyed in a human being through the craft of the evil spirit, and by the abundance of fuller grace renews and reforms it for the better.

This too had been signified by the restoration of the temple of Jerusalem, which is read as having been accomplished under Darius, king of the Persians, by Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, the leader of Judah, and Jesus (Joshua) son of Jehozadak, the high priest, 386 (I Esdr. III). For just as Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had then destroyed the temple of Jerusalem by taking the people captive, so the spirit of wickedness, who possesses inward confusion, [Col. 0911B] often takes the human soul captive from its freedom and thus pollutes God’s temple with the filth of perverse desire.

And just as the temple was then restored through Zerubbabel and Jesus, representing the royal and priestly persons respectively, so the soul of a human being, overthrown by the fury of the ancient enemy and shamefully violated through his cunning, is raised up by the power of our Redeemer, who descended from both lines; and it is reformed not only into what it had been, but also into the fullness of a greater grace.

Hence the prophet Haggai said concerning that stone temple: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than the former; and in this place I will give peace, says the Lord God of hosts” (Agg. II). Then that Priest of priests and King [Col. 0911C] of kings enters to possess his temple forever. He not only purifies it from the contamination of the crime committed, but also illumines it thereafter with the continuing glory of his indwelling. As the same prophet says: “And the Desired One of all nations shall come; and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts” (ibid.).

Therefore, dearly beloved, we exhort you and beneficially admonish the wisdom of your holy devotion: if you recognize that the temple of your heart has been corrupted either by the craft of the ancient enemy or even polluted by the stain of some extremely grave crime that has been committed, approach that Priest who principally possesses the power of restoration and of the whole salvation of humanity. Cast out from the chamber of your mind the filth of wicked desire [Col. 0911D]; moderate the goads of fury and anger through the gentleness of patience; drive out the poison of wanton lust; remove, by contemplating what is above, the darkness of vain thoughts. Thus, when all the filth of vices has been cast far away, let the adornments of spiritual virtues take their place. Then almighty God, delighting sweetly in them, may build in you that dwelling in which he himself is both summit and foundation.

The summit, as it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII). The foundation, as it is said: “For no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Cor. III).

[Col. 0912A] Therefore, dearly beloved, let your mind not be a storeroom of merchandise, nor a treasury of greed, nor a battlefield of warriors. For whatever you diligently turn over in your conscience, that same thing you are in the divine judgment. Indeed, every desire of ours, whether good or evil, is seen depicted in our mind before the divine gaze.

But if the flame of lust burns within you, your mind is a house of fornication, not a house of prayer. If the tinder of envy and hatred is present, it appears to be not a dwelling of peace but a field of battle. Therefore let our mind not be a furnace of obscene lust, nor a sewer of carnal passions, nor finally a wallow of vices; rather, with the help of almighty God, let it be a hall of spiritual virtues, 387 which [Col. 0912B], the heavenly inhabitant himself may deign to visit and dwell in the temple of the breast dedicated to him, just as he promises through the prophet, saying: “I will walk among them, and I will dwell in them, and I will be their God” (II Cor. VI), who lives and reigns, one true God, in perfect Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

## MORAL SERMONS

A sermon on the vice of the tongue. A sermon on spiritual combat. A synodal sermon.

## SERMON LXXIII. ON THE VICE OF THE TONGUE

When a kindly creditor accepts whatever payments are offered under a written bond of security, the debtor who is bound is confident. So, dearest brothers, so indeed [Col. 0912C], when I see you attentive and willing to hear what is put forward from the poverty of my rustic inadequacy, I grow more ready and stronger to discharge to you the debt of the sermon I have promised.

And because throughout the whole course of the week, living separately in your cells, you have been nourished with the abundant banquets of sacred Scripture, let your spirit now receive from the hands of our service something like humble apples for eating, so that afterward you may return to the former feasts with all the greater hunger and eagerness.

Therefore, my brothers, when you come together, take care to walk honorably, gravely, and with restraint, so that, bearing the marks of due self-mortification, you may be able to agree among yourselves in quiet and peaceful brotherly love, and offer those who come from outside examples of holy conduct [Col. 0912D]. Above all, however, resist severely and watchfully the vice of talkativeness, and apply the bridle of sober restraint to your itching tongue. Otherwise, God forbid, in the space of a brief hour you may lose through idle speech what you acquired through many prayers, and what now flows lightly from the tongue may afterward weigh heavily upon the mind in repentance.

Often, among other foods, something is perhaps swallowed by the eater which, occupying the stomach for many days afterward, is not digested at all. So, among the many words that we utter indiscriminately, it is impossible that something should not sometimes emerge by which we feel the stomach of our mind weighed down, and which therefore cannot easily be digested, because what has been consigned to memory cannot be erased from thought.

[Col. 0913A] Some of the brothers, after remembering that they have kept silent for a somewhat longer time, immediately—presuming upon a kind of security arising from that very silence—drift into uttering all sorts of vain and frivolous things. They loosen their undisciplined mouths not to indicate necessity but rather to indulge pleasure and wantonness. Such men must greatly fear that they offend God more through the vice of their empty verbosity than they had previously pleased him by the discipline of their silence. 388 For they do not fear to persecute, through leisure spent in gossip and idle talk, all the more dangerously because all the more closely, the God whom they may previously have deserved to receive within themselves by keeping silent and persisting in prayer.

Let them therefore hear what Paul says to the Ephesians [Col. 0913B]: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only whatever is good for the edification appropriate to faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV). And because some first gladden God by living well, but afterward grieve him by speaking whatever is superfluous and perverse, he immediately added: “And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (ibid.).

Let wretched men consider what joy can insinuate itself into them, flattering them through vain words, when they know that they are grieving not some powerful person of this world, nor even merely any holy human being, but the Holy Spirit himself, who is undoubtedly God.

[Col. 0913C] If anyone wishes to know with what vigilance the tongue’s insolence must be restrained, let him consider among what crimes the same teacher of the nations places it. He says: “Fornication and all impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor coarse joking, which is out of place” (Eph. V). There, where he included fornication, impurity, and greed, he also indiscriminately named coarse joking and foolish talk, so that it may clearly be understood that the evil of the tongue is joined in offense to the gravest crimes and is not distinguished from them in the prohibition itself.

What can be worse than empty talk? It not only weighs down the unhappy soul lethally through itself, but also empties the religious life of integrity which has joined a person to God. James bears witness to this when he says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his heart, his religion is vain” (James I). From these words it is clearer than light that all our religion is reduced to nothing unless the wantonness of an uncontrolled tongue is carefully restrained.

[Col. 0913D] Again he says: “The one who does not offend in speech is a perfect man” (James III). If human perfection consists in guarding one’s speech, it is plainly evident that through the negligence of unbridled talkativeness the entire structure even of a perfect life is dispersed.

And if we wish to examine the matter carefully, the tongue often sins more seriously than life. For even if we intend to guard our soul with watchful care, nevertheless, because we have been propagated from flesh together with sin, we sin frequently through the hindrance of the weakness of that very flesh [Col. 0914A]. But whatever is committed in human conduct is expiated by the fruitful remedy of repentance and by frequent prayers.

Let us therefore consider, dearest brothers, how serious it is to sin with the tongue. The tongue, moved by a contrite and bitter heart, is accustomed to pray effectively for our sins, yet through the vice of the most empty talk it makes itself guilty and liable before the divine gaze. Remaining pure in its own cleanliness, it could have obtained pardon for our offenses.

Hence it is not without reason that the Wise Man says: 389 “The blow of a whip makes a bruise; but the blow of the tongue crushes bones” (Eccli. XXVIII). Behold: the tongue has no bones, yet it crushes bones, because when it flows lightly through windy words, it corrupts the strong and robust deeds of our virtue.

[Col. 0914B] Since “death and life are in the hand of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII), the vice must be greatly feared which is said to use its hand to strike, so that the soul of one who speaks emptily may be slaughtered. Hence, not without reason, the same Wise Man mentioned above says: “Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not so many as those who have perished through their tongue” (Eccli. XXVIII).

Two things are necessary for anyone who wishes to guard himself from the plague of this wickedness: he must restrain his own mouth from superfluous speech and also close his ears to the foolish chatter of another’s talkativeness. For this poison infects lethally not only those from whom it arises, but also those into whom it is poured, corrupting them with destructive disease.

[Col. 0914C] Hence it is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue; make doors for your mouth and bolts for your ears. Melt down your gold and your silver, make a balance for your words and straight bridles for your mouth, and take care lest you slip with your tongue, fall before enemies lying in wait for you, and your fall be incurable unto death” (ibid.).

[Col. 0914D] Solomon says: “Whoever guards his mouth guards his soul; but whoever is inconsiderate in speaking will experience evil” (Prov. XIII). Nor should we believe, my brothers, that the holy teachers of the New and Old Testament brought forward so many sayings against the vice of the tongue without reason. If they had not recognized that immense danger lay in this disease, they would never have argued against it so sternly, so incisively, so variously, and with such unanimity.

[Col. 0914D] To pass over the other testimonies of sacred Scripture, whom would that apostolic trumpet not terrify, when it thunders so dreadfully concerning this destruction, saying: “Behold, how great a fire kindles how great a forest! And the tongue is a fire, the universe of iniquity. The tongue is placed among our members; it stains the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth, being set on fire by Gehenna” (James III).

[Col. 0915A] The tongue is not without reason called a fire, because, as Solomon says of the fool: “The opening of his mouth is a burning” (Eccli. XX). If, then, the tongue is a fire that burns the entire forest of our virtues; if it is the universe of iniquity; if it contaminates the whole body with its foulness; if it sets on fire the wheel of our birth—that is, if it devours the whole merit of this unstable life of ours in the fire of its condemnation—unless someone guards his tongue with measured restraint, who can presume upon sobriety or chastity? Who can boast of fasts, vigils, or any good work?

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, place a bridle on our mouths. Let no coarse words come forth from them; let no fuel for frivolous amusement burst out. Let our tongue not bite the life of a weak brother by slander. Let it not rashly exalt the deeds of one who is running well, in the uncertainty of this life. Let it not idly recite past actions or words. Let it not maliciously report among the brothers what is being done by worldly people. 390

Let us also observe what Paul commands the Colossians, saying: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. IV) [Col. 0915B]. Therefore let our tongue be modest, sober, discerning, and chaste. Let the saliva of our mouth remain virgin as the day advances, and, unless an occasion of usefulness arises, let it remain uncorrupted until tomorrow or even the day after tomorrow.

[Col. 0915C] My brothers, you carry with you the key to your cell; carry also the key to your tongue. You put a bolt on the door; apply salutary restraints to your mouth. A fowler does not release his hawk unless he sees a goose; will a monk release his tongue if no necessity for speaking is present? A hunter disdains to set loose his hound unless a hare appears; should a monk hold his tongue so cheaply that he releases it uselessly for no one’s salvation or benefit? A stone sweats in the hand of those attacking walls; shall a word fly forth in vain from the mouth of one standing under the discipline of holy warfare? A bow is not stretched needlessly with its horns bent; shall a rational mouth be opened indiscriminately to pour forth superfluities? The quiver is spared so that an arrow does not lightly fly from it; shall the tongue not be spared, so that it does not inflict upon anyone a biting word like the blow of a wound?

[Col. 0915D] What shall we say to this, brothers? By what argument can we defend ourselves? By what artful excuse can we cleanse ourselves? Is it not easier and more peaceful to act than to speak? Is it not more laborious for the tongue to travel through so many words of extended talk than to remain quiet in its silence? Hence it is not without reason that Jeremiah says of certain people: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jer. IV). They are said to have labored to act wickedly because, by keeping silent, they would have rested better and without sin.

And if anyone happens to take delight in constantly tiring himself through speech, let him hear Paul say to the Corinthians: “What then, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation: let everything be done for edification” (I Cor. XIV).

If anyone, then, is troubled by restraining his tongue through the stern discipline of silence, let him diligently exercise it in prayer, psalmody, reading, or even in words that edify [Col. 0916A], lest the tongue that now burns with desire for speaking should afterward be burned in the punishment of its condemnation.

For we must not heed carelessly what that rich man sought: that his tongue might be cooled, because he was being tormented in the flame (Luke XVI). Since, according to the apostolic statement, the human tongue is now said to be set on fire by Gehenna—that is, by the inhabitants of Gehenna (James III)—it is not without reason that afterward, when delivered to avenging flames, it deserves to be burned together with them.

[Col. 0916B] Hence the Wise Man appropriately says of the perverse tongue: “In its own flame, it will not burn the just. Those who abandon God will fall into it; it will blaze against them and will not be extinguished, and it will be sent against them like a lion and like a leopard; it will wound them” (Eccli. XXVIII).

391 Let us also consider how much fear and terror should be aroused in us by what the Truth says: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII).

[Col. 0916C] Let the tongue that speaks emptiness hear; let the idle tongue hear; let the diseased tongue hear. I call it a diseased tongue because it suffers, as it were, from a kind of itch and scurf unless it is constantly scratched with the sharp nail, so to speak, of superfluous speech. Let it hear and tremble; let it understand and shudder at so terrible a sentence. Let it hear the terror of judgment from the mouth of the one who will himself judge.

Does it not have ears to hear, when it also has a hand with which it can kill? “For death and life are in the hand of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII). Let it therefore hear what is spoken by the mouth of the Truth, and let it examine through subtle meditation the threat: “Every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII).

Let us suppose that an idle word—if it is lawful to say this contrary to the judgments of sacred Scripture—is a light and altogether insignificant sin. But what is shorter than millet? What is lighter than a feather? Nevertheless, if an innumerable multitude of feathers or grains of millet is heaped together, the neck of the bearer must be broken, pressed too heavily as though beneath a great stone.

From damp rocks, too, a thin and scanty drop trickles; but if a vessel is allowed to remain beneath it for a longer period, it is found as full as though flowing water had poured into it. Tiny but innumerable gnats overcame the power of proud Pharaoh and all Egypt (Exod. II). An hour is a brief time; but as hour is joined continuously to hour, the whole course of our life is completed.

[Col. 0916D] Therefore let no one deceive himself, my brothers. While weighing the sin he considers light, let it appear heavy in his estimation when he counts it. For what is harder than stone? What is more fluid than water? And yet a certain wise man—Ovid—says:

> A drop hollows the stone; a ring is worn away by use.

[Col. 0917A] In the same way, all the solidity and strength of our soul is destroyed if it is worn down by the constant streams of words that pour forth and fall, as it were, like rain—even if someone claims that he has sinned only lightly—when the Apostle says: “Whoever transgresses the law dishonors God” (Rom. II).

Moreover, one accustomed to idle words plainly appears liable to a double fault: he both rejects the divine praises to which human nature is constantly summoned and persists in the superfluous talkativeness from which he is forbidden, just as Jeremiah says of certain people: “My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. XII).

These words of the prophet can also appropriately be understood of those who speak idly. Having abandoned the fountain of living water—that is, having set aside the word of life—they make their mouths into cisterns from which they bring forth not the words of the new but of the old person; like people drawing not fresh water from a fountain but rather foul water from a cistern. And because they do not know how to restrain their lips with discerning moderation, their broken cisterns cannot hold water.

[Col. 0917B] 392 It should certainly be noted that, just as a flying bird settles upon a branch of any tree, so the malignant spirit often comes and sits upon the tongue of one who speaks without thought. Through stealth it persuades something disorderly to flow forth in the course of speech, and afterward, when it comes as though with material for battle heaped up, it is able to attack the human heart.

Let each one of you, dearest brothers, return within his own conscience and recognize what we are saying. Often we speak something carelessly; afterward, when we return to guard our silence, we suffer such a great assault of invading thoughts [Col. 0917C] that we can scarcely endure it. We are altogether sorry to have uttered something harmful so incautiously, but no remedy presents itself, because what has once been sent forth we cannot recall.

As Flaccus says:

> And once sent forth, the word flies irretrievably.

[Col. 0917D] We pray and sing psalms, but we cannot tear from our heart the thorn’s embedded barb. Then, when the aged enemy sees our mind tossed about in such a great whirlpool, he rejoices as a victor, exulting that he is gathering, as it were, the fruits of his labor—the seeds that he remembers having sown in the ill-productive soil of our tongue.

In this deed, what else do they imitate but the thrush, which dies from what it digests? From its dung a plant grows; from its moisture birdlime is made, by which it is later captured. Thus it is driven by what had previously been its food, so that afterward it itself becomes another’s food.

[Col. 0918A] Therefore, when we utter whatever is impure and vain, what else do we do by speaking than weave snares for ourselves, by which we are afterward captured by cunning fowlers—that is, by malignant spirits? Often our speech generates battle not for the speaker but for the hearer, so that it inflames his heart intensely with hatred against the one who uttered the opposing words; and, if he has the means, he prepares to answer not words with words but deeds with an evil return.

These things seem to us, during the very conversation, trivial and light; but when we withdraw to the secret places of prayer, recalled immediately to memory, we judge them altogether harsh and intolerable.

Therefore, my dearest brothers, let us strive to restrain ourselves within the enclosures of silence and to hold our tongues back from vain and useless speech. For our soul is the bride of the heavenly King, endowed with the pledge of the Holy Spirit and dowered with the seal of faith.

Let her therefore remain a virgin in her inner chambers; let her not indecently go out in public; let her not cross the threshold of her mouth and pour herself vainly into superfluous and worldly words. Otherwise, if the Bridegroom should see her straying from the grave modesty of her chastity, he may at some time rebuke her, saying: “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks” (Song II).

[Col. 0918B] Let her therefore remain in her chamber in virginal fashion, keep the door of her mouth closed, and never go forth to speak except of what concerns awaiting the arrival of the heavenly Bridegroom. Let her restrain herself beneath the shadow of silence, lest she appear discolored; let her hide herself from every heat of worldly business, so that she may deservedly sing with an eager voice: “Under the shadow 393 of him whom I desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat. The king brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered love within me” (ibid.).

The brides of nobles commonly roll various kinds of spices about in their mouths as they chew them, so that they may be able to smell more fragrantly and sweetly [Col. 0918C] to their approaching suitors. Let our soul utterly shun onions, garlic, and everything that burns with the sharpness of earthly wisdom. Rather, let it continually strive to breathe forth cassia, the fragrance of constant prayer; stacte, the fragrance of sacred reading; cinnamon, the fragrance of psalmody; and every spice of spiritual perfume.

Let Christ be everything that it speaks, everything in which it delights, everything that it tastes, everything by which it lives. Let it breathe Christ, implore Christ, burn with Christ, pronounce Christ with its mouth, and handle Christ through constant meditation of the heart. Let it know no love for another; let it burn toward him alone with all its inmost being.

Let it call upon him with the loudest cries of desire; let it summon him to come to it through sighs and frequent groans. Adorned with various virtues and with its own beauty, let it invite him to enter it [Col. 0918D]. When it perceives that the one for whom it burns, for whom it is anxious, and for whom it longs has come to it, let it immediately cry out joyfully and eagerly:

“The voice of my beloved, knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my friend, my undefiled one.’” Then she adds: “I arose to open to my beloved.”

Happy is the soul into whose bridal chamber that heavenly Bridegroom enters and to which he is joined by an unbreakable bond of perpetual love. Without interruption it celebrates the wedding feast and enjoys, in unfailing abundance, the banquets of heaven.

Happy, I say, is the soul which, while it is drenched with the dew of divine grace, is immediately made fruitful with heavenly offspring. Thus, dried up toward the flesh, it produces fruit for itself; dead to the world, it lives for the living God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXIV. ON SPIRITUAL COMBAT

[Col. 0919A]

If we wish to consider carefully, dearest brothers, from where we have come and to where we are called, we have no strength by which we can adequately give thanks to God. For we are the children of Israel who served Pharaoh in Egypt (Exod. III), oppressed by the most grievous command of the proud king.

The prince of this world rejoiced to wear us down without ceasing beneath the iron yoke of his servitude and to occupy us always with the duties of servile labor. He compelled us to make bricks because he commanded us to construct for God not a temple from precious stones of virtue, but rather to fabricate an earthly building for himself.

But behold: the God of our fathers, the God blessed forever [Col. 0919B], has brought us out of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of the former life. He has released us from the bondage of tyrannical domination and has faithfully led us into the promised land.

394 We have already entered the promised land from the moment when, having rejected the desire of the world, we placed the confidence of firm hope in eternity. We already possess it in hope, and later, by God’s grace, we shall possess it in reality. By the grace of hope, those to whom Peter said had already been brought into this land: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light” (I Pet. II).

But because, under the guidance of divine grace, we have entered this land, we must no longer give ourselves to idleness [Col. 0919C], nor yield to sluggishness or negligence; it is not good for us to indulge sleep or careless security. It is therefore expedient that, always girded with the arms of virtue, we keep constant watch over our protection and fight fiercely against our most savage enemies.

Through war one reaches peace; through labor one passes into rest. There is no victory without combat, nor does anyone reach the crown without victory. We have internal enemies with whom, if we do not wish to perish, we are compelled to fight tirelessly and without any interruption whatsoever.

The enemies against whom we always stand in battle are not separated from us by ramparts interposed between us; fortified walls do not divide us; deep rivers do not flow between us; steep mountains do not stand in the way of close engagement [Col. 0919D]. They are always with us because they dwell in the inner chambers of our mind.

There are seven principal vices, from whose viperous seed the other plagues of the vices arise as poisonous offspring. They are pride, avarice, vainglory, anger, envy, lust, and sadness. We omit discussing them carefully here because we find that many interpreters of sacred Scripture have left numerous statements concerning them.

For now, it is enough to affirm this: whoever fails, with God’s help, to overcome these things will never be victorious in spiritual warfare and will never be able to attain the crown of victory: “For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Tim. II).

[Col. 0920A] These, finally, are the nations that Moses commanded the Israelite people to exterminate and to erase from the face of the earth without any treaty intervening: “When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are entering to possess, and has destroyed before you many nations—the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites—seven nations more numerous than you and stronger than you, and when the Lord your God has delivered them to you, you shall strike them down to destruction. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor show them mercy” (Deut. VII).

Behold, dearest brothers, you have heard that almighty God has delivered into our hands the nations hostile to us and, in the disposition of his providence, has already destroyed them from before us [Col. 0920B]. Why then do we grow sluggish through degenerate weakness? Why do we not seize the victory granted to us from heaven? Why do we not fulfill what pertains to us in that which has already been established in the heavenly judgment?

For if we carefully weigh the sequence of the words, we already see those nations prostrate before the divine judgment—those whom we ourselves are commanded to strike down and destroy. 395 When it says, “When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are entering to possess, and has destroyed the nations,” and shortly afterward adds, “You shall strike them,” it is clearer than light that almighty God has already extinguished in his foreknowledge our adversaries, whom he has appointed us to extinguish.

[Col. 0920C] He himself fights and invites us to conquer; he himself destroys the strength of the enemies and attributes the name of victory to us. He wants us to become victorious through his power, so that he may rightly crown us as triumphant.

Therefore, let no despair break us, since the exhortation of heavenly power summons us to act bravely. Let no weakness of human condition hinder us where the authority of divine command strengthens us for combat.

[Col. 0920D] Let us also hear what was said to them: “If you say in your heart, ‘These nations are more numerous than I; how can I destroy them?’ do not be afraid, but remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all the Egyptians: the great plagues that your eyes saw, the signs and wonders, the strong hand and outstretched arm by which the Lord your God brought you out. So will he do to all the peoples whom you fear” (Deut. VII).

Why then do we distrust because of our weakness, when we have the very Author of strength preceding us and leading our engagement? The one who is the leader and author of the battle is bound by his promise to grant victory.

Therefore let the mind be kindled with love of combat and let it go forth to the field to fight. Let sluggish spirits grow hot for routing the enemy’s ranks. Let no treaty intervene between us and our adversaries; let no terms of an intermediate peace reconcile us.

For not going to battle is inglorious; but to go and act sluggishly is altogether dangerous to life. It is better not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.

[Col. 0921A] Some, after taking up the rudiments of the sacred warfare, become so softened as their spirit grows lukewarm that, even if they appear not to do evil, they nevertheless make no effort to labor for any progress of their soul. They do not strive to overcome hunger through fasting; they do not resist the pleasures of offered banquets; they do not endure the harshness of cold; they do not take care to anticipate the common vigils.

Although they reject the use of what is unlawful, they nevertheless enjoy pleasantly whatever is lawful. These men have indeed been enrolled within the sacred army, but they do not know what spiritual combat is. They are counted among the number of soldiers, but they are proved ignorant of military duty.

Indeed, among armed men they are not ashamed to walk unarmed; among the armored battle-lines of warriors they do not blush to move about slack and unbelted [Col. 0921B]. And therefore they fall at the first blow of any hurled spear, because they are fortified by no shield of vigilance. It would have been better to live ingloriously within the enclosure of one’s house than, unarmed amid battles, to perish amid warfare without any titles of praise.

Indeed, those who seek the delight of the flesh while wearing the monastic habit desire to extract sap from dry wood. From this softness and laxity of life it happens to many that, although they know much, they do not know themselves, and do not fully recognize what degree of austerity they themselves are capable of enduring. Thus it comes about that those who have been granted knowledge of many external things still appear to need testing in order to know themselves.

For we have seen many long established in the sacred order who still did not know what they were capable of bearing in fasts, vigils, and the other practices of heavenly discipline. And since Scripture says, “Whoever is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. XIV), how can one who is convicted of being ignorant of himself in God’s service deserve either to be known by God or to know God himself?

Moreover, the fervent warrior who surrounds a fortress with a siege, strives to approach the earthworks, attempts to seize the ramparts, and amid the very hailstorms of missiles examines how far he may violently break in—

Therefore, whoever wishes to conquer himself ought to be ashamed not to know the measure of his own strength. Hence the Lord says: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate.” Yet that soldier of God had not received experience of himself, of whom Scripture says: “He placed a bronze helmet upon his head, clothed him in a coat of mail, and also girded him with a sword over his armor; he began to test whether he could walk while armed, for he had no practice in it. And he said: ‘I cannot walk in this way, because I have no experience of it’; and he removed them” (1 Sam. XVII).

But he had already proved himself skillfully when he took the sword of Goliath the Philistine, wrapped in a cloak behind the ephod, and carried it with him as he fled from the face of Saul who was pursuing him, saying: “There is no other sword like it” (1 Sam. XXI).

Here lies the test: the person who has advanced in the contest of spiritual warfare feels that the obstinacy of vices against him has become weaker; easily restrains the movements of the flesh rising within him; suppresses the tumultuous noise of thoughts with less effort than before; cuts away the thorns of carnal enticement as soon as they begin to grow; and immediately severs with the sword of divine fear the swelling necks of pride, lust, and the other vices.

But what benefit is there in anyone’s long participation in the sacred warfare when, as though still at the very beginning of his first training, he is seen limping with slackened hands and knees still weak? From this dissolution of negligence the excellent preacher forbids his disciples, saying: “Raise your slack hands and weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray” (Heb. XII).

A trained hand readily reaches battle and triumph; a body worn by its armor is borne ready into combat. What else is to be said of a monk who is still unable to crush pride, restrain avarice, extinguish the torches of envy, guard a pure mind from the wantonness of lust; who cannot drive out the poison of malice against one who has offended him; who, for the sake of preserving the rule of justice, succumbs to enduring injury—except that, as far as his profession is concerned, he has already enlisted in the sacred warfare, but has not yet at all recognized what spiritual combat is?

Indeed, those who strive toward perfection must apply all their strength to this: that, with salutary rigor, they learn rather not to know these things than to overcome them. Let those who profess themselves dead with Christ be ashamed that rebellious movements of the flesh and passions of the mind still live brazenly within them—passions against which it is necessary to fight as though at the very beginning of the engagement, lest, when the time comes that veterans may rightly be permitted to rest, they should still be serving among the battles as recruits.

Let the soldier of Christ, while still new, learn therefore to join battle; let him learn to confront each vice as it emerges, according as circumstances dictate. Let him turn himself prudently, keeping the lively eyes of experience directed here and there; and let him oppose a shield of defense to each of the arrows that are shot, so that he may cast down pride by humility, restrain gluttony by sobriety, trample anger by gentleness, curb avarice by generosity, extinguish the heat of lust by dread of everlasting fire, and burn up the beam of hatred with the flame of the sweetest charity.

Certainly God delights in this contest, for he considers subtly and profoundly everything that moves within the mind. The angels rejoice at such a spectacle, seeing that human nature, in fighting against itself, restores itself to their fellowship, from which it had been expelled; and by quarreling with itself it undoubtedly strives toward the true peace that it once lost through wicked self-agreement, because it did not resist.

Let us not complain, my brothers, if we do not immediately conquer everything as we wish; if, in the struggle of this combat, we endure hardships, labors, distress, and often the gravest weariness of a wavering soul. For divine providence looks after us in this way, lest our spirit be lifted into arrogance by sudden victory and fall more deeply from its height if it attributes the strength of its victory not to God its author but to itself.

Hence it is said through Moses to the Israelite people: “After the Lord afflicted you and tested you, he finally had mercy on you, lest you should say in your heart: ‘My strength and the power of my hand have accomplished all these things for me’; but you should remember the Lord your God, because he himself gave you strength” (Deut. VIII).

Hence also it often happens that a mind which overcomes many strong things within itself cannot defeat one perhaps very small thing, however carefully it keeps watch. This is done by divine providence, so that the human condition, shining everywhere with virtues, may not be lifted up in elation; so that, when it considers that it has overcome the strongest things, yet cannot subdue the small thing despite long effort, it may attribute the victory not to itself but to him whose gift enabled it to overcome what was conquered. Therefore it is said there: “These are the nations which the Lord left, in order to instruct Israel through them” (Judg. III). Israel is instructed through the nations that have been left behind, when our mind learns from the small things resisting it that it certainly did not subdue the greater things by its own power.

Here, dearest brothers, lies the whole substance of our undertaking, for which we abandoned the world; here our entire attention must be directed. We rejoice that we have come to the sacred order precisely so that our mind, girded with the armor of virtues, may always exercise itself in spiritual combat and strive with ardent spirit to destroy the monstrous forms of vice that do not cease to rage around us.

For what would it have profited the Israelite people merely to abandon the fields of Egypt, unless they had struck the necks of their enemies with the slaughter of war, so that afterward they might possess the excellent land in peaceful leisure? What benefit, finally, would it have been if they had escaped Pharaoh’s yoke, under which they were permitted to live in some fashion, if through sluggish negligence they had exposed themselves to the swords of the Canaanites?

Let us therefore shake off, dearest brothers, the degenerate inertia of a withered laxity, since we wish to reach the crown through the strength of vigorous combat. Let us always be ready to drive from the field of our heart the attacking wedges of vices and the roaring beasts, and let us permit them no place in what belongs to us from which they may bring about a perverse condemnation.

May our enemies not see us—God forbid—yielding weakly, lest they soon applaud themselves and be able to exult in our retreat. For we have as the unconquered commander of our warfare one to whom we confidently say: “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight those who fight against me; take up arms and shield, and rise to my assistance” (Ps. IX).

Happy is that spiritual warrior who follows such a commander in battle, who deserves to have such an author of his struggle—one who grants boldness to the presumptuous, victory to the fighter, and advances the victor to the crown; indeed, he himself is the donative for those on campaign, citizenship for veterans, and the everlasting reward for those who triumph: Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, the same blessed God forever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXV. FRAGMENTS OF THE FIRST SYNODAL SERMON

Just as on Mount Sinai the Lord, through Moses, set forth the decrees of the law to the Israelite people (Exod. XIX and following), so in the holy Church the same lawgiver and judge, through the ministry of priests, discloses to the Christian people the commandments by which they must live.

Sinai is interpreted as “bush” or “temptation.” For, as Scripture testifies, the Lord appeared from the bush and commanded Moses to carry his instructions to the children of Israel. And without doubt God is also seen in the Church, just as he promised Moses when Moses asked him to show himself to him, saying: “Behold, there is a place beside me; you shall stand upon the rock, and when my glory has passed by, then you shall see my back” (Exod. XXXIII).

But since Sinai is also called “temptation,” what else should this signify except that in the Church, where the law is given, the temptation of the evil spirit sometimes arises pestilentially? At one moment the hope of profit steals in to violate the rule of righteous judgment; at another, praise or human favor softens the rigor of justice; at another, anger or the resentment of hatred drives one to do harm; at another, fear restrains the heart from judging rightly with freedom; and at another, cruelty exceeds the measure of deserved punishment.

“Behold, there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock, and then you shall see my back.” What is this place, where the Lord is immediately seen standing upon [or: above] the rock, except the holy Church? There, while she stands firmly upon the rock of faith, we contemplate, together with the Apostle, the glory of the Lord. For this is the Church of which it is said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI).

“Earth up to the windows, and the windows closed” (Ezek. XLI). The Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. III). The windows of this temple are the priests, who pour the light of holy preaching into the people of the faithful. But when earth is piled up to the windows, the temple is immediately darkened by the closed windows. And when priests entangle themselves in earthly affairs, the temple, as though its windows were closed, is darkened because it loses its light.

Therefore, as far as we can, we must abstain from earthly activities so that we may continually devote ourselves to sacred utterances. As the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and dwelling beside the fullest-flowing streams” (Song V).

# HISTORIES OF THE SAINTS BY ST. PETER DAMIAN, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

## LIFE OF SAINT ODILO, ABBOT OF CLUNY AND CONFESSOR, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT  
*(A.D. 1049, 1 January.) With notes by André Duchesne and the Anonymous author.*

**400 Peter Damian sends greetings in Christ Jesus to the holy churches established in the western regions of Gaul.**

[Note: Hugo was the sixth abbot of Cluny and was also illustrious for his holiness.]

Hugh, rector of the monastery of Cluny and commander and chief instructor of the spiritual army, imposed upon me the task of briefly treating in my own style the Life of Blessed Odilo, his predecessor, and of selecting in a short abridgment the more useful and necessary elements from what had been set out at greater length on the preceding pages.

Compelled by his command, I shall not pursue the elegance of a polished eloquence; rather, as I am able to discover from the written materials presented to me, I shall attempt, with the help of almighty God, to serve pure truth. It is superfluous to bring a lamp in one’s hands when one is trying to distinguish the signs of shining stars. So too, while I display the deeds of this remarkable man as though they were stars in a clear and transparent sky, I have no need of the embellishments of urbane eloquence.

The life of the saints itself, faithfully narrated, shines so brightly that it does not require the brilliance of carefully wrought speech to illuminate the hearts of the faithful. Moreover, rusticity of unpolished speech commonly dispels suspicion of falsehood. For one who scarcely manages to produce even a polished expression—how would he know how to fabricate a fiction? And certainly it is more honorable for you to have brought a king in iron than a servant in gold; clear water in an earthen vessel is more useful than muddy or foul water, whose external ornaments commend not its own flavor but what is outside it.

So truth in simple words is better than falsehood in the elaborated beauty of speech. But let the matter itself now be brought forward, and let us invoke the help of that supreme Truth of whom the abbreviated Word is promised through the prophet (Isa. X), so that in the execution of this writing he may show us both concise in suitable brevity and free from the charge of falsehood.

Blessed Odilo—

[Note: Concerning this Odilo, besides Peter Damian and the anonymous monk of Souvigny, who committed his Life and miracles to writing, mention is also made by the Chartulary of St. Honoratus of the island of Lérins; Claber Rodulfus, *History*, books I, chapters 5 and 8; book III, chapter 3; and book V, chapters 1 and 4; Ademar of Chabannes in his *History of Aquitaine*; the Council of Limoges, session 3; the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapter 58; Fulbert of Chartres, bishop, letters 31 and 66; the Eighth Provincial Council of Chalon; the continuator of Hermannus Contractus; Sigebert under the year 993; Peter of Blois, letter 133; the *Book of Customs of the Monastery of Cluny*; the *Fasciculus temporum*; Vincent of Beauvais, book XXVI of the *Mirror of History*, chapter 102 and following; the *Chronicle of Limoges*; Bernard Gui; the *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living*; Platina; the *Chronicle of Chronicles*; Lupold of Bebenburg, book *On the Faith and Religion of the Ancient Princes of the Germans*, chapter 13; Trithemius, book II of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 75; book III, chapter 235; and the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Antony, archbishop of Florence, in his *Chronicles*; Philip of Bergamo in his *Supplement*; Volaterranus in his *Anthropology*; the *Chronicle of Burgundian Affairs*; Guillaume Paradin in the *Annals of Burgundy*; Peter San-Julian in *The Antiquities of Mâcon and Chalon*; Richard Wasseburg in his *History of Belgic Gaul*; Caesar Baronius in the *Annals* and in his notes to the *Roman Martyrology*; Alfonso, bishop of Albi, in his book *On the Kingdom of Transjurane Burgundy*; Chopin in his *Monasticus*; and many others, both ancient and modern.

To these must also be added John of Paris in his *Memorial of Histories*, where he says:

“After Blessed Maiolus, Odilo became the fourth abbot of Cluny. He was from Auvergne and descended from the equestrian order. Having become a Cluniac monk under St. Maiolus, he remained there in quietness, simplicity, humility, and holy conduct. When he had already attained the standard of perfection, scarcely four years had passed when St. Maiolus rested in the Lord. Then, with all the brothers’ wishes converging upon Blessed Odilo, he was appointed in his place to pastoral care.

“He presided for fifty-six years and never ceased celebrating Mass on any day, however greatly he was hindered. In distributing alms he was so generous that some called him not a steward but a spendthrift. During a famine, after the church’s treasures had been consumed for the use of the poor, he also distributed many sacred vessels and ecclesiastical ornaments to them. He did not even spare the crown that Emperor Henry II had sent to him as a memorial of himself.

“He weakened his body not only with severe fasts and subdued it with the harshest hair shirts, but also constricted it with certain iron bonds. He was temperate in eating and compassionate in pitying others. Among the other saints, he burned with the most ardent devotion toward the blessed Mother of God. When he was criticized because he seemed more merciful toward penitents than justice required, he replied: ‘If I must be condemned, I would rather be condemned for mercy than for harshness or cruelty.’

“Peter Damian wrote his Life at the command of Hugh, his successor. Thus illustrious for miracles during his life, he departed to Christ on the vigil of the Circumcision. While laboring in his final illness, he saw the devil standing by and drove him away after adjuring him.

“The *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon* also remembers him. It records that in the year 1014 King Robert entered Burgundy with a very large army and came to the fortress of Dijon, devastating and plundering the surrounding region. Fearing his anger, Abbot William ordered all the monks to withdraw from that place into other monasteries; some, together with all the church’s adornment, he made remain in the fortress of Dijon and in the church of St. Vincent, which the monks of that place then possessed in undisturbed right. Only a few brothers were left in that place for the protection of the site and the service of St. Benignus, together with Lord Abbot Odilo.

“But when the king, being benevolent in disposition, learned that the monks had been scattered because of him, he was deeply grieved. After a few days had passed, he returned to France.

“They all unanimously call this man Odilo the abbot; nor has the present writer seen his name written otherwise anywhere, except in a single diploma of Emperor Otto, which gives *Odilus* instead of *Odilo*.” **DUCHESNE.**

He was from Auvergne and descended indeed from the equestrian order, **401** but he surpassed the nobility of his earthly lineage by the nobility of his heavenly life.

[Note: The same authors, and most of those already cited, write this as well, though they leave the name of his nation or family unmentioned. I suspect, however, that it was Mercorii and that Saint Odilo was surnamed “of Mercorio,” supported by the testimony of the calendar of the Church of Clermont, which was supplied through the courtesy of D. Savaron and reads as follows:

“On the fourth day before the Nones of January, the octave of St. Stephen, and of Odilo, abbot and confessor: for celebrating the feast, Odilo of Mercorio, canon of Clermont and provost of Brioude, promised forty solidi annually, or to pay forty pounds once for all; and they are to be paid at Mass and at Vespers of the said feast.”

For what reason would Odilo of Mercorio have promised money for celebrating the feast of St. Odilo the abbot unless he had been his relative and descended from the same family? **ID.**]

While he was still held in the weakness of childhood, he was suddenly so afflicted by a weakness of nearly all his limbs that he completely lost the ability even to walk. It furthermore happened [the text reads *accedit*, corrected to *accidit*] that his nurse left him before the door of a certain basilica dedicated in honor of the blessed Mother of God and, intent on her own errands, went far away in different directions.

The boy, seeing that he had been left without a guardian and deprived of the attentive service of his nurse, prompted by a certain divine impulse, began to test whether by any effort he could reach the church doors. Thus the innocent child, yet one accused before God and placed under divine chastisement, wavered and did not know what to do. Innocent, I say, because he had not sinned; yet accused before God because he was being struck by a heavenly scourge.

At last, crawling forward and supporting himself, as it were, by the rowing of his hands and feet, he scarcely reached the door and gradually entered. Then, having conceived hope, he openly grasped the altar screen and began to raise himself by whatever efforts he could make. But while he attempted this prematurely, he was still constrained by the knots of the weakness that had not yet been loosed.

What more need be said? At last he felt the aid of divine power; the whole weakness was laid aside, he became well, and he moved the minds of those who saw him to give thanks to God. Since at that time there was no one else to intercede for him, the saint himself—as I may put it—displayed in himself a sign of power: he intervened for himself and, by making the miracle itself into a medicine, obtained divine healing.

This is an outstanding and remarkable miracle: when a person, not through another but by himself, calls upon the aid of divine power.

**402** Moreover, as he advanced toward a more mature age, he first became a cleric at St. Julian the Martyr—

[Note: Namely, in the town of Brioude. Hence the anonymous monk of Souvigny says in his Life: “Consecrated to Christ like another Isaac or Samuel, he was assigned by clerical lot at Brioude to St. Julian, the glorious martyr.” **ID.**]

—and afterward entrusted himself to the instruction of Blessed Maiolus, the distinguished confessor, and received the habit of holy religion in the monastery of Cluny. While he remained there quietly and simply, humbly persevering in the holy religious life, and while certain signs of perfection were already shining forth in him at the very beginning of his inexperienced and novice conduct, barely four years had passed when Blessed Maiolus fell asleep in the Lord.

Before he paid the debt of human nature, though the moment of his blessed death was already near, he appointed Blessed Odilo in his place to oversee the pastoral office and left him as his vicar in the guardianship of the Lord’s flock. At once all the brothers’ wishes converged upon him; all submitted themselves to his authority with unanimous devotion. Those who had lamented that they were left bereft compensated for the loss of their father by the restoration of an equal vicar.

Now established in the care of the government entrusted to him, he began to flourish in many virtues of holy religion: he devoted himself watchfully to psalmody, disciplined his body with severe fasting, and, never withdrawing from the sacred altars, offered the sacrifice of praise to almighty God almost every day. Amid these vigils of pious devotion he was often overflowing with abundant tears of compunction.

Moreover, Adrald—

[Note: Concerning him, the writer of the *Chronicle of Cluny* also speaks, though corruptly calling him Adraud, abbot of the monastery of Uzerche. **ID.**]

—the abbot of the monastery of Breme, a religious man conspicuous for the integrity of his holy conduct, who had been his disciple, once related to us that, when the man of God was lying ill with the sickness from which he later died, he ordered him to calculate, using the reckoning of an abacus, what might be the total number of Masses he had celebrated during the fifty-six years in which he governed the monastery. This clearly reveals how long-lasting and unceasing was the flame of divine love that consumed the blessed man’s breast: the anxiety of so many concerns and pressing affairs could not restrain him from offering saving sacrifices every day.

In distributing alms he was also so generous that some, seeing him scatter everything without hesitation, judged him not a steward but a spendthrift. This was especially so at a certain time when a severe famine afflicted the regions of Aquitaine and pestilentially oppressed many provinces of Gaul. After the treasuries had already been exhausted for the use of the poor and the granaries had been considerably depleted of every kind of produce, he immediately broke up many vessels from the sacristy, sold the church’s distinguished ornaments, and did not spare even the crown that the emperor Henry had sent him as a memorial of himself.

[Note: The generosity of this Henry toward the Cluniacs, although without the crown being expressly mentioned, is also praised by the monk of Limoges in his *History of the Aquitanians* in these words: “Emperor Henry bestowed many gifts upon the monastery of Cluny.”

This was Henry II, the son of Conrad—or, according to others, his son-in-law. After Odilo’s death, as Bishop Hildebert of Le Mans relates, Henry desired to see the face of St. Hugh, Odilo’s successor in the abbacy of Cluny, and to obtain his friendship; he therefore requested in a suppliant voice that Hugh come to him. The holy Father granted the request. He entered Saxony and was received with the highest honor and joy. After spending a few days there, at the king’s request he lifted his son from the sacred font, giving the child his father’s name. He celebrated Easter with the emperor at Cologne, while the Germans marveled at his youthful age yet gray-haired wisdom, the gentleness of his conduct, the grace of his countenance, and the mildness of his speech.

By these signs of virtue the king’s soul became so bound to him and to the monastery of Cluny as though the king himself had made a perpetual treaty of friendship with them. Henry’s son, called Henry III, fathered Henry IV, who himself, as some say in Martin of Troppau’s fourth book of the *Chronicle*, eventually abandoned the imperial office and became a Cluniac monk.

The crown that Damian says his grandfather destined for Odilo is also mentioned by the anonymous monk of Souvigny in the Life of that same Odilo, where he says that Odilo broke up many church vessels for the use of the poor, together with distinguished ornaments, among which was also the imperial crown of Emperor Henry. **DUCHESNE.**]

Thus, in order to relieve as much as he could the poverty caused by so severe a famine—

[Note: A letter of Blessed Odilo to García, king of Navarre, exists in volume II of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, in which he seeks his aid during a famine. For this reason Mabillon believes that it was written on that occasion. **ANONYMOUS.**]

—he gave whatever resources he could scrape together from here and there for the support and nourishment of the needy.

One day, as the compassionate horseman was traveling along a public road, he found two boys on the way who had died of hunger. Immediately dismounting from his horse, he stripped off the woolen under-tunic which he wore next to his flesh and, wrapping each corpse with it as far as the quantity of cloth permitted, provided burial for the dead. He also hired gravediggers for a fee and followed the funeral rites all the way to the grave, fulfilling toward the deceased brothers the duty of human compassion.

It is also recorded among his deeds that he was accustomed not only to weaken his body with severe fasts and subdue it with the harshest hair shirts, but also to constrict it with certain iron bonds. In taking food he exercised such moderation that, touching each item placed before him and serving natural necessity only with due measure, he both avoided the vanity of superstition and preserved the restraint of sobriety.

In issuing judgments and assigning forms of penance he was so compassionate and showed such humanity toward those who mourned that he displayed not the stern authority of a father but rather the affection of a mother. Therefore, in response to those who criticized him, he would elegantly allude to the matter in words such as these: “Even if I must be condemned,” he said, “I would nevertheless rather be condemned for mercy than for harshness or cruelty.”

Among the other saints, he burned with such ardent devotion toward the blessed Mother of God that, while standing in the choir of those singing psalms, when the following verse came to him through the alternating chant:

> You, who were about to take up human nature in order to liberate humankind,

he would prostrate himself upon the ground, thereby showing through his body with what flames of heavenly desire he was burning in his mind.

Thus, as the holy man grew in good morals through the daily increase of his pious conduct and each day more fervently aspired to the summit of perfection, he began to shine with certain miracles. He who was illustrious in moral integrity became illustrious also in the manifestation of signs; and he who was a burning lamp in the sight of almighty God became also a light shining before human beings (John V).

By divine judgment it therefore came about that, because he belonged to those to whom it was said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V), he first displayed a miracle of light. Once, while he was at a certain estate belonging to him called Bersoniacum, he saw a boy handsome in appearance but blind from birth. On making inquiries about him, he learned that he was the son of the estate manager and had never possessed sight at all.

Taking pity on him immediately with kindly compassion and secretly persisting in silent prayer before God—for he had not yet experienced such things—he finally summoned the little boy, traced the sign of the life-giving cross upon his forehead, and at once the boy received the sight that nature had denied him.

On another occasion, when the man of God was at one of his monasteries called Vallis Aurea—

[Note: Damian himself later writes of this place: “Moreover, when the venerable man was taking food beside a certain church of the monastery called Vallis Aurea.” **DUCHESNE.**]

—it was Wednesday of the first week of Lent, the day called the beginning of the fast. When the brothers rose from the table, he secretly filled his hand with ashes and sat down with a piece of bread. As he ate the ashes as though they were bread, wishing also, according to the prophet, to temper his drink with weeping (Ps. CI), he signaled to a brother to bring him water secretly, without anyone observing.

The brother did as he had been ordered and brought water; but when it was brought to the lips, it was perceived to smell strongly of wine. The man of God therefore restrained his hand, pushed the cup away, and by clear signs ordered the servant to bring him water. The servant was astonished, and the one who had poured water wondered and was frightened that he had brought wine from the table.

Nevertheless, he repeated the service, poured out the wine, filled the vessel with water, and again offered it to the man reclining at table. But behold, when the water was taken up for drinking a second time, wine was again found in the cup. The holy man, recognizing the benefit of divine mercy toward him, did not refuse to receive with thanksgiving what he understood God mercifully to be granting him.

Moreover, when the man of God was staying in the city of Ticinum together with King Henry, who afterward became emperor, and they were celebrating the glory of the Lord’s Nativity, it happened that the tablecloth, remarkable for its skillful textile workmanship, was stolen by sacrilegious fraud.

After the man of God had departed with the king, the thief who had stolen it, now secure, put the cloth up for sale in the marketplace. But heavenly providence opposed him, and the sacred object could not be sold. Three times he displayed what he had stolen among the merchandise of the fair and three times made the attempt discreetly; but he could not agree on a price with the buyers, nor could a sale be arranged between seller and purchaser, because divine providence denied success to human efforts.

Meanwhile divine vengeance seized the author of this crime. It dried up the hands that had committed the sacrilege and the feet by which the thief had fled, constricting them with intolerable pain. Compelled by his illness, he was then carried by the hands of others to the church of Blessed Maiolus. The stolen cloth was hung up before everyone as evidence of his guilt, and divine mercy was implored by the entire people who, stirred by the report of this event, had gathered there.

Thus, made sound and unharmed through the merits of Blessed Maiolus and the prayers of the brothers serving him, he returned the stolen cloth and recovered himself. He thereby proved what punishment one deserved who offended Blessed Odilo.

Another thief, while the man of God was staying in the same city, broke into his stable at night and cautiously stole the horse that Odilo himself was accustomed especially to ride. But because the sacrilegious thief feared being caught in that region, he hurried away to the town of Laon.

There, confident that no one would recognize him, he offered the horse for sale, invited buyers, praised the animal, and demanded a transaction. But divine providence so obstructed the man that he could neither reach an agreement with any buyer nor exchange the animal for money. At last he came to his senses and, moved by repentance, led the beast back to the place that knew of his crime. He did not conceal what had happened to him, but made it known for his own humiliation and for the glory of almighty God.

The same venerable man, while traveling, wished to pass quickly and without delay through Ticinum, as the circumstances required. But when the waters had swollen, there was not even a boat available. Immediately, therefore, trusting in God, he summoned one of his servants and ordered him to go ahead through the riverbed in the name of Christ.

The servant obeyed at once and did not hesitate to enter the foaming heaps of the flowing waves. Then the holy man followed with the whole company of travelers, and all were conveyed to the farther bank of the riverbed without any obstacle or inconvenience whatsoever.

When some who were present marveled at this, they began, as though rivals of those who had gone before, to attempt the passage themselves. But as soon as they undertook it and reached the outermost waves of the nearer bank, they would undoubtedly have suffered shipwreck in the abyss of the flowing water had they not rapidly restrained their horses.

One of those who were present, when he saw so remarkable a miracle, was astonished and humbly obtained through earnest prayers that the man of God would deign to enter his house as a guest.

On another occasion, in the silence of the dead of night, a violent force of wind suddenly arose and extinguished the lamp that hung in the bedchamber of those who were sleeping. When the chamberlain awoke and realized that the light had gone out, he asked that the brightness of divine light should shine forth to drive away the darkness of the night.

“Almighty God,” he said, “who are the true light, for the love of your servant Odilo remove the darkness from this house and flood it with the light of your grace.”

Immediately the splendor of flashing light shone forth from heaven, and the entire house was illuminated by the radiance of heavenly brilliance. If Odilo accomplished this while then weighed down by sleep, what do you think he can now do with God, freed from the corruption of the burden of the flesh?

Shortly before the Lord’s Nativity, during the harshness of the winter rains, the holy old man hastened to the monastery of the blessed martyr Marcellus, which [Note: King Guntram of Burgundy founded near Chalon, as Fredegar records in his Appendix to Gregory in these words: “In the twenty-fourth year of his reign, out of divine love he ordered the church of the blessed Marcellus, where that precious body itself rests, to be magnificently and carefully built. It lies indeed in the suburb of Chalon, but nevertheless in the territory of the Saône. There, having gathered monks, he founded a monastery and endowed that church with very many possessions.” Much later, says Theobaldus, the most noble count of Chalon, Gaufredus—himself also count of Chalon—in a charter which we printed in full on p. 314 (in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*), approached the abbot Maiolus of blessed memory and entrusted this monastery to him. It had been magnificently built in the suburb of the city of Chalon by the aforementioned most noble and religious king Guntram, and there the body of the blessed martyr Marcellus rested. He entrusted it to him on the condition that he restore the monastic order, which had almost been abolished; cultivate the rights and possessions belonging to that place; and ensure that he and his successors, the abbots of Cluny, should have and possess it perpetually. DUCHESNE.] It was hurrying on.

They came, however, to a certain river which had become so terrifying through its overflowing waves that it seemed altogether impassable. Trusting in the Lord, he sent ahead a guide to test the fords; then, following immediately with his companions, he crossed unharmed. Yet something marvelous occurred during this crossing: although the water reached the thighs of the others, not even the strap of the holy man’s foot was wetted by the flood. In him alone the water lost the power of its wetness; in the others it displayed the natural force inherent in its nature. The water could touch him but could not wet him; the others it thoroughly soaked, as nature prescribed. 407

Moreover, while the man of God was staying at the monastery of the blessed Martin, which is called “at the Public Road” [Note: In the *Life of Jotsaldus*, Book II, chapter 8, we read: “Near Saint-Denis there is a little monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Martin, commonly called ‘at the Public Road.’” The learned Mabillon added this note to those words: “The church of Saint-Denis de Strata, commonly Saint-Denis de l’Estrée, still stands today. There the most ancient tombs of Saints Dionysius and his companions are seen. No monks live there, although its revenues are very rich and are collected by the commendatory prior. Beside this church there is another, bearing the title of a parish church, under the patronage of Saint Martin.” ANONYMOUS.] he was received as a guest. As was customary, wherever he stayed and wherever he turned, a company of monks immediately gathered around him; and no small group of brothers came to him. He received them cheerfully, first sharing with them the intimacy of his ineffable speech, and afterward inviting them, out of charity, to dine with him.

But as the conversation continued at length, he took aside certain servants from his household and carefully inquired whether there was enough food to refresh the brothers whom he had invited. They replied that there was an adequate quantity of the other foods, but almost no fish sufficient for so large a multitude. To them he said: “In the name of him who knew how to feed five thousand men with a little bread and two fish (Luke 9; John 6), provide us and our guests not with ‘almost nothing,’ as you say, but with an abundant supply of fish.”

When the few fish available were brought to the table by the servers for those who were reclining, the food began to increase in the hands of the diners; and the more the assembled guests consumed it, the more abundantly it multiplied, so that, after everyone had been satisfied, a great quantity remained—enough not only for all the servants but also for others, had they arrived.

Immediately the servants said to him: “Behold, Father, what our faintheartedness did not believe, the merit of your faith has obtained from God. We have now learned not to doubt whenever we hear your promise in a moment of difficulty.” But he, as he was always gentle and humble, did not ascribe what had been divinely accomplished to his own faith; rather, he attributed it to their obedience and to the merits of the holy guests.

A similar event also occurred when the servant of God was staying in the city of Rome and lodging on the Aventine Hill at the monastery of the blessed Mother of God. It happened—as is common in that city—that no wine could be found of a quality suitable in taste for the holy man. He therefore asked the abbot of the place whether he had any better wine. The abbot immediately declared that he did, and willingly promised to bring as much as he himself ordered.

The man of God gave him the small vessel that stood before him and asked that it be brought back full. When it had been brought and placed before him, he acted like a cupbearer and poured wine chiefly for himself and for the abbot, who was reclining beside him. When the meal was complete and it was time to rise from the table, a little wine still remained in the vessel. The holy Father smiled gently and said: “My brothers, I have not fully shown you the service of charity, since I have neglected to share with you the wine that tasted good to me.”

Taking the cup, he poured the wine and gave a single cupful to each as a blessing. The event was marvelous: although the brothers numbered nearly twelve, the supply of drink did not fail while they drank, and when their number had been served, absolutely nothing remained. As they marveled at what had happened, the man who truly guarded humility, wishing both to direct the gift of divine grace toward another and to avoid human praise, attributed the miracle of heavenly blessing solely to the charity of the one who had supplied the wine.

Afterward, as he was returning from Rome to his own region, a certain man within the city of Turin was suffering from an exceedingly severe fever. Secretly, through attendants, he obtained water in which the man of God had washed his hands, drank it faithfully, and without delay recovered completely, every trace of fever having departed.

[Col. 0934C] As he was already climbing the steep slopes of Mount Jovinus, he encountered poor people who, exhausted by the difficulty of the road, were urgently asking for drink to quench their burning thirst. The compassionate Father, neglecting himself and showing pity to those in need, ordered that whatever wine was in his own vessels should be given to the needy without any attempt at reservation or fear that the drink would run out.

A little later, when nature’s need compelled them, everyone reclined to take food. And behold, the wineskins, which had been emptied through an act of pious compassion, were found filled with wine—God thereby paying what was owed. For, according to Scripture, “He who gives to the poor lends to the Lord” (Proverbs 19). In this fortunate exchange, where the Lord was the debtor and the servant the lender, what had been faithfully deposited by the servant was promptly repaid by the good debtor.
