Once, while Emperor Henry was reclining at a prepared table, a very costly glass vessel, crafted with Alexandrian artistry, was brought to him together with pounded spices. He immediately summoned two chaplains of the royal court, namely Alberic and Landulf, [Note: That is, the man from Como, who is also often called *Cumanus*. Como, commonly Como, is a city of Insubria; Cumae, in Italian Cuma, is in Campania. No Alberic appears among the bishops of Cuma; the contrary is true among those of Como. Alberic was indeed famous in those times, having rendered excellent service to the Church and to the monastic order. See Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V. ANONYMOUS.] one of whom was from Como, while the other later became bishop of the Church of Turin. He handed the vessel to them, and through them sent the blessed man Odilo a gift of fragrant nectar.

The chaplains humbly presented the vessel to the holy man as was fitting, and afterward returned to the king’s banquet, intending to come back for it. A little later, as is the custom of human curiosity, which eagerly gazes at anything new and unfamiliar, the monks began to handle the aforementioned vessel admiringly and to pass it carefully from hand to hand for inspection. Then, behold, it slipped from the hands of those who were holding it carelessly and, being fragile by nature, immediately broke. As soon as the holy man learned what had happened, he was deeply distressed, and he felt especially paternal compassion for the clerics who had committed the offense, lest they should offend the emperor while innocent of intent and suffer not only the loss of favor but also the danger of royal anger.

The pious Father therefore immediately entered the church with the brothers. So that those who were free from blame might not incur the displeasure of the king, he devoted himself to prayers and psalms and implored the mercy of the Godhead. When his prayer was complete, the man of God ordered that the broken vessel be brought to him. He handled it, examined it carefully on every side with his eyes, and behold, he found no trace whatsoever of a fracture in it.

Then, indignant with the brothers, he rebuked them sternly for complaining that the vessel had been broken when it had remained entirely uninjured. They, however, greatly astonished by the manifest display of the miracle, gladly accepted the sternness of his rebuke and were inflamed with greater fervor to give thanks to almighty God.

Moreover, a certain religious man from the district of Roten [*de Rolez*] was returning from Jerusalem. As he crossed the sea, which extends from Sicily toward Thessalonica through many places dangerous because of the waves, the terror of raging winds drove him and many others toward an island—or perhaps a rock—where a certain servant of God lived in seclusion.

The man from Roten remained there for some time, awaiting a calm in which the sea might subside, and delighted in frequently conversing with the servant of God. As they exchanged some words on one side and many on the other, the host asked the man where he came from by birth. He replied that he was originally from Aquitaine.

He was further asked whether he knew that monastery called Cluny and its abbot Odilo. He declared that he knew very well the person and place about which he was being asked. The man inquired why this servant of God was asking him about them.

He replied: “Near us there are places from which exceedingly fierce fires burst forth [Note: Sigebertus, Vincentius, John of Paris, Bernard Gui, and others report the same thing. But to elucidate both their account and that of our Damianus concerning those fires—in which, they say, the souls of the reprobate undergo diverse torments according to the quality of their merits—no examples are more useful than those recounted by Damianus himself in Letter 9, Book I, concerning Pandulf, prince of Capua, and John, commander of the soldiers of the city of Naples. “After they died,” he says, “Mount Vesuvius in Sicily, from which hell frequently belches forth, erupted in flame. For whenever a reprobate rich man dies in those regions, fire seems to burst forth from that mountain; and so great a mass of sulphurous resin immediately flows from Vesuvius that it forms a torrent and, rushing downward, descends into the sea. There one may see bodily what is said in the Apocalypse of John concerning the reprobate: ‘Their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.’” And shortly afterward: “Indeed, when the prince of Salerno once saw from afar pitchy and sulphurous flames suddenly burst from the aforesaid Mount Vesuvius, he immediately said: ‘Beyond doubt some wicked rich man is about to die and descend to hell.’ But, O blind mind of a reprobate man! For on the following night, while he lay unsuspectingly with a harlot, he died. DUCHESNE.]—flames in which the souls of the damned suffer torments according to the measure of their merits. [Note: Damianus himself, in Letter 9, Book I, calls these places Mount Vesuvius, as is clear from the preceding note; the inhabitants, however, call them, as Sigebertus says, the Pots of Vulcan. ID.] Countless demons have been assigned to intensify their punishments; they renew their intolerable pains every day and continually restore them to renewed torments.

“Yet I have often heard those demons wailing in plaintive lamentation and weeping with tearful cries because, through the prayers and almsgiving of certain people who wage an implacable struggle against them, the souls of the condemned are frequently snatched from their hands.” [Note: Not forever, that is, but for a time; these were the condemned—or rather, those assigned to purgatorial punishments, which are sometimes also called infernal, as when, in Sigebertus, Pope Stephen said that he was tormented by infernal punishments but hoped to obtain pardon through the intervention of Abbot Odilo. Blessed Augustine is likewise sometimes said to understand condemnation in this sense, as appears from chapter 110 of the *Enchiridion*. ID.]

“Among other things, they make a very great complaint about the community of the Cluniacs and its abbot, because through them they very often lose their native servants who are subject to their jurisdiction. Therefore, by the terrible name of God, I adjure you to report faithfully to the holy brothers there what I have told you. Tell them also from us that they should devote themselves more and more earnestly to almsgiving and prayers, and especially, for this purpose, that they should lead out of the demons’ hands those who are tormented by them, so that the enemy of the human race may suffer grief from the daily plundering of his victims, while joy is multiplied in heaven.”

Some time afterward the man returned to his homeland and faithfully related to the blessed Father and the holy community everything he had learned from the man of God. Then the venerable Father Odilo established throughout all his monasteries a general decree [Note: The Cluniacs call this decree the “Statute concerning the Dead”; it is found on p. 330 of this *Bibliotheca*. DUCHESNE.] that, just as on the first day of November, according to the rule of the universal Church, the solemnity of All Saints is celebrated, so on the following day the memory of all who rest in Christ should be celebrated with psalms and almsgiving, and especially with the solemn offering of Masses. [Note: This rite later passed from the monasteries of the Cluniac order to many churches, causing the memory of the faithful departed to be solemnly celebrated everywhere, as Sigebertus adds. ID.]

If anyone, however, is not content with this general account and asks specifically whom the blessed Odilo rescued from avenging punishments, let him clearly learn, from Pope Benedict, what he should think concerning the rest [Note: He means Benedict VIII, concerning whom the same Damianus writes in Book I, Letter 9, and Sigebertus in his *Chronicle*, although Sigebertus incorrectly calls him Stephen. John, bishop of Porto, to whom he appeared after death, was not the brother of Stephen but of Benedict VIII, as Baronius teaches under the year 1024. ID.]. Thus, from the Roman pontiff, who is the head of all Christians, one may plainly infer what ought rightly to be judged concerning others.

This Apostolic [Note: That is, the pope, or Roman pontiff. The author of the *Life of Charlemagne* writes: “After the praises, he was worshiped by the lord Apostolic according to the custom of the ancient princes.” Likewise, Pippin writes in the foundation charter of Figeac: “It also pleased us and the lord reverend Apostolic.” Hence the old vernacular writers commonly called him *apostole* or *apostoile*. Guido’s *Bible* has:

> “Of our father, the Apostle,  
> I would have him resemble the star.”
>
> (*De nostre pere l’apostoile / Voulsisse qu’il semblast l’estoile.*)

And Guillelmus of Nangis writes in his *Chronicle*: “This King of France, Pippin, first anointed and crowned Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, by the authority of Pope Zachary.” But this expression is so frequent and customary that it seems to require no further proof. ID.] whom we have mentioned, while he was still alive, loved the blessed man affectionately, honored him reverently, and often supplied excellent assistance for the necessary expenses of his journeys to the tombs of the apostles.

Immediately after his death, his brother John succeeded him in the Apostolic dignity. After he had departed from human affairs and a considerable period had elapsed, the aforementioned pope appeared in a nocturnal vision to John, bishop of Porto, and to two others whose names are unknown to us. He revealed to them that he had been placed in penal darkness, adding that the heavenly judgment had determined to free him from his torments through the venerable merits of the blessed Odilo.

He therefore entreated and humbly begged them to send a swift messenger to his brother, the aforementioned man of singular compassion, and to ask him earnestly to pray for him. Immediately John, bishop of Porto, supported by letters of Apostolic authority, hastened as far as Pavia. There, exhausted by the long and perhaps excessively hurried journey, he sent through the monks of the monastery of blessed Maiolus [Note: The monastery at Pavia, which was greatly enlarged through Odilo’s efforts, as the anonymous monk of Silviniacum states. He calls it “the most noble place of blessed Maiolus near Pavia.” ID.] the documents of his Apostolic mission and explained through them the entire account of the vision he had seen.

It was clearly arranged by divine judgment that the bearer of the Apostolic mission should find him at the monastery of Cluny. The venerable Father therefore ordered that psalms and prayers be offered for him by everyone, privately and publicly, that alms be distributed to the needy, and that the sacrifice of the saving mystery be offered to God. He was not content to establish this only in that place; he also sent an edict of the same sanction throughout all the monasteries under his governance.

While the brothers were carrying this out with the greatest devotion, and while the flame of fraternal charity sprang forth from the altar of their holy hearts and penetrated the sanctuary of divine mercy, the appointed time was already drawing near. And behold, a monk of holy conduct, named Heldebertus, whose duty was to feed the poor and provide assistance to the needy, saw during sleep a certain man of handsome and serene appearance, conspicuous with a solemn radiance, entering the monastery cloister accompanied by a great throng of men clothed in white.

He then entered the chapter house, where Brother Odilo was sitting with the brothers, bowed his head humbly to Odilo’s knees, and, as his bodily gesture indicated, gave him thanks. When the brother who was observing this vision asked who this man so beautiful and radiant might be, who was offering the holy man the service of greeting, he was told that it was Benedict, bishop of the highest see. He was giving thanks to the man of God because, through the pious prayers of Odilo and the holy brothers, he had escaped the destruction of Tartarean torment and had merited entrance into the heavenly Jerusalem, where he would rest with the blessed citizens.

From this it can plainly be discerned what opinion may rightly be held concerning the merits of blessed Odilo. He who, by the privilege of Apostolic dignity, held the keys of the Church above all mortals, and who possessed the power of binding and loosing by a pre-eminent right, when placed in that invisible judgment, could be released either from sins or from penal punishment only through the prayers of this man.

At another time, while he was staying in the monastery called Paterniacum [Note: This monastery was founded by the empress Adalheidis in the diocese of Lausanne and entrusted to Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors. Odilo himself reports this in the *Life of Saint Adalheidis* in these words: “In the reign of her father—namely, the most noble king Rudolf—and of her brother Lord Conrad, at the place called Paterniacum, where she committed her mother, Queen Berta, devoted to God in every goodness, to burial, she founded a monastery in honor of the Mother of God and, through her generosity and by the command of her brother King Conrad, entrusted it perpetually to the most holy Father Maiolus and his successors for its governance.” He adds later: “At that same time she visited the monastery of Paterniacum, which she had nobly founded from her maternal possessions in honor of the Mother of God and for the remedy of the soul of her mother, who rested there.” Indeed, during the time of Abbot Odilo, this Paterniacum, as the monk of Silviniacum says, grew very greatly in buildings, possessions, and ornaments, as a place dear to the Mother of God and to him, through love of God. DUCHESNE.] there was a certain young monk named Rodulfus. A swelling goiter had disfigured his throat to such an extent that it took away the clarity of his voice and, in addition, seemed in some way to threaten that it would eventually deprive him even of his hearing.

The truly merciful man of God summoned him, felt the place of the swelling with his hand, then impressed the sign of the cross upon the afflicted throat. After saying certain divine words, he immediately allowed him to leave. Then, in a remarkable reversal—for in others that disease, once it appears, normally grows day by day and miserably occupies the entire throat—in this boy it began from that moment gradually to subside each day, until the disease vanished completely and the boy’s throat was restored in every respect to its natural appearance.

At another time, the holy man had left the monastery [Note: I suspect that the Roman monastery is intended; it too was situated in the diocese of Lausanne and perhaps was entrusted by Adalheidis, the sister of King Rudolf, to Odilo and his successors in the monastery of Cluny. In the Cluniac *Chartulary* there is a royal charter in which King Rudolf granted this monastery to his sister Adalheidis during her lifetime, with the power after his death to leave it to whomever she wished. The text of the charter is as follows:

**Concerning the Roman Monastery**

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Rudolf, by the merciful favor of God king. Since it is fitting for royal eminence to lend a kindly ear to its subjects and to bring their just requests to fulfillment, it is especially appropriate that it should graciously bestow generosity upon those who devote themselves with the utmost readiness to its service. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know that my sweetest and beloved sister Adalheidis came into the presence of our majesty, asking and supplicating that we grant her, by a charter of our royal dignity, during her lifetime the abbey of the Roman monastery, which has been built in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and is situated in the county of Vaud; and that after her death she should have the power to leave it to whichever of her heirs she wished.

“We have received this petition from the depth of our heart, and by the sovereign authority we possess we grant the aforementioned Roman abbey to her for as long as she lives. When God deigns to call her from the body, she shall have permission and every power to leave it to whichever of her heirs she chooses. And so that this gift of ours may be regarded as more secure and preserved inviolate throughout all ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

“Sign of Rudolf, most pious king.

“Berengar, notary, in place of Theodoric, archbishop and chancellor, have acknowledged this.

“Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the tenth year, with Rudolf I, most pious king, reigning favorably; in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 988, indiction six. Done at Vabres, in the name of God. Amen.”

Whatever the case may be, the date of the charter proves that the Roman monastery could not have become a member of the Cluniac monastery at any time other than Odilo’s; and the anonymous monk of Silviniacum testifies that it was rebuilt from its foundations by that same Odilo. ID.] which is situated in the territory of the Jura. The holy man went out and set out on the journey toward the city of Geneva [Note: In it stands the ancient and noble church of Saint Victor, which also belongs to Cluny and was again repaired by Odilo himself, as the same monk affirms.

Duchesne reads “toward the city of Genoa,” which could be understood as Genoa, also called Janua and commonly Genova. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently clear from what Mabillon says in the *Eulogy of Saint Odilo*, no. 74, sixth century, part I, that the city of Geneva, commonly Genève, is intended here. ANONYMOUS.].

When he came to a river of considerable depth, it happened that a mule carrying the man of God’s belongings—namely, books and a bed—strayed far from the public ford and fell into a deeper chasm in the riverbed. It was swept away by the whirlpool, with no part of its body appearing above the waves except its head.

At last it was pulled out of the wreck and brought ashore, and an examination was made to determine whether the belongings, especially the books, had perished. By a marvelous arrangement of heavenly providence, the books, together with the bed, were found untouched by the waves, so that they did not appear to have been sprinkled with even a thin drop of water. The cloths and hand towels, however, were found completely wet on every side.

Here one should observe how watchful divine protection was toward its servant: it permitted those things which more frequently require washing to become wet, while it kept from contact with the waves those which cannot be wetted without damage.

At another time, while the man of God Odilo was staying in the same monastery in the Jura, he found a boy named Gerardus afflicted with the terrible disease of epilepsy. He repeatedly fell as though lunatic, and the attack of that deadly illness used to overwhelm him so completely that neither voice nor memory nor any function of his limbs remained in him, and he scarcely differed from a dead man.

The man of God compassionately condescended to him and instructed the brothers to pray to God’s mercy on his behalf. He himself approached the most holy altar to celebrate Mass and instructed the sick boy also to be present. He immediately gave him the sacrament of the saving Eucharist; then, as was his custom, he gave him sanctified water to drink from the chalice of blessed Maiolus. 414 Without delay, all the boy’s illness departed, the desired health returned, and, through the merits of the blessed man, he remained sound in the strength restored to him.

At another time, the man of God was traveling through the steep paths of the Jura Alps. Suddenly a pack animal laden with various burdens fell down the mountain slopes and was dragged through the rugged precipices of rocks and crags into the depths of the valley below.

The attendants immediately descended into that slippery ravine. They found some of the small packages, which had been scattered here and there, undamaged; but they judged that a book of the Sacraments written in golden letters, together with certain glass vessels carved with embossed ornamental work, was missing. Leaving these aside for the time being, they went to their lodging, refreshed their weary bodies, and rested in the silence of the night.

When morning came, they rose early, quickly returned to that place, and carefully searched every side path. They found everything they had suspected was lost: the glass vessels, of course, were found unbroken; and the gilded book, although the rainy season was becoming threatening, had not been touched by any flood of rain. Thus, through the merits of the blessed man, the headlong fall could not break the glass, nor could the abundance of the pouring rain soak the codex.

A certain nobleman was lying beneath a tree when a piece of bark fell into his eye. It not only greatly disturbed his sight but also brought upon him a manifold burden of other afflictions. Since what had once lodged in his eye could not in any way be expelled, sleep fled from his eyes; and the man was not only unable to sleep but could not even take nourishment from food. 415

The holy man led him aside, made the sign of the cross over him, and then breathed over the place of pain. He promised that he would offer saving sacrifices for him and departed. As soon as the man of God had gone, the nobleman fell into a gentle sleep. When he awoke, he expelled the piece of bark from his eye, together with a certain small tuft, and immediately became well; thereafter he felt no further trouble from that pain.

A deadly ulcer had grown pestilentially on the arm of a cleric of the Church of Tours, so that it now threatened him not merely with the illness of suffering but with death itself. While the man of God was being hosted at Lucense [Note: He says “at Lucense,” which Rodulfus Glaber and others interpret as *Lucense*, from Lucis or Loches, a town in the district of Tours, called Loches in French. DUCHESNE.—Nevertheless, Mabillon holds that the city of Lucca is intended, a republic in Etruria, commonly called Lucca. ANONYMOUS.], the cleric approached and displayed the danger of so pestilential an affliction.

The holy man pretended not to see it, secretly took hold of the arm, impressed upon it the sign of the life-giving cross, and, dismissing him, ordered him to take prudent care of himself. A little later, when the cleric examined the place of the ulcer more carefully, he found no trace whatever of the illness that had been destroyed.

Astounded by the novelty of the miracle, he immediately returned to the man of God. He confessed what had happened, not so much by a verbal account as by displaying his arm with complete clarity. The holy man was deeply displeased by this and angrily drove him from his presence. For he fled human rumors as one flees the poisons of serpents. He maintained that, however lofty the structure of holy works might be, it could suddenly collapse through the desire for empty glory.

Moreover, a certain soldier had become so deprived of his senses that, entirely abandoning every concern, private or public, he wandered naked and alone through byways, uttered incoherent sounds, and displayed himself as though possessed by a demon through the madness of his disordered gestures.

The man of God, moved by paternal compassion for him, prostrated himself with the brothers before the altar of Saint Peter and implored divine mercy with psalms and litanies, asking that God not permit His creature to perish under the madness of this frenzy. Then, rising from prayer, he approached the sufferer, sprinkled him with sanctified water, and urged him to drink from it.

Not long afterward the man came to Cluny sound and unharmed. He brought gifts of fish and reported, with thanksgiving, that he had been restored to himself in every respect.

Another soldier had lost the ability to produce effective speech. He was admonished in a vision that, if he drank the water with which the blessed Odilo had washed his hands, the power of speech and the function of his lost tongue would certainly be restored to him.

Water was therefore secretly taken by the attendants in faithful theft; another water, blessed by the man of God from the chalice of Saint Maiolus, was sent to the mute man. He received both with great devotion, changed his clothes, and entered the church. Since he could not pray with his tongue, he prayed with the mouth of his heart. After receiving the cup of blessing, he recognized that the function of speech had been restored to him. He immediately began speaking fluently and provided a marvelous spectacle to those who witnessed it, making clear what the blessed Odilo could accomplish with God. 416

Moreover, when the venerable man was taking food at a certain church of the monastery called Golden Valley, he learned that the place was suffering from a great shortage of wine. So as not to burden the brother who had received him cheerfully, he established this rule for the community: each of those reclining at table should be content with only one cup, while the cupbearer should pour a double measure for the monks alone.

The measure was nevertheless exceeded, and a generous quantity of drink was provided to all the diners. Indeed, although the wine vessel was only one and was small, the wine not only did not fail despite so many drinking without restraint, but after they had departed it was found full, without any diminution. This makes clear by evident signs that the man of God was able to obtain from God not only what he asked, but also that through him certain signs of power were divinely displayed of which he himself was unaware.

These accounts of the signs and powers that the holy man displayed while he was still in the body are sufficient. We must now, with the Lord’s help, approach the account of his blessed death.

Although the man of God raised himself loftily through spiritual pursuits and divine contemplation, in bodily works he also labored with no little practical diligence. He built certain monasteries from their foundations; others, already half-ruined or perhaps threatening collapse, he repaired. He enlarged their estates and bestowed distinguished ornaments on some of them.

We have therefore postponed enumerating in order which monasteries he founded anew, and which he restored at great expense when they consisted only of ruins and patched roofs, lest the length of our writing appear to weave together mere scraps of discourse—especially since the eyes experience the truth of these deeds in their living works far more clearly than any speech can relate it.

A distinguished administrator of this twofold stewardship, he shone before the divine gaze in spiritual discipline and flourished no less conspicuously in the diligent execution of earthly labor.

Moreover, when the man of God was already in the final stages of life, he was compelled for nearly five years to suffer the affliction of a most serious illness. He therefore hastened to visit the thresholds of the blessed Apostles, so that, as if beneath their feet, he might depart from this world if he were granted what he had always desired. Yet because “a man’s way is not his own” (Jeremiah 10), matters turned out otherwise than he had hoped. For four full months he languished there, detained by illness; afterward, recovering somewhat contrary to expectation, he returned to his own places. Arriving at Cluny, he remained almost entirely engaged in prayer for about a year and, as far as his illness permitted, afflicted himself severely with fasts and vigils. He resolved, before paying the debt owed by human nature, to visit each of his monasteries in turn, going around them in a spirit of holy admonition. Having therefore begun this holy journey of edification, he reached Silviniacum,417 and there he plainly declared that he would depart from this world around the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision. But when he had already been brought into the anguish of his final struggle, he saw the devil standing before him and sternly rebuked him, invoking the name of the fearsome Judge, so that he might depart.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1048 [Note: [Col. 0943C] Jotsald places the death of Saint Odilo in the following year, 949. ANONYM.], at the age of eighty-seven, and in the fifty-sixth year of his ordination, on the night preceding the solemn feast of the Lord’s Circumcision, he received the sacrament of the saving Eucharist [Col. 0943C] and thus gave his blessed spirit back to God.

A short while afterward, on that same night, when the body of the blessed man had already been carried into the church, a certain brother named Gregory, a native of Juveneta [perhaps Venetus] [Note: Mabillon, in the Life of Saint Odilo written by Jotsald [Col. 0943D], calls him a Ninivite by nationality; the manuscripts read *Ninevita*, although Bollandus reads *Juveneta*. “Could it be from Ninivia,” Mabillon says, “a town of Flanders midway between Brussels and Oudenarde in the county of Aalst?” ID.], a man of simple nature and innocent life, overcome by the fatigue of the funeral rites, sought his own bed in the same cell in which the saint had died. Throwing himself down upon it, he tried to sleep. But before he had completely fallen asleep, he saw the blessed Odilo standing before him. Immediately he addressed him in a ready voice:

“What are you doing, Father?”

And he replied:

“Well, brother—very well indeed. For my Lord Jesus has deigned to come to his servant in person and mercifully to make his presence known. But at the very hour of my departure, in that corner there”—for he pointed to the place as though with his finger—“I saw a certain figure, exceedingly savage and terrifying, which tried to inflict upon me the horror and dread of its most dreadful appearance. But, because the power of Christ strengthened me, it could harm me by no assault.”

In the following Lent, Laurence, of holy and venerable memory [Note: The Martinian manuscript calls him Archbishop of Malsia, in these words: “There was also frequent and welcome visitation by monks and clerics, among whom Lord Laurence, Archbishop of Malsia, a man most holy in every respect and most eloquent in the writings of both languages, Greek and Latin, often visited him.” Unless *de Malfia* should rather be read. There is a see at Amalfi, or the Amalfitan see, in the kingdom of Naples; commonly Amalfi. DUCHESN.], archbishop of the Amalfitan see, who was learned in letters and bilingual, knowing Greek and Latin—and, what is far more excellent, distinguished by the brightness of an exemplary life—was then residing at Rome and fell asleep in the Lord. When his body had been carried into the church, a certain respectable cleric named Albero, tired, laid his limbs down to sleep in a corner of that same church. While he was still almost awake, the blessed man suddenly appeared to him. The cleric immediately said:

“My lord, when did you come here, and why?”

“I have come,” he replied, “for the funeral rites of my once dearest friend, Lord Laurence the bishop. When they have been completed, I did not wish to depart before seeing you.”

After he had said this, the appearance of the speaker vanished.

The man of God, then, because he lived rightly, died happily; and because he led a wondrous life, he rightly shone forth in miracles. The life of this blessed man is like a golden tablet, into which we set, as it were, pearls and gems when we intermingle with his deeds the miracles of virtues that shine through them [Col. 0944C]. New signs of virtue still gleam at his venerable tomb. We consider it superfluous to insert them here, since we see them recorded by others. Therefore, wishing to spare our readers’ weariness, we are content with what we have touched upon in concise brevity, to the honor and glory of our Redeemer Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Let those who wish to learn the deeds of this same saint consult the fuller Life of Saint Odilo written by Jotsald—not Lotsald, as some incorrectly state—a Cluniac monk and Odilo’s own disciple. At the urging of Abbot Hugh, Odilo’s successor, Saint Peter Damian abridged Jotsald’s work, cutting away what was superfluous. Duchesne published a fragment of this Life in the appendix to the Cluniac Library under the name of the anonymous author of Silviniacum, and Bollandus under another form of the name, Lotsald. Mabillon, however, published it in full in part II of the sixth-century Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict and supplied notes; in particular, he prefixed to it a eulogy, or rather a commentary, on Saint Odilo, in which, with remarkable learning, he assembled much material especially suited to illuminating the history of that saint and of the Cluniac congregation. ANONYM.]

[Col. 0945]

# LIFE OF SAINT MAURUS, BISHOP OF CESENA AND CONFESSOR, TAKEN FROM THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT  
*(20 January.) With notes by John Bollandus, S.J.*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0945A]

Desiring to write something for the glory of our God concerning the blessed bishop Maurus, we wish to satisfy our hearers’ desire in such a way that, in accordance with the method of an orderly account, we safeguard truth in every respect. For a cupbearer is contemptible who, while boasting of an abundance of wine, also serves dregs with blameworthy rashness. A caterer is wicked who prepares a banquet for others with such ambition that he permits the fire of raging hunger to rage within himself. Likewise, a narrator is reckless who, while striving to exalt others by proclamations of praise, does not fear to be himself plunged into the abyss of falsehood. For some think that they render honor to God if, in setting forth the marks of his praise, they concoct proofs of falsehood; yet if they carefully attended to the words of the excellent preacher, they would not think such things. For he says to the Corinthians: “But if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is vain and your faith is vain; moreover, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we gave testimony against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise” (1 Corinthians 3). According to these apostolic words, therefore, one who lies while indiscreetly wishing to praise God is rightly called a false witness against God; and without doubt, whoever devises a fabrication by perverse art in God’s praise bears testimony against God. The Prophet also thunders terribly, saying: “You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak lies” (Psalm 5). He plainly declares, indeed, that just as it is less serious to hate than to destroy, so it is more tolerable to commit iniquity through weakness than deliberately to fabricate lies.

Hence it is said through Jeremiah of liars: “They have taught their tongues to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jeremiah 9). Those who could easily have presented the simple truth freely offered to them take pains to invent lies with labor. And if anyone perhaps rebukes us here for a long preface, and as a severe critic objects to what is written in the book of Maccabees—“It is foolish,” he says, “to be diffuse before the history and concise in the history itself” (2 Maccabees 2)—we give this reason: where an abundance of material is available, the very length of the style prevents one from lingering over such matters. But here, where few things concerning the blessed man’s virtues are at hand that ought to be written, we judge it more useful, for the edification of hearers, to which all ecclesiastical Scripture is directed, to write in the preface against falsehood than, for want of narrative, to prolong the history itself to the limits of falsehood.

Therefore, whatever concerning the life or miracles of blessed Maurus could come to our knowledge, so far as we have been able to infer it from the account of certain monks not wholly contemptible, we faithfully make known to Christ’s faithful.

# CHAPTER ONE. Saint Maurus’s Episcopate and His Deeds

[Col. 0946B]

At that time, when the Roman Church extended the rights of its possessions much more widely than it does now, and among other places also possessed the town of Cesena [Note: Leander Albertus: “During the times of the Lombards, the people of Cesena remained steadfast in allegiance to the city of Rome.”], it happened that Cesena was deprived of its bishop. When the Roman pontiff [Note: Ferrarius reports that this was John IV, as previously written.] saw his nephew, the blessed Maurus, ascending through the ranks of virtue to lofty heights and keeping vigilant watch with no slackness in the pursuit of holy conduct [Note: Menardus attempts from this passage to prove that Maurus was a monk.], he judged it fitting to promote such a man to the summit of priestly office, so that the lamp of the Holy Spirit would not remain hidden beneath a bushel but, placed upon a lampstand, would illuminate all who are in the house of God with the rays of sacred teaching.

Why say more? At last, by the ordering of divine providence, blessed Maurus received the chair of the Church of Cesena. We have omitted to insert here the name either of the king who was then ruling or of the apostolic bishop himself [Col. 0946C], because, along with those who supply the rest of our account, we likewise do not know them. They report that they saw their names in ancient volumes [Note: In Surius and in the codices.], but they also state that, since the city had previously been consumed by fire, its records were destroyed at the same time.

When the man of God Maurus saw that a burden of such demanding care had been laid upon him, he did not, as is written of blessed Paul (Galatians 1), yield to flesh and blood. Instead, he began to make himself all the more vigilant in divine service, knowing that the guardianship of so many subjects was incumbent upon him. Reflecting that the governance of souls is an art above all arts, he judged it fitting neither to diminish care for interior matters through preoccupation with exterior affairs, nor, conversely, to abandon concern for exterior affairs completely because of anxiety over interior matters. Otherwise, devoted to external matters, he might collapse altogether in his inner life; or, occupied only with inward concerns, he might provide too negligently for his neighbors what he owed them outwardly.

Often certain people, as though forgetting that they have been placed over their brothers for the sake of their souls, serve worldly concerns with such an effort of heart that, when these concerns are present, they rejoice to be engaged in them, and, when they are absent, they pant after them amid turbulent waves of thought. When perhaps circumstances give them respite from these matters, they are worn down even more severely by the respite itself. They regard it as pleasure to be weighed down by activities, and consider it labor when they are not laboring at earthly business.

Others, by contrast, undertake the care of the flock but desire to devote themselves to spiritual things in such a way that they are not occupied at all with exterior affairs. Since they completely neglect care for bodily needs, they fail to meet the necessities of their subjects. Their preaching is often despised, because, while they correct the deeds of sinners, they do not provide them with what is necessary for the present life, and so they are not willingly heard. The word of instruction does not penetrate the mind of the needy if the hand of mercy does not commend it to that person’s heart. The seed of the word germinates easily when the preacher’s compassion waters it in the listener’s breast.

We speak of these different pastoral dispositions in order to demonstrate how prudent and how balanced was the discernment of blessed Maurus. He neither abandoned the active life altogether by pursuing the leisure of contemplation, nor withdrew from contemplation by moving freely amid the weariness of active work [Note: Surius reads *latitudinem*, “breadth,” instead.]. Thus, so to speak, he penetrated by the golden path to the height of the heavenly kingdom.

Finally, while he lived in his episcopal residence and vigorously governed the Church entrusted to him, he began to search with anxious attention for a place where, for a time, he could withdraw from the crowd of worldly people and cling more especially to God alone. He was an earnest imitator of his Lord, who preached in the cities by day but devoted himself to prayer on the mountain by night (Luke 21).

As the concern caused by this anxiety grew daily more intense, he finally turned his eyes toward a small promontory, about four stadia distant from a little town. It was called the Spatian Forest, a place neither raised aloft by steep peaks nor wholly sunk into the depths; it seemed level with the flatness of a cultivated hollow [Note: *Lama* means a hollow or a collection of waters.]. Rather, it stood at a suitable elevation midway between these extremes, so that it offered those stationed above it a clear view of almost the entire diocese, while those ascending it were not wearied by any excessively steep slope.

That mountain was covered with a wooded density of various trees. This mountain pleased the blessed man’s eyes as though he saw Mount Olivet beside the city of Jerusalem, and he could rightly have sung with the Prophet this psalm:

“I shall remember you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain” (Psalm 41:7).

He first requested this mountain from the Roman pontiff, under whose jurisdiction it was held; then he built himself there a small cell with a little church. He remained there during Lent, devoting himself to fasts and prayers, and whenever he could steal time away from ecclesiastical business, he returned to the same cell as to a banquet of sweet food.

There he drank in the stream of divine contemplation with the eager thirst of his mind, so that afterward he might refresh the parched breasts of his neighbors with the cup of holy preaching. He used that place, in a sense, as a bath. There he sought to wash away any stain of word or thought that he might have contracted through conversation with worldly people; and he cleansed there, with frequent fountains of tears, the dust of worldly conduct, without which no one traverses the road of human mortality.

That place, therefore, which had been so dear and familiar to the holy man during his life, deserved to be honored as his burial place after his death. For his body, placed in a stone coffin, was laid beside the small basilica that he himself had built.

# CHAPTER TWO. The Translation of the Body; Miracles

These matters concerning the life of the blessed man that have come to our knowledge were not seen by our own informants, but were disseminated through the celebrated memory of succeeding generations.

There was, however, in our own recent times a very old man, already trembling with a body wasting away, who testified that he had seen the nephew of this blessed Maurus, namely Constantius, bishop of the Church of Cesena. But since we have set down in running prose what we happened to hear concerning the life of blessed Maurus, let us now briefly explain how almighty God revealed his merits for the glory of his name.

[Note: Leander. In the interior of Emilia, especially among the Apennine hills, which are thickly covered with vines, fig trees, olive trees, and other fruit-bearing trees, there is near Cesena a magnificent monastery with a church dedicated to the Queen of Heaven, whom they call Saint Mary of the Mountain. The place is called Mount Maurus, after Saint Maurus, bishop of Cesena, who led a most holy life there. It faces west and north and is inhabited by monks of Saint Benedict.]

There is now a famous monastery on the mountain mentioned above, where the man of God used to pray. It is dedicated to the blessed Mother and Virgin of God, and by an ancient popular custom the mountain is called Mount Maurus, because the place is rightly honored by the name of the holy man.

When the coffin enclosing the little body of the blessed man lay hidden beside the aforementioned church beneath earth that had accumulated all around it, so that scarcely the top of the stone rose above the ground, it happened that a certain man arrived with litanies. The thong of his sandal having come loose, he suddenly placed his foot there and, suspecting nothing, securely fastened it.

When his ankle had been bound and he wished to depart, he could not move his foot in any way. Although he struggled for a long time, trying everything and turning this way and that, his foot nevertheless remained immobile, held fast to the stone as though by nails. The wretched man stood there guilty of an unknown crime; he had intended to tie his sandal, but lamented that he had instead tied himself to the stone.

He wanted to stand, but could not do so supported on only one foot; he wished to lie down, but could not fall because of his own foot. At last, when a crowd of people suddenly rushed together, some wielding hammers and others axes, they cut away part of the stone and, after much effort, were scarcely able to free the man from it.

Immediately the cry of the rejoicing crowd arose, the wondrous power of God was extolled, and the tomb of blessed Maurus was judged worthy of reverence.

The same monk of the monastery mentioned above, named Teuzo [Note: Surius reads *Tenzo*.], now very old and venerable by reason of his gray hair, from whose account we learned these things, reported another miracle, which we shall by no means pass over in silence.

At one time that same brother was oppressed by a violent attack of fever. Since he could not return to a state of health through any medical treatment or any human effort whatsoever, blessed Maurus appeared during the silence of night to one of his maternal aunts, a religious woman and nun, and said to her:

“If you wish your nephew to recover from the illness he is suffering, tell him to set the sign of the holy cross above my burial place and to vow that he will celebrate my solemnity throughout the entire year.”

When he gratefully fulfilled the blessed man’s oracle, which he learned from the nun’s report, as soon as he fixed an iron cross above the tomb, he suddenly vomited violently, his entrails convulsed; thus he immediately cast off all the affliction of the fiery illness, as though the vomit itself had expelled it. Restored completely to his former health, he gave worthy thanks to God the Savior and took care to proclaim to many, for the glory of God’s name, the miracle of blessed Maurus that he had experienced in himself.

Thus, as the celebrated fame of both signs flew among the people, many began devoutly to hasten to the sacred relics of the blessed man and to commend their souls more attentively to his pious merits. Others, suffering from various bodily ailments, either drank the worn dust from the marble of the tomb or merely implored the mercy of the blessed confessor with an outpouring of prayers; they returned home healthy and unharmed, whatever bond of illness had held them captive.

You might see the limp bodies of pitiable invalids carried in, previously supported by the assistance of others; soon afterward they returned with great exultation and rejoicing, restored to their former health.

As the fame of blessed Maurus grew ever more renowned through the shining of so many miracles, and as the wonders that the Lord displayed through him resounded not only throughout the neighboring regions but also across more distant places, at last, after the bishops of the neighboring cities had been summoned and large crowds of people had flocked together from every direction, the coffin in which the blessed man’s patronage is preserved was excavated in eager rivalry. A breach was made in the church wall, and the coffin was placed with hymns and praises, with the greatest care, between the apse and the altar.

In the course of time the same basilica was enlarged and, as it may be seen today, more festively adorned. There, to make known the merits of the blessed confessor, many miracles continue to occur through God’s agency even to the present day. We touch upon a few of them, which those who report them to us testify that they saw.

# CHAPTER THREE. Various Miracles at the Relics

Pope Gerbertus [Note: Gerbertus was first archbishop of Rheims, then archbishop of Ravenna; he became Roman pontiff in the year 999 and was called Sylvester II. He died in 1003.] had encamped near Cesena, and armies surrounding its town were hemming it in under siege [Note: Rubeus, book V: “In the following year (1000), Sylvester surrounded Cesena after bringing up an army; what cause impelled the pontiff is uncertain.” Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book VII, on the same year: “Sylvester, having set out from Orvieto, bound the state of that city with many salutary laws and surrounded Cesena after bringing up an army.”].

At that time a certain peasant was brought to the tomb of blessed Maurus, afflicted by a double disease, namely paralysis and blindness. But after prayers had been offered, the lost light returned to his eyes and the illness that had stiffened his limbs released them.

When the man saw himself so wondrously restored to health, he gave thanks as best he could and surrendered himself to blessed Maurus as his perpetual servant by an everlasting right. He vowed that he would remain in his service as long as he lived.

For almost a decade he enjoyed the gift of the health he had received. Then he weakly yielded to the frailty of the flesh and joined himself to a wife in an ill-omened marriage. As soon as he had indulged in the pleasure of lust, he completely lost the light of his eyes and remained blind for as long as he lived.

It was certainly fitting that one who withdrew from the authority of blessed Maurus, to whom he had enslaved himself [Note: Surius observes that *se subtrahens*, “withdrawing himself,” or something similar, seems to be missing.], and shamefully placed his neck beneath the yoke of lust should lose the gift with which the good Lord had enriched him; and that one who had voluntarily fallen into inward darkness should unwillingly incur outward darkness.

At another time a certain demoniac woman was brought to the altar of the blessed man. The destructive spirit had filled her with such fury that, making her into an instrument of itself, it uttered many sacrilegious and insane things through her mouth, emitted dreadful cries, and barked like a rabid dog with repeated yelps [Note: The edition of Surius had *naubatibus*, through a copyist’s error; *baubant* or *baubantur*, “they bark,” corresponds to Greek *βαύξουσι* and *βαύνξουσι*, used of dogs.]. Three days after she had been brought there, she vomited blood in a violent spasm and thus expelled the evil spirit that held her.

Another woman, excessively devoted to the demands of her household affairs, did not fear to clean wheat on the feast of Saint Rophillus [Note: Saint Rophillus, or Rofilus—or, as Leander Albertus writes, Rofillus—is celebrated on 18 July.]. But because she failed to show the blessed confessor the reverence due to him, she did not escape a deserved sentence of punishment.

For immediately, struck by divine judgment, her arms were drawn tight and stiffened; she began wretchedly to tremble as though she were still winnowing with a grain shovel [Note: An old manuscript glossary: “A *capisterium* is a vessel with which grain is cleaned.” The word is also used by Columella, book II, chapter 9.].

She was therefore led before the altar of blessed Maurus and, during the solemnity just mentioned, earnestly promised that she would never again do anything of that kind. At once the most abundant mercy of almighty God mercifully came to her aid and completely restored the woman’s rigid arms to freedom and the full use of their natural strength.

Again, another woman suffered from a flow of blood. Since she was continually tormented by an incurable wound and, trying this and that, could find no remedy for her health, at last, placed in the extremity of distress, necessity itself found counsel for her.

She covered the mausoleum of blessed Maurus with a clean linen cloth, as far as her means permitted, and was thus divinely freed, escaping entirely the distress of her foul illness. For since the Apostle says, “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9), because she touched the tomb of the blessed man with a pure heart, being full of faith, she deservedly obtained release from the uncleanness of flowing blood.

Likewise, another woman was twisted by the violence of an exceedingly severe illness to such a degree that, the natural order being undone, she held her face behind her and carried her neck before her. She too placed a linen cloth upon the memorial of blessed Maurus, and immediately, once health had been restored, nature returned each limb to its proper function and adjusted the organs of her arteries to sustain their proper strength.

Another woman, having lost her sight, was brought from the regions of Aquitaine. Preserving the temperament of the Gallic character and violently mangling her words in the manner customary to her homeland, she obstinately declared that she would never leave unless, through the merits of blessed Maurus, she recovered the light she had lost.

Thus, inflamed with great fervor of faith, she put together a small hut beside the church wall, so that she seemed to be preparing a dwelling rather than merely lodging. After prayers had been offered with the greatest insistence for eight days, she received the sight she sought through the gift of divine grace and gave worthy thanks to God her illuminator and to his servant Maurus.

A crowd from the diocese of Popiliensis [Note: Forum Popilii is a town on the Via Aemilia, called by others Forum Pompilii and, corruptly, Forum Populi in various itineraries; today it is Forlimpopoli, often Forlipiccolo, that is, “the lesser Forum Livii.” Not without reason, since, according to the author Leander, it was utterly destroyed around the year 1370 and rebuilt twenty years later by Sinibaldo Ordelaffi, prince of the people of Forlì, in the form in which it is now seen. It lies six miles from Cesena. The episcopal see of Forum Popilii of the Brittones—or Forum Fruentinorum or Druentinorum—was transferred to the nearby city.] was traveling to the shrine of blessed Arduino [Note: We shall discuss blessed Arduino, a priest of Rimini, on 15 August.] for the sake of prayer. As they passed by the oratory of blessed Maurus, it happened that one of the women humbly kissed the knee of the abbot of that monastery and asked permission to continue her journey.

She had scarcely gone the distance of one arrow-shot when she was suddenly seized by a demon, thrown to the ground, shaken, and rolled about. She spewed many biting insults against that same abbot. She was therefore brought before the altar of blessed Maurus and, not long afterward, was freed by the command of divine power. When her companions returned, she had already regained possession of herself and returned home with them, healthy and unharmed.

Dearest brothers, we have written down these few accounts of the virtues that almighty God has deigned to work through his blessed confessor Maurus, in order to stir the devotion of your charity toward glorifying the power of the divine majesty.

While he deigns to display to us, who are still placed on the road, the power of his miracles, through them he invites and urges us to obtain the inheritance of our heavenly homeland. The Psalmist bears witness, saying: “He will proclaim to his people the power of his works, to give them the inheritance of the nations” (Psalm 110:6–7).

Thus, when we see the very tombs of the saints shining with so many miracles, we may have no doubt about their immense glory, in which they already reign with Christ. Then, despising earthly things, may our mind already transfer itself through desire to the place where it hopes to rejoice forever; may the spirit freely direct itself to the place where Christ, the Emperor of heaven, reigns ineffably with the senators of the heavenly court. To him be glory and dominion, with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0953]

# LIFE OF SAINT ROMUALD, ABBOT AND CONFESSOR, FOUNDER OF THE CAMALDOLESE CONGREGATION OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT  
*(A.D. 1027, 19 June.) With annotations by an anonymous author.*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0953A]

We complain directly against you, filthy yet clean one [Note: The edition printed in Florence in 1513 by Filippo Giunta, as well as another printed at the monastery of Fontebuono near Camaldoli in 1520 by Bartholomew of Zanetti of Brescia, does not contain the emphatic particle *prorsus*, “directly” or “altogether.”], because you have an intolerable crowd of foolish wise men who are eloquent toward you but mute toward God.

You have men who, through vain eloquence and empty philosophy, know how arrogantly to raise themselves upon the horns of pride; but you do not have men who wish to record in written pages something beneficial to the edification of their neighbors and posterity [Note: In Vatican codex no. 3797, written in the year 1113, as Fontanini believes in his dissertation on Saint Peter of Urs, page 30, which contains the whole of this Life of Saint Romuald, the reading is: “who wishes the memory of posterity to be entrusted to the pages.”].

You have, I say, men who can plead in the courts of judges the lawsuits of secular affairs and the quarrels of cases through continual declamations; but you do not have anyone who can describe in holy Church even the virtues and glorious deeds of a single saint.

For “they are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jeremiah 4).

Behold, nearly three lustrums have already passed since blessed Romuald, laying aside the burden of the flesh, migrated to the heavenly kingdoms, and no one among these so-called wise men has yet appeared who would set down, in even a brief historical account, a few of the many praises of his wondrous life and, satisfying the faithful’s most eager devotion, hand them over to the reading stand of Holy Church for the common benefit [Note: From this it is possible to infer the truth and sincerity of this history, written by the otherwise most learned and holy man Peter Damian: it was composed so soon after the holy man’s death that it could have, and indeed did have, eyewitnesses furnished with a recent memory of events—namely, Saint Romuald’s own disciples, as he himself testifies below.].

For us, however, sitting in the cramped corner of a cell, it was more useful, as we had resolved, constantly to recall our own sins before the eyes of our mind than to weave the history of another’s virtue; it seemed more expedient to lament the darkness of the guilt entrusted to us than to obscure the splendid marks of holiness with unskilled words [Note: The Fontebuono edition reads: “and hand it over to the assembly of Holy Church,” that is, to the gathering of the faithful meeting together. In the Vatican codex, however, the reading is *legivo*, which Saint Benedict, in chapter 9 of the Rule, calls the reading stand or lectern.]. The Vatican codex has *expediret*, “it would be more expedient”; the Fontebuono edition has *magis expedire videbatur*, “it seemed more expedient to do so.” Both are correct; otherwise another verb governing the infinitive *expedire* would be lacking.

Nevertheless, since throughout the year, and especially on his feast day, a multitude of the faithful gathers at his tomb from distant regions of the earth, sees the miracles divinely performed through him, and eagerly seeks to hear the history of his life—but cannot hear it because no such history exists—we greatly fear that his most celebrated fame, still uttered by the mouth of the whole people, may, as time passes, be entirely erased from human memory.

Therefore, compelled by this fear and bound by the prayers and genuine affection of many brothers, I shall undertake, with God as my guide, to describe what I learned about that remarkable man from his distinguished disciples. An unskilled man, I shall attempt to set down the beginning, course, and end of his life in a few written lines—not weaving a history, but making something like a brief memorandum.

I wish my reader to know this above all: I shall not gather in this little account many miracles performed through him; rather, I shall strive to recount the order of his way of life, which is wholly directed toward edification. For the blessed man so guarded himself under the cloak of humility from the wind of vainglory that whatever might have appeared wondrous to human eyes, wherever it occurred, he suppressed with the greatest care.

Yet even if he had performed no miracles at all, he would not have been worthy of less veneration, since he led a wondrous life. For we do not read that the Lord’s Forerunner performed miracles, although Truth itself testifies that no one greater than he arose among those born of women (Matthew 11).

Some people think they honor God if, in extolling the virtues of the saints, they invent lies. Ignorant that God has no need of our falsehood, they abandon the truth—which is God himself—and imagine that they can please him through a fabrication.

Jeremiah rightly rebukes them, saying: “They have taught their tongues to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jeremiah 9). They could easily have reported the simple truth freely offered to them, but they sweat through futile labor composing what they do not know; and insofar as they claim to stand for God as his assistants, they in fact stubbornly fight against God as false witnesses, as the Apostle bears witness to the Corinthians:

“If Christ has not been raised, our preaching is empty and your faith is empty”; and then he adds: “We are found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise” (1 Corinthians 15).

But since necessity compelled us to write, and these remarks, as though stirred up, have made us begin with a preface, let us now, with the help of God and through the prayers of him about whom we speak, proceed to the order of the narrative.

## 428 CHAPTER ONE. The Cause of Romuald’s Conversion

Romuald, therefore, born in the city of Ravenna, was descended from the most illustrious line of its dukes [Note: That Romuald’s origin was most noble is plainly understood from Damian’s description of it as an illustrious lineage. The distinguished V. Muratori, in Dissertation 5 of volume I of *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, p. 158, wrote—according to his custom—with great erudition about this most noble ducal family of Ravenna. It died out around the year 1180, when Duke John was taken from the living without offspring, and Peter Traversaria, a Ravennate patrician, and Taurello, a noble citizen of Ferrara and father of the famous Salinguerra, were called to his inheritance, as is perfectly clear from two charters that he presents in that dissertation. “Although it is credible,” he says, “that these dukes in ancient times assumed this distinguished title from some splendid magistracy, whether from the government of the city of Ravenna or of some other city situated in the exarchate, nevertheless I am inclined to think that, as time went on, they obtained at least the continued honor of the title after being removed from that office, and that for this reason the designation ‘ducal’ was imposed upon their estate, just as the name ‘count,’ once given only to the rectors of some city, gradually began to be applied to the lords of castles and villages.”].

When he had reached adolescence, he began to be inclined toward the sin of the flesh, a vice by which that age commonly attacks people, especially the wealthy, with particular force [Col. 0955B]. Yet devoted in mind to God, he frequently tried to raise himself up and resolved that he would accomplish something great [Note: This is how it is read in the Vatican manuscript no. 3797, mentioned above; but in a certain fragment of this Life written perhaps in the eleventh century, preserved in manuscript no. 5411 of the Vatican Library, the reading is: “he frequently proposed something great against himself,” as also appears in several editions.].

For whenever he prepared himself for the pursuit of hunting, wherever in the woods he was able to find a pleasant place, his mind immediately grew ardent with a desire for the desert, and he would say within himself: “How well hermits could live in these recesses of the woods! How suitably could they rest here, free from all disturbance caused by worldly noise!” Thus his mind, inspired from heaven, was already divining in love what he would later fulfill in action.

He had a father named Sergius, intensely devoted to the world and wholly entangled in secular affairs. When he was waging hostilities against a certain relative of his after quarrels had arisen over the ownership of a meadow [Note: The fragment of the Vatican manuscript cited above adds *fraudulenter*, “fraudulently.”], and saw his son Romuald growing hesitant in the dispute and deeply fearing the crime of fratricide, he began to threaten that he would disinherit him if he persisted any longer in the same opinion.

Why say more? At last both parties of the enemies rushed out of the city toward the disputed matter, seized their weapons, and engaged in civil warfare. While they were fighting hand to hand on either side, Sergius’s enemy and relative by marriage were suddenly killed by Sergius’s hand [Note: The word *affinis* is absent from the same fragment and from the older printed manuscripts. Hence Rubeus says in *History of Ravenna*, book V, that there was a dispute between Sergius the father and his neighbor. Fortunius, however, in part II, book I, chapter 7, using an ambiguous expression, writes that a dispute over a certain meadow arose between Sergius the relative and another kinsman.].

Although Romuald had inflicted no wound on the slain man, nevertheless, because he had been present, he undertook penance for so great a crime. He immediately hastened to the monastery of Blessed Apollinaris at Classe, intending to remain there in mourning for forty days, according to the custom for homicides [Note: Ractius, in *Description of the Holy Desert*, chapter 2, and Lucas Barchinonensis, *Roman History*, book II, chapter 4, attribute this to a particular custom of the people of Ravenna. Rubeus, however, in book V, says that he went to Classe in order to undergo there the punishment customary in that age. In the fragment mentioned above, the reading is *in luctu*, “in mourning,” rather than *in luctibus*.].

## 429 CHAPTER TWO. The Conversion Itself, and That the Body of Blessed Apollinaris Lies Without Doubt in the Monastery at Classe

There, constantly chastising himself with severe penance, he began to hold daily conversation with a certain convert [Note: The ancients called *conversi* those who, as adults, embraced the monastic discipline. Here, however, the subject seems to be a lay brother, as Mabillon observed.]. From him, according to the modest measure of his understanding, he often heard good counsel of exhortation [Col. 0956B]. The convert frequently admonished him to set aside secular life entirely and hasten toward the order of holy conversion [Note: The Fontisboni edition reads: “so that he might set aside secular life entirely and hasten toward the order of holy conversion.”], but was utterly unable to humble his mind for this purpose [Note: In the fragment of the Vatican manuscript the reading is: “but when he could in no way humble his mind for this purpose.”].

On one occasion, among other things, he said—as though rejoicing—“If I show you Blessed Apollinaris in bodily form, so that you can see him clearly, what reward will I receive from you?”

Romuald replied: “I bind myself by a firm and inviolable obligation: as soon as I see the blessed martyr, I will remain no longer in the world.”

The convert therefore urged Romuald not to go to sleep that night, but to keep vigil with him in prayer inside the church. When both had persevered patiently in prayer through the silence of the night, behold, around cockcrow, Blessed Apollinaris emerged—clearly visible to both—from beneath the altar that stands constructed in the middle of the church in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary. He seemed to come out from the eastern side, namely from the place where the porphyry marble lies.

Immediately such radiance filled the entire church as though the sun were confining the rays of its brightness within those very walls. Then the most blessed martyr, marvelously adorned in priestly vestments and carrying a golden thurible in his hand, incensed all the church’s altars. When this was done, he at once returned to the place from which he had emerged, and immediately all that radiance, following him, ceased to appear.

The convert then began to press Romuald—clearly a stern exactor—with great insistence and anxiously demanded that he fulfill what he had freely promised. When Romuald still resisted and asked to see the same vision again, they likewise persevered in prayer on another night and saw the blessed martyr in every respect as before.

For this reason, whenever a question later arose concerning the body of the aforesaid martyr, Romuald firmly asserted that it was reposed in that very church; and throughout the time that the holy man lived, he never ceased to bear this testimony [Note: The body of Apollinaris, the most holy first shepherd of the people of Ravenna and apostle of Emilia, is still venerated with the greatest devotion in the basilica at Classe.].

Romuald also had the practice of frequently devoting himself to prayer before the church’s principal altar. There, after the brothers had departed, he strove with many groans to entreat God. When he was doing this one day after the vision with greater attentiveness, the Holy Spirit soon kindled his mind with so great a fire of divine love that he suddenly burst into tears and could not restrain abundant streams of them. He threw himself prostrate at the monks’ feet and begged with indescribable longing to be given the monastic habit.

The monks, however, fearing his father’s harshness, did not dare to open the way to his conversion [Col. 0957C]. Honestus [Note: See the distinguished V. Guido Grandi’s *Camaldolese Dissertation* II, chapter 3, where he attempts, with considerable erudition, to prove that Honestus at that time was only the coadjutor, or co-bishop, of Peter, archbishop of Ravenna.] then held the archiepiscopal see at Ravenna and had formerly been abbot of the monastery at Classe. Romuald therefore promptly approached him and disclosed to him the entire desire of his heart [Note: Here the aforementioned fragment of the Vatican manuscript, no. 5411, ends.].

Honestus, becoming eager, added the spurs of exhortation to his chaste desire and commanded the brothers to admit him without hesitation into their community. Supported, therefore, by this patronage, the monks received Romuald with fearless confidence and gave him the habit of holy religious life.

In that monastery [Note: It was called the monastery at Classe because of the nearby city of Classe, of which no trace now remains. But because of wars and the unhealthy climate, the monks moved to the city of Ravenna in the sixteenth century, where they built a new and beautiful monastery and dedicated it to their holy father Romuald, although it continued commonly to be called by the same name, Classe. The extremely ancient basilica of Classe still exists and is preserved by those same monks with the greatest care and reverence.] he spent approximately three years.

## CHAPTER THREE. How the Monks, Having Been Rebuked, Tried to Throw Romuald from the Upper Gallery

[Col. 0958A]

But when he saw that some men there lived more carelessly along the broad road, while he was not permitted to take up the arduous path of perfection that his mind dictated, he began anxiously to inquire within himself what he ought to do and was compelled to seethe amid many waves of thought.

He presumed to rebuke harshly those who lived laxly and often summoned the precepts of the Rule as witnesses to their disgrace. When he persisted vehemently in reproving their faults, while they regarded the words of a younger man and novice as worthless [Note: The Fontisboni edition reads: “as the words of a younger man and novice.”], at last, unable to endure this reproach, and disdaining to correct their own lives, they began to plot the death of the one who rebuked them [Col. 0958B].

Romuald customarily rose during the night earlier than the other brothers. If the door of the oratory was still closed, he would keep vigil in prayer inside the dormitory. The building mentioned above had been constructed high, in the manner of an upper gallery or terrace.

The sons of Cain therefore found this plan, dictated by the devil: when Romuald rose before the others in his usual manner, they would throw him headfirst through the window of the upper chamber [Note: We do not recall finding this word used elsewhere among Latin writers to signify a window. The reading *per speculam* is therefore preferable. This word is ordinarily used for a part of an elevated place from which something can easily be viewed or observed, and from which access is consequently provided for throwing things down, as in Virgil, *Eclogue* VIII:

“Headlong from the airy watchtower of the mountain  
I shall be carried down into the waves.”].

When this plot became known to Romuald through one of the conspirators, he thereafter avoided the imminent danger by praying to his Father within the chamber of his heart, with the door of his mouth closed. Thus, while he guarded himself against bodily ruin, he closed for the brothers the abyss of iniquity, lest they fall into the death of their souls [Col. 0958C].

## CHAPTER FOUR. How Romuald Went to the Desert

As the love of perfection grew stronger each day in his soul, and his mind found no rest, he heard that in the region of Venice there was a certain spiritual man named Marinus [Note: The place was that which is still called the Tower of Darkness, commonly Torre di Caligo, where the remains of the once-abandoned ancient city of Heraclea could be seen.], who led the life of a hermit [Note: Sigonius, *Kingdom of Italy*, book VII, calls Marinus a Ravennate; Ferrarius and others make him a Venetian.].

With the abbot and brothers’ consent very easily obtained [Note: Perhaps this was that abbot Dominic whom Rubeus mentions in the *Acts of the Council of Ravenna* of the year 995.], he reached the aforesaid venerable man by boat and undertook to live under his direction with the humblest devotion of mind.

Marinus was, among his other virtues, a man of simple character and exceptionally sincere purity. He had not been trained by any instruction in the eremitical way of life, but had been moved toward it solely by the impulse of good will.

His manner of life was as follows: throughout the year, on three weekdays each week he tasted half a morsel of bread and a handful of beans; on three others he took wine and pottage with measured moderation. He sang the entire Psalter every day [Note: On hermits reciting the complete Psalter privately, see Peter Damian, work XV, chapter 18, and Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book III, chapter 27, concerning Egbert.].

But because he was untrained and in no way instructed in the ordering of the solitary life [Note: “The solitary life,” that is, the eremitical life, as in the following chapter and chapter 9.], as Blessed Romuald himself later cheerfully recounted, he would often leave his cell and wander about with his disciple, singing psalms across the broad expanse of the desert: now singing twenty psalms beneath one tree, now thirty or forty beneath another.

Romuald, however, because he had left the world unlearned, could scarcely sound out, syllable by syllable, the notes of his verses with an open Psalter. His keeping his eyes fixed downward produced in him an unbearable oppression of acedia. Marinus, meanwhile, carried a rod in his right hand and very often struck the left side of Romuald’s head while Romuald sat opposite him.

Afterward, when Romuald was compelled by very serious necessity, he humbly said: “Master, if it pleases you, strike me from the right side from now on, because I am already completely losing the hearing of my left ear.”

Then Marinus, astonished at such patience, moderated the discipline of his excessive severity.

## CHAPTER FIVE. How Peter Urseolus Was First Made Duke and Afterwards Converted

At the same time Peter [Note: This Peter, from the ancient Participatian family, was surnamed Urseolus, or Ursiolus, as in the Vatican manuscript and elsewhere, instead of Ursio and Urso, by which names he is also called in many places. Participatia and Ursona were the same clan; from this most holy man Peter propagated a second Urseolan family, just as Justinian and Baduarius, likewise Participatii, produced the Justinian and Baduarian families respectively. See the Preface to the distinguished V. Justus Fontanus’s Dissertation no. 2, *On Saint Peter Urseolus*.], surnamed Urseolus, held the reins of the duchy of Dalmatia [Note: Although Damian attributes the duchy of Dalmatia, and consequently the principality of the kingdom of Dalmatia, to Saint Peter Urseolus, the Venetians first acquired dominion over Dalmatia under his son, Duke Peter Urseolus II. This is shown by Dandulus, book IX, chapter 1, part XV, who later, in part XXXI, adds concerning Peter Urseolus II: “By the unanimous consent of all, he first called himself Duke of Dalmatia.”].

He had deserved to rise to this height of dignity because he had been a supporter of the killers of his predecessor, namely Vitalis Candianus [Note: Read “Peter Candianus”; Vitalis Candianus succeeded Saint Peter Urseolus, rather than preceding him. It was easy for Damian, writing in solitude, to err concerning names. Hence, in letter 10 of book I, he candidly noted: “We are not particularly concerned to appear as hunters of names, provided that the sequence and order of events do not disappear.” This may also be a copyists’ error.] [Note: Here too the most devout writer was mistaken, deceived by a false report. From childhood Saint Peter Urseolus had sought nothing but to please God and had disdained climbing to so great a dignity, fearing that he would lose his purpose of holiness through ambition for secular honor. At last, when the people pressed him insistently, he did not refuse to accept the summit of this principate—not out of human favor, but for the good of the entire republic. So reports the ancient Venetian Chronicle and other manuscripts.].

Why that man was killed by his own people, I think it worthwhile to explain briefly, without departing from the concision I have preserved.
