He had taken as his wife the sister of that great marquis Hugh [Note: She is called Valdrada and Valderada, as well as Gualdrada or Valderta and Walderta, by various writers. She was the sister of Hugh and daughter of the marquis and prince of Tuscany, Ubertus. On Hugh and Ubertus, or Oberto, see Damian, work XVII, dissertation 2, *On the Office of a Prince*, addressed to Marquis Gothifredus, chapter 3.]. At the urging of his brother-in-law, he was acquiring many soldiers from the regions of Lombardy and Tuscany by distributing monetary pay.

The inhabitants of Venice could not endure this. They secretly formed a plan to burst violently, in a sudden armed attack, into the duke’s palace and kill him, together with his entire household, without any hesitation, by the sword.

When Duke Vitalis discovered this conspiracy, he surrounded himself with watches by night and day and reduced the hostile ambushes to nothing. As they tried this and that but could not bring their faction’s undertaking to completion, they finally decided first to set fire to Peter’s house, which adjoined the duke’s palace, so that in this way they might both capture the duke and burn all his household.

When they sought Peter’s agreement for carrying out this plan—Peter having been a participant in their counsel—they finally made a pact with him on these terms: in exchange for one house of his, which they would consume by fire, they would place the whole of Venice under his rule and, once the duke whom they hated had been destroyed, immediately install Peter in his place.

In this way Peter obtained the principate of the kingdom of Dalmatia. Later, after he had attained the pleasure of his ambition, he was at last pierced in heart with regard to divine grace [Col. 0960C].

A certain venerable abbot named Guarinus [Note: Guarinus, or Warinus—which is the same name—was a most holy man. The monk Gartia wrote of him in a certain letter, reported by Balutius in the Appendix to *The March of Spain*, title 222: “The angel, or heavenly man, Warinus.” In the Acts of the consecration of the basilica at Cuxa, as read in the cited Appendix, title 119, it is said that Prince Seniofred appointed there an excellent abbot named Guarinus, who, like a bright star, strove to shine abundantly throughout the world.] was accustomed, for the sake of prayer, to travel as a pilgrim through various regions of the world from the farthest parts of Gaul.

When he too came to the duke, the latter immediately demanded that he provide counsel by which he might escape the danger of so great a crime. Marinus and Romuald were therefore summoned, and by their common judgment he was ordered to abandon the world together with the duchy that he had wickedly seized. Since he had unjustly rushed toward the citadel of another’s dominion, he was to subject himself to the rule of another’s authority.

That man, however, being plainly a person in power, did not dare to make his conversion openly. He thought it safer to use the following plan. As the feast of a certain martyr approached, a basilica named after that martyr still being in his private possession, he sent his wife there the day before, while he himself pretended that he would soon follow. He instructed her both to see that the church was furnished with the utmost care and to prepare sumptuous banquets for those who would come with her on the following day.

He himself remained behind his wife and, taking from his treasures whatever seemed appropriate to him, boarded a ship with one of his retainers, namely John Gradenicus [Note: John, from the equally ancient and noble Gradonica family, was a nephew of Saint Peter Urseolus. He, like Urseolus himself, had never been involved in the killing of Peter Candianus.], who had been aware of the aforementioned conspiracy, and with the three blessed men whom we mentioned above [Note: To these must be added John Maurocenus, a companion of equal nobility and piety, and Urseolus’s son-in-law. After completing the monastic life at the monastery of Cuxa, he returned to Venice and founded the monastery of Saint George there, now inhabited by monks of the Congregation of Saint Justina, or Monte Cassino.].

He then fled to Gaul, to the monastery of Abbot Guarinus, as a great convert [Note: Namely, the monastery at Cuxa, presided over by Abbot Guarinus, situated in the diocese of Elne. Damian above places it in the farthest parts of Gaul, and not incorrectly, for the distinguished V. Mabillon, in his observations on the Life of Saint Peter Urseolus, no. 4, noted: “The monastery of Saint Michael at Cuxa, although situated in Catalonia, was properly located within the boundaries of Gaul, since the territory of Barcelona, Cerdanya, and other counties along the Llobregat River had long before come under Gallic rule.”].

After Peter and John had become monks in the monastery of Saint Michael, Marinus and Romuald, living not far from the monastery, returned to the solitary life to which they had been accustomed. After scarcely a year had passed, the brothers just mentioned joined them in bearing the strictness of that same solitude.

## CHAPTER SIX. How Romuald Lived for One Year on a Handful of Chickpeas per Day and for Three Years on His Own Agriculture

[Col. 0961C]

Meanwhile Romuald, with the desire of his mind inflamed, began to grow marvelously from virtue to virtue and to outstrip the other brothers by far in the steps of holy conduct. Thus, whatever he decided among the brothers, whether concerning spiritual or even bodily matters, his judgment prevailed entirely, with everyone willing.

Marinus himself rejoiced to be devoted to Romuald, over whom he had recently presided. For an entire year Romuald had nothing else for food; each day he lived only on a single handful of boiled chickpeas.

For three years, however, he and John Gradenicus broke the soil with hoes, sowed wheat, and lived from the labor of their hands. While they practiced agriculture, they doubled the burden of their fasting.

## 435 CHAPTER SEVEN. The Various Battle with the Devil That He Endured

The devil nevertheless attacked Romuald with many and varied assaults of temptation, especially at the beginning of his conversion. He dragged his mind about through many incentives to vice: sometimes recalling to him what and how much, as a vigorous man, he could have acquired in the world; sometimes what he had left behind for ungrateful relatives to inherit after him with covetous desire; sometimes accusing him that the things he was doing were insignificant and of no merit; sometimes, by impressing upon him the honor of so great a labor, promising him a long span of life.

Oh, how often, striking his cell, did he rouse him when he had scarcely fallen asleep and, as though twilight were already approaching, force him to pass the whole night in vigil! For almost five continuous years the devil lay at night upon his feet and legs and, so that he could not easily turn here or there, weighed him down with the appearance of a phantom burden.

Who could explain how many roaring beasts of vice he endured? How often did he drive away present evil spirits with the harshest rebukes? Hence, if one of the brothers, compelled by some necessity, entered his cell during the hour of silence, the soldier of Christ, ready for battle, immediately assumed that he himself was the devil and rebuked him in a loud voice, saying:

“Where are you going now, most disgraceful one? What business have you in the desert, you who have been cast down from heaven? Begone, unclean dog; vanish, sluggish serpent!”

By these and similar words he showed that he was always standing in battle formation against the evil spirits and, girded with the arms of faith, immediately went forth into the field to confront the enemies who challenged him.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. One Form of Romuald’s Life; and the Penance of Duke Peter and His Prophecy

It happened once that, while reading a book on the lives of the Fathers, he came upon the passage [Col. 0962D] stating that certain brothers, fasting individually throughout the entire week [Note: See Palladius, chapter 24 and chapter 106. This severe custom of fasting is established by chapter 2 of the Rule of Saint Antony and observed by Saint Athanasius in the *Summary of Doctrine for Monks*.], would meet together on Saturdays; on Saturday and Sunday they would relax the strictness of their fast and live on a less austere diet.

Romuald immediately adopted this way of life and remained in it with continuous austerity for nearly fifteen years or more.

Duke Peter, however, because he had been accustomed to being raised amid many delicacies, was now on the point of collapsing under the burden of such a strict fast. Therefore he humbly prostrated himself at Blessed Romuald’s feet [Note: This is unquestionable evidence that Saint Peter Urseolus was his disciple and spiritual son, since he humbly prostrates himself before his feet, as before those of his teacher, and asks for help.].

When ordered to rise, he was compelled by shame to disclose his need. “Father,” he said, “because I have a large body, I cannot sustain myself on half this piece of *paximatium* [Note: In the eremitical Rule edited by Blessed Paul Justinianus in 1520 at the monastery of Fontisboni near Camaldoli, chapter 28, it says: “Their daily measure of food was half a portion of *paximatium* for each day, that is, half of dry or twice-baked bread.” Among some people *paximatium* means bread baked beneath ashes or barley bread.], for the sake of my sins.”

Romuald, therefore, compassionating his weakness with piety, added a quarter-piece of *paximatium* to the customary measure [Note: Blessed Paul Justinianus, in the eremitical Rule mentioned above, says: “That is, a fourth part of this kind of bread.”]. Thus he extended the hand of mercy to the brother who was already failing, lest he perish entirely, and strengthened him to complete the path of good living that he had begun [Col. 0963B].

His son, who bore the same name, a man very prudent according to worldly standards, visited him on one occasion. To him the Father foretold whatever would happen to him, whether by the spirit of prophecy or by some revelation—I do not know which.

“My son,” he said, “I know without any doubt that they will make you duke and that you will prosper. Take care only that you preserve the rights belonging to Christ’s churches and do not turn aside from justice toward your subjects, whether through love or hatred of anyone.”

[Note: This prophecy was fulfilled after the dukedoms of Vitalis Candianus and Tribunus Memmi, when, in the year 991, Peter Urseolus II was made duke in the thirtieth year of his age, in accordance with the prophecy of his holy father, as Dandulus writes, book IX, chapter 1.]

## CHAPTER NINE. Another Form of Romuald’s Life

After this, Romuald again read that Saint Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, had instituted the fasting of Saturday [Col. 0963C], truly as a vigil for holy Easter [Note: See Peter Damian’s letter to the hermits of his congregation, volume I, book VI, letter 35, where this judgment of Blessed Sylvester concerning fasting on Saturday is discussed.]. He immediately changed the relaxation of Saturday to Thursday and, thus taking account of the weakness of the sick, made the long fast easier through the exercise of discretion.

He established this rule of life [Col. 0964A] for all followers of the solitary life: each person should recognize that he is observing the fast of the eremitical life when, throughout the week, he fasts for three days and for two days [Note: These words are frequently used in ancient constitutions. Lucas Barchinonensis, also called the Spaniard, discusses their meaning and use at length in *The History of Romuald*, book V, chapter 3. In ancient times *biduana* and *triduana* were the names given to fasts when one fasted on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, and afterward on Friday and Saturday, on bread and water. Thus the abstinence of the first three days was called *triduana*, and that of the following two days *biduana*, as Blessed Paul Justinianus explained in the eremitical Rule, chapter 27. On these fasts see also our Peter Damian, work XV, chapter 6, and work XIV, where he says concerning the meaning of fasting: “We call those people fasting who take bread with salt and water; but when anything else is added beyond these, it is not called a complete fast.”], while on Thursday and Sunday he may take vegetables or any kind of broth with thanksgiving, except during the two Lents of the year. During those periods, not only he himself but also many of his disciples were accustomed to continue the fast throughout the entire week.

And certainly it was fitting that he who always strove to praise God with choir and timbrel should continually make the principal consonances of harmonic melody—namely the diapason, diapente, and diatessaron [Note: Musicians use these terms to signify the principal, or, as they call them, perfect, consonances of harmonic melody. The *diapason* is the octave, the *diapente* signifies the fifth, and the *diatessaron* the fourth. Since during Lent Blessed Romuald and his disciples postponed their meal from one Sunday until the next, they rightly sounded the harmonic *diapason*, an octave, in the ears of divine light. When at other times they relaxed the weekly fast on Thursday, they divided that *diapason* into the lower *diapente*, extending from the first Sunday to Thursday, and the higher *diatessaron*, extending from Thursday to the following Sunday. Thus their fasts were recognized as distinguished by the principal consonances through a mystical melody.]—should continually resound before the ears of unbounded light.

Although he himself very often fasted completely—that is, passed the day without any food—he absolutely forbade others to do so. For he said that, for one striving toward perfection, it was supremely fitting to eat every day and always remain hungry, so that through habit the flesh might become lighter in what appears burdensome to novices at the beginning of their conversion.

He thought little of anyone beginning something great for a time if he did not also persevere in it with patience.

He strongly recommended that vigils be performed moderately and with great discretion, lest someone perhaps fall into sleep after completing the nighttime offices. Indeed, the holy man hated this kind of sleep so much that if someone confessed to him that, after keeping vigil through twelve psalms, he had fallen asleep—especially near dawn—he could not, with Romuald’s permission, celebrate the solemn rites of Mass on that day.

He also said that, if possible, it was better to sing one psalm by heart and with compunction than to run through a hundred while the mind was engaged in chatter. But whoever had not been given this grace perfectly, he nevertheless urged not to despair and not to grow lukewarm in bodily exercise itself, until the one who had given the will should at some time also grant the ability.

Only let the mind’s intention, once fixed upon God, preserve the incense of prayer; for the breeze of thoughts entering from outside disturbs it. Where the intention is upright, a thought arriving against one’s will need not be greatly feared.

## 438 CHAPTER TEN. Concerning the Count Who Seized a Cow and Was Killed While Eating It
At a certain time, while he was still dwelling within the borders of Gaul [Note: Namely, in the solitude of the monastery of Cuxanum.], he had as a close acquaintance a certain farmer who sometimes made for him the utensils he needed in his cell and, if he needed anything, cheerfully supplied it from the scant resources of his poverty, richer in charity than in possessions. A certain proud and swollen-headed count, sending his retainers, seized this man’s cow with barbarous violence and ordered its flesh to be prepared for his dinner, with great eagerness of appetite. Behold, the peasant hastened to Romuald’s cell and, with loud wailing, cried out the misfortune of his loss; he complained that the hope of himself and his household had been taken away. Saint Romuald therefore quickly sent a messenger to that same count and with the most humble entreaty begged him to return the poor man’s animal [Note: Blessed Jerome of Prague, illustrious for holiness and learning, a Camaldolese ascetic who flourished in the fifteenth century, adds in his *Life of Saint Romuald* that Romuald threatened the count with divine vengeance, which later followed.]. But the slippery count rejected his pleas with a defiant spirit and declared that he would taste that very day what flavor the flanks of the fat cow might have.

When the hour of dinner arrived, the table was set and the cow’s flesh was brought in; and, as the sentence of divine vengeance was already impending, at the very beginning of the meal the count cut off a piece of the cow’s kidney [Note: Jerome himself writes “a piece of cow’s flesh.” Peter of Natalibus, however, says plainly: “A bone suddenly turns in the throat of the robber, and he is immediately suffocated.”] and put it into his mouth. It suddenly stuck so immovably in his throat that, despite every effort, it could neither descend inward nor be expelled outward. Thus, while his companions stood around him, with the passage of breath blocked, he was killed by a dreadful death; and from the very thing by which, against God’s servant, he had desired to satisfy his fleshly appetite to satiety, by God’s just judgment he lost his bodily life while still fasting.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Olibanus, who promised conversion

There was another count in the same regions of Gaul, named Olibanus [Note: The encomiast of Urseolus, in Mabillon, calls this Olibanus the lord of the territory in no. 18 and the duke of that province in no. 19. He held under his authority Narbonese Gaul—namely, Catalonia, where Cuxanum is situated.], under whose jurisdiction the monastery of the aforementioned abbot Guarinus had also been placed [Col. 0965D]. Though raised high upon the lofty summit of earthly power, he was heavily burdened by many masses of sins. At one time he visited Romuald for the sake of a visit; while the others remained outside the cell, he began, alone with the solitary, to recount, as though in confession, the sequence of his deeds. When the venerable man had heard what he related, he answered that he could in no way be saved unless, abandoning the world, he hastened to a monastery.

The count, immediately troubled in mind, said that his spiritual advisers, who knew his deeds, certainly did not think so and would never urge him to undertake something so intolerable. He therefore summoned the bishops and abbots who had come with him and began jointly to inquire whether matters truly stood as God’s servant testified. They all confirmed Blessed Romuald’s judgment with one voice, but excused themselves for not previously having said this to the count, since they had been restrained by fear. Then the count, after dismissing everyone, made this secret agreement with Blessed Romuald: he would go to Mount Cassino under the pretext of prayer and irrevocably devote himself to divine service in the monastery of Saint Benedict.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Sergius, who wished to return to the world

Meanwhile Sergius, Romuald’s father, became a monk; but some time afterward, persuaded by the devil and repenting of his conversion, he attempted to return to Egypt. The monks immediately tried to report this to Blessed Romuald—namely, the monks of the monastery of Saint Severus [Note: The monastery of Saint Severus, once famous, rises between Classe and Ravenna; its church survives to this day. Fortunius discusses it at length in *History of Camaldoli*, part II, book I, and it has been united with the monastery of Classe.], which lies not far from the city of Ravenna, where Sergius dwelt bodily but not in heart.

Struck by this unfavorable report, Romuald decided that Abbot Guarinus and John Grandenicus should go with the count to further his conversion, while he himself should come to the aid of his failing father as quickly as possible. Duke Peter, however, had already happily ended his final day. Romuald therefore entrusted the count to these two men, to both of them but especially to John, who was subject to him, commanding him in particular under obedience that, even if Guarinus departed, he himself should never separate from the count.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Romuald’s prudence, the hardship of his journey, and his discipline of his father

When the inhabitants of that region heard that Romuald intended to leave, they were disturbed by excessive grief. Considering among themselves how they might restrain him from this intention, they finally thought the following course best: to kill him through an impious act of piety by sending assassins, so that, since they could not retain him alive, they might at least possess his lifeless corpse as a protection for the land. When Romuald learned of this, he shaved his head completely on every side. As the agents of this deed were already approaching his cell, at almost the first light of day he began to eat as though out of greed [Note: A similar example occurs in the *Book of the Sayings of the Fathers*, no. 8.]. Seeing this, they believed him insane and, judging that his mind was deranged, disdained to injure his body.

Thus, the prudent spiritual David overcame by madness the cunning of those who were carnally wise in folly (1 Kings 21). For he both restrained them from committing sin and, without fear of death, escaped the danger of death, thereby adding to the accumulation of his merits. Then, once he was permitted to use his freedom, he reached Ravenna from the innermost regions of Gaul—not supported by a horse, not carried in a vehicle, but bearing only a staff in his hand and traveling barefoot. There he found his father wishing to return to the world, bound his feet firmly in a wooden device, tied him with heavy chains, and afflicted him with hard beatings. He subdued his body with pious severity until, with God’s healing assistance, he restored his mind to the state of salvation.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Sergius saw the Holy Spirit

Sergius, therefore, having at last recovered sound judgment, later corrected whatever he had previously done wrong through his backward-turning will by taking many upright steps in holy conduct. Among his other practices, he was accustomed to stand frequently before a certain image of the Savior; there he prayed with particular devotion and sacrificed himself with abundant tears and much contrition of heart.

One day, while he was remaining there more attentively in prayer—a new and unheard-of event in our times!—the Holy Spirit suddenly appeared to him in some form unknown to me. When Sergius immediately asked who he was, the figure plainly asserted that he was the Holy Spirit, and then, suddenly, as if passing by, escaped from the eyes of the one who was looking at him. At once Sergius was carried into ecstasy and, set aflame by the fire of the one he had seen, began to run rapidly after him through the monastery cloister, asking the brothers who were there, with great fervor, where the Holy Spirit had gone.

Because they thought that he had fallen into madness and rebuked him harshly, Sergius maintained that without any doubt he had seen the Holy Spirit and that the Spirit had visibly passed before his eyes. Immediately afterward he was seized by illness, took to his bed, and within a few days ended his life in a blessed consummation. Here it is clearly proved what is said to Moses by the divine voice: “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exodus 33). Hence Daniel, when he said that he had seen not God but a vision of God, added: “I languished and was sick for many days” [Note: The Vulgate lacks the word “many.”] (Daniel 8). Rightly, therefore, after Sergius had been permitted to behold eternal life, which is God, he soon failed from temporal life.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning John’s leg, which was broken because of disobedience

The count Olibanus [Note: Namely, Olibas or Oliva, which is the same name—one frequent in those regions. He too became a monk, was appointed abbot of Cuxanum and Ripoll, and was subsequently made bishop of Ausona.], leaving his possessions to his son together with a great abundance of wealth—specifically, fifteen pack animals loaded with treasure [Note: “Pack animals” or “beasts of burden” are what *sagmarii* means, as both Leo of Ostia, who relates this same event, and Peter Damian himself use the term in the *Life of Saint Odilo* and in his letters]—went with Guarinus and John, as well as Marinus himself, to the monastery of Blessed Benedict. Taking leave of those who had accompanied him, who until then suspected nothing of this plan, he compelled them to return home, afflicting themselves with many groans and bitter tears.

Marinus soon afterward went toward Apulia and, living there later in solitude, was killed by Saracen brigands [Note: In the manuscript of the *Life of Blessed Marinus* it reads: “He was attacked by Saracen brigands whose vices he sharply rebuked; for the sake of Christ he himself was seized and impiously slaughtered, and was deemed worthy to obtain the crown of martyrdom.” Around the year 1000, the Saracens established a camp on the summit of Mount Gargano, where Blessed Marinus had founded his hermitage, and in savage raids they ravaged all Italy and the shores of Gaul and Spain as far as the Ocean.].

A short time later, Guarinus, who was accustomed to travel about for the sake of prayer, and John, encouraged by his brother’s example to undertake the same religious duty, decided by common agreement to travel to Jerusalem. When Olibanus learned this, he began sadly and tearfully to beg them most devoutly not to abandon him after breaking faith, but, as Blessed Romuald had ordered, to guard him in God’s service. He added: “At least remember this, John: your master entrusted me especially to your faith and, if you depart, has laid upon you the charge of disobedience.”

But they persisted in their purpose with stubborn determination and, finally leaving Olibanus, set out on their pilgrimage. When they had descended from the mountain and turned toward the plains, they stopped at a place and began to discuss among themselves something they considered necessary. While they were engaged in this, Guarinus’s horse suddenly wheeled away with a furious rush and, against the rider’s will, turned in another direction; striking John’s shin with its iron-shod hoof, it broke the leg.

Immediately thrown to the ground by the immense pain, John at last remembered and recalled his master’s commands to mind. In words of public confession he accused himself of faithlessness and of being guilty of disobedience. From the broken leg he learned that breaking faith had been a sin. And because he, endowed with reason, had been disobedient to his master, an irrational animal did not know how to obey its rider in order to preserve his safety.

Afterward, returning to the place from which he had set out, he asked that a cell be built for him near the monastery. There he remained in holy conduct for nearly thirty years, as long as he lived. He possessed great charity and wondrous humility, but his abstinence was exceedingly strict and cautious, so that no one even within the monastery cloister knew how the holy man fasted [Note: We have a sufficiently learned commentary on Blessed John Grandenicus, written by the religious man Amedeo Lutius, a Venetian Minorite.].

Among his other gifts of virtue, he so detested the vice of backbiting that, as soon as someone opened his mouth to disparage another, the person’s slander was immediately driven back by him, like an arrow rebounding from a stone with the force of its impact [Note: These words—“the person’s slander was immediately driven back by him”—are absent from the Vatican manuscript.]. After his death, God performed through him a number of miracles.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Romuald, who was struck by demons

After correcting his father, Romuald established a cell in the marshes of Classe and lived in a place called Peter’s Bridge. Later, fearing neither bodily illness nor the stench’s nausea, but lest, under the pretext of weakness, he relax even slightly from the rigor of abstinence, he moved to the estate of Classe, where there is the church of Blessed Martin called “in the Wood” [Note: This not insignificant place is still counted among the estates of Classe and preserves the ancient name of Saint Martin; nevertheless, no remains of the ancient church survive there.].

One day, while he was singing Compline [Note: Some writers have said that, among the many commendable institutions the universal Church received from monks, it also received this part of the divine office from the Benedictines, as the epilogue and summary of the daytime praises. In truth, Saint Benedict gave it only the name “Compline,” for this canonical hour was already in use before his time. See Martène and Calmet, chapter XVII; and Mege, chapter XVI, in the commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict.], because there had formerly been an ancient cemetery there, the thought of this suddenly came to him, as often happens; immediately a great horror of phantasmal illusion seized his mind.

As he turned this over in his mind more and more frequently, behold, evil spirits entered his cell with a sudden assault, immediately threw him to the ground, battered him with monstrous violence, and inflicted the most terrible blows upon his limbs, exhausted by a long fast [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “very severe blows.”]. At last, while he was being visited by divine grace amid the blows of the assault, Romuald cried out: “Dear Jesus, beloved Jesus, why have you abandoned me? Have you handed me over entirely into the hands of my enemies?” At this, all the wicked spirits were driven away by divine power.

Immediately such a profound compunction of divine love inflamed Romuald’s breast that his whole heart melted into tears like wax, and he felt nothing of the many wounds inflicted upon his battered body. Soon he rose from the ground sound and strong, and, although blood still hindered him, returned to the same verse of the psalm where he had left off. For, as the demons entered, the window of the cell struck him on the forehead; afterward a visible scar hardened there, displaying clear evidence of the wound for as long as the holy man lived.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the wicked spirits who appeared to him like dreadful birds

Thus the soldier of Christ, strengthened by becoming accustomed to battle, strove daily to advance toward greater things, to grow from strength to strength, and, always stronger than his former self, could no longer fear any ambushes of the enervated enemy. Often, as he sat in his cell, the wicked spirits seemed to him to stand there like the most hideous ravens or vultures; and, as though they were watching over the corpse of an animal, because they did not dare approach, they were compelled to gaze from a distance.

Often they displayed themselves in the forms of Ethiopians; often they showed themselves in the shapes of various animals. The renowned triumphator of Christ mocked them, saying: “Behold, I am ready; come! And if there is any strength in you, show it. Are you now completely failing? Have you already been defeated, and have you no stratagems left with which to contend against God’s servant?” With these and similar words he put the wicked spirits to shame and immediately drove them away, as though he were shooting just as many arrows at them.

When the devil therefore saw that he could not prevail against God’s servant by himself, he turned to cunning devices. Wherever the holy man went, he stirred the minds of his disciples into hostility against him, so that, since it had been impossible to restrain Romuald from the impulse of his inflamed fervor, he might at least check him from caring for the salvation of others; and, since he himself could not be overcome by the enemy, he might at least not be denied victory through others.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the monks who beat Romuald and were struck by divine wrath

At one time he went to a place called Bagno [Note: Bagno is a town in Romandiola under the temporal rule of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, but under the spiritual rule of the Camaldolese monks, who inhabit there an abbey dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary. In the vernacular it is called Bagno. It is situated on the Apennine mountain, not far from the Camaldolese Hermitage, in the territory of the city of Sarsina, which in antiquity was called Saxena, Saxina, and Sassina.], situated in the territory of Saxena. While he remained there for some time, he built a monastery in honor of Blessed Michael the Archangel, and entered a cell not far away in which he was to live [Note: Blessed Jerome of Prague says: “He built a monastery in honor of Saint Michael, in which he appointed monks and an abbot; he himself entered a reclusion in a small cell not far from the fortress of Vergaretum.” Vergheretum, or Vergaretum, and Verghereta, are an Apennine fortress not far from Bagno, near the sources of the Sapis River, commonly called the Savio.].

Hugh, the margrave [Note: Concerning this Hugh, prince of Tuscany, see above, chapter 5, note 5.], sent him seven pounds of coin for his needs. Romuald accepted them so that, as a good spendthrift, he might distribute them mercifully. When he heard that the monastery of Palatioli had been consumed by fire [Note: There are several places in Italy with this name: one between the rivers Bedesis and Candianus above the monastery of Classe; another in the marshes between Ravenna and the mouths of the Po, which I think is meant here and was dedicated to Saint Mary; another at Monteverdi in the diocese of Populonia in Tuscany; and another in Latium, four thousand paces from Albano.], he sent sixty solidi from the money mentioned above to the brothers as assistance and kept the remainder to spend on a similar work.

When the monks of Saint Michael learned this, they were stirred against him with bestial fury, both because he had already opposed their wicked customs in many ways [Note: Surius reads: “for many years already.”] and because he did not spend everything brought to him on them, but used some of it for others. They therefore formed a conspiracy and unanimously broke into his cell with clubs and poles [Note: He uses *phalangas* for poles. This is a word familiar among Africans, as appears in Pliny, book VII, chapter 56; Saint Augustine, *Sermon* 100, *On Time*, 12, Tuesday after the fourth Sunday of Lent; Saint Prosper, *On Promises and Predictions*, part II, chapter 9. Honnius, however, drops the aspiration and calls them *palangas*; this is also how the word appears in Varro, book IV, *On the Life of the Roman People*.]. They beat him repeatedly and, after plundering everything, shamefully dishonored him and drove him from their territory.

As he departed, expelled in this way [Note: The edition of Fontisboni reads: “When he had thus been expelled.”], and the force of his excessive sadness had already descended into the depths of his mind, he deliberated within himself that from then on he would be content with his own affairs and would completely abandon concern for the salvation of others. A terror so great seized his mind with this thought that he had no doubt that, if he persisted stubbornly in what he had conceived, he would perish and be condemned by divine judgment.

The monks, however, having obtained the fulfillment of their long-desired vengeance and, as though relieved of a heavy burden [Note: That is, “lightened” or “relieved.”], praised among themselves what they had done against God’s servant and, with joy flattering them, gave themselves over to excessive revelry and laughter. Then, to make the celebration of such great joy especially delightful, they prepared an expensive abundance of delicacies for a feast.

It was winter, a season most fitting not only to the changing times but also to their cold minds. One of them, who had been more savage toward the most blessed servant of Christ [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “soldier.”], was trying to obtain honey with which to make mead for the diners. As he crossed the Sapin River for this purpose, his feet struck against planks [Note: *Plancae* are flat boards that formed the bridge of the river from which he was thrown; the word is also found in Pliny, book VIII, chapter 43, where he says that even asses cross bridges, while rivers gleam through the gaps between the planks.]. Suddenly he was thrown from the bridge, dragged down, and completely swallowed up by the river’s whirlpool.

It was plainly by God’s just judgment that the troubled water satisfied him unto death, because, where he ought to have wept, he had desired the sweetness of honey for the pleasure of life.

At night, while all were resting as usual, a great quantity of snow began to fall, and suddenly the entire structure of the common building collapsed upon them. It crushed one man’s head, another’s arms, another’s legs, and yet another’s various limbs. One of them even had an eye torn out. Rightly did he suffer the division of bodily light, because, separated from his neighbor, even if he had retained the other eye, he had lost the single light of the twofold charity.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the command of Saint Apollinaris to Romuald

At one time the holy man remained not far from Catria [Note: Mount Catria is a very lofty peak among the Apennines, piercing the clouds; it lies in the duchy of Urbino, in the diocese of Gubbio, between the city of Cagli and the town of Sassoferrato. At its foot stands the monastery called the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana, long famous for the holiness of so many monks. At that time Blessed Lodulphus, the founder—or rather instigator—of this monastery or hermitage, was living there; he is said to have received the laws of the eremitical life from Lord Romuald.]. While he stayed there for some time, Blessed Apollinaris appeared to him visibly and, with great authority, ordered him to go to his monastery [Note: That is, the monastery of Classe, in which he had been clothed in the monastic habit.] and live there instead. The holy man considered this command by no means to be neglected, and without delay left the place where he was staying and hastened energetically to the place to which he had been sent.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning his dwelling at Origarium

At another time the venerable man was enclosed in the marsh of Comacchio [Note: Read “of Comacchio.” Comacchio is an episcopal city of Emilia, commonly called Comacchio, famous for fishing because of the stagnant waters there. It lies below Ferrara at the mouths of the Po.], which is called Origarium. Later, because of the excessive stench of the marshy mud and the corrupted air, he emerged so completely swollen and hairless that he no longer seemed to have the same appearance as when he had entered. His entire flesh had even become so green that he scarcely differed in color from a *stellio* [Note: A *stellio* is an animal somewhat resembling a lizard, with a back marked by certain shining spots. Pliny discusses it in book III, chapter 10.].

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the cell that caught fire and was extinguished by prayer

At another time he lived on an island called Pereum [Note: This island lay at the mouths of the Po. It was formerly called Pyretum and later also Peretrum. Blessed Jerome of Prague calls the hermitage “of Peretello.” The place is now commonly called Saint Albert.]. The island lies approximately twelve miles from the city of Ravenna.

While he was staying there in a cell with a certain venerable man, namely his disciple William, the narrow walls of the dwelling suddenly caught fire. Then, rising upward, the flame began with unrestrained force to dominate the roof. The holy man immediately resorted to his usual means of defense: he did not drag outside the things stored there; he did not, as is customary, scatter the roof’s shingles [Note: Some read *scandulas*. These are wooden boards split into thin strips, with which buildings were roofed before tiles were invented. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 19: “*Scindulae*, because they are split and divided.”]; he did not pour out an abundance of water, nor did he strain with any effort to extinguish the flames. He simply poured out a prayer, and at once divine power extinguished the hissing masses of fire.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning King Otto, Romuald’s guest, and how Romuald accepted the abbacy

At the same time the younger Otto [Note: Namely, Otto III, who came to Italy in the year of Christ 996 to aid the Apostolic See, which was being harassed by the tyranny of the duke Crescentius, according to Baronius.] the Emperor, wishing to appoint an abbot for the monastery of Classe, gave the brothers the option of electing without hesitation whomever they wished. They immediately and unanimously chose Romuald.

The Emperor, doubting that the blessed man could be summoned to the royal court by a messenger, wished to go to him in person and arrived at his cell as the sun was setting. Since Romuald had received a great guest in a small house, he graciously offered him his own little bed for rest. The king, however, refused the covering because he considered it extremely rough.

In the morning the king took him with him to the palace and at last began, with many entreaties, to press him to accept the abbacy. When Romuald resisted and absolutely refused to consent to the royal request, the king, on the contrary, threatened him with excommunication and anathema from all bishops, archbishops, and the entire synodal council. At last, overcome by the urgency, Romuald yielded and was compelled to accept the governance of souls.

He said that this did not seem new to him at all, but that it had been divinely revealed to him five years earlier [Note: The Vatican manuscript nevertheless reads: “He said.”]. He therefore governed the monks under the strict discipline of the rule, and no one was permitted to turn aside from it with impunity. Neither a nobleman nor an educated man dared, through unlawful actions, deviate to the right or the left, or depart from the straightness of upright conduct.

Finally, the holy man fixed the eyes of his heart upon heaven so that he might obey God in all things, and did not fear displeasing human beings. Considering this, the brothers first blamed themselves for having requested that he be placed over them; then they tore him apart with many whispered slanders and harassed him with the harsh goads of scandal [Note: The same manuscript reads: “But the brothers, considering this too late,” and so forth.].

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the abbacy that was relinquished, and the peace made between the king and the Tiburtines

Romuald, seeing that his own perfection was being diminished to some extent and that their conduct was turning more readily toward worse things, went promptly to the king. Although the king resisted him not lightly, Romuald, together with the archbishop of Ravenna [Note: Gerbert, who later became Pope Sylvester II.], threw down his staff in the presence of both men and relinquished the monastery.

At that time the king was besieging the city of Tibur. The citizens had killed its illustrious duke, named Mazolinus [Note: The Vatican manuscript has *Mazolinum*. Surius reads *Matholinum*; Jerome of Prague, *Masolinum*; and the old edition, *Mamolinum*.], and, taking up arms, had driven the king himself away from their walls [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “from their own,” and so forth.]. It is therefore beyond doubt that Blessed Romuald was sent there by divine providence, to remove the impending danger to so many souls by establishing peace [Note: See Baronius under the year 996, no. 77, concerning the siege of this city of Tibur—commonly called Tivoli—situated approximately eighteen miles from Rome. The Tiburtines, mindful of the great benefit conferred upon them by Lord Romuald, still venerate him as their patron.].

He arranged this agreement between them: the Tiburtines were to demolish part of their walls in honor of the king and give hostages; and they were to send the killer of the duke, in chains, to the duke’s mother. She, softened by the holy man’s prayers poured out to God, though cruelly offended, forgave the crime and permitted him to return safely to his own people.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Saint Venerius [Note: The Vatican manuscript also calls him a saint, although chapters XXVII and XXVIII lack this title; those chapters are “Concerning Boniface the Martyr” and “Concerning John and Benedict, Martyrs,” who have been entered by the Church in the catalogue of saints. From this the sanctity of Venerius may be inferred.]

The venerable man also produced another fruit of good work at Tibur, which I do not think should be passed over in silence. A certain blessed man named Venerius initially began to live in the monastery with such humility and simplicity that all the brothers despised him with mockery and thought him delirious and demented. Some of them often slapped him; others poured over him the dirty water in which they washed their kettles [Note: A *lebes* was an ancient garment of monks, also called a *colobium*, without sleeves and with some covering for the head. Thus an anonymous writer from Ripoll wrote of Saint Peter Urseolus that he had placed a *lebes* upon his head.]; others habitually lacerated him with various abusive insults.

When he realized that amid so many adversities he could not preserve a tranquil state of mind, he abandoned their company and fled into the solitude. There he remained for six years in the dryness of an exceedingly strict discipline, without wine or any prepared dish.

When Romuald heard of his reputation, he therefore sought to visit him [Note: The following words are missing from the Vatican manuscript: “Romuald, having heard of his reputation, sought to visit him.”]. Romuald asked under whose rule he lived and to whose authority he submitted the obedience of his way of life. Venerius replied that, freed from another’s command, he followed whatever seemed more useful to him.

Romuald said to him: “If you carry the cross of Christ, it remains for you not to abandon Christ’s obedience. Go, therefore, and, having obtained your own abbot’s consent, return and live humbly under his authority, so that the structure of sacred work, which good will builds, may be raised by humility [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “may be erected”] and lifted up by the virtue of obedience.”

After offering this and many other admonitions for his edification, Romuald taught him how he could resist his thoughts and how he could oppose the assaults of wicked spirits. Having strengthened and instructed him in this way, he left him with great cheerfulness.

Venerius gratefully embraced the holy man’s teachings, immediately went to his abbot, obtained his consent, and returned as quickly as possible to the solitude he loved. Wishing to live within the possession of his monastery, he climbed onto a certain rock inaccessible to human footprints and completely removed from human company. There he lived alone for four years, deprived of every human comfort. Apart from three small loaves that he had brought with him from the monastery, he ate no bread, drank no wine, and tasted nothing cooked at all; he lived only on the fruits of trees and the roots of plants.

There was a hollow in that same rock where water collected in winter; the holy man drank all summer from this supply. At last, when it became known that God’s servant lived there, many people began to gather around him, bringing supplies of food and providing whatever they thought he needed. Since he himself lacked nothing, he gave everything to shepherds, herdsmen, and other needy people.

At the urging of the local bishop, he permitted a basilica to be built and consecrated for him. He died there some time afterward, and was found by certain people who were looking for him lying inclined before the altar, resting on his elbows and knees as though engaged in prayer. There the Lord deigned to perform through him various signs of miracles.

Thus, indeed, the good earth returned abundant fruits after receiving the seed of the word multiplied from Romuald’s mouth.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning Tammo and King Otto’s religious devotion

In the aforementioned city the most blessed man, Romuald, also converted a certain German named Tammo [Note: The edition of Fontisboni has “a certain German named Tamum.” Jerome of Prague calls him Thanius and a military commander.]. He had been, as is said, so close and dear to the king that the clothing of each covered both of them, and their hands were often joined together at a common meal by a single dish.

The Roman senator Crescentius [Note: Concerning the history of this Crescentius, see Baronius under the year 996, no. 7 and following. Lambert of Hersfeld, however, a monk who lived in the eleventh century, places the beheading of Crescentius in the year 998 in the *Annals of Germany*.], having incurred the king’s anger, fled for refuge to the mountain called Saint Angelo. Because its fortification was impregnable, he prepared himself confidently to defend it while the king laid siege.

At the king’s command, Tammo gave him an oath guaranteeing his safety [Note: Namely, Pope Gregory V, the emperor’s relative, against whom Crescentius had set up the antipope John XVI [Col. 0976D], formerly bishop of Piacenza.]. Deceived in this way, Crescentius, with the cooperation of the pope who was his enemy, underwent a capital sentence as guilty of treason against the majesty. The emperor afterward took his wife as a concubine.

Since Tammo was both aware of the fraud and bound by guilt for perjury, Blessed Romuald therefore ordered him to abandon the world. Tammo immediately asked the king for permission; he found the king not merely willing to grant it but exceedingly eager to do so. For the aforementioned emperor was very favorably disposed toward the monastic order and devoted with excessive affection to the servants of God.

The king himself, however, having confessed the same crime to the blessed man, set out from the city of Rome barefoot for the sake of penance and proceeded in this manner as far as Mount Garganus, to the church of Saint Michael. [Cols. 0976B–D]

[Note: Lucan sings of the location of this mountain in Book V:

“Garganus, Apulian, rises out into the Adriatic waves.”]

He also remained throughout the whole of Lent in the monastery of blessed Apollinaris at Classe, with only a few companions adhering to him. There, devoted to fasting and psalmody as far as he was able, he wore a hair shirt next to his skin, while above it he was covered with gilded purple. Although a bed had been spread with shining coverings, he himself wore down the tender limbs of his delicate body [Col. 0976B] upon a mat made of papyrus. He therefore promised blessed Romuald that, abandoning the imperial dignity, he would assume the monastic habit; and although innumerable mortals had been subject to him, he himself had now begun to be subject to a poor man and to owe obedience to him.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How Romuald fell ill at Cassino and afterward came to Pereum [Cols. 0976B–0977D]

Romuald, then, together with the aforementioned Tammo, with the most renowned Boniface, a man 450

[Note: This blessed Boniface is none other than Saint Bruno, concerning whom the Monastic Breviary speaks on 15 October. Mabillon is to be consulted, sixth century, part I, under the year 1009; and from there the new commentary of Conrad Janning in the Bollandist *June*, vol. VI, part I, p. 27.]

whom the Russian Church now proudly possesses as its most blessed martyr, and with other converted Teutons, descended from the town of Tibur to the monastery of blessed Benedict established on Mount Cassino. [Col. 0976C] There he was indeed seriously ill, but soon recovered through divine mercy.

He had a rather excellent horse, which Busclavus, son of the Slavic king, had given him after becoming his monk.

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript the name is written *Bluscavi*; some maintain, however, that this name is corrupt.]

The holy man exchanged it out of a desire for humility, and, in a profitable bargain, received a donkey, like the praiseworthy merchant (Matthew XXII). For, because of his excessive longing for our Redeemer, who had sat upon the back of a she-ass, the venerable man preferred to ride this same animal.

With all those mentioned above, Romuald returned to Pereum, where he had formerly lived. There, after many other brothers had joined them and had been assigned to individual cells, he maintained the strictness of the eremitical way of life, both in himself and in others, with such fervor that their life was regarded as marvelous by all to whom the report of it could reach.

For who would not be astonished? Who would not proclaim the transformation wrought by the right hand of God, when he had previously seen men clothed in silken, indeed gilded, garments, crowded by frequent throngs of attendants and accustomed to an abundance of every luxury, but now saw them content with a single rough tunic, enclosed, barefoot, unkempt, and worn down by such severe abstinence? [Col. 0977A]

They all performed manual labor: some made spoons, others spun, others wove nets, and others made hair shirts.

[Note: A *birrum* is a shaggy, unpolished tunic; see Cange’s *Glossary*.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the martyr Boniface [Cols. 0977B–0979D]

The manner of life of blessed Boniface, however, surpassed that of all the others by far. He had been a kinsman of the king

[Note: The emperor Otto III, whom Damian often calls only “the king.”]

and was so dear to him that the king called him by no other name than “My Soul.”

He was exceptionally learned in the doctrines of the liberal arts and especially distinguished in the study of musical composition. While he was therefore staying in the royal chapel, he saw the church of the ancient martyr Boniface

[Note: Namely, the church seen on the Aventine Hill at Rome, dedicated to Saints Alexius and Boniface, archbishop of Mainz and apostle and martyr of Germany. Formerly monks of the Order of Saint Benedict served it, but at present it is served by members of another order, that of Saint Jerome.]

and, immediately inspired by the example of his namesake to desire martyrdom, said: “I too am called Boniface. Why, then, should I not also be a martyr of Christ?”

Later, once he had become a monk, he bound himself to such frugal abstinence that he often ate only on Sundays and on Thursday during the week. Sometimes, if he saw a dense patch of nettles or even brambles, he would throw himself into it and roll about.

When a brother once reproved him for this, saying, “Hypocrite, why do you do this publicly, to win reports of popular approval?” he answered nothing except: “Let confessors be yours; let martyrs be mine.”

When, after a long life of eremitical observance, he was preparing to go forth to preach, he made his way to Rome and received from the Apostolic See the consecration of the archbishopric. An old monk told me—he had accompanied him there from the territory of Ravenna—that throughout the entire journey the venerable man walked on foot with all who followed him, but that he himself, constantly singing psalms and far ahead of the others, always went barefoot. He ate daily because of the labor of the journey; yet he lived each day on half a loaf of bread and water. On feast days, with every drink excluded, he supplemented his daily fare with whatever fruits or roots of herbs were available.

After he had been consecrated, he observed daily both the monastic and the canonical order in the celebration of the offices of the hours. When he was now proceeding beyond the mountain regions, he traveled on horseback, but the venerable bishop, as it is said, endured the bitter cold of that extremely frigid region with bare legs and feet, so intolerable that, when he wished to dismount, he could scarcely detach his foot from the adhering iron unless warm water first came to his aid. At last, when he reached the pagans, he began to preach with such steadfastness of fervent heart that no one could doubt that the holy man was seeking martyrdom.

They, however, fearing that the same thing might happen to them as had happened after the martyrdom of blessed Adalbert—when many of the Slavic people were converted by the conspicuous signs of miracles—held back their hands from the blessed man by an artful malice for a long time. Though he passionately desired to die, they cruelly spared him because they did not wish to kill him.

When the venerable man reached the king of the Russians and insisted vigorously upon preaching with steadfast courage, the king saw him dressed in filthy garments and walking barefoot. He supposed that the holy man did not present himself in this way for religious reasons, but rather for the purpose of collecting money. He therefore promised that, if Boniface would abandon such vanity, he himself would enrich his poverty with the most lavish generosity.

Boniface immediately returned without delay to his lodging, put on the most precious episcopal vestments in a dignified manner, and thus presented himself again at the king’s palace. When the king saw him adorned in such splendid clothing, he said: “Now we know that it was not poverty’s lack but ignorance of the truth that impelled you toward your vain teaching. Nevertheless, if you wish what you assert to be believed as true, let two tall piles of wood be raised, separated from each other by the narrowest interval; and when, with fire placed beneath them, they have been filled with smoke and flame so that the two heaps appear to be one fire, pass through the middle. If you are harmed in any way, we shall hand you over completely to those fires to be consumed; but if—something that cannot be believed—you emerge unharmed, we shall all believe in your God without any difficulty.”

When this agreement pleased not only Boniface but all the peoples who were present, Boniface, dressed as though he were about to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, first walked all around the fire with holy water and incense, then entered the hissing globes of flame, and emerged unharmed, so that not even the smallest hair of his head appeared to have been burned.

Then the king and the others who had witnessed this spectacle threw themselves in crowds at the feet of the blessed man, tearfully sought pardon, and urgently begged to be baptized.

A multitude of peoples therefore began to flock to baptism, so great that the holy man went to a certain spacious lake and baptized the people in the abundance of its waters. The king resolved that, leaving the kingdom to his son, he himself would never separate from Boniface as long as he lived.

The king’s brother, however, who lived with him and refused to believe, was killed by the king in Boniface’s absence. Another brother, who had already separated himself from the king’s household, came to him soon afterward.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “as soon as he came to him.”]

The venerable man’s words he refused to hear; instead, inflamed by excessive anger against him because of his brother’s conversion, he immediately seized him. Then, fearing that, if he kept him alive, the king might take him from his hands, he ordered him to be beheaded in his presence, while a considerable crowd of people stood around.

Immediately he himself was struck blind, and such stupor overcame him, together with all who were standing there,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “so that they could in no way speak, feel, or perform any human function.”]

that they could neither feel nor perform any human function at all, but all remained rigid and motionless like stones.

When the king heard this, he was struck with immense grief and resolved not only to kill his brother but also to slaughter with the sword all who had supported him in so great a crime. But when he came there at once and, with the martyr’s body still lying in the midst, saw his brother standing stupefied, together with the other men, without sensation or movement, it seemed best to him and all his companions that prayer should first be offered for them, in case divine mercy might restore to them the sense they had lost. Then, if they agreed to believe, they would live with their crime pardoned; but if not, they would all perish beneath avenging swords.

After both the king himself and the other Christians had prayed for a long time, not only was their former sense restored to the stupefied men, but their resolve to seek true salvation was also increased. Immediately they tearfully sought penance for their crime, received the sacraments of baptism with great joy, and built a church over the body of the most blessed martyr.

Yet if I attempted to recount all the gifts of virtue that can truthfully be told about this remarkable man, my tongue would perhaps fail, though the material would not. Since, therefore, the virtue of Boniface requires a work of its own, we nevertheless take care to mention him briefly here together with Romuald’s other disciples, so that from their praise we may show how great was their glorious Master. Thus, while the eminence of his disciples sounds in the ears of the faithful, it may become known from the school he directed how exalted their Teacher was. 453

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the martyrs John and Benedict [Cols. 0979C–0981D]

Meanwhile, while Romuald was still living at Pereum, King Busclavus sent petitions to the emperor asking him to send spiritual men who might call the people of his kingdom to the faith.

The emperor then approached Romuald and begged him to grant some of his monks who might suitably be sent there. Romuald, however, did not wish to command any of his monks as though by the authority of a superior; instead, leaving the matter to their own decision, he gave them the choice either to remain or to depart.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript has “to all of them.”]

For he did not know God’s will concerning so fearful an undertaking and therefore entrusted it not to his own judgment but rather to that of the brothers.

When he questioned them

[Note: The same manuscript adds: “the king questioning them.”]

and humbly entreated them, only two among them all were finally found who voluntarily offered themselves as ready to go to him. One was called John, the other Benedict.

They therefore went to Busclavus, first remaining in the wilderness that sustained them, and laboriously applying themselves to learn the Slavic language so that afterward they might preach. In the seventh year, when they fully understood the speech of the land, they sent a monk to the city of Rome and through him asked the bishop of the Apostolic See for permission to preach. They also instructed him to bring with him some of blessed Romuald’s brothers who, knowing the eremitical way of life, might live together with them in the regions of the Slavs.

Busclavus, wishing to receive the crown of his kingdom from Roman authority, began earnestly to beg the venerable men to carry many of his gifts to the pope and bring back for him a crown from the Apostolic See. They entirely refused to consent to the royal request, saying: “We have been placed in the sacred order; it is not at all permitted to us to handle secular affairs.” Thus they left the king and returned to their cell.

Certain men who understood the king’s plan, but did not know what the holy men had answered, imagined that the monks had brought with them to their cell the large quantity of gold that was to be sent to the pope. They then made an agreement among themselves to enter the wilderness secretly at night, kill the monks, and carry off the money.

When the blessed men perceived them attempting to break in, immediately recognizing the reason for their arrival, they began to make confession to one another and to arm themselves with the banner of the holy cross. Two boys were also there, assigned from the royal court to serve them, who, as far as their strength allowed, tried to stand in defense of the holy men and resist the thieves.

At last the thieves found an entrance, burst in with drawn swords, and killed them all together. Then, anxiously searching for the treasure but finding nothing after turning everything upside down, they attempted to set fire to the cell and burn the martyrs’ corpses with it, so that they might conceal the crime of their great offense and cause human suspicion to attribute what had happened to flames rather than weapons.

But when the fires were brought near, their natural force failed, and they could consume nothing at all despite every human effort. Indeed, the very material of the walls repelled them as though it were composed of the hardest flint instead of wood.

The frustrated thieves therefore attempted to flee, but divine providence denied them this as well. Throughout the entire night they anxiously sought a path through the forest thickets, across the breadth of the wilderness, and through the darkness of the woods; yet, wandering about, they could not find one at all. Nor could they put their daggers back into their sheaths, their arms having become paralyzed.

Where the bodies of the saints lay, a brilliant light shone abundantly until daybreak, and the sweetness of angelic song did not cease to resound.

When day arrived, the king could not remain unaware of what had happened. He immediately hastened to the wilderness with a great multitude of people and, forming a ring of men, surrounded the whole forest on every side so that the thieves might not escape. At last they were found, plainly guilty of the crime, and, by divine vengeance, still bound to their swords.

After considering and deliberating what he should do with them, the king finally decided not to order them killed, as they deserved, but to send them bound in iron chains to the martyrs’ graves. There they would either live miserably in chains until death or, if the holy martyrs judged otherwise, the martyrs themselves would release them through their mercy.

When, by the king’s command, they had been dragged to the saints’ tomb, they were immediately freed from their bonds by the ineffable omnipotence of God, the chains having been broken.

Afterward, a basilica was built over the saints’ bodies, and innumerable miracles have occurred there through divine power, not only then but also now.

[Note: The Camaldolese celebrate the feast of these saints on 16 November.]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the monk released from prison by an angel [Cols. 0981B–D]

Emperor Henry, aware of Busclavus’s plan, had ordered the roads to be guarded everywhere so that, if Busclavus sent messengers to Rome, they might immediately fall into the emperor’s hands.

The monk

[Note: Ractius, Minius, and other writers call this monk blessed Barnabas. Together with Saints Andrew, Benedict, Justus, and other illustrious followers of the Camaldolese institute, he shone with great holiness. Martin Baronius published their Lives at Kraków in 1610, printed by Basilius Skalski.]

who had recently been sent by the holy martyrs was therefore finally captured and immediately handed over to prison custody. During the night, however, an angel of the Lord visited him in prison and informed him that those whose embassy he was conducting had met their end

[Note: Instead of *admonuit*, the Vatican manuscript reads *innotuit*.]

and immediately declared that, by divine opening of the prison, a boat had been prepared for him on the river that he was to cross. The monk hastened there and proved the angelic promise true.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the monastery built for Saint Adalbert and Romuald’s prophecy against the king [Cols. 0981C–0982B]

While Romuald was still staying at Pereum, the emperor Otto, at his suggestion, built there a monastery in honor of Saint Adalbert.

[Note: Not even a trace of this monastery now remains. In that place there is a church, not ancient, dedicated to the same holy martyr; in the corrupt speech of the common people it is called Saint Alberto.]

He assigned to it the adjoining possessions of the monastery at Classe and compensated himself for them from his fiscal estates in the regions of the Firmian domain.

[Note: In the province that we call the March of Ancona, where the city of Firmum, commonly Fermo, is situated.]

After appointing one of Romuald’s disciples as abbot there and gathering brothers around him, Romuald began to keep them under strict supervision and taught them to live according to regular discipline. He also instructed the abbot, when withdrawing into the wilderness, to remain in his cell throughout the week and, on Sundays, to come to the monastery to visit the brothers.

The abbot, however, disregarding the holy man’s orders, began to live like a secular person. Having once strayed in practice from the path of righteousness, he soon departed farther and farther from it.

Romuald therefore saw that he could not labor there according to the ardor of his own will. He immediately went to the king and, as one demanding fulfillment of the promise he had received, began to press him more urgently to become a monk.

The king replied that he would indeed do what was required, provided that he first attacked Rome, which was in rebellion against him, and, after conquering it, returned victoriously to Ravenna.

Romuald answered him: “If you go to Rome, you will never see Ravenna again.” He declared to him most plainly that death was near. Since he could not recall him, being undoubtedly certain of his death, Romuald boarded a ship while the king was hurrying to Rome and crossed over to the city of Parentium.

[Note: This is a city in Istria under Venetian rule, commonly called Parenzo.]

Thus, in accordance with the blessed man’s prophecy, scarcely had the king begun to return from Rome when he was seized by illness and died at Paternum.

[Note: Several cities and castles are recorded under the name Paternum; here, however, we believe that the castle situated in the territory of Todi is intended, as Cosmas de Arena observes in his *Series of the Dukes of Etruria*, p. 183.]

## CHAPTER XXXI. How the grace of perfection was divinely granted to Romuald [Cols. 0982C–0983D]

Romuald lived for three years in the territory of the city of Parentium. There he built a monastery

[Note: A church dedicated to Saint Michael the Archangel still stands near Parentium, where tradition says that Saint Romuald lived. Because of the unhealthiness of the air, the monks cannot live there; they have nevertheless been transferred to the monastery of Saint Matthew at Murano near Venice. Apart from the church, the entire surrounding territory, called Lemmi after the nearby river Lemmus, is now held under the jurisdiction of the abbot of Samathia, who enjoys the title of Count of Lemmi, recently confirmed by the Venetian Republic in the year 1040. The illustrious Wilpurga, countess of Istria, with the consent of Lord Uxelin, Lord Vedoxicus, and their sons and daughters, donated a large part of the county of Lemmi to the aforementioned church, which had been built in honor of God, the holy Virgin Mary, and blessed Michael the Archangel by Abbot John and consecrated by Hengalmer, bishop of Parentium. This appears from the deed of donation, transcribed in 1305 at the command of Lord Boniface, bishop of Parentium, by Andrew, notary of Parentium. A copy written by the distinguished Peter Delphinus, abbot of Camaldoli, is preserved in the archive of Saint Michael of Murano, chapter 66, no. 1.]

and appointed an abbot over it together with the brothers. He himself, however, remained enclosed in two [cells].

[Note: Perhaps in a certain crypt, which the inhabitants of Lemmi still recognize as the place inhabited by Saint Romuald.]

There, divine grace advanced him to the summit of great perfection, so that, inspired by the Holy Spirit, he foresaw certain future events and penetrated many hidden mysteries of the Old and New Testament by the rays of understanding.

At times he was anxious to burst into tears there, but was unable by any effort to attain the compunction of a contrite heart. It happened one day, as he was singing psalms in his little cell, that he came upon this verse of the psalm:

“I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk; I will fix my eyes upon you” (Psalm XXXI).

Suddenly such an outpouring of tears arose in him, and his mind was so illumined for understanding the meanings of Holy Scripture, that from that day onward, for as long as he lived, whenever he wished, abundant tears flowed from him with the greatest ease, and many mysteries of Scripture were not hidden from him.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads *mystica* (“mystical things”).]

Often such contemplation of divinity carried him away that, as though wholly dissolved in tears and burning with the indescribable heat of divine love, he would cry out: “Dear Jesus, dear one, my sweet honey, ineffable desire, sweetness of the saints, delight of the angels,” and other expressions of this kind.

He uttered these words under the prompting of the Holy Spirit; we cannot express such things with merely human understanding. For, as the Apostle says: “We do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit himself prays for us with unutterable groanings” (Romans VIII).

For this reason Romuald never wished to celebrate Mass before many people, because he could not restrain himself from the flood of tears. Later, because of his excessive familiarity with this gift, the simple-hearted man thought that the grace divinely granted to him had been granted to everyone and often said to his disciples: “Take care not to shed many tears, because they weaken the eyesight and injure the head.”

Wherever the holy man decided to live, he first built an oratory with an altar in his cell; then, shutting himself in, he sealed the entrance.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning Romuald’s prophecy by which he foretold the arrival of his disciples [Cols. 0983C–0984D]

On one occasion, brothers living in the solitude called Bifurcum sent to him asking for advice about how they ought to conduct themselves in the wilderness and how they might resist the assaults of the devil.

[Note: Bifurcum is a place in the Alps within the Florentine domain, toward Faenza, where a monastery dedicated to Saint Benedict was situated and was fully called Saint Benedict in the Alps.]

When their messengers had reached the monastery, from which Romuald’s cell was some distance away, the venerable man immediately recognized their arrival through the spirit. He ordered Abbot Anso, who was then attending him, saying: “Go and prepare a meal for the brothers who have come from distant regions.”

[Note: Damian mentions a certain Aso in this volume, in the Life of Saints Rudolph and Dominic. I do not know whether he is the same man who transferred from monastic to eremitical life, as often happened at that time.]

Anso immediately began to mock him and say that he was truly a false prophet. Nevertheless, at last, as though compelled, he came to the monastery and found those whom the holy man had foretold already praying in the church.

Romuald seasoned them with much salt of saving doctrine, armed them with many virtues against the snares of the ancient enemy, and, after carefully teaching them about everything, sent them back to the wilderness with great joy.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning his return from Parentium and the sailors rescued from danger through his merits [Cols. 0984A–0985D]

At another time the aforementioned brothers again sent messengers to him and sought advice concerning the same matter with even greater anxiety.

The venerable man said to them: “I am now writing a little book about the battle with demons, which I will give you when you return; or perhaps I myself will come with you.”

[Note: If only that book still existed!]

When they heard this, they immediately prostrated themselves on the ground and begged him with very persistent entreaty to deign to go with them. The next day he declared without hesitation that he would go with them and ordered them to seek a ship.

When the bishop of Parentium heard this, he was struck with immense sorrow. Finding the monks running about in search of a vessel, he subjected them to many insults and disgraced them with abusive words. He also proclaimed this edict to everyone staying near the harbor: whoever dared to give Romuald a ship would himself depart irrevocably together with him and would never return to Parentium.

A messenger was therefore sent hastily to the bishop of Pola

[Note: This bishop of Pola was perhaps Bertaldus. Pola, an ancient city of Istria, is now commonly called Pula.]

so that he would not delay sending a vessel to the blessed man. The bishop mentioned above had often urged Romuald never again to remain hidden, enclosed in so obscure a retreat, but rather to go where he could gain a richer harvest of souls—so that he might not burn like a coal only for himself, but, like a lamp truly placed upon a lampstand, pour out the rays of his light upon all who were in the house of God.

While they were waiting for the messenger who had been sent, Romuald said to the brothers who were with him: “Know beyond doubt that that brother will come late, and that we must go in another ship before he returns.”

When the holy Sunday arrived, at the first dimness of dawn he said to a brother attending him, named Ingelbert, who afterward became archbishop among the pagans: “Look far out over the sea and see two ships, still at a great distance, moving toward us with equal speed. One of them must certainly receive us.”

The brother gazed more intently, carefully inspecting everything with his eyes wide open, but could see no sign at all of rowing. When the day was already beginning to brighten, however, behold, at the furthest limit of his sight he saw two ships approaching from afar, appearing, because of their great distance, almost like two birds.

When at last they entered the harbor, the rowers were asked whether they wished to take Romuald and his companions aboard their own ship. Immediately filled with a new joy, they placed themselves and all they possessed at his disposal and declared that they would be blessed to bear the weight of so precious a pearl.

That day they refused to depart because they feared the threatening weather. Romuald, however, encouraged them to begin the journey at once in hope of divine grace, promising that they would suffer no danger whatsoever. They nevertheless remained there throughout the day and began to sail by night.

Toward dawn the winds suddenly raged, a storm arose, and the sea was churned from its deepest foundations. Violent squalls now flew at the rowers from every side, striking the ship back and forth and loosening almost all its planks.

You might see the men: some stripping themselves in preparation for swimming, others tying themselves to various floating objects, and still others grasping oars or some solid piece of wood so that they might remain afloat on the waves.

When, in such danger, with everything desperate, shipwreck no longer seemed doubtful but imminent, Romuald immediately hastened to the familiar weapons of prayer.
