Leaning his head slightly forward and lowering it into his lap, he poured out prayers silently to the Lord. Then he securely instructed Abbot Anso, who was sitting close beside him, saying: “Tell the sailors not to fear at all, but to know without any doubt that they will all escape unharmed.”

Scarcely had he said this when, beyond all expectation and without any human assistance, the ship itself set its course and soon slipped rapidly into the harbor of the city of Capreola.

[Note: For *Capreola*, read *Caprulensis*. Caprula, commonly Caorle, is a city about forty miles from Venice and is very sparsely inhabited because of the unhealthiness of its air. Nevertheless, it has a bishop who is suffragan to the patriarch of Venice.]

Then they all gave worthy thanks to God their deliverer and openly acknowledged that they had been snatched from the jaws of death through Romuald’s merits.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning Romuald’s arrival at Bifurcum [Cols. 0985C–D]

When Romuald arrived at Bifurcum and saw all the brothers’ cells, he thought that they appeared somewhat ostentatious because of a certain superstition. He therefore did not wish to lodge in any of them except the one in which the venerable Peter, his disciple, lived.

[Note: Writers, especially Camaldolese ones, record this venerable man under the title “Blessed Peter of Bifurcum.”]

He was a remarkable man of great abstinence and extraordinary austerity, who scarcely ever allowed his cell to be made wider than four cubits, following the example of Saint Hilarion.

The same venerable man reported that, while blessed Romuald was staying with him and the two of them alternated psalm verses by turns, Romuald pretended to go out to relieve nature thirty times during the night, or even more, because he could not restrain the flood of tears and sobs that poured from him.

When Romuald had remained there for some time and admonished the brothers not only concerning spiritual combat but also to place an abbot over themselves and do everything in common, they paid little attention to Romuald’s instructions. Each of them had his own means of support, and each followed the freedom of his own judgment as he pleased.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning his arrival in the valley of Castro and the great harvest of souls produced through him [Cols. 0986A–D]

Romuald, therefore, unable to endure such barrenness, began anxiously and eagerly to seek where he might find land suitable for producing a harvest of souls.

He sent messengers to the counts of the province of Camerino.

[Note: Camerino is an episcopal city situated near the borders of Picenum and Umbria, called Camerino by the Italians. The province took its name from Camerino; Damian, in Letter 12 of Book VII to Duke Gotifredus, calls it the “domain,” that is, the March of Camerino. After reserving the dominion of Etruria for himself, Hugh ceded this province of Camerino, together with the duchy of Spoleto, to the emperor, as Damian himself relates in the letter cited above.]

When they heard Romuald’s name, they were filled with immense joy and offered him all the estates belonging to their power—not only forests and mountains, but also fields, if he desired them.

At last a place was found in their possession quite suitable for the eremitical way of life, surrounded on every side by mountains and forests. In the middle lay a broad plain, suitable not only for producing crops but also watered by clear springs.

[Col. 0986B]

This place had long been called the valley of Castro. There was already a small church there

[Note: Dedicated to the Most Holy Savior and blessed Mary.]

in which there appeared to be a community of certain converted women.

After these women had been settled elsewhere, the venerable man began to live there with his disciples, having constructed cells.

Who could describe with ink or proclaim with speech how many fruits of souls the Lord acquired through him there? People began to flock from every direction to penance and to distribute their possessions mercifully to the poor. Others abandoned the world entirely and hastened with fervent spirit to the way of holy life.

The most blessed man was like one of the Seraphim, for he himself burned incomparably with the flame of divine love and, wherever he went, set others aflame with the torches of holy preaching.

Often, while he was delivering words of preaching, such compunction stirred him to tears that he would suddenly abandon his interrupted sermon and flee somewhere in a sudden rush, as though out of his mind.

Even when he sometimes rode with the brothers, coming far behind the others and always singing psalms, he nevertheless did not cease continually shedding tears, as though he were sitting in his cell.

Among the others, however, he rebuked with especially harsh severity those secular clerics who had been ordained through payment, and he asserted that, unless they voluntarily abandoned their order, they were altogether condemnable and heretical. Hearing this novel claim, they plotted to kill him. For throughout that entire realm, down to the time of Romuald, scarcely anyone knew, according to widespread custom, that the Simoniacal heresy was a sin.

He said to them: “Bring me the books of the canons, and let the pages of your own books attest whether what I say is true.” After they had carefully examined them, they acknowledged the crime and lamented their errors. The holy man therefore appointed several canons and clerics who had been living in a secular manner, like laymen, and taught them to obey superiors and live communally in a congregation.

[Note: Damian imitated this institution of St. Romuald’s: canons living communally in a congregation under superiors. Indeed, he not only rebuked the canons of his own Church of Velitrae but voluntarily brought them back to a strict rule of life, as he reports in his letter that is Opusculum 34.]

Some bishops, too, who had invaded sacred sees through the Simoniacal heresy, flocked to him for the sake of penance. Entrusting themselves to the venerable man, they promised both to leave the episcopate at a fixed time and to hasten to the order of holy religious life. Yet of these, while the holy man lived, I do not know whether he was able to convert even one. That poisoned heresy, especially in the episcopal order, is so hard and rigidly resistant to conversion that, always making promises, always putting matters off from day to day and postponing them to the future, it is easier for a Jew to be converted to the faith than for a heretical robber to be brought fully to repentance.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### Of the thief whom he saw in spirit breaking into Gregory’s cell and dismissed unharmed

[Col. 0987B]

In those same regions the holy man also founded a monastery for maidens. On a certain solemn day, while the venerable man was sitting there with the brothers in chapter and satisfying them with the nourishment of salutary teaching, he suddenly interrupted his discourse and began to cry out with anxious concern, saying: “Come now, come now, and hurry as quickly as possible, for a thief is already breaking into Brother Gregory’s cell.”

This Gregory was afterward consecrated archbishop among the nations.

[Note: He too, like St. Boniface and Ingelbert, was consecrated by the supreme pontiff only with the title of archbishop, in order to preach the Gospel of Christ to the nations.]

They immediately leapt up, ran swiftly to the cell, and found the thief already breaking through the walls. They seized him, dragged him before the master, and asked what should be done with so sacrilegious a plunderer. The holy man began cheerfully to say to them:

“And I, brothers, do not know what we can do with so evil a man. Shall we tear out his eyes? But afterward he will not see. Shall we cut off his hand? But he will no longer work, and perhaps as a result he will perish from hunger. If we cut off his foot, he will not be able to walk. But lead him inside and first set food before him, while in the meantime we consider what should be done with him.”

And so, rejoicing in the Lord, after the holy man had had the robber fed, he gently rebuked him, admonished him with kind words, and allowed him to return home in peace.

## 461 CHAPTER XXXVII  
### Of the monastery of the Old City which he built

At last, leaving some of his disciples in the valley of Castro, he went to the region of the Old City and built a monastery on the estate of Count Pharulphus, with the support of many people, but especially with Pharulphus providing the expenses.

[Note: Augustine of Florence, together with not a few other writers, incorrectly renders this as Civita Vecchia, formerly Centumcellae. In reality, it refers to the region of Urbevetana, commonly called Orvieto, a city of some distinction in Etruria under the dominion of the Church; no one but an uninformed person can doubt this.]

[Note: Pharulphus was count of the Old City, as Damian himself reports in Letter 19 of Book VI. He is said to have belonged to the celebrated family of the counts of Monte Martino, or Monte Martini, which some regard as the family of the counts of Corbara. That monastery appears to have been the monastery of Blessed Mary in Silva, mentioned in a papal diploma of Alexander IV and elsewhere.]

For such an ardor for producing fruit had blazed up in the holy man’s heart that, never satisfied with what had been accomplished, while doing one thing he immediately hurried on to do another. He seemed almost to wish to turn the whole world into a desert and to join the entire multitude of the people to the monastic order. Finally, he withdrew many people there from the world and distributed them among several holy places.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### Of the count’s son who restored sight to a blind man after his death

Some sons of nobles, too, despising their parents, fled to the most blessed man. Among them was the son of Count Guido.

[Note: This is also how the Vatican manuscript reads. In the Appendix to the Life of Blessed Guido of Monte Martino, written by Francesco Lollio of Ravenna and published at Bologna in 1659 together with other Lives of Blessed Reginald of the Order of Preachers and Blessed Angelina of the Third Order of St. Francis, both from the same family of Monte Martino, this entire thirty-eighth chapter of the Life of Romuald is reproduced, where we read: “Among them was also Guido, count, son of Count Pharulphus.” Jacobilli, who included the history of this most holy monk in volume II, page 215, of the Saints of Umbria, and the Camaldolese and other writers, always identify him as Guido, son of Count Pharulphus. If this is correct, it must be said that in Damian’s passage the word “son” means grandson, for on the page concerning the donation of Valliscastrum—if the whole document published by Augustine of Florence in Part II, page 37, of the Camaldolese History is entirely trustworthy—we read: “I, Count Pharulphus, son of Count Guido.”]

This Guido, while still a boy, became a monk and, not long afterward, as death approached, saw two evil spirits, like very black vultures, fixing terrifying eyes upon him. When the boy told this to Blessed Romuald, who was attending him, he immediately added: “Look, master: so many Ethiopians are entering now that they already fill the entire building.”

Romuald urged him to confess what he had done wrong. The fortunate sinner confessed, with great terror, only this crime: he had been ordered by his prior to take an unspecified number of bundles of switches, which he had not yet received.

[Note: Blessed Dominic Loricatus turned bundles of rods into scourges of thongs; our Damian records this in his Life.]

After Romuald had granted him forgiveness for so great a transgression, he died in peace. On the following day, a certain blind man—specifically, his father’s prebendary—came to his tomb and cried out in a loud voice:

“Ah, my lord,” he said, “if you are with God, as I believe, pray to him for me and restore the light of my eyes.”

After saying this, he was immediately given sight. Several sick people, too, came to his tomb and were restored to health. His tomb itself also gave off a fragrance as though it were filled with many spices. Thus God deemed him worthy of honor after death, because, while alive, for love of God, he had despised the inheritance of his earthly parents.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### Of the three monasteries which Romuald built, and of his journey to Hungary

Meanwhile Romuald, hearing that the most blessed man Boniface had suffered martyrdom, was inflamed with an immense desire to shed his blood for Christ and at once resolved to go to Hungary.

[Note: Jerome of Prague, in The Life of St. Romuald, chapter 8, section 49, adds: “Hearing that his disciples Adalbert and Boniface had been crowned with glorious martyrdom, he himself was inflamed with an immense desire for martyrdom,” and so forth.]

While he persisted in this intention, however, he established three monasteries within a short time: one in the valley of Castro, where his most holy body is now buried; another near the river Isino; and a third near the town of Asculum.

[Note: That is, the monastery of St. Helen, near the river Aesis, of which only the church now remains, under the jurisdiction of a commendatory abbot. Aesis is a river in the territory of Camerino, formerly the boundary between Umbria and Picenum; through the confusion of local speech it is called il Fiumesino by the inhabitants. How famous this monastery was in ancient times is made perfectly clear by a diploma issued at the Lateran in 1199, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, by Pope Innocent III to Nicholas, abbot of this Camaldolese monastery, and to his successors. Besides confirming numerous possessions, the document also confirmed its rights over more than forty churches and five castles. Moreover, if Jacobilli is to be believed, St. Romuald first established nuns there. See volume II, page 27, of the Saints of Umbria.]

[Note: Formerly called Esculum, but now Asculum, commonly Ascoli, an episcopal city in the province of Picenum. No one has yet determined with sufficient certainty what kind of monastery this was.]

Then, having received permission from the apostolic see, and having had two of his disciples consecrated archbishops,

[Note: Evidently Gregory and Ingelbert, as above.]

he set out with twenty-four brothers. For such an ardor to die for Christ burned in them all that it was difficult for the holy man to go on such an undertaking with only a few. As they traveled and had already reached the borders of Pannonia, Romuald was suddenly seized by illness and could go no farther. Whenever he considered turning back, he promptly recovered from his sickness. But if he tried to go farther, his entire face immediately swelled up, and, as his stomach grew weak, he could no longer retain food.

He summoned the brothers and said to them:

“I perceive that it is in no way the judgment of the divine will that I proceed farther. Nevertheless, since I do not fail to recognize the desire of your intention, I compel none of you to turn back. Many before us have striven through vows and efforts to reach the summit of martyrdom, but because divine providence judged otherwise, they were forced to remain in their own station. Although I do not doubt that martyrdom will be lacking to all of you, let each person’s own judgment determine who wishes to go on and who wishes to return with me.”

Thus, when fifteen went on into Hungary and two had already been left elsewhere, scarcely seven disciples remained with their master. Some of those who continued were flogged, sold, or—more numerous—entered the Lord’s service; yet, as the holy man had foretold, they did not attain martyrdom.

Romuald then returned to the monastery he had built in the region of the Old City, after converting a certain most noble man, a kinsman of Duke Adhelberon, who later became a monk and remained in holy religious life until his death, and other Germans.

It should therefore be noted that the holy man could not have been deceived through mere fickleness, as though he had acted frivolously. In accordance with his own intention, he did indeed suffer martyrdom; but in accordance with the divine plan, he was sent for the salvation of those whom he converted.

In the monastery mentioned above he endured many scandalous persecutions. He wanted the abbot, as a true monk, to love the lowest place, not handle secular matters out of desire, not spend the monastery’s goods for empty glory, and provide what was necessary for the brothers’ use. While the abbot ignored all these things with deaf ears, Romuald, leaving the place with his disciples, lived not far from Castro on the estate of Rainerius, who later became margrave of Tuscany.

[Note: That is, on his estate, as Damian says in chapter 35 of this Life: “They offer all the estates of their property.” At times virtutes meant rights and privileges; at other times, the relics of saints, and so forth. See Du Cange’s Glossary, second edition.]

## CHAPTER XL  
### Of Margrave Rainerius

This Rainerius had repudiated his wife on account of their kinship and had married the wife of his kinsman, whom he himself had killed, though somewhat unwillingly, when the man was pursuing him.

[Note: Damian sent Letter 17 of Book VII to Rainerius, margrave of Tuscany, who had married Countess Gilla, and the following letter, Letter 18, to Gilla herself. In this chapter, however, the reference should probably be to Rainerius’s father, who had also been margrave and duke of Etruria and who, according to Cosmas de Arena, page 155, had Walderada as his wife.]

For this reason Romuald, so as not to become a participant in his crime, refused to remain on his estate without payment. Instead, he set aside one gold coin for water and another for wood. Although Rainerius completely rejected these payments, preferring to give his own things rather than receive anything from the holy man, he finally agreed, lest Romuald depart.

When he already held dominion, Rainerius used to say: “Neither the emperor nor any other mortal can instill in me as much fear as the sight of Romuald terrifies me. In his presence I neither know what to say nor find any excuses with which I can defend myself.”

Indeed, the holy man had received this grace from God: whenever sinners, especially the powerful of this world, came into his presence, they immediately trembled and feared as though before the majesty of God. The Holy Spirit, who dwelt within his heart, divinely inspired this terror in the unjust.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads intentabat, “threatened” or “imposed.”]

## CHAPTER XLI  
### Of the abbot of Classe who tried to strangle Romuald

At that time the venerable man built a monastery not far from the fortress of Massiliano.

[Note: Peter de Natalibus gives Castrum Maximianum, while some editions have Maxiliano and Mariliano.]

On one occasion he heard that a certain Venetian had seized the abbacy of Classe by purchasing it through the Simoniacal heresy and was also sinning wickedly against his own body. The soldier of Christ hastened there at once and tried in various ways to purge the monastery of him.

But the reprobate man, while fearing to lose the abbacy, did not fear to commit murder. In the dead of night, while Romuald was resting safely in bed, he secretly attacked him and began to squeeze his throat with his wicked fingers, attempting to suffocate him cruelly. But while the holy man, his breath not yet completely cut off, was rasping as he struggled to breathe, Ingelbert was immediately awakened by his master’s gasps, seized a log from the smoldering fire, and drove the devil’s servant away from his attempt at that unspeakable crime.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### Of his departure and return again from Parentium

After this Romuald sailed once more to Parentium, but the pontiff of the Apostolic See and the Roman citizens sent an embassy to him to return. They promised that, if he came back, they would carry out all his commands; otherwise, they threatened him with a sentence of excommunication. In this way Italy, his foster-mother, succeeded in recovering her Romuald.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### Of the miracle performed for a robber on Mount Petrano

At that time he remained for some while in the passes of the Callian Mountains.

[Note: The Apennine Mountains near Cagli, a city of no small distinction in Umbria, called Callium in Latin and Cagli in Italian.]

Then he moved to Mount Petrano, not far from the monastery of St. Vincent, which is situated near the river Candilianus.

[Note: This is the same place as Petra Pertussa, or Pertusa, as it is written in Peter Damian’s Life, chapter 5. Some also call it Petralata; today it is commonly called Petrolata. Some report that St. Romuald lived on that mountain, formerly called Petrano, but now called by the inhabitants of the region il monte de’ Cavalli. It is in the same area where the church of St. Nicholas stands above the Boasi River; that church is united to the priory of Secchiano, while another church of St. Bartholomew above the Burano River is attached to the provostship of the Church of Cagli.]

Wherever the holy man went, he always bore fruit, always increased the gain of souls more and more, and drew people away from the world. As though entirely transformed into fire, he kindled human hearts with the desire for heaven.

At that time, wishing to find a place suitable for establishing a desert, he ordered a certain priest, when returning to his own house, to bring food for himself and for those accompanying him. Then, carefully exploring the mountain, he finally found a certain monk living near a small basilica. He immediately demanded that the monk go with him and show him where water could be found.

The monk refused, saying that he could not leave his house without a guard, because he feared an attack by lurking robbers. Romuald promised to make full restitution if anything of the sort occurred. Thus, having made himself responsible for another person’s loss, he took the monk with him.

While they were searching for a place, behold, the priest, bringing the meal as he had been ordered, found a thief already breaking into the house. He seized him, kept him under guard until Romuald returned, and then handed him over. When Romuald found him, he first sought to rebuke him with the compassionate severity of his words; then, gently admonishing him, he allowed him to return home unharmed.

Thus, indeed, divine providence preserved unharmed what had been left in the custody of the absent Romuald.

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### Another miracle concerning other robbers

Again, while he was building cells in the same region—for some baggage had been placed some distance away beneath a rock—the venerable man suddenly sent a certain brother there with something like an urgent shove, ordering him to hurry with the greatest anxiety.

When the brother arrived, he found thieves already attempting to carry the things away, but discovered that nothing of what had been deposited was yet missing. From this it is rightly inferred that the blessed man sent the brother with such urgency under the impulse of divine revelation, at precisely the moment when the thieves happened to reach the unguarded property.

## CHAPTER XLV  
### Why and how Romuald was expelled from the Valley of Castro

After this Romuald returned to the monastery of the Valley of Castro and immediately urged the abbot to govern the others in such a way that he did not neglect himself. He also wanted him not to abandon altogether, because of his administration, the cell he had used, but to live there spiritually and visit the brothers only on the principal feast days, for the sake of admonition.

That manner of life among abbots, which we see, was so hateful to the blessed man that he would have rejoiced no less if he could have torn an abbacy from anyone’s hands than if he had been given the opportunity to summon any powerful secular person to the order of holy religious life.

But, as Solomon says, “As vinegar upon nitre, so is one who sings songs to a perverse heart” (Proverbs 25), this man, made worse in his evil by the preaching of the venerable man, immediately went to the countesses, the ladies of the place,

[Note: The Valley of Castro is a place in the territory of Camerino; it is easy to conclude that the ladies of that place were the countesses of Camerino.]

and sacrilegiously suggested that they order the wood intended for the construction of Romuald’s cell to be cut into small pieces. In this way the tall cedar of paradise was driven out from the forests of earthly men.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
### Of the miracle he performed at Aqua-bella by healing a priest

From there he proceeded and decided to remain not far from Mount Apennine, at a place called Aqua-bella.

[Note: Aqua-bella is the same place as Vallis Umbrosa, in the diocese of Fiesole. There St. John Gualbert built a very famous monastery after his departure from Camaldoli; it gave its name to the congregation of Vallombrosa of the Order of St. Benedict.]

While certain secular people were building dwellings there with his disciples, Romuald was no longer able to work because of his advanced age and remained alone to guard the lodging. A certain priest, suffering intolerable pain in his teeth, unwillingly left the building work and, having obtained permission from the brothers to return home, began to depart with miserable cries.

Since his route of return took him past Romuald, Romuald asked him why he was leaving. The priest immediately explained the nature of his suffering. Romuald touched with his finger the place where the priest was in pain and said to him:

“Put a glowing awl into a reed, so that it does not injure the lip, and place it here; the pain will flee.”

The priest had scarcely gone farther than the space of one iugerum when, at once, with all pain gone, he returned healthy and unharmed to the work he had abandoned. He cried out in a loud voice:

“We give thanks to you, almighty God, who have deigned to illumine our region with the splendor of so great a star. Truly an angel of God, truly a holy prophet, and a great light hidden from the world has appeared in our land.”

Shouting these and many other praises to God, he was scarcely compelled to be silent by the disciples of the blessed man. For if such words reached Romuald’s ears on any occasion, they would strike his heart with the most severe indignation.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### Another miracle concerning the beech tree cut down near his cell

At another time, while he was staying in a very beautiful and excellent desert called Camaldoli, which he himself had built, he was seated in his cell and ordered a large beech tree standing near his cell to be cut down.

[Note: Some editions read “a very beautiful and splendid place, called Camaldoli.” In the Vatican manuscript, as also in the copy edited by Mabillon in the Acts of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict, some words are missing, and the passage reads only: “At another time he ordered a certain large beech tree, which stood near his cell, to be cut down.”]

[Note: Some editions read “called Camaldoli,” as though it meant the field of Maldulus, after a certain Maldulus, lord of the place. But it was also called the pleasant field at that time, as appears in the bulls of Alexander II, issued in 1072, and of Gregory VII, issued in 1074, and elsewhere. From this desert, situated among the Apennine Mountains in the diocese of Arezzo, the Camaldolese Benedictine congregation took its name. Among all the deserts and monasteries founded by St. Romuald or brought by him back to regular discipline, it has always been and remains the most distinguished.]

The beech was so inclined toward and overhanging the cell that, according to human judgment, if it fell, it would unquestionably bury the entire building at once. The workers wanted to carry out his orders but feared the tree’s collapse; he insisted that they should not be afraid.

When, therefore, they had driven axes into it on every side and were already reaching the tree’s very heart, while the tree threatened to fall upon the holy man with an unmistakable force, everyone began to plead and urge him loudly that, if he would abandon the cell, he should at least leave it and save himself.

He did not yield at all to their cries but firmly ordered them to complete what they had begun without delay, making the sign of the cross against the tree.

[Note: The words “making the sign of the cross against it” are absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

At last the beech fell with a tremendous crash, but by divine power it was thrown in the opposite direction, so that, to everyone’s amazement, the cell remained completely unharmed. All, astonished at so great a miracle, raised joyful voices to heaven and gave immense thanks to God.

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
### Of the holm oak that fell upon a peasant without injuring him

But why should we speak of the divine protection shown toward the venerable man, when we know that others, too, were often rescued from great dangers through his presence? It is enough to mention one of them here, so that the prudent reader may recognize that there were many more.

On one occasion he was staying with the workers and having a holm oak of enormous size cut down on Mount Petrano. The tree hung over the steep slope of the mountain and leaned toward the depths below. A certain peasant was standing somewhat farther down.

When the cut tree fell heavily and rolled headlong down the mountain slope, it suddenly encountered the peasant and began to roll him toward the lower ground with a violent force. Everyone immediately cried out in grief and supposed that the man was not merely dead but that his entire body had been torn to pieces.

But, wonderful power of God! He was soon found so healthy and unharmed that it was as though not a tree but a leaf of the tree had fallen upon him. From this it may rightly be understood how much weight the holy man’s merit had before God, in whose sight the massive weight of the tree was unable to retain its weight.

## CHAPTER XLIX  
### Of the insult he suffered from his disciples at Sytria

Later, when Romuald left the Apennines,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “when he left.”]

he climbed Mount Sytria to live there.

[Note: Mount Sytria is not far from the hermitage of Avellana, where a famous monastery of St. Mary formerly stood. Today only a few traces of it can be seen, for it is held by a commendatory abbot.]

Great care must be taken lest anyone, hearing that the holy man changed so many places, attribute the burden of a pious work to the fault of fickleness. The undisputed reason for these changes was that, wherever the venerable man lived, an almost innumerable crowd of people gathered to him. Reason therefore required that, whenever he saw one place filled with inhabitants, he should appoint a prior there and hurry on to fill another place.

At Sytria he suffered insults and scandals beyond our ability to set forth from his disciples. We shall relate one of them and pass over the rest for the sake of brevity.

He had a certain disciple named Romanus, noble by birth but utterly degenerate in conduct. The holy man rebuked him not only in words for the uncleanness of his flesh but often also restrained him with severe beatings. This diabolical man dared to turn the title of his own offense against Romuald and shamelessly bark with a sacrilegious mouth against the temple of the Holy Spirit, claiming that the holy man had sinned together with him in the same pollution.

Immediately all the disciples became angry and hostile toward him. Some cried that the impious old man ought to be hanged; others judged that he deserved to be burned together with the cell itself.

This was exceedingly astonishing, especially since spiritual men could have believed such a monstrous crime of an extremely old man, more than a hundred years of age.

[Note: This is the expanded reading throughout the Vatican manuscript and everywhere else. I therefore do not know by what argument those who reduce Romuald’s life to only seventy years reject this clear statement of Damian concerning the saint’s age.]

Even if he had possessed the will, nature itself, his cold blood, and the dryness of his emaciated body would have made the act utterly impossible. But it must undoubtedly be believed that, for the sake of increasing the holy man’s merit, this scourge of such grave adversity came upon him from heaven.

For he himself asserted that he had truly recognized this in the desert from which he had recently departed and that he had come eagerly to undergo this disgraceful reproach.

That reprobate Sarabaita who had brought the accusation against the holy man later acquired the bishopric of Nocera through the Simoniacal heresy and occupied it for two years.

[Note: A class of monks who are known to lie to God through their tonsure, as St. Benedict says in chapter 1 of his Rule, and so forth. See also our Damian, Letter 9 of Book V.]

[Note: Nocera is a city of Umbria called Nocera Camellaria, to distinguish it from the other Nocera, called Nocera dei Pagani, situated in the province of Campania.]

In the first year, because of his merits, he saw a church set on fire together with its books, bells, and other sacred ornaments; in the second, by a divine sentence striking him, he miserably lost both his dignity and his life.

## CHAPTER L  
### Of the divine command given to Romuald to celebrate Mass and expound the Psalms

[Col. 0995D]

The disciples therefore imposed a penance upon the holy man as though he had committed the alleged crime and completely took away his permission to celebrate the sacred mysteries. He willingly accepted this judgment, observed the penance as though he really were guilty of the crime, and for nearly six months did not presume to approach the most holy altar.

At last, as he later reported to those same disciples, he was divinely commanded that, if he feared losing divine grace, he should entirely set aside his undiscerning simplicity and confidently celebrate the solemnities of the Mass.

The next day, when he began to offer the sacrifice and had reached the second secret prayer of the Mass, he was carried into ecstasy and remained silent for so long that all who were present were astonished.

Later, when asked why he had taken so much longer than usual in offering the sacrifice, he replied:

“I was carried up into heaven and presented before God, and immediately I was commanded by a divine voice to expound the Psalms according to the understanding God had infused into me, and to commit them in order to written pages according to the measure of my intellect.

“But I, overcome by immense and indescribable terror, could answer nothing except: ‘Let it be done, let it be done.’”

Afterward the holy man lucidly expounded the entire Psalter and several of the songs of the prophets. Although he violated the rules of grammar, he everywhere preserved a sound meaning.

[Note: This venerable codex, written by Blessed Romuald himself, is still kept in the Camaldolese treasury. See Mabillon, Italian Journey.]

## 471 CHAPTER LI  
### Of Romuald’s soul, which was carried before God white as snow

The disciples once asked him:

“Master, of what age does the soul appear to be, or in what form is it presented for judgment?”

He replied:

“I know a man in Christ whose soul was carried before God, radiant like snow, in human form but of the stature of full maturity.”

When they asked again who this man was, he refused, in indignation and embarrassment, to tell them. The disciples immediately reported the matter to one another as it truly was, and by clear disclosure recognized that he himself was the man.

## CHAPTER LII  
### Of the excessive strictness of the life he maintained at Sytria

At Sytria the venerable man remained enclosed for nearly seven years and inviolably maintained continuous silence. Nevertheless, though his tongue was silent and his life preached, scarcely anywhere could he have labored so greatly, either in converting people or among those flocking to him for repentance.

Although his old age was already advancing, he lived with excessive strictness, even at a time when perfect men themselves usually live more leniently and relax something of the rigor of their commitment.

For the length of an entire Lent he consumed nothing at all, whether food or drink, except a thin broth made from a little flour and a few herbs; he lived on this in imitation of Hilarion. For five weeks, eating nothing else, he restricted himself to a small quantity of soaked chickpeas.

Thus, through many other forms of life, Romuald continually tested what his strength could accomplish, exercising himself in one practice after another.

[Note: Read our Peter’s Opusculum XV, chapter 16.]

As a disciplined soldier of Christ, he always sought to prepare himself for a new contest; and whenever he seemed about to fall,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “whenever he seemed to be hard-pressed.”]

he immediately applied mercy and raised up his faltering little body.

At times he wore two or even three hair shirts because of the body’s growing importunity. He never allowed them to be washed but would throw them into the rain and customarily change them after thirty days.

He never permitted a razor to touch his head. Instead, very rarely, he used tongs to cut the excess hair of his head and beard himself.

If at any time the vice of gluttony provoked him through some more appetizing food, he immediately ordered it to be carefully prepared, placed it before his mouth and nostrils, and, merely savoring its odor, said:

“O gluttony, gluttony, how sweet and pleasant this food would now taste to you! But woe to you! You will never taste it.”

Then he sent it untouched back to the storeroom.

## 472 CHAPTER LIII  
### Of the miracle by which he healed Gregory by blowing upon him
But although the holy man maintained such austerity toward himself, he nevertheless always displayed a cheerful expression and a serene face. For a certain brother named Gregory once complained that he was suffering from a very severe headache. When he came with intense lamentation to the blessed man’s cell, where other brothers were also present, as soon as the venerable man saw him, he unequivocally attributed the pain not to an imbalance of humors but to the plots of the ancient enemy. Then, as though mocking him, he blew through the cell’s window upon his forehead, with the lively expression he always wore, and signaled that all the others present should do likewise. Once this had been done, Gregory was so completely healed that he felt no trace of pain remaining in his head. I think that the holy man wished to do this because, through the Holy Spirit who presided in his heart, he believed that the most wicked enemy, the instigator of the pain, had to be driven away. To avoid personal praise, he pretended that it was a game and sought companions. For our Redeemer too is read to have breathed upon the apostles when he is said to have given them the Holy Spirit (John 20).

### CHAPTER LIV. On the madman whom he cured with a kiss

A certain man suffered from madness of the head, so that, having lost the power of reason, he had no understanding whatever of what he was doing or saying. Romuald did nothing for him except offer him a kiss, and immediately restored him to his former soundness. By making peace with the disturbed man, he brought him back to peace of mind.

Later, the man who had been cured related the matter, saying: “When I was deemed worthy to touch the holy lips of the blessed man, I immediately felt a breath issue from his mouth like a powerful breeze. It passed over my entire face and finally over the crown of my head, and at once drove away all the heat of my fevered brain.”

### CHAPTER LV. Likewise, on Gregory, whom cold water freed from a serious illness

[Col. 0998A]

At another time, the same Gregory mentioned above endured such a foul and festering itch on his legs that he already believed so severe a swelling to be arising from elephantiasis.

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Elephantia, or elephantiasis, is a kind of leprosy; see Celsus and others. [Col. 0998D]]

Romuald prescribed for him this particular kind of treatment: namely, that he should pour cold water over his legs for three days, promising that in this way he would recover his former health. Gregory nevertheless undertook to fulfill the command, evidently more from the necessity of obedience than from confidence in recovering his health. It was a remarkable event, attributable solely to divine power: immediately the swelling of his shins subsided, all the infection dried up, and, with every trace of illness entirely removed, the brother was restored to complete health. It may therefore reasonably be believed that Romuald ordered his disciple to pour water over his swollen legs three times by the same Spirit through whom Elisha commanded Naaman the leper to wash seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5).

### CHAPTER LVI. On the disciple whom he recognized by the spirit while going to Rome, and on the man who, disparaging him, broke out of his enclosure

Certain carnal men, however, did not fear maliciously to criticize him and to attribute his words or deeds to the fault of frivolity. One of his disciples lived in a distant desert. At one point, yielding to the needs of his relatives, he finally consented—though apparently unwillingly—to go to Rome during Lent for their benefit. The holy man immediately recognized this through the spirit and, as though indignant, wrote to a brother who was standing nearby that this good man had presumed to go to Rome on such business. The brother wondered how his master could know this, since no one had come from elsewhere to speak with him. He carefully investigated the matter and confirmed that it was exactly as the venerable man had said.

He went to another of his fellow disciples, namely Ingelbert, who was living enclosed, and emphatically affirmed both that the master had said this and that he unquestionably possessed the spirit of prophecy. Ingelbert, however, detesting and utterly denying the claim, rebuked the brother and bound himself by an imprecation, saying: “If he said this through the spirit of prophecy, and not rather through the devil, may almighty God not permit me to remain in this enclosure.”

What he said was done. For scarcely a few days had passed when Ingelbert broke out of his enclosure and departed without the master’s permission; and, as the story goes, he never again saw him in this life.

### CHAPTER LVII. On Gaudentius, Berard, and a monk who was healed

Another brother, named Gaudentius, the father—that is, the abbot—of this monastery of Saint Vincent,

[Note: [Col. 0998D] The monastery of Saint Vincent of Petra Pertusa is meant here; it was also mentioned above, in chapter 43. Since the blessed writer adds “of this monastery,” although he had not mentioned it immediately beforehand, the demonstrative expression plainly indicates that this was the very monastery in which he was then writing and living. John, the author of Damian’s Life, reports that Damian was sent to this monastery twice. Those who think that “of this” belongs with the word “abbot,” rather than with “monastery,” must surely believe that Damian addressed this history of Romuald to the monks of Saint Vincent—a view entirely without foundation. Peter Damian mentions this monastery in Letter 32 of Book IV and again in Letter 15 of Book VII. It lies midway along the road between Cagli and Fossombrone, and the canons of Urbino enjoy its revenues. [Col. 0999D]]

after embracing the religious life with great fervor, afterward lived in God’s service with still more ardent devotion. At one point he asked the blessed Romuald for permission to give up all cooked food and, content with bread and water, to live also on fruit or raw vegetables. After obtaining this permission and remaining indefatigably committed to the same resolve, another brother, Tedaldus, indiscreetly sympathizing with his weakness, tried to approach the master and suggested that the brother could not carry so heavy a burden and that his obstinacy ought by all means to be broken.

Romuald, being a man of simple disposition, accepted Tedaldus’s words and withdrew from Gaudentius the permission to live in this manner. Gaudentius took this very badly and would no longer tolerate living with Tedaldus in the desert where Romuald had placed them. Instead, he submitted himself to Ingelbert, who had been separated from Romuald, and received from him approval for the way of life described above.

Not long afterward Gaudentius died, and he was buried in the cemetery of Saint Vincent beside the body of the venerable Berard, who had likewise been a disciple of Romuald. Because Gaudentius had ended his life in the transgression of disobedience, Romuald completely forbade prayers to be offered for him.

Some time later, a monk of that monastery, while celebrating the morning office with the other brothers, suddenly began to feel such a sharp pain in his teeth that he could no longer stand in the choir to chant. He immediately went out, threw himself lamenting upon the tomb of Berard and Gaudentius, and, hoping to receive healing through them, placed himself between the two.

[Note: [Col. 1000D] The words “and, hoping to receive healing through them, placed himself between the two” are absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

As he lay there praying for some time, sleep soon overcame him. At once he saw Berard, splendidly adorned in priestly vestments, standing before the altar and celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, holding in his hands a book written in golden letters. But he saw Gaudentius mourning, sad, and standing far behind Berard with downcast face; like an excommunicated man, he did not dare approach the sacred mysteries.

Gaudentius immediately spoke to him, saying: “Do you see, brother, that wondrously gilded book of Berard’s? I too would now have one exactly like it, unless the monk Tedaldus—alas, alas!—had taken it from me.”

The brother immediately awoke and rose healthy and unharmed, all pain having disappeared. He then joyfully related his vision in order to the brothers. When Romuald heard it, he immediately ordered the brothers to show Gaudentius fraternal charity and to pray for him more earnestly.

It is therefore reasonably concluded that the man who, deprived of Romuald’s fellowship, lost the book he had deserved, once restored to Romuald’s favor and assisted by prayers, deserved to recover that same book. What Tedaldus had taken from him only through Romuald, Romuald now, by praying for him together with all the brothers, restored.

### CHAPTER LVIII. On the disciple beaten by demons in Romuald’s bed

Once, when the venerable man was preparing to set out on a journey for a necessary purpose, he entrusted his cell to one of his disciples and ordered him to remain there until his return. But the rash man, failing to show his master the reverence due to him, did not hesitate boldly to lie down in his bed.

Behold, during that very night, evil spirits violently attacked him, battered him with the severest blows, and, throwing him out of the bed, left him almost half dead. He deservedly suffered such arrogant avengers of his offense, since he had sinned against such a man after setting humility aside; and because he had not shown reverence to his pious master, he experienced discipline at harsh and impious hands.

Later, when the venerable man was again about to travel, he left another disciple in the same cell. When the disciple said to him, “Master, I will not lie in your bed, because I fear that what happened to the other man might happen to me as well,” he replied: “My son, lie down and sleep without fear. The other man fell into the hands of the enemy because he had not obtained permission to use my insignificance in this way. You, however, having received my consent, place your hope in God and rest without fear.”

He lay there as he had been ordered and suffered no misfortune whatever.

### CHAPTER LIX. On the woman who was driven mad and healed by Romuald’s blessing

A certain secular man named Arduinus gave himself to Romuald to receive the habit of holy religious life. He then returned home in order to arrange his affairs. When his wife saw him arriving, inflamed, as women are, with fury, she cried out against him, saying: “So, good man, you have come from that heretic and ancient seducer, and now you are abandoning me, poor woman, deprived of every human comfort?”

Having said this, she immediately became insane and began to rage and convulse as though she were plainly being tormented by a demon.

The holy man had this custom: whenever he sent brothers on a journey, he gave them a blessing—whether bread, an apple, or something else. His disciples, having often experienced the effect, firmly believed that if they gave some sick person anything touched by the master’s blessing, they would restore him unharmed to health. Many sick people were also frequently restored through the water in which he washed his hands. This had to be done with the greatest caution, lest the holy man discover it and fall into profound sadness.

Since the woman had already been miserably afflicted for a long time, some brothers who were present gave her a piece of the blessed bread they had received from the master. After the woman had eaten it, her mind was immediately calmed, and she was completely freed from the fury of insanity. She promptly gave thanks to almighty God and to his servant Romuald for her restored health, and no longer refused her husband permission to enter the religious life.

### CHAPTER LX. On the demoniac whom he cured

At another time a demoniac boy was brought to the blessed man. He did nothing for him except give him a piece of bread as a blessing. As soon as the boy had been refreshed by it, he was immediately freed from the demon. Rightly indeed: once Romuald’s blessing had entered the body under evil possession, the malign spirit immediately departed, scorched by it.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] “Scorched,” that is, burned; see Du Cange’s Glossary.]

### CHAPTER LXI. On the devil who threatened Romuald with death and broke the wall of his cell

[Col. 1001C]

The devil, however, could never cease attacking the holy man. Since he could accomplish nothing against him by hidden fraud, he did not cease visibly displaying the poison of his malice. Once, while the venerable man was standing in his cell, behold, the evil spirit—truly hideous, hairy, and horrible—began to inspire the holy man with immense terror. In an excessive frenzy he threatened and menaced him with death.

While Romuald, undaunted, sought help from heaven and confidently cried out for Christ to come to his aid, the ancient enemy fled. But he struck the wall of the cell with such a burst of furious rage that he split a heavy beech plank to a length of one cubit or more.

Thus he plainly showed in the dwelling how great a fire of cruelty had blazed against its inhabitant, and in a manner left written on the wall what he carried hidden in his mind.

### CHAPTER LXII. Likewise, on the devil who tried to drown Romuald by frightening his horse

On another occasion, while the venerable man was riding with his disciples, behold, the evil spirit, assuming the shape of a red dog, rushed upon them with great force and so frightened the horse on which the holy man was riding that he nearly fell into the water.

When the disciples were asked whether they had seen it, they acknowledged that they had seen the horse shying in terror, but testified that nothing of the sort had appeared to them. He replied: “That wretched being, who was once known to have been a glorious angel, now does not hesitate to display himself in the form of an unclean dog.”

### CHAPTER LXIII. Likewise, on the devil who beat a cask when discord arose among Romuald’s disciples

Again, at another time, when he had decided to build the monastery of the Handmaids of God at Vallebona, discord immediately arose among the holy man’s disciples. Some did not want the monastery built, while others vigorously insisted that it should be.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] The location of this monastery is still unknown. A certain Martin, abbot of Vallisbona, who preached after Saint Ambrose of Camaldoli at the Council of Ferrara in 1438, on 8 January, is mentioned in the Acts of the Council of Florence edited by Horatius Justinianus, Part I, no. 20. [Col. 1002D]]

While both opposing parties argued before the venerable man, each using different claims, the devil began incessantly to beat a cask before the little door of the cell, as though with a mallet. Through the echoing forest he could be heard booming with repeated blows.

Then, when everyone had unanimously agreed that the monastery should be built, behold, the evil spirit, heard by all, continued to howl and weep and to utter mournful cries. Finally, when the brothers, now divided, were each returning to his own lodging, the ancient enemy pursued them with such a storm and whirlwind, stirring up, as it were, every kind of wind, that he seemed intent on uprooting the entire forest from its foundations.

One of the brothers rebuked him, saying: “I command you in the name of the Holy Trinity, unclean spirit, to stop following us.” And so he was driven away.

Rightly, then, the author of discord, once peace had been established, was compelled to burst into tears. Earlier he had been heard rejoicing as the quarrel grew; now, having tried to draw out the circular band of an empty vessel and scatter the parts by which it had been held together, he departed sadly when the disciples had been bound together in the structure of peace and charity.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] The better explanation of this word seems to be the one given by Du Cange under the word *veges*: a wine cask, which the devil continuously beat or threw down before the little door of the cell.]

### CHAPTER LXIV. On the strict life then led in Sytria

Such was the life then led in Sytria

[Note: [Col. 1002D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “the life then led in Sytria.”]

that, by the likeness not only of its name but also of its practice, it seemed once again to be another Nitria. Everyone walked barefoot; everyone was unkempt, pale, and content with the utmost austerity in all things. Some, shut in behind barred doors, appeared so dead to the world, as though already placed in a tomb.

No one there knew wine, even if he suffered from the gravest illness. But why am I speaking of the monks, when even their servants—the monks’ own herdsmen—fasted, observed silence, disciplined one another, and demanded penance for any idle words?

[Note: [Col. 1002D] In the same manuscript: “for any idle words.”]

O golden age of Romuald! Although it knew nothing of the torments inflicted by persecutors, it was nevertheless not without voluntary martyrdom. A golden age, I say, which among the wild beasts of the mountains and forests nourished so many citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

When the brothers had become so numerous that they could scarcely all live there, Romuald built a monastery there and appointed an abbot; then, preserving unbroken silence, he withdrew to Bifurcum to live. There, because he wished the abbot to live spiritually and to maintain a life of uprightness,

[Note: [Col. 1003D] The same place reads: “the way of uprightness.”]

he suffered much injury from his persecution.

### CHAPTER LXV. On Romuald’s prophecy and his conversation with King Henry

Meanwhile the emperor Henry, coming from the transalpine regions into Italy,

[Note: [Col. 1003D] Baronius assigns Henry’s arrival in Italy to the year 1022.]

sent a petitionary embassy to the blessed man, asking him to deign to come to him and promising that he would do whatever Romuald commanded if only he would not refuse him an interview.

Since the venerable man absolutely refused to break his silence, all the disciples began unanimously to beg him, saying: “Master, you see that we who follow you have now become so numerous that we cannot suitably live here. Go, then, if it pleases you, and ask the emperor for a great monastery, and establish there the multitude who follow you.”

To them the holy man confidently wrote—I do not know whether he had already received a revelation or whether this came from a sudden inspiration of God: “Know that you will have the monastery of Mount Amiata as a gift from the king. Consider only whom you ought to appoint abbot there.”

He therefore went to the king without breaking his silence. The king immediately rose to greet him and, with great affection of heart, burst out with these words: “Would that my soul were in your body!” The king then humbly begged him to speak, but could not obtain this favor that day.

The next day, when Romuald came to the palace, behold, a crowd of Germans rushed eagerly from every side. They humbly bowed their heads in greeting, and anxiously plucked hairs from the fur garment he wore, carefully storing them to carry back to their homeland as sacred relics.

This so overwhelmed the venerable man with grief that, had his disciples not restrained him, he would have immediately returned to his cell. He entered the king’s presence and spoke at length about restoring the rights of the churches, the violence of the powerful, and the oppression of the poor. After much else, he asked the king for one monastery for his disciples.

The king then gave him the monastery of Mount Amiata and expelled its abbot, since he was subject to many vices.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] The monastery meant here seems not to be the celebrated monastery of Saint Savior, now inhabited by Cistercian monks, but another one called Saint Peter at Vivo, in the Sienese territory and situated in the region of Mount Amiata. Its deed of donation, by which Saint Henry the Emperor bestowed it upon Saint Romuald in 1004, is mentioned in the notes appended to the treatise on the *Pandects*, p. 228, Class V, by Guido Grandi, abbot of Camaldoli. [Col. 1004D]]

How many adversities the holy man endured there—not only from the man who had been expelled but also from the man whom he himself had appointed abbot from among his disciples—we cannot recount, even if eloquence were available to us. But one example will suffice to show how God assisted him in everything, so that any prudent person may understand what happened in the other matters as well.

### CHAPTER LXVI. On the monk whom the devil began to strangle, but whom Romuald rescued

A certain monk, inflamed with mad fury against him, secretly sharpened a *pilum* and, hiding it away, began to await a suitable opportunity to kill the holy man.

[Note: [Col. 1004D] A *pilum* is a type of weapon with a shaft bearing a pointed iron head of triangular shape, according to Vegetius. In the second edition of Du Cange’s Glossary, however, an example is given for a meaning equivalent to a small lance, which could more easily be used secretly.]

One night, while he lay resting, overcome by sleep, behold, an evil spirit violently attacked him. Throwing a twisted cord around his neck,

[Note: [Col. 1004D] That is, a rope.]

it tried with such ferocity to tighten his throat that he was already being forced to breathe his last.

Then, the monk, already at the point of death, begged Romuald to come to his aid. As it seemed to the monk, Romuald immediately rushed up and snatched him from the hands of the wicked enemy.

When he awoke, he hurried to prostrate himself at the feet of the venerable man and begged him to witness the injury to his neck. He did not hesitate to confess the crime of his malice. Finally, he gave thanks for the life that had been preserved for him and accepted penance for so great a fault.

Thus the man who had plotted to take Romuald’s life deserved, through that same most holy man, to preserve his own; and he who had tried to inflict death upon Romuald escaped through him the danger of his own death.

[Note: [Col. 1004D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “who had plotted.”]

### CHAPTER LXVII. On Romuald, who, surrounded by waters, learned from heaven that food was to be brought to him

When the Saint was in charge of a monastery, he had the custom of coming daily to the common table with the brothers—unless he was fasting—and eating one cooked dish; afterward, occupied with reading or with whatever was happening among the individual brothers, he would taste nothing else.

[Note: [Col. 1004D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “the holy man.”]

During Lent, unless unavoidable necessity compelled him, he remained continually in his cell.

When the most blessed man was governing the monastery mentioned above, and the Lenten fast was already approaching, he searched with his disciples through the neighboring mountain regions for a place where he could establish a hermitage. As they prolonged their search for a long time, they were suddenly enclosed by waters flowing all around them, so that they could neither return nor could anyone from the monastery cross over to them in any way.

They lived on a small quantity of chestnuts that they had brought with them. When Sunday arrived and no other hope of food remained, the brothers began to peel the few chestnuts left and, already somewhat doubtful, to prepare what would in a sense be their final meal.

Romuald, however, always cheerful in appearance, confidently said that unless God sent him bread through someone, he would not eat anything that day. The disciples wondered among themselves on what basis he could make such a claim, yet they were certain that their master could not rashly make a vow. They therefore began confidently to await food appropriate to so great a solemnity.

As the sixth hour of the day was approaching, behold, three men arrived, laden with bread, wine, and other foods. They said that they had come from distant regions after much toil.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] In the same place: “had come to them.”]

Then all, filled with spiritual joy, blessed God, and took the food together. They recognized without doubt that the blessed man had learned through revelation from heaven that it was coming.

### CHAPTER LXVIII. On the fish found in a dry stream through Romuald’s merits

At a certain time the venerable man came to Sytria. Since he was still fasting, and the brothers, living as they did in rugged mountains, had no fish to set before him, they began to blush with embarrassment among themselves and anxiously consider what they could obtain for so venerable a guest.

Then one brother, I think divinely inspired, hurried to an almost dry stream that flowed nearby. There was scarcely any water in it, and no fish had ever been seen there. The brother therefore began devoutly to ask God that he who had been able to bring water from a dry rock for the Israelite people (Numbers 20; Exodus 17) might deign to show him a fish in the dry stream.

Immediately he put his hand into the little water and found a fish, which was more than sufficient to refresh the blessed man. God was providing a banquet for his servant: on a rocky and arid mountain, a fishpond had been found, as though in a valley full of fish.

But since we believe that these matters from the life of the blessed man—few as they are among many—are sufficient, let us now come to his departure.

### CHAPTER LXIX. On Romuald’s departure

[Col. 1005D]

The holy man ultimately lived in many other places and endured many other evils, especially from his disciples; many more miracles were also performed through him. We omit them from our account in order to avoid the excessive length of a more extended work.

After all the places in which he had lived, when he saw that his end was approaching, he finally returned to the monastery he had built at Valle de Castro. There, confidently awaiting his approaching death, he arranged for a cell with an oratory to be built for him, in which he could be enclosed and preserve silence until death.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] He dedicated it to Saint Blaise; hence the hermitage was called Saint Blasiolus. It was one mile distant from the monastery of Valle Castrense. [Col. 1006D]]

Twenty years before the end of his life, he had plainly foretold to his disciples that he ought to rest in the monastery mentioned above and that it would be fitting for him to breathe forth his spirit with no one present and no one performing the funeral rites.

Once the enclosure had been built, and while his mind was set on being enclosed in it immediately, his body began to grow increasingly burdened by ailments and to decline downward, as though not so much from illness as from the prolonged debility of extreme old age. For nearly half a year, an excessive abundance of phlegm had flowed from him together with the decay of his damaged lung, and he was afflicted by severe coughing and labored breathing.

Nevertheless, the holy man would not on that account lie down in bed or, insofar as possible, agree to relax the rigor of his customary fast.

One day he gradually began to lose his bodily strength and was more severely wearied as his illness advanced. As the sun was already inclining toward sunset, he ordered the two brothers who were present to go outside and close the cell door behind them; at dawn they were to return to him to celebrate the morning hymns.

Concerned about his death and leaving reluctantly, they did not immediately go to rest. Anxious lest the master should die, they kept watch near the cell, like men guarding a treasure of precious worth.

After remaining there for some time, they listened more attentively with alert ears. When they heard neither movement of the body nor sound of the voice, they correctly supposed what had happened, pushed open the door, hurried inside, lit a lamp, and found the holy corpse lying on its back, the blessed soul having been carried away to heaven.

Thus lay the heavenly pearl, apparently neglected at that moment, but afterward to be honorably placed in the treasury of the supreme King. Indeed, since he died as he had foretold, he passed to the place for which he had hoped.

The most blessed man lived for 120 years: twenty of them he spent in the world, three in a monastery, and ninety-seven in the eremitical life. Now he shines ineffably among the living stones of the heavenly Jerusalem; he rejoices with the ranks of the spirits of the blessed, wears the purest robe of immortality, and is crowned forever by the King of kings, whose diadem flashes eternally.

### CHAPTER LXX. On a demoniac healed by a piece of his hairshirt

[Col. 1006D]

After the most sacred death of the venerable man, who would seek to read how many signs of miracles God displayed through him, when new ones can frequently be seen even now?

Since the miracles that occur at his tomb are so numerous that we think it better to pass over them all in silence than to recount only a few, let it suffice for us to relate only two miracles performed elsewhere through that same most blessed confessor.

A certain brother who had been a disciple of the holy man had given a small basilica to the monastery for the sake of his soul. To this basilica he sent a strip cut from the edge of the sleeve of the blessed man’s hairshirt and ordered that it be honorably placed beneath the altar.

The attendant, however, failed to place it beneath the altar as he had been ordered. Instead, he carelessly left it in a crack in the wall.

Later, a certain demoniac was brought to the church mentioned above. As he stood in the middle, rolling his head from side to side and looking all around, he finally fixed his fierce eyes terrifyingly upon that very wall. Staring at the place where the piece of the holy man’s hairshirt lay, he did not cease crying out repeatedly: “It is driving me out! It is driving me out!”

And so, while he was shouting, the demon was immediately expelled from him.

From this it may rightly be inferred what he himself can obtain from divine mercy, before even the smallest piece of whose clothing the demon could not stand. And if he performed such things while absent, what could he not accomplish through the presence of his body?

### CHAPTER LXXI. On the steward who stole a cow and was immediately struck dead

At another time, a certain Castaldius

[Note: [Col. 1007C] Among the Lombards, this was the name given to the guardians and administrators of farms, estates, or places; indeed, not rarely to the prefects of castles, cities, and even provinces. See Du Cange’s Glossary.]

violently took a cow from a poor woman and refused to listen to her cries and many entreaties. She immediately ran to the church mentioned above and brought two hen-chicks. Throwing them down with her before the altar, she began tearfully to cry out in these words:

“Ah, Saint Romuald, hear me in my misery; do not despise me in my desolation, and return to me my provider, unjustly taken away.”

A remarkable event! The steward had scarcely left the woman’s house with the stolen animal when he was immediately struck by the discharge of an arrow. He abandoned the cow on the spot and, reaching home, immediately expired.

[Note: [Col. 1007C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “He had left the woman’s house with the stolen animal, at the discharge of an arrow, and, immediately struck, he abandoned the cow,” etc. [Col. 1008C]]

### CHAPTER LXXII. On Romuald’s body, found intact after five years

[Col. 1008A]

Five years after the holy man’s death, the apostolic see granted the monks permission to build an altar above his venerable body. A certain brother named Azo therefore went into the forest to make a small chest capable of holding only the bones and dust of the holy confessor.

During the following night, a venerable old man appeared to a sleeping brother. The brother immediately asked him: “Where is the prior of this monastery?” When the brother said that he did not know, the old man at once added: “He has undertaken to go into the forest to make a chest, but the body of the blessed man will not fit into so small a vessel.”

The next day the prior returned with the chest completed. The brother who had seen the vision asked him what had taken him into the forest. The prior, as though wearied by his labor, was unwilling to say. The brother then recounted the reason for his journey and, explaining in order what he himself had seen, concealed nothing.

They dug up the tomb and found almost the entire body of the holy man sound and undefiled, just as it had been when they first entrusted it to burial, except that a thin kind of mold-like down appeared to have grown on some of his limbs.

They therefore discarded the small chest that had been made and immediately prepared a vessel suited to the dimensions of the blessed body. In it they placed the protection of the sacred relics, and above it solemnly consecrated an altar.

The most blessed man Romuald died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July,

[Note: [Col. 1008C] On this day the feast of Saint Romuald is celebrated in the Camaldolese congregation and also in some other places. By the universal Church, however, it is celebrated on 7 February, the day of the translation of Saint Romuald’s body, since 29 June is occupied by the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.]

under the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1007]

# LIFE OF SAINT RODULPH, BISHOP OF GUBBIO, AND OF SAINT DOMINIC LORICATUS

(26 June, in the year of Christ 1063; 1 October, in the year of Christ 1062.) With notes by an anonymous writer.

## SUMMARY

The supreme pontiff Alexander had ordered him to write something memorable for him, something that, because of its usefulness, deserved to be preserved in public records.

[Col. 1009]

He therefore writes about the character, life, and most holy deeds of Rodulph, bishop of Gubbio, and of Dominic Loricatus. He had recently learned that both had died, and had been greatly distressed by the death of each. He also touches briefly upon Peter, Rodulph’s brother, and upon other monks of his monastery, renowned for the holiness of their lives and conduct.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1009A]

To the most blessed Pope Alexander, from Peter, a sinful monk, submission.

Your Beatitude, venerable father, instructed me never to send you letters containing anything trivial, forgettable, or frivolous—letters which, as soon as a reader has skimmed them, are consumed by devouring flame—but always to write something that might be received for the edification of readers and deserve to be preserved among authoritative writings. Therefore thanks must be given to the Father of lights, who has kindled the sanctuary of your heart with the fire of his love, so that you continually rest in the studies of the ancient Fathers and, moreover, do not neglect to urge those whom you consider suitable to write.

[Col. 1009B] Having recently departed from you, when I entered the walls of the city of Florence, a sudden messenger immediately hurried to me and turned midday into darkness, filling the veins of all my inward parts with the gall of a most bitter message: namely, that the bishop of Gubbio had died. His way of life, if recalled, can certainly provide no slight edification to those who hear of it. For it is useful both for expressing the proper form of living and for applying discipline to correct morals. Nearly seven years ago, when he and his mother, together with two brothers slightly older than himself, and with slaves who had merely been granted their freedom, gave me his castle, fortified with an impregnable defense, along with all the estates belonging to it, and came to the desert, he assumed the monastic habit [Note: [Col. 1009D] Some writings attest that these venerable men were descended from the most noble Gubbian family of the Gabrielli. Damian here speaks of Rodulphus and of his brother Peter, but says nothing about the other. It nevertheless perhaps cannot be denied that this man was Blessed Fortis, since he is found in Jacobillus, Ferrarius, and others to have lived in the same century and in the same Avellanese monastery, and to have belonged to the same Gabrielli family. See the Bollandists’ note on him for May.] [Col. 1009C] of the monastic profession [Note: [Col. 1010D] Add *accepit* (“he assumed”), as in the Mabillon edition.].

## CHAPTER I. Saint Rodulphus Becomes a Monk

We built a monastery on their property, and we now rejoice sufficiently in the Lord over its holy community, which lives there according to the rule. With his mother and his weaker brother established there, this Rodulphus—who was later raised to the summit of the episcopate—and his firstborn brother Peter led an eremitical life with such constancy and severity that their reputation proclaimed them extraordinary to those who heard of them, while their life displayed their excellence to those who lived with them.

Indeed, if I wished to recount everything that can be told about Peter, this little sheet might run out before the material for speaking did. To mention briefly at least one example from many: once, while we were sitting in the chapter-house and discussing the monastic disciplines, he, being still a novice, uttered an undisciplined expression drawn from worldly custom. Then I, as though moved by anger, rebuked him with a sufficiently harsh attack. After a long scourging of reproaches and corrections, as though delivering a sentence to one who had been examined under interrogation, I ordered him to abstain from wine for forty days. My intention, however, was merely to deter him, for the present, together with the others, from careless speech, and afterward to temper the sentence through the moderation of a considered remission.

But it happened that I was occupied with various affairs, and no one recalled this matter to me. When the prescribed period of days had already elapsed, I finally remembered and was terrified; astonished, I asked what Peter had done with the penance imposed upon him. From the brothers’ report I learned that the penance had been completed. I regretted, I confess, the sentence I had pronounced, but I rejoiced and marveled at the brother’s great penance: for a single word uttered thoughtlessly, he had undertaken so long a penance and had asked for no indulgence either personally or through others.

## CHAPTER II. Saint Rodulphus Relaxes Nothing of Monastic Severity in the Episcopate

Let the discourse now return to the bishop with whom it began. Although Peter, being older, always went before him no less in the path of an arduous purpose and strict life, Rodulphus, once promoted to the rights of priestly office, did not abandon in the Church what he had learned in the desert.

He continually wore the same hairshirts over his limbs and was content with the same exceedingly scanty and contemptible garments. When the nature of youthful age brought upon him a very severe [Col. 1010C] acedia, he tied cords to the ceiling of his cell and, inserting his arms into them, remained suspended while applying himself to the chanting of the psalms.

He never consumed fat, eggs, or cheese. Even with the same foods that were served, his restraint tormented him, so that when he reclined at table he seemed not so much to refresh himself as to engage in combat; what appeared outwardly to be a meal was rather an inward war against gluttony.

I often struggled to persuade him, at least during the harshness of winter, either to place beneath himself bedding made of papyrus matting or to sleep clothed at night. But he lay naked on a bare wooden board, content with only an under-tunic. He assigned the church as his lodging and designated his solitary cell as his dwelling. For the rough manners of the people, their undisciplined necks, and the easy yoke of the Lord (Matthew 11) would not allow themselves to be imposed upon them. Intent on earthly gifts, they waited for advantages not from the bishop’s mouth as the word of God, but as though from the hands of a governor. For this region, the more it is found to be alien to riches, the more abundantly it overflows with vices. Gubbio itself seems to have been named from *egenus*, “needy,” or “lacking in goodness.” Therefore, compelled by my insistence, he retained by official duty the Church he had abandoned by his vow; nevertheless, he continued to dwell more assiduously in the desert.

## CHAPTER III. Rodulphus’s Abstinence

Whenever he could arrange for such bread to be made in the desert, he ate bread not intended for the brothers, nor even for children, but bread made either from pure barley or, rather, from *cantabrum*—what remained from the children’s loaves and was fit to be thrown to dogs. Although, apart from the more solemn days, he was content with this bread every day, he nevertheless weighed out his portion carefully on the scales of equity.

Once he complained to me [Col. 1011B] that, if a larger measure were allowed him, he would indulge his itching appetite more generously in this same bread. Hunger chastised the young man so severely that, whatever food he received as relief, his stomach did not care, with its belly empty.

At times, even on Sundays, knowing no cooked dish, he lived only on apples and bread with water. He was continually girded about the chest with an iron ring; yet he carefully concealed the ring, sunk beneath his loins, whenever he stripped before the brothers.
