He never attended the chapter-house as a confessor without receiving discipline, and then rejoiced festively if he was ordered to be scourged not by only one brother but by two.

He often accepted a penance of a hundred years, which he discharged over twenty days by striking himself with bundles of rods [Col. 1011C] and by other remedies of penance. Every day he did not neglect to complete the Psalter: when he could not complete two, he completed at least one. While in his cell, he customarily continued the whole of it with discipline, armed with a broom in each hand.

When he was on some expedition, however deep the darkness of the untimely night, he would rise and continue singing psalms with bare legs and feet until dawn. While he remained in his cell, he kept this custom without interruption by day and night. However severely the bitter winter froze, he protected his feet with simple socks, whereas his brother was content with shoes alone.

Often he adjured me solemnly, by the mercy of Christ, that if he should ever perhaps go too far, I must not withdraw from correcting him but must fulfill toward him every measure of discipline owed to monks. Thus he laudably observed both the monk’s rule and the bishop’s authority in alternating succession.

At suitable and unsuitable times alike he persisted in the word of preaching, and whatever he could take away from his household expenses he scattered, very generously, among the poor. When he annually convened a synod, he did not permit the clergy to be required to pay any customary canon of offerings or gifts, nor did he demand any payment from the fallen, apart from penance alone. “Far be it from me,” he said, “to sell a synod; I would rather raise up the fallen than grow fat, like a raven, on their corpses.”

I am weary of proceeding further in writing, and Icarian grief seems to restrain my paternal hands, as it were, from painting [Note: [Col. 1011D] Icarus, son of Daedalus, perished miserably because he did not obey his father’s warnings, according to Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII; Mabillon.].

## CHAPTER IV. His Blessed Death

Adorned with these and similar flowers of virtue, he was, like a shining lily, scorched by the frost of premature death. Although he seemed scarcely to be about thirty years old, he departed from this unhappy light to the Author of true light [Note: [Col. 1011D] The Bollandists note under 26 June that the people of Gubbio show no veneration for Rodulphus. Nevertheless, his memory appears in Menard’s Benedictine martyrology, in Bucellinus’s menology, and in Ferrarius’s catalogue; in notes to that catalogue Ferrarius indicates that he was honored by public cult among the people of Gubbio. Jacobillus repeats this, adding that his body was buried in the old Gubbian church, then transferred to another and placed beneath an altar dedicated to his name.] [Col. 1012B].

For, having been made perfect in a short time, as Scripture says, he fulfilled many times. His soul was pleasing to God (Wisdom 4). And rightly is one who was made perfect in a short time said to have fulfilled many times, because, while he followed the path of justice during the brief life he possessed, he spent all time, so far as he was concerned, in the service of the Creator.

Everything that Wisdom says there about the holy man fits this man in every respect, as though it had been said about him specifically:

“Old age is honorable, not because of length of time nor reckoned by number of years. The understanding of a person is gray hair, and an undefiled life is the age of old age, pleasing to God.”

And it continues:

“Having become beloved, and living among sinners, he was taken away. He was snatched away lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit mislead his soul. Therefore he hastened to lead him out from the midst of iniquity” (ibid.) [Col. 1012C].

## CHAPTER V. The Life of the Venerable Man Dominic Loricatus

But behold: while a messenger for this letter, one who might come to you, is being sought and cannot be found, something else suddenly occurs to me which, if written, may contribute more abundantly to edification. Perhaps the messenger is withheld from me by a heavenly arrangement for this reason: so that, while I am free for the moment, my pen may be transferred to something else.

The man of God, Dominic, my father and lord, died a year ago. If his life is written, I fear that some brothers may perhaps judge it incredible. But far be it from me to write a lie. For I honor truth truthfully, to the best of my ability, and I admit no fabrication of deceit.

We are not unaware of the Apostle’s statement. After saying, “If Christ has not risen, then our preaching is empty,” he immediately added: “We are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if the dead do not rise” (1 Corinthians 15) [Col. 1012D].

Without lingering longer over these apostolic words, the reader readily understands that anyone who invents the claim that God or God’s servant has done something marvelous not only deserves no reward for a fabricated proclamation, but is also convicted of having borne false witness against the one whom he praised.

## CHAPTER VI. He Becomes a Hermit Monk

When Dominic was a cleric in the world, because the heresy of Simony was then flourishing—would that it were now entirely extinguished!—his parents gave the bishop a tanned goatskin so that Dominic might become a priest. For, as the Apostle says, “All things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8), this one fault of the blessed man proved to be the source of many subsequent goods.

Terrified by this event, he despised the world, put on the monastic habit, and immediately undertook the arduous institution of eremitical life like an undaunted soldier. But because he had been wrongly promoted, he never presumed, as long as he lived, to exercise the ministry of the holy altar.

He remained a virgin until death and did not abandon the eremitical life. There, under the direction of the holy man John, who was called “of Montefeltro,” he lived for many years.

In that desert, which was situated in the region called Luceoli [Note: [Col. 1013D] Luceolum was a very ancient city of Umbria, formerly situated between the cities of Cagli and Gubbio. It is now commonly called Ponterezzoli, or Ponte Riccioli, through corruption of the name, in place of the bridge of Luceoli. A note in the manuscript chronicle of Fonte Avellana records that this monastery was built by Saint Romuald, the father of the Camaldolese, near the end of the tenth century.], there appeared to be eighteen cells assigned for the brothers to inhabit. They lived under this rule: they never drank wine and never seasoned their food with fat; they took one cooked dish on Sunday and also on Thursday; for five days of the week they practiced fasting on bread and water.

Devoting themselves only to prayers or persisting in manual labor, they did not practice agriculture, nor did they possess estates or any property, except one pack animal. One servant accompanied this little ass or horse, constantly traveling either to acquire or to grind grain, and alone sustained them in all their needs. This was John, who later became abbot of the place and governed the community under an honorable administration.

Throughout the week they maintained silence under strict discipline. On Sunday, after vespers and the breaking of their fast, they had freedom to speak with one another until the office of compline. Moreover, they continually remained in their cells with bare feet and legs.

He told me that, when he lived with Anso—a religious man whom I myself also saw—they inflicted discipline upon each other every day throughout all the canonical hours with blows from brooms. This Anso once complained to him that he had nine daily measures of bread in his stomach. They were so weakened by hunger that dry bread became packed into their intestines and could scarcely be digested.

There was also a certain brother there who had often attempted to leave his cell as a vagrant. John, the prior of the desert, first rebuked him sternly, as was fitting, and then ordered him to be beaten in his presence. When, at his master’s command, he began to dress, he spoke arrogantly. The master again ordered him to strip and again commanded that he be beaten.

Yet even as he began to dress again, he did not cease uttering something arrogant. Thus a third time, thus a fourth, and, if I remember correctly, he was beaten as many as six times without being corrected. Stripped and redressed, he could not answer humbly.

But when he was scourged for the seventh time and began to dress, he started to cry out in a loud voice, saying [Col. 1014B]:

“Behold, the devil has gone; behold, the most wicked inhabitant of my heart has fled and, breaking the bonds by which I was bound, has left me free. Now, now I gladly obey my lord and master, and I promise in every respect to submit myself to his laws.”

In this way that brother returned to the guardianship of humility and, remaining constantly in his cell, lived thereafter irreproachably.

## CHAPTER VII. He Becomes a Disciple of Blessed Peter Damian

Much later, with his master’s consent, the aforementioned holy man deigned to entrust himself, in his astonishing humility, to me, a wretched and unworthy man whom he himself had chosen to receive, and to subject himself to me as a monk to an abbot.

He gave himself to me; he did not receive me. I had accepted him as a dependent client, but I rejoice that in Christ’s school I truly received a philosophical teacher. His entire life was preaching and edification, teaching and discipline.

But because we have scattered some sayings and deeds of this holy man through various little works already composed by us, it does not seem absurd to append here the same material, which is at hand, in the very style in which it was written.

It is easier to build a house from hewn timber than to multiply the labor by hewing and building at the same time. For it is also written of Solomon’s temple:

“The house, when it was being built, was built of stones prepared and finished; and neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house when it was being built” (1 Kings 6) [Col. 1014D].

We too have, according to the inadequacy of our hands, polished stones which it is enough for us simply to arrange in the structure just as they were found.

## CHAPTER VIII. Saint Dominic Wears an Iron Cuirass Next to His Flesh

In the letter sent to Lord Teuzo [Note: [Col. 1013D] This is opusculum 51. Teuzo was a monk of Saint Mary’s near Florence. He had disagreed with his abbot Albizo and left the monastery; later, when Peter Damian came to him to reconcile him with the abbot, Teuzo drove Peter and the abbot together from his cell. Peter therefore wrote to him in order to recall him to better fruitfulness through the sayings and examples of the saints. So the learned Mabillon explains in his notes on this Life, century 6, part 2.], I find that I wrote the following:

“But why do I roam through various places in recalling holy men, when I have one within my threshold and at hand, before whose worthy praises I cannot rise, unequal to the task? Indeed, with cells situated opposite one another and separated only by the intervening space of the basilica, he and I are divided.

If I devote myself to counting his virtues, the days will pass before the material for writing seems capable of running out. I mean Dominic, my teacher and lord, whose speech is rustic but whose life is sufficiently skillful and graceful. That life preaches far more profitably for the edification of the living by its works than the sterile tongue of certain people, which vainly weighs carefully polished words of courtly elegance.

For many years now, wearing an iron cuirass next to his flesh, he has waged an unbreakable battle against wicked spirits. Always ready for combat, this fervent soldier advances with his body as well as his heart fortified against hostile ranks.

He maintains this practice throughout his life without distinction: scarcely any day passes on which, chanting two Psalters, he does not beat his naked body with brooms held in both hands. And this is during a more relaxed period. During the cycles of Lent, or when he has to perform penance—for he frequently undertakes a penance of a hundred years—then, while afflicting himself daily with blows from brooms, he completes at least three Psalters in meditation.

As we learned from the man himself, a penance of a hundred years is completed in this way. Since three thousand broom blows regularly complete one year of penance among us, and the chanting of ten psalms, as has often been tested, permits a thousand broom blows, while it is beyond doubt that a Psalter consists of one hundred and fifty psalms, those who calculate correctly find that five years of penance are contained in the discipline of one Psalter.

Whether you multiply five by twenty or twenty by five, the result is one hundred. It follows, therefore, that whoever chants twenty Psalters with discipline may confidently say that he has completed a hundred years of penance.

Yet in this too our Dominic surpasses most people. While some use only one hand in performing discipline, he, truly a son of Benjamin, fights tirelessly with both hands against the rebellious allurements of the flesh.

As he himself declared to me, he easily completes this hundred-year penance in six days according to his custom. I also remember that, at the beginning of a certain approaching Lent, he asked us to impose a thousand years of penance upon him; he completed nearly all of them before the time of the fast had ended [Note: [Col. 1016D] He adds several things in the work itself in defense of the use of such disciplines, which Saint Dominic Loricatus promoted in a remarkable way.].”

A little later I continued as follows:

“Let the discourse now return to Dominic, with whom it had begun. Although bowed old age already weighs him down and frequent illnesses often waste him away, it is astonishing from where such fervor burns within him, making him always unconquered and tireless in spiritual exercises.

For, as I learned from his own account, he often continues two Psalters while standing and performing discipline, so that he neither sits during the interval nor rests for even a moment from the blows, with an incredible ardor of mind.

Once, when I asked whether he could endure for a while bending his knees beneath the weight of his iron garment, he gave me this obscure answer:

‘When my health answers my wish, I sometimes customarily bend my knees a hundred times through each successive group of fifteen psalms of the entire Psalter.’

At the time I did not attend carefully to this, but afterward, turning his words over in my mind, I was astonished and terrified to realize that, with one Psalter, this bent old man performed a thousand prostrations (*metanoeas*) [Col. 1016B] (consult the scholia at the end of the Life).

One day after vespers, he entered my cell and said: ‘Master’—for in his humility he addresses me by this unworthy title—‘today I did what I do not remember having done before: I completed eight Psalters in chanting between day and night.’

At that time his entire face appeared so rubbed by brooms and so bruised by certain furrowing welts that it looked as though he had been pounded like grain in the manner of a medicinal gruel.

The chanting of psalms comes so easily to him because, as he himself says, he does not so much repeat the words with his resounding tongue as pass through the meaning with the vitality of his mind.”

## CHAPTER IX. His More Generous Food: Bread with Fennel

“Once he lived at some distance from me. When I entered and asked under what rule of life he was then living, he answered that he was living according to the flesh and that on Thursdays, as always on Sundays, he relaxed the usual severity of his abstinence.

When I asked whether he ate any cooked dish, eggs, or cheese, he denied it. Again I asked whether he ate fish or apples.

‘Fish and apples,’ he said, ‘if there are any, I provide for the sick. I lament that in our regions an exceedingly large number of them lie ill.’

When I pressed him like a harsh examiner, enclosing him in a narrow question, and said, ‘How then do you live more indulgently on those days, if you eat none of the things that must either be cooked over fires or found on trees?’ he replied:

‘I gladly eat fennel with bread.’

I immediately understood how carnally a man lived when he had placed his delicacies in fennel.

He certainly possesses an abundant grace of tears, but one that alternates. When he restrains himself, shut away under strict silence, he soon weeps abundantly whenever he wishes. But if conversation is frequent, he complains that he has lost his tears.

I too often reproach him for the poverty of my own dryness, saying: ‘Alas, father, your tears are unfruitful, since they cannot give birth to other tears through prayer. I would wish—as follows naturally—that just as you are my father, so your tears might likewise become the mothers of my tears.’”

I also remember inserting this in the eremitical rule:

“I shall say it. But who knows whether faith will be given to so faithful an assertion? It is of little importance if human rashness accuses one whom supreme truth excuses from falsehood.

There is among us a man who sometimes spends one day joined continuously to the night, passing through nine Psalters in meditation, while almost always afflicting his naked body with brooms held in both hands.

It must be noted that, while he strives to perform these things, he has no leisure to sleep by night or day. Sometimes, bending his knees and lowering his head to the ground, sleep suddenly steals upon him while he is naked; he is content with that alone.

This brother once complained to me with fraternal intimacy that, although he often completed nine Psalters in this way, he had never been able to reach the tenth.”

In the letter that we sent to Countess Blanca, we seem to have inserted this:

“If only you could now be granted the opportunity to see my lord Dominic, who would teach and form you by the far more effective and radiant example of his life in what we attempt to accomplish through an unskilled tongue.

For about three periods of five years now he has worn an iron cuirass next to his flesh. Two iron rings gird his body, and two more constrict him around the upper arms [Note: [Col. 1017D] This is opusculum 50.].”

## CHAPTER X. He Completes Twelve Psalters Continuously, Meanwhile Beating Himself with Rods

Since we have already arranged much about him in other little works of ours, let us now report what he told us when he came to us scarcely six days ago.

He said:

“I happened to learn what you had written: that I had chanted nine Psalters in one day with bodily disciplines. When I heard this, I trembled, was terrified, and groaned with a remorseful conscience.

‘Woe is me,’ I said. ‘Behold, this has been written about me without my knowing it. Yet I do not know whether this could have been done by me. Therefore I shall try again and learn without doubt whether I was able to accomplish it.’

On Wednesday, therefore, I stripped off my garments, armed with a broom in each hand, and did not cease keeping vigil throughout the whole night, chanting and beating myself. On the following day, having completed twelve Psalters according to custom, I continued crawling on the third day as far as the thirteenth psalm, ‘Blessed are those whose…’

Now, by one example let us show how childish and contemptible he considers what often seems harsh and difficult to us. A certain brother greatly shrank from wearing himself out with blows from brooms and considered it most grievous to inflict and endure blows upon himself. At last, however, he yielded to the frequent urging of Lord Dominic, and he did not cease to impose discipline upon himself with his own hands through the chanting of the entire Psalter and, in addition, fifty psalms.

[Col. 1018A] That night preceded Sunday and the feast of Blessed Michael. When morning came, that brother went to the aforementioned old man. Fearing a rebuke for lack of discretion, he recounted in order what he had done. The old man replied:

‘Do not be faint-hearted, brother, nor lose confidence because of the weakness you now possess. God can raise you from the depths to higher things and strengthen the infancy of your milk-white way of life for the growth of youthful vigor.’

Then he added:

‘We too began gradually at first and little by little reached what divine mercy wished to lead us toward, although we were brought forth weak and fragile.’

Thus it happened that he did not rebuke him for excessive fervor, as the brother had feared, but, so that he would not succumb to despair, refreshed his courage as though he had done something very small.

By the example of this holy old man, the practice of performing discipline became so deeply established in our regions that not only men but also noble women eagerly undertook this kind of purgatory. The wife of Tethbald, a woman of exalted lineage and certainly not low rank, once told me that, by the rule prescribed for this discipline, she had completed a hundred years of penance.”

In the letter also to John, the prior of the desert situated near Mount Suavicino [Note: [Col. 1017D] The desert of Suavicino was built by Damian in the territory of Septempeda, commonly called San Severino, as he himself testifies in opusculum 15, chapter 6. It is now called Frontale in Italian. Only the church dedicated to Saint Dominic remains there; it preserves an ancient painted image of the holy man dressed in a white hood, together with his sacred relics. Through the negligence, it is said, of the commendatory abbots, little is maintained with proper reverence.], when I was exhorting him and his subjects to extend their arms in prayer, I first spoke of a very fervent brother of ours in the love of Christ, Adam by name, and then added Dominic as an example, saying:

“We have a certain young brother who confessed to me that, while chanting the Psalter, he keeps his arms raised from the beginning to the end, so that his hands often touch the ceiling of the cell. He observes this discretion, however: after every fifty psalms, he lowers his relaxed arms for a moment and immediately raises them again.

We also have another man of more advanced age, a bent old man—and, to confess to you secretly, this is Dominic. He found a little written text stating that if anyone sang the twelve psalms marked there twenty-four times, with his hands raised in the form of a cross, he could regularly compensate for one year of penance.

Immediately he took up what was written as an exercise and, with his arms extended in the form of a cross as prescribed, sang those twelve psalms twenty-six times every day, without any interval at all, but in a single continuous effort.”

I have written about this in other little works also, perhaps; but since they are either unavailable for the present or do not readily come to mind, let the discussion now pass from repeating what has been written to anything new.

A kind of divine fire continually burned in his breast [Col. 1019A], never permitting him to rest from the labor of spiritual exercise.

Once, when I asked him on the holy day of Easter whether he too had slept while the other brothers, according to custom, were resting at midday, he said:

“Certainly, father. I said in my heart: ‘Why should I sleep during the day when there are still such long nights for me?’”

Then, stretching his arms in the form of a cross, I began the Psalter. When I had completed it while standing in that position, the signal for the ninth hour immediately sounded. In this way I joined the victory of the cross with the glory of the Resurrection.

On another occasion, when we were speaking together, as is customary, about our daily works, he said:

“I shall make clear what happened to me this night. When I rose, freed from sleep, I immediately stretched out my arms in the form of a cross and began the Psalter. When I had completed all the psalms, the following canticles, and the hymns, I had reached the point at which I had only to conclude everything with the psalm of the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 1019D] Mabillon says that this means, if I am not mistaken, the creed commonly known under the name of Athanasius.] and the litanies.

Then it occurred to me to set these aside for the moment and chant the Psalter for the dead. Without lowering my arms, I therefore turned to the Psalter for the dead, which, according to custom, I divided into three sections by interspersing the readings after every fifty psalms.

When I had completed it, I immediately returned to what I had omitted and finished what remained of the first Psalter. As I was considering beginning the third Psalter in succession, the signal for the nocturnal assembly suddenly sounded—as I may put it, a good deed had been accomplished—and compelled me, with my arms lowered, to celebrate the office with the brothers. Certainly, at that time—I do not know in what season of the year—the nights were shorter.”

## CHAPTER XI. He Scourges Himself Wonderfully with a Leather Whip
Some years before his death, as though inventing a new kind of punishment, he changed his brooms of rods into whips of leather thongs; and, having once tasted them—for they are harsher—he made a habit of flogging himself with them. Whenever he went out into the world, he carried this whip in his bosom, so that wherever he happened to lie down, he would not be without blows. Sometimes, when circumstances did not allow him to strip himself completely, he never ceased afflicting himself at least across his legs and thighs, his head and neck.

Because four iron rings had, through his long custom, become almost worthless to him, he added four more, so that two might be fastened around his hips and two, in succession, around his legs. Indeed, the coats of mail that he wore like hair shirts or any woolen garments, he washed after a month—or after a longer interval—in order to remove the rust, so that they would not cause a burning irritation to be inflicted upon his dry limbs. Moreover, while all of us who live in cells strive to make our clothing fall all the way to the floor for the protection of our feet against the cold, this too seemed intolerable to us in his case: for, since he always lived in the wilderness and knew nothing of boots or shoes, his garments nevertheless descended scarcely to the middle of his shins. When he stripped himself to receive discipline in the chapter—which he never wished to omit—and his limbs, wasted by fasting and worn down by the weight of the hooked coat of mail, were exposed, he seemed to have acquired an Ethiopian blackness. His clothing, too, appeared, if I may put it so, yellowed and worm-eaten, consumed by age.

He often said this to me: “In psalmody, a person who sings quickly makes progress if he holds his heart to the words, if his mind truly grasps what his tongue utters; otherwise, if his heart wanders, the course of the psalms is brought to its end slowly, with the tongue now deceiving, now growing slack.” He also used to say that sleep feeds sleep, and vigils produce vigils. For the human body is afterward strengthened by gradual increase in that in which it is first gradually nourished.

But perhaps someone will reproach me here, someone who is eager to hear not so much what manner of life the holy man had, but by what miracles he became famous in this life. To him it should briefly suffice for me to reply that neither Mary nor John the Baptist is read to have worked a miracle, although their lives are narrated not by some ordinary Scripture but by the testimony of the Gospel. Yet Mary, in the single birth that she brought forth, unquestionably surpasses the virtues and signs of all the saints. I will also add this, because the wondrous life of holy men provides richer fruit for those who hear it than the miracles displayed by them. [Col. 1020C] The former demands imitation; the latter brings only amazement. Miracles teach how those saints became holy; their life, however, suggests how people even now may become holy. Besides, you who seek a miracle: does it not seem wondrous to you that a human being, still enclosed in fragile flesh, so to speak, should live like an angel, to such a degree that among so many thousands of people you can scarcely find one like him? And certainly there are many even today of inferior manner of life through whom almighty God deigns to display his powers.

With Jesus as my witness, I am not lying: not yet three months have passed since two young monks came to me while I was staying in the wilderness of Gamugni. One of them said that he came from the territory of Spoleto; the other, from the regions of Venetia, namely from the city of Pola.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] That is, from the duchy of Spoleto.]

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Pola, an episcopal city of Istria under Venetian rule; [Col. 1020D] therefore Damian calls this monk a Venetian. He is mentioned in the Martyrologies of Menard and Bucellini.]

But the Venetian, whose name was Michael, as he admitted to us in confession, at the very beginning of his conversion bound himself with an iron ring under this pledge of his desire: he earnestly begged the mercy of almighty God that, when he found a place suited to his salvation, that ring might immediately break. On the very day, however, when this new guest entered the wilderness, scarcely three hours later, while he was reading syllable by syllable, as an uneducated man, more or less, in the Rule of Saint Benedict, suddenly the spirit of compunction dissolved him in tears, and at that same moment the ring appeared broken. Since we remember having already described this miracle elsewhere, we will pass over it quickly and set out more fully the following miracle, which has not yet been committed to writing.

## CHAPTER XII. The holy man’s excesses in the subjugation of his flesh

A short time afterward, at my command, he went to the city of Ravenna to bring away his little belongings and bundles, which he had left there when he came ashore from the ship. There, at a smith’s workshop, he had new equipment of iron bonds made, and, acting as both judge and defendant against himself, violently fastened himself with many chains around various parts of his body. Two chains hung down from his neck over his shoulders on either side, one reaching to his groin and the other all the way to his thigh; he also placed two rings around his hips and two around his arms.

Thus surrounded on every side by such manifold restraints, he returned to us secretly and showed what had been done to him. He obtained, only with difficulty and at last, the fulfillment of his wish, lest I alter what he had done. But when these tortures burdened him beyond his strength, and stench was already beginning to emerge from his abraded flesh, something else was added that disturbed more sharply the heart of the brother who rejected glory. For the report of this secret began to break out, first flying about among the brothers, and then through the mouths of anyone who came to visit.

He therefore begged the mercy of almighty God to show clearly, through a sign of his power, whether he approved of what he had begun. Meanwhile, while he frequently persisted in prayers of this kind, he heard twice in a dream, as a consolation, that those iron implements had already been loosed by divine power. Then, on the feast of the blessed apostles Simon and Jude, which we celebrated very recently, while he was attending the nocturnal office with the brothers, those two pieces of iron that had been placed over his shoulders and hung downward on both sides, constricting his belly and kidneys, were suddenly completely broken: one into two pieces and the other into three.

The remaining rings were not broken into pieces, but were loosened and softened by a certain pliancy, so that they seemed in some way not so much iron as lead. Indeed, even if he had wished to fasten himself with them as they slipped down and fell away, he could no longer do so. Thus, thus the brother who had been bound by the burning ardor of holy devotion was wonderfully released by God’s merciful judgment.

What wonder, then, if God had wished to display some sign through Dominicus, that remarkable man, when at the very beginning of his apprenticeship he deigned to exhibit two miracles through this young man—since it is more praiseworthy to accomplish difficult deeds than novel ones? Hence, after David had said, “God is wonderful in his saints,” he immediately added, “He himself will give strength and power to his people” (Psalm 67). He did not say “signs” or “wonders,” but “he himself will give strength and power.”

Moreover, when a certain Roman named Stephen was administering the highest judicial office at Auximum, Dominicus came to him, compelled by the circumstances, and earnestly petitioned him concerning a certain possession in the wilderness that he held by right of the apostolic see. Stephen, despising him because his clothing was in no way elegant, rejected him contemptuously and granted him none of what he requested. When those standing nearby said to Stephen, “Do not receive him so harshly; he is a holy man,” he replied, as though vomiting bile: “Let him be holy, as you wish; but blessed Peter is certainly holier, whose cause I am defending in this administration.”

Thus Dominicus, unsuccessful in his undertaking, returned to his cell, and Stephen shortly afterward returned to Rome. A contemptible young servant, who had remained in the administration to carry out any business, reverently fulfilled everything that Dominicus had requested from the judge.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Mabillon notes that here the word “boy” should be understood as referring to a servant of lowly condition.]

Not long after the judge had returned to his own home, he was pierced by hostile swords and died. Since he had no offspring, he left many riches to heirs outside his family.

Dominicus was also extremely careful in his speech, so that the saying of the apostle James suited him well: “If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (James 3). For whenever someone asked what hour of the day it was, he never answered without qualification, “It is the whole hour”; rather, he always added, “It is nearly the third hour,” or “It is nearly the sixth hour.” When I asked him why he always spoke in this way, he replied: “By this I guard against lying. For whether the hour has already passed or perhaps is still approaching, it is nevertheless near, since it is not far removed from the moment at which we are speaking.”

At one time he had a cell beside the monastery called Conjunctuli. On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, after he had remained enclosed throughout the preceding Lent and had been severely afflicted by such fasts and labors, he went out, drawn by the splendor of the solemnity, humbly prostrated himself before the abbot of the place, asked pardon, and tearfully confessed his actions and thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] This “Lent” must be understood as the Lent of Saint Martin, which extended from the octave of All Saints to Christmas. In its place the Church now observes the fast called Advent.]

But the abbot, being a young man, frivolous in character and unaccustomed to spiritual counsels, content with imposing a single psalm or some very small penance, ordered him to sing thirty psalters for what he had confessed. Struck by this sentence as by an arrow, Dominicus returned to his cell and judged that this had occurred by the disposition of divine judgment. Therefore, after returning to his cell, he did not come out until he had paid the prescribed rule of the imposed penance with the most diligent perseverance.

## CHAPTER XIII. His blessed departure from this life

[Col. 1023A]

He used to drink wine occasionally, though very sparingly; but long before he died, he resolved to abstain from it completely. To come now, then, leaving the other matters aside, to his death: he suffered from heaviness of the stomach and was additionally tormented by frequent headaches. Since one condition often results from the other, he decided to take a draught of medicine to cleanse his stomach.

Accordingly, throughout Friday he scarcely ceased either to devote himself to chanting psalms or to scourge himself with blows from leather thongs. At night, after setting aside sleep, he took the medicine; then he began to suffer distress and complained bitterly of pain in his stomach. After the office of the nocturnal assembly had ended, after the morning hymns, while the brothers who were present were already singing the first hour for him, he returned his holy spirit to God.

They also found a second coat of mail, besides the one he had been wearing, laid beneath his sides in the manner of a winding sheet. The brothers therefore suspected that this had by no means happened to him contrary to his custom, since when well he had been accustomed to keep himself beneath it, and he had lain upon it also in his illness.

At that time, a certain brother dreamed of me that I had lost the light of my eyes. When I had related this to the venerable Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, in the Lateran palace, he said: “It is by no means, as you fear, an indication of your imminent death; rather, someone close to you will be extinguished—someone who is dear to you as your eye and your light, and who appears to you as a splendor in good works.”

And, oh, true—but more bitter than any gall—was the prophecy! On the third day after I had left the walls of Rome, a cruel report met me, declaring that I had been left blind, when I suspected nothing less: namely, that my lord and illuminator, Dominicus, had recently departed from this world. At once it became clear to me that, when he sought the author of light, I had remained in the darkness of blindness.

The brothers, fearing that neighboring monks might snatch his body from their hands, quickly buried it in dug earth in the very cell in which he had died. But on the Sunday itself on which we entered the wilderness, we reverently removed the holy body from there and buried it in the chapter house, as was fitting. On the ninth day after its burial, we found the body sound and intact.

Let those who delight in the allurements of their flesh go now; let them absorb the marrow of pleasures and be nourished for the eternal fire as victims of slaughter; let them raise themselves on the horns of pride, insult the innocent, and live softly according to their desire, so that afterward their inward parts may grow bitter amid ever-avenging punishments. Let them now run about like unbridled horses through the meadows of their pleasures, so that afterward the ultimate cords of discipline may restrain their hands and arms (Galatians 8).

But our Dominicus carried the marks of Jesus in his body, and he depicted the standard of the cross not only upon his forehead, but also impressed it upon all his limbs on every side. Scorched and dried out by the moisture of the reed and rush, he deserved to be watered by the abundant rains of heavenly grace. Here he is girded with an iron coat of mail; there he is adorned with the snow-white garments of angelic glory. Here he is worn down by the hardness of his bed; there he is cherished in the gentle bosom of the patriarchs. This entire life became for him a preparation for the cross; there, festive and splendid, he celebrates the eternal glory of the resurrection. Now he shines among the fiery stones of the heavenly Jerusalem; now, adorned with the titles of his victories, he triumphs in eternal praise and rejoices together with the blessed citizens in their joyful fellowship.

Blessed Dominicus died on the day before the Ides of October.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] He is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on this day; but the Camaldolese celebrate his feast on the seventeenth of the same month.]

Our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1024B] A thousand *metanoeae* are performed by a prostrate person in one psalter. Here *metanoea* does not mean the term that Ausonius describes in verse: “which,” as he says, “demands punishment for what was done and not done,” although that is the true and proper meaning of the word among reputable authors. For *μετάνοια* (*metanoia*) means repentance, a change of mind, when after the deed we come to understanding.

Here, however, it denotes what later Greek ecclesiastical writers called by that name: the prostrations of the body that Christian believers performed publicly or privately, either voluntarily or according to the prescriptions of the canons of the saints. Those who formerly performed public penance were called *μετανοῦντες* (*metanoountes*), or “those who are in *metanoia*,” *οἱ ἐν μετανοίᾳ ὄντες* (*hoi en metanoia ontes*).

Frequent prostrations upon the ground were in use, as can be gathered from Sozomen; and among the Greeks such prostrations were imposed upon penitents, so that for this reason prostrations upon the ground could be called by a virtually proper name, *μετάνοιαι* (*metanoiai*), or *στρωταὶ μετάνοιαι* (*strotai metanoiai*). Others are *ἐδαφιαῖαι* (*edaphiaiai*), which are completed without prostration, with the knees merely bent. Such is the passage in Gregory against the Jews: *Κλίνας τὸ γόνυ ἕως ἐδάφους τρίς, καὶ ἀναστὰς, καὶ ἐκτείνας τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν, εἶπε*—that is, “bending the knee three times all the way to the ground, then rising and stretching his hands toward heaven, he said.”

Many further examples are available in Chrysostom, Basil, Evagrius, and other writers who have treated the affairs and deeds of monks, but the limits of a note do not permit us to cite them here. [Col. 1024D] Those writers, however, called these acts by the purer and more polished term *γονυκλισίαι* (*gonuklisiai*), “genuflections.”

Finally, let us add in passing something that makes the matter clearer: among monks, greetings are made either by lowering and bending the body or even by bending the knees; for this reason *μετάνοια* (*metanoia*) means “greeting.” We read this in John of Jerusalem’s Life of John of Damascus, in Damascus’s Book I, *On Images*, and in Maximus’s scholia on the Areopagite. A certain recruit asks the elder in Anastasius of Sinai’s *Guide* whether it is religious to greet someone who has offended him: “I make a *metanoia* to him,” he says. “Am I to greet him?”]

[Col. 1025]

# THE PASSION OF THE HOLY VIRGINS FLORA AND LUCILLA (29 July)

With annotations by William Cuper, S.J.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1025A]

We have learned from the testimony of the Psalmist that God is wonderful in his saints (Psalm 67), not only because he works wondrous signs through them in those who are sick, but also because, through him, those who recover from the common sickness of humanity are made strong in battle. Human weakness desires to flee death, especially when death is to be inflicted amid tortures. But the holy martyrs, overcoming this weakness through God’s grace, not only endured the torments offered to them and poured out their lives through them; they also voluntarily offered themselves to tyrants and executioners for the most atrocious punishments.

I would rightly say that this class of human beings, by divine gift, changed the direction of their natural strength. They lay down, without compulsion, what nature loves, and of their own accord pursue what nature naturally shudders at. Although such strength of mind is wondrous and worthy of the highest praise in men themselves, it is far more wondrous and praiseworthy in the female sex, which is timid and soft because of the coldness of its nature; and just as it is most unsuited to warfare, so it hates swords and weapons, and shudders not only at the sight but even at the memory of blood.

I have prefaced this so that you may understand, dearest brothers, what kind and how great are the virgins to whose solemn feast you have gathered. [Col. 1025C]

[Note: [Col. 1025C] From this I infer that this narrative was composed for the annual feast of these virgins. [Col. 1025C] It is extant in volume 7 of the Bollandists’ July.]

In them we ought to venerate not only religion, nor virginity alone, but also martyrdom itself—not just any kind of martyrdom, but one to which they themselves ran from distant regions no less eagerly than to the greatest delights. In this act of supreme courage they not only shone forth, but also, by the example of their virginity, brought the barbarian king, who had not yet been reborn in the waters of baptism, to the same contest, to undertake it with the same disposition, in a most holy emulation.

If we compare these virgins and the king with one another in an act of such virtue, they surpass him in sex, piety, and example; yet they are surpassed by the king in this respect: although he had not yet been regenerated in Christ, he began his apprenticeship at such a height of perfection that he became a martyr before receiving the sacrament of faith, and, although he had not been washed with water, he was washed in his own blood.

O truly a great spectacle: to see one who was not a Christian stretch out his neck for Christ, and one who had not yet been reborn through baptism placed, by the palm of martyrdom, before many who had been baptized! But let the history itself now speak to us; let it itself set before us the origin of the saints, the progress of their life, and the glory of their completed contest.

[Note: [Col. 1025C] It is not stated whether this history was written at that time or merely received by tradition. See what I said about a similar text of Peter Damian in the preceding commentary, no. 30. [Col. 1026C]]

## CHAPTER I. The piety, captivity, and freedom in captivity of these holy virgins

It is evident that the city of Rome surpassed all cities in every kind of nobility and was the head of the world. For if you consider the period before the birth of Christ the Lord, you find the Romans masters of affairs; but if afterward, you see that through the see of blessed Peter she became the head of the world. If you review in your mind the men who arose in her, you will find them cautious in counsel, vigorous in arms, supreme in courage, distinguished in justice, and moderate in all things.

One thing had been lacking before Christ—the piety of faith, that is—but when it was brought in through Peter, it ennobled the city that until then had surpassed other cities in every other respect, so that in this too she might take precedence over them. What need is there to count how many natives of this city have shone in Christian times, in war and in peace? Their number surpasses belief, and it surpasses even credibility.

But among those who purchased the kingdom of heaven through their torments, these women, to whose solemn feast you have gathered, possess a special dignity. Assuming a manly spirit, born in Rome, they deserved to live in Rome with the greatest devotion and finally to die in Rome with the utmost constancy.

Therefore the glorious virgins Flora and Lucilla, sisters, in the time—as far as can be understood and established—of Antoninus, surnamed Pius, while they burned before the divine gaze in Rome with their holy conduct, and outwardly, in accordance with the meaning of their names, flourished and shone, chose the apostolic life. Through it they withdrew themselves from love of earthly things and consecrated the vessels of their bodies by the sanctification of chastity; and, knowing that angels had fallen through pride, they prepared for themselves an ascent to heaven through humility.

[Note: [Col. 1026C] Antoninus Pius held the Roman Empire from the year 138 to 161 after Christ, as stated in the preceding commentary, no. 7.]

Since through these and other good works they pleased God and human beings, the Lord wished to test them through tribulations, like gold through fire, so as to make them more glorious in his sight. For although God had equipped the holy virgins with the virtue of courage, he did not wish them to remain hidden, but to go out into the field of battle: so that those who had conquered the sufferings of their bodies and the temptations of the devil might also overcome the world itself.

Therefore, beginning with lighter trials according to his holy plan—by which he draws good even from evils—he allowed the holy women to be taken from their own country, so that they might receive the merit of patience, announce the name of Christ to foreign peoples, and bring them to his worship.

At that time there was in the regions of Africa a barbarian king named Eugegius.

[Note: [Col. 1027D] The homeland of this petty king is not mentioned in the three manuscript copies of the acts, as we observed in the preceding commentary.]

He was hostile to the Roman territories and attempted to lay them waste.

[Note: [Col. 1027D] This devastation can readily be understood in light of what we noted in the preceding commentary, nos. 48 and 62. [Col. 1028D]]

Among the other captives, by God’s will, he brought the holy virgins into his own country. When he saw that they were outstanding in youthful age and beauty, he burned with love for them. While he arranged for them to be supplied with royal clothing and women’s finery, the virgin Flora wisely perceived what the barbarian intended and said to him:

“Consider what you are doing. For we have a most powerful bridegroom, who, moved by the injuries done to us and to his own people, will stir up his fury against you.”

The barbarian raged when he heard this; swollen with the empty pride of his arrogance, and not thinking that anyone could be found who might exact vengeance upon him, he replied with troubled mind and haughty voice:

“And who is this bridegroom of yours, and what power does he possess, that he could avenge his own injuries or yours against me?”

But the virgin of the Lord, Flora, without any fear and infusing manly confidence into a woman’s mind, said:

“We have God and the Lord Jesus Christ as our bridegroom, who created heaven and earth from nothing, and all that is contained within the compass of heaven. Everything serves him; nothing can be difficult for him. To this Lord God we have pledged ourselves; to him we serve with an immaculate heart and body.

“You can see how abhorrent, impious, and impossible it would be for us to be violated, polluted, or made subject to your lust. For if you attempt to violate the temple of God—which we are—you must not imagine that you will escape unpunished (1 Corinthians 3:16); rather, you must know with absolute certainty that you will immediately be destroyed by him whom you provoke through the injuries done to us.”

When the invincible king heard this, he marveled at the woman’s constancy, eloquence, and love of chastity. By the Lord’s will he was terrified, and, changing the impure desire with which he had prepared rape for the virgins into religious devotion, he worshiped the supreme and true God in their hearts.

At once he ordered a private and well-appointed chamber to be prepared for them, to which no man would have access, but only the virgins whom he had dedicated perpetually to the service of the saints. He also commanded that attendants should not withdraw from their service, but minister to them with the greatest reverence, as to servants of God who dwells in heaven.

When the holy sisters saw such providence from God toward them—who had changed a plunderer into their protector, a violator into the defender of their chastity, and a royal court into a monastic enclosure—they marveled at the divine plan and gave immense thanks to the author of every good. He had caused them, though held in captivity, to find such favor with a foreign king. They frequently prayed to God, as was right, both for his safety and for his eternal salvation, lest they be marked by any stain of ingratitude.

Meanwhile the king’s mind was being shaped toward faith, and he trusted so greatly in their holy prayers that, whenever he was about to go to war, he most earnestly commended himself to them. When they ordered him to be of good courage, or told him that he would return home safely, he went down into battle as though fortified by a heavenly oracle, conceiving a firm hope of victory; and by God’s will he always brought back victory.

Understanding through these most evident signs of their holiness that he was protected by God through their prayers and aided in all his undertakings, the king honored the virgins more greatly and regarded them as mothers. He considered himself blessed, and his kingdom blessed, because it was protected by the merits of Christ’s handmaids and strengthened by their prayers.

[Note: [Col. 1028D] Here the dominion of this ruler is called a kingdom, although Dinus, on the basis of the Aretine acts, argues from the omission of that word and tones down the title “king,” as may be seen in the preceding commentary, no. 42.]

## CHAPTER II. The virgins’ liberation from captivity, return to Rome, and martyrdom together with their captor

[Col. 1028C]

The holy virgins had now been living religiously and devoutly in the African region under King Eugegius, while the king attended them with constant services and benefits, for their twentieth year since they had been taken captive from their own city was passing.

After this period of time, the Lord Jesus, wishing to rescue his most faithful brides from the present world through a laborious contest, bring them into the heavenly bridal chamber itself, and knowing that they were most ready to undergo martyrdom, did not wish them to be adorned only with domestic triumphs. Rather, he wished them to go out into the field, increase the contest, and end their glorious life with the triumph of glorious martyrdom.

For our king does not gird his soldiers with the strongest weapons without reason. He would certainly do so at that time if he strengthened people for martyrdom but did not set a contest before them, allowing them to depart peacefully according to nature.

Their bridegroom therefore appeared to them in a vision during the deep silence of night and addressed them in these words:

“Beloved brides, remain no longer in these regions. Rise and return to your homeland, where you must be brought to completion through martyrdom.”

When they heard this, the virgins rejoiced with great joy at such a message and favor, gave the bridegroom Christ the highest thanks, and in the morning told their ruler, asking permission to return to their homeland, according to the oracle given to them, in order to attain the palm of martyrdom.

When the king heard this, he understood that it was both impious and impossible to resist divine commands. Reflecting deeply, he also considered that through the presence of the virgins he had not only been preserved in his military affairs but had prospered, and that through them he had been made glorious in everything. Fearing destruction for himself and his life because of their absence, he resolved to appoint himself their companion on the journey and said to them:

“Since you must depart, and since it would not be right for me to remain in these regions after your departure, if you permit it, I too will come with you.”

When they indicated their consent and desire that this should happen, and further declared that he would most certainly be joined to the Christian flock, he seemed moved by a divine response. He left behind his kingdom, children, and wife, became the companion of Christ’s handmaids, and the man who had once carried the virgins from their own regions in barbarian fury now brought them back like a most loving father.

If you compare the two situations, you behold a transformation wrought by the right hand of God. There you find Eugegius a most savage wolf; here, a most gentle lamb. Then he attempted to seize what belonged to others, violate virginity, and kill the innocent; now he considers his own possessions worthless, defends chastity, desires to die for Christ, and of his own accord hastens from distant regions to lay down his life for Christ.

Let pagans and unbelievers marvel at these things—those who do not know that God is wonderful in his saints (Psalm 67), as we have said above.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] Similar miracles of divine grace are still found in sacred Scripture and ecclesiastical history.]

We, however, ought not to marvel at such things but to love them, knowing that all things are possible for the faithful.

When Marcus Antoninus Verus and Commodus Aurelius were ruling at Rome—namely, in about the one hundred and eightieth year of our Lord—the holy sisters Flora and Lucilla entered the city of Rome with King Eugegius to receive martyrdom for Christ. They found that, under the city prefect named Helius, the fury of the pagans was raging against Christians.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] Concerning these emperors, whose names here have been dislocated or transposed, see Tillemont, volume II of the *History of the Emperors*, pages 562 and following. [Col. 1030D]]

The virgins were not at all afraid of him. They showed themselves openly, were seized by the soldiers, and brought before the city prefect Helius.

[Note: [Col. 1030D] The city prefect Helius appears everywhere, although some place the martyrdom of these virgins at a much different time.]

Questioned by him about Christian worship, they unhesitatingly declared themselves Christians, adding that after twenty years of captivity they had returned to Rome at Christ’s command for martyrdom.

Helius asserted and repeated that the emperors’ order was that Christians should sacrifice to the gods or be killed by severe punishments. The virgins replied that they were ready to lay down their lives for the living and true God, and that they had come from the distant regions of the world to do so by divine revelation.

Then the impious Helius, seeing that he could not move them from their holy purpose, ordered them to be condemned to a blessed death. In accordance with his command, while Eugegius stood by and marveled at their constancy, they were beheaded by the executioners and gained the crown of martyrdom.

After their departure, King Eugegius saw that Flora and Lucilla—his mothers and his ladies—had been crowned through such constancy, while he had been left alive. Burning with love of martyrdom, of which examples had already appeared in the female sex, he voluntarily presented himself to the prefect, saying:

“Lay me down with them also, since both are my ladies, and I refuse to live after their departure.”

When asked who he was, he gave his name and homeland, and revealed the whole history of the virgins and of himself, adding that he desired death for the name of Jesus Christ.

Helius hesitated and doubted that this man, who had not been a Christian, wished to die for Christ. King Eugegius said to him:

“The shedding of my blood will make me a worshiper of Christ, who will not consider me alien from his grace.”

After this confession of faith, the venerable man was beheaded at the prefect’s command.

Thus the glorious virgins Flora and Lucilla, together with King Eugegius, acquired immortality through beheading and death on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. Angelic spirits led them to the bridal chamber of the supreme Bridegroom, whom they had pursued throughout life and in death with the whole desire and love of their minds. For him they most willingly despised riches, pleasures, honors, and life itself, than which nothing is dearer to human beings.

Resting there and blessed, they acquired immeasurable and true riches in place of voluntary poverty; eternal banquets in place of temporal fasts; honor and perpetual pleasures in place of contempt for the foulest lusts; true, solid, and everlasting honors in place of the ridiculous and childish things of this life; and, in place of a momentary and fragile life, they earned everlasting life.

## CHAPTER III. The burial and translation of the holy bodies
The bodies of these saints were gathered by the faithful and buried with Christian reverence in the suburb of the city of Ostia, where they rested for [506] more than seven hundred years, that is, until the year of the Lord 901. At that time the religious father John, bishop of Arezzo and palatine chancellor, requested and received from Benedict III, Roman pontiff of that name, the sacred bodies of Saints Flora, Lucilla, and King Eugegius. Having devoutly arranged for them to be carried by his household toward Arezzo, he himself returned by another route, lest the Romans cause him any hindrance.

But since God wished the names and merits of the virgins to be made known for his own glory and theirs, it happened one day that the bishop’s attendants, carrying the holy bodies, lodged between a lake called Disortium and the marsh of Arezzo. The local inhabitants—and especially their lords—recognizing, out of reverence for the place and for the religious character of the household, the sacred relics, obtained from them, by God’s will, a certain portion. In order to show gratitude, in accordance with the apostolic admonitions, for such great benefits of God, they built a basilica in honor of God, Blessed Mary, and Saints Flora and Lucilla, and had it consecrated through their holy relics. They also ordered that the name of the town and of their principality should be derived from Saint Flora’s name, since previously the town had been called Amia and they themselves had been called counts of Amiata.

Leaving, therefore, the town of Saint Flora and its devout counts, they continued the journey they had begun and were already approaching the plain of Arezzo when, behold, by God’s design, the beast carrying the sacred bodies refused to be led any farther, despite every exhortation and beating. The attendants were astonished; they waited for one another and did not understand what the martyrs intended. They did not fail to inform the bishop, who had already reached Arezzo, of what had happened to them.

Then the devout bishop, having received the news and accompanied by a very large multitude of clergy and people, went to meet the saints. After offering sacred prayers and shedding tears, he himself tried to move the animal. When he too was unable to do so, he took counsel with his companions and allowed the beast to go, knowing for certain that the saints had chosen the place to which the aged animal would hasten of its own accord. Once this was done, the brute animal, led by God’s angels and the holy martyrs, ascended at the swiftest pace the mountain then called Titanus, as though breaking out of prison, and stopped at the place appointed from heaven for the saints, about two miles from the city of Arezzo.

There, soon afterward through the devotion of the faithful, a basilica was built, together with a monastery, which, through the holiness of those dwelling there and through the intercession of the virgins, wonderfully flourished for many years through frequent and great miracles. Because of the fame of this monastery and the devotion shown to the holy women, a fortress was built there. It received its name from Saint Flora, as did the entire mountain, and flourished for many years.

[Note: [Col. 1031] These additions concern entirely the ruin of the monastery and fortress of Saint Flora.]

The monastery, however, was destroyed in the year of the Lord 1193 by the factions of the Guelphs and Ghibellines of Arezzo. After this [507] desolation had taken place, it was transferred, together with the holy relics, into the city of Arezzo, where the holy virgins are venerated to this day with great devotion by the people. The fortress, however, was later destroyed, in the year of the Lord 1196, on account of the same factions, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1031]

## EXPOSITION OF THE VISIONS OF THE HOLY MARTYRS MARIANUS AND JAMES  
*(30 April)*

Henschenius published and illustrated with notes, among the Acts of the Saints for 30 April, the Life of these saints, written by an author who was an eyewitness. Their sacred bodies are preserved in the church of Gubbio, which bears their dedication; their martyrdom is traditionally said to have occurred around the year 259 of Christ.

[Col. 1031C] Now, to treat briefly of some aspects of the visions of these saints: who was the judge whom blessed Marianus had seen on the tribunal, except the one who presides in heaven and, having received judgment from the Father, judges the living and the dead? As it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). He appeared with an honorable and handsome face, because he is the one of whom it is said: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44 [45]). Thus he ordered the confessors to ascend to the torments, because however furiously the madness of persecutors may rage, and however ardently the devotion of the faithful may burn to suffer for Christ, no one rises to the height of martyrdom unless that judge, by his hidden judgment, has raised him there. The ascent to the summit of the scaffold was by many steps, because by many steps of virtue one climbs to the summit of perfection; and only then, through divine grace, does one reach the height of martyrdom.

[Col. 1032C] But when the martyr Cyprian raised Blessed Marianus to a higher place on the scaffold, we must understand that the Lord exalted him among the martyrs with a special dignity of martyrdom. But what does it mean that, at the Lord’s command, the blessed martyr ascended to the place of his passion, yet did not then receive the martyrdom of passion? It means that every perfect man who has already raised himself to the citadel of virtue, and who has firmly fixed the intention of his mind, with all his strength, upon dying for Christ, is nevertheless delayed until his desire may increase daily still more.

Hence it is rightly said in this vision: “The judge rose and went to his praetorium, and we followed him together.” For the martyrs to follow the judge from the place of torment to his praetorium means that the Lord temporarily suspends his chosen ones from the consummation of martyrdom and meanwhile raises their minds, through contemplation, to heavenly joy. It should be noted that Marianus said that he followed together with the other martyr, but asserted that the judge did not go with them at the same time, but went ahead of them. For whoever is journeying toward the rest of the heavenly dwelling, whoever is hastening by holy conversion to the fellowship of the blessed, can keep to the paths of the saints with God going before us; but we can imitate Christ’s footsteps, while in no way can we fully overtake them.

For those who confess truthfully say: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). But Christ says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). It is fitting also that the one who has a martyr as companion on the journey has the judge as his guide, since he is that Prophet to whom the Prophet says: “For your name’s sake you will be my guide and nourish me” (Psalm 30 [31]).

[Col. 1033B] But when he says: “Our journey was through a meadow,” what is signified by the meadow, which is called a field, except this world? Thus it is rightly said that he did not remain in the meadow but had a journey through the meadow, because whoever belongs to that desirable city, the heavenly Jerusalem, has in this world not a dwelling but a journey.

But what does it mean that he is said to have journeyed through a meadow and to have seen there not grass but tall trees, arranged in orderly fashion? What, finally, are these trees except holy and righteous men, who in the loftiness of their minds despise all that is lowly and, firmly rooted in the foundation of fraternal charity, do not confuse their order?

Finally, what is drinking from a bowl of spring water except tasting the cup of passion? Hence David says: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115 [116]). It should be noted how beautifully the vision agrees with the Prophet by means of this likeness. He took the cup and called upon the name of the Lord; the martyr drank from the bowl and gave thanks to God. The spring from which he filled the bowl poured forth clear waters, and through the Psalmist it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (ibid.).

Here one may ask what it means that this Judge went before the blessed martyrs throughout the entire journey as far as the spring and then immediately vanished from their sight. Are we to believe that the Lord, who leads his chosen ones through hidden grace to the crown of martyrdom, abandons them as soon as he withdraws, amid the very distress of their tribulations? But it should be noted that the Lord seems in a certain way to abandon the saints when he permits them to be scourged by the wicked. Hence our Redeemer cried out to the Father on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27; Mark 15). Thus all these secret mysteries, which almighty God daily bestows through his chosen ones by hidden dispensation, he showed especially to this man in an open vision, so that he might deserve to see here what is secretly accomplished in others.

Now, whom did James see as a young man, except the one whom Marianus saw as Judge? He appeared as a young man because the Mediator between God and human beings, having lived among human beings, reached indeed the age of youth and did not decline into old age. He was of lofty stature because “he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18 [19]). He had raised his head above the clouds because, through his majesty, “his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his meeting-place is even to its summit” (ibid.).

And because, as Paul says, “the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11), while Christ is the head of his body, which is the Church, he had raised his head above the clouds because, through the majesty of his divinity, by which he is always one with the Father, he reigns equally with him in heaven together with the substance of the humanity he assumed.

Although the head is raised above the clouds, the body is nevertheless seen on earth, because all the saints, who are the Redeemer’s body, remain on earth through the condition of mortality so long as they bear this flesh, although they are shown already to dwell in heaven through the freedom of the spirit, saying with Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). Hence it is rightly said that his body was seen on earth but was not said to touch the earth, because holy men appear indeed to live on earth, but are not entangled by desire in earthly actions; and while they raise themselves upward with all their strength, they suspend the feet of their minds from the earth.

He is rightly said to have been clothed in shining garments, because of him it is said through the Prophet: “You are clothed with light as with a garment” (Psalm 103 [104]). By the shining garments with which he is clothed, the holy Church is undoubtedly signified. This garment is radiant through the purity of holy works and is stretched out in adherence to the Lord through hope of future blessedness. Of it the Apostle says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5). And it is fitting that he is remembered as clothed in gleaming garments, because the Lord says of his chosen ones: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matthew 13).

Nor is it without mystery that these garments are described as distinguished by different colors. For holy men, when they abound in many virtues, are distinguished, as it were, by a variety of colors. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “The queen stood at your right hand, in gilded clothing, surrounded by variety” (Psalm 44 [45]).

This young man was seen not to stand but to pass before the faces of the martyrs, because the Lord was already preparing to take them from this world and lead them to the contemplation of his majesty, as he himself says in the Gospel: “And passing by, he ministered to them” (Luke 12).

But what does it mean that he casts individual purple belts into the bosom of the martyrs, except that he makes known that they are to be surrounded on every side by the distresses of suffering? This belt of passion becomes purple when blood is shed. By casting them into their bosom, he showed with what certainty he strengthened them concerning their own passion. For we believe that nothing is held with greater certainty than what we hold in our bosom. Hence blessed Job says concerning the hope of the resurrection: “This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom” (Job 19).

Nor is it without mystery that the boy carries a rose-colored necklace around his neck and a very green palm branch in his hand. By the necklace, which is encircled around the neck, the blessedness of eternal life is appropriately signified, for whoever receives it is surrounded on every side by ineffable joy. Just as no end or beginning is found in a necklace, so eternal life neither begins with a beginning nor is concluded by an end. The necklace appeared rose-colored because this boy, who had received the necklace of eternal life, was to be crowned with martyrdom after his blood had been poured out.

In his hand he carried a very green palm branch because, as the Psalmist says, “The righteous will flourish like the palm tree” (Psalm 91 [92]). And John says: “In the presence of the Lamb they are clothed in white robes, and palm branches are in their hands” (Revelation 7).

Appropriately he did not say, “You will have lunch,” but rather, “Tomorrow you will sup with us,” because the Lord himself calls heavenly joy not lunch but supper (Luke 12; John 13). For just as after supper no further banquet remains, so after that banquet of everlasting happiness nothing further can be found to follow it.

What do we understand by the young men seated on white horses except the holy angels prepared to receive the souls of the blessed martyrs? Blessed John also declares that he saw angels seated on white horses (Revelation 19). A horse is an animal suited to war. Those who return victorious from worldly wars lead their triumphs to the capitol on white horses yoked to a chariot. Thus the horses suggest the strength of the combatants, while the whiteness suggests the glory of the triumphant. Therefore the angels were rightly seen on white horses, because they were to lead those who had fought in Christ’s battle, after their victory, to the heavenly citadel with the triumph of glory. Thanks be to God.
